title: dsid_0dd4dcc98daa4a81896c79c0ca232a30__service-traffic-topology-and-adaptive-shaping-guide-2026.txt
text:
Service Traffic Topology and Adaptive Shaping Guide

Overview

This guide documents the platform-level approach for mapping service traffic topology and applying an adaptive request-shaping layer to guarantee latency SLOs, control cost exposure, and preserve fairness across tenants and feature priorities. It covers topology discovery, shaping algorithm design, configuration examples, dashboards and alerting, an operational runbook for degraded conditions, retrospective observations from the Q4 2025 trial, and a short roadmap for next steps.

Motivation and goals

- Problem: Multi-tenant inference traffic causes unpredictable tail latency and sudden cost spikes when bursty workloads align with cold caches or concentrated GPU affinity.
- Goals:
  - Keep 99th percentile inference latency below configured SLOs per tenant (default 500ms for interactive endpoints).
  - Limit per-tenant burst cost to committed budget (burst credit model).
  - Prevent head-of-line (HOL) blocking between latency-sensitive and batch/background workloads.
  - Provide operators clear observability and safe rollbacks.

Scope and assumptions

- Applies to all platform ingress proxies and the request router layer that makes placement decisions.
- Assumes existing tokenized SLI metrics (p95/p99 latency, token cost, KV cache hit rate) are available per-tenant and per-model.
- Does not replace model-level QoS (quantization/cost tuning) but complements it by shaping at the network/runtime boundary.

Design summary

1) Topology mapping: Build a dynamic graph that tracks traffic flows between logical request sources (tenants/routes) and serving clusters (model-version pools, GPU pools, regional endpoints).

2) Shaping primitives:
  - Rate limit (requests/sec) with elastic burst credits.
  - Concurrency cap (active requests) per tenant+route.
  - Priority queueing with preemption hints for emergency-fallback routes.
  - Cost-gated admission based on token budget windows.

3) Adaptive controller: Uses short-term telemetry (30s, 1m windows) to adjust shaping parameters: lower concurrency when p99 rises or cache hit-rate drops; replenish burst credits gradually; move low-priority traffic to cooler pools.

Topology mapping details

We maintain three primary maps:
- Source map: tenant -> active routes -> origin region
- Pool map: GPU pool -> region -> served model-variants -> current utilization and evictable slots
- Link map: measured latency and KV-hit statistics for source->pool pairs (updated continuously)

These maps are stored in the platform catalog service and replicated to the request-router sidecars (read-only primary) every 15s. Topology reconciliation frequency is configurable (default 15s) and should balance staleness risk vs. control-plane load.

Adaptive shaping algorithm (high level)

Inputs (per-request window): p99_latency_source, pool_utilization, kv_hit_rate, token_cost_rate, tenant_priority, burst_credit_balance.

Algorithm steps (per control interval, default 10s):
1) Compute violation_score = w1 * (p99_latency_source / p99_slo) + w2 * (1 - kv_hit_rate) + w3 * pool_utilization
2) If violation_score > threshold_high: tighten shaping for that source by reducing concurrency_cap by 20% and draining 1/3 of available burst credits to the shaping bucket.
3) If threshold_low < violation_score <= threshold_high: reduce concurrency_cap by 10% and mark lower-priority routes for cold-pool migration.
4) If violation_score <= threshold_low for 3 consecutive intervals: relax shaping (increase concurrency_cap up to configured max) and slowly replenish burst credits at configured refill rate.

Default weights and thresholds (can be tuned per tenant):
- w1=0.6 (latency importance), w2=0.2 (cache health), w3=0.2 (utilization)
- threshold_high = 1.2, threshold_low = 0.8

Configuration examples

Below is an example tenant policy YAML applied at the router: 

policy: "interactive-standard"
settings:
  p99_slo_ms: 500
  concurrency_max: 50
  concurrency_min: 2
  burst_credit_initial: 1000
  burst_refill_per_min: 50
  cold_pool_migration_enabled: true
  weights: [0.6, 0.2, 0.2]
  thresholds: [0.8, 1.2]
  control_interval_secs: 10

CLI (example):
- Apply policy: 
  rctl policy apply --tenant=acme --policy-file=interactive-standard.yaml --env=prod
- Query topology: 
  rctl topology describe --tenant=acme --format=table

Dashboard and alerting guidance

Recommended dashboard panels (per-tenant / per-model):
- Real-time topology heatmap: source -> pool latency (color-coded)
- SLI trend: p50/p95/p99 latency (1m, 5m), with SLO lines
- Burst credit balance and refill rate histogram
- Concurrency cap and current active requests
- KV cache hit rate and model load trend

Suggested alert rules (Prometheus-style expressions):
1) High p99 breach:
  expr: max_over_time(p99_latency_ms[5m]) > tenant_p99_slo_ms * 1.2
  for: 3m
  severity: P1
2) Rapid burst depletion:
  expr: rate(burst_credit_balance[1m]) < - (burst_refill_per_min / 60) * 2
  for: 2m
  severity: P2
3) Cold-pool overload:
  expr: avg_over_time(pool_utilization[2m]) > 0.85 and avg_over_time(kv_hit_rate[2m]) < 0.6
  severity: P2

Alert routing: P1 -> oncall SRE + platform pager; P2 -> platform channel + ticketing. Include tenant owner in notifications for P1 and require explicit acknowledgement in the incident runbook.

Operational runbook (degraded latency event)

1) Triage (owner: platform oncall)
  1. Check dashboards: identify affected tenants and serving pools.
  2. Inspect topology map: are many sources draining to the same pool?
  3. Check KV cache hit rate and recent rollouts for model variants.

2) Immediate mitigation (if p99 > slo * 1.5):
  a. Apply emergency shaping for impacted tenants: reduce concurrency_cap by 50% and set burst_refill_per_min to 0.
     Command: rctl policy override --tenant=<T> --concurrency-cap=<value> --reason="emergency-latency"
  b. If eviction is required, move non-priority traffic to cold pools: rctl migration start --from=<hot-pool> --to=<cold-pool> --selector='priority<50'
  c. If persistent, enable temporary fallback to model-variant with lower memory footprint: rctl model fallback --tenant=<T> --variant=quantized-v2

3) Root cause analysis (owner: platform reliability team)
  - Collect traces and tail logs for sample requests.
  - Compare recent deployments, kernel changes, and topology reconciliation events.
  - If hardware saturation suspected, coordinate with GPU-ops to inspect node health.

4) Post-incident follow-up:
  - Publish incident notes with timeline, actions, and suggested policy tweaks.
  - Adjust default weights or thresholds if event tied to algorithm mis-calibration.

Retrospective: Q4 2025 trial summary

What we did: Deployed adaptive-shaping to 20% of production traffic for non-enterprise tenants in 3 regions. We collected 6 weeks of telemetry and ran 4 injected workload bursts to exercise cold-pool transitions.

Key findings:
- Adaptive shaping reduced p99 tail by median 38% for affected tenants.
- Inaccurate topology mappings (stale link map entries) caused two unnecessary migrations; lowered reconciliation interval from 30s to 15s resolved this.
- The default burst refill rate was too aggressive, producing oscillations; we replaced instantaneous refill with token-bucket smoothing.

Action items from retrospective:
- Add canary tests for topology reconciliation when control-plane changes are released.
- Introduce synthetic KV-hit probes per pool to better predict cold transitions.
- Provide a per-tenant tuning page in the Redwood Console showing how weights affect behavior.

Roadmap (next 12 months)

- Q2 2026: Apply tenant-level machine-learning model to adapt weights (w1/w2/w3) instead of static values.
- Q3 2026: Integrate shaping decisions with cost-optimization engine (link tags for billable credits).
- Q4 2026: Expose self-serve shaping policy editor in console with simulation mode.

Ownership and contacts

- Design and implementation: Platform Traffic Team (primary owner).
- Observability dashboards: Telemetry Platform Team.
- Runbook maintenance: SRE Team.

Appendix: Example topology table (text)

| Source (tenant) | Region | Preferred pool | p99_ms (1m) | KV_hit_rate | Burst_balance | Notes |
| ACME | us-west-2 | gpu-pool-3-hot | 430 | 0.78 | 640 | interactive-heavy |
| acme-dataflow | us-west-2 | gpu-pool-5-cold | 1200 | 0.22 | 50 | background batch, migrate |
| betacorp | eu-central | gpu-pool-2-hot | 210 | 0.92 | 1200 | high-priority, SLA-99 |

If you have questions or propose policy changes, comment on this page or ping the Platform Traffic Team in #platform-traffic.

Change log:
- 2025-11-12: Drafted initial design (Aisha Patel).
- 2026-01-15: Incorporated telemetry team feedback; tuned thresholds (Marco Ruiz).
- 2026-02-03: Added Q4 2025 retrospective and roadmap (Sophie Chen).

title: dsid_8b58fca07ca34699bb2cce932e3dd24d__forensic-ready-compliance-playbook-for-emergency-deployments-2025.txt
text:
Forensic-ready Compliance Playbook for Emergency Deployments

Overview

Purpose:
This playbook describes the combined technical and procedural controls required to remain forensically and legally compliant when performing emergency or out-of-band deployments, regional failovers, or temporary entitlement exceptions that cross normal RBAC, data residency, and SDLC boundaries. It prescribes: who may authorize an emergency deployment, what audit evidence must be captured, how to preserve data residency guarantees, and how to assemble a compliance evidence package suitable for regulators and internal audit.

Scope:
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem) Redwood deployments.
- Covers emergency code releases, rollback operations, region-to-region failover, and temporary role escalations lasting <= 72 hours.
- Excludes planned maintenance with advance approval from Change Control.

Key Principles:
1) Forensic readiness: any emergency action must be captured end-to-end with immutable audit records, cryptographic verification where applicable, and a minimal evidence manifest.
2) Least privilege + compensating controls: temporary exceptions must be timeboxed, scoped, and paired with increased telemetry and monitoring.
3) Data locality preservation: customer residency SLAs must be honored or explicitly waived and logged in the evidence bundle.
4) Post-fact governance: all emergency actions require retrospective review, remediation, and either a permanent policy change or revocation.

Roles & Ownership:
- Incident Commander (IC): Security & Compliance oncall (sec-oncall). Authorizes emergency exception and certifies the evidence bundle.
- Deployment Lead: Eng-Platform owner of the deployment-pipeline service (service: deployment-gate). Executes the emergency deploy.
- Auth Owner: Eng-Auth (service: authz-service). Applies temporary role grants and records RBAC deltas.
- Audit Custodian: Eng-SRE (service: audit-collector + evidence-orchestrator). Ensures immutable storage and artifact packaging.
- Legal/Privacy Reviewer: Legal team. Consulted when cross-border data movement occurs.

Pre-deployment Checklist (must be completed before executing emergency action):
- IC approval recorded in the incident ticket (Jira ID required).
- Timebox declared (default: 72 hours).
- Affected customers/tenants enumerated and residency requirements noted.
- RBAC deltas planned and scoped. Use short-lived groups (prefix: emergency-YYYYMMDD).
- Audit pipeline health check: audit-collector retention tier \u003e= 30 days and append-only store reachable.
- Snapshot: automated snapshot of configuration and model artifacts stored with SHA256 checksums in artifacts-bucket (kms-integrator).

Emergency Exception Workflow (step-by-step):
1) Request & Approval
   - Requester opens incident ticket and selects template: Emergency Deployment – Compliance Evidence.
   - IC confirms necessity on #sec-incident and records explicit authorization: UTC timestamp, approver, reason, scope.
2) Scoped RBAC Grant
   - Auth Owner creates temporary role in authz-service with TTL <= declared timebox. Naming: emergency-grant-<ticket>.
   - All role creations/assignments must include originator, justification, and correlating ticket id.
3) Audit Hardening
   - Turn on verbose auditing for involved services: deployment-gate, model-serving, data-proxy.
   - Increase retention for the incident partition to legal_hold by toggling retention-tag via audit-collector API.
4) Deployment & Data Controls
   - Deployment Lead performs deploy through deployment-gate using --evidence-manifest flag.
   - If cross-region movement occurs, data-residency waiver must be recorded and signed-off by Legal.
5) Evidence Packaging (see Evidence Collection section).
6) Revoke & Remediate
   - Immediately after stabilized: revoke emergency roles, rotate affected keys, revert any temporary config flags that broaden access.
   - Open a post-incident CR for permanent remediation if needed.

Evidence Collection (minimum artifact set):
- Immutable audit log slice (start_ts..end_ts) for: authz-service, deployment-gate, audit-collector, data-proxy, model-serving-runtime. Format: JSONL, signed at storage by evidence-orchestrator.
- RBAC delta manifest: CSV listing grants, principal, scope, TTL, created_by, created_at.
- Deployment manifest: git SHA, image digests, environment variables with redaction markers for secrets, and operation transcript.
- Data residency waiver (if applicable): PDF signed by Legal with timestamp and list of affected tenant IDs.
- Snapshot of configuration plus SHA256 of model artifacts and schema versions.
- Incident ticket & approver log (Jira export).
- Chain-of-custody log for any data extracts (who accessed, purpose, retention).

Audit Logging Configuration (operational details):
- Required fields: timestamp (ISO8601), service, operation, principal_id, request_id, correlation_id, before/state deltas, after/state deltas, outcome, region, retention_tag.
- SLOs: audit ingestion 99.99% availability; mean ingestion latency \u003c= 2s; immutable store replication across 2 regions for hosted deployments.
- Retention mapping: default customer-audit: 1 year; legal_hold: 7 years; ephemeral_debug: 30 days.
- Immutable storage: evidence-orchestrator writes a signed bundle to s3://evidence-locked/{ticket}/bundle-{timestamp}.tar.gz with kms-integrator envelope encryption.

RBAC Adjustments & Controls:
- All emergency grants must be implemented via authz-service API with the header X-Incident-ID set. Ad-hoc console grants are forbidden.
- Short-lived credentials must be provisioned via the service-token-exchange (max TTL 8 hours).
- Deprovisioning hook: revocation events are automatically recorded and a revocation-proof object is attached to the evidence bundle.

Data Residency and Retention Considerations:
- If data must cross jurisdictional boundaries during failover, the Legal/Privacy Reviewer must approve and sign a waiver before the action proceeds. The waiver must state the minimal subset of affected data and retention/erasure commitments.
- For private deployments, customers must be notified within SLA windows specified in their contract (default: 24 hours). Notification artifacts are included in the evidence bundle.
- All temporary copies created for forensic or rollback purposes must be tagged with retention_tag=ephemeral_debug and auto-deleted after 30 days unless escalated to legal_hold.

SDLC Gating and Emergency Releases:
- Deployment-gate has two distinct flows: normal (CI->canary->gradual) and emergency (IC-authorized single-step). Emergency runs must still produce the same artifacts as the normal flow (build manifest, test run ids) and include rationale for bypassing gates.
- Code review exemptions are conditional: emergency PRs must be triaged and tagged emergency-pr and undergo retrospective code review within 5 business days.

Evidence Packaging & Submission (artifact manifest format):
- evidence-manifest.yaml (top level):
  - ticket_id: STRING
  - ic_approver: STRING
  - start_ts: ISO8601
  - end_ts: ISO8601
  - artifacts: [list of artifact filenames]
  - retention_policy_applied: STRING

Example evidence-manifest.yaml snippet:

```yaml
ticket_id: INC-2025-1234
ic_approver: a.kapoor@redwood.com
start_ts: 2025-09-12T14:03:21Z
end_ts: 2025-09-12T14:21:09Z
artifacts:
  - audit-slice-authz-20250912.jsonl
  - rbac-delta-INC-2025-1234.csv
  - deployment-manifest-20250912.json
retention_policy_applied: legal_hold
```

Evidence submission process:
1) Audit Custodian runs evidence-orchestrator --package --ticket INC-2025-1234.
2) The orchestrator validates signatures, computes checksums, uploads to s3://evidence-locked/ and writes a pointer to the internal evidence index (immutable).
3) Notification sent to Legal + Compliance channel with secure link (signed URL TTL: 7 days).

Post-incident Review & Remediation:
- Conduct a Post-Incident Compliance Review (PICR) within 10 business days. Required attendees: IC, Deployment Lead, Auth Owner, Audit Custodian, Legal Reviewer, and the affected product owner.
- Deliverables: updated incident timeline, lessons learned, concrete remediation tickets, confirmation of role/secret rotation, and closure of temporary artifacts or escalation to legal_hold.

Escalation & Exceptions Register (risk and exceptions):
- Any emergency action that increases cross-border data exposure beyond the approved waiver must be escalated immediately to the Head of Security and the Chief Privacy Officer.
- Maintain an Exceptions Register (sheet-id: protect://exceptions/registry) that captures: ticket, approver, business rationale, risk_assessment_score (1-100), expiration, and artifacts. Entries are audited quarterly.

Operational Runbook Snippets (CLI examples):
- Create a timeboxed role (Auth Owner):

```bash
curl -X POST https://authz.internal.redwood/v1/roles \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"name":"emergency-grant-INC-2025-1234","ttl_seconds":259200,"scopes":["deploy:execute","config:write"] ,"metadata":{"incident_id":"INC-2025-1234","created_by":"deployment-lead@redwood.com"}}'
```

- Package evidence (Audit Custodian):

```bash
evidence-orchestrator package --ticket INC-2025-1234 --output /tmp/INC-2025-1234-bundle.tar.gz \
  --sign-key /var/secrets/evidence-signing-key.pem --upload-bucket evidence-locked
```

Appendix A — Artifact retention table:
| artifact_type | default_retention | legal_hold_retention | storage_location | notes |
|---------------|-------------------|----------------------|------------------|-------|
| audit-jsonl | 1 year | 7 years | s3://audit-archive/{region}/ | signed by evidence-orchestrator |
| rbac-deltas | 1 year | 7 years | s3://audit-archive/{region}/rbac/ | CSV with principal hashes |
| deployment-manifest | 90 days | 7 years | s3://artifacts/ | digest-signed |
| waiver-pdf | 90 days | 7 years | s3://legal/waivers/ | must include Legal signature |

Appendix B — Quick decision checklist (for IC):
- Is emergency action the only viable path to meet customer SLAs or safety?
- Has Legal been contacted for cross-jurisdictional data movement?
- Are audit pipelines green and archivable?
- Is there a clear rollback plan and timebox?

References & Links:
- deployment-gate README: internal link /confluence/eng-platform/deployment-gate/README
- authz-service API spec: /confluence/eng-infra/authz-service/api-spec
- audit schema & ingestion runbook: /confluence/security-and-compliance/audit-logging/event-schema-contract-and-retention-runbook-2025

Revision History:
- 2025-09-12: Created by Aisha Kapoor.
- 2025-10-01: Added data-residency waiver template (Legal review).
- 2026-02-01: Clarified RBAC delta manifest format and added evidence-orchestrator CLI examples.

Contact: sec-oncall@redwood.com (for IC handover)

title: dsid_64e231c0e0d54447a5168e2da24bd3be__field-handoff-tenant-surgery-and-safe-cutover-playbook-2027.txt
text:
Field Handoff, Tenant Surgery, and Safe Cutover Playbook

Summary
This playbook describes the operational pattern we call 'tenant surgery' — a safe, auditable process for making targeted changes to a single tenant or a small tenant cohort in a Redwood Private deployment (VPC or on‑prem). It focuses on three phases: field handoff to customer operators, pre-cutover compatibility validation (packaging + network + KMS), and staged cutover with guaranteed rollback. Use this for major model swaps, KV cache migrations, network boundary changes, or tenant-level capacity rebalancing.

Audience
- Field engineers and customer operators performing tenant cutovers
- Platform SREs owning rollback automation and observability contracts
- Solutions engineers validating customer compatibility and acceptance criteria

Assumptions and scope
- Applies to Redwood Private (VPC and air‑gapped on‑prem) deployments managed under our operator handoff contract.
- Assumes existing telemetry ingestion and per-tenant tracing are active.
- Not for full fleet upgrades (see incremental-stateful-upgrade strategy doc).

High-level goals
1) Minimize tenant downtime: target < 2m P99 for ephemeral cutover operations, non‑disruptive where possible.
2) Provide deterministic rollback with preserved evidence for compliance.
3) Ensure customer-run acceptance tests are reproducible and auditable.
4) Limit blast radius: one tenant or tenant cohort at a time unless explicit approval.

Ownership and roles
- Field Lead (owner): executes cutover with customer operator present.
- SRE Oncall: watches platform SLOs and has escalation rights to abort cutover.
- Release Engineer: prepares artifacts, signs images, and validates compatibility gates.
- Customer Operator: performs network/KMS handshakes and runs acceptance tests.
- Compliance/Support: receives evidence bundle on completion for audit.

Prerequisites (checklist)
- Release artifacts: image SHA, signature, bill of materials (BOM), and quantization profile.
- Compatibility matrix: CPU/GPU arch support, CUDA/cuDNN versions, container runtime.
- Network proofs: BGP peering or VPC peering established, IP allowlists updated.
- KMS/HSM keys: test wrap/unwrap confirmed in staging.
- Telemetry: per-tenant metrics (latency, token rate, error rate) streaming to observability.
- Acceptance tests: deterministic prompt set, expected output hash range, latency budget.

Pre‑field handoff tasks (release engineer)
1. Generate evidence bundle: artifacts list, checksums, container image signature, upgrade checklist.
2. Run deterministic offline simulation against cached KV snapshots (if model change touches KV layout). Store results and diffs.
3. Publish canary/compatibility policy (YAML) to operator API and attach to evidence bundle. Example policy:

---
canary: 
  cohort_size: 1
  success_criteria:
    p50_latency_ms: 120
    error_rate_pct: 0.5
    semantic_regression_score: 0.95
  max_duration_minutes: 30
---

4. Verify signed images on target runtime: run sha256sum and container-sig verify.

Field handoff checklist (operator + field lead)
- Confirm maintenance window and customer notifications sent.
- Confirm access: operator SSH jumpbox, RBAC token, KMS policies.
- Validate telemetry forwarders are healthy (last 5m data present).
- Confirm snapshot of tenant state and KV cache created and archived.

Staged cutover procedure (step by step)
Stage 0 — Preflight validation (non-disruptive)\1. Run acceptance smoke tests against a mirrored staging path:
   - run: ./rci acceptance-run --tenant <tenant-id> --suite smoke
   - verify output hashes within tolerance.\2. Confirm routing policy: requests destined for tenant traffic must be tag‑routed to a canary host pool.

Stage 1 — Canary (single tenant instance)\1. Deploy artifact to canary host pool with prefix canary-<tenant>-<ts>.
   - kubectl apply -f canary-deployment.yaml --namespace=tenant-<id>
2. Observe telemetry for max_duration_minutes from canary policy. Key metrics:
   - inference_latency_p50/p90/p99
   - inference_error_rate
   - kv-cache-hit-rate
   - cost_per_token_estimate
3. Run customer acceptance suite: run canonical prompts and match semantic_regression_score >= threshold. Use eval harness sample command:
   - python -m redwood.eval.run --tenant <tenant-id> --suite canary_prompts --baseline /evidence/baseline.json
4. If criteria pass, promote to cohort. If not, trigger immediate rollback (see rollback cookbook).

Stage 2 — Cohort expansion (progressive ramp)
1. Expand from 1 -> 5 -> 20% -> 50% of tenant traffic using traffic-steering policy with 30m stabilization windows. Example traffic policy fragment:

trafficRouting:
  - step: 1
    weight: 1
    durationMinutes: 30
  - step: 2
    weight: 5
    durationMinutes: 30
  - step: 3
    weight: 20
    durationMinutes: 60
  - final
    weight: 100

2. At each step verify acceptance tests and SLOs; preserve evidence bundle of metric snapshots.
3. Pause and investigate if p99 latency exceeds target or error rate spikes > 2x baseline.

Rollback cookbook (deterministic, auditable)
Principles:
- Rollback must be automatic for safety-critical thresholds or manual with documented approval otherwise.
- Preserve post-failure evidence: traces, per-token logs (redacted), and the artifact that caused the failure.

Automatic rollback triggers\- inference_error_rate > 5% sustained for 5 minutes\- p99 latency > 5x baseline for 3 consecutive windows\- semantic_regression_score < 0.85 on canary prompts

Rollback steps\1. Set traffic weight back to last stable target (or 0 for immediate cutover abort).
   - CLI: redwoodctl traffic set --tenant <id> --policy previous-stable\2. Drain canary hosts: kubectl cordon/evict with grace period 30s.
3. Revert routing tables and BGP announcements if changed.
4. Run integrity validation: KV snapshot replay and state hash comparison.
5. Archive evidence and open a postmortem ticket with initial severity and impact.

Postcutover validation and evidence package
- Deliverable artifacts to customer and compliance: signed image SHA, canary run results, metric snapshots, logs (redacted), and rollback timeline.
- Postcutover acceptance: customer to run full acceptance suite within 24 hours.
- SRE to monitor SLOs for 72 hours and sign off.

On‑prem packaging compatibility notes
- Minimal runtime footprint: ensure staging images are built with BUILD_TAG=runtime-minimal to avoid optional tools requiring internet.
- FIPS/KMS: ensure our kmod/driver versions match vendor HSM firmware versions documented in the BOM.
- Airgap Caching: provide a tarball of container layers and a checksum manifest. Import steps for customer operator:
  1. scp layers.tar.gz to jumpbox
  2. ctr -n moby images import layers.tar.gz
  3. container-sig verify --artifact <image>.sha256

Telemetry and alert thresholds (operator defaults)
- p50 latency: baseline + 30ms alert (warning)
- p99 latency: baseline + 200ms alert (critical)
- error_rate_pct: > 1% warning, > 3% critical
- kv_cache_hit_rate: < 70% warning
- token_consume_5m_rate: sudden drop > 50% -> investigate routing 

Testing matrix and customer acceptance criteria (table)
| Test | Purpose | Pass criteria | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke prompts | Verify liveness and basic correctness | 100% run success | Field Lead |
| Regression eval | Semantic parity against baseline | cosine >= 0.95 | Customer + SE |
| Latency profiling | Validate tail latency | p99 <= 250ms | SRE |
| KV replay | Ensure stateful requests return consistent results | state_hash match | Release Eng |

Communication templates
- Precutover notification: include maintenance window, risk, rollback plan, contact list.
- Abort notification: time of abort, reason, immediate impact, next steps.
- Completion note: duration, artifacts delivered, request for customer sign-off.

Recordkeeping and compliance
- All cutovers must have a ticket in the deployment tracker with linked evidence bundle.
- Evidence retention: 12 months for regulated customers, 90 days default.
- For restricted data workloads, export telemetry at reduced fidelity and include data handling justification.

Common failure modes and mitigations
- Failure: semantic regression on edge prompts. Mitigation: roll back and schedule a targeted fine-tuning or prompt-filter patch.
- Failure: KMS unwrap errors post-cutover. Mitigation: revert key policy change, re-run test unwrap flow, escalate to KMS vendor.
- Failure: slow p99 due to KV cache cold start. Mitigation: pre-warm cache with synthetic traffic to reach target hit rate.

Appendix A — Useful CLI commands
- redwoodctl image verify --image my-image:sha256 --signature my-image.sig\- redwoodctl traffic set --tenant tenant-123 --policy canary-to-stable\- rci kv snapshot --tenant tenant-123 --out s3://evidence/tenant-123/snap-20261115.tar.gz

Appendix B — Minimal canary deployment YAML (example)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: canary-tenant-123
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        tenant: tenant-123
        rollout: canary
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: runtime
        image: registry.redwood.internal/tenant-runtime:sha256-abcdef
        resources:
          limits:
            nvidia.com/gpu: 1
        env:
        - name: TENANT_ID
          value: "tenant-123"

Appendix C — Postmortem checklist
- Timestamp of failure and automated trigger logs
- Evidence bundle id and storage location
- Scope of impact (tenants, requests/minute, time window)
- Root cause hypothesis and next steps

Frequently referenced docs
- Private deploy operator handshake and runtime guardrails (link)
- Tenant bootstrapping and immutable upgrade playbook (link)
- Observability contracts and log sampling strategy (link)

Revision history
- 2026-11-15: Draft created (Priya Nair)
- 2026-12-02: Added canary policy and rollback triggers (Diego Alvarez)
- 2027-02-03: Expanded telemetry thresholds and evidence retention guidance (Maya Chen)

title: dsid_bbe88e43700e44b4897c8757a039eb81__adr-structured-embeddings-and-streaming-contract-2026.txt
text:
ADR: structured-embeddings-and-streaming-contract-2026

Summary:

This ADR records a cross-domain decision to standardize a lightweight contract for combined streaming generation and embeddings requests. The goal is to enable safe, predictable evolution of the API surface used by: the edge-proxy, model-router, embed-service, stream-gateway, and telemetry-pipeline.

Decision:

We adopt a dual-track contract: a strict structured payload (JSON Schema v1) for non-streaming embeddings and metadata, and a chained streaming envelope for long-running generation that can optionally carry incremental embedding updates. Both tracks share a compact version header and a capability bitset so routers and sidecars can negotiate fallback behavior.

Motivation and context:

- Customers increasingly send mixed workloads (short embeddings, long-chat streaming) through a single integration.
- We observed inconsistent handling of incremental embeddings in streaming sessions (loss of context, inconsistent attribution to requests), leading to troubleshooting overhead and customer-facing AE cases.
- Current ad-hoc approaches create high coupling between model variants and clients, making model version rollouts risky.

Constraints and non-goals:

- Non-goal: This ADR does not redesign the SDK; it constrains server-side contracts that SDKs will implement.
- Constraint: Must be implementable without rewriting the existing stream-gateway; changes should be additive with config flags.
- Constraint: Must preserve per-tenant billing attribution and SLO observability (no silent sampling of embeddings).

Alternatives considered:

1) Do nothing: continue with ad-hoc incrementals. Rejected — causes operational burden and regressions during rollouts.

2) Separate endpoints: force embeddings and streaming to different endpoints. Rejected — breaks customer ergonomics and increases egress/ingress complexity for private deployments.

3) Heavyweight protobuf/RPC contract with binary frames and full schema registry. Rejected — too heavyweight for quick iteration and cross-region private deployments that prefer JSON.

Chosen approach (details):

- Contract header: Every request MUST include a top-level header object "ri_contract" with fields: version (semver string), capability_mask (integer bitmask), request_id (UUID), tenant_id (string).

- Two tracks: 
  - Structured track (embeddings): a single JSON payload with schema 'embedding_request' (see example). This is the canonical path for batch or single embeddings.
  - Streaming track (generation + optional incr-embeds): an envelope with newline-delimited JSON frames. Each frame MUST include a frame_type field ("init", "token", "embed_delta", "final"). embed_delta frames carry embedding vectors for the partial text prefix with provenance metadata.

Examples:

Structured embedding request (HTTP POST):

POST /v2/structure/embeddings
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "ri_contract": {"version": "1.0.0", "capability_mask": 0, "request_id": "b4d3-...", "tenant_id": "acme-corp"},
  "input": ["How to tune batching for latency?", "Redwood inference architecture"],
  "model": "redwood-emb-1.2",
  "response_options": {"normalize": true, "vector_format": "float16"}
}

Streaming envelope (HTTP chunked or WebSocket NDJSON):

{"ri_contract": {"version":"1.0.0","capability_mask":2,"request_id":"req-123","tenant_id":"acme-corp"}, "frame_type":"init","params":{"model":"redwood-gen-7b"}}
{"frame_type":"token","token":"Hello"}
{"frame_type":"token","token":" world"}
{"frame_type":"embed_delta","cursor":11,"embedding": [0.12, -0.03, ...], "provenance": {"prefix":"Hello world","prefix_len":11}}
{"frame_type":"final","completion_metadata":{"tokens":12}}

Capability mask bitset (initial):

- 0x01: supports_structured_embeddings
- 0x02: supports_streaming_embeds
- 0x04: accepts_incremental_routing_hints

Compatibility matrix (text table):

| Component | v1.0.0 header | streaming frames | embedDelta support | notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| edge-proxy | yes | passthrough | no | will add validation at parse step |
| stream-gateway | yes | must parse | yes | will buffer and validate embedding vectors |
| model-router | yes | understands frame_types | yes | may drop embed_delta when model variant cannot produce vects |
| telemetry-pipeline | yes | will accept event stream | yes | tag-based attribution required |
Implications:

API standards:
- Add ri_contract header to API spec and SDK generator templates.
- Register new endpoints (/v2/structure/embeddings and /v2/streaming/ndjson) in the public API catalog with stable docs.

Coding standards & infra:
- Server-side JSON parsing must be tolerant: accept unknown fields but fail-fast on missing ri_contract.
- Add a lightweight request validator library (go/python) packaged as an internal pip/go module. This module will implement schema checks and capability_mask helpers.
- Stream-gateway will implement adaptive backpressure: if embed_delta frames exceed 1MB/s per-request, gateway returns 429 with a structured retry-after JSON.

Model-serving and runtime behavior:
- Model variants that cannot produce embedding deltas must advertise capability_mask bit 0x02 == 0; model-router will fall back to post-hoc embeddings via embed-service and mark the request with a routing_reason header.
- For private deployments the runtime-sidecar will expose a toggle (ENV REDWOOD_ACCEPT_EMBED_DELTAS) defaulting to true for compatibility, but constrained by CPU caps.

Observability standards:
- New metrics: ri.requests_total, ri.stream.frames_by_type{frame_type}, ri.embed_vectors_bytes, ri.embed_generation_latency_ms (percentiles P50/P95).
- Tracing: Every frame must propagate the request_id and a frame_sequence integer. Spans must be created per-stream with child spans for embed-generation and model-inference.
- Alerts: if ri.embed_vectors_bytes per-tenant > 10GB/day unexpected, trigger investigate-embed-surge playbook.

Performance standards and SLOs:
- Streaming request p95 end-to-end latency (first token) must remain under 150ms for hosted-critical tier.
- Embedding generation SLO: 99th percentile per-item embedding time < 80ms for small models and < 250ms for large batch variants.
- The stream-gateway should enforce a soft limit of 100 embed_delta frames per minute per request by default.

Migration and rollout plan (phased):

1) Stage 0 (feature-gated dev): ship request validator library and unit tests; default flags off in prod.
2) Stage 1 (internal rollout): enable header validation in internal staging, update stream-gateway to parse frame_type but continue passthrough behavior. Add telemetry dashboards.
3) Stage 2 (public opt-in): publish API docs; SDKs add header template; allow customers to opt into streaming embed deltas via account flag.
4) Stage 3 (enforce): require ri_contract for all v2 endpoints; stream-gateway returns 400 on missing header.

Testing and validation:
- QA harness: replay 10M historical requests through a staging stream-gateway to validate parsing and observe embed vector distribution.
- Perf test matrix: small (redwood-emb-1), medium (redwood-emb-1.2), large (redwood-gen-7b) across GPU types (A100, L40s) with synthetic loads.
- Backwards-compat tests: simulate model-router fallback and validate billing attribution remains correct.

Operational runbooks and playbooks:
- Investigate-embed-surge: steps to identify tenant, disable embed_delta via tenant feature toggle, revert model-variant if sudden surge coincides with recent rollout.
- Fallback-to-post-hoc: how to rehydrate missing embed_delta frames by re-sending final text to embed-service and adding mapping metadata.

Open questions and future work:
- Schema: whether to move from JSON Schema to a compact CBOR wire format after initial stabilization for bandwidth savings.
- Delta compression: research efficient lossy compression for embed_delta frames to reduce network cost for high-frequency partials.

Owners and contacts:
- RFC author / primary owner: Aisha Patel (serving-runtime)

title: dsid_0e0ac7276c864c63a02586fa07ae85e1__latency-regression-tokenizer-update-2026-01-27.txt
text:
Postmortem: Latency regression after tokenizer update (2026-01-27)

## Summary
On 2026-01-27 we observed a significant p95 latency increase for chat completions on several popular models. The regression began shortly after a tokenizer library update was rolled out to the hosted fleet.

## Customer impact
- Duration: 58 minutes
- Symptoms: p95 end-to-end latency +38% for affected routes; some customers hit client-side timeouts
- Scope: Hosted API traffic in us-east-1 and eu-west-1

## Detection
- Alert: route latency SLO burn for /v1/chat/completions
- Perf dashboards showed elevated CPU in prefill pipeline

## Timeline (UTC)
- 19:11: SLO burn alert fired
- 19:18: On-call correlates onset with tokenizer update rollout
- 19:30: Mitigation: rollback tokenizer update
- 20:09: Latency returns to baseline

## Root cause
A tokenizer update changed default normalization behavior, increasing average token counts and causing additional CPU overhead in request preprocessing. The change was not detected in canary because the canary prompt set did not include multi-language and emoji-heavy inputs that are common in production.

## Contributing factors
- Canary prompt set coverage gap
- Lack of automated guardrail on average tokens/request
- Rollout checklist did not include a CPU budget validation

## Follow-up action items
1. Expand canary prompt sets to include multilingual and special-character heavy inputs representative of production. Owner team: Applied ML. Priority: P0.
2. Add automated guardrail: alert when avg input tokens per request changes by >10% for a route/model over 15 minutes. Owner team: SRE. Priority: P1.
3. Add perf CI check for tokenizer updates (CPU per 1k chars, tokens per 1k chars) and require approval on regressions. Owner team: Serving Runtime. Priority: P0.
4. Update rollout checklist to include "tokenization cost" section and explicit rollback criteria. Owner team: Platform. Priority: P2.
5. Add a dashboard panel tracking avg tokens/request by top 20 customers (anonymized) to catch distribution shifts. Owner team: Observability. Priority: P1.

## Lessons learned
Seemingly minor preprocessing changes can have first-order latency impact. Production-like prompt sets and token-count guardrails are necessary for safe rollouts."

title: dsid_15584be40f5444c980658a5857816adb__operator-autonomy-economic-signal-roadmap-2029.txt
text:
Operator Autonomy & Economic Signal Roadmap (2029)

Overview

This roadmap defines a 12–18 month program to increase platform operator autonomy while surfacing and acting on economic signals from the runtime. The goal is to reduce operator cognitive load, reclaim 20% of operational time spent on manual capacity adjustments, and improve token-unit marginal cost by 12% across hosted and dedicated deployments.

Why this matters
- Operators currently execute frequent manual interventions during regional surges and quantization rollouts; these interventions are a major source of error and time-to-stable.
- The platform lacks unified economic signals (cost-per-token, burst cost delta) in operator tooling and dashboards, so decisions are conservative and expensive.
- Increasing autonomy reduces MTTI for common degradations and enables predictable capacity scaling that lowers unit economics.

Objectives (measurable)
1. Operator time reclaimed: reduce manual intervention mean time per week from ~8 hours to <=2 hours for routine events.
2. Cost efficiency: lower marginal token cost by >=12% for top-10 tenants through policy-driven routing and prefetch optimization.
3. Alert fidelity: reduce false-positive operator alerts by 40% through telemetry fusion and economic thresholds.
4. Safety: maintain customer-facing SLOs (P99 token latency and error rate) within current bounds during all automated actions.

Key results / success metrics
- Operator MTTR for cache-miss storms: <=25 minutes.
- Percentage of capacity adjustments automated: >=65% for non-PSL (pre-specified level) tenants.
- Cost delta dashboard: visible cost savings of >=12% for at least 50% of tested workloads within 3 months of rollout.
- False alert rate on operator channels: <=10% of alerts after tuning.

Milestones & timeline (high level)
- Q1 2027: Baseline measurement & pilot design. Instrument cost-per-token pipelines, create synthetic workloads for burst economics lab.
- Q2 2027: Economic signal schema and API. Implement cost-synthesis service (service name: cost-synth) and expose signals to operator UIs and runtime-allocator.
- Q3 2027: Autonomy primitives v1. Safe autoscale and prefetch hints enforced by operator-guard rails (runtime-allocator v2, prefetch-service).
- Q4 2027: Canary automation for low-risk tenants. Integrate with rollout DSL and operator-approval queue.
- Q1–Q2 2028: Expanded automation and operator UX improvements. Replace manual change templates with guided automation workflows.
- Q3 2028: Cross-region economic fallback policies and full rollout.

Dependencies
- Telemetry: High-fidelity cost attribution (token attribution across models and routes). Owner: billing-infra.
- Runtime: runtime-allocator changes to accept economic-weighted routing. Owner: eng-serving-runtime.
- Prefetch & KV cache: prefetch-service readiness for operator-safe hints. Owner: eng-platform.
- RBAC & approvals: fine-grained operator roles in console. Owner: eng-platform + security.

Phases & implementation details
Phase 0 — Baseline (Q1 2027)
1. Run cost-sensitivity experiments for 30 representative tenants (open-source workloads + enterprise traces).
2. Create baseline dashboards: cost-per-tenant, cost-per-model-version, cold-cache cost multipliers.
3. Document operator workflows and current manual decision trees.

Phase 1 — Signal & UI (Q2 2027)
1. Implement cost-synth (stateless microservice) that aggregates request traces, token counts, GPU-time, and memory residency to produce per-request cost estimate. API: /v1/cost-signals {tenant_id, model, route, window, cost_est}.
2. Add a new dashboard panel: Operator Economic Lens (operator-dashboard:econ-lens).
3. Roll out read-only visibility to operators and SREs; collect feedback.

Phase 2 — Safe Autonomy Primitives (Q3 2027)
1. Extend runtime-allocator to accept "economic-weight" in placement decisions. Default multiplier = 1.0; can be scaled down for cheap model variants.
2. Implement prefetch-service hooks: hint priority, TTL, and eviction-safeguards.
3. Safety net: all automated actions create operator-tickets with auto-rollback predicates (error_rate > 0.5% OR P99 latency degrade > 10% for 5m).

Phase 3 — Canary & Operator Workflow Automation (Q4 2027)
1. Create an operator-approval queue with progressive automation (manual -> semi-auto -> fully-auto).
2. Integrate rollout DSL to run small-scale economic experiments (cohort size 2–5%) and collect A/B metrics: token-cost, QPS, error-rate.

Phase 4 — Scale & Cross-region Policies (2028)
1. Extend policies to regional-fallbacks and preemptible capacity pools.
2. Add multi-tenant fairness constraints to avoid negative externalities.

Monitoring, dashboards & alerting changes
- New dashboards to create/update:
  - Operator Economic Lens (operator-dashboard:econ-lens): cost-per-token heatmap, model-variant deltas, marginal GPU-minutes per 1k tokens.
  - Automation Safety Console (operator-dashboard:auto-safety): active automations, rollbacks, recent ticketed actions.
  - Prefetch Efficacy (prefetch-metrics): hit-rate change vs. cost delta, eviction churn.
- Alert thresholds and SLO checks to add:
  - Auto-action abort alert: when an automated action triggers rollback predicate (severity P1 if customer SLO violated).
  - Economic regression alert: sustained cost-per-token increase >8% over baseline for 15 minutes.
  - Prefetch-exhaustion alert: tenant prefetch queue >90% capacity for >10 minutes.

Runbook updates required (high priority list)
- operator-autonomy-fallback-runbook (new): how to pause/revoke automation, manual rollback steps, and emergency revert to conservative routing.
- kv-prefix-cache-eviction-troubleshoot (update): add sections on prefetch hint burnout and recommended TTL tuning.
- operator-oncall-cost-blast-response (new): triage steps when automation causes unexpected cost spikes.

Operational SLOs and safety constraints
- Maintain existing customer-facing SLOs: P99 token latency <= 600ms for hosted small models; error-rate <= 0.5% across cohorts.
- Automation safety guard: any automated change must run a 10-minute synthetic smoke test that verifies no SLO regressions before being promoted.

Ownership & stakeholders
- Program lead: Maya R. Chen (eng-platform).
- Runtime changes: Kairos Gomez (eng-serving-runtime).
- Cost pipeline & billing telemetry: Priya Nambiar (billing-infra).
- Operator UX + Console changes: Diego Alvarez (eng-platform UI).
- Security & RBAC: Sara H. Morgan (security).
- SRE validation & oncall playbook: Evan K. Li (eng-sre).

Budget & resource estimate (rough)
| Item                                   | FTE months | One-time infra | Notes                             |
|----------------------------------------|------------|----------------|-----------------------------------|
| cost-synth service                      | 4          | $12k           | instrumentation + storage         |
| runtime-allocator changes               | 6          | $8k            | kernel selection and QA           |
| operator UI and dashboard               | 3          | $5k            | dashboarding and access controls  |
| prefetched cache improvements           | 4          | $10k           | eviction/ttl tuning + experiments |
| Safety & testing harness                | 2          | $6k            | synthetic labs and canary infra   |

Total (approx): 19 FTE-months, $41k infra.

Rollout checklist (pre-canary)
1. Unit & integration tests for cost-synth API.
2. Synthetic workload runbook and baselines captured in dashboards.
3. Operator training session and playbook distribution.
4. RBAC roles for automation toggles verified.
5. Canary cohort selection criteria documented and approved.

Safety, risks & mitigations
- Risk: Automation causes unintended cross-tenant latency regressions.
  - Mitigation: automatic abort predicates + immediate rollback; restrict early automations to low-risk tenants.
- Risk: Cost signal inaccuracies lead to harmful routing changes.
  - Mitigation: conservative confidence intervals; require 2 independent signal windows before action.
- Risk: Operator trust erosion from noisy automations.
  - Mitigation: progressive rollout with human-in-the-loop, clear audit trail in tickets and dashboards.

Post-rollout retrospectives & checkpoints
- 30-day retrospective: operator time metrics, SLO adherence, cost delta analysis.
- 90-day deep dive: fairness impact on multi-tenant workloads, cross-region cost shift analysis.
- Quarterly: evaluate whether automation should be extended to enterprise/dedicated tiers.

Appendices & references
- Related runbooks: operator-runbook-templates (link internal id: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/operator-runbook-templates).
- Related dashboards: operator-dashboard:econ-lens (internal).
- Draft API spec: /api/internal/cost-synth/v1/spec (internal reference).

Action items (next 30 days)
1. Kickoff meeting with owners (Maya) and telemetry team to finalize cost signals schema.
2. Instrument three pilot tenants and publish baseline dashboards.
3. Draft operator-autonomy-fallback-runbook and circulate for review.

Contact
- Program lead: maya@redwood.ai
- Slack channel: #platform-operator-autonomy

This document will be updated after the Q1 2027 kickoff and after the initial pilot is complete.

title: dsid_63fc83f403f34016b63d368060adada5__stakeholder-advocacy-dossier-pilot-economics-and-security-scripts-2026.txt
text:
stakeholder-advocacy-dossier-pilot-economics-and-security-scripts-2026

Overview
========

This dossier is a compact, cross-functional playbook for activating and scaling a Redwood inference pilot with enterprise prospects. It combines concise positioning for each stakeholder (CISO, CTO, Platform/Infra, Product, Finance), a competitive snapshot you can share during discovery, scripts for short elevator and objection handling, sample pricing scenarios with transparent math, and a targeted security FAQ for prospects evaluating embedded or private deployments. Use this as the single-page advocacy brief in workshops, executive previews, and technical pilots.

Executive summary
-----------------

- Goal: Convert a 6–12 week pilot into an enterprise deployment by aligning evidence across security, platform, product, and finance stakeholders.
- Outcome metrics to prove: end-to-end P99 latency under target, cost per 1,000 tokens vs. incumbent, error rate <0.1% for production routes, and successful audit of data residency/KMS controls.
- Suggested pilot scope: 2 production routes (low latency + high throughput), up to 500k tokens/day, SLA-backed dedicated capacity for peak test windows.

Who to engage and why
---------------------

1) CISO / Head of Security
- Primary concerns: data residency, encryption-at-rest/in-transit, key management, audit logs, and supply-chain risk.
- One-line pitch: "Redwood Private gives you a customer-managed control plane with KMS/HSM integrations and full audit trails so security decisions remain in your hands."

2) CTO / VP Engineering
- Primary concerns: operational predictability, deployability, compatibility with infra, rollback safety.
- One-line pitch: "Same API and rollout primitives across hosted, dedicated, and private modes — minimize app changes while gaining predictable inference economics."

3) Platform / SRE
- Primary concerns: autoscaling behavior, observability, SLOs, tracing hooks, and cost controls.
- One-line pitch: "Per-route dashboards, token-level cost attribution, and configurable autoscale/burst policies so platform teams can enforce economics without developer changes."

4) Product / ML Engineers
- Primary concerns: quality regressions, model versioning, latency, and prompt experiments.
- One-line pitch: "Model pinning, canary rollouts, and integrated evaluation hooks guard quality while you iterate on prompts and model variants."

5) Finance / Procurement
- Primary concerns: TCO, commitment flexibility, pilot-to-production migration costs, and auditability of usage.
- One-line pitch: "Transparent per-token economics, optional reserved capacity for predictable unit costs, and migration credits for pilots that convert."

Tailored messaging snippets (short scripts)
------------------------------------------

- 30s CISO elevator: "For customers that cannot have vendor-managed keys or need region isolation, Redwood Private runs with a customer control plane and integrates with your KMS/HSM. We provide an audit log export and a prescriptive SOC2/ISO evidence package for pilots."

- 45s CTO elevator: "You can swap your model endpoint to Redwood with minimal SDK changes and benefit from deterministic batching and fallback policies. During pilot we'll instrument one critical route to measure production SLOs and cost delta."

Objection handling (concise scripts)
-----------------------------------

- Objection: "We can't trust vendor-managed data flows."
  - Script: "Understood — we recommend Redwood Private with VPC-only egress, customer-managed KMS, and an initial SOC2 evidence review. We can provide an engineering runbook and a 2-week on‑site/remote security validation window."

- Objection: "This will be too expensive compared to our internal GPUs."
  - Script: "We’ll run an apples-to-apples throughput and latency benchmark against your baseline (same prompts/seq lengths). Redwood Optimize then simulates batching and quantization profiles; typical pilots see 20–50% per-token cost improvement for production workloads."

Competitive snapshot (one-paragraph)
------------------------------------

Redwood positions between large managed API vendors and self-hosted inference runtimes: we provide the developer velocity and integrations of a hosted API, but with a deterministic, production-grade serving runtime and options for dedicated or private deployments. Notable differentiators for buyers: clear per-route cost attribution, automated fallback policies for reliability, and first-class model lifecycle controls (pinning, canary rollouts). For buyers leaning toward full self-hosting, highlight Redwood’s private deployment patterns and our migration credits for enterprise conversions.

Pilot configuration templates (recommended)
-----------------------------------------

Template A — Latency-focused pilot (recommended for consumer-facing UX)
1) Routes: 1 conversational route with streaming enabled; 1 reranking route for post-processing.
2) Traffic: mirror 5–10% of production traffic or simulate 100 concurrent sessions.
3) Targets: P50 < 150ms token, P95 < 350ms, model quality delta <2% from baseline.
4) Observability: tracing enabled, token-level cost export, and error-rate alert at 0.1%.

Template B — Throughput-focused pilot (recommended for batch/embedding workloads)
1) Routes: batch-embeddings, bulk-generation.
2) Traffic: 500k embeddings/day simulated with mixed vector sizes.
3) Targets: CPU/GPU utilization 60–85% during peak; throughput > target per commit.
4) Observability: queue latency histogram, batch sizing reports, and cache hit metrics.

Pricing guidance and worked examples
----------------------------------

Assumptions for worked scenarios:
- Unit costs used in examples are illustrative — adapt to current rate card during quotes.
- Pilot discount: 25% off hosted list for pilot periods under an MSA that converts.

ASCII pricing table (example math)

| Scenario | Mode | Usage | Example unit price | Monthly cost estimate | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Small pilot | Hosted API | 10M tokens | $0.0008 / token | $8,000 | Basic integration, no reserved capacity |
| Dedicated pilot | Dedicated | 50M tokens | $0.00045 / token (committed) | $22,500 | Reserved pool, predictable throughput |
| Private PoC | Private | 50M tokens | $0.00035 / token (incl. infra credit) | $17,500 + infra | Includes on-prem packaging and limited support |

Worked example: If a platform route uses 5M tokens/month and you aim to scale to 50M:
- Hosted list: 5M * $0.0008 = $4,000/month
- Reserved (dedicated) forecast: 50M * $0.00045 = $22,500/month (but unit cost decreases with higher commitment)
- Recommendation: start with hosted for 4–8 weeks to validate SLOs, then move to a modest reserved pool sized for 2–4x peak if conversion probability >40%.

Success criteria and metrics
---------------------------

- Technical success: P95 latency below agreed threshold, error rate <0.1%, model parity within guardrails on evaluation prompt set.
- Financial success: measured per-token cost delta vs. incumbent <= target threshold (e.g., 20% improvement or breakeven after reserved capacity).
- Business success: conversion to a 6–12 month reserved commitment or signed Private license.

Security FAQ for prospect meetings (ready-to-read answers)
---------------------------------------------------------

Q: Where is customer data stored during the pilot?
A: For Redwood Private, all persistent data remains in customer-controlled storage in the selected region. For Dedicated/Hosted pilots we can configure VPC peering and enable strict retention policies; short-lived token caches are stored on encrypted local volumes and rotated per best practice.

Q: Do you support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM)?
A: Yes. Private deployments and Dedicated customers can use customer-managed KMS or HSM. Keys can be rotated under customer policy and access is limited to approved operator roles.

Q: Can we run a vendor security review / on-site audit?
A: Yes. We have a standardized audit package (SOC2 summary, threat model, patching cadence) and an accelerated review process for pilot conversions. For Private pilots we support scheduled remote validation and a 2‑week engineering validation window.

Q: How do you handle secrets, tokens, and telemetry?
A: Secrets are stored encrypted at rest with strict RBAC controls. Token-level telemetry is anonymized by default for hosted deployments; for Private deployments telemetry can be forwarded to customer observability endpoints without vendor retention.

Rollout & escalation playbook (brief)
------------------------------------

1) Week 0: kickoff — align SLOs, success metrics, and security checklist.
2) Week 1–2: integration — instrument one critical route, enable tracing, and run baseline load tests.
3) Week 3–5: validation — run 2 production-like windows, capture metrics, and run Redwood Optimize suggestions.
4) Week 6–8: decision — present success evidence to stakeholders, propose conversion options (reserved capacity or Private license).
5) Escalation path: bench-level SRE -> Platform eng lead -> CTO/CSO. Include on-call contact from Redwood engagement team.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------

- Deal owner (Redwood): [RM assigned at time of engagement — replace before sharing].
- Technical lead (Redwood): Solutions Engineer — Marcus Green (marcus.green@redwood.ai).
- Security liaison (Redwood): Priya Shah (priya.shah@redwood.ai).

Appendix: quick checklist to attach to customer workshops
-------------------------------------------------------

- Signed NDA and SRA (security review annex)
- Pilot MSA with pilot discount clause
- List of evaluation prompts and sample payloads
- Expected peak hours and representative traffic patterns
- Contact list for escalation and weekly sync cadence

Notes on sharing: This dossier is intended to be shared with prospect buying committees during pilot negotiation, and adapted per vertical (finance/healthcare/legal) by appending any vertical-specific evidence or compliance artifacts. For restricted or customer-sensitive pilots mark this file as restricted and attach compliance artifacts from the security vault.

Related resources
-----------------

- Platform adoption decision playbook (internal)
- Pilot activation playbook and technical economics (internal)
- Security evidence package: SOC2/ISO/PCI summaries (security vault)

Document history
----------------

- 2026-04-02: Draft created by Leah Kim
- 2026-04-10: Added pricing worked examples and security FAQ (reviewers: Marcus Green)
- 2026-04-15: Incorporated reviewer feedback; prepared for go-to-market review

title: dsid_9070c2525f7f48489478992e2f5932d1__continuous-authorization-audit-streaming-playbook-2028.txt
text:
Continuous Authorization Audit Streaming Playbook

Overview

This playbook defines Redwood's approach for continuous authorization (authz) audit streaming: producing, transporting, storing, and using fine-grained authorization events across RBAC/ABAC systems, service meshes, and platform control planes to satisfy operational, forensic, and compliance evidence requirements. The goal is a reliable, low-latency audit stream that supports live detection, long-term retention for regulatory evidence, and automated packaging for audits.

Scope

- Systems in scope: API gateway, token service, identity provider integrations (OIDC/SAML), service control plane (sidecar/mesh), internal admin consoles, Dedicated/Private proxy layers.
- Event types: authorization_decision, privilege_escalation, permission_change, role_binding_change, delegated_access_grant, service_account_key_ops.
- Out of scope: application-specific business logs (those remain with product teams), PII-only event content (see data handling).

Objectives

1. Ensure every authorization decision that affects multi-tenant isolation or privileged actions emits a structured audit event.
2. Maintain an immutable, tamper-evident audit stream with metadata to support chain-of-custody evidence requests.
3. Provide streaming and historical query interfaces for SRE, Security, and Compliance.
4. Automate evidence bundles for scheduled audits and ad-hoc legal requests.

Key roles and ownership

- Security (owner): authz schema, evidence packaging templates, periodic review of retention policies.
- Eng Platform (producer owners): instrumenting libraries, SDKs, and gateway integration.
- Eng SRE (stream operator): pipeline SLAs, alerting, retention enforcement.
- Legal/Compliance (consumer): audit requirements, evidence acceptance criteria.
- Product teams (local owners): ensure application-level authorizations produce required events when applicable.

Design and data model

- Event transport: Kafka (primary), with fallback to object-store batched uploads for long-term archival in regions without streaming persistence.
- Immutable append-only event format with signed envelopes (HMAC using service key) to ensure tamper evidence during transit and at rest.

Minimum audit event schema (line-delimited JSON, example):

{
  "event_type": "authorization_decision",
  "timestamp": "2028-01-12T14:23:09Z",
  "request_id": "req_8f3a1b9c",
  "principal": {
    "id": "user:alice@example.com",
    "type": "user",
    "auth_method": "mfa"
  },
  "resource": "/v1/projects/1234/secret",
  "action": "read",
  "decision": "deny",
  "policy_id": "policy-tenant-isolation-v2",
  "reason": "role-mismatch",
  "signature": "hmac:v1:BASE64SIG=="
}

Note: the event JSON above is included verbatim for operators. Producers must ensure that PII elements are either pseudonymized or excluded unless approved by Security and Data Privacy.

Stream topology and guarantees

- Producers (gateway, token-service, control-plane) -> Kafka topics partitioned by tenant-id -> Stream processors for enrichment (geo, device, risk signals) -> Cold-tier: encrypted object store (daily batches signed) -> Evidence API for packaging.
- Guarantees: at-least-once delivery to Kafka, idempotent enrichment processors, daily signed manifests that map topic offsets to archived batches.

Retention and data residency

- Default retention: 2 years in hot+warm tiers for global logs; 7 years archival for regulated customers on contract.
- Residency: Events are stored in region of origin by default. Cross-region replication requires an approved Data Residency Exception.
- Redaction policy: PII fields are redacted at producer if the tenant has chosen privacy shielding. Redaction must be reversible only by Compliance with a legal process when reversible encryption is used.

Evidence packaging workflow

1. Request intake: Legal/Compliance opens an evidence request ticket referencing tenant and time window.
2. Evidence API call: Evidence service composes manifests mapping topic offsets, enrichment snapshots, and archived batches.
3. Signing and hash: Package is signed with organizational signing key and hash chain published to the evidence index.
4. Delivery: Secure transfer (SFTP or customer-configured cloud bucket with pre-signed URL and access logs) and audit of delivery recorded.

Operational runbook (SRE + Security)

- Alerting thresholds:
  - Consumer lag > 30 minutes -> P1 to SRE-runbook.
  - Failed manifest generation -> P1 to Security and SRE.
  - Archive write error -> P0 (investigate immediate write path and fallback uploads).

- Incident triage steps (numbered):
  1. Confirm scope: which topic(s) and tenants affected, determine last known good offset.
  2. If producer outage: engage owning service team, toggle short-term diagnostic sampling to avoid noise.
  3. If integrity suspected (e.g., signature mismatch): freeze further ingestion for affected partitions and create a chain-of-custody ticket.
  4. For retention misconfiguration: run targeted rehydration from cold backups and replay into append-only archive with new manifest.

Sample queries and investigator tools

- Example KSQL query to find denial spikes for a tenant over 1 hour:

SELECT tenant_id, COUNT(*) AS denials, WINDOWSTART, WINDOWEND
FROM authz_events_stream
WHERE event_type = 'authorization_decision' AND decision='deny'
GROUP BY tenant_id, TUMBLINGWINDOW(hour, 1)
HAVING denials > 100;

- Investigator checklist: correlate request_id across gateway trace, authz_event, and application logs; validate HMAC signature on event envelope; locate archived batch using manifest ID.

Secure SDLC gating and automation

- Producer changes that modify schema or event semantics require:
  1. ADR describing schema change and rollover plan.
  2. Contract tests (producer + enrichment consumer).
  3. Canary rollout to subset of tenants with monitoring: schema conformance, consumer lag, and sample evidence package verification.
- CI step: run schema-registry validation + integration test that produces synthetic events and verifies evidence packaging end-to-end.

Risk exceptions and compensating controls

- Temporary disablement of streaming (e.g., for an emergency patch) requires:
  - Approved exception ticket recorded in the risk register with rationale and end-date.
  - Compensating control: enable buffered file-based signed uploads, increase retention of local queues, and schedule manual evidence packaging.

KPIs and SLOs

- Stream availability SLO: 99.95% weekly availability of the write path.
- Evidence packaging latency: 95th percentile < 30 minutes from request to signed manifest for hot-tier queries.
- Integrity SLO: 100% of archived daily manifests must have verifiable signatures; any failure triggers immediate remediation.

Testing and validation

- Quarterly: cryptographic signature verification audit and end-to-end evidence drill with Compliance.
- Annual: simulated legal hold request and full-chain-of-custody demonstration with independent witness (internal audit).

Appendix: Implementation checklist (short)

- [ ] Identify producers and integrate SDK (library: platform/authz-audit-sdk v1.3).
- [ ] Register topic naming convention: authz.events.{region}.{tenant_hash}.v1
- [ ] Deploy enrichment processors with idempotency keys.
- [ ] Configure archival buckets with KMS encryption and signed manifests.
- [ ] Add CI integration tests and ADR templates.

Contact and escalation

- Security on-call: pagerduty/team-security-oncall
- SRE stream owner: streams-sre@redwood.example.com
- Evidence intake (Compliance): compliance-evidence@redwood.example.com

Related pages and references

- See: Structured Audit Pipeline and Query Playbook (audit-logging) for topic-level query examples.
- See: Entitlement Provisioning and Evidence Automation (rbac-and-auth) for role-change event producers.

End of playbook

title: dsid_57b5f77726da4c0586d6619307e4bce5__kernel-stability-siege-testing-and-metrics-manifest-2026.txt
text:
Kernel stability siege testing and metrics manifest

Summary:

This document defines the 'siege testing' program for runtime kernel components: a repeatable, low-variability stress protocol designed to exercise kernel hot paths, handoff/fallback logic, allocator behavior, and scheduler admission/signaling. The goal is to produce deterministic signal surfaces and a small set of stable metrics that correlate with production regressions and that can be used as gates for kernel changes and experimental rollouts.

Scope:
- Components: kernel dispatcher, prefetch/hint path, batch slicer, KV cache eviction function, tensor allocator, cooperative preemption shim.
- Environments: synthetic lab cluster (staging-fidelity-1), canary pool, and a shadow-prod replay mode.
- Exclusions: network stack-wide failures, hardware thermal throttling (handled separately).

Why 'siege' testing?
- Traditional microbenchmarks miss cross-component contention; siege runs sustained, controlled contention across shared resources to reveal systemic instabilities (oscillation, runaway backpressure, allocator landlocks).

Testing matrix and workload catalog:

1) Workload classes (representative):
   a) Short-chat burst (seq_len 32, reply tokens 32): high qps, small KV reuse.
   b) Long-completion (seq_len 1024, reply tokens 512): memory-heavy, long kernel occupancy.
   c) Mixed-concurrency (50% short, 25% long, 25% moderate): mimics PLG mixed surface.
   d) Cold-start storm (many first-frame requests with empty caches).
   e) Model-switch churn (frequent model variants and quantization profile swaps).

2) Siege axes (vary these orthogonally):
   - Concurrency (clients): 100, 500, 2000
   - Batch-intent randomness: deterministic vs jittered arrival
   - Kernel variant set: baseline, opt-kernel-A, fallback-emu
   - KV cache hit ratio: 10%, 50%, 90%
   - Quantization mode: fp16, int8-quantized

Metrics manifest (canonical signals) - interpreted as single-line CSV-compatible columns for dashboards:

| metric_name                          | description                                                   | unit    | sampling_window |
|--------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|---------|-----------------|
| kernel_dispatch_latency_p50          | kernel dispatcher processing latency (p50)                    | ms      | 1m              |
| kernel_dispatch_latency_p95          | p95 latency for kernel dispatch                               | ms      | 1m              |
| kernel_dispatch_latency_p99          | p99 (captures microbursts / hitch)                            | ms      | 1m              |
| kernel_cpu_busy_ratio                | % time CPU-bound in kernel control loops                      | pct     | 1m              |
| kernel_gpu_occupancy_ratio           | % GPU occupancy recorded during runs                          | pct     | 1m              |
| allocator_fragmentation_score       | normalized score (0..1) indicating fragmentation severity     | unitless| 5m              |
| kvcache_eviction_rate                | evictions per second                                          | /s     | 1m              |
| backpressure_retry_rate              | fraction of requests retried due to admission                 | pct     | 1m              |
| kernel_fallback_count                | number of fallback activations (kernel -> software-path)      | count   | 1m              |
| input_tail_response_time_p999        | e2e input->final-token latency p999                           | ms      | 1m              |
| kernel_stall_incidents               | counted 10s+ stalls identified by watchdog                     | count   | 1m              |
| error_budget_consumed_rate           | % of configured SLO budget used due to this test              | pct     | 1m              |

Pass / fail and stability criteria:
- Green: All p99 latencies < target for workload class, allocator_fragmentation_score < 0.3, kernel_fallback_count == 0 during steady-state 30m window.
- Amber: Any single metric crosses warning threshold (p99 > target*1.5 or fragmentation > 0.6), or >5 fallback activations in 30m. Requires immediate engineering review and localized bisect.
- Red: Recurring oscillation (latency spikes followed by capacity collapse) or kernel_stall_incidents > 3 in 10m. Block rollout and open P1 triage.

Example thresholds (should be tuned per-model):
- Short-chat: p99 < 120ms (green), warning if >180ms, critical >400ms.
- Long-completion: p99 < 900ms (green), warning if >1400ms, critical >3000ms.

Run procedure (operator-run; 20–60 minutes per configuration):
1) Pre-checks:
   - Ensure staging-fidelity-1 node labels and quotas are provisioned: 
     * kubectl get nodes -l env=staging-fidelity-1
   - Confirm telemetry ingestion: grafana/ingest check 'kernel_dispatch_latency_p95' has fresh datapoints.
2) Deploy test harness (siege-runner):
   - git clone git@internal:redwood/siege-runner.git && cd siege-runner
   - kubectl apply -f deploy/siege-runner-staging.yaml --record
3) Load scenario selection:
   - Edit scenarios/config.yaml: set workload_class, concurrency, kv_hit_target.
   - Example snippet:
     workload: short-chat
     concurrency: 500
     batch_jitter_ms: 5
     kv_hit_ratio: 0.5
4) Start run and tag with experiment metadata:
   - ./bin/siege-runner --scenario scenarios/config.yaml --tags kernel-experiment=stable-2026 --duration 30m
5) Observe live dashboards: grafana dashboard id: runtime-kernel-siege-v2 (owner: eng-serving-runtime)
6) Collect artifacts at end: traces archive (traces.tar.gz), perf profiles (perf.data), allocator heap dumps (allocator-heap-*.bin), and the siege-runner events.json.
7) Upload to artifact store: rclone cp traces.tar.gz remote:kernel-siege/2026-02-03-<runid>

Instrumentation and telemetry guidance:
- Required tracing spans: kernel.dispatch, kernel.batch_slice, allocator.malloc, kvcache.evict, scheduler.admit. Ensure spans include kernel_variant, model_id, request_cohort labels.
- Sampling policy: 100% for p99 tail-trace capture during siege; annotated with 'siege_run_id'.
- Lightweight task-level counters should be emitted at 1s resolution to Prometheus push gateway for short retention.

Dashboards and alerting (deliverables):
- runtime-kernel-siege-v2 (Grafana): combined heatmap of p99 over concurrency sweep, allocator fragmentation trend, fallback waterfall chart.
- Alerts (temporary during siege): alert if kernel_stall_incidents > 1 in 2m or backpressure_retry_rate > 2%.

Analysis checklist (post-run):
1) Verify steady-state window (last 20m) has stable request rates.
2) Correlate p99 spikes with kernel_fallback_count and allocator_fragmentation_score.
3) Inspect traces for sequential blocking patterns (allocator->dispatcher->kvcache).
4) Run deterministic replay of top-5 tail traces with kernel variant toggles.
5) If amber/red observed, run a binary bisect: isolate last change (kernel commit range) and re-run siege with single-commit rollback.

Binary bisect protocol (fast safety bisect):
1) Narrow candidate commits to the minimal set by commit-time ordering and previous green runs.
2) Deploy candidate commit to a 2-node canary pool with identical siege workload.
3) Run 10m micro-siege focused on reproducing failing signal.
4) If failing, mark commit as suspect and iterate; if green, exclude commit and continue.

Artifacts to archive per run (minimum):
- siege-metadata.json (scenario + tags)
- traces.tar.gz (all collected spans)
- perf-summaries.csv (per-node p50/p95/p99)
- allocator-heap-*.bin
- kube-state-dump.yaml

Ownership and cadence:
- Program owner: runtime-reliability (eng-serving-runtime) — primary contact: Asha Patel (author).
- Siege maintenance: rotate workloads quarterly and review thresholds after each major kernel merge.
- Scheduled runs: weekly smoke (short 20m mixed-concurrency) and monthly deep-siege (full matrix).

Runbook: interpreting common failure modes:
- Symptom: p99 spikes + immediate kernel_fallback_count increase. Likely cause: kernel invariant assertion or slow path fallback. Action: check kernel logs (grep "fallback-activated" /var/log/kernel/*.log), collect first-tail trace, disable canary kernel variant.
- Symptom: allocator_fragmentation_score rising steadily with long-completion workloads. Likely cause: allocation patterns + tensor pinning. Action: trigger allocator-compact routine, capture heap dump, run reproducer with slab debugging flags.
- Symptom: oscillation between high occupancy and near-zero throughput. Likely cause: admission controller thresholds too aggressive combined with eviction storm. Action: reduce admission aggression, increase kvcache size for test, re-run.

Security and data handling:
- Siege runs must not use customer data. All test corpora reside in 'siege-corpus/public' and are sanitized.
- Artifacts containing telemetry are internal-only; upload paths are restricted to eng-serving-runtime group.

Appendix: example CLI recipes
- Start a short-chat siege locally (developer):
  ./bin/siege-runner --scenario scenarios/short-chat.yaml --concurrency 100 --duration 20m --local-debug

- Replay a trace against a kernel variant under test:
  ./bin/trace-replay --trace traces/tail-1234.json --kernel-variant opt-kernel-A --replay-speed real-time

Notes and future work:
- Add thermal/NRM (non-replayable memory pressure) axis to catch hardware-coupled flakes.
- Integrate automated bisect with CI as an optional post-merge siege gate for high-risk kernel changes.

References:
- See related: controlled-kernel-perturbation-playbook (link in related_pages).
- Runtime telemetry data model: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-telemetry-sampling-cost-aware-profiling-manual-2027.json

Document change log:
- 2024-11-12: Created by Asha Patel.
- 2025-07-10: Added allocator_fragmentation metric and bisect protocol (reviewers: Marco Li).
- 2026-02-03: Formalized pass/fail thresholds and added artifact manifest (reviewers: Priya Nambiar, Ethan Cole).

title: dsid_faa411f37bb4427d934512b92f46a483__playground-patterns-support-sherpa-2026.txt
text:
Playground patterns and support sherpa

Overview:

This page collects pragmatic developer-experience patterns (the "playground") and a compact support 'Sherpa' that engineers can use to onboard, iterate, and troubleshoot SDK integrations with Redwood’s inference API. The goal is to reduce time-to-first-success for integrators, and provide a single reference for reproducible canonical fixes for the most common edge cases.

When to use this doc:
- Teams building or embedding Redwood SDKs to iterate quickly in a local or CI sandbox.
- Customer success and support engineers troubleshooting reproducible failures.
- Docs site authors writing quickstarts and snippet bundles.

Quick start patterns (recipes):
1) Minimal local playground (good for debugging auth and streaming):
   - Create a sandbox project directory and add the sample .env (API_KEY, REDWOOD_ENV).
   - Run the local proxy (see sample below) to capture requests & replay.
   - Use the minimal client snippet to assert connectivity and token usage.

2) Batch vs streaming toggle test (validate latency-cost behavior):
