- If the incident involves EU-only tenants (residency label present), evidence must remain in EU zone buckets and access must be granted only to staff with EU processing authorization. See label: residency:EU.
- For hybrid-residency customers, coordinate with Privacy & Legal before any artifact transfer outside permitted zones.

Chain-of-evidence steps (recommended):
1) Assign evidence custodian: security investigator (primary) and SRE (secondary).
2) Create evidence record in internal tracker: evidence-id, artifacts list, custodian, custody log.
3) Collect artifacts using read-only copies and compute SHA256 hashes.
4) Upload to evidence bucket with encryption and immutability flags (if supported).
5) Update custody log with date/time, operator, action, and destination URI.

Secure-SDLC integration and remediation gating:
- All code changes intended to remediate segmentation incidents must pass an elevated review: security-review required + automated policy tests for RBAC regression.
- Pull request checklist additions for remediation PRs:
  - unit/regression tests covering the RBAC policy paths
  - canary rollout plan with feature flag and fallback
  - performance backstop to ensure latency SLOs not violated (99th percentile token latency must remain within baseline + 30%).
- Release blocking criteria: failing evidence-preservation steps or incomplete audit captures are release-blocking until resolved.

Notifications and stakeholders (communication):
- Pager duty groups: sec-oncall-tenant, platform-oncall.
- Slack channels (restricted): #sec-tenant-incidents (read-only for non-stakeholders).
- Notification cadence: initial triage within 15 minutes for Sev1 to legal, C-level ops; hourly updates until containment.

Regulatory and compliance packaging (what to provide to auditors):
- Evidence manifest (CSV) with artifact URIs, hashes, custodian signatures, residency assertions, and legal hold tags.
- Signed preservation affidavit from custodian describing actions taken and timing. Template available as /templates/preservation-affidavit.md.
- Redacted sample of impacted request/response pairs with consistent redaction rules documented in /security/redaction-guidelines.md.

Operational templates and automation (location):
- Collection scripts: /infra-scripts/evidence-collector.sh (invoked with --evid-id).
- Custody tracker template: internal jira template 'EVID-TRACKER'.
- S3 lifecycle and replication manifests: terraform modules under infra/terraform/modules/evidence-buckets.

Post-incident review and risk/exceptions handling:
1) Within 7 days: post-incident review (owner: security manager) with attendees: SRE, product, legal, affected OEMs/customers as needed.
2) Document root cause, sequence-of-events, and permanent remediations in the RCA page.
3) If remediation requires an exception to existing controls (temporary entitlements, expanded cross-region access), file a risk-and-exceptions request using the template at /confluence/security-and-compliance/risk-and-exceptions/exception-request-template. The request must include compensating controls and an explicit expiration time.

Monitoring and regression detection after remediation:
- Add continuous evals to detect recurring policy overrides: daily authz-audit queries for anomalous policy evaluations.
- Include synthetic tests in the perf suite that simulate tenant boundary checks (see eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/tenant-isolation-tests).

Appendix A — Example commands and snippets:
- Export authz events: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $LOG_API_KEY" "https://log-api.internal/v1/stream?tenant=t-012345&service=authz-audit&from=2026-02-10T09:50:00Z" | jq . > authz-stream.ndjson
- Snapshot KV store (GCP datastore example): gcloud datastore export --kinds=redwood_kv --namespaces=t-012345 gs://temp-evidence/kv-export-20260210
- Evidence upload (AWS example): aws s3 cp authz-events.json s3://redwood-evidence-prod/evid/EVID-20260210-authz-9f3a/ --sse aws:kms --sse-kms-key-id arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111122223333:key/abcd-efg

Appendix B — Ownership and contact matrix:
- Security-oncall: PagerDuty sec-oncall-tenant, primary investigator.
- SRE: platform-oncall, assists with snapshots, network captures, and kube-level containment.
- Privacy & Legal: consult for residency, cross-border transfer, and regulatory notifications.
- Customer Success: coordinates customer communication for Dedicated and Private deployments.

Revision history:
- 2025-11-18: Initial draft (Marta Ruiz).
- 2026-01-09: Added retention policy examples and cross-region replication controls (Ethan Zhao).
- 2026-02-12: Finalized severity SLA and secure-SDLC gating (Priya Menon).

Related artifacts and links:
- /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/least-privilege-evidence-and-access-risk-playbook-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/known-issues/tenant-isolation-regressions-2025
- /infra/terraform/modules/evidence-buckets (internal repo)

Contact for questions: Marta Ruiz (security) — mruiz@redwood.example.com

title: dsid_ccef2cc20569412994ad9c68223054cb__operator-readiness-smoke-tests-and-ops-simulations-2025.txt
text:
Operator Readiness: Smoke Tests & Ops Simulations

Overview:
This document defines a standardized program for operator readiness driven by automated smoke tests and scheduled operations simulations (ops-sims). The program's goal is to reduce time-to-detect, improve first-response accuracy, and validate runbook/automation effectiveness before customer impact. It complements regular game-days by focusing on repeatable, measurable smoke-test workflows that run as part of CI and during oncall rotations.

Scope:
- Services: inference-api, routing-service, kv-cache, model-proxy, quota-gateway
- Operators: first-responder oncall, SRE bridge, service owner, customer success liaison (for customer-facing scenarios)
- Test types: fast smoke (30s–5m), stability smoke (5m–30m), degraded-path simulation (15m–2h)

Why this matters:
1) Catch regressions in alarm-to-remediation flows before production impact.
2) Ensure runbooks are executable by new responders.
3) Validate automation (auto-scaling, fallback routing, cache warming) under realistic load patterns.
4) Produce reproducible evidence for post-incident retros and regulatory audits.

Program Components:
1) Smoke-test harness and CI integration
   - A small Go-based test runner (cmd/smoke-runner) executes scenario scripts against test and staging clusters and publishes results to the Operator Dashboard.
   - CI jobs: smoke-fast (on PR to infra/runtime), smoke-nightly (staging), smoke-full-weekly (multi-region)
   - Failure policy: failing smoke-fast blocks merges to main for changes touching runtime infra.

2) Ops-sim calendar and cadence
   - Mini-sims: 1-hour focused sims run weekly per service team (first-responder + owner).
   - Full-sims: 4-hour cross-functional sims (SRE, runtime, customer success, product) run quarterly and are scored.
   - Post-sim retro and action tracking mandatory within 72 hours.

3) Runbook validation matrix
   - Every critical runbook is assigned a verification frequency: smoke (weekly), quarterly sim (quarterly), code-coupled test (on PR).
   - Owners maintain a checklist in the runbook header indicating last-verified date and verifier.

Minimum Acceptance Criteria (table):
| Item | Threshold | Evidence |
|---|---:|---:|
| Alert generation latency | <= 60s from fault injection | Alert ID + timestamp in Operator Dashboard |
| First ack time (sim) | <= 5 min | Pager event + oncall ack log |
| Runbook reproducibility | 90% steps succeed in staging | Step-level pass/fail artifacts (logs/screenshots) |
| Automated fallback success | 95% for injected failure mode | Traffic routing logs, request success % |

Triggering smoke tests (how-to):
1) Via CI: push to repo that contains change to runtime/core triggers smoke-fast.
2) Manual run: use smoke-runner CLI per section below for ad-hoc validation during oncall handoff.

Smoke-runner CLI examples:
- Quick check (fast smoke): 
  ./smoke-runner --scenario basic-echo --target staging --timeout 60s
- Degraded-path sim (full): 
  ./smoke-runner --scenario kv-eviction-and-slow-proxy --target staging --duration 20m --collect-traces

Sample smoke scenario (YAML):
---
name: kv-eviction-and-slow-proxy
steps:
  - id: priming-traffic
    type: traffic
    qps: 20
    duration: 60s
    assertion: 99th_p99_latency < 200ms
  - id: evict-kv
    type: fault-inject
    service: kv-cache
    action: evict-keys
    keys: sample-key-prefix*
  - id: slow-proxy
    type: fault-inject
    service: model-proxy
    action: add-latency
    milliseconds: 300
  - id: validate-fallback
    type: assertion
    query: /healthz?route=fallback
    expected_status: 200
---
(Place scenario files in repo: infra/op-sims/scenarios/)

Escalation & Communication Flow (numbered run):
1) Detect: Monitoring fires alerts into PagerDuty, with tags: service, region, impact-lanes.
2) Acknowledge: First-responder acknowledges in <5 min, posts short status in Slack #ops-bridge and creates a sim ticket if running test.
3) Assess: Triage & impact classification by owner using the Decision Ladder (see below).
4) Execute: Follow validated runbook steps; invoke automation where safe.
5) Bridge: If >30 minutes without resolution or cross-service impacts, open a bridge and invite SRE and CS.
6) Customer Notice: For customer-affecting incidents, use the Customer Comms Template below within 60 minutes of bridge formation.

Decision Ladder (triage rubric):
- Step 1: Is the alert actionable? (yes -> proceed, no -> adjust alert)
- Step 2: Scope: single-tenant, multi-tenant, whole-region
- Step 3: Severity: S1 (outage), S2 (degraded), S3 (no customer impact)
- Step 4: Containment strategy: throttle, fallback, rollback, capacity add

Customer Comms Templates (short and long):
- Short status (initial, internal copy to CS):
  Subject: Redwood inference — Investigating elevated latency in <region>
  Body: We are investigating reports of increased latency affecting inference requests in <region>. We have opened a bridge and are working to identify the root cause. We will provide updates every 30 minutes. Impacted customers: <list>.

- Public status page template (for StatusPage):
  Title: Degraded inference latency — <region>
  Summary: We are currently experiencing elevated latency for inference requests in <region>. Traffic is being routed to fallback hosts where possible.
  Latest update: <time> — Engineers have identified a cache eviction pattern and are running mitigations.

Ops-sim Scoring Rubric (full-sim):
- Detection score (30 pts): alerts produced and routed correctly (0–30).
- Response score (30 pts): ack time, runbook execution completeness (0–30).
- Communication score (20 pts): bridge establishment, customer notice cadence (0–20).
- Remediation score (20 pts): solution correctness, post-sim artifact quality (0–20).
A passing sim requires >= 75 total points and no critical gaps in runbook steps.

Post-sim Retro Template (actionable):
1) Summary of scenario and timeline (who, what, when).
2) Findings (what worked, what failed).
3) Actions (owner, due date, validation step).
4) Evidence (logs, CI smoke link, runbook version).
5) Policy changes (alert tuning, runbook edits).

Ownership matrix (table):
| Role | Primary responsibilities | On-sim expectation |
|---|---|---:|
| First-responder | Ack, initial triage, runbook start | Execute first two runbook blocks |
| Service owner | Deep troubleshooting, code rollbacks | Lead root cause analysis |
| SRE bridge | Bridge coordination, cross-service calls | Maintain timeline + status page updates |
| Customer Success | Customer notices, FAQs | Draft public messaging and CS Q&A |

Runbook Quality Checklist (to be in every runbook header):
- [ ] Has a clear owner and last-verified date
- [ ] Steps are executable by a non-owner operator
- [ ] Includes safe-rollback instructions and automation guardrails
- [ ] Contains smoke-test scenario name and repo path
- [ ] Links to related dashboards and traces

Operational SOPs (short):
- Oncall handoff: outgoing oncall runs smoke-fast against staging with scenario: handoff-sanity within 15 minutes of the handoff window and attaches result to handoff note.
- New runbook onboarding: new runbooks must pass a first verification smoke within 7 days of creation.
- Runbook pruning: owners should remove/annotate steps that are no longer valid during quarterly review.

Evidence retention and compliance:
- Smoke-test logs retained for 90 days in logstore.
- Full sim artifacts (videos of bridge, timing spreadsheets, scored rubric) retained for 12 months in the retro archive.
- Regulated-customer scenarios tagged and stored separately with restricted access.

Appendix A — Example Post-sim Action (realistic):
- Action: Add a cache-warming preflight when restarting proxy pods
- Owner: Marcus Chen
- Due: 2025-07-01
- Validation: smoke-runner scenario kv-eviction-and-slow-proxy passes in staging with fallback success >95%

Appendix B — Quick links and commands:
- smoke-runner repo: git@github.com:redwood-inference/op-sims.git
- Operator Dashboard: https://ops.redwood-inference.internal/dashboard/smoke-tests
- Runbook location: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbook-library/

Contact and escalation list:
- SRE Pager: pagerduty://team-sre
- Ops Slack channel: #ops-bridge
- Incident executive contact: exec-oncall@redwood-inference.com

Document maintenance:
This doc is owned by engineering (oncall program). Review cadence: 6 months. Update the header in any change and record the verifier.

title: dsid_5e65a1cb22b6464e9f36d0fa2d1f4317__2026-02-09-sev2-dedicated-autoscaler-stuck.txt
text:
Postmortem: SEV-2 Dedicated autoscaler stuck at min capacity (2026-02-09)

The Dedicated autoscaler stopped scaling above min due to a metrics query change that returned empty series for a subset of clusters.
Two Dedicated customers in us-west experienced sustained queueing and timeouts. p99 latency exceeded 6s for ~70 minutes; timeout rate peaked at 3.2%.
13:22 UTC: Support escalated customer reports of timeouts on Dedicated pools (us-west).
13:28 UTC: SRE on-call confirmed queue depth rising and no scale-out events.
13:40 UTC: Identified autoscalermetrics query change deployed earlier that day.
14:05 UTC: Hotfix applied to autoscaler query; scale-out resumed.
14:20 UTC: Queue depth normalized; timeouts subsided.
14:47 UTC: Incident resolved.
A refactor in the autoscalerPromQL query switched label matching from cluster_id to cluster. Some clusters emitted cluster_id only, causing the query to return no data and preventing scale decisions.
Primary detection was via customer escalation; internal alerting on scale-out suppression was missing.
Rolled forward a hotfix restoring label compatibility and added a fallback query when no series are returned.
Once identified, the fix was small and low risk. Capacity was available to scale immediately.
Insufficient alerting on autoscaler making no decisions; canary did not include clusters with legacy labels.
Add alert: autoscaler decision loop sees empty metrics for >5 minutes (SRE; due 2026-02-25).
Add integration test covering both cluster and cluster_id labels (Infrastructure; due 2026-03-05).
Update Dedicated release checklist to require canary across at least one legacy-labeled cluster (Infrastructure; due 2026-02-22).

title: dsid_af07f94d81764b1fa7ddcf8412037685__serving-consumption-experiments-framework-prd-and-co-packaging-playbook-2029-11-20.txt
text:
serving-consumption-experiments-framework-prd-and-co-packaging-playbook-2029-11-20

Title: Serving Consumption Experiments Framework — PRD and Co-Packaging Playbook

Summary:
This document defines a repeatable experimentation framework and associated commercial packaging guidance to evaluate and commercialize consumption-side interventions on Redwood’s inference platform. It covers goals, core experiments, instrumentation requirements, acceptance criteria, rollout safety checks, and recommended pricing/packaging patterns for successful experiments that bridge product, commercial, and engineering stakeholders.

Problem statement:
- Teams need a standardized way to run controlled consumption experiments (e.g., batching defaults, cache-enabled tiers, adaptive SLOs) that: (1) surface measurable cost and latency impact, (2) preserve customer experience, and (3) produce artifacts that map directly to pricing & packaging options.
- Ad-hoc experiments produce inconsistent metrics, avoidable regression risk, and unclear commercial signal.

Goals (what success looks like):
- Reproducible experiments with end-to-end instrumentation across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Clear mapping from experiment outcome to at least three commercialization levers: credits/discounts, fidelity tiers, and SLO-backed bundles.
- Safety-first rollout with automated rollback triggers and guardrails to prevent customer impact.
- Baseline experiment-to-packaging lead time <= 8 weeks (from hypothesis to commercial pilot).

Non-goals:
- This is not a customer-facing SLA document.
- It does not prescribe model-level optimizations (quantization kernels live in eng-serving-runtime docs).

Scope:
- Applicable surfaces: Hosted API (primary), Redwood Dedicated (secondary), Redwood Private (limited: requires opt-in telemetry).
- Workstreams covered: experiment infra, metrics schema, agent orchestration, product UX for opt-ins, pricing templates, and sales enablement collateral.

Key definitions:
1) Consumption experiment — a controlled change in the serving stack or defaults intended to influence unit economics (examples: prefetching, adaptive batching, cached prefixes, quantization-policy assignment).
2) Fidelity mapping — classification of output fidelity policies (high / medium / economize) and their observable quality metrics.
3) Commercial packaging — charging construct offered to customers (token-based credits, fidelity add-ons, SLO bundles).

Success metrics (for an experiment run):
- Primary: delta tokens/second cost (% reduction) and 95p latency change (ms).
- Quality guard: no more than 1.0% increase in top-line regression for evaluated prompt set (measured by automated evals).
- Adoption metric: 3% of eligible customers opt-in during pilot or assigned in commercial trial.
- Risk control: automated rollback executed < 2% of runs due to regression signals.

Experiment framework requirements (high level):
- Instrumentation and telemetry:
  - Emit experiment_id and treatment tag for every request.
  - Token-level cost attribution (per-request token_count, compute_ms, cached_hit boolean).
  - Quality capture: 1:1 eval harness capture for a configurable prompt set (up to 5k prompts/day for pilot).
- Experiment orchestration:
  - Support traffic split (0-100%) by percent and by customer cohort (tenant-aware).
  - Built-in ramp schedule (stages: canary 0.5% -> ramp 5% -> broad 25% -> commercial).
  - Fallback policy: automatic model variant fallback and cross-region failover when SLO violation threshold exceeded.
- Data storage and retention:
  - Experiment metadata retained for minimum 180 days.
  - Aggregated experiment summaries available in Console and API for 365 days.
- Access controls and confidentiality:
  - Experiment results classified internal; customer-specific metrics may be flagged restricted and require legal sign-off to share.

Functional requirements (numbered):
1) FR-001: Experiment API — A REST endpoint to create/update/terminate experiments with fields: name, hypothesis, treatment_config, allocation_rules, safety_config, observability_config.
2) FR-002: Console UI — Visual experiment builder with pre-filled templates for common experiments (batching, caching, quantization policy).
3) FR-003: Metrics export — Per-experiment export to S3/BigQuery with schema versioning.
4) FR-004: Prompt-set manager — Attachable prompt sets for quality validation; support fingerprinting and diff reports.
5) FR-005: Auto-rollback engine — Rule-based engine with threshold config (e.g., quality_regression > 0.5% AND latency_increase > 15% -> rollback).

Non-functional requirements (NFR):
- NFR-001: Observability latency — experiment tagging and metric emission must add < 0.5ms p95 overhead to request path.
- NFR-002: Scalability — support concurrent experiments across 10k tenants without > 2% throughput degradation.
- NFR-003: Privacy — for Private deployments, telemetry is optional; experiments requiring telemetry must have an opt-in SDK.

Design considerations and trade-offs:
- Per-tenant vs global experiments: per-tenant yields cleaner commercial signal but increases complexity for capacity planning; global experiments are cheaper to run but noisier for billing signals. Recommendation: start with per-cohort experiments mapped to buying personas.
- Instrumentation cost: token-level tracking increases storage cost. Use sampled token traces for long tail while keeping full traces during canary windows.

Experiment templates (examples):
- Template A: Adaptive batching default change
  - Hypothesis: Increasing default batch_size from 8 -> 12 for short-context requests reduces per-token cost by >= 12% with < 5% 95p latency increase.
  - Metrics: cost_per_1k_tokens, 95p latency, cache_hit_rate.
  - Ramp: 0.5% -> 5% -> 20%.
- Template B: Prefix KV caching for conversational flows
  - Hypothesis: Keeping KV cache warm for recurrent session IDs reduces compute_ms by >= 20% for returning sessions.
  - Metrics: compute_ms, kv_cache_hit_ratio, quality eval delta.
- Template C: Mix of quantization profiles by tenant size
  - Hypothesis: Small tenants can use quantized variants (4-bit) without measurable quality loss on curated prompts.
  - Metrics: eval score delta, error_rate, latency p50/p95.

Safety and rollback playbook (procedural):
1) Define safety thresholds in the experiment creation flow.
2) Run canary at 0.5% for minimum 24 hours with full trace capture.
3) Evaluate automated quality reports and run manual spot checks.
4) If rollback triggers fire, auto-rollback and notify triage channel (eng, product, support).
5) Post-mortem required for any rollback that hit > 1% of traffic.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Pilot (internal + 2–5 trusted customers): 4 weeks. Goal: validate metrics and guardrails.
- Commercial beta (opt-in by customers + sales-assisted): 8 weeks. Goal: 2–3 pilots converted to paid offering.
- GA packaging: ship as add-on or default change accompanied by migration credits.

Commercial packaging recommendations (patterns):
1) Experiment-to-Addon path: successful experiments become optional add-ons that customers can enable; price as % discount on per-token price while ensuring margin floor.
2) Fidelity bundling: map experiment outcomes to fidelity-graded SKUs (e.g., Economy, Balanced, Premium) with explicit SLO descriptions.
3) Trial credits and pilot discounts: provide 6–8 weeks of offset credits to early adopters; capture conversion rate as commercial KPI.

Pricing guardrails and cost modelling:
- Minimum margin floor: expected unit-cost reduction from experiment must sustain a 15% gross margin before packaging as discount.
- Price/discount table example:
  | SKU | Unit price delta vs base | Packaging notes |
  | Economy-Cache | -20% | Requires opt-in caching; not available for customers with restricted data policies |
  | Balanced-Batch | -12% | Default for small tenants; includes canary monitoring |

Console & sales enablement deliverables:
- Console: experiment history, outcome dashboard, commercial suggestion card (maps results to recommended SKU).
- Sales: pitch templates, ROI calculator (spreadsheet), customer migration checklist.

Release notes template (for GA of an experiment-based feature):
- Feature: name, short description, availability (regions, tiers), experiment-to-SKU mapping, migration steps, known limitations, contact for support.
- Migration guidance: timeframe for auto-migration (if any), customer opt-out instructions, credits/grace period.

Operational runbook highlights for SRE & Support:
- Alerting: define experiment-specific alerts (quality_regression_pct, latency_p95_delta_ms, error_rate_increase).
- Escalation path: on critical alarm, page SRE -> product -> assigned account owner.
- Post-release validation: run curated prompt-set eval daily for 14 days post rollout.

Ownership and governance:
- Product (owner): experiment catalog, hypothesis approval, commercial mapping.
- Engineering: experiment infra, auto-rollback engine, telemetry.
- Applied ML / Evals: prompt-set curation and quality gates.
- Sales / RevOps: packaging, pricing, pilot conversion tracking.

Next steps & timeline (quarterly milestones):
1) Q4 2029: Build Experiment API and Console MVP; create 3 template experiments.
2) Q1 2030: Run internal pilots and instrument conversion metrics.
3) Q2 2030: Commercial beta and packaging pilots with 5 customers.

Appendix A — Example Experiment API payload (YAML):
---
name: "adaptive-batching-default-12"
hypothesis: "Increase batching for short-ctx reduces unit cost >=12%"
treatment_config:
  batching_default: 12
  kv_cache: false
allocation_rules:
  percent: 5
  cohort: "small-tenant-cohort"
safety_config:
  quality_regression_pct: 0.5
  latency_p95_delta_ms: 50
observability_config:
  prompt_set_id: "pilot-2029-batching"
  trace_sample_rate: 1.0
---

Appendix B — Minimum data schema (CSV export):
- experiment_id, treatment_tag, tenant_id, request_id, timestamp_utc, tokens_in, tokens_out, compute_ms, kv_hit, latency_ms, eval_score_delta

Appendix C — FAQ (short):
Q: Will Private deployments be forced to participate?
A: No. Private deployments require explicit opt-in for telemetry and experiments.

Q: How do we prevent cross-tenant billing confusion?
A: All experimental metrics are per-tenant and exported to RevOps; commercial mapping requires a signed pilot agreement before offering discounts.

Approvals: product and engineering leadership sign-off required before GA.

Document history:
- Created: 2029-10-15 by Aisha Patel
- Reviewed: 2029-11-05 by Marco Li, Sofia Nguyen
- Updated: 2029-11-20 — added pricing guardrails and rollout timeline.

title: dsid_c5b919deea7f429c96ccfba5ec746bef__prd-cost-simulator-and-visibility-ux-sdk-2026-08-01.txt
text:
PRD: Cost What‑If Simulator and Consumption Visibility (Console + SDK)

Summary

This document describes the product requirements, UX flows, backend contracts, rollout plan, and success metrics for the "Cost What‑If Simulator and Consumption Visibility" feature. The goal is to give developers and platform engineers a unified, low‑friction way to understand the cost and performance impact of configuration choices (model variant, batch size, quantization, KV cache, routing policy, SLO targets) before they hit production. The feature includes: a Console wizard, a headless SDK for automation, and a simulation API that mirrors Redwood's runtime economics models.

Audience

- Product and engineering teams evaluating migration from hosted to dedicated/private.
- Customer SREs and platform engineers tuning SLOs and cost budgets.
- Solutions/SEs running onboarding cost projections for enterprise deals.

Goals (What success looks like)

1. Developers can generate an end‑to‑end cost/latency estimate for a defined traffic profile within 30 seconds (interactive mode) or via batch simulation (background jobs).
2. Simulator predictions are within +/- 15% of observed cost for representative workloads across 30 customer pilots after 3 months.
3. 40% reduction in onboarding time for Dedicated customers who use the simulator during migration (measured by time from sales handoff to first production traffic).
4. Expose per‑route and per‑model cost drivers in Console with actionable optimization recommendations (top 3).

Out of scope

- Billing system changes to invoices or contractual language (this is an insights and estimation tool; final billing remains authoritative).
- Real‑time prediction for live production requests (simulator is offline or best‑effort background).

User personas and primary flows

- Developer (self‑serve): Uses Console QuickStart, uploads a small representative trace (or selects a template), toggles model variant and quantization, gets immediate cost/latency delta and a short list of recommended configs.
- Platform Engineer (bulk): Uses SDK to run nightlies that simulate 7 day/30 day traffic windows across multiple affinity policies and produces CSV reports for finance/infra planning.
- Solutions Engineer (sales assist): Runs an onboarding scenario with realistic QPS and gets a packaged recommendation for Dedicated capacity and expected monthly spend range.

Functional requirements

1. Console Wizard
   - Input: traffic profile (QPS, percentiles of sequence length, mix of embeddings vs generation vs chat), optional sample requests (JSON), time window, region.
   - Controls: model variant selector, quantization toggle, batch target, KV cache enabled/disabled, routing policy (latency|cost|affinity), preferred capacity tier (hosted|dedicated|private).
   - Output: interactive dashboard with: estimated tokens/month, estimated monthly cost range (min/median/max), latency P50/P95/P99 estimates, expected GPU hours, confidence band, and top 3 cost drivers with suggestions.
   - Export options: PDF executive summary, CSV scenario results, SDK JSON payload for re‑run.

2. Simulation API / SDK
   - POST /api/v1/simulate with body (see API contract below) that returns a simulation id and async results endpoint.
   - Support synchronous mode for small traces (<= 1000 requests) and asynchronous for larger runs.
   - SDK bindings in Python and TypeScript mirroring Console options.

3. Fidelity to Billing Model
   - Simulator uses the same unit economics as billing metadata service v2 to ensure consistent cost factors (token types, per‑model multipliers, embedding unit conversion).
   - Simulator must include a configurable safety margin (0–20%) to account for variability; default 10%.

4. Recommendation Engine
   - Returns ranked suggestions (e.g., lower precision quantization, smaller model variant, enable prefix caching) with estimated delta to cost and latency and an approximate impact score.

5. Audit & reproducibility
   - Every simulation run is stored with a hashable scenario id, inputs, simulator version, and a reproducible command (SDK CLI example). Runs are retained for 90 days in the Console.

Non‑functional requirements

- Latency: interactive synchronous simulations should return within 30 seconds for small traces; async jobs should complete within 4 hours for 7‑day traffic windows of up to 10M tokens.
- Accuracy: mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) <= 15% against observed charges in pilot customers within first 90 days.
- Cost: simulator compute should be subject to internal quota; typical runs should not exceed 1 vCPU and 512MB memory for small scenarios.
- Security & privacy: sample traces must be optional and scrubbed by default. Customer can opt into retention for reproducibility with explicit consent.

API contract example (JSON payload)

- Request example (Console/SDK submits this):

{
  "scenario_name": "chat-service-migration",
  "region": "us-west-2",
  "time_window_days": "30",
  "traffic_profile": {
    "qps": "12",
    "mix": "{\"chat\":0.7, \"embeddings\":0.2, \"generation\":0.1}",
    "seq_len_p50": "128",
    "seq_len_p95": "1024"
  },
  "models": [
    "redwood-1.5b-fp16",
    "redwood-1.5b-4bit-q"
  ],
  "kv_cache_enabled": "true",
  "batch_target_tokens": "64",
  "safety_margin_pct": "10",
  "billing_reference": "customer-1234"
}

- Response (async):

{
  "simulation_id": "sim-20260720-7a3b",
  "status": "queued",
  "results_url": "/console/simulations/sim-20260720-7a3b"
}

Console UX specification

- Entry points: per‑tenant Overview page (quick card), per‑route settings (simulate this route), and a top‑level "Cost Studio" in product nav.
- Primary visualization panels:
  1) Summary card: tokens/month | est. cost | est. latency P95 | recommendation badge.
  2) Waterfall: cost breakdown by model, request type, batching, caching, and region.
  3) Sensitivity slider: allow interactive adjustment of QPS or batch target and see live cost delta.
  4) Scenario comparison: pin up to 3 scenarios side‑by‑side.
- Accessibility: keyboard navigable controls, color palette meets AA contrast.

Data model and example table (described)

Every scenario persists a flat record with columns: scenario_id, name, owner_user_id, created_at, simulator_version, model_list (comma separated), qps, time_window_days, estimated_tokens, est_monthly_cost_usd_min, est_monthly_cost_usd_median, est_monthly_cost_usd_max, latency_p95_ms, top_cost_drivers (comma separated), exported_files (urls, comma separated).

Recommendation ranking algorithm (high level)

- Score each suggestion by a combined metric: impact_score = normalized_cost_delta * 0.7 + normalized_latency_delta * 0.3 - confidence_bonus.
- Only show recommendations with confidence > 0.5 and expected cost saving > 2%.

Telemetry and observability

- Events emitted: simulation.submitted, simulation.completed, simulation.failed, recommendation.clicked, scenario.exported.
- Required telemetry fields: simulation_id, user_id, tenant_id, simulator_version, runtime_ms, tokens_processed_estimate, models_considered_count.
- Alerts: more than 3 failed simulations in 10m across a tenant triggers pager for infra oncall.

Rollout plan and milestones

1. Alpha (internal): 2026-07-01 to 2026-08-01
   - Console prototype with single model type and static unit economics. Internal testing only.
   - Owners: Asha Patel (product), Daniel Weber (backend), Priya Singh (UX).

2. Private Beta (select customers): 2026-08-15 to 2026-10-15
   - Add SDK, async jobs, recommendations, support for multiple model variants and safety_margin. Pilot with 6 customers (mix of start‑ups and 2 Dedicated customers).

3. General Availability: 2026-11-10
   - Full Console surface, export capabilities, telemetry, stored runs. Public docs and SDK packages.

Operational playbook (day‑to‑day)

- Troubleshooting checklist:
  1) simulation failed -> check simulator logs (service: cost-sim-engine), validate input schema, check billing-meta service connectivity.
  2) large latency -> check async worker queue depth and resize worker pool if > 80% utilized.
  3) accuracy drift -> run monthly calibration job that re‑trains multipliers against observed billing for pilot clients.

- Ownership and escalation:
  - Product owner: Asha Patel (product).
  - Backend owner: Daniel Weber (eng-infra).
  - Observability: SRE oncall; alert channel #prod-cost-sim-alerts.

Security and compliance notes

- Sample traces: scrub PII by default using redaction rules (regex patterns for emails, keys, tokens).
- Simulator does not persist raw request bodies unless customer opts in; opt‑in must be explicit and accompanied by retention TTL.
- All exported artifacts are subject to tenant RBAC and the same SSO policies as Console.

Open questions and risks

1) How to map simulator outputs to invoiceable line items for customers that have custom discounts? (Risk: expectation mismatch). Proposed mitigation: UI callout and additional "apply discount" input for SE workflows.
2) Simulator accuracy on multimodal pipelines is untested. Priority: run focused pilots with multimodal customers in Beta.
3) Potential for customers to rely on simulator for exact billing — clearly label this as "estimate" and add confidence bands.

Appendices

A. CLI/SDK example (Python)

from redwood_sdk import CostSimulator

sim = CostSimulator(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY")
scenario = {
  "scenario_name": "migration-test",
  "region": "eu-central-1",
  "time_window_days": 30,
  "traffic_profile": {"qps": 8, "mix": {"chat": 0.8, "embeddings": 0.2}, "seq_len_p95": 512},
  "models": ["redwood-7b-compat-4bit", "redwood-7b-fp16"],
  "kv_cache_enabled": true
}
run = sim.create_simulation(scenario)
print(run["simulation_id"])

B. Acceptance criteria

- All UI controls work end‑to‑end in Console and produce a valid downloadable summary.
- SDK functions available and pass integration tests against staging billing metadata.
- Pilot accuracy MAPE <= 15% across at least 5 pilot customers.

References and related docs

- Serving economics decision guide (internal): /confluence/product-docs/product-overview/serving-economics-decision-guide-2029-02-14
- Offline cost estimator prototype: /confluence/product-docs/requirements/prd-offline-cost-estimator-sdk-and-simulation-playground-2025-10-12

Owners and contacts

- Product: Asha Patel (asha@redwood.example)
- Backend & Modeling: Daniel Weber (daniel@redwood.example)
- UX: Priya Singh (priya@redwood.example)
- SRE: Liam O'Connor (liam@redwood.example)

Document history

- 2026-06-15: Draft created by Asha Patel.
- 2026-07-05: Internal review updates and added telemetry section (reviewer: Rita Gomez).
- 2026-07-20: Incorporated backend feasibility notes and updated rollout timeline (last_updated by Daniel Weber).

title: dsid_ec41b0ed6a22408aa8ef1807a6a012e9__gpu-provisioning-rate-limit-and-iac-throttling-policy.txt
text:
GPU Provisioning Rate Limits and IaC Throttling Policy

Summary
This page defines Redwood's standardized policy for rate limiting GPU provisioning operations and the corresponding IaC (Terraform) throttling patterns. The goal is to protect global capacity pools, avoid cross-account supply storms, reduce noisy-neighbor incidents, and ensure predictable oncall behaviour when provisioning pressure spikes.

Context and motivation
- We operate multi-account, multi-region GPU pools with a mix of on-demand, reserved and spot-backed capacity.
- Provisioning is a high-impact control plane activity: simultaneous requests can saturate cloud quotas, exhaust IP/EIP pools, and trigger eviction cascades across tenants.
- Prior incidents stemmed from unconstrained CI pipelines, self-serve onboarding flows, and bulk repo migrations that created large, parallel terraform apply operations.

Goals
1) Limit blast radius from mass-provisioning operations by enforcing global and per-tenant request caps.
2) Provide predictable throttling primitives in IaC modules so teams can safely self-serve.
3) Integrate throttling with CI/CD to gate large changes behind canary windows and operator approval.
4) Ensure transparent telemetry and runbook-able thresholds for oncall.

Policy overview (short)
- Global provisioning concurrency cap: 30 concurrent machine create operations per region across all accounts.
- Account-level concurrency cap: 8 concurrent machine create operations per account per region.
- CI/CD pipeline burst cap: 4 concurrent terraform apply jobs per repo in a single region (enforced by the shared CI runner queue).
- Daily provisioning budget per team (non-reserved): 120 nodes total (soft quota, alerts at 80% and hard block via CI gating at 100%).
- Spot fallback window: if >50% of queued requests fail due to capacity for 10 minutes, automatically route new requests to spot-backed warm pools with agreed fallbacks.

Technical design
1) Rate-limiter service: centralized lightweight service (gpu-provision-limiter) that exposes an API used by Terraform provisioner hooks, internal provisioning SDKs, and CI runners. Implements token-bucket per (region, account, team, repo).
2) Terraform module integration: modules call a provisioner hook that checks the limiter API and waits/queues before starting create operations. The module supports a "throttle_strategy" variable with values: "blocking", "queued", "fail-fast". Default: "queued".
3) CI/CD integration: shared Buildkite queue contains a rate-limiter step that consults gpu-provision-limiter and denies starting apply jobs when per-repo or per-account caps are hit.
4) Remote-state lock awareness: limiter integrates with remote-state lock TTLs to prevent deadlocks; locks are annotated with expected create counts.

Configuration matrix
| Scope | Metric | Default threshold | Enforcement action | Owner |
|-------|--------|------------------:|-------------------|-------|
| Global (per-region) | concurrent_creates | 30 | queue new requests (60s backoff) | infra-sre |
| Account (per-region) | concurrent_creates | 8 | queue or fail based on module setting | cloud-accounts team |
| Team (daily) | daily_create_count | 120 | alert @ 80%, CI gated at 100% | capacity-planning |
| CI Repo | concurrent_applies | 4 | block new jobs in Buildkite queue | eng-dx |
| Egress IP pool | ephemeral_ips_requested | 50 | block provisioning until IPs freed | network-ops |

Terraform module example (recommended pattern)
```hcl
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules.git//gpu-pool"

  region            = var.region
  desired_count     = var.desired_count
  throttle_strategy = "queued" # options: queued | blocking | fail-fast
  throttle_group    = "team-${var.owner_team}"
  tags = {
    Owner = var.owner_team
    Purpose = "inference-pool"
  }
}

# hook (executed as null_resource local-exec) will call internal limiter API before create.
```

Limiter API contract (example)
- POST /v1/allocations -> body: {"scope":"region:us-west-2","count":3,"meta":{"team":"vision"}}
- Response: {"status":"granted","token":"abc123","expires_at":"2025-02-20T12:34:00Z"} or {"status":"queued","eta_seconds":45}
- Clients must supply token when performing cloud create operations to allow accounting and idempotency.

CI/CD pipeline integration snippet (Buildkite step)
```yaml
steps:
  - label: ":terraform: apply"
    command: ./ci/terraform-apply-wrapper.sh
    parallelism: 1
    concurrency: 1
    agents: ["gpu-provisioner"]
```
Where terraform-apply-wrapper.sh calls limiter and aborts if the limiter returns "fail-fast".

Observability and metrics
Instrument these key metrics into Prometheus/Telemetry platform:
- gpu.provision.request.count{scope,team,region}
- gpu.provision.request.latency_seconds
- gpu.provision.concurrent_creates{region,account}
- gpu.provision.queue_depth{region,account}
- gpu.provision.daily_count{team}
- terraform.apply.blocked_by_throttle{repo}
Alerting rules (examples)
- P1: gpu.provision.queue_depth > 60 for 5m in a region -> page infra-sre and cloud-accounts.
- P2: terraform.apply.blocked_by_throttle spikes by >200% over baseline -> page eng-dx and capacity-planning.
- P3: daily_create_count for team > 120 and continues growing -> notify team-owner and capacity planner.

Runbook: typical oncall flow for a provisioning storm
1) Triage: check Prometheus dashboards (GPU Provisioning Overview) and limiter health endpoint /healthz.
2) If queue_depth > 60: open a slack #infra-incident channel, page infra-sre.
3) Check recent CI runs to identify a noisy pipeline (filter terraform.apply.blocked_by_throttle metric).
4) If noisy repo identified: temporarily increase its per-repo burst cap by +1 via limiter UI (requires cloud-accounts approver) and instruct the team to linearize their applies.
5) If cloud provider quota exhaustion is suspected: run quick checks: aws ec2 describe-instances quota and ENI usage; check ephemeral IP pool usage.
6) Fallback: enable spot-warm-pool routing (toggle in limiter) for new requests and communicate expected P99 latency increase.
7) Post-incident: require a retro and request a remediation plan from the owner (e.g., change module to use smaller batches or use instance reuse patterns).

Operational considerations and best practices
- Prefer desired_count adjustments (scale-up within a pool) over creating many independent node pools. This reduces per-create overhead and throttling pressure.
- When doing large migrations, break work into windows and request a temporary quota bump from capacity-planning at least 48h in advance.
- Use the module variable throttle_strategy to set fail-fast for automated tests and queued for production rollouts.
- Annotate terraform runs with `throttle_group` so accounting is available in the limiters.

Security and RBAC
- Limiter UI/API is protected via OAuth with short-lived tokens. Only cloud-accounts, capacity-planning, and infra-sre roles can adjust global caps.
- Per-repo burst increases require an approver from eng-dx or cloud-accounts. Approvals are recorded in audit logs.

Ownership and roadmap
- Owner: infra-sre (primary), cloud-accounts (secondary)
- Next roadmap items: automatic machine-type selection when capacity low, adaptive backoff algorithms using historical fill-rate, and terraform-provider plugin for native limiter checks.

Appendix A: Example incident timeline (short)
- 2024-05-03 02:12 UTC: CI bulk migration runs 24 concurrent applies in us-west-2.
- 02:15 UTC: queue_depth spikes to 180, many creates fail due to ENI exhaustion.
- 02:18 UTC: infra-sre pages team; temporary block placed on CI pipeline and spot-warm routing enabled.
- 03:00 UTC: queue drains; partial restores initiated; retro mandated.

Appendix B: Troubleshooting snippets
- Check limiter status: curl -sS https://limiter.redwood.internal/healthz
- Inspect current allocations: curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://limiter.redwood.internal/v1/allocations?region=us-west-2
- Force-read cloud ENI counts: aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=availability-zone,Values=us-west-2a | jq '.NetworkInterfaces | length'

Contact and escalation
- Primary oncall: infra-sre rotation (pager duty link in internal wiki)
- Slack channels: #infra-oncall, #cloud-accounts, #capacity-planning

Change history
- 2024-09-12: Document created by Aisha Patel (initial policy draft).
- 2024-11-05: Added CI gating examples and daily team budgets (reviewers Marco Chen, Lina Rodriguez).
- 2025-02-20: Formalized API contract and added remote-state lock awareness notes.

Related templates and modules
- terraform-modules/gpu-pool (recommended)
- ci/terraform-apply-wrapper.sh (example script)

End of document

title: dsid_bff1f4054a1c4a00b13962af8818d3de__operator-training-synthetic-experiment-catalog-2027.txt
text:
Operator Training: Synthetic Experiment Catalog & Metrics Contract

Summary

This catalog documents a curated set of synthetic experiments and operator exercises aimed at validating platform fallback behavior, SLI sensitivity, and operator handoff procedures for LLM inference services. It is intended for platform operators, SREs, and platform engineering leads responsible for regional resilience and tenant isolation.

Background

We run synthetic experiments regularly to: 
- Ensure safe fallbacks between model variants and regions.
- Validate automated prefetch/prefix-cache heuristics.
- Measure SLI sensitivity to token-burst and cold-cache scenarios.
- Train operators on triage flows and decision heuristics.

This document combines: an experiment catalog, expected metrics/dashboards, runbook snippets for operator drills, an exercise planner template, and retrospective questions used after each lab.

Experiment Catalog (top-level)

1) Cold-cache token-burst (Tiered degradation)
- Objective: Validate warmup paths and synthetic warm-start improvement when a cold prefix cache receives a 10k-request burst.
- Preconditions: deploy synthetic workload generator in us-west-2, target model: "redwood-open-7b-v2" (can be swapped to quantized variant).
- Injection steps:
  1. Create cohort of 500 synthetic tenants with cold KV prefixes.
  2. Ramp to 10k QPS over 60s, sustain 120s, then ramp down.
  3. Enable predictive prefetch hints for 20% of tenants mid-burst.
- Success criteria:
  - 95th percentile frontend latency does not exceed 1.8x normal baseline for more than 3 minutes.
  - KV-prefetch hit rate increases by >= 30% for hinted cohorts.
  - No sustained SLO burn (error budget < 1% consumed per 10-minute window).

2) Model-variant fallback misfire
- Objective: Confirm that an automated model-variant fallback triggers and that synthetic QA prompts show no catastrophic regression in semantic quality beyond alert thresholds.
- Preconditions: Canary the lower-cost variant "rw-open-7b-q4" in regional fallback policy.
- Injection steps:
  1. Force model variant exhaustion on primary pool via quota exhaustion script.
  2. Observe routing to fallback variant and record outputs for a fixed prompt suite (see prompt-set ID: PS-regen-2026-14).
- Success criteria:
  - Fallback occurs within configured 2s routing window.
  - BLEU-like regression metric (internal eval) <= 10% drop vs primary model baseline.
  - Alerts: quality-regression SLI triggers if >20% of prompts exceed threshold.

3) Regional-degradation graceful routing
- Objective: Validate that soft-failover to secondary region preserves 99% of throughput for Tier-1 tenants and that billing attribution and backfill queues behave correctly.
- Preconditions: Synthetic cross-region latency emulator engaged.
- Injection steps:
  1. Introduce 250ms additional egress delay on primary region for 5 minutes.
  2. Shift routing weight by policy to secondary region using canary stage.
- Success criteria:
  - Throughput for tier-1 tenants maintained at >= 99% of baseline within 120s of cutover.
  - Cost-accounting tags preserved for billing reconciliation.

Metrics and Dashboards (contract)

All experiments must populate or validate the following dashboards and queries. Dashboard names assume the prefix "Platform Lab/". Operators should add experiment tag "lab:<experiment-id>" to all synthetic traffic for traceability.

Key metrics (names used in telemetry):
- platform.request.latency_ms (histogram)
- platform.request.errors (counter, labeled by error_type)
- platform.kv_cache.hit_rate (gauge, per-promoted-prefix)
- platform.routing.fallback_rate (counter, per-tenant)
- platform.model.quality_regressions (counter, per-prompt-suite)
- platform.billing.metered_tokens (counter, per-tenant)

Required dashboard panels (minimum):
- Latency heatmap (p50/p90/p95/p99), split by region and tenant tier.
- KV-prefetch hit-rate trend and per-prefix breakdown.
- Fallbacks: rate and latency delta for requests that fallback.
- Quality regression panel showing prompt-suite pass/fail and semantic-diff histogram.
- Billing spike detector showing token volume by tenant and lab tag.

Alerting rules to validate (example PromQL / alert text):
1) Latency surge (informational):
Expression: increase(platform_request_latency_ms_bucket{le=\"500\"}[5m]) / increase(platform_request_latency_ms_count[5m]) > 0.2
Alert: "Lab: High fraction of requests <500ms dropping — investigate cold-starts and prefetch"

2) Fallback rate spike (actionable):
Expression: increase(platform_routing_fallback_rate[2m]) > 50
Alert: "Fallback surge — routing policy in effect, confirm model pool health and canary config"

3) Quality regression (critical):
Expression: increase(platform_model_quality_regressions{lab=~\"lab-.*\"}[10m]) > 5
Alert: "Quality regressions detected in synthetic prompt-suite; abort rollout and notify ML oncall"

Runbook snippets (operator play flows)

A) Cold-cache token-burst quick triage
1) Confirm lab tag on incoming traces and isolate synthetic tenant IDs.
2) Inspect platform.kv_cache.hit_rate for the prefix cohort. If hit_rate < 15% and latency delta > baseline: run warming job:

Command (example):

curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/v1/prefetch?action=warm&prefix_id=prefix-2026-09 -H 'Authorization: Bearer $OPERATOR_TOKEN'

3) If warming job fails or queue length grows > 2000, escalate to runtime-owner and open an Incident with severity: P2.

B) Model-variant fallback misfire triage
1) Validate routing policy: /ops/routing/policies/<policy-id> shows fallback windows configured (expected 2s).
2) Pull prompt-suite results and run quick diff:

python tools/quality_diff.py --baseline baseline.json --sample lab-output.json --threshold 0.10

3) If regression > 10% and >20% of prompts fail, trigger rollback of auto-fallback (set fallback_weight=0) and notify ML and Product for evaluation.

Exercise Planner (template)

Use this template to schedule and score operator drills. Fill fields and attach experiment run logs to the lab ticket.

- Experiment ID: lab-2027-05
- Owner: @platform-ops (team alias)
- Duration: 90 minutes
- Pre-reads: link to model baseline, prompt-set PS-regen-2026-14, and dashboard links.
- Tasks (timed):
  1. 0–10m: Preflight checks and tagging.
  2. 10–30m: Run injection step.
  3. 30–60m: Triage and mitigation.
  4. 60–80m: Postmortem writeup draft.
  5. 80–90m: Scorecard and lessons.
- Scoring rubric (operator-focused):
  - Detection (0-3): Did operator detect the injected failure via dashboard/alert?
  - Isolation (0-3): How quickly did operator narrow to cause (region, model, prefix)?
  - Mitigation (0-4): Quality of mitigation decision (prefetch, rollback, routing adjust).
  - Communication (0-2): Did operator update incident channel and paging appropriately?

Retrospective checklist (post-exercise)

- What worked well?
- What were signal blind spots? (missing metrics, noisy alerts)
- Were playbook steps clear and executable?
- Actions (owner + due date) — add to backlog with priority tag lab:action.
- If regression observed, create quality-guardrail ticket with prompt-suite and sample outputs attached.

Appendix: Example PromQL and SQL queries

PromQL: 5m prefetched hit rate by prefix

sum by(prefix_id)(increase(platform_kv_cache_hit{lab="lab-2027-05"}[5m])) / sum by(prefix_id)(increase(platform_kv_cache_lookup_total{lab="lab-2027-05"}[5m]))

SQL: retrieve lab-tagged billing for reconciliation

SELECT tenant_id, sum(tokens) as tokens, lab_tag
FROM billing.events
WHERE lab_tag LIKE 'lab-%' AND ts >= '2027-02-01T00:00:00Z'
GROUP BY tenant_id, lab_tag
ORDER BY tokens DESC

Ownership and scheduling

- Platform Ops (oncall alias: "platform-ops") - experiment owner and scheduler.
- Runtime Team - responsible for kernel/quantization rollbacks and prefetch API.
- Observability - dashboard and alerting steward.
- Applied ML - quality metrics, prompt-sets, and regression thresholds.

Schedule recurring exercises quarterly and after any significant runtime change (kernel swap, quantization rollout, routing policy update). For high-risk rollouts, run a focused experiment 48–72 hours prior to customer-impacting deploy.

Glossary and resources

- lab:<id> — tag applied to synthetic traffic to trace experiments.
- prefix — KV cache prefix used for warmup.
- prompt-set PS-regen-2026-14 — canonical prompt suite for regeneration quality checks.

Useful links:
- Dashboard: Platform Lab / Synthetic Experiment Overview -> https://grafana.internal/d/PLAB/synthetic-overview
- Prefetch API docs: https://docs.internal/prefetch-api
- Playbook generator: /eng-platform/runbooks/playbook-generator

Revision history

- 2026-11-15 (Maya Chen) — created initial catalog and contract.
- 2026-12-20 (Arjun Patel) — added exercise planner and PromQL examples.
- 2027-02-10 (Maya Chen) — updated success criteria for regional failover and added billing reconciliation query.

title: dsid_5be046d07c25458997dfc60c8ced2609__procurement-contract-approval-matrix-and-billing-trigger-guide-2026.txt
text:
Procurement Approval Matrix and Billing-Trigger Guide

Purpose
-------
This page defines Redwood Inference's standardized procurement approval matrix, the lifecycle steps for contract execution, and the precise billing triggers that feed the revenue recognition (revrec) process. It is intended for Finance, Legal, Procurement owners, and Engineering or Product teams who initiate supplier commitments. The goal is to reduce cycle time, ensure correct accounting treatment at go-live, and avoid revenue/billing misalignment across hosted, dedicated, and private product lines.

Scope
-----
Applies to: all third-party software and hardware purchases, cloud/hosted commitments, professional services, and vendor contracts that create a legal obligation or financial commitment for Redwood Inference (including pilot agreements and proof-of-concept statements of work).
Excludes: petty cash, employee expense reimbursements, and subscriptions procured on employee cards under $500 (see petty-expense policy).

Key Definitions
---------------
- Commitment: any signed agreement or PO that obligates Redwood to pay or receive services.
- Billing Trigger: the event which causes the vendor to generate invoices and which typically corresponds to the point at which Redwood recognizes expense or revenue impact.
- Effective Date vs. Service Commencement: Effective Date is when the contract is executed; Service Commencement is when vendor obligations start (these can be different).

Summary of Approval Matrix
--------------------------
Approval thresholds are financial (total contract value over term) and categorical (SaaS, infra, professional services, capital equipment). Routing times assume standard 5 business day SLA for each approver unless flagged. Use the Procurement Portal to initiate all requests.

Table: Approval Matrix (text tabular view)
Value band / Category | Requestor -> Approvers (order) | Required Attachments | Typical SLA
---------------------|--------------------------------|----------------------|---------
<$25k (non-capex) | Requesting Manager -> Procurement -> Finance (inform) | Quote, business justification | 3–7 days
$25k–$150k | Requesting Manager -> Procurement -> Finance -> Legal (if T&C change) -> Procurement Head | Quote, ROI or cost-center approval, security checklist | 7–12 days
$150k–$750k | Requesting Director -> Procurement -> Finance -> Legal -> Head of Product/Eng -> CFO (if multiyear) | Contract redline, SOC/attestation, procurement risk assessment | 10–20 days
>$750k or capital equipment | VP-level sponsor -> Procurement Director -> Legal -> CFO -> CEO (if > $2M/3yr) | Full diligence pack, board notice (if required) | 15–45 days
Special categories: any contract involving customer data residency, on-prem deployment, or KMS/HSM access must route to Security & Compliance prior to Legal review (add 5 business days).

Roles & Responsibilities
------------------------
- Requesting Manager: complete procurement request in portal, attach justification, and define cost-center and budget tag.
- Procurement: primary owner of vendor selection, PO issuance, and supplier onboarding checklist.
- Finance: verifies budget availability, assigns GL codes, and confirms revrec/billing implications.
- Legal: reviews and negotiates T&Cs; signs if within delegated authority.
- Security & Compliance: performs data-security risk review for relevant categories.
- Contracts Admin: executes signature workflows and uploads countersigned agreement to contract registry.

Standard Contract Lifecycle (5-step process)
-------------------------------------------
1) Intake & Business Justification
   - Requestor opens procurement ticket (Portal -> New Request) and attaches: vendor quote, scope of work, cost-center approval, and expected go-live date.
2) Risk & Compliance Screening (automatic)
   - Procurement auto-runs vendor risk checks (sanctions, AML, basic security posture). If flagged, Security & Compliance engages.
3) Negotiation & Approvals
   - Legal negotiates commercial terms and redlines. Approvers are notified in the order defined by the Approval Matrix.
4) Signature & PO Issuance
   - Contracts Admin finalizes signature (DocuSign). Procurement issues PO referencing contract ID and expected billing trigger.
5) Onboarding & Accounting Setup
   - Vendor is added to AP, GL mapping applied, invoicing instructions recorded, and revrec treatment confirmed in the contract registry.

Billing Triggers and RevRec Alignment
------------------------------------
Each contract requires an explicit Billing Trigger field to be set at signature. Typical triggers and how Finance treats them for expense recognition and billing purposes:
- Invoice on execution: vendor invoices after signature. Finance posts expense when invoice received; revrec not applicable (vendor expense only).
- Monthly in arrears based on usage: vendor invoices monthly for actual usage. Finance accrues monthly; for Redwood customer-facing revenue (if vendor pass-through), match usage reports to invoiced amounts.
- Milestone-based invoicing: vendor invoices on achievement of defined milestones. Finance recognizes expense as milestones are met; procurements that create customer billable services must map vendor milestones to customer billing milestones in product contracts to avoid mismatched revenue timing.
- Delivery + Acceptance: hardware or on-prem appliances invoiced on delivery and customer acceptance. Capitalization policy applies for items meeting fixed-asset thresholds (see capitalization policy).
- Supply or Capacity Reservation (committed capacity): vendor invoices per agreed commitment schedule even if unused. Finance treats unused commitment as expense on vendor invoice date unless contractual credits or rollovers exist.

Examples (practical scenarios)
----------------------------
1) Dedicated GPU pool reserved capacity (3-year commitment)
   - Approval: VP of Engineering -> Procurement -> Legal -> CFO.
   - Billing trigger: quarterly in advance per committed capacity.
   - Finance treatment: expense recognized when billed; related customer revenue recognized when we host customer workloads (ensure internal transfer pricing mirrors committed schedule).
2) Professional services (integration) tied to a customer implementation
   - Approval: Director Product -> Procurement -> Legal.
   - Billing trigger: milestone-based.
   - Finance treatment: vendor expenses recognized per milestone; Redwood invoices customer per product contract milestone — Product and Legal must ensure milestone definitions match.

Checklist for Requestors (minimum attachments)
--------------------------------------------
- Vendor quote or SOW
- Business justification and expected ROI or product impact
- Cost center and budget approver name
- Expected service commencement date and billing trigger recommendation
- Security questionnaire (if handling customer data)
- Any required export-control or compliance notes

Delegated Signature Authority (summary)
-------------------------------------
- Legal Counsel: up to $500k for standard SaaS templates (with no high-risk clauses)
- VP/Director of Finance: approve non-binding MSA addenda < $250k
- CFO: approves multiyear commitments > $250k and <= $2M
- CEO: approvals > $2M or any arrangement with strategic/board impact
Full authority matrix and delegation letters are in the Contracts Admin folder.

SLA Targets and Escalation Path
-------------------------------
- Standard legal review (non-complex): 7 business days.
- High-risk contracts (data residency, HSM, on-prem): 15 business days.
- If any stage exceeds SLA, Procurement will escalate to the approver’s manager and add an expedited tag. For > 10 business day delays in total, the Procurement Director performs a weekly review with stakeholder owners.

Common Pitfalls & Mitigations
----------------------------
- Mismatched milestones between vendor invoice schedule and customer billing: mitigation — require cross-signed milestone appendix and Finance sign-off pre-execution.
- Hidden termination or auto-renew clauses without notice periods: mitigation — Legal to enforce 30–90 day advance notice for renewals and include renewal reminders in contract registry.
- Security attachments missing: mitigation — block signature until Security & Compliance clears or issues a formal exception.

Operational Templates and Tools
------------------------------
- Procurement Portal: https://procurement.redwood.internal (internal) — use for all intake and auto-routing.
- Contract Registry spreadsheet / Confluence index (Contract-ID lookup) — upload signed agreements and set Billing Trigger field.
- Standard SOW and SaaS MSA templates are available in the Contracts library (link in related pages).

Change Log
----------
- 2025-11-12: Document created by Priya Natarajan (initial published).
- 2026-02-08: Updated approval thresholds and added committed capacity guidance for dedicated GPU pools; minor SLA adjustments.

Appendix: Example Billing Trigger JSON (for Contract Registry)
---------------------------------------------------------
Use the following example when filling the Billing Trigger field in the registry:

{
  "contract_id": "RWI-2026-0123",
  "billing_trigger": "quarterly_in_advance",
  "service_commencement": "2026-04-01",
  "revrec_note": "expense recognized on invoice; customer revenue recognized per usage"
}

Contact
-------
Procurement team (procurement@redwood.ai), Finance contracts (finance-contracts@redwood.ai), and Legal (legal-ops@redwood.ai). For urgent escalations, contact the Procurement Director (procurement-director@redwood.ai).

References
----------
- Capitalization policy (finance-and-legal/capitalization-policy-2025)
- Contract registry process (finance-and-legal/procurement/contract-registry-howto-2025)
- RevRec principles (finance-and-legal/revrec-and-billing/revrec-principles-2024)

title: dsid_6a8960473c834e90937c940c221bf958__first-contact-flowbook-and-csr-bridge-handshake-2026.txt
text:
First-Contact Flowbook and CSR Bridge Handshake

Summary:
This page documents the "first-contact" operator flow for any production incident affecting customer-facing inference (hosted API / Dedicated). It codifies the handshake between the first on-call operator and Customer Success/CSR (the "CSR Bridge"), an evidence snapshot format, the triage decision ladder, and templated customer status messages.

Audience:
- SREs, on-call engineers, incident commanders, CSR/Support L1-L3, and Product PMs responsible for customer comms.

Scope:
- Applies to P0/P1/P2 severity events touching API availability, major latency regressions, KV cache corruption, or model-quality regressions that generate customer tickets.
- Does NOT replace component-specific runbooks (see linked runbook library).

Quick reference: severity to action map
1) P0 (outage impacting >10% requests or control plane failures) — immediate bridge, page on-call IC, open incident bridge, status page 15-minute notice.
2) P1 (significant degradation, customer-facing but partial) — notify CSR bridge, open short bridge, begin mitigations within 30 minutes.
3) P2 (minor service regression / performance variance) — ticketed, track in backlog, notify stakeholders if customer-reported.

1) First-contact operator flow (step-by-step)
A. Acknowledge alert (0–2 minutes):
  - Confirm alert source (metric alert, external customer report, Sentry/trace).
  - Set working hypothesis label on incident channel: "latency","errors","capacity","quality".
B. Rapid evidence snapshot (2–8 minutes): collect the Evidence Snapshot (table below).
C. Initial mitigation attempt (8–20 minutes):
  - For latency: apply emergency routing to region fallback OR scale up critical pools as allowed by autoscale policy.
  - For errors: enable guarded fallback model (quantized variant) if validated in service matrix.
  - For KV cache or state corruption: isolate nodes and enable read-only fallback; do not evict caches unless instructed by runtime owner.
D. CSR Bridge handshake (10–25 minutes) — see Handshake script below.
E. Decide: containment vs escalate (20–30 minutes): if mitigation removes >50% customer errors/latency within 20 minutes, continue containment and move to stabilization; otherwise escalate to IC and call for cross-team bridge.

2) The CSR Bridge handshake (objective: align external comms and customer impact quickly)
- Who: first-contact operator (on-call), CSR bridge lead (L2), incident commander (if IC present).
- When: invoked by the on-call operator once an evidence snapshot and a working mitigation attempt are in place (recommended within 25 minutes of first alert).
- Goals:
  1) Confirm which customers are impacted (tenant list or telemetry-derived list).
  2) Agree on an initial public status message and cadence.
  3) Determine whether affected customers need immediate 1:1 outreach.
  4) Assign CSR owner(s) for ongoing inbound customer questions.

CSR Bridge handshake script (copy-paste during bridge):
"Hey CSR team — operator here. We have a [P0|P1|P2] impacting [region / hosted / dedicated / model-serving]. Current hypothesis: [latency / errors / quality / capacity]. Evidence snapshot attached. Initial mitigation: [scaled up pool / routed traffic / enabled fallback model / isolated nodes]. Estimated first stabilization check: T+20 minutes. Recommended customer message: 'We are investigating degraded performance affecting inference in REGION. We will update in 15 minutes.' Assigning CSR owner: @Name. Any immediate customer escalation requests?"

3) Evidence Snapshot format (copyable checklist)
- Incident ID: INC-YYYYMMDD-<short>
- Time range observed: UTC timestamps
- Primary symptom: high 5xx rate / p95 latency climb / model-quality mismatch / etc.
- Service(s) affected: api-gateway, route-engine, runtime-pool-{region}, model-store
- Top three error traces (trace_id list, sample stack/message)
- Recent deploys (last 60 minutes) and rollback flag
- Autoscale events (scale up/down timestamps)
- Affected tenants (derived from routing logs) — list up to 10
- Customer tickets opened (IDs)
- Temporary mitigations applied and who performed them (operator name + time)
- Link to runbook(s) consulted

Table: Minimum evidence payload (paste into incident channel)
| Key | Value | Notes |
| --- | ----- | ----- |
| Incident ID | INC-20260214-ashp-01 | generated by incident-bot |
| Window | 2026-02-14T15:02Z — ongoing | UTC |
| Symptom | p95 latency > 1.2s | threshold breach: p95 > 800ms |
| Services | api-gateway, runtime-pool-eu | see service map |
| Mitigation | routed traffic to dedicated-fallback | operator: Asha Patel |

4) Triage decision ladder (short rules)
- If > 10% global request failure OR control plane unresponsive -> P0 and immediate IC.
- If single-region hit with automatic fallback available -> attempt fallback, notify CSR bridge, escalate only if fallback fails.
- If model-quality regression (LLM hallucinations or top-k shift) -> sample outputs, open model-quality ticket, engage Applied ML and Product.
- If degradation tied to recent deploy -> mark deploy as suspect and initiate rollback if rollback window open.

5) Escalation matrix (contacts & when to pull them)
| Role | Typical contact | Escalate when |
|---|---:|---|
| Incident Commander | oncall-ic@redwood.com | P0 or P1 failing containment |
| Runtime Owner | runtime-team@redwood.com | persistent latency after fallback |
| Networking | infra-net@redwood.com | region connectivity anomalies |
| Model Onboarding | model-onboard@redwood.com | quality regressions |
| CS/Support Lead | cs-lead@redwood.com | customer escalations requested |

6) On-call rotation continuity rules (prevent single-point handoffs)
- Warm handoff required for all incidents longer than 1 hour: outgoing on-call must provide a 5-minute verbal summary and the Evidence Snapshot.
- Cold handoff only allowed when incident < 30 minutes and no customer escalations.
- Shadowing windows: new oncall must shadow for two weeks with a mentor.
- Handoff checklist (must be posted in channel before sign-off): incident ID, symptom, actions taken, next immediate steps, CSR owner, escalation contacts.

7) Game day and simulation template (scripting a 90-minute lab)
Objective: validate first-contact flow and CSR bridge within SLA.
Preconditions:
- Synthetic traffic generator configured to hit model variant A/B
- Test tenants: test-tenant-1..5 with simulated alerts enabled
- Observability toggles: inject p50/p95 latency anomalies and 5xx spikes

Scenario script (90 minutes):
  0–10m: alert fires, on-call acknowledges and posts Evidence Snapshot
  10–25m: operator attempts fallback & scales pools; CSR Bridge handshake executed
  25–40m: fallback partially restores; simulate a deploy that increases errors -> operator must detect and rollback
  40–60m: IC declared, cross-team bridge called, customer status update posted
  60–90m: restore and closure; postmortem quick-rubric completed within 48 hours

8) Postmortem quick-rubric (48-hour initial doc, full postmortem within 7 days)
Minimum fields for the 48-hour quick doc:
- Executive summary (1–2 sentences)
- Impact (customers affected, duration, SLO breaches)
- Root cause hypothesis (short)
- Immediate remediation performed
- Next steps / action owners (owner + due date)
Full postmortem must include timeline with evidence, change history, RCA analysis, and actions with measurable success criteria.

9) Status page & customer comm templates
Template: initial 15-minute status (public)
Title: 2026-02-14 — Degraded inference performance in REGION
Body: We are investigating degraded inference performance for customers in REGION. Our engineers have identified an issue affecting request latency for some workloads and have implemented temporary mitigations. We will provide an update within 15 minutes.

Template: internal CSR one-to-one outreach (when customers request direct contact)
Subject: Immediate update: temporary mitigation applied for your traffic
Body: Hi <Customer Name>,
We’re actively investigating elevated latency affecting inference requests for your account (observed T+...). Our engineers have routed traffic to a fallback pool and are monitoring. You may see reduced throughput for complex requests while we stabilize. We will reach out with a follow-up within 1 hour. If you observe errors, please reply with example request IDs.

Template: substantive post-incident customer update (24–72 hours)
Subject: Incident summary and next steps — [INC ID]
Body: Hi <Customer Name>,
Summary: On <date> between <start> and <end> UTC, you may have experienced increased latency/errors for inference requests routed to REGION. Root cause: [brief]. What we did: [actions taken]. What we will do to prevent recurrence: [list of engineering actions + ETA].

10) Evidence retention and regulatory notes
- Save snapshots, traces, and deployment artifacts to the incident evidence bucket under path s3://inc-evidence/YYYY/MM/DD/INC-<id>. Only attach sanitized customer-identifying data.
- For enterprise customers requiring audit evidence, note the evidence ID in the postmortem and copy legal/compliance.

11) Ownership and SLAs for this flowbook
- Document owner: eng-sre (oncall-runbooks owner).
- Review cadence: bi-annual and after every P0.
- Training: new SREs and CS leads must complete the First-Contact Flow lab during onboarding.

Appendix A — Quick command snippets
- Open new incident in incident-bot: /incident start "INC-<short>" --severity P1 --owner @oncall
- Snapshot traces: curl -sS "https://obs-api/trace?from=...&to=..." | jq '.' > evidence.json
- Route traffic to fallback (example): infractl route set --service runtime-pool-eu --target dedicated-fallback --session 30m

Appendix B — Example timeline (sample)
- 15:02 UTC — Alert: p95 spike detected
- 15:04 UTC — Acknowledge, Evidence Snapshot posted
- 15:10 UTC — CSR Bridge handshake, initial public status posted
- 15:18 UTC — Fallback routing applied; errors drop 65%
- 15:35 UTC — IC declared for persistent error traces; model-onboard alerted
- 16:40 UTC — Rollback of suspect deploy; gradual recovery
- 17:10 UTC — Stabilized, bridge closed; post-incident actions assigned

Notes and related runbooks:
- See runtime-pool-eviction-runbook, model-quality-triage, and api-gateway-throttle-runbook for component-specific remediation steps.

Feedback / improvements: email oncall-runbooks@redwood.com or add comments to this page.

title: dsid_0af523d62c7647318a9afcf9d021d50e__concurrent-tenant-quota-and-fairness-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Concurrent Tenant Quota and Fairness Playbook for Private Deployments

Summary:

This playbook describes Redwood's recommended policies, configuration patterns, and operational procedures for enforcing concurrent-tenant quotas and fairness in private (VPC / on-prem) deployments. It focuses on multi-customer sharing of GPU pools, predictable latency for tenant SLAs, cost transparency, and safe escalation paths for quota-related incidents. The guidance applies to both hosted control-plane-managed private deployments and fully air-gapped on-prem bundles.

Scope and intent:
- Prevent noisy-neighbor effects in shared inference pools while preserving utilization.
- Provide a clear mapping from business-level entitlements (committed vCPU/GPU units, burst windows, priority tiers) to runtime enforcement knobs.
- Offer deterministic operational procedures for emergency throttling, quota adjustments, and fairness audits during incidents and capacity changes.

When to use this playbook:
1) Customer requests: shared-GPU private deployment where multiple internal teams or customer tenants run inference workloads on the same cluster.
2) Observed tail latency or token throughput variance correlated with tenant workload spikes.
3) Pre-launch capacity validation for new tenant onboarding to identify fairness violations.

Definitions:
- Tenant: A logical customer (could be an internal business unit or external customer) with an isolated API key and billing account.
- Entitlement: Contractual or configured resource allocation (e.g., 2 reserved GPUs, 10 max concurrent generation requests).
- Soft quota: Dynamic throttling thresholds that can be exceeded briefly by burst policy.
- Hard quota: Enforced reject/fail path when exceeded.
- Fairshare window: Time window used to calculate proportional resource distribution (default: 5 minutes).

Design principles:
- Favor proportional fairshare over strict absolute caps to maximize utilization while bounding worst-case interference.
- Expose transparent metrics and quota usage per tenant to customers where allowed by confidentiality agreements.
- Provide graceful degradation: fall back to lower-cost model variant or lower max tokens before rejecting.
- Separate priority (SLA) from entitlement; priority affects preemption/reservation, entitlement is billing/accounting.

Configuration reference (example YAML snippet for quota controller):

quotaController:
  fairshare_window_seconds: 300  # 5 minutes
  per_tenant:
    default:
      max_concurrent_requests: 8
      max_total_tokens_per_minute: 20000
      soft_burst_multiplier: 2
      hard_reject: true
    enterprise-tier:
      max_concurrent_requests: 32
      max_total_tokens_per_minute: 200000
      soft_burst_multiplier: 3
      hard_reject: false
  eviction_policy:
    - name: low_priority_preempt
      priority_threshold: 20
      actions:
        - reduce_batch_size: 0.5
        - lower_model_variant: amd/quantized-8bit

Notes on fields:
- max_concurrent_requests: concurrency at the inference request level (requests that are currently holding KV-cache slots).
- soft_burst_multiplier: allows short bursts; quota controller will apply backpressure via 429 + Retry-After when sustained.

Monitoring & observability:
Essential metrics (Prometheus names given):
- tenant_quota_utilization{tenant_id} = gauge of usage / entitlement
- tenant_concurrency_active{tenant_id} = number of in-flight requests
- tenant_token_rate{tenant_id} = tokens/sec rolling mean
- quota_controller_rejections_total{tenant_id,reason}
- fairshare_score{tenant_id} = internal calculated fairness factor

Example PromQL alerts:
- High sustained concurrency for tenant:
  sum by (tenant_id) (tenant_concurrency_active) > 0 and avg_over_time(tenant_concurrency_active[10m]) > 0.9 * on(tenant_id) group_left() tenant_entitlement_concurrency
- Quota rejections spike (indicative of misconfigured entitlements):
  increase(quota_controller_rejections_total[5m]) > 10

Operational procedures (step-by-step):
1) Detection: automated alert triggers on quota rejections spike or sustained tail-latency across tenants.
2) Triage: on-call reviews Grafana dashboard: per-tenant concurrency, fairshare_score, model_variant distribution, node GPU load.
3) Fast mitigation (first 15 minutes):
