   a) Enable global soft-throttling (reduce default soft_burst_multiplier to 1).
   b) If a single tenant is responsible, apply per-tenant temporary hard cap (e.g., set max_concurrent_requests=2) with a TTL of 30 minutes. Record change in incident channel.
   c) If cluster-wide contention, trigger autoscale (if allowed) or move low-priority pods to reserve pool.
4) Customer communication: Send templated status update to affected tenants with observed metrics, mitigation steps, and ETA for resolution.
5) Root cause & remediation (post-30 minutes):
   a) If a tenant is misbehaving repeatedly, schedule a billing/entitlement review.
   b) Adjust fairshare_window_seconds or reserve capacity for enterprise-tier tenants.
   c) Update runbook with any new thresholds discovered.

Safe rollback and escalation:
- Immediate rollback of quota controller changes: use the controller's versioned configstore. Command example:
  # rollback to previous config version
  rcli quota-config rollback --to-version=v21 --env=prod
- If config rollback fails or controller is unreachable:
  1) Flip global feature-flag to bypass fairshare controller and fall back to absolute per-tenant hard-caps (emergency limit).
  2) If the API gateway shows overload, enable 503-fastfail for non-enterprise tiers for 3 minutes while mitigation runs.

Sample CLI snippets for on-prem appliance (control-plane managed):
- Inspect current per-tenant usage:
  rcli tenant list-usage --format=table --filter="tenant:acme-corp"
- Apply a temporary hard cap:
  rcli quota set --tenant acme-corp --max-concurrent-requests 4 --ttl 30m --reason "Emergency mitigation"

Fairness audit and monthly reconciliation:
- Run monthly audit job to detect persistent unfairness (script runs nightly and emits a report):
  1) Compute 95th-percentile fairshare_score per tenant for the month.
  2) Flag tenants with score < 0.6 and > 3 incidents for manual review.
  3) Generate CSV for billing and product ops to reconcile entitlements vs usage.

Capacity planning knobs (recommendations):
- Reserve 10% of physical GPU capacity as "headroom" for eviction/burst handling.
- For mixed workloads (short chat vs long-completion), isolate long-token workloads into a dedicated node-pool labeled "long-running" and enforce stricter per-tenant token-rate caps.
- Use multi-queue scheduling: separate small-batch low-latency queue vs large-batch high-throughput queue, and map tenants based on SLAs.

Security, privacy, and compliance considerations:
- Do not expose per-tenant payloads in shared dashboards; only surface aggregated quota and latency metrics unless customer consent exists.
- Store quota change audit logs in the control plane KMS-encrypted audit store (retention 13 months for enterprise customers).

Ownership and escalation matrix:
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments Day-2-ops (owner: Asha Patel)
- SRE escalation: eng-sre on-call (pager rotation)
- Product/billing reviews: customer-success and finance-legal for entitlement disputes

Post-incident analysis checklist:
- Time-series graphs: fairshare_score, per-tenant concurrency, node_gpu_utilization for the incident window.
- Configuration diffs: compare quota controller versions and list any manual per-tenant overrides.
- Customer impact: enumerated tenants affected, duration, tokens lost or rejected.
- Action items: carry-forward changes, timeline for reserved capacity purchase, API changes if necessary.

Appendix A — Example fairshare calculation (simplified):
- For N tenants, each tenant i has entitlement E_i. Compute weight w_i = E_i / sum(E). Over fairshare_window_seconds, allocate capacity proportionally by w_i. If tenant exceeds 2x w_i in any sub-window, apply soft throttle.

Appendix B — Emergency contact templates:
- Slack: "@channel Incident: quota rejections spike. Mitigation: per-tenant caps applied to tenant=acme-corp. Owner: Asha Patel. ETA 30m. See dashboard: <grafana-link>"
- Email: short templated incident summary to customer-facing leads for affected tenants.

Appendix C — Related configuration files and locations:
- /etc/redwood/quota-controller/config.yaml (cluster-local copy)
- s3://redwood-controlplane/backups/quota-configs/ (retention 90 days)

Revision history:
- 2025-09-12: Initial draft and trial runbook (Asha Patel).
- 2025-11-03: Added PromQL alert examples and soft_burst semantics (Liam Chen).
- 2026-02-08: Hardened rollback steps and added per-tenant TTL policy for overrides (Sofia Martinez).

End of document.

title: dsid_2a1e3c46331c4b16ad4455d9f395636d__tenant-heavy-ingest-surge-mitigation-connector-patterns-2027.txt
text:
Tenant-heavy Ingest Surge Mitigation: Connector Patterns and Operational Playbook

Overview

This playbook documents proven connector integration patterns and operator runbooks for handling tenant-heavy ingest surges against Redwood inference endpoints (hosted, dedicated, and private). It is intended for solutions engineers, customer success, SREs, and partner integrators who build connectors or bridges that forward high-volume telemetry, batched requests, or streaming job workloads into Redwood.

Goals
- Prevent noisy-tenant surges from degrading other tenants or customer SLAs.
- Provide single-source connector configuration templates for backpressure, graceful degradation, and safe failover.
- Define operational checks, monitoring signals, and an on-call escalation ladder.

Scope
- Applies to connectors that: ingest text payloads for generation, embeddings, or reranking; proxy tenant traffic; or batch large historical backfills.
- Covers both synchronous (API) and asynchronous (job/batch) ingestion patterns.
- Does NOT cover hardware-level GPU autoscaling (see eng-infra docs).

High-level Patterns (when to use each)
1) Client-side rate shaping (ideal for SaaS partners)
   - Best when you control the client SDK or agent.
   - Enforce tenant-level QPS/TPU caps and token limits proactively.
2) Connector-side adaptive throttling (recommended default)
   - Connector maintains per-tenant token counters and request queues; adjusts ingress windows based on downstream latency and error rates.
3) Burst cache + queueing with prioritized dispatch
   - For bursty workloads: short-term KV/prefix cache for repeated prompts + prioritized consumer queue to dispatch high-value requests first.
4) Degraded-mode fallback to lower-cost model variants
   - Fall back to quantized or smaller model variants when latency SLOs break. Useful in Dedicated and Private where model variants are available.
5) Backfill and bulk job isolation
   - Run large backfills on isolated routing paths and quota pools; never share production routing with real-time traffic.

Connector Architecture (text diagram)
- Ingress -> Per-tenant ingress limiter -> Priority queue (hot/warm/cold) -> Dispatch worker pool -> Redwood proxy (smart routing) -> Redwood inference endpoints
- Optional: Local caching layer and metrics exporter between queue and dispatch.

Required Preconditions
- Tenant quotas configured in Redwood console or via API (min and max token caps).
- Observability hooks configured: request tracing, per-tenant latency histograms, error counters, and token-metering.
- Circuit-breaker library available in connector runtime (examples use circuitbreaker v1.2).

Connector Configuration Examples
1) Per-tenant sliding window token limiter (pseudo-YAML)
---
# tenant rate limiter
window_seconds: 60
max_tokens_per_window: 10000
burst_allowance: 1.5
priority_buckets:
  - hot: 0.6    # 60% capacity reserved for high-priority routes
  - warm: 0.3
  - cold: 0.1
---

2) Adaptive dispatch strategy (pseudo-config)
---
autoscale:
  enabled: true
  target_latency_ms: 200
  min_workers: 2
  max_workers: 100
  cooldown_seconds: 30
backoff:
  initial_ms: 100
  max_ms: 5000
  factor: 2.0
---

Implementation recipes
A) Synchronous connector (recommended) - Validate incoming request size and tokens; reject with 429 when tenant quota exceeded.
- Maintain a token bucket per tenant persisted in Redis for cross-instance coordination.
- If downstream latency > target_latency_ms for 3 consecutive windows, reduce per-tenant throughput by multiplier 0.5 and emit event to telemetry.

B) Asynchronous large-batch worker - Accept job payloads, store in durable queue (SQS/Kafka), run preflight estimator that calculates token estimate, and schedule against a backfill queue with dedicated capacity pools.
- Mark job "low-priority" when it would exceed daily tenant quota; schedule to off-peak windows.

C) Prioritization example
- Tags: critical (SLAs), interactive (real-time), background (backfills).
- Dispatcher policy: always reserve 30% of capacity for critical and interactive. Background only consumes spare capacity or dedicated backfill pool.

Monitoring & Telemetry (what to track)
- Per-tenant token consumption (tokens/min, tokens/day)
- 95th/99th latency per tenant and per route
- 429 rate and quota rejections per tenant
- Queue depth by priority bucket
- Dispatch worker saturation (gpu_utilization, inflight_requests)
- Model fallback events and quality-regression alerts
- Cost metrics: estimated tokens billed vs allowed

Suggested SLOs and thresholds (connector owner to adopt)
- Target P95 end-to-end latency: 300ms for interactive routes, 1.5s for batch submission acceptance.
- Queue depth alert: queue_depth > 500 for 5m -> page oncall.
- Token spike alert: tenant token rate > 3x baseline for 5m -> create incident priority P2.
- Error ratio alert: 5xx_rate > 2% over 3m -> page P1.

Runbook: Surge detected (step-by-step)
1) Detection: Alert triggered (token spike OR queue_depth OR p99 latency).
2) Triage: Oncall examines per-tenant metrics, request traces, and Redwood console SLO page.
3) Immediate mitigation (5–15 minutes):
   - Throttle the offending tenant to safe cap (e.g., 50% of capacity) using Redis token bucket override.
   - If available, shift tenant to a dedicated low-priority pool or pause background jobs.
   - If customer has a go-live playbook, contact CS lead to coordinate intentional throttling.
4) Short-term containment (15–60 minutes):
   - Enable degraded-mode: route tenant to smaller model variant or quantized profile.
   - Add temporary rule in gateway to drop non-critical requests (e.g., trace-only or sampling).
5) Recovery & Postmortem (>60 minutes):
   - Maintain reduced cap until token rate returns to baseline for 30m.
   - Open RCA with customer and document actions in ticket; include traces and telemetry snapshots.

Escalation & Communication matrix
- If mitigation fails in 30 minutes escalate to Tier 2 SRE and CS Director.
- Customer communication template (first 30 minutes): acknowledge the surge, confirm an active mitigation, and provide ETA 60–90 minutes.
- Post-incident follow-up: share RCA and recommended client-side changes (e.g., batching, retry backoff).

Quality safeguards for degraded-mode fallbacks
- If switching to smaller model variant, run a validation prompt set (20 representative prompts) and measure fidelity threshold (>= 90% acceptable). If below threshold: avoid fallback and instead tighten throttling.

Testing & QA checklist before enabling connector in production
- Load test with per-tenant mix: 80% interactive, 15% background, 5% critical.
- Verify token metering persists across restart and multiple instances.
- Chaos test: simulate network partition to Redis; ensure connector fails open-to-safe-mode (reject new requests with 503 rather than silently accept).
- Confirm alerts and dashboards surface tenant attribution in < 60s.

Operational notes and best practices
- Always prefer rejection (429) with clear error body for quota vs silent delay.
- Maintain a customer-specific throttle override table for known forged bursts (e.g., scheduled batch imports).
- Store per-tenant historical baseline metrics for anomaly detection rather than relying on global thresholds.
- Keep model fallback as a last-resort; measure downstream quality drift and notify customer when used.

Customer Success Playbook (how CS teams should engage)
- Pre-onboarding: document expected daily token volume and peak profile; agree on backfill windows.
- Go-live: run a pre-go-live surge simulation with the customer (30–60 minutes) and validate connector behavior.
- Post-incident: recommend engineering changes (batching, client SDK backoff), and schedule a follow-up health QBR focusing on inference economics.

Appendix: sample 429 response body
{
  "status": 429,
  "error": "quota_exceeded",
  "message": "Tenant token quota exceeded. Retry after backoff or contact your account team for quota increase.",
  "retry_after_seconds": 60
}

Owners and contacts
- Primary owner: Solutions Integration (Aisha Patel)
- Secondary owner: Customer Success Oncall (pager: #cs-oncall)
- Escalation: Eng SRE (pager: #eng-sre)

Related reading
- event-driven-batch-ingest-connector-guide-2026 (integration guide)
- tenant-stability-predictive-signals-runbook-2026 (support process)

Document history
- 2026-11-15: Created by Aisha Patel
- 2027-02-10: Expanded with runbook steps and testing checklist (reviewers: Marcus Lee, Elena Gómez, Samir Mehta)

title: dsid_aaaf6ae3258d4fe2a6883f2cc58e7360__quickstart-templates-launch-metrics.txt
text:
Quickstart Templates v1 — Launch Metrics & Telemetry Specification

## Overview
This document defines the metrics, telemetry events, and traffic tagging required for the **Quickstart Templates v1** launch (RAG + Agents templates across Python and TypeScript). The goal is to measure adoption, activation, and ongoing retention while respecting privacy constraints and avoiding high-cardinality analytics.

**Primary use cases**
- Measure funnel from docs/CLI to “first successful request”.
- Attribute API traffic to template-generated apps (opt-in) to assess retention and quality.
- Quantify support deflection (lower ticket rate / faster time-to-resolution) over time.

**Non-goals (v1)**
- User-level session replay, prompt content capture, or any collection of customer data beyond minimal operational/attribution fields.
- Perfect causal attribution across all acquisition channels (we will prioritize docs → CLI → API request instrumentation).

**Owners**
- Spec owner: Nikhil Sharma (Hosted API PM)
- Implementation liaison: Logan Wright (Telemetry platform)
- DevEx implementation: Monica Patel (templates), Dana Lo (TS)
- Privacy/Security review: Marcus Lin
- Support KPI alignment: Dev Patel / Priya Shah

---

## Success metrics (KPIs)
### North Star KPI
**Time-to-First-Success (TTFS)**
- **Definition:** time between a developer starting a template (CLI init or repo template usage) and their first **successful** Redwood API request from that template app.
- **Target (launch):** p50 ≤ 15 minutes, p90 ≤ 45 minutes (internal beta baseline to be captured).

### Activation KPIs
1) **Template Activation Rate**
- **Definition:** % of template starts that reach First Success within 24 hours.
- **Segments:** language (py/ts), template type (rag-agent), acquisition channel (docs vs github).

2) **Doctor Pass Rate**
- **Definition:** % of `doctor` runs that end with “healthy” status (API connectivity + env validated + collector reachable when configured).

3) **Streaming Readiness Rate (where applicable)**
- **Definition:** % of first success requests using streaming that complete without disconnect/reconnect errors.

### Retention KPIs
1) **Template-tagged Weekly Active Apps (WAAs)**
- **Definition:** number of distinct template app install IDs that generate ≥ 1 successful request in a rolling 7-day window.
- **Note:** Requires opt-in traffic tagging (see “Traffic tagging”).

2) **D7 / D30 Retention (tagged apps)**
- **Definition:** % of apps active in week 0 that are active again in week 1 (D7) / week 4 (D30).

### Support & Quality KPIs
1) **Support Ticket Rate per 1k template starts**
- **Definition:** count of template-related tickets / (template starts / 1000).
- **Source:** Support tagging + analytics.

2) **Top Failure Modes (by event + error taxonomy)**
- **Definition:** distribution of failure categories for first-run requests (auth, quota, network, tool schema, retrieval empty, exporter misconfig).

---

## Funnel definition (canonical)
We will measure the following funnel steps. Each step is backed by one or more telemetry events.

1) **Discovery**
- Developer views template docs page or README.

2) **Start**
- Developer scaffolds a project via CLI or GitHub template.

3) **Configure**
- Developer sets API key and required env (model, base URL, etc.).

4) **Verify (Doctor)**
- Developer runs `doctor` to validate env/API connectivity (recommended but not required).

5) **Run Local**
- Developer starts the app locally and makes a request.

6) **First Success**
- The template app makes its first successful inference request to Redwood.

7) **Ongoing Usage**
- Subsequent successful requests in later days/weeks.

---

## Telemetry principles & constraints
1) **Opt-in traffic tagging**
- Template-origin tagging MUST be **off by default** for requests that traverse customer corporate proxies that may reject unknown headers.
- Templates SHOULD provide a simple switch (env var) to enable tagging.

2) **Privacy + data minimization**
- Do NOT send prompts, tool arguments, retrieved documents, PII, or customer identifiers.
- Do NOT log API keys or bearer tokens.
- Any “install/app identifier” must be a randomly generated UUID stored locally in the template project.

3) **Cardinality control**
- No dynamic IDs in metric label sets.
- Any identifiers used for analytics must be stored in event payloads (analytics system), not as metric dimensions.

4) **Consistency across languages**
- Python and TypeScript templates MUST emit the same core event names and required fields.

---

## Event taxonomy
All events are emitted to Redwood’s analytics pipeline (Console/Analytics) as discrete events.

**Naming convention**
- Prefix: `quickstart_` for template/quickstart events.
- Use snake_case.

**Field conventions**
- `template_id`: stable string identifier for template family, e.g. `rag-agent`.
- `template_language`: `python` | `typescript`.
- `template_version`: semver string (e.g. `1.0.0`).
- `scaffolder`: `cli` | `github`.
- `install_id`: random UUID generated on init; stored in local project file (e.g. `.redwood/template.json`).
- `project_hash`: optional stable hash derived from (install_id + repo path) used only for dedupe; must not contain user path strings.

### Event list (v1)
#### 1) Docs / discovery
**Event:** `quickstart_docs_view`
- **When:** docs page for templates is loaded (docs-site instrumentation).
- **Required fields:** `page_path`, `referrer_domain` (domain only), `utm_source` (if present), `utm_campaign` (if present)
- **Notes:** avoid full URLs beyond path; do not capture query strings other than UTM.

**Event:** `quickstart_docs_click_install`
- **When:** user clicks CLI install / repo link.
- **Required fields:** `target` (`cli_install` | `github_repo` | `walkthrough`), `page_path`

#### 2) Start / scaffold
**Event:** `quickstart_template_init`
- **When:** CLI `init` completes successfully OR (if feasible) a first-run script in GitHub template runs.
- **Required fields:** `template_id`, `template_language`, `template_version`, `scaffolder`, `install_id`
- **Optional fields:** `os_family` (windows/macos/linux), `node_major` or `python_major_minor`

**Event:** `quickstart_template_init_failed`
- **When:** CLI init fails.
- **Required fields:** `template_id` (if known), `scaffolder`, `error_category`, `error_code`
- **Allowed categories:** `dependency_install`, `filesystem_permissions`, `network`, `unknown`

#### 3) Configuration / environment
**Event:** `quickstart_env_check`
- **When:** template app starts up and validates required env vars.
- **Required fields:** `template_id`, `template_language`, `template_version`, `install_id`, `env_status` (`ok` | `missing_required` | `invalid_value`)
- **Optional fields:** `missing_fields` (comma-separated allowlist: `REDWOOD_API_KEY,REDWOOD_MODEL,REDWOOD_BASE_URL,OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`)

#### 4) Doctor
**Event:** `quickstart_doctor_run`
- **When:** CLI `doctor` is executed.
- **Required fields:** `template_id`, `template_language`, `template_version`, `install_id`
- **Optional fields:** `checks_run` (comma-separated), `duration_ms`

**Event:** `quickstart_doctor_result`
- **When:** `doctor` finishes.
- **Required fields:** `install_id`, `result` (`healthy` | `degraded` | `unhealthy`)
- **Optional fields:** `failed_checks` (comma-separated allowlist: `api_key,api_reachable,model_access,otel_collector_reachable,dns,tls,clock_skew`)

#### 5) API request outcomes (template app)
**Event:** `quickstart_first_success`
- **When:** first successful inference request is completed from a given `install_id`.
- **Required fields:** `install_id`, `template_id`, `template_language`, `template_version`, `request_mode` (`sync` | `streaming`)
- **Optional fields:** `model_family` (e.g. `llama`, `qwen`, `mistral`), `region` (Redwood region code), `latency_ms_bucket` (bucketed)

**Event:** `quickstart_request_failed`
- **When:** a request fails before first success (or any time, sampled).
- **Required fields:** `install_id`, `template_id`, `template_language`, `template_version`, `error_category`, `http_status`
- **Allowed `error_category`:** `auth`, `quota`, `rate_limit`, `network`, `timeout`, `stream_disconnect`, `tool_schema`, `tool_execution`, `retrieval_empty`, `retrieval_error`, `otel_export_error`, `unknown`
- **Optional fields:** `retry_attempts` (bucketed: 0,1,2,3+)

**Event:** `quickstart_request_success`
- **When:** successful requests after first success; sampled to control volume.
- **Required fields:** `install_id`, `template_id`, `template_language`, `template_version`
- **Sampling:** 1% default (configurable); always emit `quickstart_first_success` regardless of sampling.

#### 6) Deploy / upgrade
**Event:** `quickstart_deploy_selected`
- **When:** user selects a deploy recipe (e.g. Fly.io, Render, Docker, k8s) from README or CLI.
- **Required fields:** `install_id`, `deploy_target` (`docker` | `flyio` | `render` | `kubernetes` | `other`)

**Event:** `quickstart_template_upgrade`
- **When:** CLI upgrade command runs successfully (v1 may be deferred; include only if shipped).
- **Required fields:** `install_id`, `from_version`, `to_version`

---

## Traffic tagging (API gateway attribution)
Traffic tagging is used to allow Console analytics to filter and report on template-generated traffic.

### Requirements
- Must be **opt-in** and easy to disable.
- Must not include sensitive data.
- Must be stable across retries and streaming reconnect.
- Must be compatible with Redwood Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private when possible.

### Header conventions (v1)
When tagging is enabled, the template app will include the following headers on Redwood API requests:
- `X-Redwood-Template-Id: rag-agent`
- `X-Redwood-Template-Version: 1.0.0`
- `X-Redwood-Template-Lang: python` (or `typescript`)
- `X-Redwood-Template-Install-Id: <uuid>`

**Important:** `X-Redwood-Template-Install-Id` is used for analytics correlation and MUST NOT be promoted to metric dimensions.

### Enable/disable behavior
- Env var: `REDWOOD_TEMPLATE_TELEMETRY=1` enables header tagging.
- Default: disabled.
- If a request fails due to proxy/header rejection (4xx at proxy), templates should log a user-facing warning suggesting disabling tagging.

### Gateway handling
- Gateway will allowlist these headers and persist them into request metadata for analytics (not logs by default).
- For Private deployments, customers can choose to drop these headers at ingress; templates should continue functioning.

---

## KPI dashboard definitions (Console)
Dashboards will be built in Console/Analytics and must be reviewable by DevEx, PM, and Support. This section defines each dashboard, required charts, and filters.

### Dashboard 1: “Quickstart Templates — Adoption & Activation”
**Primary questions:** Are templates being started? Are users reaching first success quickly?

**Charts**
1) Template Starts
- Metric: count of `quickstart_template_init`
- Breakdown: `template_language`, `scaffolder`

2) Activation Rate (24h)
- Metric: % of `install_id` with `quickstart_first_success` within 24h of init
- Breakdown: `template_language`

3) TTFS (p50/p90)
- Metric: distribution of (first_success_ts - init_ts)
- Breakdown: `template_language`

4) Doctor Health Outcomes
- Metric: count of `quickstart_doctor_result`
- Breakdown: `result`

**Filters**
- Date range
- Language
- Template version

### Dashboard 2: “Quickstart Templates — Failure Modes (First Run)”
**Primary questions:** Where do users fail before first success and how do we fix it?

**Charts**
1) Top error categories
- Metric: count of `quickstart_request_failed` before first success
- Breakdown: `error_category`

2) Rate limit / quota issues
- Metric: count of `quickstart_request_failed` where `error_category in (rate_limit, quota)`
- Breakdown: `http_status`, `template_language`

3) Streaming disconnect rate
- Metric: `stream_disconnect` / total streaming attempts
- Breakdown: language

4) Tool schema failures
- Metric: count of `tool_schema`
- Breakdown: template_version

### Dashboard 3: “Quickstart Templates — Retention (Tagged Apps)”
**Primary questions:** Do template apps keep using Redwood?

**Prereq:** tagging enabled by developer (header-based attribution).

**Charts**
1) Weekly Active Apps (tagged)
- Metric: distinct `install_id` with ≥ 1 successful request (rolling 7d)

2) D7 / D30 retention
- Metric: cohort retention based on first success week

3) Token economics (tagged traffic)
- Metric: tokens in/out aggregated for tagged traffic
- Breakdown: model_family (coarse)

---

## Sampling & rate limits
To avoid excessive telemetry volume:
- `quickstart_request_success`: sampled at 1% (configurable).
- `quickstart_request_failed`: emit at 100% until first success; after first success sample at 10%.
- `quickstart_first_success`: always emit.
- CLI events: always emit (low volume).

---

## Data sources & implementation notes
### Sources
- Docs-site analytics: `quickstart_docs_*` events.
- CLI telemetry: `quickstart_template_init`, `quickstart_doctor_*`.
- Template runtime telemetry: `quickstart_env_check`, `quickstart_first_success`, `quickstart_request_*`.
- Gateway attribution: header allowlist and metadata persistence for Console filtering.

### Correlation strategy
- Primary key: `install_id` (UUID, generated at init).
- We DO NOT attempt to correlate to a Redwood user identity at v1 in this spec. Account-level rollups can be derived from request auth on the backend (internal only).

---

## Privacy, security, and compliance checklist
**Must-haves**
- No prompts, documents, tool args, or file paths in telemetry payloads.
- No full URLs (only docs page path + referrer domain).
- No IP addresses captured in template-side telemetry.
- Install ID is random UUID; not derived from hostnames, usernames, or repo paths.

**Review gates**
- Security review sign-off (Marcus Lin) for field allowlist.
- Observability review sign-off (Allison Grant) to ensure no high-cardinality metric labels.
- Support review (Dev Patel) to ensure error categories align with troubleshooting taxonomy.

---

## Open questions (to resolve before GA)
1) GitHub template starts: do we have a reliable mechanism to emit `quickstart_template_init` without CLI? (Option: a one-time “postinstall” script that is clearly disclosed and can be disabled.)
2) Private deployments: do customers want the ability to disable all analytics events while still allowing OTel traces/metrics? If so, define `REDWOOD_TELEMETRY_MODE=off|minimal|full`.
3) Versioning: confirm whether template version should reflect repo release tag or CLI scaffold version stamp (prefer scaffold stamp written into project).

---

## Changelog
- 2025-03-11: Made traffic tagging explicitly opt-in; clarified header set and proxy compatibility rationale.
- 2025-03-03: Added retention dashboard definitions and sampling guidelines.
- 2025-02-14: Initial v1 spec drafted for PM-912.

title: dsid_2995c19427744884bbd5e6bb32759dea__prd-developer-cohort-telemetry-and-cost-triangulation-2028-02-14.txt
text:
Developer Cohort Telemetry and Cost Triangulation PRD

Overview:

This PRD describes the Developer Cohort Telemetry and Cost Triangulation feature. The goal is to provide product and go-to-market teams with automated, reliable mappings from developer cohorts (by onboarding path, SDK usage, integration type, and region) to normalized runtime cost signals and consumption patterns. The feature will enable pricing experiments, onboarding funnels optimizations, and early detection of high-cost adoption patterns.

Problem statement:

- We lack a standard, low-friction way to link developer onboarding cohorts to downstream consumption economics.
- Current cost signals are per-tenant and noisy; it is time-consuming to reconcile cost drivers with SDK/feature choices.
- Sales and Growth teams run ad-hoc analyses; a repeatable product-grade pipeline will increase iteration velocity and reduce billing disputes.

Objectives (success metrics):

1) Provide cohort-level cost reports with 95% reproducibility for the top 80% of cohorts by volume.
2) Reduce time-to-answer for cohort-cost questions from days to < 2 hours for standard queries.
3) Surface early-warning signals for cohorts whose cost-per-active-dev increases > 30% week-over-week.

Non-goals:

- This PRD does not change billing semantics or invoices. It is analytics and decisioning only.
- Not intended to replace low-level per-token billing exports.

User stories:

- As a Growth PM, I want to compare 7-day and 30-day cost-per-active-dev between email-onboarded users and self-serve API key users so I can prioritize onboarding fixes.
- As a Solutions Engineer, I want to see which SDK versions are associated with higher KV cache misses and token churn so I can recommend runtime config changes.
- As a Pricing Analyst, I want cohort elasticity curves (price vs usage) for cohorts that adopted the 'warm capacity' option.

Feature scope (MVP):

- Cohort definition engine: allow cohorts by attributes (signup_channel, onboarding_flow, SDK_version, tenant_size, region, first_route).
- Telemetry ingestion: lightweight SDK tags + server-side enrichment to attach cohort_id to runtime traces and cost events.
- Normalization layer: map raw cost events to normalized cost buckets (compute, storage, network, prefetching) and apply cohort weighting.
- Query surface: precomputed cohort dashboards and a permissive ad-hoc query API for product/finance users.
- Alerting: cohort-cost anomaly alerts (email/Slack) with suggested root-cause pointers.

Out of scope (MVP):

- Auto-enforced pricing changes.
- Deep ML-driven attribution beyond heuristics.

Telemetry contract (example payload):

POST /telemetry/cohort-event  HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "event_type": "runtime_cost_event",
  "timestamp": "2028-02-14T15:04:05Z",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_12345",
  "cohort_id": "cohort_email_2028_q1",
  "route": "/v1/generate",
  "tokens_in": 24,
  "tokens_out": 180,
  "compute_ms": 720,
  "kv_cache_hit": true,
  "quant_profile": "q4_8bit",
  "region": "us-west-2"
}

Normalization rules (explicit):

- compute_cost = compute_ms * per_ms_rate(region, instance_class)
- storage_cost = embedding_storage_bytes * storage_rate_tier
- network_cost = bytes_out * egress_rate(region)
- discounted_cost_for_warm_capacity applied at cohort attribution step (not invoice).

Data model (fields required for cohort mapping):

| field             | required | description |
|-------------------|----------|-------------|
| tenant_id         | yes      | unique tenant id |
| cohort_id         | conditional | assigned by onboarding pipeline or fallback to derived_cohort |
| signup_channel    | optional | web_console | sdk | partner |
| sdk_version       | optional | semantic version string |
| region            | yes      | AWS/GCP region |
| event_timestamp   | yes      | ISO8601 UTC |
| compute_ms        | yes      | runtime compute in milliseconds |
| tokens_total      | yes      | tokens_in + tokens_out |

Privacy and retention:

- Cohort identifiers must not contain PII.
- Retention defaults: raw runtime events retained 30 days; precomputed cohort aggregates retained 18 months.
- For regulated tenants (confidentiality: restricted), only aggregated, anonymized cohorts are stored.

Security and compliance considerations:

- SDK tags are optional and default to "no-cohort" when disabled.
- Cross-check with privacy/legal to ensure cohort granularity does not enable deanonymization.
- Audit logs for cohort assignment changes stored for 7 years (audit-only, restricted access).

UX and dashboards:

- Prebuilt dashboard tiles: cohort summary, cost-per-active-dev trend, cost component breakdown (compute/storage/network), SDK-version heatmap, onboarding funnel overlay.
- Drilldown: click a cohort -> open route-level and tenant-sample views; do not expose raw tenant IDs unless user has "finance_analyst" role.

APIs and exports:

- GET /api/v1/cohorts/{cohort_id}/metrics?window=30d&granularity=1d -> returns precomputed timeseries.
- CSV export for finance with column-level hashed tenant ids.

Rollout plan and milestones:

1) 3-week discovery: finalize cohort attributes and sample SDK tagging. (Owner: Product, 2027-11-08 to 2027-11-29)
2) 6-week implementation: ingestion pipeline, normalization, and initial dashboard (Owner: Eng-Platform, 2027-12-01 to 2028-01-12)
3) 2-week limited beta: opt-in tenants and internal finance testing (Owner: Customer Success, 2028-01-16 to 2028-01-30)
4) Production rollout: dashboard enabled for Product and Finance (Owner: Product, 2028-02-14)

Ownership and stakeholders:

- Product: Priya Nair (PRD owner)
- Eng-Platform: Owen Zhang (ingestion + normalization)
- Eng-Data: Sara López (aggregation and retention)
- Finance: Ethan Ramirez (use cases + acceptance)
- Customer Success: Leah Morgan (beta coordination)

Monitoring, SLOs and alerts:

- Ingestion SLO: 99.9% of telemetry events processed within 120s.
- Dashboard freshness: precomputed cohorts available within 10 minutes for 99% of events.
- Anomaly alert precision target: > 70% true positive rate on simulated anomalies.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):

- Cohort definitions UI exists and saves definitions to the cohort registry.
- Telemetry SDK or server-side enrichment can attach a cohort_id and the payload accepted by ingestion API.
- Precomputed cohort dashboard with cost-per-active-dev and component breakdowns accessible to Product and Finance roles.
- Export CSV contains reproducible, hashed tenant references for reconciliation.
- Beta cohort anomaly alerts deliver examples to Slack channel #cohort-cost-alerts with a sample precision >= 70% on test data.

Open questions and risks:

- How to map legacy tenants lacking SDK tags to cohorts reliably? Proposed mitigation: derived cohort heuristics (first_route, signup_timestamp) and a manual mapping UI.
- Potential for cohort identifiers to leak business-sensitive adoption patterns. Mitigation: enforce access controls and aggregation thresholds (min 5 tenants per cohort before cohort-level export).
- Billing disputes: ensure documentation that this product is analytics-only and not a billing source.

Appendix: sample cohort definition YAML

---
name: "email_onboard_q1_2028"
description: "Users who completed email verification and used SDK v2.x within 7 days"
filters:
  - field: signup_channel
    operator: equals
    value: email
  - field: signup_date
    operator: between
    value: ["2028-01-01","2028-03-31"]
  - field: sdk_version
    operator: starts_with
    value: "2."
aggregation_window: 1d
min_tenants: 5
---

Appendix: sample alert rule (pseudocode)

IF cohort.cost_per_active_dev(7d) / cohort.cost_per_active_dev(14d) > 1.3 AND cohort.volume(7d) > 50 THEN alert("cohort_cost_spike", severity=high)

Related artifacts and next steps:

- Product to approve final cohort attribute list and retention windows.
- Engineering to provide SDK tagging examples and a lightweight server-side enrich endpoint.
- Finance to identify first three canonical cohort reports for reconciliation.

Contact: Priya Nair (priya@redwood.ai)

title: dsid_de6b49c261c64af3885c8d0603ef134d__incident-commander-checklist-platform-degradation.txt
text:
Incident Commander checklist: platform-wide degradation (Hosted API)

h1. Goal
Provide a fast, repeatable checklist for Incident Commanders responding to platform-wide degradation of the Hosted API.

h1. Declare + organize (first 5 minutes)
1) Create incident channel and set severity (P0/P1).
2) Assign roles:
- IC
- Ops lead (SRE)
- Comms lead
- Liaison to Support
3) Start a shared timeline doc (link in channel).
4) Confirm paging of required oncalls:
- SRE
- Infra
- Gateway
- Serving runtime
- (If auth suspected) Security

h1. Triage + stabilize (minutes 5-20)
1) Confirm user impact:
- 5xx rate
- latency
- streaming disconnects
2) Determine blast radius:
- single region vs global
- one route vs multiple
- specific model vs all models
3) Apply quick mitigations (if available):
- tighten rate limits
- disable recent feature flags
- pause deploys
- re-route only a subset of traffic

h1. Decision: do we initiate regional failover?
You should ask three questions:
1) Is this clearly regional? (e.g., only us-east-1 is failing)
2) Is the secondary region healthy and has headroom?
3) Is recovery in the primary likely within 30 minutes?

If (1) and (2) are YES and (3) is NO/unknown, instruct Ops lead to initiate failover per the failover runbook.

*Documentation requirement:* If we are cutting over global traffic, this is an Emergency Change. Capture second-person sign-off in the channel per policy.

h1. Comms
- Update status page at incident start, at major state changes (failover started, failover complete), and at resolution.
- For enterprise customers, coordinate with Support on direct outreach.

h1. Resolution + wrap-up
1) Confirm stability for at least 30 minutes.
2) Announce "resolved" and note whether we remain failed over.
3) Assign postmortem owner and due date.
4) Ensure the exact traffic routing commands used are in the timeline.

title: dsid_007cbc5fb0fd42a49290950884e2b72a__emergent-tenant-behavior-simulation-and-operator-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Emergent Tenant Behavior Simulation and Operator Playbook

Summary:
This runbook describes the Emergent Tenant Behavior Simulation (ETBS) harness, the operator playbook for diagnosing and mitigating cross-tenant emergent failures, and the dashboards/alerts recommended for early detection. ETBS is a lightweight lab and production-adjacent simulator used to reproduce tenant interactions that cause unexpected resource contention, KV-prefix cache thrashing, and indirect latency spikes. The goal is to reduce time-to-mitigate for hard-to-reproduce degradation patterns and to provide prescriptive operator actions tied to observable signals.

Scope:
- Systems covered: LLM inference runtime, KV prefix cache, batching layer, tenant priority queue, regional routing, and serving-side prefetch components.
- Environments: non-prod simulation cluster (primary), canary region, and production operator-guided sandbox.
- Not covered: client-side application bugs, upstream model weight corruption (separate model-onboarding flow).

Owner and Contacts:
- Runbook owner: Maya Patel (Platform Reliability)
- Primary on-call owner: Platform Operators (eng-platform oncall rotation)
- Secondary escalation: Runtime Team (eng-serving-runtime)
- Pager duty runbook link: /runbooks/oncall-platform
- Slack channel: #platform-ops (include tag @runtime-leads when escalating)

Why this matters:
Emergent tenant behavior is typically a multi-signal failure: small, coordinated changes across tenants can push the runtime from healthy to high-tail-latency or high-cost degenerate modes. By codifying simulation inputs, telemetry contracts, and operator playbooks we: 
- Shorten detection and triage time for cross-tenant regressions
- Provide a safe, reproducible path to validate mitigations (prefetch tuning, eviction adjustments, batch-size caps)
- Create an evidence trail for post-incident regressions and roadmap items

Detection: key signals and thresholds
- Token tail latency 95/99/99.9 percentiles per-tenant and per-region (Prometheus metrics: llm_token_latency_p95_seconds, llm_token_latency_p99_seconds)
- KV prefix cache eviction rate: kv_evictions_total by prefix shard > 500/min sustained for 5 minutes
- Continuous batching wait time: batch_wait_seconds p90 > 200ms
- Tenant queue depth: tenant_queue_depth{tenant=~".*"} > 300 for more than 3 minutes
- Cost spike proxy: token_cost_rate_usd_per_minute > baseline * 4 for any single tenant

Suggested alerting rules (Prometheus-style):
- Alert: EmergentTenantLatencySpike
  Expr: sum by(tenant, region)(increase(llm_token_latency_bucket{le="0.05"}[5m])) / sum by(tenant, region)(increase(llm_token_requests_total[5m])) > 0.25
  For: 3m
  Labels: severity=high, owner=platform-ops
  Annotations: summary = "High token latency fraction for tenant {{ $labels.tenant }} in {{ $labels.region }}"

- Alert: KVPrefixEvictionStorm
  Expr: increase(kv_evictions_total[5m]) > 500
  For: 2m
  Labels: severity=critical

- Alert: SustainedBatchWait
  Expr: histogram_quantile(0.9, sum(rate(batch_wait_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, instance)) > 0.2
  For: 5m

Dashboard panels (Grafana recommendations):
1) Cross-tenant latency heatmap: rows = tenant, columns = region, color = p99 token latency.
2) KV prefix churn timeline: stacked area by shard showing evictions and allocations.
3) Batch latency distribution: density plot with tiered SLO lines (p90/p99).
4) Tenant cost rate and request rate scatter: identify high-cost low-throughput tenants.
5) Synthetic prefetched-key hit ratio: higher granularity for prefetch subsystem.

Pre-run checklist (operator before running ETBS):
1) Notify customer-success for tenants that will be included in the production-guided sandbox.
2) Verify operator lab cluster has the latest runtime commit matching the target environment.
3) Confirm telemetry retention and synthetic tenant tagging are enabled.
4) Snapshot routing config and prefetch profiles: config snapshot stored in S3 path s3://redwood-internal/etbs/snapshots/{{date}}.json
5) Ensure rollback plan is documented and oncall is available for 1 hour post-test.

Simulation harness overview (how-to):
- The harness is located in repo infra/simulation/etbs. It runs synthetic clients that: 1) send request distributions (prompt length, frequency), 2) vary attachment of function/tool calls, 3) simulate prefix-key overlap among tenant cohorts, and 4) exercise tokenization edge cases.
- CLI quick example: 
  $ ./etbs/run --config=configs/high-churn-prefetch.yaml --target=canary --duration=30m --output=results/2026-02-01

- Example config (YAML snippet):
  tenant_groups:
    - name: cohort-alpha
      tenants: [tenant-a, tenant-b]
      qps: 120
      prompt_length_mean: 800
      prefix_overlap: 0.38
    - name: cohort-beta
      tenants: [tenant-c]
      qps: 40
      prompt_length_mean: 160
      prefix_overlap: 0.02
  prefetch_profile: aggressive
  runtime_flags:
    enable_jit_kernel_switch: true
    batch_size_cap: 64

Operator Diagnosis and Mitigation Steps (ordered):
1) Confirm the alert and scope (single tenant vs multi-tenant). Use the latency heatmap and request rate panel.
2) If KVPrefixEvictionStorm alert triggered, run: 
   - Query: sum(increase(kv_evictions_total[5m])) by (shard) and identify top-3 shards.
   - Action: Apply temporary per-shard eviction smoothing (API: POST /admin/prefetch/eviction-smoothing?shard={id}&factor=0.5).
   - Monitor for 2 minutes. If evictions drop > 60% and latency improves, promote to a 30m scheduled policy.
3) If SustainedBatchWait is high, cap batch size and enable jittered batching: 
   - API: PUT /admin/batching/config {"batch_size_cap":32, "jitter_ms":50}
   - Note: capping reduces throughput; coordinate with capacity team if throughput SLOs may be violated.
4) If a single tenant is driving cost spikes, apply soft tenant throttling: 
   - POST /admin/tenant/{tenant}/soft-throttle {"qps": 20, "duration_minutes": 15, "cascade": true}
   - Communicate to Customer Success and create a temporary billing note.
5) For model-variant fallback misfires (multi-model routing causing oscillation), pin affected tenants to a stable model variant: 
   - PUT /admin/routing/tenant/{tenant}/pin {"model": "redwood-open-stable-v2"}

Escalation matrix:
- After 20 minutes of mitigation without improvement: page Runtime Team (pager duty) and open an incident with title: Emergent tenant degradation — {region} — {top-tenant}.
- After 60 minutes without improvement: page Engineering Leadership and Customer Success for outbound comms.

Post-run verification and evidence capture:
1) Export time series windows (start -10m to +30m) for all relevant metrics: llm_token_latency_*, kv_evictions_total, batch_wait_seconds*. Store in s3://redwood-internal/etbs/results/{{run_id}}.tar.gz
2) Run reproducibility checklist: if the simulation is reproducible in non-prod, mark as 'reproducible' and assign to the Runtime backlog with labels: regression, preftech, reproducible.
3) Populate a short incident note (Confluence page template link provided) with: summary, timeline, actions taken, mitigation effectiveness, and recommended follow-ups.

Guidance for mitigations selection (decision canvas):
- If evictions are root cause -> prefer smoothing + prefetch-profile adjustment.
- If batch waits dominate -> prefer batch-size caps and jitter.
- If single-tenant cost spike -> soft throttle + CS communication.
- If oscillation between model variants -> pin variant + schedule controlled rollout of a new variant after testing.

Maintenance and roadmap items (short-term backlog):
- Instrument per-tenant prefix overlap metric (ETA Q2 2026).
- Build automated mitigation playbook that can apply smoothing heuristics under operator supervision.
- Integrate ETBS harness into CI job that runs pre-rollout for runtime changes (goal: catch regressive behavior before canary).

Retrospective template (to be completed after each significant exercise):
1) Problem statement and impact (who, what, when).
2) Hypothesis and root cause.
3) Actions taken and evidence.
4) What went well / what didn't.
5) Owner and timeline for follow-ups.

Runbook upkeep cadence:
- Owner review every 90 days.
- Simulation config refresh aligned with capacity planning cycles (quarterly).
- Dashboard and alert tuning review after every substantive runtime release.

Appendix A: Quick queries
- Top offender tenants by eviction rate: 
  topk(10, sum(increase(kv_evictions_total[5m])) by (tenant))
- Prefetch hit ratio per tenant: 
  sum(prefetch_hits_total{tenant=~".*"}) by (tenant) / sum(prefetch_requests_total{tenant=~".*"}) by (tenant)

Appendix B: References and links
- Simulation repo: git@github.com:redwood/infra-simulation/etbs
- Prefetch API docs: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/prefetch-api-spec-2025
- Incident template: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/incident-note-template

If you have questions or want the on-call to run a guided ETBS sandbox, ping Maya or @platform-ops in #platform-ops. This playbook is intended to be operator-friendly and to provide a reproducible path from detection to safe mitigation.

title: dsid_c89cc8e839d64b00a4a471ad87ea41ce__sdk-breaking-change-mitigation-matrix-and-hotpatch-playbook-2026.txt
text:
SDK breaking change mitigation matrix and hotpatch playbook

Overview
--------
This document defines a practical mitigation matrix and hands-on hotpatch playbook for SDK breaking changes that affect customer integrations. It is intended for DX engineers, SDK maintainers, and on-call support engineers who need reproducible steps to triage, mitigate, ship a hotpatch, and verify compatibility with minimal customer impact.

Scope and goals
----------------
- Scope: client-side SDKs maintained by eng-developer-experience (JS, Python, Go) and ancillary adapter libraries produced by partners.
- Goals:
  - Triage breaking changes within 60 minutes of detection (severity-critical)
  - Ship a validated hotpatch inside a 4-hour window for customer-impacting regressions
  - Provide clear communication to customers and internal teams within 90 minutes
  - Reduce recurring break incidents through postmortems and improved tests

When to use this playbook
-------------------------
Use this flow for any of the following detection signals:
1) Automated integration test failures that started occurring after a dependency bump in the SDK CI pipeline.
2) Production error spike with >=5% of customer requests failing due to SDK client exceptions.
3) Multiple customer support tickets reporting the same reproducible error tied to a released SDK version.

Severity classification matrix
------------------------------
The following table maps observable symptoms to severity, SLA, and immediate action. Apply the first matching row.

| Symptom | Severity | Target MTTA | Immediate action owner | Temporary mitigation pattern |
|---------|----------|-------------|------------------------|-----------------------------|
| SDK throws exception on auth handshake for 100% of requests | critical | 15m | On-call DX engineer | Revert client-facing release or publish patched minor with compatibility shim and rollback policy |
| Tokenization/requests get garbled causing model misrouting for many customers | high | 30m | SDK lead + SRE | Enable server-side fallback to previous model route; advise customers to pin model version |
| Non-fatal response shape change (missing optional field) | medium | 4h | SDK maintainer | Release patch with backward-compatibility layer and deprecation notes |
| Performance regression < 2x latency for a minority of customers | low | 24h | Performance owner | Deploy client-side option to disable new optimization, gather telemetry |

Owners and communication matrix
-------------------------------
- Primary: eng-developer-experience SDK on-call (pager duty: dx-sdk-oncall).
- Secondary: eng-platform SRE for rollout and traffic shaping.
- Stakeholder notifications: product (PM), support, developer-advocate, security (if auth implicated).
- Customer comms owner: Customer Success (for named accounts) + Support (public issue tracker).

Triage checklist (first 60 minutes)
----------------------------------
1. Confirm signal provenance:
   - Verify Sentry/Errbot alerts, reproduce against latest published SDK version, and run the failing test in local sandbox.
   - Use reproducible request body and logs from the customer or synthetic harness.
2. Scope impact:
   - Use telemetry dashboards: percent of requests failing, top 10 customer IDs, geographic spread.
   - Check CI: which PR or dependency change landed last 24–72 hours.
3. Temporary mitigation decision (yes/no):
   - If severity is critical or high and mitigation possible, escalate to hotpatch flow.
4. Communicate initial status (within 90 minutes):
   - Post to #dx-incident channel with short summary, severity, impacted versions, and next ETA.

Hotpatch flow (shipable within 4 hours)
-------------------------------------
Step 0 — Pre-conditions: confirm reproducible failing test and safe rollback path exists (git/release tags).

Step 1 — Create minimal patch branch
- Author: SDK maintainer. Branch naming: hotpatch/sdk/<package>-<version>-<YYYYMMDD>-<short>
- Keep change small: compatibility shim, defensive null checks, or revert of recent commit.
- Example minimal change (JavaScript):

```js
// compat-shim.js
if (!response.parsedContent) {
  // fallback to older field name
  response.parsedContent = response.content_v1 || '';
}
```

Step 2 — Local and CI validation
- Run unit tests and full integration suite against the reproducible scenario.
- Add one targeted acceptance test in the patch branch that reproduces the bug.
- If integration tests are flaky, record run artifacts and proceed with conservative rollout.

Step 3 — Code review and quick sign-off
- Use expedited reviewers list (owner + one reviewer). PR label: hotpatch/expedite.
- If release manager approves, merge to main with commit message referencing the incident ID.

Step 4 — Release and canary
- Build artifact and publish to canary channel (npm tag: canary-<incident-id>, pip: pre-release wheel).
- Canary rollout plan:
  - 0–5% of downloads for 15 minutes
  - 5–25% for 30 minutes if no regressions
  - 25–100% after 1 hour with monitoring green
- For public package registries where immediate download % control is limited, issue clear advisory and provide patched package URL and pin instructions.

Step 5 — Verification and rollback criteria
- Metrics to watch during canary:
  - error rate for the failing endpoint (target: <25% of prior spike)
  - latency P95 should not degrade more than 20% relative to baseline
  - customer-reported reproduction count should drop to zero for confirmed customers
- Rollback if any of the following triggered:
  - new critical exceptions introduced within canary window
  - customer complaint rate increases after patch
  - test-suite failure in post-release smoke checks

Step 6 — Publish stable release
- After canary success, promote artifact to stable channel and publish changelog entry with clear migration guidance and API contract notes.
- Add deprecation timeline if behavior intentionally changed.

Communication templates
-----------------------
Use these snippets for rapid updates. Replace placeholders in brackets.

Initial status (internal):
"Incident [INC-YYYYMMDD-###]: SDK exception observed in [package-name] v[semver]. Impact: [X%] of requests failing. Triage in progress. Owner: [name]. ETA for next update: 60 minutes."

Customer advisory (public):
"We are investigating an issue impacting the [package-name] SDK v[semver] that may cause client errors during requests to the Redwood API. A mitigated release is available at [URL]. For immediate relief, pin to [previous-version] or install the patch with `npm i @redwood/sdk@[patched-tag]`. We will follow up when fully resolved."

Post-incident follow-up (24–72 hours)
-------------------------------------
- Run a blameless postmortem documenting root cause, timeline, and decisions.
- Required action items (assign owners and due dates):
  1. Add an automated integration test that reproduces the regression (owner: SDK QA) — due in 7 days.
  2. Add canary telemetry dashboard and alert with runbook link (owner: SRE) — due in 14 days.
  3. Review dependency upgrade policy to include staged rollout for critical transitive deps (owner: platform) — due in 21 days.

Prevention and engineering improvements
--------------------------------------
- Recommended CI gates:
  - Block dependency updates if integration tests are red for any supported runtime.
  - Require a locally reproducible acceptance test before merging changes that touch serialization, auth, or network layers.
- SDK design guidance:
  - Favor additive changes: add new fields under clearly namespaced keys, avoid renaming top-level fields.
  - Implement feature flags in SDKs for opt-in behavior changes.

Runbook quick commands and examples
----------------------------------
- Reproduce failing call (Python example):

```py
from redwood_sdk import Client
c = Client(api_key='REDACTED')
resp = c.generate(prompt='hello', model='gpt-lite')
print(resp.raw)
```

- Publish canary npm tag:

```bash
npm publish --tag canary-INC-20260210
```

- Tag for stable release after verification:

```bash
git tag -a v1.4.7 -m "hotpatch for INC-20260210" && git push origin v1.4.7
```

Appendix: additional references
--------------------------------
- SDK changelog conventions: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/sdk-patch-release-playbook-and-compat-rules-2026
- Support canonical fixes index: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/support-top-issues/sdk-telemetry-mismatch-canonical-fixes-2026
- Incident template and postmortem form: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortem-template

Contact and escalation
-----------------------
- DX on-call group: dx-sdk-oncall (PagerDuty)
- Slack channels: #dx-incident, #sdk-release, #support
- Pager escalation: 1st on-call -> SDK lead -> Eng Platform SRE

End of document

title: dsid_b9e4f67455d7490584b315b4468750e2__kernel-compat-matrix-and-rolling-upgrade-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Kernel compatibility matrix and rolling upgrade playbook

Summary:
This document defines the kernel compatibility matrix and the step-by-step rolling upgrade playbook for Redwood's serving runtime kernels. It codifies preflight checks, compatibility rules, canary and phased rollout procedures, automated and manual verification gates, telemetry thresholds, rollback criteria, and post-rollout validation. The goal is to enable safe roll-forward of kernel builds across heterogeneous GPU pools with minimal customer impact.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers
- SREs and oncall
- Release and QA engineers
- Integrations/Private deployment teams

Owners and escalation:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-scheduling team (oncall: @kernel-scheduler)
- Release coordinator: Maya Thompson
- SRE escalation: Pager duty (SRE-oncall)

1) Compatibility matrix (purpose and format)
The compatibility matrix captures which kernel binary versions are allowed to run against which runtime control-plane versions, model-ABI versions, and accelerator families. It is the single source of truth for rollout decisions.

Matrix columns (canonical):
- kernel_version (e.g., kv1.4.2)
- runtime_api_version (e.g., rapi-2.1)
- model_abi_tag (e.g., v10-kv-shape)
- supported_accelerators (comma-separated; e.g., A100-80GB, H100-80GB)
- mandatory_feature_flags (comma-separated; e.g., async-handshake, prefetch-v2)
- safe_for_canary (yes/no)
- known_incompatibilities (short note)

Example row (ASCII table):
| kernel_version | runtime_api_version | model_abi_tag | supported_accelerators | mandatory_feature_flags | safe_for_canary | known_incompatibilities |
| kv1.4.2 | rapi-2.1 | v10-kv-shape | A100-80GB,H100-80GB | async-handshake,prefetch-v2 | yes | none |

Location:
- Canonical file persisted in git: infra/serving/kernel-compatibility/canonical-matrix.csv
- A human-readable exported copy lives in Confluence attachments and the release ticket.

Maintenance rules:
- Any kernel build must include a compatibility entry before scheduling to production pools.
- Entries are created by the kernel owner and reviewed by the runtime API owner (two approvals).
- When a control-plane change increments runtime_api_version, affected kernel entries must be audited within 48 hours.

2) Preflight checklist (automated + manual)
Automated checks (CI must pass):
- Unit and integration test suite: PASS
- Kernel self-smoke: can load model artifacts and run a short end-to-end generation for 512 tokens with NVTX tracing enabled
- ABI verifier: static check for model_abi_tag compatibility
- Telemetry instrumentation present: success/failure counters, heap/gpu mem gauges, and critical trace spans
- Artifact signing and provenance: SHA256 + build metadata present

Manual checks (release engineer):
1. Confirm compatibility matrix entry and required feature flags.
2. Verify canary image tag exists in registry and matches signed SHA256.
3. Confirm automated preflight reports are green and that a representative model from the canary corpus completes end-to-end generation within baseline latency + 15%.
4. Check known-issues tracker for regressions against this kernel family.

3) Canary rollout plan (recommended default)
Objective: validate new kernel in small, representative traffic with full observability and automatic halt on regressions.

Phases:
- Phase A (lab canary): 0% production. Deploy to lab pool with synthetic traffic generator. Duration 4 hours. Gate: no critical errors, tail latency p50/p95 within target, no increase in GPU OOM events.
- Phase B (shadow canary): shadow production traffic (mirror) to canary instances; no responses used for serving. Duration 6 hours. Gate: match semantic outputs for a 1k prompt sample (fidelity >= 98%), no unbounded latency spikes.
- Phase C (live canary): route 3% of production requests by weighted routing to canary nodes. Duration 2 hours. Gate: token error rate < 0.05%, p95 latency within 1.2x baseline, no kernel-level panic or GPU watchdog events.
- Phase D (ramp): if gates pass, double canary traffic every 30 minutes (3% -> 6% -> 12% -> 24% -> 48% -> 100%). Each step has a 30-minute observation window and explicit automated checks.

Automated gating checks (examples):
- Error budget burn for the kernel cohort: > 10% of allocated error budget -> halt and rollback
- Token-level error rate delta > 0.02% above baseline-> halt
- SLO latency p95 delta > 25% -> halt
- GPU memory OOM events rate > 0.01 per 10k requests -> halt

4) Roll-forward and fallback mechanics
Artifact naming and deployment:
- Kernel artifacts use a deterministic tag: <kernel_version>-<build_date>-<sha8>
- Release job publishes signed artifact and updates a canary deployment manifest in k8s (or internal deployment coordinator for Dedicated pools)

Routing controls:
- Weight-based routing controlled by the routing-service with per-pool overrides. Canary group is isolated by pool labels (kernel:kv1.4.2-canary).
- Fallback policy: on detection of a kernel-level failure, the router automatically re-routes impacted requests to the last-known-good kernel version in the same pool (prefer local fallback) and triggers enrichment events.

State and KV cache handling:
- New kernel must be able to reconcile KV cache formats. If cache format changes are non-backward-compatible, the canary entry must include a migration plan (see section "KV migration patterns").
- Best practice: versioned cache keys and a two-step reconciliation where new kernels accept old keys and write with a new versioned prefix for a configurable warmup window (default 1 hour).

5) KV migration patterns (examples)
- Read-compatible migration: new kernel reads both old and new key namespaces; writes only new namespace. Safe for rolling upgrade without global cache flush.
- Full rekey migration: requires coordinated drain-and-repopulate. Procedure:
  1) Schedule maintenance window for dedicated pools.
  2) Drain incoming new sessions, allow existing sessions to finish.
  3) Run rekey job that migrates hot keys first (top 5% heat).
  4) Bring new kernels online and monitor cache hit rate and latency.

6) Observability and runbook automation
Essential dashboards and alerts (owner: telemetry/runtime-observability):
- Kernel cohort dashboard: p50/p95/p99 latency, token error rate, GPU OOMs, CPU steal, nvml_temperature, kernel_crash_count
- Canary gating dashboard: automated gate results, canary routing weight history, payload fidelity scorecards
- Deployment health alerting rules (examples):
  - kern_crash_rate > 0.5 per minute for 5m -> Sev-1
  - token_error_rate_delta > 0.02% for 15m -> Sev-2
  - canary_p95_latency_delta > 25% for 10m -> Sev-2

Standard automated remediation play actions (CI/CD hooks + operator):
1. Automatic immediate weight rollback to previous kernel on kern_crash detection.
2. Create a rollback release ticket with diagnostics bundle (trace samples, nvml counters, kernel logs, artifact sha).
3. If rollback fails or broader pool degradation observed, escalate to oncall SRE and initiate incident process per oncall-and-incident-response docs.

7) Rollout validation checklist (post-100%):
- 24h stability: no Sev-1 incidents tied to kernel, <10% error budget burn vs baseline
- 72h fidelity: sample prompt set outputs validated against golden set for regression drift (automated diffing)
- Cost/efficiency check: per-token GPU time within expected envelope (±10%)
- Telemetry maturity: histogram buckets for latency show no new unexpected long tail spikes

8) Rollback decision tree (condensed):
- Immediate rollback triggers (automated): kernel_crash_rate spike, GPU driver panic, mass OOM, unhandled kernel watchog reset
- Conditional rollback (requires manual review): sustained p95 latency > 1.5x baseline for 30m, widespread fidelity regressions on important customers
- If rollback performed, collect a full post-rollback artifact bundle and open a postmortem if incident severity >= Sev-2.

9) Testing matrix (must be green before canary):
- Unit tests: 100% green
- System tests: conv/generation/embeddings path tests with sample models on each target accelerator type
- Interop tests: runtime_api_version compatibility tests across last 3 API versions
- Chaos tests: simulated GPU preemption, NVLink transient error replay, kernel-level random failures (in lab)

10) Release notes content model (what goes into the release ticket and Confluence excerpt):
- What changed: brief bullet list of functional changes and safety mechanisms
- Compatibility impacts: matrix excerpt showing affected runtime_api_versions, models, and accelerators
- Known limitations: short list and mitigation recommendations
- Migration steps: KV migration or config toggles required
- Owners and rollback instructions

11) Examples: quick commands and verification queries
- Check canary weight: curl -sS https://routing.internal/api/v1/weights | jq '.pools["kv1.4.2-canary"]'
- Fetch kernel logs: rlog fetch --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --since 1h --grep kern_crash
- Automated gate status: /infra/cicd/gates/latest?artifact=kv1.4.2

12) Post-deployment retrospective checklist (within 7 days):
- Release owner schedules a 30m review: verify metrics, confirm no hidden regressions, and capture lessons learned
- Update compatibility matrix if any implicit constraints were discovered
- If migration was required, document performance delta and any customer communication that occurred

Appendix A: Emergency rollback quick commands
1) Immediate zero-weight (global): routingctl set-weight --cohort kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --weight 0 && routingctl promote --cohort kernel:kv1.3.9-stable
2) Force restart pool nodes: deployctl restart --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --grace 30s
3) Collect diagnostics bundle: diag-collector --pool kernel:kv1.4.2-canary --out /tmp/diag-kv1.4.2.tgz

Appendix B: Glossary
- Kernel: native GPU execution binary and support shim used by the serving runtime
- Model ABI: serialized contract between runtime and model execution kernels
- Canary cohort: isolated set of nodes running a target kernel for validation

References:
- infra/serving/kernel-compatibility/canonical-matrix.csv (git)
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-upgrade-validation-and-canary-matrix-2026 (related runbook)
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-handshake-and-adaptive-fallback-patterns-2026 (handshake spec)

Contact: Maya Thompson (mthompson@redwood.ai) for questions or to request a matrix exception.

title: dsid_01f4ce1ac9ca4b85a471d39960e6be37__post-incident-action-triage-and-continuous-remediation-2026.txt
text:
Post-Incident Action Triage and Continuous Remediation Playbook

Purpose:
This playbook defines a standardized, SLO-driven process for triaging post-incident actions and executing continuous remediation across Redwood Inference services. It focuses on converting incident findings into prioritized, time-boxed work items tied to SLOs, capacity commitments, and automated validation using our operational tooling. The goal is to reduce repeat incidents, lower SLO regression risk, and shorten mean time to fix for systemic causes.

Scope:
- Applies to incidents with customer-facing impact (Pages SEV-2/SEV-1) and any SLO breach event detected by the SLO observability pipeline.
- Covers immediate action triage, remediation planning, rollouts, validation, and runbook/tooling updates.
- Not a replacement for the incident commander or postmortem — this is the actionable remediation workflow that starts at the end of the incident timeline.

Key principles:
- SLO-first prioritization: Actions are prioritized by their expected reduction in SLO burn and customer impact, not by ease of implementation.
- Time-boxed remediation: Every remediation is assigned a remediation class (hot, fast, normal) with target SLAs.
- Evidence-driven verification: Automated, reproducible checks must validate each remediation before and after rollout.
- Continuous improvement: Runbooks and tooling are updated as part of the remediation and are included in the completion criteria.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Incident owner / service owner: Ensures the produced action list is accurate and assigned.
- Remediation owner: Implements the fix, drives rollout and validation.
- SLO steward (SRE): Scores each action against SLO impact and approves prioritization.
- QA / Canary owner: Builds canary tests and validation jobs in the observability pipeline.
- Product stakeholder: Confirms business risk/priority when remediation conflicts with roadmap.

Remediation classification and SLAs:
1) Hot (P0): Immediate engineering change required; target remediation window = 72 hours. Examples: misconfiguration causing sustained SLO breach, runaway process consuming KV cache.
2) Fast (P1): High-reduction action; target window = 30 days. Examples: model quantization profile regression identified; autoscaling rule mis-tuning.
3) Normal (P2): Improvements with clear benefit but lower urgency; target window = 90 days. Examples: telemetry gaps, non-critical refactors.

Triage procedure (step-by-step):
1. Populate the Post-Incident Remediation Board (Jira project: SRE-REM) within 24 hours of incident close. Use the template `SRE-REM - Remediation Template`.
2. For each action, the remediation owner provides: summary, technical cause, estimated effort (T-shirt size), mitigation steps, validation criteria, and rollback plan.
3. SLO steward runs the SLO impact scoring worksheet and assigns an SLO impact score (0-10).
4. Prioritize backlog by: 
   - SLO impact score (desc)
   - Customer exposure (desc)
   - Cross-service blast radius
   - Implementation effort (asc)
5. Assign remediation classification (Hot/Fast/Normal) and set target completion date.

SLO impact scoring quick reference (worksheet excerpt):
- 8-10: Immediate SLO breach or recurring >50% daily burn
- 5-7: Noticeable burn, intermittent customer impact, potential to escalate
- 1-4: Low immediate risk; candidate for batching with other tasks

Action ticket template (required fields):
- Title (short)
- Severity class (Hot/Fast/Normal)
- SLO impact score
- Affected services/components
- Detailed technical summary
- Proposed change (PR/infra change/service config)
- Validation plan (canary + synthetic checks)
- Rollback plan and guardrails
- Estimated effort and owners
- Link to incident postmortem

Validation and automated checks (required before marking remediation complete):
- Canary job in CI/CD that mimics incident traffic profile (minimum 2 repeats).
- Pre/post metric snapshots for SLOs and error budget burn rate. Include: p50/p95/p99 latency, success rate, token-level rejection rates.
- Synthetic test run showing no regression for the relevant prompt sets (if applicable).
- Telemetry ingestion sanity: logs, traces, and sampling for the change must be available for 14 days.

Example validation checklist (table-like):
| Check | Owner | Pass condition | Evidence required |
|--|--|--|--|
| Canary passes under incident-profile load | QA/Canary owner | 0 failures for 1 hour | Canary run ID, logs |
| Latency p99 <= SLO threshold | SRE | p99 <= 1200ms for model-generation svc | Metric snapshot link |
| Error budget burn halts | SRE | Burn rate reduced by >= 60% | Burn-rate graphs |
| No increase in downstream errors | Service owner | Downstream 5xx under baseline | Traces + logs |

Rollout and gating policy:
- All Hot remediations require: canary (10% route), feature-flagged rollout, and automated rollback at 5% error-rate delta or 2x burn-rate.
- Fast remediations require a staged rollout (canary -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with 24-hour hold windows and metric checks.
- Normal remediations follow a regular deployment cadence but must include synthetic validation post-deploy.

Runbook and tooling updates (completion criteria):
- Update the affected runbook with a reproducible reproduction section and new remediation steps.
- Add a diagnostic checklist to the runbook that is no longer >3 manual steps without an automated check.
- If the remediation introduced new observability, add dashboards and alerts to the SRE Dashboard catalog.

Capacity and provisioning considerations:
- If remediation touches autoscaling or capacity configuration, include a capacity rehearsal step: simulate expected traffic for 30 minutes at projected peak and validate scaling events.
- Reserve a temporary capacity pool for Hot remediations that require burst testing. Open a capacity request ticket to infra with the tag `sre-capacity-test` and provide expected GPU/CPU and duration.

Incident review linkages and metrics to track post-remediation:
- Time to remediation (TTRem): time between incident close and remediation completion. Target medians: Hot <= 7 days, Fast <= 45 days, Normal <= 120 days.
- Remediation effectiveness: % of remediations that prevent recurrence within 90 days. Target: >= 85%.
- Runbook coverage: % of incidents where runbook was updated as part of remediation. Target: >= 95%.
- Mean validation automation: percent of remediations with automated validation pipelines. Target: >= 90%.

Escalation and arbitration process:
1. If remediation target date will be missed, remediation owner must file an `SRE-REM` update and notify SLO steward within 48 hours with a mitigation plan.
2. If product or legal constraints block a remediation, tag the ticket with `blocked-by-policy` and route to Product or Legal for decision within 5 business days.
3. Arbitration: SRE lead + Product manager + Infra lead decide priority tradeoffs for any Hot remediations that compete for capacity or runway. Decision recorded on the remediation ticket.

Playbook templates and automation hooks (examples):
- Jira template: `SRE-REM - Remediation Template` (fields are enforced via Jira schema).
- CI job: `remediation-canary-test` (parameters: service, profile, run-id).
- Observability job: `slo-impact-snapshot` (outputs a JSON artifact attached to ticket). Example CLI: 
```
$ infra-cli remediation-canary --service model-gen --profile incident-2026-01 --duration 60m --notify SRE
$ observability-cli slo-impact-snapshot --service model-gen --since incident-start --until now --out artifact://sre/12345.json
```

Post-mortem to remediation handoff checklist (immediate tasks after incident close):
- Confirm incident entry in postmortem repo and link (owner).
- Create SRE-REM board entries for all actionable items (owner).
- SLO steward assigns impact scores (within 48 hours).
- Initial prioritization meeting (weekly SRE triage) adds Hot items to the next sprint if not already scheduled.

Reporting and governance cadence:
- Weekly SRE remediation triage meeting: review Hot items, stalled tickets, and capacity conflicts. Attendees: SRE leads, service owners, product liaisons.
- Monthly metrics review: TTRem, effectiveness, and tooling coverage to Engineering leadership.
- Quarterly remediation audit: random sample of remediations audited for evidence, validation artifacts, and runbook updates.

Appendix A — Ticket lifecycle sample (narrative):
- Incident closes on 2026-01-10; postmortem authored and links 4 technical findings. By 2026-01-11, SRE-REM board has 6 tickets. Two items classified Hot (misconfigured autoscaler, missing KV cache TTL), both assigned and given 72-hour windows. By 2026-01-14 both have canary validation passing and are rolled to 100% with no regression. Evidence artifacts are attached and runbooks updated.

Appendix B — Example SLO impact statement (to include in ticket):
"This remediation addresses an autoscaler misconfiguration that caused sustained p99 latency breaches for the model-generation service, burning ~65% of the daily error budget during the incident window. Implementing the corrected scaling policy is expected to reduce p99 latency by 35-50% under current traffic profiles and eliminate the observed error-budget spike."

Related pages and artifacts:
- Link to SLO observability pipeline (internal): /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/slo-observability-pipeline-design-and-validation-2025
- Remediation board: Jira project SRE-REM
- Postmortem template: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/postmortem-template

Change history:
- 2026-01-15: created by Anika Shah
- 2026-02-10: clarified validation checklist and added capacity rehearsal requirement (Ravi Patel)

Contact:
- For questions about this playbook, contact the SRE guild (sre-guild@redwood-inference.internal) or the author.

title: dsid_7b606edaac794ccc94a5c269d7f1f510__incident-play-catalog-and-rotation-succession-plan-2029.txt
text:
Incident Ecosystem Catalog and Rotation Succession Plan

Summary:

This document defines the Incident Ecosystem Catalog (the canonical inventory of services, dependencies, and runbook ownership), the runbook lifecycle (creation, validation, maintenance, retirement), and a rotation succession plan tied to training/game-day cadence. It also contains templated status-page and customer communication artifacts and a repeatable post-incident follow-through process.

Scope:

- Applies to all production-facing services under Redwood Inference (hosted API, dedicated fleet, private control plane).
- Primary consumers: SRE, Serving Runtime, Platform, Customer Success.
- Excluded: non-production experimental feature branches and personal projects.

1) Incident Ecosystem Catalog (IEC)

Purpose: keep a small, queryable index of services, critical thresholds, primary/secondary owners, and an accession link to the authoritative runbook. Update cadence: weekly sync from service owners; audited quarterly by SRE.

Minimum IEC entry fields (single-line CSV allowed):
- service_name, tier (critical/high/medium), primary_owner, secondary_owner, sla_target, p99_latency_threshold_ms, error_rate_threshold_pct, runbook_path, alert_channel, data_sensitivity

Example entries (CSV):
"runtime-router,critical,serving-runtime@redwood.com,platform-oncall@redwood.com,99.95,800,0.5,sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/runtime-router-ops.json,#svc-runtime-router,internal"
"kv-cache,high,serving-runtime@redwood.com,eng-sre@redwood.com,99.9,120,1.0,sources/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/kv-cache-eviction.json,#svc-kv-cache,internal"

Where to find the catalog: Confluence index + canonical YAML at git://infra/configs/incident-catalog.yaml (read-only for non-SRE teams).

2) Runbook lifecycle and governance

Principles:
- Runbooks are living, tested playbooks for common faults. They must be concise (<= 6 steps for first-responder play), include mitigation commands, known-safe rollbacks, and postmortem hooks.
- Every runbook must have an owner and a quarterly reviewer.

Stages and required artifacts:
1. Draft: create markdown in the runbooks repo under /runbooks/{service}/prod.md. Add IEC reference.
2. Review: assign two reviewers (1 owner-team, 1 SRE). Use the PR template checklist: alerts, mitigation, rollback, comms template, test plan.
3. Validation: perform a tabletop or runbook test during a game day within 30 days of merging. Attach test notes to the PR.
4. Published: add confluence link and tag version (vYYYYMMDD).
5. Maintenance: owner signs off quarterly; automated stale runbook reminder after 90 days without edits.
6. Retirement: deprecate with 90-day notice window; redirect IEC entry to replacement or archive.

Runbook content template (top-of-file):
- title: short service identifier
