- impact_summary: one-sentence impact profile
- when_to_run: bullet list of alert signatures
- immediate_actions: numbered steps for first 10 minutes
- mitigation_commands: shell/cli commands (tested)
- rollback_instructions: how to undo risky steps
- owner: person/email/team
- last_tested: YYYY-MM-DD
- metrics_to_capture: list of Grafana dashboards/alerts

Sample mitigation_commands snippet:
```
# fetch last 30m errors for runtime-router
rbx logs query --service runtime-router --since 30m --severity error --limit 200
# temporarily disable model-fanout path
kubectl -n serving patch svc model-fanout --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/type","value":"ClusterIP"}]'
```

3) Alerting thresholds and immediate SLO triggers

Standard thresholds (service owners may set stricter values in IEC):
- Availability SLO breach: 5m of sustained failing health checks across >= 3 regions. Escalation: auto-page SRE and owner.
- Latency SLO degradation: p95 > 500ms for more than 5 minutes or p99 > 800ms for more than 1 minute -> consult oncall, consider fallbacks.
- Error rate: 0.5% error rate sustained for 10 minutes -> page.
- KV cache eviction storm: eviction_rate > 1000/s for > 2 minutes -> page.

Example alert rule (YAML):
```
alert: RuntimeHighP99
expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="runtime-router"}[2m])) by (le)) > 0.8
for: 1m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:
  summary: "runtime-router p99 > 800ms"
```

4) On-call roles & Succession ladder

Roles (primary responsibilities):
- Incident Commander (IC): owns prioritization, customer comms, and decision to rollback.
- Bridge Operator (BO): manages the incident bridge, records timeline, runs shared commands, and updates status page.
- Service Owner (SO): subject-matter expert for the affected service; leads mitigation steps.
- Customer Liaison (CL): coordinates CS/Sales/Legal comms, templates, and escalations.
- Artifact Scribe: collects artifacts and ensures evidence is attached for postmortem.

Succession & escalation ladder (automated paging):
1. Primary oncall page (IC) -> 5 minutes -> secondary oncall (IC2) -> 10 minutes -> oncall lead -> 15 minutes escalate to Eng Director.
2. If BO does not join within 3 minutes, the first responder must declare a bridge and assume BO duties.

Succession plan for rotations:
- Each rotation is 2 weeks for SRE ICs, with an overlap (shadow) week.
- Every third rotation the secondary is required to shadow the primary for at least one incident.
- Rotation handoff checklist (short): latest flagged runbooks, active alerts, outstanding action items, customer-impacting incidents in last 7 days. Store as /handovers/{oncall}-handover-YYYYMMDD.md.

5) Training and game-day schedule

Cadence:
- Quarterly global game day (all responder roles): full 6-hour scenario simulating a multi-region model-serving degradation including KV-cache thrash and failover to dedicated.
- Monthly focused drills (2 hours) for a single failure class: latency spike, memory pressure, or model quality regression.
- New-oncall ramp: 1-week shadow + 1 simulated incident inside first 30 days.

Game-day deliverables:
- A play-by-play timeline (shared in the bridge)
- Evidence capture (logs, heap dumps, tracer snapshots) and upload location (s3://incidents/game-days/{date}/)
- Post-exercise retro with action owners and deadlines (must be closed within 30 days).

6) Status page and customer communications

Status page taxonomy (internal canonical):
- Operational, Degraded Performance, Partial Outage, Major Outage, Under Maintenance.

Customer comms templates (short form) - use Customer Liaison to fill contextual fields.

Immediate acknowledgement (within 30m):
Subject: Redwood Inference — Service Disruption Acknowledged
Body:
We’ve detected elevated errors impacting the Redwood Hosted API. Our SRE team is investigating. Affected customers may experience increased latency or errors. We will post updates every 30 minutes or when there is material progress.

Status update (every 30–60m):
Subject: Redwood Inference — Update on Ongoing Disruption
Body:
Summary of impact (services/regions affected), actions taken to date, next steps and ETA if available, mitigation in place (e.g., routing to fallback region), any customer workarounds.

Resolution notice (post-resolution):
Subject: Redwood Inference — Incident Resolved
Body:
Root cause summary (high level), impact window, customer mitigation steps if action required, link to postmortem, and SLA/credit guidance if applicable.

Template examples (copyable):
```
Subject: [Incident #{INCIDENT_ID}] Redwood Inference — Partial Outage (runtime-router)
Body:
Hello,

We are currently investigating elevated 5xx errors from runtime-router affecting requests routed to us-east-1. Our mitigation steps include throttling large-batch requests and routing traffic to a healthy model-fanout pool. We will send updates every 30 minutes.

Regards,
Redwood SRE
```

7) Postmortem and action tracking

Minimum postmortem content:
- incident_id, time_window, impact_summary, timeline (minute granularity for first 60 minutes), root_cause_analysis, contributing_factors, corrective_actions (owner + due date), detection_time, mean_time_to_recovery (MTTR), customer_impact_summary, SLA impact.

Postmortem process:
1. Draft within 72 hours by Artifact Scribe.
2. RCA workshop within 7 calendar days with SO and IC.
3. Publish postmortem (Confluence) within 14 days.
4. Track corrective actions in a shared board (JIRA project: INF-INC). Actions must be tagged with severity and closed within agreed timelines (critical: 14 days, high: 30 days, medium: 90 days).

8) Runbook retirement checklist (appendix)

When to retire: service removed, replaced, or runbook obsolete for >180 days.
Checklist (mark each):
- [ ] Confirm IEC entry marked deprecated
- [ ] Notify stakeholders and open retirement PR (90-day notice)
- [ ] Migrate any linked alerts to replacement runbook
- [ ] Archive runbook to /runbooks/archive with explanation and final test logs
- [ ] Update redirect in Confluence to replacement or archive note

9) Evidence and compliance notes

- For any incident involving customer data, attach audit logs + KMS access records to postmortem. Security must be CC’d for restricted incidents.
- For enterprise customers impacted, attach the customer notification log and timestamps for regulatory review if requested.

10) Appendix — Quick commands and dashboards

- Logs: rbx logs query --service {svc} --since 60m --severity error --json > /tmp/{svc}-errors.json
- Traces: open https://tracing.redwood.company/trace?q=service:{svc}&since=30m
- Dashboards to bookmark: Runtime Overview (grafana id: infra-rt-01), KV Cache Health (infra-cache-02), Ingress Errors (infra-ingress-04)

Revision history:
- 2028-11-01: created by A. Patel
- 2029-01-15: updated succession ladder and game-day cadence after SRE retrospective
- 2029-02-12: added runbook retirement checklist and sample alert YAML

Questions or change requests: ping #ops-governance or open a PR in git://infra/runbooks.

title: dsid_a62bf0ab014c427799c670aa62f1b074__benefits-activation-and-eligibility-playbook-2024.txt
text:
Benefits activation and eligibility playbook

Overview

Purpose: This playbook documents how Redwood Inference activates, verifies, and maintains employee benefits eligibility across role changes, onboarding events, leaves, and internal transfers. It is intended for people-ops partners, hiring managers, and enrollment specialists.

Scope: medical, dental, vision, retirement (401k), paid time off (PTO), parental leave, tuition & professional development stipends, commuter/office stipends, and company sabbatical programs.

Quick summary of owner and SLA
- Owner: People Operations Benefits & Enrollment (people-ops-benefits@redwood.ai)
- Escalation: benefits-ops-lead -> Head of People Ops -> General Counsel (for exceptions)
- SLA: new-hire benefit provisioning within 5 business days after first-day completion; eligibility disputes resolved within 10 business days.

Eligibility rules (high-level)
1) New hires\   - Regular full-time employees (FTE) are eligible for core benefits (medical, dental, vision, 401k) on the first of the month following 30 days of service unless local country rules require earlier coverage.\   - Part-time employees: eligibility follows the part-time policy table below.\   - Contractors: contractors are eligible for limited programs (commuter, learning stipend) only when explicitly stated in the contract.

2) Role changes and promotions\   - If a role change does not involve a break in service, benefits continue uninterrupted. People-ops must be notified via the Role Change Form (HR-ROLE-REQ) within 3 business days.\   - Compensation level changes do not change medical eligibility; however, certain perks (executive coaching, expanded stipend) may require manager-requested provisioning.

3) Internal transfers between legal entities or regions\   - Transfers that change the legal employing entity require benefits re-enrollment. The transfer coordinator (hiring manager + people-ops reps) must initiate cross-entity enrollment at least 30 days before the target start date in the new entity.

4) Leaves of absence\   - Short-term leaves (<= 30 days): benefits remain active; payroll deductions continue per normal cadence.\   - Medical/parental leaves > 30 days: people-ops will notify benefits carriers and provide options for paid/unpaid continuation; employees are sent a Benefits Continuation Packet with deadlines and payment instructions.

Table: Eligibility summary by worker type\| Worker type \| Medical \| Dental \| Vision \| 401k match \| PTO accrual \n|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FTE (full-time) | Yes (after 30 days) | Yes | Yes | Yes (up to company cap) | Standard accrual |
| Part-time (>=20 hrs/week) | Yes (subject to local law) | Yes | Optional | Pro-rated | Pro-rated |
| Fixed-term contractor | No | No | No | No | No |
| Contractor (engagement clause) | Limited (see contract) | Limited | No | No | No |

Activation checklist (new hires) — step-by-step
1. Hiring manager: submit New-Hire Ticket with candidate start date and working location at offer acceptance.
2. HRBP: verify offer details and confirm start date in HRIS.
3. On employee first day: people-ops sends enrollment packet and credentials for benefits portal.
4. Employee: completes benefits elections within 30 days (default plan applied if no election).
5. People-ops: confirms enrollment with carriers and verifies access to ID cards within 5 business days of election.
6. Payroll: validates first payroll deduction; report any discrepancies to benefits@redwood.ai.

Manager responsibilities during onboarding and role changes\- Ensure the New-Hire Ticket is accurate and includes relocation or cross-entity details.\- Complete the Role Change Form for promotions/transfers within 3 business days.\- Approve one-time requests tied to role level (e.g., onboarding relocation top-ups, special equipment allowances).

Special programs and eligibility triggers\- Professional Development Stipend: All FTEs at level IC2 and above receive a $1,200 annual stipend; managers may allocate additional budget for role-critical certifications. Stipend requests must be submitted via the Learning Portal and approved by the manager.
- Sabbatical (Service-based): Employees are eligible for a 6-week paid sabbatical after 6 years of continuous full-time service, or a 12-week unpaid sabbatical after 10 years, subject to product/people operations approval.
- Returnship & phased reboarding: People-ops offers a 12-week phased return for employees returning from extended leave; managers should pair returning contributors with a reboarding buddy.

How benefits change with role level (rules of thumb)
- Level IC1–IC2: core benefits and standard stipends.
- Level IC3–IC4: increased professional development budgets and eligibility for expanded coaching programs.
- Manager levels (M1+): access to leadership development stipend and executive health screening (where available by region).
- Executive/Director: eligible for supplementary financial planning sessions and elevated relocation allowance.

Examples: common scenarios and resolution steps\- Scenario A: New hire misses the 30-day election window.\  Resolution: Default plan assigned. Employee can change plans during next open enrollment or within 60 days if a qualifying life event occurs. Submit a Benefits Exception Form to people-ops for retroactive change requests.\- Scenario B: Employee transfers from US entity to UK entity effective July 1.\  Resolution: Initiate cross-entity transfer 30 days prior. Employee completes local enrollment; benefits in the old entity end the day before new entity start. Coordinate tax withholding and payroll timing with finance.

Systems and artifacts (where to do work)
- HRIS: Workday (enrollment triggers, role-change forms)\- Benefits portal: [CarrierPortal.example.com] (login via SSO)\- People-ops tracker: internal sheet (managed by people-ops-benefits) for SLA and audit trails

Table: System responsibilities\| System \| Primary owner \| Purpose \n|---|---|---|
| Workday \| People Ops HRIS \| Role records, leave of absence, enrollment triggers |
| Payroll (Gusto/ADP region-specific) \| Finance Payroll \| Deductions, employer contributions |
| Carrier portal(s) \| People Ops Benefits \| Claims, ID card issuance |

Operational runbook: benefits enrollment exception workflow
1. Employee requests exception via Benefits Exception Form (people-ops) with supporting documents.\2. People-ops triages request; if standard exception (e.g., late enrollment within 60 days due to documented IT outage) approve within 5 business days.\3. For non-standard exceptions (policy deviation, cross-entity legal issues), route to benefits-ops-lead for review and escalate to Head of People Ops with recommended compensating controls.\4. If exception approved, create audit log entry and notify payroll to process any retroactive adjustments.

Audit & compliance notes\- Quarterly audits: benefits-ops runs a quarterly reconciliation comparing HRIS enrollments to carrier rosters and payroll deductions. Discrepancies > $500 per employee must be investigated and resolved within 30 days.\- Documentation retention: benefits enrollment forms and exception approvals are retained for 7 years for tax and audit purposes.

Communication templates (copy-paste ready)
- New hire enrollment reminder:
  Subject: Action required: Complete your Redwood benefits enrollment
  Body: Hi {FirstName}, welcome to Redwood! Please complete your benefits elections by {deadline}. Log into our benefits portal with your SSO: {link}. Contact people-ops-benefits@redwood.ai with questions.

- Manager reminder for role change:
  Subject: Role change submitted for {EmployeeName} — action needed
  Body: Please confirm the role change details in Workday for {EmployeeName}. If the change crosses legal entities, coordinate with people-ops to start cross-entity enrollment.

Escalation contacts\- Benefits ops lead: benefits-ops-lead@redwood.ai\- People Ops general: people-ops@redwood.ai\- Payroll (US): payroll-us@redwood.ai

Appendix A — Common forms and links\- New-Hire Ticket (internal): /forms/new-hire-ticket\- Role Change Form: /forms/hr-role-change\- Benefits Exception Form: /forms/benefits-exception\- Learning Portal (stipend requests): /learning/stipend-request\\n
Appendix B — Revision history\- 2024-03-12: Created by Mariana Ortiz.\- 2024-07-07: Clarified 30-day re-enrollment rule after region transfer (reviewer: Ethan Park).\- 2025-11-04: Updated professional development stipend levels and sabbatical timelines; added quarterly audit SLA (reviewer: Sana Malik).

title: dsid_2ee7b031b5504f09b3eec777c8ded8d6__mixed-precision-token-billing-and-telemetry-playbook.txt
text:
Mixed-Precision Token Billing and Telemetry Playbook

Summary

This playbook defines the telemetry, tagging, measurement, and investigation process required to bill GPU inference usage at token granularity for mixed-precision and quantized execution paths. It is intended for infra engineers, billing/data platform, and SREs who operate the inference runtime and chargeback pipeline.

Goals

- Produce accurate token-level billing that reflects real execution cost differences between FP16/FP32/BF16 and INT8/4-bit quantized paths.
- Map runtime telemetry to billing dimensions without double-counting KV-cache reuse, cached prefixes, or streaming re-requests.
- Provide a reproducible investigation checklist for cost anomalies and reconciliations.
- Minimize instrumentation overhead and avoid exposing customer prompt text to billing systems (PII-sensitive).

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: hosted & dedicated deployments; applies to on-prem when telemetry bridge is enabled.
- Non-goals: prompt content collection, model-quality metrics, or per-token content inspection. This playbook is strictly about resource attribution and cost telemetry.

Ownership

- Runtime telemetry schema and collectors: infra/serving-runtime team (owner: Aisha Patel)
- Billing pipeline mapping & ETL: finance-data (owner: Marcus Lee)
- Billing validation & reconciliation: infra-sre + finance ops (owner: Sofia Gomez)

High-level approach

1) Emit a compact per-request telemetry envelope from the runtime that includes resource-attribution fields (not raw text). Telemetry must be signed and batched to avoid high cardinality.
2) Enrich telemetry in the ETL with model flavor, quantization profile, and effective execution kernel.
3) Convert tokens to a normalized token-charge unit using a kernel-cost table and per-region GPU cost factors.
4) Post-process to deduplicate cached tokens (prefix/kv hits) and to apply tenant-level discounts/credits.

Telemetry envelope (contract)

- Emit at request completion and for mid-stream checkpoint (for long streaming sessions). Envelope fields (compact):
  - request_id: opaque UUID
  - tenant_id: tenant-opaque-id
  - model_id: model name + pinned version (e.g., "llama-2-70b-v1")
  - kernel_id: runtime kernel identifier (e.g., "attn_v2_bf16_k8")
  - precision_path: one of [FP32, BF16, FP16, INT8, INT4]
  - input_tokens: integer (tokens in prompt sent to runtime)
  - output_tokens_emitted: integer (tokens emitted to user)
  - tokens_served_from_kv_cache: integer
  - continuous_batch_group: optional string (if request batched)
  - seq_len_distribution: short histogram string (buckets: <=32, 33-128, 129-512, 513+)
  - gpu_micros: integer (microseconds spent on GPU kernels attributable to request)
  - gpu_memory_bytes_peak: integer
  - region: cloud region code
  - instance_flavor: e.g., "p4d.24xlarge" or on-prem SKU
  - timestamp: ISO8601

Example (JSON emitted by runtime):

{"request_id":"f83c9a1e-...","tenant_id":"t-acme-42","model_id":"redwood-rlm-30b@v3","kernel_id":"attn_v2_bf16_k8","precision_path":"BF16","input_tokens":48,"output_tokens_emitted":96,"tokens_served_from_kv_cache":12,"gpu_micros":230000,"gpu_memory_bytes_peak":2147483648,"region":"us-west-2","instance_flavor":"g5dn.12xlarge","timestamp":"2025-10-05T17:12:09Z"}

Note: Runtime MUST NOT emit user prompt text or raw outputs in this envelope. Any enrichment requiring prompt length should only use token counts.

Kernel cost table and normalized token units

- Maintain a kernel cost table (canonical source: infra-config repo) that maps (kernel_id, instance_flavor, region) -> cost_per_micros and amortized overhead_per_request.
- Billing unit: normalized_token_cost = base_token_charge * precision_multiplier * kernel_efficiency_factor
  - base_token_charge is a global value per model family and region (configurable)
  - precision_multiplier examples: FP32=1.0, BF16=0.75, FP16=0.7, INT8=0.42, INT4=0.29 (numbers derived from profiling; updated quarterly)
  - kernel_efficiency_factor is derived from gpu_micros / output_tokens_emitted to capture kernel-level variance

Telemetry to billing pipeline mapping (ETL steps)

- Ingest raw envelopes into telemetry lake (Kafka -> minio).
- Enrich with model family tags and quantization profiles (from model-service metadata).
- Convert per-request fields into normalized_token_cost and token_count_for_billing = output_tokens_emitted - tokens_served_from_kv_cache.
- Aggregate per tenant per day/hour and write to billing ledger (append-only).

Deduplication & KV-cache handling

- Rule: Tokens served from KV cache do not incur full generation cost; they are charged at cache_retrieval_rate (configurable, default 10% of base token charge) unless the KV cache warmup was a paid generation by another tenant.
- If tokens were seeded by the same tenant earlier in the session, mark as internal cache hit -> charge at cache_retrieval_rate.
- If tokens were restored from a global warm-pool seeded by evaluation infra (non-customer), the ETL should flag this and drop charges (or route to evaluation billing codes) using warmpool_tag in telemetry.

Chargeback reconciliation rules

- Daily reconciliation: compare telemetry-derived spend vs. GPU utilization cost allocation. If delta > 3% absolute or > $2,500/day, trigger an automatic investigation ticket.
- Weekly sampling audit: pick 0.1% of requests, validate telemetry fields against raw runtime logs (only counts, never text).

Alerting thresholds (SRE + Finance)

- anomaly_spend_rate: 20% increase in normalized_token_cost per tenant vs. 7-day rolling baseline -> create high-priority alert.
- kernel_efficiency_regression: a kernel_id with median gpu_micros/output_token > baseline * 1.35 over 30 minutes -> pager to runtime-oncall.
- telemetry_backfill_lag: if ETL ingestion lag > 2 hours for > 10% partitions -> page data-platform.

Investigation runbook (step-by-step)

1) Triage ticket created automatically by reconciliation or manual alert.
2) Owner: infra-sre oncall. Attach tenant_id and the offending time window.
3) Query examples:
   - Prometheus: GPU kernel micros per request: sum(rate(runtime_gpu_micros_total{tenant_id=~"t-.*"}[5m])) by (kernel_id, tenant_id)
   - SQL (bigquery-like): SELECT tenant_id, SUM(gpu_micros) as gpu, SUM(output_tokens_emitted) as tokens, kernel_id FROM telemetry_enriched WHERE timestamp BETWEEN X AND Y GROUP BY tenant_id,kernel_id
4) Calculate normalized_token_cost_delta = current_cost_per_token / baseline_cost_per_token. If delta > 1.2, proceed.
5) Check for: model change (new model_id), kernel rollout, quantization override, instance flavor change (spot->on-demand). Cross-check with deploy history and rollout tags.
6) If kernel_efficiency_regression: roll back kernel rollout (see kernel rollback playbook) or engage runtime engineers.
7) If billing mis-attribution suspected: freeze ledger writes for the tenant for the time window and perform manual discounts/adjustments. Finance ops to approve crediting.

CI/CD & Terraform patterns for instrumentation rollout

- Instrumentation code lives in serving-runtime repo. Releases must follow canary promotion policy: 5% canary -> 25% -> 60% -> 100% with 12-hour observation windows.
- Terraform: add option to enable/disable enriched telemetry at tenant scope via terraform module parameter (module: tenant-gpu-config.enable_cost_telemetry).
- A sample Terraform snippet (HCL):

resource "redwood_tenant_config" "acme" {
  tenant_id = "t-acme-42"
  enable_cost_telemetry = true
  telemetry_retention_days = 30
}

Performance and privacy constraints

- Telemetry aggregation must be batched with max payload size 512KB and no more than 1 request/sec per inference process to the telemetry endpoint.
- All telemetry must be obfuscated at source: tenant IDs are hashed with a rotating salt when exported to datasets used by non-finance teams. Full tenant mapping is restricted to finance-data.

Operational play scenarios

- Scenario A: Sudden spike in per-token cost for a single tenant -> run Investigation runbook; if caused by accidental model pin to FP32, recommend a customer-facing configuration change and offer temporary credit.
- Scenario B: Kernel rollout caused fleet-wide 10% cost uplift -> immediate rollback and create postmortem with cost delta table.
- Scenario C: ETL lag causes underbilled tenants -> run backfill procedures (see "backfill-procedure" internal doc id) and communicate adjustments with finance ops.

Metrics dashboard (recommended widgets)

- Per-tenant normalized token cost (7d, 30d)
- Kernel efficiency heatmap (kernel_id x model_family) showing median gpu_micros/output_token
- KV-cache hit ratio by tenant and by model
- Daily delta: telemetry-derived spend vs. infra allocation cost

Quarterly governance

- Every quarter: update precision_multiplier table based on micro-benchmarking across representative model families.
- Finance and runtime lead to sign-off on multiplier changes; changes are annotated and backdated for historical comparability.

Appendices

A. Example ETL pseudo-SQL for deriving billing rows

INSERT INTO billing_ledger (tenant_id, day, normalized_tokens, amount_usd)
SELECT tenant_id, DATE(timestamp) as day, SUM((output_tokens_emitted - tokens_served_from_kv_cache) * precision_multiplier * kernel_efficiency) as normalized_tokens, SUM((output_tokens_emitted - tokens_served_from_kv_cache) * precision_multiplier * kernel_efficiency * base_rate) as amount_usd
FROM telemetry_enriched
WHERE timestamp BETWEEN @start AND @end
GROUP BY tenant_id, day;

B. Common troubleshooting checks (quick list)

- Did the tenant pin to a new full-precision model?
- Was a kernel rollout in the affected region?
- Did instance flavor change to an expensive SKU (spot->on-demand)?
- Are cache warmups being misattributed as paid generations?
- Is ETL normalizing tokens incorrectly (off-by-one in output token counts)?

C. Contact matrix

- runtime-oncall: #runtime-oncall (pager)
- infra-sre: infra-sre@redwood.com
- finance-data: finance-data@redwood.com
- billing-ops (customer credits): billing-ops@redwood.com

D. Change log

- 2024-11-12: Document created (Aisha Patel)
- 2025-04-01: Added kernel_efficiency_regression alert thresholds (Marcus Lee)
- 2026-01-20: Updated precision_multiplier recommendations after Q4 benchmarking (Sofia Gomez)

End of document

title: dsid_b062ce0f769944d4bb63560dee21efe3__operator-multisignal-triage-lattice-and-decision-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Operator multisignal triage lattice and decision playbook

Summary:
This playbook defines a single operator-facing triage lattice that combines telemetry from cost, latency, model-quality, and infrastructure signals into an actionable decision flow. It is intended for platform operators, oncall engineers, and SREs who need to rapidly triage multi-signal incidents affecting Redwood Inference runtime and customer-facing SLAs.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: Hosted and Dedicated inference endpoints, per-region operator dashboards, and the routing/eviction control plane.
- Intent: Reduce mean time to correct action (MTCA) by providing deterministic prioritization rules, concrete thresholds, and a step-by-step decision lattice operators can follow for common multi-signal incidents.

Audience:
- Platform operators and oncall SREs
- Service owners for serving-runtime, routing, and caching components
- Solutions engineers supporting enterprise customers during incidents

Owners and primary contacts:
- Playbook owner: Ravi Patel (eng-platform)
- Escalation owner: Leah Gomez (eng-sre)
- Oncall Slack channel: #platform-operators
- Pager duty: Platform SRE escalation policy (PD -> Level 1/2)

When to use this playbook:
1) An alert triggers with a combined signal score >= 7 (see "Signal scoring" below).
2) Multiple alerts across cost, latency, and quality fire within a 10-minute window for the same tenant/region.
3) Customer-facing complaints that map to token cost spikes, tail-latency, or degraded model outputs.

Signal taxonomy and scoring (operator quick reference):
| Signal category | Example metrics / alerts | Typical thresholds | Operator severity weight |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Latency | p95_token_latency, p99_tail_latency | p95 > 350ms or p99 > 800ms | 4 |
| Cost / Tokens | token_rate, cost_per_1k_tokens | 2x baseline token_rate or cost spike > +40% 10m | 3 |
| Model quality | eval-regression-rate, semantic-error-rate | regression > 3% over baseline on golden prompts | 5 |
| Infrastructure | GPU_util, pod_restart_rate | GPU_util > 95% for 5m or >3 restarts/5m | 3 |
| Availability | 5xx_rate, timeouts | 5xx_rate > 1% or timeout_rate > 2% | 4 |

Signal scoring rules:
- For a given incident window (10 minutes), assign the weight for each signal category observed and sum to create a combined signal score.
- Combined score buckets: 1–3 (note), 4–6 (action recommended), 7+ (immediate remediation + pager).

Decision lattice (step-by-step):
1. Observe: Check the incident dashboard and collect top 3 anomalous series by tenant and region.
2. Attribute: Use token cost attribution and trace links to map the anomaly to service islands (model-serving, prefetcher, router, customer batch job).
3. Score: Compute combined signal score. If score < 4, record and monitor; if 4–6 proceed with local mitigations; if >= 7 escalate per Escalation rubric.
4. Local mitigations (ordered):
   a) Apply per-tenant soft throttles / soft-quota cut to reduce token_rate by 30% for 5 minutes.
   b) Toggle caching profile to serve from prefix/KV cache (if cache hit ratio < 70% but warmups available).
   c) For model-quality regressions, roll back to last verified model variant or enable scripted post-processing heuristics (sanitizers).
   d) For tail-latency due to queueing, temporarily increase burst capacity (if available) or move low-priority tenants to a preemptible pool.
5. If local mitigations do not reduce score within 5–10 minutes: escalate to Level 2 and open an incident channel.

Escalation rubric:
- Combined score 7–9: Notify Level 1; create incident; L1 to perform triage and applies local mitigations.
- Combined score >=10 or customer-impacting model-quality regression: Page Level 2 immediately and engage product-owner and solutions-engineering for coordinated customer comms.

Concrete runbook examples (copyable actions):
- Query: top 10 tenants by token_rate in last 5m (PromQL):
  sum by (tenant) (rate(inference_tokens_total[5m])) | topk(10, sum)
- Query: p95 token latency for model-serving (PromQL):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(token_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le,service))
- Quick k8s command to identify pod restarts in serving namespace:
  kubectl -n serving get pods -o wide --sort-by=.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount | head -n 20

Alert rule examples (recommended minimal set):
1) token-burst-guard: triggers if token_rate > 2x baseline AND token_rate delta sustained for 5m. Severity: P2.
2) p99-degradation: triggers if p99_token_latency_in_region > 800ms for 3m. Severity: P1.
3) model-quality-regression: triggers when eval_regression_window(30m) > 3% (golden prompt baseline). Severity: P0 (page).
4) gpu-saturation: GPU_util > 96% for 5m AND pod_restart_rate > 2/5m. Severity: P1.

SLO impact mapping (operator table):
| Incident class | SLO affected | Immediate target action |
|---|---|---|
| Tail latency spike | generation latency p95/p99 | Open fast rollback or model-shed to CPU-backed instances |
| Token surge | cost SLO per-tenant | Soft-throttle, engage billing-policy to prevent runaway costs |
| Model-quality regression | quality SLO (eval pass rate) | Revert model variant and kick off canary re-eval pipeline |
| Infrastructure exhaustion | availability SLO | Burst scale or region-failover per capacity playbook |

Short checklist for the oncall operator (5-min quick run):
1) Identify top-3 affected tenants and whether there are VIP customers.
2) Compute combined signal score.
3) Apply the highest-priority local mitigation (soft-throttle or rollback).
4) Observe telemetry for 5 minutes. If no improvement, escalate.
5) Annotate incident with decisions and set follow-up actions.

Dashboard and alerting templates to maintain:
- Multi-signal incident view: Cost (top-10 tenants) + p95/p99 latency (by model) + model-regression heatmap + GPU utilization map.
- Tenant detail page: token-rate, cache hit ratio, recent model variants, recent evals.
- Incident timeline: correlated alerts, mitigation actions, and automated rollback events.

Operator quick commands and scripts (examples):
- Soft-throttle CLI: redwoodctl tenant throttle --tenant-id $TID --pct 30 --duration 5m
- Rollback model variant: redwoodctl model set-active --model $MODEL_ID --variant $LAST_KNOWN_GOOD --reason "triage rollback"
- Re-enable cache prefetch: redwoodctl cache profile apply --tenant $TID --profile prefetched-warmup

Post-incident: retro and ticketing guidance:
1) Severity owner files incident document within 24 hours. Include timeline, mitigation steps, and SLO burn.
2) Action items must be triaged within 3 working days and assigned an owner.
3) If model-quality regressions are frequent, add coverage to the evaluation harness and block automated rollouts until regression is resolved.

Operational metrics to track for playbook effectiveness:
- Mean time to first mitigation (MTFM) after alert: target < 6 minutes.
- Mitigation efficacy rate: % incidents resolved by local mitigations within 10 minutes: target > 70%.
- False-positive rate of multi-signal pager: target < 5%.

Roadmap and improvements to this playbook (quarterly):
- Q4 2026: Add ML-powered incident classifier to map alert clusters to recommended mitigations automatically.
- Q1 2027: Integrate per-tenant cost guardrails into automated soft-throttle to reduce human-in-loop for cost spikes.
- Q2 2027: Expand model-quality golden prompt coverage and tie regression thresholds to severity dynamically.

Appendix A — Example incident vignette (short):
- 09:12 UTC: token-burst-guard fires for tenant T-314 (token_rate 3x baseline).
- 09:14 UTC: p99_degradation and gpu_saturation alerts for region us-west-2. Combined score = 10 -> immediate page.
- Actions: L1 applied soft-throttle 40% and moved low-priority tenants to preemptible pool; L2 initiated model rollback after golden prompt shows 4.2% regression. Incident resolved 09:29 UTC.

Appendix B — Links and related runbooks:
- Runtime emergency model swap: /eng-platform/runbooks/emergency-model-swap-and-token-surge-mitigation-2026
- Token forensic cookbook: /eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/token-burst-forensics-and-debugging-workflow-2026

Document maintenance:
- Review cadence: quarterly. Next review: 2027-01-10.
- Ownership: eng-platform (Ravi Patel).

If anything in this playbook conflicts with customer-specific runbooks (customer-managed routing or dedicated private deployments), follow the customer runbook first and notify platform via #platform-ops.

title: dsid_246208905f6f404495e503b2f931550b__streaming-fidelity-handshake-and-progressive-degradation-protocol-2027.txt
text:
Streaming Fidelity Handshake and Progressive Degradation Protocol

Summary

This document defines the Streaming Fidelity Handshake and Progressive Degradation Protocol (SF-Handshake). SF-Handshake is an API-level contract between clients, edge proxies, and the streaming runtime that enables: negotiation of output fidelity and cost/latency tradeoffs, progressive degradation when capacity or latency constraints are hit, and traceable fallbacks with deterministic observability hooks.

Motivation

As Redwood serves a spectrum of applications (interactive chat, embedders, high-volume summaries), we need a common, lightweight mechanism for clients to express fidelity preferences and for the runtime to respond with deterministic degradation steps rather than opaque failures. Existing streaming contracts either assume fixed fidelity or rely on ad-hoc headers. SF-Handshake standardizes the capabilities, signals, and telemetry so downstream systems (billing, routing, caching) can make consistent decisions.

Scope

- Applies to: hosted API streaming endpoints (edge-proxy -> stream-gateway -> runtime).
- Not in scope: non-streaming batch RPCs, internal-only debug hooks (these remain separate).
- Backwards compatibility: servers must accept requests without SF-Handshake fields and use safe defaults.

Owner and Contacts

- Document owner: eng/runtime-platform
- Primary implementation owners: service-edge team (edge-proxy), stream-runtime team (stream-gateway).
- Pager: eng-sre rotation (see runbook link in related pages).

Protocol overview

High-level flow:
1) Client sends an initial negotiation envelope as the first message or as request headers.
2) Edge validates the envelope, applies client-tier policies (quota, tenant SLOs), and forwards a server decision object.
3) Runtime executes generation respecting the decision and emits streaming tokens with fidelity annotations.
4) If the runtime must degrade, it emits a deterministic degradation event and updates the decision path; clients can optionally request a retry or accept degraded output.

Core concepts

- Fidelity Vector: A small typed set of dimensions describing desired result quality and cost: {accuracy, verbosity, creativity, safety_strictness, latency_priority}. Each dimension is an integer 0..100.
- Decision Envelope: Server-side response containing: selected fidelity vector, reason_code, allowed_cost_multiplier, degradation_plan (if applicable), observable_keys.
- Degradation Plan: Ordered instructions the runtime may apply in sequence (e.g., reduce creativity -> truncate output -> switch to cached summary).
- Observable Keys: Set of short opaque strings used to link tokens/events to telemetry traces and billing entries.

Negotiation surface (HTTP + streaming)

- Endpoint: POST /v1/stream/generate (existing streaming endpoint). SF-Handshake may be provided either as headers or as a JSON negotiation preamble.
- Headers (optional, lightweight):
  - X-RW-Fidelity: base64url(JSON) — compact fidelity vector when using headers.
  - X-RW-Client-Tier: free | standard | enterprise
  - X-RW-Negotiate-Mode: prefer | require | best-effort

- JSON preamble (recommended for full expressivity). Example: 

Preamble JSON example:
{
  "handshake_version": "1.0",
  "fidelity_vector": {"accuracy": 80, "verbosity": 60, "creativity": 40, "safety_strictness": 90, "latency_priority": 70},
  "budget_usd": 0.02,
  "client_tier": "standard",
  "request_id": "cli-1234-ctx-7890",
  "negotiate_mode": "prefer"
}

Server Decision object (example returned synchronously or as the first streamed control event):
{
  "decision_version": "1.0",
  "selected_fidelity": {"accuracy": 75, "verbosity": 55, "creativity": 35, "safety_strictness": 90, "latency_priority": 80},
  "allowed_cost_multiplier": 1.2,
  "reason_code": "latency_slo_adjustment",
  "degradation_plan": ["prune_long_form_summaries","early_token_exit","quantize_hidden_states"],
  "observable_keys": ["ok_47f3","path_99b1"]
}

Client behavior and expectations

- Conservative clients: set negotiate_mode=require. If the server cannot honor the request, the request should fail with 422 /error {"reason":"UNABLE_TO_SATISFY_FIDELITY"}.
- Opportunistic clients: set negotiate_mode=prefer or best-effort. They should accept decision objects with lower fidelity.
- Clients should always correlate server observable_keys to local telemetry and include request_id in logs.

Server behavior and enforcement rules

- Edge-proxy must validate handshake_version and apply tenant policy (quota, minimum fidelity floor for enterprise tier).
- If negotiate_mode=require and constraints cannot be met, reject early with detailed reason_code and allow clients to retry with altered fidelity/budget.
- When allowed_cost_multiplier > 1.0, billing signals must be emitted to the cost pipeline; stream-gateway must annotate tokens with the chosen multiplier.

Degradation semantic primitives (order matters)

1) Soft downgrades (non-destructive): reduce creativity, shorten verbosity, increase repetition penalty.
2) Structural downgrades: switch to a lighter head model (same family), reduce sequence rematerialization.
3) Performance tradeoffs: enable aggressive KV-cache eviction policies or turn on quantized kernels.
4) Fallbacks (last resort): return cached or synthetic summary, mark response as degraded=true, attach degradation_plan_trace.

Concrete headers and token annotations (stream payload)

- Control event structure (first stream event):
  - type: "decision"
  - payload: <Decision object JSON above>

- Token annotation envelope (attached to token frames):
  - token_text: "..."
  - fidelity_annotation: "f:75,v:55,c:35,l:80,s:90"
  - trace_key: "ok_47f3"

Observability and SLOs

Minimum telemetry required for each SF-Handshake request (emitted as structured events):
- handshake.received (tags: request_id, client_tier, hashing of fidelity_vector)
- decision.emitted (tags: decision_version, reason_code, allowed_cost_multiplier)
- degradation.event (tags: plan_step, runtime_node, latency_ms)
- token.emitted (tags: trace_key, fidelity_annotation)

SLOs (service-level guidance):
- handshake latency (time to first decision event): p95 <= 30ms for edge-proxy local decisions; p99 <= 120ms globally.
- faithful-degradation response time (time between decision to degrade and first degraded token): p95 <= 40ms.
- correctness alerting: if more than 2% of standard-tier requests receive a degradation_plan with step "fallback_cached" for 12h window, create an incident.

Billing and cost signals

- If allowed_cost_multiplier != 1.0, stream must emit cost.multiplier events to the billing pipeline.
- Offline aggregator will compute unit-cost adjustments; design of the billing pipeline is outside this doc but streams must contain observable_keys for correlation.

Testing, rollout, and compatibility

- Feature gate: SF-Handshake is gated via feature-flag edge.synthetic.sf_handshake. Default off for free-tier.
- Canary plan: enable for 5% of traffic with negotiate_mode=prefer, collect metrics for handshake.latency, degradation.rate, billing.adjustments.
- Backwards compatibility: if client sends no handshake, runtime must behave as if fidelity_vector={accuracy:70,verbosity:60,creativity:50,safety_strictness:80,latency_priority:50}.

Operational runbook (high-level)

1) Detect spike in degradation.event rate (dashboard alert).
2) Validate whether increased degradation correlates with capacity events, policy changes, or a new model rollout.
3) If caused by model rollout, trigger automatic rollback to previous variant and alert product/ML.
4) If caused by tenant quota misconfiguration, apply tenant-specific temporary uplift and notify billing.

Security and privacy considerations

- Fidelity Vector values are not PII but may correlate with business-critical usage. Mark handshake events as internal.
- Observable_keys must be short opaque tokens; do not encode tenant or user IDs directly.

Compatibility matrix and decision rationale

- Rationale: We prefer an explicit JSON preamble to allow extensibility; header form remains for low-bandwidth clients.
- Compatibility: Servers will maintain a mapping layer to translate legacy headers into the fidelity_vector shape for at least 12 months.

Open questions and follow-ups

- Should we define a canonical set of degradation_plan steps and identifiers across runtime teams? (Action: convene engineering standards working group Q1 2026).
- How granular should cost multipliers be (per-token vs per-request)? Current recommendation: per-request multiplier with downstream prorated attribution.

Appendices

A. Example client curl (preamble body approach)

curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"handshake":{ "handshake_version":"1.0", "fidelity_vector":{"accuracy":85,"verbosity":50,"creativity":30,"safety_strictness":95,"latency_priority":40}, "negotiate_mode":"prefer" }, "prompt":"Summarize the following..." }' \
  https://api.redwood.example/v1/stream/generate

B. Short glossary

- handshke_version: version string for ability to evolve envelope schema.
- negotiate_mode: how strict the client is about fidelity.
- observable_keys: short opaque tokens for telemetry/billing correlation.

Change log

- 2025-11-12: Initial draft authored.
- 2026-02-03: Added SLOs and example decision object; reviewer feedback incorporated.

Related references

- See related cost-aware streaming payload schema guideline for details on token framing and billing annotations.
- See runtime observability contract for event naming and ingestion paths.

title: dsid_f76ba3bc1db340d1bea261cc24cfd32d__multi-signal-prefetch-governance-and-telemetry-contract-2027.txt
text:
Multi-signal prefetch governance and telemetry contract

Summary
This page defines the governance model, telemetry contract, and operational playbook for multi-signal prefetching in the runtime. It standardizes the signals we will accept, the scoring formula, the telemetry schema, dashboard/alert mappings, experimentation requirements, rollout safety gates, and post-rollout validation steps. This doc is meant to be the single source of truth for teams that build or operate prefetch/warmer logic (platform, runtime, operator tools).

Goals
- Reduce cold-start tail latency for interactive LLMs without increasing GPU token-cost by more than 8% at steady state.
- Make prefetch decisions auditable and debuggable with a stable telemetry contract.
- Provide a safe experiment and rollout pathway to tune prefetch behavior per-tenant and per-region.

Scope
Applies to: KV/prefix prefetcher, edge-warmers, region-local cohort prefetching, and operator-triggered warmup scripts. Does NOT cover proactive model weight loading (separate infra).

Definitions
- Signal: any input used to score a candidate for prefetch (history access, tenant SLA, synthetic ranking).
- PrefetchCandidate: a unique key (tenant_id, model_id, prefix_hash).
- PrefetchScore: single numeric score (0-100) computed using the telemetry signals and feature weights.

Approved Signals (canonical names and description)
1) recent_prefix_count_1h — count of requests matching the prefix in the last hour
2) tenant_priority_score — static tenant weight from billing/contract (0-1.0)
3) kv_cache_hit_rate_24h — recent hit-rate for same tenant/model
4) projected_token_savings — approximate tokens saved if cache-hit occurs
5) synthetic_sla_risk — risk signal from synthetic lab (0-1.0)
6) op_manual_inhibit — operator override (boolean)

Scoring formula (canonical)
- PrefetchScore = clamp(0,100, 20*normalize(recent_prefix_count_1h) + 30*tenant_priority_score + 25*normalize(kv_cache_hit_rate_24h) + 15*normalize(projected_token_savings) + 10*(1 - synthetic_sla_risk) - 50*op_manual_inhibit)
- Normalization functions MUST be the canonical helpers in infra-libs/prefetch (v2.1).

Telemetry contract (required fields)
All prefetch decisions MUST emit a structured event to telemetry with the following keys (JSON schema):
| field | type | description | example |
| tenant_id | string | canonical tenant id | t-01234 |
| model_id | string | model version id | llama-13b-vq-2026-11 |
| prefix_hash | string | sha1 of prefix | 3f2a... |
| decision_ts | iso8601 | timestamp of scoring | 2027-02-09T14:22:00Z |
| score | number | computed prefetch score (0-100) | 73.2 |
| signals | map<string,number> | raw normalized signals used in scoring | see example |
| decided_action | enum | {no-op, prefetch-queued, prefetch-executed, inhibit} | prefetch-queued |
| reason | string | human-readable rationale (optional) | high recent_prefix_count |
| operator_run_id | string | optional, if triggered by operator | run-20270201-42 |

Implementation notes
- Event emission must be idempotent for a given (tenant_id, model_id, prefix_hash, decision_ts). Use event deduplication key: <tenant_id>::<model_id>::<prefix_hash>::<minute-ts>.
- Signals must be calculated from the canonical time-windowers (1h,24h) and should not sample from offline backfills during normal scoring.

Dashboard and alert mappings
- Dashboards (must ship before rollout):
  - Prefetch Decisions Overview: timeseries of decisions/second, queued vs executed, mean score distribution (by model tier).
  - Cost Impact Viewer: token-cost delta attributable to prefetch (daily) with tenant breakdown.
  - Prefetch Reliability: event success rate, dedupe rate, and failure reasons.
- Alerts (initial thresholds):
  1) prefetch-error-rate > 1% sustained for 15m -> P3 alert to platform-ops.
  2) cost-delta > +12% across >24h -> P2 alert and rollback candidate.
  3) automated-prefetch-fallbacks > 0.5% -> investigate kernel/IO contention (P2).

Experimentation and rollout checklist (required for all changes to weights, new signals, or new prefetch actor)
1) Write experiment spec: hypothesis, target metric (tail P99 latency for interactive routes), safety metric (token-cost delta), cohorts, duration.
2) Synthetic validation: run the new scoring function in the synthetic lab for at least 48h across representative tenants and sequences.
3) Shadow run in production (no-op decisions logged) for 7 days; gather telemetry and cost projection.
4) Canary rollout to 5% of traffic in a non-critical region for 72h; monitor SLOs and cost.
5) Ramp to 25% if canary green for 72h; run retrospective.
6) Full ramp to 100% with automated rollback gates (see safety gates).

Safety gates (automated)
- If cost-delta > +10% sustained 2h => auto-disable prefetcher for the cohort and raise P1.
- If tail latency (P99) for interactive route degrades > 10% vs baseline for 30m => auto-disable and roll back weights.
- If prefetch-error-rate > 5% in 10m window => throttle queue drain and notify platform-ops.

Operator runbook (short)
1) Investigate: open Prefetch Decisions Overview for the region/tenant, filter by operator_run_id or prefix_hash.
2) If cost spike: throttle prefetch queue (CLI: infractl prefetch throttle --tenant t-... --percent 0) and open incident.
3) If latency spike: disable prefetch scoring (infractl prefetch set-mode --mode off) and route tenant to warmset fallback.
4) Postmortem: capture the score distribution, synthetic_sla_risk trend, and tenant_priority changes into the incident doc.

Ownership and SLAs
- Owner: platform-prefetch team (primary), eng-sre (oncall escalation).
- Oncall SLA: P1 response target 15 minutes, P2 2 hours.
- Telemetry retention: decision events retained at full fidelity for 90 days, aggregated rollups for 2 years.

Schema examples
- Signals payload example (JSON string emitted as signals field):
{"recent_prefix_count_1h": 42, "tenant_priority_score": 0.8, "kv_cache_hit_rate_24h": 0.24, "projected_token_savings": 1200, "synthetic_sla_risk": 0.12, "op_manual_inhibit": 0}

FAQs and non-goals
- Q: Can teams add arbitrary signals? A: Not without a governance review. New signals must be registered, have owner, unit tests for normalizers, and pass synthetic lab validation.
- Non-goal: This doc does not specify runtime kernel selection or hardware affinity for executed prefetch tasks. Those remain in eng-serving-runtime docs.

Related artifacts and follow-ups (action items)
1) Create dashboard templates in Grafana: pref-prefetch-overview, cost-impact-viewer (owner: telemetry-bench). Due: 2027-02-20.
2) Add canonical normalizers to infra-libs/prefetch v2.1 (owner: runtime-lib eng). Due: 2027-02-15.
3) Run a company-wide triage tabletop for prefetch-induced cost vs latency tradeoffs (owner: platform-ops). Due: Q2 2027.

Appendix: quick CLI snippets
- Throttle prefetch queue: infractl prefetch throttle --tenant t-01234 --percent 10 --region us-west-2
- Disable scoring (unsafe immediate): infractl prefetch set-mode --mode off --region eu-central-1

Change history
- 2026-11-15: initial draft (Priya Anand).
- 2027-01-05: added synthetic_sla_risk and operator_run_id fields (reviewers: Maria, Ethan).
- 2027-02-10: finalized scoring weights and rollout thresholds after synthetic lab run.

title: dsid_27d930fbdbc445c99c9461421c644a1d__evidence-assembly-matrix-for-regulatory-audits-2026.txt
text:
Evidence Assembly Matrix for Regulatory Audits

Summary
-------
This page defines the Evidence Assembly Matrix (EAM): a concise, repeatable format for collecting, validating, and packaging technical evidence for regulatory audits (SOC 2, GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS) and customer compliance requests. The EAM prioritizes reproducibility, minimal manual steps, and verifiable provenance for each artifact.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: Redwood Inference platform components that generate or control security-relevant artifacts: API control plane, serving runtime, infra provisioning, audit pipelines, RBAC systems, and private deployment connectors.
- Audience: Security Engineers, Compliance Engineers, SREs, Incident Response, Legal/Security review, and Customer Trust teams.

Why we use an Evidence Assembly Matrix
-------------------------------------
- Single canonical source mapping regulations to artifacts and concrete collection steps.
- Reduces ad-hoc evidence requests during audits.
- Provides verifiable provenance and chain-of-custody metadata for each item.
- Enables automation where possible and clearly documents manual steps where automation is not feasible.

How to read the matrix
----------------------
Each row in the EAM corresponds to a single piece of evidence. Columns are: Regulation, Evidence ID, Artifact Type, Source Service, Collection Method, Retention Window, Custodian, Verification Procedure, Storage Location, Proof-of-Presence artefacts (hashes/logs). Example matrix rows are below. Use the "Evidence Collection CLI" (see section) to automate fetching when supported.

Evidence Matrix (examples)
--------------------------
| Regulation | Evidence ID | Artifact Type | Source Service | Collection Method | Retention Window | Custodian | Verification Procedure | Storage Location | PoP (proof-of-presence) |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|----------------|-------------------|------------------|-----------|------------------------|------------------|-------------------------|
| SOC2 | EAM-API-01 | Authz policy snapshot | IAM / RBAC service | automated: iam-export --date=YYYY-MM-DD | 3 years | security-team | verify sha256, diff against last snapshot | s3://redwood-compliance/soc2/api-polices/ | sha256:abc123, manifest.log |
| GDPR | EAM-DR-04 | Data residency map | Config DB (vault). | manual: export via admin UI & validate | 7 years | data-privacy | cross-check with infra tags and region ACLs | s3://redwood-compliance/gdpr/data-residency/ | manifest.log, signed-metadata.txt |
| PCI-DSS | EAM-LOG-12 | Immutable audit stream | Audit-logging pipeline (kinesis -> long-term) | automated: aws-kinesis-dump --range | 6 years | eng-sre | run query to ensure event types present; validate retention confirmation | gs://redwood-logs/pci/ | event-hashes.json |

Note: The above table is illustrative. The canonical EAM is maintained as a CSV in the compliance repo and exported to this page via automation.

Evidence collection procedures
-------------------------------
1) Identify audit scope and required regulations. Confirm with Legal/Compliance what evidence IDs are required.
2) Retrieve EAM rows relevant to the scope. Filter by Regulation and Source Service.
3) For each Evidence ID:
   a) Attempt automated retrieval using Evidence Collection CLI.
   b) If automation is unavailable, follow the explicit manual steps recorded in the EAM row. Document the operator and timestamp.
   c) Compute and record cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of each artifact.
   d) Generate a manifest entry containing: Evidence ID, artifact filename, sha256, collected_by, collected_at (UTC), collection_method.
   e) Upload the artifact and manifest to the ephemeral evidence bucket for audit assembly.

Evidence Collection CLI (examples)
----------------------------------
- Purpose: standardize automated retrieval for supported sources (IAM, audit pipeline, config DB exports, console logs).
- Location: git@redwood:infra/compliance/evidence-cli.git
- Quick example:
  # export RBAC snapshot for a given date
  ./evidence-cli iam-export --date 2026-02-15 --output /tmp/eam-iam-20260215.json

  # pull audit logs for a 1-hour window (UTC)
  ./evidence-cli logs-dump --service api-gateway --start 2026-02-14T10:00:00Z --end 2026-02-14T11:00:00Z --out /tmp/gateway-logs-1000-1100.jsonl

Manual collection guidance
-------------------------
- Always use a separate workstation with MFA and compliance-approved device posture.
- For UI exports: capture a video (screen recording) of the export operation if the service does not provide an automated export; attach the recording to the manifest.
- Do not sanitize logs unless explicitly instructed by Legal; instead, request a filtered export with the Compliance Engineer present.

Manifest format (plain text)
---------------------------
- Example manifest line (one-per-artifact) – store in UTF-8 text: 
  EvidenceID: EAM-API-01 | Filename: iam-snapshot-2026-02-15.json | SHA256: <sha256sum> | CollectedBy: a.patel | CollectedAt: 2026-02-15T18:05:12Z | Method: automation | Location: s3://redwood-compliance/tmp/eam-20260215/iam-snapshot-2026-02-15.json

Verification and signing
------------------------
1) After artifacts are uploaded, run the verify-manifest tool: ./evidence-cli verify-manifest --manifest /path/to/manifest.txt
2) Verify-manifest performs: sha256 validation, schema sanity checks, and cross-checks expected artifact counts for the audit scope.
3) The Security Custodian signs the manifest with a GPG key and stores the signed manifest alongside artifacts. Example: gpg --sign --armor --output manifest.txt.asc manifest.txt

Chain-of-custody and immutable storage
-------------------------------------
- All artifacts intended for long-term retention must be copied into the immutable evidence bucket: s3://redwood-evidence-immutable/<regulation>/<year>/
- Immutable bucket has MFA-delete enabled and lifecycle rules to transition to cold storage after 180 days.
- Each copy operation must be recorded in the chain-of-custody log (COC), which is an append-only audit stream (Kafka topic: coc-evidence-events). The Evidence CLI automatically emits COC events on successful uploads.

Retention and purge controls
----------------------------
- Default retention per regulation: SOC2=3 years, PCI-DSS=6 years, HIPAA=6 years, GDPR=7 years for residency-related artifacts. See the EAM retention column for exceptions.
- Purge requests must follow the Data Retention Exception process: file a request in the Risk and Exceptions portal with explicit business justification and legal approval. Purge actions are recorded and require a two-person approval from Security + Legal.

Audit-ready packaging checklist
------------------------------
Before handing artifacts to auditors or legal, confirm:
- [ ] Manifest present and signed
- [ ] sha256 hashes verified
- [ ] Chain-of-custody entries present for each upload
- [ ] Access control on the package limited to the audit team and Security Custodian
- [ ] Any redaction or PII handling steps documented and approved by Legal

Escalation and SLAs
-------------------
- Evidence retrieval SLA for external audits: 72 business hours for standard requests, 24 business hours for executive-critical escalations (requires Legal approval).
- If evidence collection cannot meet SLA due to technical gaps, notify Compliance@redwood.com with a remediation plan within 8 business hours.
- Owner escalation chain: Security Custodian -> Head of Security (Lena Ortiz) -> Chief Security Officer (Rahul Sharma).

Periodic maintenance and audits of the EAM
-----------------------------------------
- The EAM CSV and automation scripts are reviewed quarterly by Security and Compliance.
- Run an internal mini-audit every six months: select a random subset of 10 Evidence IDs and validate collection, verification, and archival end-to-end. Failures must be remediated within 30 days with a postmortem.

Change history and approvals
----------------------------
- 2026-01-18: Initial published by Aisha Patel (Security). Reviewed by Marco Nguyen and Lena Ortiz.
- 2026-03-02: Clarified immutable bucket lifecycle and added Evidence CLI examples (updated by Aisha Patel).

Related resources
-----------------
- Compliance repository: git@redwood:infra/compliance
- Evidence CLI project: git@redwood:infra/compliance/evidence-cli.git
- Chain-of-custody topic: kafka://coc-evidence-events
- Contact: compliance@redwood.com (for process questions), security-oncall@redwood.com (for urgent evidence preservation during incidents)

Appendix A: Example queries for audit-logging verification
---------------------------------------------------------
- Verify presence of service restart events:
  Elastic search query: service:runtime AND event:restart AND @timestamp:[2026-02-01 TO 2026-02-28]
- Verify RBAC change events (sample KQL):
  event.type: "rbac.change" AND user.role: ("admin","infra-admin") AND timestamp >= "2026-02-01"

Appendix B: Example minimal manifest snippet
------------------------------------------
- manifest.txt content (3 lines):
  EvidenceID: EAM-API-01 | Filename: iam-snapshot-2026-02-15.json | SHA256: <sha256> | CollectedBy: a.patel | CollectedAt: 2026-02-15T18:05:12Z
  EvidenceID: EAM-LOG-07 | Filename: gateway-logs-2026-02-14.jsonl | SHA256: <sha256> | CollectedBy: s.sre | CollectedAt: 2026-02-15T20:12:55Z
  EvidenceID: EAM-DR-04 | Filename: data-residency-map-2026-02-14.csv | SHA256: <sha256> | CollectedBy: d.privacy | CollectedAt: 2026-02-16T09:30:01Z

End of document

title: dsid_7bed0739a8f241219e4f3ab0304916bb__enterprise-severity-matrix-and-customer-communication-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Enterprise Severity Matrix and Customer Communication Playbook

Overview

Purpose
This playbook defines a standardized severity matrix for enterprise customers during onboarding and production, and prescribes customer-facing communication workflows for each severity. The goal is to ensure consistent, transparent, and timely communications while aligning engineering, SRE, and customer success actions with contractual SLAs and business expectations.

Scope
- Applies to Redwood-hosted API, Dedicated, and Private deployments for enterprise customers.
- Covers incidents affecting availability, correctness of outputs, performance regressions, and billing/quotas that materially impact customer business outcomes.
- Does NOT replace product-specific runbooks or legal escalation paths for data breaches (see security-and-compliance incident playbooks).

Definitions and Severity Matrix
Use the following table and criteria to classify customer-impact incidents. Classify on customer-visible impact; escalate by highest impacted customer tier when multiple tenants are affected.

Severity Levels (quick reference)
- P0 (Critical): Customer-facing outage or corrupted responses that prevent core business flows, repeated for >5 minutes, affects 25%+ of requests or one or more high-value tenants.
- P1 (High): Significant degradation in throughput/latency or consistent quality regressions affecting >10% of requests for a specific tenant or features used in production.
- P2 (Medium): Partial feature outage, degraded quality with mitigations available, or single-tenant rate limiting causing customer-visible errors but with fallback.
- P3 (Low): Minor functional issues, intermittent errors, non-urgent quality differences, or documentation gaps.
- P4 (Informational): Non-customer-impacting background issues, upcoming maintenance notices, or low-risk changes.

Severity Scoring Criteria (short form)
1. Impact: % of requests affected or number of customers/tenants impacted.
2. Business Criticality: Revenue at risk, compliance implications, or go-live status.
3. Duration: Time since onset without effective mitigation.
4. Reproducibility: Deterministic vs intermittent.

SLA and Target Responses
- P0: Acknowledge to customer within 5 minutes. Formation of incident bridge with engineering and SRE within 10 minutes. Initial public-facing or customer-facing update within 15 minutes. Target time-to-recover (TTR) depends on root cause; communicate ETA if >30 minutes.
- P1: Acknowledge within 15 minutes. Bridge within 30 minutes. Customer-facing update within 60 minutes and then every 2 hours until resolved.
- P2: Acknowledge within 1 business hour. Customer update within 4 hours and daily status until resolved.
- P3/P4: Acknowledge within 24 business hours. Weekly or as-needed updates.

Owner and Escalation Roster
The following ownership matrix is used when classifying and communicating incidents. Replace names with on-call rotation contact where appropriate.
- First responder: Support Tier 1 (CS Operations)
- Technical owner: SRE / Runtime on-call
- Product owner: Product Manager assigned to the affected feature
- Account lead: Customer Success Manager (CSM) for the tenant
- Executive notify: VP Customer Success (for P0 and repeated P1 on production customers)

Contact escalation paths (order)
1. Support Tier 1 -> 2. SRE on-call -> 3. Runtime engineering -> 4. Product -> 5. VP Customer Success / Head of Eng (as needed)

Operational Checklist by Severity (numbered steps for responders)
P0 (Critical)
1. Classify severity and escalate to SRE immediately.
2. Launch incident bridge (Zoom/Slack/Bridge) and add: Support lead, SRE on-call, runtime eng, product PM, account CSM, and communications.
3. Stabilize traffic: enable fallback model, route to standby region, or activate quota protections. Document actions in the bridge.
4. Craft initial customer-facing update (see templates). Post to customer’s preferred channel (email + support portal ticket + CSM slack).
5. Track metrics and logs: error rate, 95/99th percentile latency, tail drop %, model output error metrics. Attach graphs to updates.
6. Confirm mitigation, run customer verification steps, and coordinate rollback if change-induced.
7. After resolution, run RCA and share timeline within 48 hours and a corrective action plan in the QBR cadence.

P1 (High)
1. Acknowledge and open incident ticket. Notify SRE and product.
2. Attempt quick mitigations (scaling, model fallback, rolling to previous model checkpoint).
3. Provide updates every 2 hours until stable.
4. If unresolved after 6 hours, escalate to executive notify list.

Customer Communication Templates
Use the templates below and customize per tenant (replace tokens in {{braces}}). Always coordinate final messages with the CSM and legal when regulatory language or credits are discussed.

P0 Initial Notification (email/portal)
Subject: URGENT: Incident affecting Redwood Inference API for {{customer_name}} ({{incident_id}})
Body:
Hello {{customer_name}} team,

We are aware of a critical incident affecting {{feature_or_api}} that is impacting production traffic for your account (incident ID: {{incident_id}}). Our on-call engineering and SRE teams have launched a bridge and are actively investigating.

What we know now:
- Time detected: {{iso_timestamp}}
- Observed impact: {{brief-impact-summary}}
- Immediate mitigation actions: {{mitigations}}

Next update: We will provide an update within 15 minutes or sooner. Your Customer Success Manager {{csm_name}} is available at {{csm_contact}} for direct coordination.

We understand the urgency and appreciate your patience.

— Redwood Inference Support

P1 Update Example
Subject: Update: Ongoing service degradation for {{customer_name}} ({{incident_id}})
Body:
Hello {{customer_name}} team,

Status update ({{iso_timestamp}}):
- Current impact: {{current-impact}}
- Actions taken: {{actions}}
- Next steps / ETA: {{eta}}

Assignee: {{technical_owner}}

Regards,
Redwood Inference Support

P2 Customer Guidance (short)
Subject: Notice: partial functionality impacted for {{customer_name}}
Body:
We identified an issue affecting {{feature}}. A workaround is available: {{workaround_steps}}. We will update you by {{next_update_time}}.

Incident Posture and Tone Guidance
- Tone: factual, empathetic, and action-oriented. Avoid speculative technical claims.
- Transparency: If unknowns remain, state what is unknown and planned investigative steps.
- Credits/Compensation: Route any compensation requests to Billing and legal. Do not promise credits in customer message; escalate to finance for approval.

Onboarding-specific Escalations and Go-Live Safeguards
During enterprise onboarding and initial cutover, apply a lower tolerance for regressions and ensure the following:
- Pre-cutover: confirm runbook and contact list, stomping on-call handoff validation.
- Canary phase: require minimum 24-hour monitoring with dedicated telemetry dashboards and synthetic checks for edge-cases.
- Cutover hold gate: no model or config changes that impact the tenant for 72 hours post go-live unless approved by the CSM + SRE.
- Onboarding rapid response team: Onboarding PM, CSM, SRE representative, and runtime eng must be on-call during cutover windows.

Telemetry and Dashboard Recommendations (examples)
- Ingress: request/sec, 50/95/99 latency, HTTP error 5xx/4xx by route.
- Model: token generation rate, kv-cache hit ratio, GPU utilization, OOM events, and per-tenant queue length.
- Quality: perplexity drift, top-1 response divergence from baseline evaluation set, and customer feedback rate.

Example monitoring queries (PromQL-like pseudocode)
- api_errors_total{tenant="{{tenant_id}}"} / api_requests_total{tenant="{{tenant_id}}"} > 0.05
- histogram_quantile(0.95, api_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate"}) > 1.2

Escalation Communication Channels
- Primary: Customer ticketing portal + dedicated support email.
- Real-time: Slack DM to CSM and customer production channel (if provisioned).
- Bridge: Zoom + pinned Slack incident channel.
- Public status: status.redwood.ai for multi-tenant incidents.

Post-Incident Activities and QBR Integration
1. Within 48 hours: publish timeline, mitigation steps, and next actions to the customer and internal ticket.
2. Within 7 days: share a draft RCA and proposed corrective actions.
3. In next QBR: include incident summary, SLA impact table, and long-term remediations (owners and milestones).
4. For repeated issues: propose permanent routing or quantization changes via Redwood Optimize recommendations and include cost/latency tradeoffs.

Runbook Snippets (copyable checklist for responders)
- Confirm impact and severity.
- Validate customer's on-call and preferred communication channel.
- Collect: logs, trace IDs, example request payloads and model outputs.
- If code/config change suspected: capture deployment IDs and roll back marker.
- For Private deployments: verify network connectivity and customer firewall rules before code rollback.

Templates and Forms
- Incident ticket tags: severity:P0|P1|P2|P3, tenant_id, impacted_feature, psa_required:true|false.
- Customer update subject prefix: [Incident][P{n}] or [Maintenance][Info] for scheduled events.

Related pages
- /confluence/customer-success-and-support/enterprise-onboarding/onboarding-handback-and-first-90-days-ops-guide-2026
- /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/incident-bridge-template
- /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/major-incident-classification

Change log
- 2026-02-15: Created by Samantha Lee.
- 2026-04-02: Revised response SLAs and added onboarding cutover gates (reviewers: Jordan Kim, Priya Nair).
- 2026-07-12: Added telemetry query examples and post-incident QBR integration guidance.

Ownership and Review
- Document owner: Samantha Lee (Customer Success Operations)
- Review cadence: Quarterly or after any P0/P1 incident affecting enterprise customers.

Appendix: Example short-form verification checklist for customers to run after mitigation
1. Send 5 canonical requests used in production and compare outputs to baseline.
2. Verify 95th percentile latency improvement.
3. Confirm no new 5xx errors for 30 minutes.
4. Confirm billing/quotas unchanged (if relevant).

End of document

title: dsid_117e5a150aa94adc86295786bd6b7843__hosted-api-model-intake.txt
text:
Hosted API model intake: third-party LLM onboarding request

# Purpose
This page describes the *intake* process for launching a new third‑party LLM in the Redwood Hosted API model catalog. It defines what the requester must provide, who owns each step, and what artifacts are required before engineering work starts.

# When to use
Use this process for any new entry in the Hosted API model catalog, including:
- New upstream model families (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral)
- New sizes or instruction variants
- New upstream releases that change tokenizer, weights, or license

# Roles
- Requester: typically Product or Solutions Engineering
- Intake owner: Applied ML Onboarding (Applied ML)
- Runtime owner: Serving Runtime
- Release owner: Release Engineering
- Security gate owner: Security & Compliance
- Docs owner: DevEx / Docs

# Intake ticket and required fields
Create a Linear ticket in *ENG* with label `model-onboarding` and include the following fields (copy/paste section):

## 1) Model identity
- Upstream model name and version tag
- Model type: `chat` | `completion` | `embeddings` | `rerank`
- Upstream repo / source URL
- Tokenizer type and expected special tokens

## 2) Intended catalog surface
- Proposed Redwood model ID (e.g., `rw/llama-3.1-70b-instruct`)
- Compatibility target: `redwood` native | OpenAI-compatible endpoint
- Any planned aliases (e.g., `rw/llama-3.1-70b`)

## 3) License and redistribution
- License name + link to full text
- Redistributable weights: yes/no/unclear
- Any use restrictions that must be enforced in ToS / UI (e.g., geo, user class)

## 4) Data and policy
- Safety/policy concerns (e.g., uncensored, adult content)
- Any known PII or training data controversies (link sources)

## 5) Target customers and workload
- Example customer workloads (prompt length distribution, expected max tokens)
- Regions required (US/EU/APAC)
- Any explicit SLO expectations (latency, availability, streaming)

# Intake gates (must all be satisfied to proceed)
1. **License pre-check** (Owner: Finance-Legal liaison + Security)
   - Outcome: `approved`, `approved w/ restrictions`, or `blocked`
   - Artifact: link to Security risk review page entry (see Security space)
2. **Baseline evaluation plan** (Owner: Applied ML)
   - Outcome: evaluation suites selected + success criteria
   - Artifact: eval plan comment in Linear + link to eval harness run(s)
3. **Feasibility / runtime fit** (Owner: Serving Runtime)
   - Confirm tokenizer handling, KV cache behavior, and kernel coverage
   - Artifact: short feasibility note + any required runtime flags

# Artifacts produced during intake (and where they live)
- Model intake summary: Linear ticket (single source of truth)
- Eval plan + results: Eval harness run links and Confluence (Applied ML and Evals)
- Performance benchmark results: Confluence Performance Standards page + attached benchmark run IDs
- Quantization plan/results: Confluence Quantization Profiles space
- Security risk review: Confluence Security & Compliance space
- Rollout plan and fallback: Confluence Eng Platform runbook
- Model registry change: GitHub PR in `redwood-model-registry`

# Definition of “ready for implementation”
A model is ready to move from intake to implementation when all of the following are true:
- License is approved (or approved with documented restrictions)
- Eval plan includes at least one internal prompt set and one public benchmark
- Runtime owner has stated no known blockers
- A rollout owner is named (release + platform)

# Related pages
- Eval gates for model launch (Applied ML and Evals)
- Hosted model performance bar (Architecture and Standards)
- Quant profile requirements for catalog (Applied ML and Evals)
- Third-party model risk review workflow (Security and Compliance)
- Hosted model rollout and fallback runbook (Eng Platform)

title: dsid_d7c1267719e849bc8fdc670a798b6f64__slice-drift-sentinel-quant-hedging-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Slice Drift Sentinel and Quant Hedging Playbook

Overview

This playbook describes the Slice Drift Sentinel system and the Quant Hedging policy used across Redwood's eval harness to maintain user-visible fidelity while maximizing cost savings from quantized deployments. It covers detection signals, thresholds, automated hedging (fallback) rules, how to allocate cost 'shields' to high-risk slices, and the operational runbook for regression triage and rollback.

Motivation

- Quantized model variants decrease serving cost but occasionally produce regressions that are slice-specific (e.g., domain jargon, long context).
- We need automated, explainable controls to detect quality shifts at slice granularity and to migrate affected traffic to higher-fidelity variants with minimal manual intervention.
- The sentinel also provides cost accounting so product teams can accept controlled quality trade-offs.

Scope

Applies to: hosted and dedicated inference fleets, hybrid private deployments where telemetry is available.
Not covered: full retraining workflows, human annotation pipelines (see related pages).

Key concepts

- Slice: a workload partition (intent, tenant cohort, locale, prompt family) defined in the probe registry.
- Sentinel score: a composite signal combining fidelity delta, confidence calibration shift, and embedding drift (0-100).
- Quant hedging: automated rule set that routes a percentage of slice traffic to a higher-precision variant when sentinel score exceeds thresholds.
- Cost shield: per-slice budget to allow temporary hedging without blowing team-level cost targets.

Telemetry and metrics

Primary metrics (per slice, computed hourly):
- fidelity_delta_pct: relative drop in oracle-aligned metric (e.g., BLEU/QA-F1/Instruction-adherence) vs baseline (rolling 7d).
- topk_confidence_shift: change in average model token confidence or logit gap.
- embedding_drift_cosine: mean cosine distance between recent embeddings and baseline centroid.
- user_apdex_change: change in product Apdex correlated with quality signals.
- hedged_traffic_pct: percent of slice routed to higher fidelity.

Detection algorithm (high level)

1. Compute normalized z-scores for fidelity_delta_pct, confidence_shift, embedding_drift using slice historical window (90th percentile to reduce noise).
2. Sentinel score = weighted sum: 0.5*fidelity_z + 0.3*confidence_z + 0.2*embedding_z, clipped to 0-100.
3. Apply hysteresis: require sentinel score > threshold for 3 consecutive hourly bins before triggering hedging.
4. Raise severity levels: informational (20), guarded (40), hedging (60), immediate rollback (85).

Quant Hedging Policy (config example)

policy_name: slice_quant_hedge_v1
priority: high
thresholds:
  informational: 20
  guarded: 40
  hedging: 60
  rollback: 85
actions:
  guarded: notify-steward, increase-probe-frequency
  hedging: route-percent: 25; 50; 100 by step; duration: 2h-auto-evaluate
  rollback: immediate-shift-to-fp16, open-incident
cost_shield:
  default_monthly_credits_usd: 1500
  per_slice_max_pct_of_shield: 20
  auto-replenish_policy: manual

Policy semantics

- Hedging ramps are conservative: start with 25% traffic to higher-fidelity for 2 hours, evaluate fidelity_delta and user_apdex; if improved, escalate to 50% then 100%.
- Shielding prevents unlimited hedging: when a slice's cumulative hedging cost exceeds its allocated shield, the policy falls back to alert-only and requires steward approval.

Cost accounting model (table)

Slice metric | baseline cost/token | hedged cost/token | expected monthly delta
--- | ---: | ---: | ---:
default-chat | 0.0012 | 0.0025 | +$320
enterprise-forms | 0.0020 | 0.0040 | +$1,200
longcontext-recalls | 0.0009 | 0.0021 | +$480

Onboarding checklist for a new slice

1. Register slice in probe registry with owner, intent, and canonical prompt set.
2. Define baseline (rolling 14d) fidelity metric and target SLO.
3. Assign cost shield and steward approver.
