Journal entry examples (simplified)
- On receipt of prepaid committed capacity (example Tier 2):
  DR Cash 100,000
  CR Deferred Revenue 100,000

- On recognition of first month of service (amortized):
  DR Deferred Revenue 8,333
  CR Revenue 8,333

Implementation notes and next steps
- Engineering: add contract metadata fields (tier, amortization_schedule_id, deferment_days) to contract ingestion webhook by 2026-07-01. (Owner: Platform Eng)
- Procurement: update internal procurement form to collect capacity plan and provisioning lead times for tier 2/3 requests by 2026-05-01. (Owner: Procurement Ops)
- Finance: publish standard amortization schedule templates for Tier 2 by 2026-04-01 and configure weekly reconciliation job. (Owner: Revenue Ops)

Contacts and ownership
- Procurement lead: Jon Patel (procurement@redwood.ai)
- Revenue Ops: Sofia Martinez (revops@redwood.ai)
- Legal contract owner: Liam O'Connor (legal@redwood.ai)
- Platform Eng (webhook owner): Priya Ramesh (eng-platform@redwood.ai)

Revision history
- 2026-02-15: Document created by Maya Thompson; initial draft.
- 2026-04-06: Added CLI examples and webhook schema; updated Tier numeric thresholds. (Reviewer: Jon Patel)
- 2026-06-10: Published; added Appendix A amendment flow and example GL mappings. (Reviewer: Sofia Martinez)

title: dsid_92bf997794b046c892bf1f210b9aee09__anticipatory-degradation-lab-curriculum-and-dashboard-templates-2026.txt
text:
Anticipatory Degradation Lab: Curriculum and Dashboard Templates

Summary

This page defines a repeatable, instructor-led curriculum and a set of dashboard + alert templates to run "anticipatory degradation" labs for Redwood's platform operators and platform engineers. The labs simulate slowdowns, token surges, cache thrash, and region-level partial outages so teams can practice detection, mitigation, and graceful degradation.

Goals

- Teach operators to detect early signals of SLO drift using dashboards and enriched traces.
- Validate alert thresholds and escalation flows before production incidents.
- Exercise fallback policies (model swap, region failover, reduced-batch mode) with minimal customer impact.
- Improve postmortem fidelity by codifying measurement and regression checks.

Audience and prerequisites

- Audience: platform-operators, oncall-eng, runtime-engineering, SREs, and solutions engineers.
- Prereqs: access to staging tenant, synthetic traffic harness (load-generator), Grafana + Prometheus test instance, ability to run controlled traffic through routing policies, and a disposable GPU pool in a sandbox region.

Instructor notes

- Keep experiments constrained to the staging environment and pre-approved tenants.
- Each lab run must have a designated "control" observer who does not touch remediation steps; their role is to adjudicate timing and to measure detection latency.
- Expected run length: 60–120 minutes depending on scenario complexity.

Scenario Catalog (short)

| id | name | injected signal | expected SLO impact | median run | primary owner |
|----|------|-----------------|---------------------|------------|---------------|
| S1 | KV cache thrash | sudden drop in KV cache hit rate (simulate re-shard) | p95 latency up, token cost up | 45m | runtime-engineering |
| S2 | Token surge (burst) | 5x request rate to single model variant | queue depth increase, tail latency | 60m | eng-platform |
| S3 | GPU interference | background noisy process on one GPU node | increased variance in latency, dropped async batches | 30–45m | gpu-fleet |
| S4 | Model worker OOMs | controlled process kills for a subset of workers | service errors, failovers to fallback model | 45m | serving-runtime |
| S5 | Region partial outage | network partition to approx 20% of API nodes | increased cross-region routing, cost spike | 90m | infra |

Detailed Scenario Example: S1 - KV Cache Thrash

Purpose: Validate detection when prefix/KV cache coherence breaks and evaluate fallback to cold-cache warmup policy.

Preflight checklist:
1) Ensure staging metric collection is enabled for token-level telemetry and KV cache metrics (kv_cache_hit_rate, kv_cache_evictions, kv_prefix_miss_count).
2) Provision 2 synthetic tenants: one control, one experiment.
3) Confirm canary routing policy points to an alternate model variant for fallback.
4) Schedule the run and notify oncall (Slack #platform-gameday).

Execution steps:
1) Baseline collection: run synthetic traffic for 10m and capture p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec, and kv_cache_hit_rate.
2) Trigger: run a script to delete cache shards for experiment tenant (sample command):
   kubectl -n sandbox exec deploy/cache-controller -- ./scripts/delete-shards --tenant=exp-01 --shards=3
3) Observe dashboards for: kv_cache_evictions > 100/min, kv_cache_hit_rate drop > 20% absolute, p95 latency increase > 30%.
4) If p95 > SLO threshold for > 3 minutes, initiate fallback: set routing policy to reduced-batch and model-variant B. CLI example:
   redwood ctl route set --tenant exp-01 --policy reduced-batch --variant model-B
5) Continue observation until metrics return to within 10% of baseline.
6) Run postmortem checklist and collect traces for the 30m window surrounding the trigger.

Observation metrics (canonical)

- latency_p50_request_ms, latency_p95_request_ms, latency_p99_request_ms
- token_rate_per_tenant (tokens/sec)
- request_rate_per_model_variant (req/s)
- kv_cache_hit_rate, kv_cache_evictions, kv_prefix_miss_count
- queue_depth_by_shard, worker_error_rate, worker_restart_count
- gpu_utilization_percent (per instance), bg_process_load

Dashboard template library (summary and example queries)

Each template is a collection of small panels (3–7) that should be combined into a single Grafana dashboard. Use panel IDs in the runbook for quick reference. Recommended tags: team=platform, lab=scenario-id, env=staging.

Template A: Degradation Early-Detection (panels)
- Panel 1: SLO burn rate (line)
  Query: sum(rate(errors_total[5m])) / sum(rate(requests_total[5m])) * 100
  Thresholds: warning 0.5%, critical 1.5%
- Panel 2: p95 latency (line)
  Query: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket[1m])) by (le, service))
  Thresholds: warning = 0.8 * SLO_ms, critical = SLO_ms
- Panel 3: kv_cache_hit_rate (single stat)
  Query: avg(kv_cache_hit_rate{tenant=~"exp-.*"}) by (tenant)
  Thresholds: warning drop > 10pt, critical drop > 20pt
- Panel 4: queue_depth_by_shard (bar)
  Query: sum(queue_depth) by (shard)
- Panel 5: token_rate_heatmap (heatmap)
- Panel 6: backend_error_rate_by_code (table)

Template B: Operator Triage View (short)
- Overview: top 5 p95 latency contributors (by route and model)
- Dependency graph snapshot (static image updated every minute)
- Recent deploys and model-version rollouts (events panel)

Alert rule examples

- Simple Prometheus alert for sustained p95 breach (YAML style):

alert: SustainedP95Breach
expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket{env="staging"}[2m])) by (le, route)) > 1.0 * scalar(SLO_MS_BY_ROUTE{route="/v1/generate"})
for: 5m
labels:
  severity: page
annotations:
  summary: "p95 latency > SLO for /v1/generate in staging"

- Cost-aware alert for token surge:

alert: TokenBurstDetected
expr: increase(token_count_total{tenant=~"exp-.*"}[5m]) > 50000
for: 3m
labels:
  severity: ticket
annotations:
  summary: "Sudden token volume increase for experimental tenant"

Alert playbook (on-page quick actions)

When page triggered:
1) Confirm alert validity by checking token_rate_per_tenant and request_rate_per_model_variant.
2) Identify the top five routes and the top model variants serving the spike.
3) If token surge exceeds auto-burst threshold, apply tenant soft-throttle:
   redwood ctl throttle set --tenant exp-01 --limit 0.6
4) If fallback is needed, trigger model swap or region failover per runbook.
5) Document actions in the incident timeline and tag the run with lab scenario id.

Runbook snippets (copyable)

- Capture a trace window around the event (example):
  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" \
    "https://traces.internal.redwood/api/v1/query?start=$(date -d \"-10 minutes\" +%s)&end=$(date +%s)&trace_filter=tenant:exp-01"

- Apply reduced-batch routing:
  redwood ctl route set --tenant exp-01 --policy reduced-batch --reason "lab:kv-thrash"

- Redeploy cache-controller with forced warmup:
  kubectl -n sandbox rollout restart deploy/cache-controller --timeout=5m

Cleanup and post-lab actions

- Revert any routing policies and throttles applied during the lab.
- Rebuild the cache from snapshots where relevant:
  kubectl -n sandbox exec deploy/cache-controller -- ./scripts/warmup-from-snapshot --tenant=exp-01
- Tag the run artifacts and dashboards with labels: lab=scenario-id, run=YYYYMMDD-HHMM, facilitator=name.

Postmortem checklist (template)

- Timeline with timestamps (detection, remediation start, remediation complete)
- Detection latency: time from injection to alert firing and time from alert to operator acknowledgement
- Actions taken and who performed them
- SLO impact: delta p95/p99 and token-cost delta during window
- Lessons learned and next steps (three concrete follow-ups)

Measurement of success & continuous improvement

- Aim to reduce mean detection latency by 25% quarter-over-quarter for the lab scenarios.
- Maintain a runbook coverage metric: 100% of scenarios must have an owner and a dashboard within 2 weeks of addition.
- Track run friction on a simple score (0–5) where operators rate whether the dashboards and alerts made triage straightforward.

Cadence and governance

- Labs run monthly by platform team with rotating facilitator and a different tenant each run.
- Quarterly cross-functional review (runtime + infra + sres + solutions) of dashboards and alert thresholds.
- Change control: any alert threshold changes discovered during a lab must be submitted as a small PR to the alert rules repo and reviewed by at least one SRE.

Appendix: useful queries and quick references

- Top p95 contributors by route (PromQL):
  topk(5, histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_bucket{env="staging"}[2m])) by (le, route)) )

- KV cache hit rate (per-tenant):
  avg_over_time(kv_cache_hit_rate{env="staging", tenant=~"exp-.*"}[5m])

- Queue depth alert example (PromQL):
  sum(queue_depth{env="staging"}) by (shard) > 100

- Quick contact list for a lab run: #platform-gameday (Slack), oncall duty phone, runtime-engineering@redwood.example

End of document."

title: dsid_461a0b4330144f4ba82c4da1919f279e__local-data-sovereignty-fallback-orchestration-runbook-2026.txt
text:
local-data-sovereignty-fallback-orchestration-runbook-2026

Summary:
This runbook documents the local data sovereignty and fallback orchestration pattern used for Redwood Private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It defines when and how tenant traffic should be routed to local model variants, what safeguards to use to preserve data residency guarantees, operator procedures to trigger and recover from fallbacks, and telemetry & SLO thresholds that drive automation.

Goals:
- Maintain data residency: ensure PII and regulated data never leaves customer-controlled networks during fallback.
- Preserve availability: keep inference capacity online with best-effort local models when control-plane or cross-region links are impaired.
- Ensure safe rollbacks: provide clear operator steps to revert automated actions with minimal config drift.

Scope:
- Applies to Private deployments that run a hybrid control plane (customer control plane + Redwood managed components) or fully air-gapped on-prem stacks.
- Covers network partition/failure, control-plane outage, upstream model catalog unavailability, and degraded cross-region links.
- Does NOT cover hardware-level GPU failures or kernel-level runtime bugs (see hardware failover docs).

Assumptions and prerequisites:
- Private deployment runs these services: redwood-control-agent, private-operator, edge-proxy (service-lb), rt-inference, kvcache-service.
- Customer has configured a local model cache (min 1 warm model per critical route) and an allowlist of model IDs that are permitted to be used in-scope for local processing.
- KMS/HSM keys for local encryption are available and reachable from the compute tier.

Ownership:
- Incident owner: oncall-private-ops (primary).
- Fallback orchestration: infra-platform-team (automation).
- Security & data residency validation: security-compliance (review and approval).

Key SLOs and thresholds that drive fallback:
- Control-plane API error rate > 2% sustained for 5 minutes -> begin staged local fallback (step 1).
- Cross-region bandwidth degradation > 60% of baseline for 10 minutes -> prepare local routing but do NOT fail traffic until control-plane errors observed.
- Local model cold-start time > 10s at 95th percentile after priming -> raise playbook alert to operator.
- Local inference latency p99 must remain < 600ms post-fallback for critical routes; if exceeded, trigger degradation policy to reduce response size or invoke cached responses.

High-level orchestration patterns:
1) Passive priming: maintain a warm local model cache for critical tenant routes. Regularly refresh KV-caches and checkpoint files during low-traffic windows.
2) Staged activation: fallback occurs in stages: traffic shadowing -> partial routing (10-30%) -> full cutover. Each stage waits for health gates.
3) Policy guardrails: use the allowlist and residency rules to prevent models that require external telemetry or third-party calls from being used during offline mode.

Configuration snippets (example automation policy YAML):

automation_policy: |
  name: "local-fallback-policy-tenant-critical"
  triggers:
    - type: control_plane_error_rate
      threshold_percent: 2
      window_sec: 300
    - type: bandwidth_degradation
      region: "primary->secondary"
      threshold_percent: 60
      window_sec: 600
  stages:
    - name: shadow
      traffic_percent: 0
      verify_health: true
      wait_sec: 120
    - name: partial
      traffic_percent: 20
      verify_health: true
      wait_sec: 300
    - name: full
      traffic_percent: 100
      verify_health: true
      wait_sec: 180
  residency_enforcement: "strict"
  allowed_models: ["local/gptx-small-v1", "local/embedding-sparse-1"]

Operator runbook: step-by-step for automated fallback:
1) Alert triage (0-5 min): confirm control-plane error alerts (redwood-control-plane) and cross-region telemetry. Check grafana dashboard: "Private / Control Plane / Errors" and "Network / Inter-region Throughput".
2) Verify residency policy: ensure allowed_models list is intact in /etc/redwood/private-config.yaml and that KMS is reachable.
3) Kick off shadowing stage if automation did not start: run CLI on private-operator box:
   - sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl begin-shadow --tenant $TENANT_ID --policy local-fallback-policy-tenant-critical
4) Monitor shadowing: verify shadow profiles in the "shadow-traffic" table on the operator UI and confirm no data egress events in the telemetry stream.
5) If shadowing healthy for 2 minutes (no model exceptions, p95 latency stable), progress to partial routing:
   - sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl set-traffic-split --tenant $TENANT_ID --percent 20
6) Health gates at each stage:
   - error-rate (local inference) < 1%
   - KV cache hit rate > 70%
   - p99 latency < configured limit (default 600ms)
7) If any gate fails, rollback one stage and re-prime model caches (see Cache re-priming below). Notify security-compliance if data residency policy was close to violation.
8) When full routing completes, mark incident: annotate runbook in incident tracker and set recovery actions.

Manual fallback: when automation is disabled or unsafe
- If automation is off, follow the CLI steps above; for emergency full cutover run:
  - sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl emergency-cutover --tenant $TENANT_ID --force --reason "$INCIDENT_ID"
- Emergency cutover requires two approvers from infra-platform-team and security-compliance.

Cache re-priming procedure:
1) Stop inference endpoints for the tenant on a single node: systemctl stop redwood-rt-inference@$TENANT_ID
2) Remove stale KV entries: /opt/redwood/bin/kvtool prune --tenant $TENANT_ID --older-than 72h
3) Start priming job (background): /opt/redwood/bin/priming-job --tenant $TENANT_ID --model local/gptx-small-v1 --concurrency 4 --duration 10m
4) Verify KV hit rate > 70% and memory usage within expected bounds.

Rollback & upgrade coordination (day-2 guidance):
- Rollback policy: prefer configuration rollback over model rollback. Revert operator policy first, then restore traffic split to last known good value.
- If rollback involves a model swap (hot-swap), use staged rollbacks: partial -> shadow -> off. Do NOT revert to hosted-only mode in restricted residency customers without explicit approval.
- Upgrade windows: schedule control-plane upgrades during low-traffic windows and ensure warm models are available in at least two zones. Communicate planned maintenance at least 72 hours in advance to the customer.

Telemetry, alerts and dashboards (key metrics):
- control_plane_api.error_rate (by tenant)
- network.region_throughput (primary->secondary)
- local_inference.latency.p95/p99
- kvcache.hit_rate
- data_egress.events (counts of external egress attempts)
- operator.automation.stage (current fallback stage)
Alert routing:
- PAGER: private-ops@pagerduty (severity P1 for control_plane_api.error_rate > 5% for 2 minutes)
- EMAIL: infra-platform-team for warnings

Security and compliance considerations:
- Enforce strict residency_enforcement during fallback: all outbound connectors disabled by policy; no telemetry with PII forwarded outside the VPC.
- KMS rotations: local key rotations MUST be applied before any model priming job if rotation occurred in the previous 24h.
- Audit: record the full operator CLI transcript and store in secure evidence bucket with retention 7 years for regulated customers.

Testing and validation matrix (recommended):
1) Simulation: emulate control-plane errors by returning 5xx for 6 minutes; verify runbook triggers and staged cutover completes.
2) Network: throttle inter-region link to 40% bandwidth for 15 minutes and validate that fallback does not trigger until control-plane errors occur.
3) Residency: run a synthetic PII query and confirm no egress logs recorded during fallback.
4) Load: run 1k QPS synthetic load during partial routing and verify p99 latency stays within SLA.

Post-incident checklist and evidence capture:
- Timestamped incident timeline (UTC).
- Snapshots of dashboards and operator logs (redwood-control-agent, private-operator).
- Copy of automation policy used and final allowed_models list.
- Post-incident review: assign owners, list root causes, and planned mitigations.

Appendix A: quick CLI commands
- Check policy status: sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl policy-status --tenant $TENANT_ID
- Start priming job: sudo /opt/redwood/bin/priming-job --tenant $TENANT_ID --model $MODEL --duration 10m
- Emergency rollback: sudo /opt/redwood/bin/operator ctl rollback --tenant $TENANT_ID --to-tag $TAG

Appendix B: common failure modes and mitigations
- Problem: local model OOM after cutover -> Mitigation: reduce concurrency, enable quantized model profile, evict non-critical tenants.
- Problem: KMS unreachable during priming -> Mitigation: fall back to cached DEKs for 15 minutes and run health-checks that require KMS unavailable flag.

References and links:
- Private deployment control plane topology (reference architecture)
- Operator CLI reference: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-operator-cheat-sheet-for-field-installations-2027
- Security policy: private-deploy-telemetry-data-classification-policy-2026

Change log:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft (Ava Kim).
- 2026-02-10: Added automation policy examples and security gating (Priya Nambiar).
- 2026-03-02: Reviewed and published; updated SLO thresholds and CLI paths (Diego Ramos).

title: dsid_db405adbc9a242658289b0fbb085f34f__postmortem-writeup-style-guide-and-exec-summary-templates-2026.txt
text:
Postmortem Writeup Style Guide and Executive Summary Templates

Purpose
This document defines the standard structure, language guidance, and templates for producing postmortem writeups and short executive summaries at Redwood Inference. Our goal is faster, higher-quality postmortems that surface actionable remediation, respect blameless culture, and provide concise executive-ready summaries suitable for customers and leadership.

Scope
- All incidents that meet the postmortem threshold (see "Incident Triage and Postmortem Thresholds" below)
- Game-day exercises where a formal writeup is required
- Customer-impacting outages and incidents requiring external communication or regulatory evidence

Quick reference: When to write a postmortem
1) Severity P1 or P2 incident that impacts >1% of customers or violates an SLO for >10 minutes.
2) Any incident with regulatory evidence requirements (enterprise customers, data residency, security incidents).
3) Any game day or chaos experiment that requires lessons learned.

1. Required structure of a postmortem page (order matters)
- Title: short, specific, include incident date and primary symptom (e.g., "2026-02-18 — Multi-region KV-cache Eviction Causing 5xx Spike")
- Severity and duration: single line (Severity: P1, Start: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC, End: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM UTC, Duration: 00h00m)
- Executive summary (one paragraph + 3 bullets) — see template below
- Impact summary: number of customers, affected routes, estimated error budget/percentage, and key metrics (e.g., 95th latency, error rate)
- Timeline: ordered, timestamped events (ISO 8601) and short descriptions; include detection, mitigation, and closure events
- Root cause analysis: concise causal chain (not a laundry list) with evidence links (logs, dashboards, traces)
- Mitigations applied during the incident (with timestamps and owners)
- Long-term corrective actions: 90-day plan with owner and target completion date (format: ACTION — OWNER — ETA)
- Verification plan: how we will validate the fix (synthetic tests, load tests, monitoring checks)
- Lessons learned / Preventative measures: short list, prioritized
- Postmortem checklist and artifacts: list of evidence files retained and retention policy
- Distribution list and stakeholder notifications: who was informed and when
- Closure criteria and sign-off: product, SRE, and legal (if required) approval

2. Executive summary template (target length: 3–6 sentences + up to 3 bullets)
- One-line incident description: what happened and when.
- Top-level impact: number of customers or percentage affected, and key metric delta (e.g., "peak error rate 18% (baseline 0.3%)").
- Root cause (one sentence): the proximate failure in plain language.
- Short statement of immediate mitigation and current state.
- Bulleted quick actions: 2–3 highest-priority next steps with owners.

Example executive summary (copyable)
"On 2026-02-18 at 14:02 UTC a multi-region KV-cache eviction path was triggered during a rolling kernel update, causing sustained 5xx errors on text-generation routes for ~72 minutes. Approximately 12% of production requests experienced errors at peak; SLOs for 99th percentile latency and error budget were violated. The proximate cause was a race condition in the cache eviction handler under parallel evacuation; a mis-sized eviction window was exposed by the higher-than-expected GC pressure. Immediate mitigation reverted the kernel update and scaled replicas to drain hot partitions; customer-facing traffic is back to nominal. Short-term actions: 1) Fix eviction race (owner: Sasha) — ETA 2026-03-15; 2) Add synthetic canary for kernel-update path (owner: Infra Team) — ETA 2026-02-28."

3. Blameless language checklist (must be enforced)
- Use facts, not attributions. Replace: "Engineer X deployed a bad patch" with "A patch containing an eviction-window change was deployed during maintenance".
- Avoid "caused by" that implies intent. Use "contributed to" or "exposed".
- Attribute systemic factors (process, tests, monitoring, documentation), not people.
- Include timeline evidence that supports statements.

4. Incident triage and postmortem thresholds (short table in text)
- P1 (complete service outage or major data loss): postmortem required and must be published within 5 business days.
- P2 (partial degradation impacting many customers): postmortem required within 10 business days.
- P3 & below: postmortem encouraged where cross-team learning is likely; product or incident owner can opt-in.

5. Evidence and artifact retention (minimums)
- Full APM trace export for the incident window (retain 90 days)
- Raw logs for implicated services (retain 30 days unless regulatory hold)
- Correlated metrics, synthetic test outputs, and timeline screenshots (retain 180 days)
- Incident bridge recording and decision artifacts (retain 365 days)
- For enterprise customers or regulatory incidents, follow the Incident Evidence Chain runbook for extended retention and legal hold.

6. Timeline guidance (best practice)
- Use ISO 8601 timestamps (UTC).
- Each event row: TIMESTAMP — ROLE — ACTION/OBSERVATION — LINK TO EVIDENCE.
- Distinguish detection vs mitigation events.
- Annotate who made the decision and why (brief rationale).

Sample timeline fragment (text table)
2026-02-18T14:02:12Z — Monitoring — Spike detected: 5xx rate > 10% on /v1/generate — link: grafana/dashboard/err-rate
2026-02-18T14:05:30Z — Oncall — Opened incident bridge (bridge-id) and paged Platform team
2026-02-18T14:12:10Z — Platform — Scoped to kv-eviction logs; identified eviction storms — link: logs/query?id=evict
2026-02-18T14:25:00Z — SRE — Rolled back kernel update in eu-west-1; began draining replicas — link: deploy/rollback/1234

7. Action item format and tracking (required fields)
- Each action must be entered into the action tracker (JIRA) and referenced in the postmortem using JIRA-ID. Required fields in the tracker: Summary, Owner, Risk/Impact, ETA, Acceptance Criteria, Verification Plan.

8. Customer and status-page messaging templates (short, adjustable by severity)
A) P1 public status-page (initial notice)
- Title: "Service disruption affecting text-generation routes — investigating"
- Body: "We are investigating elevated error rates for text-generation routes (v1). Affected customers may experience 5xx errors. Our engineers have opened a bridge and are actively investigating. We will provide an update by [time]."
- Follow-up updates: factual, timestamped, short; avoid technical blame in public messages.

B) P2 customer email (post-incident summary)
- Subject: "Incident summary: Partial degradation impacting inference latency (YYYY-MM-DD)"
- Body: Short executive summary + impact bullets + what we did to resolve + link to full postmortem page + next steps and contact for support.

C) Enterprise sensitive notice (when legal or customer data exposure is suspected)
- Contact: CSM and Legal must be looped immediately using the enterprise incident escalation matrix. Do not send external text until Legal approves.

9. Postmortem workflow and SLAs
- Owner assignment: The incident commander (IC) assigns the postmortem author within 24 hours of incident closure.
- Draft: Author produces a complete draft within the SLA window (5 or 10 business days depending on severity).
- Peer review: Two reviewers (one SRE, one Product) must provide comments within 48 hours.
- Publication: Postmortem page is published and linked from the incident tracker; exec summary is emailed to leadership and attached to the incident.
- Closure: Postmortem is closed only after all action items have owners and an initial verification test is scheduled.

10. Examples: poor vs. improved phrasing
- Poor: "Alice's deploy broke the cache and caused the outage."
- Improved: "A deploy that modified the cache eviction parameters coincided with increased GC pressure; the change was a proximate factor in exposing an eviction race."

11. Game day specific guidance
- If a game day triggers a postmortem requirement, label the page with the game-day tag and include: exercise hypothesis, injected fault, expected outcome, observed outcome, and recommended changes to the runbook.
- Always include a dedicated section "What behaved as expected" to keep the learning balanced.

12. Publishing checklist (confluence-specific quick steps)
1) Create page under /oncall-and-incident-response/YYYY/MM/ with title format above.
2) Paste executive summary at the top and pin the page to the incident tracker.
3) Add labels: postmortem, incident, severity-P1/P2, owner-[team].
4) Attach artifacts (screenshots, recordings) and add evidence links (do not paste large logs inline).
5) Assign reviewers and request comment turn-around of 48 hours.
6) After reviewers sign off, set status to "published" and notify distribution list.

13. Metrics and dashboards to include in every postmortem (minimum)
- Request volume (qps) and error rate time series for implicated endpoints
- 50/95/99/99.9 latency percentiles for inference routes
- Pod/node-level resource utilization (GPU/CPU/memory) for implicated clusters
- Cache hit ratio and eviction counts (if applicable)
- Autoscaler events and queue length

14. Ownership and escalation for postmortem defects
- If a defect spans multiple teams, the service owner nominates the primary assignee; SRE co-owns verification.
- For regressions that impact customers repeatedly, the head of SRE sponsors an incident review (30-day retro) and may escalate to leadership for additional resourcing.

15. Frequently asked questions (short)
Q: Who writes the postmortem?
A: The IC assigns the primary author; typically an oncall SRE or the service owner.
Q: Can we redact internal names before publishing externally?
A: Yes — redact PII and internal-only notes. Use the public executive summary for customers.
Q: How do I request extended evidence retention?
A: Follow the Incident Evidence Chain runbook and open a legal hold ticket via the runbook link.

Appendix: Quick CLI snippets and pointers
- Export traces for incident window (example: jaeger)
$ jaeger-export --start 2026-02-18T14:00:00Z --end 2026-02-18T15:30:00Z --service inference --output ./traces.json
- Query logs (example using our internal logs service):
$ logs query "service:inference AND status:5xx" --start 2026-02-18T14:00:00Z --end 2026-02-18T15:30:00Z --save evict-logs.ndjson
- Snapshot dashboards: open Grafana panel and click "share -> snapshot"; attach link to postmortem.

Contact and governance
- Postmortem process owner: Marcus Chen (SRE) — process@redwood.com
- Escalation: see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/escalation-lattice-restoration-blueprint-2026 for the escalation matrix and legal contacts.

Revision history
- 2026-01-12: Created (Marcus Chen)
- 2026-02-10: Clarified retention and added game-day guidance (Anika Patel)
- 2026-03-02: Updated review SLAs and added sample CLI snippets (Rohit Singh)

End of document

title: dsid_a043ee4ad3a64469b4ec9e385cd7a292__kms-iam-baseline-and-rotation-roles.txt
text:
KMS IAM Baseline and Rotation Roles (Terraform/IaC Standard)

## Purpose
This document defines Redwood Inference’s baseline IAM posture for interacting with customer-managed KMS/HSM-backed envelope encryption across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

It standardizes:
- A least-privilege role model for runtime KMS calls vs administrative/rotation operations.
- Per-environment identity separation (dev/staging/prod) and blast-radius constraints (region/account/project/tenant).
- Break-glass access patterns that are auditable, time-bound, and safe.
- A repeatable process to rotate roles/credentials without causing KMS storms, decrypt outages, or prolonged dual-access windows.

This standard is the infra companion to:
- ADR-007 (KMS client wrapper + failure policy)
- ADR-008 (dual-read rotation strategy)
- Key Management Standard (controls + review checklist)

---

## Scope
### In scope
- IAM roles/policies used by Redwood services that call KMS (Encrypt/Decrypt/GenerateDataKey/DescribeKey).
- IAM roles/policies used to validate KMS access during installation/preflight (Private) and ongoing health checks.
- Separation of duties for rotation/cutover operations.
- Break-glass access for incident mitigation and evidence gathering.
- Terraform modules and patterns used to generate and enforce the above.

### Out of scope
- New cryptographic primitives or changes to encryption algorithms.
- Customer-specific key policy authoring (we provide guidance, but customers own their KMS key policies in Private).
- Broad authentication refactors unrelated to KMS.

---

## Principles (non-negotiables)
1) **Runtime decrypt is sacred.** Only the minimum set of principals needed to serve traffic may call `Decrypt`.
2) **Separate runtime from rotation.** Roles used to change key versions/config must not be able to decrypt customer data by default.
3) **Short-lived credentials only.** No long-lived access keys for services. Prefer OIDC/IRSA/workload identity.
4) **Environment + tenant isolation.** Dev/staging/prod separation, and isolate by customer deployment where applicable.
5) **Deny-by-default guardrails.** Use permission boundaries and explicit denies to prevent privilege creep.
6) **Auditable access.** Session tags, CloudTrail/Audit Logs, and Redwood audit events must identify who/what/when.
7) **Break-glass is time-bound + approved.** Must be issued via ticket, with expiry and post-incident review.

---

## Terminology
- **KEK**: Key Encryption Key (KMS key used to wrap/unwrap DEKs).
- **DEK**: Data Encryption Key (generated via KMS `GenerateDataKey`, used for envelope encryption).
- **Runtime role**: Used by data-plane services to decrypt/encrypt payloads and generate DEKs.
- **Rotation operator role**: Used by humans/automation to update config, aliases, or key version references (no decrypt).
- **Validation role**: Used by installers/preflight checks to prove access and report actionable failures.
- **Break-glass role**: Exceptional access for incident mitigation; time-bound and heavily logged.

---

## Role model (baseline)
We standardize on four role categories. Names below are canonical; per-repo modules may apply prefixes/suffixes.

### 1) Runtime KMS Client Role (service identity)
**Used by**: Data-plane services (e.g., `inference-gateway`, `embedding-worker`, `control-plane-secrets`, `private-agent`).

**Allowed actions (minimum)**:
- `kms:Decrypt`
- `kms:Encrypt` (only if service performs encryption; otherwise omit)
- `kms:GenerateDataKey`
- `kms:DescribeKey`

**Prohibited by default**:
- Any key policy mutation (`PutKeyPolicy`, `UpdateAlias`, etc.)
- Key state changes (`DisableKey`, `ScheduleKeyDeletion`, etc.)

**Notes**:
- Runtime roles should be scoped to a specific key ARN (or alias) and, when possible, to a specific encryption context.
- Runtime roles must be deployed per-environment and per-deployment boundary (Hosted vs Dedicated vs each Private cluster).

### 2) KMS Validation Role (installer/preflight)
**Used by**: Private installer, CI validation, and “validate KMS access” workflows.

**Allowed actions (preferred)**:
- `kms:DescribeKey`
- `kms:Decrypt` and `kms:GenerateDataKey` *only when required to validate end-to-end envelope flows*.

**Guidance**:
- Prefer `DescribeKey` for early failure detection.
- If `Decrypt` is needed for validation, use a dedicated “validation ciphertext” generated for testing, not production data.

### 3) Rotation Operator Role (human/automation)
**Used by**: Controlled rotation workflows (quarterly/annual) that update configuration and cutover flags (ADR-008).

**Must NOT include**:
- `kms:Decrypt`
- `kms:GenerateDataKey`

**Allowed actions (typical)**:
- Redwood control-plane admin actions (e.g., update key reference, enable dual-read window) via internal APIs.
- Read-only KMS introspection:
  - `kms:DescribeKey`
  - `kms:ListAliases` (AWS only; optional)

**Rationale**:
Rotation is primarily a *configuration and rollout* process, not a runtime decrypt operation. Decrypt access should remain limited to runtime services.

### 4) Break-glass Roles (exceptional)
We define two break-glass variants; choose based on the task.

**A) Break-glass Auditor (read-only)**
- For evidence gathering and triage: read-only views into KMS metadata and logs.
- Allowed: `kms:DescribeKey`, list operations (as needed), access to log sources (CloudTrail/Audit Logs) via separate log-reader roles.

**B) Break-glass Decrypt (extremely restricted)**
- Only when required to mitigate an active incident where runtime access is failing and customer impact is severe.
- Must be time-bound (hours, not days) and limited to the smallest set of keys and environments.

**Approval + tracking**:
- Requires an access ticket with approvers per the Security & Compliance process.
- Must include an expiry timestamp and post-incident review notes.

---

## Per-environment separation requirements
**Minimum**: separate identities and policies for `dev`, `staging`, `prod`.

**Hosted/Dedicated**:
- Separate AWS accounts/projects/subscriptions per environment.
- Separate KMS keys per environment.

**Private**:
- Each customer cluster should have a distinct identity boundary:
  - Separate IAM roles (or workload identities) per cluster.
  - Scope policies to that customer’s key(s) only.

**Never**:
- Reuse prod runtime roles in staging.
- Allow wildcard `Resource: *` for decrypt in prod.

---

## AWS implementation guidance (primary reference)
### A) Prefer role assumption with OIDC/IRSA (no long-lived keys)
- EKS-based services: use IRSA and a dedicated role per service.
- Self-managed Kubernetes/VMs: use OIDC federation where possible.

### B) Policy scoping
**Resource scoping**
- Scope KMS access to explicit key ARNs:
  - `arn:aws:kms:<region>:<account-id>:key/<key-id>`
  - Prefer alias ARNs only if alias management is well-controlled.

**Encryption context scoping (recommended)**
Where supported by the integration, require an encryption context that binds ciphertexts to:
- `deployment_id`
- `customer_id` (Private/Dedicated)
- `service` name (optional)

Example condition (illustrative):
- `kms:EncryptionContext:deployment_id = <expected>`

### C) Canonical runtime policy (AWS IAM JSON snippet)
Use as a starting point; apply strict resource and condition scoping.

```
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "KmsRuntimeDataKeyAndDecrypt",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "kms:Decrypt",
        "kms:GenerateDataKey",
        "kms:DescribeKey"
      ],
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/aaaaaaaa-bbbb-cccc-dddd-eeeeeeeeeeee"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Do not** add:
- `kms:*`
- `kms:CreateKey`, `kms:PutKeyPolicy`, `kms:DisableKey`, `kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion`

### D) Permission boundaries (recommended for prod)
All KMS-capable roles in prod must attach the org-approved permission boundary. The boundary should explicitly deny:
- KMS administrative actions
- Cross-account key access not explicitly allowed
- Any use of `Resource: *` with `kms:Decrypt`

### E) Key policies vs IAM policies
- For AWS KMS, access is the intersection of the key policy and IAM policy.
- For Private deployments, customers control key policies. Our installer should validate that the customer key policy allows the runtime principal.
- Avoid placing broad principals in key policies; prefer explicit role ARNs.

---

## GCP and Azure implementation guidance (high-level)
We support multiple clouds, but our baseline separation-of-duties model remains the same.

### GCP Cloud KMS
- Prefer Workload Identity for GKE.
- Separate service accounts:
  - `svc-runtime-kms` (decrypt/data key generation)
  - `svc-rotation-operator` (no decrypt)
- Use IAM roles aligned to minimum permissions (e.g., CryptoKey Decrypter/Encrypter as needed) and scope to specific CryptoKeys.

### Azure Key Vault / Managed HSM
- Use Managed Identity for workloads.
- Separate identities for runtime vs rotation.
- Scope access policies/RBAC roles to specific vaults/keys and restrict “key management” actions from runtime identities.

---

## Terraform module expectations
### Required module capabilities
Our standard Terraform module(s) for KMS IAM must:
- Generate separate roles for runtime, validation, rotation operator, and break-glass.
- Enforce per-environment naming and tagging.
- Support optional encryption context conditions.
- Emit outputs used by installers and control-plane config (role ARN, principal IDs).
- Provide safe defaults (least privilege) and require explicit opt-in for expanded permissions.

### Naming + tags
**Naming**
- `redwood-<env>-<deployment>-kms-runtime-<service>`
- `redwood-<env>-<deployment>-kms-validate`
- `redwood-<env>-<deployment>-kms-rotation-operator`
- `redwood-<env>-<deployment>-kms-breakglass-auditor`
- `redwood-<env>-<deployment>-kms-breakglass-decrypt`

**Required tags/labels**
- `owner_team=eng-infra`
- `system=kms`
- `env=<dev|staging|prod>`
- `deployment=<hosted|dedicated|private-<customer>>`
- `data_classification=<internal|customer-sensitive>`

---

## Break-glass access process (operational standard)
Break-glass is not a shortcut for missing permissions.

### When break-glass is allowed
- Active incident with customer impact where normal runtime access is failing.
- Evidence gathering required for audit/customer security review (read-only variant).

### Required controls
- Ticketed request with business justification, scope, and duration.
- Approval: Security Engineering + SRE on-call lead (or delegate).
- Time-bound access (prefer 1–4 hours; max 24 hours without re-approval).
- Session must be attributable (SSO, MFA, session tags).
- Post-incident note: what actions were taken, and how we prevent recurrence.

### Logging requirements
- Cloud provider audit logs (e.g., CloudTrail) must be enabled for the account/project/subscription.
- Redwood audit events must capture:
  - who granted access
  - who assumed role
  - scope (key IDs, environment)
  - start/end time

---

## Rotating roles/credentials safely (no downtime)
This section covers rotating *identities* (roles/service accounts/managed identities) and any associated credentials/trust configs.

### Rotation triggers
- Scheduled rotation (at least annually for trust relationships and access boundaries; more frequently if policy is).
- Suspected credential compromise.
- Policy drift or privilege creep.
- Cloud provider best-practice updates.

### Standard rotation procedure
1) **Create new role/service account**
   - Apply least-privilege policy.
   - Attach permission boundary (prod).
   - Configure trust (OIDC/IRSA/workload identity) with required conditions.

2) **Deploy to staging first**
   - Update service configuration to assume/use the new identity.
   - Validate KMS preflight and runtime behaviors.
   - Monitor KMS metrics: latency, error rate, throttling.

3) **Canary in prod**
   - Enable for a small percentage of traffic or a subset of pods.
   - Confirm:
     - No increase in `AccessDenied` / `InvalidCiphertext`.
     - No retry amplification (ADR-007 failure policy).

4) **Full rollout**
   - Roll out by service and region.
   - Keep old role enabled during the rollout window to avoid partial cutovers.

5) **Disable old role**
   - Remove from trust policy / detach from workloads.
   - Validate that no principals are still assuming it.

6) **Delete old role (after cooldown)**
   - After a defined cooldown (recommended: 7–14 days), delete.
   - Retain policy and audit artifacts as evidence.

### Rollback
- If KMS `AccessDenied` spikes or health checks fail, roll back to the previous identity immediately.
- File a follow-up task to understand missing permissions; do not “temporarily” broaden runtime permissions in prod without Security review.

---

## Common anti-patterns (do not do these)
- Using a single shared “kms-admin” role for runtime and rotation.
- Granting `kms:Decrypt` to humans as a convenience.
- Allowing `Resource: *` on `kms:Decrypt` in prod.
- Reusing the same principal across multiple Private customers.
- Relying on long-lived access keys for services.

---

## Review checklist (for new/changed KMS IAM)
- [ ] Roles separated: runtime vs rotation vs validation vs break-glass.
- [ ] Per-environment identities and keys.
- [ ] Runtime policy contains only required KMS actions.
- [ ] `kms:Decrypt` scoped to specific key resources.
- [ ] Permission boundary applied in prod.
- [ ] Logging enabled and role sessions attributable.
- [ ] Rotation plan documented (create → stage → canary → rollout → disable → delete).
- [ ] SRE sign-off for prod changes that affect runtime decrypt.

---

## Ownership and change management
**Owner**: Eng-Infra (Terraform/IaC), with required review from Security Engineering for any prod policy changes.

**Material changes** (e.g., adding `Decrypt`, widening resources, changing trust conditions) require:
- Security review
- Staging validation
- Canary rollout plan
- Updated runbook notes if operator behavior changes

---

## Appendix: Suggested role-to-service mapping (typical)
- `kms-runtime-inference-gateway` → decrypt/generateDataKey for request/response envelope payloads
- `kms-runtime-control-plane-secrets` → decrypt for control-plane stored secrets (where applicable)
- `kms-validate-private-installer` → describeKey + optional decrypt on validation ciphertext
- `kms-rotation-operator` → call Redwood control-plane APIs to stage/cutover key version references (no decrypt)
- `kms-breakglass-auditor` → read-only metadata + audit logs access
- `kms-breakglass-decrypt` → exceptional decrypt scoped to specific incident keys (time-bound)

title: dsid_eaea2c6a20134dd8a83d1bbac4189e2e__safemode-degrader-and-fallback-orchestration-playbook-2026.txt
text:
SafeMode Degrader and Fallback Orchestration Playbook

SUMMARY

This document describes the SafeMode Degrader (SMD) — an operator-facing and automated orchestration subsystem used in Redwood private deployments to gracefully degrade service capabilities under capacity, thermal, or upstream network stress. It defines the decision trees, policy primitives, SLO thresholds, observability signals, deployment & testing steps, and rollback guidance for on-prem and VPC installations.

Use case and scope

- Primary goal: keep customer-facing APIs available and predictable by trading off non-essential or expensive work (large-model variants, long-context requests, non-critical caching) when infrastructure signals indicate imminent SLO violations.
- Scope: tenant-level and node-level degradation for Private (VPC/on-prem) control planes and runtime nodes. Not intended for hosted API mode.
- Audience: field operators, SREs, account engineers, and partner integration engineers.

Key concepts

1) Safemode Degrader (SMD)
- Lightweight policy engine that executes ranked degradation actions (degraders) when configured triggers fire.
- Runs as part of the operator agent on each control-plane node and as a central orchestrator in customer-managed control planes.

2) Degrader (action) examples
- reject-large-requests: drop or 429 requests exceeding configured token length per tenant.
- downgrade-model-variant: route new requests to quantized or smaller model family.
- kv-prefetch-disable: disable aggressive prefix/KV prefetch to reduce memory pressure.
- batch-size-limit: cap continuous-batching window to preserve latency.
- soft-throttle-embeddings: reduce embedding concurrency.
- cost-airgap: suspend non-essential billing-intensive background jobs.

3) Policy primitives
- trigger: metric + comparator + duration (e.g., node_gpu_util > 92% for 30s).
- priority: integer ranking of degraders; lower = higher precedence.
- scope: tenant | node | control-plane | region.
- duration: intended degrade duration and max_auto_rollback window (e.g., 5m, 30m, 2h).
- cooldown: minimum time after an auto-rollback before re-applying same policy.

SLOs and thresholds (recommended defaults)

- Availability SLO (API): 99.95% per tenant per 30d (target for Dedicated/Private).
- P50 latency (token response): <40ms local GPU workloads.
- P95 latency: <150ms; escalate to SMD if approaching 200ms sustained over 60s.
- GPU util: soft-trigger at 85% sustained 120s (candidate for preemptive degradation). Hard trigger at 95% sustained 30s (immediate action).
- KV cache evictions: >12 evictions/s per node sustained 60s = trigger.
- Swap/IO wait time: >20ms per second sustained 30s = trigger for throttling background tasks.

Observability signals and dashboards

- Required metrics (per node, per tenant): gpu_util, gpu_memory_free_mb, kv_evictions_per_sec, request_rate_rps, avg_tokens_per_request, p95_latency_ms, error_rate_5m, cold_start_count_1h.
- Derived signals: tenant_pressure = weighted(gpu_util, kv_evictions, request_rate).
- Alerts (suggested):
  - SMD:policy_fired (severity: warning) when any policy enters active state.
  - SMD:degrader_escalation (severity: critical) when primary degraders cannot restore SLOs and fallback to more impactful actions.
  - tenant:safemode_active (severity: info) with list of active degraders per-tenant.

Dashboard layout (recommended):
- Top row: cluster GPU utilization heatmap, node-level active policies, rolling error rate.
- Middle: tenant pressure scatter, per-tenant active degraders, latency P95.
- Bottom: recent auto-rollbacks, manual overrides, and operator notes.

Operator procedures

1) Pre-install checklist (field handoff)
- Confirm SMD version matches runtime compatibility matrix.
- Verify telemetry: required metrics exported and sampled at 10s resolution.
- Ensure RBAC: operators with "smd.operator" role and read-only auditors.
- Confirm emergency escape hatch: operator can force global-safemode-off with 2-person approval.

2) Deployment steps (central orchestrator + agent)
- (A) Stage: deploy SMD central controller in a tenant-isolated namespace.
- (B) Validate: run `redwoodctl smd validate --telemetry-endpoints` to confirm metrics ingestion.
- (C) Promote: enable dry-run mode for 24h to record policy triggers without enforcement.
- (D) Enable enforcement: flip `enforce: true` with staggered rollout to 10% of control-plane nodes for 15m, then 50% for 30m, then 100% if no regressions.

3) Runbook: responding to an SLO incident with SMD firing
1. Triage: identify affected tenant(s) using dashboard.
2. Check active degraders: `smdctl active --tenant <id>` (lists actions, priority, since).
3. Evaluate metrics: confirm the trigger condition and scope (node vs tenant).
4. If degraders restored latencies: monitor for 15m then mark incident resolved.
5. If not restored: escalate to next-priority degrader (see escalation table below) or perform manual intervention (model swap to smallest) and notify customer success.
6. Document operator action in incident log and add tags for post-incident review.

Escalation matrix (example)

- Stage 0 (preemptive): limit-batch-window -> reduces throughput, low customer impact.
- Stage 1 (non-disruptive): soft-throttle-embeddings, kv-prefetch-disable -> impacts throughput/accuracy slightly.
- Stage 2 (moderate): downgrade-model-variant -> lower token quality/latency improvements.
- Stage 3 (high-impact): reject-large-requests, global-rate-limit -> more customer-visible but preserves core availability.

Configuration examples

- Sample policy YAML (flat fields only):

  policies:
    - id: node_gpu_pressure_preemptive
      scope: node
      trigger:
        metric: gpu_util
        comparator: GT
        threshold: 85
        duration: 120s
      actions:
        - name: limit-batch-window
          priority: 10
          duration: 15m
          cooldown: 5m
    - id: tenant_severe_capacity
      scope: tenant
      trigger:
        metric: p95_latency_ms
        comparator: GT
        threshold: 200
        duration: 60s
      actions:
        - name: downgrade-model-variant
          priority: 30
          duration: 30m
          rollback_on: p95_latency_ms_LT_150
        - name: reject-large-requests
          priority: 40
          duration: 10m

- CLI sample: `redwoodctl smd apply policies.yaml --namespace redwood-smd --mode enforce`

Testing and validation

- Unit tests: policy evaluation functions, comparator math, cooldown logic.
- Integration: simulate node pressure using synthetic GPU-util generator and confirm action ordering.
- Chaos test: run controlled chaos where 2/3 nodes in a zone hit 98% GPU util for 90s and assert availability remains >99.5.
- Acceptance: run a 24h dry-run during a low-traffic window and review recorded actions before enabling enforcement.

Operator scripts and utilities

- smdctl (examples)
  - `smdctl list-policies` -> prints effective policy per-scope.
  - `smdctl simulate --policy-id tenant_severe_capacity --simulate-duration 120s` -> local dry-run trigger.
  - `smdctl active --tenant <id>` -> list active degraders for tenant.
  - `smdctl override --tenant <id> --degrader reject-large-requests --action disable --reason "Customer in maintenance window"`

Permissions and safety controls

- Two-person approval is required for: disabling all degraders in a customer environment, globally turning off enforcement, or forcing a stage-3 degrader.
- Audit logs: every automatic change and manual override must write an immutable audit event to the telemetry lake (retention 2y for enterprise customers).

Rollback and post-incident work

- Auto-rollback: configured by policy via `rollback_on` expression. Example: rollback when p95_latency_ms < 150 for 10m.
- Manual rollback: `smdctl rollback --policy-id <id> --reason "post-fix validation"` with a 2-person signoff annotation.
- Post-incident: run a root-cause analysis template that records root cause, which degraders triggered, why, and proposed config changes. Attach sample telemetry: time-series charts, raw logs (redact PII), and request traces.

Customer communication templates

- Notice for scheduled safemode trial: short email template with date/time, expected impact, and how to opt-out by requesting a maintenance window.
- Incident FAQ snippet: brief explanation of degraded features, expected customer-visible differences, and estimated restoration steps.

Compatibility and integration notes

- Runtime compatibility: SMD v2.1+ required for quantized-model routing. See compatibility matrix in referenced page.
- Private control-plane note: when running fully air-gapped, ensure time synchronization (NTP) across nodes; policy windows rely on consistent clocks.

Appendix A — Example operator checklist (quick)

1. Confirm telemetry ingestion and sampling rates.
2. Switch SMD to dry-run for 24h and collect triggers.
3. Review triggers and update priorities where actions are too aggressive.
4. Enable enforcement to 10% nodes for 15m, verify no SLO regressions.
5. Ramp enforcement as noted in deployment steps.

Appendix B — Example incident run record fields

- incident_id
- start_time
- affected_tenants
- active_degraders
- metrics_at_start (p95_latency, gpu_util, kv_evictions)
- manual_actions
- rollback_actions
- root_cause
- follow_up_tasks

Ownership and contacts

- Primary: Serving Runtime (pager: #serving-runtime-oncall).
- Secondary: Eng SRE (pager: #eng-sre-oncall).
- Escalation: Solutions Engineering (for customer comms).

Related pages and references

- See also: Private deploy observability contracts, tenant-failure-quarantine procedures, and operator field-handbook.
- Compatibility matrix: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging/package-compatibility-license-audit-playbook-2026

Change log

- 2026-03-15: created by Aisha Raman (initial draft).
- 2026-05-08: added escalation matrix and sample policies (review by Diego Martinez).
- 2026-06-20: final edits and published; added auto-rollback expressions and two-person approval notes.

End of document

title: dsid_a5b2109e90b14ba6ac841ff8dec11073__subscriber-impact-notification-orchestration-and-verbatim-scripts-2026.txt
text:
Subscriber impact notification orchestration and verbatim scripts

Summary:
This playbook standardizes how we detect customer-impacting incidents, decide who gets notified, and craft clear, consistent messages for status pages, email, and account managers. It focuses on orchestration (who sends what, through which channel and when), escalation criteria tied to SLOs, and ready-to-send verbatim templates to reduce cognitive load during a high-severity incident.

Goals:
- Ensure stakeholders (customers, CS, Sales, Legal) receive timely, accurate information with minimal fragmentation.
- Reduce time-to-first-notice to under 10 minutes for Severity 1 incidents.
- Maintain a single source of truth (the incident bridge and the status page).

When to use this document:
- Any incident classified Severity 1–2 with measurable customer impact (errors, increased latency, failed requests, or degraded embeddings).
- Silent degradations that cross alert thresholds defined below.

Severity definitions and notification triggers:
1) Severity 1 (S1) — Platform outage or severe degradation affecting >10% of requests or any major enterprise customer. Trigger: SLO breach for 5 continuous minutes or on-call pager fire.
2) Severity 2 (S2) — Partial degradation affecting isolated regions or customers, increased error-rate >3x baseline for 15 minutes.
3) Severity 3 (S3) — Minor, intermittent customer impact, limited feature subset.

Notification thresholds (table):
- Metric / Threshold / Action
- 99th latency > 4x baseline for 5m / Open bridge and page customers (S1) / Page on-call + CS_alert
- Error rate > 3x baseline for 15m / Targeted customer notices + status page note (S2) / Page on-call and notify affected accounts
- KV cache miss storm causing token cost >2x for 30m / Internal ops note + product review (S3) / Triage in next shift

Ownership and channels:
- Incident Commander (IC): engineering SRE on-call — owns single source-of-truth and approves public messaging.
- Bridge Operator: opens/hosts bridge (Zoom/Slack/Google Meet), posts timeline, toggles status page drafts.
- Customer Success (CS) Liaison: crafts account-specific notices and coordinates PM/AM outreach.
- Legal/Compliance: review if sensitive customer data or regulatory scope.
- Channels: status.redwood.ai (status page), customer-email, in-app notices, enterprise Slack/Teams, account manager call.

Immediate on-call actions (first 10 minutes):
1) Acknowledge pager and join bridge.
2) Assign an IC and Bridge Operator in the bridge banner.
3) Determine preliminary severity and impacted surface area (use the Impact quick-check checklist below).
4) Post first-look line to status page (Draft) with timeframe, scope, and next update ETA.
5) Notify CS Liaison for S1/S2.
6) Begin evidence collection: logs, traces, metric graphs, request IDs.

Impact quick-check checklist (use rapid one-liners):
- Is production traffic failing or timing out? (yes/no)
- Are multiple regions affected? (list regions)
- Any enterprise customer alerts? (list accounts)
- Is degradation reproducible via synthetic tests? (yes/no)

Status page lifecycle template:
- Draft posting: short title, affected components, impact (e.g., Degraded / Partial outage), scope estimate, and ETA for next update.
- Update cadence: every 15 minutes while S1; every 30–60 minutes for S2 until mitigated.
- Resolution: clear recovery summary and steps taken; link to postmortem when available.

Verbatim message templates (replace placeholders {incident_id}, {component}, {eta}, {workaround}, {customer_list}):
- Initial public status page (S1):
  Title: {component} — Partial outage
  Body: We are investigating an issue impacting {component}. Some requests may fail or experience elevated latency. We have opened an incident ({incident_id}) and are actively working to restore service. Next update: {eta}.

- Initial customer email (enterprise-facing, S1):
  Subject: Immediate notice — service disruption impacting {component} ({incident_id})
  Body: Hi {customer_contact},

  We are actively investigating a service disruption that may affect your requests to {component}. We have opened incident {incident_id}. At this time we believe the impact is: {scope_summary}. The SRE team is working on mitigation. We will provide a status update by {eta}. For urgent concerns, reply to this email or contact your AM/CS lead.

  Apologies for the interruption — we will follow up with a root cause analysis after recovery.

- Update for status page / customer email: 
  Subject (email): Incident {incident_id} — update
  Body (status page): Update: We have identified the likely root cause (summary) and are testing a rollback/mitigation. Current impact: {impact_now}. ETA for next update: {eta}. Workaround: {workaround} if available.

- Resolution notice (status page + email):
  Title: Resolved — {component} incident {incident_id}
  Body: The incident affecting {component} has been resolved as of {resolved_time}. Summary of impact: {brief_impact}. Actions taken: {mitigation_steps}. If you observe ongoing issues, please contact support. A post-incident report will be published at {postmortem_link}.

- Escalation note for regulatory/PII exposures (internal only):
  Subject: URGENT — Potential data exposure {incident_id}
  Body: IC: please notify Legal and Security immediately. Do not send external notices until Legal clears messaging. Summarize: what data classes, affected customer list, logs/IDs collected, retention concerns.

Account-specific outreach guidance:
- For named enterprise customers (contracted SLAs): send targeted email + AM call within 15 minutes for S1. Use the enterprise email template above and include {customer_list}.
- For broad multi-tenant impact: use status page as canonical source and avoid multiple conflicting emails. CS should prepare account-specific context packs for any inbound AM/CS requests.

Post-incident actions and postmortem checklist:
1) Capture timeline in incident document (bridge transcript, key timestamps).
2) Collect evidence artifacts (logs, dashboards, runbooks used).
3) Assign authors and reviewers for the postmortem within 48 hours.
4) Publish a public-facing summary for customers within 72 hours for S1 incidents.
5) Identify action items, owners, and target dates. Track in the Operational Reliability board.

Game day exercises tied to this playbook (quarterly):
- Scenario A: Silent throughput regression (KV cache misconfiguration) — test detection-to-notice time under 15 minutes and validate customer email flow.
- Scenario B: Multi-region outage — validate cross-region routing fallback and enterprise AM call procedure.
- Scenario C: False-positive alert — practice rollback of premature customer notice and retraction messaging.

Templates and automation tips:
- Store canonical templates in the incident tool (PagerDuty templates) with variables.
- Automate initial status page draft via webhook from the bridge when IC is assigned.
- Keep an account-impact list updated in CRM with contact emails and escalation phone numbers.

Related pages and references:
- Link to oncall-bridge-operator-cheatsheet (internal) and incident-comm-tonebook. Use those as low-level operator guides.

Appendix — Example timeline (S1):
- T+0m: Pager fires, on-call joins bridge, IC assigned. Draft status posted (10m).
- T+10m: CS notified and AMs briefed. First customer emails queued.
- T+30m: Mitigation tested (rollback/traffic shift). Update status page.
- T+90m: Service restored. Postmortem assigned.

Contact and escalation matrix (quick list):
- On-call SRE: oncall+primary@redwood.ai
- CS Liaison: cs-liaison@redwood.ai
- Legal (on-call): legal-oncall@redwood.ai
- Status page owner: status-owner@redwood.ai

Document governance:
- Review cadence: annually or after every S1 incident.
- Owner: SRE Operations (oncall process lead).
- Change process: PR to this doc and two reviewers required (SRE lead + CS lead).

End of playbook.

title: dsid_4372cc67130c478ba9a9eee68bdab0fe__graceful-fidelity-degradation-prd-2026-09-07.txt
text:
Graceful fidelity degradation PRD

Title: Graceful fidelity degradation PRD

Overview:
This PRD describes the user-facing and technical requirements for a Graceful Fidelity Degradation feature: a platform-level capability that reduces model output fidelity in controlled ways when customer-configured SLOs (latency, error rate, cost budget) are at risk. The objective is to preserve availability and acceptable latency by switching to lower-fidelity model variants, structured output with summarization, or token-budgeted responses while guaranteeing predictable cost and automated rollback when pressure abates.

Background and problem statement:
- Problem: Production applications using Redwood Inference occasionally face capacity or latency pressure (regional outages, batch-surge traffic, cold-starts for private deployments). Current fallbacks are coarse (full model variant swap or throttling) and can cause large quality regressions or customer surprise.
- Opportunity: Provide a predictable, observable, and recoverable fidelity-degradation surface that application teams can opt into per-route to maintain availability and aligned unit economics.

Goals (success criteria):
1. Preserve availability for 99.9% of routed requests under transient capacity pressure by reducing per-request compute in controlled steps.
2. Provide measurable fidelity/quality delta metrics (ROUGE/BLEU/embedding-similarity or custom eval sets) exposed in Console for every degradation step.
3. Ensure automated rollback to full-fidelity within 30s once SLO metrics return to normal.
4. Surface cost delta and estimated token savings in the Console and usage APIs.
5. Allow per-tenant and per-route policy configuration with sensible defaults.

Non-Goals:
- This feature is not a substitute for long-term capacity provisioning. It will not change billing semantics for token accounting; it surfaces estimated savings but does not change metering.
- It does not implement model training or quality-improvement techniques beyond variant selection and structured output templates.

Target personas and use-cases:
- Product engineers building chat assistants who require high availability across regions.
- Platform/infra teams wanting graceful SLO-preserving behavior without manual playbooks.
- Customer success teams enabling this for enterprise customers with strict uptime SLAs.

User stories:
- As a product engineer, I want to configure a per-route fidelity policy so my chat route degrades to a summarization-only response when latency SLO is threatened.
- As an SRE, I want automated, observable rollback so I do not need to manually re-enable full-fidelity.
- As a product manager, I want Console charts that show quality delta for each degradation step compared to golden prompts.

High-level approach and design summary:
- Policy model: per-tenant, per-route JSON policy with prioritized ordered steps (e.g., model-variant -> quantized-variant -> structured-output -> token-cap). Each step includes trigger conditions, max duration, and permissible quality-budgets.
- Runtime enforcement: Serving runtime will evaluate policies in a sidecar decision path before scheduling a request. Decisions are tagged in traces and logs for observability.
- Observability: New Console widgets, structured event logs, and trace spans for decisions. Quality metrics are computed asynchronously via lightweight eval proxies and batched against stored prompt-sets.

Functional requirements (must-have):
1. Policy schema (example) - stored in Config Service and exposed in API:

Example policy JSON (user-visible):

{
  "max_latency_ms": 250,
  "steps": [
    {"id": "variant-a-quant", "type": "model_variant", "variant": "llama-70b-q4a", "triggers": {"p95_latency_ms": 300}},
    {"id": "summarize-only", "type": "structured_output", "template": "summarize_first_paragraph", "triggers": {"p95_latency_ms": 400}},
    {"id": "token-cap-200", "type": "token_cap", "max_tokens": 200, "triggers": {"region_capacity_utilization": 0.85}}
  ]
}

2. API: PATCH /v1/routes/{route_id}/fidelity-policy to create/update policies.
3. Console: a policy editor UI with preview of expected behavior for each step and simulated quality deltas using tenant prompt-sets.
4. Runtime tags: Every degraded request must emit a decision tag with step id and rationale.
5. Rollback: automatic step reversal when trigger conditions clear for 3 consecutive evaluation windows (configurable, default 3 x 10s).
6. Opt-in: Default tenant state = disabled. Admins can enable per-tenant compliance mode (required by some enterprise customers).
7. Observability: Time-series metrics: fidelity.degradation.count, fidelity.degradation.duration, fidelity.quality.delta.mean, fidelity.rollback.count.
8. Alerts: SLO burn alert when automated degradation triggers > 10% of requests for > 5 minutes for a tenant.

Non-functional requirements (NFRs):
- Latency overhead: decision layer must add <= 3ms p95 to overall request path when policy checks are cached.
- Storage: Config entries per route should be < 5KB.
- Security: Policies are tenant-scoped; only route owners or org admins can modify. Policy changes produce audit log entries.
- Scalability: Decision service must support 10k policy evaluations/sec in hosted control-plane.

Quality and evaluation metrics:
- Primary: % availability preserved during simulated pressure (target 99.9%).
- Secondary: mean quality delta measured by tenant eval-set (target median delta <= 12% for first fidelity step).
- Cost: estimated per-request compute savings aggregated over a week when enabled.

Policy schema and validation rules (table):
| Field | Type | Description | Constraints | Default |
|-------|------|-------------|-------------|---------|
| max_latency_ms | int | Target latency SLO for route | >50 and <5000 | 250 |
| steps | list | Ordered degradation steps | 1..5 steps | n/a |
| step.id | string | Unique step id | Alphanumeric + dashes | required |
| step.type | enum | model_variant, structured_output, token_cap | one of allowed types | required |
| step.triggers | object | Trigger predicates | See triggers table | required |

Triggers supported (examples):
- p95_latency_ms > X
- region_capacity_utilization > 0.Y
- error_rate_5m > Z

Rollout plan and milestones:
1. Discovery & API design (4w): finalize schema, UX mockups, security review. Owner: Product.
2. Control-plane implementation (6w, parallel): policy store, validation, audit logs. Owner: Eng - Platform.
3. Runtime integration (8w, parallel): sidecar decision path and tagging. Owner: Eng - Serving Runtime.
4. Telemetry & Console (6w): ingest metrics, add Console charts, preview. Owner: Eng - Platform + DX.
5. Canary (4w): enable for 5 pilot tenants (internal and 2 customers) with manual ops rollout.
6. GA and docs (2w): runbook, migration guide, public docs.

Total expected lead time to GA: ~6 months when run in parallel across teams.

Canary strategy and criteria:
- Canary targets: internal app (redwood-console), two low-risk customers (consent obtained).
- Success criteria: degrade invocation latency saved >=20% on average when triggered, quality delta within targets on golden prompts, rollback operates within 30s.

Observability and traces:
- Trace annotation: fidelity.step_id, fidelity.trigger_reason, fidelity.pre_estimated_cost_savings.
- New dashboards: Per-tenant fidelity events, per-route decision timelines, quality-delta over time.
- Light eval proxy: asynchronously scores a sample of degraded responses vs golden outputs and writes fidelity.quality.delta metrics.

Console UX and admin surfaces:
- Policy editor (advanced mode) + simple toggle view for quick enable/disable.
- Preview pane that runs 10 selected tenant prompts through simulated steps and highlights the expected change and calculated similarity score.
- Billing view: projected weekly savings and number of degraded requests.

Pricing & packaging considerations:
- Feature will be available to Dedicated and Hosted customers; Private customers require on-prem runtime compatibility (see Dependencies).
- Default offering: included for paid hosted accounts.
- Enterprise add-on: compliance-mode support (audit retention > 1 year) and SRE-assisted rollout for a fee.
- Pricing note: this feature only provides estimated savings; it does not change per-token metering. For enterprise contracts that purchase Dedicated reserved capacity, assist with a consultancy bundle to define safe policies and guardrails.

Migration guidance for existing customers:
1. Audit existing fallback policies and route-level fallbacks.
2. Create tenant fidelity policy in a staging environment and run Console preview.
3. Schedule controlled canary; monitor fidelity.quality.delta metrics and SLO burn.
4. If unacceptable quality delta, tighten triggers or reduce allowed steps.

Operational runbook (short):
1. Detect: Alert fires when fidelity.degradation.count ratio > 0.1 for 5m.
2. Investigate: Check Console traces for step IDs and triggers.
3. Mitigate: If quality regressions exceed thresholds, temporarily set route.policy = disabled for tenant via PATCH API.
4. Remediate: If regional capacity is the root cause, trigger cross-region failover per existing runbook.
5. Postmortem: Capture decision timeline and attach to incident.

Security, privacy, and compliance considerations:
- Policies are tenant-scoped with RBAC. Audit logs record author, timestamp, and diff.
- For regulated customers, disabling automated degradation is permitted via compliance-mode.
- The light eval proxy only uses anonymized prompt-sets unless tenant opts in to provide labeled prompts.

Dependencies and risks:
- Control-plane policy store and Config Service availability.
- Serving runtime integration complexity (must maintain <=3ms added latency).
- Risk of customer surprise: need strong Console previews and defaults.

Open questions (to resolve in discovery):
- Should token-cap steps be metered differently in billing reports? (Finance)
- What are acceptable default quality deltas per model family? (Applied ML)
- How to limit cross-tenant test data exposure for light eval proxy? (Security)

Ownership and contacts:
- Product Owner: Maya Thompson (product)
- Eng - Platform: Owen Martinez
- Eng - Serving Runtime: Ethan Park
- Applied ML / Quality: Rhea Kapoor
- Customer Success contact for pilot: Priya Desai

Appendices:
A. Example CLI to preview a route policy:

$ curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/routes/rt-123/preview-fidelity \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \
  -d '{"policy": {"max_latency_ms":250, "steps": [{"id":"summ","type":"structured_output","template":"summarize_first_paragraph","triggers": {"p95_latency_ms":350}}]}}'

Returns: JSON with simulated outputs, similarity scores, and estimated cost delta.

B. Minimal policy validation pseudo-rules:
1. steps.length between 1 and 5.
2. each step.id unique.
3. triggers reference only supported telemetry keys.
4. total allowed token caps cannot be lower than 32 tokens.

C. Glossary:
- Fidelity step: an ordered transformation with lower compute or stricter output budget.
- Light eval proxy: asynchronous scoring service for quality delta estimation.

Document change log:
- 2026-09-07: Draft created (Maya Thompson).
- 2026-09-14: Added policy schema and rollout timeline (Ethan Park).
- 2026-09-21: Updated console UX notes and canary criteria (Rhea Kapoor).

title: dsid_beb19079228343409daf97737c1c765f__runbook-interoperability-decision-exchange-retrospective-2026.txt
text:
Runbook Interoperability and Decision Exchange Retrospective

Summary:

This retrospective summarizes the 10-week program to standardize runbook formats, build a "Decision Exchange" API for cross-operator coordination, and validate machine-readable runbook execution in the operator UI. The goal was to reduce mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for multi-service incidents and decrease cognitive overhead during cross-team escalations.

Why we did this:
- Repeated friction during cross-service incidents: multiple teams maintained incompatible runbook formats (Markdown, Google Docs, and ad-hoc checklists).
- Operators spent an average of 12 minutes just locating the canonical remediation step during multi-tenant KV prefix cache incidents.
- Lack of a standard resulted in inconsistent automation integration (PagerDuty, CLI, and operator UI).

Timeline and scope:
1. Week 1–2: discovery and inventory of 87 runbooks across platform services (allocator, prefetch, kv-cache, router).
2. Week 3–4: design of runbook schema (YAML-first) and Decision Exchange API v0.1 (GET /decisions, POST /decisions).
3. Week 5–7: prototype integration with Operator UI and PagerDuty webhook enrichment.
4. Week 8–10: canary validation during two synthetic cross-region degradations and one real incident (prefetch feedback-loop regression 2026-11-28).

Key artifacts produced:
- runbook-schema-v1.yaml (YAML schema with fields: id, intent, preconditions, steps[], automated_actions[], rollback_steps[], runbook_owner, sla_impact_estimate).
- decision-exchange-api.md (open API spec with example payloads).
- operator-ui-integration.md (how-to for embedding machine steps into the UI).

What we measured (metrics):
- MTTA (multi-service incidents) dropped from 8.6 min -> 5.1 min (40% improvement).
- Mean time to remediation (MTTR) for the prefetched cohort improved 18% in canary windows.
- Number of manual copy-paste steps during operator handoff decreased from median 3 -> 0.
- False-automation-trigger rate: 0.6% (target < 1%).

Principal findings and root causes:
- Fragmented formats: 52% of runbooks were not parsable without manual normalization (HTML exports, images-as-steps).
- Missing preconditions: 34% lacked explicit guardrails; automated actions ran in unsafe states.
- Ownership ambiguity: 9 runbooks pointed to deprecated pagerduty services causing stale escalation paths.
- UI/automation mismatch: Operator UI displayed steps but had no canonical action IDs. That prevented safe idempotent automation.

Decisions taken during the program:
- Adopt YAML-first machine-readable runbook schema as the canonical repository format (human-authorable, machine-validated). Owner: eng-platform/runbooks team.
- Introduce Decision Exchange API v1 with explicit decision objects that can be referenced in runbooks by ID. Owner: eng-platform/systems-and-services.
- Deprecate Google Doc canonical runbooks by 2027-02-01; migrate to git-backed runbook repo with CI validation (see rollout steps).
- All automated_actions must include a safety_check expression and a post-check step (schema mandatory fields).

Rollout and migration plan (high-level):
1. Create a git repo: git@internal:runbooks/canonical.git with a protected main branch and CI that lints runbook-schema-v1.yaml.
2. Bulk normalization: scripts/normalize_runbooks.py converts Markdown/HTML to YAML and raises a migration ticket per runbook.
3. Two-week canary: onboard allocator and router runbooks to Decision Exchange API (traffic routed to canary tenant IDs).
4. Complete migration: all platform runbooks on canonical.git; deprecate older sources with redirect pages.

Sample runbook schema (excerpt):
```yaml
id: runbook-alloc-prefetch-001
intent: "Recover prefetch feedback loop when latency spike > 200ms for 3m"
preconditions:
  - metric: prefetch.latency_p50
    operator: '>'
    value: 200
    window: 180
steps:
  - id: s1-check-queue-depth
    description: "Confirm queue depth and correlate tenant traffic"
    manual: true
  - id: s2-disable-prefetch
    description: "Toggle prefetch cohort to read-only"
    automated_action: "/api/v1/operator/actions/disable-prefetch?cohort={{cohort}}"
    safety_check: "prefetch.in_flight_tokens < 10000"
rollback_steps:
  - id: r1-reenable-prefetch
```
