```yaml
    description: "Re-enable prefetch after metrics normalize"
owner: team-sdk/allocator
```

Operator playbook changes (how-to snippets):
- PagerDuty webhook enrichment: include decision_id and runbook_id in the incident payload. Example payload snippet: {"incident": {"id": "P12345", "runbook_id": "runbook-alloc-prefetch-001", "decision_ids": ["dec-20261128-01"]}}
- CLI helper to fetch the latest runbook and render actionable steps: `ri runbook fetch runbook-alloc-prefetch-001 --format=tty`
- Safe-automation invocation example: `ri runbook exec --action s2-disable-prefetch --dry-run`

Compatibility matrix (summary text table):
- Services tested: allocator, prefetch, kv-cache, router, regional-allocator.
- Supported pipelines: operator-ui (v2.3+), pagerduty-enricher (v1.5+), cli-tooling (ri v0.9+).

Lessons learned (opportunities and cautions):
- Start with schema-first: earlier attempts to retrofit parsers were far more expensive than agreeing on a minimal schema.
- Human readability matters: templates must include natural-language step descriptions, not just machine fields.
- CI linting is critical: first week of migration caught 17 runbooks with missing safety_check fields.
- Backwards compatibility: keep an adapter service for 6 months to translate old Google Doc links for on-call flows.

Action items (owners and deadlines):
- [eng-platform/runbooks] Create canonical.git and CI pipeline (owner: Jordan Li) — due 2026-12-20.
- [eng-serving-runtime] Add safety_check telemetry and post-action assertions (owner: Priya Rao) — due 2027-01-10.
- [eng-platform/systems-and-services] Ship Decision Exchange API v1 and documentation (owner: Miguel Torres) — due 2026-12-31.
- [eng-platform/operator-tools] Add `ri` CLI runbook commands and dry-run support (owner: Ethan Brooks) — due 2027-01-15.
- [platform-ops] Migrate top 20 high-frequency runbooks (allocator, router, kv-cache) and validate canary metrics (owner: Runbook Migration Squad) — due 2027-02-01.

Risk register and mitigations:
- Risk: Automated actions run during partial preconditions leading to degradation. Mitigation: Safety checks mandatory + CI enforcement + canary gating.
- Risk: Team pushback on moving away from Google Docs. Mitigation: Provide a thin UI that renders YAML as a readable document and export back to PDF for stakeholders.

Follow-up experiments (next 3 months):
1. Decision Exchange subscription model: allow teams to subscribe to decisions for their services and auto-populate incident timelines. Metric: reduction of duplicate manual steps.
2. Automated precondition simulator: a test harness that runs safety_check expressions in a sandbox against synthetic telemetry. Metric: percentage of false-positive safety checks detected.
3. Runbook “confidence” scoring exposed as a dashboard panel in Platform SLOs (scale 0–100).

Owner contacts and escalation map:
- Program lead: Asha Patel (asha@redwood.ai)
- API owner: Miguel Torres (miguel@redwood.ai)
- Runbook CI: Jordan Li (jordan@redwood.ai)
- Operator tooling: Ethan Brooks (ethan@redwood.ai)

Appendix: sample Decision Exchange payloads and CI lint rules
- Decision object example (JSON):
```json
{
  "id": "dec-20261128-01",
  "title": "Disable prefetch cohort B",
  "rationale": "prefetch.latency_p50 > 200ms for 3m",
  "actions": ["/api/v1/operator/actions/disable-prefetch?cohort=B"],
  "author": "jordan@redwood.ai",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-28T03:41:00Z"
}
```
- CI lint checks (examples):
  - schema:valid -> runbook must validate against runbook-schema-v1.yaml
  - fields:owner -> owner must be a team alias in TEAM_ALIASES.yaml
  - safety:present -> any automated_action must include a safety_check expression

Conclusion:
The runbook interoperability program achieved meaningful operator efficiency wins and created a repeatable pattern for machine-readable runbooks tied to a Decision Exchange. The next quarter focuses on completing migration, hardening safety checks, and exposing runbook confidence to platform dashboards so product teams can prioritize remediations that reduce operational toil.

Related documents and links:
- See runbook-schema-v1.yaml (attached in canonical.git)
- Decision Exchange API spec: /internal-api/specs/decision-exchange-v1
- Operator UI integration how-to: /confluence/eng-platform/how-tos/operator-ui-integration-guide-2026

title: dsid_803c1c97739d4bef99720d3d08f9c62d__vpc-terraform-modules-alpha-overview.txt
text:
VPC Terraform modules (alpha) – suite overview (AWS / Redwood Private)

## Summary
This page provides a high-level overview of the **VPC Terraform modules (alpha)** shipped in the `redwood-terraform` repository for **Redwood Private (AWS VPC + optional on-prem connectivity)** deployments.

The intent is to reduce networking variability during customer discovery/pilots by providing **Redwood-validated defaults** for:
- VPC + subnet layout
- routing + NAT strategy
- VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) + DNS behavior
- baseline security group patterns
- flow logs + log destinations
- IAM scaffolding (permission-boundary-friendly) for installer execution
- integration hooks for VPN / Direct Connect (placeholders)

This is **foundational infrastructure only**. Cluster install and application components are handled by **redwood-private-installer / Helm**.

---

## Goals (alpha)
1. Provide opinionated, composable modules with safe defaults that work for most Private deployments.
2. Expose a controlled set of inputs/overrides with clearly documented constraints.
3. Standardize outputs that the **Redwood Private installer** can consume (or preflight-validate).
4. Ship a repeatable validation pipeline (fmt/validate/tflint/checkov + integration tests).
5. Make Solutions Engineering/Pro Services successful in POCs with reference examples.

### Non-goals (alpha)
- Multi-cloud parity (GCP/Azure) beyond stubs/roadmap notes.
- Turnkey “one click” end-to-end environment + cluster install.
- Supporting every enterprise topology; instead we document **supported extension points** and anti-patterns.

---

## Where these modules fit in Redwood Private
**Typical flow (AWS):**
1) Customer (or SE/PS) runs Terraform modules to create the networking + foundational IAM/logging.
2) Terraform outputs are used to configure and run `redwood-private-installer`.
3) Installer performs preflight checks (endpoints, DNS, egress) and then installs cluster add-ons / Redwood services.

**Key integration points with the installer:**
- Subnet IDs for worker/node groups (private subnets) and (optional) ingress subnets
- VPC endpoints presence + Private DNS behavior (ECR is the most common failure mode)
- Egress strategy and allowed destinations (NAT vs proxy patterns)
- Log destinations for auditability (Flow Logs -> CloudWatch or S3)
- IAM execution role for installer with permission boundaries

**Design principle:** Modules must produce a predictable, supportable footprint that aligns with the reference architecture and installer assumptions.

---

## Module suite (alpha)
Modules are designed to be composable. You can use the full suite, or bring your own VPC and only use endpoints/logging/IAM patterns.

> Naming note: module source paths below reflect the `modules/` layout in `redwood-terraform`. Actual module names in docs/examples should match the repository README for the released tag.

### Module list and responsibilities
| Module | Primary responsibility | Key resources created | Typical inputs (high-level) | Key outputs (for consumers/installer) | Primary owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `modules/vpc` | Opinionated VPC + subnet topology + routing defaults for Private deployments | VPC, subnets (public/private), route tables, IGW (optional), NAT gateways (default per-AZ), NACL defaults | `vpc_cidr`, `az_count`, `private_subnet_cidrs`, `public_subnet_cidrs` (optional), `nat_mode` (default: per_az) | `vpc_id`, `private_subnet_ids`, `public_subnet_ids`, route table IDs | Infra Eng (Networking): Victor Alvarez |
| `modules/vpc-endpoints` | Required/recommended VPC endpoints + Private DNS controls | Interface + gateway endpoints (S3 gateway; ECR API/DKR; STS; CloudWatch Logs; EC2; EKS; SSM/SSMMessages; KMS as needed) | `vpc_id`, `subnet_ids`, `endpoint_policy_mode`, `private_dns_enabled` per-service | `endpoint_ids`, `endpoint_sg_id`, resolved endpoint service set | Infra Eng (Networking): Victor Alvarez |
| `modules/logging-flow-logs` | Flow Logs defaults and destinations for auditability | VPC Flow Logs, IAM role/policy (CW option), CW Log Group or S3 target wiring | `destination_type` (cloudwatch|s3), `retention_days` (CW), `s3_bucket_arn` (customer-owned recommended), `traffic_type` | `flow_log_id`, destination identifiers, IAM role ARN (CW) | Security Eng + Infra: Kevin Osei / Irene Choi |
| `modules/security-groups` | Opinionated SG patterns for Private EKS footprints | SGs for nodes, control plane access patterns (where applicable), endpoint SG, egress SG patterns | `vpc_id`, `cluster_cidr`, `allowed_admin_cidrs` (optional), `egress_mode` | SG IDs for nodes/endpoints/ingress, egress rule summaries | Infra Eng + Private Deployments: Nina Petrova / Victor Alvarez |
| `modules/iam-installer` | IAM scaffolding for installer execution with permission boundaries | IAM role, policies, optional permission boundary attachment points | `role_name`, `permission_boundary_arn`, `tags`, `policy_mode` | `installer_role_arn`, policy ARNs, external ID placeholders (if used) | Security Eng: Marcus Lin / Hanae Suzuki |
| `modules/connectivity-hooks` | Placeholders/outputs for VPN/DX integration without encoding enterprise-specific assumptions | Minimal route propagation hooks, output structure for VGW/TGW attachment IDs (if supplied) | `tgw_id` (optional), `customer_cidrs`, `route_table_ids` | route table IDs, attachment placeholders, documented extension points | Solutions Eng + Infra: Markus Klein / Irene Choi |

### Recommended consumption patterns
**Pattern A (most common): Full suite**
- Use `vpc` + `vpc-endpoints` + `logging-flow-logs` + `security-groups` + `iam-installer`

**Pattern B: Customer-managed VPC**
- Customer provides `vpc_id`, subnets, route tables
- Use `vpc-endpoints` + `logging-flow-logs` + `iam-installer` (and optionally `security-groups`)

**Pattern C: Strict enterprise connectivity (TGW/VPN/DX)**
- Use Pattern A or B
- Add `connectivity-hooks` and follow documented extension points (customer network team implements attachments and routing)

---

## Supported topologies (alpha)
Supported topologies are intentionally narrow for supportability.

### Baseline topology
- **2 or 3 Availability Zones** (3 recommended)
- **Private subnets** for cluster nodes and internal services
- Optional **public subnets** for managed ingress where customer policy permits (otherwise use private ingress + customer-provided LBs)
- **NAT gateways**:
  - Default: **per-AZ NAT** (resilience)
  - Supported override: **single NAT** (cost optimization; lower availability)

### DNS assumptions
- VPC DNS support and hostnames **enabled**.
- Interface endpoints often rely on **Private DNS** for “just works” behavior.
- If Private DNS must be disabled (rare), the deployment guide requires explicit endpoint-specific DNS handling and installer preflight will warn.

### Endpoint expectations
- At minimum, endpoints required to avoid image pull / control-plane dependencies in private subnets:
  - **ECR (api + dkr)**
  - **S3 (gateway)**
  - **STS**
  - **CloudWatch Logs** (if using CW logging destinations)
- Additional endpoints may be required depending on cluster setup and customer controls (SSM, KMS, EKS, EC2).

---

## Ownership, support model, and escalation
**Primary ownership:** Infrastructure Engineering (AWS networking + IaC)
- Tech lead: **Irene Choi**
- Networking: **Victor Alvarez**

**Security reviews and defaults:** Security Engineering
- IAM boundaries: **Marcus Lin**, **Hanae Suzuki**
- Logging/SIEM guidance: **Kevin Osei**

**Private deployment constraints:** Private Deployments Engineering
- Topology constraints + installer integration: **Nina Petrova**

**Field enablement:** Solutions Engineering / Pro Services
- Field feedback + pilot readiness: **Markus Klein**

**Escalation path (alpha):**
1) #eng-infra (first response; triage)
2) #eng-private-deployments (installer constraints / cluster topology)
3) #eng-security (IAM/logging/security posture)

---

## Compatibility matrix (alpha)
This matrix defines what we test in CI and what we will support during alpha pilots.

| Component | Supported (alpha) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Terraform CLI | `>= 1.6.x` | CI pins to a minimum version and also runs a “latest stable” lane when feasible. |
| AWS Provider | `~> 5.x` | Provider versions are pinned for reproducibility; update requires CI green + security scan review. |
| Target AWS partitions | `aws` (commercial) | GovCloud is not validated in alpha; track separately with Security/Compliance. |
| Regions | Common commercial regions (us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-west-1) | Others may work; not all are covered by integration tests. |
| EKS assumption | Yes | Reference architecture assumes EKS; modules are networking-first, but defaults align with EKS private cluster patterns. |

---

## Interfaces: inputs/outputs (design intent)
The module interfaces are designed around:
- **Minimal required inputs** for the happy path
- **Explicitly documented extension points** for enterprise needs
- **Stable outputs** that other modules and the installer depend on

Output stability is critical during alpha because customers will pin module versions and wire outputs into their own pipelines.

See: ADR-027 for module boundaries and the public interface philosophy.

---

## CI, validation, and integration tests
CI is designed to catch the most common failure modes before they reach pilots.

**Per-PR checks (gated):**
- `terraform fmt` and `terraform validate`
- tflint (AWS ruleset)
- checkov (baseline IaC security scanning)
- docs lint (where applicable)

**Integration tests:**
- Ephemeral environment tests (create/destroy) validate:
  - subnet + route table wiring
  - NAT assumptions across AZ counts
  - endpoint creation + Private DNS toggles
  - expected outputs exist and are non-empty

Heavier integration tests may be scheduled nightly to manage cost/time; PR gating remains focused on fast feedback.

See: ADR-028 for full acceptance criteria.

---

## Versioning and releases (alpha expectations)
- Semantic versioning is used (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).
- During alpha, we will avoid breaking changes, but **breaking changes may occur** if required for security/supportability.
- Design partners should pin exact tags and coordinate upgrades with Redwood.

Release process details are documented in the Terraform module versioning and release standard (see related pages).

---

## Known limitations (alpha)
- Not validated for GovCloud or air-gapped on-prem-only environments.
- DNS edge cases (custom resolvers, split-horizon) require careful design; we provide guidance but do not encode enterprise DNS appliances in modules.
- Connectivity (VPN/DX/TGW) is supported via hooks/outputs and patterns, not as a full turnkey module.
- Flow Logs cover VPC-level traffic; workload/cluster logs are handled by installer/cluster tooling.

---

## Getting started
1. Read the reference architecture: **AWS Private VPC reference architecture (EKS)**.
2. Follow the deployment guide: **Terraform VPC deployment guide (alpha)**.
3. Use the quickstart template (DevEx) to structure customer repos and tfvars.

If you are onboarding a design partner, align early on:
- CIDR ranges and subnet counts
- NAT strategy (per-AZ vs single)
- Required endpoints and Private DNS policy
- Logging destinations + retention
- IAM boundaries / execution role constraints

---

## Appendix: What “opinionated defaults” means here
These modules default to:
- private-by-default subnet usage
- endpoint-first access to AWS services to reduce public egress reliance
- logging enabled with explicit destinations
- least-privilege scaffolding with customer-managed permission boundaries

If a customer’s baseline violates one of these assumptions, treat it as an architecture review item and involve Infra + Security early.

title: dsid_95a841e7b302416b82dbe635f09788a1__audit-proofchain-temporal-binding-guideline-2024.txt
text:
Audit Proofchain: Temporal Binding and Authorization Evidence Guidelines

Summary:
This guideline defines the Audit Proofchain pattern: a tamper-evident, timebound method for synthesizing authorization (RBAC), audit logs, SDLC gate artifacts, and data residency assertions into a single evidence package suitable for compliance reviews and incident response. The goal is to make cross-domain verification deterministic for auditors and automated verification tooling.

Scope:
- Applies to hosted and private model-serving environments, CI/CD pipelines that touch model artifacts, and legal/regulatory evidence requests.
- Covers evidence collection, temporal binding (hashing + timestamping strategy), packaging, retention stamps, verification procedures, and exception handling.
- Not intended to replace the audit logging schema; it augments existing logs with cross-source correlation and proof packaging.

Terminology:
- Proofchain: an ordered chain of evidence artifacts with cryptographic hashes and timestamps that proves sequence and integrity.
- Residency Stamp: a metadata token asserting data-at-rest or data-in-motion residency constraints (region, tenancy, encryption key id).
- SDLC Gate Artifact: CI/CD output (build ID, test summary, security scan result) attached to a deployment.
- Evidence Package (EP): ZIP/LTSV container including metadata.json, provenance ledger, signed-hash index, and raw artifacts (logs, manifests).

Ownership and Roles:
- Security (owner): overall guideline steward, verification tooling, and auditor liaison.
- Eng-SRE: responsible for runtime log retention and initial proofchain anchoring.
- Eng-Serving-Runtime: supplies model-serving traces and KV cache snapshots when requested.
- Eng-Private-Deployments: enforces residency stamping for on-prem and VPC deployments.
- Legal/Compliance: defines evidence retention periods for each jurisdiction.

Prerequisites (technical):
- Centralized immutable audit stream (Kafka or Kinesis) with event IDs and logical clocks.
- Object storage with object immutability / WORM capabilities for long-term evidence packaging.
- HSM or KMS for signing index manifests (recommended).
- SDLC pipeline hooks that store gate artifacts in the same artifact registry used for releases.

Evidence sources (examples):
- RBAC change events: role grants/revocations, service-account provisioning, JIT activations.
- Authorization decision logs: grant/deny with reason and policy id.
- Access tokens and session lifecycle events (issuance, revocation).
- Audit logs: API calls, model invocation traces, configuration changes.
- SDLC artifacts: build id, commit hash, dependency SBOM, SCA scan, test-suite summary.
- Data residency metadata: storage region, encryption key id, residency policy id.
- Incident attachments: snapshot IDs, forensic captures, human-written investigator notes.

Proofchain creation (high-level steps):
1. Identify scope window: define start_ts and end_ts for the evidence window (e.g., 2025-02-01T00:00:00Z to 2025-02-01T04:00:00Z).
2. Collect canonical artifacts from each source. Use event IDs and logical clocks to avoid duplication.
3. Normalize artifacts to canonical form (JSONL for logs, canonicalized manifest for SDLC outputs).
4. Compute SHA-256 for each artifact and record: {artifact_path, sha256, size_bytes, source_service, event_id}.
5. Create provenance ledger (ordered list) that binds sequence using a parent hash field (proofchain): ledger[i].parent = ledger[i-1].entry_hash.
6. Timestamp the ledger using internal authoritative clock and submit ledger root hash to an external timestamping service (optional; recommended for legal non-repudiation).
7. Sign the signed-hash index with KMS/HSM key and persist signature metadata (key_id, sig_algo, sig_ts).
8. Package artifacts and manifests into Evidence Package (EP) and write to WORM storage with object metadata including residency stamps and retention policy id.
9. Emit an evidence-registration event to the central catalog (catalog_id) with EP location and summary.

Detailed packaging template (metadata.json fields):
| field | description | example |
|---|---:|---|
| ep_id | canonical evidence package id | ep-20250201-ff12 |
| scope_start | window start ts (ISO8601) | 2025-02-01T00:00:00Z |
| scope_end | window end ts (ISO8601) | 2025-02-01T04:00:00Z |
| artifacts_count | total artifacts included | 46 |
| ledger_root_hash | SHA-256 hex of provenance ledger root | 3f8a... |
| signed_index_sig | base64 signature of signed-index | AQAB... |
| residency_stamps | list of residency stamps (see below) | [us-west-2:KMS:arn:..., eu:...] |
| retention_policy_id | compliance retention policy id | retention-2027-default |
| created_by | service or user that created EP | eng-sre/evidence-batcher |

Residency stamping rules (table):
| scenario | stamp required | mandatory fields | retention baseline |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Hosted model invocation (US customer data) | region-stamp | region=us-west-2, key_id, tenant_id | 7 years |
| Private VPC on-prem | locality-stamp | dc_id, physical_location, cust_contact | per-customer policy |
| Cross-border inference | geo-proof | origin_country, transit_countries, residency_exception_id | consult Legal |

Automated CLI example (proofchain-batcher) (pseudo):
$ proofchain-batcher \n  --scope-start 2025-02-01T00:00:00Z \n  --scope-end 2025-02-01T04:00:00Z \n  --sources audit,k8s,svc-auth,ci \n  --sign-key arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:123:key/abcd1234 \n  --output s3://evidence-bucket/ep-20250201-ff12.zip

Verification checklist for auditors (procedural):
- Confirm EP metadata.json fields match requested scope.
- Verify signed_index_sig using the KMS public key (rotate key check).
- Recompute SHA-256 for a 10% random sample of artifacts and compare hashes.
- Confirm residency stamps: query storage object metadata and encryption key residency.
- Cross-check RBAC events against authorization decision logs (timestamps within scope).
- Ensure ledger parent hashes form an unbroken chain and root hash equals ledger_root_hash in metadata.json.

Incident response integration:
- When a security incident is created, responders must:
  1) Tag the incident with ep_id(s) capturing the pre-incident snapshot window.
  2) Generate a rapid evidence snapshot (rapid-ep) using the same proofchain flow but set retention to incident-retain-30d.
  3) If changing production for containment, record an explicit deployment gate SDLC artifact and append to EP with a new ledger entry.
  4) Preserve the signed-index and timestamp anchor as primary artifacts for any future investigation.

Risk and exception handling:
- Risk register: every exception that relaxes retention, stamping, or signing MUST be recorded in the Evidence Exceptions register with: exception_id, owner, justification, compensating controls, expiration_ts, and approver.
- Emergency exception flow (short-lived): on-call must file a fast-approval entry in the register within 4 business hours and create a compensating proof (e.g., notarized external timestamp).
- Common accepted exceptions: temporary replay of logs from ephemeral cache when persistent logs are not immediately available (max 72h).

Retention and SLAs:
- Baseline retention: 7 years for customer-facing access logs (unless legal dictates otherwise).
- Evidence packaging SLA: evidence package for a given window must be created and cataloged within 14 days of window end unless explicitly flagged for accelerated build (incident, audit request).
- Verification SLA for auditor requests: 3 business days for basic EP validation, 10 business days for deep verification.

Operational playbook (step-by-step):
1. Request initiation: Security or Compliance opens evidence request in the central catalog and assigns scope.
2. Batcher run: Eng-SRE runs proofchain-batcher for scope window.
3. KMS signing: Eng-SRE ensures signed-index signature recorded by KMS and key rotation is documented in register.
4. WORM persist: Store EP into evidence-bucket with residency tags and immutability flags.
5. Catalog update: Evidence catalog receives event and attaches EP to request and incident objects as needed.
6. Auditor verification: Compliance runs the verification checklist and records the result as pass/fail in the catalog.

Appendix A — Example provenance ledger entry (canonicalized JSONL line):
{
  "entry_hash": "af3b...",
  "parent": "d94c...",
  "artifact_path": "logs/k8s/api-server-20250201-0001.jsonl.gz",
  "sha256": "0f4b...",
  "source": "k8s-audit",
  "event_id": "kube-evt-9876543",
  "ts": "2025-02-01T00:01:12Z"
}

Appendix B — Related pages and references:
- /confluence/security-and-compliance/audit-logging/event-schema-contract-and-retention-runbook-2025 (event schema)
- /confluence/eng-private-deployments/customer-requirements-library/ (private deployment residency matrix)
- /confluence/security-and-compliance/secure-sdlc/sdlc-security-gates-rbac-audit-residency-checklist-2026 (SDLC gating)

FAQs (short):
Q: Can we omit SDLC artifacts for low-risk deployments?
A: Only with an approved exception recorded in the Evidence Exceptions register. Compensating controls (e.g., additional log retention or external timestamping) should be applied.

Q: How do we handle rotated keys for historical EPs?
A: The signature metadata must include the public key fingerprint and key rotation history. Old keys remain available in the key archive to allow signature verification.

Contact and escalation:
- Primary: Maya Chen (security) — maya.chen@redwood.ai
- On-call evidence engineer: eng-sre/evidence-batcher (pager)
- Legal/Compliance liaison: Arjun Patel — arjun.patel@redwood.ai

Change log:
- 2024-11-06: Draft created (initial pattern and packaging template).
- 2025-03-12: Revised residency stamping rules and incident integration flow.

title: dsid_9b12aabe7e854ee3acc02de71d3b11ba__slice-driven-eval-strategy-and-coverage-matrix-2026.txt
text:
Slice-Driven Evaluation Strategy and Coverage Matrix

Summary:
This doc defines a practical, repeatable approach to slice-driven evaluation for model onboarding, continuous monitoring, and regression triage. We introduce a standardized coverage matrix that maps user-visible subpopulations to concrete prompt templates, input transformations, expected metrics, and alerting thresholds. The procedure integrates with the eval harness, prompt catalog, and regression playbooks so slices can be exercised automatically during promotion and production monitoring.

Goals and scope:
- Provide a cataloging format for slices (why they matter, how to generate them, golden labels or heuristics).
- Define minimum coverage required before model promotion to canary and production tiers.
- Standardize metric families and thresholds (quality, latency, cost, safety) at slice granularity.
- Describe triage and escalation paths when slices fail or regress.
- Integrate with eval harness scheduling, annotation workflows, and prompt augmentation pipelines.

Definitions:
- Slice: a reproducible subpopulation of inputs defined by data attributes, prompt structure, user intent, or model behavior fingerprints.
- Coverage unit: a prompt variant + conditioning context + (optional) metadata filters used to exercise a slice.
- Reference distribution: the production-like distribution used for sampling each slice (deterministic or stochastic).
- Critical slice: a slice whose failure would cause user-visible loss or compliance exposure; requires strict gate thresholds.

Slice taxonomy (examples):
1) Demographic edge slices: short/long utterances with named-entity patterns, non-native idioms, locale-specific date formats.
2) Formatting robustness: inputs with broken markup, mixed-language code+text, or very long preambles.
3) Safety-sensitive: prompt templates likely to elicit policy-sensitive content (medical, legal, personal data).
4) Systemic failure modes: cache-eviction on long-context, kv-cache collision patterns, prefix-only prompts that rely on hidden state.
5) Business-critical intents: payment instructions, authentication flows, and billing queries.

Coverage matrix (canonical columns):
- slice_id: short-id used in eval harness (e.g., SLC-003-locales)
- description: plain-language slice description
- generators: prompt templates / sampling recipe (file paths or template ids)
- sample_size_promote: minimum sample count for promotion (canary/production)
- metrics: list of metric keys (e.g., exact_match, BLEU, toxicity_score, p95_latency)
- thresholds: per-metric pass/fail criteria (numeric or rule)
- priority: critical | high | medium | low
- owner: individual/team owning slice

Example coverage matrix rows (ASCII table):
| slice_id | description                       | generators                      | sample_size_promote | metrics                            | thresholds                                 | priority | owner            |
| SLC-001  | Short-utterance intent ambiguity  | prompt-templates/short-intent   | 100                 | exact_match, confusion_rate         | exact_match >= 0.9, confusion_rate <= 0.05 | high     | applied-ml       |
| SLC-012  | Non-English romanized names       | generators/romanized-names.yaml | 200                 | accuracy_top1, toxicity_score       | accuracy_top1 >= 0.85, toxicity_score < 0.02| critical | trust-safety     |
| SLC-021  | Billing flow canonical responses  | scenarios/billing-flow-v2       | 300                 | intent_accuracy, p95_latency_ms     | intent_accuracy >= 0.95, p95_latency_ms < 400| critical | product-payments |

(Maintain this table as CSV in the prompt catalog; the eval harness ingests it during scheduled runs.)

Metric families and recommended thresholds (default guidance):
- Quality: exact_match / intent_accuracy / semantic-similarity. Promotion gates: critical slices >= 95% (intent_accuracy) and non-critical >= 85%.
- Safety: toxicity_score / policy_violations. Gate: no policy_violations within sampled set for critical slices; toxicity_score median < 0.02.
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 in ms measured under canary traffic pattern. Gate: p95 <= 2x baseline for canary; p99 <= 4x baseline.
- Cost/efficiency: average tokens-per-inference and token-rate. Gate: tokens-per-inference should not regress >12% vs baseline without quality improvement.

Procedures:
1) Slice definition and registration (owner responsibility):
   a) Author a slice YAML in prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/slices/ with fields: slice_id, description, tags, generator_refs, sampling_policy, canonical_labels (if available), and owner.
   b) Add entry to coverage CSV and assign priority.
   c) Add human-readable examples (min 10 positives, 10 negatives) to the annotation queue.

2) Pre-promotion evaluation (on dev model):
   a) Run the eval harness scheduled job for candidate model across all slices with sample_size_promote.
   b) Produce slice-level report: metric deltas vs baseline, failure cases (10 worst), and suggested mitigations (prompt re-write, quant config, safety filter adjustment).
   c) If any critical slice fails gate, block promotion and route to model-onboarding owner for mitigation.

3) Canary / production monitoring:
   a) Instrument streaming sampling of production traffic by slicing heuristics (10% sample for non-critical, 100% of flagged critical events).
   b) Maintain rolling 24h and 7d slice-level dashboards with alerts:
      - Alert if intent_accuracy delta <= -5% absolute for critical slices over 24h.
      - Alert if p95_latency delta >= +40% over baseline for any slice.
   c) On alert: create regression ticket with auto-attached worst 20 examples and model fingerprints.

4) Regression triage flow (linked into regression-triage playbook):
   a) Initial responder (applied-ml) reproduces failure in eval harness by replaying examples and checking quantization, KV-cache behavior, and kernel traces.
   b) If reproducible in harness: create an action plan — either revert to prior model, apply prompt shim, or schedule targeted retraining/augmentation.
   c) If not reproducible: escalate to eng-serving-runtime to collect runtime traces (batching patterns, GPU kernel mismatches, memory pressure).

Generator and sampling recipes (implementation notes):
- Generators should be idempotent and parameterized. A recipe must specify seeding strategy, slot variables, and post-processing steps (e.g., normalize whitespace, simulate user typos).
- Use the existing prompt catalog format. Example generator snippet (YAML):

  name: romanized-names-v1
  seed: 1234
  slots:
    - name: name
      source: samples/romanized-names.txt
  post_process:
    - lowercase: true
    - inject_typo: 0.12

- Sampling policy should include rarity multipliers for long-tail slices and a production-weighted sampling option for continuous monitoring.

Integration with eval harness scheduling and priorities:
- Each slice row contains schedule metadata: nightly | weekly | on-demand.
- Critical slices: nightly full run + real-time sampling. High: nightly partial run (50% samples). Medium: weekly. Low: on-demand.
- The eval harness must tag results with model_version, quantization_profile, and execution_profile (batch_size, nvlink topology) to aid kernel-level correlation.

Ownership, SLAs, and backlog:
- Owners are responsible for: keeping generator recipes runnable, maintaining 20 example golden set, and responding to slice alerts within 8 business hours for critical slices and 3 business days for non-critical.
- Applied-ML team SLA: initial triage within 4 business hours for critical slice alerts during business hours; 12 hours off-hours.
- Eng-serving-runtime SLA: provide runtime traces and kernel logs within 24 hours of escalation.

Operational considerations and pitfalls:
- Beware of overlapping slices: maintain a slice-priority resolution policy to avoid duplicate alerts. Match examples to a single primary slice for ownership clarity.
- Avoid synthetic-only slices without production validation: flag these as research-only and run at reduced frequency.
- Quantization sensitivity: add a quant-profile column to the matrix so slices known to be quant-sensitive are tested under every promoted quant profile.

Onboarding checklist for adding a new slice (summary):
1) Draft YAML generator + 50 seed examples.
2) Add CSV row to coverage matrix with sample sizes and thresholds.
3) Run one-off eval harness job and confirm example coverage.
4) Add golden examples to annotation tool and label 10 positives/10 negatives.
5) Assign owner and set schedule.

Appendices:
- A: Example slice YAML (path: prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/slices/SLC-012-romanized-names.yaml)
- B: Example eval harness command: 
  ./harness/run_eval --model vX.Y --coverage-file coverage.csv --slices SLC-001,SLC-012 --output reports/vX.Y/slice_report.json
- C: Recommended labels taxonomy: accessibility, performance, safety, locale, intent, long-context, quant-sensitive

Contacts and escalation map:
- Applied ML (owner): maya.patel@redwood.ai
- Trust & Safety: trust-safety@redwood.ai
- Runtime: runtime-observability@redwood.ai

Revision history:
- 2025-11-03: created (Maya Patel)
- 2026-01-10: updated thresholds and added generator policy (Liam O'Connor)
- 2026-02-14: adjusted SLAs and incorporated triage links (Aisha Khan)

Related artifacts (where to store supporting files):
- prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/slices/ (YAML generators and examples)
- prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/coverage.csv (canonical table)
- eval-harness/reports/slice_reports/ (historical runs)
- regression-triage/cases/ (auto-created tickets and evidence)

title: dsid_0b1807249cc04a02a141b07d2bb09b19__zero-trust-inference-mesh-and-authz-policy-2024.txt
text:
Zero-Trust Inference Mesh and Authorization Policy

Overview:

This document defines Redwood's zero-trust service mesh and authorization policy tailored for inference workloads. It covers authentication, per-request authorization, sidecar behavior, and operational constraints that preserve latency and throughput SLOs for model serving. The goal is to provide a repeatable, secure pattern that applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment modes while minimizing change to inference runtime paths.

Goals:
- Guarantee mutual authentication between edge and inference runtime with short-lived credentials.
- Enforce least-privilege per-request authorization for sensitive operations (model downloads, cache priming, admin endpoints).
- Limit auth-related latency impact on P95/P99 token generation and validation to within budget.
- Provide an auditable trail for data access tied to request metadata and tenant identifiers.

Scope:
- Applies to: edge-proxy -> gateway -> model-router -> runtime sidecar -> model process flow.
- Not in scope: developer local environments (see local-dev-auth.md), CI systems (see infra/cicd-authz).

Key constraints and rationale:
- Inference paths are latency sensitive: auth verification must not add more than 2ms median and 8ms P99 on top of baseline CPU-bound path for small requests (<=128 tokens). Where strict cryptographic checks add overhead, use a hybrid approach (local cache + async audit).
- Private deployments must support customer KMS-provisioned signing keys for identity issuance. Hosted and Dedicated deployments will use Redwood KMS and short-lived certificates.

Authentication model (workload identity):
1) Workloads obtain identities via a short-lived certificate issued by Redwood Identity Service (RIS) or customer KMS in Private mode. Certificates TTL default = 5 minutes.
2) Sidecars validate peer certificates using mTLS on all intra-cluster RPCs.
3) For cross-region/gateway calls, TLS with JWT delegation tokens is used (see JWT section).

Authorization model (per-request):
- Authorization decisions are made by the runtime sidecar using a local policy cache (sync'd from central Policy Store) and request attributes: tenant_id, model_id, route, cost_tier, and request_tag.
- Use a simple allow/deny policy language that supports attribute match, TTL, and rate-limited allow exceptions for emergency fallbacks.

Service and policy names (examples):
- redwood-identity-service (RIS) - issues short-lived certs and JWTs
- redwood-policy-store - canonical source of RBAC/ABAC policy for sidecars
- redwood-sidecar-authz - local enforcer embedded with runtime
- redwood-audit-collector - consumes signed request logs

Operational SLOs and thresholds:
- auth.cert_issue_latency.p95 <= 40ms
- sidecar.authz_check.p95 <= 5ms
- auth.failure_rate (production traffic) <= 0.01% per day
- audit.log_delivery_success >= 99.5% over 24h window
- sidecar.cpu_overhead median <= +6% vs. baseline; sidecar.mem_overhead <= +80MB per replica

Metrics to emit (suggested):
- auth.cert_issue_latency_p50/p95/p99
- sidecar.authz_check_latency_p50/p95/p99
- authz.decision.allowed_count, authz.decision.denied_count
- auth.token_replay_detected_count
- audit.log_enqueued_count, audit.log_delivery_latency_p95

Policy sync and cache semantics:
- Policy Store publishes delta snapshots every 30s; sidecars fetch full snapshot every 15m.
- Policy cache TTL default = 60s; stale-while-revalidate applies for 5s to reduce blocking on transient connectivity.
- If policy validation cannot be performed and request is critical (health-check, internal-mgmt), default to deny but trigger emergency fallback policy if configured by owner.

Example Authorization Rule (pseudocode):
- allow if tenant_id == request.token.tenant and model_id in tenant.allowed_models and request.route != admin_endpoint
- deny otherwise

YAML example: (Envoy JWT + simple RBAC mapping)
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-inference-calls
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inference-sidecar
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        requestPrincipals: ["spiffe://redwood/tenant/{{tenant_id}}/workload/*"]
    to:
    - operation:
        paths: ["/v1/generate", "/v1/embed"]
    when:
    - key: "model_id"
      values: ["model-*-public", "model-tenant-*"]
---
# JWT validation snippet (gateway)
jwt_validation: |
  {
    "issuer": "https://ris.redwood.internal/",
    "audiences": ["redwood-inference"],
    "jwks_uri": "https://ris.redwood.internal/.well-known/jwks.json"
  }

Performance and runtime considerations:
- Use local cache of JWT public keys and cert chains; rotate keys with grace_period = 30s.
- Offload heavy crypto to a shared crypto worker pool accessible by sidecars (gRPC interface). This avoids per-pod CPU spikes.
- For small requests, prefer symmetric MAC verification for internal delegation tokens to reduce cost; asymmetric signatures remain for cross-boundary calls.

Audit and signing requirements:
- Every inference request that touches models marked PII or regulated must record a signed audit entry containing: timestamp, tenant_id, model_id, request_hash, auth_decision, sidecar_id.
- Audit entries are batched and pushed to redwood-audit-collector; batch max interval = 5s, max size = 200 entries.
- In Private deployments, customers may opt-in for on-prem audit storage; sidecars must support local filesystem buffer + forwarder.

Rollout plan (gated):
1) Canary 1 (internal infra): deploy sidecar authz to 2% of traffic on non-critical models. Run for 48h.
   - Verification checks: authz.allowed_rate ~ expected, authz.denied_rate ~ 0, auth.latency overhead < 5ms P95.
2) Canary 2 (customer-facing read-only routes): increase to 10% for 72h.
   - Add synthetic traffic with edge-case JWTs (expired, malformed, tenant-mismatch).
3) Partial rollout: 50% of inference pods, 7 days. Monitor CPU and latency budgets.
4) Full rollout: all inference pods; enable audit batching.

Rollback criteria:
- sidecar.authz_check_latency_p95 increases > 8ms continually for 1h
- increased 5xx rate on runtime endpoints by > 0.2% absolute
- audit.log_delivery_success < 98% for 1h

Operational runbook (high level):
1) If sidecar authz failures spike: check policy-store connectivity, RIS health, cert TTLs.
2) For token replay: identify sidecar_id and revoke the token series via RIS; initiate tenant notification if necessary.
3) If audit backlog grows > 10k entries: temporarily drop non-regulated audit entries and prioritize PII/regulatory audits.

Permissions and ownership:
- Policy Store: eng-platform (primary), security (secondary)
- RIS (identity service): eng-infra (primary), security (secondary)
- Sidecar authz enforcer: eng-serving-runtime (primary), security (secondary)
- Audit collector and retention policy: security (primary), eng-sre (secondary)

Testing checklist before promotion:
- Unit tests for policy compile/parse and edge cases (missing attributes, wildcard matching).
- Integration tests: sidecar with a local Policy Store (simulate 30s delta + full snapshot).
- Load test: sidecar under synthetic mixed traffic at production QPS for 2h.
- Chaos: simulate policy-store partition and verify stale-while-revalidate behavior.

Related pages and references:
- /confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026
- RIS design doc (internal link: ris/design-2024)

Appendix: short JWT validation example (pseudo-CLI)
$ curl -s -X POST https://ris.redwood.internal/token 
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
  -d '{"aud": "redwood-inference", "sub": "tenant:acme:router"}'

Response: {"access_token":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...","expires_in":300} 

Table: example policy attributes and defaults:
Attribute | Default | Notes
--------- | ------- | -----
policy_cache_ttl | 60s | sidecar-side default
cert_ttl | 5m | short-lived to reduce key compromise window
audit_batch_interval | 5s | max buffering before push
crypto_worker_pool_size | 8 | adjustable per-node based on CPU

Contact and escalation:
- Security on-call: security-oncall@redwood.ai
- Policy Store owner: eng-platform@redwood.ai
- Runtime sidecar owner: eng-serving-runtime@redwood.ai

Document lifecycle:
- Review cadence: quarterly for threat model updates and annually for retention and TTL defaults.
- Primary reviewer for next revision: Liam O'Connor.

End of document.

title: dsid_988d5adb48064bf1a8d4b3300ab1924f__gpu-burst-simulation-lab-playbook.txt
text:
GPU burst simulation lab: canary & capacity safety playbook

Overview

This playbook describes the GPU burst simulation lab: a reproducible, CI-driven environment for exercising burst scenarios across networking, tenant routing, and the GPU allocator. The lab is used by infra, SRE and runtime teams to validate autoscaler policies, egress/fair-share shapers, and fallback behavior before capacity changes or kernel/runtime rollouts.

Goals

- Provide a repeatable CI job that simulates tenant-level bursts with controllable demand profiles.
- Validate safety gates: preemptive warm-pool seeding, spot fallback, and network egress shaping.
- Measure SLO impact (p50/p95 latency, tail queuing, eviction rate) and billing/backpressure signals.
- Ensure Terraform/IaC promos and CD pipelines require an acceptance signal from the lab for changes touching allocator, egress, or tenancy modules.

Scope

- Included: simulated multi-tenant traffic (small, medium, large), allocator scaling behavior, cross-account egress shaping, and kernel rollout fallback.
- Excluded: hardware firmware upgrades, long-running production migrations, customer data.

High-level architecture

1) Lab control plane (k8s in staging account) — runs orchestrator, metrics collection, and synthetic tenants.
2) Workload generators — containerized drivers that spawn inference sessions across hostnames, varying sequence lengths and concurrency.
3) Allocator & Autoscaler (staged TF modules + runtime canary) — deployed from CI pipelines into the staging account.
4) Egress shaping sidecar — simulates network throttles and NAT pool exhaustion.
5) Verdict engine — aggregates metrics and decides pass/fail for CI gate.

Key SLOs and thresholds (lab failure triggers)

| Metric | Baseline | Failure threshold (lab gate) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| p50 gen latency (ms) | 35 | > 70 (avg across tenants) | measured at model route level |
| p95 gen latency (ms) | 120 | > 250 | includes queuing and network penalty |
| eviction rate (%) | 0.2 | > 2.0 | evictions / active sessions per 10m window |
| request error rate | 0.1% | > 1.0% | endpoint-level 5xx + transport errors |
| egress queue depth | N/A | sustained > 80% of NAT pool | indicates egress saturation |

Prerequisites

- Staging AWS account with cross-account roles: arn:aws:iam::STAGING:role/lab-deployer
- Terraform workspace named ci-lab-staging and a branch-per-change policy (see TF snippet below)
- Buildkite pipeline: gpu-burst-lab (concurrency limited to 2)
- Canary model bundle published to staging S3 (s3://redwood-staging-models/canary/).

CI Integration (recommended flow)

1) Developer opens PR that touches: allocator TF, egress sidecar, gpu-node profile, or canary runtime kernel.
2) CI runs unit tests + linter.
3) CI applies TF to an isolated tf workspace (plan + apply) in staging (requires manual approval if change touches allocator policies).
4) CI triggers lab runkite job: run-lab --scenario=burst-20p-tenants --duration=30m.
5) Verdict engine collects metrics and posts verdict to PR (pass/fail + artifacts).

Acceptance criteria (pass)

- No lab failure triggers within the configured scenario window.
- Performance regressions (p95) < 10% vs baseline.
- No increase in eviction rate > 0.5 percentage points.
- Artifacts (profiles, telemetry snapshots, heap/kv-cache sketches) attached to CI run.

Runbook: starting a canonical burst scenario

1) Checkout branch and ensure the TF plan is green: terraform -chdir=iac/allocator workspace select ci-lab-staging && terraform plan -var-file=staging.tfvars
2) Apply plan (CI will normally do this): terraform apply -auto-approve -var-file=staging.tfvars
3) Trigger a lab run (from staging bastion): ./labctl run --scenario burst-20p-tenants --duration 30m --tag $BUILDKITE_BUILD_URL
4) Monitor dashboards:
   - grafana/staging/gpu-burst-sim (p50/p95, eviction_rate, egress_queue)
   - loki/staging/gpu-burst-sim (allocator events, preempt logs)
5) If failure triggers: capture traces (otel collector) and snapshot KV cache warmup state: ./labctl snapshot --kvcache --name failure-$(date +%s)
6) Rollback TF changes if allocator misconfigured: terraform apply -refresh=false -var-file=rollback.tfvars

Simulations & parameterization

- Tenant mixes: 80% small (1-2 concurrent requests), 15% medium (5-10 concurrent), 5% large (40+ concurrent).
- Sequence length distribution: short (avg 32 tokens), medium (avg 256), long (avg 1024) — tuned by --seq-dist flag.
- Burst shape templates: step, ramp, poisson. Use step for worst-case admission spikes.

Safety gates and canary policies

- Always run lab with a seeded warm-pool for preflight if TF change modifies hot-pool parameters.
- Kernel rollouts must go through a 3-stage canary: unit-tests -> lab burst (this doc) -> blue/green with traffic slicing 5/20/100%.
- TF changes that adjust tenant priority weights require manual approver from SRE.

Terraform/IaC example (minimal allocator override)

```hcl
module "allocator" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.ai/infra/terraform//modules/allocator?ref=${var.branch}"
  instance_type = "g5.48xlarge"
  warm_pool = {
    size = 10
    preseed = true
  }
  priority_weights = {
    tenant_default = 100
    tenant_eval = 10
  }
}
```

Buildkite snippet (trigger lab)

```yaml
steps:
  - label: "Run GPU burst lab"
    command: |
      ./ci/trigger_lab.sh --scenario burst-20p-tenants --duration 30m
    agents:
      queue: gpu-ci
    concurrency: 1
    concurrency_group: "gpu-burst-lab"
```

Diagnostics & artifacts to collect (automated)

- Telemetry: perf traces (OTEL), allocator metrics (prom counters), GPU telemetry (nvml summary).
- Snapshots: kv-cache TTL histograms, warm-pool inventories, node placement maps.
- Heap dumps for runtime if OOM observed (limit: 1 per run).

Post-failure triage checklist

1) Attach lab run id and timeframe to PR and Slack #infra-oncall.
2) Run combiner to align traces and metrics: ./labctl combine --run <id> --out combined-<id>.tar.gz
3) Look for correlating events: kernel rollout, TF plan apply, egress spikes.
4) Re-run smaller scoped scenario isolating the failing subsystem (e.g., only egress shaping).
5) If allocator policy is root cause, revert to previous TF module tag and run lab again.

Promotions & gating policy (CD)

- All TF changes to allocator/egress modules require a green lab verdict. PRs without verdict auto-block and flag to owners.
- Non-blocking changes (docs, comments) skip lab runs.
- For emergency hotfixes to production allocator, a short-circuit path exists but must be followed by a mandatory lab recreation within 48 hours.

Ownership & contacts

- Lab owner: infra-cicd (pager: #infra-oncall)
- Allocator module owner: runtime-team (runtime-owner@redwood.ai)
- Networking & egress: cloud-net (cloud-net@redwood.ai)

Appendix: common troubleshooting commands

- List active synthetic tenants: kubectl -n gpu-burst get pods -l app=workgen
- Tail allocator logs: kubectl -n allocator logs -l app=allocator --follow --tail=200
- Download artifacts: aws s3 cp s3://redwood-staging-burst-artifacts/<run-id> ./ --recursive

Notes and maturity

This playbook started as an SRE/infra experiment in 2023 Q4 and was formalized into CI gates in 2024 Q1. We expect to iterate on tenant mixes and threshold tuning; when changing thresholds update the thresholds table and capture a 10-run baseline.

title: dsid_7254c2a134f34c2598ef1d452f12c159__tenant-airlock-commissioning-and-operator-safety-playbook-2029.txt
text:
Tenant Airlock Commissioning and Operator Safety Playbook

Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines the commissioning pattern we call a "tenant airlock" — an isolated, auditable staging path used during initial tenant onboarding, major configuration changes (network/KMS), and sensitive model swaps. The airlock provides predictable safety gates for operators, reduces blast radius for misconfiguration, and produces artifacts required for compliance evidence. This document covers prerequisites, step-by-step commissioning procedures, automated validation checks, escalation and rollback steps, SLOs and audit artifacts, and recommended operator CLI snippets.

Intended audience: Field operators, SREs supporting private deployments, solutions engineers running customer handoffs, and compliance reviewers.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to VPC-based private deployments and VPC-connected airgapped on-prem variants.
- Assumes the control plane and tenant data plane are installed and reachable via management jump host or operator bastion.
- Assumes operators have RBAC role "operator.airlock.commit" and access to tenant evidence bucket and KMS stamping keys.
- Not covering hardware provisioning steps (see field-installation guide).

Key goals
1) Minimize human blast radius during tenant commissioning.
2) Produce deterministic acceptance artifacts: smoke tests, telemetry samples, and signed evidence bundle.
3) Ensure immediate safe rollback path before any customer traffic flows into production.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: Private Deployments Field Engineering (onboarding squad).
- Emergency escalation: oncall-private-deploy (pager duty) -> eng-platform oncall -> customer success lead.
- Compliance evidence owner: security-ops (verifies evidence bundle).

Airlock Architecture (conceptual)
- Airlock control plane: temporary namespace in customer VPC with restricted egress (HTTP/S to allowed endpoints only) and dedicated service account for operator actions.
- Staging runtime: reserved GPU pool with pinning to non-production models and quantization profiles to test performance under realistic load.
- Traffic gating: operator-approved route table that either points to the staging runtime (airlock) or to tenant production endpoints.
- Evidence store: encrypted object store (customer S3 or operator-managed evidence bucket) with KMS envelope encryption.

Pre-commission checklist (must pass before starting)
- Network: BGP/route validation completed and ACLs verified (CIDR whitelist for operator bastion).
- KMS: operator key present, policy allows encryption:Encrypt and Decrypt for evidence bucket.
- Quotas: reserved GPU capacity for staging assigned and tested with synthetic load.
- Telemetry: observability pipeline subscriptions created (sampling 1:10 for traces, 1:1 for errors).
- SME approvals: Solutions Engineer and Security reviewer signed off in ticketing system.

Commissioning procedure (operator steps)
1) Open onboarding ticket and attach pre-commission checklist. Record ticket ID in evidence bundle.
2) Create airlock namespace: run terraform module or operator CLI: 
   - terraform apply -var 'env=airlock' -target=module.airlock_namespace
3) Provision temporary service account and apply fine-grained RBAC: 
   - rbacctl create --role operator.airlock.commit --namespace tenant-airlock --expiry 72h --notes 'onboard-<ticket>'
4) Mount evidence bucket with KMS: 
   - operator-cli evidence mount --bucket s3://evidence-<tenant> --kms-key arn:aws:kms:...
5) Deploy staging runtime and default model variant: 
   - deployctl apply -f airlock/staging-runtime.yaml --wait 600s
6) Run automated validations (see next section). Do not proceed until all pass.
7) Manual performance verification: operator runs three controlled synthetic scenarios: 
   a) Low-latency conversational burst (95th percentile latency target <= 120ms)
   b) Batch-embedding throughput (tokens/sec target within 15% of benchmark)
   c) KV cache warmup and cold-start latency profile measured over 1 hour
8) Sign and upload evidence bundle: operator-cli evidence sign --ticket <id> --attach ./validation-report.json
9) If all validation gates pass, open ticket for production flip with proposed window and rollback conditions.

Automated validation checks (must be automated where possible)
- Network sanity: traceroute to control-plane endpoints, TLS cert validation, and egress firewall policy conformance.
- KMS and secret access: attempt envelope encrypt/decrypt roundtrip and verify rotation policy existence.
- Runtime health: all runtime pods at 1.0 readiness for 5 continuous minutes.
- Model correctness: 20 predefined prompt-set evaluations run; pass rate >= 98% for syntactic correctness checks and semantic match thresholds.
- Latency SLO smoke: 95th percentile response time <= target defined in tenant SLA matrix.
- Telemetry sampling: a minimum of 100 traces and 100 events ingested into observability backend.

Validation report contents (artifact)
- Ticket ID, operator name, timestamp
- List of checks run with pass/fail and deterministic logs/links to traces
- Synthetic workload artifacts: raw latency histograms, token counts, and CPU/GPU utilization samples
- Signed KMS envelope metadata and evidence bucket object IDs

Decision gates and criteria
- Gate A (Network & KMS): required. Any failure -> STOP and open incident labeled "airlock.network-kms-failure"
- Gate B (Runtime & Model): required. Minor failures in model match may proceed only with SE approval and a documented mitigation plan.
- Gate C (Performance & Telemetry): if latency or telemetry targets fail, operator must schedule an additional tuning iteration. Production flip is blocked until Gate C passes.

Rollback / safe-fail strategies
- Immediate rollback (fast path): if any catastrophic failure observed during commissioning or the first 10 minutes after production flip, execute: 
  1) operator-cli route set --tenant <id> --target staging (re-point traffic away from newly swapped variant)
  2) scale down new model pods: deployctl scale --name model-swap --replicas 0
  3) re-enable previous pinned model variant and confirm traffic flows correctly
- Evidence-first rollback: when compliance evidence required before rollback, capture a final evidence bundle before any destructive change.
- Graceful degrade: for partial performance regressions, enable rate-limiting or throttling policies to bound user impact while rolling back.

Upgrade and long-lived change coordination
- For scheduled upgrades (runtime, model, control plane) use airlock to validate each major change. Each upgrade must include: 
  - Upgrade runbook: planned steps, pre-checks, blackout windows, backout commands
  - Canary policy: start with 1% traffic directed to the upgraded runtime for 30 minutes observation, then 10% for 60 minutes, then 100% after final sign-off
  - Automated rollback trigger thresholds: error rate > 1.5x baseline OR 95th percentile latency increase > 30% -> automatic rollback
- State migration: when moving KV caches or model state, perform transactional snapshot, checksum verification, and a dry-run restore into airlock environment.

Operator safety checklists (quick reference)
- Before any change: verify RBAC and ephemeral credential expiry times
- Before flip: ensure at least two operators are available and at least one has production revert permissions
- After flip: remain on-call for 60 minutes and monitor defined dashboards (latency, errors, cpu_gpu, kv_hit_rate)

Runbook snippets and CLI commands
- Mount evidence: operator-cli evidence mount --bucket s3://evidence-tenantX --kms-key arn:aws:kms:region:acct:key/abcd
- Trigger validation suite: operator-cli validate --suite airlock-onboard --output ./validation-report.json
- Route flip to production: operator-cli route set --tenant tenantX --target production --window 2027-02-11T02:00Z/2027-02-11T03:00Z
- Emergency rollback: operator-cli emergency rollback --ticket <id> --reason "latency-regression" --confirm

SLOs and monitoring thresholds (recommended)
- Latency: 95th percentile <= tenant-SLA-95 (default 120ms for small conversational workloads)
- Error budget burn: automated alert when 1h burn-rate > 20% of hourly budget
- Telemetry fidelity: fewer than 0.5% missing traces across the sampling window
- Evidence retention: signed evidence bundles retained for minimum 180 days for regulated customers

Evidence and audit artifacts (what to store)
- validation-report.json (signed), signed KMS envelopes, a copy of deployed manifests with checksums, route-change audit log, operator action log (who/when/what), and observability links to recorded traces and dashboards.

Post-commission acceptance and handoff
1) Compile the evidence bundle and upload to evidence store with tags: tenant:<id>, ticket:<id>, type:commissioning, status:accepted
2) Notify customer success and provide handoff notes with SLA expectations, known limitations, and tuning suggestions
3) Schedule follow-up QBR with customer within 14 days to review performance and handle any model-quality concerns

Common failure modes and remediations
- KMS permission denied: verify IAM policies and check key policy for operator principal. Temporary mitigation: use operator-managed ephemeral key while key policy is updated.
- Trace ingestion gap: check observability sampler configuration and network egress rules to telemetry backend. If backlog grows, increase sampling temporarily to capture sufficient traces.
- GPU OOM during synthetic test: reduce batch size and restart staging runtime; record OOM logs and escalate to runtime-kernel team if recurrent.

Appendix A — Staging runtime manifest (example)
# YAML excerpt (operator should validate before apply)
# deploys a minimal staging runtime with pinned model variant
apiVersion: redwood/v1
kind: StagingRuntime
metadata:
  name: tenantX-airlock-runtime
spec:
  gpuPool: reserved-small
  modelPin: openmodel-compat-v2-quant
  kvCachePolicy: ephemeral
  observability:
    traces: sampleRate: 0.1
    logs: level: info

Appendix B — Evidence bundle file list (example)
- validation-report.json
- deployed-manifests.tar.gz (sha256)
- runtime-metrics.tar.gz
- kms-envelope.json
- route-audit.log

Appendix C — Troubleshooting checklist (operator quick commands)
- Check runtime pods: kubectl -n tenant-airlock get pods -o wide
- Confirm GPU utilization: nvidia-smi on runtime node or metrics query: sum(container_gpu_utilization) by (node)
- Recreate ephemeral service account: rbacctl rotate --name operator-airlock --namespace tenant-airlock

Related reading
- See "private-deploy-operator-handshake-and-runtime-guardrails-2026" for operator preconditions and guardrail definitions.
- See "tenant-bootstrapping-and-immutable-upgrade-playbook-2026" for upgrade patterns and immutable image guidance.

Change history
- 2026-11-01: Created by Marisol Chen (initial draft)
- 2027-02-10: Updated automation checks and added evidence-first rollback guidance (reviewers: Arjun Patel, Lena Vogel)

Contact
- Onboarding squad Slack: #onboard-private-deploys
- Emergency pager: oncall-private-deploy

title: dsid_19ad34685e004d74a944327a524ed255__runtime-circuit-observability-and-safety-test-plan-2027.txt
text:
Runtime circuit observability and safety test plan

Overview:

This document defines the observability signals, safety checks, and automated test plan for runtime circuit constructs used across Redwood’s inference serving stack. It applies to the runtime components that can engage in circuit-style behavior: inference-router, batcher, kv-coordinator, model-worker, fallback-orchestrator, and edge-proxy adapters. The goal is to ensure that circuit transitions (open / half-open / closed), shed decisions, and graceful degradation behaviors are visible, tested, and safe to roll out in production.

Audience:
- Runtime engineers
- SREs and oncall
- Release owners for serving runtime features

Scope and definitions:
- Circuit: any runtime control that can stop or alter request processing for a class of traffic (examples: kernel-shed, variant-fallback, batcher-queue-cutoff, model-quantize-fallback).
- Safety check: deterministic assertions executed before a circuit is flipped in production (e.g., minimum healthy model-worker count, KV cache warmness).
- Observability signal: telemetry that must be emitted to correlate circuit events with customer-visible impact (latency, error rates, token drop).

Non-goals:
- Design of new circuit types (covered by ADRs). This plan describes testing and telemetry for circuits that are already implemented.

Principles:
1) Explicit, machine-readable circuit events with stable schema for correlation.
2) Safe, automated rollback gates driven by SLO regressions and saturation signals.
3) Deterministic test harnesses that run in CI and as scheduled synthetic checks in staging and canary clusters.
4) Single source of truth for circuit metadata to drive dashboards and incident playbooks.

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: Runtime Reliability (runtime-sre)
- Engineering owner: Maya Chen (runtime-platform)
- Pager: eng-sre rotation (see oncall roster link)

SLOs and safety thresholds used by circuits:
- 99th percentile inference latency (regional): must not increase by >20% after a circuit flip during canary window.
- Error rate (5xx and inference-failures): must remain below baseline + 0.5 percentage points over 5m window.
- Token throughput: maintain at least 60% of baseline for dedicated capacity plans when shedding non-critical paths.

Observability contract (event schema and metrics):
All runtime components that alter request flow must emit the following signals with exact keys to the telemetry pipeline. Consumers (dashboards, SLOs, rollback automation) depend on the exact keys.

Required Event fields (log or structured event):
- event_type (string): one of [circuit_open, circuit_half_open, circuit_closed, circuit_probe, shed_start, shed_end]
- circuit_id (string): canonical id, e.g. runtime.kernel_shed.v2
- reason_code (string): classification of why the circuit fired (e.g. GPU_OOM, KV_STALE, LATENCY_BREACH)
- source_service (string): service name emitting the event
- affected_route_hint (string): optional, route id or product hint
- timestamp (ISO8601)
- metadata (stringified map): freeform diagnostic kernel (must include shard_id and available_gpu_count)

Required Metrics (time-series):
- runtime.circuit.{circuit_id}.state (gauge): 0=closed, 1=half-open, 2=open
- runtime.circuit.{circuit_id}.latency_delta_pct (gauge): measured percent latency change attributed to circuit actions
- runtime.circuit.{circuit_id}.error_delta_pp (gauge): change in error percentage points
- runtime.shed.{reason_code}.count (counter)

Tracing requirements:
- Any request that triggers a circuit action must include a trace span named runtime.circuit.action with attributes: circuit_id, reason_code, pre_action_latency_ms, post_action_latency_ms. Span must link to the original request span_id.

Test harness specification:
The harness has three layers: unit-level simulators, integration artifacts in CI, and scheduled synthetic canary runs.

1) Unit simulators (local):
- Goal: verify circuit state machine, deterministic transitions, and basic metrics emission.
- Implementation: python/golang harness located at infra/tests/runtime-circuits/simulators. Tests must cover: open->half-open->closed transitions with timeouts, probe success/failure paths, and manual override.
- Example CLI: 
  ./circuit-sim --circuit=kernel_shed --open-after=5 --probe-interval=30 --simulate-load=high

2) Integration tests (CI):
- Goal: validate observable side effects across services (router -> batcher -> worker -> fallback).
- Setup: deploy a mini-cluster in CI that includes a real batcher and a mock model-worker that can be toggled to induce GPU_OOM and latency conditions.
- Checks: event emission schema, metrics ingestion (prometheus-style), and trace linking.
- Pass criteria: all required events are present, metrics have expected deltas, and no silent failures.

3) Canary / scheduled synthetic checks (staging and prod-canary clusters):
- Goal: exercise circuits under production-like traffic and validate SLO gating works.
- Traffic shape: 5 steady-state minutes followed by burst scenarios (spikes at 3x baseline) and slow-path heavy token streams.
- Automation: Canary orchestrator runs the plan and collects pre/post SLO snapshots.
- Gate: circuit flips are only allowed if pre/post delta checks remain within thresholds for the canary window (see rollout checklist).

Test matrix (examples):
| Test scenario | Trigger | Expected events | SLO gate |
|---------------|---------|-----------------|---------|
| GPU OOM spike | Model-worker returns OOM | circuit_open, shed_start | 99p latency < +20% and error_delta < +0.5pp |
| KV stale after deploy | KV warming fails | circuit_open, circuit_probe | Error rate unchanged; probe must succeed within 10m |
| Batcher backlog growth | queue depth > 80th percentile | shed_start, shed_end | Token throughput >=60% |
| Canary probe success | half-open probe passes | circuit_closed | No increase in 5xxs during 5m window |

Automation and tooling:
- Rollback automation: A script (runtime/tools/circuit_guard.py) subscribes to newly emitted circuit events and can automatically mark a rollout for rollback if SLO gates are broken. The script requires a signed release token for any automated revert.
- Dashboard: a prebuilt dashboard (Runtime / Circuits) shows live state, sustained open durations, and correlated SLO deltas per circuit_id.
- Test data capture: all canary runs create an artifacts bundle (metrics, events, traces, request samples) stored in s3://redwood-ci/circuit-artifacts/<run-id>/ for 90 days.

Rollout checklist for circuit changes (feature flag / runtime deploy):
1) ADR completed and linked in related_pages.
2) Unit and integration tests added to CI and passing.
3) Canary harness test plan configured with expected baselines.
4) Observability contract validated in staging (events + metrics + traces present).
5) Oncall and release manager notified; rollback plan pre-registered.
6) Health gates configured in rollout system (canary window length, SLO delta thresholds).
7) Post-rollout smoke run scheduled for 30 minutes.

Safe flip procedure (manual override):
1) Pause traffic to edge-proxy for the target region (if supported).
2) Engage the circuit in half-open mode with probe rate = 1% of requests.
3) Monitor latency and error telemetry for 10 minutes.
4) If metrics within thresholds, incrementally increase probe rate to 10% then 50% with 5-minute holds.
5) If at any step SLOs breach, immediately revert to closed and escalate.

Incident triage and postmortem trigger conditions:
- Any automated rollback triggered by runtime.tools/circuit_guard.py
- Sustained open period > 30 minutes with customer-visible SLO breach
- Unexplained increase in shed_start counts > 2x baseline in 1h

Playbook links and related pages:
- Related ADRs: link to ADRs for specific circuit designs must be added in related_pages metadata.
- Runbooks: oncall runbook for circuit incidents (see security-and-compliance/runbooks or eng-sre/runbooks).

Appendix: Example probe config (JSON used by canary harness)
{
  "circuit_id": "kernel_shed.v2",
  "probe_mode": "half_open",
  "initial_probe_rate": "0.01",
  "probe_increase_schedule": "0.01->0.10->0.50",
  "hold_seconds": "300",
  "slo_latency_pct_99_threshold": "20",
  "slo_error_delta_pp_threshold": "0.5"
}

FAQ (short):
Q: Who can flip a circuit manually?
A: Release owners + oncall SRE with release token. Manual flips must be recorded in the incident log.

Q: How long are artifacts retained?
A: Canary artifacts retained for 90 days; production incident artifacts archived per compliance retention policy.

Changes and revision history:
- 2024-10-10 (Maya Chen): Initial draft and unit simulator design.
- 2025-06-18 (Arjun Patel): Added CI integration requirements and metric keys.
- 2026-02-20 (Sofia Martinez): Updated SLO gating thresholds and canary schedule to align with new canary orchestrator.

Contact and escalation:
- Runtime Reliability (runtime-sre) mailing list: runtime-sre@redwood.example.com
- Pager: eng-sre rotation (see internal oncall)
- Doc owner: Maya Chen (maya.chen@redwood.example.com)

title: dsid_f78e91b3e6854c5c8db4213238b3d1ab__error-budget-billing-reconciliation-and-priority-credit-runbook-2026.txt
text:
Error budget billing reconciliation and priority credit runbook

Summary:

This runbook defines the deterministic process for reconciling SLO-driven error budget burn with customer billing and for issuing priority credits (temporary elevated capacity or monetary credits) when SLO violations materially impacted customer SLAs. It covers detection, verification, audit evidence retention, automated reconciliation jobs, manual approval flows, credit issuance, and post-action review. The intent is to provide a reproducible, auditable, and customer-safe process that minimizes manual disputes and protects the platform’s cost model.

Audience:
- SRE oncall and escalation engineers
- Revenue operations and billing team (Finance)
- Customer Success managers
- Account execs for enterprise customers

Scope and goals:
1) Map SLO violations and error budget consumption to customer-facing impact windows and quantify eligible credits.
2) Provide an end-to-end automated reconciliation pipeline that produces an evidence bundle for Finance and Customer Success.
3) Define safe, time-bounded priority credits (capacity reservation) to maintain customer experience while minimizing platform cost.
4) Ensure all credits are traceable, approved, and reversible.

Key definitions:
- SLO incident window: contiguous period where a service-level metric (e.g., p99 latency or availability) is below target per the SLO definition.
- Error budget consumption (EBC): fraction of budget consumed in a rolling 28-day window attributable to platform service degradation.
- Impact-adjusted customer exposure (IACE): portion of EBC attributable to a given customer based on routing, region, and tenancy.
- Priority credit: temporary reservation of dedicated capacity or monetary credit applied to billing.

Ownership matrix:
- Detection & telemetry: Eng-SRE Observability team (primary)
- Reconciliation automation and evidence packaging: Eng-SRE Operational Tooling (primary) + Finance (consumer)
- Credit approval: Finance (final), CS (customer notification), SRE (technical justification)
- Priority capacity execution: Eng-Platform (implementation), Eng-SRE (validation)

Trigger conditions (automated):
1) Any SLO incident with severity >= P2 and duration >= 10 minutes triggers a partial run of the reconciliation pipeline.
2) Aggregate EBC > 12% during a 28-day window flags automated credit calculation.
3) Customer-specific telemetry indicates >10% request routing loss to fallback model/region during the incident window.

High-level workflow (steps):
1) Detection: Observability alerts populate a reconciliation ticket in the SRE Reconciler queue (Jira label: sb-reconcile).
2) Evidence collection (automated): run evidence collector job that pulls traces, token-level sampling, traffic routing logs, KV cache miss rates, model fallback metrics, and tenant routing records for the incident window. Evidence saved to S3 with 90-day retention (see retention policy).
3) Impact attribution: run impact calculator to produce IACE per customer. The calculator uses routing logs and token counters to weigh per-tenant exposure.
4) Credit calculation: apply the credit rules table (below) to compute recommended monetary credit and/or priority-capacity minutes.
5) Approval: packet with recommended amount sent to Finance + CS + SRE owner for sign-off via Slack workflow + Jira approval step.
6) Execution: Finance issues billing credit or Eng-Platform provisions priority capacity as agreed.
7) Customer notification: CS sends templated explanation and remediation notes.
8) Post-action review: SRE leads a 2-week follow-up to confirm incident remediation and avoid duplicate credits.

Credit rules (config):
- Monetary credit = floor(IACE * Customer-monthly-recurring-revenue * adjustment-factor), where adjustment-factor defaults to 0.2 for availability incidents and 0.1 for latency incidents unless escalated.
- Priority capacity credit = min(1200 minutes, IACE * 2880 minutes) — expressed as reserved GPU-minutes on Dedicated or ephemeral priority tokens on Hosted.
- Minimum credit threshold: $50 or 100 GPU-minutes. Events below threshold require manual review before crediting.

Example credit matrix (text table):
- Small customer (MRR < $5k): IACE 20% during 2h outage -> monetary credit = floor(0.2 * $2,000 * 0.2) = $80 -> Issue monetary credit + 240 GPU-min priority if requested.
- Enterprise customer (MRR > $100k): IACE 5% during sustained 24h degradation -> monetary credit = floor(0.05 * $150,000 * 0.2) = $1,500 -> Offer priority capacity + account-level remediation SLA.

Automation implementation notes (CLI & SQL snippets):
1) Evidence collector (example CLI trigger):
- ./reconciler collect --service=model-serving --window-start=2026-05-18T03:12Z --window-end=2026-05-18T05:22Z --out-s3=s3://reconciliation-evidence/incident-20260518-0312

2) Sample SQL to compute per-tenant token exposure (Postgres / analytics DB):
- SELECT tenant_id, SUM(tokens) as token_count
  FROM token_usage
  WHERE ingest_ts >= '2026-05-18T03:12:00Z' AND ingest_ts <= '2026-05-18T05:22:00Z'
    AND route in (SELECT route FROM route_table WHERE service='model-serving')
  GROUP BY tenant_id
  ORDER BY token_count DESC;

3) Impact attribution (pseudo):
- For each tenant: IACE = tenant_token_count / total_token_count * incident_service_degraded_fraction

4) Automated approval Slack workflow (example payload to /slack/workflows):
- POST /api/workflows/trigger
  {"trigger_id": "reconcile-12345", "approvers": ["finance@redwood.com","cs@redwood.com"], "summary": "Recommended credit: $1,500 for tenant ACME (IACE 5%)"}

Evidence retention policy:
- Raw telemetry (traces/metric-series/raw-logs): retain 30 days by default; extend to 90 days for incident evidence bundles linked to reconciliations.
- Aggregated reconciliation artifacts (impact reports, SQL extracts, approval history): retain 3 years for audit and accounting.
- Access controls: evidence buckets are restricted to Eng-SRE, Finance, and CS with read/write auditing enabled.

Monitoring & alerts for the pipeline itself:
- Reconciler job failures: PagerDuty to Eng-SRE Operational Tooling (P1 if collection fails for critical incidents).
- Evidence-packaging delays > 30 minutes: Email + Slack to SRE tooling owners.
- Drift between automated recommended credit vs. Finance manual: Weekly reconciliation report and retraining of adjustment-factor.

Escalation & manual override guidance:
- Finance has authority to override automated monetary credits but must add a reason to the approval ticket and attach manual calculation.
- Eng-SRE can request priority capacity without monetary credit for short-duration critical production incidents; Finance must be notified within 24 hours.
- Any override that increases credit above 2x automated recommendation requires Director-level sign-off from Finance.

Rollback and reversal:
- Credits issued in error: Finance will reverse via billing system and create a reversal ticket with reason. All reversals must include the reconciliation artifact.
- Priority capacity revocation: Eng-Platform will de-provision reserved capacity and log the action to the incident ticket. If the customer incurred costs externally (rare), CS and Finance coordinate remediation.

Telemetry queries (examples to paste into Grafana or Observability):
