- Availability SLO: query service_health.policy('model-serving', 'availability', '28d') to see rolling window.
- Tenant exposure: custom panel that joins token usage and route health during the incident window; pre-built panel id: sre.impact.tenant-exposure. Note: panel references require SSO access.

Checklist for initiating a reconciliation (quick reference):
1) Confirm incident window and severity.
2) Kick evidence collector (automated if trigger conditions met).
3) Validate impact attribution outputs (top 10 tenants).
4) Review recommended credit and compare to SLA in customer contract.
5) Create approval ticket and trigger Slack approval workflow.
6) After approval, notify CS to coordinate customer communication.

KPIs & telemetry for continuous improvement:
- Mean time from incident detection to recommended credit (target < 4 hours).
- Percentage of automated recommendations accepted by Finance (target > 85%).
- Number of credit disputes raised by customers per quarter (target < 2% of credits).
- Cost delta introduced by priority capacity credits as % of platform spend (target < 1.5% monthly).

Post-incident review template (to attach to Jira ticket):
- Incident summary and timeline (UTC)
- SLO metrics and graphs for the window
- Evidence bundle S3 path
- Per-tenant IACE table and credit recommendation details
- Approvals and execution evidence (Finance ticket ids, Slack approvals)
- Lessons learned and follow-up actions (owners + due dates)

Security and compliance notes:
- Do not include PII in evidence bundles. Strip or redact any request payloads before archiving.
- All evidence access is logged; Finance access is time-limited to relevant artifacts.

Appendix: troubleshooting common failure modes
- No token entries for tenant in incident window: confirm routing TTLs and whether tenant was served by a fallback region; check ingress proxies for sampling.
- Evidence collector times out: increase collector parallelism for large incidents and file a tooling incident.
- Discrepancy with Finance ledger: run the monthly reconciliation audit job and attach delta report to the ticket.

Revision history:
- 2026-01-15: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2026-03-02: Added Slack approval workflow and CLI examples (reviewers: Diego Ramirez, Priya Singh).
- 2026-06-02: Updated retention and approval thresholds; elevated confidentiality to restricted.

Contact and escalation list:
- Eng-SRE Observability: observability-oncall@redwood.com
- Eng-SRE Operational Tooling: tooling-oncall@redwood.com
- Finance billing lead: billing@redwood.com
- Customer Success: cs-ops@redwood.com

End of runbook.

title: dsid_e5235bfb4db94a12a69d08fcf0338bdc__integrated-control-taxonomy-and-exemption-workflow-2025.txt
text:
Integrated Control Taxonomy and Exemption Lifecycle

Overview

This playbook defines a unified control taxonomy across RBAC, audit logging, data residency & retention, secure SDLC gates, incident-response evidence collection, and the lifecycle for risk exceptions. The goal is to make control ownership, expected evidence, and exception handling consistent and auditable across Redwood Inference deployments (hosted, dedicated, and private).

Scope

- Applies to all services and teams that operate customer-facing inference workloads, control planes, and observability pipelines.
- Covers preventative controls (RBAC, gated releases), detective controls (audit streams, alerts), and compensating controls used when short-lived exceptions are granted.

Definitions

- Control: A specific security or compliance requirement (e.g., "Authorization decision logging").
- Evidence bundle: Packaged artifacts used to prove a control was operating (logs, screenshots, attestations, config snapshots).
- Exception: An approved, time-bound deviation from a control or requirement.

Principles

1. Single source of truth: Every control is mapped to an owner, control-id, expected evidence types, and a review cadence.
2. Least privilege baseline: Default system roles are narrowly scoped and require explicit justification for widening.
3. Time-bound exceptions: Exceptions must include mitigation, acceptance criteria, and an expiration date.
4. Auditability: Every exception and control change must produce an immutable record that can be assembled into an evidence bundle for auditors.

Control Taxonomy (high level)

| Control ID | Domain | Owner | Expected Evidence | Review cadence | Criticality |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|
| C-RBAC-001 | RBAC & Auth | IAM Team | Role definitions (YAML), policy diffs, entitlement audit log | Quarter | High |
| C-AUD-002 | Audit Logging | Observability | Immutable audit stream sample, retention config, ingestion metrics | Month | High |
| C-RES-003 | Data Residency | Legal/Privacy | Residency config, access logs, DPA references | Quarter | Medium |
| C-RET-004 | Retention | Compliance | Retention schedule, purge job runbook, verification snapshot | Month | High |
| C-SDLC-005 | Secure SDLC | EngSec | Release gate checklist, signed commit metadata, SCA report | Release | High |
| C-IR-006 | Incident Response | SRE/Security | Incident timeline, forensic snapshots, evidence bundle | Post-incident | Critical |

RBAC baseline and evidence requirements

- Baseline roles (applies to hosted, dedicated, private):
  - viewer: read-only access to dashboards and non-sensitive metrics. Evidence: role assignment records, last-change diff.
  - operator: runbooks, restart/scale, non-privileged routing changes. Evidence: assignment audit trail, JIT activation logs.
  - platform-admin: deploy builds, manage model artifacts, secret rotation. Evidence: multi-approver change record, credential issuance logs.

RBAC review cadence and automation

1. Monthly entitlement exports produced by IAM service and deposited to secure evidence bucket.
2. Automated drift detection: compare current role bindings to the baseline; generate anomalies.
3. Quarterly manual certification: team leads attest to required roles and approve or request removals.

Audit logging: schema, retention, and evidence packaging

- Minimum logged events (all services): authn events, authz decisions (allow/deny and policy reason), administrative changes (role create/delete/attach), model deployment/rollback, evidence-handling actions (export/create/delete), and alert acknowledgements.
- Event schema (example):
  {
    "timestamp": "2026-02-14T15:04:05Z",
    "service": "inference-gateway",
    "event_type": "authz_decision",
    "principal": "svc:platform-admin:srv-42",
    "action": "model.deploy",
    "resource": "model:v1.43",
    "decision": "DENY",
    "policy_id": "policy-deploy-3",
    "request_id": "req-6f7a2c"
  }

- Retention minimums: control C-AUD-002 requires raw immutable stream retention for 90 days in hot tier, 2 years in cold storage; aggregated event indices 12 months.
- Evidence packaging: when auditors request artifacts, assemble: schema contract, representative event samples (filtered by timeframe), retention config snapshot, and ingestion metrics. Include hash manifest signed by Observability owner.

Data residency and retention schedule (example table)

| Data type | Default residency | Minimum retention | Purge action | Owner |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Inference request logs (redacted) | US/EU region matching customer | 90 days hot, 2 yrs cold | automatic purge job (30d TTL after retention end) | Platform Data |
| Customer PII (when present) | Customer-specified region | As contractually required (e.g., 7 yrs) | Legal-approved manual purge | Legal/Compliance |
| Model artifacts (serving binaries) | Global (indexed) | 365 days | archival + checksum verification | Model Ops |
| Audit stream (raw) | Primary region, replicate to cold region | 2 yrs cold | immutable archive rotation | Observability |

Secure SDLC gates (release checklist)

For a release to progress from staging -> canary -> prod the following controls must be true: 
- C-SDLC-005 checklist satisfied:
  1. Passing unit/integration tests and security SCA scan (zero critical vulnerabilities).
  2. Signed commit metadata and verifiable author identity.
  3. Feature flags in place for quick rollback and telemetry toggles.
  4. RBAC changes included as declarative policies in the release (no manual console grants).
  5. Evidence bundle (SCA report, pipeline signature, canary metrics snapshot) stored in evidence bucket.

Incident response (security-specific steps and evidence capture)

1. Triage: capture immutable copies of relevant audit partitions (timestamped, hashed).
2. Containment: if a privileged token is suspected, enact immediate token revocation and record revocation action in the audit log.
3. Forensic snapshot: record process lists, container images, model artifacts touched, and network flows.
4. Evidence packaging: assemble incident bundle with chain-of-custody manifest, hashes, observer notes, and access-control changes.
5. Legal/compliance engagement: trigger Data Residency review if data egress is suspected.

Exception (exemption) lifecycle: procedure

1. Request: team files an Exception Request using the central form (fields: control-id, justification, compensating controls, mitigation, expected expiration date, roll-forward plan).
2. Initial review by control owner within 3 business days.
3. If risk > medium, Security Risk Committee review required; if < medium, owner may approve with mitigation.
4. Approval artifacts: signed exception record, acceptance criteria, monitoring tasks, and expiration reminder entry.
5. Automated enforcement: where possible, exception approvals inject timebound feature flags and monitoring policies (e.g., increase audit sampling to 100% for the affected scope).

Approval matrix (simplified)

| Risk level | Approver(s) | Max duration |
|---|---|---:|
| Low | Control Owner | 30 days |
| Medium | Control Owner + Security Manager | 90 days |
| High | Security Risk Committee + Head of Product | 180 days (requires quarterly re-approval) |

Compensating controls examples (must be documented in request)

- Increase audit sampling and retention for the targeted resource.
- Isolate the resource into a temporary tenancy or constrained network ACL.
- Add automated regression/e2e checks to detect specific drift symptoms.

Evidence bundle template (minimum contents)

- control-id and exception id (if applicable)
- time-window covered by artifacts
- hashed archives: role-dump.zip (roles YAML), audit-sample.jsonl (filtered), retention-config.yaml, release-signature.txt
- attestation: named approvers and timestamps (SAML assertion or signed ticket)
- verification checklist and manifest with SHA256 hashes

Operationalizing and automation priorities

- Priority 1: automated entitlement exports and drift alerts (monthly -> daily).
- Priority 2: exception request API so approvals are machine-actionable and inject temporary mitigations.
- Priority 3: evidence bundling API to produce auditor-ready bundles on demand.

Metrics / KPIs to monitor program health

- Percentage of exceptions with compensating controls documented (target: 100%).
- Mean time to approve exception (target: <= 5 business days).
- Number of entitlement drifts detected per week (trend downward).
- Percentage of releases with complete SDLC evidence bundles (target: 100%).

Appendix A: Example exception request payload (JSON form)

{
  "control_id": "C-RBAC-001",
  "requester": "team:models/platform",
  "justification": "Emergency migration to new key manager requires temporary broad role attach for migration tool.",
  "compensations": ["increased-audit-sampling", "temporary-network-isolation"],
  "expiration": "2026-03-01",
  "approvals": []
}

Appendix B: Quick checklists

- Pre-approval checklist for exception reviewers:
  1. Verify mitigation is actionable and measurable.
  2. Ensure monitoring (alerts, dashboards) is enabled for the scope.
  3. Confirm expiration is set and automated reminder exists.
  4. Confirm evidence bucket path and manifest pattern.

- Post-incident evidence checklist for on-call:
  1. Preserve raw audit partitions (hash + store).
  2. Snapshot RBAC bindings and any policy diffs.
  3. Capture release pipeline logs and SCA artifacts.
  4. Tag evidence bundle with incident ID and legal hold flag if requested.

Related links

- RBAC playbooks and automation: /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/entitlement-provisioning-and-evidence-automation-2026
- Audit schema and retention runbook: /confluence/security-and-compliance/audit-logging/event-schema-contract-and-retention-runbook-2025

Revision history

- 2025-10-20: Drafted by Maya Gomez.
- 2025-11-15: Reviewed by Liam Patel (IAM) and Rosa Alvarez (Observability).
- 2026-02-14: Published with clarifications to retention schedule and exception automation steps.

title: dsid_17f616be6a3445a09c08bf2715d2a067__permissioning-procurement-lifecycle-patterns-2026.txt
text:
Permissioning and Procurement Lifecycle Patterns

Overview

This page describes a compact, company-wide set of patterns and templates for: access & permissions, lightweight change management, data classification and handling, procurement & expenses, vendor onboarding, and travel approvals. The goal is to provide reproducible, low-friction flows that meet security and finance controls while minimizing friction for product and platform teams.

Principles (high level)
- Least privilege by default; temporary elevation when necessary.
- Single, auditable approval path for spend and access changes.
- Separation of duties between requestor, approver, and implementer.
- Risk-based variance: low-risk changes follow a lightweight path; high-risk changes get formal review.
- Templates and automation reduce clerical errors and speed approvals.

Scope
- Applies to all Redwood employees, contractors, and vendor integrations.
- Covers: account-level permissions, service/role grants, infrastructure change requests, data access and handling, procurement and vendor onboarding, travel and expense reimbursements.

Quick reference: ownership and SLAs
- Access Requests: owner_team = people-ops; SLA for standard requests = 2 business days.
- Elevated Privilege (temporary): owner_team = security; SLA = 4 business hours for urgent, 24 hours otherwise.
- Infrastructure Change Requests: owner_team = eng-platform; change validation window = 3 business days for non-urgent.
- Procurement Requests < $5k: owner_team = finance-legal (delegated approvers); SLA = 48 hours.
- Procurement Requests >= $5k: owner_team = finance-legal; requires manager + finance approval; SLA = 5 business days.

Roles and RACI (text table)
- Requestor: person initiating the request.
- Approver: manager or role-specific approver (see approval matrix).
- Implementer: engineer/admin performing the change.
- Reviewer/Auditor: security or finance reviewer for high-risk items.

Approval matrix (summary)
- Access:
  - Org-level or admin roles: Manager + Security review.
  - App-level read-only: Manager.
  - Service principal/automation keys: Security + Eng-platform.
- Spend:
  - <= $500: Manager.
  - $501–$5,000: Manager + Finance delegated approver.
  - > $5,000: Manager + Finance + Procurement lead.
- Vendor onboarding: All vendors with access to sensitive data require Security + Legal sign-off.

Access request flow (recommended lightweight pattern)
1) Requestor submits an Access Request using the ACCESS REQUEST template (link in templates section). Include reason, duration (if temporary), and resource.
2) Automated validation checks (IAM policy, resource tags, existing grants).
3) Manager receives approval email + one-click approve/deny.
4) If approval granted and role is standard, system auto-applies role and records audit event. If temporary, auto-expiry ticket created.
5) Security is notified for elevated roles or unusual patterns (out-of-band notification).
6) Requestor receives confirmation with audit ticket ID.

Change management (lightweight pattern for infra and config changes)
- When to use this pattern: routine configuration updates, non-invasive infra adjustments, runtime parameter tweaks.
- Minimal required artifacts: short description, impact analysis, rollback plan, scheduled window.
- Flow:
  1. Create a CHANGE REQUEST (CR) in the Change Tracker with: title, owner, change window, rollback steps, and validation checks.
  2. Automated linting checks: CI config, Terraform plan diff, linter output.
  3. Approvals: Manager + Eng-platform for infra; Manager + Security for security-affecting changes.
  4. Implementer executes change during scheduled window.
  5. Post-change validation: smoke tests, metrics (latency/error thresholds), and a 1-hour monitoring watch.
  6. Close CR with links to deployment logs and verification artifacts.
- High-risk changes: require a 3-day review and a canary deployment with rollback triggers.

Data classification and handling summary
- Classification tiers: PUBLIC, INTERNAL, CONFIDENTIAL, RESTRICTED.
- Handling rules (short):
  - PUBLIC: No controls required.
  - INTERNAL: Use company accounts; avoid sharing outside Redwood without approval.
  - CONFIDENTIAL: Encrypted at rest and in transit; access on a need-to-know basis; logged.
  - RESTRICTED: Strictly limited to named individuals/roles; key management with KMS/HSM; contractually controlled.
- Examples:
  - Customer PII: CONFIDENTIAL or RESTRICTED depending on contractual terms.
  - Model weights + sensitive prompts: CONFIDENTIAL (treated as IP).
  - Audit logs: INTERNAL (retention per policy).

Procurement and vendor onboarding (concise lifecycle)
- Pre-qualification checklist for vendors:
  - Business need justification and estimated annual spend.
  - Security posture summary: SOC2 or equivalent, encryption at rest/in transit, subprocessor list.
  - Privacy terms and DPA if processing customer data.
  - Insurance and indemnity (where applicable).
- Onboarding flow:
  1. Requestor opens a PROCUREMENT REQUEST with cost center, estimated spend, contract term, and vendor security info.
  2. Finance validates budget and assigns spend code.
  3. Legal or finance triggers Vendor Intake if the vendor handles regulated data.
  4. Procurement lead negotiates terms (if > $5k or non-standard).
  5. Contract signed, vendor record created, and bill-to/PO details stored.
- Vendor recurring review cadence: annual for production vendors, biennial for low-risk SaaS.

Expenses and travel (policy highlights)
- Employees should use corporate card when available; otherwise submit EXPENSE REPORT within 10 business days.
- Per diem and limits:
  - Domestic travel lodging: up to $300/night unless pre-approved.
  - International lodging: submit estimated cost; finance will review for reasonableness.
  - Meals: up to $75/day.
  - Ground transportation: ride-share or taxi; rental car requires prior manager approval.
- Travel approval flow:
  1. Employee creates a TRAVEL REQUEST with destination, dates, estimated cost, and business justification.
  2. Manager approves or requests changes.
  3. Finance may require additional approval for international travel or costs > $2,500.
  4. After travel, submit receipts and expense report.

Templates (examples and machine-friendly snippets)
- ACCESS REQUEST template (fields): requestor, resource, role, justification, duration, manager, impact, related_ticket.
- CHANGE REQUEST template (fields): title, owner, change_window, impact_summary, rollback_plan, risk_level, approvers, validation_checks.
- PROCUREMENT REQUEST example (YAML):
  requestor: "name@redwood.com"
  vendor: "Acme Vector"
  estimated_annual_spend: "$3,200"
  contract_term_months: "12"
  cost_center: "platform-research"
  security_posture: "SOC2 Type II"
  business_justification: "GPU monitoring and alerting for runtime"
  approvers: ["manager@example.com","finance@example.com"]

- EXPENSE REPORT example (JSON):
  {
    "employee": "name@redwood.com",
    "trip": "SFO-SEA 2025-02-10",
    "items": [
      {"type": "lodging", "amount": "275.00", "currency": "USD"},
      {"type": "meals", "amount": "45.00", "currency": "USD"}
    ],
    "total": "320.00"
  }

Operational controls and automation suggestions
- Integrate access requests with the IAM system (SCIM/OKTA) to auto-provision standard roles.
- Enforce temporary tokens for elevated access via a Time-Bound Elevation service with automatic revocation.
- Automate procurement threshold checks and route to the appropriate approvers.
- Store vendor artifacts (contracts, SOC reports) in a central, versioned repository and link them in the vendor record.

Escalation and exceptions
- Exception handling: submit an EXCEPTION REQUEST with rationale and compensating controls.
- Escalation path for blocked approvals:
  - Day 0–2: Manager follow-up.
  - Day 3–5: Owner_team lead engages.
  - After Day 5: Head of People-ops or Finance engages depending on domain.

Related pages and references
- See the Security "RBAC and auth" page for technical IAM role names and SCIM sync instructions.
- See Finance "Procurement" for vendor payment onboarding and PO templates.

Appendix A: Example vendor onboarding checklist (short)
- Business justification and owner.
- Data handling: does vendor process customer data? (yes/no).
- Contract status: DPA required? (yes/no).
- Security artifacts: SOC2 / penetration test summary.
- Insurance certificates.
- Assigned account owner and billing code.

Appendix B: Common Q&A
- Q: Who can request admin-level access?
  A: Any employee can request admin-level access, but approval requires manager + security and a documented business justification.
- Q: How long do temporary elevations last?
  A: Default = 8 hours. Requests for longer duration require manager & security approval.

Change log
- 2024-11-12: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2025-06-03: Updated approval thresholds and procurement SLA; added YAML procurement example.

Contact
- For process questions: people-ops@redwood.com.
- For security-related approvals: security-approvals@redwood.com.

title: dsid_39d72f8c93ce4a1cad9dfa0e08b4e5a9__parameterized-endpoint-hinting-and-fidelity-bridging-guidelines-2026.txt
text:
Parameterized Endpoint Hinting and Fidelity Bridging Guidelines

Summary

This document defines a lightweight, consistent standard for parameterized endpoint hinting (client-supplied signals) and the server-side fidelity-bridging behavior that uses those hints to balance latency, cost, and output quality. The goal is to provide a predictable, testable contract that SDKs and platform components can implement to enable graceful degradation, cost-aware routing, and safe rollouts of new fidelity tiers.

Scope and motivation

- Applies to public and private Redwood inference endpoints that accept narrative/text generation, chat, or structured-response requests.
- Covers: request surface (headers/query/payload hints), server routing decisions, recording telemetry, contract tests, deprecation semantics, and rollout / rollback procedures.
- Motivation: customers and internal services need explicit controls to trade fidelity for latency/cost without opaque behavior or hard failures. This reduces emergent faults where mixed client expectations and runtime capacity produce surprising outputs.

Terminology

- Fidelity hint: optional client-provided signal that expresses a preference for latency/cost vs. quality (e.g., high, balanced, low).
- Bridge variant: a runtime-selected model or config that provides a fidelity tier (for example, quantized small-model, full-precision large-model, cached-prefix-boost).
- Degradation plan: the observable path the service takes when capacity or SLO pressure requires lowering fidelity.

Surface contract (required fields)

All endpoints must accept fidelity hints and a stability header. The server MUST treat the absence of a hint as "balanced" and continue to serve. The canonical names and allowed values are: 

| Field | Location | Allowed values | Default | Description |
|-------|----------|----------------|---------|-------------|
| X-Redwood-Fidelity | request header | low, balanced, high | balanced | Client preference for latency vs. output fidelity |
| fidelity_hint | JSON body / top-level | "low"/"balanced"/"high" | balanced | Mirrors header for clients that cannot set headers |
| X-Redwood-Stability | request header | experimental, stable, pinned | stable | Signals client expectation about API/format stability |
| X-Redwood-Return-Variant | request header | variant-id (string) | unset | If provided, server should attempt to route to exact variant or return 412 if incompatible |

(Represented here as a plain-text table; servers should include these names verbatim.)

Behavior rules (server-side)

1. Respect hints: The server SHOULD attempt to honor X-Redwood-Fidelity when selecting a bridge variant. Hints are advisory, not authoritative; servers may choose a higher fidelity than requested but must never silently drop from high to low without telemetry and a routed reason code.
2. Capability negotiation: If a requested fidelity or variant is impossible for the tenant (e.g., regulatory pinning, private deployment constraints), the server must return 412 Precondition Failed with a machine-parsable JSON explaining the allowed options and the owner link. Example: 

```json
HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "error": "fidelity_not_available",
  "allowed": ["balanced"],
  "message": "Tenant policy pins model to balanced. Contact infra@redwood.example.com for exceptions.",
  "owner": "/teams/eng-serving-runtime"
}
```

3. Deterministic bridging: When routing to a bridge variant because of capacity or cost policies, routing must use deterministic keys (tenant id, request hash, or session id) to avoid flapping across sequential requests in a session.
4. Circuit transparency: If the runtime degrades fidelity due to SLO pressure, the response MUST include the applied_variant and fidelity_reason fields in the response metadata. Example response snippet: 

```json
{
  "output": "...",
  "meta": {
    "applied_variant": "gptx-lite-q4_5",
    "fidelity_reason": "slo_pressure::cpu_90pct"
  }
}
```

Telemetry and SLI obligations

- Every request must emit telemetry with dimensions: tenant_id, fidelity_hint, applied_variant, latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, tokens_generated, and fidelity_reason (when applicable).
- SLOs tied to fidelity tiers: each fidelity tier must declare a latency SLO and a quality SLI (see Quality monitoring section). Example: balanced: p95 < 450ms, quality_score >= 0.92 on canonical tests.
- Sampling guidance: For 'low' hints, record 100% of telemetry for the first 72 hours after a new bridge variant is introduced, then reduce to 10% unless anomalies are detected.

Contract testing and SDK expectations

- SDKs must expose an enum for Fidelity {LOW, BALANCED, HIGH} mapped to the header/value strings. SDKs should provide a default of BALANCED.
- Contract tests (run in CI) must include:
  1) Round-trip test asserting that sending fidelity_hint results in either the same applied_variant or a deterministic and documented alternate.
  2) Compatibility test asserting 412 behavior when tenant policy forbids a fidelity.
  3) Telemetry hook test verifying presence of applied_variant and fidelity_reason in response metadata for degraded paths.

Quality monitoring and regression gating

- Each bridge variant must have an associated prompt-suite (subset of the canonical eval harness) and a quality baseline.
- Changes to bridge variants must pass: automated regression checks (no >2% drop in baseline metric) and a manual signoff from the model steward.
- Degradation alerts: if the quality metric for any fidelity tier drops below its baseline by threshold (configurable; default 3%) for a 1-hour window, trigger P1 alert and automatically mark the variant as quarantined for rollback.

Rollout and rollback playbook (high level)

1. Preflight (local + staging): run full contract tests and the variant-specific prompt-suite.
2. Canary release: route 1–5% of traffic using deterministic bucketing tied to tenant or API-key. Monitor fidelity-specific SLIs for 24 hours.
3. Incremental ramp: increase to 20% and then 50% only if no quality/latency regressions.
4. Full release: after 72 hours with stable telemetry, mark variant as default for the target fidelity hint.
5. Hot rollback: on P1 or automated quarantine, switch deterministic routing to previous stable variant and open an incident with the serving-runtime on-call.

Each rollout step must annotate the release with: owner, targeted tenants (if any), monitoring playbook link, and a revert tag. Use the release metadata schema: 

```yaml
release_id: r-2026-xxxx
owner: eng-serving-runtime
canary_fraction: 0.01
start_time: 2026-02-01T15:00:00Z
revert_to: gptx-lite-q4_4
notes: "introduce q4_5 for low fidelity to reduce cost for short conversations"
```

Runtime and infra safeguards

- Cost cap: bridge variants labeled "low" must have a budget tag and be subject to daily spend caps enforced by the quota controller.
- Preemption policy: instances running high-fidelity variants must register preemption handlers; during forced preemption the service should attempt to complete in-flight tokens up to a safety cutoff (e.g., 50 tokens) and emit fidelity_reason = "preempt_shutdown".
- Cache-awareness: when applying a cached-prefix-boost as a bridge variant, ensure the cache TTL respects data retention policies and is tagged with the tenant id and prompt-suite hash.

Security and privacy considerations

- Any bridge variant that uses external retrieval or tool-calling must verify tenant authorization for external calls and redact telemetry fields that may contain PII before export.
- For Private deployments, the runtime MUST honor tenant-configured accepted_fidelities and may reject hints that would route traffic outside approved artifact manifests.

Observability: dashboards and alerts (example)

- Dashboard: Fidelity Overview (filters: tenant, variant, hint) showing applied_variant distribution, p95 latency per variant, tokens per request, and quality_metric trendlines.
- Alert examples:
  - fidelity_quarantine_trigger (P1): quality_metric_deviation > 3% for 1h on any fidelity tier.
  - fidelity_unexpected_variant (P2): >0.5% of 'high' hint requests served by 'low' variants without explicit fidelity_reason tag.

Appendices

A. Example request/response (full)

Request:
```http
POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redwood.ai
Content-Type: application/json
X-Redwood-Fidelity: low
X-Redwood-Stability: stable

{
  "model": "text-creative-v2",
  "prompt": "Summarize the release notes in 3 bullet points.",
  "fidelity_hint": "low"
}
```

Response (degraded path):
```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "output": "- Released performance improvements.
- Fixed bug in telemetry.
- Improved deployment safety.",
  "meta": {
    "applied_variant": "text-creative-v2-q4_5",
    "fidelity_reason": "slo_pressure::gpu_85pct",
    "latency_ms": 312
  }
}
```

B. Quick CLI checks for on-call

Run a fidelity-bridge health check against a tenant: 

```bash
# requires REDWOOD_API_KEY set
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \ 
  -H "X-Redwood-Fidelity: low" \ 
  -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/debug/bridge-health \ 
  -d '{"tenant_id":"t-1234"}' | jq
```

Interpret output: presence of "quarantined": true indicates the variant is currently blocked.

C. Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (oncall: runtime@sre.redwood.example.com)
- Quality steward: applied-ml-and-evals (evals@redwood.example.com)
- Infra quotas: eng-infra (quota-owners@redwood.example.com)

D. Migration notes for clients

- SDKs: add Fidelity enum and expose a client flag `auto_fidelity_fallback` (default true). If set to false, client must handle 412 responses.
- Backwards compatibility: servers must accept legacy header X-RW-F (values numeric 0/1/2) mapping to low/balanced/high for at least 18 months and emit a deprecation header: X-Deprecation-Notice: "X-RW-F is deprecated; use X-Redwood-Fidelity".

E. Open questions (to be reviewed quarterly)

- Should fidelity hints be weighted by account spend tier? (Pros: better UX for premium customers. Cons: coupling billing to model quality.)
- How to standardize quality_score computation across very different prompt suites?

Related pages and references

- See also: contract-driven-client-simulator-and-compat-test-spec (integration with contract tests)
- See also: model-invocation-stability-and-tooling-contract (runtime variant stewardship)

Conformance checklist (copy this into PRs that add a bridge variant)

- [ ] Variant has a prompt-suite and baseline quality metrics
- [ ] Contract tests included in CI
- [ ] Telemetry dims emitted and validated
- [ ] Cost cap and quota tags set
- [ ] Rollout metadata created and linked

Contact and feedback

For feedback or proposed changes, open an issue in the architecture repo and tag @eng-serving-runtime.

title: dsid_a4d925705ccb4b079d9872a2e9a8067a__prd-session-anchored-embeddings-cache-and-metering-2026-04-07.txt
text:
PRD: Session-Anchored Embeddings Cache and Metering

Summary
-------
This PRD defines a productized feature: a session-anchored embeddings cache with integrated metering and TTL tiers. The feature provides low-latency, cost-efficient vector retrieval for conversational and transactional workloads by keeping short-lived, session-scoped vectors hot while retaining an economical long-term tier for reuse and billing reconciliation. The goal is to reduce per-request embedding compute, improve tail latency for conversational flows, and introduce clear metering semantics for session-resident vectors.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
- Many customers run conversational agents that repeatedly re-query or augment a short-lived context (e.g., user session, chat thread). Generating embeddings repeatedly for the same context increases token and compute costs and increases latency.
- Existing incremental embeddings tiering work focuses on storage durability and long-term retention; there is a gap for short-lived, session-anchored caches that are both performance-optimized and correctly metered.
- Business asks: 1) reduce host inference spend for ephemeral high-QPS sessions, 2) offer predictable billing for cached embeddings (distinct from permanent storage), 3) instrument quality and eviction metrics for SRE/product monitoring.

Goals
-----
- Provide an in-platform session-anchored cache with three TTL tiers (session-hot: 0-30 minutes, session-warm: 30m-24h, persistent: >24h) configurable per-tenant.
- Expose a clear metering model: cached-hit credits for session-hot/warm usage and standard embedding credits for persistent or cache-miss generation.
- Keep additional tail latency for embed requests under 20ms P95 for session-hot cache on Dedicated and Hosted tiers.
- Provide SDK primitives and server-side hooks so customers can opt into session anchoring with a single flag (session_id + anchor=true).
- Emit telemetry to reconcile cache hits/misses with billing and to detect quality regressions due to TTL/quantization interactions.

Non-goals
---------
- This PRD does not introduce cross-tenant shared caching.
- Not handling GDPR data-deletion workflows beyond standard deletion APIs (deletion and retention policies handled by separate compliance playbooks).

User stories
------------
1) As a product engineer at a messaging startup, I want repeated assistant-context embeddings during a user conversation to be served from a session cache so the assistant responds faster and my bill decreases.
2) As a platform engineer at a regulated enterprise, I want to configure session TTLs and disable the persistent tier, preventing long-term retention of session vectors.
3) As a finance analyst, I want a daily report that attributes credits consumed to (a) hot cache hits, (b) cache warms (migrated to warm/persistent), (c) cache misses (fresh embedding generation).

Requirements (functional)
------------------------
- API changes:
  - New embedding API parameter: session_anchor: boolean (default false), session_id: string (optional), ttl_override: string (optional human duration).
  - Example request snippet:

```json
POST /v1/embeddings
{
  "model": "redwood-embed-2-sim",
  "input": "user message",
  "session_anchor": true,
  "session_id": "chat-12345"
}
```

- Cache behavior:
  - On session_anchor:true and a provided session_id, the runtime attempts to read the session-hot cache. If miss, compute embeddings and write to session-hot with default TTL 30m (configurable at tenant level).
  - Access frequency moves objects between tiers: >5 hits in 30m -> promote to session-warm (TTL 24h), explicit customer opt-in can promote to persistent (billed as persistent embeddings).
  - Eviction policy: LRU within session scope, configurable max bytes per-session (default 16MB).

- Billing model:
  - Cache hit in session-hot: minimal or zero embedding generation credits; bill a small per-hit metadata credit (to account for bandwidth/storage) as defined in the pricing matrix.
  - Promotion to persistent triggers an embedding-generation charge at prevailing rates plus storage crediting.
  - Cache miss: standard embedding generation credits.

- Admin controls:
  - Tenant-level toggles: enable_session_cache (bool), max_session_cache_bytes (int), session_hot_ttl, session_warm_ttl, allow_persistent_promotion (bool).
  - RBAC: only admin roles may change TTLs / persistent promotion setting.

- Observability and reconciliation:
  - Telemetry events: session_cache_read, session_cache_hit, session_cache_miss, session_cache_promote, session_cache_evict, session_cache_write. Each event must include tenant_id, session_id (hashed for PII), vector_id, tier, and latency_ms.
  - Daily billing reconciliation job must consume these events to attribute credits to customers.

Non-functional requirements
---------------------------
- Latency targets: P95 read latency for session-hot on hosted must be <= 20ms, P99 <= 50ms.
- Throughput: support 10k concurrent session caches per host in Dedicated targets with graceful degradation.
- Durability: session-hot/warm should be stored in-memory + replicated to local node persistent store for fast warm-up across container restarts; persistent tier uses existing embeddings store.
- Security: session_id must be accepted only over authenticated requests; if session_id is not present, behavior falls back to standard embedding generation.

Architecture and integration
---------------------------
- Components:
  - Session Cache Master (SCM): lightweight orchestrator per-host that coordinates TTLs, promotions, and eviction signals. Owned by eng-serving-runtime.
  - Local In-Memory Cache: per-runtime process LRU store for session-hot.
  - Warm Store: SSD-backed per-host store for session-warm tier.
  - Persistent Embeddings Store: existing global embeddings store for long-term retention.
  - Metering Bridge Service: receives telemetry events, aggregates, and forwards to billing pipeline and cost-analysis systems.

- Data flow:
  1. Request with session_anchor arrives at edge -> routed to preferred runtime.
  2. Runtime queries Local In-Memory Cache. If hit -> return vector and emit session_cache_hit.
  3. If miss -> compute embedding, write to Local Cache and Warm Store, emit session_cache_miss & session_cache_write.
  4. Promotion process runs asynchronously in SCM; on promotion to persistent, emit session_cache_promote and trigger billing event for generation+storage.

SLOs and monitoring
-------------------
- SLOs:
  - Session-hot read latency: 95th percentile <= 20ms (hosted), 99th <= 50ms.
  - Cache correctness: typed mismatch or corruption rate < 0.01% per 1M ops.
  - Billing-metering accuracy: discrepancy between aggregated telemetry-derived usage and billing pipeline < 0.5% over 7-day window.

- Key dashboards and alerts:
  - Session Cache Health: hit rate, average TTL remaining, eviction rate, memory pressure per-host.
  - Billing Reconciliation: daily variance, un-attributed credits, top tenants by promotions.
  - Regression detectors: sudden drop in hit-rate or spike in cache misses after rollout (auto alert and rollback path).

API and SDK changes (developer experience)
-----------------------------------------
- SDKs (Python/Node/Go) shall add a single optional parameter: session (object) with fields id and ttl_hint. Example (Python):

```py
client.embeddings.create(model="redwood-embed-2-sim", input="...", session={"id": "chat-12345", "ttl_hint": "15m"})
```

- UX guidance in docs: recommended pattern is to scope session_id to a conversation thread and to avoid using PII; SDK will automatically hash session_id for telemetry.

Telemetry and billing reconciliation
----------------------------------
- Event schema (flattened JSON per event):
  - event_type, timestamp, tenant_id, session_id_hash, vector_id, tier, latency_ms, host_id, model_name
- Reconciliation flow:
  1. Metering Bridge aggregates per-tenant daily counts for hits/misses/promotions.
  2. Aggregates fed into billing engine; promotions and misses are billed as embedding generation events.
  3. Daily report emailed to tenant admin and surfaced in Console under "Embedding Usage > Session Cache".

Security and compliance considerations
-------------------------------------
- Session identifiers are treated as potentially sensitive. We will store only hashed session_id in event logs.
- Tenants may opt-out of persistent promotions to meet retention regulations.
- Data deletion: explicit delete requests from tenant must remove all session-warm and session-hot records for that tenant; persistent tier deletion flows handled by existing embeddings retention APIs.

Rollout plan and migration path
------------------------------
1. Alpha: internal-only on staging, limited to internal tenants, no billing hooks enabled; telemetry only. (2 weeks)
2. Beta: opt-in for Hosted (small cohort) and Dedicated (selected customers) with billing hooks in dry-run mode (reconciliation only). (4 weeks)
3. GA: billing hooks enabled, SDK docs published, Console UI for session cache toggles. Gradual rollout with canary ratio 5% -> 25% -> 100% across tenancy segments. (4–6 weeks)
4. Post-GA: observe billing variance, iterate pricing if needed, add migration scripts for customers who want to port persistent vectors out. (Ongoing)

Migration considerations for existing customers
---------------------------------------------
- For tenants already using persistent embeddings for conversational workloads, recommend a migration plan: enable session cache opt-in, set conservative TTLs, monitor hit-rate for 2 weeks, then consider promotion policy.
- Provide a one-click Console toggle to opt-in with recommended defaults and a simulator that shows estimated cost impact (savings vs promotions).

Open questions (product / engineering)
------------------------------------
1. What is the exact per-hit metadata credit (business must set a pricing floor)? Suggested: 0.01x of standard embedding credit per hit for session-hot.
2. Promotion heuristics: should we use purely frequency-based criteria, or model access patterns and semantic stability?
3. Cross-region session affinity: how to handle when a session’s traffic shifts region mid-conversation? (fallback to recompute).
4. Measuring vector quality drift across caches with quantized warm store. Need an eval harness hook.

Ownership and next steps
------------------------
- Product lead: Elena Morales (author).
- Engineering owners: eng-serving-runtime (runtime + SCM), eng-infra (warm store integration), eng-platform (console + billing integration).
- Milestones:
  - Design review complete: 2026-04-21
  - Implementation spike (runtime & SDK): 2026-05-05 -> 2026-06-02
  - Beta cohort start: 2026-06-15

Appendix: sample billing table (illustrative)
--------------------------------------------
| Item | Charge basis | Example rate (illustrative) |
|------|--------------|-----------------------------|
| Embedding generation (standard) | per request token/compute | 1.0 credit per 1k tokens |
| Session-hot cache hit | per-hit metadata credit | 0.01 credit per hit |
| Session-warm access (read) | per-read warm tier | 0.05 credit per read |
| Promotion to persistent | generation + storage | generation charge + storage baseline |

Appendix: example telemetry event (newline-delimited)
----------------------------------------------------
{"event_type":"session_cache_read","timestamp":"2026-05-15T12:00:00Z","tenant_id":"t-123","session_id_hash":"sha256:...","vector_id":"v-abc","tier":"hot","latency_ms":12,"host_id":"host-9","model_name":"redwood-embed-2-sim"}

References and related pages
----------------------------
- Incremental embeddings storage tiering (design) – /product-docs/requirements/incremental-embeddings-storage-tiering-prd-2026-12-10
- Billing bridge and reconciliation playbook – /product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/predictive-bundling-and-sla-credit-algorithm-playbook-2027-06-18
- Developer SDK session patterns – /eng-developer-experience/quickstarts-and-templates/session-patterns-overview (internal link)

This document is intended to be reviewed by the serving runtime, infra, billing, and product teams. Feedback requested on promotion heuristics and initial pricing floor for per-hit credits.

title: dsid_c41ef7a99a6348beaaa083f4e86613e3__onboard-slo-first-playbook-2026-12-13.txt
text:
Onboard: SLO-first Packaging Playbook

Summary

This playbook describes the SLO-first packaging model for onboarding new developer and mid-market customers to Redwood Inference. It provides a prescriptive set of packaging defaults, onboarding steps, telemetry and rollout guidance designed to reduce cost uncertainty while guaranteeing customer-facing latency/availability objectives. Use this when negotiating early SLAs, designing onboarding flows, or creating customer-specific packaging addenda.

Goals

- Make service-level objectives the primary axis for packaging and entitlements.
- Reduce cost uncertainty by exposing clear tradeoffs between SLO tiers and cost levers (batching, KV caching, quantization).
- Provide a repeatable onboarding checklist that product, solutions, and customer success can follow for 48–72 hour time-to-first-SLO (customer-visible).
- Ensure safe rollouts with telemetry, rollback triggers, and canary guardrails.

Audience

Product managers, solutions engineers, customer success, account executives negotiating Dedicated/Private contracts, and developer onboarding engineers.

Scope and non-goals

In scope:
- Hosted and Dedicated onboarding paths.
- Default packaging configurations and SLO mappings.
- Onboarding runbook and telemetry requirements.
- Pricing buckets tied to SLOs and predictable capacity commits.

Out of scope:
- Detailed legal contract language (finance/legal will publish templates).
- Deep runtime kernel tuning steps (see eng-serving-runtime docs).

SLO-first packaging model overview

We define three canonical SLO tiers customers can select during onboarding. Each tier maps to a set of default runtime and packaging configurations, and a cost multiplier relative to baseline usage pricing. Teams can override defaults for enterprise customers with Dedicated or Private deployments.

Table: Canonical SLO tiers

| Tier name | Availability SLO | P95 latency target (text gen) | Default runtime profile | Typical customer size | Notes |
|-----------|------------------:|-----------------------------:|------------------------|---------------------|------:|
| Bronze    | 99.5%             | 800 ms                      | shared-hosted, opportunistic batching | small dev teams, PoC | cost-first, longer coldstart windows |
| Silver    | 99.9%             | 350 ms                      | hosted with prefix-KV cache, medium batching | early production apps | balanced cost/latency |
| Gold      | 99.99%            | 120 ms                      | Dedicated warm capacity, reserved KV, strict batching caps | mission-critical, scale | SLA-backed availability and latency |

Defaults and packaging primitives

Each tier exposes configurable primitives that materially impact unit economics. Default values for each tier are documented in the table below. These defaults are opinionated; use engineering review for bespoke allocations.

Table: Default primitives by tier

| Primitive | Bronze | Silver | Gold |
|-----------|--------|--------|------|
| Max batch size | 64 | 32 | 16 |
| Prefix KV cache TTL | 10m | 60m | 6h |
| Quantization profile | fp16 | int8-mixed | int8+llm-quant |
| Warm capacity percent | 0% | 30% | 80% |
| Reserved concurrency | burst | 200 r/s | 2k r/s |

Pricing model and packaging SKUs

High-level pricing approach: map expected steady-state consumption to an SLO SKU. Each SKU consists of: base monthly fee (for dedicated/warm guarantees), per-token variable price, and an SLO credit that limits behavior under overload. Example SKU (Silver):

- base_fee_monthly: $1,200 (stringified in contract)
- per_token_rate: $0.0006 per token
- on_slo_mitigation: traffic reprioritization + adaptive batching

Note: Concrete USD values are negotiation starting points — product/pricing must sign off on any discounting above 15%. Finance owns final published SKUs.

Developer onboarding checklist (48–72 hour target)

1. Initial scoping call (owner: solutions engineering).
   - Confirm target SLO tier, expected peak qps, concurrency pattern, and security requirements.
   - Capture model family and sequence length distribution.
2. Provisioning (owner: infra ops/product).
   - For Hosted: allocate namespace, default runtime profile per chosen tier.
   - For Dedicated: reserve GPU pool and warm capacity; create tenant routing policy; configure KMS if requested.
3. Baseline traffic replay and smoke tests (owner: onboarding eng).
   - Run synthetic traffic generator with representative prompts (use playbook prompts-store).
   - Verify p95 latency and error budget burn over 1–4 hours.
4. Telemetry and tracing hooks (owner: observability/product).
   - Ensure tenant export of token-level telemetry, p95/p99 latency metrics, and request traces to customer's telemetry workspace (if configured).
5. Cost forecast and packaging sign-off (owner: solutions/product).
   - Use the cost simulator (CLI example below) to estimate 30/60/90 day spend given projected traffic.
6. Go-live and canary (owner: SRE/onboarding eng).
   - Canary 5% traffic for 2 hours with active rollback monitors.

Example: cost simulator CLI snippet

# CLI: simulate cost for 10M tokens/month at Silver defaults
redwood-cost-sim --tokens 10000000 --tier silver --sequence-avg 128 --output report.json

Output (example JSON):
{"scenario":"silver-default-10m","monthly_cost_usd":"7200","base_fee":"1200","variable":"6000"}

Telemetry, observability and rollback triggers

Required telemetry exports for onboarding must be configured before removing canary protection. At minimum:

- token_count (per request), request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), request_error_count, kv_cache_hit_rate, batch_size_distribution, warm_capacity_utilization.
- SLO burn rate alert: when error budget consumption > 10% per 10-minute window for > 2 windows, trigger automated rollback to previous runtime profile.
- Cost-exposure alert: projected monthly cost increase > 15% vs signed forecast for sustained 60 minutes.

Table: Alert thresholds (recommended)

| Alert | Threshold | Action owner | Automated action |
|-------|----------:|--------------|------------------|
| P95 latency > target + 20% | sustained 5m | SRE | throttle and scale-up signal |
| Error rate > 0.5% | sustained 10m | Oncall | fallback to lower fidelity variant |
| KV hit rate < 10% | 30m window | Runtime eng | suggest cache-warm job |
| Cost drift > 15% projection | 60m | Customer success | send usage hold and flag to AE |

Rollout phases and gating

Phase 0 — Discovery: collect traffic patterns, negotiate tier.
Phase 1 — Provisioned canary: 5% traffic routed for 2–4 hours, full telemetry.
Phase 2 — Gradual ramp: 20% for 12 hours, then 100% if stable.
Phase 3 — Harden + review: 72-hour post-go-live review with performance and cost readouts.

Gates before moving from Phase 1 to Phase 2:
- P95 and error budget within 125% of target for duration of canary.
- No more than 5% cost overshoot vs forecast during canary.

Engineering contacts and ownership

- Product owner: Aisha Patel (product) — overall playbook steward.
- Solutions eng lead: Diego Martinez — onboarding scoping and customer templates.
- Runtime liaison: Elliot Ng (eng-serving-runtime) — implementation of tiered defaults and rollback hooks.
- Observability: Priya Raman (eng-platform) — telemetry export onboarding.

API example: SLO binding request (HTTP JSON)

POST /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/slo-binding
Content-Type: application/json

Request body example:
{"slo_tier":"silver","target_p95_ms":"350","max_monthly_tokens":"20000000","preferred_runtime_profile":"silver-default-2026-11"}

Operational notes and known tradeoffs

- Stronger SLOs (Gold) typically increase unit cost by 2–4x for the same token volume due to warm capacity and reduced batching. Communicate this clearly during pricing conversations.
- For customer workloads dominated by long sequences (avg sequence > 1024 tokens), Gold may require model variant pinning or quantization profile adjustments.
- On Dedicated, reserved KV cache TTLs should be conservatively lowered before any mass migration to avoid cache stampedes.

Open decisions

- Whether to expose an automated SLO-negotiation UI in Console that maps observed workload to a recommended tier (product to decide by 2027-01-15).
- How to standardize discounting policy tied to multi-year Dedicated commitments (finance/product ongoing).

KPIs and success metrics

- Time to first customer-visible SLO (target <= 72 hours).
- Fraction of onboards that hit forecasted cost within ±15% at 30 days (target >= 80%).
- Post-onboard SLO compliance at 90 days (fraction of customers meeting their tier's SLOs, target >= 95%).

Related docs

- /confluence/product-docs/requirements/hosted-to-private-migration-performance-playbook-prd-2026-05-17.json
- /confluence/product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/migration-pricing-pathways-hosted-to-dedicated-2027-11.json
- /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/tenant-onboarding-telemetry-template.json

FAQ

Q: Can a customer change tiers mid-cycle?
A: Yes. Tier changes are permitted at the start of the next billing cycle unless otherwise negotiated. Mid-cycle emergency downgrades may be applied with prorated credits.

Q: What happens if SLOs are violated due to third-party model regressions?
A: We route to fallback variants and open an incident. The SLO review will distinguish between platform and model-level causes; customer credits follow the contractual SLA process.

Appendix: minimal JSON contract snippet for SKU assignment

{"sku_id":"silver-onboard-2026-1","tier":"silver","base_fee_monthly":"1200","per_token_usd":"0.0006","slo_p95_ms":"350"}

If you have questions about tailoring this playbook for a customer, contact the product owner or add to the playbook issues tracker (link: /confluence/product-docs/roadmap-and-themes/playbook-issues).

title: dsid_fc9fa49f6ec642848ccd1c35c43b729e__regional-oncall-rotation-simplification-retrospective-2026.txt
text:
Regional On-call Rotation Simplification — Retrospective

Summary:

Background: In H2 2025 the platform team expanded regional coverage to three additional cloud regions (eu-west-3, ap-southeast-2, and us-west-3). The on-call rotation grew organically: separate regional rotations, multiple overlap windows, and bespoke escalation rules for legacy services. By late 2025 we observed higher page fatigue, increased cross-region handoffs, and slower mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) for multi-region incidents.

This retrospective reviews the simplification project (Project ROTA-SIMP) that ran from 2025-11-02 to 2026-01-28 with the goal to reduce operational cognitive load while preserving SLOs and regional ownership.

Scope and goals:
- Reduce the number of distinct rotations covering core platform services from 6 to 3.
- Reduce cross-region handoffs during incidents by 50% within 2 months of rollout.
- Maintain or improve 99th percentile page-to-acknowledge (P2A) latency.
- Document and publish updated runbooks and dashboard views.

Timeline and milestones:
1. 2025-11-02: Project kickoff; stakeholders: Eng-Platform, Eng-SRE, Eng-Infra, Product.
2. 2025-11-16: Audit of existing rotations and escalation graphs completed.
3. 2025-12-01: Prototype unified regional rotation design approved by oncall leads.
4. 2025-12-15: Small internal pilot with us-central and eu-west on core infra services.
5. 2026-01-05: Gradual rollout to remaining teams and regions.
6. 2026-01-28: Formal project close and start of monitoring phase.

Data and key metrics (pre vs post, baseline window: 2025-09-01 — 2025-11-01; post window: 2026-01-01 — 2026-02-15):
- Number of distinct rotations covering core services: 6 -> 3
- Average page-to-acknowledge (median): 2.4 min -> 2.1 min
- 99th percentile page-to-acknowledge: 18.2 min -> 12.7 min
- Cross-region handoff rate (incidents requiring >1 region team): 34% -> 14%
- Paging noise (pages per oncaller per week): 18 -> 13

Root causes identified:
- Over-specialization: Many rotations were scoped to single-region operational tasks; as services became globally routed, incidents crossed boundaries and required multiple teams.
- Divergent escalation trees: Small, ad-hoc differences in escalation (who to call at 15 vs 20 minutes) created inconsistent behavior.
- Tooling configuration sprawl: Pager and roster configurations lived in multiple spreadsheets and two different PagerDuty teams.
- Insufficient runbook normalization: Runbooks used different naming conventions and inconsistent troubleshooting steps, increasing cognitive load during high-pressure incidents.

What worked well:
- Cross-team working group: Weekly cross-functional syncs (Platform, SRE, Infra) accelerated decisions and surfaced edge cases early.
- Pilot-first rollout: A conservative pilot reduced blast radius and produced real production data.
- Observability changes paired with rota changes: Updating SLO dashboards and adding region labels to alerts made responsibilities clearer.

What didn't work / surprises:
- Short-term increase in duplicate notification noise during reconfiguration windows due to overlapping schedules in PagerDuty. Mitigation required three emergency rollbacks and a follow-up cleanup job.
- Underestimated training time: New oncall run-throughs and handover docs took two additional weeks of SMEs' time.
- A handful of legacy services required custom escalation rules which complicated consolidation.

Decisions made:
- Consolidation model: Adopt a hybrid regional-owner model — three rotations (Americas, EMEA, APAC). Each rotation owns initial triage for services routed to that region; for cross-region stateful failures the owning region coordinates fixes with a designated global follow-up (Global-Fix rotation).
- Standard escalation windows: 0/5/15/30/60 minutes for first/second/tech-lead/engineering-manager/exec escalation respectively for critical SLO breaches.
- Centralized roster storage: Single source of truth in the platform team repo: infra/oncall/roster.yml with automated PagerDuty sync.
- Runbook normalization: All core runbooks must conform to the runbook template (section table below) and include explicit 'handoff' steps.

Runbook template (mandatory fields):
- Service name
- Region labels (Americas/EMEA/APAC/global)
- Owner (primary, secondary)
- Symptoms and first checks (bullet list)
- Quick mitigation steps (ordered)
- Escalation path with contact links and time windows
- Post-incident checklist and RCA pointer

Operational changes to deploy (action items):
- A1: Implement roster.yml and PagerDuty sync automation (owner: Infra-Automation, due 2026-02-15).
- A2: Migrate 42 runbooks to normalized template; prioritize core services (owner: Platform-Docs, due 2026-03-01).
- A3: Update SLO dashboards: add rotation-aware widgets and handoff metrics (owner: Observability, due 2026-02-10).
- A4: Add a dedicated 'Global-Fix' weekly rotation (owner: Eng-SRE, due 2026-02-01).
- A5: Run four 60-minute playbook drills (regional and cross-region scenarios) across Q1 2026 (owner: Eng-Platform, due 2026-04-30).

Risk assessment and mitigations:
- Risk: Single roster source is a single point of configuration failure.
  - Mitigation: GitOps workflow with required PR approvals from two distinct oncall leads and automated unit tests for roster sanity (e.g., coverage by role, no overlapping primary slots).
- Risk: New rotation boundaries might reduce local oncall domain knowledge in small regional teams.
  - Mitigation: Pairing windows and weekly 'regional clinic' office hours during the first 8 weeks after rollout.

Dashboard and alert changes (examples):
- New dashboard panels: 'Active incident by rotation', 'Handoff count (last 24h)', 'Pages per oncaller (7d rolling)'.
- Alert label changes: add label rotation=americas|emea|apac. Use this label in the Alertmanager routing tree to control deduplication and notification channels.
- SLO watchlist: For the first 60 days after rollout, add SLOs for page-to-acknowledge 99th percentile to the daily ops digest.

Communication and rollout plan summary:
- Week 0 (pre-rollout): Publish runbook guidelines and hold two 1-hour training sessions.
- Week 1 (pilot): Enable merged rotations in PagerDuty for two non-critical services. Monitor for 7 days.
- Week 2–3: Iterate on config and runbooks based on pilot findings.
- Week 4 (full rollout): Switch remaining eligible services during low-traffic window and trigger verification playbooks.
- Week 5–12: Monitoring phase and weekly status updates to platform leadership.

Follow-ups and measurement plan:
- Weekly post-rollout review for first 8 weeks focusing on: handoff rate, paging noise, MTTA percentiles, pager overlap incidents.
- After 8 weeks produce an outcome memo with updated metrics and recommended further changes.

Owners and stakeholders:
- Project lead: Asha Patel (Eng-Platform)
- Infra-Automation: Ethan Morales
- Observability: Sofia Chen
- Eng-SRE liaison: Priya Nair
- Platform docs: Liam O'Connor
- Product stakeholder: Maya Rodriguez

Participants in retrospective workshop:
- 14 total: representatives from Platform (6), SRE (3), Infra (2), Product (2), Support (1).

Appendix — sample roster.yml schema (example snippet):

# roster.yml (example)
# Note: actual file is in infra/oncall/roster.yml in the platform repo
- rotation: americas-core
  primary: ["alice@example.com", "bob@example.com"]
  secondary: ["carol@example.com"]
  regions: ["us-central", "us-west"]

- rotation: emea-core
  primary: ["dan@example.com"]
  secondary: ["eve@example.com"]
  regions: ["eu-west-3", "eu-central-1"]

(Operational team: Do not edit roster.yml directly in PagerDuty. All changes must be PR -> CI -> PD-sync.)

Lessons learned (top three):
1. Simplify first, automate second: consolidations without automated, testable configuration caused the largest operational headaches.
2. Pilot in production at small scale is invaluable — it uncovered unexpected notification duplication caused by historic PD integrations.
3. Documentation and runbook normalization are as important as technical changes; consistent language reduced cognitive load during incidents.

Open questions / parking lot:
- Should the Global-Fix rotation be staffed by a smaller, dedicated cross-functional team or a larger on-call pool? (Decision required by 2026-03-15).
- How should we handle customer-facing incident comms when multiple regions are involved? Propose a templated comms flow tied to rotation ownership.

Tags and archival notes:
- Retrospective created as part of continuous reliability improvements; archive after 18 months unless requirements change.

If you have updates to the action items or metrics, add a comment on this page and tag the owner.

title: dsid_1e9c815541314824aba32a8babdea641__cross-functional-slas-and-capacity-delegation-guide-2026.txt
text:
Cross-functional SLAs and Capacity Delegation Guide

Summary:
This guide defines a cross-functional approach to SLAs, SLOs, error budgets, and capacity delegation between SRE, product/owner teams, and tenant/platform teams. The goal is predictable reliability while giving product teams responsibility for feature-level availability and SRE responsibility for fleet-level capacity and safe-guards.

Scope:
- Applies to all customer-facing inference services (hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments) operated by Redwood.
- Includes multi-tenant services (model serving, embedding pipelines, batch/streaming inference) and their associated supporting infra (gateway, routing, cache).

Definitions and principles:
- SLA: A contractual commitment (external). Handled by Sales/Legal with SRE input.
- SLO: A measurable service objective used internally to guide operations (e.g., 99.9% successful-gen within latency target).
- Error budget: The allowed rate of SLO violations over a rolling period (commonly 30d).
- Delegated capacity: Reserved capacity quota entrusted to a product/tenant team for guaranteed throughput.
- Capacity escrow: A short-term set-aside of physical capacity for rapid use during incidents or launches.

Key design principles:
- Clear ownership: SRE owns platform capacity envelope; product teams own feature-level SLOs and alerts.
- Transparent economics: Per-tenant cost impact of delegated capacity must be visible in console.
- Fail-open vs fail-safe: Default is fail-open for non-critical features (best-effort); critical features must declare fail-safe fallbacks.
- Single source of truth: SLO definitions, runbooks, and capacity reservations live in the Redwood Console and this repo of playbooks.

Ownership matrix (high level):
| Concern | Primary owner | Secondary owner | Decision authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fleet capacity provisioning | SRE | Eng Infra | SRE (with Product consult) |
| Model selection/rollout | Product/ML | SRE | Product/ML |
| Feature SLO definitions | Product/Owner team | SRE | Product/Owner team |
| Emergency capacity release | SRE | Product | SRE (operational) |
| Error budget arbitration | SRE & Product | Customer Success | Cross-functional committee |

SLO and error-budget governance
1) SLO template (required fields):
- service_name (string)
- objective (e.g., 99.9%)
- metric (e.g., successful_generation / total_requests)
- latency_bound (ms) or qualitative outcome (e.g., correctness threshold)
- evaluation_window (30d default)
- alert_thresholds (burn_rate > 2x for 1h, 4x for 30m)
- owner (email/alias)

2) Example SLO (text):
- Service: hosted-text-generation
- Objective: 99.9% of requests return a completion within 300ms p50 and 1.5s p95, and successful token stream without error
- Error budget: 0.1% daily allowance, evaluated on rolling 30d window

3) Error budget banking and cross-tenant pooling:
- Per-tenant error budgets are primary. Teams may opt into a limited pooled budget for burst events (max retention 7 days) to facilitate controlled launches.
- Banking rules: unused daily error budget can be banked up to 3x daily allowance; banking beyond that requires SRE approval.
- Pooling rules: a tenant can request temporary access to pool; SRE will authorize if pool health (available capacity headroom > 15% and fleet burn_rate < 0.8).

Capacity delegation protocol
Phase A — Request and justification:
1. Product/tenant files a capacity-delegation request via the Console form including expected QPS, percent of/p95 tail, time window, and expected duration. Attach load-test artifacts.
2. SRE reviews request within 48 business hours, verifying load profile against historical telemetry.

Phase B — Approval and configuration:
1. SRE may approve one of: a) Dedicated quota (hard limit), b) Burst escrow (temporal cushion), c) Managed shared quota (soft limit with throttling policies).
2. Configuration includes: reserved GPU count, routing policy ID, admission controller tags, and cost center assignment. SRE provides IaC fragment to commit to tenant config.

Phase C — Operational handoff:
1. SRE publishes a delegated capacity dashboard (latency, queue-depth, token-rate, error-rate) scoped to the tenant.
2. Product owners are added to the capacity-alerting rotation and must maintain runbook readiness.

Operational tooling integrations
- Telemetry hooks required for delegation: request_id propagation, tenant_id tag, model_variant, routing_path, queuing_time_ms, GPU_util_pct, kv_cache_hit_rate.
- Console views: per-tenant headroom, projected burn-rate, cost-per-1000-tokens, active-reservations.
- Automation: Accepts CLI commands for emergency-release and escrow-expansion with RBAC (examples below).

Runbook excerpts (emergency capacity bind)
1) Trigger: product reports sustained p95 latency > target for 10m and queue-depth increase > 2x baseline.
2) Triage steps (chronological):
   a) Confirm telemetry: open tenant dashboard, confirm latency and GPU_util_pct.
   b) Check model variants: is there an older quantized variant available for fallback? If yes, set routing policy to fallback (see routing-policy CLI sample).
   c) If fallback insufficient, SRE evaluates emergency escrow release:
      - Verify pool health: overall fleet error_rate < 1% and available physical headroom >= requested GPUs.
      - Run preflight scaling canary (deploy 1 pod to a target host and validate latency with synthetic tracer).
   d) Execute emergency-release CLI (RBAC) with annotation linking to incident ID.
   e) Communicate to product and CS: update incident ticket with release time and expected impact.

3) Post-incident reconciliation:
- SRE and Product complete an incident-initiation form in Retroboard within 48h.
- Any escrow usage beyond 8 hours triggers chargeback or repatriation plan (see Cost and chargeback table).

Incident review and evidence standards
- Evidence required for incident review:
  * telemetry snapshot (30m pre/post),
  * request traces (sampled set, min 100 requests),
  * model input corpus snippet (redaction required),
  * configuration changes (IaC commits) and rollout timeline,
  * error budget burn reports.
- Postmortem checklist (deliverables within 72h):
  1) Annotated timeline (ISO timestamps)
  2) Root cause hypothesis and verification steps
  3) List of corrective actions with owners and ETA
  4) SLO recalibration proposal (if applicable)

Decision and arbitration process
- Minor disputes (e.g., short-term escrow denials) resolved by SRE lead + product manager.
- Material disputes (affecting contracts or multi-tenant guarantees) escalate to Reliability Council (SRE director, Head of Product, Head of CS, Finance rep).
- Arbitration signals include: >3 tenants requesting emergency escrow within 24h, sustained fleet burn_rate > 1.5 for 4h, or cross-region failure correlation.

Cost and chargeback (summary table)
| Item | Trigger | Billing rule |
|---|---:|---|
| Escrow use (short) | < 8h | No immediate charge; internal AR ticket created |
| Escrow use (long) | >= 8h | Automated charge by cost-center; prorated GPU-hours at committed rate |
| Dedicated delegated quota | Reservation commit | Monthly invoice based on reserved GPU-hours |

CLI / IaC examples (samples)
- Emergency release (RBAC required):
  redwoodctl capacity release --tenant tenant-42 --gpus 4 --reason "p95-latency-surge" --incident-id INC-2026-1543

- Example reservation fragment (YAML):
  reservation:
    tenant_id: tenant-42
    reserved_gpus: 8
    routing_policy: "policy-ml-fastpath-v2"
    escrow_expiry: "2026-03-01T08:00:00Z"

Observability and analytics requirements
- SRE will maintain a "capacity forecast" job that projects required headroom for the next 14d with daily cadence. Inputs: historical QPS, trending growth, scheduled launches, and pooled banking levels.
- Alerts must include: burn_rate(1h) > 2x, headroom < 10% for two consecutive evaluation windows, and sustained queue_depth_growth > 50% for 30m.

Templates and attachments (stored in Console):
- Delegation request form template (JSON schema)
- Incident evidence submission checklist (CSV)
- IaC sample repo link: git://git.redwood/services/capacity-delegation/examples

Appendix A — Quick decision matrix (condensed)
- Is the request predictable? -> Yes -> request Dedicated quota; No -> request Burst escrow + managed throttling.
- Is the pool healthy? -> No -> SRE denies escrow and offers staged canary.

Appendix B — Example SLO JSON (copy into console):
{
  "service_name": "hosted-text-generation",
  "objective": "99.9%",
  "metric": "successful_responses / total_requests",
  "latency_p95_ms": "1500",
  "evaluation_window": "30d",
  "owner": "team-hosted-ml@redwood.com"
}

Contact & escalation paths:
- Primary SRE oncall alias: sre-oncall@redwood.com
- Capacity governance mailbox: capacity-gov@redwood.com
- Reliability Council chair: lina@redwood.com

Revision history:
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft by Asha Verma
- 2025-12-02: Added banking rules and pooling criteria (reviewers: Diego Morales)
- 2026-02-03: Updated CLI samples and incident evidence standards (reviewers: Priya Nair)

title: dsid_2ff741df6d7c4d8aa80a17b381bbb653__preemption-aware-batch-slicing-spec-2026.txt
text:
Preemption-aware Batch Slicing: Spec and Operational Playbook

This document defines the design and operational guidance for "preemption-aware batch slicing" — a kernel-scheduler-adjacent feature that slices large inference batches into smaller execution windows aligned to expected preemption boundaries and GPU occupancy windows. The goal is to reduce tail-latency spikes caused by mid-kernel preemption, long-running kernels blocking higher-priority work, and KV-cache warmup penalties while preserving throughput and unit-cost efficiency.
Large requests and long-sequence generation can produce kernel executions that exceed preemption windows on shared GPU pools. When preemption occurs mid-kernel, it can cause: lost progress for KV cache priming, long tail latencies for higher-priority requests, and noisy GPU utilization signals that complicate autoscaling. Preemption-aware batch slicing inserts low-overhead slice boundaries and scheduling hints so the kernel mapper and dispatcher can make better trade-offs between latency and efficiency.
- Applies to: runtime dispatcher + kernel mapper + per-shard executor on heterogeneous GPU fleets (hosted and Dedicated modes).
- Not in scope: model-architecture-level sequence truncation, offline compilation changes, or business-layer client batching policies.
- Reduce 95th/99th percentile latency regressions caused by preemption during long kernels.
- Minimize KV-cache thrash from repeated long preemptions.
- Preserve (or gracefully trade) throughput for improved latency predictability.
- Provide knobs for operations to tune behavior per service / customer tier.
- Non-invasive: default behavior should be conservative (opt-in per route or model bundle).
- Scheduler hints: expose slice boundary hints to kernel mapper and GPU dispatcher rather than forcing a single global policy.
- Cheap slicing: slices add minimal overhead (<2–4% per-token CPU overhead in microbenchmarks) and leverage existing continuous-batching state (KV cache re-use across slices).
- Observability-first: emit slice metrics (counts, preemptions, latency per slice, warmup penalty) for actionable alerts.
1. Request classification: the dispatcher categorizes incoming requests by expected kernel duration (microbenchmark model estimate + runtime sampler). If estimated kernel > slice_threshold_ms, candidate for slicing.
2. Slice generation: generate a sequence of slice descriptors. Each slice descriptor contains: slice_token_budget, expected_execution_ms, priority_hint, and cache_warmup (boolean).
3. Execution model: slices are enqueued to shard executors. The kernel mapper may coalesce slices from different requests if compatibility and priority allow, subject to slice size upper bounds.
4. Preemption and recovery: if a slice is preempted mid-execution, runtime records a "preempted_slice" event and restarts the slice respecting cache_warmup. Recovery strategy prefers resuming from last KV checkpoint if supported; otherwise slice is retried and warmup penalty is recorded.
5. Completion semantics: final response is reassembled from slice outputs. The runtime ensures deterministic ordering and idempotency of slice execution.
- KV cache: slices should be sized to preserve meaningful KV reuse. The runtime tags warmup slices to avoid evicting critical entries.
- Adaptive kernel mapper: uses slice.expected_execution_ms to choose different kernel implementations (fast-preemptible kernels vs high-throughput kernels).
- Priority and credit accounting: slice_priority is charged against the original request budget and interacts with kernel-credit-accounting and fairness systems.
- Autoscaler: emits slice-level throughput and preemption rates to autoscaler to help scaling decisions (see metrics section).
Parameter | Default | Description
slice.enabled | false | Master kill-switch. Must be enabled per route or model via config blob.
slice.threshold_ms | "120" | Estimate threshold above which requests become slicing candidates (ms).
slice.max_tokens | "2048" | Maximum token budget for a single slice; influences kernel execution time.
slice.min_tokens | "16" | Minimum slice token size to avoid excessive overhead on tiny requests.
slice.timeout_ms | "200" | Wall-clock timeout to cut a running slice for fairness and preemption sensitivity.
slice.priority_policy | "inherit" | inherit | explicit-priority | preemptible-first — how a slice chooses priority.
slice.warmup_policy | "sticky" | sticky | fresh — whether slices assume prior KV warmup is valid.
slice.coalesce_window_ms | "10" | Micro-window where compatible slices can be coalesced by the dispatcher.
slice.metrics_sampling | "1.0" | Fraction of slices for detailed telemetry (0.0–1.0).
route: /v1/generate-heavy
model: redwood/turbo-large-8k
slice:
  enabled: true
  threshold_ms: 120
  max_tokens: 1024
  min_tokens: 32
  timeout_ms: 250
  priority_policy: inherit
  warmup_policy: sticky
  coalesce_window_ms: 8
Emit the following metrics (prometheus-style names):
- runtime_slice_total{route,model,priority}
- runtime_slice_preempted_total{route,model}
- runtime_slice_latency_ms_p50/p90/p95/p99{route,model}
- runtime_slice_warmup_penalty_ms_avg{route,model}
- runtime_slice_coalesce_rate{route,model}
- runtime_slice_resume_success_ratio{route,model}
- runtime_slice_estimation_error_ms{route,model}
1) High preempted slice rate
- Trigger: increase in runtime_slice_preempted_total over 5m such that rate > 0.5% of runtime_slice_total AND p95 latency for route increases > 30% relative to baseline.
- Severity: P2
- Action: follow "slice preemption triage" runbook (below).

2) Warmup penalty regression
- Trigger: runtime_slice_warmup_penalty_ms_avg > 30ms for 10m for a paid-customer route.
- Severity: P3
- Action: Consider increasing slice.min_tokens, enabling sticky warmup, or moving customer to dedicated pool if persistent.
1. Identify affected routes
- Query: top 5 routes by runtime_slice_preempted_total in last 30m and correlated p95 latency.
2. Verify cluster-level preemption activity
- Inspect kube/gpu-proxy preemption events and cloud provider preemption logs.
3. Inspect slice metrics
- Check slice_estimation_error_ms; if high, the estimator is underpredicting kernel duration.
4. Interim mitigations (in order):
  a) Reduce slice.max_tokens for the route to favor smaller slices.
  b) Increase slice.coalesce_window_ms to allow the dispatcher to recombine smaller slices into more efficient kernels when preemption risk drops.
