   - Add explicit “anti-flap guardrails enabled + validated in staging” to go/no-go checklist.
   - Owner: **Talia Benson** (Program) + **Tomáš Novák** (Runbooks)
   - Target: **2026-02-07**

11) **Customer comms targeting**
   - For production tests, proactively notify a small set of enterprise accounts with strict HA expectations if their traffic might be in scope, even when blast radius is limited.
   - Owner: **Dev Patel** (Support escalation) + **Lauren Bishop** (Dedicated PM)
   - Target: **2026-02-14**

## Success criteria (for declaring this class of regression “fixed”)
For two consecutive production game days with scoped blast radius:
- No more than **one** routing policy transition per policy (flip only; rollback only if explicitly invoked by on-call).
- No customer-visible 5xx increase above agreed threshold for scoped tenants.
- p99 latency in target region remains within defined tolerance band during convergence.
- Audit events and dashboard annotations allow reconstruction of the decision timeline within 10 minutes.

## Appendix A: Key lessons
- “Reachability > 5xx burn” is correct only if reachability is truly authoritative; without corroboration, it can be the noisiest signal.
- Rollback is not inherently safe; rollback without stabilization can create a control loop that is worse than staying failed over.
- Controlled tests must be treated like real incidents operationally: annotations, clear decision authority, and customer comms preparedness.

## Appendix B: Open questions
- Should we treat reachability as authoritative only when multiple independent vantage points fail, or when combined with provider status signals?
- For Hosted API streaming, do we want a first-class “resume token” pattern to reduce user impact during redirects?
- What is the right default DNS/traffic-steering posture for faster failover without amplifying transient network noise?

## Owner
- Primary owner for follow-through: **Rafael Mendes (SRE delivery lead)**
- Architecture owner: **Miles Thornton (Failover architecture lead)**

## Status
- This postmortem is complete. Action items are tracked in **ENG-2426** and linked sub-issues. Updates should be reflected here if any CPA materially changes scope or target dates.

title: dsid_298465b56d664ab9b22678d74630c484__quantized-serving-slo-cost-tradeoff-runbook-2026.txt
text:
Quantized Serving: SLO–Cost Tradeoff Runbook

Summary
-------
This runbook describes the operational procedure, telemetry, and decision heuristics SREs and on-call owners should use when trading off SLOs for lower unit cost via quantized model serving. It focuses on production-facing inference (latency SLOs, error budgets, throughput) and ties the quantization decision to capacity planning, rollout, and incident review. The guidance applies to Redwood-hosted and Dedicated deployments; private deploys should adapt network/KMS specifics but follow the same decision logic.

Goals
- Provide clear, auditable steps for enabling, throttling, or rolling back quantized serving profiles (e.g., int8, int4, hybrid).
- Define required telemetry and alerts to ensure cost optimizations do not silently breach customer-facing SLOs.
- Offer a decision matrix mapping SLO tiers to allowed quantization, autoscaler targets, and emergency fallbacks.

Audience
- SRE on-call and capacity engineers
- Runtime engineers responsible for compiling/serving kernels
- Product/Platform managers approving cost experiments

Prerequisites and ownership
- Owner (primary): eng-sre/model-serving-capacity
- Secondary owners: eng-serving-runtime (kernel/quant), eng-platform (observability)
- Required telemetry: per-model and per-route histograms for latency (P50/P95/P99), per-token CPU/GPU time, request success rate, model_variant label (fp16/int8/int4), batch_size distribution, KV cache-hit ratio, and per-tenant error budget burn rate.

SLO and cost signals to monitor
1) SLOs (example):
   - Tier 1 (critical): P99 latency <= 250ms, availability >= 99.95%
   - Tier 2 (standard): P99 latency <= 500ms, availability >= 99.9%
   - Tier 3 (best-effort): P99 latency <= 1s, availability >= 99.0%
2) Cost signals: GPU-seconds per 1k tokens, average tokens-per-request, cost per inference (derived from reserved GPU hourly rate + amortized infra).
3) Quality signals: upstream regression flags, customer-reported hallucination/score regressions (from Redwood Optimize / evals).

Decision matrix (SLO -> allowed quantization and constraints)
| SLO Tier | Allowed quantization profiles | Max batch size | Cache policy | Fallback policy |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| Tier 1 | fp16 only; quantized only in canaries with strict perf testing | 4 | aggressive KV preservation; do not evict on cold start | Route to reserved fp16 pool; circuit-break quantized traffic |
| Tier 2 | int8 (production); int4 in short canaries if quality passes | 8 | standard KV TTLs | Fallback to int8 or slower fp16 variant |
| Tier 3 | int4 / aggressive mixed quantization allowed | 16 | permissive eviction | Degrade to int8 or enqueue to best-effort queue |

Telemetry and dashboards (minimum)
- Dashboards per-model: latency P50/P95/P99 by model_variant label, batch_size heatmap, per-request token count distribution, cache-hit ratio timeseries.
- Error-budget burn panels: 1h/24h/7d burn rates, per-tenant contributors.
- Cost dashboard: GPU-seconds per 1k tokens, GPU-utilization per cluster, and forecasted monthly unit-cost delta when changing quantization.

Prometheus/Query examples
- P99 latency for model X (int8):
  sum(rate(latency_histogram_bucket{model="model-x", variant="int8", le="0.99"}[5m]))
- Token GPU walltime per 1k tokens (approx):
  sum(rate(gpu_walltime_seconds_total{model=~"model-.*"}[1m])) / (sum(rate(request_tokens_total[1m])) / 1000)

Alerting thresholds (examples)
- Alert: quantized-p99-exceed: triggers when P99 for a quantized variant exceeds permitted SLO by >20% for 5m.
- Alert: quantized-quality-regression: triggers when eval job on canary shows >2% degradation on critical prompt set.
- Alert: quantized-cost-anomaly: triggers when cost delta vs baseline >30% in 6h window.

Operational procedure: enabling a quantized profile (canary -> ramp -> audit)
1) Pre-checks (done by eng-serving-runtime + SRE):
   - Confirm quantization profile is uploaded and listed in model catalog (profile id, quant bits, kernel flags).
   - Ensure canary MLP has traffic shadowing enabled and telemetry ingestion for variant label.
   - Produce offline quality evaluation on the model's critical prompt sets. Quality pass required for production ramp.
2) Canary stage (0.5% traffic, 2h minimum):
   - Enable profile for a specific route with traffic weight 0.5%.
   - Verify P50/P95/P99 and quality metrics remain within SLO-band for Tier.
   - Check cost delta estimate on running traffic (projected GPU-seconds saved).
3) Gradual ramp (0.5% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50%):
   - At each step: 30m steady-state minimum, review P99 and error budget, run automated quality sampling (1000 senarios).
   - If an alert fires at any step, immediately step down to previous stable weight and open an incident review.
4) Full roll (>=75%):
   - Only after 24h of stable performance at >=50% and sign-off from product SLO owner.

Rollback and emergency mitigation
- If any of the following are observed: sustained P99 exceedance >20% over SLO for 10m, quality regression flagged by evals, or error-budget burn spikes, then perform the following: 
  1) Trigger traffic-weight decrease to 0% for the quantized variant (automated via rollout manager).
  2) If traffic cannot be shifted quickly (backend constraint), enable rate-limiter at gateway to reduce QPS for affected routes.
  3) If rollback causes capacity shortage (more GPU load than expected), escalate to capacity team to activate burst-reserved pool or notify customers per SLA.

Capacity planning heuristics when adopting quantized serving
- Baseline capacity model should include two working scenarios: 
  A) Reduced-cost steady-state (quantized enabled): calculate expected GPU-seconds reduction and adjust reserved capacity commitments conservatively by 60% of the estimated savings (leave 40% slack).
  B) Failure/rollback mode: assume full traffic routed back to fp16; maintain a capacity buffer equal to the differential GPU-seconds for peak 99th percentile traffic for 1h.
- Schedule a capacity rehearsal: simulate traffic returning to fp16 for 30 minutes during a low-traffic window monthly for the first 3 months after major rollouts.

Incident review guidance specific to quantized regressions
- Required evidence for a post-incident analysis: request ids (sampled), per-request variant and batch_size, GPU utilization and walltime for affected traces, KV-cache hit rates, evaluation prompt-run logs comparing normal vs quantized outputs.
- Triage checklist: 
  1) Did the incident begin after a quantization rollout or autoscaler change?
  2) Is the failure a latency tail, correctness regression, or degraded availability?
  3) Correlate the incident window with model_variant label, batch_size, and host kernel versions.
  4) Capture a rand-100 sample of requests spanning cold/hot sequences to replay in the perf-lab.

Automation and operational tooling recipes
- Minimal CLI examples (hypothetical)
  * Enable canary: redwood-rollout apply --model model-x --variant int8 --weight 0.005 --route chat.generate --note "canary int8"
  * Query P99: redwood-metrics query "p99(latency{model=\"model-x\",variant=\"int8\"})"
  * Force rollback: redwood-rollout set-weight --id <rollout-id> --weight 0.0 --urgent
- Observability instrumentation: ensure span/resource tags include model.variant, quant_profile_id, kernel_version, batch_size. Add lightweight sampling for full request payloads for the runbook's evidence collection (rotate retention policy to 7d for on-call review).

Testing and validation playbook
- Offline regression: run the canonical prompt set at n=10k examples comparing fp16 vs quantized variant. Acceptable thresholds are model-dependent but baseline: perplexity delta < 1.5% and critical-prompt accuracy delta < 1%.
- Perf profiling: run synthetic ramps with batch-size envelope from 1–max_batch and measure P99 and GPU-seconds. Feed results into the cost estimator to produce forecasted monthly savings.

Runbook examples and checklist (quick reference)
1) Before enabling: quality pass, telemetry flagged, notification to stakeholders.
2) Canary: 0.5% traffic, 2h minimum, monitoring on-call.
3) Ramp steps: 0.5% -> 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 75% (sign-offs at 50% and 75%).
4) Post-roll: schedule capacity rehearsal within 72h.
5) If rollback: collect evidence bucket and open post-incident review within 48h.

Post-incident review template items
- Incident summary (what changed, when)
- Timeline of traffic weights and SLO breaches
- Root cause hypothesis (e.g., kernel mismatch for int8 GEMM on A100 driver X.Y)
- Remediation and long-term action items (e.g., require perf-bench signatures for new quant kernels)
- Cost impact analysis (savings vs. rollback cost)

Appendix A: Example config snippet (rollout manifest)
---
rollout: 
  model: model-x
  variant: int8-v2026-03
  route: chat.generate
  initial_weight: 0.005
  step_durations: [120m, 60m, 30m]
  metrics_watchlist: ["latency_p99", "eval_quality_delta", "error_budget_burn"]
  auto_rollback: true
---

Appendix B: Quick decision checklist for product managers
- Is the expected cost savings >10% for the tenant's forecasted usage?
- Can we accept a temporary quality delta at or below the pre-agreed threshold?
- Is there capacity slack to absorb a rollback to fp16 without violating SLOs?

References
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/quantization-profiles
- /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-onboarding-runway-and-slo-admission-playbook-2026
- Internal perf-lab runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/latency-degradation-policy-and-recovery-cookbook-2026

Ownership and review cadence
- Primary owner: eng-sre/model-serving-capacity
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major quantization kernel change
- Required sign-off for Tier 1 exposed experiments: eng-sre lead + product SLO owner

Contact
- For questions or emergency escalations, ping #sre-model-serving and the on-call rotation via PagerDuty.

Document history
- 2026-02-18: created by Emily Chen
- 2026-04-12: added rollback automation notes (Asha Patel)
- 2026-08-03: updated capacity rehearsal guidance and example queries (Liam O'Connor)

title: dsid_1c89bb2a56cc4f06a8ca93bead56e8c9__developer-integration-checklist-and-examples-2026.txt
text:
Developer Integration Checklist and Example Patterns for SDKs and Docs

Overview

Purpose: This page is a single-stop checklist and pattern catalog for SDK authors, docs authors, and on-call engineers who publish or maintain SDKs, quickstarts, API examples, and docs-site content. It combines a publishing checklist, snippet library governance, example API patterns (good + bad), docs-site operating commands, and canonical fixes for the top support issues we observe in the DX queue.

Audience: SDK engineers, developer-docs authors, support engineers, and release owners.

Quick links
- Snippet registry: dx-snippets-registry (internal)
- Docs CI pipeline: docs-ci.redwood.internal
- Docs preview host: preview.docs.redwood.internal
- SDK package repo: packages.redwood.dev

1) Publishing checklist (SDKs, quickstarts, snippets)
Follow these steps before merging a PR that changes public-facing SDK code or docs snippets. Fail-open items block CI if missing: unit tests, snippet lint, docs preview.

Required (pre-merge):
1) Confirm API contract: update openapi/schema if the surface or request/response shape changed. Include example payloads in examples/ directory.
2) Unit and integration tests: >= 90% coverage for new modules + stable CI runs.
3) Snippet validation: run tools/snippet-lint --path <changed_files>. Ensure snippet passes naming and size limits.
4) Docs preview: create a docs preview build and attach the preview URL in the PR. Command: 
   - make docs-preview || ./scripts/docs_build.sh --pr $PR_NUMBER && ./scripts/publish_preview.sh --pr $PR_NUMBER
5) Backward-compatibility note: include a short migration note if behavior or defaults changed. Add a ‘breaking-change’ label if needed.

Optional (recommended):
- Add or update a quickstart in quickstarts/ with step-by-step copy/paste commands.
- Add a minimal e2e example using the client in examples/ with a small recorded golden output.

2) Snippet library governance
Naming conventions (enforced by snippet-lint):
- category/feature-language-variant.extension; example: auth/getting-started-python.py, chat/stream-js.js
- Max snippet length: 60 lines. If longer, break into multiple focused snippets.
- Metadata header required: // owner: team-name | tags: sdk, quickstart | expires: YYYY-MM-DD

Snippet registry table (owner + expectations):
| Category | Registry path prefix | Owner | Review cadence | Example tags |
|---------|----------------------|-------|----------------|--------------|
| Auth | auth/ | eng-platform | quarterly | auth, quickstart |
| Chat + Streaming | chat/ | eng-developer-experience | monthly | streaming, samples |
| Embeddings | embeddings/ | applied-ml | quarterly | vector, embeddings |

Snippet review checklist:
- Small focused unit tested example exists
- No production secrets or hard-coded keys
- Uses canonical SDK patterns (timeouts/retries)
- Includes expected output or response sample

3) Canonical API examples: good vs bad patterns
Example: simple text generation (pseudocode).
Bad pattern (anti-pattern): blocking call with long timeout + no retry/backoff
```
# bad: blocks for 60s, no retry
response = client.generate(prompt, timeout=60000, retries=0)
print(response.text)
```
Good pattern (recommended): explicit shorter network timeout, streaming when appropriate, retry with exponential backoff, and per-request idempotency token when applicable
```
# good: streaming + retry policy + timeout
with client.stream.generate(prompt, stream_handler=on_token) as s:
    s.configure(timeout_ms=5000, retry_policy="exponential", max_retries=3)
    s.start()
```
Python example (curl + minimal):
```
# Python example: safe generate
from redwood_sdk import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key="$REDWOOD_KEY", default_timeout_ms=5000)
resp = client.generate("Translate to French: Hello world", max_tokens=80)
print(resp.text)
```
Curl example for support reproduction:
```
curl -sS -X POST "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"rwd-small-1","prompt":"Summarize: ...","max_tokens":120,"timeout_ms":5000}'
```
Notes: always include model name and a numeric timeout_ms in reproducible examples; this minimizes triage time.

4) Docs-site operating procedures (authors + release ops)
Short runbook: update -> preview -> smoke -> release.
- Local build: npm run docs:dev (runs mkdocs + local snippets watcher)
- Preview build (CI): docs-ci pipeline will run on PR. Required checks: snippet-lint, link-check, spell-check, accessibility-check.
- Smoke checklist for preview reviewers:
  1) Validate key quickstarts run end-to-end in the preview (copy commands and run locally)
  2) Validate code snippets execute (use snippet-runner container)
  3) Verify tables render correctly and images are present
- Release: after two approvals and passing CI, merge to main triggers docs-ci -> publish to docs.redwood.ai. For hotfixes, set #hotfix label and tag the release: git tag -a docs-hotfix-YYYYMMDD && git push origin main --tags && docs-ci trigger --hotfix

5) Top DX support issues and canonical fixes (triage + known remediation)
Issue pattern: streaming disconnects under TLS + intermittent 50x from runtime.
- Symptom: client receives partial stream, then socket closes.
- Triage steps:
  1) Reproduce with curl using --no-buffer to see chunking: curl --no-buffer ...
  2) Check client network (proxy / corporate TLS interception). If corporate proxy, suggest bypass or increase keepalive.
  3) Check runtime logs for connection resets (service: rwd-runtime-streaming) and correlate request_id.
- Canonical fix for SDKs: implement automatic reconnect with resume token and idempotency. Example pattern:
```
# SDK pseudocode: resume tokens
stream = client.stream.start(prompt)
for token in stream:
    if connection_lost:
        new_stream = client.stream.resume(resume_token=stream.resume_token)
        stream = new_stream
```
Issue pattern: high token cost from accidental greedy loops (prompting bug).
- Symptom: unexpectedly high cost spike traced to a client that repeatedly called generate in a loop.
- Canonical remediation:
  - Add safeguards in quickstarts: show how to set max_tokens and stop sequences.
  - Add quota-friendly example using lower temperature and max_tokens, and show batch sampling if many prompts are required.

Issue pattern: timeouts on long context window requests (>= 32k tokens).
- Symptom: request times out; logs show memory pressure in serving runtime.
- Triage steps:
  1) Ask customer for sample prompt + model. Reproduce in perf lab with rwd-large-32k profile.
  2) If reproducible, suggest chunked generation or streaming.
- Canonical fix: update quickstarts to include chunking example (split into context windows and rehydrate KV cache). Example pseudo-command:
```
# chunking pattern: pseudo
chunks = chunk_prompt(large_prompt, window=8192)
state = None
for c in chunks:
    resp, state = client.generate_chunk(c, kv_state=state)
```

6) Support triage template for PRs and incidents
Include these fields when filing a DX support ticket or creating a regression PR:
- Title: short summary + reproducible phrase (e.g., "stream disconnects when using corp-proxy")
- Steps to reproduce: minimal curl + environment (OS, node/python version, proxy true/false)
- Expected behavior vs actual behavior
- Request ID(s) / timestamps (if available)
- Attach reproduction snippet (no secrets) and a brief smoke test script that the reviewer can run in <5 minutes
- Suggested fix and rolling strategy (canary percent, config to change)

7) Templates and snippets to include in quickstarts (copy/paste)
- Minimal auth example (LANG: python, js)
- Streaming safe consumer (resume token pattern)
- Batching example for embeddings (batch size, parallel worker pool)
- Local mock server for offline docs dev (mock-server config snippet)

Example: embeddings batching (NodeJS)
```
// embedding-batch.js
const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY, timeout: 10000 })
async function embedBatch(lines){
  const batchSize = 64
  const batches = chunkArray(lines, batchSize)
  const results = []
  for(const b of batches){
    const resp = await client.embeddings.create({ model: 'rwd-embed-2', input: b })
    results.push(...resp.data)
  }
  return results
}
```

8) Ownership and escalation
- Owner for SDK patterns and snippets: eng-developer-experience (primary)
- Escalation path for production-facing regressions: devx-oncall -> eng-sre -> eng-platform.
- SLA for DX triage in paid tiers: initial response 2 business hours, triage commit/mitigation in 48 hours (for dedicated/private customers).

Appendix A: Common CLI commands
- lint snippets: ./tools/snippet-lint --changed
- build docs locally: npm run docs:dev
- run docs CI (manual trigger): curl -X POST https://docs-ci.redwood.internal/trigger -H "Authorization: Bearer $CI_TOKEN" -d '{"branch":"main"}'
- publish preview: ./scripts/publish_preview.sh --pr 123

Appendix B: Example PR description template (copy into PR body)
- One-line summary
- Which packages/docs were changed
- Preview URL(s)
- Tests run and results
- Backwards compatibility notes
- Migration steps (if applicable)

If you are publishing a new snippet or quickstart and want assistance, ping @eng-developer-experience in Slack or open a review request with the ‘dx-snippet-review’ label.

Change log
- 2025-08-18: created by Alexis Morgan
- 2025-11-02: added snippet-lint rules and python streaming resume example (reviewer: Ravi Patel)
- 2026-02-20: expanded top support issues and added templates for chunking and embeddings batch patterns (reviewer: Marina Lopez)

title: dsid_9316d58c7198464a85329ef8121ce237__automated-customer-incident-reporting-and-slo-impact-generator-2026.txt
text:
Automated Customer Incident Reporting and SLO Impact Generator

Summary:

This document defines the design, operational runbook, verification checks, and customer-facing templates for Redwood's Automated Customer Incident Reporting and SLO Impact Generator (ACIR-SIG). ACIR-SIG produces standardized, auditable customer incident summaries within a defined SLA window after an incident is classified as customer-impacting. The system computes SLO impact automatically from telemetry and timeline evidence, assembles a concise narrative, and supports automated delivery to customers (via Console, email, or support ticket) with human-in-the-loop gating.

Goals and scope:
- Goal: Reduce time-to-customer-summary while preserving accuracy, traceability, and blameless language.
- Scope: infra and inference incidents that affect production API responses (latency, availability, errors). Excludes: billing, account-level policy, or non-production incidents.
- Output: structured incident summary (human-readable + machine JSON payload) and an SLO impact statement.

Ownership and roles:
1) SRE oncall: responsible for verification and approval when gating is required.
2) Incident commander (IC): final sign-off for any customer report that contains mitigation details or security-sensitive statements.
3) Customer Success (CS): decides routing and cadence for customer notifications and escalations.
4) Reporting service (service-owner: ops-tooling): implements ACIR-SIG automation and maintains templates.

Key constraints and principles:
- Always calculate SLO impact from the canonical SLO aggregator (slo-aggregate-service) and telemetry (tracing, api-metrics, regional-health). Do not use local approximations.
- Maintain a human-in-the-loop for incidents where the automated confidence < 92% (see confidence rules).
- Use standardized, blameless language and give measurable impact (requests affected, time windows, and computed %SLO burn).
- Store evidence pointers (trace IDs, query snippets, dashboards) in the report payload for audits and follow-ups.

SLO impact computation (algorithm):
- Inputs:
  - timeseries of successful requests S(t) and total requests T(t) at 1s aggregation or the highest fidelity available.
  - policy: SLO target (e.g., availability 99.9% over 30d) and SLO window used for customer-facing burn calculation (typically rolling-30d).
  - incident window [t_start, t_end] defined by timeline service.
- Steps:
  1) Compute baseline SLO compliance before the incident: baseline_compliance = sum_{t < t_start}(S(t))/sum_{t < t_start}(T(t)) over a baseline period (default 24h).
  2) Compute incident compliance: incident_compliance = sum_{t in [t_start,t_end]}(S(t))/sum_{t in [t_start,t_end]}(T(t)).
  3) Convert to SLO burn for the rolling window:
     - delta_unavailability = max(0, target - incident_compliance) * (duration_of_window_weight)
     - approximate SLO%_burn = (sum_{window} expected_bad_seconds_from_incident) / (total_window_seconds * (1 - target)) * 100
- Simplified formula (used by ACIR-SIG for short reports):
  SLO_burn_percent = round(100 * ((target - incident_compliance) * incident_duration_seconds) / (rolling_window_seconds * (1 - target)), 2)
- Example:
  - target = 99.9% (0.999), rolling_window_seconds = 30*24*3600 = 2,592,000s, incident duration = 900s, incident_compliance = 0.95.
  - SLO_burn_percent = 100 * ((0.999 - 0.95) * 900) / (2,592,000 * (1 - 0.999)) = 100 * (0.049 * 900) / (2,592,000 * 0.001) = 100 * 44.1 / 2592 = 1.70% (rounded).

Confidence scoring and gating rules:
- Confidence inputs (scored 0–100):
  - telemetry_coverage (percentage of requests covered by high-fidelity metrics): weight 40
  - timeline_agreement (percent overlap between automated detection and timeline boundaries): weight 20
  - anomaly_correlation (correlation of errors/latency with topology/event): weight 20
  - evidence_linkage (presence of traces/logs matching top error signatures): weight 20
- Final confidence = weighted_sum(components).
- Gating thresholds:
  - confidence >= 92: auto-generate and auto-send short customer summary (no mitigation detail) after 2h post-incident verification window.
  - 75 <= confidence < 92: auto-generate draft; require SRE oncall verification and IC approval.
  - confidence < 75: do not generate automated customer content; produce internal report only.

Automated customer summary template (short):
- Title: (Service) Incident Summary — (YYYY-MM-DD) — (region)
- One-line impact: During (time window), customers experienced increased (errors/latency/availability) affecting approximately N requests (~X% of requests) in (region).
- What happened: brief description of root cause or leading hypothesis (automated, with confidence).
- What we did: mitigation steps taken and timeframe.
- SLO impact: SLO_burn_percent for rolling window and absolute requests affected.
- Links & evidence: dashboard links, trace IDs, support ticket link for follow-up.
- Next steps: planned remediation and expected ETA when available.

Full machine payload (JSON) — example snippet for automation (ACIR-SIG sends this to CS or support):
{
  "incident_id": "INC-2026-1234",
  "service": "inference-api",
  "region": "us-west-2",
  "window": "2026-08-14T15:12:00Z/2026-08-14T15:27:00Z",
  "requests_affected": "18234",
  "approx_pct_requests": "3.6",
  "slo_burn_pct": "1.7",
  "confidence": "94",
  "evidence": ["dash://api-availability/overview", "trace://abc123"],
  "narrative": "A partial control-plane configuration regression caused router miss-paths leading to elevated 5xxs for 15 minutes. Mitigation: rollback of config at T+6."
}

Automation architecture (high level):
- Inputs:
  - slo-aggregate-service (canonical SLO metrics)
  - telemetry-mesh (metrics/traces/logs)
  - timeline-service (incident boundaries and annotations)
  - incident-bus (events from PagerDuty/ops)
- Components:
  - generator-worker: computes SLO burn and assembles payloads.
  - confidence-evaluator: calculates confidence and determines gating.
  - draft-store: stores auto-drafts for human review (if needed).
  - delivery-orchestrator: posts to Console, creates CS ticket, or sends email.
- Safety layers:
  - rate limiter: ensures only one auto-customer report per incident, and no more than one per hour for the same customer group.
  - redaction module: strips PII or security-sensitive fields per policy.
  - audit logger: immutable storage of generated payloads and final send event (retention policy defined below).

Runbook: step-by-step operator flow when a draft is generated and human gate required:
1) Alert: oncall receives automated draft notification (Slack + Console).
2) Quick checks (5–10 min): verify top evidence links, ensure traces contain indicative errors, confirm region and affected customers.
3) Approve or reject: Approve via Console button to publish; reject sends back to draft with reason.
4) If approved, CS will receive the published summary and follow-up engagement steps are initiated automatically.
5) If rejected, SRE tags draft with notes and sets auto-resend window to 2h.

Manual override and safety escalation:
- IC can hold customer notifications for up to 24h for incidents involving legal, compliance, or high-sensitivity customers.
- If an automated summary is already sent and later found inaccurate, publish a correction using the same payload schema and include a clear correction header.

Verification checklist (pre-send):
- [ ] Evidence pointers present (>=2 of {dashboard, trace, logs})
- [ ] SLO computation cross-checked by slo-aggregate-service snapshot
- [ ] PII redaction module passed (redaction=false means pass)
- [ ] Confidence >= configured threshold for auto-send or IC approval obtained
- [ ] Delivery channel contact list validated for affected customer segments

Operational observability and metrics for ACIR-SIG itself:
- Metric: acir.reports.generated (count) — label by outcome: auto_sent/draft/rejected/corrected
- Metric: acir.processing.latency (ms) — time from incident-closed to draft ready
- Metric: acir.confidence.distribution — histogram of confidence scores
- Alert: if acir.processing.latency P95 > 45min for 3 hours => paging to ops-tooling

Retention and audit policy:
- Generated payloads and evidence pointers retained for 365 days in immutable audit store.
- Access to full payloads limited by RBAC: engineering/incident-review and CS lead roles, security/legal by approval.

Security and privacy notes:
- Redaction rules are centrally controlled: do not include customer payloads, secrets, or raw logs in customer-facing narrative. Evidence pointers are allowed but must not embed credentials.
- For incidents involving regulated customers, default confidentiality escalates to 'restricted' and a manual IC approval is required before any outgoing message.

Testing and validation cadence:
- Quarterly TT (tabletop) exercises: validate automated outputs against mock incidents.
- Monthly synthetic incidents: run ACIR-SIG in shadow mode to measure drift in confidence and SLO calculation correctness.

Rollout and migration plan for first production release:
1) Phase 1 (shadow): 2 months, run in draft-only mode for a subset (20%) of incidence types.
2) Phase 2 (co-pilot): human-in-the-loop gating required for all drafts; telemetry and metrics validated.
3) Phase 3 (autorelease): enable auto-send for confidence >= 92; monitor metrics and enable roll-back flag for first 30 days.

Appendix A — Example customer-facing short summary (final):
Service: Redwood Inference — Hosted API
Date: 2026-08-14
Impact window: 15:12–15:27 UTC
Summary: Between 15:12–15:27 UTC customers in us-west-2 experienced elevated 5xx errors affecting approximately 18k requests (~3.6% of normal request volume). We rolled back a recent control-plane configuration change at 15:18 which restored normal routing by 15:18:30 and fully recovered by 15:27.
SLO impact: Estimated to consume 1.7% of the 30-day availability budget for Hosted API (99.9% target).
Links: Dashboard: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/incident-1234 Trace: trace://abc123 Ticket: https://support.redwood.ai/t/INC-2026-1234
Next steps: Root cause analysis in progress; RCA will be published within 72 hours.

Appendix B — Quick references:
- SLO aggregation playground: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/slo-aggregate-playground
- Incident timeline canonicalization: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-review/incident-hypothesis-repro-environment-spec-2024
- PII redaction policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-management/redaction-policy

Questions or feedback: reach out to the ops-tooling owners (ops-tooling@redwood.ai) or file improvements via the Console suggestions flow.

title: dsid_3d9521c633a54699b5ab2f1d2765017d__evaluation-federation-onboarding-and-tenant-safety-guide-2026.txt
text:
evaluation-federation-onboarding-and-tenant-safety-guide

Overview:
This playbook defines the processes, contractual artifacts, telemetry gates, and safety controls for onboarding federated evaluators (internal teams, channel partners, and third-party annotator pools) into Redwood's eval-harness. The goal is to enable distributed evaluation capacity while preserving tenant isolation, model and data confidentiality, and consistent quality guarantees across federated runs.

Intended audience:
- Applied ML engineers running evaluation orchestration
- Eval platform operators and privacy engineers
- Solutions/Customer engineering teams onboarding partner evaluators
- Security/compliance reviewers for third-party evaluators

Goals and non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Provide a repeatable onboarding checklist that ensures privacy-safe federation of evaluators.
  - Standardize eval contracts and runtime gating to protect tenant telemetry and artifacts.
  - Define SLOs, telemetry, and remediation steps for federated evaluation runs.
- Non-goals:
  - This document does not replace formal legal contracts (NDAs/SOWs) but provides the operational artifacts needed for them.

Scope:
- Applies to: shadow, synthetic, and targeted-slice evaluation runs executed outside the central eval-fleet (including cloud-hosted partner pools and air-gapped contractor environments).
- Out of scope: live production inference serving, customer-facing A/B experiments, and on-device user telemetry.

Key definitions:
- Federated evaluator: any non-central evaluator (external contractor, partner, or separate internal org) that receives probes and returns annotations or metrics.
- Tenant-safe run: an evaluation run guaranteed not to leak identifiable tenant data, metadata distributions, or telemetry that can be re-linked to production traffic.
- Eval contract: a machine-readable manifest and runtime policy (YAML) that declares allowed inputs/outputs, retention, and privacy parameters.

Roles & ownership:
- Eval Platform (owner: eval-harness team): provides the federation APIs, contract verification, and telemetry gating.
- Privacy & Security: signs off on contracts, DP parameters, K-anonymity thresholds.
- Onboarding Lead (customer/product engineering): coordinates partner onboarding and verifies artifacts.
- QA/Evals steward: validates annotation quality and sample representativeness.

Onboarding checklist (step-by-step):
1) Intake & classification:
   - Collect evaluator identity, jurisdiction, and infrastructure class (cloud/shared / dedicated / air-gapped).
   - Classify evaluator into risk tier: low, medium, high based on access, data sensitivity, and past audits.
2) Contract & artifacts:
   - Exchange NDAs and SOWs as required by Legal.
   - Produce an eval contract (see template below) signed by both parties.
3) Technical attestation:
   - Validate the evaluator can run the assigned harness (version compatibility).
   - Confirm cryptographic keys (if using encrypted payloads) and key rotation cadence.
4) Privacy controls setup:
   - Configure differential-privacy (DP) parameters or k-anonymity masking per the contract.
   - Set telemetry redaction rules and retention TTL.
5) Sandbox trial runs:
   - Run a minimum of 3 seed experiments using synthetic probes and noise-injected inputs.
   - Verify outputs against a golden-checker within the central eval-harness.
6) Quality calibration:
   - Run annotator calibration tasks and compute Krippendorff's alpha or Cohen's kappa.
   - Define per-slice pass/fail thresholds.
7) Production gating:
   - Gradually increase sample volume and remove synthetic-only constraints after 48 hours of stable output and telemetry.

Safety & privacy controls (table):
| Control | Purpose | Default threshold | Owner |
|---|---|---:|---|
| DP epsilon | Limit information leakage from outputs | 1.0 (high-risk slices 0.5) | Privacy |
| K-anonymity masking | Remove identifier granularity | k>=50 | Privacy |
| Telemetry sampling | Reduce exposure of token-level logs | 0.1% by default | Eval Platform |
| Retention TTL | Max stored artifact lifetime | 30 days (reviewed per contract) | Legal/Eval Platform |
| Output watermarking | Tag outputs generated by federated runs | required | Eval Platform |

Eval contract (example YAML manifest):
```yaml
contract_version: 1.0
evaluator_id: "partner-acme-annotators"
jurisdiction: "EU"
risk_tier: "medium"
allowed_probe_types:
  - synthetic
  - shadow
  - slice_specific
max_sample_rate_per_tenant: 0.002
privacy:
  differential_privacy:
    enabled: true
    epsilon: 0.8
  k_anonymity_min_k: 50
retention:
  artifacts_seconds: 2592000  # 30 days
telemetry:
  sample_rate: 0.001
  redaction: ["user_id", "ip", "session_token"]
signatures:
  eval_platform_sig: "sha256:..."
```

Telemetry & gating:
- Pre-flight checks (automated): contract schema validation, signature verification, and DP parameter sanity checks.
- Runtime gates (must pass to proceed):
  - No-probe-leak test: candidate run must not include raw tenant IDs in any return channel.
  - Output-consistency test: sampled outputs compared to central golden-checker; divergence > delta triggers fail.
  - Latency anomaly detection: sudden latency variance indicates environment instability; pause run for investigation.

Quality metrics and SLOs:
- Annotator agreement: Krippendorff's alpha >= 0.70 on core slices.
- Coverage: federated pool must cover 95% of assigned slices within agreed TTL.
- Stability: output distribution divergence (JS distance) to central harness < 0.05 for 24h.

Failure modes and triage steps (numbered):
1) Privacy gate fail (e.g., epsilon too large / identifiers detected)
   - Immediate: halt run, revoke evaluator tokens, notify privacy owner.
   - Follow-up: run artifact redaction and re-run synthetic-only checks.
2) Low annotator agreement
   - Immediate: reduce sample volume and require calibration tasks.
   - Follow-up: impose retraining and re-certification for the annotator pool.
3) Telemetry spike or exfil suspicion
   - Immediate: isolate network access and snapshot evaluator workspace; escalate to Security.
   - Follow-up: forensic log review, legal notification if required.

Rollout & certification checklist (table):
| Step | Artifact required | Pass condition |
|---|---|---|
| Contract signed | Signed eval contract (YAML + signatures) | Present and verified |
| Sandbox trial | 3 trial runs with synthetic probes | No privacy gate failures |
| Calibration | Annotator calibration report | Agreement >= 0.7 |
| Telemetry | Telemetry gating logs | Sampling and redaction confirmed |
| Production ramp | Gradual sample increase plan | Stable for 48h |

Operational playbooks (quick commands):
- Generate an eval contract skeleton:
  - CLI: redwood-eval contract create --evaluator partner-acme --jurisdiction EU --risk medium > contract.yaml
- Validate contract schema locally:
  - CLI: redwood-eval contract validate contract.yaml
- Run a gated sandbox job:
  - CLI: redwood-eval run create --contract contract.yaml --mode sandbox --probes probes/synthetic-seed-01.json

Appendix A — audit evidence bundle requirements:
- Signed YAML contract with platform and partner signatures.
- Snapshot of trial run outputs (redacted) and golden-checker diffs.
- Annotator calibration artifacts (raw annotations, agreement metrics).
- Telemetry gating logs and sampling snapshots.

Appendix B — recommended DP & privacy presets by slice sensitivity:
- High-sensitivity (PII or proprietary content): epsilon <= 0.5, k>=100, telemetry sample_rate <= 0.0005
- Medium-sensitivity (business intent, non-identifying): epsilon <= 1.0, k>=50, telemetry sample_rate <= 0.001
- Low-sensitivity (public content): epsilon <= 2.0, k>=20, telemetry sample_rate <= 0.01

References & related pages:
- See the Eval Harness orchestration spec: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/eval-mesh-and-workload-fingerprinting-2026
- Privacy budgeting playbook: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/quality-guardrails/probe-privacy-budget-and-annotation-retention-playbook-2024

Change log:
- 2026-01-15: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-10: Added DP presets and contract YAML example (review: Priya Nair).
- 2026-03-01: Finalized gating sequence and telemetry thresholds (review: Liam O'Connor).
