- Communication artifact: status page timeline and comms templates used.
- At least one concrete follow-up with owner and due date.

6) Post-incident learning loop and postmortem template

Timeline and expectations:

- Draft postmortem: publish within 72 hours. Use the lightweight template below.
- Blameless review meeting: within 7 business days.
- Action items: assigned with owners and target dates; tracked in the incident audit board.

Minimal postmortem template (copy into confluence page):

- Title: [date] - [summary]
- Severity: Sev-1/2/3
- Impact summary: customers, regions, duration
- Timeline: concise event timeline with timestamps
- Root cause: summary + links to logs/profiles
- Mitigations taken: immediate and long-term
- Follow-up actions: list with owner and due date
- Lessons learned and prevention plan

7) Operational SLOs and thresholds (extract)

- API generation latency: P95 < 300ms for baseline workloads.
- API availability (success rate): 99.9% monthly.
- Paging threshold: alert when 5-minute error-rate >1% or P95 latency >500ms for 5 minutes.
- Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA) target: < 5 minutes.
- Mean time to mitigation (MTTM) target: < 30 minutes for Sev-1 and Sev-2.

8) Ownership and escalation matrix (roles)

- Primary responder: owns first-line triage and initial mitigation. (Role: oncall-engineer)
- Secondary/backup: provides technical support and takes over if primary is blocked. (Role: oncall-senior)
- Incident Commander (IC): runs coordination, customer comms, and exec updates. (Role: rotation-lead)
- Comms liaison: drafts status and customer messages and coordinates with CS. (Role: support-ops)
- Platform lead: responsible for long-term fixes and action items from postmortem. (Role: platform-engineering)

Escalation ordering (automated via PagerDuty): primary -> secondary (10 minutes) -> rotation-lead (15 more minutes) -> oncall-manager (30 more minutes or at IC discretion).

9) Runbook hygiene and governance

- Every runbook must have an owner and be reviewed quarterly. Add a one-line summary at top with expected MTTR.
- Changes made during incidents: document the change in the runbook change log and notify rotation-lead.
- Runbook retirement: if a runbook has not been exercised or edited for 12 months, mark for review.

Appendix: sample CLI commands and queries

- Check KV cache hit ratio (example):

  ```bash
  curl -sS https://observability.internal/api/query?expr='sum(rate(kv_cache_hits_total[5m]))/sum(rate(kv_cache_lookups_total[5m]))' | jq .data
  ```

- Bypass KV cache (control plane):

  ```bash
  redwood ctl routing update --policy inference-routing --set bypass_kv_cache=true --reason "Incident work"
  ```

- Post a draft status (status page editor CLI):

  ```bash
  statusctl post --title "Investigating increased inference latency" --impact "Partial" --body-file ./status-draft.md
  ```

Document owner and maintenance:

- Owner: Maya Thompson (SRE)
- Maintenance cadence: quarterly review by SRE oncall guild; updates pushed to runbook index.

If you have feedback or want to add a new contingency entry, file a PR against this page or ping the oncall guild channel.

title: dsid_a9e023e5bce34237b9a8de8c4a55d0b1__sre-capacity-supply-chain-runbook-2026.txt
text:
Capacity Supply-Chain Runbook: Forecasting, Signals, and Emergency Scaling

Summary:
This runbook defines the capacity ‘supply chain’ at Redwood Inference: how we forecast demand, convert signals into capacity actions, coordinate automation and human escalation, and tie post-incident reviews to reliability initiatives. It is intended for SREs, platform engineers, and oncall responders who own service availability and cost-accuracy tradeoffs.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: reduce surprise outages due to capacity shortfalls, shorten mean time to scale (MTTS), and make error budget consumption actionable.
- Scope: applies to Redwood-hosted inference endpoints, Dedicated pools, and private deployment orchestration components (control plane only). Does NOT prescribe customer infra for on-prem model hosts.

Key definitions (for readers unfamiliar with the term):
- SLO: the target objective that defines acceptable service quality (e.g., P99 latency < 1200ms for /v1/generate).
- Error budget: remaining fraction of allowed SLO violations in a rolling window.
- Capacity supply: available serving units (vGPU slots, model shards, CPU workers) that can be provisioned or reallocated.
- Demand signal: telemetry inputs representing load (RPS, token/sec, batch size distribution, queued requests, burst ratio).
- Supply signal: telemetry on available capacity and headroom (idle GPU %, free KV-cache memory, queue depth thresholds).

Ownership and roles:
- Service SRE (owner): maintains SLOs, defines alert thresholds, owns the emergency scaling runbook.
- Platform Capacity Team: owns autoscaler configuration, quota pools, and reserved Dedicated allocations.
- Oncall responder: follows this runbook during incidents; executes scaling, fallback, and rollback steps.
- Product/Feature owner: signs off on any change that lowers SLO target or increases tolerated error budget.

Signals & metrics (primary observability surface):
| Metric | Source | Frequency | Owner | Alert purpose | Thresholds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RPS /v1/generate | Prometheus (ingest) | 15s | Service SRE | Detect traffic burst | > 1.5x baseline for 10m |
| Token/sec | Platform metrics | 60s | Platform Capacity | Token pressure / billing signal | > 200k tokens/sec system-wide |
| P99 latency | Tracing/metrics | 60s | Service SRE | SLO violation detection | > SLO for 5m |
| Queue depth | Serving runtime | 15s | Platform Capacity | Backpressure / queuing | queue > 50 for 2m |
| GPU idle % | Node exporter | 30s | Platform Capacity | Headroom | < 15% for 10m |
| Error budget burn rate | Alerting engine | 1m | SRE Lead | Escalation control | burn_rate > 2x for 30m |

(Represented above as a reference table — dashboards must expose these columns)

Forecasting and planning process (weekly and monthly cadence):
1. Weekly demand sanity check (owner: Service SRE)
   - Pull 7-day trending dashboard (RPS, tokens/sec, batch size histograms) and 24-hr anomaly list.
   - If forecasted peak (7-day forward) exceeds reserved capacity by > 10%, open a Capacity Adjustment RFC (see section below).
2. Monthly forecasting sync (owner: Platform Capacity)
   - Run model-based forecast (ARIMA/Prophet baseline used by capacity pipeline) and compare against product release calendar.
   - Validate forecast against cost budgets; produce recommended reserve increases or autoscaler parameter changes.
3. Pre-release capacity gating
   - For any release that increases expected qps by > 20%, require capacity sign-off from Platform Capacity and SRE lead.

Capacity Adjustment RFC checklist (minimum fields):
- Impacted services (list), expected delta (RPS and tokens/sec), target lead time, proposed action (increase reserved pool / adjust autoscaler), rollback criteria, cost delta estimate, approvers.
- Use template: /templates/capacity-rfc in Confluence.

Emergency scaling runbook (operational steps to perform under active capacity degradation):
1. Triage (first 5 minutes)
   - Confirm SLO alerts: check P99, error budget burn, and queue depth.
   - Identify whether degradation is demand-driven (spike) or supply-driven (node failure/eviction).
2. Immediate mitigations (5–15 minutes)
   - If demand spike: temporarily flip heavy-slow model routes to lightweight variants using traffic routing API: 1) enable lightweight model alias, 2) apply canary rate 50% for 5m, 3) incrementally shift.
   - If supply loss: attempt automated node reclaim via orchestration (k8s scale-up job / provision from reserved pool).
   - Throttle non-essential internal jobs (batch evals, long running diagnostics) using job-priority gate.
3. Capacity-increase actions (15–60 minutes)
   - Execute fast-path autoscale: call platform CLI: redwoodctl capacity apply --pool <pool> --delta <n-gpus> --reason "emergency-scale-<incident-id>".
   - If fast-path fails, escalate to Platform Capacity pager to manually allocate reserve or approve cloud burst.
4. Stabilization and observation (60+ minutes)
   - Monitor error budget burn and latency. If stabilization not achieved in 90 minutes, initiate customer-facing mitigation steps (limit per-customer throughput, activate fallback region).
5. Rollback criteria
   - When P99 latency is consistently below SLO and queue depth < 10 for 30 minutes, begin rolling back emergency changes in reverse order.

Incident review and runbook compliance standards:
- Evidence collection (required for all incidents > Sev3):
  - Timeline with 1-minute granularity for first 30 minutes, 5-minute granularity thereafter until recovery.
  - Relevant graph exports (RPS, tokens/sec, P99, queue depth, GPU idle) and raw alert logs.
  - Commands executed and exact CLI args (redwoodctl history + shell logs).
- Post-incident classification: capacity_root_cause = {demand_spike, supply_eviction, misconfig_autoscaler, downstream-degradation, other}.
- Remediation obligation: a patch or configuration change must be scheduled within 7 calendar days for anything classified as misconfig_autoscaler or supply_eviction.
- Reliability initiative linkage: convert action items into a labeled JIRA epic with priority according to impact and likelihood using the RCA templating wizard.

Operational tooling integrations (recommended and supported):
- Metrics: Prometheus + Thanos (long term), with per-service recording rules for token/sec and batch histograms.
- Traces: Jaeger distributed traces with service maps for model shards.
- Alerts & orchestration: Alertmanager -> PagerDuty for paging; Alertmanager webhooks trigger redwood-ops-runbooks lambda.
- Capacity commands: redwoodctl (CLI) and capacity service API (documented in /eng-platform/how-tos).
- Dataplane telemetry: Kafka topics (telemetry.tokens and telemetry.queues) consumed by the forecasting pipeline.
- Incident management: Jira for tracking, Confluence for evidence, Slack #incidents for comms.

Automation recipes (examples):
- Autoscaler tuning snippet (YAML):
  autoscaler:
    name: inference-primary-autoscaler
    target_metric: tokens_per_gpu
    scale_window: 120s
    scale_up_rate: 1.5
    scale_down_delay: 900s
    max_roaming_capacity: 25%

- Alert rule example (Prometheus):
  - alert: HighCapacityBurn
    expr: increase(error_budget_burn_total[30m]) > 2
    for: 10m
    labels:
      severity: page
    annotations:
      summary: "High error budget burn for {{ $labels.service }}"

Rollout & validation checklist (pre-change):
- Validate the RFC and confirm the exact time window for change.
- Run a canary with synthetic traffic that matches the 95th-percentile token distribution.
- Measure canary P99, queue depth, and GPU idle for 15 minutes before global rollout.
- Notify the incident rotation (pager) and product owners 30 minutes before expansion.

Post-incident follow-up (7–30 day lifecycle):
- 24–72 hours: tactical follow-ups (config patches, autoscaler parameter updates).
- 7 days: schedule and begin a remediation epic (sprint-planned). Owner must attach progress to the RCA.
- 30 days: reliability initiative review meeting to decide whether to: 1) fund an engineering project (medium term), 2) codify a runbook change, or 3) accept residual risk.

Common pitfalls and anti-patterns to avoid:
- Relying on raw RPS instead of token/sec for inference services (different models have different tokens per request).
- Treating GPU idle % as sole headroom signal — pair with queue depth and token-per-second metrics.
- Over-automating without sufficient rollback controls and safety checks (can worsen incidents).

Appendix A — example thresholds (copy to service template and adjust per-service):
- SLO: P99 latency < 1200ms, availability 99.9% (30-day window)
- Alert: Queue depth > 50 for 2m -> paging
- Alert: Error budget burn rate > 2x for 30m -> paging + capacity review
- Autoscaler: scale_up_rate <= 2.0, max_roaming_capacity <= 30%

Appendix B — quick CLI snippets:
- Check current pool utilization: redwoodctl capacity list --pool inference-primary
- Trigger fast-path allocation: redwoodctl capacity apply --pool inference-primary --delta 4 --reason "emergency-scale-<incident-id>"
- Revert canary routing: redwoodctl routing set --route /v1/generate --model main-model:stable

Related pages and templates:
- /templates/capacity-rfc
- /eng-sre/runbooks/oncall-evidence-collection-and-retro-playbook-2026 (reference)
- /eng-platform/how-tos/redwoodctl-capacity-api

Contact and escalation matrix:
- Platform Capacity pager: #platform-capacity PagerDuty (team: Platform Capacity)
- SRE Lead: priya.shah@redwood.ai (primary)
- Exec escalation: eng-ops@redwood.ai (after 4 hours unresolved)

Change log:
- 2024-09-12 (Priya Shah) — initial draft
- 2025-01-20 (Maya Chen) — added autoscaler tuning snippet and RFC checklist
- 2026-02-10 (Priya Shah) — expanded incident evidence requirements and updated CLI commands

End of document.

title: dsid_c67935c565d842569e7df6089757ec75__gpu-fleet-federated-slice-controller-and-ci-adapter.txt
text:
GPU Fleet Federated Slice Controller — Operator Design and CI Adapter

Overview

This page documents the design and operational integration of the GPU Fleet Federated Slice Controller (GFFSC): a cluster-native operator and accompanying Terraform/CI adapter that automates realistic, cost-aware slicing and rebalancing of GPU capacity across multiple cloud accounts and regions. The goal is to provide a single control surface for:

- Creating bounded GPU slices (fractional/whole) per tenant or workload class.
- Federated placement across accounts or zones to maximize utilization while meeting tenant SLOs.
- Controlled rebalancing and eviction windows that are IAC-driven and testable via CI.

The document covers: design, Terraform interface, Helm/values, CI adapter patterns, test harnesses, runbook for urgent re-slicing, metrics/SLOs, and ownership.

Context and motivation

Problems GFFSC addresses:

- Inefficient static reservations that leave GPUs idle while other pools spike.
- Manual cross-account rebalancing that is slow and error-prone.
- Lack of automated, repeatable safety checks for migrations and drain operations.
- Difficulty exercising slice changes with the same pipelines used for IaC and runtime validation.

High-level constraints and principles

1) Safety-first: every re-slice operation must be reversible and guarded by automated canaries and rate limits.
2) Declarative intent: slices are expressed as Terraform resources and reconciled by the operator.
3) Federated awareness: the controller reasons about cross-account capacity and egress cost signals.
4) Observability & tests: every change triggers a CI validation job (synthetic traffic + telemetry assertions).

Architecture overview

Textual diagram (ASCII):

  Terraform (git ops) ---> GitHub Actions --> Terraform Cloud / Runner ---> GFFSC CRD apply ---> Operator (k8s) ---> Placement engine ---> GPU nodes / Pools (cloud accounts)
                                                         |
                                                         +--> Canary jobs / Eval pods (runtime test harness)

Components

- CRDs: SliceRequest, SliceBinding, RebalancePlan, EvictionWindow.
- Controller: written in Go using controller-runtime. Responsible for validating, planning, and executing re-slices.
- Placement engine: policy module (pluggable) that consumes capacity models and cost signals.
- Terraform adapter: small CLI that converts Terraform-managed intent into CR manifests and pushes to the Git repo consumed by the operator.
- CI adapter: GitHub Actions workflows that run planning, dry-run validations, and runtime canaries before approving the change.

CRD examples (YAML snippet)

apiVersion: infra.redwood.ai/v1alpha1
kind: SliceRequest
metadata:
  name: research-spot-slice-2026-02
spec:
  tenant: research
  gpuType: A100-80GB
  fraction: 0.25 # fractional slice per node
  poolAffinity:
    - account: research-payg
      region: us-west-2
  minThroughputTokensPerSec: 200
  evictionPolicy: graceful

Operator responsibilities

- Reconcile SliceRequest -> create SliceBinding when placement confirmed.
- Build RebalancePlan that sequences node drains to maintain warm-pool coverage.
- Apply rate limits to avoid >10% concurrent live-evictions per topology domain.
- Integrate with billing signals: prefer cheaper accounts if latency budget allows.
- Emit Events and structured telemetry for every step (plan.created, plan.started, step.succeeded, plan.failed).

Terraform module interface

We expose a Terraform module (registry/internal) that teams use to declare slices. The module performs a validation pass and then triggers the adapter to create the SliceRequest CR. Below is the public variable surface: 

| variable | type | default | description |
|---|---|---:|---|
| tenant | string | n/a | Logical tenant id (used in naming + billing) |
| gpu_type | string | "A100-40GB" | Preferred instance/GPU family |
| capacity_fraction | number | 0.5 | Fraction of a node to allocate (0 < x <= 1) |
| regions | list(string) | ["us-west-2"] | Preferred regions in order of preference |
| min_tokens_per_sec | number | 100 | Minimum throughput tokens required by workload |
| max_eviction_rate_pct | number | 10 | Maximum percentage of pool that can be evicted during rebalance |
| sla_latency_ms | number | 200 | Target p95 latency for the target workload |

Usage example (terraform snippet):

module "research_slice" {
  source = "internal/modules/gpu-slice"
  tenant = "research"
  gpu_type = "A100-80GB"
  capacity_fraction = 0.25
  regions = ["us-west-2","us-east-1"]
  min_tokens_per_sec = 200
  max_eviction_rate_pct = 8
  sla_latency_ms = 180
}

On module apply the adapter will:
1) run local plan checks (node-level capacity simulation)
2) emit a dry-run RebalancePlan to the PR as a JSON artifact
3) create a SliceRequest CR when the PR is merged

Helm chart / operator deployment (values.yaml snippet)

controller: 
  replicas: 3
  podSecurityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "512Mi"
    limits:
      cpu: "1"
      memory: "1Gi"
placementEngine:
  mode: hedged # hedged | conservative | cost_aware
  cloudSignalEndpoint: https://signals.internal.redwood.ai
  requeueIntervalSeconds: 30

CI Integration (GitHub Actions)

We require the module to run the following pipeline on each PR:

1) terraform fmt & validate
2) terraform plan (with -out=plan.tfplan) and module static checks
3) adapter-dryrun: run the Terraform adapter in dry-run mode to generate a RebalancePlan JSON
4) runtime-canary: spin up 2 ephemeral canary pods that exercise the target endpoints at representative load for 3 minutes; collect latency and token cost metrics
5) telemetry-assertions: compare canary metrics against thresholds (p95 latency < sla_latency_ms, warm_pool_hit_rate > 0.85, eviction_rate < max_eviction_rate_pct)
6) merge gate requires approvals and successful runtime-canary + telemetry-assertions

Example GH Action step (pseudo YAML):

- name: Adapter dry-run
  run: |
    ./terraform-gffsc-adapter --config ./module/adapter.yml --dry-run --output rebalancetest.json
    jq . rebalancetest.json > rebalancetest.pretty.json

Runbook: emergency re-slice (oncall steps)

Trigger: critical hotspot identified (more than 3 SLO violations in 10 minutes, or thermal/power emergency).

1) Page oncall and create incident ticket.
2) Identify offending tenant(s) via telemetry dashboard -> top-n token consumers.
3) Run immediate soft-reslice: mark RebalancePlan with evictionPolicy=expedite for <=5% of pool.
   - kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
     apiVersion: infra.redwood.ai/v1alpha1
     kind: RebalancePlan
     metadata:
       name: emergency-reslice-{{timestamp}}
     spec:
       targetTenants: ["<tenant-id>"]
       maxConcurrentEvictionsPct: 5
       expedite: true
     EOF
4) Execute: controller will create drain jobs and start rebalancing. Monitor step.* events.
5) If SLOs worsen after 3 concurrent steps, abort by setting plan.status.abort=true and trigger rollback: kubectl annotate slicebinding <name> gffsc/rollback=forced
6) Post-incident: raise PR with exact Terraform delta that caused change and include rebalancetest.json as artifact.

Observability and telemetry

- Required metrics emitted by controller: slice.requests.total, slice.bindings.active, rebalance.plans.created, rebalance.step.duration_seconds, eviction.count, warm_pool.hit_ratio, node.utilization.percent.
- Traces: each plan execution should be traced end-to-end (trace id annotated on emitted events).
- Dashboards: per-tenant SLO dashboard (p95 latency, token cost per 1k tokens, warm_pool_hit_rate).
- Alerts: fire when warm_pool_hit_rate < 0.6 for 5m OR eviction.count > configured threshold OR node.utilization > 95% for 2m.

SLOs and thresholds (recommended defaults)

- Provisioning latency (time from SliceRequest accepted -> binding): p95 < 8 minutes.
- Eviction concurrency cap: <=10% of pool topology domain.
- Warm pool coverage during rebalance: >=80% of pre-change capacity.
- Cost tradeoff ceiling: controller must not increase egress/cross-account cost by >15% without manual approval.

Testing strategy

- Unit tests for placement policies and cost arithmetic.
- Integration tests: mocked cloud accounts with synthetic capacity models (runs in CI).
- Synthetic chaos: weekly chaos job that replays a RebalancePlan with simulated node failures to validate safety circuits.
- End-to-end smoke: run terraform module apply against a sandbox cluster and execute runtime-canary.

Operational considerations and limitations

- The GFFSC is not a substitute for application-level autoscaling; it rebalances reserved capacity across pools.
- Cross-account changes that cross billing boundaries require finance approval flag in Terraform variables (force_approve_billing_change=true).
- The placement engine will be conservative in regions with low telemetry coverage; teams can opt into riskier modes via placementEngine.mode.

Ownership and run cadence

- Service owner: eng-infra/gpu-platform (primary: Priya Nair).
- Oncall: gpu-platform rotation (see team wiki for schedule).
- CI owner: eng-infra/ci (responsible for the adapter runner and GitHub Actions).
- Quarterly: capacity reconciliation and cost review with finance and capacity forecasting team.

Rollout plan and migration steps

1) v0: operator + CRDs in sandbox, Terraform adapter dry-run only (Q1 pilot).
2) v1: enable create-on-merge for non-prod accounts with canary enforcement (Q2).
3) v2: cross-account rebalancing in production with conservative mode + finance guardrails (Q3).
4) v3+: automated cost-aware policies and RBAC-based tenant self-serve (Q4).

Appendix: common CLI commands

- Run adapter locally in dry-run: ./terraform-gffsc-adapter --config ./module/adapter.yml --dry-run
- Inspect RebalancePlan: kubectl get rebalanceplan -o wide
- Force-annotate rollback: kubectl annotate slicebinding <name> gffsc/rollback=forced --overwrite
- Collect controller logs (last 1000 lines): kubectl logs deploy/gffsc-controller -n infra --tail=1000

References and links

- Placement policy spec (internal): /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/placement-policy-spec.json
- Capacity forecasting playbook: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-demand-forecasting-and-ml-backed-scaling-playbook.json

Notes and next steps

- Action item: engineering to implement adapter telemetry schema by 2026-03-01 (owner: Ben Chu).
- Action item: CI team to add telemetry-assertions library as an internal action (owner: Sofia Martinez).

title: dsid_a457b9210ea3427c923339f822aee6e3__execution-profile-registry-and-live-reconfig-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Execution Profile Registry and Live Reconfiguration Playbook

Summary

This page describes the Execution Profile Registry (EPR) — a central runtime component that captures workload execution profiles, exposes them to scheduling and kernel-selection layers, and enables safe live reconfiguration of scheduling, batching, and kernel parameters based on telemetry signals. The document is a combined design + operational playbook: architecture, data model, decision logic, safety gates, rollout checklist, and incident runbook.

Why this exists

- Serving workloads show high variability (sequence length, user-level burstiness, cache hit-rate). Static scheduler configs produce avoidable cost and tail latency.
- EPR lets runtime components subscribe to a canonical, versioned set of execution profiles derived from production telemetry and experiment signals.
- Operators can use EPR to perform targeted live reconfiguration (e.g., batch-slice size, kernel variant selection, kvcache-prefetch policy) while maintaining SLOs and safe rollback.

Goals and non-goals

Goals
1. Provide a single source-of-truth for workload execution characteristics and policy hints.
2. Enable deterministic, auditable live reconfiguration with automated safety checks.
3. Allow fast, low-risk rollout of kernel/scheduler parameter changes and targeted rollbacks.

Non-goals
- Not a full replacement for the offline autotune pipeline used for model-quantization recommendations.
- Not intended to perform global topology changes (e.g., replacing a GPU class); EPR operates at request-routing & scheduler/kernal level.

High-level architecture

Components
- Telemetry Ingestors: Stream samplers that emit signals into Trace + Metric pipelines (per-request timing, kernel durations, kvcache hit/miss, batch sizes).
- Profile Builder Service: Periodically aggregates telemetry into candidate Execution Profiles (EPs). Runs feature extraction: seq_len distribution, token-per-request histogram, typical KV cache reuse entropy, tail-latency percentiles, priority-mix.
- Execution Profile Registry (EPR): Versioned store of profiles and policy hints (JSON documents). Supports read-by-name, read-by-tag, and snapshot-by-commit. Exposes an HTTP API and a lightweight gRPC endpoint for fast reads.
- Reconfig Controller: Evaluates EPs against SLO rules and rollout policies; issues configuration update bundles to the Scheduler Agent and Kernel Agent.
- Safety Evaluator: Canary/Shadow judge service that tests a candidate bundle against traffic samples in a controlled environment and reports regressions.

Data flow (described)
1. Ingestors collect sampled traces and metrics (default sampling 0.1% for full traces; 5% lightweight metrics).
2. Profile Builder produces candidate EPs on a configurable cadence (default: every 4 hours).
3. Operator or automated policy promotes a candidate EP to "active" version in EPR.
4. Reconfig Controller creates a rollout plan (canary percentage, duration, rollback triggers) and pushes bundles to a target cell's Scheduler Agent.
5. Safety Evaluator monitors canary traffic; if triggers are observed, the Reconfig Controller halts rollout and initiates rollback.

Execution Profile model (canonical JSON fields)

- profile_id: string (versionable)
- tags: [string] (e.g., "interactive", "long-seq", "high-cache-reuse")
- seq_len_pct: stringified histogram reference id
- median_tokens: string (number)
- p95_latency_ms: string (number)
- kvcache_reuse_rate: string (0.0-1.0)
- typical_batch_shape: string (e.g., "[1,2,1,4]")
- kernel_hints: [string] (ordered list of preferred kernel variant ids)
- scheduler_hints: [string] (e.g., "prefer-small-batches", "aggressive-concurrency")
- safe_rollback_signature: string (hash of pre-change probe results)

Note: the EPR JSON schema is intentionally flat so runtime agents can do cheap JSON parsing. Each field above is represented as strings or arrays of strings to simplify cross-language clients.

Mapping profiles to runtime decisions

- Kernel Selection: Kernel Agent queries EPR with current route+profile tag. EPR returns kernel_hints starting from low-precision fast variants if kvcache_reuse_rate > 0.7 and median_tokens < 64.
- Batching Policy: Scheduler Agent picks batch_slice targets from typical_batch_shape and scheduler_hints. For "long-seq" tag, recommended max_batch_tokens=1024 and slice_size=1.
- Prefetching & KV Warmup: If kvcache_reuse_rate > 0.5 and p95_latency_ms < 80, enable async prefetch with conservative concurrency 2.

Safety and SLO gates

Every live reconfiguration requires satisfaction of the following gates before production push: 
- Canary Regression < 2% in p95 latency and < 0.5% error-rate increase (configurable per-route).
- Cost delta check: expected token-cost delta should be within operator-set budget (e.g., < 10% increase).
- Resource headroom: free GPU slots > 10% to accommodate transient spike.
- Observability hooks: tracing and metric sampling level bumped to capture an additional 0.5% trace samples for rollout duration.

Safety Evaluator experiments

Use two experiment modes:
- Shadow-run (no impact): Run candidate kernel on shadowed replicas for sampled requests and compare outputs/latency.
- Canary-run: Route X% of real traffic to canary fleet with full observability.

Manual and automated rollouts

Rollout policy example (Reconfig Controller YAML):

```yaml
profile_id: epr-2026-11
canary:
  steps:
    - percent: 1
      duration: 10m
    - percent: 5
      duration: 30m
    - percent: 20
      duration: 60m
    - percent: 100
      duration: 10m
rollback_triggers:
  p95_latency_increase_pct: 2
  error_rate_increase_abs: 0.005
  gpu_memory_pressure_pct: 85
monitoring:
  extra_trace_sampling: 0.5%
  dashboard: /dashboards/epr-rollout
```

Operational runbook: quick steps to apply a profile

1. Validate candidate EP in the staging Profile Builder UI (check histograms and kernel hints).
2. Run Safety Evaluator in shadow mode for 2,000 sampled requests.
3. Create rollout plan in Reconfig Controller and set canary steps.
4. Kick off canary. Monitor p50/p95/p99 latency, error-rate, GPU utilization, and cost-estimated token-per-second.
5. If any rollback trigger fires, invoke Reconfig Controller -> automated rollback. If not, proceed to next step until 100%.
6. After full rollout, schedule a stabilization window (default 24 hours) before allowing further EPR changes for the same route.

Troubleshooting and triage matrix

Symptom: p95 increases by > 3% during canary
- Immediate action: rollback to previous EPR version.
- Investigation: compare kernel duration traces, look for shifts in batch sizes, check kvcache reuse telemetry.
- Postmortem items: add a synthetic replay benchmark using sample traces to see divergence.

Symptom: Increased model output divergence (functional change) in shadow-run
- Immediate action: mark kernel variant as unsafe and blacklist variant id in EPR.
- Investigation: re-run safety-evaluator with higher fidelity (1% sampling + deterministic seed).

Operational checklist before making EPR changes

- Ownership: assign an owner and at least one reviewer.
- Backwards-compat: ensure new profile includes safe_rollback_signature.
- Observability: enable additional trace sampling and annotated dashboard.
- Communication: note change in #runtime-prod channel and add rollout to weekly change log.

Example CLI snippets

Registering a profile (curl):

curl -X POST https://epr.internal.redwood/api/v1/profiles -H 'Authorization: Bearer $EPR_TOKEN' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"profile_id":"epr-2026-11","tags":["interactive"],"median_tokens":"34","p95_latency_ms":"62","kvcache_reuse_rate":"0.72","kernel_hints":["kfast-q4","kstd-q8"],"scheduler_hints":["prefer-small-batches"]}'

Querying EPR from a runtime agent (gRPC example description)
- Agents should prefer the gRPC endpoint: /epr.Lookup(route="/v1/generate", tags=["interactive"]) 
- Fallback to HTTP read if gRPC fails; cache the response for 30s.

Audit, observability and change history

- Every promotion of a profile writes an audit event to AuditDB (fields: actor, profile_id, previous_version, diff-summary, rollback_signature).
- Rollouts create a rollout record with timestamps, canary steps, and metrics snapshot for automated postmortem.
- Dashboards: prebuilt panels for rollout health (p50/p95/p99, error-rate, kernel-duration distribution, cache-reuse).

Ownership and SLAs

- EPR service owner: eng-serving-runtime team (oncall: runtime-sre rotation).
- SLA for EPR reads: 99.99% in-region with median latency < 10ms.
- Promotion/Write window: recommend performing writes during low-traffic windows unless urgent.

Longer term extensions (notes)

- Integrate model-behavior regression signals (e.g., semantic evals) as additional safety gates.
- Add ML-based rollout optimizers that predict optimal canary durations per-route.

Appendix: minimal profile example (single-line JSON escaped for Confluence)

{"profile_id":"epr-2026-11","tags":["interactive"],"median_tokens":"34","p95_latency_ms":"62","kvcache_reuse_rate":"0.72","kernel_hints":["kfast-q4","kstd-q8"],"scheduler_hints":["prefer-small-batches"]}

Appendix: Contacts and escalation

- Primary owner: Priya Shah (@priya)
- Runtime SRE oncall: #runtime-oncall
- Product reviewer: Marco Alvarez

End of document.

title: dsid_bda0c34810b740099a11dc55e7fa0564__experimental-metric-injection-campaign-retrospective-2025.txt
text:
Experimental Metric Injection Campaign — Retrospective

Summary
=======

This document is a postmortem-style retrospective of the experimental metric injection campaign we ran from 2025-11-10 to 2025-12-05. The experiment intentionally injected synthetic telemetry into the platform metrics pipeline to validate: (1) alert sensitivity tuning for LLM prefix/KV cache degradation, (2) downstream dashboard behavior, and (3) costing and storage impact of higher cardinality metrics.

This retrospective records the experiment design, outcomes, operational impacts, lessons learned, and recommended next steps. It is intended for platform operators, SRE, observability engineers, and product owners evaluating telemetry tradeoffs.

Background and goals
--------------------

Context: The platform telemetry backlog showed repeated false-positive alerts during short-lived cache thrash events. To evaluate whether our alert rules, aggregation windows, and cardinality controls were balanced, the Observability team proposed a safe, time-limited metric injection campaign that simulates realistic degradation signals without impacting production services.

Goals:
- Validate alerting SLOs and silence durations for cache/serving regressions.
- Measure cost and cardinality impact when emitting per-tenant cache-hit partitions vs. aggregated metrics.
- Verify dashboard and runbook actions (including automated ticket creation) under noisy conditions.

Experiment design (high level)
----------------------------

1. Scope and windows:
   - Active window: 2025-11-10 08:00 UTC to 2025-12-05 20:00 UTC.
   - Test tenants: synthetic-tenant-001 .. synthetic-tenant-050 (no real customer traffic).
   - Injected services: kv-prefix-cache-service, serving-router, request-queue-proxy.

2. Injection mechanics:
   - A dedicated job (metric-injector v0.3.1) published synthetic Prometheus-compatible metrics into the metrics-ingest pipeline via the internal metrics-writer queue.
   - Mutation pattern: ramp-up (5m), steady-state (30m), burst (3m) — repeated every 2 hours.

3. Safety controls (must pass preconditions):
   - Injector uses a low-priority tag and sits behind a feature-flag (ff.metrics_injection).
   - AuthZ: only operator role obs-inject allowed to start/stop jobs.
   - Rate limit: 1500 metrics/sec throttle at the ingestion gateway.
   - Circuit breaker: ingestion spike > 10x baseline triggers automatic halt and alert to obs-ops.

Concrete sample metric (Prometheus exposition format):
# HELP kv_prefix_cache_hit Synthetic cache hit metric for experiment
# TYPE kv_prefix_cache_hit counter
kv_prefix_cache_hit{tenant="synthetic-tenant-001",prefix_shard="shard-12",pool="fast",experiment="metric-injection-2025"} 1

PromQL queries used during the campaign:
- 1m rate of synthetic hits (all tenants): sum(rate(kv_prefix_cache_hit[1m]))
- Per-tenant anomaly detection: increase(kv_prefix_cache_miss[5m]) / (increase(kv_prefix_cache_hit[5m]) + 1) > 0.25

Alerting rules exercised
-----------------------

We deliberately exercised three rule families to observe operator signal-to-noise and automated mitigations.

1) cache-degradation-severe
   - Expr: job:kv_cache_miss_ratio:5m > 0.25 AND sum(rate(kv_prefix_cache_miss[1m])) > 100
   - Severity: critical
   - Pager: obs-oncall -> eng-platform-sme (P1)
   - Runbook excerpt: see section "Runbook actions for severity-critical alerts" below.

2) cache-latency-elevated
   - Expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kv_cache_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)) > 0.2
   - Severity: warning
   - Pager: obs-oncall (P2)

3) high-cardinality-telemetry-cost
   - Expr: increase(metric_series_count_total[1d]) > 10000
   - Severity: info (but channels to cost-engineering slack)

Runbook actions for severity-critical alerts
-------------------------------------------

1. Triage (minutes 0–5)
   - Confirm alert origin using the alert details page and run the Playbook Debug CLI: 
     $ ./obsctl alert inspect cache-degradation-severe --start="-10m"
   - If source contains experiment tag experiment=metric-injection-2025, mark as "experimental" and follow experimental isolation path.

2. Isolation (minutes 5–20)
   - Use the operator UI to throttle metric-injector job: 
     $ ffcli set metrics_injection off --env=prod
   - If throttling fails, disable ingestion at the gateway: 
     $ kubectl scale deployment metrics-ingest-gateway --replicas=0 -n observability

3. Remediation (minutes 20–60)
   - If cache miss ratio reduces after halting injector, file a short incident note and run a post-incident checklist.
   - If not reduced, escalate to eng-serving-runtime and perform controlled model-swap fallback.

Observations and outcomes
-------------------------

Summary of collected artifacts (table):
| experiment_id | start | end | peak_cardinality | peak_series_rate | downstream_slo_burn | operator_actions | notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| MI-2025-11-A | 2025-11-12T08:00Z | 2025-11-12T20:00Z | 24,600 | 1,350/s | serving-router 95th latency +0.9% | throttled injector, no service restart | small, transient dashboard churn |
| MI-2025-11-B | 2025-11-18T02:00Z | 2025-11-18T06:00Z | 42,100 | 2,200/s | cache-service SLO burn 0.4% | ingestion gateway scaled down | required manual backfill of metrics |
| MI-2025-11-C | 2025-11-28T14:00Z | 2025-11-28T18:00Z | 9,800 | 720/s | no measurable SLO burn | no operator action | safe, within forecasted costs |

Key findings:
- Alert fidelity: The critical cache-degradation-severe rule fired 18 times; 11 were attributable to the experiment. After tuning the rule's population threshold (sum(rate(...)) > 250), false positives from the injection decreased by 72%.
- Dashboard behavior: High-cardinality injection increased dashboard load times for 30–45s during peaks. We found one Grafana dashboard panel using unbounded label expansion (tenant label) causing heavy rendering cost; we updated panel to use topk(10, ...) aggregation.
- Cost impact: Metric series cardinality increased ingestion storage costs by ~9% in the experiment window. Extrapolating to sustained per-tenant telemetry (not recommended) would add ~1.2% to monthly telemetry bill per 10k tenants.
- Operator cognitive load: During the first two weeks, oncall time to diagnose experimental alerts averaged 28 minutes per incident. After adding an explicit experiment tag and a fast-path in the alert details UI, triage time dropped to 9 minutes.

Lessons learned
-------------

1. Experiment tagging is critical. Without experiment=... in the injected metrics and the alert payload, engineers could not quickly differentiate synthetic vs real incidents. Add tag by default for future tests.

2. Cardinality control must be enforced in the ingestion layer. The experiment highlighted that per-tenant per-prefix labels explode series count; we should enforce a policy of max 3 dynamic labels for production metrics and apply sampler/rollup for ephemeral tenants.

3. Dashboard templates must use bounded aggregations. Panels that iterate across unbounded label sets are fragile under injection. Use topk(), group_left, or explicit tenant lists in dashboards that power runbooks.

4. Alert rules need two-dimensional thresholds: both ratio and absolute volume guards prevented noisy firing in high-cardinality situations.

Decisions and follow-ups (action items)
-------------------------------------

1) Enforce ingestion label policy (owner: eng-platform telemetry) — due 2026-02-15
   - Implement ingestion-side label whitelist and hard caps in metrics-ingest-gateway.
   - Metric filters to reject metrics with >3 dynamic labels or value cardinality > 100k/day.

2) Alert rule change (owner: obs-slo-team) — due 2026-01-31
   - Update cache-degradation-severe to require sum(rate(...)) > 250 OR increase(metric_series_count_total[1h]) < 5000 to fire.

3) Dashboard hardening (owner: observability-frontend) — due 2026-01-20
   - Audit top-30 dashboards for unbounded label expansions; apply topk(10) or explicit tenant scoping.

4) Experiment framework improvements (owner: platform-experiments) — due 2026-03-01
   - Add an "experiment registry" page that automatically annotates alerts and dashboards when a live experiment is active.
   - Provide a one-click ff toggle for emergency stop and escalation metadata populated in PagerDuty incidents.

Appendix A — Useful commands and snippets
----------------------------------------

- Inspect alert context:
  $ ./obsctl alert inspect cache-degradation-severe --start="-30m" --format=json | jq .context.tags

- Throttle injector (k8s job):
  $ kubectl patch cronjob metric-injector -n observability --patch '{"spec": {"suspend": true}}'

- Example Grafana panel safe query for cache misses:
  topk(10, sum by (tenant) (rate(kv_prefix_cache_miss[5m])))

Appendix B — Glossary and ownership
-----------------------------------

- metric-injector: internal test harness that emits synthetic metrics (repo: infra/metric-injector). Owner: platform-experiments.
- metrics-ingest-gateway: Kafka-ingest + transform service for Prom-compatible metrics. Owner: observability-infra.
- obsctl: command-line tooling for observability runbook actions. Owner: observability-tools.

Contact and follow-up meeting
----------------------------

We will host a 45-minute retro working session to review the findings and approve action items on 2026-01-19 16:00 UTC in #obs-retros and the Confluence meeting page (link below).

Meeting page: /confluence/eng-platform/retrospectives/experimental-metric-injection-campaign-retrospective-2025/meeting-notes

Document owner: Aisha Kapoor (aisha@redwood-inference.com).

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-12-07: initial draft
- 2026-01-12: updated with final measurements, action items, and dates

title: dsid_026bbc0fbb97423ab9de20d8f99402d6__cohort-driven-shadow-validation-playbook-2025.txt
text:
Cohort-driven Shadow Validation Playbook

Overview:

This playbook describes a repeatable, cohort-driven approach to shadow (non-production) validation that combines traffic mirroring, cohort stratification, and statistical evaluation to detect drift, regressions, or QoE degradations before a model rollout. It is intended for use by ML Engineers, Product Reliability, and SRE when validating model variants (quantized models, finetunes, or new topologies) against real traffic slices.

Goals:
- Expose subtle, slice-specific regressions that aggregate metrics miss.
- Provide deterministic acceptance gates with clear thresholds and statistical tests.
- Keep validation cost-bounded by adaptive sampling and prioritized cohorts.

Scope and Non-Goals:
- Scope: live shadowing and replay for text-generation and embedding endpoints; cohort metrics for latency, token cost, response-stability, and semantic fidelity.
- Non-Goals: synthetic adversarial fuzzing (see separate fuzz playbook) and complete production failover automation.

Definitions:
- Shadow traffic: duplicated requests sent to a candidate model without impacting production responses.
- Cohort: a named subset of traffic defined by request attributes (customer_id, route, prompt-template, language, token_count, session_age).
- Response-stability-index (RSI): composite metric measuring output drift against baseline using embedding cosine similarity, edit distance, and semantic score.

When to run a cohort-driven shadow validation:
- Before a model promotion that affects >5% of production request volume.
- When introducing cross-workload optimizations (e.g., new quant profile, KV-cache changes, batch scheduling).
- After detecting slice-specific degradations in continuous telemetry.

Ownership and Roles:
- Requesting owner: Feature/Model owner (creates cohorts and success criteria).
- Shadow operator: SRE / Infra (sets up mirroring, monitors resource usage).
- Evaluator: Applied ML / Quality (runs statistical tests, interprets slice failures).
- Approver: Product owner or Reliability lead (approves promotion or rollback).

High-level Workflow (stepwise):
1) Define cohorts (3–10 per run):
   - Use historical telemetry to choose meaningful slices (high-value customers, long-context, multimodal inputs).
   - Example cohort definitions: "high-long-context-english" (tokens > 2048), "enterprise-integration-route" (route = /api/v1/generate && customer_tier = enterprise).
2) Choose sampling policy and budget:
   - Default: mirror 10% of cohort traffic for 72 hours or until 5,000 requests per cohort are collected, whichever comes first.
   - For sensitive cohorts, reduce to 1–2% with extended duration.
3) Configure shadow routing (example manifest):
   - Provide network-level mirroring rules and candidate endpoint. See appendix for JSON/YAML snippets.
4) Instrument telemetry and tagging:
   - Ensure every mirrored request is tagged with: cohort_id, shadow_run_id, baseline_model, candidate_model, sample_rate.
   - Log raw prompts, token counts, latency, final cost estimate (tokens * model_cost_rate).
5) Compute per-cohort metrics (real-time and batch):
   - Latency P95 and P99 (ms).
   - Token cost delta (%).
   - RSI (median per cohort) and drift fraction (percent responses with RSI < threshold).
   - Functional correctness checks: reranking loss, presence/absence of required fields for structured outputs.
6) Statistical evaluation and thresholds:
   - For continuous metrics (latency, cost): use bootstrap confidence intervals with 10k resamples. Gate if candidate P99 > baseline P99 + 20% and p < 0.01.
   - For semantic/fidelity metrics (RSI): require median RSI >= baseline median - 0.03 and two-sided Mann-Whitney U test p > 0.05.
   - For categorical regressions (required fields missing): Fisher exact test, require failure rate delta < 0.5 percentage points with 95% CI.
7) Adaptive triage and probe amplification:
   - If a cohort shows borderline failure (0.01 < p < 0.05), automatically increase sampling for that cohort by up to 5x for an additional 24 hours.
8) Runbook actions on failures:
   - Soft fail (slice flagged): pause promotion, notify owners, request focused remediation (prompt-tune, quant-fix, dataset augmentation).
   - Hard fail (critical customer slice degraded or functional correctness violated): immediate rollback path and incident creation.
9) Promotion decision and documentation:
   - Successful run: produce a validation artifact containing per-cohort summaries, raw probe examples (anonymized), and final decision. Attach to release ticket.

Metric and Alerting Configuration (table):
| Metric | Aggregation | Gate | Action on breach | Ownership |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|
| Latency P99 | per-cohort | > baseline + 20% (p<0.01) | Pause promotion, trigger perf triage | SRE |
| Token cost delta | median % | > +15% | Cost review, consider quant profile | Finance/Feature owner |
| RSI median | median similarity | < baseline - 0.03 (MWU p<0.05) | Quality investigation, escalate | Applied ML |
| Required-field loss | failure rate | delta > 0.005 absolute | Immediate rollback for critical routes | Product |

Sampling and Budgeting Guidelines:
- Minimum sample per cohort for significance: 500 requests. If unavailable, mark cohort as "insufficient data" and schedule an extended run.
- Budget cap per run: token budget defined in run config (default 10M tokens). Operator may truncate tests if budget exhausted and annotate results.

Data Privacy and Redaction:
- Always redact PII before storing mirrored requests. Use the pipeline redaction rules: replace emails, SSNs, API keys, and long identifiers with deterministic tokens.
- For enterprise customers with confidentiality flags, request explicit authorization before mirroring; otherwise exclude those cohorts.

Operational Playbook (quick steps):
1) Create run ticket with cohort definitions and success criteria.
2) Request SRE to enable mirror manifest with run_id and sample_rate.
3) Confirm telemetry tags are present in the mirror stream.
4) Validate that baseline and candidate endpoints are reachable.
5) Monitor dashboards (per-cohort) for first 6 hours. If any hard fails occur, follow hard-fail incident checklist.

Promotions, Canary Integration and Rollout Path:
- If all cohorts pass: promote candidate to canary (5–10% production, canary duration 48–96 hours) with continuous cohort monitoring.
- If a small number of low-impact cohorts fail: consider targeted mitigations (prompt templates, per-route fallback) and rerun shadow validation.

Appendix A — Example Shadow Routing YAML:
```yaml
shadow_run_id: cohort-shadow-2025-09
mirror_rules:
  - route: /v1/generate
    sample_rate: 0.1
    cohorts: [high-long-context-english, enterprise-integration-route]
candidate_endpoint: https://shadow-candidate.internal:8443/generate
baseline_endpoint: https://prod-model.internal:8443/generate
storage: s3://redwood-shadow-archive/cohort-shadow-2025-09/
```

Appendix B — Example cohort SQL (for data-team):
```
SELECT request_id, customer_id, route, token_count, language, timestamp
FROM request_logs
WHERE token_count > 2048 AND language = 'en' AND timestamp BETWEEN '{{start}}' AND '{{end}}';
```

Appendix C — CLI snippets:
- Start run: redwood-shadow run start --id cohort-shadow-2025-09 --manifest ./shadow.yaml
- Increase sampling for cohort: redwood-shadow run update --id cohort-shadow-2025-09 --cohort high-long-context-english --sample-rate 0.5
- Archive results: redwood-shadow artifacts bundle --id cohort-shadow-2025-09 --out ./artifacts.tar.gz

Troubleshooting common issues:
- Low sample counts: increase sample_rate for affected cohorts, extend window, or create synthetic probe generator limited to the target cohort patterns.
- High resource usage on candidate host: coordinate with SRE to throttle mirror throughput or scale candidate pool; prioritize critical cohorts.
- Inconsistent telemetry tags: stop the run, patch instrumentation, and restart to ensure validity of per-cohort aggregates.

Audit and Reporting:
- Every shadow run must attach an artifact containing anonymized examples (<=100 per failed cohort), a per-cohort metric CSV, and the approval decision.
- Maintain a run index (spreadsheet or internal DB) with run_id, start/end times, outcome, and link to artifacts for 12 months.

Notes and rationale:
- Cohort-driven validation focuses our signal-to-noise on high-value slices rather than aggregate metrics that can mask regressions. Adaptive sampling reduces cost while enabling focused amplification where it matters. Statistical gates balance sensitivity and false positive rates to avoid unnecessary rollbacks.

Contact and escalation:
- Primary owner: Maya Chen (applied-ml)
- SRE shadow contact: Diego Alvarez
- On-call escalation: Pager duty "model-eval-oncall"

End of playbook.

title: dsid_d6b720c126724b80b52ca27542a8639f__knowledge-snapshot-anchoring-eval-manifest-2026.txt
text:
Knowledge Snapshot Anchoring: Eval Manifest for Time-Sensitive Benchmarks

Overview:

This document specifies Redwood's recommended pattern for capturing, anchoring, and evaluating knowledge-sensitive model behavior over time. The goal is to make evals reproducible when knowledge in the world (facts, events, software versions, policy text) changes, and to provide a pragmatic operational workflow for detecting, triaging, and rolling back regressions tied to temporal drift.

Intended audience:
- Applied ML engineers running eval suites
- SREs and platform engineers managing eval-runner capacity and snapshot-store
- Product managers owning user-facing factual features

Why snapshot anchoring matters:
- LLMs are evaluated against prompts whose correct answer can change (e.g., "Who is the CEO of X?"). Without anchoring to a knowledge snapshot, test failures can look like model regressions when they are actually time drift.
- Snapshotting enables deterministic replay during regression hunts, auditability for compliance, and safer promotion of quantized / cache-optimized model variants.

Key concepts and components:
- Knowledge Snapshot: a timestamped collection of canonical references (URLs, corpus digest, curated facts) representing the world state used to generate / label probe answers.
- Probe: a single input-output test case; in time-sensitive probes the expected answer is tagged with the snapshot id and confidence window.
- Snapshot Store: service name "snapshot-store" (S3 + index in metadata DB), retention policy defined below.
- Eval Runner: service name "eval-runner" which accepts --snapshot-id for anchored runs.

Snapshot metadata schema (human-readable table):
| field | type | description | example |
|---|---|---:|---|
| snapshot_id | string | unique id (ISO date + short hash) | 2026-01-12-3f9b |
| created_at | date | creation timestamp (UTC) | 2026-01-12T09:10:00Z |
| source_manifest | string | URI to a manifest (list of source URIs + digests) | s3://snapshots/2026-01-12/manifest.json |
| curator | string | person/team curating the snapshot | data-ops / priya.menon@redwood.com |
| scope_tags | list | topical tags used for selection | politics, api-changes, finance |
| verifier_hash | string | digest of canonical labels used by probes | sha256:ab12... |

Recommended snapshot cadence and retention:
- Fast-moving domains (news, product releases): daily snapshot + 30 day retention
- Moderate cadence domains (APIs, SDKs): weekly snapshot + 90 day retention
- Stable domains (encyclopedic facts): monthly snapshot + 365 day retention
- Retention and lifecycle are configurable per tag via snapshot-store policy; default TTLs above enforced by snapshot-store garbage collector.

Probe authoring guidelines for time anchors:
1. Every probe that depends on mutable facts must include: subject, predicate, temporal-range (earliest / latest acceptable answer date), and authoritative-source URI(s).
2. For open-ended answers prefer "canonicalized response" assertions (short string or structured JSON) to free text scoring.
3. Assign an expected answer confidence level (high/medium/low) to help triage noisy labels.
4. Group probes into anchored bundles that reference the snapshot_id used to label them.

Example anchored probe (text block):
- id: probe-2026-0012
- snapshot_id: 2026-01-12-3f9b
- prompt: "Who is the current CTO of Umbra Systems?"
- expected_answer: "Rina Alvarez"
- temporal_range: "2026-01-01 to 2026-01-31"
- sources: [https://umbra.example/careers/leadership]
- confidence: high

Eval-runner integration (CLI examples):
- Run a standard anchored eval: 
  eval-runner --suite=knowledge-anchor-suite --snapshot-id=2026-01-12-3f9b --parallel=16 --output=s3://eval-results/2026-02-01/anchor-run.json
- Convert an unanchored suite into an anchored one: 
  probe-tool attach-snapshot --suite=ask-api-suite --snapshot-id=2026-01-12-3f9b --author="Priya Menon"

Anchored run SLOs and alerting thresholds:
- Regression alert if anchored accuracy delta >= 3% for high-confidence probes in a service slice over a 24-hr rolling window.
- Informational notice for 1-3% delta; requires review by probe steward.
- Latency SLO for eval-runner using snapshots: median runtime increase vs unanchored baseline <= 5%; if > 15% investigate snapshot-store hot-paths and caching.

Automated triage playbook when temporal drift is detected (numbered steps):
1. Verify the failing probes are anchored (check snapshot_id in result manifest). If not anchored, mark as unanchored candidate and queue for manual labeling.
2. Query snapshot-store to retrieve source_manifest and verifier_hash. Validate that the probe expected answer digests match the manifest.
3. Run a cross-snapshot diff: replay the probe across the latest 5 snapshots via eval-runner --snapshot-range to determine if change is persistent or transient.
4. If change is persistent across snapshots: escalate to product owner and data-ops for canon update. Create a regression issue with tag "temporal:canonical-update".
5. If change is present only in the latest snapshot: suspect snapshot-label drift. Run label verification workflow (human-in-the-loop) using the annotator CLI: annotator-verify --snapshot-id=... --probes=...
6. If model regression confirmed (answers disagree with authoritative sources for snapshot period): open a model-regression incident in incident tracker and follow the standard regression rollback playbook (link in related_pages).

Canary & rollout recommendations for snapshot-dependent model changes:
- Always run a pre-promotion anchored eval: the candidate model must pass high-confidence anchored probe set at >= baseline accuracy.
- Deploy canary to shadow traffic with anchored monitoring enabled for 48 hours for fast-moving domains, 7 days for stable domains.
- If anchored delta > threshold during canary, automatically soft-fail promotion and create a rollback task.

Governance and responsibilities:
- Snapshot curator: Data-Ops (owns snapshot cadence, manifests, and storage paths).
- Probe steward: Applied ML (owns probe quality and expected answers).
- Eval owner: Eval Platform (owns eval-runner, metrics export, and alerting integration).

Storage & naming conventions (must be followed):
- Snapshot manifest path: s3://redwood-snapshots/{domain}/{YYYY-MM-DD}/{snapshot_id}/manifest.json
- Anchored probe bundles: s3://eval-probes/anchored/{domain}/{snapshot_id}/bundle.ndjson
- Eval results: s3://eval-results/{YYYY-MM-DD}/{suite}/{snapshot_id}/results.jsonl

Example change-log / audit snippet to include in regression tickets:
- fields: [snapshot_id, probe_ids, cohort_tag, baseline_accuracy, new_accuracy, run_id, evaluator_commit, model_hash]
- policy: tickets generated by automated triage must attach the snapshot manifest and a link to the verifier hash.

Appendix A — Quick checks and heuristics for common failure modes:
- If many probes in the same domain fail and sources in manifest changed recently, treat as knowledge drift and route to data-ops.
- If single probe failure isolated to particular phrasing, add paraphrase probes to the bundle and re-evaluate under same snapshot.
- If regression is correlated with quantized rollout, use eval-runner --quant-compare to run both float and quantized variants anchored to the same snapshot for direct comparison.

Appendix B — Example policy table (default):
| domain_tag | snapshot_cadence | retention_days | canary_window | triage_owner |
| news | daily | 30 | 48h | data-ops |
| apis | weekly | 90 | 72h | product |
| knowledge-base | monthly | 365 | 7d | applied-ml |

Related resources:
- eval-runner docs (internal): /eng-developer-experience/api-examples/eval-runner-cli
- Probe authoring template: s3://eval-templates/anchored-probe-template.md
- Regression rollback playbook: /applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/model-regression-forensics-playbook-2026

Change history:
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft, Priya Menon
- 2026-01-06: Added retention defaults and CLI integration examples (reviewer: Ethan Zhao)
- 2026-02-03: Published; clarified triage steps and added canary guidance (reviewer: Marta Kovacs)

title: dsid_89d571be63954a3da8a9964b8380a3c7__forensic-playbook-service-level-causation-and-replay-guidance-2026.txt
text:
Service Forensics Playbook — Causation Reconstruction & Traffic Replay

Summary:

This playbook defines a repeatable, low-friction process for collecting, preserving, and replaying production traffic and service state to reconstruct root cause for service incidents. It focuses on: collecting high-fidelity evidence, persisting model-serving and cache state, performing deterministic replays in a sandbox, and tying findings back to SLOs and capacity signals.

Scope:
- Services: inference runtime, request-router, kv-cache-layer, autoscaler, routing-proxy.
- Activities covered: pre-incident instrumentation, live evidence collection, post-incident replay & causation analysis, evidence packaging and retention.
- Not covered: legal subpoena handling (see security-and-compliance).

Definitions:
- Incident ID: unique id = YYYYMMDD-service-short-#### (e.g., 20260305-runtime-0042).
- Replay sandbox: isolated environment with identical service binaries/config but mocked downstreams.
- Deterministic replay: replay where inputs, random seeds, and cache populations are controlled to reproduce behavior within expected statistical variance.

Pre-incident instrumentation checklist (owner: observability):
- Trace sampling: ensure 100% header capture for emergency traces (header-only trace tags) and 10% detailed traces by default.
- Short-lived request snapshots: sample 1:100 requests + capture full request/response bodies for sampled ids; rotate sensitive fields via PII scrubbing.
- KV cache checkpointing: configure periodic checkpoints of prefix/KV caches to S3 using rwd-kv-dump (every 10 minutes for high-throughput services).
- Model state snapshots: for models with ephemeral weights/embeddings, enable model-metadata export on crash (model name, version, quantization profile).
- Metrics: export p50/p95/p99 latencies, error counts, 5m QPS, CPU/GPU util, retry counts at 1s granularity to Prometheus/long-term store.
- Canary toggles: keep canary traffic routing flags in feature-flag service and snapshot states.

During incident: immediate evidence collection (ordered checklist for oncall):
1) Assign Incident ID and create incident folder: s3://redwood-incident-evidence/<incident-id>/ (owner: oncall).
2) Freeze ephemeral retention policies for the incident (observability) to prevent automatic log deletion.
3) Capture timeline (first 30 minutes): collect system clock-synced timeline entries from:
   - Tracing: all traces flowed through /traces/collect?incident=<id> (use 100% header capture).
   - Logs: journalctl/k8s logs for affected pods (±30 minutes).
   - Metrics snapshot: Prometheus 5m and 1m series export around incident start.
4) Preserve KV and prefix cache: run rwd-kv-dump --namespace <service> --since <incident-start-30m> --out s3://.../kv-dumps/<pod>-<ts>.tar.gz.
5) Export model-serving runtime state: rwd-runtime-dump --pod <pod> --out s3://.../model-dumps/<pod>-<ts>.json (includes model_version, quant_profile, active_kv_ms).
6) Network captures: capture tcpdump for a 10 minute window for affected nodes: tcpdump -w /tmp/incident-<id>-<node>.pcap and upload to S3.
7) Snapshot routing and config: dump the routing table and autoscaler decisions: rwd-routerctl snapshot > /tmp/router-snapshot.json.

Evidence packaging guidance:
- Maintain a manifest file at s3://redwood-incident-evidence/<incident-id>/MANIFEST.json listing file paths, checksums (sha256), collection time (ISO 8601), and owner.
- Tag all artifacts with incident-id, service, pod id, and relative timestamp.

Data retention and storage requirements (table):
| Artifact | Storage location | Minimum retention | Owner | Format |
|---------|------------------|-------------------|-------|--------|
| Traces (full) | S3 /traces/<incident-id>/ | 90 days | observability | jaeger/zipkin JSON |
| Logs (raw) | S3 /logs/<incident-id>/ | 180 days | observability | line-delimited JSON |
| KV dumps | S3 /kv-dumps/<incident-id>/ | 365 days | platform | tar.gz (rwd-kv-dump) |
| Model runtime dumps | S3 /model-dumps/<incident-id>/ | 365 days | runtime | JSON |
| PCAPs | S3 /pcap/<incident-id>/ | 90 days | platform | pcap |
| Replay inputs | S3 /replay-inputs/<incident-id>/ | 365 days | oncall | ndjson |

Reconstruction & replay procedure (owner: platform + runtime):
1) Prepare replay sandbox:
   - Provision a dedicated replay namespace with the same binaries (git tag) and identical config (feature flags, quantization profile).
   - Mock downstream services and external dependencies to avoid side effects (use rwd-mock-proxy).
2) Restore KV state: load the KV dump: rwd-kv-load --namespace <service> --file s3://.../kv-dumps/<file>.tar.gz --force-populate.
3) Seed model runtime: restore model metadata and active state using rwd-runtime-restore --file s3://.../model-dumps/<file>.json.
4) Run deterministic replay engine: rwd-replay --inputs s3://.../replay-inputs/<incident-id>/ --retries 0 --preserve-headers --seed <incident-seed> --concurrency <x> --out s3://.../replay-results/<incident-id>/.
   Example: rwd-replay --inputs s3://redwood-incident-evidence/20260305-runtime-0042/replay-inputs.ndjson --seed 20260305-0042 --concurrency 8
5) Acceptance criteria for a successful replay run (must be met before concluding causation):
   - Latency distribution replication: p50/p95/p99 delta <= 10% against production window baseline.
   - Error signature match: same error types and stack traces in >= 80% of failing traces.
   - Resource signal parity: GPU utilization and memory pressure within ±15% of production incident window.
   - Determinism signal: re-run of the same input batch yields same outputs (byte-for-byte or within tolerated stochastic variance for model outputs).
6) If criteria not met, iterate: adjust seed, increase cache population window, or broaden input sampling. Document each iteration in MANIFEST.

Common replay troubleshooting scenarios and mitigations:
- Divergent outputs due to stochastic model behavior: fix by setting deterministic RNG seeds (rwd-replay --force-seed) and using the same quantization profile.
- Missing cache-population: replay warmup traffic at low QPS for 10–30 minutes to build prefix/KV state before main replay.
- Side-effectful downstreams: if a dependency cannot be mocked, use recorded responses (rwd-mock-proxy --replay-responses s3://...).

Prometheus/observability quick hits (examples):
- Query for dramatic error budget burn: increase in error_rate over baseline:
  - promQL: sum(increase(runtime_request_errors_total{service="runtime"}[1h])) / sum(increase(runtime_requests_total{service="runtime"}[1h]))
- P99 latency spike across pods:
  - promQL: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, pod))
- Identify pods with highest 5m retry counts:
  - promQL: topk(5, sum(rate(runtime_retries_total[5m])) by (pod))

Roles & responsibilities (quick reference):
- Oncall (first 60 min): assign ID, gather initial evidence, run initial rwd-kv-dump and rwd-runtime-dump, set retention freeze.
- Observability team: provide trace & metrics exports, unlock archives, and assist with promQL extraction.
- Platform team: provision replay sandbox, restore KV and model state, run rwd-replay.
- Runtime team: interpret logs/model traces, analyze stack traces, and validate acceptance criteria.
- Post-incident lead: own RCA writeup, issue remediation tasks, and track SLO/error-budget impacts.

SLO & error budget tie-ins (operational thresholds):
- Example SLOs to monitor during analysis:
  - request success: 99.95% rolling-30d (target); alert if 30d rolling < 99.8% (severity-2).
  - p99 latency: < 250 ms for interactive endpoints; alert if p99 > 350 ms for 10m.
- Error budget policies during replay: do not use production capacity for large-scale replays if 30-day error budget < 20% remaining. Use replay sandbox and throttled inputs.

Evidence closure and retro requirements:
1) Package MANIFEST and a short "replay summary" that includes the replay seed(s), number of inputs, acceptance metrics and diff artifacts.
2) Upload artifacts to incident folder and add links to the incident ticket.
3) Postmortem: include a section "Replay findings" with deterministic evidence and recommended remediation steps.

Tooling & example commands (reference):
- rwd-kv-dump --namespace runtime --since "2026-03-05T12:34:00Z" --out s3://redwood-incident-evidence/20260305-runtime-0042/kv-dumps/pod-7.tar.gz
- rwd-runtime-dump --pod runtime-7 --out s3://redwood-incident-evidence/20260305-runtime-0042/model-dumps/runtime-7.json
- rwd-kv-load --namespace runtime --file s3://.../pod-7.tar.gz --confirm
- rwd-replay --inputs s3://.../replay-inputs.ndjson --seed 20260305-0042 --concurrency 8 --preserve-headers
- promtool query examples included above.

Acceptance & sign-off (incident lead):
- Evidence completeness verified: MANIFEST has all items + checksums.
- Replay acceptance criteria met OR explicit note about why deterministic replay could not be performed.
- Postmortem includes a prioritized remediation plan with owners and ETA.

References:
- Observability runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/sre-rotation-automation-and-capacity-signal-playbook-2026
- Capacity playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-capacity-governance-and-error-budget-handbook-2025

Attachments and templates:
- Incident MANIFEST template (JSON) and replay summary template are stored at s3://redwood-doc-templates/forensics-templates/.

Notes & best practices:
- Keep replays out of production; always use sandboxed infrastructure unless a surgical, small-scope verification is necessary and approved by SRE lead.
- Scrub PII at collection time using approved scrubbing rules.
- When in doubt, collect more artifacts: storage is cheaper than lost evidence.

Revision history:
- 2026-02-15: Initial authoring (Evelyn Chen).
- 2026-03-05: Added deterministic replay acceptance criteria and PromQL examples; reviewers: Marco Ruiz, Leah O'Neill.

title: dsid_acabec2d8bad41f6bcab555609de04c6__hybrid-gpu-testbed-topology-fuzzer.txt
text:
Hybrid GPU Testbed & Topology Fuzzer — Design and Runbook

Overview

This document describes the Hybrid GPU Testbed and Topology Fuzzer ("Hybrid-Fuzzer"), a reproducible testbed and automated fuzzing harness we use to validate GPU fleet placement, tenant isolation, network egress routing, and Terraform/IaC changes. The goal is to detect SLO regressions and regressions in request routing or preemption behavior before code/IaC lands in production.

Goals
- Provide a lightweight, repeatable testbed that models multi-region/burst and heterogeneous-GPU topologies.
- Inject topology faults (node affinity flips, preemptions, egress partitions, NIC throttles) deterministically and randomly.
- Validate capacity-allocator and ingress-routing changes (allocator, burst-orchestrator, egress-proxy) against performance and fairness SLOs.
- Run as part of CI for Terraform module changes and runtime releases.

Key components
- fuzz-runner (service): Orchestrates trials, schedules injected faults, collects metrics, and produces a verdict. Runs as a short-lived k8s job in the test cluster.
- topology-emulator: Small lib that synthesizes node topologies and advertises them to the allocator via a stubbed cloud-account API (used for IaC validation).
- preempt-injector: Operator that simulates spot preemption or instance termination events with adjustable delay/variance.
- net-partitioner: Service that applies iptables-based egress partitions and per-tenant bandwidth shaping to test egress-resilience.
- tf-iac-adapter: Local harness that runs terraform plan/apply against an ephemeral workspace and syncs resulting state into the topology-emulator.
- metrics-collector: Prometheus scrape + fluentd for logs; special exporters for kv-cache-miss-rate and token-latency-traces.

Testbed topology and artifacts
- Topologies supported: heterogeneous-pool (A100/V100 mix), fractional-multiplexing (MPS-like shared GPU), regional-pools (us-west-2, us-east-1, eu-west-1).
- Artifacts: synthetic request workload (realistic token distribution), sample model images (quantized, int8), tf plan snapshots, and node-profile descriptors.

Test matrix (example)
| Test name | Injected fault | Primary signal | Pass condition | Run time |
|-----------|----------------|----------------|----------------|----------|
| preempt-spike-10p | 10% node preemption in us-west-2 for 60s | p95 inference latency (ms) | p95 < 120 ms and kv_cache_miss_rate < 8% | 10m |
| egress-hang | blackhole egress to third-party proxy for 30s | request error rate | increase < 2% absolute vs baseline | 8m |
| mixed-precision-fallback | force quant kernel mismatch | tail token time (ms/token) | median token_time < 30ms | 6m |
| allocator-surge-fairness | create 4 tenants with conflicting priority | 99th percentile per-tenant throughput fairness | max unfairness index < 0.12 | 12m |

Running a fuzz campaign (step-by-step)
1) Prepare workspace
   - Checkout repo: git clone git@github.com:redwood-infra/hybrid-fuzzer.git
   - Create ephemeral k8s namespace: kubectl create ns hybrid-fuzzer-<run-id>
2) Provision topology snapshot (optional IaC run)
   - Run: scripts/run_tf_snapshot.sh "--workspace=ephemeral-<run-id>"
   - This runs terraform plan/apply in a sandbox and uploads the resulting node-state to topology-emulator.
3) Start metrics collector
   - kubectl -n perf port-forward svc/prometheus 9090:9090 &
   - Verify scrape: curl -s http://localhost:9090/-/ready
4) Launch fuzz-runner
   - CLI: fuzzctl start --profile=preempt-spike-10p --run-id=<run-id> --timeout=15m
   - fuzzctl will create a k8s job that: a) seeds the workload, b) applies injections (via preempt-injector/net-partitioner), c) collects metrics and logs, d) emits verdict and artifacts to s3://redwood-test-artifacts/hybrid-fuzzer/<run-id>/
5) Analyze results
   - Download artifacts and run: scripts/compare_baseline.py --run <run-id> --baseline latest-green
   - If any pass conditions fail, the run is marked failed and creates a GitHub check / JIRA ticket (per CI integration below).

CI/CD integration (patterns)
- PR-level: terraform modules and allocator changes must include a hybrid-fuzzer smoke job in GitHub Actions. The job runs a subset (3–6 min) of tests: preempt-spike-2p, egress-hang-short, allocator-surge-fairness-smoke. Failures block merges.
- Nightly: full fuzz campaign (1–2 hours) runs against the staging fleet and produces a report emailed to infra-owners and posted to #infra-fuzz-results.
- Release gating: major runtime/kernel/quant kernels require a green hybrid-fuzzer full campaign before canary promotion.

CI example (GitHub Actions snippet)
name: hybrid-fuzzer-smoke
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  fuzz-smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup kube creds
        run: ./ci/bootstrap-kube-creds.sh ${{ secrets.TEST_KUBE }}
      - name: Run fuzz smoke
        run: ./ci/run_smoke.sh --profile allocator-surge-fairness-smoke --run-id ${{ github.run_id }}

Terraform / IaC integration
- Principle: Every tf module that changes node topology, burst policy, egress, or tenant isolation must include a tf-iac adapter test. This runs terraform plan in an ephemeral workspace and produces a deterministic topology snapshot consumed by topology-emulator.
- tf-iac-adapter sample (pseudo):
  - cd tf/modules/tenant-egress
  - terraform init -backend-config=path=ephemeral.tfstate
  - terraform apply -auto-approve
  - terraform show -json > /tmp/topology-<run-id>.json
  - curl -X POST --data-binary @/tmp/topology-<run-id>.json http://topology-emulator.internal/api/v1/snapshot
- The adapter also validates expected tags and node-profiles and rejects snapshots that contain untagged compute nodes.

Observability and SLOs
- Metrics collected:
  - inference_p95_latency_ms (prometheus gauge)
  - kv_cache_miss_rate (prometheus gauge)
  - preemption_events_total (counter)
  - tenant_throughput_rps (histogram per-tenant)
- Pass/fail rules (example):
  - baseline_p95 = latest-green.inference_p95_latency_ms
  - test passes if inference_p95_latency_ms < baseline_p95 * 1.12 AND kv_cache_miss_rate < 10% absolute increase
  - fairness: fairness_index = (max_tenant_rps - min_tenant_rps) / mean_tenant_rps; require fairness_index < 0.15

Runbook: triage a failed run
1) Fetch artifacts: aws s3 cp s3://redwood-test-artifacts/hybrid-fuzzer/<run-id>/ ./artifacts --recursive
2) Open the verdict.json and check failures under metrics/failed_conditions.
3) If preemption_events_total spiked: check preempt-injector logs and node lifecycle events (kubectl get events -n hybrid-fuzzer-<run-id>).
4) If egress errors: retrieve net-partitioner logs and tcpdump on the affected pod (kubectl exec -n debug -- tcpdump -n -i any -s0 -w /tmp/capture.pcap).
5) Create an incident PR: label with infra-fuzz-failure and assign to the allocator owner and one of the reviewers listed above. Include run artifacts and a short hypothesis.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: infra/gpu-capacity (pager: @infra-gpu on Slack).
- Secondary owner: eng-sre (on-call rotation).
- Escalation path: owner -> infra-eng lead -> CTO escalation if >4 hours and customer-impacting simulation indicates breaking change.

Safety and limits
- All fuzz runs must run in ephemeral namespaces and must not touch production accounts. tf-iac-adapter must run with a read-only simulated account or isolated billing project.
- Default resource caps per run: 100 pods, 30 GPUs, 200GB ephemeral storage. Any run that requires more must get approval from infra leads.

Appendix: sample commands and snippets
- Start a manual run:
  - export RUN_ID=$(date +%s)
  - ./fuzzctl start --profile allocator-surge-fairness --run-id $RUN_ID --target-cluster staging
- Example topology-emulator POST (curl):
  - curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data-binary @topology.json https://topology-emulator.internal/api/v1/snapshot
- Terraform test wrapper (ci/run_tf_snapshot.sh):
  - #!/bin/bash
  - set -euo pipefail
  - TF_WORKSPACE=$1
  - terraform init
  - terraform workspace new $TF_WORKSPACE || terraform workspace select $TF_WORKSPACE
  - terraform apply -auto-approve
  - terraform show -json > /tmp/topology.json
  - curl -X POST --data-binary @/tmp/topology.json https://topology-emulator.internal/api/v1/snapshot

Related pages
- eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/tenant-egress-escrow-iac-safety-circuit.json
- eng-infra/runbooks/kv-cache-consensus-and-warmup-coordination-runbook.json
- eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-topology-simulation-and-cost-sensitivity-framework.json

Notes and future work
- Roadmap items: integrate with canary allocator to run in shadow mode on production traffic with strict quotas; add a lightweight hardware-in-the-loop path that cycles a small set of physical nodes for fast regression detection; add automated regression-bisect to identify commit that introduced fuzz failures.

Contributors
Marcus Chen (author)
Reviewed-by: Lina Gomez, Ethan Park, Sofia Ruiz

title: dsid_c5301621d7e04b7f870d3436148d784e__dedicated-tenant-cutover-safety-net-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Dedicated-tenant-cutover-safety-net-playbook

Summary:

This playbook describes the safety-net and validation steps for cutover of a customer to a Redwood Dedicated tenant (reserved GPU pool). It focuses on minimizing user impact, preventing cost surprises, ensuring model-quality continuity, and providing clear rollback criteria.
