  - Show error banner at top.
  - Provide retry button.
  - Provide a fallback list of recommended docs links (static) so the page is still useful.

### Partial data / delayed instrumentation
If we detect user activity but step completion is missing due to delayed events:
- Show non-blocking info text in the step detail: “This step may take a few minutes to update after you complete it.”
- Provide “Refresh” button and last updated timestamp.

---

## Copy guidance (content design)
### Tone
- Developer-first, factual, and action-oriented.
- Avoid judgmental language (“You forgot…”).
- Prefer “Recommended” over “Required” except for truly required steps (e.g., API key).

### Length constraints
- Step title: max 48 characters
- Step row description: max 90 characters
- Detail “Why this matters”: max 240 characters
- Troubleshooting bullets: max 5 bullets before linking to docs

### Terminology standards
- Use “API key” (not “token”).
- Use “project” consistently (not “workspace”) unless the Console IA uses “workspace” elsewhere.
- Use “streaming” not “SSE” unless in a technical snippet.

### Example copy (recommended)
- Blocked due to auth:
  - Title: “Check your API key setup”
  - Body: “We’re seeing authentication failures. Verify the key and environment variable in your app.”
  - CTA: “Open API keys”

- Rate limiting warning:
  - “If you hit 429s, use exponential backoff and set a budget/quota before launch.”

---

## Accessibility requirements (must-haves)
The onboarding checklist must meet Redwood Console accessibility standards (WCAG 2.1 AA target).

### Keyboard & focus
- Full checklist page is fully navigable by keyboard.
- Step list rows must be focusable and selectable via Enter/Space.
- When opening step detail (panel or full-screen), focus moves to the detail title.
- Closing the detail view returns focus to the previously selected step row.

### Screen readers
- Step list uses semantic structure (list with listitems).
- Status icon includes accessible label (e.g., “Completed”, “Not started”, “Attention needed”).
- Progress summary is announced as text (e.g., “3 of 10 steps completed”).

### Color and contrast
- Do not rely on color alone to communicate status (icon + label in detail view).
- Warning states must meet contrast requirements.

### Motion and animations
- Avoid auto-advancing animations.
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion settings; progress transitions should be instant or minimally animated.

---

## Analytics hooks (UX + funnel)
### Required UI analytics events
These are Console UX events (distinct from server-side onboarding progress events). They are used to understand engagement with the checklist UI.

Event: console_onboarding_checklist_viewed
- Trigger: checklist page loaded (success state)
- Properties: project_id, cohort, checklist_version, steps_total, steps_completed

Event: console_onboarding_checklist_step_selected
- Trigger: user selects a step row
- Properties: project_id, step_id, step_state

Event: console_onboarding_checklist_cta_clicked
- Trigger: user clicks the primary CTA from step detail
- Properties: project_id, step_id, cta_type (console|docs|quickstart|example), destination

Event: console_onboarding_checklist_refresh_clicked
- Trigger: user clicks refresh
- Properties: project_id, data_age_seconds

Event: console_onboarding_checklist_error_shown
- Trigger: progress service error state displayed
- Properties: project_id, error_category (timeout|5xx|auth|unknown)

### Attribution requirements
- Any deep link from onboarding must include query params: from=onboarding and step=<step_id>.
- Destination pages should emit a lightweight “landed_from_onboarding” UI event to validate navigation success.

### Privacy constraints
- Do not include API keys, request payloads, prompts, or user content in Console UX events.
- project_id/tenant_id are allowed (internal identifiers); ensure logs follow retention policy.

---

## Wireframes / visual references
- Linear: DES-418 “Onboarding checklist Console wireframes”
- Key screens:
  1) Project Overview card (collapsed + expanded)
  2) Full checklist page (two-column)
  3) Step detail panel (with troubleshooting)
  4) Error states (service failure)
  5) Mobile layout (single column + full-screen step detail)

Implementation must match wireframe intent; minor spacing adjustments can be made to align with Console component library.

---

## Component & design system notes
- Use standard Console components for:
  - Progress ring/indicator
  - List rows with leading icon
  - Right-side panel/drawer (desktop)
  - Banners (info/warning/error)
- Ensure empty/error banners support inline links and a single action button.

---

## Edge cases & UX decisions
1) **User completes steps outside Console**
- Checklist should update via events even if user never visits Console pages.
- UI should not require manual confirmation.

2) **Usage dashboard lag**
- The “View usage dashboard” step should never show as “blocked”.
- Include explanatory copy: “Usage may take a few minutes to appear.”

3) **Multiple projects per account**
- Checklist is scoped per project/tenant.
- Navigation must not leak progress across projects.

4) **Admin/support overrides**
- No end-user UI for overriding step state in MVP.
- If a step is overridden, end-user sees the resulting state only.
- Support UI (internal) can surface an audit note; outside this spec.

---

## QA acceptance checklist (UX)
- [ ] Checklist visible in correct cohorts under feature flag; hidden otherwise
- [ ] All step states render correctly (not started, in progress, completed, attention needed)
- [ ] Deep links include from=onboarding and step params
- [ ] Loading skeleton shows before data
- [ ] Error state: retry works; fallback links visible
- [ ] Mobile: step detail navigation works and preserves context
- [ ] Keyboard navigation + focus management passes audit
- [ ] Screen reader labels present for status and progress
- [ ] UI analytics events fire once per intended interaction

---

## Open questions (tracked in Linear)
1) Should we show “Attention needed” for streaming disconnects in MVP, or defer until SDK reconnect guidance ships across all languages?
2) Do we want a persistent “Back to onboarding” breadcrumb on destination pages, or rely on browser back + nav item?
3) What is the final naming in navigation: “Onboarding” vs “Checklist”?
4) Should we allow users to dismiss the overview card after completion?

Owners:
- Product: Marissa Cole (Console)
- Design: Kenji Nakamura
- Engineering: Dylan Brooks / Chloe Martin
- Telemetry: Logan Wright
- Support enablement: Dev Patel

title: dsid_ff73d3cd66c84794a9f482d52ba07124__observability-conformance-and-failover-certification-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Observability Conformance and Failover Certification Playbook

Overview:

This playbook defines a standardized certification process for enterprise onboarding focused on observability conformance and failover simulation. The goal is to provide a repeatable, auditable test-suite that validates a tenant's integration with Redwood's telemetry, alerting, and failover behaviors before and during go‑live.

Why this exists:
- Ensure consistent telemetry quality and signal availability for QBRs and SLO enforcement.
- Reduce post‑go‑live escalations by pre‑validating failure modes and remediation paths.
- Provide a clear sign‑off for both Customer Success and the customer’s engineering team.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: Customer Success engineers (CSEs), Onboarding architects, Customer reliability engineers, SRE on-call.
- Applies to: Dedicated and Private tenants (VPC/on‑prem), customers with reserved capacity, and any Hosted customers requesting enterprise SLA/observability contracts.
- Not in scope: low‑volume self‑serve signups unless otherwise requested.

Certification objectives (pass criteria):
1) Observability conformance: required metrics, traces, and logs are present, correctly tagged, and within fidelity bounds.
2) Alert and paging behavior: alerts fire at configured thresholds and route to intended escalation targets.
3) Failover simulation: tenant can gracefully fallback to configured model‑variant and/or region policy without data loss or broken requests within SLOs.
4) Performance parity: tail latency and 95p token throughput are within 10% of the accepted baseline for the tenant profile.

Prerequisites (customer and Redwood):
- Customer provides: representative API keys, ingress IP ranges, and a traffic seed (synthetic workload or production snapshot).
- Contracted observability level agreed (metrics retention window, trace sampling rate).
- Access: cross-account metrics forwarding set up (if Dedicated/Private), service account for telemetry validation, and customer contact list for paging.
- Baseline established: a 24h baseline run capturing normal traffic characteristics and sequence length distribution.

Conformance test suite (run by CSE):
- Metrics coverage checklist (automated assertions):
  - Per-tenant request count (counter)
  - Per-model token count (counter)
  - Per-route 95th and 99th percent latency (histogram)
  - Inference errors by class (5xx, 4xx, model-timeout)
  - KV cache hit ratio (gauge)
  - Batching statistics (avg batch size, dropout count)
  - Memory/GC and GPU memory pressure (hosted or dedicated telemetry exporters)
- Tracing:
  - Root span includes route, model.id, request.id, tenant.id, and sequence_len tags.
  - KV cache warmup and cache-miss traces for long‑running sessions.
  - Downstream service spans (e.g., affinity proxy, telemetry bridge) present and correlated.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, severity, tenant_id, request_id, model_variant, error_code.

Telemetry assertion examples (fail/pass matrix):
- Metric emission: per-tenant request counter emits once per request -> pass if >=99.9% of sampled requests have metrics.
- Tag fidelity: model_variant tag present -> pass if present in >=99% of traces.
- Sampling: trace sampling at configured rate within ±2% of target.

Failover simulation scenarios (minimum required):
1) Model variant degradation: simulate a regression in primary model (increased generation time or error rate). Expected behavior: automatic traffic shift to fallback variant within configured rollout window; client-facing failures <=0.1% during switch.
2) Regional outage: simulate region R failover to R2. Expected behavior: DNS/Anycast routing handoff, warming of KV cache for hot prefixes, and latency impact within contractual SLOs (95p latency < 2x baseline or configured threshold).
3) GPU node eviction (Dedicated): simulate node preemption and validate autoscaler rehydration, batch redistribution, and request retry behavior.
4) Telemetry bridge loss: simulate loss of telemetry export for 5 minutes and validate local buffering, partial metrics backfill correctness, and alert suppression mechanisms.

Detailed runbook (step-by-step):
1) Preparation (T-72 to T-1 days):
  - T-72: Confirm prerequisites, sign OSS (if applicable), and create certification ticket in JIRA (label: obs-cert).
  - T-48: Customer provides traffic seed and auth tokens for test harness.
  - T-24: Baseline run completed and validated; acceptance thresholds documented.
  - T-1: Final smoke test and contact list validated.
2) Execution day (D):
  - 09:00: Kickoff call with stakeholders.
  - 09:30–11:00: Run observability conformance scripts (see commands below).
  - 11:00–12:30: Run failover scenario 1 (model variant). Monitor telemetry and collect traces.
  - 13:30–15:30: Run region failover simulation with staged traffic migration.
  - 15:30–16:30: Run node eviction and telemetry bridge tests.
  - 16:30–17:30: Analyze results, compile pass/fail, and agree next steps.
3) Post-exec (D+1 to D+7):
  - D+1: Deliver certification report and recommended remediations.
  - D+3–D+7: Re-run specific tests on fixes and mark items closed in certification ticket.

Automation commands and snippets (examples):
- Run metric smoke test (CLI):
```
redwoodctl observability assert --tenant $TENANT_ID --duration 15m --checks metrics,logs,traces --out results.yaml
```
- Inject model latency fault (test harness uses canary traffic):
```
redwoodctl inject fault --target model:$MODEL_ID --type delay --p50 200ms --p95 1200ms --duration 10m
```
- Simulate region drain (staged):
```
redwoodctl region failover --from us-east-1 --to us-west-2 --staged 50,75,100 --monitoring-window 5m
```

Pass/fail reporting and artifact collection:
- Artifacts required for sign-off: results.yaml (assertions), raw trace archive (.zip), sample logs (masked PII), screenshots of dashboards showing baseline vs test windows, and a short executive summary (1 page).
- Pass requires: all high-priority conformance checks passed AND no more than 2 medium severity failover gaps (with tied remediation plan).

Remediation and escalation matrix:
- Severity classification:
  - P0: cert-blocker (missing tenant id tags, missing request counter, or failover causes >1% client errors) -> Engineering oncall + CSE triage within 1 hour.
  - P1: degraded observability signals (missing noncritical tags, sampling misalignment) -> Owner team fix within 72 hours.
  - P2: cosmetic issues (logging format differences) -> backlog item for future patch.
- Escalation flow: CSE -> Platform Oncall -> Runtime Engineering -> Head of SRE. Use the internal pager channel #obs-cert-paging for P0.

Sign-off and handover:
- Sign-off stakeholders: Customer Success Manager, Customer Reliability Lead, Onboarding Architect, and SRE certifier.
- Sign-off artifact: single JSON certificate stored in the ticket with fields: tenant_id, cert_date, results_uri, signer_emails, scope (observability/failover), and expiry (90 days).

Operational notes and cautions:
- For Private deployments with air-gapped telemetry, ensure local artifact encryption and transfer controls are in place.
- Avoid running production traffic seeding during business critical windows; prefer weekend or agreed maintenance windows.
- When simulating paid capacity changes (autoscaler stress), ensure commercial approval for potential billing spikes.

Ownership and contacts:
- Playbook owner: Morgan Reyes (Customer Success – Observability Lead).
- Primary engineering contact: Kai Huang (Runtime Engineering).
- SRE escalation: Oncall rotation (see /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/oncall-rotation).

Templates and checklists (appendix):
- Preflight checklist (checkbox list):
  - [ ] Traffic seed uploaded and validated
  - [ ] Cross-account metrics forwarding configured
  - [ ] Pager rotations updated
  - [ ] Baseline run completed
  - [ ] JIRA ticket created and stakeholders invited
- Certification report template (fields to populate):
  - Tenant ID, Customer contact, Certification date, Tests run, Pass/fail summary, Remediation items, Signers.

QBR integration and recurring validation:
- If certified, tenant will be enrolled in a quarterly telemetry health check. The certification expiry triggers a reminder 30 days before expiry to schedule a re-certification window. Failures found during QBR health checks feed back into the remediation board and may require out-of-band recertification.

Related resources and references:
- Observability contract template (product-docs/pricing-and-packaging)
- Telemetry exporters and agent configuration examples (integration-guides/telemetry-onboarding)
- Oncall runbooks and escalation playbooks (oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process)

Revision history:
- 2026-02-14: Draft authored by Morgan Reyes.
- 2026-04-02: Added telemetry bridge simulation details. Reviewer: Kai Huang.
- 2026-06-01: Updated pass criteria and automation commands; added private deployment note. Reviewer: Leah Thompson.

End of document.

title: dsid_7754cd5d7b4d4a7ea217f1c09c28ef3c__contributor-toolflow-and-privileges-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Contributor Toolflow and Privileges Playbook

Overview

Purpose: This playbook documents the standard tool access lifecycle for contributors at Redwood — from first-day provisioning through promotions, cross-team rotations, and final deprovisioning. The emphasis is on fast enablement, least-privilege by default, auditable changes, and clear manager/engineer responsibilities.

Audience: people-ops, hiring managers, engineering managers, IT, security reviewers, and new contributors.

Summary of goals:
- Ensure 95% of new hires have usable accounts and core tool access within 8 business hours of start.
- Enforce least-privilege role assignments for 90% of contributors by role templates.
- Complete deprovisioning within 24 hours for offboarded contributors (per security SLA).

Key principles
- Least privilege: grant only the roles required for the contributor’s current responsibilities.
- Role templates: use standardized permission packages (see Role → Tool mapping).
- Manager-driven exceptions: any deviation requires manager justification and a 90-day review.
- Auditability: every access change must be recorded in Okta and the access-request ticket.

Role → Tool mapping (canonical templates)
| Role | GitHub | GCP (project) | Datadog | Jira | Slack | Console/Secrets | Notes |
|------|--------|----------------|---------|------|-------|----------------|-------|
| IC-Engineer-Level-1 | repo:read | viewer | dash:read | dev-project | full | vault:read | Standard new-hire dev access (no prod) |
| IC-Engineer-Level-2 | repo:write | dev-editor | dash:read | dev-squad | full | vault:read | Can merge to non-protected branches; needs sprint leads approval for protected branches |
| IC-Engineer-Level-3 | repo:admin* | staging-editor | dash:write | squad-admin | full | vault:deploy | Elevated staging access; production access by exception and 90-day review |
| Platform-Engineer | repo:admin | multi-project | dash:write | infra | full | vault:admin | Broad access required for ops teams; requires security onboarding checklist |

*repo:admin for Level-3 is scoped to staging and infra-adjacent repos only.

Provisioning process (first-day onboarding)
1) Hiring manager creates a People Ops onboarding request in Workday/HRIS and links the candidate start date.
2) Manager files an Access Request ticket in Jira using template: "Access Request: New Hire - <NAME> - <TEAM> - <ROLE TEMPLATE>". Include start date and required projects.
3) people-ops triages: validates manager, picks correct role template, and initiates Okta provisioning flows.
4) Core accounts to create: Okta account, GitHub account (SAML link), Slack, GCP IAM invite, Datadog, Confluence.
5) Owner (people-ops) confirms repo and project invites; manager completes the New Hire Checklist and schedules Security Onboarding session.

Expected times:
- Okta and Slack: within 2 hours of ticket acknowledgement.
- GitHub & GCP invites: within 4 hours.
- All core tooling active and verified: target within 8 business hours.

Manager checklist for first 3 days
- Verify that the contributor can clone the repo and run the local dev script (tools/dev-setup.sh).
- Confirm access to Jira board and Datadog dashboards used by the team.
- Run through the security checklist: 2FA enforced, passwordless keys setup, vault read only.
- Submit permission escalation requests for protected branches if needed (see Escalation flow).

Permission escalation flow (protected or prod access)
1) Engineer or manager opens a "Privilege Escalation" Jira ticket with justification, duration, and list of specific resources.
2) Security reviews and responds within 2 business days. If approved, a scoped temporary role is created (max 90 days).
3) Audit log entry created; approver is added as owner.
4) 7 days before expiry, system sends reminders to the owner and manager to extend or revert access.

Cross-team rotations and role transitions
- When a contributor changes teams, the new manager must:
  - Open a change request ticket to add new role template and remove prior team templates.
  - Schedule a knowledge transfer and update on-call and pager duty rosters if applicable.
  - Verify completed de-escalation of previous team secrets and remove access to prior projects.
- people-ops will run an automated script (rotation-reconcile) that compares current Okta groups to team rosters and flags mismatches weekly.

Promotion-specific tool changes
- Promotion to IC-3 or above triggers a permissions review: expected changes include elevated staging permissions and write access to internal infra repos.
- Manager must document the promotion in the "Promotion Access" ticket and indicate any necessary temporary exceptions.

Deprovisioning (offboarding)
1) Offboard event triggers: manager submits Offboard ticket in Jira or HRIS marks termination/leave.
2) Immediate actions (within 2 hours): suspend Okta session, remove Slack privileges, revoke long-lived GitHub tokens.
3) Secondary actions (within 24 hours): remove GCP and Datadog access, rotate any secrets where the contributor was a maintainer.
4) Final reconciliation (within 72 hours): people-ops confirms all access removed and produces an audit report attached to the Offboard ticket.

Escalation playbook for stuck provisioning
- If new hire lacks access after 8 business hours: manager escalates to people-ops-ops channel and pings the people-ops oncall.
- If an access change is refused by security for unclear reasons: open a security-appeal with evidence and invite the security reviewer to a 30-minute working session.

Audit and quarterly clean-up
- Quarterly automated audit runs across Okta, GitHub org, GCP IAM, and Datadog.
- Flags generated: stale groups (>90 days), inactive users with elevated roles, long-lived tokens.
- people-ops and security jointly triage and close flags within 30 days.

Tooling snippets and examples
- Access request JSON example (paste into Jira ticket):
  {"candidate": "First Last", "team": "Platform", "role_template": "IC-Engineer-Level-2", "projects": ["project-dev-a", "project-infra-test"], "start_date": "2026-11-01", "justification": "Standard onboarding for backend engineer"}

- CLI to verify GitHub team membership (example):
  gh api repos/org/repo/teams --jq '.[] | select(.name=="platform") | .members_count'

Ownership and SLAs
- people-ops: primary owner for provisioning and deprovisioning SLAs.
- Security: owner for privilege escalations and audits.
- Team manager: owner for role correctness and business justifications.
- SLA targets: provisioning complete within 8 business hours (95%), deprovisioning within 24 hours (100% for suspension).

Templates & attachments
- New Hire Access Request (Jira template): create issue type ONBOARD-ACCESS with fields: name, start_date, role_template, projects, repo_list, manager_approver.
- Offboard checklist (attached to offboard ticket): suspend Okta session, revoke tokens, rotate secrets, remove from oncall, archive workspace.

Common FAQs
- Q: What if the new hire needs production access on day 1?
  A: Production access requires an explicit Privilege Escalation ticket plus security approval. Expect 48–72 hour lead time.
- Q: Who can request temporary elevated roles?
  A: Only the hire’s manager or a Director-level approver; all requests create audit trail entries.

Change history
- 2026-03-15 — initial draft (Asha Patel).
- 2026-07-07 — added rotation-reconcile automation notes (reviewers: Evan Liu).
- 2026-10-02 — tightened escalation SLA and clarified deprovisioning target windows (Priya Kapoor).

Related resources
- Security onboarding checklist: /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security/security-onboarding-checklist-2025
- Onboarding toolchain mapping: /confluence/company-handbook/05_internal-tools/onboarding-toolchain-access-and-career-checkpoints-2025.json

Contact
- people-ops oncall: #people-ops-urgent (Slack).
- Security escalation: security-escalations@redwood.ai

End of playbook

title: dsid_3addd624e0894a01a6cfb0147a6d571d__rapid-sla-triage-runbook-and-external-briefing-templates-2026.txt
text:
Rapid SLA Triage Runbook and External Briefing Templates

Summary:
This document defines a compact, operator-focused runbook for rapid triage of SLA-impacting events (availability, latency, throughput regressions) and provides tested external briefing templates for customers and execs. It is optimized for the first 30/60/180 minutes of an incident where the primary goal is to stabilize SLAs and communicate clearly.

Scope and intent:
- Scope: multi-region inference control plane and serving stack (hosted API + Dedicated routing).
- Non-scope: billing pipeline, long-term capacity planning (see related pages).
- Intent: provide a predictable, low-cognitive triage path that on-call responders, bridge operators, and customer success can adopt with minimal prep.

Key definitions:
- SLA-impacting: any event causing a measurable drop below an SLO threshold for availability or 95th/99th latency for a paid customer tier.
- Triage Owner: primary on-call for the service indicated by PagerDuty alert tag (e.g., inference-runtime-prod).
- Bridge Lead: SRE on the active bridge who owns external comms until handed to Customer Success.

SLO thresholds (quick reference):
| Metric                     | Target        | Alert threshold (auto-trigger) | PagerDuty severity |
|---------------------------|---------------|-------------------------------|--------------------|
| API availability (global) | 99.95% monthly| < 99.9% (15m window)          | Sev 1              |
| 95th latency (text gen)   | < 300ms       | > 350ms (5m window)           | Sev 2              |
| 99th latency (embeds)     | < 1200ms      | > 1600ms (10m window)         | Sev 1              |
| Error rate (5m)           | < 0.1%        | > 0.5%                        | Sev 1              |

Ownership matrix (quick):
- Triage Owner: fix-forward actions, log collection, scope.
- Bridge Lead: status cadence, external messages.
- Model/Serving Owner: kernel/quantization teams for model regressions.
- CS Liaison: customer notices and ticket updates.

Rapid SLA Triage: 0–30 minutes (stabilize & estimate)
1) Acknowledge and create the bridge (Triage Owner / Bridge Lead):
   - Create an incident bridge: #oncall-bridge-<service>-<ts>. Invite CS and PM if > 30 customers impacted.
   - Confirm severity via the SLO dashboard and metric snapshot.
2) Immediate controls (first 5–10 minutes):
   - Apply emergency mitigation(s) prioritized by lowest-customer-impact first:
     a) Route traffic to healthy region: runbook command: curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/routing/shift -d '{"region":"us-west-2","service":"inference"}'
     b) Temporarily increase fallback model capacity: ops-cli models set-capacity --model redwood-v1-small --pool dedicated --scale 2
     c) Toggle caching layer to read-only mode to reduce write pressure: redis-cli -h cache-main CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
3) Rapid evidence capture (parallel):
   - Export traces for 15 minutes around alert: 
     - tracing-cli export --service inference-runtime --since "-15m" --out /tmp/trace-<incident>.zip
   - Grab top error logs: kubectl -n inference logs -l app=inference-runtime --tail=500 > /tmp/errors-<incident>.log
   - Snapshot autoscaler and pool metrics: ops-monitor snapshot --pools inference* --out /tmp/pools-<incident>.json
4) Estimate impact & ETA (10–20 minutes):
   - Use dashboard: open /dashboards/slo-latency?window=15m and capture 1m/5m/15m deltas.
   - Bridge Lead gives initial ETA: stabilize estimate (e.g., 30m) and next update cadence (10m).

Triage: 30–60 minutes (diagnose & mitigate)
5) Narrow root cause hypotheses (30–45 minutes):
   - Common buckets: noisy neighbor (GPU saturation), kernel regression (recent runtime release), networking (regional AZ issues), model size/kv-cache eviction.
   - Quick checks: GPU utilization (nvidia-smi via fleet-agent), kernel-level error traces, and latest deploy tags: git rev-parse --short HEAD on runtime node.
6) Apply scoped mitigations (45–60 minutes):
   - If deployment suspect: rollback runtime: ops-deploy rollback inference-runtime --to-tag v2025.04.12 || kubectl rollout undo deployment/inference-runtime -n inference
   - If noisy neighbor: isolate offending instance pool and evict pods: kubectl cordon <node>; drain --ignore-daemonsets
   - If model quality regression: route traffic to previous model variant and throttle new variant: ops-cli models route --from new-variant --to old-variant --weight 0.9
7) Confirm SLO recovery and document evidence (60 minutes):
   - Once SLOs back above alert thresholds for 15m window, declare partial mitigation. Capture recovery artifact IDs and evidence bundles.

Escalation ladder and when to involve execs (decision rules):
- Escalate to on-call manager & PM if: 2 hours elapsed with no sustained SLO recovery or > 5% of paid customers impacted.
- Engage Legal/Comms if incident is customer data exposure or regulatory risk.
- For cross-region outages, engage Cloud Ops and network providers immediately.

Customer and executive briefing templates (copyable)
- Initial acknowledgement (within 10 minutes):
  Subject: [Redwood] Incident affecting inference API — we’re investigating
  Body: Hello — we are aware of an issue affecting inference API performance for some customers. Our engineers have opened an incident and are investigating root cause. We're prioritizing SLA stability and will provide an update by <ETA in minutes>. Bridge ID: #oncall-bridge-inference-<ts>.

- Status update (10/30/60 minute cadence):
  Subject: [Redwood] Update — inference API incident — progress update
  Body: Current status: Mitigations in progress (routing changes / temporary capacity increases). Impact: X% of requests affected; primary symptom: increased 95th/99th latency. Next update: in 20 minutes. For urgent support, reply to this message or open a support ticket: <link>.

- Resolution notice (post-stabilization):
  Subject: [Redwood] Resolved — inference API incident — summary and next steps
  Body: The incident affecting inference API performance has been resolved as of <timestamp>. Root cause: <brief cause>. Actions taken: list of mitigations/rollbacks and timeline. Customer impact: estimated duration and affected customers. If you saw persistent issues, please contact your CS rep. We will publish a post-incident summary within 72 hours.

- Executive brief (if escalated):
  - One-line: Major SLA-impacting incident affecting inference API, partial customer impact, mitigation in place.
  - Metrics snapshot: availability pre/post, peak error rate, affected regions.
  - Next steps: timeline for RCA, compensatory credit assessment, and product/infra remediation plan.

Game day and simulation checklist (pre-run):
- Objectives: validate bridge process, verify external templates, practice three mitigations (route shift, runtime rollback, pool isolation).
- Participants: SRE, runtime team, CS, PM, legal (optional).
- Pre-reqs: synthetic load harness, shadow customer, snapshot restore point.
- Day-of script: 1) Inject latency to us-west-2 pool. 2) Trigger pager and follow the 0–60 minute runbook. 3) Time each step, capture gaps.

On-call rotation guidance (practical rules):
- Primary on-call should be reachable for 15 minutes for SEV1 pages and start bridge within 10 minutes.
- Handoff template (two lines): current active mitigations; next steps; outstanding manual actions.
- Shadow to primary progression: shadow for 3 rotations, then co-take for 2, then primary.

Post-incident writeup / evidence checklist (what to attach to the postmortem):
- Incident timeline with wall-clock stamps.
- Evidence bundle IDs (traces, logs, snapshots).
- Root cause hypothesis and confirmation steps.
- Customer impact list and support ticket IDs.
- Action items (owner + due date) and severity remediations (quick/medium/long term).

Technical play snippets and commands (copy/paste):
- Check SLOs: curl -s "https://ops-monitor.internal/api/v1/slo?service=inference&window=5m" | jq .
- Route traffic to a region (API): curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/routing/shift -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPS_TOKEN" -d '{"service":"inference","target_region":"eu-west-1","drain_seconds":30}'
- Runtime rollback (k8s): kubectl -n inference rollout undo deployment/inference-runtime --to-revision=3
- Snapshot traces: tracing-cli export --service inference-runtime --since "-30m" --out s3://incidents/trace-<id>.zip

Runbook maintenance and ownership rules:
- Every play must have a single owner listed in the runbook header (owner_name@example.com). Owners must review the play annually and after any SEV1 incident.
- After each game day run, update the playbook with any temporary hacks that became standard operating practice or remove them if unsafe.

Decision log (quick ADR entries for this playbook):
- 2024-11-05: Adopted 10/30/60 minute cadence as default for SLA incidents.
- 2025-03-18: Added customer-facing templates and mandatory CS liaison for incidents > 30m.

Related artifacts and page links:
- SLO library (link): /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets
- Incident evidence standard: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-evidence-collection-standard-2025.json

Appendix: Example customer acknowledgement (multi-tenant sample)
---
Hello <CustomerName>,

We detected elevated latency for inference requests affecting some tenants between <start> and <end>. Our engineers mitigated the issue by shifting traffic and performing a controlled rollback. We estimate <percent> of your requests were affected for <duration>. A detailed post-incident report will follow.

Regards,
The Redwood Inference Reliability Team
---

Notes and housekeeping:
- Keep this runbook concise — long investigations belong in the postmortem.
- If you're unsure which mitigations to use, prioritize actions that reduce customer-visible impact over full root-cause proof.

Maintenance log: last reviewed by Maya Chen on 2025-06-12.

title: dsid_aca3c58497ec4182b8df9c0d6f2e9f89__ensemble-eval-orchestration-and-weighting-guidelines-2026.txt
text:
Ensemble evaluation orchestration and weighting guidelines

Overview
=======

Purpose
-------
This document specifies a standard for orchestrating ensemble-style evaluations in Redwood's eval harness. It covers how to configure multi-metric evaluation jobs, how to compute a single acceptance score from heterogeneous metrics, recommended weighting strategies, and the operational rules used for model acceptance, canary rollouts, and automated rollback triggers. The goal is consistent, explainable production decisions across different product use-cases (chat, summarization, reranking, embeddings).

Background and motivation
-------------------------
Teams frequently need to combine multiple eval signals (e.g., BLEU/ROUGE-like n-gram overlap, semantic similarity, safety pass rate, latency percentiles) into a single decision for model promotion or rollback. Without a standard approach:
- teams create ad-hoc weights that are hard to justify
- comparisons across workloads are inconsistent
- drift or slice regressions are missed when only aggregate metrics are considered

Scope
-----
This guide applies to:
- All evaluation jobs run through eval-harness-runner and eval-orch services.
- Post-training checks that feed Redwood Optimize and model-onboarding pipelines.
- Production acceptance gates tied to rollout automation in the deployment orchestration layer.

Terminology
-----------
- eval job: a single run that produces a set of metrics for a model version on a prompt set.
- slice: an orthogonal data subset (e.g., low-resource queries, long-contexts, legal-phrasing).
- metric vector: the set of scalar metrics produced by one eval job.
- ensemble score: a normalized, weighted aggregation of metrics used for acceptance decisions.

High-level orchestration
-----------------------
1) Eval job submission: developers submit an eval job YAML to eval-orch. Jobs declare model id, dataset id, slices, metrics, and desired aggregations.
2) Parallel runners: eval-harness-runner scales horizontally to execute slices in parallel. Per-slice results are written to metric-store with a unique job id.
3) Post-processing: a standardized post-processing step normalizes raw metrics, computes slice-level z-scores or bounded transforms, and produces the ensemble score.
4) Decision hooks: the ensemble score is compared against the configured acceptance matrix (thresholds and weights). If the score passes, the model progresses to canary rollout; otherwise it triggers triage.

Orchestration diagram (text)
---------------------------
- user -> eval-orch -> queue (kafka) -> runner pool -> metric-store (timeseries + artifacts) -> postproc -> decision-service -> deployment-orch

Weighting and aggregation strategies
----------------------------------
We provide three canonical strategies. Choose the simplest that satisfies your product requirements; prefer reproducibility over complexity.

1) Equal-weight normalized aggregation (default)
- Use when metrics are commensurate after normalization (e.g., all are percentages or bounded scores).
- Steps: compute per-metric min/max clipped to historical percentiles (5th/95th), rescale to [0,1], average.
- Pros: simple, transparent.
- Cons: can under- or over-emphasize rare but critical metrics.

2) Priority-weighted aggregation
- Use when one metric is safety-critical (e.g., toxicity, hallucination rate).
- Steps: assign integer priority weights (example: safety=5, accuracy=3, latency=1), normalize weights to sum to 1, compute weighted sum of normalized metrics.
- Documentation: every priority weight must have an author and justification recorded in the eval job metadata.

3) Dynamic frequency-weighted aggregation (recommended for customer-facing embeddings/reranking)
- Use when production slice frequencies differ significantly from training/test distributions.
- Steps: estimate slice frequencies from production telemetry (last 30 days), compute per-slice weight proportional to frequency, and combine slice-level metric aggregates into a global metric before normalization.
- Important: frequency estimates are clipped to [0.01, 0.5] per slice to avoid domination by a single slice.

Normalization and transforms
---------------------------
We standardize on the following transforms before aggregation:
- bounded metrics in [0,1] (no transform)
- unbounded error metrics (e.g., MSE): apply inverse transform 1/(1+log(1+value)) then rescale to [0,1]
- latency percentiles: map P50/P95 to score = 1 - min(latency / latency_slo, 1) (SLOs stored in product-config)
- safety/failure rates: use 1 - rate so higher is better
- For metrics with heavy tails, use winsorization at 99th percentile prior to normalization

Scoring formula (canonical)
--------------------------
Given normalized metrics m_i in [0,1] and weights w_i that sum to 1:
ensemble_score = sum_i w_i * m_i

When combining slices, compute slice_score_j first (per-slice aggregation across metrics), then global_score = sum_j slice_weight_j * slice_score_j where slice_weight_j is chosen per weighting strategy.

Config examples
--------------
Example eval job YAML (submit to eval-orch):

---
job_name: "chat-v2-ensemble-eval"
model_id: "m-redwood-chat-v2-2026-03"
dataset_id: "chat-production-sim-2026-01"
metrics: ["semantic-similarity", "toxicity_rate", "response_length_variance", "p95_latency_ms"]
slices: ["all", "long_context_>2048", "low_english_proficiency"]
weighting_strategy: "dynamic-frequency"
weights: {} # optional for dynamic; required for priority-weighted
postproc:
  normalization: "percentile-clip-5-95"
  latency_slo_ms: 150
notify_on_fail: ["ml-evals@redwoodeval.internal"]
---

Example postproc snippet (pseudo-YAML) for priority-weighted:

weights:
  semantic-similarity: 0.4
  toxicity_rate: 0.4
  p95_latency_ms: 0.2
normalization: "1/(1+log(1+value))"

Acceptance matrix and thresholds
--------------------------------
Acceptance matrices must be checked into model-onboarding metadata and include:
- minimum safety pass rate by slice (e.g., safety >= 0.995 on all slices),
- global ensemble_score threshold (default 0.82),
- latency SLO tolerances (P95 <= configured SLO),
- allowed per-metric regressions from baseline (e.g., no more than 2% drop in semantic-similarity).

Default baseline policy (applies if team does not provide custom matrix):
- safety pass rate >= 0.998 on all slices
- ensemble_score >= 0.80
- no metric regressions > 3% compared to production baseline
- canary rollout limited to 5% traffic for 48 hours with monitoring hooks

Canary and rollback rules
------------------------
Canary rollout: on pass, deployment-orch will deploy model to canary cluster at 5% traffic. During canary the following automated checks run every 15 minutes:
- Production sampler run: compare online metrics with eval predictions for a random sample of requests (1 per 1000 requests or at least 1000 samples/day).
- Alert conditions: ensemble_score drop > 0.05 vs baseline OR safety failure spike > 0.01 absolute OR P95 latency increase > 25% -> trigger rollback.

Automated rollback sequence (executed by deployment-orch):
1) Pause canary traffic.
2) Demote model from canary and switch traffic to previous stable model.
3) Create incident and assign to on-call owner of model-service (see runbooks).
4) Persist failing eval artifacts and logs under job id for triage.

Regression triage flow
---------------------
1) Triage owner reviews per-slice deltas and pulls failing examples (eval-harness provides direct links).
2) If failure is dataset-related (label drift), tag dataset and schedule augmentation.
3) If failure is model-related (systematic hallucination/safety), open ModelRegression ticket with: baseline artifacts, counterexamples, per-slice metrics, and suggested mitigation (prompt tuning, quantization rollback, smaller context window).
4) For performance regressions, check runtime config (quantization profile, batching settings) and revert to last-known-good profile if needed.

Operational considerations and do's/don'ts
----------------------------------------
Do:
- Record weight justifications in job metadata.
- Use production frequency data for dynamic weighting when available.
- Always include safety metrics as separate slices (do not absorb safety into a single aggregate without explicit weight).
- Keep acceptance matrices in model-onboarding for auditability.
Don't:
- Hard-code weights in deployment scripts without provenance.
- Use raw latency numbers directly without mapping to SLO-based scores.
- Rely solely on aggregate scores; always require per-slice checks for safety and critical business slices.

Metrics and observability
------------------------
- metric-store: stores per-job, per-slice metrics with job_id and model_id tags.
- dashboards: ensemble-over-time, per-slice-breakdown, canary-sampler-comparison.
- alerts: configured in deployment-orch and routed to ml-evals and eng-sre channels.

Ownership and SLAs
------------------
- Eval orchestration (eval-orch, runner): team = applied-ml (owner: Priya Menon).
- Post-processing & scoring library: team = applied-ml, SLAs for processing of a single job <= 30 minutes for medium datasets (<=100k examples).
- Decision-service and deployment hooks: team = eng-platform.

Required artifacts for onboarding a new model using ensemble evals
----------------------------------------------------------------
- eval job YAML and historical weight justifications (checked into model PR)
- acceptance matrix (JSON) checked into model-onboarding metadata store
- baseline production metrics snapshot (timestamped)
- list of critical slices and slice definitions

Appendix: example of normalized score calculations
------------------------------------------------
Given metrics: semantic_sim=0.78 (higher better), toxicity_rate=0.002 (lower better), p95_latency_ms=120 (SLO=150)
Transform toxicity: 1 - toxicity_rate = 0.998
Transform latency: 1 - min(120/150, 1) = 0.2
Assume weights [0.5, 0.3, 0.2] -> ensemble_score = 0.5*0.78 + 0.3*0.998 + 0.2*0.2 = 0.39 + 0.2994 + 0.04 = 0.7294

Links and references
--------------------
- eval-harness-runner README: internal link (eval-harness-runner)
- model-onboarding checklist: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/production-model-certification-checklist-2026
- regression triage playbook: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/model-regression-forensics-playbook-2026

Contact and escalation
----------------------
For questions about weighting strategy or to request new slice definitions, open an issue in the Applied-ML backlog and assign to the evals owner (Priya Menon). For production incidents related to canary rollouts, follow eng-sre oncall escalation documented in: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/oncall-escalation.

Change log
----------
- 2026-02-15: initial published draft by Priya Menon.
- 2026-03-01: clarified dynamic weighting clipping rules; added default baseline policy.

title: dsid_af2d62f228a54a36965d7506c657beb6__route-experiments-integration-notes.txt
text:
Route Experiments (A/B testing) – SDK integration notes (stickiness keys, headers, docs plan)

## Purpose
These notes describe how Redwood SDKs and examples should integrate with **Route Experiments** (route-level A/B/n testing in Console Rollouts), with specific focus on:
- How customers provide **deterministic stickiness keys** (so a user consistently receives the same variant)
- How SDKs should expose and document **experiment/variant response headers**
- A documentation + examples plan for beta → GA

This page is DX-facing (SDKs, docs, examples). It is not the source of truth for routing semantics; see ADR-047 / ADR-048.

---

## Customer-facing mental model (what we want users to understand)
1. An experiment is attached to a **route** (endpoint / routing policy).
2. Each request is assigned to a **variant** based on a stable **stickiness key**.
3. Redwood returns optional **debug headers** so customers can tell which variant they hit.
4. Console shows per-variant metrics (latency/cost/error/quality) using experiment attribution emitted by the platform.

In docs and SDKs, we should present experiments as “**routing-layer experiments**” (not application-layer experiments). Customers do not need to run their own bucketing logic.

---

## Stickiness keys (SDK guidance)
### Why stickiness keys matter
Deterministic assignment requires a key with adequate entropy and stability. If customers omit a stable key, they can observe:
- Variant skew (one variant accidentally getting most traffic)
- Assignment churn (same end-user bouncing between variants)
- Harder-to-interpret metrics and regressions

### Recommended key choices (in priority order)
SDK docs should recommend one of the following, in this order:
1. **A customer-defined stable end-user identifier** (e.g., internal user UUID)
2. **Account/tenant identifier** (B2B SaaS) if experiments are intended to be “per-tenant”
3. **Session identifier** (only if the experiment is short-lived and per-session consistency is acceptable)

Avoid:
- Random UUID generated per request
- Raw IP address as the only identifier (low quality, NAT/shared IP issues, privacy concerns)
- Email address in plaintext (PII). If email is the only available stable identifier, recommend hashing on the client side before sending.

### SDK parameter and header names
We should support a first-class, consistently named option in SDKs.

**Canonical name (docs):** `experiment_sticky_key`

Transport:
- If the API supports explicit fields on the request body, pass it as a request field.
- Otherwise (or additionally), pass as a header.

**Request header:** `x-redwood-experiment-sticky-key`

Notes:
- The stickiness key is used only for experiment bucketing. It is not a security boundary.
- SDKs should treat the stickiness key as **potentially sensitive**, and should not log it at INFO by default.

### Precedence rules (what SDKs should document)
Platform-side precedence (high level, aligned with ADR-047):
1. `x-redwood-experiment-sticky-key` (explicit)
2. Authenticated `customer_id` / `tenant_id` if available
3. End-user identifier passed via customer application (if explicitly mapped by the customer)
4. Fallback: request-derived identifiers (discouraged; may be disabled or changed)

Docs should emphasize: **If you care about determinism, set the explicit sticky key.**

---

## Response headers (how customers interpret variant assignment)
### Required-to-document headers
When a request is eligible for a route experiment, the gateway/router may attach:
- `x-redwood-experiment-id`: Stable experiment identifier
- `x-redwood-variant-id`: Assigned variant identifier (e.g., `control`, `v1-quantized`, `new-model`)

Recommended additional headers (where available):
- `x-redwood-experiment-config-version`: Helps support debug config propagation issues
- `x-redwood-route-id`: Normalized route identifier (template form; may differ from raw URL path)

When no experiment applies, headers may be omitted. SDKs should expose a convenient way to read these headers without forcing customers to parse low-level HTTP objects.

### SDK ergonomics goal
For each SDK, support:
- Access to raw headers (existing behavior)
- A small helper to parse experiment info into a typed structure

Example structure to document:
- `experimentId: string | null`
- `variantId: string | null`
- `configVersion: string | null`

### Troubleshooting guidance to include in docs
If a customer reports “my experiment isn’t splitting traffic” or “variant is always control”, ask them to capture:
- Their configured `experiment_sticky_key` logic (is it stable? is it always present?)
- One request/response showing returned `x-redwood-experiment-id` and `x-redwood-variant-id`
- Region and route name
- Whether they are using streaming + retries (older SDKs may drop headers if they only surface the streaming iterator)

---

## SDK implementation notes
### TypeScript SDK (redwood-sdk-typescript)
**Add to request options:**
- `experimentStickyKey?: string`

**Behavior:**
- If set, add header `x-redwood-experiment-sticky-key: <value>`
- Parse response headers and expose them on the response object (non-breaking):
  - `response.experiment = { experimentId, variantId, configVersion }`

**Example (TypeScript):**
```ts
import { Redwood } from "@redwood-inference/sdk";

const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY! });

const userId = "user_2f3a9c1b"; // must be stable

const resp = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: "redwood/llama-3.1-70b-instruct",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Summarize this article..." }],
  // New SDK option
  experimentStickyKey: userId,
});

console.log(resp.experiment?.experimentId, resp.experiment?.variantId);
```

**Streaming note:** ensure the first response chunk (or stream wrapper) includes the parsed experiment headers; do not drop them when returning an async iterator.

### Python SDK (redwood-sdk-python)
**Add to request options:**
- `experiment_sticky_key: Optional[str] = None`

**Behavior:**
- If set, add header `x-redwood-experiment-sticky-key`
- Expose parsed headers:
  - `response.experiment_id`
  - `response.variant_id`
  - (optional) `response.experiment_config_version`

**Example (Python):**
```py
from redwood import Redwood

client = Redwood(api_key=os.environ["REDWOOD_API_KEY"])

user_id = "user_2f3a9c1b"  # must be stable

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="redwood/llama-3.1-70b-instruct",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this article..."}],
    experiment_sticky_key=user_id,
)

print(resp.experiment_id, resp.variant_id)
```

### Backwards compatibility
- Adding the request option is backward compatible.
- Adding response fields is backward compatible if we avoid breaking existing response types and keep raw header access unchanged.

### Logging defaults (privacy + support)
SDK defaults:
- Do not log the sticky key at INFO.
- If customers enable debug logging, redact or hash the sticky key in logs.
- It is OK to log `experiment_id` and `variant_id` (not typically PII), but treat them as customer-sensitive in shared logs.

---

## Documentation plan (beta → GA)
### Docs artifacts to ship
1. **Customer Guide:** “Route experiments (A/B testing) in Console”
   - What it is, when to use it
   - Creating an experiment (Console workflow)
   - Choosing stickiness keys (with examples)
   - Reading variant headers / debugging
   - Guardrails + stopping semantics (soft-stop vs optional hard-stop)

2. **SDK reference additions:**
   - `experiment_sticky_key` / `experimentStickyKey` option in the API reference
   - Response header fields / helper structure

3. **Example app updates (redwood-examples):**
   - A minimal route experiments demo showing:
     - Passing a stable stickiness key
     - Printing assigned variant
     - A note on stable routing keys in multi-tenant apps

4. **Troubleshooting page / section:**
   - “Variant skew / always control”
   - “Headers missing”
   - “Streaming retries missing attribution”
   - “Results in Console not updating (propagation lag / aggregation delay)”

### Beta documentation constraints
- Avoid promising advanced statistics/significance analysis in GA (out of scope).
- Be explicit that metrics may take time to appear due to aggregation windows.

### GA readiness checklist (DX-owned)
- SDKs released with stickiness key option in TS + Python
- Example app merged and referenced from docs
- Customer guide includes a “How to pick a stickiness key” section with at least 3 concrete patterns
- Docs reviewed by:
  - Policy Engine (assignment semantics)
  - Telemetry (header naming + attribution correctness)
  - Security (PII guidance / redaction)

---

## FAQ (for SDK/docs authors)
### Do customers need to implement their own bucketing?
No. Bucketing is performed by Redwood’s routing layer.

### What if the customer cannot provide a stable user identifier?
Recommend tenant-level stickiness or session-level stickiness depending on product needs. Explicitly warn about churn/skew if they cannot provide any stable key.

### Are headers always present?
Only when a request is eligible for an experiment and the request path surfaces headers. Some intermediaries can drop headers; if customers are behind proxies, advise them to allowlist the Redwood headers.

### Can customers force a variant?
Not in GA docs. Any internal override mechanism should be treated as restricted/internal-only and gated by RBAC/feature flags.

---

## Open items / follow-ups
- Confirm final header names with Observability + Policy Engine owners (align with OTel tag naming conventions).
- Finalize copy for Console tooltips explaining headers and stickiness.
- Add a short section in docs on hashing PII identifiers before using them as sticky keys.
- Ensure streaming clients surface response headers consistently (prior issues observed with retries).

title: dsid_49bf1d6e143d4003b7fb765dfbd78a51__aws-marketplace-offer-preflight-playbook-2026.txt
text:
AWS Marketplace offer preflight playbook (2026): launch checklist + hero copy templates

h1. Purpose
This playbook is the standard preflight packet for an AWS Marketplace offer (new listing or major revision). It covers:
- The required artifacts to unblock Procurement/Legal review
- Recommended SKU structure and metering defaults
- Approved hero copy templates (with compliance-safe language)
- A one-page co-sell blurb template for AWS Partner Ops

This page was created after repeated partner asks for a “short checklist + 2–3 hero copy options” to speed internal alignment.

h1. When to use
Use this playbook when:
- A partner requests an AWS Marketplace listing (public listing, private offer, or both)
- A deal is targeting AWS co-sell registration
- Procurement requests a “preflight checklist” before engaging Legal/Security

h1. Owners and turnaround expectations
- DRI (Partners/Marketplace): Partnerships Director (default)
- Messaging: Product Marketing
- Packaging/Metering: Platform GTM + Product
- Co-sell: Partner Ops enablement

SLA targets (typical):
1) Preflight checklist + draft hero copy within 2 business days
2) Consolidated partner packet within 3 business days

h1. Preflight packet contents (send as one consolidated PDF or folder)
Deliverables to include:
1) Offer preflight checklist (see below)
2) Hero copy options (2–3) + subheadline
3) SKU + metering summary (1 page)
4) Co-sell one-pager blurb (paragraph + value props + use cases)
5) Image guidance notes (or link to latest design guidance)

h1. Offer preflight checklist (required artifacts)
The table below is the canonical “what we need” list. If a partner asks for a checklist, copy/paste this section into email and offer to provide a filled-in version.

h2. Checklist table
| Category | Item | Required for | Notes / tips |
|---|---|---|---|
| Listing basics | Product name + short description | All offers | Keep description consistent with website naming; avoid unverified superlatives. |
| Listing basics | Category + keywords | All offers | Use stable keyword set across AWS + website + decks. |
| Packaging | SKU names + SKU descriptions | All offers | See recommended SKU set below; keep names stable for billing mappings. |
| Metering | Metering dimension(s) + unit definitions | SaaS offers | Prefer token-based metering where applicable; define rounding/minimums explicitly. |
| Pricing | Public price card | Public listing | Include any volume tiers and minimum monthly commits if applicable. |
| Pricing | Private Offer readiness | Enterprise deals | Confirm discount bands and approval path; define start/end dates and renewal term language. |
| Legal | EULA/contract addendum link | All offers | Confirm latest template; avoid partner-specific edits without Legal review. |
| Security | SOC 2 / ISO status statement | Most enterprise deals | Provide the “what we can share” summary and the evidence request process. |
| Support | Support tiers + response times | All offers | Provide business hours, P1 expectations, and escalation channel. |
| Images | Hero image(s) + logo usage approval | Public listing | Follow AWS image constraints; do not use customer logos without written permission. |
| Sales enablement | Value props (top 3) + ICP | Co-sell | Must map to measurable outcomes; avoid hard performance numbers unless approved. |
| Implementation | Getting started steps + prerequisites | All offers | Include IAM/network prerequisites and onboarding timeline ranges. |

h1. SKU and metering guidance (2026 standard)
This section supersedes older notes that used different metering for dedicated capacity.

h2. Recommended SKU set
Default recommendation is 3 SKUs (use 2 only if product scope is narrow):
- Standard (Shared hosted): best for trials, dev/test, and smaller workloads
- Dedicated (Reserved capacity): best for predictable production workloads needing isolation
- Enterprise (Private Offer only): used when commercial terms require custom commitments, add-ons, or bundled support

Important: Some partners will ask whether “standard/dedicated” is final so their billing team can map the catalog. For 2026, these names are the preferred defaults; only change if there is an existing contracted naming scheme.

h2. Metering and pricing defaults
- Primary usage metric (preferred): tokens-in/tokens-out (or “total tokens processed” if a single dimension is required)
- Dedicated capacity: prefer token-based metering plus a minimum monthly commit rather than vGPU-hour metering, unless Finance explicitly requires capacity-based billing for that product line
- Pricing footnotes to include:
  1) Clear definition of what counts as input vs output tokens
  2) Rounding behavior and any minimum billable unit
  3) Overages/burst behavior (if enabled)

h2. Private Offer guidance
- Default: enable Private Offer for initial enterprise customers to accelerate procurement and ensure predictable billing
- Include in partner packet:
  - Proposed term (12/24/36 months)
  - Discount band (if pre-approved)
  - Start date, renewal behavior, and any ramp schedule

h1. Hero copy templates (compliance-safe)
Keep hero copy short (target: <= 85 characters for the main line). Avoid unapproved hard claims (exact latency, “X% cheaper”) unless Product + Legal sign-off is recorded.

h2. Options (2026)
Option A — "LLM inference, production-grade: predictable latency and cost at scale."
Subline — "Run open and custom models—fast, reliable, and cloud-ready."

Option B — "Ship AI features with zero ops friction: high-throughput inference for teams."
Subline — "Dedicated capacity, private options, and integrated cost controls."

Option C — "Cut inference costs. Keep quality. Scale confidently."
Subline — "Unified runtime across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments."

Notes:
- Option B text reflects the preferred legal-friendly wording (“with zero ops friction”) and replaces older phrasing (“without the ops”).
- If a partner requests stronger performance language, route to Product for claim substantiation and approval.

h1. Co-sell blurb template (AWS Partner Ops)
Provide AWS Partner Ops a single paragraph plus 3 value props and 3 use cases.

h2. One-paragraph template
"Redwood Inference helps teams ship production AI features by providing reliable, cost-controlled model inference across shared hosted and dedicated capacity. Customers use Redwood to reduce operational overhead, improve predictability for latency-sensitive workloads, and scale usage with clear commercial terms through AWS Marketplace."

h2. Top 3 value props (edit to fit product scope)
- Predictable performance for production inference workloads
- Cost controls and transparent metering aligned to usage
- Flexible deployment options (shared, dedicated, private offer commercial paths)

h2. Top 3 use cases (choose the most relevant)
- Agentic workflows and RAG applications in customer support and knowledge search
- Real-time personalization and recommendation inference
- Internal copilots and document automation for operations teams

h1. Email-ready response (copy/paste)
Subject: AWS Marketplace preflight pack: checklist + hero copy + SKU guidance

Body:
"Thanks—attached is our AWS Marketplace offer preflight pack. It includes (1) the required artifacts checklist, (2) 3 hero copy options with sublines, (3) recommended SKU/metering defaults, and (4) a co-sell one-paragraph summary + value props/use cases. If Procurement/Legal needs MSA redlines or security evidence, tell us what format they prefer and we’ll prioritize."

h1. Change log
- 2026-12-10: Updated Option B hero copy to “with zero ops friction” and clarified SKU/metering default to prefer token-based metering for dedicated offers unless Finance requires capacity-based billing.
- 2026-11-05: Initial publication based on partner request pattern (checklist + 2–3 hero copy options + SKU guidance + co-sell blurb).

title: dsid_3bc44c4b81ff49ecaa19f7e2671ec7a0__multi-tenant-canary-eval-privacy-anchoring-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Multi-tenant Canary Eval: Privacy Anchoring & Probe Design Playbook

Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines a reproducible, privacy-preserving approach for running multi-tenant canary evaluations of model and serving changes. It describes probe design, anchoring strategies, acceptance criteria, telemetry schema, and rollback procedures tailored for shared evaluator fleets and tenant isolation constraints.

Why this doc exists
- Multi-tenant canaries enable fast feedback but increase privacy risk and cross-tenant interference.
- We need deterministic, auditable probes that exercise production traffic slices while bounding leakage and differential privacy (DP) exposure.
- This playbook standardizes the orchestration (evaluator-orch, canary-operator), probe provenance (probe-store), and decision gates used by model promotion and runtime rollouts.

Scope and audience
- Audience: Applied ML engineers, evaluation owners, SREs operating the evaluator fleet, privacy-compliance reviewers.
- Scope: Canary evaluation of model binaries, quantization variants, routing policies, and KV-cache configurations in environments that host multiple tenants. Not intended for offline-only evals or external benchmark runs.

Key definitions
- Probe: A synthetic or sampled input designed to exercise a targeted failure mode or slice. Probes carry provenance metadata (seed_id, tenant_guard, probe_ttl).
- Anchor probe: A small subset of probes designated as high-trust references (no PII, stable expected outputs) used to detect drift or regressions without exposing tenant data.
- Privacy anchor: A probe or probe-set paired with DP noise parameters and an access policy used to bound leakage across runs.
- Canary slice: A set of tenants or traffic percentage routed to the candidate model variant during the canary window.

Goals and acceptance criteria
- Detect regressions in fidelity (semantic delta, BLEU/ROUGE proxies, task-specific accuracy) within the canary window.
- Maintain isolation: no probe should reveal PII or customer-identifiable artifacts.
- Privacy budget: per-candidate canary epsilon <= 2.0 for public-anchor aggregates; delta <= 1e-6. For tenant-level metrics, use aggregated reporting only.
- Latency and reliability SLOs: p95 latency delta <= 20ms; error-rate delta <= 0.5 percentage points.

Ownership and roles
- Eval owner: creates canary config, defines probe set and success / failure thresholds. (Team: applied-ml)
- Canary operator: schedules the canary via canary-operator and coordinates telemetry capture. (Team: eng-platform)
- Privacy reviewer: verifies that the probe-set and DP parameters meet the privacy policy. (Team: security-and-compliance)
- SRE: monitors infra signals and executes rollback if infra thresholds are violated. (Team: eng-sre)

Probe design principles
1) No-PII-by-construction: All anchor probes must be synthetic or redacted. For sampled probes from production, apply automated redaction and a secondary human privacy review for any sample used as an anchor.
2) Slice coverage: Build probes to cover long-tail slices (rare intents), latency-sensitive paths, and heavy-token sequences. Prioritize probes flagged by the stability index and production-hotspot telemetry.
3) Deterministic seeds & provenance: Store seed_id, generator version, and fixture parameters in probe-store. Each probe run must be reproducible using these fields.
4) Anchors vs. field probes: Keep anchor probes stable across promotions and use field probes for exploratory detection. Anchors are permitted in automatic gating; field probes require manual review if they signal failure.

Probe categories and examples
- Anchor synthetic: templated multi-turn tasks with fixed random seed (e.g., code-refactor instruction templates).
- Sanitized sample: production user query with PII redacted and paraphrase applied.
- Stress probe: artificially long context, heavy function-calls, or many-shot priming.
- Cache-sensitive probe: sequences designed to stress KV cache reuse patterns.

Telemetry schema (table)
Columns to capture per-probe-run:
- run_id (string)
- probe_id (string)
- seed_id (string)
- tenant_guard (string, e.g., "public_anchor" | "tenant_agg")
- model_variant (string)
- route (string)
- tokens_in (int)
- tokens_out (int)
- latency_ms (float)
- p95_latency_ms_by_route (float)
- semantic_score (float)  # per-task similarity metric
- error_tag (string, optional)
- dp_noise_eps (float, optional)
- sample_timestamp (ISO8601)
- provenance_sha (string)

Minimum retention: 90 days for aggregate metrics; probe input text retention limited to 30 days for sanitized samples unless explicitly approved by privacy.

Differential privacy guidance
- Use Gaussian mechanism for aggregate telemetry where we report counts, averages, or semantic-score histograms.
- Default per-run epsilon: 0.5; allow up to 2.0 for tightly-scoped internal canaries only after Privacy review. Report epsilon and delta in telemetry headers.
- DP implementation checklist: prove mechanism via unit tests, attach randomness source (kms-wrapped seed), and include reproducible audit logs.

Canary orchestration: step-by-step
1) Prepare probe-set and canary-config in evaluator-orch repository. Canary-config fields:
   - model_variant: identifier (e.g., redwood-model-x-v3-q4)
   - traffic_percentage: 1-5% initially
   - tenant_selectors: explicit tenant list or hashed namespace selectors
   - duration: 2h default for multi-tenant canaries
   - metrics_and_thresholds: list of metric keys and thresholds
2) Run privacy pre-check: privacy reviewer approves probe-set and DP params.
3) Schedule canary via canary-operator: attach canary-config and probe manifest.
4) Start telemetry capture: canary-operator toggles evaluator-orch telemetry API and streams to probe-ingest pipeline.
5) Monitor primary gates (automated) for the canary window:
   - Quality gate: semantic_score delta <= 0.02 (relative) on anchor set
   - Latency gate: p95_latency delta <= 20ms
   - Error gate: 4xx/5xx increase <= 0.5pp
6) If all gates pass for the stable window (configured contiguous 30 minutes), promote model to broader rollout.
7) If any gate trips, mark canary as failed and escalate to evaluation owner + SRE.

Automated gate thresholds (default)
- anchor_semantic_delta_pct <= 2%
- anchor_confidence_drop >= 5% triggers manual triage
- p95_latency_delta_ms <= 20ms
- top-10-slice-degradation > 3% triggers failure

Rollback and remediation flow (triage playbook)
1) Automated rollback: canary-operator immediately routes traffic back to baseline variant and records the rollback event (run_id, triggered_gate, top failing probes).
2) Post-rollback triage steps (ordered):
   a) Capture failing probe set snapshot and delta metrics.
   b) Reproduce failure locally using probe-store seeds and evaluator-orch local-run mode.
   c) Check quantization/serving differences: kernel fallbacks, heterogenous device dispatch, and cache warming state.
   d) If failure is model-quality: run the regression triage checklist and notify applied-ml on-call.
   e) If failure is infra: route to SRE incident playbook (latency or memory errors).
3) Report: create a canary-incident ticket with attached artifacts: telemetry export, probe snapshots, provenance_sha, and privacy approval stamp.

Operational best practices and tips
- Canary window sizing: for multi-tenant shared fleets prefer shorter windows (1–2 hours) with repeated micro-canaries instead of one long run.
- Tenant selection: prefer hashed namespace selectors to avoid tenant identity in configs. Example selector: tenant_hash_mod(1024) in range [0..10) to pick ~1% of tenants.
- Reserve a small pool of "quiet" tenants used exclusively for privacy anchors; rotate quarterly and record human approval for any changes.
- Maintain a canary catalog: each run should append to a central registry with run metadata and results for auditability.

Example canary-config (YAML)
---
model_variant: "redwood-llm-v2-q4a"
traffic_percentage: 2
duration_minutes: 120
tenant_selector: "hash_mod(1024) in [0..20)"
probe_manifest: "s3://probe-store/canaries/anchors/2026-01-07.json"
metrics_and_thresholds:
  - key: "anchor_semantic_delta"
    threshold: 0.02
  - key: "p95_latency_delta_ms"
    threshold: 20
  - key: "error_rate_delta_pp"
    threshold: 0.5
---

Example CLI (create canary)
# register canary (evaluator-orch)
curl -X POST 
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer $EVAL_ORCH_TOKEN' 
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
  -d @canary-config.json 
  https://evaluator-orch.internal/api/v1/canaries

Audit and compliance
- Every canary run must include an attached privacy stamp (reviewer name, approval timestamp, epsilon/delta values).
- Audit logs: canary-operator writes a signed event to audit-log service with run_id and provenance_sha. Keep logs for minimum 1 year for compliance reviews.
- For any canary that used sanitized samples, store redaction diffs and the redaction tool version in probe-store.

Appendices
A. Quick checklist before running a canary
1) Build probe-set with anchors and field probes.
2) Run privacy pre-check and attach DP params.
3) Validate probe reproducibility using probe-store seeds.
4) Define automated gates and acceptance windows.
5) Confirm telemetry retention and data access policies.

B. Troubleshooting hints
- If p95 latency spikes only on the candidate variant, check kernel selection logs and quant fallback traces.
- If semantic_score shifts inconsistently across anchors, verify tokenizer/version mismatch and prompt priming.

C. Related tooling and services
- evaluator-orch: canary scheduling and local-replay runner.
- canary-operator: Kubernetes operator handling traffic splits.
- probe-store: canonical repository of probe manifests, seed_ids, and provenance.
- probe-ingest: topology for streaming probe telemetry into the eval-metrics pipeline.

Contact and escalation
- Primary owner: applied-ml@redwood.com (Mariana Ortiz)
- Platform coordination: eng-platform@redwood.com
- Privacy escalation: privacy-team@redwood.com

title: dsid_fafc6b7b4e86492b8336f6b317cf44b5__privilege-approval-safeguards-and-evidence-manual-2027.txt
text:
Privilege Approval Safeguards and Evidence Manual

Overview:
This manual defines Redwood Inference’s standard safeguards for privileged access approvals, the associated audit evidence requirements, and operational procedures that span RBAC, audit logging, data residency, secure SDLC gates, incident-response integration, and exception handling. The goal is to create a single reference that engineering, security, and compliance teams can use to approve, document, and retain proof for any high‑risk entitlement change.

Scope:
- Applies to all identity and authorization changes that grant: cluster-admin, service-account wide-scope roles, production secrets access, direct access to customer-resident datasets, or any action classified as "privileged" by Product Risk Classification (PRC) level 3 or higher.
- Covers approvals in hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Does not replace team-level ACLs for low-risk developer tooling (PRC level 1).

Key Principles:
- Principle of least privilege: Every grant must be scoped to the minimum resources and time window required.
- Evidence-first approvals: No privileged change is considered approved without an attached evidence bundle (see Evidence Requirements).
- Auditability: All actions in the approval workflow must be logged to the centralized immutable audit pipeline.
- Separation of duties: Approval and provisioning must be owned by different roles for level 3+ grants.

Ownership and Roles:
- Requestor: Engineer or operator who needs the privilege. Responsible for justification and evidence submission.
- Approver: Designated approver from Security or Product (for infra or product-scoped grants respectively).
- Provisioner: System or operator who executes the grant after approval.
- Compliance Custodian: Security engineer responsible for packaging and retaining evidence for audits.

Approval Categories and Required Approvals:
1) Level 1 (Low): short-lived non-production roles, auto-approvable by team leads.
2) Level 2 (Medium): production read access, customer metadata, requires peer approver + audit log check.
3) Level 3 (High, Privileged): write access to production systems, key material, data residency overrides, requires Security approver + Product approver (if customer impact) + SRE signoff.

Evidence Requirements (manifest):
Each approval must include the following evidence bundle items. The Compliance Custodian will index these into the evidence store.
| Manifest field | Required? | Example/Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Requestor identity + employment ID | Yes | SSO username + employee ID; include OKTA session id |
| Timeboxed scope (start, expiry) | Yes | ISO8601 timestamps; <= 30 days for level 3 unless approved exception |
| Justification statement | Yes | One-paragraph summary of business need; link to ticket |
| Related change ticket/PR | Yes | JIRA ID or repo PR link |
| Approval chain (names + timestamps) | Yes | Approver SSO + approval e-signature id |
| Audit-log extract | Yes | Query snippet + associated event IDs (see Audit Log Requirements) |
| Data residency coordinate | Conditional | If access touches customer data with residency constraints, include region + legal basis |
| Proof of roll-back plan | Conditional | Short steps to revoke, and test steps |

Audit Log Requirements:
- All approval workflow steps must emit structured events to the centralized audit topic with these fields: event_id, actor_id, action, target_resource, request_id, timestamp, outcome, audit_context.
- Immutable retention: approval events are retained for a minimum of 7 years in cold storage for high‑risk customers (per contract), 3 years default for internal.
- Extraction template (CLI):
  rlog query --start 2027-02-01T00:00:00Z --end 2027-02-10T23:59:59Z --filter 'request_id:ABC123' --format json > approval_audit_extract.json
- The audit extraction must include chain-of-custody headers (collector-node, sign-of-copy) for evidence packages used in regulatory submissions.

Data Residency and Retention Considerations:
- Any approval that grants access to data with residency constraints must explicitly list the affected residency zone(s).
- Evidence bundles for residency-bound access must include the legal basis (contract clause or data processing agreement) and a mapping to storage buckets or VPC endpoints used.
- Short table of default retention mappings:
| Data Type | Default Retention | Notes |
| Customer PII | 7 years (or contractual) | Retention overrides require Legal concurrence and explicit evidence |
| Operational telemetry | 1 year | Aggregated metrics kept longer in roll-ups |
| Audit logs (privileged) | 3—7 years | Per above, default 3y; extend per customer SLAs |

Secure SDLC Gate Integration:
- Privileged code or deployment changes that introduce new privileged capabilities must go through an elevated PR checklist:
  1) Threat model update (owner: submitter)
  2) Security review (owner: Security reviewer)
  3) Test plan for rollback and fail-open/fail-closed behavior (owner: SRE)
- The PR must attach the same evidence manifest schema as the runtime privilege request. The CI pipeline will reject merges without a valid manifest JSON attached.

Incident Response Tie‑ins:
- If a privileged approval is created during incident mitigation, label the request with INCIDENT=true and include incident ID and timeline. Evidence requirements remain the same but a post‑incident retrospective must evaluate whether the temporary grant should have been issued.
- Rapid revocation play:
  1) Provisioner issues revoke via IAM CLI with request_id.
  2) Audit pipeline flags revoke event and notifies SRE/security pager.
  3) Compliance Custodian attaches revoke evidence to original manifest.
- For incidents that cross data-residency boundaries, notify Legal immediately and preserve all evidence under legal hold.

Exception and Risk Handling:
- Exceptions to the policy (timeboxed >30d, residency overrides, or role-broadening) require an exception request filed to Risk Board with: risk rationale, compensating controls, and a sunset plan.
- Exception evidence template (minimal): requestor, business case, compensating controls (monitoring/playbooks), duration, approvers.
- Risk Board cadence: fortnightly; emergency ad-hoc approvals require 2/3 voting quorum from Board members for immediate exceptions.

Operational Runbook: Approving a Level 3 Grant (step-by-step)
1) Requestor creates ticket: include manifest.json with required fields.
2) Ticket auto-assigns to Approver group; approver validates justification and checks active SLOs.
3) Approver records e-signature in approval platform; system emits audit event.
4) Provisioner applies grant via IaC or impersonation flow; emits provisioning events.
