Pre-engagement checklist: 1) workload profile (tokens/request, concurrency, seasonality), 2) security needs (residency, KMS, DPA), 3) success criteria and rollback triggers. Pilot activation script (1–3 business days): 1) create trial/Dedicated slot and scoped API keys, 2) deliver SDK quickstart and logging samples, 3) enable dashboards and alerts (p95 SLA and token-cost thresholds), 4) run synthetic traffic and KV cache validation, 5) run <1% real-traffic canary and evaluate quick-evals, 6) test rollback to quantized variant and verify continuity. Post-pilot: deliver 1-page exec report with cost per 1k tokens, p95 latency, quality regression delta.
Q: How is customer data isolated in Hosted mode? A: Logical isolation by project and customer ID; recommend Dedicated/Private for regulated data.
Q: Which KMS/HSM integrations are supported? A: AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault, optional Cloud EKM and customer HSM appliances for Private.
Q: Can we export raw audit logs and traces? A: Yes — logs/traces/cost events can be exported to S3/GCS/Azure Blob or SIEM via syslog/EventHub.
Q: Is encrypted inference (BYOK for model weights) supported? A: Supported in Private via EKM-managed decryption and secure enclave workflows; hosted uses provider-managed model keys.
Q: Certifications and pen tests? A: SOC2 Type II; ISO 27001 in targeted regions; annual third-party pen-test reports available under NDA.
Q: Patch and CVE management for Private? A: Scheduled patch cadence, security bulletins, offline signed artifact bundles and migration/rollback instructions for air-gapped customers.
Marketplaces startup (mid-market): Problem—peak search latency hurt conversions. Outcome—moved to Dedicated pool with autoscaling and prefix caching; conversion +3.8% at peak, token cost −26% vs prior endpoints.
Healthcare regulated partner (enterprise): Problem—required customer-managed keys and audit trail. Outcome—Private deployment with KMS integration and evidence pack; passed security review and went to production in 14 weeks.
One-page pitch bullets: 1) Predictable inference economics and latency across hosted/dedicated/private; 2) Reduce unit cost via batching, KV caching, quantization guidance; 3) Ship safely with canaries, prompt-set regression alerts, and automated fallback. Sample SLA excerpt: Uptime 99.95% for Dedicated (monthly), p95 <= 2x agreed baseline for provisioned capacity, P1 acknowledgement within 15 minutes and two-hour mitigation path for production-impacting regressions.
Internal benchmarks Q3–Q4 2025, anonymized telemetry from pilot customers, public feature scans of major cloud providers (market scan 2025).
Primary AE contact: Priya Nair (priya.nair@redwood-inference.com) — include SE handoff in initial email and attach trial spreadsheet estimate.

title: dsid_feec3f6f71f04949a2cb9fcdf099a8bc__slice-synthesis-governance-and-localization-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Slice Synthesis Governance and Localization Playbook

Summary:
This playbook describes the governance process and technical procedure for synthesizing evaluation slices and localized derivative probes used in continuous evals, stress benchmarks, and production shadowing. It defines responsibilities, sampling budgets, quality gates, telemetry contracts, and localization constraints to ensure probes remain representative and safe across languages, regions, and product features.

Audience:
- Applied ML engineers
- Evaluator / probe authors
- Product QA and Safety stewards
- Model-onboarding owners

Scope:
This document covers:
- Derivative probe generation (seed mutation, paraphrase, noise injection).
- Cross-locale and dialect localization rules.
- Sampling governance (budgets, quotas, retention).
- Telemetry and metadata contract for probes and synthetic examples.
- Quality guardrails and automatic rejection criteria.
Not in scope: human annotation instructions (see related annotation charters) and private customer data handling (see privacy-first-shadow-eval-and-dp-certification).

Definitions:
- Seed: a canonical prompt or user-exemplar used to generate derivative probes.
- Derivative probe: any synthetic or transformed prompt created from a seed (paraphrase, translation, noise-perturbed, adapter-context).
- Slice: a labeled subset of workload defined by intent, complexity, or locale (e.g., billing-clarification, spanish-colloquial, long-context).
- Localization family: group of locales/languages sharing a translation and cultural adaptation policy (e.g., en-US/en-GB -> English family).

Governance principles:
1) Traceability: Every derivative probe must include provenance metadata: seed_id, generator_version, transformation_chain, author, and creation_timestamp.
2) Minimal human cost: Favor automatic synthesis when quality gates pass; preserve human review for high-risk slices or customer-impacting features.
3) Budgeted sampling: Each team has a monthly synthesis budget in tokens and probe-counts; budget exhausted => escalation to evaluator lead.
4) Local fidelity: For localization families, include at least one native-speaker validation sample per slice for languages with >1% of traffic.

Metadata (telemetry) contract (required fields):
- probe_id (string)
- seed_id (string)
- slice_tags (list)
- generator (string) e.g. "paraphrase-v2" or "translate-bridge-en-to-es"
- generator_version (string)
- transform_chain (string) e.g. "seed->synonym-perturb(0.2)->paraphrase-v2"
- locale (string) e.g. "es-419"
- estimated_token_cost (int)
- human_review_status (enum) {none, sampled, approved, rejected}
- provenance_url (string) link to source artifact in eval-mesh or storage
- safety_review_tag (string) optional safety label if flagged

Sampling and budget rules:
- Default budget per owning team: 5k probes / month or 1M tokens, whichever is first.
- High-risk slices (financial instructions, legal guidance) capped at 500 auto-synth probes / month unless human-reviewed.
- Localization multiplier: for locales marked as "high fidelity" (top 10% traffic), synthesize a 1:1 ratio to en seeds; for low-traffic locales, cap at 10% of en volume.
- Retention policy: keep synthesized probes and metadata for 24 months. Older probes must be archived with audit trail.

Quality gates (automated):
Run in order; failure at any gate marks the probe as "rejected-automated" and triggers triage.
1) Tokenization sanity: probe must tokenize without OOV errors and token count <= 4x seed length.
2) Semantic-presence check: intent classifier confidence >= 0.7 for target slice.
3) Toxicity filter: run safety classifier v3; toxicity score < 0.2 or flagged for human_review_status.
4) Model-consistency smoke: run lightweight evaluator (evaluator-lite) against production model and baseline model: normalized response similarity >= 0.65 (unless slice expects diversity).
5) Locale fluency spot-check: language identification must match locale with confidence >= 0.9.

Quality gates (human):
- Any probe failing automated gates but within salvage thresholds (e.g., toxicity between 0.2-0.35) is queued for human review.
- Human review checklist: fluency, cultural appropriateness, PII leakage, and instruction preservation. Use the HumanReview UI in eval-mesh (link in related_pages).

Derivation strategies (examples):
- Paraphrase ensemble: 3 paraphrase models (paraphrase-v1/v2/paraphrase-light) with disagreement pruning: keep probes where at least 2 models agree on intent classifier.
- Translation bridge: seed->translate(en->pivot_lang)->paraphrase->back-translate->normalize. Include intermediate artifacts for audit.
- Noise injection: controlled character/token-level perturbations to simulate ASR/typo errors; parameterize by noise_rate (0.01, 0.05, 0.1).

Procedure: Creating a new localized slice (step-by-step)
1) Define slice in the slice registry: slug, owner_team, acceptance_criteria, and initial seed list (minimum 20 seeds).
2) Create a synthesis job in probe-orch with parameters: generator_set, locale_targets, noise_profile, and sampling_budget. Example CLI: 
   probe-orch create --slice billing-clarification --seeds seeds/billing-clarity-2025.json --generators paraphrase-v2,translate-bridge --locales en-US,es-419 --budget 200
3) Probe-orch emits artifacts to s3://eval-mesh/synth/{slice}/{job_id}/ including metadata.json and samples.csv.
4) Run auto-gates: call eval-harness auto-gate --input s3://eval-mesh/synth/{job_id}/metadata.json --out s3://eval-mesh/synth/{job_id}/gated.json
5) If any probes are queued for human review, assign to a reviewer via the HumanReview UI and mark status.
6) Approve and promote a subset (minimum 200 approved probes) to the probe registry for continuous evals.

Role and ownership matrix:
- Slice owner: owns definition, acceptance criteria, and seed list. (Team-level)
- Probe author: initiates synthesis jobs and triage. (Applied ML / Evaluator)
- Quality steward: signs off on human-reviewed probes for high-risk slices. (Safety / Product)
- Telemetry owner: ensures probes emit required metadata. (Observability / Eng-DE)

Metrics and SLOs for synthesis pipeline:
- Gate processing latency: 95th percentile <= 2 minutes per probe for automated gates.
- Human review turnaround: median <= 48 hours for sampled probes.
- Rejection rate (automated): target < 12% for low-risk slices; < 6% for seeded QA sets.
- Localization coverage: top-10 locales must reach 95% of planned probe volume within 7 days of job completion.

Example metadata JSON (single-line, stored in metadata.json):
{"probe_id":"probe-20260115-0001","seed_id":"seed-billing-0007","slice_tags":["billing","clarification","long-context"],"generator":"paraphrase-v2","generator_version":"2.1.0","transform_chain":"seed->paraphrase-v2->noise(0.01)","locale":"es-419","estimated_token_cost":18,"human_review_status":"none","provenance_url":"s3://eval-mesh/synth/billing-20260115/job-7/probe-0001.txt"}

Interoperability notes (integration with quantization profiles and runtime):
- Mark probes with a "quant_sensitivity" tag when probes exercise long-context or high-precision numeric outputs. This flag must trigger the quant-impact-synthesis pipeline (see quantization-profiles directory) to validate behavior under int8/int4 artifacts.
- For probes in dedicated/private workloads, ensure the provenance_url points to private storage and that telemetry respects customer-data redaction policies.

Triage playbook for regression signals (quick steps):
1) Alert from evaluation-dashboard identifies a slice-level quality drop > 5% compared to baseline.
2) Kick off synthetic-bisect: re-run the slice with multiple random seeds and generator_versions to determine whether regression is generator- or model-driven.
3) Check derivation metadata for generator_version drift or locale mapping changes.
4) If candidate root cause is quant-related, add quant-sensitivity-tagged probes to the failing cohort and re-evaluate under quantized artifacts.
5) If human-safety issue found, escalate to Safety oncall and freeze synthetic generation for affected slice.

Rollout and deprecation policy:
- New slice must run in shadow for 2 weeks with continuous monitoring and a minimum of 1k interactions.
- Deprecate a slice only after: owner_team sign-off, archival of artifacts, and update to slice registry.

Appendix: example slice registry table (column descriptions)
- slug: short identifier for the slice (string)
- owner: Owning team
- seeds_count: initial seed count
- target_locales: comma-separated locale list
- risk_level: low|medium|high
- last_audit: YYYY-MM-DD

References and links:
- Eval Mesh: internal portlet for artifact storage and orchestration.
- HumanReview UI: link in top nav > Evaluations > HumanReview.
- Related docs: localization-translation-guidelines, probe-curation-stewardship-and-annotation-charter.

Contact:
For questions or to request increased synthesis budget, open a ticket in #eval-synthesis-support or email maya.singh@redwood-inference.com.

title: dsid_6ce194cd02b7424e9100c5d7136e61f0__optimize-conductor-3-0-live-fidelity-advisor-release-notes-2027-01-15.txt
text:
Optimize Conductor 3.0 — Live Fidelity Advisor and Distributed Quant Profiles (Release Notes)

Optimize Conductor 3.0 introduces the Live Fidelity Advisor, distributed quantization profiles, and a telemetry-normalization pipeline designed to reduce per-token cost while preserving response quality. This release focuses on runtime coordination between Optimize and the serving runtime, migration tooling for customers, and a new pricing addendum for fidelity-as-a-service. Rollout begins 2027-01-20 with progressive canaries.
Purpose and scope:

This page documents the 3.0 release of Optimize Conductor (internal name: OC-3.0). The release bundles three product features and operational changes: (1) Live Fidelity Advisor (LFA), (2) Distributed Quantization Profiles (DQP), and (3) Telemetry Normalization v2 (TN-v2). The target audience is product, SRE, eng-serving-runtime, solutions engineering, and enterprise customers migrating to the new optimizer.

Highlights:
- Live Fidelity Advisor: a real-time signal generator that recommends per-request fidelity hints (quantization level, kv-cache retention, token budget preference) back to the serving runtime and SDK. LFA aims to lower unit cost by 10–30% on mixed conversational workloads while keeping quality regression below 1.5% on monitored eval sets.
- Distributed Quantization Profiles: allow customers to opt into per-tenant quant profiles that are coordinated across dedicated pools and private deployments. Profiles are stored in a signed, versioned manifest and can be roll-forward/rollbacked via the Optimize Console.
- Telemetry Normalization v2: reduces noise in cost attribution by 40% for batched streaming workloads; includes provenance tagging for per-prefix caching and fallback decisions.

Compatibility and footprint:
- Supported runtimes: Serving Runtime >= v5.4.0 (kernel and KV cache changes required).
- SDK changes: No breaking API changes. New thin SDK patch (client 2.5.0) exposes fidelity hints and local prefetch toggles.
- Deployment modes: Hosted API (immediate rollout), Dedicated (opt-in scheduled upgrade), Private (release bundle + migration script for on-prem appliances).

SLO & safety targets for rollout:
- Fidelity regression guardrail: end-to-end quality delta <= 1.5% as measured by tenant-controlled eval sets.
- Availability target during canary: 99.9% for canaries; 99.95% for full rollout windows.
- Reconciliation latency for advisor signals: median <= 120ms, p99 <= 450ms.

APIs and contract changes (developer-facing):
1) New SDK callbacks and headers (client 2.5.0):
   - x-rw-fidelity-hint: enum (high, balanced, low, custom).
   - fidelity_hint_callback(config) — library hook that surfaces LFA recommendations and decision metadata to the client app.
2) Admin endpoints (Optimize Console):
   - POST /orgs/:org/profiles/_apply — atomically apply a quant profile to a tenant.
   - GET /orgs/:org/profiles/:id/manifest — signed manifest for verification.

Operational rollout plan (high level):
1) Internal staging (2027-01-10 to 2027-01-17): run daily simulated traffic with chaotic fidelity toggles. Owners: eng-serving-runtime + Optimize infra.
2) Developer canary (2027-01-20 to 2027-02-03): opt-in for developer sandbox tenants. Monitor quality gates and cost curves. Owners: product + developer relations.
3) Controlled enterprise pilot (2027-02-07 to 2027-03-07): 5–8 enterprise customers invited; Dedicated customers can schedule upgrades; Private customers receive migration bundle. Owners: customer-success + eng-private-deployments.
4) Gradual ramp (from 2027-03-10): expand to broader hosted tenant population with automatic rollback thresholds configured. Owners: eng-sre + product.

Migration and customer guidance (checklist):
- Pre-migration:
  1. Ensure serving runtime >= v5.4.0 is available to your region or pool.
  2. Run the "OC-3 compatibility scanner" against your tenant workload samples (cli: rwd-compat-scan --profile oc3).
  3. Confirm client SDK 2.5.0 adoption schedule for your application teams.
- During migration:
  1. Enable LFA in balanced mode for 48–72 hours.
  2. Push a non-blocking sampling route (5% traffic) to collect fidelity decisions and retrain local pref cure heuristics.
  3. Validate no more than 1.0% increase in customer-reported error rates or timeouts.
- Post migration:
  1. Review the fidelity decision audit logs (Optimize Console -> Telemetry -> Fidelity Decisions).
  2. Consider customizing quant profiles for high-SLA routes.

Pricing and commercial notes:
- For hosted customers: LFA and TN-v2 included in Optimize Conductor base for all paying tiers. DQP is a paid add-on (per-tenant profile seats).
- DQP commercial model: $X/month per active profile + usage-based fraction for per-token quantization overhead. Finance has published the vendor-facing addendum (see related_pages).
- Trial path: customers can run a 30-day DQP pilot with up to 3 profiles; billing triggers only after pilot ends.

Monitoring and observability changes:
- New dashboards shipped under Optimize -> Fidelity Ops:
  - LFA Decision Distribution (bucketed by endpoint).
  - Profile Impact Heatmap (quality delta vs cost delta).
  - Telemetry Normalization Drift (per region).
- Alerts:
  - fidelity.regression.high — fires when end-to-end eval delta > 1.5% for 15m window. Severity: P1. Owner: eng-sre.
  - fidelity.advisor.latency.p99 — fires when p99 > 600ms for 5m window. Severity: P2. Owner: eng-serving-runtime.

Security and compliance notes:
- DQP manifests are signed with org-specific keys; private deployments must import org public keys into Appliance KeyStore.
- Telemetry Normalization v2 scrubs PII by default; customers with strict retention rules can opt into a redaction-only mode.

Operational runbooks (quick pointers):
- Rollback fidelity advisor to safe-mode: Console -> Fidelity -> Global -> safe-mode -> enable. This switches all hints to "balanced" and disables per-request experimentation.
- Emergency rollback of DQP: POST /orgs/:org/profiles/_rollback with profile_id. This immediately reverts to last stable manifest.

Known issues (v1):
- In some mixed-batch streaming scenarios (large batch sizes > 128 tokens on older kernels) the advisor may under-estimate cache retention leading to 5–8% higher latency spikes. Workaround: temporarily pin profile to "low" on heavy streaming routes.
- Private deployment migration script requires curl >= 7.68; older appliances will need an update before migration.

Telemetry and evaluation methodology (how we measure fidelity regressions):
- Eval sets: tenant-provided representative prompts + standard reference sets (conversational-commons-1000, summarization-200).
- Metrics: BLEU/ROUGE variants for structured tasks, embedding-sim delta for semantic parity, and human raters for a 200-sample audit per tenant.
- Measurement windows: rolling 7-day and 30-day with anomaly-detection baseline.

Release owner and contact info:
- Release owner: Asha Menon (Product Manager, Optimize).
- Technical lead: Evan Kim (Eng, Optimize Conductor).
- Oncall rotation for rollout window: optimize-oncall@redwood.internal.

Post-release follow-ups (action items):
1. Run a 30-day post-launch quality audit and publish a summary report by 2027-02-20. Owner: product.
2. Evaluate cost impacts per major customer segment and propose pricing adjustments if DQP trial uplift > 20% cost savings. Owner: finance + go-to-market.

Appendix: CLI snippets and example manifests
- Example apply command (hosted):
  rwd-optimize apply-profile --org acme --profile-file acme-dqp-v1.json --mode progressive

- Example profile manifest (text summary):
  - profile_id: acme-dqp-v1
  - model_compat: [rw-llama-13b-quant, rw-gpt-6b-8bit]
  - quant_strategy: dynamic-int8
  - fallback: balanced
  - signed_by: optimize-team@redwood.internal

Change log (brief):
- 2026-12-20: initial internal staging build (v3.0.0-rc.1).
- 2026-12-28: added TN-v2 telemetry pipeline improvements and SDK hook iteration.
- 2027-01-07: hardened rollout thresholds and added DQP manifest signing.
- 2027-01-15: final docs and publish.

Document history and maintenance:
- Owner: product/optimize. Update cadence: as-needed during rollout, quarterly thereafter.

Related pages and references:
- See related product brief for Optimize Conductor (internal) and quantization coordination spec (links in metadata).

If you need migration assistance or a pilot slot, contact customer-success-optimize@redwood.internal.

title: dsid_7c52f59a57b9405a9fd26c83d43bd2f9__comp-and-bands-review-playbook-and-merit-process-2026.txt
text:
comp-and-bands-review-playbook-and-merit-process-2026

Summary
This playbook describes Redwood Inference’s annual compensation band review and merit cycle, plus the operational steps managers and people-ops must follow for offer approvals, pay adjustments, and pay-equity checks. It combines timeline, approval matrix, calibration guidance, communication templates, and escalation paths. Purpose: ensure fair, defensible, and timely compensation decisions that align with performance, market data, and budget constraints.

Scope
Applies to all full-time and permanent part-time employees in North America and Europe for Redwood-hosted payroll. Contractors and third-party temps follow separate vendor-pay guidelines (see vendor-finance). Covers base salary, spot bonuses, title changes tied to band movement, and merit increases. Does not cover equity refreshes or promotion bonus programs (handled by Total Rewards special programs).

Principles
- Market-driven: use up-to-date benchmark data (Mercer/Levels.fyi/internal comp bands).
- Pay-equity first: ensure adjustments reduce documented gaps by role, gender, and region before discretionary over-target increases.
- Manager accountability: managers own calibration preparation and written justification for out-of-band decisions.
- Transparency: employees receive clear rationale and timing for changes; non-confidential summaries published for org-level trends.

Definitions
- Band: pay band range for a role/level (e.g., ENG-3: $140k–$200k USD).
- Target midpoint: market-aligned midpoint used for benchmarking.
- Merit pool: team-level budget allocated for salary increases (percentage of payroll).
- Out-of-band increase: raise that would move base outside the role band or above the established band cap. Requires escalated approvals.

Compensation Bands (example table)
Role/Level | Region | Band Min | Band Midpoint | Band Max
ENG-2 | US (CR) | $110,000 | $135,000 | $160,000
ENG-3 | US (CR) | $140,000 | $170,000 | $200,000
SWE-Staff | US (CR) | $200,000 | $235,000 | $280,000
Product-PM-2 | US (CR) | $120,000 | $150,000 | $185,000
Note: Bands vary by region currency and cost-of-labor adjustments. Always reference the latest band CSV in People-ops -> Compensation -> current-bands.csv.

Annual Merit Cycle Overview (timeline)
1) Planning (Q4 prior fiscal year): People-ops publishes budget guidance and merit pool % targets to Heads of Org. Example: company target merit pool = 6% of base payroll for FY26; teams may be allocated between 3%–9% depending on performance and hiring posture.
2) Calibration & Manager Prep (Jan): Managers prepare draft increases, linking to performance reviews and calibration docs. People-ops schedules calibration windows by department.
3) Executive Calibration (Feb): Cross-org calibration meetings with Director+ to review above-target requests and out-of-band moves.
4) Final Approvals (early Mar): Finance and People-ops finalize budgets and sign off.
5) Payroll Cutover (mid Mar): HR inputs finalized changes to payroll provider; effective date is first full pay period in April.
6) Employee Communications (same week as cutover): Managers deliver 1:1 messages with pay letters and FAQs.

Manager Checklist (before submitting increases)
- Confirm employee's band and current comp vs midpoint and market comp.
- Attach performance summary: top 3 accomplishments, evidence of impact, and rating.
- Show proposed increase, new base, and % of merit pool used.
- For out-of-band requests, include business rationale, retention risk analysis, and suggested alternate mitigations (bonus, promotion timeline).
- Check for potential pay-equity regressions in your team (people-ops will run automated checks but managers should flag anomalies).

Calibration & Decision Rules
- Standard increases: up to 6% for most employees (guided by band position and performance rating).
- High-performer increases: 6%–12% with documented impact and peer calibration support.
- Promotions with role/level change: typically include base increase of 10%–20% depending on band movement; must be accompanied by new role description and promotion packet.
- Out-of-band (above band max): CTO or People Ops VP approval required + Director-level justification.
- If requested increase exceeds available merit pool, managers must prioritize based on retention risk and business criticality and provide rebalancing plan.

Approval Matrix (who signs what)
- Manager (team level): sign-off on proposed increases and file documentation.
- Director: approves standard increases and promotions within team budget.
- People-ops Lead: approves calibration exceptions up to $X total additional spend per month (internal threshold).
- VP People Ops + Finance: signs off on out-of-band moves, comp compression resolutions > 10% gap, and region-level policy changes.

Offer & Hiring Exceptions (fast-track rules)
- Standard offers: within band and sign-on threshold require Manager + Recruiter approval.
- Above-band offers <= 10% above band max: Director + People-ops approval (expedites available for time-sensitive hires).
- Critical hires or counteroffers that exceed 10% above band max: require VP People Ops + Finance and an approved business case.
- Emergency retention increases: documented retention risk, attempted interventions (bonus, non-monetary), and a 6-month follow-up plan.

Pay Transparency Guidance (manager-facing)
- Public information: high-level band ranges and compensation philosophy are published internally.
- Private information: individual salary numbers are confidential and should not be disclosed by managers except to payroll, finance, or people-ops staff with legitimate business need.
- Manager talking points for 1:1s: focus on performance impact, development plan, and timing. If asked directly about peer salaries, defer to People-ops and offer to explain band structure instead.

Template: Manager 1:1 Pay Conversation
1) Affirm contribution and context: "I appreciate your work on X; because of the impact on Y, we've recommended..."
2) Explain change succinctly: "Your new base will be $XXX, effective April 1. This reflects performance/market/promotions."
3) Next steps: "We'll update payroll and you’ll see the increase on your next paycheck; here's the development plan that supports continued growth."
4) If asked about colleagues: use band-level and philosophy language; do not disclose numbers.

Escalations and Appeals
- Employee questions escalate to manager -> People-ops rep -> HRBP -> VP People-ops. People-ops maintains an appeals log.
- Appeals must be submitted within 30 days of communication and should include the employee’s rationale and supporting evidence.
- People-ops will respond with a timeline for review (typical response: 10 business days).

Operational Runbook: Submitting a Request
1) Manager completes the Compensation Worksheet (People-ops -> Templates -> comp-worksheet.xlsx).
2) Attach performance summary and promotion packet (if relevant).
3) Submit via People-ops compensation portal by the calibration deadline.
4) People-ops runs automated equity and compression checks and returns an exception flag report.
5) If exception flagged, manager addresses or escalates with added justification.

Data & Reporting Requirements
- Every increase must be recorded in the compensation ledger with: employee ID, current/base salary, new salary, effective date, approver names, and justification.
- People-ops publishes anonymized quarterly compensation health dashboards (labels: median-to-midpoint ratio, gender pay gap by level, out-of-band %).

Common Scenarios & Guidance
- Compression (junior > senior): file a compression mitigation plan; prioritize critical cases for immediate adjustment.
- Cross-region adjustments: use regional cost-of-labor multiplier table; consult People-ops for exchange-rate locked effective dates.
- Promotion denied after performance rating improved: provide written developmental plan and reassessment timeline (usually next 6 months).

FAQs
Q: When will I see my increase?
A: Effective date aligns with payroll cutover (first full pay period in April).
Q: Can managers give raises outside the merit cycle?
A: Spot increases are rare — limited to retention or market-correction situations and require documented exception.

Appendix: Useful Links
- Compensation band CSV: People-ops -> current-bands.csv
- Compensation worksheet template: People-ops -> Templates -> comp-worksheet.xlsx
- Appeals form: People-ops -> Compensation Appeals -> submit-a-claim
- Payroll provider integration docs and cutover checklist: Finance -> Payroll -> payroll-cutover.md

Ownership & Contacts
- Document owner: Aisha Patel (People Ops Manager)
- Operational contact: Marcus Chen (Total Rewards Sr. Analyst)
- Policy steward: VP People Ops (for policy changes and executive approvals)

Revision history
- 2025-04-15: Created (initial framework and band examples).
- 2026-02-12: Updated merit pool guidance and approval thresholds; added remote-region multiplier note.

This playbook is the authoritative guidance for compensation and merit processes at Redwood Inference. For exceptions or region-specific questions, contact the operational contact listed above.

title: dsid_2b85fd14da474f0d93b15dac96a7034d__gpu-plugin-release-gatekeeper-and-experimentation-runbook.txt
text:
GPU plugin release gatekeeper and experimentation runbook

Overview

This runbook describes the release gatekeeper and experimentation workflow for GPU runtime plugins and related IaC/CI artifacts. It consolidates the safe rollout patterns we use when introducing new kernel changes, operator plugins, and Terraform module updates that affect GPU allocation, scheduling, or runtime behavior. The goal is to enable frequent, measurable experiments while minimizing blast radius and providing an operator-focused rollback path.

Scope

- Applies to changes that touch: runtime plugins (CUDA/cuDNN wrappers, mixed-precision kernels), scheduler hooks, kube-device-plugin updates, device-plugin CRDs, and Terraform modules that change GPU pool topology or autoscaling policies.
- Not for model weights or purely application-level changes (those follow application release processes).

Motivation

GPU plugin changes can produce subtle performance regressions or availability problems (OOMs, kernel timeouts, NVLink saturation). We need a single, well-documented path for CI gating, canary experiments, and rapid rollback so SRE and infra engineers can act quickly during incidents.

Key concepts and definitions

- Gatekeeper: the CI pipeline stage (and human review step) that prevents unsafe changes from reaching production GPU pools.
- Canary cohort: a reserved subset of tenants and runtime instances used for early verification.
- Fractional routing: traffic split controlled by traffic router to send X% of inference requests to new plugin variant.
- Safe-mode: a runtime fallback that disables the plugin and uses a verified baseline kernel path.

Design overview

1) Preflight validations (automated): unit tests, kernel-level microbenchmarks (latency and memory), IaC plan diffs, and model smoke evals ran against canary images.
2) CI gate: artifact promotion blocked unless benchmarks meet thresholds and all checks pass. Human reviewers can override with documented justification.
3) Canary rollout: staged policy that attaches new plugin to a reserved canary GPU pool, backs up KV caches, and enables fractional routing.
4) Observation window & experiment metrics: performance, error rates, OOMs, and cost delta tracked for a minimum observation window (see thresholds).
5) Decision and rollout: promote to broader pools only when success criteria met. If not, automated rollback to baseline.

Preflight checklist (automated + manual)

- CI must run kernel microbenchmarks (P50, P95 latency for 128/512/2048 token sequences) comparing new plugin vs baseline.
- Terraform plan must be approved; diff must not modify production GPU pool sizes without explicit capacity sign-off.
- Smoke eval: run 3 representative prompts per model family for deterministic regressions.
- Security scan of plugin binary for SLSA provenance and signatures.
- Disk and NVMe throughput tests on sample nodes.

Thresholds (gates)

- Latency regression: P95 increase <= 10% for 512-sequence workloads.
- Error rate: increase <= 0.5 percentage points over traffic baseline.
- OOMs: zero OOMs during a 30-minute stress run on canary nodes.
- Resource delta: GPU utilization increase <= 15% at equivalent throughput.

CI/CD pipeline steps (numbered)

1. Developer opens PR that includes: code, changelog, and an integration test manifest (test cluster config reference).
2. CI runs unit tests and builds plugin artifact (container + signed checksum).
3. CI executes microbenchmarks in an ephemeral GPU sandbox and posts results to PR.
4. IaC job runs terraform plan against a dry-run workspace. Changes to production pools trigger a blocked state requiring "infra-approver" review.
5. If automated gates pass, PR enters "gatekeeper_pending" and sends reviewers. Reviewer must: check logs, confirm canary plan, and approve within 48 hours or request more tests.
6. On approval, CI publishes canary artifact tag (e.g., plugin:v2025-01-18-canary) and kicks off canary rollout pipeline.

Canary rollout procedure

1. Provision canary GPU pool using a stable IaC module and tag nodes with `canary=true`. Keep pool size small (3-6 GPUs).
2. Deploy plugin container to canary pool using the runtime operator with feature flags: enable plugin behind runtime flag `runtime.pluginX.enabled=true`.
3. Seed canary cohort: attach 3 internal tenants + 1 synthetic load generator to canary pool. No production customer traffic unless explicit opt-in and written consent.
4. Set fractional routing to 10% initially for 2 hours, 25% for next 2 hours, then 50% for 4 hours if metrics stable.
5. Observation window: minimum 8 hours total with at least one daily peak.

Metric dashboards and SLOs to monitor

- Throughput (tokens/sec) and per-request latency P50/P95/P99.
- GPU metrics: SM utilization, memory alloc failures, GPU temperature, NVLink error counters.
- Node metrics: CPU steal, network egress, disk IOPS.
- Application error budget: 5-minute rolling error-rate and 1-hour rolling error-rate tracked.
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - P95 latency increase > 15% over baseline for 10 minutes -> SEV-2.
  - Any new OOM on canary pool -> SEV-1.
  - GPU ECC errors or NVLink CRC errors -> SEV-1.

Automated rollback and safe-mode activation

- If any SEV-1 condition fires: immediately flip feature flag to disable plugin and re-schedule nodes to baseline runtime. CI pipeline will mark the canary tag as failed.
- For SEV-2 conditions: hold rollout, pause fractional routing at current level, run targeted diagnostics scripted below.

Rollback steps (ordered)

1. Disable fractional routing: set traffic-split to 0% for plugin variant.
2. Flip runtime flag to baseline: `kubectl patch deployment runtime-operator -n redwood --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/0/value","value":"false"}]'` (example).
3. Drain canary pool and cordon nodes for postmortem.
4. Re-deploy baseline plugin from signed artifact.
5. Run immediate smoke evals and validate metric baseline is restored.

Incident diagnostic checklist (for SRE oncall)

- Collect plugin container logs from all canary pods: `stern plugin -n runtime --selector=canary=true`
- Pull kernel messages on host: `sudo journalctl -k --since "-30m" | grep -i nv`
- Query GPU counters via nvidia-smi and nvprof where available.
- Check recent Terraform apply runs and IaC diffs for accidental topology changes.
- Capture top models causing spikes and isolate via routing.

Experimentation guidance (AB tests and QoE measurements)

- Use multi-arm experiments: compare baseline vs pluginX vs pluginY with traffic-split and hypothesis-driven metrics (latency and quality proxies).
- Randomization: route based on request id hash to avoid correlated traffic.
- Minimum sample sizes: ensure at least 50k requests per arm for high-traffic endpoints; scale down for low-volume endpoints but extend observation window.
- Quality proxies: use eval prompts tied to model outputs and automated regression detectors (token-level divergence, repetition metrics).

Example GitHub Actions snippet (canary publish job)

```yaml
name: Publish Canary
on: [workflow_dispatch]
jobs:
  build-and-publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build plugin container
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/redwood/pluginX:${{ github.run_id }} -f docker/Dockerfile .
      - name: Sign artifact
        run: |
          cosign sign --key ${{ secrets.COSIGN_KEY }} ghcr.io/redwood/pluginX:${{ github.run_id }}
      - name: Publish canary tag
        run: |
          docker tag ghcr.io/redwood/pluginX:${{ github.run_id }} ghcr.io/redwood/pluginX:canary-${{ github.run_id }}
          docker push ghcr.io/redwood/pluginX:canary-${{ github.run_id }}
```

Terraform module example (version pin and safety flags)

```hcl
module "gpu_pool_canary" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-iac/gpu-pool.git//module?ref=v1.14.2"
  name   = "canary"
  size   = 3
  labels = { canary = "true" }
  lifecycle = {
    prevent_destroy = true
  }
}
```

Rollout governance and approvals

- Any plugin that modifies kernel launch parameters or memory pooling must have a TL or SRE approver in the PR.
- Changes that increase GPU pool max size or modify subnet routing require cloud-networking approval and billing sign-off.

Ownership, contacts and escalation

- Primary owner: infra-runtime team (oncall channel #infra-runtime).
- Secondary owner: gpu-fleet team.
- Oncall escalation: PagerDuty rotation `infra-runtime-pager`. If SEV-1, page the primary and the platform-engineering manager.

Postmortem and learnings

- Failed canaries require a postmortem within 5 business days with root cause analysis, impact timeline, and preventive actions. Share postmortem link on the PR and tag `release-failure`.

Appendix: common debugging commands

- `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv -l 5`
- `kubectl describe pod <pod> -n runtime`
- `stern runtime -n runtime-logs --selector=canary=true`

Change log

- 2024-09-12: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2024-11-05: Added automated microbenchmark gates and CI snippet.
- 2025-01-18: Formalized rollback procedure and fractional routing cadence.

Related docs and links

- See IaC module compatibility matrix and deprecation plan for module pinning guidance.
- See runbook: preflight-gpu-deployment-validation-and-rollback-playbook for preflight checklist details.

This document should be used by engineers and oncall responders as the canonical guide for safely releasing GPU runtime plugins and conducting controlled experiments on production-grade inference workloads. For process changes, update this page and notify the infra-runtime mailing list.

title: dsid_ba9518f1c10344b4a0fb5f7d82ca070b__prd-quantization-profile-library-opt-in.txt
text:
PRD: Quantization Profile Library (Opt-in, Route-level Enablement)

h1. Summary
Redwood Inference will launch an *opt-in Quantization Profile Library* that publishes *per-model, versioned quantization profiles* and enables customers to turn them on *per route* (and optionally scoped by region and/or deployment tier) to reduce inference cost while preserving quality and meeting latency SLOs.

This PRD defines user stories, product scope, API + Console requirements, rollout plan, and success metrics for v1.

h1. Goals (v1)
*G1. Stable, versioned profile schema per model variant*
* Profiles are stored in the model registry with validation and compatibility metadata.
* Profiles are versioned and immutable once published.

*G2. Safe route-level enablement controls*
* Customers can enable/disable a specific profile per route.
* Optional scoping by *region* and/or *deployment tier* (Hosted, Dedicated, Private) where supported.
* Changes are auditable and reversible.

*G3. Deterministic runtime selection and safe fallback*
* Runtime applies an approved profile deterministically when enabled and compatible.
* If incompatible or unavailable, system safely falls back to baseline (default precision) and emits clear signals.

*G4. Quality guardrails and rollout safety*
* Offline eval harness gates profile publication.
* Canary enablement + telemetry to detect regressions quickly.
* Rapid rollback (route-level disable + global kill-switch).

*G5. Documentation and support readiness*
* Clear customer docs for enablement, limitations, and troubleshooting.
* Support playbook and internal runbooks are ready before Beta.

h1. Non-goals (out of scope for v1)
* Fully automated per-customer profile recommendations or “auto-enable.”
* Online auto-tuning in production.
* Making quantization default-on across all routes/models.
* Guaranteeing bit-identical outputs between baseline and quantized modes.

h1. Background / Problem
Customers increasingly ask for concrete levers to reduce cost/token while maintaining production latency and quality. Quantization is a high-leverage technique, but in production it introduces risk:
* model/hardware incompatibilities,
* quality regressions on specific tasks,
* tail-latency changes due to kernel selection or memory/KV-cache behavior,
* operational complexity when rolling changes across fleets.

The Quantization Profile Library provides an approved and observable path to enable quantization in production safely, with deterministic behavior and strong rollback.

h1. Users and Personas
h2. Primary personas
1) *ML Engineer / Applied ML (customer-side)*
* Wants lower cost while maintaining eval scores.
* Needs ability to A/B compare baseline vs profile on a subset of traffic.

2) *Platform / Infra Engineer (customer-side)*
* Owns route configuration, latency SLOs, and incident response.
* Needs guardrails, compatibility warnings, audit logs, and quick rollback.

3) *Redwood internal operators*
* Applied ML: generate and publish profiles.
* Runtime + Platform: ensure deterministic apply/fallback and stable ops.
* SRE/Release: safe rollout and monitoring.

h1. User Stories
h2. Customer stories
*US-1 (Enablement):* As a platform engineer, I can enable a specific quantization profile on a route, so that only traffic to that route uses quantization.

*US-2 (Safety/Validation):* As a platform engineer, I receive a compatibility validation result (model + hardware + max context constraints) before enabling, so that I do not accidentally break production.

*US-3 (Auditability):* As a platform engineer at an enterprise, I can see who changed quantization settings, when, and what changed, for change-control and compliance.

*US-4 (Rollback):* As an oncall engineer, I can quickly disable the profile for a route and confirm the runtime has reverted to baseline.

*US-5 (Scoped rollout):* As an ML engineer, I can enable a profile for a specific region and/or tier first, so that I can canary in a low-risk environment before expanding.

*US-6 (Observability):* As a platform engineer, I can see applied vs fallback rates and cost/latency deltas for the route, so I can verify savings and detect regressions.

h2. Redwood internal stories
*US-7 (Publishing lifecycle):* As Applied ML, I can publish a new profile version after it passes the required eval suites and perf checks.

*US-8 (Kill-switch):* As SRE, I can globally disable quantization profiles during an incident and verify resolution.

h1. Definitions / Terminology
* *Quantization profile:* A versioned configuration + artifacts describing a quantized execution mode for a specific model variant, including constraints and known caveats.
* *Baseline:* Default serving precision for a route/model when no profile is enabled.
* *Profile ref:* The identifier stored in route config referencing a specific published profile version. (v1 requires explicit, versioned IDs.)
* *Compatibility:* Deterministic evaluation that the profile can be applied for the current request context (model variant, GPU class/SKU family, deployment tier, max context, etc.).
* *Fallback:* When enabled but incompatible/unavailable, system uses baseline and emits signals.

h1. Requirements
h2. Product requirements (functional)
1) *Profile library visibility*
* Customers can list available profiles for a given model/variant.
* Profiles include:
  * profile_id (versioned), quantization method, supported hardware classes, max context/sequence constraints, and status (published/deprecated).
  * “known caveats” and “recommended use cases” text.

2) *Route-level config*
* Route config supports an optional field:
  * quantization_profile_ref: "default" | <profile_id>
* Default behavior remains unchanged when unset or "default".
* Support optional per-region/per-tier overrides:
  * If implemented in v1: route-level base setting + override blocks by region/tier.
  * If not implemented for a specific deployment mode, API returns a clear error and Console hides/locks the control.

3) *Deterministic selection*
* For a given request context, the resolved outcome must be deterministic:
  * applied(profile_id) OR fallback(baseline) OR disabled.
* No “silent” changes: v1 does *not* auto-advance to newer profile versions.

4) *Compatibility guardrails*
* Control plane must validate at write-time:
  * route model_id/variant is compatible with the profile’s model_id/variant
  * deployment tier compatibility
  * GPU class/SKU family compatibility where known
  * max context constraints and any “blocked” contexts
* Runtime must validate at apply-time as a second line of defense and safely fallback.

5) *Audit logs and RBAC*
* Enabling/disabling/changing profile ref must produce an audit event containing:
  * actor identity, route identifier, before/after diff, timestamp, and effective scope (global/region/tier)
* RBAC: only users with appropriate permissions can modify quantization settings.

6) *Emergency controls*
* Global kill-switch to disable profile application platform-wide.
* Optional per-tenant “disable all profiles” override (if approved for v1; otherwise tracked as follow-up).

h2. API requirements
Note: endpoint names are representative; exact paths owned by Platform Control Plane (Ethan Park / Benji Okafor).

*Read APIs*
1) List available profiles for a model variant
* GET /v1/models/{model_id}/variants/{variant}/quantization-profiles
* Response includes profile_id, status, quant_method, precisions, constraints summary, and “known caveats”.

2) Get resolved quantization setting for a route
* GET /v1/routes/{route_id}/quantization-settings
* Returns stored configuration and effective resolved setting per scope (default + overrides).

3) Validate compatibility (preflight)
* POST /v1/routes/{route_id}/quantization-settings:validate
* Input: profile_id + optional region/tier scope
* Output: compatible=true/false, reasons[], and suggested remediation.

*Write APIs*
4) Update quantization setting
* PATCH /v1/routes/{route_id}/quantization-settings
* Supports:
  * set quantization_profile_ref to "default" or <profile_id>
  * optional region/tier override blocks (if in v1)
* Must be idempotent and write an audit log event.

*Error and safety semantics*
* Incompatible enablement returns 4xx with structured error codes (e.g., QUANT_PROFILE_INCOMPATIBLE, QUANT_PROFILE_NOT_FOUND, QUANT_PROFILE_DEPRECATED).
* “Write-time validation” failures must be explicit; do not accept config and rely on fallback.

*Caching and resilience*
* Profile metadata fetches must be cached and rate-limited to protect the model registry under high QPS.

h2. Console UX requirements
Owned by Console & Tooling (Dylan Brooks / Chloe Martin / Tessa Morgan).

1) *Placement and discoverability*
* Route detail page includes a “Quantization” section under Performance/Cost controls.

2) *Enablement flow*
* Dropdown/select to choose a profile version (profile_id) or Default.
* Compatibility preflight runs before allowing save.
* Confirmation modal includes:
  * Selected profile_id
  * Model variant and scope (route, region, tier)
  * Warning that outputs may change
  * Link to docs and recommended eval playbook

3) *Warnings and guardrails*
* Surface compatibility warnings with clear reasons:
  * hardware unsupported
  * max context exceeded
  * profile deprecated/blocked
* If the global kill-switch is active, show a banner and disable the toggle.

4) *Change history*
* Route shows a “Change History” panel with:
  * timestamp, actor, change diff, and links to audit event ID.

5) *Observability affordances*
* After enabling, Console presents quick links to dashboards filtered by route/model/region:
  * applied vs fallback rate
  * p95 latency
  * cost/token deltas
  * error rates

6) *Canary support*
* v1 requirement: Console supports staged enablement by scope (region/tier) as the primary canary mechanism.
* (Optional follow-up) Traffic-percentage splitting is out of scope unless already supported by existing route canary primitives.

h2. Documentation requirements (customer-facing)
Owned by DevEx (Alex Martinez / Elliot Price).
* Explain:
  * what a quantization profile is
  * how to enable per route (API + Console)
  * how to run A/B evals and monitor quality
  * troubleshooting: how to confirm applied vs fallback; common incompatibilities
  * rollback steps and kill-switch behavior (high level)

h1. Quality and Safety Guardrails
h2. Publication gates (before a profile is “published”)
Owned by Applied ML & Evals (Arjun Desai / Jonas Weber / Selene Huang).
* Required eval suites per quantization-regression-thresholds policy.
* Statistical testing and acceptable deltas by task family.
* Perf benchmark suite across key GPU SKUs for cost/token and tail latency.
* Explicit “blocked contexts” recorded in profile constraints (e.g., max context).

h2. Runtime apply/fallback rules
Owned by Serving Runtime (Noah Patel / Hiro Tanaka / Omar El-Sayed).
* Must annotate traces/logs with:
  * quant_profile_id
  * resolution outcome: applied | fallback | disabled
  * fallback reason (enum)
* Must not enter fallback loops; fallback is single-step to baseline.

h2. Rollback triggers
Owned by SRE/Release (Connor O'Brien) + Telemetry (Paula Mendes).
* Automated alerts (examples; final thresholds set in SRE dashboards):
  * fallback_rate > 1% sustained over 10 min on an enabled route
  * p95 decode latency regression > 10% vs baseline for 15 min
  * 5xx error rate increase > 0.2% absolute vs baseline
  * quality guardrail alert fired (per eval harness or online proxy metrics where available)

h1. Success Metrics
h2. Primary (must-hit)
* *Cost reduction:* Demonstrated cost/token reduction on targeted models with enabled profiles (goal: meaningful savings; tracked per model/profile, not a single global number).
* *Quality:* No statistically significant quality regression beyond agreed thresholds on Redwood prompt sets/eval suites for published profiles.
* *Latency:* Stable p95 latency for enabled routes within SLO and within acceptable regression bounds.
* *Operational overhead:* Rollback within minutes via route disable; clear diagnostics for applied vs fallback.

h2. Secondary
* Adoption: number of customers/routes enabling profiles during Beta and within 30/60 days post-GA.
* Support: low ticket volume per enabled route; time-to-resolution < 1 business day for common issues.
* Internal velocity: cadence for publishing new profiles (weekly or biweekly target during initial expansion).

h1. Rollout Plan
h2. Phase 0 — Discovery & Design (Complete/In progress)
Deliverables:
* ADR confirming route-level enablement strategy.
* Schema v1 finalized and validated.
* Threat model and safety analysis (quality regressions, incompatibility, metadata fetch amplification).

h2. Phase 1 — Implementation (Engineering)
Deliverables:
* Model registry storage, signing/integrity checks, versioning.
* Control plane APIs and policy evaluation with compatibility checks.
* Runtime load/apply + deterministic signals.
* Console UI and backend wiring.
* Audit events + RBAC.
* Kill-switch.

h2. Phase 2 — Validation (Internal)
Deliverables:
* Offline eval harness and perf suite run for initial set of models.
* perf-canary scenarios and automated regression checks.
* Game-day rollback drill (route disable + kill-switch).

h2. Phase 3 — Beta (2–3 design partners)
Target: Hosted + Dedicated, allowlisted tenants.
* Explicit opt-in per route with published profile versions.
* Close monitoring dashboards and weekly check-ins.
* Rollback criteria defined per partner.

h2. Phase 4 — GA
* Expand availability to self-serve customers with appropriate RBAC.
* Publish docs and support playbook.
* Ongoing profile publishing cadence and deprecation policy.

h1. Dependencies
* Model Registry (Quentin Harris): schema + storage + caching.
* Control Plane + Routing (Ethan Park, Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon): route config field + policy evaluation.
* Runtime (Noah Patel, Hiro Tanaka): kernel selection guardrails, KV-cache interactions.
* Observability (Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman): metrics and dashboard panels.
* Security (Marcus Lin, Naomi Feldman): RBAC/audit requirements.
* DevEx (Alex Martinez): docs + SDK examples.

h1. Risks and Mitigations
1) *Quality regressions on narrow prompt sets*
* Mitigation: strict eval gates; label profiles experimental; block publication if borderline.

2) *Incompatibility leading to silent performance changes*
* Mitigation: write-time validation + runtime validation; explicit fallback signals; no silent version advances.

3) *Metadata fetch spikes causing registry load*
* Mitigation: caching/rate-limiting in control plane and runtime; prefetch on rollout.

4) *Operational confusion (is it applied? why fallback?) *
* Mitigation: consistent error codes, Console warnings, trace/log annotations, dashboard panels.

h1. Open Questions
1) Should we support a “recommended” alias in v1?
* Current v1 stance: *No* (avoid silent changes). Re-evaluate after GA with explicit customer opt-in for alias semantics.

2) Do we ship per-tenant global disable override in v1?
* Proposed: include if low engineering risk and requested by enterprise security reviews; otherwise track as v1.1.

3) What is the minimal set of regions/tiers for scoped rollout in v1?
* Proposed: region scope first (Hosted), tier scope for Dedicated where routing primitives exist.

h1. Launch Criteria (Beta → GA)
* At least 2 design partners have successfully enabled profiles on production-like traffic with measured savings and no unresolved regressions.
* Console enable/disable works with audit logging and RBAC.
* Dashboards and alerts are live.
* Kill-switch tested in a rollback drill.
* Docs published with troubleshooting and rollback guidance.

h1. Appendix: Example Console copy (high level)
* “Quantization profiles can reduce cost/token but may change model outputs. Enable only after evaluating on your prompt set. You can roll back instantly by switching to Default.”

h1. Owners
* Product: Marissa Cole
* Program Management: Talia Benson
* Applied ML sponsor: Dr. Maya Srinivasan
* Runtime sponsor: Mateo Alvarez
* Platform sponsor: Priya Natarajan
* Rollout/Telemetry PM: Paula Mendes

title: dsid_038086c2041043ddb619843d47a7c601__probe-pruning-and-adaptive-sampling-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Probe Pruning and Adaptive Sampling Playbook

Summary

This playbook defines the probe pruning and adaptive sampling system used by the Eval Harness to keep continuous evaluations cost-effective while preserving signal for regression detection. It formalizes: probe scoring, pruning thresholds, an adaptive sampler that reallocates budget to high-variance slices, scheduler policies for burst/steady modes, and a safe rollout path for any changes.

Motivation

Large-scale continuous evaluation produces a long tail of low-value probes (very stable slices, duplicated semantics, or highly correlated prompts) that consume budget and increase noise in alerting. By pruning probes and adaptively sampling, we achieve:
- 30–60% reduction in probe execution cost for stable workloads
- Faster regression detection on volatile slices
- Lower false-positive alert rates from noisy low-variance probes

Scope

This document applies to:
- The Eval Harness scheduler (service: eval-sequencer)
- Probe catalog artifacts (probe registry and metadata)
- Continuous monitors and alerting rules tied to eval-sentinels

Not in scope: manual one-off experiments, offline research-curated benchmark runs.

Definitions

- Probe: a single stimulus (prompt + context) executed against a model variant and recorded with outputs and telemetry.
- Slice: logical grouping of probes (e.g., language, intent, length bucket).
- Stability score: running statistic (0..1) where 1 == perfectly stable across N recent runs.
- Importance score: business-weight multiplier (0.1..10) assigned by owners.

High-level architecture

1) Probe registry enriches probes with base metadata (slice, created_at, owner_team, importance).
2) Eval-sequencer assigns probes to worker queues according to adaptive-sample policy.
3) Pruner service periodically marks probes as "prune_candidate" based on scoring rules and retention config.
4) Audit logger records all prune actions and supports rehydration for 90 days.

Key metrics and thresholds (recommended defaults)

- Metric: Stability score (rolling 30-day window)
  - Thresholds: stable if >= 0.98, semi-stable if 0.95–0.98, unstable if < 0.95
- Metric: Sample variance (per-slice)
  - Action: reallocate +20% budget to slices with variance in top 10%
- Metric: Duplicate similarity (embeddings cosine)
  - Prune if cosine >= 0.995 to a higher-ranked probe in same slice
- Minimum retained probes per slice: 50 (unless slice cardinality < 50)

Pruning ruleset (ordered)

1) Structural deduplication: within a slice, group probes with embedding cosine >= 0.995 and keep the highest-importance/most-recent item.
2) Stability floor: for probes with stability >= 0.99 and age > 21 days, mark prune_candidate.
3) Low-importance culling: importance <= 0.2 and stability >= 0.97 -> prune if slice has > minimum retained probes.
4) Manual holdouts: probes with flag "do_not_prune" are preserved.

Adaptive sampling algorithm (overview)

The adaptive sampler reallocates probe budget per scheduling epoch (default 24h) based on per-slice signal. Steps:
- Compute per-slice priority = mean(importance * max(1, variance_score * 10)) * recent_violation_factor
- Normalize priorities to available budget (tokens / probe cost estimate)
- Ensure hard floor: every slice must receive >= 1% of epoch budget unless explicitly disabled

Pseudocode:

for each epoch:
  load slices S
  for s in S:
    compute importance_s, variance_s, violation_factor_s
    priority_s = importance_s * max(1, variance_s * 10) * violation_factor_s
  scale priorities so sum(priority) == epoch_budget
  assign probes to queue respecting per-slice minimums and per-probe dedup constraints

Scheduler policies

- Steady mode: evenly distributed probes across 24h with jitter; used for baselining.
- Burst mode: directed execution for top-K priority slices when on-call triage requests immediate re-eval or after new model rollout. Burst windows capped at 2h and require SRE approval.
- Canary mode: small fraction (default 2%) of new probe templates are exercised for 72h before being added to main catalog.

Configuration example (YAML snippet)

# eval-sampler-config.yaml
epoch_period: 24h
min_slice_budget_pct: 0.01
min_probes_per_slice: 50
stability_window_days: 30
dedup_cosine_threshold: 0.995
burst_mode_max_window: 2h
canary_fraction: 0.02
prune_scan_interval: 48h
prune_retention_days: 90

Rollout and change control

Any change to pruning thresholds or adaptive sampler weights must follow this path:
1) Draft change proposal in the eval-harness repo with benchmarks (description, config diff, expected savings/risks).
2) Submit PR and tag reviewers from applied-ml-and-evals and eng-sre.
3) Run controlled experiment (A/B) for 7 days: 10% traffic on new config vs 90% control. Record: detection latency for seeded regressions, cost delta, alert noise.
4) If experiment meets pass criteria (<=5% degradation in detection latency, >=10% cost improvement, no increase in high-severity alerts), schedule staged rollout: 10% -> 30% -> 60% -> 100% over 7 days with monitoring gates.
5) Post-rollout retrospective and update playbook if necessary.

Pass/fail gate checklist for A/B

- Regression detection latency: no more than 5% worse than control
- Alert precision on top-10 slices: not decreased by >3 percentage points
- Cost per epoch: >=10% improvement expected; if less, require product sign-off
- No increase in customer-facing incidents attributed to eval changes

Operational runbook (quick actions)

- If critical slice goes missing from schedule:
  1) Query pruner audit logs: "pruner.events?probe_id=<id>"
  2) Rehydrate probe from archival store (rehydrator CLI): "rehydrator restore --probe <id> --reason emergency"
  3) Temporarily mark slice as "holdout" in probe registry and set min_slice_budget_pct to 0.05
- If adaptive sampler is starving a high-importance slice:
  1) Pause prune job: "kubectl scale deployment/pruner --replicas=0 -n eval"
  2) Manually bump importance for affected slice in registry UI or via API
  3) Re-run epoch with debug logging enabled and capture schedule plan

Observability and alerts

Monitor these dashboards and alerts:
- Dashboard: Eval Sampling Overview (latency, cost, per-slice budget allocation)
- Alert: eval-sampler:budget-deviation > 25% for 2 epochs -> paged to applied-ml-oncall
- Alert: prune:unexpected-retention-drop when retained_probes_count < 60% expected -> pager
- Alert: canary-failures: > 3 seeded-regressions missed in 72h -> paged to product-owner and applied-ml-oncall

Data retention and auditability

- Pruner decisions are logged in audit store for 90 days.
- Full probe artifacts (inputs, outputs, embeddings) retained for 365 days for investigations.
- Rehydration API supports re-executing archived probes against historical models for reproducibility.

Safety & false-positive mitigation

- Never prune a probe used in a currently open incident ticket.
- Prioritize retention of probes tagged as regulatory or compliance-critical.
- For any prune action that would drop a probe with importance >= 5, require two approvers (applied-ml lead + product).

Troubleshooting checklist

- Symptom: sudden drop in per-slice probe count
  - Check prune job logs for recent sweeps and decisions.
  - Verify dedup threshold change in config history.
- Symptom: missed seeded regression in canary
  - Inspect canary fraction; confirm canary traffic was delivered.
  - Increase canary_fraction to 5% for next experiment if flakiness persists.

Ownership and contacts

- System owner: applied-ml-and-evals team (oncall: applied-ml-oncall rotation)
- Pruner service owner: runtime-quality squad (primary: Marcus Nguyen)
- Scheduler owner: eval-platform squad (primary: Aisha Patel)
- SRE escalation: eng-sre oncall (see runbook for page routing)

Appendices

A. Example dedup query (CLI)

# Find duplicates within slice=faq
probe-embeddings search --slice faq --similarity-threshold 0.995 --output csv | head -n 50

B. Example schedule inspection API

GET /api/v1/scheduler/plan?epoch=2026-02-09T00:00:00Z
Response fields: slice_id, assigned_probes, estimated_cost_tokens, priority_score

C. Change log
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft and internal review (Priya Shah)
- 2026-01-05: Added burst/canary policies and safe rollout gates (Liam O'Connor)
- 2026-02-10: Tightened dedup cosine default to 0.995 and clarified rehydration retention (Sofia Martinez)

If you have questions, file an issue in the eval-harness repo and tag @applied-ml-and-evals.

title: dsid_0b72a868b885486b91f3531a54a4d786__multi-vector-authz-incident-evidence-and-restoration-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Multi-Vector Authorization Incident: Evidence, Containment, and Restoration Playbook

Summary

This playbook defines the triage, containment, evidence collection, and restoration workflow for multi-vector authorization (authz) incidents affecting Redwood Inference services (hosted, dedicated, private). A multi-vector authz incident is any event where authorization failures or entitlements (RBAC/attributes/roles) are implicated across more than one boundary: user-facing API, internal service-to-service, and/or administrative control plane. The goal is to preserve provable evidence, contain blast radius, restore least-privilege state, and produce a compliance-grade evidence bundle within SLA.

Scope and non-goals

- Scope: incidents where authorization decisions, entitlement changes, or privileged token misuse lead to unauthorized data access, model invocation, or administrative actions. This includes combined failures with audit logging gaps or cross-region residency concerns.
- Non-goals: application-layer privilege bugs not involving RBAC policy (these belong to product bug triage).

Ownership and roles

1) Incident Commander (IC): Security on-call. Responsible for overall coordination and final evidence sign-off.
2) Authz Forensics Lead: Security engineer specializing in RBAC and identity stores (owner of evidence bundle).
3) Audit/Telemetry Lead: Observability engineer for log retrieval and retention snapshots.
4) Network & Residency Lead: Infra engineer responsible for geo/residency containment and data egress checks.
5) SRE/Platform Lead: Executes runtime containment (feature flags, policy rollbacks).
6) Legal & Compliance: Notified for incidents with cross-border data movement or customer scope.

Alerting and initial triage (first 60 minutes)

1) Triage checklist (IC or primary on-call):
   - Confirm alert source(s): SIEM, WAF, anomaly detector, or customer report. Note time and detection signals.
   - Capture scope: affected customer tenants, namespaces, models, and services.
   - Determine blast radius: user requests, service tokens, admin console actions.
   - Immediately preserve clocks and offsets: note UTC epoch, host times, and time sync status.

2) First-hour objectives (SLOs):
   - Contain obvious ongoing exploitation: 1 hour
   - Initial evidence snapshot captured and immutable: 1 hour
   - Legal notified if PII or cross-border data potentially exposed: 2 hours

Containment play (technical steps)

- Short-term containment (fast, reversible):
  - Revoke active session tokens for affected service/tenant. Example (internal token service):
    curl -X POST https://auth.redwood.internal/v1/sessions/revoke -d '{"scope":"tenant:abcd"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $IC_TOKEN'
  - Apply deny-listing policy to the implicated role(s) in the attribute broker (example):
    # One-line: set-role-state --role devops/cluster-admin --state suspended --reason "incident"
  - Deploy emergency feature flag to disable high-risk endpoints (console write actions, model rollouts).

- Medium-term containment (safe, audited):
  - Create scoped ACL overrides that restrict privileged operations to IC and Authz Forensics Lead for the investigation window.
  - Enable immutable logging for queues/runtimes where KV cache or model artifacts could be exfiltrated.
  - Preserve database snapshots (read-only) for affected tenants in a write-blocked storage bucket.

Evidence collection and preservation

Principles: collect chronological, provable, and tamper-evident artifacts. Prefer immutable exports, signed manifests, and checksums. Do not modify original artifacts; only create read-only copies.

Required evidence components (minimum):
- Entitlement change log (authorization graph deltas) for 90 days prior to incident start.
- Authentication/session tokens timeline (session create/revoke) and token binding info.
- Audit event stream for the affected services (application, control plane, admin console).
- Network flow metadata for cross-region endpoints and egress hosts.
- Model invocation logs (model id, prompt hash, output hash), if model-serving involved.
- Storage object access logs (S3/GCS access entries) and object checksums.
- KMS/HSM signing events and key-access logs if keys were used by any privileged ops.

Evidence snapshot procedure (step-by-step)

1) Create a forensic staging bucket (immutable) in the same region as data residency requires. Naming convention: redwood-forensics-<incident-id>-<region>.
2) Run audit export queries and stream to staging bucket with object-level metadata and sha256 checksums. Example query for clickhouse-style audit index:
   SELECT timestamp, tenant_id, actor, action, resource, decision, reason FROM authz_audit WHERE tenant_id IN ('t1','t2') AND timestamp >= '2026-02-20T10:00:00Z' ORDER BY timestamp ASC;
   Pipe output to: gzip | tee >(sha256sum > /tmp/audit.sha256) | aws s3 cp - s3://redwood-forensics-INC123/audit/audit-20260220.gz
3) Collect host-level forensic snapshots (memory/disk) only after Legal approval if required; otherwise collect process-level logs and syscalls.
4) Pull index of entitlements from attribute store: export attributes in CSV with schema header and sign the file with key-capture utility.
5) Export and sign any CI/CD release artifacts that coincide with suspicious admin actions (commit SHA, release id).

Audit log discovery queries (examples)

- Service audit events (Elasticsearch/Kibana DSL):
  {
    "query": {
      "bool": {
        "must": [ { "term": { "tenant_id": "t-123" } }, { "range": { "@timestamp": { "gte": "now-14d" } } } ]
      }
    }
  }
- Postgres for entitlement deltas: SELECT * FROM role_changes WHERE role_name = 'admin' AND created_at >= '2026-02-20' ORDER BY created_at;

Evidence packaging and chain-of-custody

- Forensic bundle manifest fields (text file): incident_id, collector, collection_time_utc, region, object_paths, sha256s, signature_key_id, legal_hold_flag, hashing_algorithm.
- Every artifact must be accompanied by a signed manifest entry. Use the internal signing tool:
  sign-artifact --key-id=forensics-2026 --file=/tmp/audit-20260220.gz --out=/tmp/audit-20260220.gz.sig
- Maintain chain-of-custody log in our case management system (security-incidents/INC-123) recording who accessed each staging object and when.

Data residency and cross-border considerations

- If evidence contains residency-restricted customer data, keep copies only in regionally compliant forensics buckets and set confidentiality=restricted.
- If a copy must be moved for law enforcement or cross-region analysis, the Network & Residency Lead must record the legal basis and update the manifest with destination region and legal approval ID.

Restoration, remediation, and authorization hardening (post-containment)

1) Determine rollback vs. patch: if entitlement change was human error (e.g., bad rollout), prefer rollback to last-good policy snapshot. If root cause is a policy enforcement bug, deploy an annotated patch with tests.
2) Enforce short-term role rotation: rotate secrets for any service account that had elevated access (SLO: rotation within 4 hours for direct compromise suspects).
3) Reapply least-privilege baseline and run the entitlement conformance test-suite (see SDLC section below).

Post-incident evidence workflow and compliance deliverables

- Deliver an evidence bundle within 72 hours containing: manifest, signed audit exports, signed entitlement snapshot, network metadata, and a remediation timeline.
- For incidents impacting customers, produce a customer-facing summary template and a redacted evidence bundle scoped to the customer and approved by Legal.

SDLC integration and forward controls

- All authorization policy changes must pass the pre-deploy policy static analysis and test-suite (policy-lint, policy-simulate, policy-e2e). The incident should seed new unit/integration tests that replicate the failure vector.
- CI gate: policy changes touching high-privilege roles require two approvers from the security rota and a signed justification comment in the PR.
- Release-time evidence hook: any admin console change triggers an automatic audit snapshot that is stored for 180 days.

Automation snippets and useful commands

- Create immutable S3 object with retention (example):
  aws s3api put-object --bucket redwood-forensics-INC123 --key audit/audit-20260220.gz --body ./audit-20260220.gz --metadata file-signer=EvelynPark --object-lock-mode GOVERNANCE --object-lock-retain-until-date 2030-12-31T00:00:00Z
- Query session store for active tokens (redis example):
  redis-cli -h session-cache.redwood keys 'session:*tenant:t-123*' | xargs -L1 redis-cli -h session-cache.redwood ttl > /tmp/session-ttls.txt

Retention, legal hold and evidence lifecycle

- Default evidence retention: 7 years for high-severity incidents; 3 years for moderate incidents unless Legal extends.
- Legal hold takes precedence over normal retention; manifests must include legal_hold_flag=true.

Reporting and postmortem requirements

- Trigger post-incident review (PIR) for Sev 1/2 incidents within 7 calendar days. PIR deliverables: timeline, root cause, remediation verification, regression tests added to CI, and evidence bundle index.
- Update risk register entry for the affected entitlement patterns and track mitigation completion in the quarterly roadmap.

Appendix: quick-reference checklist

1) Triage & notify: IC, Authz Lead, Audit Lead, Legal (if PII) — within 1 hour.
2) Contain: revoke tokens, suspend implicated roles, feature-flag endpoints — within 1 hour.
3) Snapshot evidence to immutable staging bucket with sha256 and signatures — within 1 hour.
4) Package manifest, sign artifacts, log chain-of-custody — within 24 hours.
5) Deliver compliance-grade evidence bundle and customer communications (if applicable) — within 72 hours.

Appendix: contacts & escalation

- Security on-call: security-oncall@redwood.example (primary pager)
- Legal emergency: legal-oncall@redwood.example
- SRE paging: sre-pager@redwood.example

Document history and references

- Created: 2025-11-18 by Evelyn Park
- Major revision: 2026-03-01 expanded residency guidance and added signature workflow
- Related: see entitlements test-suite in eng-platform/team-wiki and audit-schema contract pages listed in Related Pages section.

End of playbook

title: dsid_50f8bc252e104f678d0b61ffe3e562c3__access-change-data-procurement-handbook-2024.txt
text:
Access, Change, Data, and Procurement Operational Handbook

Purpose
-------
This handbook consolidates company-wide policies and standardized processes for access & permissions, change management, data management, procurement & expenses, vendor management, travel, and the canonical templates used across Redwood Inference. It is intended for managers, approvers, engineering leads, security, finance, and people-ops staff responsible for compliance and day-to-day operations.

Scope
-----
Applies to all Redwood employees, contractors, and third-party vendors with accounts on company systems or who perform work on behalf of Redwood. This document covers:
- Identity lifecycle (onboarding, role changes, offboarding)
- System and infrastructure change controls (standard and emergency)
- Data classification, handling, and retention
- Procurement, purchase orders, and expense reconciliation
- Vendor onboarding, due diligence, and SLA expectations
- Business travel approvals and allowable expenses
- Reusable templates for requests and approvals

Principles (applies to all sections)
--------------------------------
- Least privilege by default: grant the minimal access necessary and approve broader access only with documented justification.
- Separation of duties: no single individual should both request and permanently approve high-impact changes or vendor payments.
- Traceability: every access grant, change, and procurement action must be auditable with an owner and timestamped approval.
- Risk-based controls: higher sensitivity data and critical infrastructure require elevated review and approval paths.

Roles & Responsibilities
------------------------
- Requester: initiates access/change/procurement/travel request with justification and required attachments.
- Approver: business manager and/or owner of the resource; approves only requests within their authority.
- Security/Compliance: performs risk assessment for access to sensitive data and vendor security reviews.
- Finance/Procurement: validates budgets, issues POs, and processes vendor payments.
- IT/Platform: performs technical implementation for access and change requests; records implementation notes.
- People-Ops: ensures identity lifecycle aligns to employment status and schedules access reviews.

Access & Permissions
--------------------
Access categories:
1) Standard Access — tools for daily work (Slack, Email, Confluence). Granted by manager approval, auto-provisioned via Okta groups. SLA: 1 business day.
2) Elevated Access — production consoles, admin roles, database access. Requires manager approval + technical owner approval + security review. SLA: 3 business days.
3) Temporary/Emergency Access — timeboxed elevated access for incidents or critical work. Must be requested with explicit expiry and post-action audit.
4) Service Accounts — machine/service identities used by infrastructure. Managed via identity-service (idp-redwood) with lifecycle tags.

Access request process (standard)
1. Complete Access Request template (see Templates section). Include justification, data sensitivity level, and expected duration.
2. Manager approves in JIRA access-requests board.
3. Technical owner (resource owner) reviews and verifies minimal required scope.
4. Okta automation adds user to the relevant group; IT documents the change in the ticket.
5. Requester confirms access and closes ticket.

Access review and attestation
- Quarterly automated reviews for all admins and service accounts.
- Semi-annual attestation by resource owners for access to systems categorized as "sensitive" (see Data Classification).
- Revocation target: access flagged for removal should be revoked within 5 business days.

Change Management
-----------------
Change categories:
- Low-risk (configuration tweaks, documentation updates): owner approval + single approver. Target lead time: ad-hoc.
- Standard (non-breaking infra changes, deployment to staging): change request submitted, business owner approval, SRE review. Planned maintenance windows preferred.
- High-impact (schema migrations, production DB changes, network changes, model rollout with >10% customer impact): change advisory board (CAB) approval required and rollout plan + rollback plan + monitoring checklists. Notice period: 72 hours.
- Emergency: use Emergency Change procedure; must be declared by on-call SRE or engineering lead. Follow-up: retrospective within 48 hours and formal change record within 5 business days.

Standard change request workflow
1. Create a JIRA change-ticket using the Change Request template.
2. Attach runbook/rollout plan: steps, expected timeline, feature gates, metrics to watch, rollback steps.
3. Triage by platform on-call; categorize risk.
4. If required, schedule for CAB review; CAB meets Tue/Thu 09:00 PT for high-impact windows.
