5. After approvals, schedule rollout in maintenance window and coordinate with SRE and support.
6. Post-deploy: run smoke tests, annotate incident metrics, and close change ticket with results.

Emergency change handler (minimum fields)
- Declaration by: name, role, time, and incident ID.
- Reason and risk summary.
- Actions taken and owners for each step.
- Post-change review owner and timeline.

Change metrics & thresholds
- Percentage of emergency changes (target < 5% of changes per quarter).
- Rollback rate (target < 1% of standard changes).
- Change-related incidents within 30 days (target: zero high-severity incidents).

Data Management & Classification
--------------------------------
Data sensitivity categories:
- Public: meant for public consumption, no protections required.
- Internal: company information not for public release but not legally protected. Basic access controls.
- Restricted: PII, financials, customer data (non-aggregated), model training datasets with customer content. Requires encryption at rest and in transit, limited access, and audit logging.
- Regulated: data subject to legal/regulatory controls (HIPAA, PCI, regional data residency). Requires additional contractual and technical controls; contact Security & Legal before processing.

Handling rules (restricted/regulatory)
- Storage: only approved storage classes in GCP/AWS with encryption and logging enabled.
- Transfer: use secure channels (TLS 1.2+) and SFTP/transfer appliances where required.
- Masking/Anonymization: remove or tokenize PII prior to use in development or eval environments.
- Backups: encrypted backups with retention per retention table below and periodic restore tests.

Retention & deletion
- Default: 3 years for internal operational logs; 7 years for financial and contract records unless otherwise stated.
- Personal data: retention driven by legal requirements and data subject requests.
- Deletion process: submit Deletion Request template, include scope, datasets, and retention justification. Implement and verify deletion with a checksum audit.

Data access controls & monitoring
- All access to Restricted/Regulated datasets must be logged and reviewed monthly for anomalies.
- Anomaly thresholds: more than 10 distinct data exports by one user in 7 days triggers an investigation.

Procurement & Expenses
----------------------
Procurement tiers and approval thresholds (USD):
- Tier 0 (<= $1,000): Requester + Manager approval. Credit card purchase allowed.
- Tier 1 ($1,001 - $25,000): Requester + Manager + Finance approval. PO required for vendors.
- Tier 2 ($25,001 - $250,000): Procurement + Legal + Finance + Exec Sponsor approval. Competitive bidding encouraged.
- Tier 3 (> $250,000): Board-level notification & multi-vendor RFP recommended.

Vendor onboarding checklist
1. Business justification + budget code.
2. Vendor security questionnaire (standard vendor-security-questionnaire.pdf).
3. Contract review: Legal must sign off.
4. PO issuance and finance coding.
5. Technical integration plan and data flow diagram if vendor handles company data.
6. SLA and monitoring expectations documented and owner assigned.

Expense policy highlights
- Airfare: economy for domestic; business class allowed for flights >8 hours with Exec approval.
- Lodging: reasonable single room rate in line with corporate travel band.
- Meals and incidentals: per diem or receipts (choose one per trip); private events require advance approval.
- Personal expenses are not reimbursable (e.g., family upgrades, leisure).
- Receipts required for all expenses > $25; card statements alone are insufficient.

Payment and reconciliation
- Net 30 standard for vendor invoices unless contract specifies otherwise.
- Finance performs monthly reconciliation of POs and expense reports. Discrepancies > $500 require escalation to the requester’s manager.

Vendor Management & SLAs
-----------------------
- Security due diligence: all vendors with access to Restricted data must complete security questionnaire and a pen-test summary where required.
- SLA minimums: uptime targets, response time objectives, and incident escalation paths. Critical vendors must provide four-hour incident response commitments and a 99.9% monthly uptime objective unless otherwise negotiated.
- Contract clauses required: data residency, breach notification (<=72 hours), liability limits, SLAs, and termination/exit clauses for data extraction.

Vendor review cadence
- Annual security review for vendors handling Restricted/Regulated data.
- Quarterly performance review for top 10 spend vendors.

Travel Policy (business travel)
-------------------------------
Pre-approval: all trips > $500 must be pre-approved in Concur (or approved travel tool) with estimated budget and duration.
Booking guidelines:
- Use corporate travel portal where available.
- Schedule meetings to maximize overlap and reduce duplicate trips.
Safety & emergency: travelers must enroll in Redwood travel safety program and share itinerary with People-Ops.
Domestic per diem example:
- Meals: $60/day
- Incidentals: $10/day
International per diem: varies by country; use Finance country band lookup.

Templates (canonical, copy/paste to JIRA/Confluence)
--------------------------------------------------
1) Access Request (short):
- requester: NAME
- role: requested-role
- system: e.g., "prod-db-redwood"
- justification: Business reason (link to ticket)
- duration: e.g., 7 days (for temporary)
- approvals required: Manager; technical owner; security if Restricted
2) Change Request (short):
- change-summary: brief description
- risk-category: Low/Standard/High
- owner: implementer name
- planned-start: YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM TZ
- rollback-plan: steps to revert and verification
- monitoring: metrics to watch and thresholds
3) Vendor Onboarding:
- vendor-name, service-description, data-handled, contract-owner, PO-required(Y/N), security-questionnaire-complete(Y/N)
4) Travel Expense:
- traveler, dates, purpose, itinerary, total-amount, receipts-attached(Y/N), policy-exception(Y/N)

Appendix A — Retention table (examples)
- Contracts: 7 years
- Financial records: 7 years
- Access logs (standard): 90 days online, archived for 3 years
- Audit logs (sensitive infra): 1 year online, archived 7 years

Appendix B — Quick CLI snippets and examples
- Add Okta group (example):
  curl -X POST https://idp-redwood.example/api/groups -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"name":"prod-readonly","description":"Prod readonly group"}'
- Exporting dataset (must be approved):
  gsutil cp gs://redwood-restricted-datasets/experiment1.tar.gz /secure-transfer/

Governance & Review cadence
---------------------------
- This handbook is owned by Finance-Legal and reviewed quarterly by a cross-functional governance committee (Finance, Security, People-Ops, Platform, Product).
- Major policy changes require a 30-day comment period and approval from Exec Leadership.

Contact & escalation
--------------------
- Policy owner (Finance-Legal): finance-ops@redwood.ai
- Security intake: security-intake@redwood.ai
- Procurement: procurement@redwood.ai
- People-Ops (travel & onboarding): people-ops@redwood.ai

Change log
----------
- 2024-09-15: Initial published draft.
- 2024-12-10: Added emergency change procedure and updated access review cadence.
- 2025-02-10: Clarified procurement thresholds and vendor SLA expectations.

End of document

title: dsid_42bff1d59d404db5b5becf1b03ce720f__local-developer-runtime-sandbox-design-spec-2026-02-12.txt
text:
Local Developer Runtime and Sandbox – Design Spec

Overview

This design spec describes the Local Developer Runtime (LDR) and Sandbox: a lightweight, offline-capable packaging of Redwood inference primitives intended for fast iteration, reproducible QA, and preflight performance/cost simulation. The LDR lets developers run a constrained subset of Redwood features locally or in CI with realistic latency and cost signals while preserving safety and telemetry guarantees for product analytics.

Goals

- Provide a low-friction developer experience for prototyping integrations, prompt engineering, and tests without requiring hosted credentials or GPU access.
- Surface representative latency and token-cost estimates that are consistent with hosted Redwood economics for small-scale workloads.
- Support parity with a subset of API features: text generation, chat, embeddings, and function/tool calling.
- Enable CI/integration tests to run deterministically using recorded sample models or micro-models.
- Offer clear upgrade paths to Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes.

Non-Goals

- The LDR is not intended to replicate production throughput or horizontal scalability.
- It will not expose reserved capacity management, multi-tenant billing, or SLA-backed telemetry retention.
- It is not a vehicle for serving customer traffic in production.

User Personas

1) Product Engineers: rapid prompt iteration and local experiment harnesses.
2) Platform Engineers: CI validation of integration and telemetry.
3) Solutions Engineers / SEs: demoing to customers in air-gapped environments.

High-level Architecture

The LDR is a single-package distribution composed of three layers:

1. Core runtime shim: a small, CPU-optimized binary that implements Redwood API compatibility (request/response shapes, streaming hooks, function-calls). The shim routes requests either to: a) bundled micro-model (small distilled model for deterministic output) or b) a remote-hosted proxy when the developer chooses to exercise hosted models.

2. Model artifacts: one or more pinned micro-model weights (quantized FP16/INT8 where license allows) plus a test catalog (prompt sets, sample KV-cache dumps).

3. Developer tooling: CLI, local dashboard (single-page static UI), and test harness libraries for Node/Python to simulate token accounting and telemetry in alignment with backend heuristics.

Data and Control Flow (textual diagram)

- Developer client (SDK/CLI) -> LDR runtime shim -> (bundled micro-model | remote proxy) -> LDR telemetry sink (local file / optional forwarded telemetry).

Compatibility and Feature Matrix

| Feature | LDR v1 | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Text generation (sync) | Supported | Uses micro-model; deterministic sampling by default. |
| Streaming responses | Supported | Buffered streaming emulation with configurable latency knobs. |
| Chat state management | Supported | In-memory conversation storage; optional KV-cache snapshot load. |
| Embeddings | Supported (reduced-dim) | Must flag `--low-dim` to match offline models. |
| Function/tool calling | Supported (sync) | Handler hooks mirror production API; no external tool sandboxing. |
| Adaptive batching | Not supported | Out of scope for V1. |
| Quantization profiles | Supported | Shipping INT8 profiles for CPU inference as examples. |

Security and Licensing

- All included model artifacts will be cleared by Legal and Research before release. Only models with redistributable licenses will be bundled.
- The runtime will validate API keys for remote proxy calls; local mode can be started without keys but will emit an audit banner.
- Telemetry is opt-in by default. When enabled, telemetry is scrubbed of PII and batched locally. A clear `--telemetry=off|local|forward` flag controls behavior.

Developer UX: CLI and SDK

1) CLI quickstart:

- Install: pipx / npm / brew package (packaging TBD).
- Start local sandbox: `rdw sandbox start --mode local --port 8080`
- Send a request via curl:

```
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/generate -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"model":"ldr-micro-v1","input":"Summarize: Redwood Inference platform"}'
```

2) Python SDK snippet (local):

```
from redwood_sdk import Client
client = Client(endpoint="http://localhost:8080", api_key=None)
resp = client.generate(model="ldr-micro-v1", prompt="Explain caching in one paragraph")
print(resp.text)
```

Telemetry and Cost Simulation

- Token accounting follows the hosted token model. LDR exposes a `--cost-extractor` service that logs token counts and maps them to a local cost estimate using the same per-token formulas used in Redwood pricing (configurable in `cost.yaml`).
- Default `cost.yaml` (example):

```
per_token_generation_usd: 0.0000025
per_token_prompt_usd: 0.0000010
embedding_unit_usd: 0.00005
```

- Telemetry events: request_start, request_end, token_count, sampled_output_hash. Events are JSON lines written to `~/.redwood/ldr/telemetry.log` when local forwarding is disabled.

Acceptance Criteria (MUST for GA)

1. Startup on macOS/Linux with no external GPU dependency.
2. SDK compatibility: Node 18+ and Python 3.10+ example apps run without code changes.
3. Cost estimates within ±20% of hosted micro-benchmark for sample prompts (documented sample set).
4. Deterministic outputs for the provided canonical prompt set at default settings.

Packaging, Distribution, and Licensing Options

- Freemium model: LDR binary + micro-models distributed under open license; free for individual developers.
- Enterprise bundle: additional sample datasets, longer KV-cache snapshots, and an offline telemetry-forwarding plugin under commercial license.

Pricing table (proposed)

| SKU | Distribution | Price | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| LDR Community | Binary + micro-models | Free | Individual developers, redistributable. |
| LDR Enterprise | Binary + extended artifacts + plugin | $12k / year | Includes support, license to use extended artifacts in air-gapped demos. |

Roadmap and Phases

- Phase 0 (Q4 2025): internal alpha for SEs and Platform.
- Phase 1 (Q1 2026): external beta, packaging improvements, telemetry opt-in UX.
- Phase 2 (Q2 2026): enterprise bundle and onboarding playbook; marketplace listing.

Rollout and Migration Plan

1. Internal dogfood: SE demos and developer productivity teams (2 weeks).
2. Private beta: 10 strategic customers (4 weeks) — collect feedback on model fidelity and license implications.
3. Public beta: open to wider community with clear license and telemetry defaults (6 weeks).
4. GA: announce in Console and Docs; provide migration checklist for customers moving from LDR proxy to Hosted/Dedicated/Private endpoints.

Operational and Support Considerations

- Support: Developer experience first-line with escalation to Research for model fidelity questions.
- Metrics to track: installs (opt-in), telemetry forward rate, mismatch rate between LDR cost estimate and hosted cost for matched prompts.
- Known limits: LDR does not emulate preemption behavior or dedicated GPU latency characteristics.

Open Risks and Mitigations

- Licensing risk: Mitigation — Legal signoff and conservative model selection; feature flags to remove suspect artifacts quickly.
- Customer confusion about production-readiness: Mitigation — Strong UI/UX banners and docs emphasizing LDR as not-for-production.
- Telemetry privacy concerns: Mitigation — default off and local-first design; clear docs and opt-in prompts.

Acceptance Tests and QA Checklist

1. End-to-end sample app runs locally and matches snapshot responses.
2. Cost estimator exercised with 1000 sample prompts; error within acceptance bounds.
3. SDK examples run in CI containers (Linux) and report telemetry to local file.

Owners and Next Steps

- Product lead: Maya Chen (owner).
- Engineering lead: Rafael Ortiz.
- Research lead: Priya Nair.
- Next steps: finalize packaging format, complete legal/model clearance, and schedule private beta for 2026-03.

Appendix: Configuration Reference (example)

- ldr.yaml (example):

```
mode: local # local | proxy
port: 8080
telemetry: local # off | local | forward
cost_config: ./cost.yaml
model: ldr-micro-v1
```

- FAQ (short):

Q: Can I use LDR to benchmark Dedicated capacity?
A: No. LDR provides representative cost/latency signals for development and should not be used for production capacity planning.

Q: Will LDR outputs match Hosted exactly?
A: Not necessarily. LDR uses distilled micro-models and deterministic sampling to offer reproducible behavior; fidelity will be documented per prompt set.

End of spec.

title: dsid_5ed6adf60d144850824a7bc602d3f37e__adaptive-operator-feedback-and-deploy-safety-roadmap-2028.txt
text:
Adaptive operator feedback and deploy safety roadmap — 2028

Summary
-------
This roadmap describes a cross-team program to reduce operator cognitive load while improving deployment safety for the LLM inference platform. The program combines tightly instrumented telemetry, an operator feedback loop (OFL) service, and safe deploy controls so operators can act faster, with higher confidence, during both planned rollouts and unexpected regressions.

Background
----------
We have recurring cost and latency incidents where operator intervention is necessary (examples: KV-cache misbinding, sudden p95 token latency regressions after a model variant rollout). Current runbooks are detailed but rely on manual signal correlation across multiple dashboards. The goal of this initiative is to build a set of primitives and a staged rollout plan that: 
- Provides automatic signal synthesis and prioritized playbooks to the oncall UI.
- Introduces deploy-time safety checks and soft-guards that prevent high-risk rollouts from progressing.
- Collects structured operator feedback to continuously improve alert routing, dashboard relevance, and automatic remediations.

Goals and success criteria (measurable)
-------------------------------------
1) Reduce average operator action time (OAT) for platform-degradation incidents from 18m to <=10m within 12 months.
2) Reduce high-severity deploy regressions (SEV impacting >1 customer) due to model swap or kernel switch by 50% year-over-year.
3) Increase precision of high-priority alerts (true-positive rate) seen by operator UI from ~58% to >=75%.
4) Ship the OFL service with a minimum viable telemetry-synthesis pipeline and expose it in the operator console by Q2 2027.

Scope and non-goals
------------------
In-scope:
- Instrumentation taxonomy and dashboard templates for operator-facing signals (latency, token cost spikes, eviction rates, prefetch misses).
- The OFL service (signal fusion + ranking + suggested playbook).
- Deploy safety gates integrated with the canary orchestration service (canary-policy-enforcer).
- Operator UI panels and a small set of automated corrective actions (cache-reset, model-variant-rollback).

Out-of-scope:
- Full autonomous remediation for all regressions (we will limit automated actions to safe, idempotent ops).
- Rewriting existing model serving runtime kernels; instead we will provide stronger guardrails around kernel-swaps.

Timeline & milestones (high-level)
----------------------------------
- Q4 2026: Pilot instrumentation taxonomy and 3 operator dashboard prototypes (regional and global views).
- Q1 2027: Launch telemetry-synthesis pipeline (Kafka -> fusion -> ranked-events) and OFL alpha in staging.
- Q2 2027: Operator console integration; pilot with Platform oncall team; gating prototype added to canary-policy-enforcer.
- Q3 2027: Expand pilots to three customer-facing regions; add automated cache-reset action and rollback playbook.
- Q4 2027: Ramp to beta; run live gamedays and chaos scenarios; validate success criteria.
- Q1 2028: GA for OFL + deploy-safety feature set.

Implementation details
----------------------
1) Telemetry taxonomy and dashboards
   - Core signals to collect (metric names and intent):
     * platform.token_latency_ms.p50/p95/p99 (latency SLI)
     * runtime.kv_cache_hit_rate (cache health)
     * runtime.eviction_rate_per_min (eviction pressure)
     * orchestrator.deployment_canary_error_rate (canary health)
     * billing.token_rate_change_pct_1h (cost surges)
   - Dashboard templates: a regional operator view (per-region heatmap), a global regressions page (ranked regressions), and a deploy-safety cockpit.

   Example SLOs and thresholds (for dashboard alerting and OFL ranking):
   | SLO id | Metric | Target | Warning | Trigger |
   |--------|--------|--------|---------|---------|
   | SLO-LLM-LAT-P95 | platform.token_latency_ms.p95 | <=200 ms | 200-350 ms | >350 ms for 5m |
   | SLO-KV-HIT | runtime.kv_cache_hit_rate | >=92% | 85-92% | <85% for 10m |
   | SLO-EVICT | runtime.eviction_rate_per_min | <=5/min | 5-15/min | >15/min for 10m |

   Note: thresholds will be parameterized by region and tenant tier.

2) Operator Feedback Loop (OFL) service
   - Purpose: fuse telemetry signals, enrich with recent deploy context (committer, variant, kernel flags), run heuristics and ML-based classifiers to produce a ranked list of prioritized events and suggested playbooks.
   - Ingestion: Kafka topics (metrics, traces, deploy-events). Fusion layer will attach a TTLed context object per tenant/region.
   - Output: ranked-events API (JSON) consumed by the operator UI and by canary-policy-enforcer webhooks.

   Minimal OFL API example (HTTP):
   POST /v1/fusion/query {"region":"us-west-2", "window":"5m"} -> returns [{"event_id":"evt-123","score":0.94, "suggested_playbook":"cache-reset-v1","confidence":0.88}]

3) Deploy safety gates and canary-policy-enforcer integration
   - Extend canary-policy-enforcer with:
     a) preflight checks (synthetic smoke metrics, dependency-liveness, model-compatibility matrix)
     b) mid-canary automatic hold when OFL reports high-risk ranked-events (score > 0.8)
     c) staged rollback automation (first attempt: automated rollback trigger with manual confirmation window default 3 minutes for non-critical tenants).

Operator workflows and runbook changes
-------------------------------------
- New operator console panels: "Ranked Regressions", "Deploy Safety Cockpit", and "OFL Playbook Suggestions".
- Example operator flow for a canary hold:
  1. Operator receives a high-priority ranked-event in console (score>0.8).
  2. Console displays: top 3 signals, likely root cause, suggested playbook, and one-click actions (cache-reset, pause-canary, rollback).
  3. Operator either authorizes an automated action or escalates to L3.
  4. Automated action is executed and result recorded as structured feedback back to OFL for future tuning.

Runbook snippet (human-readable):
1) If p95 latency rises above 350ms and kv_cache_hit_rate < 80% within 10m:
   - Pause canary (canary-policy-enforcer -> pause)
   - Run cache-reset action for the affected shard(s) (operator console -> cache-reset)
   - If latency does not recover in 5 minutes, trigger model-variant rollback.

Telemetry & dashboards (implementation notes)
---------------------------------------------
- Use high-cardinality metrics sparingly; prefer aggregated telemetry with dimensions [region, tenant_tier, model_variant].
- Add a "regression fingerprint" field to fused events to allow quick deduplication of signals across tenants.
- Dashboards will include a single boolean column "OFL-suggested" to surface events already triaged by the service.

Owner matrix and responsibilities
---------------------------------
| Area | Primary owner | Secondary owner |
|------|----------------|-----------------|
| OFL service | eng-platform/fusion (Marina Kovács) | eng-serving-runtime (Ethan Zhao) |
| canary-policy-enforcer changes | eng-platform/orchestration (Luis Herrera) | eng-infra (Priya Nair) |
| operator console UI | eng-developer-experience (Priya Nair) | eng-platform/product (Marina Kovács) |

Risk register & mitigations
---------------------------
- False positives from OFL: roll out scoring conservatively; provide "dismiss and teach" operator actions to improve classifier.
- Hard fails during automated rollback: enforce canary-size limits on automated rollback; require manual confirmation for high-revenue tenants.
- Data lag causing stale decisions: instrument end-to-end latency for telemetry pipeline and surface metric in console; default to manual hold if data freshness < 30s.

Validation and experiments
-------------------------
- Phase 1 (staging): run seeded regressions and measure OAT and precision.
- Phase 2 (limited production): opt-in tenants and region for 4 weeks, run canary-hold experiments, track false-positive and false-negative rates.
- Phase 3 (beta): widen to 50% of regions, run gamedays with simulated multi-region degradations.

Appendix: operator CLI examples and safe automations
---------------------------------------------------
# Pause canary for rollout id
redwoodctl rollout pause --id rlt-20270901 --reason "OFL:high-score"

# Trigger cache-reset action (idempotent)
redwoodctl runtime cache-reset --shard us-west-2-a --force --dry-run=false

# Query OFL ranked events (example JSON output):
# [{"event_id":"evt-123","score":0.94,"suggested_playbook":"cache-reset-v1","confidence":0.88}]

Related artifacts and links
--------------------------
- Playbooks: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/operator-safe-mode-and-manual-intervention-playbook-2026
- Dashboards: Platform/Operator Feedback (dash-id: dash-ops-feedback-usw2)
- Canary service: canary-policy-enforcer (repo: github.com/redwood/platform-canary-enforcer)

Next steps (immediate actions for Q4 2026)
-----------------------------------------
1) Align instrumentation taxonomy with eng-serving-runtime and SRE (owner: Marina Kovács). Deadline: 2026-10-15.
2) Kickoff OFL alpha prototype sprint and define minimal fusion schema. Deadline: 2026-11-30.
3) Create operator console mockups and run two user interviews with oncall rotation members. Deadline: 2026-12-10.

Contact and ownership
---------------------
Primary contact: Marina Kovács (marina.kovacs@redwood.ai)
Secondary: Luis Herrera (luis.herrera@redwood.ai)

title: dsid_046bfb4c350a48a390e4ac33b03b0ecb__fidelity-migration-impact-matrix-and-pricing-heuristics-2027-08-09.txt
text:
Fidelity migration impact matrix and pricing heuristics

Playbook and decision matrix to guide product and commercial teams when migrating customers between fidelity tiers (e.g., high, standard, low). Includes impact matrix, quantitative heuristics used for pricing adjustments, rollout steps, telemetry requirements, and risk mitigations.
Overview:

Purpose
This document provides a repeatable playbook for assessing the customer and system impact when migrating a tenant’s inference consumption between fidelity tiers. It combines an operational impact matrix (technical and customer-facing effects) with concrete pricing heuristics and a phased migration plan. The goal is to enable predictable economics while limiting customer disruption and preserving SLOs.

Scope
- Applies to migrations across fidelity bands within Redwood’s consumption model (e.g., High-Fidelity -> Standard, Standard -> Low-Fidelity).
- Relevant to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments; where private deployments have separate contractual constraints, use the appendix guidance.
- Intended audience: product managers, solutions engineering, account teams, billing, and SRE.

Definitions
- Fidelity tier: Operational profile that trades response quality characteristics (sampling, decoding, quantization, KV cache aggressiveness) for cost/latency. Typical tiers: High, Standard, Low.
- Migration: A change to the effective fidelity tier for a tenant (per-route or global).
- Fidelity delta: Observable changes in output quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE proxy, hallucination rate, perplexity drift, or domain-specific accuracy).

Impact Matrix (technical / customer / commercial)
Format: rows = Migration type, columns = Expected system CPU/GPU impact, Latency, Token cost delta, User-facing quality risk, Customer billing change, Recommended guardrail.

| Migration | GPU utilization | 95p latency | Cost per 1k tokens | Output quality risk | Billing delta | Guardrail |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| High -> Standard | -20% to -35% | -10% to -25% | -28% | Small drop; risk on long-context summarization | -25% | Canary 1% traffic, track domain prompts |
| Standard -> Low | -30% to -50% | -15% to -40% | -40% to -55% | Medium; increased token repetition, factuality regressions | -45% | Run A/B on synthetic prompts, revert on >5% metric degradation |
| High -> Low (fast path) | -45% to -70% | -25% to -60% | -60%+ | High; possible unacceptable regressions for sensitive workflows | -60%+ | Only for non-transactional routes or explicit customer opt-in |
| Low -> Standard | +15% to +30% | +8% to +20% | +30% | Quality improvement measurable; risk of increased cost | +28% | Phased uplift with cost alerts and budget caps |

Note: values above are workload-sensitive. Always run synthetic replay (see telemetry section) before schedule.

Quantitative Pricing Heuristics
We use a set of heuristics to translate expected runtime delta into an adjustment to per-token pricing or to recommended credits/discounts for migration windows. Heuristics are intentionally conservative to avoid revenue loss from quality-related churn.

1) Baseline compute cost mapping
- Measure steady-state per-token GPU seconds over representative 24h window.
- Map GPU seconds to unit cost using committed pricing for the deployment (hosted vs dedicated).

2) Apply fidelity multiplier (example):
- High: 1.00 (reference)
- Standard: 0.72 (+/- 0.06)
- Low: 0.42 (+/- 0.08)
These multipliers are validated monthly against production telemetry; treat as soft knobs.

3) Convert to billable price adjustment
- If migration reduces compute by X%, then per-token price is reduced by max(X - 5%, floor 10%), where 5% accounts for overheads not realized as direct savings.
- For increases in fidelity, recommend a surcharge calculated as ceil((observed cost increase + 3% ops premium) * 100)/100 to nearest cent per 1k tokens for advertised pricing.

4) Migration crediting
- For customer-facing migrations (where perceived drop might reduce retention), offer a one-time credit sized at 10% of the first-month expected spend differential for migrations that exceed a projected 20% quality regression risk.

Decision rules (binary)
- If projected output-quality delta (measured by the evaluation harness) > 7% on critical prompt set => require explicit customer approval and Solutions Eng sign-off.
- If projected cost savings < 8% => do not auto-migrate; consider opt-in only.

Telemetry & Evaluation Requirements
Before approving a migration produce:
- Synthetic replay of at least 50k representative requests or 72 hours of sampled production traffic (whichever is larger).
- Evals: domain prompt set (owner-provided) + Redwood baseline prompt set. Key metrics: fidelity_score, hallucination_rate, latency_p95, token_cost_estimate.
- Dashboard: per-route change visualization, diff histograms for token counts and latency, sliding 24/168h windows.

Migration Playbook (operational steps)
1) Prepare:
  - Owner: Product / Solutions Eng
  - Collate domain prompt set (min 100 canonical prompts) and representative traffic sample (see telemetry).
  - Estimate cost delta via offline simulator (use cost-sim SDK v2).
2) Synthetic run (preflight):
  - Run A/B: 10% traffic routed to candidate tier for 48 hours. Capture fidelity metrics and customer-facing regressions.
  - Monitor: fidelity_score drop, error rates, latency p95, requests with >3 repeated tokens.
3) Canary expansion:
  - If preflight passes thresholds (fidelity_score drop <= 4% and no customer errors) expand to 33% for 72 hours.
4) Billing and pricing action:
  - Apply temporary dual-billing window: customer billed at midpoint price for 2 billing cycles while retention and usage observed; credit if churn signals triggered.
5) Full rollout:
  - Increase to 100% in 24-48 hours with automated rollback triggers.
  - Post-rollout: 14-day monitoring window with weekly review.

Rollback triggers (automated):
- fidelity_score drop > 7% sustained for 6 hours
- new error.rate increase > 2x baseline
- customer-initiated escalation recorded

Customer communication templates
- Pre-migration (email/in-console): clear summary of expected changes, scheduled window, cost impact (estimated), opt-out instructions, contact for support.
- Post-migration: operational summary with before/after metrics and applied credits if any.

Pricing examples (scenarios)
- Scenario A: Customer A (Standard -> Low): baseline monthly spend $50k. Projected token cost reduction 45%. Heuristics: reduce per-token price by 40% (since >8% and accounting for overheads). Offer 10% one-time credit ($5k) if fidelity delta on domain set >10%.
- Scenario B: Customer B (High -> Standard, non-critical): baseline $12k. Projected compute saving 30%. Per-token price reduced by 25% and no credit; add a 2-month observation billing band and telemetry reports.

Risk & Mitigations
- Regressions for long-context chains: use targeted fallback policy for routes with long sequences (route-level 'high-fidelity' pin).
- Unexpected billing disputes: require ledger export and spend-simulator runbooks to be part of migration packet.
- Model drift: include monthly re-eval cadence for migrated tenants for first 6 months.

KPIs to evaluate migration program
- Migration success rate: % migrations completed without rollback within 14 days (target >= 90%).
- Net dollar retention impact for migrated customers at 90 days (target >= -2%).
- Average cost savings realized vs simulated (target within +/- 8%).
- Time to rollback when automated trigger fires (target < 10 minutes).

Operational ownership and contacts
- Product (Fidelity Programs): Maya Chen (owner) — maya@redwood.example.com
- Solutions Engineering: Liam Patel — liam@redwood.example.com
- Billing & Revenue Ops: Sofia Martinez — sofia@redwood.example.com
- SRE escalation: Ethan Brooks — ethan@redwood.example.com

Appendix A — Private deployments and contractual constraints
- Private deployments may require contract amendment for any fidelity-based pricing changes. Work with Legal and Commercial to produce one-off amendments. For on-prem, the migration must be scheduled with a 4-week lead time and a signed change order.

Appendix B — Example cost-sim snippet (pseudo-JSON)
{
  "route": "chat-v1/assistant",
  "baseline_seconds_per_token": "0.0032",
  "candidate_multiplier": "0.72",
  "estimated_monthly_tokens": "1_200_000_000",
  "projected_monthly_cost": "$X"
}

Appendix C — Fast checklist (one-pager)
- [ ] Domain prompts collected and validated
- [ ] Synthetic replay configured (>=50k requests)
- [ ] Preflight A/B run (10% traffic) complete and passing
- [ ] Canary (33%) complete and passing
- [ ] Billing plan updated and communications drafted
- [ ] Rollback configured with automated alerts

Notes and change log
- 2027-08-09: Initial draft and internal review.
- 2027-10-01: Added explicit billing band and credit heuristics after pilot with three customers.
- 2028-01-15: Clarified rollback thresholds and added private-deploy constraints.

Related artifacts
- Cost-sim SDK v2 runbook (internal link)

title: dsid_205fb3a403c2459e978b5ede8d0e5f96__approval-timestamping-and-evidence-chain-for-delegations-2024.txt
text:
Approval Timestamping and Evidence Chain for Delegated Access

Overview

Purpose: This runbook defines the architecture, operational procedures, and compliance packaging for approval timestamping and end-to-end evidence chains when access is delegated (temporary privileges, approved service delegation, or emergency access) across Redwood Inference services. The goal is to make every delegation auditable, tamper-evident, residency-aware, and queryable for regulatory audits and incident response.

Scope: Applies to all delegated access flows that grant elevated privileges for >5 minutes or that provide access to customer data, keys, or private deployment configuration. This includes: just-in-time (JIT) elevation, short-lived service tokens, delegation via ticketing systems, and emergency bypass workflows.

Key design goals
- Strong provenance: cryptographically verifiable timestamps and chaining between approval records and resulting credentials/actions.
- Auditability: every step is correlated across RBAC, audit logs, and evidence bundles with a stable correlation ID.
- Residency-aware packaging: evidence bundles preserve locality metadata for cross-border deployments and include residency policy tags.
- Operational resiliency: fallbacks when primary evidence capture fails (e.g., network partition, logging store outage).
- SDLC alignment: automated checks to ensure delegation logic is exercised in CI and gated in releases.

Definitions
- Delegation: granting temporary authority to a principal (human or service) to perform actions outside their default entitlement.
- Approval record: signed statement that documents who approved a delegation, scope, duration, and reason.
- Evidence bundle: a packaged artifact containing approval records, audit-log excerpts, credential issuance records, and residency metadata used for audits.
- Correlation ID (correlation_id): a UUID used to connect the approval, issuance, and audit trail for a single delegation incident.

Architecture and data flow (textual diagram)
1) User/Service requests delegation -> 2) Approval flow (UI/ticketing/JIT) -> 3) Approval service timestamps & signs approval (approval-service) -> 4) Credential issuer generates ephemeral credential -> 5) Audit-logging service captures the issuance event and links correlation_id -> 6) Evidence assembler compiles a signed bundle and stores it in evidence-store (geo-tagged).

Component responsibilities
- Approval-service: generate approval_id, attach approver identity, scope, duration, and create a signed approval object using KMS-backed signing keys. (Owner: Security Engineering)
- Credential-issuer: mint ephemeral tokens/credentials, include approval_id and correlation_id in credential metadata. (Owner: Identity Service)
- Audit-logging: ingest issuance events with correlation_id and context, forward to immutable-audit-store and stream to evidence-assembler. (Owner: Observability Platform)
- Evidence-assembler: assemble the evidence bundle (see packaging spec below), compute bundle hash, timestamp with approved signer, and store in evidence-store with residency tags. (Owner: Compliance Platform)

Concrete service names and endpoints
- approval-service: https://internal.approvals.redwood/api/v1/approve
- identity/issuer: https://internal.issuer.redwood/api/v1/issue
- audit-ingest: kafka-topic audits.high; http-ingest at https://internal.audit.redwood/api/v1/ingest
- evidence-store S3 buckets: evidence-us-west-2, evidence-eu-west-1 (encrypted, versioned)

Evidence bundle schema (flat key-value manifest)
- bundle_id: string (UUID)
- correlation_id: string (UUID)
- approval_id: string
- approver_principal: string (email/SERVICE_ACCOUNT)
- approval_signed_at: ISO8601 timestamp
- approval_signature_kid: string (KMS key id)
- issuance_record_id: string
- credential_id: string
- credential_ttl_seconds: integer (as string)
- audit_log_excerpt_ids: list of strings (comma-separated when stored in the manifest)
- residency_tag: one of [US, EU, APAC, MULTI]
- bundle_hash: sha256 hex string
- retention_policy: string (e.g., "evidence_standard_7yrs")
- stored_location: s3://bucket/path

Retention and residency mapping (table)
- Evidence type: Approvals for privileged access -> Retention: 7 years -> Residency: follows resource location (if customer-specific, match customer region)
- Evidence type: Emergency-bypass approvals -> Retention: 10 years -> Residency: store in multiple regions (primary + mirrored region)
- Evidence type: Routine JIT approvals -> Retention: 2 years -> Residency: single-region per policy

Operational SLOs and thresholds
- Approval record signed and emitted: P99 <= 2s
- Correlation ID present in audit ingest: P99 <= 10s after issuance
- Evidence bundle assembled and stored: P95 <= 300s (5 minutes)
- Evidence-store put_object success rate: >= 99.9% over 30d

Procedures: Delegation approval flow (step-by-step)
1) Requestor initiates delegation (UI/API) with requested scope, justification, and desired duration. Correlation ID is created client-side if possible; otherwise the approval-service issues it.
2) Approval-service validates request against policy engine (policy-service) and escalates if above thresholds (e.g., >24h or access to production keys).
3) Approver performs review; approval-service records approver identity, signs the approval payload using KMS sign key (key rotation required annually).
4) Approval-service emits approval_event to audit-ingest with correlation_id.
5) Credential-issuer listens for approval_event, issues ephemeral credential embedding approval_id + correlation_id, and emits issuance_event.
6) Audit-ingest links issuance_event to the approval_event by correlation_id.
7) Evidence-assembler subscribes to audit streams and, once all required pieces (approval, issuance, log excerpts) are available or after 5 minutes, assembles the bundle and writes to evidence-store.

Failure modes and fallback steps
- If audit-ingest is unavailable: approval-service persists signed approvals in a local queue and retries ingestion. Runbook: page oncall and trigger audit-ingest escalation (link: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/audit-ingest-outage).
- If evidence-assembler timed out: create provisional evidence bundle with a note "partial" and set follow-up job to reconcile within 24h. This provisional artifact must be retained and labeled.
- If approval signature key is unavailable: fallback to secondary KMS key; record key rotation/cross-signing proof in evidence bundle.

Evidence verification (for auditors and IR)
- Use the evidence verifier CLI: redwood-evidence verify --bundle s3://...
- Verification steps the CLI performs: 1) validate bundle_hash; 2) validate approval signature with provided KMS key id; 3) confirm presence of approval_id in audit logs (query via audit-search API); 4) confirm residency tags match customer deployment metadata.

Example: evidence bundle ingestion CLI snippet

$ redwood-evidence assemble --correlation-id 3f8b2a4e-9d6a-4f9e-bd2a-6c4a3e512c7e --output s3://evidence-us-west-2/bundles/3f8b2a4e.json

Example: internal JSON manifest (flattened for compliance auditors)
{
  "bundle_id": "3f8b2a4e-9d6a-4f9e-bd2a-6c4a3e512c7e",
  "correlation_id": "3f8b2a4e-9d6a-4f9e-bd2a-6c4a3e512c7e",
  "approval_id": "apr-20240610-451",
  "approver_principal": "security-approvers@redwood.com",
  "approval_signed_at": "2024-06-10T14:12:33Z",
  "approval_signature_kid": "kms://aws/us-west-2/keys/abcd-1234",
  "issuance_record_id": "iss-20240610-990",
  "credential_id": "cred-xyz-0001",
  "credential_ttl_seconds": "3600",
  "audit_log_excerpt_ids": "log-20240610-01,log-20240610-02",
  "residency_tag": "US",
  "bundle_hash": "e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb924...",
  "retention_policy": "evidence_standard_7yrs",
  "stored_location": "s3://evidence-us-west-2/bundles/3f8b2a4e.json"
}

Testing and SDLC gating
- Unit tests: policy-engine rules that gate approvals must have >= 90% rule coverage and explicit negative tests for cross-region delegations.
- Integration tests (pre-prod): simulate approval -> issuance -> audit -> evidence assemble pipeline using test KMS and ephemeral S3.
- Release gate: changes to approval-service or credential-issuer require a Security Review and inclusion in the compliance test harness (PR checklist item: "evidence-assembly test case added").

Incident response integration
- If a suspected misuse is reported, IR runbook should: 1) identify correlation_id(s) for the suspect window; 2) retrieve evidence bundles and audit logs; 3) validate approval signatures; 4) freeze evidence-store objects for legal hold (see retention policy).
- Legal hold: evidence bundles tied to an active investigation get an additional tag: legal_hold:true and are excluded from normal deletion TTL jobs. (Owner: Legal + Security)

Audit readiness checklist (pre-audit)
- All delegation evidence bundles for sample period are present and verifiable via redwood-evidence verify.
- All approval signer KMS keys used during sample period are listed with rotation events.
- Residency tags on bundles match customer region metadata for each sampled item.

Operational rollout plan
1) Pilot (2 weeks): instrument approval-service and credential-issuer in staging; verify end-to-end assembly for 100 simulated delegations.
2) Canary (4 weeks): enable in production for a subset of teams (internal infra and one customer integration).
3) Full rollout (2 months): enable globally with monitoring dashboards and alerting for evidence-assembly failures.

Monitoring and dashboards
- Dashboard tiles: evidence-assembly latency histogram, failed-bundles counter (24h), audit-ingest lag (P99), evidence-store put_object errors.
- Alerts: evidence-assembly failure rate > 0.25% sustained for 15m -> pager to Security Oncall.

Governance and review cadence
- Quarterly review of retention policies and residency mappings.
- Annual audit of approval key material and KMS access lists.
- Post-incident reviews to update failure fallbacks and retention exceptions.

Appendix: quick references and links
- Evidence assembler runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/evidence-assembler
- Audit ingest outage runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/audit-ingest-outage
- Evidence verifier tool (internal): https://git.internal.redwood/tools/redwood-evidence

Contact and ownership
- Doc owner: Ava Martinez (Security Engineering)
- Operational owner: Observability Platform (pager: #observability-oncall)
- Compliance owner: Legal & Compliance team (legal@redwood.com)

Revision history
- 2024-06-10: created by Ava Martinez
- 2024-09-05: added residency tagging rules (Priya Kaur)
- 2025-02-14: finalized SLOs and rollout plan (Daniel Cho)

title: dsid_22d482b83ba9406b93e52c73a758e1f6__gpu-tenant-backpressure-and-queue-smoothing-runbook.txt
text:
GPU tenant backpressure and queue-smoothing runbook

Summary

This runbook describes the design, detection, mitigation, and long-term fixes for tenant-level backpressure and request-queue smoothing in Redwood's GPU serving fleet. It covers the runtime components, SLO-oriented thresholds, automated mitigation policies, emergency manual steps for oncall, Terraform/Helm snippets for rate-limiter configuration, and guidance for post-incident follow-up.

Objectives

- Maintain per-tenant 99th-percentile request latency SLOs under mixed workloads.
- Prevent noisy tenants from causing cascading queuing and eviction events.
- Provide deterministic short-term mitigations and a path to corrective changes (rate limits, scheduling, capacity).
- Make runbook steps executable by oncall engineers with minimal blast radius.

Applicability and scope

- Applies to hosted and dedicated GPU pools managed by eng-infra.
- Focuses on inference serving paths (text generation, chat streaming, embeddings).
- Not a replacement for billing/fraud investigation - those runbooks are in customer-success.

Key concepts and components

- Frontline queue: per-host in-memory FIFO with configurable max-concurrency and max-queue-length.
- Tenant router: request router that tags requests with tenant_id and route metadata.
- Per-tenant rate limiter: token-bucket-based limiter with burst allowance and steady-rate target.
- Global admission controller: enforces cluster-wide soft caps and triggers fallback routing to warm-pools or cheaper model variants.
- Warm pool: pre-warmed containers/GPUs with shorter start latency used for smaller bursty requests.
- Eviction controller: removes low-priority tasks when memory or GPU RAM pressure is detected.

SLOs and thresholds (operational values)

- Service SLOs (runtime team): P50 < 40ms, P95 < 200ms, P99 < 600ms for short-generation requests (<512 tokens).
- Soft backpressure threshold: per-host queued requests > 200 or per-tenant concurrent requests > 120 => throttle advisory.
- Hard backpressure threshold: per-host queued requests > 500 or per-tenant concurrent > 300 => automatic throttling and priority demotion.
- Eviction trigger: GPU memory pressure > 92% for > 30s or OOMs > 3/min => start eviction policy.

Metrics to monitor (critical dashboards)

- gpu.request.latency.{p50,p95,p99} (tagged by tenant, model, region)
- gpu.queue.length.host and gpu.queue.length.tenant
- gpu.concurrent.requests.tenant
- gpu.mem.usage.percent.host and gpu.mem.usage.percent.pod
- gpu.eviction.count and gpu.preemption.count
- admission.throttle.actions and admission.throttle.rejections
- tokenbucket.fill.rate and tokenbucket.dropped.requests

Detection: triage checklist (first 10 minutes)

1. Confirm symptom: customer tickets or alerts showing elevated p95/p99 latency or queue backlog.
2. Look at cluster-level dashboard for sudden spikes in gpu.queue.length.host and gpu.mem.usage.percent.host.
3. Group by tenant_id: identify tenants with disproportionate request rate or sustained long-running sessions.
4. Check admission.throttle.rejections for which tenant was first rejected.
5. Correlate with recent deployments (ci-cd) or model rollouts: use /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build to verify canary promotions in last 30m.
6. If noisy tenant(s) identified, verify request patterns (burst vs sustained) and model variant sizes (512 vs 4096 context).

Automated mitigations (behavior we expect to run)

- Step A (soft): per-tenant token-bucket reduces effective refill rate by 20% for tenants exceeding soft threshold for > 60s.
- Step B (fallback): route new requests to warm-pool or cheaper quantized model variant when hard threshold reached.
- Step C (preempt): demote low-priority background eval workloads and evict them from GPUs.

Manual rapid mitigations for oncall (ordered)

1. Announce: post on #oncall with cluster and region (e.g., us-west-2-gpu-pool-1) and attach key metrics screenshots.
2. Temporarily increase per-tenant rate-limiter denominator (reduce allowed concurrency) for the noisy tenant:

   CLI example (internal admin):
   rcli tenant update-rate --tenant-id tenant-123 --concurrency 80 --burst 120

3. If step 2 insufficient, enable forced fallback to warm-pool for that tenant:

   rcli routing set-fallback --tenant-id tenant-123 --fallback-target warm-pool-usw2 --duration 15m

4. If the cluster is memory pressured, mark non-critical nodes for cordon and drain of background workloads only:

   kubectl cordon worker-gpu-045 -n gpu-serving
   kubectl drain worker-gpu-045 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data -n gpu-serving

5. As last resort, trigger capacity burst (if dedicated account permits) following the burst runbook: raise capacity request to 1.5x and notify capacity-oncall. See related page: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-scaling-decision-framework-and-burst-policy

Short-term rollback (if mitigation causes regressions)

- Revert rate-limiter change with the audit id printed by rcli.
- Remove forced fallback and allow gradual roll-back over 10 minutes to avoid thundering herd.

Kubernetes/Helm/Terraform snippets (examples)

- Sample token-bucket Helm values (values.yaml fragment):

  tokenBucket:
    enabled: true
    defaultRefillRate: "100r/s"
    tenantOverrides:
      tenant-123:
        refillRate: "60r/s"
        burst: 120

- Terraform resource example (rate-limiter config):

  resource "redwood_rate_limiter_config" "tenant_123" {
    tenant_id = "tenant-123"
    refill_rate = 60
    burst = 120
    enforcement = "soft"
  }

- Admission controller config (K8s CRD pseudo):

  apiVersion: serving.redwood.ai/v1
  kind: AdmissionPolicy
  metadata:
    name: global-backpressure
  spec:
    queueLimitPerHost: 500
    tenantConcurrentLimit: 300
    fallbackTargets:
      - warm-pool
      - quantized-variant

Testing and pre-deployment checks

- Canary pattern: deploy rate-limiter changes to 5% of hosts behind a feature flag for 1 hour; monitor queue length and latency.
- Load test: run tenant-level simulated burst test (loadgen) that replicates 2x expected peak for 15 minutes against a staging cluster.
- CI checks: ensure terraform plan shows only rate-limiter changes for tenant configs and Helm charts include admission policy updates.

Post-incident analysis (PI) checklist

1. Collect traces (request IDs and tenant_id), CPU/GPU utilization, queue metrics for the incident window.
2. Identify root cause: noisy tenant, model size change, regression in admission controller, or capacity shortage.
3. Quantify impact: affected tenants, p99 delta, cost of burst capacity used.
4. Action items (prioritized):
   - Implement per-tenant adaptive refill that uses moving-average request rate.
   - Add preflight CI test to simulate model-context jumps (512->4096).
   - Update onboarding templates to set sensible tenant defaults (max concurrent, burst).
5. Schedule a retrospective with runtime, infra, and product leads; publish summary to /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/postmortems (link incident id).

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owners: eng-infra/gpu-fleet team (Page owners list in the console).
- Secondary owners: eng-platform (routing/admission), eng-serving-runtime (model variant fallback).
- Pager escalation: oncall -> senior-infra -> runtime-lead -> eng-sre director.

Operational tips and lessons learned

- Prefer progressive throttling over blunt rejects; gradual reductions avoid thundering herd.
- Warm-pools are effective for short bursts but must be sized carefully to avoid cost leak.
- Model size changes (context length) are a frequent root cause; include context-length in deployment metadata.
- Automate tenant whiteboard: maintain a small spreadsheet of tenants with known high-burst patterns and runbook contact points.

Related pages and artifacts

- Capacity burst policy: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-scaling-decision-framework-and-burst-policy
- Warm-pool sizing guide: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/warm-pool-sizing-and-cost-model
- CI/CD canary checklist: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/canary-gpu-provisioning-safety-net-pipeline.json

Appendix: example incident timeline (condensed)

- T+00:00 Alert fires: p99 latency for us-west spikes to 1200ms.
- T+00:03 Identified tenant-123 responsible for 70% of new queue entries.
- T+00:06 Soft rate-limiter lowered for tenant-123 (20% reduction). P99 improved to 900ms.
- T+00:12 Forced fallback to warm-pool enabled for tenant-123. P99 dropped to 340ms.
- T+00:35 Background eval jobs were demoted; cluster memory pressure subsided.
- T+02:00 Post-incident actions initiated (PI items list created).

Contact list

- gpu-fleet oncall: #gpu-oncall (pager)
- runtime-engineering: runtime-team@redwood.ai
- capacity-ops: capacity@redwood.ai

This document is authoritative for tenant-level backpressure and queue smoothing procedures. Review quarterly or after any major changes to the admission controller, warm-pool sizing, or rate-limiter implementation.

title: dsid_43d5e54548ef45f491f9d46ec144994f__dynamic-gpu-pool-affinity-and-topology-orchestration.txt
text:
Dynamic GPU Pool Affinity and Topology Orchestration

Summary:

This document describes the design, IaC patterns, CI/CD controls, and runbook for Redwood's Dynamic GPU Pool Affinity and Topology Orchestration system. The goal is to enable workload-aware placement across heterogeneous GPU types (preemptible and reserved), maintain tenant isolation (network and iSCSI/NFS mounts), minimize tail latency for inference workloads, and provide clear operational steps for scaling and incident response.

Audience:
- Infra engineers running GPU fleet capacity and scheduling
- Platform engineers integrating routing and autoscaling policies
- SRE / oncall for operational playbooks
- IaC/CI teams responsible for module changes

Goals and non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Maintain placement SLO: 99th percentile queue-to-start <= 150ms for burst-critical inference routes
  - Ensure predictable cost by tagging and affinity (reserved vs spot)
  - Support multi-tenant network fencing per tenant VPC overlay
  - Provide safe rollout path for topology and affinity changes via CI/CD canaries
- Non-goals:
  - This is not a guide for model-level kernel tuning or CUDA runtime internals. See runtime docs.

Design overview:

1) Key concepts and terminology:
- Logical GPU pool: an abstract grouping of nodes with similar capabilities and SLO characteristics (e.g., "reserved-a40", "spot-h100-preemptible").
- Affinity policy: a declarative mapping that prefers or pins workloads to pools based on labels (model-size, latency-sensitivity, tenant-tier).
- Topology hint: per-request metadata used by scheduler to pick nodes that minimize inter-process communication latency (eg. NUMA locality, same rack).
- Fencing profile: network & mount isolation controls applied at pool creation (VPC peering, egress rules, persistent volume access control).

2) High-level control plane components:
- PoolManager service (internal): maintains pool metadata, health, and capacity targets. Exposes HTTP API used by autoscaler and Scheduler.
- Scheduler extension (kube-scheduler plugin + custom extender): consumes affinity and topology hints to make placement decisions.
- Autoscaler (FleetAutoscaler): converts workload signals to desired counts per pool using padded headroom and safety margins.
- Overlay Network Controller: configures tenant overlay routing and egress slices for pools that require isolated egress.

3) Placement flow (simplified):
1. Client request arrives at serving gateway with metadata (tenant, route, latency-class, model-id).
2. Gateway queries PoolManager for candidate pools matching route policy and affordability profile.
3. Scheduler evaluates node-level topology hints and current KV-cache state to prefer warm nodes; respects preemption preference.
4. If no eligible node is available within placement SLO, request falls back to a slower but more available pool (fallback policy).

SLOs and monitoring:
- Target SLOs:
  - Placement latency (enqueue->container-start): p50 < 20ms, p95 < 65ms, p99 < 150ms
  - Cold-launch token penalty (additional startup for model load): tracked separately; aim to keep < 30% of requests experiencing cold-launch during normal traffic
- Key metrics to emit:
  - pool.capacity_target (gpus), pool.available_count, pool.headroom, pool.spot_preemptions_total
  - placement.latency_ms (histogram), placement.fallback_rate
  - node.numa_locality_score, node.kv_cache_freshness
- Dashboards (per-pool): capacity chart, placement latency histogram, egress error rate, preemption events timeline.

IaC patterns and Terraform module examples:
- Module goal: create a single reusable Terraform module that provisions a logical GPU pool and its networking fencing. Module inputs should be explicit and idempotent.

Required inputs (table described):
- name: string (pool name)
- gpu_type: string (e.g., a40, h100)
- capacity_target: number (desired number of GPUs)
- preemptible: boolean
- vpc_overlay_id: string (ID of tenant overlay or shared overlay)
- egress_policy: string (none|shared|private-nat)
- tags: list of strings

Sample Terraform usage (snippet):

module "pool_reserved_a40_us-east-1" {
  source        = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.ai/infra/terraform-modules.git//gpu_pool"
  name          = "reserved-a40-us-east-1"
  gpu_type      = "a40"
  capacity_target = 64
  preemptible   = false
  vpc_overlay_id = "overlay-prod-1"
  egress_policy = "private-nat"
  tags          = ["env:prod", "team:platform"]
}

Network and storage considerations:
- Pools with "private-nat" egress_policy must include NAT gateways in the pool's subnet and explicit egress ACLs in the overlay controller.
- NFS/iSCSI mounts used for model artifacts must be mounted with per-tenant access controls and use volume encryption. Mounts must be defined in the pool module and set to ReadOnly unless model pre-loading requires write access.

CI/CD and rollout strategy:
- Branching policy: Changes to the gpu_pool module require a TF plan published in CI and a manual approval for production changes.
- Canary rollout steps for topology/affinity changes (automated pipeline):
  1. Create a canary pool with identical module inputs but capacity_target = 5% of desired final size and label canary=true.
  2. Run integration tests: placement latency, preemption simulation, network egress test.
  3. Promote canary: gradually increase capacity in 3 steps (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with 30-minute observation windows.
  4. If any critical metric crosses thresholds (see "Safety thresholds" below), rollback via terraform apply to previous module state.

Safety thresholds:
- placement.fallback_rate > 2% for 10 continuous minutes -> pause rollout and scale up warm pool
- pool.preemptions_per_minute spike to > 0.5% of pool.size -> pause canary and notify SRE
- network.egress_errors_rate > 0.2% -> rollback egress policy change

Runbook: common operational procedures

A) Routine scale-up (capacity request from demand planner)
1. Verify demand trend in dashboard and cross-check cost impact in billing dashboard.
2. Create TF change for pool capacity_target delta. Run CI plan and ensure no other pending changes.
3. Apply to staging/canary pools first and observe 2x placement latency and headroom for 2 hours.
4. Apply to production pools during a low-traffic window (if possible) and monitor. Notify oncall via Slack channel #infra-gpu.

B) Fast mitigation for sudden preemption storm or network isolation failure
1. Pager triggers: alert from preemption-rate or egress-errors. Acknowledge alert within 5 minutes.
2. Run the diagnostic commands: 
   - kubectl get nodes -l pool=<pool-name> -o wide
   - curl -sS https://poolmanager.internal/api/v1/pools/<pool-name>/health | jq
   - aws ec2 describe-instance-status --filters "Name=tag:pool,Values=<pool-name>"
3. If preemption spike is detected, run autoscaler emergency policy: increase reserved fallback pool target by 30% and enable temporary routing to fallback pools. Command:
   - aws autoscaling set-desired-capacity --auto-scaling-group-name reserved-fallback-<region> --desired-capacity <new-capacity>
4. If network egress issues are root cause, switch pool egress to shared-egress path (short term) by updating Overlay Controller and re-applying config: 
   - overlayctl set-egress --pool <pool-name> --policy shared 
   - Wait for config propagation (<= 90s) and validate with `curl --fail -I https://egress-test.<tenant>.internal`
5. Post-incident: run postmortem and capture affected tenants, preemption counts, time to mitigation, and steps taken.

C) Rollback procedure for a failed canary (quick rollback)
1. Run `terraform workspace select production` and `terraform apply -target=module.pool_canary -var capacity_target=0` to drain canary capacity.
2. Trigger scheduler to demote canary nodes: `kubectl label nodes <node-list> canary=false --overwrite` and gracefully evict pods with `kubectl drain` preserving disruption budgets.
3. Roll back module change in source branch and open emergency PR to restore previous module inputs if CI failed to block the change.

Operational ownership and run windows:
- PoolManager service owner: platform-team (primary) and infra-oncall (secondary).
- Terraform module owner: infra-iac team.
- Oncall rotation: infra-gpu oncall 24/7; weekend escalation to core-sre if incident impacts > 5% of capacity for > 30 minutes.

Testing and validation matrix (short table described):
- Unit tests: terraform module unit checks, network ACL static validation
- Integration tests: small infra cluster deploy, mount tests, model pre-load latency test
- Chaos tests: simulated spot preemption, simulated NAT gateway failure, mount latency injection

Example scheduler plugin config (YAML snippet):

apiVersion: scheduler.redwood.io/v1
kind: AffinityPolicy
metadata:
  name: latency-sensitive-affinity
spec:
  preferredPools:
    - name: reserved-a40-us-east-1
      weight: 100
    - name: spot-h100-preemptible-us-east-1
      weight: 30
  topologyHints:
    numaLocalityPreferred: true
    sameRackBonus: 20
  fallbackPools:
    - name: reserved-fallback-us-east-1
      maxFallbackPct: 10

Notes and gotchas:
- Avoid mixing heterogeneous GPU families in a single logical pool; this increases scheduling complexity and cache inefficiencies.
- When adding a new NUMA-aware placement rule, verify kernel module versions and drivers across node images. Mixed drivers can lead to failed CUDA calls.
- Tagging discipline is critical: billing and cost-allocation depend on tag accuracy. Tagging errors will surface as billing mis-attribution.

Appendices:
A) Useful CLI snippets
- List pool nodes and their NUMA affinity summary:
  - kubectl get nodes -l pool=reserved-a40-us-east-1 -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}	{.metadata.labels.numa}
{end}'
- Simulate preemption of a spot node (chaos):
  - aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1

B) Example alert thresholds (Alertmanager rules description):
- ALERT PoolPreemptionHigh
  IF increase(pool.preemptions_total[5m]) / sum(pool.size) > 0.005
  FOR 5m
  LABELS {severity="critical", team="infra-gpu"}

C) Related reading:
- Link: Runtime kernel selection and batching (internal doc)
- Link: IaC module lifecycle and migration guidelines (internal doc)

Document change history:
- 2025-11-03: Drafted initial design and runbook (Asha Patel)
- 2026-01-20: Added CI/CD canary automation steps and safety thresholds (Riley Chen)
- 2026-02-10: Added fast mitigation commands and clarified ownership (Marta Kovacs)

title: dsid_d3daada29415432da9d60846860125c9__pricing-contract-ingestion-and-billing-rulebook-2028.txt
text:
Pricing, Contract Ingestion, and Billing Rulebook for Capacity & Usage Agreements

Summary

This document defines the single source of truth for how pricing terms and signed contracts are ingested into billing systems, how contract rules map to billing triggers, and the guardrails for revenue recognition for Redwood Inference capacity, reserved, and usage-based agreements. It codifies ingestion workflows, mapping templates, automated sanity checks, handoff steps, and escalation paths for exceptions.

Scope

- In scope: enterprise capacity reservations (Dedicated), hosted usage-based plans, overage/burst rules, marketplace/integration partner chargebacks, and enterprise amendments that change billing start/stop or unit economics.
- Out of scope: employee expense reimbursements, vendor payments, one-off professional services invoices (unless tied to a contract change).

Goals

1. Ensure every signed commercial agreement results in an accurate billing contract record within 3 business days.
2. Prevent revenue leakage and mis-billing with automated pre-bill checks (coverage, unit price, effective dates).
3. Provide a deterministic mapping from contract clause → billing trigger → revenue recognition rule.
4. Minimize exceptions via standardized ingestion templates and templates for common commercial constructs.

Definitions

- Contract Record: canonical record in the Contract DB that contains commercial fields used by billing and revrec.
- Billing Trigger: an event or schedule (e.g., start_date, monthly_recurring_invoice, usage_reported) that causes invoice creation.
- Commitment Window: time period where reserved capacity pricing applies.
- Decommitment: customer-initiated early termination or capacity downscale with contractual penalties.
- Price Component: atomic billable item (e.g., reserved_gpu_hour, token_generation_unit, model_fanout_fee).

Ownership & Roles

- Sales (Contract Owner): deliver fully executed contract PDF and the signed commercial term summary in SAP/CRM.
- Finance - Contract Intake (Owner): validate commercial terms, create Contract Record, assign pricing component IDs. Primary contact: Priya Kapoor.
- Billing Ops: configure billing product catalog entries and ensure invoicing schedule aligns with trigger rules.
- RevRec (Revenue Recognition): validate recognition start/end dates and amortization schedule; responsible for ASC 606 mapping.
- Platform (Eng): provide capacity allocation IDs for Dedicated contracts and API to feed usage data into billing pipeline.

High-Level Process (Step-by-step)

1) Sales executes contract and uploads signed PDF to CRM within 24 hours.
2) Sales fills the standardized Commercial Term Summary (CTS) form in the CRM including: customer_id, product_line, commitment_quantity, unit_price, start_date, end_date, billing_frequency, cancellation_clause, acceptance_criteria (if any), discount_codes, and related SOW IDs.
3) Contract Intake validates CTS within 48 hours and creates a Contract Record using the ingestion template. Validation checklist: signed PDF present, effective date matches CTS, pricing math verified, SLA-bounded credits/penalties documented, and data residency flags set.
4) Contract Record is emitted to Billing Ops via message queue (topic: contracts.ingested) with payload following the canonical mapping (see Mapping Template).
5) Billing Ops maps the Contract Record to Product Catalog entries and schedules the first invoice. For reserved capacity, allocate capacity_id and tag with the customer’s project.
6) Pre-bill automation runs 3 business days prior to invoice period to detect mismatches (see Pre-bill Checks). Exceptions are routed to Finance - Contract Intake and Sales for resolution.

Canonical Mapping Template (example YAML-ready fields)

Note: this is the canonical set Billing expects. All keys are required unless marked optional.

---
contract_id: "<string>"
customer_id: "<string>"
contract_type: "reserved|usage|hybrid"
product_line: "hosted|dedicated|private"
price_components:
  - component_id: "reserved_gpu_hour"
    unit: "gpu_hour"
    unit_price_usd: "<decimal>"
    quantity_committed: "<number>"
billing:
  billing_frequency: "monthly|quarterly|annual"
  billing_trigger: "advance|arrears|usage_reported"
  first_invoice_date: "YYYY-MM-DD"
term:
  start_date: "YYYY-MM-DD"
  end_date: "YYYY-MM-DD|open"
  auto_renew: "true|false"
cancellation:
  notice_period_days: "<int>"
  early_termination_fee: "<decimal>|none"
revenue_recognition:
  recognition_policy_id: "capacity_reservation_scheduled|usage_immediate|one_time"
  recognition_start_date: "YYYY-MM-DD"
  recognition_end_date: "YYYY-MM-DD|as_billed"
acceptance_criteria: "<string>|none"
special_terms: "<string>|none"
---

Ingestion automation will reject the record if required keys are missing or dates are inconsistent. The intake team will correct rejected records or escalate to Sales.

Billing Trigger Rules

- Reserved (prepaid or committed): Invoice cadence follows billing_frequency. Billing_trigger=advance unless explicitly contract-specified as arrears. Revenue recognition uses scheduled amortization over the commitment window (see RevRec rules).
- Usage-based: Billing at arrears with usage_reported triggers; system expects daily usage exports with timestamped ingestion. If usage exports are >24h delayed, Billing Ops must set a tentative bill hold and notify Platform and Sales.
- Hybrid: Reserved baseline invoiced in advance; overage invoiced in arrears. Overage rates default to the contract’s overage_component if present or fallback pricing in product catalog.

Pre-bill Sanity Checks (automated)

The following checks run automatically 72 hours before invoice generation for each active Contract Record:

1. Date consistency: first_invoice_date within [start_date, end_date].
2. Price math: unit_price * quantity matches contract_summary_total (tolerance 0.5%).
3. Coverage: for reserved capacity, allocated_capacity_id exists and is tagged to customer project.
4. Usage feed health: for usage-based contracts, last_received_usage_timestamp within 48 hours.
5. Exchange rate lock: for multi-currency contracts, FX rate applied matches the FX capture date.
6. Revenue policy set: recognition_policy_id populated and verified against RevRec catalog.

Any failed check raises a ticket in Finance-Triage queue with severity: P1 (billing impact >$10k), P2 ($1k–$10k), P3 (<$1k). P1 tickets require Finance Lead and Sales Director acknowledgement within 4 business hours.

Revenue Recognition Rules (high level)

- Reserved capacity: ASC 606-compliant deferred revenue amortized on a straight-line basis over the commitment window unless contract specifies usage-based acceptance or tied SOW milestones. Revenue start_date = max(contract.start_date, service_delivery_date).
- Usage-based: Recognize revenue as usage is billed (billing-at-arrears). For multi-period usage invoices, split recognized revenue to match measured usage timestamps.
- Upfront fees (e.g., onboarding): allocate to distinct performance obligations; if service spans multiple periods, defer and amortize unless explicitly consumable on receipt.
- Amendments: if price or quantity changes mid-term, calculate prospective vs. retrospective treatment per accounting guidance; default: prospective unless contract indicates restatement. Document restatement calculations in the Contract Record note.

Special Cases & How to Handle Them

1) Early Decommitment (customer reduces Dedicated capacity before term end)
   - If contract includes a fixed early_termination_fee, Billing Ops invoices the fee on the next invoice cycle.
   - Finance - RevRec computes immediate acceleration of deferred revenue related to cancelled capacity portion in the month of termination.
   - Process: Sales files a Decommitment Form -> Contract Intake updates Contract Record -> Billing Ops issues invoice -> RevRec posts adjustment entry.

2) Overuse Detection with No Overage Clause
   - If usage exceeds committed baseline and no overage_component defined: Billing Ops applies the fallback overage pricing defined in product_catalog.fallback_rates and notifies Sales for contract amendment.

3) Marketplace Resale/Channel Billing
   - Channel partners must provide usage reports and invoice reconciliation files in the marketplace ingestion format. Billing Ops reconciles partner invoices to usage ingestion daily; differences >5% open a reconciliation ticket.

Example SQL Checks (for Billing Ops)

-- Find contracts with mismatched first invoice date\SELECT contract_id, start_date, first_invoice_date FROM contract_records WHERE first_invoice_date < start_date OR first_invoice_date > COALESCE(end_date, '9999-12-31');

-- Price mismatch tolerance check\SELECT cr.contract_id, cr.unit_price, calc.price_calc_total, cr.summary_total FROM contract_records cr JOIN (SELECT contract_id, SUM(unit_price * quantity) price_calc_total FROM contract_price_components GROUP BY contract_id) calc ON cr.contract_id = calc.contract_id WHERE ABS(calc.price_calc_total - cr.summary_total) / cr.summary_total > 0.005;

Automation & Integration Points

- Ingestion API: POST /v1/contracts/ingest (auth: api_key). Returns 202 with ingestion_id. Payload must follow Canonical Mapping Template.
- Event bus topics: contracts.ingested, billing.prebill_alerts, revrec.adjustments. Use message schema versioning (v1, v2).
- Usage feed formats: newline-delimited JSON with fields: timestamp, metric_id, quantity, capacity_id (optional), customer_id.

Sample ingestion curl (example)\curl -X POST https://internal-api.redwood.company/v1/contracts/ingest -H "Authorization: Bearer ${INGEST_KEY}" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"contract_id":"C-2027-888","customer_id":"cust_42","contract_type":"reserved","product_line":"dedicated","price_components":[{"component_id":"reserved_gpu_hour","unit":"gpu_hour","unit_price_usd":12.5,"quantity_committed":100}],"billing":{"billing_frequency":"monthly","billing_trigger":"advance","first_invoice_date":"2027-03-01"},"term":{"start_date":"2027-03-01","end_date":"2028-02-29","auto_renew":false},"revenue_recognition":{"recognition_policy_id":"capacity_reservation_scheduled","recognition_start_date":"2027-03-01","recognition_end_date":"2028-02-29"}}'

Exception Escalation Matrix

- P1 Pre-bill Failure: notify Finance Lead (Priya Kapoor), Sales Director, Billing Lead. 4-hour SLA to acknowledge; 24-hour SLA to remediate or apply interim mitigation (e.g., bill hold).
- P2: 1 business day acknowledgment; 3 business day remediation.
- P3: 3 business day acknowledgment; 10 business day remediation.

Audit & Controls

- All Contract Record changes must be auditable (who/when/what). DO NOT edit contract financial fields in the DB without creating a Contract Audit entry.
- Quarterly sample audit: RevRec team picks a random 20 contracts to validate contract→billing→revrec flow; results reported to Head of Finance and Internal Audit.

Reporting & Dashboards

Essential dashboards (Billing Ops):
- Contracts pending ingestion >72h
- Pre-bill failure rate by error class (date, price, usage feed)
- Deferred revenue schedule rollforward (monthly)
- Top 25 customers by committed spend (current quarter)

Change Log & Maintenance

- Any change to the Canonical Mapping Template requires approval from: Finance - Contract Intake, Billing Lead, and RevRec.
- Versioning: mapping templates and event schemas use semantic versioning. Update the mapping version in Contract Records when ingesting from a new template.

Appendix A — Common Clause Translations (examples)

- "Committed 50 GPU-hours/month at $10/hour": contract_type=reserved; price_component.quantity_committed=50; billing_frequency=monthly; billing_trigger=advance; revenue_policy=capacity_reservation_scheduled.
- "Monthly usage billed in arrears at $0.0002/token": contract_type=usage; billing_trigger=usage_reported; price_component.unit=token; unit_price_usd=0.0002; recognition_policy=usage_immediate.

Appendix B — Contact List

- Finance - Contract Intake: Priya Kapoor (priya.kapoor@redwood.com)
- Billing Ops Lead: Ethan Brooks (ethan.brooks@redwood.com)
- RevRec Manager: Marisol Vega (marisol.vega@redwood.com)
- Platform Billing API: billing-api-team@redwood.com

Document History

- 2026-11-15: Created by Priya Kapoor (initial draft).
- 2027-02-02: Updated with pre-bill automation thresholds and escalation SLAs.

Related policies & references

- Contract Change Financial Impact Playbook (contracts-and-legal-process/contract-change-financial-impact-playbook-2026)
- Commitment Usage Reconciliation SOP (revrec-and-billing/commitment-usage-reconciliation-sop-2026)

End of document.

title: dsid_54a31045f6f149d58a1350ff8d697815__forecast-aligned-purchasing-authorization-framework-2027.txt
text:
Forecast-Aligned Purchasing Authorization Framework

Summary
------
This document defines the Forecast-Aligned Purchasing Authorization Framework (FAPAF): a single, auditable process that ties purchase approvals to active budget forecasts and anticipated revenue recognition timelines. The goal is to reduce off-budget spend, improve procurement predictability, and ensure finance has timely inputs for RevRec and billing handoffs.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all Redwood Inference employees and contractors initiating purchase requests (POs, contracts, reserved capacity, and subscriptions).
- Covers capital (CapEx) and operating (OpEx) purchases that affect monthly/annual forecasts or revenue recognition timelines.
- Integrates Budget Owners, Procurement, Legal, and Revenue Operations (RevOps).

Key principles
--------------
1. Forecast-first approvals: every purchase > $10k USD or that creates a multi-period obligation must reference a forecast line and variance rationale.
2. Approval ceiling tiers are aligned to forecast buckets and owner responsibilities (see Approval Matrix).
3. RevRec-aware commitments: any purchase that creates customer-facing billing or deferred revenue consequences must include RevRec tagging and an expected recognition schedule.
4. Single source of truth: all approvals occur through Redwood Finance Portal (RFP) or integrated procurement system and must include a forecast ID.

Approval matrix (summary)
------------------------
- Tier 0: < $2,500 — Manager approval (no forecast match required).
- Tier 1: $2,500–$25,000 — Department Head approval + budget line reference.
