- Tier 2: $25,001–$250,000 — Budget Owner + Procurement + Legal (if contract) approvals + forecast variance note.
- Tier 3: > $250,000 or multi-year commitment — CFO approval + Procurement Director + Legal + RevOps review.

(For international purchases convert to USD at the finance daily FX rate and use same thresholds.)

Purchase lifecycle (step-by-step)
--------------------------------
1. Request initiation: Requestor files a Purchase Request (PR) in RFP with a short description, vendor, amount, supplier TIN, forecast ID, forecast impact (one-line), and requested delivery/term dates.
2. Automated validation: RFP checks forecast ID validity and existing commitments for the forecast line. If forecast capacity is insufficient, the PR is routed to Budget Owner for an uplift/exception.
3. Approvals: Required approvers are determined by the Approval Matrix. Legal is auto-requested for any contract or SOW.
4. Procurement execution: Procurement issues PO / negotiates contract and records supplier metadata.
5. RevRec tagging & billing handoff: For purchases that affect billing or deferred revenue (for example, customer pass-throughs, third-party services billed to customers), RevOps assigns RevRec tags (revenue category, recognition start, recognition pattern) and creates the RevRec ticket.
6. Close & record: Finalized PO/contract attached to PR, finance records commitment for forecast consumption and posts to commitments ledger.

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Requestor: completes PR accurately; provides justification and forecast ID.
- Manager / Department Head: confirms business need and policy compliance.
- Budget Owner: verifies forecast alignment and approves or requests uplift.
- Procurement: negotiates terms, issues PO, maintains vendor onboarding checklist.
- Legal: reviews contracts, ensures clause templates and data-residency/KMS requirements are satisfied.
- RevOps / Finance: tags commitments for RevRec, reconciles forecast consumption weekly, and updates billing teams.

Forecast integration rules (operational detail)
----------------------------------------------
- Every PR must reference an active forecast line (forecast ID). If no appropriate line exists, Budget Owner creates a forecast movement request with expected GL mapping and submits to Finance within 3 business days.
- Commitments reduce available forecast capacity as soon as PR is approved by Procurement. This ensures downstream teams see true available headroom.
- Monthly cutoffs: PRs approved after the 20th of a month but with vendor start dates in the next month must be included in the next month’s forecast update package.

Revenue recognition (RevRec) and billing impact
------------------------------------------------
- When purchases create deferred revenue or influence customer billing (e.g., third-party service resold to customers, prepaid support included with client contracts), RevOps must be looped in during the procurement review.
- RevRec tagging fields required on the PR: "revrec_category", "recognition_start_date", "recognition_pattern" (e.g., immediate, monthly_pro_rata, straight_line). Example: 

```
{
  "revrec_category": "prepaid_support",
  "recognition_start_date": "2026-04-01",
  "recognition_pattern": "monthly_pro_rata"
}
```

System configuration and automation notes
----------------------------------------
- RFP must enforce forecast ID presence via a mandatory field and reject PRs without it.
- Integrations: RFP <-> Procurement System (PO issuance), RFP <-> RevRec system (ticket creation and tag sync), RFP <-> ERP (commitment posting).
- Webhook example (Procurement -> RevOps) payload: use JSON snippet above with PR id and PO id.

Exceptional approvals and off-cycle requests
------------------------------------------
- Off-cycle purchases (urgent security, compliance, or production hotfixes) may be approved by the CTO and CFO jointly up to $500k; Procurement and Legal follow-up must occur within 5 business days.
- Emergency spend must still be logged into RFP with an "emergency" flag and retroactive forecast alignment submitted within the same fiscal quarter.

Control and auditability
-----------------------
- Every PR/PO/contract must contain the forecast ID and the approval path; missing metadata is a policy violation and will be flagged by internal audit.
- Finance runs weekly commitment reports and a monthly reconciled commitments-to-forecast report; exceptions are escalated to Finance Leadership.
- Retention: procurement records and RevRec tags are retained for 7 years per finance policy.

Implementation roadmap
----------------------
1. Q1 2025: Policy ratification + RFP adjustments to require forecast ID and add RevRec fields.
2. Q2 2025: Procurement systems integration (PO automation) and Legal template updates.
3. Q3 2025: RevOps integration and end-to-end testing using three pilot teams (Infrastructure, Product, Sales Ops).
4. Q4 2025: Full company rollout and training.

Helpful reference links
-----------------------
- Contract templates: confluence://finance-and-legal/contracts-and-legal-process/contract-clauses-escrow-kms-data-residency-2026
- Monthly forecast cadence: confluence://finance-and-legal/budgeting-and-forecasting/monthly-forecast-process-2025
- RFP user guide (Procurement system): confluence://eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/rfp-integration-guide

Appendices
----------
A. Sample PR summary (text to paste into RFP)
- Title: Reserved GPU capacity for Q3 campaign (3-month burst)
- Vendor: RedCloud Compute, Inc.
- Amount: $72,000 USD; multi-month prepaid
- Forecast ID: INFRA_Q3_2025_BURST
- RevRec Category: prepaid_infrastructure
- Recognition: straight_line from 2025-07-01 to 2025-09-30

B. Commonly used GL mappings
- CapEx: 6000-Equipment
- OpEx – Cloud compute: 6200-CloudServices
- Professional services: 6400-Consulting

Questions and feedback
----------------------
For questions or to request an exception, contact Procurement (procurement@redwood.com) or Finance (finance-ops@redwood.com).

title: dsid_a1db7929fff849349197e74ac03f7a31__incremental-kv-cache-migration-with-zero-query-loss-playbook-2026.txt
text:
incremental-kv-cache-migration-with-zero-query-loss-playbook

Overview

Purpose: This playbook describes a step-by-step, operator-focused procedure for migrating KV (key-value) cache state across private deployments with the objective of zero query loss for live traffic. It is intended for field operators, SREs, and the runtime team executing stateful rollforwards when model artifacts, runtime versions, or topology changes require an in-place KV cache migration.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Private (VPC / on-prem) deployments managed by Redwood Operator.
- Target runtime supports snapshot-and-restore of per-tenant KV cache (runtime version >= 3.9.0).
- Customer traffic must be routable through an operator-managed proxy that supports request mirroring and short-circuit quiescing.
- Operators have access to the control plane and the field operator toolkit (kvctl).

When to use this playbook:
1. Upgrading runtime where KV cache format changed (compatible-by-conversion).
2. Moving tenant state between clusters or AZs for capacity rebalancing.
3. Performing a live model swap that requires warm KV cache on the new model variant.

Owners and roles:
- Run: Field Operator (runbook executor)
- Validation & Escalation: Runtime SRE (on-call)
- Customer liaison: Solutions Engineer (if customer-visible windows are needed)

Prerequisites and checklist (must pass before initiating):
- [ ] Current SLOs and traffic windows approved by customer (if applicable).
- [ ] Snapshot storage bucket reachable and encrypted (KMS key id provided).
- [ ] kvctl >= 1.12 installed on operator host.
- [ ] Canary tenant traffic generator available.
- [ ] Baseline telemetry captured (latency / error / cache hit-rate) and uploaded to evidence bucket.

Key safety principles:
- Always prefer staged, shard-by-shard migration over big-bang for tenant-level isolation.
- Keep a forensic snapshot at every phase boundary (before any irreversible change).
- Use traffic quarantine (mirror-and-divert) to validate correctness before switching live traffic.
- Automate verifications and make thresholds explicit.

High-level approach (phases):
1) PREPARE: Validate topology, take global snapshot, set safe circuit-breakers.
2) WARMUP: Stream historical prefixes and replay hot keys to target cache (shadow writes).
3) INCREMENTAL MIGRATE: Move cache shards one-by-one with live validation and mirrored read-checks.
4) QUARANTINE CUTOVER: Divert a small percentage of live traffic to the migrated shard and confirm parity.
5) FINALIZE: Promote migrated shards to live, remove mirror, and retire source shard.
6) POST-VALIDATION: Run extended check and collect forensic evidence for rollback readiness.

Detailed procedure

Phase 0 - Safety gates (operator must complete these first)
- Confirm operator-host clock synced (NTP).
- Ensure control-plane connectivity: kubectl get pods -n redwood-control
- Confirm snapshot bucket ACL and KMS access: aws s3 ls s3://redwood-kv-snapshots/ --profile fieldops
- Set service-level circuit breaker: PATCH /api/operator/config {"kv.cache.migration.safe_mode": true, "traffic.diversion_threshold": 0.0}

Phase 1 - Global forensic snapshot
1. Create a read-consistent snapshot for the tenant(s) in scope:
   kvctl snapshot create --tenant tenant-42 --output s3://redwood-kv-snapshots/tenant-42/pre-migrate-20260301.tar.gz --encrypt --kms-key arn:aws:kms:region:acct:key/xxxx
2. Verify checksum and retention: kvctl snapshot verify --uri s3://...
3. Record the snapshot id and manifest in the runbook evidence section.

Phase 2 - Warmup (shadow writes + prefix replay)
- Goal: Populate hot keys on the target runtime without changing live responses.
- Steps:
  a) Enable mirror mode on the proxy for tenant-42: proxyctl route update --tenant tenant-42 --mirror-target cluster-B --mode read-write-mirror
  b) Run prefix replay using historical logs (or synthetic generator):
     ./tools/prefix-replayer --source logs/tenant-42/ --target cluster-B --concurrency 16 --rate 500rps
  c) Monitor mirrored write success and error ratio for 30 minutes. Acceptable thresholds: mirror-write-error < 0.2% and mirror-latency P95 < baseline+50ms.

Phase 3 - Incremental shard migration (repeat per shard)
1. Select one shard (shard-id from topology map).
2. Lock routing for that shard to a fenced operator path (prevent autoscaler evictions):
   operatorctl shard lock --shard shard-13 --reason "kv-migrate-2026-03-01"
3. Create shard-level snapshot:
   kvctl snapshot create --shard shard-13 --output s3://.../shard-13-pre.tar.gz
4. Restore into target nodes and validate checksum: kvctl restore --shard shard-13 --from s3://... --nodes node-a,node-b
5. Run read parity checks:
   - Configure mirrored read-checks: proxyctl readcheck enable --shard shard-13 --comparison-mode strict
   - Send 1,000 sampled reads with span distribution that targets hot keys.
6. Tolerances for progress: read-parity mismatches <= 0.05% for 10m window. If mismatch rate exceeds threshold, mark shard as degraded and escalate to runtime SRE.
7. If parity passes, proceed to quarantine cutover for that shard (Phase 4).

Phase 4 - Quarantine cutover (canary live traffic)
1. Shift 1% of real traffic to the new shard using the operator traffic-steering controller:
   trafficctl steer --tenant tenant-42 --shard shard-13 --percentage 1 --duration 10m
2. Monitor metrics (live request latency, error rate, generated tokens, cache hit-rate).
3. Automated gating rules (fail if any triggered):
   - live-error-rate increase > 0.5% absolute over baseline
   - P95 latency regression > 150ms over baseline
   - cache-hit-rate drop > 10%
4. If all gates pass for 10 minutes, increment to 10%, then 25% with 10m stabilization windows.
5. On successful 25% window, promote shard to 100% and remove mirror for that shard.

Phase 5 - Finalize and retirement
- Mark source shard retired: operatorctl shard retire --shard shard-13 --retain-snapshot s3://.../shard-13-post.tar.gz
- Rotate any shard-specific routing config and update runbook evidence with final metrics.

Rollback decision matrix
- Soft rollback (fast revert): if live error-rate > 1.5% within a 5m window OR parity mismatches persist > 0.25% -> divert traffic back to source for affected shard and stop migration.
- Hard rollback (forensic restore): if data divergence is large or snapshot corrupted -> restore source from pre-migration snapshot and open a P1 incident.
- Escalation path: Runtime SRE -> Head of Platform -> Customer Solutions if customer impact > 10% traffic.

Rollback steps (soft revert)
1. trafficctl steer --tenant tenant-42 --shard shard-13 --percentage 0 --target source --immediate
2. operatorctl shard unlock --shard shard-13
3. Re-enable mirror mode for diagnostics for 30 minutes and capture parity logs.
4. If necessary, restore from pre-migration snapshot:
   kvctl restore --shard shard-13 --from s3://redwood-kv-snapshots/tenant-42/pre-migrate-20260301.tar.gz --force

Forensic snapshot and evidence collection
- Always collect:
  * operator logs: kubectl logs -n redwood-tenant-ops controller --since=2h > evidence/controller-logs.txt
  * parity snapshots: kvctl parity dump --shard shard-13 --out evidence/parity-shard-13.json
  * telemetry export: metrics-exporter --range "2026-03-01T00:00:00Z/2026-03-01T02:00:00Z" --tenant tenant-42 > evidence/metrics.json
- Tag evidence in S3 under runbook id and notify oncall via #ops-incident with presigned links.

Operational thresholds and example config table
| Parameter | Recommended value | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Mirror concurrency | 16 | Increase for fast warmup; watch I/O on target nodes |
| Mirror error threshold | 0.2% | Fail if exceeded during warmup |
| Read parity tolerance | 0.05% | Strict parity required for zero-loss goal |
| Canary step sizes | 1% -> 10% -> 25% -> 100% | 10m stabilization windows between steps |
| Snapshot retention | 30 days | Longer retention for regulated customers |

CLI examples and snippets
- Create tenant snapshot:
  kvctl snapshot create --tenant tenant-42 --output s3://redwood-kv-snapshots/tenant-42/pre-migrate-20260301.tar.gz --encrypt --kms-key arn:aws:kms:...
- Start prefix replayer (local):
  ./tools/prefix-replayer --tenant tenant-42 --from logs/ --target cluster-B --rate 500rps --concurrency 16
- Enable strict read-checks:
  proxyctl readcheck enable --tenant tenant-42 --shard shard-13 --comparison-mode strict

Monitoring and verification (automate where possible)
- Dashboards to monitor during migration:
  * tenant-42: Live latency by shard (P50/P95/P99)
  * parity-checker: mismatch-rate by shard
  * cache-hit-rate: 1m and 5m windows
- Required alerts:
  * parity-mismatch > 0.1% for 5m -> auto-pause migration and page SRE
  * live-error-rate delta > 0.5% absolute for 1m -> auto-revert to previous traffic steering

Common failure modes and remediation
- High mirror-write errors: reduce concurrency, validate network egress path, check disk IOPS on target.
- Persistent parity mismatches: run kvctl parity dump for a sample keyset, compare values, and escalate to runtime engineering.
- Latency regressions: disable mirror write, revert shard traffic, and capture heap/GC diagnostics from target nodes.

Post-migration checklist
- [ ] All shards promoted and mirrors removed.
- [ ] Final forensic snapshots stored and checksums verified.
- [ ] Post-migration metrics show no sustained SLO regressions for 24h.
- [ ] Customer notified with runbook evidence bundle (signed off).

Appendix: Helpful commands and links
- kvctl docs: internal link /confluence/eng-infra/team-wiki/kvctl-docs
- Traffic controller API: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/traffic-controller-api
- Incident template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems/incident-template-2025

Summary
This playbook provides an operator-centric, low-risk path to migrate KV cache shards with minimal customer impact. The emphasis is on repeated verification (parity checks), short staged cutovers, and clear rollback decision points. Operators should practice this playbook in a staging environment before running in customer production.

Adaptive Embeddings Fidelity Packaging and Onramp Brief

h1. Adaptive Embeddings Fidelity Packaging and Onramp Brief

Summary

This brief describes a product packaging and onboarding proposal for "Adaptive Embeddings": a set of SKU and fidelity controls that let customers trade storage cost, retrieval latency, and vector fidelity for embeddings-powered features (search, rerank, semantic matching). The document covers target users, concrete packaging options, pricing heuristics, SLO/telemetry requirements, an onboarding checklist, and rollout recommendations for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Problem statement

As more customers integrate high-cardinality embeddings stores into production applications, we observe three common pain points:

- Unpredictable storage costs driven by retention and dimensionality.
- Latency and throughput regressions at scale when embeddings are hot or when retrieval patterns spike.
- Difficulty mapping model fidelity (float/quantized, dimensionality, index recall) to commercial tiering and SLOs.

Goals

1. Create a small set of packaging tiers that are simple to understand and map to unit economics.
2. Expose fidelity knobs (dimensionality, quantization, retention tiers, index type) to customers through API and Console UX.
3. Provide an onramp that means small customers can self-serve while enterprise customers can request assisted migration paths.
4. Instrument SLOs and telemetry so we can correlate fidelity choices to real cost and quality outcomes.

Target users

- Product teams adding semantic search or recommendation features to customer-facing apps.
- Data platform teams that need predictable billing and multi-tenant isolation.
- ML engineers experimenting with quantization, dimensionality reduction, and hybrid indexes.

Packaging proposals (summary table)

| Tier name | Typical use-case | Dimensionality & storage | Index defaults | Throughput SLA | Monthly price anchor |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|---:|
| Starter | Prototype / dev | 128-d, float16 (no compression) | IVF/PQ small shards | Best-effort | $0.03 per 1k vectors stored |
| Balanced | Production search & rerank | 256-d, int8 quantization option | HNSW default | 99.9% query P95 < 200ms | $0.09 per 1k vectors stored + query units |
| High-Fidelity | High recall, embeddings experiments | 1024-d, float32, no quant | IVF+HNSW hybrid | 99.95% P95 < 120ms | $0.35 per 1k vectors stored + higher query unit rate |
| Archive | Long-term, infrequent recall | 64-d projection, lossy compression | Flat files / cold index | Best-effort (async) | $0.005 per 1k vectors stored (cold retrieval fees apply) |

Notes on the table:

- Prices are anchors for packaging discussion and must be validated in billing experiments.
- Query units: a separate metered quantity that charges per thousand vector-scoring operations with tier-based discounts.
- Index defaults are suggestions customers can override but may incur higher cost or relaxed SLAs.

Pricing model mechanics

- Two primary meters: storage-per-1k-vectors-month and query-units-per-1k-ops. Storage accounts for dimensionality and quantization factor (e.g., int8 reduces storage by ~4x relative to float32).
- Add-on meters: warm-capacity (reserved shards), fast-prefix-cache (per-seat), and snapshot retention beyond N days.
- Overages: soft-threshold alerts and auto-repack windows (customers can opt-in to auto-compact quantized vectors during off-peak windows).
- Bundles: Developer Bundle (Starter + 5k free queries), Production Bundle (Balanced + reserved warm capacity), Enterprise Fidelity (High-Fidelity + SLA + migration assistance).

SLOs, SLIs and telemetry

Recommended SLOs (hosted and dedicated):

- Query latency SLO: 99th percentile end-to-end query time (including network) <= tier P99 target (Starter: 800ms, Balanced: 250ms, High-Fidelity: 150ms).
- Availability SLO: > 99.9% per calendar month for Balanced and >99.95% for High-Fidelity.
- Recall guardrail: for High-Fidelity tier, maintain recall@10 >= baseline model's recall@10 +/- 2% over rolling 7 days.

Telemetry requirements (must be surfaced in Console):

- Per-tenant: average vector dimensionality distribution, quantization ratio, index type, and the storage bytes per vector.
- Cost signals: tokens-equivalent estimate for query units (to help product teams reason about cost per search request).
- Quality signals: shadow-eval sampling rate that computes recall and MRR against a small promptset for regression detection.

Onboarding and self-serve flow (numbered steps)

1. Developer signs up and chooses Starter or Balanced trial from Console.
2. Quickstart: upload up to 10k vectors via REST SDK or S3 connector; default index created automatically.
3. Run the "quality preflight" (console button)  returns recall@10 against the customer's golden set or our sandbox set.
4. Console recommends fidelity adjustments (e.g., reduce dimension to 256, enable int8) and shows estimated monthly cost delta.
5. If customer chooses a higher tier (Reserved Warm Capacity), show contract UI and provisioning ETA.
6. After acceptance, the system will (a) reserve capacity, (b) run an index optimize job, and (c) enable SLA monitoring.

Migration and rollout plan

- Phase 1 (Q3 2029): Launch Starter and Balanced tiers to hosted customers with Console guidance only. Track conversion from Starter -> Balanced.
- Phase 2 (Q4 2029): Add High-Fidelity as an opt-in for selected customers and pilot enterprise pricing; introduce dedicated warm-capacity reservations.
- Phase 3 (Q1 2030): Expand to Private (VPC/on-prem) with an assisted migration service and formal runbook for data transfer and index rebuild.

Rollout safeguards and guardrails

- Automatic rollback: If the shadow-eval shows recall degradation > 3% after an index change, auto-revert index configuration and notify the customer.
- Cost caps: Default per-account monthly soft cap that halts new ingestion and sends an escalation email when crossed.
- Gradual shard rolling: rebalance index jobs to limit CPU/GPU impact (max 10% fleet disruption at a time).

Implementation notes for engineering

- Index metadata contract: store per-vector metadata (schema) with keys: tenant_id, vector_id, dimension, quantization, index_version, created_at, last_compacted_at. (Console and billing systems read these fields.)
- Storage calc equation: storage_bytes = N_vectors * dimension * bytes_per_dimension * compression_factor + index_overhead.
- Suggested default bytes_per_dimension: float32=4, float16=2, int8=1.
- Compact/repack scheduling: Background worker that runs compaction windows during tenant low-traffic windows (configurable via API).

Release notes summary (initial launch)

- Feature: Adaptive Embeddings packaging with Starter and Balanced tiers.
- UX: Console Quickstart wizard for 10k vectors and quality preflight.
- API: New endpoints: POST /v1/embeddings/import, POST /v1/embeddings/preflight, GET /v1/embeddings/cost-estimate.
- Telemetry: per-tenant vector telemetry and shadow-eval hook.

Monitoring & ops runbook highlights

- Pager thresholds: P95 query latency spike > 3x baseline for 5 minutes -> page oncall platform engineer.
- Cost anomaly detector: daily job that flags >30% day-over-day increase in query units for a tenant.
- Incident triage: steps to identify index compaction jobs, recent schema changes, and warm-cache eviction events.

Open questions (decision needed)

- Pricing experimentation: Should we prefer storage-heavy anchors or query-unit heavy anchors for initial commercial trials?
- Multi-index tradeoffs: Should Balanced default to HNSW or IVF hybrid for multi-tenant efficiency?
- Cold retrieval model: what SLA and UX guarantees do we give for Archive tier asynchronous requests?

Appendix: Example Console UX text and API snippet

Console UX snippet (quality preflight modal):

"Quality preflight will run a lightweight recall test against either your uploaded golden set or a Redwood sandbox set. This takes ~30-90s and will produce recommendations to reduce dimensionality or enable quantization with an immediate estimate of cost change."

API snippet (example cURL):

curl -X POST "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embeddings/import" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"tenant_id":"acct_123","source":"s3://bucket/prefix","index_preset":"balanced","dim":256}'

Related pages and references

- Incremental Embeddings Storage Tiering (PRD): /product-docs/requirements/incremental-embeddings-storage-tiering-prd-2026-04-20.json
- Vector consumption packaging SLA discussion: /product-docs/pricing-and-packaging/vector-consumption-packaging-slas-and-pricing-prd-2027-06-01.json

Document owner and next steps

Owner: product (Maya Chen). Next steps: 1) run pricing sensitivity experiments on a 50-customer pilot (target Q3 2029), 2) finalize index defaults and telemetry schema with eng-serving-runtime, 3) prepare a go/no-go for High-Fidelity pilot by 2029-11.

-- End of brief --

text:
Threat Model: Offline bundle signing for Redwood Private (air-gapped installs)

## Summary
This document threat-models **offline artifact bundles** for Redwood Private (VPC + on-prem packaging) that are distributed into **air-gapped** environments. The goal is to ensure **integrity and provenance** of all artifacts required to install/upgrade Redwood Private, and to ensure the installer **fails closed** when verification fails (with an explicit, audited break-glass path).

This threat model covers:
- Offline bundle tampering (manifest/artifact modification, deletion, insertion)
- Replay and downgrade attacks (reusing old but valid bundles/signatures)
- Key compromise scenarios (signing key, build keys, trust root distribution)
- Build and release pipeline threats (CI runner compromise, artifact substitution)
- Verification flow threats in the on-prem installer (time skew, partial verification)

Out of scope (initial phase): customer-signed bundles / delegated trust roots (tracked as a future plan).

## System overview
### High-level workflow
1. **Build**: CI produces deterministic offline bundles containing installer binaries, charts/manifests, container image references, runtime/model artifacts, and dependency packages.
2. **Manifest**: A canonical manifest is generated listing artifacts and cryptographic hashes.
3. **Sign**: Redwood signs the canonical manifest with a protected release signing key.
4. **Distribute**: Bundles are delivered via approved channels (download portal, support channels, or physical media for air-gapped customers).
5. **Verify (preflight)**: The on-prem installer (or preflight tool) verifies signature + hashes before installing.
6. **Install/upgrade**: Installer enforces downgrade prevention using signed metadata + local install state.
7. **Audit**: Verification outcomes are written to local audit logs; optionally exportable to customer SIEM.

### Trust boundaries
- **Redwood build/release environment (trusted, controlled)**: CI/CD, artifact store, signing service.
- **Transport/media (untrusted)**: download mirrors, email attachments, USB drives, customer transfer systems.
- **Customer environment (variable trust)**: air-gapped servers, admin workstations, cluster nodes.
- **Installer trust root**: public keys / trust store used to validate bundle signatures.

### Assets to protect
- Integrity/provenance of:
  - Offline installer binaries and scripts
  - Helm charts/manifests and values schemas
  - Container image references (MUST be pinned by digest)
  - Model/runtime artifacts and dependency packages
  - SBOM (or pointer + hash) and release metadata
- Confidentiality is not the primary objective for bundles (content is typically not secret), but **tampering** and **downgrade** are critical.
- Signing private key material and any CI credentials used in release.

### Security objectives
- **Fail closed**: Any signature or hash mismatch blocks install/upgrade by default.
- **Anti-replay/downgrade**: Prevent installing older signed bundles when a newer version has already been installed (unless a documented rollback procedure is used).
- **Key hygiene**: Signing keys are protected, rotated, and revocable without bricking air-gapped customers.
- **Auditability**: Verification events and break-glass usage are locally auditable and exportable.

## Assumptions and non-goals
Assumptions:
- Customer admins control the on-prem host that runs the installer, but their environment may be misconfigured (e.g., time skew).
- Bundle transport is considered hostile (bit flips, truncation, malicious replacement).
- Customers can update the installer/trust store through a controlled process.

Non-goals:
- Preventing a fully privileged customer admin from intentionally installing an untrusted build (break-glass exists). Our goal is to make this **explicit, gated, and auditable**, and to ensure the default path is secure.
- Secretless distribution: we do not rely on network calls for verification in air-gapped mode.

## Threat actors
- External attacker with access to bundle distribution channel or physical media
- Malicious insider or compromised Redwood developer workstation
- Compromised CI runner / build service account
- Customer-side attacker with access to staging machine used to transfer artifacts into the air gap
- Customer operator error (accidental corruption, wrong versions, partial transfers)

## Data flow / components (conceptual)
Components:
- Bundle builder (CI job) -> produces bundle directory and manifest
- Signing service (HSM-backed or equivalent) -> signs manifest
- Artifact repository -> stores bundles, signatures, metadata
- Installer / preflight CLI -> verifies trust store, signature, manifest hashes; enforces policy gates
- Audit log emitter -> records verification results and override usage

Primary file artifacts:
- `bundle/manifest.json` (canonical, signed content)
- `bundle/manifest.sig` (detached signature)
- `bundle/sbom.spdx.json` (or SBOM pointer + hash referenced by manifest)
- `bundle/artifacts/...` (charts, binaries, packages)

## Threat enumeration (STRIDE-style)
Below are key threats with mitigations. Severity is directional; actual severity depends on customer environment and deployment criticality.

### T1. Tampering: Modify bundle contents while keeping signature “valid”
**Scenario**: Attacker modifies `bundle/artifacts/*` (e.g., swaps installer binary or chart), but leaves `manifest.json` and signature unchanged.

**Impact**: If installer does not verify hashes for all artifacts, attacker can execute arbitrary code or deploy compromised components.

**Mitigations**:
- Manifest contains a complete inventory of required artifacts with **strong hashes** (SHA-256 minimum; SHA-512 allowed per customer crypto policy).
- Installer verifies:
  - Signature over canonical manifest (before reading artifact list)
  - Hash of each listed artifact before use
  - Refuses unknown/extra artifacts when policy is “strict” (default for GA)
- Container images must be referenced by **immutable digests** (e.g., `@sha256:...`) and those digests are included in the signed manifest.
- Integration tests cover modified file, swapped artifact, truncated file, and missing file cases.

Residual risk:
- If customers manually bypass verification (break-glass), tampering may succeed; this is logged.

### T2. Tampering: Modify manifest to exclude malicious content
**Scenario**: Attacker alters `manifest.json` to remove a hash check or to point to a different artifact set.

**Mitigations**:
- Manifest is signed; any changes invalidate the signature.
- Canonicalization rules (ordering/encoding) are fixed and versioned to avoid ambiguous verification.
- Installer verifies manifest schema version and refuses unknown future versions unless explicitly allowed.

### T3. Spoofing: Replace signature file with attacker signature + attacker public key
**Scenario**: Attacker provides a new `manifest.sig` and attempts to convince installer to trust attacker key.

**Mitigations**:
- Installer trust store contains **Redwood-controlled public keys** (or a customer-managed trust store that is populated via a documented procedure).
- Installer fails closed on unknown signing key.
- Trust store updates are treated as a privileged change with local audit logging.

### T4. Replay: Reuse an older signed bundle
**Scenario**: Attacker supplies an older bundle that is still correctly signed (e.g., contains known vulnerability), causing a rollback to a vulnerable version.

**Mitigations**:
- Signed manifest includes:
  - `release_version` (semantic version)
  - `build_id` (unique)
  - `build_timestamp` (for ordering; informational)
  - `min_installer_version`
- Installer maintains a local **install state record** (last installed version/build_id).
- Default policy: disallow installing a version lower than the recorded state.
- Explicit, documented rollback procedure requires a separate flag and is locally audited.

### T5. Downgrade: Force older key/trust root to accept compromised signing key
**Scenario**: Attacker forces customer to use an older installer/trust store that trusts a compromised key.

**Mitigations**:
- Signed manifest includes **key_id** and signature metadata to support revocation guidance.
- Trust store supports multiple keys with activation windows; installer supports key rollover.
- Key rotation runbook includes customer-facing update instructions for air-gapped environments.
- Release gating ensures new bundles require a minimum installer version that includes current trust roots.

Residual risk:
- Air-gapped customers who do not apply trust store updates are exposed until updated. This is addressed with customer communication and support runbooks.

### T6. Repudiation: Dispute about what was installed / whether verification was performed
**Scenario**: During incident response, customer or Redwood cannot prove whether a bundle was verified or whether break-glass was used.

**Mitigations**:
- Installer emits local audit events for:
  - verification success
  - verification failure (reason codes)
  - break-glass override invocation (with required annotation fields)
  - trust store updates
- Audit events include:
  - bundle build_id, release_version, key_id
  - hash of manifest
  - timestamp (local), host identifier, installer version
- Support bundle tooling includes verification output and manifest metadata.

### T7. Information disclosure: Leak sensitive metadata through logs
**Scenario**: Verification logs include full file paths, usernames, or customer internal topology.

**Mitigations**:
- Audit schema supports redaction; default is minimal fields required for troubleshooting.
- Do not log full file contents or environment variables.
- Clearly document what is logged locally and what can be exported.

### T8. Denial of service: Prevent installation via time skew / validity windows
**Scenario**: Air-gapped systems have incorrect clocks, causing signature validation to fail (“not yet valid” / “expired”).

**Mitigations**:
- Prefer signature mechanisms that do not require online validation.
- If certificate validity periods are used, choose conservative windows and clear error messages.
- Provide a diagnostic-only override for time source (does not disable signature checks; it supplies a verification time) and require explicit acknowledgement.
- Documentation includes recommended time synchronization approaches for air-gapped environments.

Residual risk:
- Some customers with strict time restrictions may require additional guidance; track as a deployment readiness item.

### T9. Elevation of privilege: Code execution via installer parsing
**Scenario**: Malformed bundle files exploit parsing vulnerabilities (path traversal, zip slip, unsafe YAML parsing) to execute code.

**Mitigations**:
- Treat all bundle contents as untrusted until verified.
- Use safe extract/untar libraries with path sanitization (no `..`, absolute paths, symlinks where disallowed).
- Validate manifest schema and size limits before processing.
- Run installer with least privilege; only escalate when required.
- Fuzzing / negative tests for malformed manifest and archives.

## Build & release pipeline threats
### P1. Compromised CI runner injects malicious artifact but signs it
**Scenario**: Attacker controls CI job that generates the manifest and artifacts; signing step produces a valid signature over compromised content.

**Mitigations**:
- Separation of duties:
  - CI build jobs cannot access signing keys.
  - Signing step runs in a restricted environment with minimal inputs (manifest only) and strong provenance checks.
- Use protected runners, hardened build images, and minimal permissions for service accounts.
- Require approvals for release signing (two-person rule for production keys).
- Generate and store provenance attestations (SLSA-aligned) and retain logs for audits.

### P2. Artifact store substitution after signing
**Scenario**: Attacker replaces published bundles in artifact storage.

**Mitigations**:
- Bundles are immutable once published (content-addressed or write-once policies).
- Publicly available checksums for bundle tarball + signed manifest.
- Installer verification ensures any substitution is detected.

### P3. Dependency confusion / external dependency drift
**Scenario**: Offline bundle includes dependencies pulled from external sources at build time; attacker poisons dependency.

**Mitigations**:
- Vendored dependencies are pinned by hash and included in signed manifest.
- Use internal artifact mirrors; forbid direct external downloads in release build.
- Reproducible build goals: deterministic inputs, pinned versions.

## Key management threat scenarios
### K1. Release signing key compromise
**Impact**: Attacker can sign malicious manifests; customers would accept them.

**Mitigations**:
- Store private keys in HSM/KMS-backed signing service with strict access control.
- Operator access via least-privilege roles; audited access requests.
- Two-person approval for signing key use in production release train.
- Key rotation cadence + emergency rotation procedure.
- Capability to distribute updated trust roots to air-gapped customers.

Detection/response:
- Monitor signing events; alert on anomalous volume/time.
- Document incident process: revoke/rotate key, publish advisory, provide updated installer/trust store, and block compromised key_id.

### K2. Trust store update tampering on customer side
**Scenario**: Attacker modifies trust store to add malicious key.

**Mitigations**:
- Trust store updates require admin privileges and are logged.
- Provide optional “pinned” mode where trust store is embedded and updates require installer upgrade.
- Document customer hardening recommendations (file permissions, integrity monitoring).

## Verification/installer threats
### V1. Partial verification (signature verified but artifact hashes not verified)
**Mitigation**: Installer must verify signature and then verify *all* referenced artifact hashes before use; tests enforce fail-closed behavior.

### V2. Ambiguous manifest canonicalization leading to signature bypass
**Mitigation**:
- Explicit canonicalization spec (e.g., canonical JSON with sorted keys, normalized UTF-8, no floats, normalized newlines).
- Reject non-canonical manifests at verification time (or canonicalize before verification, consistently).
- Version the manifest schema and canonicalization rules.

### V3. Unknown key behavior
**Risk**: If installer allows unknown keys for migration convenience, attacker could introduce malicious signatures.

**Mitigation**: Default must be **block on unknown key**; any temporary migration allowances require explicit policy flags and are tracked as exceptions.

### V4. Break-glass override abuse
**Mitigation**:
- Break-glass requires a dedicated flag and optionally a policy file (for enterprise customers) to enable.
- Installer prints explicit warnings and requires a typed confirmation.
- Audit event is emitted with mandatory annotation (ticket/customer case ID, operator identity where available).
- Support/PS runbooks require follow-up to restore normal verification.

## Risk rating (summary)
Scale: Likelihood (L/M/H), Impact (L/M/H).

| ID | Threat | Likelihood | Impact | Notes |
|----|--------|------------|--------|------|
| T1 | Artifact tampering (hash not checked) | M | H | Primary driver for manifest+hash verification. |
| T4 | Replay/downgrade to vulnerable version | M | H | Addressed by signed version metadata + local state. |
| P1 | Compromised CI signs malicious content | L-M | H | Mitigated via separation of duties + approvals + provenance. |
| K1 | Signing key compromise | L | H | Critical; requires strong custody + rotation plan. |
| V2 | Canonicalization ambiguity | M | M-H | Easy to miss; requires strict spec + tests. |
| T8 | Time skew blocks installs | H (air-gapped) | M | Operational risk; mitigations in UX/docs. |

## Security requirements (implementation checklist)
1. Installer verification MUST:
   - Validate signing key against trust store
   - Validate signature over canonical manifest
   - Validate manifest schema version and required fields
   - Validate hashes for all required artifacts prior to use
   - Validate container image references are digest-pinned and match manifest
   - Enforce downgrade prevention by default
2. Bundle build MUST:
   - Produce deterministic manifest ordering/encoding
   - Include chart tarball checksums and SBOM pointer+hash (if SBOM not embedded)
   - Produce detached signature file and publish alongside bundle
3. Release pipeline MUST:
   - Isolate signing keys from general CI
   - Require approvals for production signing
   - Store build logs and provenance artifacts for audit
4. Audit logging MUST:
   - Emit local verification events with stable reason codes
   - Emit explicit events on break-glass override and trust store changes

## Test strategy (security-focused)
Minimum set (gated in CI for Redwood Private releases):
- Tamper tests:
  - Modify artifact bytes -> verification fails (hash mismatch)
  - Modify manifest -> verification fails (signature invalid)
  - Remove artifact -> verification fails (missing required)
  - Add unexpected artifact -> policy-dependent; default fail in strict mode
- Replay/downgrade tests:
  - Install vX, attempt install vX-1 -> blocked
  - Allow rollback with explicit flag -> succeeds and logs override/rollback event
- Key rotation tests:
  - Trust store with old+new keys -> verifies both within allowed window
  - Unknown key -> blocked
- Time skew tests:
  - Simulate not-yet-valid window -> actionable error message; diagnostic override path documented

## Residual risks and follow-ups
Residual risks:
- Customers may delay trust store updates in air-gapped environments.
- A fully compromised customer admin environment can still bypass controls via break-glass.
- If a signing key is compromised, impact is high until revocation/rotation is propagated.

Follow-ups (tracked via Security review actions):
- Add stronger provenance attestations and automated verification in release gating.
- Evaluate adding transparency log for signed manifests (for non-air-gapped customers and internal auditing), while keeping offline verification independent.
- Expand documentation on air-gapped time sources and recommended operational controls.

## Operational guidance (for Support/SE)
- Always request `bundle inspect` output (manifest hash, build_id, key_id, verification status).
- For hash mismatch after transfer: validate transport tooling (zip/unzip behavior), re-transfer with checksums, avoid tools that alter line endings.
- For unknown key after rotation: confirm installer version and trust store update procedure; provide offline trust store update bundle if needed.
- For break-glass requests: follow exception process and ensure audit annotation is captured.

## Appendix A: Recommended audit event fields (minimum)
- event_type: `bundle_verification_success` | `bundle_verification_failure` | `bundle_verification_break_glass` | `trust_store_update`
- bundle_release_version, bundle_build_id
- manifest_hash (sha256)
- key_id
- installer_version
- failure_reason_code (if applicable)
- timestamp (local), host_id (or node identifier)
- redaction_mode (to indicate whether paths/usernames are suppressed)

## Appendix B: Glossary
- Offline bundle: packaged set of all artifacts required to install/upgrade Redwood Private without internet access.
- Manifest: canonical inventory of artifacts and hashes, signed by Redwood.
- Trust store: set of trusted Redwood public signing keys used by the installer.
- Break-glass: explicitly-audited override to proceed when verification cannot be completed normally.

## Change log
- 2025-11-18: Initial draft created (Security Eng).
- 2025-12-10: Added downgrade/replay section and installer local state requirement.
- 2026-01-14: Updated key rotation and trust store migration mitigations.
- 2026-01-28: Finalized audit event requirements and break-glass constraints for GA readiness.

title: dsid_265f946d7b2d4eeb8e19985466ac8b6e__bandwidth-aware-gpu-placement-and-iac-lifecycle-playbook.txt
text:
Bandwidth-aware GPU placement and IaC lifecycle playbook

Overview:
This playbook codifies an egress/bandwidth-aware GPU placement strategy and the associated Terraform/IaC lifecycle for Redwood’s multi-tenant inference fleet. The goal is to reduce noisy-neighbor egress contention, improve tail latency for latency-sensitive tenants, and maintain clear operational procedures for rollout, monitoring, and rollback.

Scope:
- Applies to all GPU clusters managed by the gpu-allocator service in public cloud regions (us-west1, us-east1, eu-west1).
- Covers node labeling, tenant egress tagging, scheduler policy, IaC module variables, CI/CD gating, and runbook actions for hotspots.
- Does NOT change model-level runtime parameters (those are handled by eng-serving-runtime docs).

Context and motivation:
- Observed incidents in 2024 where a small set of tenants with high-embedding workloads saturated node egress links, leading to 99.9th percentile generation latency spikes.
- Existing placement is GPU-count-first; we add a bandwidth signal to avoid co-locating heavy-egress workloads with latency-sensitive customers.

Key components (short):
- tenant-metadata-service: authoritative egress profile for a tenant (low/medium/high).
- gpu-allocator: placement controller that consumes tenant egress profile + node egress capacity annotations.
- egress-sharder: sidecar/proxy for shaping and tagging flows per-tenant for billing/telemetry.
- IaC modules: tf-module/gpu-node-profile and tf-module/egress-pool to manage node pools, tags, and autoscaling policies.

SLOs and thresholds:
- Per-tenant soft egress SLO: 250 Mbps sustained per GPU for "medium" profile, 50 Mbps for "low" profile.
- Node-level saturation alert: sustained >= 80% egress utilization for 60s => P3 alert (investigate).
- Tail-latency objective: 99th percentile generation latency < 450ms for latency-tier customers; placement policy aims to keep node egress headroom >= 30% for those tenants.

Node labeling and tagging conventions:
- node.kubernetes.io/gpu-type = a100|h100|t4
- node.redwood/egress-capacity-mbps = "4000" (example per-node uplink)
- node.redwood/egress-pool = "high-throughput" | "isolation" | "shared"
- Tenants are annotated via tenant-metadata-service with tenant.egress_profile = "low|medium|high". This drives placement decisions.

Placement policy rules (ordered):
1) If tenant.egress_profile == "isolation", place on nodes in egress-pool=isolation (single-tenant node pool).
2) Else prefer nodes where (node.egress_free_mbps - requested_estimated_mbps) >= 30% of node.egress_capacity.
3) When multiple candidates, prefer the node with lowest co-located "high" tenants count.
4) If no node satisfies headroom, route to dedicated burst pool (capacity permitting) or fall back to cross-region placement as configured by routing policy (costly; used as last resort).

Estimating requested_estimated_mbps (simple estimator):
- generate request: token-rate * avg-token-size-bytes * api-overhead-factor -> convert to Mbps.
- Embedding-heavy jobs include an override parameter in the request metadata to help allocator (recommended).

IaC module contract (variables and defaults):
| variable | type | default | description |
|---|---|---|---|
| egress_pool_name | string | "shared" | Name for the egress pool attached to node group |
| node_egress_capacity_mbps | number | "4000" | Advertised uplink capacity for node type |
| isolation_max_tenants | number | "1" | Max tenants for isolation pool nodes |
| enable_egress_shaper | bool | "true" | Inject egress sidecar configuration |
| autoscale_min | number | "1" | Min node count |
| autoscale_max | number | "50" | Max node count |

(Represented above as a preformatted table in Confluence - the IaC modules in the repo use these variables.)

CI/CD and gating for IaC changes:
- All changes to tf-module/gpu-node-profile or tf-module/egress-pool must have:
  - an accompanying plan that includes an estimated egress capacity delta and tenant-impact analysis.
  - at least two reviewers from eng-infra and eng-platform (automated reviewer assignment: CODEOWNERS).
  - Canary deployment: promote to a single region small pool (canary pool) behind feature-flag:placement.egress-aware=true.
- Automated tests in the CI pipeline (Buildkite):
  - terraform fmt & validate
  - unit tests for module input validation (go/py tests)
  - integration test: deploy a small cluster in ephemeral sandbox, simulate three tenant profiles and verify scheduler respects headroom constraints.

Rollout playbook (high-level):
1) Create IaC change with new variables set for isolation pools and node annotations.
2) Run CI, deploy to staging region, run integration test harness (see infra/ci-eval).
3) Enable canary pool in us-west1 with 3 nodes; route 5% of matching traffic via feature-flag routing.
4) Observe for 48 hours: target metrics (node egress utilization, 99p latency, tenant error rate).
5) Gradually ramp to 25% -> 50% -> 100% by region using rollout automation.
6) If any threshold breach occurs (see Rollback criteria), disable feature-flag and revert IaC changes.

Rollback criteria (automated):
- 99p latency for priority tenants increases > 20% over baseline for 30m.
- Node-level network saturation > 95% for 10m.
- Unbounded increase in network error rates (5xx) for any tenant > 1% of requests for 15m.

Operational runbook (responding to an egress hotspot):
1) Detect: Prometheus alert egress_node_sustained_high (>=80% for 5m).
2) Triage: identify top contributors using egress_sharder.flow_breakdown_by_tenant dashboard.
3) Immediate mitigation options (in order):
   a) Evict best-effort pods for non-isolated tenants from affected node: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=30 <node>
   b) Apply temporary per-tenant shaping via egress-sharder: redwoodctl egress-sharder throttle --tenant=<id> --mbps=100
   c) Scale up isolation/burst node pool (if autoscale_max allows): terraform apply -var="egress_pool_name=burst" -auto-approve
4) If eviction or shaping insufficient, enable cross-region fallback in gpu-allocator config for impacted tenant(s): update placement policy via config map and restart allocator (rolling): kubectl rollout restart deployment/gpu-allocator
5) Post-incident: run hotspot postmortem, capture tenant patterns, and consider promoting heavy tenants to scheduled isolation pools (owner: capacity team).

Monitoring and dashboards (recommended panels):
- Node egress utilization (per-node, 1m/5m/1h)
- Top-20 tenant egress by node
- 99p generation latency by tenant tier
- Egress sharder drop/shape rates and per-tenant throttles
- IaC drift: desired node annotations vs observed annotations

Prometheus alerts (examples):
- alert: NodeEgressSustainedHigh
  expr: node_network_transmit_bytes_rate{job="node-exporter"} / node.redwood_egress_capacity_mbps > 0.8
  for: 5m
  labels: { severity: "warning" }
- alert: PriorityTenantLatencyRegression
  expr: increase(request_latency_count{priority="high",quantile="0.99"}[30m]) > scalar(0) and (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant)) > 450)
  for: 10m
  labels: { severity: "critical" }

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: capacity@redwood (capacity team)
- Service owner: eng-infra GPU team (oncall: infra-gpu@pagerduty)
- IaC module owner: infra-iac (codeowners: @infra-iac)

Post-incident actions and continuous improvement:
- Add failing tenant patterns to synthetic load tests and CI integration tests.
- Consider quota or surcharge for sustained high egress to encourage tenant migration to isolation pools. Finance and pricing should be consulted before enforcement.

Appendix A — Example terraform snippet (gpu node pool):
```hcl
module "egress_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/tf-module/egress-pool.git"
  name   = "isolation-eu-west1"
  node_egress_capacity_mbps = 10000
  isolation_max_tenants = 1
  autoscale_min = 1
  autoscale_max = 10
}
```

Appendix B — Quick CLI commands:
- throttle tenant: redwoodctl egress-sharder throttle --tenant=tenant_123 --mbps=150
- force drain: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data
- restart allocator: kubectl rollout restart deployment/gpu-allocator -n redwood-infra

Notes and references:
- For full billing/chargeback integration see cloud-accounts-and-networking/egress-billing-clarity-and-multipath-metering-spec.json
- For scheduler internals see eng-infra/team-wiki/gpu-allocator-safety-checklist-and-iac-adapter-guide.json

Revision history:
- 2024-07-15: Drafted by Priya Patel (initial policy, metrics, and IaC contract).
- 2024-11-02: Updated SLOs and added egress-sharder integration (reviewers: Diego Morales).
- 2025-02-10: Finalized rollout playbook, CI gating steps, and example Terraform snippet.

title: dsid_71b48900e4664013bd26175b556915bb__region-sliced-gpu-allocation-operator-and-ci-guardrails.txt
text:
Region-sliced GPU allocation operator and CI guardrails

Overview

Purpose: This document describes the design and operational runbook for the Region-sliced GPU Allocation Operator (RS-GAO) and the accompanying CI guardrails. RS-GAO is an IaC + control-plane pattern used to partition global GPU fleet capacity by region, tenant eligibility, and feature flags while enforcing network egress constraints and CI-driven safety checks prior to promotion. The goal is to provide predictable tenant SLAs, safe canaries for capacity changes, and automated guardrails that reduce cross-region blast radius.

Audience
- Platform engineers responsible for GPU fleet provisioning and IaC modules
- SREs who operate capacity autoscalers and fallback routing
- CI/CD owners who maintain promotion gates for IaC changes

Context and scope
- Applies to Redwood dedicated and private deployments where multi-region capacity must be partitioned (hosted API and dedicated pools).
- Integrates with existing Terraform modules, the burst-orchestrator, and the egress-throttler sidecar.
- Not a replacement for tenant-level throttling; it operates at the cluster/pool allocation layer.

Goals and non-goals
- Goals:
  - Provide deterministic capacity slices per region and per priority class (prod/staging/eval).
  - Enforce egress accounting and rate limits at allocation time to prevent tenants from exceeding regional egress budgets.
  - Enable safe, CI-gated rollouts of allocation policy via automated policy tests.
- Non-goals:
  - Not intended for per-request routing decisions (that's handled by the smart router).
  - Not intended to replace runtime autoscaling heuristics.

Design overview

Components
1) Region-sliced Allocator (K8s operator):
   - Watches TenantAllocation CRD and ClusterCapacity CRD.
   - Enforces allocation constraints: region affinity, GPU type, burst credit, and egress budget annotations.
   - Emits allocation events to the capacity ledger (Kafka topic: capacity.allocations.v1).

2) Terraform operator manifests and module extension:
   - A Terraform module (module.rs_gao) exposes parameters for region weights, priority-class shares, and egress quotas.
   - Module outputs include allocation_policy_id and a signed manifest used as an input to the K8s operator.

3) CI Guardrails and Promotion Pipeline:
   - A pipeline that runs plan-time policy checks, synthetic allocation simulations, and a canary apply to a shadow region.
   - Failing checks block promotion to prod.

4) Runtime telemetry and SLOs:
   - Metrics: allocation.latency_ms, allocation.rejections, egress.quota_usage_pct, region.saturation_pct.
   - SLOs: allocation API P95 < 120ms, allocation success rate >= 99.5% over 24h, egress quota accounting accuracy >= 99.9%.

Allocation flow (high level)
1) Operator observes a TenantAllocation CRD created by the control plane.
2) Validates region affinity and sufficient cluster capacity.
3) Checks tenant egress budget annotation against the regional egress ledger.
4) Reserves GPUs by creating ClusterReservation objects and emits allocation event.
5) If capacity insufficient, triggers fallback routing policy (route to compatible region or downgrade priority).

Policy model and configuration table

| Key | Description | Example | Required |
| ---- | ----------- | ------- | -------- |
| region_weights | Relative allocation weights per region | {us-west: 60, eu-central: 40} | yes |
| priority_shares | Percent shares for priority classes | {prod: 70, staging: 20, eval: 10} | yes |
| egress_quota_bytes | Max egress per allocation window (24h) | 500GB | optional |
| burst_credit_seconds | Allowed burst duration before throttling | 600 | yes |

Terraform module example (snippet)

```hcl
module "rs_gao" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.internal/infrastructure/modules/rs_gao.git//module"

  region_weights = { "us-west-2" = 60, "eu-west-1" = 40 }
  priority_shares = { prod = 70, staging = 20, eval = 10 }
  default_egress_quota_gb = 300
  owner = "platform-capacity-team"
}
```

CI promotion pipeline (summary)
- Branch PR -> Terraform plan + policy check (OPA) -> Run synthetic allocation sim -> Apply in shadow region -> Integration smoke tests -> Canary apply to 5% region weight -> Promote

Example GitHub Actions stage (simplified YAML):

```yaml
name: promote-rs-gao
on: [workflow_dispatch]
jobs:
  plan-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: terraform init
        run: terraform init ./modules/rs_gao
      - name: terraform plan
        run: terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan
      - name: opa policy check
        run: opa eval -f pretty --input plan.tfplan 'data.rs_gao.allow == true'
      - name: allocation simulation
        run: ./ci/simulate_allocations.sh --policy plan.tfplan --checks smoke
  \n  canary-apply:
    needs: plan-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: apply to shadow
        run: terraform apply -target=module.rs_gao -var='canary=shadow' -auto-approve
```

Safety and rollback behavior
- All operator-initiated reservations are tagged with git revision and allocation_policy_id.
- If allocation failures > 1% in 10m for prod slices, operator triggers automatic rollback of the last allocation change and opens an incident.
- Canary policy changes are automatically reverted after 30m if egress_quota_usage_pct increases > 20% vs baseline.

Operational runbook (short form)

When an allocation rejection incident occurs:
1) Pager alerted (pager duty): alert title: "RS-GAO allocation-rejections >1% (prod)".
2) Primary oncall: check allocation.rejections and region.saturation_pct dashboards.
3) Query capacity ledger: kafka topic capacity.allocations.v1 (consumer: infra-ops).
4) If a recent Terraform promotion is present, run: terraform show -json plan.tfplan | jq '.resource_changes[].change' and identify allocation_policy_id.
5) Rollback: revert Terraform PR, apply to canary with reduced weights, and run smoke sims.
6) If failure is due to egress budgets, immediately reduce tenant egress quotas or route tenant traffic through egress-throttler sidecar.

Quick commands
- Check operator logs:
  kubectl -n platform logs deploy/rs-gao-operator -f --since=1h
- Inspect reservations:
  kubectl get clusterreservations -o wide --selector=policy_id=<policy-id>
- Revert last applied policy (Git):
  gh pr checkout <pr-number> && gh pr merge --revert

Testing and verification matrix
- Unit: CRD validation tests and OPA policies (coverage target: 90%).
- Integration: allocation simulation against synthetic cluster topologies (small/medium/large).
- Chaos: simulate region partition (netem) and ensure fallback routing engages within 60s.
- Perf: allocation P95 under 120ms at 1000 RPS simulated requests.

Telemetry and dashboards
- Core panels to add to capacity dashboard:
  - Allocation throughput (RPS), P95 latency, errors/rejections
  - Region saturation % by GPU-type
  - Egress quota burn rate (24h rolling)
  - Canary delta for egress usage and allocation success rate

Ownership and escalation
- Owner team: capacity-platform (eng).
- Oncall: infra-sre rotation for immediate paging.
- Escalation: capacity-platform lead -> infra-tools manager -> Eng VP.

Rollout checklist (for first-time promotes)
1) Author PR: update module.rs_gao with region_weights and default quotas.
2) Add simulated topology entries to ci/sim_topologies.json.
3) Ensure OPA policies updated for new keys.
4) Run pipeline: plan -> simulate -> shadow apply -> smoke test -> canary -> promote.
5) Observe metrics for 48h and confirm allocation success rate and egress quotas.

Appendix: CRD skeleton (YAML)
```yaml
apiVersion: infra.redwood/v1alpha1
kind: TenantAllocation
metadata:
  name: tenant-12345-allocation
spec:
  tenant_id: tenant-12345
  gpu_type: a100-80gb
  region_preference: [us-west-2, us-east-1]
  priority: prod
  requested_gpus: 4
  egress_quota_gb: 200
  annotations:
    requestor: team-ai
```

Notes and rationale
- Region slicing allows predictable billing and capacity runway for prioritized tenants while reducing noisy neighbor effects. Pairing the allocator with CI guardrails reduces human error during policy promotion and provides deterministic rollback behavior. The operator design keeps the control-plane decision making small (validate + reserve) and delegates runtime routing and throttling to existing runtime systems.

Related artifacts
- Terraform module repo: git@repo.internal:infrastructure/modules/rs_gao.git
- Simulation harness: /ci/simulate_allocations.sh and /ci/sim_topologies.json
- OPA policy catalog: /policies/rs_gao/*

Contact
- Primary: Evan Liu (evan@redwood.example)
- Runbook owner: Priya Desai (priya@redwood.example)

title: dsid_fe9eb6d717a5457bb6a098f1153a2233__cobalt-bridge-operator-manual-and-escalation-faq-2024.txt
text:
Cobalt bridge operator manual and escalation FAQ

Summary:
This page documents the 'Cobalt' bridge variant: a pre-authorized, lightweight incident bridge pattern for short-duration multi-team escalations (SRE + Customer Success + Platform). Cobalt is intended for events where rapid coordination and a single accountable bridge operator are required, but a full executive bridge is not yet warranted.

Goals:
- Reduce time-to-first-action for customer-impacting spikes by 40% compared to ad-hoc DMs.
- Provide a minimal, repeatable operator checklist that works across multi-tenant model-serving and dedicated capacity incidents.
- Standardize customer-facing status templates for low-latency public updates.

When to open a Cobalt bridge (criteria):
1) Any incident where a single bridge operator plus SRE and CS must coordinate live for >15 minutes and <3 hours.
2) Latency SLO breach affecting >=5% of active requests for 10 minutes.
3) Repeated 503 errors on generation endpoints with no clear single-service root cause.
4) Customer-visible errors reported by multiple unrelated tenants.

When NOT to open a Cobalt bridge:
- Regulatory/legal-impacting incidents (open a formal executive bridge).
- Long-running outages expected >3 hours (escalate to full incident command).
- Incidents confined to a single repo-level rollout where the owning team can manage via their team runbook.

Operator playbook (step-by-step):
1) Acknowledge and claim the Cobalt bridge in PagerDuty; set bridge channel to #cobalt-bridge-<region> and create the temporary bridge channel.
2) Triage initial impact: run `cobalt-scan` (internal CLI) to collect top signals: request-rate, 99th/95th latency, CPU/GPU utilization. Example: `cobalt-scan --service=serving-runtime --window=10m`
3) Post initial customer-facing status (see templates below) within 10 minutes of bridge open.
4) Convene SRE + CS + Platform in the bridge channel and assign roles: operator (single), comms, evidence collector, remediation lead.
5) Execute fast mitigations in order (see ordered checklist below). Track each action in the incident timeline.
6) If mitigations fail within 30 minutes and incident severity increases, escalate to a full Incident Command (see Escalation Matrix).
7) When service is stabilized, run the Cobalt closure checklist and schedule a 24–72 hour follow-up: short incident review (not a full postmortem unless required).

Fast mitigation ordered checklist (apply top-to-bottom until impact reduces):
- Step 1: Apply circuit-breaker routing to reduce noisy tenancy: `route-weight set --service=frontdoor --tenant=NOISY_TENANT --weight=0.0`
- Step 2: Temporarily pin affected requests to a lower-cost variant with higher concurrency limits.
- Step 3: Scale up Dedicated pool by +20% using the autoscale override API.
- Step 4: Enable KV-cache fallback for common prefixes (reduce model decode work).
- Step 5: Throttle non-critical background jobs that consume KV/cache bandwidth.

Escalation matrix (severity thresholds and handoffs):
| Severity | Trigger window | Initial responder | Escalation target |
|---|---:|---|---|
| P3 (cobalt) | 10–30m customer impact <10% | Bridge operator + SRE | Keep as Cobalt; optional EM notify |
| P2 (cobalt->ic) | >30m or impact >=10% | Bridge operator + SRE + CS | Incident Commander (IC) -> full bridge |
| P1 (exec) | region-wide outage, high business impact | IC + Exec comms | Exec bridge, on-call leadership, legal as required |

Note: escalation must be enacted automatically if metrics cross thresholds; the bridge operator declares escalation and tags PagerDuty with `escalation:automatic` when threshold is exceeded.

Roles and responsibilities (one-liners):
- Bridge operator: single point of coordination, owns the bridge lifecycle.
- Remediation lead: drives technical fixes and rollbacks.
- Comms lead: crafts public and customer notices using templates below.
- Evidence collector: captures logs, traces, and KV/cache snapshot for post-incident analysis.

Evidence collection checklist (minimum items to attach to incident):
- Timeline (UTC) of actions and observed metrics (10m resolution).
- `serving-runtime` traces for 5 example failed requests (include request_id).
- Hotspot profile: GPU/CPU per-host over the incident window (top 10 hosts).
- KV cache hit-rate and eviction logs.
- Snapshot of routing table and weight overrides.

Status page & external customer templates (use verbatim, fill placeholders):
- Initial public status (within 10m):
"We are experiencing elevated latency on model inference in <region>. Our team is actively investigating. No customer data loss is expected. Updates every 15 minutes."

- Follow-up (when mitigation in progress):
"We have applied targeted routing and capacity measures to reduce impact. Some customers may see improved latency. We will provide another update at <hh:mm UTC>."

- Resolution message:
"The service is restored in <region>. Root cause analysis will be published to affected customers within 72 hours. If you continue to see issues, please open a ticket with request_id=<REQUEST_ID>."

Customer-specific email snippet (short):
"Hi <Customer Name>,
We detected elevated latency affecting your requests originating from <region>. Our on-call team opened a Cobalt bridge and applied routing mitigations; you should see improvements. We will follow up with a root cause summary within 72 hours.
Regards,
Redwood Support"

Status page payload example (JSON, for automation):
`{
  "page": "status.redwood.ai",
  "component": "model-inference/<region>",
  "status": "degraded_performance",
  "update_body": "Elevated latency observed; mitigation in progress (Cobalt bridge open).",
  "notify_customers": ["tenant:12345"]
}`

Game day checklist (30–60 minute exercise to validate Cobalt flows):
- Pre-game: pick a low-risk service and schedule a 60m slot; notify observers.
- Inject: small, targeted latency spike via controlled canary traffic to the chosen service.
- Operator: open Cobalt bridge, run `cobalt-scan`, post initial status.
- Roles: verify SRE/CS/Platform assignment and comms cadence.
- Exercise automation: confirm `route-weight set` and autoscale override runbook succeed.
- Evidence: collect logs and validate evidence collector template.
- Retro: 30m retro using the template at the end; publish findings.

Handoff checklist (end of shift or operator transfer):
1) Update timeline and outstanding actions.
2) Confirm next check-in times and escalate points.
3) Transfer ownership in PagerDuty and Slack bridge with `@handoff` message including summary.
4) If remaining risk exists, schedule a 1-hour watch with a named owner.

Automations and tooling (quick reference):
- `cobalt-scan` — collects telemetry and writes a YAML summary to `/tmp/cobalt-<timestamp>.yml`.
- `route-weight` — routing control utility (see `route-weight --help`).
- `status-publish` — posts to status page using the JSON payload format above.
- `evidence-collector` — wrapper that bundles logs/traces and uploads to secure incident vault.

Runbook retention and post-incident follow-up policy:
- Cobalt incidents that lasted >30 minutes or resulted in customer-visible errors require a short incident review (template linked).
- If the review surfaces a systemic risk (rollout bug, scaling misconfiguration), escalate to a full postmortem and include affected model versions and rollout IDs.
- All Cobalt evidence bundles must be retained for 180 days and classified internal.

FAQ (quick answers):
Q: Can we use Cobalt for a planned maintenance window?
A: No — use maintenance channels; Cobalt is for unplanned rapid coordination.

Q: Who authorizes a Cobalt bridge closure?
A: The bridge operator closes the bridge after remediation lead confirms stable metrics for 10 consecutive minutes and comms lead has posted an external status.

Q: How do we decide between Cobalt and a full Incident Command?
A: Follow the Escalation Matrix thresholds. If impact is trending upward or customer SLA exposure is high, escalate.

Related templates and links:
- Incident timeline template: `/templates/cobalt/timeline.md`
- Evidence bundle uploader: `/tools/evidence-collector`
- Bridge operator quick-start cheatsheet: `/playbooks/bridge-quickstart`

Owner and maintenance:
- Document owner: Maya Chen (SRE, Incident Ops).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any P2/P1 escalation where Cobalt was used.

Appendix: sample incident timeline table (text representation)
Time (UTC) | Action | Actor | Notes
-----------|--------|-------|------
2024-09-14T10:02Z | Pager triggered (503 spike) | Monitoring | 5% error rate
2024-09-14T10:05Z | Cobalt bridge opened | Bridge operator | #cobalt-bridge-us
2024-09-14T10:12Z | Route weight override applied | Remediation lead | Noisy tenant pinned
2024-09-14T10:25Z | Latency reduced to baseline | Operator | Begin closure watch

End of document."

title: dsid_58937e65a65442a6935e56b1efcd642e__deployment-risk-profile-and-onboarding-runway-2025.txt
text:
Deployment risk profile and onboarding runway guide

Overview:
This guide defines a risk-based onboarding profile and an operational runway for private (VPC and on-prem) deployments of the Redwood runtime. It is intended for Customer Success, Solutions Engineering, Field Operators, and the Private Deployments engineering teams who run or validate customer installations. The goal is to align expectations, enumerate acceptance criteria, and provide a prescriptive, time-boxed plan that reduces operational surprises during the first 30 days after handoff.

Why this guide exists:
- Private deployments have heterogeneous environments (network, KMS, on-prem hardware) that significantly influence risk.
- A standardized risk profile lets us: prioritize validation work, set realistic SLAs during onboarding, and create automated evidence bundles for compliance customers.

Scope and audience:
- Scope: VPC-connected private deployments and fully air-gapped on-prem installations that run Redwood Private control plane and runtime artifacts.
- Audience: Field engineers, operator teams, customer SREs, sales engineers, and security reviewers.

High-level approach:
1) Classify customer risk across five domains: Network, Cryptography & Keys, Telemetry & Evidence, Capacity & Performance, and Change/Upgrade Surface.
2) Map a recommended onboarding runway (preflight -> install -> stabilization -> evidence delivery -> handoff) with concrete checkpoints and acceptance gates.
3) Provide templates and operator commands for evidence collection and rollback safety gates.

1) Risk profile matrix (summary):
Table: risk_domain | low | medium | high
- Network | Direct VPC peering with private subnets and predictable RTT (<10ms) | Transit via partner interconnects, occasional MTU or NAT translation | Customer-managed egress proxies, NAT with unknown middleboxes, variable WAN link >100ms
- Cryptography & Keys | KMS available with customer-managed CMKs and recorded rotation policy | KMS present but with limited audit integrations | No central KMS; hardware HSM unavailable or attestation required
- Telemetry & Evidence | Full telemetry (metrics, traces, structured logs), sample retention 90 days | Metrics only; traces sampled at 1% | Minimal telemetry; strict data-minimization or regulatory redaction constraints
- Capacity & Performance | Homogeneous GPU fleet with 10–20% spare capacity and node-level telemetry | Heterogeneous accelerators, 0–10% spare, preemptible instances | Highly constrained GPU budget, mixed architectures with warm/cold pools
- Change & Upgrade Surface | Customer agrees to scheduled maintenance windows and operator access | Limited windows and restricted operator privileges | Dynamic environment where OS/firmware changes without operator notice

Each domain above maps to mitigations and recommended operator actions later in this doc.

2) Onboarding runway (timeline & checkpoints):
- Preflight (T-minus 14 days) 
  - Deliverables: Preflight questionnaire; operator contact roster; temporary SSH bastion and agent certs.
  - Checks: Network diagram received; CIDR ranges, egress routes, and KMS endpoint listed; rack-level power/thermal info for on-prem.
  - Acceptance gate: Network trace test and remote attestation artifact received.

- Install (Day 0 to Day 2)
  - Deliverables: Signed image bundle, operator playbook, and initial model artifact SHA list.
  - Steps (numbered):
    1) Validate images and signatures on-airgap transfer checklist.
    2) Run bootstrap with operator in assisted mode: operator runbook output captured to artifact store.
    3) Smoke test: API responds to /health and sample generate request under 1s for control plane calls.
  - Acceptance gate: All smoke tests pass and a telemetry heartbeat is observed for 1 hour.

- Stabilization (Day 3 to Day 14)
  - Focus: Load profiling, KV-cache warmup, prefix caching validation, and realistic traffic replay.
  - Steps:
    1) Execute synthetic traffic at 30%, 60%, 90% of expected sustained QPS for 6h windows.
    2) Capture latency percentiles (p50/p90/p99) and GPU utilization.
    3) Validate autoscaler behavior and preemption handling for preemptible nodes.
  - Acceptance gate: No more than 5% error amplification (errors per minute increase) under 90% load; p99 under customer SLO threshold.

- Evidence delivery & compliance (Day 7 to Day 21)
  - Deliverables: Evidence bundle containing logs, telemetry config, KMS attestation, and test reports.
  - Items required for regulatory customers: egress proofing, redaction templates, signed operator runbooks.
  - Acceptance gate: Customer and security reviewer sign-off on evidence bundle.

- Handoff & burn-in (Day 14 to Day 30)
  - Final tasks: Finalize runbook for daily operator checks, schedule first QBR, and place SLO error budget in monitoring.
  - Acceptance gate: Operational readiness review completed; handover meeting recorded and owner assigned.

3) Concrete acceptance criteria and checklists (operator checklist):
- Network checklist (each item must be yes/no):
  - BGP/peer config validated (if used).
  - MTU and path MTU discovery verified for model artifact transfer.
  - TCP keepalives and idle timeouts configured per guide: idle_timeout <= 15m for long-lived KV streams.
  - Cross-AZ path measurements recorded and baseline p50/p99 RTT.

- KMS & keys checklist:
  - CMK created for tenant and key policy contains operator principal.
  - Key rotation schedule documented and a test rotation executed in staging.
  - HSM attestation (if present) exported and stored in evidence bundle.

- Telemetry & evidence checklist:
  - Metrics: Rediscovery probes, token-level counters, per-model p99 latencies.
  - Traces: Sample rate configured, at least one end-to-end trace captured.
  - Logs: Structured logs (JSON) enabled and ingestion verified to evidence bucket with retention policy.
  - Evidence: Bundle includes timestamps, SHA256 for artifacts, and operator script logs.

- Capacity & performance checklist:
  - Model artifact locality verified (weights cached locally vs. remote).
  - KV cache hit-rate measured and documented.
  - GPU telemetry available at node level and exported to metrics backend for 90 days.

4) SLOs, thresholds, and safety gates (recommended defaults):
- SLOs (can be tightened during contract negotiation):
  - Control plane API availability: 99.95% monthly
  - Serving p99 latency (short sequences): <= 350ms for small models; <= 1.2s for large models (customer defined)
  - Ingest and telemetry: metrics latency < 30s for critical counters
- Safety gates for upgrades and rollback:
  - Canary window: 1 hour at 5% traffic with synthetic checks.
  - Automatic rollback condition: error rate increases by >150% over baseline for two consecutive 5-minute windows, or p99 latency degrades by >2x.
  - Manual rollback gate: any security-critical certificate or KMS failure.

5) Upgrade and rollback playbook (short):
- Pre-upgrade: Confirm preflight snapshot is present; record KV-cache size and in-flight sessions snapshot.
- Canary rollout: 5% traffic for 60 minutes, run automated acceptance prompts and evals against canned prompt set.
- Monitoring hooks: add smoke queries for small, medium, long contexts and embed them into canary checks.
- Rollback steps (if gate violated):
  1) Disable new model/variant routing at the load balancer.
  2) Revert runtime artifact to previous SHA from artifact store.
  3) Restart minimal set of nodes (preserve KV state if possible).
  4) Run smoke tests and share evidence bundle with customer contact.

6) Telemetry evidence bundle (template of contents):
- file: evidence/metadata.txt -> short key-value manifest (install id, operator, timestamps).
