text:
Heterogeneous GPU Scheduling and Thermal Mitigation for Private Deploys

Overview

This playbook describes Redwood Inference’s recommended operational model for private deployments that use heterogeneous GPU fleets (mixed generations, memory capacities, and power envelopes). It covers scheduling policies, thermal mitigation strategies, telemetry and alerting, firmware/driver upgrade and rollback procedures, and a customer readiness checklist.

Audience

- Operators and SREs running Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem)
- Field engineers installing hardware or performing upgrades
- Customer platform engineers responsible for tenant capacity and QoS

Scope and Objectives

- Support mixed GPU fleets with minimal latency impact to inference SLOs (p95 < 120ms for interactive routes unless otherwise specified)
- Prevent noisy-neighbor thermal cascades and single-host failures from affecting tenant availability
- Provide safe firmware/driver upgrade paths with evidence-preserving rollback
- Ensure telemetry covers thermal, power, scheduler decisions, and per-tenant evictions

Background and Motivation

Many private customers prefer to incrementally add hardware (e.g., RTX A5000 with A100) for cost, procurement, or availability reasons. The runtime must:

- Map models and workload profiles to compatible hardware classes
- Respect per-tenant quotas and fairness policies (prevent a large batch job from starving low-latency tenants)
- Detect and mitigate thermal conditions proactively (avoid sudden throttling or OOM)

Key Risks

- Thermal cascade: adjacent GPUs on the same blower-based chassis heat up and trigger throttling, causing increased latency and evictions.
- Improper scheduling: assigning latency-sensitive requests to under-provisioned GPUs during bursts.
- Upgrade rollback gaps: driver or firmware upgrades that change scheduling semantics causing silent correctness regressions.

Hardware and Network Requirements (minimums)

| Category | Minimum | Rationale | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| GPU mix | homogeneous pairings preferred, support mixed generations | Heterogeneous allowed but requires explicit capacity tags | Customer / Ops |
| Interconnect | 25 Gbps per node (recommended 40 Gbps for multi-GPU NVLink traffic) | Prevent network bottlenecks during model loading and KV cache population | Customer networking team |
| Power and Cooling | per-node PDU with 20% headroom above max TDP | Allow headroom for temporary thermal spikes | Customer facilities |
| Telemetry uplink | 1 req/sec baseline agent heartbeat + burst to 10 req/sec | Ensure timely alerts during thermal events | Ops |

Scheduling and Placement Policies

1. Hardware classes: label GPUs as classes at install-time (class:a100-40gb, class:rtx-a5000, class:low-memory). The scheduler only colocates cache-heavy models on GPUs with matching class labels.

2. Latency tiering: define three tiers for routes — interactive, low-latency-background, batch. Scheduling heuristics: 
- Interactive: prefer lowest-latency GPUs (A100-family); avoid hosts with thermal risk score > 0.5.
- Low-latency-background: allow broader placement but avoid nodes with concurrent batch reservations.
- Batch: best-effort; can be scheduled onto heterogeneous cards if peak capacity is available.

3. Affinity and anti-affinity: ensure small models with heavy KV caches are anti-affinitized with large-batch workloads to reduce KV eviction churn.

4. Graceful degradation: when thermal or power headroom falls below policy, move interactive traffic to fallback model families (quantized / distilled variants) using smart routing. Include a fast-fallback tag on model versions.

Thermal Mitigation Strategies

- Node Thermal Score: computed from short-window (1m) and long-window (15m) GPU temperature, fan speed, and power draw. Values: 0.0 (healthy) to 1.0 (critical). Thresholds: 
  - warning >= 0.6 
  - mitigation >= 0.75 (start moving load)
  - critical >= 0.9 (evict best-effort workloads, signal outage)

- Proactive throttling: if node thermal score >= 0.75, stop scheduling new interactive requests; allow ongoing requests to finish with a max timeout (30s) then preempt batch tasks.

- Thermal isolation lanes: reserve 1 host per 10 nodes as a cool standby (idle slot) to absorb overflow when a rack shows sustained thermal degradation.

- Fan and PDU integration: where available, integrate chassis telemetry to increase fan RPM via automation when thermal score is between 0.6–0.75. Avoid aggressive fan curves that trigger noisy neighbor complaints from adjacent racks.

Telemetry, Metrics and Alerting

Required telemetry streams (agent names and metrics):

- gpu.temperature.C (gauge) — per-GPU temperature in Celsius (1s granularity recommended)
- gpu.power.W (gauge) — instantaneous power draw
- gpu.utilization.pct (gauge) — SM utilization
- gpu.memory.used.MB and gpu.memory.total.MB (gauge)
- node.thermal_score (derived gauge) — 1m and 15m windows
- scheduler.evictions.count (counter) — per-node, per-tenant reasons (thermal, OOM, preemption)
- model.fallback.count (counter) — counts of automatic fallback events per route

Alerting thresholds (examples):
- P1: node.thermal_score > 0.9 for 30s — page oncall, auto-evict best-effort tenants, mark node unschedulable
- P2: node.thermal_score 0.75–0.9 for 2m — message SRE Slack channel, trigger autoscale from standby pool
- P3: gpu.temperature.C > 85C for 1m — create ticket for field ops; do not immediately evict unless accompanied by thermal_score > 0.9

Dashboards (recommended tiles):
- Rack thermal heatmap (per-node 1m average)
- Evictions timeline correlated with model.fallback.count
- Scheduler decisions: placement by hardware class over the last 24h

Firmware / Driver Upgrade and Rollback Procedure

Principles:
- Upgrade in phases: staging (lab), canary (2 nodes), small canary (10 nodes), broad rollout (20% increments).
- Preserve evidence: collect driver and firmware state, driver logs (dmesg, nvidia-smi logs) and full telemetry snapshot prior to each stage.
- Automated smoke tests: model correctness, latency tail (p99) for a representative prompt set, KV cache warm-up behavior.

Step-by-step upgrade flow:
1. Prepare artifact bundle: driver+firmware image, sha256 checksum, release notes.
2. Lab validation: run full perf and correctness suite on representative models.
3. Canary (2 nodes): schedule at non-peak; run smoke tests for 6 hours.
4. Small canary (10 nodes): expand to 10 nodes across 2 racks; run extended 24h tests.
5. Broad rollout: advance in 20% increments every 24h provided no regressions.
6. Post-rollout verification: run weekly regression checks for 2 weeks.

Rollback criteria and steps:
- Rollback triggers: p99 latency regressions > 20% versus baseline, new OOM patterns, increased model inference error rate, silent correctness changes.
- Rollback steps (automated where possible):
  a. Mark affected cohort unschedulable for new traffic.
  b. Drain non-interactive workloads.
  c. Reinstall previous driver/firmware image from artifact repository.
  d. Reboot node (if required by firmware) and validate telemetry returns to baseline.
  e. Preserve and archive pre- and post-upgrade telemetry and logs in the rollback ticket.

Day-2 Operations Runbook: Thermal Event (short protocol)

1. Detection: alert triggers for node.thermal_score > 0.75 for 2m.
2. Immediate action (automated): scheduler stops scheduling interactive traffic to node; best-effort jobs are queued or drained.
3. Operator steps (manual):
  a. Check dashboard: verify neighboring nodes for rack-wide thermal trends.
  b. If single node: SSH into host, run nvidia-smi, inspect fan RPM and system logs.
  c. If firmware provides chassis controls, increase fan RPM by predefined safe step (follow per-vendor SOP).
4. If thermal_score remains > 0.85 for 10m: engage field ops to inspect cooling and PDU (file a P1 if multiple hosts affected).
5. Recovery: return node to schedulable state only after 15m of thermal_score < 0.6 and passing the model smoke test.

Customer Requirements and Acceptance Checklist

- Facility: adequate CRAC capacity to maintain inlet air <= 30C at peak loads; signed facility cooling agreement.
- Network: redundant uplinks >= 25 Gbps; documented QoS for telemetry.
- Power: PDUs with remote power cycling and 20% headroom above sustained TDP.
- Inventory: GPU inventory sheet with serials and class labels uploaded to Redwood onboarding portal.
- Telemetry: agent deployed and able to send metrics at required cadence; firewall rules allowing egress to Redwood telemetry endpoint.
- Maintenance window policy: customer must provide 4h planned maintenance windows for major driver/firmware upgrades.

Ownership and Contacts

- Primary owner: eng-sre (oncall channel #eng-sre-oncall)
- Field ops lead: Ricardo Silva (ricardo@redwood.ai)
- Customer success escalation: Priya Kapoor

Operational Tips and Traps

- Avoid aggressive packing of mixed-generation GPUs in the same chassis when possible; distribute older cards across racks to reduce correlated wear and thermal load.
- Watch for small, frequent CVM (cold-VM) model startups; they increase KV cache churn and can amplify thermal load due to repeated model initializations.
- Use the model.fallback.count metric to tune the fallback threshold conservatively during initial rollouts.

References and Related Documents

- gpu-failover-fabric-and-shared-storage-guide (operational playbook)
- hardware-root-of-trust-provisioning-and-supply-chain-playbook (onprem packaging)
- private-deploy-acceptance-and-smoke-validation-2026 (customer acceptance tests)

Appendix: Example CLI Checks

- Check GPU temperatures: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv -l 1
- Dump driver logs: journalctl -u nvidia-driver -n 500 > /tmp/driver-log.txt
- Compute node thermal score (local quick): python3 -c "print('TODO: use collector to compute thermal_score')"

Change Log

- 2026-02-12: initial draft (Maya Hernandez)
- 2026-02-20: added telemetry thresholds and dashboards (Jared Lin)
- 2026-03-01: expanded upgrade/rollback flow and added acceptance checklist (Priya Kapoor)

title: dsid_38e03f92f222429494df6a96c231cd2b__offline-upgrade-validation-harness-and-simulated-workload-suite-2026.txt
text:
Offline Upgrade Validation Harness and Simulated Workload Suite

Summary:

This page describes the offline upgrade validation harness and simulated workload suite used to validate private deployments before field upgrades or model swaps. The harness lets operators perform deterministic, repeatable validations of control-plane changes, runtime binary upgrades, model quantization swaps, and KV-cache migrations without impacting production tenants. It encodes a set of workload profiles, failure injection scenarios, telemetry assertions, and acceptance criteria required for sign-off.

Goals and scope:

- Provide an automated, reproducible validation path for upgrades that cannot be fully exercised in production canaries (air-gapped QA).
- Validate performance regressions (p50/p95/p99), correctness of model outputs for a set of golden prompts, and KV-cache consistency during stateful migrations.
- Exercise network/egress/fallback policies, tenant isolation rules, and KMS/HSM integrations in a safe sandbox.
- Produce an evidence bundle (logs, traces, metrics, artifacts) suitable for compliance audits and customer acceptance tests (CATs).

Out of scope:

- Non-deterministic A/B experimentation across live traffic.
- Long-term capacity soak tests longer than 72 hours (these are executed in separate stress labs).

Audience:

This document is intended for:
- Operators and SREs responsible for private deployment upgrades.
- Field engineers executing customer upgrades and runbook authors.
- Release engineers validating binary and package images.

High-level architecture of the harness:

1) Controller: a containerized orchestration component that coordinates profile playback, failure injection, and artifact collection.
2) Workload generator: pluggable modules that emulate request patterns for text generation, chat, embeddings, and KV-access at configurable QPS and token distributions.
3) Failure injector: network latency/jitter, process restarts, OOM simulation, GPU thermal spikes (simulated via throttling), and KMS latency stubs.
4) Telemetry validator: a rules engine that consumes traces/metrics/logs and evaluates pass/fail assertions.
5) Evidence bundler: packages logs, trace snapshots, diffs of golden outputs, and a human-friendly summary for sign-off.

Prerequisites and environment:

- Offline validation cluster that mirrors customer topology (minimum: 3 control-plane nodes, 6 worker nodes with representative GPU types).
- Ingested model artifacts: both current and candidate model binaries / quantized variants.
- Sample tenant configs and KV snapshots exported from production (sanitized).
- Network replay facility or traffic generator with TLS termination mirroring customer certs.
- Secrets: test KMS keys or HSM simulator. Ensure keys are marked test and are not customer secrets.

Workload profiles (bundled):

Each profile is a YAML file included in the suite. Profiles represent realistic mixes of requests and token distributions. Representative profiles: 

- small-text-search (embeddings-heavy): 100 QPS, 90% 128-token prompts, 10% 512-token prompts, embeddings batch size 32.
- conversational-saas (chat-heavy): 40 QPS, average 6 messages/session, 30% streaming responses, 15% function-calls.
- bursty-webhook (burst patterns): base 5 QPS with bursts to 800 QPS for 30s every 10m (tests autoscaling and burst policies).
- large-gen (long-context): 10 QPS, 80% requests with 2048 tokens output, intensive KV-cache usage.

Example profile snippet:

---
profile_name: large-gen
qps: 10
sequence_length:
  input: 512
  output: 2048
mix:
  generation: 95
  embeddings: 5
kvs:
  prefix_hit_rate: 0.65
  kv_ops_per_request: 2
---

Failure scenarios and injection matrix:

- Network partitions: simulate partial control-plane -> worker plane partitions and assert TLS fallback and routing policies.
- Slow KMS: add 200–1000ms latency to KMS calls and assert request error-rates remain below 0.5% for SLA-backed customers.
- GPU eviction simulation: sequentially drain and taint worker GPU slots and validate tenant failover and graceful degradation.
- KV inconsistency: introduce out-of-order KV-appends to check convergence and correctness of model state after catch-up.
- Model artifact corruption: feed an intentionally truncated model file and validate runtime rejects with clear error and falls back.

Telemetry assertions and acceptance criteria:

The telemetry validator enforces assertions at both service and tenant granularity. Key assertions: 

- Latency SLOs: generation p50 <= 120ms, p95 <= 420ms for small-text-search profile; p50 <= 250ms, p95 <= 1200ms for large-gen (these are validation targets, not guaranteed production SLOs).
- Error budget: end-to-end error rate (5xx or explicit runtime rejects) < 0.3% during the validation window.
- Token accounting: per-tenant token counts and cost ledger must match simulated inputs within 0.5%.
- Output fidelity (golden prompts): normalized token-level diff (BLEU-like) <= 2% on curated evaluation set after model swap. Any regression > 2% triggers hold.
- KV consistency: after simulated migration, sample 1000 state keys and assert deterministic values match pre-migration baseline.

Acceptance checklist (automated and manual steps):

Automated gating: 
1. All telemetry assertions are green.
2. Evidence bundle generated and checksum verified.
3. No fatal runtime rejects in error logs.

Manual review gating (operator):
1. Compare golden prompt diffs and confirm no semantic regressions.
2. Verify rollout playbook steps and human approvals are recorded.
3. Sign the CAT (Customer Acceptance Test) artifact when deploying to a customer.

Rollback triggers and automated backout policy:

- Immediate automatic rollback if any of the following are observed during a staged upgrade: crash-looping control-plane node, >1% sustained increase in p99 latency for two consecutive 10-minute windows, or token accounting discrepancy > 1% for billing-critical tenants.
- If rollback triggers, the harness executes these steps:
  1) Quiesce new client connections.
  2) Re-point traffic to previous model binary snapshot or previous container image.
  3) Restore KV snapshot and replay any missing operations.
  4) Re-run golden prompt set and validate parity.
  5) Generate a rollback report and mark run as failed for release dashboard.

Example rollback command sequence (CLI):

# Gracefully mark candidate version as draining
redwoodctl candidate set-drain --version v2026.03-candidate --reason "telemetry-regression"

# Roll traffic back to previous stable image
redwoodctl rollout promote --from v2026.02-stable --to production --force --note "auto-rollback"

Evidence bundle and audit artifacts:

The harness produces a bundle in S3-compatible storage (or local object store for air-gapped runs). Bundle contents:
- logs/ (structured logs from controller, generators, runtime)
- traces/ (Jaeger trace captures around failures)
- metrics/ (Prometheus scrape dumps)
- golden-diffs/ (per-prompt diffs and similarity scores)
- kv-checksums.csv (sampled pre/post migration)
- run-report.json (summary metadata, pass/fail flags, checklist status)

The run-report is machine-readable for the release pipeline; a human-friendly SUMMARY.txt is also included.

Sanitization and customer data handling:

- Use only sanitized exports from production. Replace PII using redaction toolchain (script: scripts/sanitize-export.sh).
- Generate synthetic tenant identifiers. Do not run with customer KMS keys; use test keys or HSM simulator.

Packaging and CI integration:

- The harness is shipped as a Helm chart (chart/harness/) and a CLI artifact (bin/validation-runner). CI job definitions (Jenkins / GitHub Actions) live under infra/pipelines/validate-upgrades.yaml.
- Typical pipeline steps: build artifacts -> create validation cluster -> deploy harness -> run suite -> collect evidence -> mark release pass/fail.

Runbook (step-by-step):

1) Prepare: ensure sanitized KV snapshot is uploaded and candidate images are available.
2) Bootstrap cluster: helm install harness --values ci/values-qa.yaml
3) Start profile: validation-runner start --profile large-gen --duration 60m --evidence-bucket s3://redwood-validation/runs/2026-03-01-abc
4) Monitor: tail logs and telemetry dashboard; the telemetry validator posts status to /status endpoint.
5) On success: download evidence bundle, attach to release ticket, notify release owner for manual review.
6) On failure: trigger automated rollback, collect post-rollback evidence, and open incident if regressions persist.

Operational ownership and SLAs for validation runs:

- Owner: eng-private-deployments upgrade team. Primary on-call: @upgrade-squad (rotating).
- Target run time for a standard validation (1 hour profile): full run + evidence packaging completes in <= 120 minutes. If packaging takes longer, pipeline marks run degraded.

Metrics the team dashboards should include:

- Run success rate (7d/30d)
- Median evidence bundle creation time
- Average validation runtime per profile
- Number of auto-rollbacks triggered and root-cause categories

Known limitations and future work:

- The harness currently simulates GPU thermal events through throttling rather than physical power cycling; we plan to integrate with rack-level testbeds for hardware-induced faults in 2026 Q3.
- Long-duration soak tests and regulatory customer-specific CAR tests are executed in separate labs (link to scheduling page required).

Appendices:

A. Example golden prompt verification script (bash):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
for f in golden-prompts/*.jsonl; do
  jq -c . $f | while read -r j; do
    prompt=$(echo "$j" | jq -r .prompt)
    expected=$(echo "$j" | jq -r .expected)
    got=$(curl -sS -X POST https://runtime.test.local/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer test" -d "{\"prompt\":\"$prompt\"}")
    sim=$(python3 tools/token_similarity.py --expected "$expected" --actual "$got")
    echo "$f,$sim" >> results.csv
  done
done

B. Sample profile directory layout:

/profiles/
  large-gen.yaml
  conversational-saas.yaml
  small-text-search.yaml

C. Contact and escalation:

- Upgrade lead: Aisha Kumar (aisha@redwood.ai)
- On-call rotation: upgrade-squad@pager.redwood.ai
- Security contact for sanitized data questions: Priya Shah (priya@redwood.ai)

D. Quick links:

- Release playbooks: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-onboarding-and-failover-runbook-2026
- CI pipelines: infra/pipelines/validate-upgrades.yaml
- Artifact storage policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention

title: dsid_e210c6ccf6d8490291b66113b2d87157__migration-advantage-playbook-transitioning-to-redwood-2026.txt
text:
Migration Advantage Playbook: Transitioning to Redwood Inference

A field-ready playbook that articulates Redwood's migration value for customers moving off legacy managed endpoints or DIY inference stacks. Includes positioning, competitive differentiators, pricing scenarios, objection handling, a compact pitch flow, migration milestones, and a security FAQ tailored for technical buyers.
Overview
-------
This playbook helps sales, solutions engineering, and customer success teams articulate the commercial and technical value of migrating inference workloads to Redwood Inference. It is focused on enterprise and platform teams evaluating migrations from: (a) third-party managed endpoints with opaque performance, (b) cloud-provider hosted endpoints with limited cost controls, and (c) internal DIY model-serving stacks.

Use cases covered: low-latency chat, high-throughput batch embeddings, multi-tenant customer inference, and regulated PII-sensitive workloads.

Positioning and Core Messages
----------------------------
Lead with outcomes, not features. Use these short, auditionable messages: 
- "Reduce per-token inference spend while improving 99th-percentile latency through smart batching and prefix caching."
- "Ship consistent inference across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments with the same API and rollout controls."
- "Move from brittle, ops-heavy DIY stacks to a production-grade runtime with SLAs and predictable economics."

Supporting bullet points to use in pitch: 
- Unified API for text, chat, embeddings, and reranking — reduces engineering integration time by 40–60% in our customer studies.
- Intelligent batching + KV prefix caching saves 25–60% on tokens for conversational products.
- Dedicated capacity and Private VPC options for regulated customers; HSM/KMS integrations available for secrets.

Competitive Brief (one-page)
--------------------------
Competitors in scope: CloudAI Endpoints (big cloud vendor), ModelServeCo (inference infra vendor), OpenHost (API-first LLM provider).

Comparative snapshot (simplified):
| Capability | Redwood | CloudAI Endpoints | ModelServeCo | OpenHost |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Multi-mode deployment (hosted/dedicated/private) | Yes | Hosted only | Self-host only | Hosted only |
| Predictable per-token economics | Yes (Optimize toolkit) | Limited | Variable (customer ops) | Limited |
| Latency SLOs & fallbacks | SLA + routing & model fallbacks | Region-level only | Customer-managed | Best-effort |
| Prefix/KV caching | Built-in | No | Optional (customer) | No |
| Enterprise integrations (KMS, audit) | Yes | Partial | Depends on deployment | No |
| Typical migration lift | Low to moderate (30–90 days) | Moderate | High (ops + infra) | Low (if compatible) |

Competitive talking points: 
- Against CloudAI Endpoints: emphasize cost transparency, smarter batching, and multi-deployment consistency.
- Against ModelServeCo: emphasize managed operational burden, integrated SLOs, and Redwood Optimize recommendations so customers don’t need deep infra teams to keep costs in check.
- Against OpenHost: emphasize private deployments, audit controls, and enterprise rollouts with canary/A-B policies.

Pricing and Commercial Guidance
------------------------------
High-level pricing levers to discuss: committed capacity (Dedicated), per-token rates (Hosted), model family premiums, and add-ons (observability retention, compliance).

Sample scenario templates (use during discovery):
- Conversational AI (customer support bot)
  - 1M messages/month, avg 50 tokens/request, mix of short/medium responses
  - Hosted baseline: 1M * 50 = 50M tokens -> show Hosted per-token price vs Redwood Optimize savings (assume 30% effective token reduction via caching/batching)
  - Dedicated baseline: reserved pool priced to meet 99th-percentile latency at target concurrency; present a 12-month committed cost and a per-request effective cost after queuing and utilization improvements.

- Batch embeddings (analytics pipeline)
  - 5M short documents processed in window -> emphasize throughput guarantees on Dedicated and cost reductions from quantization profiles.

Pricing playbook snippets: 
1. Start with hosted TCO to get customer using the API quickly (free credits / pilot).
2. After pilot, run a 4-week traffic profile assessment to estimate steady-state throughput and cost drivers.
3. Propose Dedicated when projected monthly spend exceeds threshold X (typical: $40k+/month) or latency consistency is required.
4. Offer migration uplift credits for first 3 months of Dedicated to offset integration effort.

Objection handling (pricing):
- "Your committed price is higher than current cloud endpoint spend." -> point to unit economics: predictable per-token after Optimize, reduced ops cost, and improved P99 latency. Provide a migration ROI slide showing 6–18 month breakeven.
- "We prefer to self-host to control costs." -> highlight hidden ops costs (engineering time, incident toil, security burden) and Redwood's Private offering with on-prem appliance.

Pitch Flow (10–12 minute engineering-focused run)
------------------------------------------------
1. Problem framing (2 mins): latency tail, unpredictable costs, and rollouts.
2. Redwood value props (3 mins): runtime optimizations, unified deployments, and observability.
3. Demo checklist (3–4 mins): API call, streaming token latencies, tracing from Console, a quick cost simulation from Optimize.
4. Migration plan & next steps (2 mins): pilot proposal and timelines.

Sales Engineering Playbook: Migration Milestones
------------------------------------------------
Minimum viable migration (30–45 day plan):
1. Pilot kickoff (Week 0): collect sample traffic, define success metrics (P99 latency, cost per 1k tokens, accuracy retention). Owner: SE + Customer Eng.
2. Integration (Week 1–2): implement API client, flush KV prefix rules, validate tokenization parity across models. Owner: Customer Eng.
3. Pilot tuning (Week 2–4): enable recommended batching/quantization profiles, run synthetic load tests, observe P99 and throughput. Owner: Runtime Eng + SE.
4. Validation & security review (Week 4–5): SOC2 evidence, KMS integration, audit log sampling. Owner: Security + Customer Eng.
5. Cutover & runbook handoff (Week 5–6): rollback plan, monitoring dashboards, on-call contacts. Owner: Customer Eng + SRE.

KPIs to capture during pilot: P50/P95/P99 latency, tokens per second, percent token savings from caching, error rates, cost per 1k tokens.

Case Study Snapshot (compact, anonymized)
-----------------------------------------
Customer: Global travel SaaS (anonymized)
Problem: High-cost conversational engine with frequent P99 spikes and inconsistent embeddings throughput.
Solution: 3-month pilot on Redwood Hosted -> moved to Dedicated (reserved capacity) with prefix caching and optimized quantization.
Outcome: 45% reduction in per-request cost, 2.5x improvement in P99 latency, and successful rollout to production across two regions.
Key quote: "Redwood cut our inference bill almost in half while giving us predictable SLAs for our support bot."

Security FAQ for Technical Prospects (concise)
---------------------------------------------
Q: How does Redwood ensure tenant isolation on Dedicated hosts?
A: Dedicated capacity is deployed as isolated GPU pools with network segmentation, customer-managed VPC peering, and per-tenant key material. Access to model artifacts and KV caches is role-based with audit trails.

Q: Can we run Redwood Private on air-gapped networks?
A: Yes. The Private deployment supports on-prem packaging and an offline installer. We provide documented checklist for secure installs and KMS/HSM integration.

Q: What evidence do you supply for compliance audits?
A: SOC2 Type II report, architecture diagrams, encryption at rest/in transit details, and sample audit logs for ingestion. Additional documentation available under NDA for regulated customers.

Q: How are model weights protected when using Hosted API?
A: Model weights are stored on encrypted volumes with strict IAM controls. For customers with strict requirements we recommend Dedicated or Private deployments.

Talk tracks for security-conscious buyers: 
- Offer a short security package: architecture review, threat model session, and 30-day security validation during pilot.
- For regulated customers, lead with Private deployment and KMS/HSM integration options.

Collateral & Pitch Assets
------------------------
- One-slide migration ROI calculator (attached in deal kit).
- 6–8 slide engineering pitch deck covering architecture differences and a short demo script.
- Security evidence packet (SOC2 summary, KMS integration guide, audit log samples).
- Migration checklist for SEs (playbook excerpt).

Owners and Contact Paths
-----------------------
- GTM owner: Lead AE (Deal origin) + Solutions Engineering (technical lead).
- SE escalation: se-oncall@redwood.ai (standard) and se-migrations@redwood.ai (migration specialists).
- Security questions: security-engagements@redwood.ai

Related pages
-------------
- link: /confluence/sales-enablement/platform-ops-inference-adoption-playbook-2026 (migration ROI calculators and templates)
- link: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/ (Private deployment runbooks)

Appendix: Quick checklist for discovery calls
-------------------------------------------
- Current monthly inference spend and 12-month trend.
- Peak concurrency and desired P99 latency.
- Whether data residency / private hosting is required.
- Existing model families in use (e.g., Llama, Falcon family, LLM-Prod-X).
- Ops team size and preferred level of managed service.

Document history
----------------
- 2026-02-15: Drafted by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-02-22: Reviewed by Jonah Reed and Mariana López, added pricing scenarios.
- 2026-03-02: Published after SE playtest and security review.

text:
Adaptive cohort probing and handoff runbook

Summary

This runbook describes the adaptive cohort probing and handoff process used by the Redwood serving runtime to detect per-cohort fidelity degradation, orchestrate kernel handoffs, and safely probe changes under production traffic. It defines telemetry signals, thresholds, automated decision steps, and operator procedures for investigation and rollback. The goal is to allow dynamic handoffs (e.g., between quantized kernel A and fallback kernel B) while preserving SLOs and minimizing cost impact.

Scope

- Applies to multi-tenant inference pools running heterogeneous kernels (FP16, 8-bit quantized, sparse-aware kernels) on GPU clusters.
- Covers automated probing, graceful handoff, telemetry required, manual intervention steps, and validation/benchmarking checklist.
- Excludes model packaging and build processes (see model-onboarding docs).

Audience

- Oncall SREs and runtime engineers responsible for scheduler and kernel rollouts.
- Benchmarking and profiling engineers validating kernel variants.

Background and motivation

Redwood supports multiple kernel implementations with different performance/cost/quality characteristics. When the scheduler considers swapping a cohort to a new kernel variant (for cost saving or fallback), naive switchovers can introduce regressions (tail latency spikes, token errors) that impact customer SLAs. Adaptive probing lets us sample production traffic for a small and controlled cohort, gather fidelity and latency signals, and make a conservative decision to expand, hold, or rollback.

Key terminology

- Cohort: A logical group of requests defined by model, route, or customer label.
- Probe window: The time-bounded sampling period used to evaluate a kernel change for a cohort (default 5 minutes).
- Handoff: The act of routing cohort traffic from one kernel variant to another.
- Fidelity regression: Any measurable reduction in output quality against a defined prompt-suite (e.g., Rouge/BLEU/embedding-similarity drop or increased hallucination rate).

Architecture overview (textual diagram)

Serving runtime components involved:

- Dispatcher: request classifier and cohort router (policy engine)
- Scheduler: allocates kernel slots and performs handoff orchestration
- Kernel Registry: metadata and compatibility matrix for kernel variants
- Probe Engine: lightweight mirroring and sampling sub-system for probe windows
- Telemetry Pipeline: streaming traces, percentile latencies, fidelity probes, error rates

(Imagine a horizontally stacked diagram: Dispatcher -> Scheduler -> Kernel instances; Probe Engine forks short-lived shadow requests to probe kernels and emits enriched traces into Telemetry Pipeline.)

Signals to collect

Collect these signals at 1s/10s/60s granularities depending on signal type:

- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for token generation and end-to-end request time
- Error rates: gRPC/HTTP 5xx, codec errors, kernel panics
- Fidelity metrics: embedding cosine similarity to baseline, token-level divergence, special token counts (UNK/UNK-like), model-specific eval score on a small prompt set
- Resource signals: GPU SM utilization, memory pressure, kernel queue depth
- Queueing indicators: queuing_time_ms, active_slots, preempt_count

Decision thresholds (defaults)

- Latency: p99 increase > 15% for probe cohort compared to baseline => fail probe
- Error rate: absolute increase > 0.5 percentage points or relative > 2x => fail probe
- Fidelity: embedding similarity drop > 0.015 absolute or relative quality delta > 5% on validation prompts => fail probe
- Resource: sustained (30s) GPU mem pressure > 90% or SM utilization pegged at 98% => fail probe

Config table (example values)

- probe_window_minutes: 5
- probing_fraction_initial: 0.01 (1% of cohort)
- probing_fraction_step: 0.05 (increase to 5% on success)
- max_probe_fraction: 0.20
- telemetry_aggregation_interval_seconds: 10
- required_consecutive_success_windows: 2

Automated probe lifecycle (high-level steps)

1) Candidate selection: Release pipeline marks kernel variant K2 as candidate for kernel K1 on cohort C.
2) Canary allocation: Scheduler selects a probe subset P (probing_fraction_initial) of cohort C and routes those requests to K2 for probe_window_minutes.
3) Shadow probing (optional): For fidelity-sensitive cohorts, the dispatcher sends a non-blocking shadow request to K2 in parallel; results are compared against the primary path.
4) Aggregation: Probe Engine aggregates telemetry for P and computes delta vs baseline.
5) Decision: If all thresholds are satisfied and required_consecutive_success_windows are met, increase probing_fraction by probing_fraction_step and continue. If probe reaches max_probe_fraction and passes final checks, promote K2 for cohort C. Otherwise, abort and revert to K1.

Manual escalation playbook (when automated probe fails but metrics are borderline)

1) Pager triggers: If failure threshold crossed for production cohort above severity threshold (see SLO incident taxonomy), page runtime-oncall.
2) Initial triage (5 min):
  - Confirm the cohort identity and affected customers.
  - Check recent kernel release events, model version swaps, infra incidents.
  - Run ktrace for an exemplar request (see commands below).
3) Containment (10 min):
  - Quarantine cohort: change cohort routing policy to pin to stable kernel K1 for all non-probe traffic.
  - Increase telemetry sampling to 100% for affected cohort for 15 minutes.
4) Root cause and remediation (30–90 min):
  - If kernel bug suspected, open kernel rollback and mark variant as unsafe in Kernel Registry.
  - If resource pressure, expand capacity or move cohort to different node pool.
  - For fidelity regressions, trigger a focused validation replay (see benchmarking steps) and notify model quality team.

Investigation commands and examples

- Capture a short trace for a failed sample:
  curl -s -H \"Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN\" \
    -d '{\"model\":\"X-small\",\"input\":\"<repro prompt>\",\"trace_id\":\"probe-debug-$(date +%s)\"}' \
    https://dispatcher.internal/v1/execute

- Query probe aggregates (PromQL example):
  sum(rate(kernel_request_duration_seconds_bucket{cohort="$COHORT",kernel_variant="K2"}[5m])) by (le)

- Compare embeddings (quick python snippet):
  from numpy import dot
  from numpy.linalg import norm
  def cos(a,b):
    return dot(a,b)/(norm(a)*norm(b))

Profiling and synthetic replay checklist

- Before large cohort promotions, run the following:
  - Microbench: run 1k synthetic requests with mixed sequence lengths (16/64/256) using the benchmark harness. Record p50/p95/p99 and compare to baseline.
  - Shadow replay: replay a 10k-sample window from production tracing storage through candidate kernel in sandbox.
  - Fidelity run: execute cohort-specific prompt set (50–200 prompts) and compute embedding similarity + model-specific metrics.

Benchmark commands (example harness invocation)

- ./bench_harness --kernel K2 --model X-small --sequences 1000 --mix \"16:0.5,64:0.3,256:0.2\" --concurrency 8 --report out/K2-microbench.json

Kernel scheduling policy examples

Use this sample policy to prefer memory-efficient kernels for cohorts with high concurrency:

- policy name: cohort_memory_preference
- selectors: cohort.labels.fidelity_tolerance <= 0.02 and avg_seq_length > 128
- preferred_kernel_order: [quantized_lowmem, fp16_sparse, fp16_full]
- admission: max_slots_per_node 32

Validation and rollout checklist (pre-promotion)

- Automated probe passed for required_consecutive_success_windows.
- Microbench p99 no more than 10% increased vs baseline.
- Fidelity metrics within thresholds on the validation prompt set.
- No related infra incidents in last 60 minutes.
- Release notes entry added to runtime release notes and Kernel Registry annotated with risk level.

Rollback policy

- Immediate auto-rollback on: p99 latency > 2x baseline or absolute error-rate jump > 2 percentage points.
- Automated partial rollback: if probe window fails but not catastrophic, revert probing_fraction to 0 and annotate Kernel Registry with failure reason.

Operational run scenarios (short examples)

- Scenario A: New quantized kernel shows 3% p99 improvement but 0.02 drop in embedding similarity.
  1) Probe small cohort (1%). 2) Fidelity delta borderline — hold probe and escalate to model-quality team. 3) After validating prompt set, either accept with a soft-fidelity gate or rollback.

- Scenario B: Kernel passes fidelity but causes GPU mem pressure.
  1) Probe fails on resource signal. 2) Quarantine cohort, move to larger nodes, re-run microbench.

Ownership and escalation contacts

- Runtime oncall: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai (primary)
- Kernel release owner: arjun.patel@redwood.ai
- Model quality: lena.rodriguez@redwood.ai

Operational metrics to track (dashboards)

- probe_success_rate by kernel_variant and cohort
- cohort_p99_latency and cohort_fidelity_delta
- kernel_panic_count and kernel_retry_rate

Safety notes and guardrails

- Never promote a kernel that showed any instance of deterministic correctness error (e.g., tokenization mismatch) in probe windows.
- For regulated cohorts (confidentiality=restricted), shadow probing is disabled unless explicitly approved by security/compliance.

Audit and postmortem requirements

- Any automated rollback must generate an incident record with: timeline, probe aggregates, decision rationale, and remediation plan.
- For rollouts that change >10% of cohort volume, perform a 72-hour post-rollout review and record in related_pages.

Appendix: troubleshooting quick hits

- If probe_latency spikes but resource signals are normal: collect detailed kernel traces and map to kernel queue depth; suspect scheduling contention.
- If fidelity drops only for long sequences: check kvcache eviction settings and kernel-specific KV handling toggles.

Related artifacts

- Kernel Registry schema: see /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/kernel-registry-spec (internal)
- Benchmark harness: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/operational-workload-simulator-and-signature-guide-2026

Change log

- 2026-01-12: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-02-10: Added kernel scheduling sample policy and expanded telemetry thresholds (review by Arjun P.).
- 2026-03-02: Clarified rollback policy and added synthetic replay checklist (review by Lena R.).

text:
Edge Request Path Cost Synthesizer and Alerting Contract

Summary:
This document specifies the Edge Request Path Cost Synthesizer (ERPCS), the associated alerting contract, and the dashboard widget library operators use to monitor and act on edge-initiated cost signals. The ERPCS synthesizes per-request cost estimates across multi-hop edge paths (edge -> regional gateway -> runtime) so we can detect high-cost request patterns early and route/mitigate before large token spend occurs.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Provide a consistent cost-estimation signal for latency-sensitive requests originating at edge proxies and define alerts and dashboards that map that signal to operator actions.
- Scope: Applies to all public and internal edge ingress paths (fast-edge, regional edge, and partner-routed) that lead to Redwood's inference runtime. Excludes: internal admin-only routes and offline batch jobs.

Background and motivation:
Redwood has increasingly diverse edge topologies and third-party routing. Token spend and backend model selection can be influenced by routing choices and prefix cache effectiveness at the edge. Operators need an early-warning synthesized cost metric that accounts for:
- estimated token emission at the runtime (model variant + expected output length),
- estimated network egress and cross-region delta, and
- cost multipliers for on-demand model swaps or quantization fallbacks.

Key definitions:
- ERPCS Score (float): normalized per-request cost estimate (USD equivalent) with a 95th-percentile bias for safety.
- Path segments: EDGE (ingress proxy) -> GATEWAY (regional routing) -> RUNTIME (model-serving).
- Cost multipliers: static factors applied for high-cost models, non-cached prefixes, and partner egress fees.

Design overview:
1) Input signals (collected at EDGE and GATEWAY):
   - request.route_id
   - request.model_hint (optional, e.g., gpt-xl-1-16k)
   - request.prompt_token_estimate (client hint; optional)
   - header: X-Request-TTL, X-Partner-Route
2) Runtime model profile: fetched from model-catalog-service: base_per_token_cost_usd, avg_output_length_tokens_by_prompt_size, cold_start_penalty_usd.
3) Cache and hit-rate model: prefix-cache-service projects cache_hit_probability for the incoming prefix window.
4) ERPCS computes:
   ERPCS = (expected_output_tokens * base_per_token_cost_usd * (1 - cache_hit_prob) + cold_start_penalty_usd) * routing_multiplier + egress_fee_estimate_usd
   - routing_multiplier = 1.0 (default) + model_variant_multiplier + partner_fee_multiplier
   - expected_output_tokens = max(prompt_token_estimate * response_factor_by_model, model_catalog.avg_output_length_tokens_by_prompt_size[bin])

Implementation notes and placement:
- Primary synthesizer runs as a lightweight sidecar inside the EDGE proxy (go service) with a policy cache.
- Gateway-level synthesizer is the authoritative aggregator that merges per-proxy scores into a single region score used for routing decisions.
- Synthesizer must be idempotent and deterministic given the same inputs for reproducible dashboards.

Metrics and telemetry emitted:
- erpcs.request_score (gauge) tagged by tenant_id, route_id, region, model_family, path_hash
- erpcs.request_components{base_cost, cache_loss_cost, cold_start_usd, egress_usd, multipliers} (gauges)
- erpcs.score_percentile.{p50,p90,p95,p99} (histograms) aggregated at 1m and 5m windows
- erpcs.high_cost_route.counter (counter) incremented when score > threshold for that tenant/route

Dashboard and widget library spec:
Provide a small library of dashboard widgets that can be composed into: tenant view, route view, and regional operator view. Each widget must include query, visualization, and suggested operator action. The spec below uses our observability query language (OQL) pseudo-syntax.

1) Widget: Route Cost Sparkline (compact)
- Query: oql:avg(erpcs.request_score{route_id="$route"}, 1m)
- Viz: sparkline + area shading for p95 band
- Threshold: warning at route-specific p95 > $route_budget_p95_usd; critical at p95 > $route_hard_limit_usd
- Suggested action: throttle route, enable cheap-model fallback, contact customer success for priority tenant

2) Widget: Distributed Cost Heatmap (regional)
- Query: oql:sum(erpcs.request_score) by (region, route_bucket) over 5m
- Viz: heatmap with topo map overlay; annotate nodes with token-rate and estimated USD/minute
- Suggested action: enable regional burst credits, divert to secondary gateway

3) Widget: Component Breakdown (per-request sample)
- Query: oql:last_values(erpcs.request_components{route_id="$route"}, 30)
- Viz: stacked bar chart showing base_cost, cache_loss_cost, cold_start_usd, egress_usd
- Suggested action: prewarm models, increase cache TTL for prefixes

Alerting contract (operator-facing):
Purpose: Alerts are actionable and map to a deterministic playbook. Alert IDs and payload must include route_id, region, top_contributing_component, tenant_id, erpcs_score_p95, and suggested_runbook_link.

1) Alert: erpcs.route_p95_degradation_v1
- Trigger: p95(erpcs.request_score{route_id="$route"}, 5m) > route_budget_p95_usd * 1.2 for 3 consecutive 1m windows
- Severity: P1 (operational) if tenant is enterprise with SLA; otherwise P2
- Pager: oncall-platform->primary if P1; email-to-route-owner if P2
- Payload fields: route_id, region, tenant_id_sample, erpcs_p95, component_breakdown_top3, correlation_links: [dashboard_url, sample_trace]
- Recommended pre-emptive actions: enable model-variant-fallback (to cheaper variant), increase cache TTL for matching prefixes, soft-throttle non-critical tenants

2) Alert: erpcs.cross_region_egress_spike_v1
- Trigger: delta(sum(egress_usd) by destination_region, 5m) > 10x baseline AND sum(erpcs.request_score) > $global_egress_alert_usd over 5m
- Severity: P1
- Pager: network-ops + platform-oncall
- Recommended actions: isolate partner egress, enforce egress caps, contact cloud provider for temporary quota boost

Runbook (short form):
1) Triage
   - Open alert payload and click sample_trace.
   - Identify tenant and route.
   - Check Route Cost Sparkline and Component Breakdown.
2) Rapid mitigations (choose one in order):
   - Enable cheap-model fallback policy for the route (if pre-approved) via runtime policy API: curl -X POST /api/v1/policy/fallback -d '{"route":"$route","fallback":"gpt-small-8k","ttl_min":30}'
   - Apply request-level soft-throttle: update route-weight in edge-routing-service to 50% for non-critical origins.
   - Pin route to regional gateway with spare capacity using routing-affinity API.
3) Recovery and verification
   - Observe erpcs.request_score p95 drop for 2 consecutive 1m windows.
   - Post-mortem note: record root cause, time-to-mitigate, and estimated USD saved.

Operational playbook for roadmap and rollout:
- Phase 0 (experiment, 2 weeks): implement synthesizer in EDGE sidecar with simulated model-catalog mock and no alerts. Gather baseline metrics.
- Phase 1 (canary region, 4 weeks): deploy synthesizer to us-west-2 edge fleet with dashboard panels. Enable low-sensitivity alerts to product owners only.
- Phase 2 (regional aggregator, 6 weeks): add gateway-level aggregator, enable routing-affinity experiments, and introduce self-serve route budgets for tenants.
- Phase 3 (global rollout, 8 weeks): enable full alerting contract and integrate with cost-optimization automation for low-priority tenants.

Governance and ownership:
- Owners: Platform Observability (primary), Edge SRE (secondary).
- SLA: ERPCS metrics must be available in dashboards with < 30s propagation to aggregation tier and 99.9% cardinality fidelity for active routes.
- Change control: Any change to routing_multiplier tables or model-catalog base_per_token_cost_usd must go through a runbooked release and have a backwards-compatible migration with a 14-day audit window.

Simulation and verification cookbook (examples):
1) Synthetic high-cost burst test
   - Steps: craft requests with model_hint set to most expensive model, set prompt_token_estimate high, tag requests with X-Partner-Route=true. Run at 250 RPS for 10 minutes.
   - Expected: erpcs.score p95 increases, cross_region_egress_spike alert (if partner egress used) should trigger in canary.
2) Cache-degradation scenario
   - Steps: artificially reduce cache_hit_probability in prefix-cache-service for a chosen prefix range and replay recorded traffic for that route.
   - Expected: component breakdown shows cache_loss_cost increase and suggested action prewarm/pin prefixes.

Troubleshooting guide (common failures):
- Missing model catalog values: ERPCS falls back to conservative defaults (high base_per_token_cost_usd) and emits erpcs.catalog_fallback counter. Action: refresh model-catalog-service and check service health.
- Divergent scores between edge and gateway: check policy cache TTL and version mismatches. Action: force policy cache refresh and reconcile tag versions.
- High cardinality explosion: if erpcs.request_score tags include highly dynamic route parameters, enable path_hash bucketing at the synthesizer to reduce cardinality.

Example queries (OQL) and saved dashboards:
- Tenant summary: oql:sum(erpcs.request_score{tenant_id="$tenant"}) by (route_id) over 1m
- Regional spend: oql:sum(erpcs.request_score) by (region) over 5m
- Cheaper fallback impact: Compare delta in p95 pre/post fallback: oql:ratio(p95(erpcs.request_score{route_id="$route", policy="fallback"},5m), p95(erpcs.request_score{route_id="$route", policy!="fallback"},5m))

Open questions / future work:
- Automating tenant-level budget enforcement vs. operator approval flow.
- Integrating client-side hints securely without opening exploitation vector for artificially low prompt estimates.
- Tighter coupling with Optimize's quantization recommendations for real-time routing decisions.

Appendix: example ERPCS JSON payload (ingress->gateway):
{
  "route_id": "public-chat-01",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-12T18:52:00Z",
  "erpcs_score_usd": 0.0124,
  "components": {"base_cost": 0.009, "cache_loss": 0.0021, "cold_start_usd": 0.0009, "egress_usd": 0.0004},
  "top_flags": ["partner_egress","no_prompt_hint"],
  "sample_trace_id": "trace-7b3a9"
}

Change log:
- 2025-11-18: Initial draft (Priya Raman)
- 2026-01-10: Added alert contract and runbook (Ethan Cole)
- 2026-02-12: Finalized dashboard widget specs and simulation cookbook (Marta Lopez)

Contacts and escalation:
- Platform Observability: observability@redwood.ai
- Edge SRE oncall: #edge-sre-oncall in Slack
- Runbook owner (primary): Priya Raman (priya@redwood.ai)

End of document.

title: dsid_43dfd9b333bf4fb4b444310398b8254c__execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026.txt
text:
Execution Stitching and Fallback Orchestration

Overview

Purpose: This document defines the execution-stitching pattern and the fallback orchestration responsible for providing graceful degradation when the primary execution path (high-throughput GPU kernel pipeline) cannot satisfy a request within SLO. It codifies the state machine, scheduling interactions, configuration knobs, observability signals, and an operational runbook for live incidents.

Scope: runtime-gateway, request-router, kernel-scheduler, kvcache-manager, fallback-router, model-variant-proxy. This guide targets on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and platform product owners.

Background and intent

- Problem: Mixed workload bursts, kernel regressions, or cache churn can cause a subset of requests to miss tail-latency SLOs. Uncoordinated retries or naive fallbacks cause thundering cascades, token-cost spikes, and model quality regressions.
- Intent: Provide a deterministic, observable orchestration that "stitches" partial progress from the primary path into safe fallback executions while minimizing cost and preserving user-visible correctness.

Architecture summary

Execution paths (logical services)
- runtime-gateway: front-door handling auth, rate limits, and per-token costing.
- request-router: classifies request by latency budget, priority, and required guarantees; assigns to execution lanes.
- kernel-scheduler: maps request lanes to kernel execution pools (low-latency, standard, background) and controls kernel handoff.
- kvcache-manager: supplies KV cache state and prefix-hinting; exposes warmup metrics.
- fallback-router: executes alternative strategies (quantized variant, truncated-response, stateless re-generation) and merges results.
- model-variant-proxy: serves model variant redirects and handles compatibility checks.

Execution stitching concept (high level)

1) Progressive execution: a request begins on the primary lane (low-latency pool). The kernel-scheduler allocates slots and attaches a progress token that represents the number of completed token-chunks and current KV epoch.
2) Checkpoints: At prescribed kernel boundaries (every N tokens or at decoder-layer boundaries), the runtime emits a "stitch-checkpoint" event with progress token, partial logits digest, and KV-origin stamp.
3) Decision point: If the primary path is delayed beyond budget T_warn (configurable), request-router consults fallback policy to decide: wait, re-route to a compatible curtailed variant, or switch to a stateless fallback.
4) Stitching: If a fallback executes, the fallback-router attempts to hydrate the fallback with the latest checkpoint (prefix/KV + partial logits) so it continues generation without repeating completed work. If KV state is incompatible, fallback falls back further to truncated restart.

State machine (summary)

- STATES: ACCEPTED -> RUNNING_PRIMARY -> CHECKPOINTED -> FALLBACK_PENDING -> FALLBACK_RUNNING -> MERGING -> COMPLETED | FAILED
- TRANSITIONS are timebox-driven and signal-driven. Key signals: KERNEL_HEARTBEAT, CHECKPOINT_CREATED, KV_WARM, SCHEDULE_PREEMPT.

Scheduling interactions and kernel implications

- Kernel preemption: kernel-scheduler must annotate preemption reasons (quota, fragmentation, safety-net) in the KERNEL_HEARTBEAT so stitching logic can choose soft vs hard fallback.
- Slice-aware execution: kernels that support incremental slice commits must expose slice boundaries to runtime-gateway via CHECKPOINT_CREATED, otherwise stitching is not possible.
- Fairness: scheduler applies a credit-based weight that factors "stitchability_score" per request; low stitchability pushes requests into conservative fallbacks early.

Configuration table (recommended defaults)

| config_key | description | default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| stitch.max_wait_ms | maximum time to wait for primary before triggering fallback_pending | "80ms" |
| stitch.warn_ms | time to emit early warning event to tracing | "40ms" |
| stitch.min_progress_tokens | minimum completed tokens to allow stitching | "8" |
| stitch.max_merge_attempts | number of attempts to merge fallback output with checkpoint | "2" |
| fallback.quantized_variant | model variant id for quantized fallback | "gptq-compat-v1" |
| fallback.truncate_heuristic | apply truncation when KV mismatch ratio > X% | "30%" |
| merge.similarity_threshold | threshold for partial-logit merge acceptance (cosine) | "0.92" |

Operational runbook: tail-latency incident (step-by-step)

1) Triage signal: alert fires on metric runtime.tail_95_ms > 1.5x SLO for 5m and stitch.fallback_rate > 3%. Channel: #oncall-runtime. Pager: primary SRE.
2) Initial checks (5 min):
   a) Verify recent deploys: check runtime-gateway and kernel-scheduler release notes for rollouts in the last 30m.
   b) Query kvcache-manager: kvcache.hit_ratio_1m and kvcache.warmup_queue length.
   c) Check kernel health: kernel.pool_fragmentation and kernel.queueing_latency.
3) Fast mitigation (10–20 min):
   a) Temporarily increase stitch.max_wait_ms to absorb transient jitter (add 20–40ms), using /admin/api/runtime/config apply --patch '{"stitch.max_wait_ms":"120ms"}'.
   b) If kernel fragmentation high, trigger node drain of <low-util> batch GPUs and rebind low-latency pools: /ops/gpu-drain --pool batch-3 --timeout 2m.
   c) If fallback rate is too high and causing cost spike, set fallback.quantized_variant to a cheaper model: /admin/runtime/set-fallback --variant gptq-compact-v2
4) Investigation (30–90 min):
   a) Correlate CHECKPOINT_CREATED rates with kernel queue depth. Low checkpoint frequency indicates slices are too large.
   b) Inspect traces: look for repeated MERGE_REJECT events (merge.similarity_threshold violations). If frequent, raise threshold or disable merging for the affected model.
5) Post-incident actions (within 5 working days):
   a) Run synthetic replay of failing traffic shape in the benchmarking suite (see: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-scaling-experiment-protocol-and-benchmark-checklist-2026).
   b) Open an ADR PR if code-level scheduler change needed.

Debugging artifacts and observability contract

Core trace fields emitted for each request (required):
- request_id (string)
- tenant_id
- execution_lane ("low-latency" | "standard" | "background")
- stitch.progress_tokens (int)
- stitch.checkpoint_ts (epoch-ms)
- kernel.heartbeat_ts
- fallback.decision ("none"|"quantized"|"truncate_restart"|"stateless")
- merge.result ("merged"|"rejected"|"not_attempted")

Metrics (minimum to alert on)
- runtime.tail_95_ms
- stitch.fallback_rate (requests/sec and %)
- stitch.merge_accept_rate
- kvcache.hit_ratio_1m
- kernel.queue_latency_p50/p95/p99

Events (audit log items)
- CHECKPOINT_CREATED: {request_id, tokens_complete, kv_epoch}
- FALLBACK_TRIGGERED: {request_id, reason, chosen_variant}
- MERGE_ATTEMPT: {request_id, similarity_score, attempt_index}

Example trace JSON (single-line)
{"request_id":"req-3f2b","execution_lane":"low-latency","stitch.progress_tokens":12,"stitch.checkpoint_ts":1700000000123,"fallback.decision":"quantized","merge.result":"merged"}

Configuration and testing guidelines

- Bench test: use the mixed-shape generator with prefix-hot distribution and KV-churn enabled. Run at 2x production QPS for 10m. Verify stitch.merge_accept_rate > 98% and stitch.fallback_rate < 2%.
- Unit tests: add deterministic checkpoint emission tests: synthetic kernel must emit CHECKPOINT_CREATED before each slice commit.
- Canary plan for changing stitch.max_wait_ms:
  1) Apply config to canary runtime-gateway cluster (10% of traffic) for 30m.
  2) Validate metrics: no increase in tail_99 or cost-per-token > 1.1x baseline.
  3) Gradually promote to 50% then 100% over 2 hours.

Known limitations and failure modes

- KV incompatibility: When model variants have incompatible KV encodings (common across quantized vs FP16 variants), stitching falls back to truncation and re-generation; expect quality delta.
- Merge false-positives: Partial-logit merging assumes consistent tokenization and output distribution; mismatch can produce incoherent continuations. Use high similarity_threshold for customer-facing models.
- Cost amplification: Aggressive fallback when primary is slow can double token costs if fallbacks re-generate long prefixes. Config guardrails must disable expensive fallback for low-tier customers.

Operational ownership and escalation

- Owner: eng-serving-runtime team
- Primary on-call: runtime-sre rotation (see /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations)
- Escalation: after 15m unresolved, page runtime-platform lead (Marco Alvarez). After 60m, involve Director of Infra.

Release and rollout notes (example change)

Change: add CHECKPOINT_CREATED to kernel v2 and enable incremental merge
- Target branches: kernel/v2, runtime/orchestrator
- Tests: kernel unit + integration with kvcache emulation
- Rollout steps:
  1) Merge to staging, run workload-sim at 1x prod.
  2) Deploy kernel/v2 to canary pool (5 nodes), enable diagnostics for 1h.
  3) If no regressions, add to low-latency pool at 10% traffic. Monitor stitch.merge_accept_rate.

Appendices

A. Sample admin CLI snippets
- Apply temporary config patch:
  curl -X PATCH -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN' \
    https://admin.internal/runtime/config \
    -d '{"stitch.max_wait_ms":"120ms"}'
- Force-stop a leaking fallback workers group:
  /ops/runtime/workerctl stop --group fallback-quantized-3 --soft

B. Recommended thresholds (summary)
- SLO: 95th percentile latency <= 120ms for low-latency lane
- stitch.warn_ms: 40ms
- stitch.max_wait_ms: 80ms (canary), 120ms (temp mitigation)
- merge.similarity_threshold: 0.92

C. Links and references
- Related ADR: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026
- Benchmarking playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/runtime-scaling-experiment-protocol-and-benchmark-checklist-2026

Contact and next steps

- For questions or to propose improvements, open a PR and tag reviewers (Marco Alvarez, Priya Shah). Planned Q1 work: increase observability of partial-logits and add a "simulated-merge" test in the CI benchmark suite.

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft (E. Tran)
- 2025-12-18: Added operational runbook and metrics (review feedback)
- 2026-02-03: Clarified kernel-heartbeat signals and added canary rollout plan

title: dsid_3ff17880925344d4b4c85042cf2c6f6d__gpu-pcie-error-isolation-and-hw-failover-runbook.txt
text:
gpu-pcie-error-isolation-and-hw-failover-runbook

Overview
======
This runbook describes operational procedures for detecting, isolating, and failing over hosts that report PCIe or downstream hardware errors affecting GPU inference capacity. It is intended for SRE and infra on-call engineers, and for infra engineers executing day-2 maintenance or emergency hardware isolation.

Goals
-----
- Detect PCIe-related degradation (corrected/uncorrected errors, link retrains, ECC counts) within 5 minutes of occurrence.
- Safely route tenant load off impacted hosts and preserve KV cache where possible.
- Quarantine or reprovision hardware with minimal disruption and within 60 minutes for high-severity incidents.
- Provide reproducible diagnostics for vendor escalation and postmortem.

When to use this runbook
-----------------------
Use this playbook when any of the following alerts fire:
1) pcie_error_rate_high (thresholds table below)
2) GPU ECC uncorrectable or frequent corrected ECC spikes
3) repeated GPU resets (nvidia-smi shows repeated GPU reset events)
4) kernel logs show PCIe AER (Advanced Error Reporting) messages or link retrain events

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Primary: infra-sre-oncall (pager)
- Secondary: gpu-fleet-team (Slack #gpu-fleet)
- Hardware vendor escalation: hw-escalations@redwood-inference.com (cc: infra-leads)
- Documentation owner: Aisha Patel

Alert thresholds and initial triage table
---------------------------------------
| Alert name | Signal | Severity | Initial triage action | SLA |
|------------|--------|----------|-----------------------|-----|
| pcie_corrected_rate | node_exporter: node_pcie_corrected_errors[1m] > 50 | Sev3 | Check dmesg and isolate flows | Detect 5m |
| pcie_uncorrected | node_exporter: node_pcie_uncorrected_errors > 1 | Sev1 | Immediate drain and quarantine | Remediate 60m |
| gpu_ecc_corrected_spike | nvml: gpu_ecc_corrected_delta > 1000/min | Sev2 | Move non-critical jobs, monitor | 30m |
| gpu_reset_count | telemetry: gpu_reset_count_in_15m > 3 | Sev2 | Reboot node if safe, otherwise drain | 30m |

Initial investigation checklist (0-10 minutes)
------------------------------------------------
- Safety: Confirm incident scope and impact in PagerDuty and Slack. Notify customer-facing channels if tenant-affecting.
- Gather quick signals:
  - dmesg | tail -n 200 | grep -iA3 -E "pcie|aer|error|link retrain"
  - sudo journalctl -k -u systemd -n 200 | grep -i pcie
  - lspci -vvv | grep -A2 -i "VGA\|3D\|NVIDIA"
  - sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,index,ecc.errors.uncorrected.volatile,ecc.errors.corrected.volatile --format=csv
  - node_exporter metrics: node_pcie_* and gpu_exporter metrics for ECC/reset counts
- Surface whether error is localized to a single GPU, host, or rack.
- If uncorrected PCIe errors or repeated GPU resets: follow the immediate isolation path below.

Immediate isolation (Sev1 path)
-------------------------------
1) Mark node as quarantined in inventory system (example tag via Terraform/CLI):
   - Terraform snippet to set quarantine tag (for manual emergency use):
     provider "aws" { }
     resource "aws_instance" "gpu_node" {
       # ... existing resource ...
       tags = {
         Name = "gpu-node-42"
         gpu_health = "quarantine"
       }
     }
   - If using our node registry API: curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' https://infra-api.internal/v1/nodes/uuid/quarantine
2) Drain workloads immediately: run the drain playbook for the cluster type (k8s, nomad):
   - Kubernetes: kubectl cordon node/<node-name> && kubectl drain node/<node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --timeout=10m
   - Nomad: nomad node eligibility -disable <node-id> and nomad run = stop allocations gracefully
3) Disable load balancing to node-level endpoints (envoy/service mesh) and remove from pool.
4) If hardware reboot is safe and no attached persistent test jobs: reboot and re-check logs (see reboot validation steps). If rebooting is not safe, preserve node for vendor escalation.

Diagnostics to collect for vendor escalation
-------------------------------------------
- dmesg output (first 5k lines) and journalctl kernel logs around the time window.
- lspci -vvv and lspci -xxxx (hex dump) for devices involved.
- nvml/pci dump: nvidia-smi -q -d ERRORS and nvidia-bug-report.sh (if allowed by compliance).
- IPMI logs / BMC event logs: ipmitool sel list && ipmitool sel get <id>
- Node telemetry snapshot (upload to secure S3 bucket):
  - /var/log/messages, /var/log/kern.log, nvml logs, node exporter metrics, kube/nomad allocation logs.
- Hardware identifiers: serial numbers, BIOS versions, PCIe link speed/width from lspci, driver versions.

Repro workflow and safe repro tips
--------------------------------
- If errors are intermittent, attempt controlled synthetic load with a non-production tenant in the same rack to reproduce under observation. Use a low-priority burst job that exercises the GPU memory and PCIe link for 10 minutes. Monitor for retries, corrected error rate, and link retrains.
- Use nvidia-smi daemon mode to increase telemetry granularity temporarily: nvidia-smi --loop-ms=1000 --query-gpu=timestamp,utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv
- When reproducing, ensure KV cache persistence strategy is documented so stateful workloads are not lost.

Remediation matrix
------------------
| Symptom | Likely cause | Remediation | When to escalate |
|---------|--------------|------------|-----------------|
| Corrected PCIe errors only | Dirty link, marginal signaling | Reduce PCIe link speed (if platform supports), update BIOS, schedule maint window | After 3 recurring incidents in 24h |
| Uncorrected PCIe errors | Faulty riser/slot or GPU | Replace GPU or move card to spare slot; vendor RMA | Immediately (Sev1) |
| Frequent GPU resets | Driver/kernel mismatch or firmware bug | Rollback driver or apply hotpatch; run canary deployment of driver image | After immediate mitigation if persists |
| ECC uncorrectable errors | Memory fault on GPU | Quarantine and replace GPU | Immediately |

Driver and kernel hotpatch/rollback guidance (CI/CD)
---------------------------------------------------
- Buildkite job naming convention: "gpu-driver-canary/<image-tag>". Canary rollout flow: 1) push image to canary pool, 2) run smoke tests (latency and token throughput), 3) monitor for 30 minutes, 4) gradual promote.
- Example Buildkite check list for driver canary:
  1. Run ci-eval-synthetic on 10 canary nodes (10M tokens).
  2. Assert gpu_reset_count_no_increase <= 0 and latency regression < 5%.
  3. If checks fail, automatically revert image tag and open incident in PagerDuty.
- Keep a pinned driver image in the Terraform node profile to allow fast rollback (ami: "gpu-runtime:v2025-02-10" style pin).

Post-quarantine validation and return-to-service
------------------------------------------------
- Before returning node to production:
  1) Run full hardware diagnostics (vendor or in-house): memtest for GPU memory, burn-in for 2 hours, PCIe stress test.
  2) Confirm no new pcie_uncorrected alerts for 24h under monitored synthetic load.
  3) Re-image node with golden image and reapply node tags.
  4) Remove quarantine tag and re-enable scheduling in a staged ramp (10% capacity first).
- Example checklist entry for re-enablement:
  - [ ] Hardware diagnostics passed (attach logs)
  - [ ] Firmware/BIOS updated to supported revision
  - [ ] Driver image validated (canary stamp)
  - [ ] No uncorrected errors on telemetry for 24h

Terraform/IaC patterns for resilience
-----------------------------------
- Node metadata tags to use (consistent naming expected by automation):
  - gpu_health: {ok, quarantine, suspect}
  - pci_lane: <x16|x8|x4|internal-bus>
  - hw_serial: <serial-number>
- IaC example to attach node pool replacement policy:
  - autoscaling_group.lifecycle_hook = true (drain before termination)
- Keep a small hot spare pool (5%) per region/zone with identical driver/kernel matrix to allow fast reprovisioning.

Telemetry and long-term detection improvements
--------------------------------------------
- Recommended derived metrics to add to Prometheus:
  - rate(node_pcie_corrected_errors[5m]) normalized by slots per chassis
  - gpu_reset_rate per GPU normalized to utilization
  - pcie_link_retrain_count by slot and vendor-reported lane width changes
- Annotate nodes with firmware and BIOS versions in node exporter to enable cross-correlation.
- Set up a daily job that finds nodes with rising corrected error trend and pre-emptively moves non-critical workloads off them.

Runbook annex: useful commands and snippets
-----------------------------------------
- dmesg | grep -iA5 -E "pcie|aer|error|uncorrected|corrected"
- sudo journalctl -k --since "15 minutes ago" | grep -i pcie
- lspci -vvv -s <bus:slot.func>
- sudo nvidia-smi -q -d ECC,RESET,PCI
- sudo /usr/bin/nvidia-bug-report.sh --logdir /tmp/bugreport-<node>
- ipmitool sel list; ipmitool sel elist
- Terraform tag update (example): terraform apply -var 'node_id=uuid' -target=module.node_registry

References and related pages
---------------------------
- GPU thermal & power guidelines: /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-thermal-and-power-management-guidelines.json
- Hotpatch safeguard and draining playbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-hotpatch-safeguard-and-rolling-drain-playbook.json

Change history
--------------
- 2024-07-15: Initial draft (Aisha Patel)
- 2024-10-02: Added CI/CD rollback and canary checklist (Marcus Lee)
- 2025-02-10: Expanded telemetry metrics and vendor escalation template (Jin Park)

Appendix: vendor escalation template (email)
-----------------------------------------
Subject: [RMA Request] GPU PCIe Uncorrected Errors - Node <node-name> - Serial <SN>
Body:
- Incident time window: <UTC times>
- Symptoms observed: uncorrected PCIe AER + GPU ECC uncorrectable + node removal required
- Diagnostics attached: dmesg, lspci -vvv, nvml error dump, IPMI event logs, node exporter snapshot
- Requested action: investigate link hardware (riser/cable/slot) and advise on replacement or firmware fix

End of document

title: dsid_174fa72d14404b7bbbeff68ac47c57d8__typed-error-model-and-client-contract-recommendations-2026.txt
text:
typed-error-model-and-client-contract-recommendations-2026

Summary
-------
This document defines the canonical, typed error model and client contract recommendations for Redwood public and internal inference APIs. It standardizes machine-friendly error schema, HTTP status mappings, retry semantics, SDK behavior, observability signals, and a migration/playbook for rolling these changes out with minimal customer impact. The recommendations apply to text generation, chat, embeddings, and management endpoints.

Goals
-----
- Provide a single parsable error schema usable by SDKs and monitoring systems.
- Make retry logic deterministic (retryable vs non-retryable).
- Ensure backward-compatible enrichment path: servers may add fields but not change semantics.
- Tie error types to SLO and alerting rules so failures surface consistently.
- Document deprecation/compatibility rules for future error code changes.

Error model overview
--------------------
All endpoints MUST return an error payload with HTTP status and the following JSON envelope when an application-level error occurs (200 responses for success remain unchanged):

Example error envelope (minimally required fields):

{
  "error": {
    "code": "MODEL_UNAVAILABLE",
    "message": "Requested model 'redwood-large-v1' is not available in region us-east-1",
    "status": 503,
    "retryable": true,
    "request_id": "req_0123456789"
  }
}

Field definitions (required):
- error.code (string): machine-readable, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE token. See taxonomy below.
- error.message (string): human-readable description for logs and developer UX. Should not be relied on for parsing.
- error.status (integer): canonical HTTP status matching the envelope. MUST match the HTTP status header.
- error.retryable (boolean): explicit recommendation whether client should attempt an automated retry.
- error.request_id (string): unique request id for support and tracing.

Optional fields (allowed but not required):
- error.meta (object encoded as string if SDKs can't handle raw objects): free-form key/value pairs for debugging (model_id, node_pool, shard).
- error.hint (string): short remediation hint for users.
- error.documentation_url (string): link to an internal/external page with more context.

Error taxonomy and HTTP mapping
------------------------------
We mandate a bounded set of canonical error codes. Each code maps to HTTP status and expected retry behavior. SDKs MUST map HTTP and transport-level failures into these codes where possible.

Table: canonical codes
- INVALID_INPUT => 400, retryable: false. Use when request payload fails schema/validation. Include field-level errors in error.meta.validation.
- AUTHENTICATION_FAILED => 401, retryable: false. Token invalid/expired.
- PERMISSION_DENIED => 403, retryable: false. RBAC/ACL error.
- NOT_FOUND => 404, retryable: false. Unknown model/resource.
- RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED => 429, retryable: true (with backoff). Provide error.meta.retry_after_seconds when available.
- QUOTA_EXCEEDED => 402 or 429 (team may choose), retryable: false. Indicates customer's billing/commit limits.
- MODEL_UNAVAILABLE => 503, retryable: true. Model runtime not available in chosen tier/region. Suggest fallback model in error.meta.fallback_model when present.
- INTERNAL_ERROR => 500, retryable: true (with capped attempts). Use for transient infra problems.
- TIMEOUT => 504, retryable: true. Long-running inference timeout.
- PARTIAL_RESPONSE => 206, retryable: false. Generation produced partial output; include meta.partial=true and best-effort continuing instructions.
- DATA_POLICY_VIOLATION => 403, retryable: false. Request triggers policy blocking; include documentation_url and policy_id.
- DEPRECATED => 299 (or 200 with warning header), retryable: false. Use to indicate deprecated parameter/route was used; include error.meta.migration_guide.

Retry semantics and idempotency
------------------------------
- Use explicit retryable boolean rather than inferring from status alone. This prevents ambiguous behavior in SDKs.
- Clients SHOULD implement exponential backoff with jitter for retryable errors. Default: initial backoff 200ms, multiplier 2, max attempts 5 for typical hosted endpoints.
- For non-idempotent operations (e.g., model fine-tuning jobs), servers MUST require an idempotency key; if provided, server must make retries safe. Document idempotency in individual route specs.

SDK requirements and behavior
---------------------------
- Language SDKs MUST expose: parsed error.code, message, status, retryable, request_id, and any meta fields.
- SDKs SHOULD surface a typed exception hierarchy (e.g., RedwoodApiError -> RateLimitError/AuthenticationError).
- SDKs MUST not make automatic retries for errors with retryable=false. For retryable=true, retries must be configurable and disabled by default in critical interactive paths.
- SDKs SHOULD provide helpers: isRetryable(err), getRetryAfter(err), getRequestId(err).

Observability and alerting
-------------------------
- All error responses MUST be instrumented with the following tags/labels: endpoint, model, deployment_tier (hosted/dedicated/private), region, customer_id (if applicable), error.code.
- Metric: inference.errors.count{code,endpoint,model} incremented for every non-2xx/non-206 response.
- SLI: 99.9% success rate (2xx) over 5m sliding window for hosted API endpoints (see performance-standards for per-route SLOs).
- Pager thresholds: sustained error rate > 0.1% for control plane endpoints or >1.0% for tenant-level endpoints over 5m should create an alert. High-severity alerts should use request samples with request_id for postmortem.

Logging and support data
-----------------------
- Error logs MUST include request_id, error.code, upstream node id (if applicable), and logged stacktrace only for internal errors. Do not log sensitive customer payloads; apply redaction rules in data-management policies.

Compatibility and evolution rules
--------------------------------
- Servers may add new fields to the error envelope at any time.
- Servers MUST NOT change meaning of existing error.code tokens. To change semantics, create a new error code and deprecate the old one via public deprecation schedule (see deprecation policy).
- New error codes MUST be introduced behind feature flags for 4 weeks with monitoring of client failures and SDK adoption.

Migration and rollout playbook
-----------------------------
1) Implement server-side error envelope in a layered rollout: production -> canary -> beta tenants. 2) Monitor client parsing failures via a synthetic test suite that validates each SDK correctly interprets the envelope. 3) Gradually enable additional metadata fields (meta, hint, documentation_url) ensuring SDKs tolerate unknown fields. 4) Announce breaking changes (if unavoidable) with 90 days notice and provide a compatibility shim for the prior behavior.

Example: client handling pseudocode
----------------------------------
try {
  const resp = await client.generate(...);
} catch (err) {
  if (sdk.isRetryable(err) && attempts < cfg.maxAttempts) {
    await backoff.wait(attempts);
