   - Phase 0 (2 weeks): library baked and unit tests; TKS prototype; no enforcement.
   - Phase 1 (4 weeks): opt-in validation for selected non-critical services (console diagnostics, model-stats). Monitor rejection rate < 0.1%.
   - Phase 2 (6 weeks): enforcement for production services (edge-proxy, runtime-coordinator). Rejection policy: quarantine + 5% sampling allowlist for backfill.
   - Phase 3 (ongoing): expand to all telemetry producers and require signatures for billing-relevant metrics.

Validation & acceptance criteria

- Producer library used by 90% of high-volume producers within 8 weeks of release.
- Telemetry-ingest signature validation latency added <= 5ms median, <= 25ms p99.
- Ingest rejection rate due to canonicalization bugs <= 0.05% in Phase 1.
- Attribution error (measured as percent of cost tokens misattributed across tenants for a weekly snapshot) reduces by >= 70% after full rollout.

Operational runbook highlights

1) Quarantine workflow:
   - telemetry-ingest writes invalid batches to topic telemetry-quarantine. An on-call rotation in eng-platform will triage.
2) Emergency bypass:
   - TKS exposes a scoped emergency token issuance endpoint to allow temporary bypass for critical deployments; all emergency issuances must be followed by postmortem and key revocation.
3) Backwards compatibility
   - For 12 weeks after enforcement, telemetry-ingest will accept unsigned events from a configured legacy-producer allowlist and mark them with tag legacy=true to prevent accidental double-counting.

Ownership and maintenance

- Primary owner: eng-platform (Telemetry Guild)
- Secondary stakeholders: eng-serving-runtime, eng-infra, eng-observability
- Documentation owner: eng-platform (responsible for SDKs, examples, and validation CLI)

Metrics and dashboards to add

- telemetry.signature.accept_rate (per-service, tenant)
- telemetry.signature.latency_ms (p50/p95/p99)
- telemetry.quarantine.count (daily)
- telemetry.enrichment.missing_fields.rate (per-field)

Appendix A: Canonicalization examples

Example signed header:
X-RDW-Telemetry-Sig: v1,hmac_sha256,key-20260305-1,9f8a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d7e8f9a0b1c2d3e4f5a6b7c8d9e0f1a

Example canonical JSON to sign (spaces removed, keys sorted):
{"envelope":{"instance_id":"host-10-2-1-7","model_commit":"f2c4a1b","model_variant":"gptx-7b-q4","request_id":"7e4a2f1c-9b6d","sample_rate_tag":"p=0.001","sequence_length_category":"short","service":"edge-proxy","tenant_id":"org-12345"},"payload":[{"metric":"inference.latency_ms","points":[[1677624000,18]],"tags":{"route":"/v1/generate","region":"us-west-2"}}]}

Appendix B: Example validation CLI (pseudo)

# validate_batch --input batch.json --sig "$X_RDW_TELEMETRY_SIG"
# exit code 0 == valid, 1 == invalid

Appendix C: Migration checklist

1) Publish libraries and TKS staging with docs and examples (eng-platform).
2) Run two-week integration pilot with model-stats and console diagnostics.
3) Add dashboards; monitor quarantine topic.
4) Communicate to all teams with timelines and support office hours.
5) Enforce for production telemetry and deprecate legacy allowlist after 12 weeks.

Related decisions

- This ADR complements: telemetry-ingestion-and-retention-guidelines-2025 and adr-telemetry-aggregation-retention-hierarchy-2026 (see Related Pages).

Questions for future work

- Evaluate asymmetric signatures for long-term archival and cross-organization sharing.
- Add cryptographic proofs linking telemetry to billing invoices.

Change log

- 2026-02-10: initial draft by Aisha Patel.
- 2026-02-24: updated key TTL and validation window after review by Diego Ramirez.
- 2026-03-05: tuned rollout phases and added quarantine handling, published.

title: dsid_4ad39c1a729b4ba98cd61fea4319315e__quota-protector-webhook-integration-and-reconciliation-guide-2026.txt
text:
Quota Protector Webhook Integration and Reconciliation Guide

Overview
--------
This integration guide describes the Quota Protector webhook used by Redwood Inference to reliably surface customer quota events and automate protective credits and throttling adjustments during anomalous billing or rate-limit events. The document explains the webhook contract, delivery guarantees, recommended reconciliation workflow for enterprise customers, on-call runbooks for mismatches, and examples for implementing a receiver and reconciliation worker in third-party billing systems.

Goals
- Reduce false-positive quota rejections for enterprise customers during bursty or partial-failure conditions.
- Provide deterministic reconciliation steps to reconcile token usage vs. billing records within a 72-hour window.
- Support automated protective credits (temporary credits) and safe rollback actions with auditability.

When to use this integration
- Enterprise customers with reserved or committed capacity (Dedicated or Private) that need automated protective measures when perceived usage spikes or system anomalies occur.
- Partners who want proactive notifications and a standard reconciliation API for invoicing systems.

Prerequisites
- Customer must have a configured webhook receiver endpoint reachable from Redwood (HTTPS/TLS).
- Shared secret (HMAC-SHA256) provisioning via the console or SRE onboarding link.
- Access to your billing system’s ingestion pipeline (batch or streaming) for reconciliation.

Webhook contract (delivery semantics)
1) Event types (payload field event_type):
   - quota.alert: short-lived alert when usage approaches a quota threshold (INFO).
   - quota.protective_action: Redwood applied a temporary protective credit or soft-throttle (ACTION).
   - quota.reconcile_request: Redwood requests reconciliation for an identified discrepancy (RECONCILE).
   - quota.reconcile_result: Customer posts back reconciliation outcome (RESULT).
2) Delivery guarantees:
   - Redwood will attempt delivery with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours.
   - Events are delivered at-least-once; receivers must be idempotent (see Idempotency section).
   - Quota.reconcile_request is guaranteed to be emitted once per discrepancy case.
3) Security:
   - Each HTTP request includes X-Redwood-Timestamp and X-Redwood-Signature (HMAC-SHA256 of body + timestamp with shared secret).
   - Request body is application/json and UTF-8 encoded.

Example payloads
- quota.protective_action (abbreviated):
```json
{
  "event_id": "e7d1f2b8-9c7a-4a4b-8a6d-2f4a1a6c9b1e",
  "event_type": "quota.protective_action",
  "tenant_id": "enterprise-42",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T21:03:12Z",
  "action": "temporary_credit",
  "amount_tokens": 250000,
  "reason": "ingestion spike during redesploy",
  "correlation_id": "ops-rollback-20260218-1",
  "metadata": {"affected_routes": ["/v1/generate"], "instance_pool": "dedicated-prod-3"}
}
```
- quota.reconcile_request (abbreviated):
```json
{
  "event_id": "r2a9b4c5-44f6-4c9b-95d6-0b9f3a2c3d7b",
  "event_type": "quota.reconcile_request",
  "tenant_id": "enterprise-42",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-18T22:00:00Z",
  "window_start": "2026-02-18T20:00:00Z",
  "window_end": "2026-02-18T21:00:00Z",
  "reported_usage_tokens": 1200000,
  "observed_usage_tokens": 980000,
  "suggested_action": "credit_25000_tokens_or_manual_review",
  "details_url": "https://console.redwood.com/tenants/enterprise-42/recon/r2a9b4c5"
}
```

Idempotency and receiver best practices
- Use event_id as the primary idempotency key. Store event_id and processing result for 90 days.
- Design reconciliation handlers to accept repeated reconcile_request events and only create a single case per unique correlation_id.
- Return standard HTTP codes: 200 for success, 202 for accepted (async processing), 4xx for client errors, 5xx for transient failures. Redwood will retry on 5xx and network errors.

Sample receiver flow (recommended)
1) Verify signature and timestamp within +/- 5 minutes. Reject otherwise with 401.
2) Check local dedupe store by event_id; if found, return 200 with existing outcome.
3) For quota.protective_action: apply temporary internal protective credit and create an internal ticket with priority=high if action==temporary_credit.
4) For quota.reconcile_request: enqueue a reconciliation job that performs matching between reported_usage_tokens and your billing records for the provided window. Post a quota.reconcile_result when complete.

Reconciliation worker design
- Match level: ingestion-level (per request ID) if available; fallback to route-level aggregation by minute.
- Tolerance band: accept discrepancies <= 2.5% as noise; >2.5% and <=10% trigger automated protective credit up to suggested_action. >10% escalates to human review.
- Audit trail: include the Redwood event_id, your reconciliation_job_id, and links to raw records.

Automated protective credits and accounting flow
1) On reconcile_request that falls into the automated band, your system should:
   - Create a refundable credit entry tied to the tenant and reconciliation_job_id.
   - Post quota.reconcile_result with fields (event_id, job_id, outcome: auto_credit_applied, credit_amount_tokens, note).
2) Finance integration: reconcile refundable credit entries weekly against Redwood billing exports.
3) Auto-expiry: credits applied as protective must be stamped with expiry (default 30 days) and a reconciliation flag to convert to permanent credit only after human approval.

SLOs and monitoring
- Delivery SLOs: Redwood aims for 99.5% successful initial delivery (non-5xx) across webhook endpoints.
- Customer receiver SLOs: process reconcile_request within 8 hours or reply with 202+job_id to indicate longer processing windows.
- Alerting: customers should alert if more than 5 reconcile_request events are queued for >24 hours for a single tenant.

On-call runbook: unresolved reconciliation mismatch
1) Redwood emits quota.reconcile_request with suggested_action. Customer system posts back quota.reconcile_result. If no result after 24 hours, do:
   a) Check delivery logs (Redwood Console -> Integrations -> Webhooks -> Delivery).
   b) Confirm webhook receiver health (CPU, request queue depth, TLS cert validity).
   c) If receiver healthy but processing stuck, escalate to internal billing ops: create ticket with tags [recon-stuck, tenant:<tenant_id>] and assign to billing-ops on-call.
2) If the reconcile_result indicates disagreement (customer refutes observed usage), run a manual audit:
   a) Export raw request logs from Redwood for the window (Console -> Tenants -> Export Usage).
   b) Crosswalk timestamps and request IDs. If discrepancies persist, open a joint investigation with Redwood SRE via the enterprise support channel.
3) If finance disputes remain after 7 days, follow the contractual dispute process (see related_pages billing-credit-policy).

Troubleshooting common errors
- 401 Unauthorized: bad HMAC signature or clock skew. Verify shared secret and sync NTP.
- 422 Unprocessable Entity: missing required fields (event_id, event_type, tenant_id, timestamp). Confirm JSON schema.
- Repeated duplicates: confirm dedupe store retention and idempotency key correctness.
- Large backlog: increase worker parallelism and consider accepting 202 with job_id for long-running reconciliation.

Implementation examples and helper scripts
- Minimal Node.js receiver skeleton (pseudocode)
```js
const express = require('express');
app.post('/webhooks/rdw', verifySignatureMiddleware, async (req, res) => {
  const event = req.body;
  if (await alreadyProcessed(event.event_id)) return res.status(200).send({status:'duplicate'});
  enqueueReconcile(event).then(jobId => res.status(202).send({job_id: jobId}));
});
```

Operational recommendations for enterprise customers
- Keep a rolling 7-day window of raw request logs for quick manual audits.
- Configure alert thresholds on per-tenant queue depth and reconcile_request age.
- Regularly rotate webhook secrets and use mutual TLS for sensitive integrations.

Privacy and audit considerations
- Webhook payloads may contain tenant identifiers and usage aggregates. Do not log PII.
- All reconciliation actions must be recorded with who/what/when for billing audit trails.

Appendix: field reference
- event_id: UUID v4, unique per event.
- correlation_id: opaque string that groups related protective actions / reconcile flows.
- reported_usage_tokens: integer, tokens Redwood observed.
- observed_usage_tokens: integer, any computed alternate observation.
- suggested_action: free-text suggestion (credit_x_tokens | manual_review).

Contact and ownership
- Integration owner: Customer Success (Elena Park) — elena.park@redwood.com
- Escalation path: first-line CSM -> Billing Ops -> Redwood SRE (via enterprise Slack channel #eng-support-enterprise).

Revision history
- 2026-01-12: Created initial draft (Elena Park).
- 2026-02-20: Clarified idempotency and added tolerance bands for automated credits (reviewers: Marcus Li, Priya Nair).

Related artifacts and links
- Console integration page: https://console.redwood.com/docs/integrations/webhooks
- Billing export schema: https://console.redwood.com/docs/finance/billing-export-schema

title: dsid_931cea2de5c741f79988b3836f08909a__traffic-smoothing-quiet-hours-and-tenant-notification-playbook-2027.txt
text:
Traffic smoothing, quiet-hours and tenant notification playbook

Summary:

This playbook defines operator and customer-facing procedures for smoothing traffic during predictable and ad-hoc tenant burst events. It covers automatic quiet-hours smoothing, tenant-level throttling/fan-out controls, notification templates, escalation ladders, telemetry queries, and rollback guidance. The goal is to preserve platform SLOs (latency/availability) while protecting customer experience and cost boundaries.

When to use this playbook:

- Planned quiet-hours or maintenance windows where we will intentionally reduce tenant throughput to conserve capacity or schedule upgrades.
- Rapid tenant traffic bursts (spikes in requests or tokens) that threaten SLOs for other tenants.
- Customer-requested temporary throttle during migration/backfill events.
- As a standard operating response prior to capacity augmentation or emergency capacity scaling.

Key objectives:

1) Maintain 99th percentile p95 token latency SLOs and >99.9% availability for host-level API endpoints.
2) Minimize customer-facing error rate and provide clear, timely communication.
3) Apply smoothing/throttles with least possible disruption using automated, observable controls.

Ownership and roles:

- Primary owner: Customer Success Operations (Customer Success) — coordinates customer comms, approves manual throttles.
- Secondary owner: Platform SRE (Engineering) — implements rate-limiter changes, monitors platform metrics, executes emergency capacity procedures.
- Response lead (oncall): person listed on the current oncall rota for Eng SRE.

Preconditions / prerequisites:

- Tenant must have telemetry forwarding enabled (tenant.metrics and tenant.traces).
- Tenant-specific quota and throttle policies must exist in the RateLimit Service (service: rate-limit-svc).
- Customer Success must have an agreed contact from the tenant (email + pager for enterprise).

SLOs and thresholds (operational):

| Metric | Threshold (trigger) | Severity | Initial action | Escalation timer |
|-------|---------------------:|----------|----------------|------------------|
| p95 token latency (global) | > 1.8x baseline for 3 consecutive minutes | Sev-2 | Auto-smooth tenants contributing >30% load | 10 min -> SRE oncall |
| error rate (5xx >= host) | >0.5% absolute increase over baseline (5 min) | Sev-1 | Immediate rollback of recent config + alert | 5 min -> Incident page |
| requests-per-min per-tenant | > 10x baseline sustained 2 min | Sev-3 | Apply per-tenant burst windowing + backpressure | 15 min -> CS PD notification |

Automated controls and tuning knobs:

- Quiet-hours smoothing: schedule-based traffic shaping that lowers max active concurrent requests by x% (default 30%) during predefined windows. Config stored as YAML in config-store:

  examples: &config-example
  - tenant_selector: "label:batching=true"
    window: "23:00-05:00 UTC"
    concurrency_limit_pct: 70
    burst_window_seconds: 60

- Tenant burst windowing: dynamic token-bucket policy applied per-API key that allows short bursts but enforces an average over a sliding 60s window.

- Graceful response headers: when rate-limited, return 429 with headers: Retry-After, X-Redwood-Limit, X-Redwood-Remaining, X-Redwood-Quota-Reset. Include optional human-readable JSON in body with guidance on next steps.

Telemetry & queries (examples):

- Grafana / Prometheus:
  - redwood.requests_total{tenant_id=~"<TENANT>"}
  - redwood.tokens_per_minute{tenant_id=~"<TENANT>"}
  - redwood.p95_token_latency{region="us-west-2"}
  - redwood.5xx_rate{host="api.redwood.com"}

- Example PromQL:
  avg_over_time(redwood.tokens_per_minute{tenant_id=~"T123"}[2m]) > 10 * avg_over_time(redwood.tokens_per_minute{tenant_id=~"T123"}[1h])

Operational runbook (step-by-step):

1) Detect: automated alert or CS report. Confirm tenant_id(s), time window, and affected routes.
2) Quick triage (5 min): verify telemetry, check deploys in last 30 min (ci-cd activity), confirm whether traffic is legitimate (backfill / scheduled job).
3) Apply automated smoothing if hit threshold: enable "quiet-hours smoothing" for tenant selector or apply per-tenant rate-limit override. Use CLI:

  # apply per-tenant override (example)
  rwctl rate-limit set --tenant T123 --max-rps 250 --burst 500 --window 60s --reason "auto-smoothing-trigger-2027-02-15"

4) Notify customer: send templated email and optional in-console banner (see templates below). Mark the change in incident tracker with runbook link.
5) Monitor 0-30 minutes: watch p95 latency, 5xx rate, and tenant error rates. If metrics improve, prepare staged rollback: reduce throttle by 20% every 10 minutes until normal.

Escalation matrix and timers:

- If p95 latency not improved after 15 minutes -> escalate to Eng SRE oncall (page) and SRE escalation Slack channel (#sre-incident).
- If 5xx error rate increases after smoothing -> immediate rollback and incident page start.
- If customer reports data loss or persistent functional errors -> raise Sev-1 and schedule cross-team warroom.

Customer communications (templates):

- In-console banner (short):
  "We are applying temporary traffic smoothing to maintain platform performance during a high-volume event. Your requests may be delayed or throttled. We will update you within 30 minutes. Contact support@redwood.ai for urgent concerns."

- Email template (first notification):
  Subject: Temporary traffic smoothing active for your Redwood tenant

  Hello <Customer Name>,

  We detected a high-volume traffic event affecting your Redwood tenant (ID: <TID>). To maintain platform stability, we've temporarily limited peak throughput for your tenant. This is a protective measure — your data is not at risk. Expected impact: brief 429s for short bursts and up-to-30s increased latency for long requests.

  What we are doing: applying per-tenant smoothing, monitoring performance, and escalating if needed.

  ETA for update: 30 minutes. Contact: <CS rep + pager>.

  Regards,
  Redwood Support

- Follow-up template (when resolved):
  Subject: Traffic smoothing removed — event resolved

  Hello <Customer Name>,

  The temporary smoothing has been removed and your normal throughput limits restored. Incident runbook: <link>. If you observed any functional problems, please reply and we will investigate further.

Configuration table (required fields for a scheduled quiet-hours rule):

| Field | Type | Description | Example | Required |
|-------|------|-------------|---------|----------:|
| rule_id | string | Unique rule identifier | quiet-window-batch | yes |
| tenant_selector | string | Selector expression (labels or tenant_id) | label:batching=true | yes |
| window | string | Time window in UTC | 23:00-05:00 | yes |
| concurrency_limit_pct | integer | Percent of normal concurrency to allow | 70 | yes |
| burst_window_seconds | integer | Sliding window for burst smoothing | 60 | no |
| owner | string | Team/owner to notify | customer-success | yes |

Rollback guidance:

- If smoothing causes unacceptable customer errors, immediately remove rule and clear rate-limit overrides using rwctl:

  rwctl rate-limit delete --tenant T123 --reason "rollback-due-to-5xx-2027-02-15"

- If rollback triggers platform instability, revert to platform-wide safe-mode throttle (config: global.safe_mode_pct = 50) and open incident page.

Post-incident actions and reporting:

1) Run a 72-hour retrospective: who acted, what thresholds fired, and whether automation behaved as expected.
2) Produce a short incident digest for the Customer (one-pager) within 48 hours.
3) Update the tenant onboarding checklist with any gap identified (telemetry, contact, agreed quiet-hours).

Observability checklist (what to capture):

- Alert triggers and timestamps.
- rwctl commands executed (audit log).
- Grafana snapshot links and PromQL used.
- Customer comms artifacts (email, banner text).

Related runbooks and docs:

- Capacity surge and degraded throughput playbook (eng/sre)
- Tenant onboarding acceptance testing (CS)
- Rate limit service configuration guide (infra)

Appendix A — Example rate-limit YAML snippet:

  - rule_id: "quiet-window-batch-2027"
    tenant_selector: "label:batching=true"
    window: "23:00-05:00"
    concurrency_limit_pct: 70
    burst_window_seconds: 60
    owner: "customer-success"

Appendix B — Short checklist for CS before applying manual throttle:

1) Confirm authorized contact and approval in CRM.
2) Validate telemetry and rule selector matches intended workload.
3) Log expected duration and rollback criteria to incident tracker.
4) Send pre-action notice to customer.

Document history and change log:

- 2026-11-10: Created by Maya Chen (initial draft).
- 2027-01-11: Added automated CLI examples and telemetry PromQL — reviewer: Ravi Patel.
- 2027-02-15: Finalized templates and escalation timers — reviewer: Elena Gómez.

title: dsid_e7de5a80bab945c5b943d8da0de38ae7__ci-gpu-interference-profiling-and-synthetic-benchmark-harness.txt
text:
CI GPU interference profiling and synthetic benchmark harness

Summary

This page documents the CI-integrated GPU interference profiling harness and synthetic benchmark suite used to characterize noisy-neighbor effects across heterogeneous GPU pools. It describes the architecture, test catalog, Terraform/CI integration examples, actionable runbook steps for triage, and rollout guidance. The goal is to make interference reproducible, measurable, and automatable in our CI/GitOps pipelines so capacity and placement decisions are evidence-driven.

Scope

- Applies to all inference and eval CI lanes that allocate shared GPU pools (ephemeral and warm pools).
- Targets heterogenous fleets (A100, H100, L40) and mixed-precision kernel rollouts.
- Not a billing / chargeback spec — this focuses on technical profiling and scheduling inputs.

Motivation

We observe intermittent latency and throughput variance when tenant workloads co-locate on the same host, particularly for prefix-heavy inference and KV-cache-intensive jobs. This harness has three purposes:

1. Reproduce interference under controlled traffic mixes.
2. Instrument and capture signals (PCIE errors, SM util skews, power/thermal throttling, memory bandwidth counters).
3. Gate CI changes (kernel rollouts, quantized runtime builds, topology-aware autoscalers) with deterministic experiments.

Architecture overview

- Harness controller: "interf-harness" service (lightweight controller that schedules synthetic workloads and coordinates telemetry collection).
- Workload runners: container images (bench-runner:audit-v1) that implement synthetic inference load (tokenised FFN hotpaths, KV cache priming, tensor-concat stressors).
- Telemetry collector: sidecar + eBPF probes + perf counters shipped to telemetry pipeline (inference-metrics).
- CI integration: Buildkite / GitHub Actions steps that start ephemeral GPU nodes via Terraform and execute a canonical experiment matrix.

Test catalog (reference)

| Test id | Workload profile | Primary stressor | Typical run (s) | Purpose |
|---------|------------------|------------------|-----------------|---------|
| IF-PRX-1 | Short prefixes (avg 16 tokens) | KV-cache churn + small batch lat | 300 | Capture latency tail under prefix-heavy routing
| IF-BULK-4 | Large sequence generation (seq 2048) | SM compute saturation | 900 | Measure throughput variance and kernel selection impact
| IF-MEM-2 | Memory-bandwidth heavy (attention-only) | PCIe+DRAM bandwidth | 600 | Detect NUMA/PCIe interference hotspots
| IF-MLP-3 | FFN stress (mixed precision) | FP16 kernel divergence | 450 | Gate quantized kernel rollouts

Runbook: reproducing interference locally

1. Provision ephemeral infrastructure (dev sandbox):
   - terraform -chdir=terraform/ephemeral apply -var="pool=dev-ephemeral" -auto-approve
2. Start harness controller: kubectl -n infra apply -f manifests/interf-harness-deployment.yaml
3. Launch target experiment: kubectl -n infra exec deploy/interf-cli -- run --test IF-PRX-1 --duration 300 --sample-label=jenkins-local
4. Collect telemetry: kubectl -n observability exec -it deploy/tlm-collector -- fetch --run=latest --type=perf,ebpf,host-sensors > /tmp/interf-artifacts.tgz
5. Interpret key signals: look at pcie_retries, sm_util_percentile_95, mem_bw_util_95, power_cap_events. If pcie_retries > 1/min, escalate to network-gpu-oncall.

CI integration: canonical pipeline steps

- Stage 1: build bench-runner image and publish to registry:
  - make bench-image VERSION=${BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER}
  - docker push $REGISTRY/bench-runner:${VERSION}
- Stage 2: terraform plan/apply ephemeral nodeset (with spot fallback knobs):
  - tf_workflow apply -var=ci_run=true -var=image=${VERSION}
- Stage 3: run matrix (parallel jobs across driver/kernel variants):
  - buildkite step matrix: 
    - kernel: [stock, quantized-canary] 
    - topology: [single-host, spread] 
- Stage 4: collect artifacts and publish a structured summary JSON to the CI artifact store.

Gating rules (example)

- Latency tail (IF-PRX-1 p99) must not regress > 15% versus baseline for canary to pass.
- Throughput (IF-BULK-4 mean tokens/sec) must be within -10%..+5% of baseline.
- If any HW telemetry shows power_cap_events or pcie_retry spikes, the pipeline fails automatically.

Terraform / IaC module example

The harness uses a small Terraform module to create ephemeral GPU node pools and to label nodes for topology tests. Example snippet:

module "ephemeral_gpu_nodes" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.redwood.ai/infra/terraform//modules/ephemeral_gpu_pool"
  name   = "ci-interf-${var.run_id}"
  region = var.region
  gpu_type = var.gpu_type # e.g., a100, h100
  count = var.count
  labels = { "bench-interf" = "true" "ci-run" = var.run_id }
  spot_fallback = true
}

Notes and constraints:
- Module sets preemptible/spot with a two-tier fallback: exact SKU -> SKU family -> on-demand.
- Provisioner attaches RBAC role gpu:harness-runner so CI jobs can create node leases.

Telemetry and metrics (what we capture)

| metric | source | alert threshold (example) | retention |
|--------|--------|--------------------------|-----------|
| p99_latency_ms(IF-PRX-1) | inference-metrics | > baseline*1.15 => FAIL | 30d |
| tokens_per_sec(IF-BULK-4) | inference-metrics | < baseline*0.9 => FAIL | 30d |
| pcie_retries_per_min | node-exporter + eBPF | > 1/min => Investigator alert | 14d |
| sm_util_95 | nvml/perf | delta > 20% between colocated tasks => Investigate | 14d |

Interference triage checklist

1. Confirm experiment reproducibility: rerun with different seed and host spread option.
2. Check node health: nvml-smi output, dmesg for GPU errors, firmware version mismatches.
3. Verify PCIe topology: run pci-topology.sh and compare against the topology baseline table.
4. Reproduce with isolation: run each workload on a dedicated host to confirm with/without delta.
5. If persistent, capture full perf profile and open an internal ticket with label "gpu-interference" including artifacts.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: infra-performance team (pager: infra-perf on-call).
- Secondary owner: gpu-runtime team (pager: gpu-runtime on-call).
- Escalations: if hardware telemetry indicates ECC errors or machine stability issues, immediately page platform-hardware and stop any CI provisioning to that region.

Rollout checklist for kernel / quantization canary

1. Run baseline matrix on stock runtime and store canonical baselines in S3 (/bench-baselines/{date}).
2. Enable canary kernel on 5% of CI ephemeral nodes (topology: spread).
3. Execute 3 consecutive matrix runs across the week during low-traffic window.
4. Compare automated summaries; if any gating rule is violated, auto-fail the canary and open an RCA ticket.

Appendix: sample commands and snippets

- Start a single test: kubectl -n infra exec deploy/interf-cli -- run --test IF-MEM-2 --duration 600 --output /tmp/out.json
- Fetch artifacts from CI: ci-artifacts fetch --run ${BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER} --path interf-summary.json

Buildkite pipeline (abridged YAML):

steps:
  - command: .buildkite/scripts/run-interf.sh ${BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER}
    agents: { gpu: "true" }
    env:
      CI_RUN_ID: "${BUILDKITE_BUILD_NUMBER}"

.manifests/interf-harness-deployment.yaml (summary):
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: interf-harness
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: harness
        image: registry.redwood.ai/bench-runner:latest
        env:
        - name: TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT
          value: https://ingest.redwood.ai/inference-metrics

Governance and data retention

- CI experiment artifacts are retained for 30 days by default.
- Baseline snapshots (S3) are versioned and immutable once published for a release window.

Related resources

- gpu-runtime team wiki: /confluence/eng-infra/team-wiki/gpu-runtime-compatibility-matrix-and-rollout-playbook.json
- Warm pool runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/warmup-sequencer-traffic-fingerprinter-iac-spec.json

Contact

For questions or to get access to the harness, contact the infra-performance team (infra-perf@redwood.ai) or open a Slack thread #infra-benchmarks.

Document history

- 2025-09-12: Initial draft by Avery Chen.
- 2025-11-08: Added Terraform module examples and CI gating rules (reviewer: Ravi Patel).
- 2026-02-03: Revised telemetry thresholds after H100 kernel rollout (reviewer: Sofia Martinez).

title: dsid_ea2a8779110d4f08addd4f875d98afe6__probe-led-quant-migration-safety-contract-2026.txt
text:
Probe-Led Quant Migration Safety Contract

Overview
This page defines the safety contract and operational playbook for rolling quantized model artifacts into production using a probe-first approach. The contract is intended for model onboarding, release engineers, and the eval-harness team. It applies to: per-layer and end-to-end quant conversions; mixed-precision fallbacks; and token/kv-cache-sensitive variants.

Goals
- Ensure user-visible quality regressions are constrained within an agreed fidelity budget.
- Provide deterministic, observable gating for canary and progressive rollouts.
- Minimize blast radius by coupling probes, telemetry, and automated fallback logic.

Scope and Risk Model
- Scope: Inference artifacts served via Redwood runtime (hosted, dedicated, private) where a quantized binary replaces a floating-point baseline. Includes customer-facing endpoints, internal eval shadows, and long-context workloads.
- Not in scope: offline batch scoring jobs (separate migration policy), model architecture changes.
- Principal risks: semantic drift, hallucination rate increase, latency regressions on small-batch/interactive tails, KV cache incompatibilities.

Definitions
- Baseline: the currently promoted (non-quant or prior-quant) model artifact used for comparison.
- Probe: a curated test case (automated or human-labeled) representing slices of production traffic used to measure quality metrics.
- Fidelity budget: numeric thresholds of acceptable deltas (see Acceptance Criteria).

Ownership
- Model owner: product/ML engineer who requests quant rollout. Responsible for probe set curation and initial evaluation artifacts.
- Eval-harness team: implements probes, schedules shadow runs, and computes metrics.
- Runtime/SRE: configures rollout routing, caching policies, and automated fallback triggers.
- Release engineer: executes promotion steps and signs off on exceptions.

Acceptance Criteria (Safety Contract)
All conditions must be satisfied for promotion from validation -> canary -> staged -> GA.
1) Functional correctness: intent-preserving metrics must remain within the fidelity budget compared to Baseline on the production-proxy probe suite:
   - Semantic Similarity (SBERT cosine) >= baseline - 0.02 OR absolute >= 0.90
   - Task Accuracy (where labeled) >= baseline - 1.5 percentage points
   - Safety/suppression tests: no new high-severity safety failures introduced (severity 1)
2) Latency & resource:
   - Median token latency <= baseline * 1.15
   - P99 token latency <= baseline * 1.5 AND absolute P99 <= 2.0s for interactive endpoints
   - GPU memory footprint reduction or within +5% of expected profile for mixed deployments
3) Stability & determinism:
   - KV-cache compatibility check: no divergence in continuation probability mass > 0.05 across 10k long-context probes
   - Determinism seeds: identical prompts under deterministic setting must match baseline behavior with <= 0.5% token edit-distance
4) Operational safety:
   - Rollout must have automated fallback route configured (quant -> baseline) with health-check cooldown of 30s
   - Telemetry events emitted for quant_migration_probe.result, quant_fallback.triggered, quant_rollout.progress

Probe Design Guidelines
- Maintain a prioritized probe portfolio:
  - Hot slices: 50K daily samples for latency-sensitive prompts (short, API-driven paths).
  - Long-context: 20K probes with >2k token histories to stress KV cache and attention speedups.
  - Function-call and structured-output probes: 5K examples covering common schema shapes.
  - Safety and red-team seeds: 10K fuzz/adversarial probes maintained by Security & Applied ML.

- Labeling and thresholds:
  - Each probe includes: prompt, expected intent, baseline response fingerprint (hash), and reference metric values.
  - Use aggregated metrics with confidence intervals (95% CI). Accept if CI upper bound meets acceptance criteria.

Rollout Plan (Procedure)
1) Local quant validation (model-owner)
   - Run local quant conversion and unit tests. Generate local evaluator report (artifact: quant_local_report.json).
   - Quick checks: shape/ops parity, seed determinism smoke tests, sample inference on 100 probes.
2) Shadow validation (eval-harness)
   - Schedule 48h shadow against production-proxy probe suite. Compare metrics to baseline.
   - Generate runbook comments and open PR to promote to canary if pass.
3) Canary (1% traffic or 0.5% depending on tenant sensitivity)
   - Duration: 4 hours minimum. Monitor metrics over 5-minute windows.
   - Automatic abort conditions:
     - Runtime error rate increase > 0.5pp absolute OR >= 2x baseline
     - Semantic Similarity delta > 0.03
     - Latency P99 increase > 2x baseline or > 3s absolute
   - If abort triggers, traffic routed to baseline immediately and release engineer notified.
4) Staged ramp (1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 50% -> 100%)
   - Each step minimum 6 hours, or longer for high-risk slices.
   - At each step, run full probe-suite and the lightweight smoke probes; require automated checks to pass.
5) GA promotion
   - Final artifact signed, release notes posted, and quant artifact retained in artifact registry with tags: quantized, promotor, baseline_hash.

Automated Fallback & Runbook
- Fallback logic (runtime): a rule set in the Router that evaluates telemetry windows and flips traffic to the configured fallback artifact.
- Emergency rollback steps (manual):
  1. Open incident on #prod-model-rollouts and tag Model Owner + Runtime oncall.
  2. Trigger immediate route reassign: curl -X POST https://runtime.internal/api/route/switch -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","to":"baseline-artifact-id"}'
  3. Validate baseline responses on 100 smoke probes.
  4. Create postmortem and hold a triage meeting within 48 hours.

Telemetry, Dashboards and Alerts
- Required telemetry exports:
  - quant_migration_probe.result: {probe_id, slice, metric_vector, delta_from_baseline, pass_fail}
  - quant_rollout.progress: {artifact_id, percent_traffic, step, timestamp}
  - quant_fallback.triggered: {artifact_id, reason, metric_snapshot}
- Dashboards (names):
  - Quant Migration Overview (team: eval-harness)
  - Quant Canary Health (team: runtime/SRE)
  - KV-Cache Divergence Monitor (team: serving)
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - ALERT: quant_canary_semantic_regression if semantic_similarity_delta < -0.03 over 10m window -> Pager to runtime oncall
  - ALERT: quant_canary_error_spike if error_rate > 1.0% for 5m -> Slack + Pager

Metrics Table (exemplar)
| Metric | Baseline target | Acceptable delta | Alert level | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Semantic Similarity (sBERT) | 0.94 | -0.02 | critical if <-0.03 | applied-ml |
| Task Accuracy (labeled) | 92% | -1.5pp | high if <-2pp | applied-ml |
| Latency P50 (token) | 12ms | +15% | medium if >+50% | serving |
| Latency P99 (token) | 180ms | +50% | critical if >2x or >2000ms | serving |
| Error rate (inference) | 0.2% | +0.5pp | critical if >1% | runtime/SRE |
| KV divergence (KL proxy) | 0.01 | +0.05 | high if >0.08 | serving |

Configuration Examples
- Canary route JSON (example):
{ "route": "/v1/generate", "artifact_id": "quant-artifact-2026-03-01", "percent_traffic": 1, "fallback_artifact": "baseline-artifact-8f9c", "health_window": 300000 }

- Probe registration YAML (example):
---
probe_id: longcontext-qual-001
slice: long-context
owner: applied-ml
metrics: [semantic_similarity, continuation_entropy]
priority: high
retention_days: 90
---

Checklist before promotion
- [ ] Probe suite completeness verified (hot, long-context, functioncall, safety).
- [ ] Shadow-run metrics uploaded and reviewed by at least one reviewer.
- [ ] Rollout route and fallback configured in Router with cooldowns.
- [ ] Dashboards created and alerts configured for the artifact.
- [ ] Artifact stored in registry with reproducibility metadata (seed, conversion script hash, quant params).

Post-promotion monitoring and audits
- Maintain probe sampling for 14 days post-GA with daily digest to model owner.
- Schedule a 7-day audit to check for slow drift in fidelity metrics; if drift > half the fidelity budget, place artifact on periodic review cadence.
- Record all incidents and anomaly detections in the migration registry and link to model promotion PRs.

Exceptions and fast-paths
- For low-risk, internal-only artifacts (non-customer-facing), expedited rollouts (shadow -> 20% -> GA in 24h) are allowed with explicit approval from Model Owner + Runtime lead. Document reason and probe subset used.

Related pages
- /applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding/inference-readiness-eval-matrix-and-promotion-playbook-2026
- /applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/shadow-orchestrator-crossmodal-stress-2026

Appendix: Typical failure modes and mitigations
- Increased continuation hallucinations on long-context: reduce quant aggressiveness, re-run with higher-precision attention layers, expand long-context probe set and rebaseline.
- Tokenization boundary drift: re-run tokenization alignment tests and validate prompt-segmentation heuristics.
- Instance OOMs after quant: tighten memory profiling in conversion and add margin to batch size scheduling.

Contact and escalation
- Primary contact: Maya Chen (applied-ml)
- Eval-harness oncall: eval-harness@redwood.internal
- Runtime oncall: runtime-sre@redwood.internal

Revision history
- 2026-02-14: Document created by Maya Chen
- 2026-03-01: Clarified automated abort conditions and added KV-cache divergence metrics (reviewers: Arjun Patel, Sofia Martinez)

title: dsid_d6363b0de8f547e1986591453d347467__benchmark-report-core-message-house.txt
text:
Benchmark Report Core Message House (Latency/$) — Sales Enablement

## Purpose
This page is the single source of truth for how Redwood talks about the **Latency/$ benchmark report** in outbound, discovery, demos, and follow-ups. It provides:
- Primary narrative (what the report means and why it matters)
- Messaging pillars + proof points (what to emphasize)
- CTA paths by audience (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private)
- Approved phrasing + required caveats
- Disallowed claims/phrasing (legal + credibility guardrails)

**Owner:** Product Marketing (Soojin Lee)

---

## One-liner (for emails, openers, and intro slides)
**Redwood’s Latency/$ Benchmark shows how much real-time performance you get per dollar across popular LLMs and regions—so you can choose the right model and deployment mode with production economics in mind.**

---

## Primary narrative (what we’re really saying)
Teams don’t win by chasing “best tokens/sec” in a lab—they win by meeting user-facing latency targets **at an acceptable unit cost**, consistently, across the regions they serve.

Redwood built and published a reproducible benchmark focused on **production inference economics**:
- **Latency** (p50/p95) and **throughput** under defined concurrency and token mixes
- **Cost efficiency** expressed as **Latency/$** (plus $/1M tokens for transparency)
- **Reliability and consistency** signals (variance gates, repeat runs, exclusions documented)
- **Regional comparability**, so you can plan global performance and capacity

The takeaway: Redwood helps you serve LLMs predictably and economically—whether you start with Hosted API, reserve Dedicated capacity, or deploy Private (VPC/on-prem) for regulated workloads.

---

## Audience framing (who cares and why)
### For builders (PLG / self-serve)
- “Pick a model + region that meets your latency target without guesswork.”
- “Use the interactive table to explore tradeoffs by context length and concurrency.”

### For platform teams / enterprise
- “Latency/$ is a better procurement and architecture input than raw tokens/sec.”
- “Dedicated capacity and Private deployment keep performance stable as usage grows.”

### For regulated industries
- “You can carry the same operational playbook into VPC/on-prem with Redwood Private.”
- “We publish methodology + retention of raw artifacts to support claims and internal reviews.”

---

## Message house (pillars + proof)
Use this structure in talk tracks, deck narrative, and discovery.

### Pillar 1 — Production Economics: Latency/$ (not vanity metrics)
**Claim (approved):** Redwood publishes and optimizes for **Latency/$** so teams can meet latency targets while controlling per-token cost.

**Proof points to use (pick 2–3):**
- Latency/$ defined as a **normalized efficiency metric** derived from measured latency under load and attributable serving cost (see Methodology page).
- Report includes supporting metrics: **p50/p95 latency, throughput, and $/1M tokens**.
- Benchmarks use a production-oriented prompt mix (prefill/decode balance) and defined concurrency, warmup, and cache/batch policies.

**Customer-impact phrasing:**
- “If you have a p95 target, Latency/$ helps you see what it costs to hit that target, not just how fast a GPU can go on a single request.”


### Pillar 2 — Predictable Performance Under Load (throughput + p95)
**Claim (approved):** Redwood focuses on **tail latency and stability** under defined concurrency so you can reason about real user experience.

**Proof points to use:**
- Runs include concurrency levels and queueing behavior; results report p95 (not only p50).
- Stability gates: repeated runs and variance thresholds trigger reruns; outliers and exclusions are documented.

**Customer-impact phrasing:**
- “Most production issues show up in p95, not in best-case single-request timings.”


### Pillar 3 — Reliability & Operational Guardrails (benchmarking and serving)
**Claim (approved):** The benchmark methodology mirrors Redwood’s production discipline: reproducibility, validation, and documented caveats.

**Proof points to use:**
- Run manifests, configs, and validation checklist are part of the approval workflow.
- Public artifacts are redacted and retained internally to substantiate published claims.

**Customer-impact phrasing:**
- “We’re not asking you to trust a screenshot—we can show the how, the configs, and what we excluded.”


### Pillar 4 — Regional Consistency & Deployment Flexibility (Hosted → Dedicated → Private)
**Claim (approved):** Redwood provides a consistent inference experience across **multiple regions and deployment modes**, with clear levers to balance cost/latency.

**Proof points to use:**
- Report spans NA/EU/APAC where available; differences are explained and caveated.
- Dedicated capacity is positioned for predictability; Private for data residency, isolation, and regulated environments.

**Customer-impact phrasing:**
- “As you expand to new regions or need isolation, you don’t need to rebuild your serving stack—your API and operational model stay consistent.”

---

## Proof assets (what to point to)
Use these in this order during conversations:
1) **Interactive benchmark table** (quick filtering by model/region/context length)
2) **Methodology summary** (short explanation + caveats)
3) **Full methodology page** (workload definitions, concurrency, caching/batching policy)
4) **PDF report** (executive narrative + charts)

---

## CTAs (what we want the prospect to do)
### Hosted API (developers / early-stage)
- “Try the models from the report in your own workload. Start with Hosted; we’ll help you tune caching/batching and pick a region.”
- CTA: **Start trial / get API key**

### Dedicated (scale / predictable throughput)
- “If you need stable p95 under sustained concurrency, we can size a Dedicated pool based on your prompt mix and SLOs.”
- CTA: **Dedicated sizing session** (Solutions Engineering)

### Private (regulated / residency)
- “If you need VPC/on-prem, we’ll map the report’s assumptions to your environment and compliance requirements.”
- CTA: **Security + architecture review**

---

## Approved language snippets (copy/paste)
### 15-second opener
“We published a Latency/$ benchmark because teams care about user latency and unit cost together. It measures p50/p95 under defined concurrency and token mixes across models and regions, with a transparent methodology so you can interpret the tradeoffs.”

### When a prospect asks “what does Latency/$ mean?”
“It’s a normalized metric that combines measured latency under a defined workload with attributable serving cost, so you can compare how efficiently different model+region options deliver responsiveness per dollar. We still show p50/p95 and $/1M tokens alongside it.”

### When a prospect asks “is this production-realistic?”
“It’s designed to be closer to production than a single-request microbenchmark: concurrency, warmups, and a prompt mix that reflects prefill/decode patterns. And we publish the methodology and caveats so you can map it to your own workload.”

### When a prospect asks “how should I use this?”
“Use it to shortlist a few model+region candidates, then we’ll validate against your real prompts and latency SLOs. If you need predictable tail latency at scale, we’ll talk Dedicated; if you need residency/isolation, we’ll talk Private.”

---

## Required caveats (must include when discussing numbers)
Use these especially in competitive contexts.
- “Results depend on workload (context length, concurrency, prefill/decode mix), region, and serving configuration.”
- “Benchmark conditions are defined and documented; numbers should be interpreted within that methodology.”
- “We report distributions (p50/p95) and run stability checks; residual variance can occur due to capacity and network conditions.”
- “Competitor baselines, if referenced, must be described with **source, date, configuration assumptions, and limitations**.”

---

## Competitive posture (safe framing)
### What we can say
- “Latency/$ helps compare efficiency for real user experience under load.”
- “Raw tokens/sec often misses tail latency and doesn’t reflect the cost to hit a p95 target.”
- “We publish methodology and caveats so teams can evaluate fit and reproduce key parts.”

### What we should do in a live conversation
- Ask for their workload: context length, concurrency, streaming vs non-streaming, p95 requirement, region(s), and traffic shape.
- Offer a “replication plan” in their environment (PoC guidance) rather than arguing over any single chart.

---

## Disallowed claims / phrasing (do not use)
These are credibility and legal risk areas. If you’re unsure, route to PMM + Legal.

### Absolute superiority claims (no)
- “Fastest / best / #1 across all models and regions”
- “Always cheaper” / “always lowest latency”
- “Guarantees” tied to benchmark outcomes (benchmarks are not SLAs)

### Unqualified comparative claims (no)
- “We beat {competitor} by X%” without specifying exact test conditions, date, and configuration caveats.
- “Competitor results are wrong” (instead: “different methodology/assumptions; here’s ours.”)

### Overstating representativeness (no)
- “This exactly matches every production workload”
- “These numbers will be identical for you”

### Misleading metric language (no)
- “Latency/$ is the only metric that matters”
- “Tokens/sec equals user latency”

---

## Quick talk track (recommended flow)
1) **Context:** “Teams need to balance p95 latency and cost under load.”
2) **What we published:** “A Latency/$ benchmark across models and regions with reproducible methodology.”
3) **Why it matters:** “Shortlists options and clarifies tradeoffs; avoids vanity metrics.”
4) **What to do next:** “Validate with your prompts; choose Hosted/Dedicated/Private based on scale and constraints.”

---

## Handling tough questions (redirects)
### “Did you cherry-pick prompts, regions, or models?”
“We published the selection criteria and methodology, and we include caveats and exclusions. If your workload differs, we’ll help run a targeted PoC with your prompts and success criteria.”

### “Were caching/batching enabled?”
“Benchmark configurations are explicitly documented. We’ll clarify the cache/batch policy used for the published numbers and can show how enabling/disabling changes outcomes depending on workload.”

### “Are these numbers an SLA?”
“No—benchmarks are measurements under defined conditions. SLAs and capacity guarantees are handled through Dedicated contracts and deployment architecture.”

---

## Internal escalation / approvals
- **Any new comparative claim or numeric claim not in the published report:** route to **Soojin Lee** + **Michael Grant/Sofia Mendes**.
- **Methodology questions beyond the summary:** route to **Jonas Weber** or **Claire Dubois**.
- **PoC replication requests:** route to **Markus Klein** (Solutions) and attach the “replication plan” template from the FAQ.

---

## Change log
- 2025-07-10: Updated disallowed phrasing list; clarified required caveats for competitor references; aligned CTAs for Dedicated vs Private.

title: dsid_36ea3683b99b4bab842777b9a48c327d__kernel-priority-calibration-lab-notebook-2026.txt
text:
Kernel Priority Calibration Lab Notebook

Summary
-------
This lab notebook documents a sequence of controlled experiments to calibrate kernel-level priorities and credit assignments in the Redwood serving runtime. The objective is to produce a repeatable mapping from request traffic characteristics to scheduler priority/weight settings that meet our latency SLOs while minimizing cost and token-level variance.

Purpose and scope
------------------
- Purpose: Establish a defensible, observable calibration process for kernel priority settings used by kernel-manager and scheduler-coordinator.
- Scope: Experiments span the dedicated GPU pool (gpool-rt-prod-sim), the local experiment cluster (lab-gpu-01..04), and the shadow-routing infrastructure used by the performance lab. This notebook does NOT change production configuration; it defines candidate settings for canary rollout.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
Over the last 18 months we've observed recurring p95 tail spikes for small interactive chat workloads when mixed with long-running batch generations. Investigation shows credit starvation and kernel handoff delays in the dispatcher + kernel pipeline. This calibration aims to:
1) Quantify how per-request weight, kernel quantum size, and preemption granularity affect latency distribution.
2) Generate recommended rule sets for the priority expression language used by kernel-manager.
3) Provide an audit trail and artifacts (traces, kernel-profiles, sample payloads) for sign-off prior to rollout.

Key concepts and definitions
---------------------------
- Kernel: GPU execution unit as exposed by kernel-agent (e.g., attn-kernel-v2).
- Priority weight: numeric weight applied by scheduler-coordinator when allocating slot quantum.
- Quantum: minimal GPU time-slice unit in microseconds (default 2000us in lab).
- Preemption point: safe boundary (KV cache alignment) where kernels can be interrupted.

Testbed and baseline configuration
----------------------------------
- Hardware: 4 x A100-80GB (lab-gpu-01..04), NVLink disabled for determinism in early runs.
- Software: runtime v3.14.2 (branch: experiment/kernel-calibration), kernel-agent v2.7.0, dispatch-service v1.22.
- Telemetry: traces via trace-proxy -> jaeger-lab, metrics to prometheus-lab, payload capture persisted to s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04.
- Baseline SLOs used in lab: p50 < 30ms, p95 < 120ms for short-chat profile; throughput target 400 reqs/s for medium packing.

Experiment matrix (summary)
---------------------------
| Run | Priority profile | Quantum (us) | Preempt? | Workload mix | Note |
|-----|------------------|--------------:|:--------:|---------------|------|
| A   | default (1,1,1)  | 2000         | no       | 80% short /20% long | baseline
| B   | favor-short (3,1,0.5) | 2000  | yes      | 80% short /20% long | test preemptive handoff
| C   | weight-linear (2,1,1) | 1000   | yes      | 50/50 mixed        | smaller quantum
| D   | conservative (1,1,0.25) | 4000 | no      | 20% short /80% long | test long-run impact
| E   | dynamic-adaptive* (see rule) | 2000 | yes | synthetic burst traces | adaptive weight function

(See "Experiment logs" below for raw outputs and links to traces.)

Calibration procedure (step-by-step)
-----------------------------------
1. Prepare lab cluster: reboot lab-gpu nodes, disable NVLink, ensure kernel-agent v2.7.0 running.
2. Load baseline model: llama-compat-13b-int8 (tag: lab-2026-02) to isolate kernel behavior from model variance.
3. Deploy traffic generator (tg-runner) with recorded production short-chat and long-burst corpora. Command: 

   ./tg-runner --target lab-gateway:8443 --corpus corpora/short-chat.json --rps 320 --duration 900 --tag run-A

4. Apply priority profile via kernel-manager CLI (example):

   rwd-kernelctl set-profile --profile-name favor-short --rules "priority(expression='request.shape == \"short\" ? 3 : 1', preempt=true, quantum_us=2000)"

5. Collect telemetry: Ensure sampling via experiment-telemetry job. Key artifacts:
   - jaeger traces: trace-id prefix "calib-2026-04-A"
   - prometheus metrics: histogram rwd_kernel_latency_{quantile}
   - captured payloads: s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04/run-A/

6. Run 1-hour trial, then a 6-hour steady-state for stability measurement.
7. Post-process: run analysis notebook /notebooks/kernel-calib-analysis.ipynb to compute p50/p95, fairness index, and variance.

Telemetry and measurement definitions
-----------------------------------
- Latency decomposition: request_total = frontend_queue + dispatch_delay + kernel_wait + kernel_exec + post_process. Each is traced and tagged.
- Fairness Index (FI): normalized Jain's index on per-cohort latency at p95 (goal >= 0.85).
- Kernel Utilization: GPU active seconds / wall-time (target 0.6-0.85 depending on workload).
- SLO thresholds: alert if burst p95 > 2x target or FI < 0.7.

Example priority rule table (recommended canonical format)
--------------------------------------------------------
| name | expression | weight | preempt | quantum_us | notes |
|------|------------|-------:|:-------:|-----------:|-------|
| favor-short | request.shape == "short" AND model.family == "llama-compat" | 3 | true | 2000 | Good for interactive agents
| default | true | 1 | true | 2000 | Fallback
| background-batch | request.type == "batch" | 0.5 | false | 4000 | Allow large runs but deprioritize

Sample kernel-manager JSON profile (apply via rwd-kernelctl)
-----------------------------------------------------------
{
  "profile_name": "favor-short",
  "rules": [
    {
      "id": "short-interactive",
      "expr": "request.shape == \"short\" and request.max_tokens < 512",
      "weight": 3.0,
      "preempt": true,
      "quantum_us": 2000
    },
    {
      "id": "batch-low",
      "expr": "request.type == \"batch\"",
      "weight": 0.5,
      "preempt": false,
      "quantum_us": 4000
    }
  ]
}

(When saving this document into kernel-manager, remember to redact any sensitive model keys.)

Experiment logs (high level)
---------------------------
- Run A (2026-04-20): baseline run, observed p95=138ms (exceeded target). Notes: dispatcher queueing prominent. Trace set: calib-2026-04-A.*
- Run B (2026-04-22): favor-short, preemption enabled, p95=86ms, FI=0.82. Short requests improved; tails reduced but long jobs saw increased runtime by 6%.
- Run C (2026-05-03): smaller quantum (1000us) reduced tail by 12% but increased kernel dispatch overhead (extra context switches). Kernel exec variance up 8%.
- Run D (2026-05-18): conservative quantum for long jobs reduced throughput by 14% with negligible improvements to short p95.
- Run E (2026-09-07): dynamic-adaptive rule using recent-ten-second-load reduced peak p95 by 20% in burst scenarios; needs further stability testing.

Decision rules and acceptance criteria
------------------------------------
Use the following rule to accept a candidate profile into canary:
1. Candidate must achieve p95 <= 1.1 * lab SLO for three independent 6-hour runs under synthetic production-mix.
2. FI >= 0.8 across cohorts for the same runs.
3. GPU utilization not below baseline by more than 10% (to avoid wasteful idle capacity).
4. No increase in observed model inference errors (model failure rate <= baseline + 0.1%).

Rollout checklist (pre-canary)
----------------------------
- [ ] Create canary plan: targeted to dedicated pool canary-nodes (2 nodes).
- [ ] Prepare automatic rollback policy in control-plane: revert-to-profile=default if p95 > threshold for 15m.
- [ ] Create dashboard: /dashboards/kernel-calibration-canary with alert rules (p95, FI, top-kernel-waits).
- [ ] Run security review for config file storage (CI secrets redaction).
- [ ] Schedule 48h passive monitoring window with oncall coverage.

Troubleshooting checklist
-------------------------
- If p95 regresses after profile apply:
  1) Re-run short deterministic microbenchmarks (script: tools/microbench/kernel_probe.sh).
  2) Collect full jaeger traces with full payload sampling for 30m.
  3) If kernel wait dominates >60% of tail, revert profile and open ticket on #sre-runtime.

Observed side-effects and mitigation notes
----------------------------------------
- Smaller quantum increases context-switch overhead. Mitigation: only use quantum <= 1000us for sub-100ms expected executions.
- Aggressive preemption can increase cache thrash for models with large KV caches; avoid preemption for models with >60M KV footprint.

Open experiments (next steps)
---------------------------
- Evaluate adaptive-weight learning that uses online p95 feedback loop with conservative damping.
- Test hardware-tiered profiles (fast-gpu vs econ-gpu) for cross-pool routing decisions.
- Validate interaction with quantization-profiles: int8 kernels show different preemption sensitivity.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Document owner: Maya Chen (serving-runtime / kernel-experiments).
- Primary contacts: Arjun Kapoor (scheduler), Lena Ortiz (telemetry), Diego Morales (SRE).
- Escalation: oncall-runtime -> #oncall-runtime -> PagerDuty escalation as per runbook.

Artifacts and storage locations
-----------------------------
- Traces: jaeger-lab (query tag calib-2026-04-*)
- Metrics: prometheus-lab (job=rwd-runtime-lab)
- Artifacts: s3://redwood-lab-artifacts/kernel-calib/2026-04/
- Analysis notebooks: /notebooks/kernel-calib-analysis.ipynb (gitlab: infra/perf-lab)

Change log (notable entries)
---------------------------
- 2026-04-15 (Maya Chen): created notebook and executed Runs A-B.
- 2026-05-03 (Maya Chen): added Run C results and small-quantum guidance.
- 2026-09-07 (Maya Chen): added adaptive profile (Run E) summary and acceptance criteria.
- 2026-11-02 (Maya Chen): consolidated logs, added rollout checklist and decision rules for canary sign-off.

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
-------------------------------------
- Apply JSON profile: rwd-kernelctl apply --file favor-short.json --target lab-kman-01
- Query p95 from prometheus-lab (example):
  curl -s "http://prom-lab:9090/api/v1/query?query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(rwd_kernel_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))" | jq

- Microbenchmark script: tools/microbench/kernel_probe.sh
  #!/bin/bash
  for i in $(seq 1 100); do 
    rwd-client --model llama-compat-13b-int8 --prompt "hello" --max-tokens 64 >/dev/null; 
  done

Related reading
--------------
- Scheduler observability contract and simulated injector (see related pages).
- Telemetry feedback & kernel autotune playbook.

Notes on document conventions
----------------------------
- This notebook is intentionally structured as a lab-first artifact: preserves time-stamped experiment runs, raw artifact locations, and decision rationale.
- When moving candidate profiles into production, create a dedicated ADR referencing this notebook and link to the canonical profile artifacts in /infra/configs/kernel-profiles/ with immutable tags.

End of notebook.

title: dsid_2f9fc4d58a7040d5be8929c9c2ef7d48__dedicated-pricing-tiers-v1.txt
text:
Dedicated Pricing Tiers v1 (Standard / Plus / Premium) — Shapes, Entitlements, and List Price Guidance

## 1) Summary
This document proposes Redwood Dedicated pricing/packaging for v1 tiered throughput guarantees. It maps (a) tier entitlements (throughput floor + burst + failover posture + support SLAs) to (b) standardized hardware “shapes” by region and (c) list price guidance + discount guardrails.

This is intended to be:
- Consistent with the Dedicated Throughput SLO definition (metric semantics, exclusions, and reporting).
- Operationally manageable (standard shapes, predictable headroom, tier-aware routing/admission control).
- Quoteable by Sales with minimal bespoke sizing work.

**Non-goals (v1):** bespoke per-customer kernel/quantization tuning commitments in the commercial package; guaranteeing quality metrics; guaranteeing throughput across arbitrary model mixes without pinning/model constraints.

## 2) Key definitions (commercial)
**Dedicated Deployment:** A customer-isolated inference pool (one or more nodes) for a single deployment_id with a pinned model version + configuration envelope.

**Committed Throughput (CT):** The customer’s purchased throughput floor for an eligible deployment, expressed as **output tokens/sec** measured at the Redwood gateway.

**Burst Throughput:** Temporary throughput above CT that may be served when capacity is available (within tier policy). Burst usage is metered separately.

**Eligible Time:** Time excluding defined exclusions (customer-side throttling/backpressure, unsupported model/config, intentional load tests exceeding published limits, control-plane maintenance windows per contract).

**Important constraint (v1):** Throughput commitments are made **per deployment** for **one pinned model version** and **one context window class** (see §4.3). Multi-model deployments require separate Dedicated deployments or an explicit exception.

## 3) Tier taxonomy (v1)
The tiers differ primarily in: (1) throughput floor strictness + headroom, (2) burst policy, (3) failover posture, and (4) support response + operational posture.

### 3.1 Tier entitlements at a glance
| Tier | Primary buyer | Throughput SLO posture | Burst policy (included) | Failover posture | Support response targets |
|------|---------------|------------------------|-------------------------|------------------|--------------------------|
| Standard | PLG→Sales assist; predictable baseline capacity | “Floor” commitment on eligible time; best-effort mitigation | Up to **1.25× CT** for **≤10%** of eligible minutes/month (when available) | Best-effort within-region capacity recovery | P1: 1 hour, P2: 4 business hours, P3: 1 business day |
| Plus | Production workloads; predictable + some spikes | Floor commitment with stronger headroom + faster remediation | Up to **1.5× CT** for **≤15%** of eligible minutes/month | In-region HA (multi-AZ) where available; faster node replacement | P1: 30 minutes, P2: 2 business hours, P3: 1 business day |
| Premium | Enterprise/regulated; strict ops expectations | Floor commitment with highest headroom + prioritized remediation | Up to **2.0× CT** for **≤20%** of eligible minutes/month | In-region HA + optional cross-region warm standby (add-on) | P1: 15 minutes, P2: 1 business hour, P3: 4 business hours |

**Notes:**
- Burst is “included” as an entitlement (no additional reservation fee), but **burst usage is billable** (see §6).
- Cross-region warm standby is **not included** in v1 base Premium; it is an optional add-on due to large COGS impact.

### 3.2 What is *contractually* promised vs. “expected”
- **Contractual:** Committed Throughput (CT) floor, measurement semantics, exclusions, support response targets, and remedy framework.
- **Not contractual (v1):** “Typical” tokens/sec benchmarks, p50 latency, or quality/accuracy.

## 4) Shape mapping and performance envelopes
This proposal uses standard Dedicated shapes. Shapes are the unit of provisioning + capacity accounting.

### 4.1 Shape naming (SKU format)
SKU format (internal + quoting):
- `DED-<REGION>-<GPU>-x<count>-<TIER>`
Examples:
- `DED-US-EAST-A10080-x8-PLUS`
- `DED-EU-CENTRAL-H10080-x8-PREMIUM`

### 4.2 Regions supported (v1 quoting)
- US: `us-east-1`, `us-west-2`
- EU: `eu-central-1`

Other regions are “exception only” until fleet supply and benchmark variance are stabilized.

### 4.3 Model/config classes supported for CT (v1)
To avoid a gamable SLO and large variance, CT commitments are only offered for these v1 classes:
- **70B dense class:** e.g., “Llama-3-70B-class” (pinned version); supported ctx: **8k** and **16k**.
- **MoE mid class:** e.g., “Mixtral-8x7B-class” (pinned version); supported ctx: **8k**.

**Out of scope for CT in v1 (exception-only):** 32k+ contexts, speculative decoding variants not in the standard runtime profile, experimental quantization profiles, and multi-model weighted routing behind a single deployment_id.

### 4.4 Proposed shapes (v1)
**Primary shapes** (recommended):
- `L40S-48GB x4` (cost-efficient; limited for 70B @16k)
- `A100-80GB x8` (stable supply; broad compatibility)
- `H100-80GB x8` (highest perf; supply constrained in some regions)

**Notes on ops posture:**
- Plus and Premium shapes are provisioned with higher headroom targets and stricter admission control to protect CT.
- Premium includes stronger spare capacity posture (warm spares / faster replacement) which drives price.

## 5) List pricing proposal (v1)
### 5.1 Pricing principles
- Price is primarily determined by **COGS + headroom** + **support/ops allocation**.
- Tiers represent increasing unit economics cost (headroom, spares, incident response), not just a “label.”
- We avoid per-customer bespoke pricing by anchoring on **shape SKUs**.

### 5.2 Monthly list price by tier and shape
**All prices below are USD/month per Dedicated deployment (shape).**

| Shape | Standard | Plus | Premium |
|------|----------:|-----:|--------:|
| L40S-48GB x4 | $24,000 | $29,000 | $37,000 |
| A100-80GB x8 | $72,000 | $86,000 | $108,000 |
| H100-80GB x8 | $132,000 | $156,000 | $195,000 |

**What’s included in monthly price (all tiers):**
- Dedicated capacity (shape)
- Standard SLO reporting (customer-visible CT compliance view)
- Dedicated operational support per tier response targets
- Standard on-call engagement for verified platform issues

**Not included (billed separately or add-on):**
- Burst usage above CT (see §6)
- Cross-region warm standby (Premium add-on)
- Extended log/trace retention beyond standard window (enterprise add-on)

### 5.3 Throughput floor guidance by shape (for quoting)
These are **commercial quoting guidelines** (not a benchmark promise) for the CT we are willing to sell on each shape for eligible model/config classes.

**70B dense class, 8k ctx (output tokens/sec):**
- L40S x4: CT up to **350 tok/s** (Standard), **400 tok/s** (Plus), **450 tok/s** (Premium)
- A100 x8: CT up to **800 tok/s** (Standard), **900 tok/s** (Plus), **1,000 tok/s** (Premium)
- H100 x8: CT up to **1,500 tok/s** (Standard), **1,650 tok/s** (Plus), **1,800 tok/s** (Premium)

**70B dense class, 16k ctx:**
- A100 x8: CT up to **550 tok/s** (Standard), **650 tok/s** (Plus), **750 tok/s** (Premium)
- H100 x8: CT up to **1,000 tok/s** (Standard), **1,150 tok/s** (Plus), **1,300 tok/s** (Premium)

**MoE mid class, 8k ctx:**
- L40S x4: CT up to **500 tok/s** (Standard), **600 tok/s** (Plus), **700 tok/s** (Premium)
- A100 x8: CT up to **1,100 tok/s** (Standard), **1,250 tok/s** (Plus), **1,400 tok/s** (Premium)
- H100 x8: CT up to **2,000 tok/s** (Standard), **2,200 tok/s** (Plus), **2,400 tok/s** (Premium)

**Guardrail:** If a customer requests CT above these bounds, require (a) benchmark validation and (b) Deal Desk + Infra sign-off.

### 5.4 Minimum contract terms (v1 defaults)
- Standard: 3-month minimum (month-to-month allowed after initial term)
- Plus: 6-month minimum
- Premium: 12-month minimum

Exceptions require VP Sales + Finance approval.

## 6) Burst packaging and metering
### 6.1 Burst policy (commercial)
- Burst is not guaranteed at all times; it is served when available subject to tier limits.
- Burst is enabled by default for Plus and Premium; Standard is “on” unless customer requests hard cap.

**Included entitlement (cap by eligible minutes/month):**
- Standard: up to 1.25× CT for ≤10% of eligible minutes
- Plus: up to 1.5× CT for ≤15% of eligible minutes
- Premium: up to 2.0× CT for ≤20% of eligible minutes

### 6.2 Burst billing (v1 proposal)
Burst above CT is billed as usage (output tokens) at a tier-specific rate.

**Proposed burst rates (USD per 1M output tokens):**
- Standard: $1.80 / 1M
- Plus: $1.60 / 1M
- Premium: $1.40 / 1M

Rationale: burst is cheaper marginally at higher tiers because the customer is paying for higher fixed headroom posture.

**Hard cap option:** Customer can request “no burst” (strict cap at CT). No price discount in v1.

## 7) Support + operational posture (packaging detail)
### 7.1 Incident communications
- Standard: incident updates at least every 4 hours for customer-impacting events
- Plus: updates every 2 hours
- Premium: updates every 1 hour; named incident commander for Sev-1

### 7.2 Remediation posture (high level)
- Standard: best-effort remediation; may require scheduled maintenance window for shape replacement
- Plus: prioritized remediation; in-region HA where shape supports it
- Premium: prioritized remediation + warm spare posture; optional cross-region warm standby add-on

## 8) Discount guardrails and Deal Desk triggers
### 8.1 Discount bands (v1)
These are guardrails for AEs; exceptions require Deal Desk and Finance.

- Standard: up to **15%** discount (AE-approved within band)
- Plus: up to **12%** discount
- Premium: up to **10%** discount

### 8.2 Deal Desk required if any of the following apply
- CT requested above §5.3 guidance
- Non-standard region or shape
- Customer requests custom exclusions/measurement windows in SLO language
- Customer requests “guaranteed burst” or burst above tier policy
- Term < minimum for Plus/Premium
- Discount above guardrails
- Any cross-region failover commitment

## 9) Assumptions (Finance + Ops)
Pricing above assumes:
- Target blended gross margin (GM) bands: Standard **~50–55%**, Plus **~55–60%**, Premium **~60%+** (Premium is higher price but also higher ops costs; GM depends on spare posture).
- Utilization targets (eligible capacity): Standard **65%**, Plus **60%**, Premium **50%**.
- Headroom allocations embedded by tier (higher tier = lower allowed saturation).
- Support cost allocation scales with tier response targets and required on-call involvement.
- Supply constraints: H100 availability may require longer lead times in `eu-central-1` and `us-west-2` (see Fleet updates); Premium H100 should be sold conservatively.

## 10) Rollout plan (commercial)
- Internal enablement: Sales cheat sheet + quoting examples + Deal Desk workflow
- Limited GA: 5–10 Dedicated accounts across Standard/Plus; 1–2 Premium pilots with explicit exclusions and weekly review
- Revisit thresholds: After 45–60 days of production data (SLO compliance, burst usage distribution, saturation signals)

## 11) Risks and mitigations
- **Benchmark variance risk:** Tokens/sec varies by model version, decoding params, and context distribution.
  - Mitigation: pin model/version; constrain config class; require benchmark for exceptions.
- **Supply risk (H100):** Over-selling Premium on H100 increases lead times and incident risk.
  - Mitigation: conservative Premium H100 allocations; warm spares only where Fleet confirms.
- **Gaming risk:** Customers might shape traffic to exploit measurement windows.
  - Mitigation: use eligible-time semantics + exclusions; monitoring for anomalous patterns; enforce admission control.

## 12) Open questions (for v1 sign-off)
1) **Burst billing:** Should burst be billed at a fixed per-token rate (proposal) or as a % uplift to monthly fee (simpler invoicing)?
2) **Cross-region standby add-on:** Do we want a standardized SKU (e.g., +35% monthly) or quote case-by-case due to region pair COGS variance?
3) **Minimum terms:** Are the proposed minimum terms acceptable for PLG conversion motion for Standard, or do we need a 1-month “starter” exception?
4) **CTX class enforcement:** Are we enforcing 8k/16k at the control plane (hard limits), or only contractually (soft limits)?
5) **Premium support scope:** Do we include a named TAM/solutions contact in Premium by default, or keep it as an enterprise add-on?

## 13) Appendix A — Example quote configurations
**Example 1 (Plus, 70B @8k):**
- Region: us-east-1
- Shape: A100-80GB x8
- Tier: Plus
- Monthly: $86,000
- CT: 850 tok/s
- Burst: up to 1.5× for ≤15% eligible minutes; burst billed at $1.60 / 1M output tokens

**Example 2 (Standard, MoE @8k, cost sensitive):**
- Region: us-west-2
- Shape: L40S-48GB x4
- Tier: Standard
- Monthly: $24,000
- CT: 450 tok/s
- Burst: up to 1.25× for ≤10% eligible minutes; burst billed at $1.80 / 1M output tokens

**Example 3 (Premium, enterprise ops):**
- Region: eu-central-1
- Shape: H100-80GB x8
- Tier: Premium
- Monthly: $195,000
- CT: 1,700 tok/s
- Burst: up to 2.0× for ≤20% eligible minutes; burst billed at $1.40 / 1M output tokens
- Add-on (optional): cross-region warm standby (requires Deal Desk + Fleet sign-off)

title: dsid_e1fe3e72263440b19a34d6dce2eb5d79__egress-bandwidth-burst-shaper-and-tenant-fairness-implementation.txt
text:
Tenant Egress Bandwidth Burst-Shaper & Fairness Implementation

Summary

This document describes a pragmatic implementation for per-tenant egress bandwidth shaping with burst allowances and fairness guarantees. The solution is intended for Redwood's multi-tenant GPU service endpoints and control-plane egress paths. It balances predictable billing/SLAs, short-term burstiness for customer UX, and efficient utilization of constrained egress capacity to reduce cross-tenant interference.

Goals

- Limit per-tenant sustained egress (Mbps) while permitting short bursts for onboarding/interactive workloads.
- Ensure fairness during contention windows (no single tenant can starve others).
- Provide Terraform modules and deployment recipes that work on AWS and GCP-hosted VPC egress gateways.
- Integrate with existing observability (Prometheus metrics + Grafana dashboards) and alerting.

Non-goals

- This doc does not attempt to replace cloud-provider traffic shaping primitives for tenant isolation at the VM hypervisor-level.
- Not a network-level DDoS defense plan; combine with DDoS protections and WAFs.

Terminology

- Tenant: Billing/identity boundary (customer account).
- Egress gateway: A NAT/egress-host responsible for routing tenant outbound flows to the internet or partner clouds.
- Shaper: Policing/queuing construct used to enforce bandwidth limits (e.g., Linux tc, cloud traffic shaping, or managed NAT gateway QoS).

Architecture overview

We operate a pool of egress gateways per-region. Each gateway services multiple tenant subnets via SNAT prefixes. The shaper is applied at the gateway host interface to enforce per-tenant limits. Key components:

- Tenant tagging: We rely on SNAT IP allocation per-tenant (or per-tenant ENI) to map flows back to tenant identity.
- Shaping plane: Linux tc qdiscs per-tenant veth/iptables mark pipeline (or cloud BPF-based filter where available).
- Controller: A Terraform-managed controller that pushes tenant quotas and burst profiles to gateways via a small control agent (grpc/HTTP).
- Telemetry: Per-tenant egress metrics exported to Prometheus (bytes/sec, drops, queue depth, burst tokens).

Design choices and rationale

- SNAT-by-tenant mapping is simpler than deep packet inspection and scales with cloud NAT design. It also aligns with billing and IPAM.
- Use Hierarchical Token Bucket (HTB) for guaranteed rates and CBQ/ fq_codel for fairness in bursts. HTB lets us set a rate and ceiling (burst).
- Keep shaper config small (<= 12 classes/gateway) to avoid control plane churn. For very high tenant counts, use per-tenant load-balancing across gateways and aggregate shaping per-tenant group.

Configuration matrix (recommended defaults)

| Parameter | Low-tier | Mid-tier | High-tier | Notes |
|-----------|---------:|---------:|---------:|-------|
| sustained_rate | 50 Mbps | 200 Mbps | 1 Gbps | Default sustained throughput per tenant class |
| burst_window | 10s | 20s | 60s | How long tenant can exceed sustained_rate up to ceiling |
| burst_ceiling | 200 Mbps | 800 Mbps | 2 Gbps | Peak allowed during burst window |
| monitoring_interval | 30s | 30s | 15s | Prometheus scrape target for egress metrics |
| enforcement_mode | shaping | shaping | shaping+policing | policing drops if exceeded beyond burst_window |

Terraform module: recommended pattern

Use a small module (egress-shaper) that manages: allocation of SNAT pools, IAM roles for gateways to fetch configs, and a configmap for the controller. Example usage (HCL-like illustration):

```
module "egress_shaper" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood/infra-modules.git//egress-shaper"
  region = "us-west-2"
  gateway_count = 3
  tenant_classes = {
    "free"  = { sustained_rate = "50mbit"  , burst_ceiling = "200mbit", burst_window="10s" }
    "pro"   = { sustained_rate = "200mbit" , burst_ceiling = "800mbit", burst_window="20s" }
```
