```
    "ent"   = { sustained_rate = "1gbit"   , burst_ceiling = "2gbit"  , burst_window="60s" }
  }
}
```

Notes: module produces: k/v store entries, gateway bootstrap userdata that includes the controller agent endpoint and a TLS client cert secret. The module does NOT deploy the controller; that is a separate service (see infra-services repo).

Linux tc example (gateway host)

Below is a tested pattern for a gateway that maps SNAT IPs to tc class IDs via iptables MARKs. The example is illustrative — production deployment should use the controller to push rules.

1) Create root HTB qdisc on eth0: 

sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1: htb default 999
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:1 htb rate 10gbit

2) Per-tenant class and filter (tenant SNAT IP = 198.51.100.42):

sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1:1 classid 1:100 htb rate 200mbit ceil 2gbit burst 1600k
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 parent 1:100 handle 1000: fq_codel
sudo iptables -t mangle -A POSTROUTING -s 10.0.42.0/24 -j MARK --set-mark 100
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 protocol ip parent 1:0 prio 1 handle 100 fw flowid 1:100

3) Token-bucket like behavior: CBQ token bucket is emulated with HTB + ceil; adjust burst and quantum for latency-sensitive workloads.

Cloud-specific notes

- AWS: Use per-tenant ENIs or Elastic IP pools for SNAT where possible. AWS-managed NAT gateways do not expose qdisc controls; forwarding through our own gateway (EC2 or ENI-based appliances) gives full control. Consider using host-based ENIs and SSM for agent orchestration.
- GCP: Use Cloud NAT or self-managed NAT instances. For very high throughput, deploy BPF-based eBPF shapers (Cilium) at the node-level.

Monitoring and observability

Export the following per-tenant metrics to Prometheus (gateway exporter):
- redwood_egress_tx_bytes_total{tenant_id, gateway}
- redwood_egress_tx_rate_mbps{tenant_id, gateway}
- redwood_egress_queue_depth_bytes{tenant_id, gateway}
- redwood_egress_drops_total{tenant_id, gateway, reason}
- redwood_egress_burst_tokens{tenant_id, gateway}
Example Grafana panels to create:
- Top 10 tenants by sustained 5m tx rate (rate(redwood_egress_tx_bytes_total[5m]))
- Tenant fairness heatmap (per-tenant deviation vs class mean)
- Gateway resource pressure (CPU, netdev qlen, socket usage)

Alerts (recommended)

- P1: Gateway queue depth > 75% for > 5m (critical) — action: scale gateways, engage networking oncall.
- P2: Tenant sustained_rate > 3x configured sustained for > 10m (billing + abuse) — action: contact CS + rate-limited throttling.
- P3: Drops rate > 5% of bytes for > 2m — action: investigate shaping misconfiguration.

Operational runbook (incident flow)

1) Detection: Alert fires for queue_depth > 75% on gateway G.
2) Triage: 
   a) Identify top 5 offending tenants: query Prometheus for top tenants by rate on G for last 10m.
   b) If a single tenant is responsible and exceeds denom thresholds, temporarily cap burst_ceiling via controller to sustained_rate for that tenant class.
   c) If multiple tenants are crowding, scale up gateway pool (see scaling section) or move noisy tenants to alternate gateways.
3) Remediation: 
   - To reduce immediate pressure: increase root HTB parent rate (if headroom on host NIC), or move tenants by updating SNAT pool allocation (Terraform plan -> apply).
   - To enforce strict limits: flip enforcement_mode to policing (drops) for offending tenant class. Coordinate with CS to notify customers.
4) Post-incident: 
   - Run a fairness report (script in infra-tools) for affected time window and attach to incident timeline.
   - Adjust default sustained_rate or burst parameters if pattern recurs.

Scaling and placement guidance

- Gateway sizing: provision NICs and instance types to support aggregated peak CEIL across tenants with 20% headroom. For example, a c6i.4xlarge with enhanced networking supports ~10 Gbps sustained; use multiple NICs for >10 Gbps.
- Tenant placement: use tenant locality to minimize cross-region egress; prefer assigning tenant's SNAT pool to gateways in the tenant's most-used region.
- Autoscaling: When CPU or netdev qlen > 70% for 2 consecutive 60s cycles, scale +1 gateway in the group (bounded by gateway_count max). Automate with controller and Terraform or cloud autoscaling groups.

Testing checklist (pre-deploy)

1) Unit tests for controller: config push, rollback, and idempotency.
2) Integration test: simulate 50 tenants with 10% noisy tenants; verify compliance with sustained and burst limits.
3) Chaos test: kill one gateway to ensure traffic reassigns and that fairness holds across remaining gateways.
4) Cost test: measure egress billing delta before/after shaping for a 72h window.

Appendix: useful commands and scripts

- psuedo-query: Top tenants by 5m rate
  curl -s "http://prometheus/api/v1/query?query=topk(10,rate(redwood_egress_tx_bytes_total[5m]))" | jq .

- Quick toggle to policing for class 1: (via controller API):
  curl -X POST https://controller.us-west-2.redwood.internal/v1/shaper/tenant/100/mode -d '{"mode":"policing"}' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

- Terraform apply sequence:
  1) terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars
  2) terraform apply -auto-approve -var-file=prod.tfvars

Owner and contacts

- Implementation owner: Maya Thompson (Networking & Infra) — maya@redwood.ai
- Oncall: infra-networking rotations (see /confluence/eng-infra/eng-sre/oncall-rotations)
- Support: infra-ops Slack channel #infra-egress

Related documents

- See GPU shared VPC egress patterns and IP management for SNAT allocation guidance.

Change log

- 2024-03-12: Initial draft and design review.
- 2024-07-09: Added Terraform module pattern and Prometheus metrics list.
- 2025-02-08: Finalized runbook steps and scaled default tier values after pilot in us-west-2.

title: dsid_e97eb6e02b934406bfff1db1c6146a46__cost-guardrails-client-rate-limit-and-grace-windows-integration-2026.txt
text:
Client-side Quota Guardrails: Rate Limiting, Grace Windows, and In-Product Nudges

Overview:

This guide explains a pragmatic pattern for integrating client-side quota guardrails with Redwood’s server-side quota and rate-limiting signals. The goal is to reduce customer-reported overage incidents, improve perceived reliability during short bursts, and give product teams an easy path to deploy polite default rate limits, local backoff, and in-product nudges (warnings) while preserving server-side SLA enforcement.

Intended audience:
- Customer-facing SDK and frontend engineers
- Solutions engineers performing integration handoffs
- Customer Success and FinOps partners who configure quotas

Scope and objectives:
- Provide a recommended client-side token-bucket configuration for typical web apps and mobile clients
- Describe soft quota (grace window) semantics vs. hard quota enforcement
- Define API headers and signals customers should consume to present accurate usage/nudge UIs
- Offer rollout, testing, and observability checklist for safe deployment

Why client-side guardrails?
- Early throttling reduces noisy retries and downstream cost spikes.
- Grace windows enable short bursts (e.g., 5–15s) without immediate hard rejections, improving UX for interactive product flows.
- Coordinated nudges reduce support tickets and unexpected billing disputes.

Architecture and signal flow (text diagram):
1) Client SDK maintains a local token-bucket governor.
2) Client sends request to Redwood ingress.
3) Redwood responds with quota headers and may apply soft-throttle or hard-429.
4) Client updates local governor (replenish / reduce) and shows in-product nudge if remaining budget is low.

Example headers (returned on every successful/failed request):
- X-Redwood-Quota-Remaining: integer (approximate remaining units for the tenant in the current window)
- X-Redwood-Quota-Window: integer (window length in seconds, e.g., 3600)
- X-Redwood-Quota-Reset-At: ISO8601 timestamp for when the window resets (optional)
- Retry-After: integer seconds (when 429 returned)
- X-Redwood-Soft-Throttle: true|false (present when server has started soft-throttling to avoid hard failover)

Recommended local governor (token-bucket) reference configuration:
- bucket_capacity: min(tenant_rate_limit * 1.5, 200) tokens
- refill_rate: tenant_rate_limit / 60 tokens per second (convert per-minute policy to per-second refill)
- max_burst_seconds: 15 (protects against 1–15s interactive bursts)

YAML example (client SDK config snippet):

client_quota:
  bucket_capacity: 120
  refill_rate_per_sec: 2
  max_burst_seconds: 15
  behaviour_on_empty: "soft-nudge" # options: soft-nudge | block | allow-with-backoff

Behavior definitions:
- soft-nudge: allow the request but surface an in-app warning and apply progressive local backoff for subsequent immediate requests (recommended default for UI-heavy flows).
- block: immediately prevent request and return local error to the UI. Use for critical cost protection on low-trust clients.
- allow-with-backoff: allow request but increase refill delay to prevent repeated bursts.

Grace window vs. hard enforcement:
- Grace window: a short period during which the server returns 200/soft-throttle but sets X-Redwood-Soft-Throttle=true. Clients should downgrade non-essential requests (e.g., analytics, background embeddings) and show a subtle UI hint if end-user action triggers repeated consumption.
- Hard enforcement: server returns 429 with Retry-After header. Client MUST respect Retry-After and stop retrying until the window expires.

Nudge examples and recommended microcopy:
- Soft nudge (UI toast): "You're sending a lot of requests right now. Some features may slow down—try again in a few seconds."
- Billing/Quota banner (when remaining < 10%): "Your team is nearing its hourly quota. Contact [billing link] to increase capacity."
- Retry modal (after 429): "We’re temporarily limiting requests. Try again at {time}."

Customer-facing telemetry and SLOs (what to track):
- Client-side: local_throttle_count, local_block_count, nudge_shown_count
- Server-side: 429_rate_by_tenant, soft_throttle_rate, quota_warning_count, overage_events
- Business SLOs:
  - Support tickets for unexpected overages: < 1 per 100 customers / month
  - False-positive hard blocks (customer experiencing 429 but expecting allowed) < 0.5% of tenant requests

Rollout plan (recommended):
1) Internal canary: ship the client governor to internal test accounts and Redwood-provided demo tenants. Monitor local_throttle_count and 429_rate.
2) Partner pilot: enable for 3–5 opt-in enterprise customers. Collect UX feedback and billing deltas.
3) Gradual ramp: enable default soft-nudge behavior for 25% of new signups, then 100% after 4 weeks of telemetry review.

Testing checklist (pre-deploy):
- [ ] Simulate short bursts (1–10s) at 2x and 5x tenant rate and verify soft-nudge behavior
- [ ] Simulate sustained high traffic for >60s and verify server 429 and client obeys Retry-After
- [ ] Validate header propagation (X-Redwood-Quota-Remaining, Retry-After) across CDN and gateway caches
- [ ] Validate mobile offline/queued requests do not bypass server quotas when network resumes

Runbook: Handling a large number of customer overage disputes
1) Detect: alert when tenant overage events spike >5x baseline or >0.5% of requests return 429 in a 10m window. Owner: Customer Success (tiered alert to SE/Escalation).
2) Initial triage: check ingress logs for header signals and client governor telemetry. If X-Redwood-Soft-Throttle was present during burst, mark as "soft-throttle UX degradation".
3) Mitigation steps:
  a) For soft-throttle cases: share nudge timeline and adjustment options (increase local bucket, raise tenant rate limit temporarily, enable burst allowance).
  b) For hard 429 errors: validate expected quota and check for config drift (tenant plan vs applied quota). If quota misconfiguration: apply emergency fix and refund/credit if customer affected.
4) Post-incident: author a short incident note, update customer with timeline and remediation, and add a follow-up item to FinOps for any necessary credits.

Compatibility notes:
- Dedicated and Private deployments: these headers and soft-throttle semantics are supported but tenant rate limits may be enforced by customer-managed policy. Coordinate with private deployment teams to ensure header passthrough.
- SDK variations: server signals are identical across SDKs; only local governor implementation differs per platform (JS, iOS, Android, backend).

Operational knobs and admin controls (product-facing):
- Tenant rate window (per-minute vs per-hour)
- Soft throttle threshold (percent of window consumption to start soft throttle; default: 85%)
- Grace window length (default: 15 seconds)
- Emergency override: temporary increase of tenant limit (owner: FinOps or Customer Success)

Metrics / telemetry export (recommended tags):
- tenant_id, region, client_sdk, flow (interactive|batch|background), plan_tier

Example SDK pseudocode (JS):

class LocalGovernor {
  constructor(cfg) {
    this.capacity = cfg.bucket_capacity
    this.tokens = this.capacity
    this.refillRate = cfg.refill_rate_per_sec
    this.behaviourOnEmpty = cfg.behaviour_on_empty
  }
  attemptRequest(cost=1) {
    this.refillTokens()
    if (this.tokens >= cost) {
      this.tokens -= cost
      return {allowed: true}
    } else {
      if (this.behaviourOnEmpty === 'soft-nudge') {
        // allow but signal UI and start backoff
        this.startBackoff()
        return {allowed: true, softNudge: true}
      } else if (this.behaviourOnEmpty === 'block') {
        return {allowed: false}
      }
    }
  }
}

Ownership and contacts:
- Primary owner: Customer Success (Ayesha K. Patel)
- Engineering contact: Mateo Ruiz (SDKs)
- FinOps contact: Hannah J. Lee

References and related reading:

- Subject: "Incident: Temporary request limits observed for {tenant} on {date}"
- Body: bullet timeline, cause (soft-throttle vs hard limit), mitigation, actions taken, expected next steps

title: dsid_5451e168fa87451a82393f6f8d085b31__corporate-controls-and-workflows-2028.txt
text:
Corporate Controls and Workflows — Policies Reference

Overview

Purpose: This handbook centralizes company-wide operational controls and step-by-step workflows for access & permissions, change management, data handling, procurement & expenses, vendor management, travel, and the canonical internal templates. Its goal is to reduce ambiguity, accelerate approvals, and ensure consistent compliance with our internal risk posture and partner requirements.

Audience: All Redwood employees, contractors, and teams owning operational changes or supplier relationships.

Scope: Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment controls, all production and non-production environments, and all vendors engaged on Redwood contracts.

Owners and escalation contacts (quick reference)
| Area | Primary Owner | Secondary Owner | Escalation | SLA for Triage |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| Access & Permissions | Security (rbac@redwood.ai) | IT Ops | Head of Security | 24 hours |
| Change Management | Eng Platform | Eng SRE | CTO | 48 hours |
| Data Management | Privacy & Legal | Eng Platform | Chief Legal Officer | 72 hours |
| Procurement & Expenses | Finance | Procurement Manager | CFO | 48 hours |
| Vendor Management | Finance-Legal | Security | Head of Partnerships | 5 business days |
| Travel & Expenses | People Ops | Finance | Head of People Ops | 3 business days |

1) Access & Permissions
Principles
- Least privilege by default.
- Role-based assignments with time-limited elevated access.
- All privileged grants require a business justification and an owner.
- Access review cadence: quarterly for production environments; semi-annually for non-production.

RBAC tiers (standardized roles)
- viewer: Read-only to logs, dashboards, and metrics.
- developer: Code and non-prod infra access; no production secrets.
- operator: Production deploy/run privileges without secret-management write.
- admin: Full control; requires 2-person approval and annual attestation.

Request and approval flow (step-by-step)
1. Submit an Access Request using the "Access Request" template (see Templates section). Include scope (systems, duration), justification, and approver (service owner).
2. Automated checks: system enforces MFA, corporate device, and current employment status.
3. Approver reviews within 48 hours.
4. If approved, Access is provisioned with a maximum duration of 30 days for elevated roles; auto-expire.
5. Requester or approver must document business rationale in the request record.

Emergency access
- For urgent operational needs, request a Break Glass session via the on-call runbook channel. A second approver must confirm the session within 8 hours. All Break Glass sessions are logged and subject to post-event review.

Periodic access audit
- Owners must attest to role membership quarterly. Audit artifacts retained for 2 years.

2) Change Management
Change classes
- Minor (low-risk): config tweaks, non-production deploys, documentation updates. No RFC required; notify owner and schedule.
- Standard (medium-risk): production config changes, model toggles, infra scaling. Requires RFC and scheduled maintenance window.
- Major (high-risk): architecture changes, schema migrations, database sharding, or anything requiring rollback coordination. Requires formal RFC, runbook, canary strategy, and SRE sign-off.

RFC template (must include)
- Title, author, date
- Change class and business justification
- Impact matrix (services, customers, data scope)
- Rollout plan (canary %, observability signals, metrics to monitor)
- Backout/rollback criteria and steps
- Validation plan and post-deploy verification checklist
- Owner and approvers

Approval cadence and SLAs
- Standard changes: approvals requested at least 48 hours in advance; approver response SLA 48 hours.
- Major changes: RFC posted and reviewed in the weekly architecture forum; approvals documented before change window.

Deployment windows and blackout periods
- Regular maintenance windows: Saturdays 02:00–06:00 UTC for non-critical infra tasks.
- Blackout: Major product launches or peak traffic periods (documented per release). No non-emergency changes during blackout.

Emergency change process
1. Triage by on-call SRE and owner.
2. Notify stakeholders via the incident channel.
3. Implement hotfix with at least one peer review and record the change per post-mortem.

3) Data Management
Classification and handling
- PUBLIC: Safe to publish.
- INTERNAL: Company information that should not be public.
- CONFIDENTIAL: Customer PII, credentials, financials. Access limited.
- SENSITIVE: Regulated data (HIPAA, GDPR PII where applicable). Additional contractual controls required.

Retention schedule (canonical)
- Application logs (non-PII): 90 days (default).
- Audit logs / access logs: 1 year (security-critical).
- Backups: 90 days snapshot, longer per retention policy for legal holds.
- Customer data: retention per customer contract; default 2 years unless specified.

Encryption and key management
- All CONFIDENTIAL and SENSITIVE data must be encrypted at rest and in transit.
- Keys must be stored in a company-managed KMS; BYOK exceptions require Legal approval.

Data deletion and subject requests
- Data deletion requests initiated via Privacy intake form. Owner: Privacy & Legal. Service owners must honor deletion within 30 days or document exception and notify Privacy.

Data access for third parties
- Only allowed after a Data Processing Agreement and Security Questionnaire are validated. Technical controls (tokenized/limited views) preferred over bulk exports.

4) Procurement & Expenses
Approval thresholds and process
- <= $5,000: Manager-level approval and corporate card use.
- $5,001–$50,000: Department head + Procurement notification; must use standard PO template.
- > $50,000: Formal Procurement RFx and Legal review; Procurement lead coordinates vendor evaluation.

Vendor selection rubric (scorecard highlights)
- Security posture (SOC2 / ISO27001): 35%
- Product fit and roadmap: 25%
- Total cost of ownership: 15%
- Reference customers and support: 15%
- Diversity and supplier risk: 10%

Contracting and payment
- Legal must review all vendor agreements prior to signature.
- Finance issues POs for contract amounts > $5k unless recurring SaaS (then follow SaaS procurement flow).
- Payment terms target: Net 30 for standard vendors; exceptions documented in the contract.

Expense policy highlights
- Receipts required for any single expense > $25.
- Per diems: domestic $75/day, international country-by-country (see Travel Appendix).
- Card misuse escalations: repeated violations may result in revocation of corporate card privileges.

5) Vendor Management
Onboarding checklist (must be completed before production work)
1. Complete Vendor Intake form and submit to Procurement.
2. Security Questionnaire AND evidence (SOC2 report or equivalent).
3. Legal reviews and signs contract template (include data handling clauses as needed).
4. Finance sets up vendor record and payment terms.
5. Technical onboarding: least-privilege credentials, IP allowlist, and expirations.
6. Kickoff meeting with success plan and QBR cadence.

Ongoing oversight
- Annual risk review for vendors with access to CONFIDENTIAL or SENSITIVE data.
- Quarterly QBRs for strategic vendors, including performance KPIs and incident review.
- Termination checklist: revoke credentials, collect data, confirm certificate of destruction when relevant.

6) Travel & Expenses
Pre-approval and booking
- All international travel requires pre-approval from People Ops and manager.
- Preferred booking channels: company travel portal. Use corporate rates where available.

Safety and compliance
- Employees traveling to high-risk countries must complete a travel risk assessment and receive security clearance before booking.
- Travel insurance and emergency contacts are provided through People Ops.

Expense submission rules
- Submit expenses within 15 days of return. Late submissions may be denied unless exception granted.
- Mandatory receipts for airfare, lodging, and meals above per-diem.

Per diem and allowable items
- Meals: up to domestic per diem. Alcohol allowed only when hosted by vendor and must be itemized.
- Ground transportation: ride-share and taxis acceptable; car rental requires justification for >4 passengers or lack of alternatives.

7) Templates and canonical artifacts
- Access Request Template: templates/access-request-2027.md
- RFC Template (Change Management): templates/change-rfc-2027.md
- Vendor Intake Form: templates/vendor-intake-2027.pdf
- Procurement PO Template: templates/po-template-2027.xlsx
- Expense Report Template: templates/expense-report-2027.csv

Example RFC snippet (minimal valid front matter)
```
Title: "Schema migration for user_profiles"
Author: "Samir Patel"
Date: "2028-01-08"
Class: "Major"
Impact: ["auth-service", "billing-service"]
Rollout: "Canary 5% -> 25% -> 100% over 72 hours"
RollbackCriteria: "Error rate > 1% sustained for 5 minutes or >20% increase in tail latency"
```

8) Governance, metrics, and reporting
- Monthly operations review: owners report on outstanding access exceptions, RFC backlog, vendor renewals, and procurement spend vs. forecast.
- KPIs to track: average access request approval time, RFC cycle time, number of vendor incidents, expense report turnaround time.

Change log (recent updates)
- 2027-11-02: Initial baseline document (created).
- 2028-01-15: Added detailed vendor onboarding checklist and scoring rubric.
- 2028-02-14: Updated access approval SLA and added emergency Break Glass procedure.

How to use this page
- Use the templates link above to raise requests and RFCs. For area-specific nuances (e.g., RBAC for Dedicated clusters, private deployment KMS requirements) follow the linked pages in Related Pages.

Questions or exceptions
- Submit exceptions to governance@redwood.ai with business justification; exceptions are time-boxed and require a sponsor and compensating controls.

Acknowledgements
- Contributors: Diego Morales (Eng Platform), Priya Nair (Security), Samir Patel (Finance), Maya Lopez (People Ops).

Appendix: Contact matrix
- Procurement: procurement@redwood.ai
- Finance: finance@redwood.ai
- Security: rbac@redwood.ai
- Privacy & Legal: privacy@redwood.ai
- People Ops: people-ops@redwood.ai

title: dsid_f5ae3d0451734792aeb8a9fd385048ea__operational-handshake-and-validator-catalog-2026.txt
text:
operational-handshake-and-validator-catalog-2026

Overview

This runbook defines the operational handshake and validator catalog used during private (VPC / on‑prem) deployments. It is intended for Operator/Field teams, Solutions Engineering, and SREs who perform acceptance, day‑2 validation, and controlled cutovers to production traffic. The goal is to provide a single, repeatable validation checklist that: (1) verifies networking, security and runtime invariants; (2) exercises the runtime and model swap paths with canary traffic; and (3) provides clear rollback triggers and remediation guidance.

Scope

- Applies to Redwood Private deployments: VPC-hosted control plane with customer-managed data plane, and air‑gapped on‑prem appliances.
- Covers pre-install validation, post-install smoke tests, canary traffic plan, performance regression checks, and rollback criteria.
- Does NOT replace security compliance evidence artifacts (see customer-requirements library) but references the minimum evidence required for acceptance.

Owner & Roles

- Owner: Deployment Engineering (eng-private-deployments)
- Primary runbook operator: Field Operator / Site Reliability Engineer
- Secondary: Solutions Engineer (customer side) for on-site coordination
- Escalation: Oncall SRE -> Runtime Lead -> Head of Private Deploys (see Escalation section)

Preflight / Prerequisites

Before running validators, confirm: 

- Customer network ACLs and BGP/VPC routes are applied per the commissioned design.
- KMS/HSM endpoints reachable from operator VLANs and test service account has encrypt/decrypt privileges.
- Minimum hardware + firmware baseline validated against the compatibility matrix (GPU driver, CUDA/ROCm version, BIOS/firmware).
- Time sync (NTP/PTP) drift < 500ms across control and data nodes.
- Inventory snapshot (serials, NIC MACs, disk UUIDs) uploaded to ticketing system for forensic traceability.

Validator Catalog (operator-friendly table)

| Check | Command / Tool | Expected Result | Remediation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Network path to control-plane API | curl -k https://{{control_plane_ip}}/healthz | 200 + JSON {"status":"ok"} | Validate route tables, firewall policy, and proxy ACLs; run traceroute and tcpdump |
| KMS envelope encrypt/decrypt | redwood-kms-tool verify --endpoint {{kms}} --key-id kv-1 | encrypt/decrypt roundtrip < 500ms and success code | Check KMS IAM, VPC endpoints, DNS, and customer firewall; fallback: use ledger-encrypted keystore for acceptance |
| GPU driver / CUDA compatibility | dpkg -l | nvidia-driver >= 525 and CUDA 12.x OR rocm >= 6.x | Reinstall certified driver image; isolate node from pool and re-run burnin |
| Image signature verification | cosign verify --key public.pem image.tar.gz | signature valid, provenance matches release tag | Re-download signed image, verify root of trust; if persistent, escalate to supply-chain security |
| Model artifact checksum / provenance | sha256sum model.tar.gz && cat provenance.json | checksums match release manifest; provenance contains signed build id | Failure -> quarantine artifact and fetch canonical artifact from model registry |
| KV cache warmup smoke | curl -X POST {{runtime}}/v1/cache/warm -d '{"prompt":"hello"}' | cache hit rate increase of >10% in 5m window | If miss-rate persists, verify model-to-cache mapping and network between workers |
| Cold start latency test | pb-runner --seq 2048 --qps 1 | p50 < 150ms, p95 < 400ms (baseline) | If regressions, collect runtime profile and compare to baseline; may require rollback of runtime build |
| TLS certificate chain validation | openssl s_client -connect {{endpoint}}:443 -servername host | full chain validated, no SHA1 intermediates | Replace cert, validate intermediates; check OCSP/CRL reachability |
| Audit log forwarding | tail -n 100 /var/log/redwood/audit.log | recent entries for install actions, no permission failures | Fix agent config and restart collector; ensure log retention policy met |

Acceptance Criteria (binary pass/fail per section)

- Critical validators (network, KMS, image signature) must pass 100%.
- Performance validators (latency/throughput) must be within defined guardrails relative to the customer profile:
  - Latency guardrails: p50 <= 120ms, p95 <= 350ms under canary load (see Performance Baseline).
  - Throughput: sustained QPS within 10% of committed throughput for dedicated pools under synthetic profile.
- Canaries: at least 30 minutes of canary traffic with < 0.5% error rate and no steady increase in 99th percentile latency.
- Security: KMS envelope rotation validated end-to-end and audit events present.

Performance Baseline (example values, tune per-customer)

- Canary profile: 10 concurrent sessions; 1.5 RPS per session; sequence length distribution 512/2048/4096 token buckets.
- Expected results for medium model (16GB KV per replica):
  - Steady-state throughput: 45 req/s per replica
  - Token generation latency: p50 90ms, p95 260ms (generator only)

Runbook: Field Validation Procedure (numbered)

1. Preflight: Review installation ticket and confirm prerequisites checklist (network, KMS reachable, inventory uploaded).
2. Smoke install: Deploy runtime image to a single validation node in the tenant pool. Run image-signature + driver + cert validators.
3. Control-plane handshake: Execute control-plane API health, and create a temporary test-tenant with restricted quota.
4. Artifact validation: Pull the model artifact and verify checksum/provenance.
5. Warmup: Trigger KV-cache warmup and confirm cache hit-rate and memory usage remain within expected bounds.
6. Canary start: Route 1% of production traffic (or synthetic canary profile defined above) to the validation tenant. Monitor for 30m.
7. Performance sweep: Run the cold-start latency and throughput synthetic tests; collect perf profiles and compare to golden baselines.
8. Security checks: Validate KMS key usage logs, certificate chain verification, and audit log forwarding.
9. Acceptance decision: If all critical validators and canary performance pass, schedule incremental traffic ramp per the traffic migration matrix.
10. Post-cutover: After reaching 100% traffic, run a second sweep of performance validators for 2 hours to detect latent regressions.

Rollback Triggers (automated + operator-observed)

- Error rate > 2% sustained for 10 minutes on production routes originating from the new deployment.
- 99th percentile latency regression > 30% compared to baseline for > 5 minutes.
- KV-cache corruption or state divergence detected (inconsistent model responses across replicas).
- Failures in KMS envelope operations or certificate chain validity errors.

Rollback Procedure (fast, auditable)

1. Initiate Safemode: operator sets tenant to safemode which pauses new model swaps: `redwood-ctl tenant update --id {{tenant}} --safemode=true`.
2. Traffic re-route: shift traffic back to previous revision via control-plane: `redwood-ctl traffic-shift --from={{new}} --to={{prev}} --weight=100` (automated orchestration preferred).
3. Verify: confirm error rate returns to baseline and latency stabilizes within 10 minutes. Collect diagnostic bundles `redwood-ctl collect-diagnostics --tenant {{tenant}} --since "-15m"`.
4. Snapshot & Quarantine: snapshot runtime state and quarantine artifact versions for forensic analysis.
5. Postmortem initiate: create incident with labels `private-deploy-regression` and assign to runtime lead.

Remediation Playbook Examples

- Networking regression: If packet loss or MTU mismatch is detected, isolate node, confirm jumbo frame settings and BGP adjacencies, then reintroduce to pool after validation.
- KMS intermittent: fallback to cached symmetric wrap with strict TTL; escalate to cryptography team if KMS SLA cannot be met for 30 minutes.
- Performance regression tied to driver mismatch: pause scheduling on heterogeneous GPU node type and trigger immutable rollback to previous image.

Telemetry & Alerts (minimum metrics to emit)

- metrics.runtime.request_count (per model, per route)
- metrics.runtime.error_count (per error class) – Alert: error_rate > 1% sustained 5m (warning), > 2% 10m (critical)
- metrics.runtime.latency_ms (p50/p90/p95/p99) – Alert: p99 > baseline * 1.3 (critical)
- metrics.kvcache.hit_rate – Alert: hit_rate drop > 20% relative to baseline during warmup window
- audit.kms.operation – Alert: KMS failures > 5 in 10m

Evidence & Reporting (for Customer Acceptance)

- Upload the following artifacts to the deployment ticket before handoff:
  - inventory.csv (hardware identifiers)
  - topology.json (VPC/BGP routes snapshot)
  - diagnostic bundle tarball from the validation node
  - signed model provenance and checksums
  - canary perf report (pdf) with latency histograms and QPS timeline

CLI & Example Commands

- Health check: `curl -sS https://{{control_plane_ip}}/healthz | jq`
- Canaries: `redwood-ctl canary start --tenant {{tenant}} --profile canary-small --duration 30m`
- Collect diagnostics: `redwood-ctl collect-diagnostics --tenant {{tenant}} --out /tmp/diag.tar.gz`

Change Log

- 2026-02-15: Created initial runbook (A. Patel)
- 2026-06-02: Added KV-cache warmup rules and canary profile updates (M. Chen)
- 2026-09-10: Tightened latency guardrails and added KMS envelope remediation (L. Rodriguez)

Related Pages & References

- Customer acceptance & smoke validation checklist (see related pages)
- Private deploy operational hardening and safe migration playbook
- Model artifact provenance and signing policy

Appendix: Quick Templates

- Minimal acceptance email snippet: "Acceptance: All critical validators passed; canary run 30m; performance within guardrails. Proceeding to staged ramp as per migration matrix. Signed: <operator>"
- Evidence bundle structure (zip): `inventory.csv`, `topology.json`, `canary_report.pdf`, `diag.tar.gz`, `provenance.json`

For questions or deviations from this runbook, open a deviation request and tag the runtime lead for approval.

title: dsid_5484981aee9b49c29167dc0b88c79dbb__slo-consumption-patterns-and-tenant-provisioning-playbook-2026.txt
text:
SLO Consumption Patterns and Tenant Provisioning Playbook

Overview

Purpose:
This playbook defines how Redwood SREs detect, classify, and act on SLO error-budget consumption patterns across multi-tenant inference services. It codifies preemptive tenant provisioning and throttling decisions to preserve service-level quality while minimizing customer impact and cost.

Scope:
- Applies to core inference endpoints (text-generation, chat, embeddings) and the routing/proxy layer (service names: rwd-proxy, rwd-batcher, rwd-router).
- Intended for on-call SREs, capacity planners, and platform owners.
- Does NOT replace product-level billing or contractual entitlements; see Finance and Customer Success for overrides.

Key definitions:
- SLO: objective for request success/latency/availability for a given route and tenant. Example: /v1/generate P50 latency < 80ms, availability 99.9%.
- Error budget: allowed SLO loss over a rolling window (typically 28 days).
- Consumption pattern: time-series shape of error-budget depletion (steady, bursty, creeping, episodic).
- Preemptive provisioning: adding capacity, warming model variants, or routing traffic to protect SLOs before hitting critical thresholds.

High-level detection and classification

Telemetry signals (priority order):
1) Error budget burn-rate (per-tenant, per-route) computed in telemetry pipeline (metric: slo:error_budget_burn_rate{tenant,route}).
2) Latency percentile shifts (p50,p95,p99) with sudden slope > threshold (metric: http_request_duration_seconds_bucket).
3) Queue/backlog growth on batcher nodes (metric: rwd_batcher_queue_size).
4) Pod/container CPU & GPU saturation (node exporter + nvidia-smi derived metrics).
5) Request/retry amplification (rate of 5xx responses and retries).

Pattern taxonomy and associated risks

1) Bursty consumption
- Characteristics: short, high-amplitude spikes in tokens or RPS (minutes).
- Risks: transient tail-latency breaches, autoscaler lag, throttling blast.
- Typical cause: customer load test, new feature rollout, upstream client bug.

2) Sustained surge
- Characteristics: elevated consumption over hours/days with consistent burn.
- Risks: prolonged SLO degradation leading to sustained availability loss and downstream throttles.
- Typical cause: marketing campaign, change in model configuration (higher temperature or longer max_tokens).

3) Creeping degradation (slow burn)
- Characteristics: gradual increase in latency and error budget depletion over weeks.
- Risks: unnoticed SLO erosion, hard to correlate to single event.
- Typical cause: model drift, unobserved config changes, billing/usage policy changes.

4) Episodic/recurring pattern
- Characteristics: predictable regular spikes (daily/weekly).
- Risks: repeated breach windows if unmitigated.
- Typical cause: scheduled batch jobs, geo/timezone-driven customer behavior.

Detection thresholds (example values)
- Burn-rate alert (warning): slo:error_budget_burn_rate > 0.2 for 30m
- Burn-rate alert (critical): slo:error_budget_burn_rate > 0.8 for 15m
- Latency slope: p95 increase > 2x baseline in 10m
- Queue growth: rwd_batcher_queue_size growth rate > 50% in 5m

Preemptive actions matrix

This matrix maps pattern -> automated/preemptive operator actions. Use the matrix to choose the lowest-impact effective action.

ASCII table (Provisioning Matrix):

Pattern | Immediate automated action | Short-term operator action (15-60m) | Medium-term action (1-24h)
---|---|---|---
Bursty | Temporary per-tenant throttling (shape to 80% of baseline) + burst-absorber routing | Warm additional batcher workers in same region; increase dispatch parallelism | Review client pattern; propose rate-limit quota change or guidance
Sustained surge | Route new requests to pre-warmed variant with quantized weights (model: gptx-quant-fast) | Trigger reserved-capacity allocation from capacity pool; enable burst credits | Open capacity ticket with GPU-fleet and negotiate commit/short-term reserve
Creeping | Emit escalation signal to capacity team and owner; flag tenant for manual review | Progressive scaling based on predicted 72h demand; adjust batching window | Evaluate model quantization or batching policy; engage Product on usage change and pricing signal
Episodic | Schedule autoscaler warm windows aligned to expected spikes | Coordinate with tenant (CS) for scheduled increases; apply per-window quota | Consider SLO tiering and time-windowed SLAs for that tenant

Concrete runbook: step-by-step for on-call

If you see slo:error_budget_burn_rate{tenant="$TENANT"} > 0.8 for 15m or matching high-severity alerts:
1) Triage in PagerDuty: acknowledge and assign (owner role: on-call SRE).
2) Query telemetry: Grafana dashboard "SLO Consumption - Tenant View" and run these queries:
   - slo:error_budget_remaining{tenant="$TENANT"}
   - http_request_duration_seconds{route="/v1/generate",tenant="$TENANT"}
   - rwd_batcher_queue_size{node=~"batcher.*"}
3) Classify pattern (use taxonomy above).
4) Perform lowest-impact automated mitigation first (runbook CLI):
   - rwdctl tenant throttle --tenant $TENANT --route /v1/generate --rate 0.8x --duration 20m
   - rwdctl routing divert --from-zone us-west-2 --to-zone us-east-1 --selectors tenant=$TENANT --duration 30m
5) If automated mitigation insufficient after 10 minutes, escalate to Capacity Pager (channel #sre-capacity) and open Capacity Incident in JIRA with tags [slo-burn, tenant:$TENANT].
6) Coordinate with Customer Success for tenant notification if any customer-visible throttling or degradation is planned.
7) Post-resolution: run Incident Review (see section below) and update tenant provisioning scorecard.

Prometheus alert rule examples (paste into alerts repo):

- alert: TenantErrorBudgetCritical
  expr: slo_error_budget_burn_rate{tenant!~"internal.*"} > 0.8
  for: 15m
  labels:
    severity: critical
    team: eng-sre
  annotations:
    summary: "High error budget burn for tenant {{ $labels.tenant }}"

- alert: BatcherQueueGrowth
  expr: increase(rwd_batcher_queue_size[5m]) / avg_over_time(rwd_batcher_queue_size[30m]) > 0.5
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: warning
    team: eng-sre
  annotations:
    summary: "Rapid batcher queue growth detected"

Ownership and decision authorities
- On-call SRE: initial triage, automated mitigations, 60-minute owner for action.
- Capacity Team: medium-term provisioning, reserved capacity commits.
- Platform Owner (rwd-router/rwd-batcher): approves routing/divert changes.
- Customer Success: customer communication and SLA exceptions.

Provisioning scorecard (use to decide when to convert preemptive actions into committed capacity)
- Key inputs: 28d burn rate trend, 7d sustained surplus RPS, predicted 72h demand, customer tier (Free/Standard/Premier), revenue impact estimate.
- Score thresholds:
  - < 30 points: use transient mitigations only
  - 30-70 points: consider short-term reserved capacity (1-7 days)
  - > 70 points: open reserved capacity/contract discussion with Sales

Runbook for planned pre-warm/provisioning (change process)
1) Owner opens a Capacity Plan PR in infra repo with: expected delta, duration, nodes required, cost estimate, rollback plan.
2) Run deployment in canary region for 30m and validate metrics (latency, burn-rate).
3) Notify #sre-capacity and #platform-runway 10m before scale-up.
4) After scale: monitor for 1h, then mark plan as effective. If instability: rollback immediately following rollback plan.

Post-incident review and KB updates
- Every time a preemptive action (throttle/provisioning) is executed, on-call must create a short Incident Log entry with: tenant, pattern classification, mitigation used, duration, and outcome.
- If mitigation used more than 3 times in 30 days for a tenant, schedule a stakeholder review with Product and CS.
- Update the tenant provisioning scorecard and archive runbook decisions in "SLO Consumption Decisions" Confluence child page.

Operational tooling and automation suggestions
- Implement a burn-rate predictor (baseline: simple exponential smoothing) that produces a 72h forecast and a provisioning recommendation.
- Provide a one-click mitigation button in Grafana dashboards that runs validated rwdctl commands (confirmation modal required).
- Maintain a staging pool of pre-warmed model variants (gptx-small-quant, gptx-medium-quant) to reduce cold-start impact.

Related runbooks and references
- Capacity governance: eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-capacity-governance-and-error-budget-handbook-2025
- Tenant gating: eng-sre/runbooks/tenant-impact-scorer-and-priority-gating-runbook-2026
- SLO triage patterns: eng-sre/incident-review/model-serving-regression-incident-review-standards-2026

Appendix: quick CLI snippets
- Throttle tenant for 20m:
  rwdctl tenant throttle --tenant acme-corp --route /v1/generate --rate 0.8 --duration 20m
- Warm model variant:
  rwdctl model warm --model gptx-quant-fast --replicas 4 --region us-west-2

Notes and revision history:
- 2026-01-15: initial draft (Ava Turner).
- 2026-02-20: added provisioning scorecard and Prometheus rules (reviewers: Ravi Patel, Lina Gómez).

Contact:
- Primary: eng-sre on-call rotation (pager duty)
