title: dsid_fd10c64adc944e5084bbaaf3e04ad858__access-ops-playbook-remote-first-and-contracts-2028.txt
text:
Access & Ops Playbook for Remote-First, Procurement, and Contract Approvals

Overview

Purpose
This playbook defines evergreen practices and step-by-step procedures covering five cross-cutting areas used by all Redwood teams: access & permissions lifecycle, approved change management pathways, data stewardship minimums, procurement & expense approvals, and vendor/travel intake templates. The goal is to reduce friction for remote-first teams while preserving least-privilege, auditability, and financial controls.

Scope
Applies to: all Redwoood employees, contractors, and vendors who request system access, submit procurement/expense requests, or manage changes impacting production systems. Exceptions must be requested via the Risk & Exceptions process (see "Requesting an Exception" below).

Key principles
- Least privilege: grant minimal access required for a task and enforce time-bounded entitlements.
- Separation of duties: approvals are split across requestor, technical owner, and finance/legal as appropriate.
- Remote-first friendliness: friction-reduced templates, automated approvals for low-risk requests, and synchronous approval SLAs for high-risk items.
- Auditability: every access and procurement action must link to a ticket (Jira ID) and include approval metadata for audits.

1) Roles and ownership
- Requestor: individual initiating access, change, or procurement. Responsible for describing business justification and SLA.
- Technical Owner: owner of the resource/service (e.g., runtime-team@redwood.com). Confirms technical validity and risk impact.
- Approver-Finance: finance-legal representative for spend > $5k.
- Approver-Security: security team member for high-scope access (data classified as PII or regulated).
- Access Steward: team responsible for periodic entitlement reviews (quarterly).

Contact matrix (examples)
- infra-prod: infra-oncall@redwood.com (Technical Owner)
- runtime-api: runtime-team@redwood.com
- procurement: procurement@redwood.com (Approver-Finance)
- security: security-ops@redwood.com (Approver-Security)

2) Access & permissions lifecycle
Minimum required fields for an access request (Jira template: ACCESS-REQ):
- Requestor name / email
- Justification & expiration date (required for contractors)
- Resource identifier (ARN, service name, dashboard link)
- Least-privilege role requested and list of actions
- Technical owner approval (required)
- Security sensitivity level: public | internal | restricted | regulated

Standard approval pathways
- Low-risk (read-only to internal services, spend < $1k): auto-approve within 8 hours if technical owner signs off via Slack/Confluence link.
- Medium-risk (write access to internal infra, non-production credentials): Technical Owner + Access Steward approval within 24 hours.
- High-risk (production write, PII access, KMS/HSM keys): Technical Owner + Security + Finance approval; must complete expansion checklist and security review; SLA 48 hours.

Entitlement management
- Time-bound access: default max duration 90 days for contractors and 365 days for employees; extensions require reapproval.
- Quarterly entitlement review: Access Stewards run reports (IAM tool: AegisIAM) and reconcile stale privileges.
- Emergency break-glass: requests via the oncall channel with post-facto Jira ticket and 24-hour incident debrief.

Example IAM policy snippet (provide in request as needed)
{\
  \"Version\": \"2023-10-01\",\
  \"Statement\": [\
    {\
      \"Effect\": \"Allow\",\
      \"Action\": [\
        \"s3:GetObject\"\
      ],\
      \"Resource\": [\"arn:aws:s3:::redwood-artifacts/*\"]\
    }\
  ]\
}

3) Change management (for infra, runtime, and customer-impacting changes)
Change classes and required artifacts
- Class A (Standard): routine config changes with a playbook, pre-approved rollback, no customer-facing impact. Requires Change Request ticket, automated CI test, and scheduled maintenance window.
- Class B (Significant): deployments that modify runtimes, stateful DB schema changes, or cross-cluster network changes. Requires Design Review (ADR link), runbook, canary plan, and request for change (RFC) with 48-hour review.
- Class C (High-risk / Emergency): production outages, security patches affecting secrets/KMS. Requires immediate oncall coordination, postmortem, and retrospective review.

Change request checklist (RFC template):
1. Summary and Jira ID
2. Owner and approver list
3. Risk classification and rollback plan
4. Pre-deploy validation steps and test commands
5. Canary rollout plan (traffic percentages and metrics)
6. Post-deploy validation metrics and SLO targets (latency, error rate)

SLOs and guardrails for deployed changes
- Production latency: no increase > 5% for 30m post-deploy relative to baseline.
- Error rate: no sustained > 2x spike in 15m window.
- If SLO breached, execute automatic rollback policy.

Automated gating examples (CI snippet)
- Run: make infra-plan && terraform apply -target=module.safe_changes --auto-approve
- Safety check: ./scripts/check-deploy-guardrails --canary 10 --observe 15m

4) Data management requirements
Classification levels
- Public: allowed to be shared externally.
- Internal: business data not intended for public release.
- Restricted: sensitive business or employee data; access limited to named roles.
- Regulated: PII/PHI/financial data subject to compliance controls (GDPR/PCI/ISO27001).

Minimum controls by classification
- Encryption at rest + in-transit: required for Restricted and Regulated.
- Audit logging: capture user ID, source IP, action, timestamp. Retain audit logs for 2 years for Regulated, 1 year for Restricted.
- Data residency: regulated datasets must be pinned to approved regions; list available in Data Residency matrix (appendix link).

Data handling checklist for projects
- Data minimization statement: why this dataset is necessary.
- Retention policy assigned & expiration date.
- Access matrix: list of users with access and justification.
- Masking/encryption strategy for non-production copies.

5) Procurement & expenses workflow
Spend thresholds and approval steps
- Under $200: manager-level approval via Expense form (automated).
- $200–$5,000: manager + finance designated approver.
- $5,000–$50,000: manager + procurement + finance.
- > $50,000: manager + procurement + finance + VP level sign-off and legal review for contract terms.

Procurement request fields (PRQ template):
- Business justification & Jira link
- Cost center and budget owner
- Preferred vendor, SOW/quote attachment, contract term length
- Security and data handling classification (is vendor processing regulated data?)
- Requested date and desired delivery/activation date

Vendor selection and negotiation guidance
- Standard vendors (SaaS infra, cloud providers) are pre-approved; use vendor-approved templates. Non-standard vendors require RFP and vendor risk assessment.
- For any vendor with access to Regulated data: require SOC 2 Type II report (or equivalent), encryption attestation, and a Data Processing Agreement (DPA).

Payment & billing
- Finance issues purchase orders (POs) for contractual spend > $5k.
- Contractors and small one-off purchases should use the corporate card with receipts uploaded to Expensify within 7 days.

6) Vendor management and contracts
Onboarding checklist for vendors with system access
- Completed vendor intake form + Jira ticket
- Security questionnaire (provided by security-ops) and evidence (SOC reports, pen test summaries)
- Contractual terms: NDAs, DPA, liability limits, termination clauses, and IP assignments as applicable
- Technical onboarding: least-privilege credentials, IP allowlists, and documented support contacts

Periodic review cadence
- Annual risk review for vendors handling Restricted/Regulated data.
- Quarterly performance review for strategic vendors (uptime SLAs, support metrics).

7) Corporate travel and remote work expense policy highlights
- Per diem and lodging caps defined by region (full matrix in appendix). Use company travel portal (TravelPortal) and preferred booking partners.
- Approval: manager pre-approval required for out-of-country travel; for trips > 5 days require People Ops sign-off.
- Expense submission timeline: receipts uploaded within 14 days of trip end. Card reconciliations within 30 days.
- Safety: employees traveling to Medium/High risk countries must register trip via TravelSafety and enroll in emergency assistance.

8) Templates and quick-start checklists (links and examples)
- ACCESS-REQ (Jira template id: ACCESS-REQ): minimal fields + IAM snippet inclusion.
- PRQ (Procurement Request): includes vendor risk section and budget owner approval.
- RFC-CHANGE: change request with canary rollout plan and rollback steps.
- VENDOR-ONBOARD: vendor intake form checklist.

Example procurement YAML (attach to PRQ):
---
vendor: \"Acme Observability\"
quote_amount: 18000
contract_term_months: 12
dpa_required: true
cost_center: \"ENG-PLATFORM\"
justification: |\
  Replace legacy tracing system with vendor-managed SaaS to reduce MTTR and support distributed tracing for Redwood services.
---

9) Requesting an exception
- Exceptions go through the Risk & Exceptions board: file EXC-{team}-{YYYY}{NN} with rationale, compensating controls, and timebox. Exceptions are time-boxed (max 90 days) and require sponsor from the owner_team.

10) Enforcement, monitoring, and continuous improvement
- Monthly dashboards: top 10 stale entitlements, open procurement requests older than SLA, vendors with expiring evidence.
- Quarterly tabletop exercises covering break-glass and vendor incident response.
- Annual policy review owned by finance-legal; suggested updates accepted via PR on the policy repo and reviewed by the board.

Appendix (links and resources)
- Standard Jira templates: /confluence/templates/access-req | /confluence/templates/prq | /confluence/templates/rfc-change
- Data residency matrix: /confluence/security/data-residency-2027
- IAM tooling: AegisIAM runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/i-am-aegis-runbook
- Contact list: procurement@redwood.com, security-ops@redwood.com, infra-oncall@redwood.com

Revision history
- 2026-07-12: Initial draft authored by Maya Chen.
- 2027-03-02: Added remote-first accelerated approval paths and IAM automation guidance.
- 2028-02-14: Published: clarified approval thresholds and vendor evidence requirements (SOC 2/DPA).

End of document

title: dsid_fd4e3fe51764479eb9012d643b8949c0__console-shadow-experiments-ux-spec.txt
text:
Console UX Spec — Shadow Experiments (Shadow Traffic Quality Metrics)

## 1. Overview
Shadow Experiments let customers mirror a sampled subset of production requests to one or more “shadow” variants (candidate model/version/quantization/prompt/routing policy), score the shadow outputs asynchronously, and surface *quality deltas* alongside cost/latency/error metrics—without affecting the response returned to the end user.

This document specifies the **Console UX** for:
- Creating and managing Shadow Experiments
- Viewing results (quality deltas, confidence intervals, segments)
- Drilling into examples with safe data handling
- Attaching quality signals to Rollouts/Canaries

### 1.1 Goals
- Make it safe and obvious that shadowing does **not** change user responses and is **fail-open**.
- Help engineers answer: “Is the candidate variant materially worse/better on quality, and are we statistically confident?”
- Provide clear integration with Rollouts so quality signals can be reviewed during canaries and (later) used for automated rollback.

### 1.2 Non-goals (v1)
- Full offline replay across arbitrary historical windows.
- Customer-provided custom code execution inside Redwood.
- Deep prompt editing / prompt version management (shadow experiments can reference prompt template IDs/versions, but prompt authoring lives elsewhere).

### 1.3 Assumptions / dependencies
- Shadow routing policy exists and is enforceable at the route/rollout level (sampling %, shadow targets, timeouts, fail-open).
- Telemetry produces control+shadow paired events with bounded cardinality.
- Scoring pipeline produces a metric bundle keyed by (experiment_id, variant_id, time_bucket, segment).
- The “default metric bundle v1” is available (format adherence, refusal/safety, instruction-following rubric, basic heuristics). Additional bundles can be introduced via rubric versions.

---

## 2. Key concepts & terminology
- **Control**: The variant serving the user response.
- **Shadow target / Variant**: Candidate configuration receiving mirrored requests (does not serve user response).
- **Shadow Experiment**: A named configuration that defines sampling, targets, metrics bundle, and retention settings.
- **Run**: A time-bounded execution of an experiment (start/stop, config snapshot). In v1, we model “run” implicitly via an experiment’s active window + config revisions; UI will show “Runs” as ranges.
- **Metric bundle**: Versioned set of quality metrics and scoring rubrics.
- **Delta**: Shadow minus control for a metric (or ratio where relevant), with confidence interval.
- **Segment**: Filterable breakdown dimension (e.g., region, request_type, route, model family bucket). Segment options are limited by cardinality rules.

---

## 3. Information architecture (IA)
### 3.1 Navigation entry points
1) **Console → Observability → Quality → Shadow Experiments**
- Landing page lists experiments and recent regressions.

2) **Console → Routes → [Route] → Quality (tab)**
- “Start Shadow Experiment” CTA pre-fills the route and control variant.

3) **Console → Rollouts → [Rollout] → Quality signals (panel)**
- Inline panel showing attached experiment status and headline deltas.

### 3.2 Pages (v1)
- Shadow Experiments (list)
- Create Shadow Experiment (wizard)
- Shadow Experiment details
  - Overview (status, config snapshot)
  - Results (delta charts, segments)
  - Examples (sampled, redacted)
  - Activity/Audit (who changed what)

---

## 4. Permissions & access model
Shadow Experiments touch production request/response artifacts and therefore require explicit RBAC handling.

### 4.1 Roles (Console RBAC primitives)
We map to existing org/project permissions; naming below reflects UI labels (final mapping owned by Console backend/RBAC).

| Permission | Who typically has it | What it enables |
|---|---|---|
| View Experiments (metadata) | Project Viewer+ | List experiments, see metrics aggregates (no raw examples). |
| Create/Modify Experiments | Project Admin, Route Editor | Create, start/stop, edit sampling/targets within guardrails. |
| View Examples (redacted) | Project Admin by default; optionally enabled for specific groups | See redacted prompts/outputs and rubric breakdowns. |
| Export Examples | Restricted; disabled by default in Dedicated/Private unless explicitly allowed | CSV/JSON export of sampled examples. |
| Attach to Rollouts | Rollout Admin | Link an experiment to a rollout/canary step. |

### 4.2 Data sensitivity guardrails (UX)
- The UI must clearly label any table that includes request text as **“Sensitive (Redacted)”**.
- For tenants with stricter settings (Dedicated/Private):
  - Examples tab may be hidden entirely.
  - Export controls may be disabled.
  - Retention defaults are displayed and cannot be extended without explicit admin approval.

### 4.3 Audit visibility
All create/edit/start/stop actions show an “Audit” drawer with:
- Actor
- Timestamp
- Fields changed
- Config revision hash
- Link to the global Audit Log entry

---

## 5. User flows

### 5.1 Flow A — Create a shadow experiment (wizard)
Entry points:
- “Shadow Experiments” list → **Create experiment**
- Route page → Quality tab → **Start shadow experiment**
- Rollout page → Quality signals → **Attach new experiment**

Wizard steps:
1) **Basics**
   - Name (required)
   - Description (optional)
   - Scope: Route (required) + Environment (prod/staging) (if applicable)
   - Control variant (pre-filled from route; editable only if user has route edit permission)

2) **Shadow targets**
   - Add 1..N shadow variants
   - Variant types (UI selection):
     - Model version (e.g., “llama-3.1-70b@2026-01-10”)
     - Quantization profile (e.g., “int8-kv-cache”) 
     - Prompt template version (reference ID)
     - Routing policy (pre-defined policy ID)
   - Show estimated incremental cost per request (rough order) when available

3) **Sampling & bucketing**
   - Sampling rate (%), default 1%
   - Bucketing mode (read-only in v1; shown for transparency): “Deterministic request fingerprinting (consistent across time)”
   - Optional: “Exclude requests with these headers/attributes” (advanced; limited to safe low-cardinality fields)

4) **Metrics & scoring**
   - Metric bundle (default “Quality v1”) + version
   - Scoring latency expectation (e.g., “Typically 2–10 minutes; may be longer under load”)
   - Warning callout: “Quality metrics are asynchronous; use confidence intervals before making decisions.”

5) **Data handling**
   - Retention window (default: 24h for examples; aggregates 30d) — exact defaults are tenant-mode dependent
   - Redaction mode (read-only default in v1; “Redact known sensitive patterns + truncate”) with link to policy
   - Examples availability toggle (if tenant policy allows)

6) **Review & start**
   - Summary of config + guardrails
   - “Start experiment” button
   - “Start in paused state” (optional for admins; to validate config without producing data)

Success state:
- Redirect to experiment details (Overview → Results)
- Show “Data will appear shortly” empty state with ETAs

Failure states:
- Validation error (e.g., sampling too high; unsupported variant type for route)
- Policy denies (e.g., retention extension not allowed)
- Partial success: experiment created but unable to start (data-plane rollout pending) → show remediation steps


### 5.2 Flow B — View experiment results (decision-oriented)
Primary questions:
- Is the candidate variant’s quality statistically worse/better than control?
- Are we segmenting by a factor that indicates localized regression?
- Is scoring healthy (lag/backlog), or are results incomplete?

Steps:
1) Open experiment → Results tab
2) Select a metric (left panel)
3) Observe headline delta + CI and sample size
4) Apply segment filter(s) to locate regressions
5) Drill into Examples for representative failures


### 5.3 Flow C — Attach quality signals to a rollout
From Rollout detail page:
- Quality signals panel shows:
  - Attached experiment(s)
  - Current status (Active/Paused/Stopped)
  - Headline metrics (top 3) with deltas
  - Scoring health (lag, completeness)

Actions:
- Attach existing experiment (must match route + environment)
- Create new attached experiment (opens wizard pre-filled)
- Define “Quality gate thresholds” (v1: advisory only)

v1 behavior:
- Quality gates generate **warnings** in the rollout timeline.
- Rollout automation (auto-pause/rollback) remains manual in v1 (future flag).

---

## 6. UI specification by page

### 6.1 Shadow Experiments — list page
**Table columns**
- Name
- Route
- Control variant
- Shadow variants (count + chips)
- Status (Active/Paused/Stopped)
- Sampling rate
- Last 24h headline: “Regressions detected” badge (if any)
- Updated

**Default sorting**: Updated desc

**Filters**
- Route
- Status
- Owner/creator
- Time range (for headline signals)

**Empty states**
- No experiments: explanation + “Create experiment”
- Permission-limited: show metadata only; hide CTAs requiring elevated roles


### 6.2 Create Shadow Experiment — wizard
**Design requirements**
- Every step includes a “Why this matters” inline helper for first-time users.
- Guardrails are shown as *constraints*, not as hidden errors:
  - Sampling max (tenant/plan dependent)
  - Shadow target concurrency max
  - Max retained examples

**Warning callouts (must-have)**
- “Shadow traffic is mirrored; it does not change user responses.”
- “Shadowing may increase compute and telemetry costs.”
- “Shadow path is fail-open; if shadow targets fail, production responses continue normally.”


### 6.3 Shadow Experiment — Overview tab
**Header**
- Experiment name
- Status pill: Active / Paused / Stopped
- Primary actions:
  - Pause / Resume
  - Stop
  - Edit (creates a new config revision)

**Overview cards**
1) Config snapshot
   - Route
   - Control variant
   - Shadow variants
   - Sampling rate
   - Metrics bundle + version
   - Retention settings

2) Health
   - Shadow dispatch success rate (last 15m)
   - Scoring lag (p50/p95)
   - Data completeness: “% of mirrored pairs scored”

3) Activity
   - Recent config changes
   - Linked rollout (if attached)


### 6.4 Shadow Experiment — Results tab (core)
The Results tab is split into three zones:
- Left: Metric selector
- Center: Chart + headline delta
- Right: Filters and segments

#### 6.4.1 Metric selector (left)
Grouped sections:
- Safety & refusal
- Format adherence
- Instruction following (rubric)
- Heuristics

Each metric row shows:
- Metric name
- Directionality indicator (higher is better / lower is better)
- Latest delta mini-sparkline


#### 6.4.2 Headline delta (top of center)
Shows selected metric’s current evaluation window:
- **Delta value** (Shadow – Control) with sign coloring
- **95% confidence interval** (always shown; never optional)
- Sample size: number of paired requests scored
- “Data freshness” indicator: last scored timestamp

Decision labels (display-only):
- “Likely regression” if CI excludes 0 in the bad direction
- “Likely improvement” if CI excludes 0 in good direction
- “Inconclusive” otherwise

Note: Labels are informational and do not imply causal proof.


#### 6.4.3 Delta chart (center)
Chart types:
- **Time series delta** (default)
  - X: time
  - Y: delta
  - Band: confidence interval
- **Distribution comparison** (secondary)
  - Control vs Shadow score distributions for the chosen window

Chart requirements:
- Confidence bands must be visually distinct and colorblind-safe.
- Hover tooltip shows:
  - Control metric value
  - Shadow metric value
  - Delta
  - CI
  - Sample size
  - Scoring completion %

Time range selector:
- 1h, 6h, 24h, 7d (availability depends on retention)

Annotations:
- Config revision changes appear as vertical markers (“Sampling changed 1% → 2%”).
- Rollout events (if attached) appear as markers (“Canary step 2 started”).


#### 6.4.4 Segments & filters (right)
Filters are limited to cardinality-safe dimensions.

Default available segments (subject to telemetry policy):
- Region
- Request type (chat/completions/embeddings where applicable; shadow experiments focus on generation endpoints)
- Model family bucket (high-level)
- Token length bucket (short/medium/long)
- HTTP status bucket (2xx/4xx/5xx)

UI behavior:
- Multi-select, with “Top N segments by volume” option.
- When segmenting, show:
  - Per-segment delta table with CI
  - Small “volume share” bar
  - Sort by worst regression first

Guardrails:
- Do not allow free-form labels.
- If a user tries to segment by a disallowed dimension, show an explanation and link to the observability standard.


### 6.5 Shadow Experiment — Examples tab
Purpose: help debug *why* a metric changed, not serve as a data export feature.

**Access**: gated by “View Examples (redacted)” permission.

**Layout**
- Top controls: time range, metric filter (optional), segment filter (optional)
- Table/list of examples with:
  - Timestamp
  - Request fingerprint (hashed)
  - Segment chips (safe)
  - Control summary (short)
  - Shadow summary (short)
  - Metric outcomes (e.g., rubric score, refusal flag)

**Example detail drawer**
- Request (redacted + truncated)
- Control output (redacted)
- Shadow output (redacted)
- Rubric breakdown (human-readable)
- Links:
  - “Open in trace” (if available)
  - “Copy redacted payload” (copy only what’s displayed)

**Safety requirements**
- Never display raw identifiers (customer_id, user_id, email) even if present in prompt.
- Prompts/outputs are truncated with a visible “truncated” indicator.
- Provide “Report redaction miss” action (creates internal ticket; does not reveal raw text).

**Export (v1)**
- If enabled by tenant policy: export current filtered view up to N rows (default N=500).
- Export includes only redacted fields and excludes any internal IDs except fingerprint.


### 6.6 Shadow Experiment — Activity/Audit tab
- Config revision history (diff view)
- Start/stop/pause events
- Attachment events (linked to rollout)
- Links to Audit Log entries

---

## 7. Rollout integration UX
### 7.1 Rollout page — Quality signals panel
Panel placement: right rail (desktop), collapsible section (mobile).

Panel shows:
- Attached experiment (name + status)
- Last 24h headline:
  - 3 selected metrics (configurable; default: refusal rate, format adherence, instruction-following score)
  - Each with delta + CI
- Scoring health:
  - Lag p95
  - Completeness %

Actions:
- “View details” (opens experiment Results tab)
- “Edit attachment” (change which experiment is attached)
- “Configure quality gate” (v1: advisory)


### 7.2 Rollout timeline annotations
When attached, the rollout timeline includes:
- Markers when the experiment starts/stops
- Markers for detected likely regressions (advisory), e.g., “Refusal rate regression (CI excludes 0)”


### 7.3 Quality gate configuration (v1)
UI is present but clearly labeled “Advisory (no automated rollback in v1)”.

Gate configuration fields:
- Metric
- Threshold type: absolute delta / relative % change
- Direction: regression only / improvement only / both
- Minimum sample size requirement
- Required confidence (fixed at 95% in v1; displayed as non-editable)

When gate triggers:
- Add warning banner on rollout page
- Add timeline event
- Optional: send notification (Slack/email integration outside scope; UI shows “Notifications configured by org admins”)

---

## 8. System states & messaging

### 8.1 Scoring lag / incomplete data
If scoring is behind, Results tab shows:
- Banner: “Scoring delayed—results may be incomplete.”
- The headline area must include completeness % and last-scored timestamp.
- Charts should visually gray out the most recent interval if completeness < X% (threshold defined by observability standard; propose X=80%).

### 8.2 Shadow dispatch degradation (fail-open)
If shadow target errors increase:
- Overview Health card shows elevated error rate.
- Show banner: “Shadow targets failing; production responses unaffected (fail-open).”
- Provide link: “How to disable shadowing” (runbook).

### 8.3 No data / low sample size
- If sample size below minimum (propose <200 pairs): show “Inconclusive—insufficient samples” and nudge to:
  - increase sampling (if allowed)
  - extend time range
  - reduce segments

---

## 9. Copy requirements (must-have strings)
These strings are specifically called out to avoid ambiguity:
- “Shadow traffic mirrors requests to candidate variants but always returns the control response to users.”
- “Fail-open: if shadowing fails, production traffic continues normally.”
- “Quality metrics are asynchronous and may lag by minutes.”
- “Confidence intervals indicate uncertainty; avoid decisions on small samples.”
- “Examples are redacted and truncated; do not use this view for data export unless explicitly enabled.”

---

## 10. Analytics & instrumentation (Console)
Console events (for product understanding; not customer-facing):
- shadow_experiments.create_started / create_completed
- shadow_experiments.pause / resume / stop
- shadow_experiments.metric_selected
- shadow_experiments.segment_applied
- shadow_experiments.example_opened
- rollouts.quality_panel_opened

Guardrails:
- Do not include prompt text in Console analytics.

---

## 11. Open questions
1) **Run modeling:** Do we explicitly create immutable “run” objects in the backend for every start/stop cycle, or infer runs from state transitions? UX can support either; preferred is explicit runs for clearer comparison.
2) **Metric directionality:** For each v1 metric, confirm “higher is better” vs “lower is better” and standardize visual semantics.
3) **Threshold defaults:** Should the UI suggest default gate thresholds per metric (e.g., +0.5% refusal) or keep entirely user-defined?
4) **Segments availability by plan:** Confirm which segments are always allowed in Dedicated/Private and which are hosted-only.
5) **Export policy:** Confirm defaults (off by default) and the approval mechanism to enable.

---

## 12. Acceptance criteria (UX)
- A Project Admin can create an experiment from a Route page in <5 minutes without docs.
- Results show delta + CI everywhere a delta is shown (no “naked deltas”).
- Rollout page displays attached experiment headline signals and health.
- Examples tab is permission-gated and clearly labeled redacted/truncated.
- All error/empty states explain what is happening and how to recover (increase time range, sampling, remove segments, check scoring health).

---

## 13. Appendix — Proposed default metric tiles (v1)
These appear in the “headline metrics” set on overview/rollout panels:
- Refusal rate (lower is better)
- Format adherence (higher is better)
- Instruction-following rubric score (higher is better)

Secondary (available in metric list):
- Safety policy violation proxy (lower is better)
- JSON/Schema validity (higher is better)
- Verbosity drift (token length delta; interpret with caution)

(Exact definitions live in Applied ML / Evals docs; UI displays names and short descriptions only.)

title: dsid_b4ccbb73fc7347749ce5c3a58aa9c588__workspace-promotion-and-fast-rollback-for-multi-region-gpu-iac.txt
text:
Workspace promotion and fast rollback for multi-region GPU IaC

Overview:

This runbook defines the canonical process for promoting Terraform changes across multiple regions that host GPU pools, and for performing an expedited rollback if a promotion causes capacity or network regressions. It focuses on safety, recovery speed, and minimal customer impact for Redwood Inference's multi-region GPU infra.

Intended audience:
- Infra engineers on-call for gpu-fleet, cloud-accounts, and terraform modules
- Release engineers operating the IaC pipelines
- SRE and capacity planners who verify post-promotion health checks

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Terraform-managed resources that affect GPU capacity, networking (VPCs, route tables, NATs), and core IAM/billing boundaries for tenant pools in all production regions.
- Backend: S3 remote state with object versioning + DynamoDB state lock (AWS).
- CI: Buildkite or equivalent pipeline that runs plan/apply per workspace and region.
- Snapshots: We maintain automated state snapshots in s3://redwood-terraform-snapshots/ and retain at least 30 days.

Goals:
1) Promote changes with clear canary and verification gates per region.
2) Make it possible to fully rollback in under 20 minutes for common failure modes (failed applies, capacity regressions, route/NAT misconfig).
3) Preserve audit trail and avoid state corruption during forced operations.

Terminology:
- workspace: Terraform workspace used to represent environment/region (e.g., prod-us-west-2, prod-eu-central-1).
- promotion: moving a module change from staging->canary->prod across regions.
- snapshot: a point-in-time export of the terraform state file (terraform state pull).

Prerequisites and safety checks before promotion:
- Confirm workspace naming: lower-case, region suffix, semantic release tag in commit message (e.g., terraform/aws/gpu: v1.23.0).
- CI pipeline green for unit tests, fmt, and terraform validate on the branch.
- Remote-state is unlocked: aws dynamodb get-item --table-name tf-locks --key '{"LockID":{"S":"<workspace>"}}' should return empty or a stale owner older than 30m.
- Verify S3 object versioning enabled for the backend bucket and the latest snapshot exists.
- Capacity freeze window check: ensure no scheduled major migrations or QBR windows.

Promotion workflow (recommended):
1) author push -> PR with module changes and description of resource impact (estimated new GPUs, expected rolling reboots).
2) automated plan in CI produces plan artifacts per region workspace. Attach plan to PR.
3) Staging apply: run apply in a non-customer-facing staging workspace backing a canary tenant pool. Verify smoke tests.
4) Canary region: pick a single low-traffic production region (by traffic matrix). Apply with limited scope (use -target for initial canary if change is large).
5) Verification gates after canary (30–60 minutes):
   - GPU warm-pool size matches intended delta (infra metric: gpu.pool.warm_count).
   - No increase in 5xxs or throttled requests for downstream serving services (api.slo.token_latency > threshold).
   - Networking path checks succeed (internal curl to service endpoints, NAT rules validated).
6) If gates pass, schedule phased promotion across remaining regions with staggered windows (min 15–30m between regions).

Terraform commands and operational snippets:
- Select workspace:
  terraform workspace select prod-us-west-2 || terraform workspace new prod-us-west-2
- Create plan file (CI):
  terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-tfstate" -reconfigure
  terraform plan -var-file=regions/us-west-2.tfvars -out=plan.prod-us-west-2
- Apply from plan with remote locking enforced in CI agent:
  terraform apply -input=false plan.prod-us-west-2
- Snapshot state (manual fast snapshot):
  terraform state pull > /tmp/prod-us-west-2-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).json
  aws s3 cp /tmp/... s3://redwood-terraform-snapshots/prod-us-west-2/ --acl bucket-owner-full-control
- Quick state restore (read-only verification):
  terraform state pull | jq '.modules[].resources[] | select(.type=="aws_instance")' > verify.json

Fast rollback procedures (common failure modes):
A. Failed apply or partial apply detected immediately after apply finishes:
1) Stop further promotions and add "rollback-in-progress" label in incident channel.
2) If apply failed and left resources partially created: run terraform apply again against the original plan if safe. If that is not safe, go to snapshot restore (see C).
3) For safely revertible changes (variable flips, scaling down new count): create a short revert commit that restores the previous module input and run plan+apply in that workspace.

B. Capacity regression (warm pool or allocations decreased / degraded):
1) Detect via alerts: gpu.pool.warm_count < expected by >10% for 10 minutes or gpu.alloc.fail_rate increased >1%.
2) If the change is a config variable (e.g., desired_warm_pool_size): revert the variable via a targeted apply. Use -target to limit scope.
3) If networking rule misconfiguration suspected, revert affected route tables / security groups via terraform apply with a revert commit. Simultaneously open routing validation job (curl tests) to confirm restore.

C. State corruption or irrecoverable dependency mismatch: snapshot restore path (slower, reliable).
1) Notify on-call SRE and create incident.
2) Acquire latest snapshot version from s3://redwood-terraform-snapshots/<workspace> using object version id.
3) Lock the workspace (DynamoDB): add manual lock owner and mark maintenance in PagerDuty incident.
4) Replace remote state object (example):
   aws s3 cp s3://redwood-terraform-snapshots/prod-us-west-2/<versioned-file> s3://redwood-tfstate/prod-us-west-2.tfstate --metadata-directive REPLACE
   (Ensure correct ACL and server-side encryption headers preserved.)
5) Run terraform plan -refresh-only and validate that drift is resolved.
6) Apply a no-op plan and then run standard smoke tests before unlocking.

Emergency fast-rollback checklist (<= 20 minutes target):
- Roles on-call: infra-oncall (primary), infra-release (secondary), platform-sre (pager).
- Step 0: Create incident channel and annotate affected regions + commit SHA.
- Step 1: If simple revert possible, merge revert commit and trigger CI apply in affected workspace with concurrency=1. (Estimated time 5–10m).
- Step 2: If snapshot needed, request snapshot restore (operator): aws s3 cp <snapshot> back to bucket (10–15m depending on region/object size).
- Step 3: Run smoke tests and confirm metrics.
- Step 4: Close incident and record actions in postmortem doc.

Observability and verification tests (automated):
- CI/Smoke jobs executed after apply per region:
  1) gpu-pool-health-check (returns 200 and expected pool sizes)
  2) internal-network-echo (connectivity over service mesh)
  3) token-latency probe (synthetic requests comparing pre/post latencies)
- Dashboards:
  - gpu-infra/Capacity Overview (gpu.pool.* metrics)
  - infra-network/Egress & NAT health (nat.errors, route.failures)
- Alerts:
  - gpu-pool-warm-count < threshold for 10m -> page infra-oncall
  - terraform-apply-error (CI) -> page infra-release slack + email

Automation and CI pipeline recommendations:
- Keep plan artifacts per region and attach to PR for review. Do not rely solely on plan logs.
- CI agents perform remote backend init with -reconfigure on each run to avoid stale state issues.
- Set pipeline concurrency to 1 per workspace to avoid accidental concurrent applies.
- Provide a manual "promote-to-region" step that requires two infra approvals for changes that touch network or IAM.
- Use the pipeline to automatically create state snapshots before each prod apply and tag snapshot with commit SHA.

Configuration table (core constraints):
- Terraform version: "1.5.x" in CI and local dev (must match exact patch for providers).
- AWS provider: pinned to a tested provider version (example: 5.17.0).
- Backend bucket: redwood-tfstate (versioning: enabled).
- Snapshot bucket: redwood-terraform-snapshots (lifecycle: 90d, encryption: SSE-KMS).
- Lock table: redwood-tf-locks (DynamoDB with TTL on lease metadata).

Roles and ownership:
- Promotion owner: infra-release team (runbook executor).
- On-call responder: infra-oncall (SRE).
- State restore approvals: require two infra-release members plus a platform-sre reviewer for region changes impacting networking.

Post-incident follow-up and metrics to record:
- Time to detect, time to rollback, time to full recovery (target: detect <10m, rollback <20m, recovery <60m).
- Root cause summary and a concrete remediation (e.g., adjust canary size to 5% of traffic).
- Update CI gating rules or module tests to prevent recurrence.

Appendix: Useful commands and examples
- List workspace versions and select:
  terraform workspace list
  terraform workspace select prod-eu-central-1
- Pull remote state snapshot locally:
  terraform state pull > snapshot.json
- Force unlock (use only with approval):
  terraform force-unlock -force <LOCK_ID>
- S3 copy for snapshot restore (example):
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-terraform-snapshots/prod-us-west-2/20250206T150000Z.json s3://redwood-tfstate/prod-us-west-2.tfstate --metadata-directive REPLACE --sse aws:kms --acl bucket-owner-full-control

Related runbooks and docs:
- remote-state-segmentation-and-cross-account-locking-primer (for backend design)
- gpu-capacity-reconciliation-audit-and-credits-ledger (for cost reconciliation after incidents)
- ci-cd-gpu-image-promotion-canary-cd-playbook (for pipeline patterns used by promotion)

Revision history:
- 2024-09-12: Created by Sofia Ramirez (initial draft).
- 2024-11-05: Added fast rollback checklist and snapshot restore steps after on-call drill.
- 2025-02-06: Clarified approval matrix and tightened snapshot retention guidance.

Contact: infra-release@redwood.example.com for questions and exceptions.

text:
Deployable Value Sprint Playbook and Technical Evidence

Summary
-------
This playbook guides a cross-functional value sprint that yields a deployable pilot of Redwood Inference in 6 weeks for midmarket and SMB product teams. The goal is to produce a working integration, measurable economic impact (latency and cost), and security evidence that satisfies a technical buyer and their CISO. Use this playbook to accelerate deal qualification, reduce risk, and shorten time from proof-of-concept to first production route.

One-line value proposition
-------------------------
Run production-grade LLM inference with predictable latency and transparent unit economics so product teams can ship conversational features without building and operating a custom serving stack.

When to use this playbook
-------------------------
- Prospects with a defined product use case and sample data (chat, summarization, or embeddings).
- Platform or product engineers willing to run a 6-week pilot.
- Security/compliance gate that requires evidence (audit logging, data residency, KMS).

Sprint overview (6 weeks)
------------------------
1. Week 0: Intake & sizing (sales + solutions)
   - Outcome: pilot statement of work (SOW) with success metrics and access plan.
   - Inputs: sample traffic shape, latency target, data sensitivity class, pilot duration.
2. Week 1: Environment & baseline
   - Outcome: baseline measurements (existing latency/cost) and minimal integration plan.
   - Tasks: provide API keys, create test dataset, configure sandbox model.
3. Weeks 2–3: Implementation & validation
   - Outcome: integrated endpoint and initial functional tests.
   - Tasks: SDK or REST integration, streaming config, fallback routing test.
4. Week 4: Performance tuning and observability
   - Outcome: configured batching and caching, dashboards for cost/latency.
   - Tasks: enable token-level cost breakdown, tracing hooks, add eval prompts.
5. Week 5: Security evidence & governance
   - Outcome: evidence pack (audit logs, KMS usage, network controls).
   - Tasks: collect logs, confirm RBAC, review data retention policy.
6. Week 6: Closure & handoff
   - Outcome: decision (scale, renew, or sunset) and cutover plan if progressing.
   - Deliverables: pilot report, recommended capacity profile, pricing scenario.

Positioning and messaging by buyer persona
-----------------------------------------
- Platform Engineer: emphasize unified runtime, predictable throughput, autoscaling controls, and clear batching knobs.
- Product Manager: emphasize time-to-market, measurable improvement in user engagement, and quick rollback paths.
- CISO/Security: emphasize data residency options, KMS/HSM integration, audit logging, and private deployment choices.
- Finance/Procurement: emphasize unit economics, pilot pricing, and reserved capacity discounts.

Competitive brief: head-to-head narrative
---------------------------------------
Key differentiators to lead with:
- Production-first controls: per-route SLOs, automatic fallback to lower-cost model variants, and token-level cost breakdowns for chargeback.
- Unified deployments: same API and rollout policies across hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem) — minimizes migration risk.
- Cost operations: built-in batching/caching suggestions with modeled cost impact and quantization guidance.

Common competitor weaknesses to exploit:
- Simpler APIs but opaque performance: many providers do not expose token-level economics or KV cache behavior.
- Limited private deployment: some vendors only offer hosted endpoints or complicated on-prem toolchains.
- Poor fallback behavior: many stacks lack automatic model variant routing and graceful degradation under pressure.

Pricing guidance and pilot scenarios
----------------------------------
Pricing principles
- Start simple for pilots: single blended per-token rate + pilot support fee.
- Show modeled cost delta: compare current infra or competitor per-token costs vs Redwood with batching enabled.

Three pilot pricing scenarios (examples)
1) Rapid evaluation (2–4 weeks)
   - Fee: $2,500 flat credit + usage at $0.0008 per input/output token.
   - Support: email + one solutions call.
2) Standard deployable pilot (6 weeks)
   - Fee: $15,000 pilot package (includes 4 support hours/week).
   - Commit: optional $10k reserved credit at a discounted rate if moving to Dedicated.
3) Enterprise sandbox (6–12 weeks)
   - Fee: $45,000 (onboarding, security review coordination, 24/7 support for the pilot window).
   - Add-ons: private control plane license, enhanced retention for observability.

Sample pricing JSON (for sales engineers)
---------------------------------------
{"pilot_type": "standard", "pilot_fee_usd": "15000", "per_token_usd": "0.0008", "support_hours_per_week": "4"}

Pitch deck outline (5 slides, executive-friendly)
-------------------------------------------------
1. Problem & customer impact: quantify user friction and missed ARR opportunity.
2. Redwood solution snapshot: runtime, deployment modes, and one-line economics.
3. Pilot plan & success metrics: latency, cost-per-call delta, and retention uplift target.
4. Security and compliance evidence: KMS, audit logs, VPC/on-prem options.
5. Commercial ask & next steps: pilot package and recommended pilot start date.

Short case study: Acme Retail (fictionalized but modeled on typical outcomes)
-------------------------------------------------------------------------
- Profile: midmarket e-commerce platform using chat-based product recommendations.
- Pilot scope: product-recommendation API (session-based chat), 10k monthly active sessions.
- Outcome in 6 weeks:
  - Latency improved from 2200ms to 350ms (95th percentile) for recommendation requests.
  - Token cost per request reduced by 38% after enabling prefix caching and optimized batching.
  - Went from pilot to dedicated capacity with a 12-month reserved commit.
- Evidence provided: configuration docs, dashboard screenshots, cost delta table, security checklist used in CISO review.

Security FAQ for prospects (short answers for field use)
------------------------------------------------------
Q: How does Redwood protect customer data in hosted mode?
A: Customer data is isolated per tenant, encrypted at rest and in transit, and can be configured to use customer-managed keys (KMS). Audit logs are retained per the agreed retention period.

Q: Can we run Redwood inside our VPC or on-prem?
A: Yes. Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane and on-prem packaging for air-gapped environments. We provide a deployment checklist and optional engineering assistance.

Q: What authentication and RBAC options exist?
A: Granular API keys, OAuth integrations for console access, and role-based access controls for team-level permissions. Integrates with SSO via SAML/OIDC.

Q: How are logs and PII handled?
A: Logs are redacted by default for known PII patterns; customers can opt into additional redaction rules. Audit logs are separate from payload storage and can be retained or forwarded to the customer's SIEM.

Q: What evidence do you provide for a security review?
A: Typical package includes architecture diagram, KMS integration proof, SOC/ISO certifications (where available), sample audit logs, network diagram, and a runbook for incident response tailored to the pilot.

Rollout checklist (minimum viable deliverables for a pilot)
---------------------------------------------------------
- Pilot SOW signed with success metrics.
- Sandbox credentials and API key exchange.
- Sample dataset and test harness (postman/pytest).
- Baseline latency and cost report.
- Observability configured (dashboards, traces, alerts).
- Security evidence pack prepared for CISO review.
- Pilot closeout report template populated with results and recommendation.

Owner & escalation
------------------
- Sales owner: account AE (named in SOW).
- Technical owner: Solutions Engineer (SE) assigned in week 0.
- Security liaison: Security Engagement lead (for enterprise pilots).
- Escalation path: AE -> SE -> Solutions Lead -> Head of Sales Engineering.

Appendix: support playbook snippets
----------------------------------
- Enable token-level cost breakdown (console): path: Console > Projects > Metrics > Token Economics.
- Configure fallback routing (YAML example):
  - name: fallback-policy-1
    route: ["gpt-variant-high", "gpt-variant-low"]
    criteria: {"latency_ms": 500}  

- Minimal eval set (5 prompts) to check quality regressions:
  1) Customer support triage (short instructions)
  2) Product summary (long product description -> short bullets)
  3) Intent classification (single shot)
  4) Embedding similarity (search task)
  5) Conversational context carryover (multi-turn)

Contact
-------
For help running the sprint or tailoring pilot economics, contact Maya Chen (mchen@redwood.ai) or the Solutions Engineering rota via SE-oncall.

Related resources
-----------------
- Pilot activation templates and SOW examples: /confluence/sales-enablement/pilot-activation-playbook-and-technical-economics-2027
- Pricing model reference for finance: /confluence/finance-and-legal/budgeting-and-forecasting/pilot-pricing-model-2028
- Private deployment checklist: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-checklist

text:
Probe Scheduling for Mixed-Precision Evaluation Orchestration

Summary
-------
This playbook defines a probe-scheduling strategy and orchestration pattern for running mixed-precision (MPX) evaluation workloads across the eval-harness. It centralizes how probes (synthetic requests, prompt slices, and adversarial cases) should be scheduled, prioritized, and routed to candidate model/quantization variants so we can detect quality regressions and quant-degradation early without overspending GPU cycles.

Goals
-----
- Detect regressions introduced by mixed-precision and quantization changes within 24 hours of a rollout candidate being staged.
- Prioritize probes that historically surface degradations while preserving sampling diversity to catch new failure modes.
- Keep incremental compute overhead <= 12% of production-like dedicated shadow capacity.
- Provide deterministic scheduling outputs for reproducible triage and automated alerts.

Scope
-----
Applies to: eval-harness orchestration, model-onboarding shadow deployments (hosted, dedicated, private), quantization profiles used by production-serving. Excludes: offline batch-only research experiments and one-off ad hoc label collections.

Definitions
-----------
- Probe: a single test case derived from the prompt catalog (single- or multi-turn) with metadata (slice, expected behavior, anchor model output).
- MPX candidate: a model variant that uses mixed-precision kernels (e.g., int8+f16 hybrid) or a quantized artifact targeted for private/dedicated deployment.
- Probe Farm: the eval-harness pool service that schedules probes to worker lanes.
- Priority Score: numeric score used by scheduler to order probes; see algorithm below.

High-level Architecture
-----------------------
1. Probe Catalog (Prompt Sets): persisted in S3 + metadata in the eval database. Each probe has tags: slice, risk_score, cost_estimate, anchor_hash, last_seen_failure.
2. Scheduler Service (probe-scheduler): computes a daily schedule manifest for each MPX candidate.
3. Orchestrator (eval-orch): reads manifests and executes probes on the shadow fleet, collecting telemetry to ingestion topic eval-telemetry-prod.
4. Analyzer (probe-analyzer): computes signal (response stability index, semantic-embedding divergence, length-normalized token-delta) and writes alerts to PagerDuty and regression-triage queue.

Probe Types and Weighting
------------------------
We categorize probes into 4 types with default target proportions for a daily run:
- High-risk regressors (15%): known slices that have produced past regressions (high precision recall).
- Random coverage (30%): uniformly sampled to detect unknowns.
- Adversarial perturbations (20%): syntactic and semantic noise variants.
- Long-context & KV-cache sensitive (35%): multi-turn sequences emphasizing cache stability.

Priority score formula (used to sort queue):
priority = clamp(0.0, 1.0, 0.5 * normalized_risk + 0.3 * age_factor + 0.2 * impact_estimate)
Where: normalized_risk in [0,1] from probe metadata; age_factor = min(days_since_last_run/30,1); impact_estimate derived from upstream product usage weight.

Scheduling Algorithm
--------------------
1. For each MPX candidate, fetch last-run outcomes and compute a reweight table for probes.
2. Reserve N high-priority slots (N = ceil(0.12 * daily_budget_slots)) for probes with last_seen_failure = true.
3. Fill remaining slots by sampling per target proportions with stratified sampling across languages, device types, and traffic cohorts.
4. Annotate schedule with preferred lane (gpu-v2, cpu-sim, or quant-sim) and estimated token-cost.
5. Persist manifest and start execution window.

Operational Runbook: daily execution
-----------------------------------
1. probe-scheduler triggers at 02:00 UTC and emits manifests per candidate.
2. eval-orch pulls manifests and runs probes over a 2-hour window. Long-context probes are rate-limited to spread memory pressure.
3. probe-analyzer runs streaming checks and posts signals:
   - Response Stability Index (RSI) drop > 0.07 -> create regression triage ticket (severity P2).
   - Embedding Cosine Drift > 0.12 on median of slice -> add to regression queue.
   - Token Delta > 20% on top-k token distribution -> flag for quantization failure-mode.
4. If more than 5 distinct probes fail automatic gates for the same candidate, automatically set deployment status to HOLD and notify Model Onboarding channel (@model-onboard).

SLOs and Alert Thresholds
-------------------------
- Coverage: At least 80% of manifest probes must complete successfully within the 2-hour window.
- Latency: median probe execution latency <= 800ms per probe on gpu-v2 lane.
- Detection window: regressions must be detected and a ticket created within 6 hours of detection.

Gates and Automated Actions
--------------------------
- Soft Gate: RSI drop between 0.03–0.07 -> create a low-priority regression ticket; schedule follow-up re-run with expanded adversarial cases.
- Hard Gate: RSI drop > 0.07 or Embedding Drift > 0.12 -> set candidate to HOLD and notify oncall and onboarding owners.
- Emergency Fallback: If an MPX candidate is promoted to dedicated and field telemetry indicates correlated errors, the Routing Service will fallback to the anchor model for 1 hour while triage proceeds.

Promotion Checklist (for MPX candidate)
--------------------------------------
- [ ] All scheduled probes pass soft gates in two consecutive daily runs.
- [ ] No hard gate triggers in the last 7 days.
- [ ] Token-cost delta within expected budget +/- 8%.
- [ ] Shadow-to-field calibration run completed (see 'shadow-rollforward' playbook).
- [ ] Owners and validators listed in onboarding ticket have signed off.

Sample manifest excerpt (YAML)
----------------------------
---
candidate: mpq-model-v3-int8-hybrid
date: 2025-02-10
slots: 1200
reserved_high_risk: 150
probes:
  - id: probe-15033
    slice: billing-invoice-extraction
    type: long-context
    lane: gpu-v2
    expected_anchor_hash: 7f2a9d
  - id: probe-1122
    slice: frontend-dialogue-clarity
    type: adversarial
    lane: quant-sim
    expected_anchor_hash: 9c4b1a

Config table: scheduler tunables
--------------------------------
| key                         | description                                    | default  | notes |
|-----------------------------|------------------------------------------------|----------|-------|
| daily_budget_slots          | total probe executions per candidate per day  | 1200     | scales with candidate priority |
| reserved_failure_slots_pct  | percent reserved for recent failures          | 12       | set to 0 for experimental runs |
| long_context_rate_limit_ms  | per-probe cooldown for long-context probes    | 1500     | avoid GPU memory thrash |
| sample_seed                 | deterministic seed for sampling               | 42       | increment per run for variance |

Telemetry and Metrics (collected per-probe)
--------------------------------------------
- run_id, probe_id, candidate, lane, start_ts, end_ts
- tokens_in, tokens_out, wall_ms, gpu_mem_peak_mb
- response_hash, embedding_vector_id, rsi_score, token_delta_percent
- annotations: human_label (if escalated), triage_ticket_id

Triage Flow and Responsibilities
--------------------------------
- Initial Triage: Model Onboarding -> verify whether difference is expected for quant profile.
- Deep Triage: Applied ML (Regression Squad) -> reproduce with debug flags, compare kernel traces, KV cache traces.
- Ops Action: If a resource bottleneck is suspected (gpu_mem_peak_mb > threshold 90%), engage eng-infra to reprofile.

Owner and Escalation Contacts
----------------------------
- Probe Scheduler (owner): Marco Ruiz (marco@redwood.ai)
- Probe Analyzer (owner): Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.ai)
- Regression Squad Lead: Priya Menon (pri@redwood.ai)
- Oncall: see eng-oncall rota (link internal)

Example CLI commands
--------------------
# Generate schedule for candidate
make run-probe-scheduler CANDIDANT=mpq-model-v3-int8-hybrid RUN_DATE=2025-02-10

# Inspect manifest
aws s3 cp s3://eval-manifests/mpq-model-v3-int8-hybrid/2025-02-10/manifest.yaml -

Appendix: common failure modes and remediation
-----------------------------------------------
1) Token distribution collapse (spike in token_delta_percent)
   - Likely cause: quant kernel top-k instability.
   - Remediation: tighten quantization calibration, run quant-sim with higher precision for top-k.
2) Embedding semantic shift
   - Likely cause: fused kernel numerical drift or tokenizer mismatch for rare unicode.
   - Remediation: run tokenizer normalization pass, add targeted probes for affected Unicode ranges.
3) Intermittent OOM on long-context probes
   - Likely cause: batch packing + long context combinatorics.
   - Remediation: reduce pack size for long-context lane and increase long_context_rate_limit_ms.

Related artifacts and references
-------------------------------
- Scheduler service repo: git@internal:redwood/eval-scheduler.git
- Probe catalog schema: s3://eval-catalog/schema/v2/probe-schema.yaml
- Regression triage template: confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/triage-ticket-template

Revision history
----------------
2025-01-15 — Dana Kim — initial draft
2025-02-12 — Dana Kim — added automated gate thresholds and sample manifest

text:
gpu-capacity-consolidation-backfill-and-safety-net-runbook

Summary

This runbook describes the playbook for planned capacity consolidation events on the GPU fleet and the automated human-in-the-loop backfill process we use to avoid customer impact. It covers preflight checks, traffic shaping and tenant draining procedures, automated backfill jobs, networking and egress considerations, Terraform/IaC change patterns, CI/CD gating, monitoring queries, rollback steps, and post-event validation. The goal is to reduce instance footprint while preserving latency SLOs and minimizing cost.

Audience

- Oncall SREs responsible for GPU fleet operations
- Infra engineers performing IaC changes and capacity consolidation
- Product/platform owners coordinating quota and customer notifications

When to use this runbook

- Scheduled consolidation of underutilized GPU pools (capacity reclamation)
- Migration from older instance families to crushed-instance families or new accelerator types
- Post-cost-optimization initiatives where we aim to reduce fleet size without degrading SLOs

SLOs and safety thresholds

- 99th percentile generation latency (per-model route): <= 250ms target, 400ms safety threshold
- Request success rate (HTTP 200/stream-ok): >= 99.9% target, 99.5% safety threshold
- Token-cost delta vs baseline: <= +5% (temporary degradation allowed for up to 2 hours)
- Automated consolidation window must not reduce available capacity below 20% headroom for regional peak demand

Preflight checklist (must be green before consolidation starts)

1. Announce maintenance window in status page and to affected tenants (if >5% of customer traffic is impacted).
2. Confirm fleet telemetry: Prometheus targets for GPU utilization, queue depth, host health.
3. CI/CD: Validate Terraform plan artifact signed and stored in S3 (artifact tag: consolidation/${date}/${change-id}).
4. Verify that model-variant fallback policies exist for all routes affected by instance family change.
5. Ensure rolling image / kernel versions are identical across nodes targeted for consolidation (avoid mixed drivers).
6. Canaries: schedule low-volume canary jobs to run for 60m prior to broad consolidation.

Key dashboards and alerts

- dashboards/gpu/region-capacity: region free GPUs, per-tenant allocations
- dashboards/runtime/latency-per-route: 50/95/99p latency trends
- alerts: GPU_POD_CPU_OVER_80 (severity P2), QUEUE_DEPTH_GROWTH_10m (P1), MODEL_INFER_ERRORS_5m (P1)

Operational steps

1) Prepare IaC and CI/CD

- Author a Terraform change that de-registers or repurposes target node pools. Use the gpu_pool_consolidation module with the following pattern: set `retain_headroom_percent = 30` and create a `consolidation_signal` feature flag.
- Run `terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan` in the consolidation CI pipeline. Attach plan artifact to the change ticket.
- Create a CD release with a single feature flag switch to flip start of consolidation. This allows fast abort via flag rollback.

2) Start canary phase (30–60 minutes)

- Flip feature flag to enable consolidation for a single low-traffic tenant with `kubectl annotate namespace tenant-ctn consolidation=canary`.
- Run heavy inference canary: `./scripts/canary/loadgen --model gpt-lite --qps 2 --duration 60m`.
- Monitor latency and error-rate PromQL: 
  `sum(rate(runtime_infer_errors_total[5m])) by (route)` and `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))`
- If 99p latency > 400ms or errors > 0.5% for the canary route, abort and rollback terraform plan; notify owners.

3) Gradual drain + backfill loop

- For each node-pool targeted for consolidation: 
  a) Identify candidate nodes using label `consolidate=true` and annotate them `drain=planned`
  b) Start tenant-aware drain: `python ops/drain_node.py --node-id <id> --max-concurrent-migrations 4 --preserve-cache=true`
  c) The drain script triggers an internal scale-up job that provisions transient backfill pods in compatible pools using the backfill scheduler (component: backfill-controller). Backfill uses KV-cache warmup and prefix caching policies to avoid cold-start latency.

- The backfill-controller behavior (configuration table):

  | setting | meaning | recommended value |
  |---|---:|---:|
  | backfill_batch_size | number of pipelines migrated in parallel | 4 |
  | kv_cache_warmup_seconds | delay to pre-populate KV cache | 120 |
  | prefer_quantized_variants | whether to use quantized model variants for cost savings | true (if within QA) |

- During each migration step: wait for health checks `runtime_probe` and model-score regression check (automated evals) to pass for 10 minutes. If any fail, the migration must be aborted for that node and marked for manual review.

4) Network and egress considerations

- Ensure cross-subnet MTU is consistent for migrated pods to avoid large-packet fragmentation. Run `ip route get 8.8.8.8` validation on target node before moving traffic.
- If consolidation involves changing NAT gateway allocation, coordinate with cloud-accounts team to pre-allocate EIPs to avoid ephemeral IP churn. Keep at least 2 NAT IPs free in each availability zone during window.

5) Terraform roll and safety switches

- The Terraform change should be applied in two phases: `apply --target=module.backfill-controller` then `apply` for pool reconfiguration. This ensures backfill-controller is live before pools are reduced.
- Maintain a fast rollback job: `terraform apply -var 'skip_consolidation=true'` is a guarded abort pattern. The deployment pipeline exposes an “abort” button to trigger this exact command.

6) CI/CD gating and automation

- All consolidation plans require a successful `consolidation-canary` pipeline run that contains: terraform plan artifact, canary loadgen results (pdf), and post-canary evals (pass/fail).
- The main apply job is gated on oncall approval with a 2-minute auto-abort if not approved. Approval must reference ticket ID and plan SHA.

Oncall runbook (P1 escalation)

- If QUEUE_DEPTH_GROWTH_10m triggers or 99p latency breaches safety threshold: 
  1. Set consolidation feature flag to `off` (fast revert).
  2. Run `backfill-controller scale --auto-heal` to increase backfill capacity by 2x.
  3. If traffic remains degraded after 10 minutes, increase dedicated pool capacity: `terraform apply -target=module.gpu_pool_adjustment -var='extra_nodes=10'`
  4. If rollback fails or Terraform is blocked, open emergency ticket to cloud-accounts and network engineering and assign severity P0.

Manual rollback steps (if automation fails)

- Re-register drained nodes: `kubectl label node <node> consolidate=false` and `python ops/rejoin_node.py --node <id>`
- Reprovision NAT/EIPs via cloud console if Terraform cannot apply. Document manual changes in the change ticket and trigger a reconciliation job later.

Post-event validation and cleanup

- Run a regression eval suite across the top 20 production routes and compare to baseline: allow <5% worsening in token-level metrics. The eval report should be attached to the consolidation ticket.
- Run cost verification job: compare hourly token-cost pre/post for 72 hours. Flag anomalies > 10% for finance review.
- Mark nodes fully decommissioned in asset inventory and update `gpu_inventory.csv` with disposition and tag `reclaimed`.

Runbook ownership and contact list

- Primary owner: eng-infra GPU team (oncall alias: eng-infra-gpu-oncall@redwood.example.com)
- Escalation: Cloud Accounts (cloud-accounts@redwood.example.com), Network Eng (neteng@redwood.example.com)

Postmortem guidance

- If the consolidation causes a P1 incident, a postmortem is required within 72 hours. Include: timeline, preflight checklist state, decision author, rollbacks attempted, metrics (latency/error/queue depth), and a remediation plan to tighten preflight gating.

Appendix: useful commands and PromQL snippets

- List nodes marked for consolidation:
```
kubectl get nodes -l consolidate=true -o wide
```
- Drain one node safely with ops helper:
```
python ops/drain_node.py --node-id i-076abc34 --max-concurrent-migrations 3
```
- Query 99th percentile latency for route `/v1/generate` (last 15m):
```
histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_latency_bucket{route="/v1/generate"}[15m])) by (le))
```
- Check queue growth over 5 minutes:
```
sum(increase(runtime_queue_length[5m]))
```
- Force feature flag off (fast abort):
```
./deploy/featureflagctl set consolidation false --env prod
```

title: dsid_79d24767cd824cfd8e1fbe46d88af5a9__support-sla-vs-engineering-slo-mapping.txt
text:
Support SLA vs Engineering SLO Mapping (Paging Thresholds + Customer Impact)

## Purpose
This page is the reference for how Support SLAs (first response + update cadence) should map to Engineering SLOs (availability/latency) and how paging thresholds should relate to *customer impact*.

This is **not** a contractual SLA document. For contract language and tier-specific coverage windows, refer to: **Customer Success & Support → SLA policy by customer tier**.

**Goals**
- Prevent mismatches where Support promises a cadence that Engineering on-call cannot meet.
- Ensure paging triggers correlate to real customer impact (not only internal “red” alerts).
- Standardize language between Support (Jira priorities P0–P4) and Engineering incident severity (Sev0–Sev3).

---

## Definitions (shared language)
**Support SLA (operational):** Response/update targets used by Support/CS for incident comms and ticket handling. These are constrained by coverage windows and the current incident process.

**Engineering SLO:** Reliability objectives for production services (e.g., request success rate, latency). SLOs drive error budgets and alerting policies.

**Customer impact:** A combination of (a) number of customers affected, (b) tier (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; Enterprise vs self-serve), and (c) degradation type (hard outage vs partial degradation vs “sharp edges”).

**Burn rate alerts:** Alerts that fire when error budget is being consumed quickly (fast burn) or steadily (slow burn). Burn rate is a more reliable paging signal than single-point thresholds.

**Time-to-triage (TTT):** Time from Support intake to a qualified owner engaged with enough context to act.

**Time-to-mitigation (TTM):** Time from detection/escalation to a customer-visible mitigation (rollback, routing change, scaling, workaround, etc.).

---

## Engineering SLOs (what we optimize for)
The exact targets may vary by region/model and are recorded in the SLO registry. The table below describes the *common SLO classes* and how they should inform Support expectations.

| SLO class | Primary metric (examples) | What customers feel | Typical mitigations | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| API availability | Request success rate (2xx/3xx), 5xx rate, auth failure rate | Outage, elevated errors, failed requests | Rollback, capacity shift, routing/fallback, dependency remediation | Availability issues generally justify rapid paging when widespread. |
| API latency | p95/p99 end-to-end latency; queue time; time-to-first-token (TTFT) for streaming | Slow responses, timeouts, UI/app slowness | Scaling, routing, batching controls, rollback, dependency tuning | Latency can be as severe as errors for synchronous apps; focus on duration + breadth. |
| Streaming health | Stream disconnect rate, truncated streams, reconnect loops | “Partial success” but bad UX; repeated retries | Gateway config adjustments, region shift, client guidance | Often appears as “works sometimes”; Support should collect request IDs + client details. |
| Control plane availability (Console/SSO/config) | Login success rate, token exchange, config API availability | Can’t log in, can’t manage keys/routes | Auth/SSO fixes, control plane rollback | Customer impact can be business-critical even if inference plane is healthy. |
| Async pipelines (e.g., audit logs) | Delivery lag (p95/p99), backlog depth, drop rate | Missing/late logs; compliance workflows blocked | Backlog drain, pipeline scaling, temporary export guidance | Typically not “Sev0” unless contractual/compliance deadlines are at risk. |

---

## Support SLAs (how we communicate)
Support SLAs are defined per tier. This mapping focuses on *how to adjust comms* based on Engineering signals and incident posture.

**Key principle:** When Engineering SLO burn indicates a fast-moving incident, Support update cadence should increase and escalation should occur even if an individual ticket is still gathering details.

The tiered SLAs (first response and update cadence) live in: **SLA policy by customer tier**. Support should follow that page for targets; this page clarifies *when to trigger paging and/or raise incident severity*.

---

## Mapping principles (Support SLA ↔ Engineering SLO)
1) **Support cadence must follow incident posture.**
   - If the issue qualifies as an incident (Sev0/Sev1), comms cadence is driven by the incident commander (IC) and comms owner, and Support should align rather than invent a parallel cadence.

2) **Page based on customer impact + burn rate, not “noise.”**
   - A single noisy host or one customer’s unusual traffic pattern should not page SRE without evidence of broader risk.
   - Conversely, a multi-customer degradation with high burn rate should page quickly even if absolute error % seems “small.”

3) **Prioritize actions that reduce TTM for the most customers.**
   - For Hosted: routing/fallback and regional traffic shifts are often the fastest mitigations.
   - For Dedicated: capacity and autoscaling controls are common mitigations.
   - For Private: diagnostics bundle + safe rollback paths reduce time-to-resolution.

4) **Support and Engineering severity must match.**
   - Support P0/P1 should not map to an Engineering Sev2 unless there is a clear reason (e.g., single-customer, self-inflicted, or no platform fault).

---

## Paging thresholds: tying SLOs to customer impact
This section defines recommended paging triggers for SRE/on-call. It is intentionally framed as **policy guidance**, not a rigid rule. Use judgment and document exceptions.

### A. Default paging triggers (broad customer impact)
Page SRE/on-call when *any* of the following is true:
- **Fast-burn SLO alert** fires for Hosted inference in a production region.
- **Multi-customer availability incident**: sustained elevated 5xx/auth failures affecting more than one customer or a material share of traffic in a region.
- **Region-level latency degradation**: sustained p95/p99 latency increase causing customer timeouts or meaningful throughput loss.
- **Streaming health regression**: elevated stream disconnect/truncation rate across multiple customers or across a region.

### B. Tier-weighted paging (Dedicated / Private)
Page the owning on-call (SRE or Platform/Private Deployments per escalation matrix) when:
- **Dedicated:** customer’s reserved capacity is not meeting contracted throughput/latency expectations due to platform-side causes (autoscaling instability, GPU pool churn, cluster issues), especially if customer cannot mitigate by retry/backoff.
- **Private:** upgrade/install failures blocking production usage or compliance obligations, or widespread control plane failures (SSO, key management, audit logs) with documented evidence.

### C. Single-customer escalation (high criticality)
A single enterprise customer can still justify paging when one or more is true:
- The issue blocks a critical workflow (e.g., production launch, compliance deadline) and there is no safe workaround.
- The ticket meets Support P0 criteria and there is evidence the platform is at fault.
- The ticket is likely an early signal of a broader incident (e.g., correlated in time with deploys, region signals, or similar symptoms in other tickets).

---

## Recommended alert posture (burn-rate oriented)
Engineering alerting should align to error budget policy. Support should understand what these alerts imply about urgency.

**Fast burn (page):** indicates we are on track to violate the SLO quickly (minutes to an hour). Support should treat this as P0/P1 depending on breadth.

**Slow burn (page during supported hours; consider after-hours based on tier/impact):** indicates sustained degradation that will consume significant budget over several hours.

**Example (conceptual):**
- Fast burn: consuming ~2% of monthly error budget in 1 hour
- Slow burn: consuming ~5% of monthly error budget in 6 hours

Support guidance:
- If Engineering declares Sev0/Sev1, **Support update cadence** should match the incident comms plan and be explicitly stated in customer emails.
- If a slow burn is detected but customers are not yet reporting, Support should prepare macros and proactively monitor incoming tickets.

---

## Mapping table: Support priority → Engineering signals → paging + comms
Use this table during triage and when deciding to page.

| Support priority | Typical customer impact | Engineering signals to look for | Paging expectation | Support comms expectation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0 | Hard outage / widespread inability to use product; severe revenue or compliance risk | Fast-burn availability alert; broad 5xx/auth failures; region down; major routing failure | Page immediately; start Slack bridge; move to #incidents when criteria met | Acknowledge fast; frequent updates; align with IC; avoid speculation; share mitigations/workarounds when validated |
| P1 | Major degradation; partial outage; many customers affected or one enterprise blocked | Elevated latency/timeouts; streaming disconnect spike; slow-burn turning into fast-burn | Page quickly if sustained; otherwise engage on-call via escalation path | Set update cadence explicitly; include what we’re measuring and next checkpoint |
| P2 | Limited degradation; workaround exists; smaller blast radius | Localized metrics; no burn-rate alerts; isolated region/model | Do not page by default; escalate via owning team queue; page if trend worsens | Provide workaround; define “when to escalate” conditions; request required diagnostics |
| P3 | Minor issue; product question; no service risk | No abnormal metrics | No paging | Macro-driven response; doc links |
| P4 | Informational / enhancement request | N/A | No paging | Route to product/feedback |

Notes:
- A P1 that is clearly caused by customer misconfiguration should not be escalated as an Engineering incident, but Support should still help the customer quickly.
- If Support is uncertain whether impact is broad, treat as **P1 with a short investigation window** (e.g., 15–30 minutes) and page if evidence suggests multi-customer impact.

---

## Symptom-driven guidance: what to collect before paging
On-call efficiency depends on Support providing consistent context. Before paging, collect what you can without blocking escalation.

**Minimum required context (copy/paste):**
- Product/tier: Hosted / Dedicated / Private (+ region)
- API surface: chat/generate/embeddings/rerank/console/audit logs
- Model + version (and whether pinned)
- Time window (UTC) + first observed time
- Request IDs / trace IDs (at least 3 examples)
- Error codes/messages or latency percentiles as observed by customer
- Any recent customer-side changes (SDK version, proxy changes, retries)
- Any observed mitigations tried (retries/backoff, region switch, smaller batches)

If the issue is streaming-related, include:
- Transport details (HTTP/1.1 vs HTTP/2; proxy/CDN; keepalive settings)
- Client language/SDK version
- Whether failures correlate with long generations or specific token counts

---

## How Support SLAs should track Engineering SLO state
### 1) When Engineering declares an incident
- Support should **stop using generic SLA language** and instead use the incident cadence (e.g., “next update in 30 minutes”).
- Support should link the bridge channel + incident ID in Jira (SUP ticket) and keep comms consistent with the status page guidance.

### 2) When there is degradation but no incident declared (yet)
- Use P1/P2 and set an explicit checkpoint: “We are investigating and will update you by <time>.”
- If Engineering signals show burn-rate risk increasing, escalate to incident posture.

### 3) When an incident is resolved but customer symptoms persist
- Treat as a new investigation unless clearly tied to known residual impact.
- Collect fresh request IDs and confirm region/model.

---

## Examples (common scenarios)
### Example A: Elevated 429s / quota confusion
- If metrics show stable availability but ticket volume spikes and headers appear inconsistent, treat as **P2** (workaround + investigation).
- Page only if there is evidence of platform-side enforcement misclassification affecting multiple customers.
- Support should link the relevant known-issue article and capture header samples.

### Example B: Streaming resets in a single region
- If multiple customers report stream disconnects and streaming-health metrics spike, treat as **P1 → page quickly**.
- If only one customer reports and no metrics show impact, treat as **P2 with a short investigation window**; page if additional evidence appears.

### Example C: Audit log delivery lag
- If lag exceeds documented expectations and affects enterprise compliance workflows, treat as **P1** (even if inference plane is healthy).
- Page Platform/SRE depending on ownership; align comms to expected delivery windows and provide temporary export/retry guidance if validated.

---

## Ownership and escalation alignment
- Follow the **Escalation paths and contacts** directory for who to page by product area.
