title: dsid_89682c439a1b44ecb75df18ee8d6b4f0__streaming-fidelity-negotiation-prd-2029-07-12.txt
text:
streaming-fidelity-negotiation-prd-2029-07-12

Overview
========

This PRD defines Streaming Fidelity Negotiation: a product capability for dynamically negotiating output fidelity versus latency/cost when serving streaming generation requests to client applications. The feature enables clients and the Redwood serving plane to agree on per-request fidelity levels (e.g., full-fidelity, low-fidelity draft, token-skim) at request time and to gracefully degrade or improve fidelity mid-stream based on real-time capacity, burst policies, and tenant SLOs.

Background and motivation
-------------------------

Customers increasingly use streaming generations in low-latency experiences (chat, code assistance, IDE autocompletion). However, fixed-fidelity models either cause high per-token cost or miss latency targets. Current options (model switching, pre-quantized variants) are coarse and happen at request boundaries. Streaming Fidelity Negotiation reduces user-facing latency and cost by:

- Allowing client and server to express acceptable fidelity ranges per request.
- Enabling mid-stream fidelity transitions when resource signals or QoS policies require it.
- Preserving a clear API contract so client SDKs can render partial outputs appropriately.

Objectives (must-have)
----------------------

1. Provide a stable, documented API for clients to request a fidelity profile when calling the streaming generation endpoint.
2. Enable the server to signal fidelity transitions mid-stream with minimal protocol changes.
3. Ensure fidelity transitions are observable in Console (per-request fidelity timeline, token-level cost estimate).
4. Maintain SLOs: median tail latency (p95) for low-fidelity requests must remain <= 150ms per token for typical short-turn workloads.

Non-goals
---------

- Automatic rewriting of prompts to match fidelity (clients must opt-in or provide fallback renderers).
- Changing model semantics beyond predicted quality trade-offs (no unsupervised content transformations).

Primary user personas and user stories
------------------------------------

- Product engineers (web/mobile)
  - "As a frontend engineer, I want to request a draft (low-fidelity) stream for quick previews and then request refinement only when the user commits, so initial latency is minimal."

- Platform/ML infra
  - "As an infra engineer, I want the serving runtime to downshift fidelity under heavy load to preserve global latency SLOs and to record the events for billing reconciliation."

- Customer success / enterprise admins
  - "As an enterprise admin, I want an SLO-driven policy that prevents fidelity degradation below a contractual floor for high-tier customers."

Functional requirements
-----------------------

Req-F1: Fidelity profile in API
- Description: Streaming generation API must accept a fidelity_profile object with the following attributes: {min_fidelity, target_fidelity, max_latency_budget_ms, allow_midstream_transition: bool}.
- Priority: P0
- Owner: API and SDK teams

Req-F2: Server-initiated fidelity change events
- Description: Server shall emit a standardized mid-stream event (EVENT:FIDELITY_CHANGE) with fields {previous_fidelity, new_fidelity, reason_code, effective_token_index}.
- Priority: P0
- Owner: Serving runtime team

Req-F3: Client SDK support and rendering guidance
- Description: Official JavaScript and Python SDKs must expose hooks for fidelity events and provide UI guidance for mid-stream render transitions.
- Priority: P1
- Owner: Developer Experience

Req-F4: Policy engine integration
- Description: Policy engine must be able to evaluate per-request signals (tenant tier, lane, current cluster CPU/GPU utilization, queued tokens) and decide to request/signal fidelity transitions.
- Priority: P0
- Owner: Routing & Policy

Req-F5: Billing and observability flags
- Description: All streams must include token-level fidelity metadata so Console and billing can attribute cost. Metadata: fidelity_label, effective_variant_id, transition_history.
- Priority: P0
- Owner: Console & Billing

Non-functional requirements
---------------------------

- NF1: Latency impact: p95 token latency for low-fidelity requests should not exceed 1.5x baseline p95 for equivalent short turns.
- NF2: Transition overhead: Emitting a fidelity change event must add <= 5ms median overhead to the streaming pipeline.
- NF3: Backwards compatibility: If a client does not include fidelity_profile, behavior defaults to target_fidelity = full-fidelity (current behavior).

API contract (summary)
---------------------

Endpoint: POST /v1/streams/generate
Request body (JSON):
```json
{
  "model": "redwood-3b-stream",
  "prompt": "Summarize the quarterly goals...",
  "stream": true,
  "fidelity_profile": {
    "min_fidelity": "draft",
    "target_fidelity": "balanced",
    "max_latency_budget_ms": 300,
    "allow_midstream_transition": true
  }
}
```

Server event sequence (example wire events):
- DATA: token chunk (fidelity_label: draft)
- EVENT:FIDELITY_CHANGE {"previous_fidelity":"draft","new_fidelity":"balanced","reason_code":"CAPACITY_PRESSURE","effective_token_index":12}
- DATA: token chunk (fidelity_label: balanced)

Fidelity taxonomy (example labels)
- draft — lowest compute path, lighter sampling, more aggressive top-k/top-p truncation.
- balanced — default production tradeoff for cost/quality.
- full — highest fidelity (longer context, temperature adjustments, ensemble/decoder variants).

SLOs, metrics and dashboards
----------------------------

Minimum metrics to implement prior to rollout:
- Median token latency by fidelity (per model): gauge
- p95 token latency by fidelity: alert on > 1.5x baseline
- Fraction of streams that experienced mid-stream fidelity transition: gauge
- Fidelity transition reasons breakdown (capacity, policy, tenant request): timeseries
- Cost delta per request attributed to fidelity (estimated per-token cost): histogram

Suggested SLOs:
- p95 token latency for balanced streams <= 200ms
- p95 token latency for draft streams <= 150ms
- Fidelity-transition event delivery success >= 99.9%

Rollout plan and feature gates
------------------------------

1. Canary (internal) — feature enabled for Redwood internal tenants and 2 pilot customers. Duration: 2 weeks.
2. Pilot customers — onboard 5-10 customers (customer success and solutions engineering manage). Duration: 4 weeks.
3. Gradual GA — traffic ramp in five steps (5%, 20%, 50%, 80%, 100%) with automated rollback on SLO/regression triggers.

Gate checks before each ramp:
- No fidelity-transition-related errors > 0.1% of streams.
- Observability metrics within expected ranges for p95 latency.
- Billing attribution present for all pilot streams.

Compatibility and migration notes
--------------------------------

- Backwards compatibility: clients not specifying fidelity_profile will see unchanged behavior.
- SDK upgrade: new SDK versions will expose fidelity hooks; server will accept legacy clients.

Operational playbook (how to investigate a migration-induced fidelity drop)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identify affected tenant(s) via Console: filter by fidelity_label and increased error/latency.
2. Check event logs for EVENT:FIDELITY_CHANGE reason_code. Common codes: CAPACITY_PRESSURE, POLICY_ENFORCED, TENANT_FLOOR_OVERRIDE.
3. If CAPACITY_PRESSURE is frequent: check cluster utilization dashboards, scale capacity or adjust batching parameters.
4. If POLICY_ENFORCED: review policy engine logs and recent rule changes.
5. Reproduce in staging: send synthetic streams with fidelity_profile and observe transitions.

Ownership and stakeholders
-------------------------

- Product lead: Ava Martinez
- Technical lead: Liam Chen (Serving runtime)
- API/SDK owner: Developer Experience (Maya Patel)
- Policy & routing: Diego Ramos
- Console & Billing: Nora Singh

Dependencies
------------

- Serving runtime: support for fidelity-labeled execution paths and in-pipeline event emission (runtime ticket: RT-3147).
- Policy engine: ability to evaluate real-time metrics and emit transition commands (policy ticket: PL-2201).
- Console: new fidelity timeline visualization (console ticket: CN-4440).
- Billing: token-level fidelity metadata ingestion and cost attribution (billing ticket: BL-758).

Open questions and tradeoffs
---------------------------

- Q1: Should fidelity profiles be expressed as continuous budgets (e.g., scaled float) rather than categorical labels? Tradeoff: finer-grained control vs. complexity for SDKs and observability.
- Q2: How do fidelity transitions interact with function/tool calling and structured outputs? Need to ensure consistency when switching mid-stream.
- Q3: Are there model classes where mid-stream transition is not safe (long-running internal state)? We need to catalog model compatibility.

Appendix: Example Console timeline (text)
---------------------------------------

Request ID: req_20290712_0001
- 00ms: request received (fidelity_profile: draft -> balanced)
- 10ms: stream started, tokens label=draft
- 110ms: EVENT:FIDELITY_CHANGE {reason: CAPACITY_PRESSURE, new_fidelity=balanced}
- 140ms: continue tokens label=balanced
- Billing: estimated cost saved vs full = 35%

Notes
-----
- This PRD intentionally focuses on streaming; non-streaming batch generation fidelity negotiation will be covered in a follow-up requirements doc.
- Implementation must prioritize observability and billing correctness to avoid disputes over billed resources.

References
----------
- Quality gates and observability contract (design-specs): /confluence/product-docs/design-specs/quality-gates-and-observability-contract-spec-2027-04-05
- Interactive inference playground PRD: /confluence/product-docs/requirements/interactive-inference-playground-prd-2028-02-15

Approval
--------

- Product: Ava Martinez (pending)
- Technical: Liam Chen (pending)
- Security review: required if fidelity signaling exposes tenant-level details (TBD).

title: dsid_a6d49acdf1214a719ef7b05f31f55c33__traffic-continuity-scorer-and-notification-contract-2026.txt
text:
Traffic Continuity Scorer and Notification Contract — Operator Handbook

Overview
========

Purpose: define the Traffic Continuity Scorer (TCS), the dashboard and alerting contract for continuity degradations, and the operator notification and triage runbook. The TCS is a single composite signal used by platform operators and downstream teams to prioritize incidents that threaten customer request continuity (e.g., token loss, model swap failures, long tail latency, partial response streams). This doc is the canonical contract for dashboards, alert rules, and runbook steps across regions.

Why we need it
---------------
- Multiple distinct symptoms (latency, 5xxs, stream truncation, model-swap misfires) historically generated noisy, disconnected alerts.
- Operators and SREs need a single, interpretable priority signal that balances severity and customer-perceived continuity.
- TCS enables consistent automation for short-circuit fallbacks and informs canary rollbacks.

Scope and boundaries
--------------------
- Applies to all hosted inference frontends and regional gateways that feed into the request routing plane.
- Not intended for batch jobs or offline ingestion pipelines.
- Each tenant, route, and region gets an independently computed TCS (scoped slices).

Design summary
--------------
1) Inputs (sampled per 1m):
   - request_success_rate (2xx/total)
   - token_deliveries_per_request (median and p90 of successfully emitted tokens)
   - long_tail_latency (p99 request duration for foreground requests)
   - model_swap_success_rate (percentage of model swap ops completed within 15s)
   - stream_close_aborts (count of client stream terminations classified as platform-initiated)

2) Normalization and weights (default):
   - request_success_rate -> 35% importance
   - token_deliveries_per_request -> 25% importance
   - long_tail_latency -> 20% importance
   - model_swap_success_rate -> 15% importance
   - stream_close_aborts -> 5% importance

3) Scoring function (interpretable 0–100):
   - Each input is mapped to a 0–100 subscore using monotonic transforms (higher = better).
   - Weighted sum gives final TCS (0 worst continuity — 100 perfect continuity).

Operational thresholds
----------------------
- Green: TCS >= 90 — normal
- Watch: 75 <= TCS < 90 — operator awareness, investigate if persistent 
- Degraded: 50 <= TCS < 75 — start mitigation (prefetch fallback, model variant swap)
- Critical: TCS < 50 — automatic escalation and region-level traffic shedding policies may be invoked

Dashboard contract
------------------
Every region/operator dashboard tile must include:
- Live TCS timeseries (1m resolution, 1h/6h/24h zoom)
- Breakdown bar chart of subscore contributions (requests, tokens, latency, swaps, streams)
- Tenant heatmap (top 50 tenants by query volume) annotated with current TCS slice and alerts
- Top 10 impacted routes and recent model-swap events

Suggested Grafana panels (panel queries are PromQL examples using our metric names):
- TCS (1m):
  sum by(region)(traffic_continuity_scorer{job="frontier"})
- Request success component (30s):
  100 * sum(successful_requests{job="frontier"}) / sum(total_requests{job="frontier"})
- Token delivery median (1m):
  histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(tokens_emitted_bucket[1m])) by (le, region))

Alerting contract and example alert rules
---------------------------------------
Alerting must follow this pattern: a Watch alert (paged to oncall) is fired at Watch threshold; a Degraded alert triggers an Incident (Slack+PagerDuty); Critical triggers regional oncall escalation and automated protective actions. Attach the TCS slice with the alert.

Prometheus alert example (YAML-like pseudocode):

- alert: TCS_WATCH_Region_eu-west-1
  expr: traffic_continuity_scorer{region="eu-west-1"} < 75 and traffic_continuity_scorer{region="eu-west-1"} >= 50
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: warning
    runbook: /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/regional-traffic-continuity-triage-runbook-2026
  annotations:
    summary: "TCS Watch in eu-west-1: {{ $value }}"

- alert: TCS_CRITICAL_Region_eu-west-1
  expr: traffic_continuity_scorer{region="eu-west-1"} < 50
  for: 2m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "TCS Critical in eu-west-1 — consider traffic shedding and automatic fallback"

Notification routing rules (contract):
- Watch -> Slack #platform-watch + email to platform-ops (no page)
- Degraded -> PagerDuty on-call for region (page), Slack incident channel created automatically
- Critical -> PagerDuty P1 flow (page + escalation), notify Product-Integrity and Customer Success if impacted tenants > 5

Runbook: operator triage checklist (ordered)
------------------------------------------------
1) Acknowledge alert and attach TCS slice and top-5 contributing subsignals.
2) Confirm scope (tenant-scoped? route-scoped? region-wide?). Use query: "traffic_continuity_scorer{route=~\"^api/.*\"}"
3) Check model-swap pipeline: exports/model-swap-events{region} for errors in last 15m. If >5 failed swaps, mark model_subsystem as suspect.
4) If long_tail_latency is primary contributor, examine recent GC / kernel/queueing events on affected nodes (node-level p99 duration dashboards).
5) If token_deliveries_per_request dropped: verify KV-prefix-cache hit rates and edge buffer backpressure metrics.
6) Apply mitigation in order of least-impactful first: increase warmset prefetch, switch to compatible lower-memory variant, enable prefix-kv-cache-read-only mode, apply tenant soft-throttle.
7) If automatic mitigation fails within 10 minutes and TCS < 50: execute region-level fallback (shift low-priority traffic to secondary region and enable model-variant fallback).
8) Post-incident: attach timeline, root-cause hypothesis and changes to the incident ticket and tag the TCS snapshot to the incident for future regressions.

Escalation and ownership
------------------------
- First responder: regional platform oncall (team: Platform-Operators).
- Secondary: Serving Runtime oncall if model-swap or kernel-level issues are implicated.
- Tertiary: Platform Engineering Pager if automated fallback fails to restore TCS in 20m.

Runbook templates and automation suggestions
------------------------------------------
- Use the incident commander CLI to capture the current TCS slice: `./inc-tools capture-tcs --region eu-west-1 --window 15m`
- Automate TCS gated runbooks as step functions with manual approvals for region-level fallbacks. The automation should expose a dry-run to estimate impact.

Retrospective and metricization guidance
---------------------------------------
- For each TCS-triggered incident, the owner must produce a short retrospective within 7 days including:
  1) TCS time-series snapshot (1h before, during, 2h after)
  2) Top-3 contributing subsignals and operator mitigations tried
  3) Regression test to prevent reoccurrence (add to preflight and synthetic checks)

- Suggested follow-ups: add a synthetic continuity test to the degradation lab that simulates token truncation and model-swap failures; track mean-time-to-recover (MTTR) from TCS_Degraded -> TCS_Green as a KPI.

Appendix: example SQL and PromQL snippets
----------------------------------------
- Tenant heatmap SQL (ClickHouse-like):
  SELECT tenant_id, avg(tcs) as avg_tcs, count(1) as qps
  FROM platform_metrics.traffic_continuity_scorer
  WHERE region = 'us-east-1' AND ts >= now() - interval 1 hour
  GROUP BY tenant_id
  ORDER BY avg_tcs ASC
  LIMIT 50;

- PromQL example: combined subscore breakdown:
  sum by (region) (
    0.35 * (100 * sum(successful_requests) / sum(total_requests))
    + 0.25 * (histogram_quantile(0.5, sum(rate(tokens_emitted_bucket[1m])) by (le)))
    + 0.2 * (100 - (100 * (increase(request_duration_seconds_bucket{le=\"0.5\"}[5m]) / increase(request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))))
  )

Related work and references
--------------------------
- This doc references and extends the platform prioritization and restoration canvas. See: /confluence/eng-platform/systems-and-services/operational-restoration-prioritization-canvas-2026
- For model-swap pipeline guidance refer to the Serving Runtime model-swap operator handbook.

Open questions and roadmap items
--------------------------------
- Automating TCS weight calibration using regression alerts and customer impact labels (Q2 2026).
- Exposing tenant-level TCS alerts to large-enterprise customers with opt-in SLA notifications (privacy and tenancy gating work required).

Contact and ownership
---------------------
- Document owner: Ava Rodriguez (Platform Reliability) — ava@redwood.example.com
- Operational contact: platform-operators@redwood.example.com

Change log
----------
- 2026-01-12: initial draft and rollout to EU region dashboards.
- 2026-02-18: updated weights and runbook step ordering after Q1 gamma trial.

title: dsid_6b62c4ece0b745d0bd35bd2892a5714e__oncall-capacity-forecasting-and-escalation-simulator-guide-2024.txt
text:
On-call capacity forecasting and escalation simulator guide

Overview

This guide defines a repeatable process for: 1) forecasting on-call staffing and GPU/serving capacity for expected traffic and failure modes, and 2) running an automated escalation simulator (a tabletop + synthetic incident harness) to validate escalation paths, runbooks, and SLO-restoration timelines. The playbook is intended for SREs, service owners, and on-call engineers who operate Redwood's inference platform.

Goals
- Produce a 13-week on-call staffing plan tied to service-level objectives (SLOs) and forecasted traffic.
- Validate that escalation policies and first-response runbooks meet the expected mean-time-to-ack (MTTA) and mean-time-to-restore (MTTR) under simulated stress.
- Provide a reproducible simulator that triggers synthetic incidents (latency spikes, cache evictions, quota storms) and exercises paging, bridge formation, and customer communication flows.

Scope
- Applied to production Redwood hosted and Dedicated control plane services and the inference routing mesh.
- Excludes detailed per-customer remediation steps for Private deployments (use customer-specific runbooks stored under eng-private-deployments).

Ownership and cadence
- Primary owner: Eng SRE (team lead: Priya Nambiar).
- Quarterly forecasting cadence: every quarter the SRE and capacity-planning owner run the forecasting model and publish staffing recommendations.
- Simulation cadence: Monthly automated game-day run + ad-hoc pre-release simulations for large infra changes.

Key inputs and signals
- Historical traffic: token/sec, requests/sec per model/version (13 weeks window preferred).
- Spike templates: 2x, 5x, 10x baseline traffic profiles per tenant class.
- Failure modes: single-region outage, KV-cache mass-eviction, GPU pool degradation (50% capacity), routing-controller lag.
- On-call constraints: max weekly shifts per engineer, paired rotation rules, escalation windows.

Forecasting model: high-level description
1) Baseline computation
   - Aggregate 13-week median and 95th percentile for requests/sec and tokens/sec per service route.
   - Compute rolling growth: week-over-week linear and exponential fits; expose high/median/low growth scenarios.
2) Capacity unit conversions
   - Convert requests/sec to GPU capacity units using benchmarked tokens/sec per GPU for the most common model families (gpt-*-8bit, llama2-13b-quant).
   - Add 25% overhead for autoscaling buffer and headroom for burst scaling.
3) Staffing need estimate
   - Derive operational headcount requirement from capacity units: one on-call rotation pod can reliably oversee X GPUs and Y services (configurable per team).
   - Adjust for scheduled releases, holidays, and hiring gaps.

Forecasting output: example table
|| Metric || Low scenario || Baseline (median) || High (95p) ||
| Projected avg tokens/sec | 120k | 210k | 380k |
| GPUs required (model-avg) | 15 | 27 | 49 |
| On-call pods required | 2 | 4 | 7 |
| Recommended reserve buffer | 10% | 25% | 35% |

Interpreting the table
- Use the baseline column for staffing commitments under normal conditions. High scenario informs hiring or short-term capacity leases for dedicated pools.

Escalation simulator: architecture and components
- Simulator repo: git@redwood:infra/oncall-escalation-sim.git (owner: eng-sre).
- Components:
  - Incident injector: creates synthetic alerts (PagerDuty events or internal alert bus messages) and synthetic SLO breaches via the observability test harness.
  - Load generator: produces traffic profiles to the serving runtime (uses internal locust-based templates).
  - Pager bridge: a test namespace integrated with the real PagerDuty and Slack channels in staging (isolated routing rules).
  - Orchestration runner: a workflow that runs a scenario, waits for acknowledgements, measures times, and records artifacts (logs, traces, recordings).

Simulator configuration table (common parameters)
|| Parameter || Description || Example ||
| scenario_name | Friendly scenario id | kv-cache-eviction-mass |
| traffic_multiplier | How many x baseline to send | 5 |
| failure_duration_sec | Duration of synthetic failure | 900 |
| expected_ack_window_sec | Expected MTTA in runbook | 300 |
| slack_channel_override | Channel to post ephemeral test notices | #ops-game-day |
| pd_dedup_key | External dedup key used by PD for this run | sim-2025-02-10-01 |

Running a monthly simulation (step-by-step)
1) Prepare environment (runbook owner, simulation lead, observers)
   - Assign roles: Incident lead, Bridge operator, Customer comms writer, Evidence collector.
   - Notify affected teams: post a 48-hour pre-notice in #ops-game-day and calendar block.
2) Start background load generator
   - CLI example: "rdw-sim load --profile kv-eviction-5x --duration 1800s --target serving-frontend.staging.redwood.internal"
3) Trigger incident injection
   - CLI example: "rdw-sim inject --scenario kv-cache-eviction-mass --pd-key sim-2025-02-10-01"
4) Measure escalation path
   - The orchestration runner captures: alert fired timestamp, pager sent, pager acknowledged, bridge created timestamp, first remediation action, and service restore timestamp.
5) Execute customer comms run through
   - Use the templates below to publish staged status updates and observe approval/clearance workflow.
6) Evidence collection and artifact upload
   - The runner uploads logs and timelines to /evidence/simulations/<sim-id>/ and creates a confluence summary stub automatically using the post-simulation hook.
7) Retro and action items
   - The simulation lead runs a 60-minute retro with assigned action owners and opens follow-ups in the incident backlog.

Acceptance criteria (what success looks like)
- SLO targets hit: MTTA <= 5 minutes for Sev-1, MTTR <= 30 minutes for canonical recoverable incidents (exclusions for multi-region outage which may be longer).
- Runbook valid: first responder follows documented sequence with no manual knowledge gaps observed.
- Paging reliability: pager delivery rate > 99% and acknowledgement rate > 90% within expected_ack_window.
- Customer comms: staged status update approved within 10 minutes of bridge creation.

Runbook health checks and pruning policy
- After each simulation, mark runbooks with one of: pass / needs-update / deprecated.
- Quarterly runbook sweep: owners must re-validate and sign-off. If owner does not respond within 14 days, runbook is flagged for escalation to the service steward.

Templates and CLI snippets
- Bridge creation (manual):
  1) Slack: /bridge create --service serving-frontend --severity Sev1 --owner @oncall-frontend
  2) PagerDuty: create incident with tag:sim-<id>, include runbook link.
- Sample customer status (initial):
  Subject: Redwood inference: elevated latency for generation API in region us-west-2
  Body: We are investigating increased latency impacting text generation calls to the public API in us-west-2. Engineers have opened an incident and are actively investigating. We will update every 15 minutes or when we have a meaningful change.
- Sample customer status (restored):
  Subject: Service restored: text generation latency back to expected levels in us-west-2
  Body: The issue has been mitigated and latency has returned to normal. Root cause analysis is in progress and we will publish a post-incident summary within 72 hours if this was a Sev-1 incident.

Evidence capture checklist (simulation + real incident)
- Timestamps: alert fired, pager sent, acked, bridge created, first deploy/rollback, restore.
- Artifacts: trace links, top N logs, autoscaler decision events, GPU utilization charts, KV-cache eviction logs, PD incident export.
- Ownership notes: incident lead, bridge operator, comms writer, follow-up assignee.

Common simulation scenarios (recommended starter set)
1) KV-cache mass-eviction + 5x traffic burst (duration 15m)
2) Routing-controller lag causing 30% request requeues (duration 20m)
3) GPU pool partial failure: 50% of GPUs offline in a region during peak (duration 25m)
4) Quota storm: single-tenant misconfiguration leading to noisy neighbor effects (duration 30m)

Data and metric dashboards to review post-sim
- SLO dashboard: MTTA/MTTR by service and by severity
- Cost dashboard: GPU-hours consumed during simulation and autoscaler actions
- Alert fidelity: alert volume, alert-to-incident conversion rate, false positive count

Post-simulation deliverables
- Simulation summary confluence page (auto-generated): scenario, timeline, measured metrics, artifacts links, action items with owners and due dates.
- Action tracking: create JIRA tickets for any remediation that requires code, infra, or runbook updates.
- Runbook update: owner must update runbook within 7 days or enter the runbook retirement process.

Appendix: quick checklist for on-call managers before quarterly forecast
- Confirm growth signals from product and usage analytics teams.
- Re-run capacity conversion benchmarks for the most used models (if new model family onboarded, include its profile).
- Verify hiring plan and contractor reserve for the forecast horizon.
- Schedule calendar windows for monthly simulations and ensure PD/Slack test namespaces are configured.

Contacts and escalation matrix
- Eng SRE lead: Priya Nambiar (priya@redwood.ai)
- Capacity planning owner: Diego Alvarez (diego@redwood.ai)
- Ops game-day coordinator: Hannah Lee (hannah@redwood.ai)

Related resources
- /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/capacity-modeling-2024
- /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbook-library-index
- /git/infra/oncall-escalation-sim

Change log
