title: dsid_569f5758f70f47cca70de64a5011ff92__gpu-checkpoint-bandwidth-gating-and-replication-runbook.txt
text:
GPU checkpoint bandwidth gating and replication runbook

Summary
-------
This runbook documents the operational procedure, Terraform/IaC patterns, CI/CD hooks, and monitoring/alerting for controlled replication of large model checkpoints across regions and accounts. It focuses on bandwidth gating (egress shaping), cost containment, replication correctness, and safe rollback on failures. Use this when moving model artifacts between regions, performing cross-region backup, or seeding private deployments.

When to use
-----------
- Scheduled cross-region checkpoint replication (nightly or weekly).
- On-demand snapshot seeding for private/on-prem deployments.
- Disaster-recovery copy to warm standby region.
- Large checkpoint promotion during model release (non-production window recommended).

Background and goals
--------------------
- Large checkpoints (tens to thousands of GB) can spike egress & saturate inter-region links. Uncontrolled transfers cause noisy neighbors and billing surprises.
- Goals: predictable egress cost, minimal impact to latency-sensitive inference traffic, retryable and observable transfers, and Terraform-managed configuration for repeatability.

Key SLOs and thresholds
-----------------------
- Replication correctness: 100% checksums match for all checkpoints copied (mandatory).
- Completion SLO (small): 95% of <500GB checkpoints complete within 2 hours.
- Completion SLO (large): 90% of 500GB-2TB checkpoints complete within 8 hours.
- Egress budget per account/region: default 1 TB/day (billing guardrails apply).
- QoS guard: background replication limited to 200 Mbps sustained per node by default; burst up to 1 Gbps allowed during low-inference windows.

Architecture and components
---------------------------
- Source store: S3-compatible buckets (hosted or on-prem object store).
- Replication controller: Kubernetes Job driven by the replication-operator. Operator accepts a Replication CRD with bandwidthQuota, schedule, and verifyChecksums flags.
- Egress shaping: egress-sideband rate limiter implemented as a sidecar (tc-based) or host-level CNI egress policy (egress-operator).
- Billing guard: Terraform-managed quotas + cloud billing alerting (daily usage anomaly detector).
- CI/CD integration: Promotion pipeline triggers a replication task in a non-production window with a canary followed by bulk copies.

Runbook: pre-flight checklist
----------------------------
1. Validate ownership and approvals
   - Confirm owner (see Ownership section). Confirm cost center and approve egress estimate.
2. Check current egress budget
   - Query billing dashboard and ensure budget has room for planned transfer.
3. Identify checkpoint size and retention policy
   - Use artifact-store metadata to determine bytes and expected runtime.
4. Pick time window: prefer low-inference window (00:00–04:00 PT) for large transfers.
5. Prepare CRD payload (sample below) and IaC changes if adjusting quotas.
6. Notify impacted teams on #infra-egress-alerts channel.

Runbook: execution steps (operator path)
-------------------------------------
1. Canary copy (small slice)
   - Create a Replication CRD with: bandwidthQuota=50Mbps, verifyChecksums=true, objectList=canary-list.
   - Apply: kubectl apply -f canary-replication.yaml
   - Wait for completion and verify checksums and telemetry (see Monitoring).
2. Safe bulk run
   - If canary passes, create bulk CRD with gradual ramp: bandwidthQuota=200Mbps, schedule with linear ramp to 1Gbps in off-peak window.
   - Apply CRD and annotate with git commit and runbook run-id.
3. Continuous verification
   - Operator will stream per-object success/failure to /metrics and a replication-log object in the destination bucket.
   - Failure policy: 3 automatic retries at exponential backoff; after that, alert and pause.
4. Post-replication validation
   - Run manifest checksum diff: aws s3api head-object / md5sum checks.
   - Ensure retention lifecycle metadata preserved.

Runbook: manual rollback and mitigation
-------------------------------------
1. If replication causes production impact (inference latency rises > 10% P99):
   - Pause replication: kubectl patch replication <id> -p '{"spec":{"paused":true}}'
   - Reduce global egress throttle via egress-operator: set globalLimit to 300Mbps.
   - Open incident and page infra-oncall.
2. If transfer stalls with checksum mismatches:
   - Mark failed objects and run targeted retransfer with verifyChecksums=true.
   - If repeated failures, escalate to storage team and preserve logs/artifacts.

Terraform / IaC patterns
-----------------------
- Principle: all egress quotas, billing alerts, and replication operator configuration must be managed through Terraform modules in infra-repo.
- Minimal recommended module outputs/inputs:
  - inputs: account_id, region, egress_daily_limit_gb, default_bandwidth_mbps, billing_alert_threshold_pct
  - outputs: quota_id, billing_alert_id, operator_config_map_name

Sample Terraform snippet (declarative quota)
```hcl
module "replication_egress_quota" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/internal-terraform-modules//egress-quota"
  account_id = "123456789012"
  region = "us-west-2"
  egress_daily_limit_gb = 1024
  default_bandwidth_mbps = 200
  billing_alert_threshold_pct = 80
}
```

Sample Replication CRD (canary)
```yaml
apiVersion: replication.redwood.com/v1
kind: Replication
metadata:
  name: canary-checkpoint-2026-02
spec:
  source: s3://checkpoints-prod/models/resnet50/2026-02-01
  destination: s3://checkpoints-usw-backup/models/resnet50/2026-02-01
  bandwidthQuotaMbps: 50
  verifyChecksums: true
  schedule: immediate
  retryPolicy:
    retries: 3
    backoffSeconds: 60
```

CI/CD integration
-----------------
- Promotion pipeline steps:
  1. Create canary artifact list and run canary replication job via kubectl or API.
  2. On success, mutate Terraform variable (if necessary) and trigger bulk replication job via a pipeline step.
  3. Post-run, publish replication manifest artifact into the release bucket and tag release branches.
- Example (Buildkite step):
  - run: ./scripts/trigger-replication --crd=bulk-replication.yaml --dry-run=false

Monitoring, telemetry and alerts
-------------------------------
- Metrics to track (Prometheus):
  - replication_bytes_transferred_total (labels: account, region, checkpoint_id)
  - replication_active_jobs
  - replication_object_failures_total
  - egress_bytes_by_account_daily
  - inference_p99_latency_by_node (to detect noisy neighbor impact)
- Alerting rules:
  - replication_object_failures_total > 5 within 10m -> pager to infra-oncall (SEV-2).
  - egress_bytes_by_account_daily > egress_quota * 0.9 -> email + Slack to cost-owners.
  - inference_p99_latency_by_node increases > 10% relative to 1h baseline during replication -> autoscale replication down and page SRE.

Monitoring queries (Grafana/PromQL)
- Bandwidth used per replication:
  sum(rate(replication_bytes_transferred_total[5m])) by (checkpoint_id)
- Egress budget remaining:
  egress_quota_gb - sum(increase(egress_bytes_by_account_daily[1d]))

Operational ownership and escalation
----------------------------------
- Replication operator maintainers: eng-infra/gpu-storage (primary).
- Oncall: infra-oncall rotation (primary).
- Escalate to storage infra lead (Meera Patel) after 30m for SEV-2 or 15m for SEV-1.

Post-incident and RCA guidance
-----------------------------
- Collect: replication logs, operator pod logs, egress-operator snapshot, cloud billing snapshots, checkpoint manifests.
- Preserve: failing objects and a 30-day snapshot of destination bucket objects (for debugging).
- Run RCA template: include timeline, impact, root cause, mitigation, owner, and follow-up actions.

Appendix: useful commands
-------------------------
- Pause a replication: kubectl patch replication <id> -p '{"spec":{"paused":true}}'
- Stream replication logs: kubectl logs -f job/replication-<id> -c replication-controller
- Check checksum remotely (S3): aws s3api head-object --bucket <bucket> --key <key> --query ETag
- Re-run targeted object copy (aws cli): aws s3 cp s3://src/key s3://dst/key --only-show-errors --region us-west-2

Appendix: quick decision matrix
- If checkpoint < 100GB and no retention change -> canary optional, proceed immediate.
- If checkpoint 100GB–500GB -> require canary + off-peak bulk.
- If checkpoint > 500GB -> require budget approval, scheduled window, and cross-team notification.

Notes and cross-references
-------------------------
- See also: egress-fencing playbook, replication operator design doc, and terraform egress quota module.
- Storage performance tips: gzip manifests, split large checkpoint objects into sharded archives to enable parallel transfer.

Document history
----------------
- 2025-11-03: Created by Aisha Khan.
- 2026-02-10: Updated SLOs and added CI/CD examples (reviewers: Diego Ramirez, Meera Patel, Jonah Li).

title: dsid_bbfa00a0e6ab439db448d33022bb1f75__sla-boundary-workbook-and-field-readiness-2026.txt
text:
SLA Boundary Workbook and Field Readiness Guide

Overview:
This workbook is designed to be used during pre-install commercial discussions and engineering handoffs for Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) customers. It defines the deployment boundary, negotiable SLA terms, objective operational readiness criteria, and the acceptance test suite used for go/no-go decisions. Use this document to align Sales, Customer Success, Solutions Engineering, and the Customer's infrastructure team before shipment or rollout.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to: VPC-hosted and on-prem deployments using the Redwood control plane or a federated control plane (customer-managed).
- Excludes: Hosted API customers and internal sandbox environments.
- Purpose: reduce ambiguity in SLAs and acceptance tests, limit scope creep, and provide a reproducible operator checklist for field teams.

Key concepts and definitions:
- Deployment boundary: the set of network segments, DNS entries, and authentication trust relationships that Redwood will operate and monitor versus those the customer is responsible for.
- Tenant SLOs: observable latency and availability targets scoped to a tenant’s ingress path and model variant.
- Evidence artifact: a saved synthetic workload run, traces, and telemetry snapshots used to demonstrate acceptance.

1) Negotiable SLA matrix (example):
- The following table is a negotiation template. Replace values per contract.

| SLA Item | Customer Tier A (example) | Measurement Window | Failure Action |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| 95th pct latency (model/generation) | 120 ms / token | 30 days rolling | Credit + failover to lower-cap model |
| Availability (control plane reachable) | 99.95% | 30 days rolling | Incident escalation + root cause report |
| Service restart MTTR | 15 minutes (stateless), 30 minutes (stateful) | per incident | Auto-rollback if >3 incidents/month |
| Telemetry retention for SLO evidence | 90 days | n/a | Extended retention add-on |

Negotiation guidance:
- Latency guarantees should be tied to a concrete model variant, sequence length distribution, and request size. Attach sample payload distributions.
- Availability guarantees differentiate between control plane, data plane (inference nodes), and customer-managed network.
- Credits and remediation steps must be explicit. Avoid language that implies unlimited retries or unconstrained rollouts.

2) Deployment boundary checklist (to be filled with customer):
- Network: list of ingress CIDR ranges, NAT/egress constraints, required ports (gRPC/HTTP), and BGP/peering expectations.
- Identity: IdP metadata, SCIM for service accounts (if used), KMS/HSM integration points, and rotation cadence.
- Storage & artifacts: snapshot locations for model artifacts, PV size expectations, and snapshot S3-compatible endpoints.
- Patching/maintenance windows: weekly and monthly windows, blackout periods for compliance.
- Operator contact list and change control flow.

Sample network boundary snippet (plain text table):
- Allowed ingress CIDR: 198.51.100.0/24 (customer), 203.0.113.0/28 (redwood ops)
- Required outbound ports: 443 (API), 5222 (internal control plane), 9000-9010 (telemetry flush)
- BGP: optional — ASN 64512 announced to customer edge for multi-region failover

3) Operational readiness acceptance tests (objective pass/fail items):
- Connectivity smoke: control plane and data plane HTTP/S gRPC handshake from three customer locations.
- Synthetic latency run: run the supplied synthetic workload for 48 hours, measure 95th/99th latency and token throughput. Evidence: load generator logs + sampling traces.
- KV cache correctness: cold-start and warm-start checks validating identical outputs for a 500-sample prompt set after model swap.
- Failover exercise: simulate a single-zone outage and validate automated fallback to regional replica with <2x latency multiplier for 90% requests.
- Rollback test: perform a dry-run rollback on canary model deployment and assert KV cache state reconciliation completes without data-loss within specified window.

Acceptance test artifacts (required):
- Synthetic workload config (attached), raw logs (gzipped), trace snapshots (zip), Prometheus/metrics snapshots (JSON), and a signed acceptance statement from the customer operator.

4) Telemetry and evidence contract (sampling & retention):
- Required metrics: per-model qps, per-tenant request latency histogram, queue depth, token generation rate, GPU util, memory pressure, and model swap events.
- Traces: capture sampling at 1% for production by default; escalate to 10% during acceptance tests.
- Logs: structured logs for request lifecycle; sensitive fields redacted per PII policy.
- Retention: default 30 days for traces and detailed logs; extendable to 90/365 days via contract.

YAML example (synthetic-workload.yaml):
---
workload_name: acceptance-synthetic-48h
seed_prompts: 1024
concurrency: 32
latency_target_ms: 120
request_distribution: 
  - prompt_length: [32, 128]
    weight: 0.7
  - prompt_length: [129, 512]
    weight: 0.3
---

CLI snippets (operator validation):
- Run a connectivity check:
  curl -s -f -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://controlplane.example.com/v1/health || echo "control plane unreachable"
- Trigger synthetic workload (field kit):
  rl-run --config synthetic-workload.yaml --out evidence/acceptance-logs.gz

5) Upgrade, rollback and constrained operations policy:
- Upgrade windows: suggested 02:00–06:00 local time, with a 2-hour canary period and automatic rollback if error budget consumed.
- State migration: stateful migrations require pre-flight snapshot and post-flight reconciliation; automated migrations off by default unless customer opts-in.
- Rollback escalation: if automated rollback does not complete within 30 minutes, operator-run rollback per documented runbook.
- Safe-mode: when network instability detected, degrade to CPU-only model variant and limit new canaries.

6) Customer-signed operational commitments (checklist for contract appendix):
- Provide a point-of-contact with SRE-level access and commit to change window notifications 48 hours in advance.
- Maintain the agreed BGP/peering or NAT configuration for failover testing.
- Allocate an operator for acceptance test execution and sign-off.

7) Example acceptance run timeline (48h):
- Day 0 (preflight): exchange SSH keys, validate network routes, import model artifact manifest.
- Day 1 (canary): run synthetic workload at 10% of target QPS for 4 hours, evaluate tail latency and error rates.
- Day 2 (full acceptance): ramp to 100% target QPS for 24–36 hours, collect evidence, perform failover and rollback drills.

8) Ownership and escalation path:
- Primary Redwood owner: Solutions Engineering (named engineer on contract).
- Secondary Redwood owner: Customer Success (technical account manager).
- Customer owner: designated SRE/Platform engineer (name and phone/email in contract).
- Escalation timeline: 15 minutes paging for Sev 1, 1 hour for Sev 2, 24 hours for Sev 3 according to the agreed SLO-criticality.

Appendix A — Sample contract clauses (language template):
- Latency SLA: "Redwood will maintain a rolling 95th percentile per-token generation latency of <=X ms for model variant Y, measured over a 30-day window using the agreed synthetic workload distribution. Failure to meet the SLA will entitle the customer to a credit defined at Z% of monthly fee per incident, up to N% per quarter."
- Evidence: "The customer and Redwood will jointly review the evidence artifact set as the authoritative record for SLA calculations. Both parties will attest to artifacts produced during acceptance runs."

Appendix B — Troubleshooting quick links and operator commands:
- Telemetry queries (PromQL examples):
  - 95th latency: hist_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, model))
  - GPU saturation: max_over_time(gpu_utilization_percent[15m]) > 90

Appendix C — Minimal attachments to include in a contract handoff zip:
- synthetic-workload.yaml, acceptance-playbook.md, operator-instructions.sh, signed-operator-acknowledgement.pdf

How to use this workbook in practice:
1. Sales/Solution engineer fills the Deployment Boundary Checklist with customer during discovery call.
2. Customer Success drives SLA negotiation using the Negotiable SLA matrix as a starting point.
3. Solutions Engineering executes preflight and acceptance tests; artifacts are uploaded to the evidence storage agreed in the contract.
4. On successful acceptance, Solutions Engineering issues an acceptance statement and hands over to Customer Success for ongoing account management.

Owner and maintenance:
- Document owner: Aisha Raman (Solutions Engineering liaison to Customer Success).
- Review cadence: biannual or after any major product change affecting deployment boundaries (e.g., new model variants, telemetry changes).

Feedback and improvements:
- If you run this workbook against a new customer and identify missing checks or unclear contractual language, add a ticket to the "private-deploy-contract-templates" board and ping the document owner for inclusion in the next revision.

End of document.

title: dsid_82c4da65fc56499b91aa659d722c3874__redwood-starter-and-career-ops-compendium-2026.txt
text:
Redwood Starter and Career Ops Compendium

Summary

This compendium is a single-page reference for new and existing Redweod contributors that ties together our approach to working at Redwood, role definitions and career ladders, benefits highlights, hiring and onboarding checkpoints, and the internal tools and access flows you will use day-to-day. It is intended to be concise, practical, and actionable — a complement to the deeper linked pages noted in Related pages.

Purpose

- Provide a unified "starter pack" for hires and managers that reduces time-to-impact.
- Map role expectations to practical first-90 actions.
- Centralize the most-used internal tools and the people-ops processes for access, privileges, and cost tagging.

Who should read this

- New hires (all levels) in engineering, product, research, GTM, and support.
- Hiring managers and people-ops partners.
- Platform and security engineers who approve access requests.

Quick start checklist (new hire)

1) Before day 1
   - Confirm offer acceptance in BambooHR and complete benefits enrollment window tasks (see Benefits Quick Reference).
   - Get SSO invite (Okta) and enable MFA.
   - Upload ID for payroll/HR verification.
2) Day 1
   - Join #new-hires Slack channel, complete the 60-minute orientation video, and meet your onboarding buddy.
   - Confirm access to GitHub org, Confluence, Jira, and your team’s Slack channel.
3) Week 1
   - Setup local dev environment using the Quickstart repo; run the smoke test.
   - Meet primary stakeholders: manager, tech lead, people-ops partner.
   - Walk through cost-center tagging and ticket templates in the Console.
4) Month 1
   - Deliver your first "small win" (bugfix, doc update, simple eval).
   - Complete the role-specific 30-day checklist (linked below).
5) Month 3
   - 90-day review prep: compile a short outcomes report, updated goals, and feedback examples for your manager.

Role & career ladder (summary)

This section summarizes expectations across common ladders. For full competency rubrics see the linked role pages.

| Ladder | Typical titles | Core expectations (summary) | First-90 focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Individual Contributor — Engineering | Associate Engineer, Engineer I, II, Senior, Principal | Delivers features, owns reliability improvements, mentors peers, influences architecture at level-appropriate scope | Ship a feature, own a post-deploy fix, start mentoring a peer |
| Individual Contributor — Product | Associate PM, PM, Senior PM, Group PM | Defines clear requirements, drives experiments, measures outcomes, partners across engineering and GTM | Deliver a scoped spec, run an experiment, present findings |
| IC — Applied ML / Research | Research Engineer, Applied Scientist, Sr Applied Scientist | Produce reproducible evals, bridge models-to-serving, present concise technical findings | Validate a small eval, document methodology, handoff to infra |
| Managerial Ladder | Tech Lead, Manager, Senior Manager, Director | Grow team outcomes, remove blockers, develop people, set priority, allocate capacity | Run 1:1s, set team goals, craft hiring plan |

Benefits quick reference (high level)

- Health & wellbeing: medical, dental, vision — standard Redwood employer contributions; enrollment within 30 days of start.
- Mental health: 8 free therapy sessions per year + employee assistance program (EAP).
- Family leave: parental leave and flexible return-to-work options.
- Remote/hybrid support: home office stipend, monthly coworking allowance.
- Professional development: learning allowance, conference budget, and internal mentorship stipends.
- Financial: 401(k) matching, equity grants, commuter benefit where applicable.

For full plan documents, carriers, and eligibility rules see the Benefits binder (HR link).

Hiring & onboarding overview (process & touchpoints)

1) Requisition to offer (hiring manager responsibilities)
   - Open requisition with people-ops using the standard job template and desired skill matrix.
   - Confirm scorecard with interview loop and rubric (technical, collaboration, growth mindset).
   - Work with recruiting to produce candidate slate and synchronized interview availability.
2) Offer and acceptance
   - People-ops generates offer letter; manager confirms start date and first-week plan; recruiter sets the candidate expectations for remote hardware, security, and documentation.
3) Pre-boarding (people-ops)
   - Initiate BambooHR onboarding tasks, send SSO invite, and assign an onboarding buddy from the team.
4) Day 0–30 (manager + buddy)
   - Ensure local environment bootstrapped, review 30-day goals, schedule cross-functional orientation meetings.
5) 60–90 day check and calibration
   - Conduct 60-day pulse, 90-day outcomes review, and either confirm ongoing role expectations or adjust a growth plan.

Internal tools mapping (most-used)

| Purpose | Tool | Primary owner | Typical access flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| Single Sign-On & MFA | Okta | Security | Provisioned by people-ops; requires SSO invite + MFA setup |
| HRIS & benefits | BambooHR | People-ops | New hires complete tasks in onboarding checklist |
| Code & PRs | GitHub | Eng-platform | Team repo invites via org; request via access ticket for private repos |
| Issue tracking | Jira | Eng-platform | Add to project at manager request; role-based permissions |
| Internal docs | Confluence | Docs & DX | Default read access; edit rights by team space membership |
| Chat | Slack | Eng-platform | Auto-join new-hire channels; request restricted channels via ticket |
| Cloud infra | GCP/AWS (via Redwood Console) | Cloud platform | Require just-in-time elevated role; must complete security checklist |
| Payroll & expenses | Ramp + Deel | Finance | Enroll in Ramp via finance; contractors via Deel |
| Observability & cost | Redwood Console (internal) | Eng-platform/FinOps | Access granted to owners; cost-center tagging required for PRs |

Access request flow (step-by-step)

1) Manager files an Access Request ticket (Jira) with: hire name, role, required systems, cost center, and justification.
2) People-ops approves identity & benefits tasks; Security reviews high-risk system requests (cloud infra, HSM, kube-admin).
3) Eng-platform or Security provisions access; engineer verifies ability to run the standard smoke test.
4) Manager confirms access in a 72-hour closure check.

First-90 plan templates (by role family)

- Engineering (IC): 30-day — local dev run, 1st small feature; 60-day — owned nontrivial bug or tiny feature; 90-day — contribute to design/ship medium-risk change.
- Engineering (Manager): 30-day — team syncs, review direct reports; 60-day — hiring priority validated; 90-day — performance calibration and plan.
- Product: 30-day — product context, 1 spec; 60-day — execute experiment; 90-day — measure and iterate.
- Applied ML: 30-day — reproduce baseline eval; 60-day — improve pipeline, 90-day — hand off model for serving.

Performance calibration & promotion rhythm (practical notes)

- Promotion cycles run quarterly. Managers collect evidence aligned to the competency rubrics. Evidence should include outcomes, technical artifacts, design reviews, mentorship examples, and customer/peer feedback.
- People-ops supports calibration panels and ensures consistency across ladders.

Manager checklist for growth-focused onboarding

- Assign an onboarding buddy and set clear 30/60/90 goals within first week.
- Schedule weekly 1:1s for the first 90 days; use the shared 1:1 template in Confluence.
- Plan for a public 30-day demo and a documented 90-day outcomes review.

Escalations and ownership

- People-ops escalation: people-ops-team@redwood.com (policy, benefits edge cases, role clarifications).
- Security escalations: sec-oncall@redwood.com (access incidents, suspicious activity).
- Payroll/Comp: payroll@redwood.com for urgent compensation issues.

Maintenance & updates

- This compendium is reviewed quarterly by people-ops with input from Eng Platform, Security, and Benefits. Any changes to access flows or benefits must be reflected here within 30 days of policy change.

FAQ (short)

Q: Who do I ask for a laptop?
A: Submit a Hardware Request via the People Ops ticketing form; your manager approves and finance orders.

Q: Where are deeper role rubrics?
A: See the linked ladder pages in Related pages; reach out to your people-ops partner for clarifications.

Q: Can I delay benefits enrollment?
A: Standard enrollment windows apply; consult benefits binder and people-ops for exceptions.

Appendix: Helpful contacts (internal)

- People-ops partner (general): people-ops@redwood.com
- Onboarding buddy program coordinator: onboarding-buddies@redwood.com
- Eng-platform: eng-platform@redwood.com
- Security (access requests): sec-approvals@redwood.com

Related pages

- Hiring templates and scorecards (linked in Related pages).
- Full benefit plan documents and carriers.
- Role competency matrices by ladder.

Revision history

- 2025-11-12 — Created by Marisol Vega.
- 2026-03-01 — Published: clarified access flow; added cost-tagging step and updated tool table.

title: dsid_fca13b5e39bc43f5abafc652df88332b__service-traffic-shepherding-and-devolution-playbook-2025.txt
text:
Service Traffic Shepherding and Devolution Playbook

Overview

Purpose: This playbook documents the design, operational guidance, dashboards, and runbooks for service traffic shepherding — the platform layer that routes customer requests across model variants, regions, and capacity tiers — and the controlled devolution behaviors used when primary paths become degraded. The approach balances latency SLOs, cost targets, and reliability.

Audience: Platform engineers, oncall, SREs, and product engineers implementing routing policies for inference endpoints.

Scope

- Systems covered: platform_router, request-mux, model-variant-proxy, cached-kv-service, per-customer-shaper.
- Environments: hosted API, dedicated GPU pools, private deployments (where the same primitives exist).
- Excludes: client-side retry strategies (refer to SDK guides).

Goals

- Maintain 99.95% request success for production endpoints with p95 latency < 120ms for short-prompt paths.
- Keep median cost-per-token within configured budget tiers by active routing decisions and quantization fallbacks.
- Provide deterministic, observable devolution (graceful downgrade) when downstream capacity or quality degrades.

Terminology

- Primary path: preferred region/model/variant for a request by policy.
- Devolution: controlled downgrade to a lower-cost or lower-latency variant or cached response when primary fails or breaches SLOs.
- Shepherding policy: a configured set of rules (latency target, cost cap, region affinity) that the router uses to pick routes.

Ownership & SLAs

| Component | Owner | SLO | Alert Owner |
|---|---|---:|---|
| platform_router (service) | eng-platform-routing | 99.95% success, p95 < 120ms | platform oncall |
| model-variant-proxy | eng-serving-runtime | 99.9% per-model availability | runtime oncall |
| cached-kv-service | eng-platform-batching | 99.99% hit availability | infra oncall |

Routing Policies (high level)

- Priority ordering: region-local low-latency variants -> region-low-cost (quantized) -> global fallback -> cached prefix -> error.
- Cost-aware decisioning: for routes tagged with budget:strict the router computes expected token-cost baseline and avoids variants with >15% expected cost overhead unless latency SLO would otherwise be missed.
- Quality guardrails: model-variant must pass recent quality checks (rolling eval failure rate < 0.5%) to be eligible.
- Affinity and stickiness: traffic is sticky by route_key (customer_id + model_id + session_id) for KV-cache warmness.

Routing Policies: Example YAML

```
policy_name: interactive-low-latency
latency_slo_ms: 120
cost_cap_pct: 15 # relative to baseline variant
variant_preference:
  - name: model-1.7b-lowlat
    region_pref: us-west-2
    quality_threshold: 0.5
  - name: model-1.7b-quantized
    region_pref: us-west-2
    quality_threshold: 1.0
  - name: model-legacy-3b
    region_pref: global
    quality_threshold: 0.8
devolution:
  cache_prefix: true
  fallback_message: "service_unavailable_try_again"
```

Implementation primitives

- feature-flag:router-devolution-enabled (per-tenant)
- sidecar:local-proxy (Envoy) that performs initial health checks and local devolution to cache.
- circuit-breakers: per-variant open when error_rate > 3% for 60s.
- tokenized-cost-estimator: microservice that estimates expected token cost and latency using request metadata and recent perf curves.

Dashboards & Alerts

Primary dashboards to maintain and review weekly:

1) Traffic Shepherding Overview (team dashboard)
   - Widgets: total routed QPS, p50/p95/p99 latency by route_key, cost per 1k tokens by variant, active devolution rate.
   - Prometheus/Tempo queries:
     - avg_over_time(request_latency_ms[5m]) grouped by variant
     - increase(routed_requests_total[5m]) by (route_key, variant)
     - sum_over_time(token_cost_cents_total[5m]) / sum_over_time(routed_requests_total[5m])

2) Devolution Heatmap
   - Widget shows % of requests devolved by hour and by customer. Use to detect noisy tenants.

Alerting thresholds (examples)

- router_devolution_rate_high: if devolution_rate > 5% for 5m for any prod tenant -> Sev2 -> paging to platform oncall.
- variant_error_spike: if variant_error_rate > 3% for 1m and p95 latency > 300ms -> Sev1 (runtime + platform)
- cost_overrun_alarm: if rolling 6h cost per token for policy > cost_cap_pct threshold -> notify cost-ops slack and product

Runbook: Active Devolution Recovery (Sev2 -> Escalate to Sev1 if unresolved)

1) Triage (0-5m)
   - Identify impacted route_keys via Shepherding Overview dashboard.
   - Check recent deploys: `git log --since=\"1 hour\" deploys/router`.
   - Verify router health: `kubectl -n platform get pods -l app=platform-router` and `kubectl logs` of failing pod.

2) Short-term mitigation (5-15m)
   - If global variant is failing, enable feature-flag `router-force-fallback-to-cache` for affected tenants: `ffcli set router-force-fallback-to-cache on --tenants tenant-id-1,tenant-id-2`.
   - Reduce routing churn: set `policy.max_retries=1` to prevent cascading retries.

3) Variant circuit-breaker action (15-45m)
   - Open the variant in the router: `POST /admin/variants/{variant}/open` (internal admin API) or use the admin console.
   - Monitor for stabilization for 10 minutes.

4) Restore & verification (45-90m)
   - Once variant metrics return to baseline, move variant to half-open and monitor for 30 minutes.
   - Roll back any temporary feature flags and verify cache warmness for sticky flows.

5) Post-incident (within 48h)
   - Populate incident timeline, attach dashboard snapshots, and run the retrospective checklist below.

Automated Remediations (playbook primitives)

- Auto-devolution rule: when variant_error_rate > 2.5% AND p95_latency > 250ms for 90s, router will automatically route 50% traffic to next eligible variant and escalate.
- Auto-warm cache: when traffic shifts to cache fallback, trigger background prefetch for top-10 prefixes per tenant.

Canary and Rollout Guidance

- Always enable flag `router-new-routing-algo` in staged mode with a 1% traffic shard for 24h, measure devolution_rate and cost impact; increase to 10% for 12h before 50%.
- Runload tests with synthetic traffic matching customer distributions (tool: load-shepherd). Use realistic token-length distributions.

Retrospective Checklist (post-incident)

- Confirm the timeline is complete and slos.
- Quantify cost impact of devolution and estimate 30-day delta.
- Identify a single corrective action owner and due date.
- Decide whether to add a new alert or adjust thresholds.

Roadmap: Next 6–12 months (prioritized)

1) Cost-informed routing 2.0: integrate per-tenant cost budgets and automatic spend throttling (Q2 2025).
2) Per-customer quality profiles: allow customers to set quality-first vs cost-first routing preferences in console (Q3 2025).
3) ML-driven prediction: use short-window ML models to predict variant degradation and proactively shift traffic (experiment Q4 2025).

Team Wiki Notes & Operational FAQs

- Q: When should we prefer cache devolution vs quantized variant?
  A: Cache devolution if prefix coverage > 30% and latency requirement <= 50ms. Prefer quantized variant when output quality must be preserved and latency SLO can be relaxed to <= 200ms.

- Q: Who can flip router-level feature flags?
  A: Platform leads + oncall SREs. For emergency toggles, product and security must be notified in the incident channel.

Appendix A: Example Envoy traffic-shift config (snippet)

```
- name: route_to_model_variants
  match: /v1/generate
  route:
    weighted_clusters:
      clusters:
        - name: model-1.7b-lowlat_us-west-2
          weight: 80
        - name: model-1.7b-quantized_us-west-2
          weight: 15
        - name: global-fallback
          weight: 5
```

Appendix B: Useful queries and CLI commands

- Check active devolution rate for tenant `acme-corp`:
  - Prometheus: `sum(rate(router_devolution_total{tenant=\"acme-corp\"}[5m])) / sum(rate(routed_requests_total{tenant=\"acme-corp\"}[5m]))`
- Open variant via admin API (curl):
```
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://admin.internal.platform/variants/model-legacy-3b/open
```
- Warm top-10 cache prefixes (example script):
```
python scripts/warm_cache.py --tenant acme-corp --top 10
```

Change Log

- 2024-09-10: Created by Priya Nair.
- 2024-12-02: Added automated remediation rules and updated runbook timelines (reviewers: Ethan Zhang).
- 2025-01-15: Expanded dashboards section and added roadmap items (reviewers: Marisol Ortega, Daniel Kim).

Notes and references

- See related: platform-sidecar-contracts-and-healthcheck-standards for local health check semantics.
- See: gpu-pool-live-shrink-and-maintenance-runbook for guidance when capacity shrink intersects with routing devolution policies.

text:
Latency-Optimized Local Model Fanout Architecture

Overview

This page documents the Latency-Optimized Local Model Fanout Architecture (LOLMFA) for Redwood Private deployments. The pattern is intended for customers who require sub-50ms median (p50) inference latency for common short requests while preserving the ability to route heavier or higher‑quality requests to central GPU pools.

Goals

- Provide a predictable low-latency path for small/short-text workloads (p50 < 50ms, p95 < 120ms) using local, quantized model shards.
- Retain correctness and quality by transparently fanouting requests to central inference for long-context or compute‑intensive queries.
- Ensure graceful degradation and clear rollback/upgrade paths for both local and central tiers.
- Minimize customer network egress and meet privacy constraints (models and tokens may remain within customer VPC).

High-level topology

1) Edge nodes (customer-managed in VPC or on-prem):
   - Small GPU or CPU instances running quantized model variants (4–8GB GPU or multi-socket CPU).
   - Serve frequent short requests locally with optimized kernels and minimal batching.
2) Regional aggregator (optional):
   - Responsible for request classification, caching, and short‑circuiting locality decisions.
3) Central Redwood Dedicated pool (hosted or customer collocated):
   - Large-GPU cluster (A100/H100 equivalents) for long-context, high‑quality responses.
4) Control plane connectors:
   - Secure control channel for model metadata, KV cache presence, and rollout policies.

Component details

- Local runtime: a stripped-down Redwood agent providing:
  - quantized-model runtime (int8/4-bit profiles),
  - prefix/KV cache with LRU TTL (default 24h),
  - small-batch path with kernel selection favoring latency.
- Classifier router: lightweight policy process that decides: LOCAL | CACHE_HIT | CENTRAL. Policies include tokens count, prompt length, customer labels, and per-route cost ceilings.
- Fallback policy: automatic reroute to central on local failure, plus degraded-mode reply when central unreachable.
- Observability: token-level traces, request sampling (1%) to central for quality checks, and latency histograms per-tier.

SLOs and thresholds (recommended starting values)

- Local path: p50 < 50ms, p95 < 120ms for requests with input tokens <= 64.
- Classification decision: < 5ms 99.9% of the time.
- Central path for long requests: p95 < 1.2s (depends on model).
- Cache hit target: >= 30% of local short requests.
- Availability: local agent SLA (operator target) 99.95% during business hours.

Customer requirements (pre-install checklist)

- Network:
  - LAN RTT to local nodes: < 2ms typical.
  - WAN RTT from edge to regional aggregator/central: < 100ms for acceptable fallbacks.
  - Ports: outbound TCP 443 to Redwood control plane and dedicated pool endpoints; open internal gRPC/TCP ports 8000–8020 for inter-agent.
- Hardware:
  - Edge GPU: minimum 4GB VRAM (recommended 8GB) for quantized variants; or 32 vCPUs with AVX512 for CPU-only sites.
  - Disk: 50GB NVMe for model shards, cache, and logs.
- Security & keys:
  - Customer KMS reachable in VPC for secret unwrap; HSM integration optional for FIPS customers.
  - Mutually-authenticated TLS between agents and central (mTLS).
- IAM & service accounts:
  - Dedicated service account with least privilege; key rotation schedule defined.

Deployment playbook (edge node)

1) Preflight (operator):
   - Validate hardware profile: run collect_hardware_profile.sh and store output.
   - Verify network rules and KMS access.
   - Ensure time sync (NTP) and kernel parameters per infra-standards.
2) Install agent:
   - curl -sSL https://packages.redwood.ai/agent/install.sh | sudo bash -s -- --profile=latency-edge
   - Configure /etc/redwood/agent.yaml with:
     - model_variant: "rw-small-quant-v1"
     - kv_cache.ttl: 24h
     - router.policy: "token-count-based"
3) Smoke test:
   - redwoodctl healthcheck --target localhost:8000
   - Run quick latency benchmark: redwoodctl bench --requests 500 --max_tokens 64
4) Canary rollout:
   - Update router policy to include 10% forced central routing to validate end-to-end. Monitor errors for 2 hours before full promotion.

Day-2 operations (operator runbook)

- Monitoring and alerting:
  - Metrics to watch: local_latency_ms (p50/p95), classifier_decision_latency_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, model_load_errors, agent_restarts.
  - Alerts: kv_cache_hit_rate < 15% sustained 30m; agent_restarts > 3 in 10m; local p95 > 200ms for 15m.
- Cache warmup strategy:
  - Scheduled synthetic workloads during quiet hours to prefill KV caches for top 200 prompt templates.
- Capacity scaling:
  - When local CPU/GPU utilization > 70% for 30m, auto-scale policy triggers adding a hot-spare agent.
- Quality checks:
  - Sampled 1% of local replies are sent to central for quality comparison; alert if semantic drift > threshold.

Upgrade and rollback procedures

- Upgrade (agent or local model):
  1. Stage new model variant in a canary edge node (1 node). Run bench and quality regression checks against a saved prompt set.
  2. Gradually increase canary percentage (1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%) over multiple hours while monitoring p95 latency and quality diffs.
  3. If quality regression or latency spike occurs, trigger rollback.

- Rollback (fast-fail path):
  - Command: redwoodctl agent rollback --target <agent-id> --to-version <previous-model-semilabel>
  - Automated safety: controller evaluates health for 10m before rolling to additional nodes; if failure persists, enact tenant traffic drain to central with retained cache headers.
  - Evidence capture: collect /var/log/redwood/agent.log, heap profiles, last 100 classifier traces. Attach to incident ticket.

Failure modes and mitigation

- Local model OOM: automatic restart into degraded/no-local mode (route to central) and notify operator.
- KV cache corruption: fallback to central until cache TTL expires and warmup job restores entries.
- Network partition (edge->central): operate in isolated mode, local-only responses; flag degraded quality for audit.

Observability and telemetry contract

- Required metrics exported via Prometheus endpoint:
  - redwood_local_request_latency_ms_bucket
  - redwood_classifier_decision_latency_ms_bucket
  - redwood_kv_cache_hit_ratio
  - redwood_model_load_duration_seconds
- Traces: OpenTelemetry spans must include decision.reason, route.tier, model.variant, and cache.hit boolean.
- Logs: structured JSON lines with request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, duration_ms, and error_codes. Retention default 30d (configurable).

Security & compliance notes

- All model artifacts signed and verified using the customer-side image attestation. See image signing playbook for commands.
- Sensitive telemetry (user prompts) must be redacted before external transmission; send only hashed prompt fingerprints when required.
- Key rotation: follow a 90-day rotation schedule and ensure agents gracefully reload keys without restart.

Ownership and contact points

- Architecture owner: Priya Natarajan (eng-serving-runtime).
- Support handoff: Private Deployments Field Team (private-deploy-support@redwood.ai).
- Oncall escalation: see eng-sre oncall roster; page: /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-rotation.

Appendix: example router policy (YAML)

---
policy_name: latency_fanout_v1
rules:
  - name: local_short_request
    condition: "input_tokens <= 64 and tenant_priority == 'standard'"
    action: LOCAL
    sampling: 0.01   # 1% sampled to central for QA
  - name: cache_only
    condition: "cache.hit == true"
    action: LOCAL
  - name: heavy_request
    condition: "input_tokens > 64 or requires_retrieval == true"
    action: CENTRAL
  - name: default_fallback
    action: CENTRAL

References and related reading

- Private deploy observability contract: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/observability-contracts-and-log-sampling-strategy-2026
- Image attestation and signing: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/onprem-packaging/image-attestation-spec-2026
- Cold start mitigation: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/cold-start-latency-mitigation-for-private-deploys-2026

Change log

- 2026-03-15: Initial draft.
- 2026-06-10: Added SLO targets and cache warmup strategy after field trials.
- 2026-10-12: Finalized rollback commands and telemetry contract.

text:
SDK Interop Patterns and Fault-Tolerant Examples for Embeddings & Streaming

Summary:
This page collects recommended interoperability patterns, canonical quickstart templates, and reproducible fixes for the top SDK/API issues we see in Support. It is intended for SDK authors, integrators, developer advocates, and SREs who ship client-side code and docs examples used by customers.

Goals:
- Provide small, copy-pasteable examples for robust client behavior across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
- Surface repeatable fixes for common support symptoms (timeouts, partial streams, tokenization mismatches, embedding drift, auth/region misrouting, 429 bursts, local vs prod config drift, telemetry gaps).
- Define Docs Site operational controls for releasing API example changes without regressions.

Quick reference: recommended runtime behaviors
1) Retry policy:
   - Idempotent (embeddings, metadata): up to 3 attempts, exponential backoff starting 200ms, max 2s, jitter multiplier 0.2.
   - Non-idempotent (generation/streaming): prefer failover to fallback model variant; limit to 1 retry.
2) Streaming: attach sequence ids to every chunk; client must drop out-of-order chunks on reconnect.
3) Backpressure: respect Retry-After header on 429/503; otherwise use exponential backoff with jitter.

Canonical SDK examples (copy-paste)
- Python: embeddings with batching + retry:
  from typing import List
  import time
  import requests

  API_URL = "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/embeddings"
  HEADERS = {"Authorization": "Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY", "Content-Type": "application/json"}

  def batch_and_call(texts: List[str], batch_size: int = 32):
      results = []
      for i in range(0, len(texts), batch_size):
          batch = texts[i:i+batch_size]
          for attempt in range(3):
              resp = requests.post(API_URL, json={"model": "open-embed-2", "input": batch}, headers=HEADERS, timeout=15)
              if resp.status_code == 200:
                  results.extend(resp.json().get("data", []))
                  break
              elif resp.status_code in (429, 503):
                  backoff = min(2, 0.2 * (2 ** attempt))
                  time.sleep(backoff + (backoff * 0.2 * (attempt + 1)))
              else:
                  resp.raise_for_status()
      return results

- Node.js: resilient streaming skeleton:
  const fetch = require('node-fetch');
  let lastSeq = -1;
  async function streamGenerate(prompt) {
    const res = await fetch('https://api.redwood.ai/v1/stream', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ model: 'redwood-chat-1', prompt }) });
    const reader = res.body.getReader();
    while (true) {
      const { value, done } = await reader.read();
      if (done) break;
      const chunk = new TextDecoder().decode(value);
      try {
        const parsed = JSON.parse(chunk);
        if (parsed.sequence <= lastSeq) continue;
        lastSeq = parsed.sequence;
        process.stdout.write(parsed.delta_text || '');
      } catch (e) {
        // fall back to buffered partial chunk handling
      }
    }
  }

Top support symptoms and direct remediations (symptom -> cause -> quick fix)
- Embedding drift between local and prod:
  Cause: unstated model version or different tokenizer pipeline in local SDK.
  Fix: pin model version in examples, use runtime check against /v1/models/{model}/meta.tokenizer_version, and add CI golden-vector assertion.

- Truncated/partial streams:
  Cause: proxy/edge idle timeout or reconnect logic that drops buffered sequence.
  Fix: require keepalive >= 120s for streaming; include sequence id in chunks; provide reconnect resume flow in examples.

- 429 bursts despite low QPS:
  Cause: short-lived worker processes each opening separate client pools or lack of shared rate limiter.
  Fix: recommend a per-host token-bucket limiter in examples; show global pool pattern for Node and Python.

- Region-specific unauthorized errors:
  Cause: credentials scoped to a region but hitting non-region-prefixed endpoint.
  Fix: recommend REDWOOD_API_REGION env + region-prefixed endpoint; SDKs should warn if token scope and region mismatch during first calls.

Diagnostics checklist for reproducing issues locally
1) Capture full request/response headers including x-redwood-request-id, x-backend-model, x-model-variant, x-cache-hit.
2) Test against both hosted public endpoint and private test image (image tag pattern: redwood/runtime:private-<git-sha>).
3) Record timing breakdown: connect, TLS handshake, first byte, per-token latency. Use curl -w or rwx diag request --url <endpoint> --save=trace.json.

Docs site change process for API examples
- Branch: docs/api-examples/<short-desc>. Add examples under docs/examples/.
- PR checklist: smoke-output.md, CI artifact proving examples ran, changelog entry.
- CI gates: syntax linting, secrets lint (no hard-coded bearer tokens), smoke execution for Python and Node examples using sandbox creds.
- Release: main merge triggers docs-publish which builds site, runs examples, uploads artifacts to S3, and invalidates CDN paths. Failed smoke tests auto-create a revert PR and notify #docs-alerts and #devx-support.

Telemetry for reproducible examples
- Include metadata fields in example logs: redwood.example.name, redwood.example.sha, redwood.example.variant.
- Store per-run trace artifact (headers + timing) in s3://redwood-docs-traces/<date>/<example>.json with default 7-day retention.

PR template checklist (short)
1) Title: docs(example): short-description
2) Attach smoke-output.md and CI green badge proof
3) Add reviewers: @devx-leads, @sdk-owner, @sre-oncall
4) Update docs/CHANGELOG.md

Escalation path for unresolved example regressions
- 0-24h: Developer Experience oncall (maya-rotation@redwood.ai)
- 24-72h: SDK owner (Sofia Nguyen) and Docs engineering lead (Liam O'Connor)
- >72h: Eng infra manager + Product manager for customer communication alignment

Related links:
- Tokenizer service: https://tokenizer.redwood.ai/docs
- Examples CI: gitlab.redwood.internal/devx/examples-ci
- Diagnostics CLI: https://internal.redwood.ai/rwx-docs

Revision history:
- 2025-02-14: created by Asha Patel
- 2025-03-01: added regional endpoint guidance and updated live examples (Liam O'Connor)

Contact:
If you encounter a new recurring customer symptom, file an issue on devx/backlog and ping the reviewer group or @devx-support on Slack.

title: dsid_162540a4f2d246658a0b7f39d9b8b92d__capacity-guardrails-multitenant-throttle-eviction-escrow-2026.txt
text:
Capacity Guardrails: Multitenant Throttle Governor and Eviction Escrow Runbook

Summary
-------
This runbook documents Redwood's operational playbook for a cluster-level throttle governor and the complementary eviction escrow mechanism used to protect SLOs during multitenant capacity shortfalls. It translates SLO and error budget signals into deterministic actions (rate-limits, admission-control, short lived evictions) while minimizing blast radius and preserving customer fairness.

Scope
-----
- Applies to multi-tenant inference clusters running the inference-serving runtime (service names: inference-gateway, kv-router, batch-allocator).
- Covers detection, automated mitigation (throttle governor), short-lived eviction via "eviction escrow", manual overrides, and post-incident verification.
- Does NOT replace tenant contract eviction policies for committed Dedicated customers; those follow dedicated-eviction-procedure page.

Objectives
----------
- Maintain customer-facing SLOs: 99th percentile latency < 350ms for standard tier; availability >= 99.9%.
- Keep error budget burn rate below 3x sustained for > 30 minutes before aggressive action.
- Ensure predictable, auditable eviction decisions with reversible escrow state.

Ownership and Contacts
----------------------
- Runbook owner: eng-sre (oncall: inference-cluster-pager)
- Primary contacts: Elena Kim (SRE), Marcus Li (Platform), Priya Nair (Runtime)
- Pager escalation: inference-pager -> platform-lead -> eng-sre-manager (see /oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations)

Key Signals and Telemetry
-------------------------
1) SLO and error budget signals
   - service.slo.latency.99p (ms)
   - service.slo.availability.rolling_1h (%)
   - service.error_budget.burn_rate.5m
2) Capacity signals
   - gpu.utilization.percent per pool
   - queue.wait_time.p95 (ms)
   - inflight_requests per tenant
3) Admission & throttling signals
   - admission.rejection.rate
   - token_bucket.fill_level (per priority-slice)

Threshold table (example)
-------------------------
| Trigger | Observed signal | Immediate action |
|---------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Warning | burn_rate >= 1.5x sustained 10m | Start telemetry shadowing; notify oncall |
| Elevated | burn_rate >= 3x sustained 30m OR latency.99p >= 350ms for 10m | Activate throttle governor (soft) for lowest-priority slice; reduce burst window by 25% |
| Severe | burn_rate >= 6x sustained 15m OR availability < 99.5% for 5m | Escalate to eviction-escrow state; apply aggressive admission limits; prepare targeted evictions |

Design: Throttle Governor and Eviction Escrow Concepts
-----------------------------------------------------
- Throttle Governor: a distributed policy engine (component: throttle-governor) that enforces per-tenant priority slices (e.g. premium, standard, best-effort). It uses a leaky-bucket algorithm with adaptive windows tuned by observed queueing latency. The governor supports a safe-decay parameter to allow recovery without manual intervention.
- Eviction Escrow: a reversible short-term marker assigned to candidate workloads/tenants when capacity is critical. Escrowed workloads are flagged for eviction but are kept in a grace state for a configurable period (default 10 minutes) during which autoscaling, routing fallback, or human remediation can prevent termination. All escrow actions are auditable.

Runbook: Automated Response Flow
--------------------------------
1) Detection and confirmation (oncall or automation)
   - Verify signals (SLO dashboards and raw metrics). If alert correlates with queue.wait_time.p95 and gpu.utilization > 85%, treat as confirmed.
2) Soft governor (automatic)
   - throttle-governor applies slice-level rate reductions: reduce best-effort to 40% of baseline, standard to 75%, premium unchanged.
   - Update oracle: post a change event to /events/capacity-governor with reason and change-id.
3) Escalation and escrow (conditional)
   - If soft governor does not restore SLOs in 10m, enter escrow evaluation.
   - Candidate selection heuristic: tenants with highest recent error-budget-burn and lowest contract-priority are shortlisted.
   - Place shortlisted tenants into eviction escrow with TTL=10min. Notify tenant owners via email/webhook and record in audit log: audit.eviction_escrow.<change-id>.
4) Forced eviction (manual or automated)
   - After TTL, if no remediation (autoscale or re-route), execute eviction handler to free nodes. Evictions should prefer ephemeral, non-critical worker pods first.
   - For each eviction, emit events, update chargeback ledger, and annotate tenant with eviction_reason and remediation_instructions.
5) Recovery and soft-restoration
   - Gradually revert governor reductions in 5-minute increments while monitoring SLOs.

Runbook: Manual Intervention Steps
----------------------------------
1) Triage (first 10 minutes)
   - Confirm cluster-level telemetry and cross-check tenant logs.
   - Run quick capacity audit: kubectl get nodes (filter: inference-enabled), check gpu health and pod eviction counts.
2) Apply targeted throttles (if automation disabled)
   - CLI: curl -X POST https://throttle-api.internal/v1/slices/adjust -d '{"slice":"best-effort","multiplier":0.4}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN'
3) Place or remove eviction escrow (manual)
   - CLI: curl -X POST https://allocator.internal/v1/escrow -d '{"tenant":"tenant-id","ttl_seconds":600,"reason":"slo_breach"}'
4) Execute safe eviction (if required)
   - Use evacuate node workflow (admin only): admin-evacuate --node <node-id> --prefer-pods ephemeral --dry-run=false
5) Communicate
   - Post update to incident channel (#inc-inference), update status page if customer-visible, and notify Customer Success for affected tenants.

Verification and Post-Action Checks
----------------------------------
- Verify SLO metrics returning to baseline for 30m window.
- Confirm eviction events are present in audit.eviction_escrow.<change-id> and reason codes match authorized triggers.
- Run smoke canaries: send 100 requests to premium/standard slices and verify p95 latency < target.

Recovery and Remediation Playbook
--------------------------------
- If evicted tenants report degraded behavior after reinstatement: collect heap traces, model cache metrics, and warm-up traffic via controlled replay (tool: canary-relay).
- For repeated escrow triggers (>3 times in 7 days): raise a reliability initiative to re-evaluate tenant assignment, capacity sizing, or pricing policy.

Auditing, Billing, and Notifications
-----------------------------------
- All throttle adjustments and eviction escrow events must be tagged with change-id and persisted to the capacity-audit-store (retention 90 days).
- Billing: evictions during non-committed windows will trigger a credit evaluation; finance notifies customers according to the Customer Impact policy.

Simulation and Playbook Validation
--------------------------------
- Test this runbook in the staging cluster monthly using the capacity-sim harness: run ./tools/capacity-sim --profile multitenant-spike --duration 20m.
- Acceptance criteria for the exercise: no committed-dedicated tenant is evicted; SLOs for premium tenants preserved; post-mortem documented within 48h.

Config reference (example JSON for throttle-governor)
--------------------------------------------------
{
  "slices": [
    {"name": "premium", "weight": 50, "min_mult": 1.0},
    {"name": "standard", "weight": 30, "min_mult": 0.5},
    {"name": "best-effort", "weight": 20, "min_mult": 0.2}
  ],
  "safe_decay_minutes": 15,
  "escrow_ttl_seconds": 600
}

Post-incident and Continuous Improvement
-----------------------------------------
- Postmortem requirements: timeline, root cause, decision rationale for throttles/evictions, missed signals, and recommended follow-ups. Owner must schedule a remediation ticket within 5 business days.
- Suggested improvements: refine candidate selection heuristic, expose per-tenant preemption risk to Customer Success, and run an AB experiment of dynamic slice weights.

Runbook Verification Checklist (quick)
------------------------------------
- [ ] Alerts validated and correlated to telemetry
- [ ] Throttle governor event has change-id and audit entry
- [ ] Eviction escrow TTL and notifications recorded
- [ ] Post-incident ticket created and assigned
- [ ] Metrics verified (p95/p99 latency, availability)

References and Related Docs
---------------------------
- /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/capacity-onboarding-checklist-for-new-model-tenants-2026
- /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/burst-absorber-architecture-and-decision-playbook-2026
- Capacity simulation toolkit: git.internal/redwood/capacity-sim

Appendix: Decision rationale for escrow TTL=10min
------------------------------------------------
- 10 minutes balances giving tenants time for autoscaling and graceful fallback while keeping the window short enough to limit exposure to prolonged SLO degradation. The TTL is tunable and should be validated in chaos drills.

title: dsid_59781d7a6d3141dda0d0d4d598d52417__slo-deprecation-and-legacy-service-retirement-runbook-2025.txt
text:
SLO Deprecation and Legacy Service Retirement Runbook

Purpose
-------
This runbook defines the standard process and gating criteria for deprecating an SLO and retiring a legacy service. It is intended for SREs, service owners, product managers, and platform engineers. The goal is to retire services safely while preserving customer-facing SLOs, minimizing capacity disruption, and ensuring clean incident evidence for postmortems.

Scope
-----
Applies to: internal and customer-facing services listed in the Redwood service catalog.
Does NOT apply to: short-lived feature flags, AB-test backends under 30 days of lifetime (use feature-flag playbooks).

Definitions
-----------
- SLO: Service Level Objective (e.g., 99.9% success rate for generate-text).
- SBI: Service Burn Indicator — combined metrics that indicate whether a service is on-track for retirement (error budget, active callers, routing weight).
- Legacy service: a service that is being retired because of replacement, consolidation, or end-of-life.

Owners and Stakeholders
-----------------------
- Primary owner: service team product lead (PL) and service oncall.
- SRE lead: responsible for runbook enforcement and capacity verification.
- Platform/Networking: routing and traffic-shift operations.
- Security/Compliance: data-retention checks for customer-sensitive data.

Prerequisites & Signals to Start Retirement
------------------------------------------
1) Product decision recorded (JIRA: RWI-####) with sign-off from PL and PM.
2) Replacement service available or confirmed migration path.
3) Metrics baseline available for 30 days: traffic, p95 latency, error budget burn rate.
4) No Sev1/2 incident in the last 7 days for the service.

Common triggers:
- Sustained <10% traffic over 60 days.
- Low active callers and deprecation announcement window passed.
- Cost/maintenance rationale accepted by product and SRE.

Gating Criteria (quick reference)
--------------------------------
| Gate | Requirement | Owner | Pass/Fail |
|------|-------------|-------|----------|
| Product sign-off | JIRA documented + roadmap removal | PL | pass |
| Migration path | Validated end-to-end tests + dry run | Eng | pass |
| SLO impact | No SLO regression > 0.1% absolute or compensatory plan | SRE | pass |
| Capacity | Capacity headroom >= projected variance + 20% | SRE | pass |
| Compliance | Data retention & audit obligations reviewed | Security | pass |

Step-by-step Runbook
--------------------
1) Pre-deprecation analysis (2-4 weeks before announce)
   - Run "service-usage" query for 90/60/30 day windows and document active callers.
     CLI example: rwi-admin metrics query --service inference-router --window 90d --metrics callers,p95,error_rate > analysis.csv
   - Calculate projected residual load if migration fails (worst-case 10% rollback).
   - SLO analysis: compute baseline and simulate removal. Use the SLO-sim tool: rwi-slo simulate --service inference-router --remove=true --horizon 30d

2) Announce deprecation (T-14 days)
   - Publish deprecation notice to product-consumers Slack channel and to the internal deprecation registry (Confluence page + tag).
   - Open a JIRA runbook ticket with checklist sub-tasks and assign owners.
   - Set the service routing flag: deprecation_notice=true (objectives: monitoring and routing behavior).

3) Canary removal and capacity verification (T-7 to T-3 days)
   - Create a 1% traffic canary to the replacement service for 48 hours. Monitor: error budget burn, p95 latency, and user-visible errors.
   - Verify autoscaling profiles on replacement to handle burst +10% traffic.
   - SRE action: if burn rate > 3x baseline or p95 regresses > 20% -> abort and investigate.

4) Phased traffic shift (T-2 to T)
   - Shift routing weights: 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 75% -> 100%, observing 2x collection window for each step.
   - Use the platform tooling command: rwi-router shift --from inference-router --to inference-v2 --steps 10,25,50,75,100 --monitoring-profile slo-critical
   - At each step validate SLO telemetry, error budget and capacity headroom. Document result in JIRA.

5) Final retirement (T+0)
   - Remove service from production routing (set weight 0).
   - Trigger infrastructure teardown plan (if applicable) after 72 hours of zero traffic.
   - Create a retirement snapshot: config export, metrics export, and logs for 90 days.

6) Post-retirement verification (T+3 to T+30)
   - Monitor for hidden callers: run daily dead-letter and 404 routing analysis.
   - Run SLO reconciliation job to ensure no downstream SLO degradation.
   - Close JIRA runbook when all artifacts and audits completed.

Rollback and Emergency Procedures
--------------------------------
- Immediate rollback condition: >5% absolute SLO regression or evidence of customer impact (SEV1).
- Rollback command: rwi-router rollback --service inference-v2 --to inference-router --until stable --reason "SLO regression"
- Post-rollback steps: create an incident, assign SRE incident commander, and follow the incident review template (see related pages).

Integration with Incident Review and SLO governance
--------------------------------------------------
- Any retirement-triggered incident must reference the runbook JIRA id and include gates that were passed.
- Incident review must include: timeline of traffic shifts, SLO telemetry graphs (p50/p95/p99, error rates), routing config, and change events.
- If an incident caused >25% of the remaining error budget to be spent in a burn window, the retirement is paused for a minimal 30-day cooldown and re-evaluated.

Operational Tooling and Automation
----------------------------------
- Automated checks: the runbook registers to-run validations with the runbook-orchestrator service (rwi-runbookd).
- Dashboard templates: create a retirement-dashboard from template 'retirement-basic' which includes: callers, traffic weight, error budget burn, p95 latency, and infra capacity headroom.
- Examples:
  - rwi-runbookd create --template retirement-basic --service inference-router --owner priya@redwood.ai
  - YAML for traffic-shift policy (example):
    policy_name: phased-shift
    steps: [10,25,50,75,100]
    validation_metrics: [error_rate,p95_latency,error_budget_burn]

Checklists and Templates
------------------------
1) Pre-deprecation checklist (must be completed before public notice):
   - [ ] JIRA decision logged and approved.
   - [ ] Replacement service end-to-end tests passing.
   - [ ] 30-day metrics baseline exported.
   - [ ] Audit & data-retention review completed.
2) Retirement execution checklist:
   - [ ] Canary run executed and monitored.
   - [ ] Phased traffic shift completed with no SLO regression.
   - [ ] Config snapshot taken and stored in artifact store.
3) Post-retirement checklist:
   - [ ] No callers detected for 30 days.
   - [ ] Teardown ticket executed.
   - [ ] Postmortem or closeout doc created and linked.

Template: SLO Change Request (example JSON)
-------------------------------------------
{
  "service": "inference-router",
  "current_slo": "99.95%",
  "requested_change": "deprecate",
  "impact_analysis": "migration to inference-v2 verified; expected drop in total capacity usage 8%",
  "owner": "priya@redwood.ai",
  "runbook_jira": "RWI-1234"
}

Monitoring and Metrics to Watch
------------------------------
- Active callers (primary leading indicator)
- Error budget burn rate (1h, 6h, 24h windows)
- p95 and p99 latency
- Request arrival distribution and sudden spike detection
- Routing 404/unknown-host spikes after weight shift

Post-retirement Incident Review Considerations
--------------------------------------------
- Include service retirement gates and timestamps in the evidence packet.
- For each incident post-retirement, verify whether callers are from deprecated clients; attach client versions.
- If retirement caused a production incident that consumed a downstream product SLO, escalate to the product SLO committee.

FAQ and Edge Cases
------------------
Q: What if we find a hidden caller 60 days after teardown?
A: Open a high-priority migration support ticket, temporarily re-enable a lightweight proxy for that caller if feasible, and run the standard canary + shift sequence targeted at that caller.

Q: Who signs off on final teardown?
A: Product lead + SRE lead + Security reviewer must sign-off in the JIRA runbook.

Appendix: Useful Commands and Dashboards
---------------------------------------
- Export metrics: rwi-admin metrics export --service inference-router --since 90d --out /tmp/inference-router-metrics.csv
- Create retirement dashboard: rwi-dashboard create --template retirement-basic --service inference-router
- Run SLO simulation: rwi-slo simulate --service inference-router --remove=true --horizon 30d

Revision history
----------------
- 2025-03-12: Initial draft (Priya Kapoor)
- 2025-05-07: Added automation patterns for rwi-runbookd (Daniel Kim)
- 2025-09-01: Publication edits and additional gating criteria (Alicia Martinez)

Related pages
-------------
- Capacity planning playbooks and SLO handbooks (see related_pages).
- Incident review standard templates in eng-sre/incident-review.

End of document.

title: dsid_6e585bf19b1848b9907b4e3aec2e61d9__inter-region-gpu-networking-privatelink-egress-playbook.txt
text:
Inter-Region GPU Networking: Egress Cost Reduction, PrivateLink Patterns, and TLS Handling

Overview

This playbook describes recommended architecture patterns, IaC snippets, operational guardrails, and an emergency runbook for inter-region GPU traffic that drives high egress costs or creates TLS/MTU problems for long-running inference streams. It targets: Dedicated and Private NVIDIA/AMD GPU pools connecting across cloud regions, cross-account PrivateLink/VPC-connector patterns, and Terraform module considerations for safe rollouts.

Goals and non‑goals
- Goals:
  - Reduce cross-region egress spend while preserving latency and throughput for inference workloads.
  - Provide safe PrivateLink / service‑mesh pattern alternatives to wide-open peering where tenant isolation and compliance are required.
  - Define TLS termination guidance for streaming tokens/KV-cache traffic and how to handle path MTU and connection affinity.
- Non‑goals:
  - This document does not cover application-level model merging or model sharding approaches.

Key concepts and tradeoffs
- Egress vs Latency:  Cross-region PrivateLink (or Cloud Interconnect) can reduce public egress but may add hop/processing cost and require cross-account endpoints. Peering is lower operational latency but can increase blast radius and egress meter complexity.
- Batching and Prefix Caching: Increasing request batching or KV cache reuse is often the highest‑ROI egress reducer at the application layer; network changes are complementary.
- TLS termination points: Terminating TLS at a regional gateway lowers CPU cost on GPU nodes and enables per-route inspection/caching. End-to-end TLS improves compliance but complicates caching and may exacerbate MTU issues on tunnels.

Recommended architectures (patterns)
1) Regional Ingress + Central Model Serving with PrivateLink (recommended for regulated customers)
- Client -> Regional API gateway (TLS) -> Regional proxy (mutual TLS to central region endpoints via PrivateLink) -> Central GPU pool.
- Pros: minimal public egress, clear ownership per-account, fine-grained IAM.
- Cons: additional proxies and potential latency.

2) Multi-region model replicas with smart routing (recommended for latency-sensitive inference)
- Deploy model replicas closer to traffic, maintain a small set of canonical models in central pool for large/batch jobs.
- Pros: low tail latency, lower cross-region streaming.
- Cons: increased republish traffic and storage sync costs.

3) Transit gateway + selective egress controls (recommended for large-scale multi-account infra)
- Use Transit/Hub + route tables to centralize control. Apply egress NATs per-tenant and enforce quotas.
- Pros: central ops, simpler routing.
- Cons: single central control plane = operational risk.

Network and TLS guidance
- TLS termination options:
  - Terminate at regional gateway when you need to inspect requests for caching or drop malicious payloads. Use mTLS between gateway and GPU nodes.
  - Keep end-to-end TLS for PII/regulated payloads; combine with token-based caching by gateway to reduce repeated decryption on GPUs.
- Connection affinity and streaming:
  - Use sticky sessions or hash-based affinity for long-lived streaming sessions (server‑sent events / chunked responses) so KV caches remain hot.
  - Prefer long-lived TCP connections with HTTP/2 or gRPC multiplexing; avoid recreating TLS repeatedly.
- MTU and jumbo frames:
  - Validate path MTU on VPN/tunnel routes. Large model payloads + gRPC streaming can hit fragmentation thresholds.
  - Recommended: 1400–1450 MTU on tunnels if path MTU discovery is flaky; enable DF detection in test harness.

Terraform / IaC patterns (examples)
- Principle: Avoid hard-coded region-to-region IDs in modules. Provide data sources that resolve correct PrivateLink endpoint IDs per-account. Use feature flags to toggle between peering and privatelink patterns.

Example snippet (Terraform pseudo-template)
```hcl
module "gpu_network_endpoint" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/internal-terraform-modules.git//privatelink-endpoint"

  region              = var.region
  service_name        = data.aws_vpc_endpoint_service.gpu_service.service_name
  allowed_account_ids = var.consumer_account_ids
  subnet_ids          = var.endpoint_subnet_ids
  tags = merge(var.common_tags, {component = "gpu-privatelink"})
}
```

- CI gating: Changes to privatelink modules must require a manual approval step in the pipeline when altering allowed_account_ids or route tables. See CI/CD section below.

Operational SLOs, metrics, and alert thresholds
- SLOs (example):
  - 95th percentile request tail latency for streaming inference <= 250ms region-local.
  - Cross-region egress cost per 1M tokens should not increase >10% month-over-month absent signed change request.
- Key metrics to export to observability:
  - network.egress_bytes_per_region (per-account, per-model)
  - network.egress_cost_estimate_per_hour (projected)
  - network.path_mtu_failures_total (per-tunnel)
  - connection.active_streams (per-node)
  - connection.stream_reconnect_rate (per-10m)
- Alert thresholds (examples):
  - network.egress_cost_estimate_per_hour > budget_rate*1.2 for 30m -> P2 paging to infra-finance oncall.
  - path_mtu_failures_total > 5 per 5m -> P1 paging to networking oncall.

Runbook: urgent egress spike (summary)
1) Detect: Pager triggers from billing-derived egress forecast alert.
2) Triage (5m): Identify top 5 (account, region, model) tuples by egress size using network.egress_bytes_per_region and query tracing.
3) Immediate mitigation (10m):
   - If PrivateLink exists: disable cross-region route propagation for the affected account via terraform toggle (see quick toggle below).
   - If peering used: remove route to expensive region and replace with reject route in Transit Gateway to force local fallbacks.
   - If neither, apply temporary token rate-limit config at regional gateway to cap requests to 10 rps per token.
4) Reduce application-level cost (15–60m): enable aggressive KV prefix caching on the gateway, increase batching window for non-interactive jobs, and re-route batch jobs to central bulk region with cheaper egress.
5) Postmortem: Create incident with cost delta analysis, deployment diffs, and retro within 7 business days.

Quick toggle example: terraform variable switch pattern
- Implement a guard variable in a small ops-only Terraform repo that flips routing from peering to blackhole for a region and is guarded by a PR that requires 2 approvers: ops_lead and finance_lead.

Operational runbooks and playbooks (short list)
- Daily checks for steady-state:
  - Top 10 accounts by egress (rollup) and delta vs baseline.
  - Path MTU probe results for all VPNs, flag failures.
- Weekly tasks:
  - Validate PrivateLink endpoint health and rotate endpoint policies in test accounts.
  - Reconcile route tables and remove stale entries older than 90 days.

Governance and ownership
- Ownership:
  - Network & Cloud Accounts Team: default owner for PrivateLink/peering configurations and Transit Gateway route tables.
  - GPU Fleet Team: owner for node-level TLS configuration, KV cache interfaces, and application-level batching knobs.
  - Infra Finance: owner for egress budgets and billing alerts.
- Change process:
  - Any change to cross-region routing or egress budget >5% must open a RFC in the infra change board and include cost projection and rollback plan.

CI/CD and deployment guidance
- Pipeline steps for terraform changes that affect networking:
  1. Static analysis (tfsec, checkov).
  2. Plan with `-out` artifact; automatic plan upload to PR.
  3. Auto-approve only for tag-only changes; manual approval required for route or account list changes.
  4. Post-deploy smoke: synthetic inference traffic from a canary region to validate MTU/TLS and measure tail latency.

Testing checklist (pre-rollout)
- Validate path MTU end-to-end with 3 packet sizes and verify that fragmentation does not occur.
- Smoke test TTL and reconnect behavior under transient 5–10s BGP flap simulation.
- Verify billing projection tool returns expected delta when toggling route to blackhole in staging.

Appendix: sample monitoring queries
- Top egress accounts by bytes (PromQL example):
  sum by (account, region) (increase(network_egress_bytes_total[1h]))
- Active streaming connections (Grafana):
  sum(connection_active_streams) by (node, region)

References and related artifacts
- See module:privatelink-endpoint in internal-terraform-modules repo for implementation.
- See existing topology diagram: /confluence/eng-infra/cloud-accounts-and-networking/gpu-network-topology-and-tenant-isolation-patterns

Revision history
- 2024-09-18: Draft created by Aaron Liao.
- 2024-11-06: Added MTU guidance and runbook steps (reviewer: Tariq Malik).
- 2025-01-10: Finalized CI gating and alert thresholds (reviewer: Evelyn Park).

Contact
- Primary oncall and owners: network-oncall@redwood.example.com, gpu-fleet@redwood.example.com

title: dsid_d726b76df4b84bec831e4f5c553c468a__entitlement-deprecation-rollforward-evidence-guideline-2027.txt
text:
Entitlement Deprecation and Rollforward: Evidence & Operational Guideline

Overview
This playbook defines the operational and audit-evidence requirements for entitlements (roles, permissions, feature flags) that are scheduled for deprecation and the controlled 'rollforward' process used to reintroduce or replace entitlement sets after a rollback. It consolidates RBAC change controls, audit logging expectations, data residency considerations, and secure-SDLC gates into a single reference for security, IAM, SRE, and compliance teams.

Audience
- IAM engineers
- Security & compliance reviewers
- SRE and platform operators
- Product owners proposing entitlement changes

Goals
1) Ensure every entitlement deprecation has an immutable, auditable evidence package that satisfies SOC-like audits.
2) Provide deterministic, tested steps for rollforward after a rollback or staged canary failure.
