   - Heuristic: sustained gpu_temp > 85C on >50% of devices in a pod -> schedule live-evacuation of affected pods to warm standby nodes, mark host for maintenance, and reduce batch size for tenants on that host. If preemption events spike, immediately migrate low-priority workloads and enable tenant burst-protections.
   - Operator actions: maintain a 5-node warm standby pool per region; use drain-with-warmup to avoid cold-start penalties.

4) Request router and routing fairness signals
   - Signals: tenant_queue_delay_ms, request_reject_rate, overflow_burst_credit_balance
   - Play ID: R-PRIOR-04 (Tenant prioritization and soft-quota enforcement)
   - Heuristic: when tenant_queue_delay > 300ms and burst_credit_balance < 0 for >2 minutes, soft-throttle best-effort tenants by returning HTTP 429 with Retry-After header and redirect high-priority tenants to dedicated capacity.
   - Automation snippet (example):
     "if tenant.priority == 'best_effort' and credit_balance < 0: return 429, Retry-After=30s"

5) Cost and token leak signals
   - Signals: token_rate_by_route, unexpected_token_spike_ratio, token_utilization_growth_24h
   - Play ID: C-LEAK-05 (Token leak detection and mitigation)
   - Heuristic: unexpected_token_spike_ratio > 3x baseline for >10m AND there is a matching increase in error_retries -> throttle route and trigger request-level debug capture for 1% of requests. Notify product owner.

Alert definitions (prometheus-style examples)
-------------------------------------------
- kv_cache_hit_rate_low: avg_over_time(kv_prefix_cache_hit_rate[5m]) < 0.7
- tail_latency_breach: (histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(inference_latency_bucket[5m])))) > 1.2 * target_95th
- gpu_temp_spike: max_over_time(gpu_temp_celsius[2m]) > 85

Decision flow (quick)
---------------------
1) Observe: which signal category is primary? Cache / Latency / GPU / Routing / Cost
2) Classify severity: P1 if SLOs are violated for >5m and >10% of tenants impacted; P2 otherwise.
3) Execute play: pick matching Play ID and follow runbook steps.
4) Escalate: if automation fails or progress < 30% within 10 minutes, page Platform Lead and Incident Commander.

Operator runbook template (what each play must include)
------------------------------------------------------
- Title and Play ID
- Observable signals and canonical Grafana dashboard links
- Step-by-step operator actions (safety-first)
- CLI commands and automation toggles with examples
- Rollback criteria and safe-stop points
- Post-incident tasks and metrics to capture
- Owner and responder contact list

Example runbook excerpt: C-REHYDRATE-01
1) Owner: kv-cache team (oncall: @kv-cache-oncall)
2) Observe: confirm kv_prefix_cache_hit_rate < 0.7 on dashboard "KV Cache Health" (region filter = EU-WEST).
3) Run: ./scripts/prefetch-prefixes --tenant-file=/tmp/top10.json --budget-tokens=20M --dry-run=false
4) Verify: monitor kv_prefix_cache_fill_latency_ms and hit_rate for 10 minutes.
5) Rollback: if hit_rate decreases or model errors increase >1% after prefetch, kill prefetch and revert retention policy.
6) Postmortem triggers: if incident lasted >30 minutes or cost delta > $1000, open a postmortem ticket.

Automation safety knobs and feature flags
----------------------------------------
- All automated remediation jobs must require one of the following: region opt-in, tenant whitelist, token budget.
- Feature flags: ff.auto_rehydrate_enabled (boolean), ff.auto_model_fallback_disabled (boolean per-customer), ff.adaptive_batching_min_ratio (float).
- Default: auto remediation disabled for Restricted tenants; enabled for public dev/test and best-effort tiers.

Roadmap and experiments (Q1/Q2 2026)
------------------------------------
- Q1 2026: ship a declarative telemetry-to-action DSL and controller that executes plays with audit trails.
- Q2 2026: integrate golden-prompt regression checks into model-fallback automation.
- Experiment: predictive rehydration using prefix access forecasting (A/B test in eu-west, success criteria: 15% token-cost reduction for top 10 tenants without latency regressions).

Retrospective notes (from regional gameday, 2025-12)
--------------------------------------------------
- What worked: targeted prefetch reduced tail-latency during simulated workload surges.
- What did not: automation assumed perfect tenant metadata; missing tenant-to-model mappings caused two false positive rehydrates. Fix: add metadata health check.
- Action items: add tenant-model mapping health check (owner: infra-metadata team), add a 60s cooldown to automated prefetches to avoid thrash.

Open ownership and next steps
----------------------------
- Owner: Platform Observability (primary) and KV Cache (secondary).
- Next step: convert this catalog to a machine-readable DSL and schedule a cross-team workshop to agree on safety gates by 2026-03-01.

Appendix: Useful CLI snippets
----------------------------
- Prefetch (dry-run): ./scripts/prefetch-prefixes --tenant-file=/tmp/top10.json --budget-tokens=1M --dry-run=true
- Evacuation (live): ./platformctl evacuate-host --host host-123 --drain-mode=warmup --notify=true
- Throttle tenant: curl -X POST https://platform-api.local/admin/tenant/throttle -d '{"tenant":"tenant-xyz","rate":10}'

Contact and escalation
----------------------
- Platform SRE primary: arjun@redwood.ai
- Platform lead pager: +1-555-0101
- Slack channels: #platform-ops, #kv-cache, #gpu-fleet

Document change log
-------------------
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft by Arjun Menon.
- 2025-12-20: Added GPU isolation play and automation knobs (reviewers: Maya Chen).
- 2026-02-15: Roadmap and retrospective updates; published.

title: dsid_c45618ed14e2472a981e12fe3a0bf6ff__attribute-access-rollout-and-evidence-retention-2029.txt
text:
Attribute-access rollout and evidence retention roadmap

Overview

This document provides a practical, phased roadmap for adopting Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) across Redwood Inference resources and services. It ties RBAC compatibility, audit logging requirements, evidence retention timelines, secure-SDLC gating, and incident-response triggers into a single operational playbook. Intended audience: security engineers, IAM owners, product platform teams, SRE, and compliance reviewers.

Goals
- Reduce over-provisioning by expressing access as attributes and policies instead of large role collections.
- Ensure auditability and compliance: every attribute evaluation must be traceable and retained per the evidence matrix below.
- Provide deterministic migration steps from existing RBAC constructs to ABAC, with explicit exception handling.
- Integrate ABAC checks into SDLC and incident response so policy drift and attribute abuse are detectable and recoverable.

Scope
- In-scope: all internal control plane services, model-serving endpoints, customer tenancy metadata, and privileged admin functions.
- Out-of-scope: ephemeral internal dev-only feature flags (will be addressed in a follow-up).

Definitions
- Attribute: a key-value pair about a subject (user/service), resource, action, or environment (e.g., department:engineering, resource.sensitivity:high, request.origin:private_vpc).
- ABAC policy: world-readable policy that combines attributes into allow/deny logic.
- Evidence artifact: packaged set of logs, policy snapshots, and attribute-change records required for audits or investigations.

Ownership and roles
- IAM Security Team (owner): policy design, central attribute catalog, evidence retention policy enforcement.
- Platform Engineering: runtime enforcement hooks, policy evaluation libraries, SDKs.
- Service Owners: map service-specific attributes to the central catalog and own migration of local roles.
- Compliance: validates evidence packaging and retention during audits.

High-level migration phases
1) Discovery (0-2 months)
   - Inventory: export current role assignments, service accounts, role-to-permission mappings.
   - Attribute catalog kickoff: seed attributes (department, tier, environment, resource.sensitivity, customer_org_id).
   - Deliverable: discovery report and attribute catalog v0.

2) Pilot (2-5 months)
   - Select 2 services (one infra service, one product-facing) for ABAC pilot.
   - Implement policy-evaluation middleware and audit hooks.
   - Run RBAC side-by-side: enforce ABAC in allow-mode while RBAC remains authoritative.
   - Deliverable: pilot runbook, sample policy set, lessons learned.

3) Gradual rollout (6-12 months)
   - Phased cutover by business unit.
   - Enforce ABAC for read-only ops first, then move to write/privileged ops after 2 weeks of stable metrics.
   - Automate attribute syncs from HR and customer directories.

4) Harden & Optimize (ongoing)
   - Enforce periodic policy review, anomaly detection, and evidence packaging for audits.

Mapping to RBAC (compatibility pattern)
- Pattern: Role -> Policy shim
  1. For each RBAC role, define an ABAC policy that reproduces permissions using subject attributes (e.g., department, job_level) and resource tags.
  2. Create a compatibility layer that evaluates both RBAC and ABAC for a transition window.
  3. Decommission roles when no bindings remain and policy test coverage shows parity.

Example ABAC policy (JSON policy snippet)
{
  "id": "policy.allow.data-read.engineering",
  "target": { "resource.sensitivity": "low", "action": "read" },
  "condition": "subject.department == \"engineering\" && subject.job_level >= 2",
  "effect": "allow"
}

Audit logging and evidence retention matrix
- All ABAC evaluations must produce an evaluation event with the following minimal fields: timestamp, request_id, subject.id, subject.attributes(snapshot_id), resource.id, resource.attributes(snapshot_id), policy_id, decision(allow|deny), decision_reason, evaluator_version.

Retention matrix (summary)
- Evaluation events: 3 years (primary evidence)
- Policy snapshots: 7 years (archival, per compliance)
- Attribute source sync logs (HR/SCIM/KMS): 1 year (sensitive PII redaction applied)
- Attribute-change records (who changed attribute, why, approval id): 7 years
- Role to policy deprecation logs: 5 years

Evidence packaging format (required fields)
- Evidence artifact must be a zipped manifest containing:
  - manifest.json (list of files, policy_ids, snapshot timestamps)
  - evaluation_events.ndjson (queryable event stream)
  - policies/ (policy snapshots in JSON)
  - attribute_snapshots/ (CSV of attribute key-values with snapshot_id)
  - acl_mappings/ (legacy RBAC role exports for the time window)
  - signer.txt (PKI-signed hash of the manifest)

Sample manifest.json (mini example)
{
  "artifact_id": "evidence-2029-01-10-0001",
  "time_range": "2028-12-01/2029-01-10",
  "included_files": ["evaluation_events.ndjson", "policies/policy.allow.*.json"]
}

Retention and storage considerations
- Primary evidence store: write-once, encrypted S3 bucket (KMS CMK: evidence-primary).
- Archival: cold store with immutability flags (7y).
- Access to evidence artifacts: RBAC+ABAC gated; access requests require documented business justification and TTR < 48 hours for compliance requests.

Secure SDLC gates
- Policy changes must follow this pipeline: dev -> peer review -> staging (test harness with replayed evaluation events) -> canary -> production.
- PR templates must include a policy-testing checklist and required unit tests for decision coverage.
- All policy PR merges trigger a policy-snapshot commit (immutable) and generate a signed manifest entry.

Incident response integration
- Attribute change anomaly detection: trigger when >5% of attributes for a domain change within 1 hour or any attribute change to resource.sensitivity:high.
- Incident playbook steps when triggered:
  1. Auto-create incident and tag with "abac-attribute-anomaly".
  2. Freeze attribute propagation pipelines (HR sync, SCIM connectors, internal APIs).
  3. Collect evidence artifact covering the 72 hours prior to anomaly and lock it for forensic analysis.
  4. Rotate any affected service credentials if policy evaluations affected privileged flows.
  5. Post-incident: run attribution analysis, policy/role rollback if required, and create a remediation timeline.

Risk exceptions and approvals
- Short-lived exceptions (<=14 days): product manager + service owner approval in ticketing system; must include compensating controls and evidence snapshot.
- Medium exceptions (15-90 days): security approver + business SLA review; artifact retention must be extended to cover exception period.
- Long exceptions (>90 days): require CISO review and recorded board-level approval.

Operational runbook (quick checklist)
- Daily:
  - Monitor ABAC evaluation error rate (<0.05% target).
  - Verify attribute sync success (last sync age < 5 minutes).
- Weekly:
  - Run policy coverage test suite for active services.
  - Review top-10 denied-but-requested cases for potential false positives.
- Quarterly:
  - Evidence retention audit (verify manifests and cold-store integrity).
  - Policy review with service owners.

Queries and dashboards to build
- Live: ABAC evaluation rate, deny-rate by service, average decision latency, evaluator version distribution.
- Forensics: event-explorer filtering by policy_id, subject.id, attribute snapshot_id, and time range.

Appendix A: SDK enforcement snippets
- Example Golang evaluator call (pseudo):
  resp, err := evaluator.Evaluate(ctx, &EvaluateRequest{
    Subject: subjectSnapshot,
    Resource: resourceSnapshot,
    Action: "write",
    RequestId: reqID,
  })
  // resp.Decision -> log to evaluation_events.ndjson

Appendix B: Policy test harness checklist
- Unit tests for deny/allow boundary cases
- Fuzz tests for unexpected attribute values
- Replay of historical evaluation events to validate decision parity with RBAC baseline

References and related reading
- Central attribute catalog (link to internal catalog)
- Event schema contract and retention runbook
- Entitlement binding and archival playbook

Document change log
- 2028-06-15: Created (Leah Nakamura).
- 2028-09-10: Pilot results and attribute catalog v1 added (Ethan Cole review).
- 2029-01-10: Clarified retention matrix and incident triggers; marked as published.

Contact
- For questions or to request a migration consult, email iam-security@redwood-inference.com or open the "ABAC Migration" Jira board and tag the IAM Security team.

title: dsid_c55ab0eb3af54bc89d6d28715a956cfe__upgrade-rehearsal-and-failover-circuit-breaker-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Upgrade rehearsal and failover circuit-breaker playbook

Summary
This playbook defines a repeatable, low-risk process for rehearsing major Private deployment upgrades and for exercising the automated failover / circuit-breaker layers that protect customer SLAs. It covers rehearsal cadence, scenario templates, instrumentation requirements, rollback triggers, and a sample circuit-breaker policy with concrete thresholds. The goal is to reduce surprise failures during live upgrades and to ensure evidence for forensic analysis is captured automatically.

Scope
- Applies to Private (VPC and on-prem) deployments across all supported architectures.
- Focus on control-plane upgrades, runtime binary/model swaps, and KV cache/stateful migrations.
- Excludes purely client-side SDK changes. For multi-tenant Hosted/Dedicated upgrades see the separate hosted upgrade playbooks.

Goals and SLOs
- Validate upgrade plan end-to-end in a staging environment that mirrors production network topology and telemetry hooks.
- Ensure automated circuit-breakers engage before customer-visible SLA impact exceeds defined limits.
- Maintain <5% error-rate delta and <25% median latency increase during a canary rehearsal for 10 minutes.
- Preserve forensic evidence for any exercised rollback (minimum: chronological logs, artifact digests, snapshot manifest).

Roles and ownership
- Upgrade Lead (owner): coordinates rehearsals, runbook gating, and customer notifications. Typical owner: release-engineering.
- Operator on-call: executes operator playbook actions during rehearsal and assesses abort/rollforward decisions.
- SRE/Telemetry: ensures traces/metrics/logs are collected and stored in the evidence bucket.
- Security/Compliance: verifies signatures and snapshot attestation where required.

Prerequisites
1) Inventory: list target clusters, tenant mappings, model variants, and control-plane endpoints.
2) Backups & snapshots: confirm last successful snapshot <24h, and that snapshot retention policy is met.
3) Telemetry hooks: traces, request-level telemetry, token-level cost logging, request IDs.
4) Circuit-breaker policies deployed and tested in dry-run mode.
5) Cross-team scheduling: at least 48h lead time and stakeholder ack.

Rehearsal types
- Canary Rehearsal: small percentage (1–5%) of synthetic or shadow traffic routed to upgraded path. Quick validation of correctness and perf.
- Fault-injection Rehearsal: induce controlled resource faults (CPU spike, GPU OOM, network blackhole) to validate degradations and failover.
- Full Swap Dry-run: perform model binary swap on staging with full KV migrations, no customer traffic, verify snapshot rehydrate.
- Multi-tenant Evacuation Rehearsal: simulate tenant migration/evacuation and verify state consistency.

Example rehearsal scenarios (prioritized)
1) Model quantized-swap + prefix cache migration under synthetic 95th percentile token load.
2) Control-plane API schema bump with canary route and automatic fallback to older schema handler.
3) Device preemption: simulate node-level GPU preempt and validate warm-start fallback.
4) Telemetry partition: drop logs to aggregator for 5 minutes and verify on-disk circular buffer retention and evidence export.

Step-by-step rehearsal runbook
1) Preflight (T-72h to T-2h)
   - Publish rehearsal window and owners.
   - Snapshot artifacts: image digests, model checksums, migration plans.
   - Validate staging mirrors: topologies, VM types, kernel versions, and container runtime.
   - Confirm test dataset and traffic generator with deterministic seeds.
2) Dry-run deployment (T-2h)
   - Deploy upgrade to staging control-plane; do not route production traffic.
   - Run the smoke-test suite (end-to-end inference, quota checks, auth paths).
   - Validate observability: dashboards update, synthetic traces appear, log retention policy applied.
3) Canary (T)
   - Shift 1%–5% of traffic or replay synthetic workload to upgraded nodes.
   - Monitor SLOs and circuit-breaker metrics for 10–30 minutes.
   - Owner accepts if acceptance criteria met.
4) Fault injection (optional; parallel)
   - Execute one fault scenario for 5–15 minutes.
   - Confirm circuit-breaker engages and traffic is routed to fallback.
5) Rollback/rollforward decision point
   - Abort and rollback if any of the failure conditions are met (see Rollback triggers).
   - When safe, rollforward with gradual ramp and increased telemetry sampling.
6) Postmortem and evidence preservation
   - Archive artifact manifests, logs, and traces to the evidence bucket.
   - Run the post-rehearsal checklist and produce a 1-page summary for stakeholders.

Rollback triggers (explicit thresholds)
- Error rate: sustained increase >5 percentage points above baseline for 5 minutes.
- Latency: 95th percentile latency > baseline * 1.8 for 5 minutes.
- Throughput: backpressure causing queue growth > 50% of buffer for 3 consecutive intervals (60s windows).
- Data integrity: any inconsistency detected between snapshot manifests and rehydrated state.
- Security: failed signature verification of artifacts or missing attestations.

Circuit-breaker design and example policy
Design principles\- Prefer fast local circuit-breakers at the node/proxy level for immediate mitigation; use global circuit-breakers at the control-plane to coordinate routing decisions.
- Circuit-breakers should act conservatively and favor preserving correctness and data integrity over latency improvements.
- Policies must be parametric with a dry-run mode to validate without impacting traffic.

Operational thresholds (suggested)
+----------------------+-------------------------------+
| Metric               | Trigger                       |
+----------------------+-------------------------------+
| Node error-rate      | > 12% sustained for 60s       |
| Route error-rate     | > 8% sustained for 120s       |
| Node GPU OOM count   | >= 2 OOMs within 10 minutes   |
| KV-consistency fail  | any detected mismatch         |
+----------------------+-------------------------------+

Example circuit-breaker policy (YAML snippet)
---
cb_policy_version: v1
name: regional-fallback-cb
scope: region
triggers:
  - metric: route_error_rate
    window_seconds: 120
    threshold_pct: 8
    action: divert_to_fallback
  - metric: node_gpu_oom_count
    window_seconds: 600
    threshold_count: 2
    action: cordon_node_and_drain
  - metric: kv_reconciliation_errors
    window_seconds: 300
    threshold_count: 1
    action: pause_model_refresh
failback_policy:
  grace_period_seconds: 300
  validation_checks:
    - smoke_tests: true
    - telemetry_lag_seconds: < 30
---

Circuit-breaker playbook steps (when CB fires)
1) Immediate notification to on-call and upgrade lead.
2) Automated action (divert to fallback model or route) executed by routing service.
3) Operator performs quick triage: check recent errors, OOM traces, and last artifact hashes.
4) If condition is transient, increase sampling and monitor for 15 minutes; otherwise progress to rollback/evacuation.

Rollback and forensic evidence requirements
- When rollback is executed, the system must capture and store the following artifacts in a tamper-evident evidence bucket:
  - Artifact digests (images, model weights) and attestations.
  - Last successful snapshots and rehydration manifests.
  - Complete logs (control-plane, node-level, and operator commands) for T-30m before trigger and T+30m after.
  - Traces for affected requests with request IDs.
- Evidence retention: retain rehearsal evidence for 90 days for internal audits; extend to 1 year for regulated customers per contract.

Acceptance criteria for a successful rehearsal
- All rehearsed scenarios completed without hitting rollback triggers, or they hit triggers and circuit-breaker behaved per policy and evidence was captured.
- Runbook acknowledgments: Upgrade Lead and Operator sign-off in the runbook journal.
- Post-rehearsal report: includes metrics table, timeline of events, root-cause hypothesis for any anomalies, and action items.

Templates and example commands
- Snapshot command (example):
  rinfctl snapshot create --cluster tenant-prod-eu --note "pre-upgrade-2026-06-15" --output manifest.json
- Evidence export (example):
  rinfctl evidence export --manifest manifest.json --bucket s3://redwood-evidence/private-rehearsals/2026-06-15
- Dry-run CB validation:
  rinfctl cb validate --policy regional-fallback-cb.yaml --dry-run

Post-rehearsal checklist (minimum)
1) Evidence export successful and checksum-verified.
2) Acceptance criteria documented and stored.
3) Action items created with owners and deadlines.
4) Dashboards returned to baseline sampling and retention.
5) Customer-impact review completed if any degradations occurred.

Appendix A — Example artifacts to attach to postmortem
- manifest.json (artifact digests)
- cb-policy.yaml (the exact policy file used)
- timeline.log (annotated sequence of operator actions)
- perf-metrics.csv (raw telemetry for the rehearsal window)

Appendix B — Quick reference: decision matrix
- If error-rate > rollback threshold AND CB failed to divert => immediate rollback and forensic snapshot.
- If CB diverted successfully and service remained within customer SLA => escalate incident for RCA but continue rollforward when safe.

Change log
- 2026-06-15: Initial published version (A. Kapoor).
- 2026-08-02: Added explicit rollback thresholds and evidence retention guidance (M. Chen).

Related policies and pages
- See the Private Deploy: Forensic rollback playbook for evidence formats and signature formats.
- See tenant-evacuation and snapshot runbooks for stateful migration commands.

Contact
- Upgrade lead: release-eng@redwood.com
- SRE on-call rotation: oncall-sre@redwood.com

title: dsid_44e3e9bc00b84beb8ada4a8b71db2fcc__discrete-stabilization-catalog-and-escape-hatch-playbook-2027.txt
text:
Discrete Stabilization Catalog and Escape-Hatch Playbook

Overview

This document is a compact, operator-friendly catalog of stabilization patterns and 'escape-hatch' procedures for on-call engineers and bridge operators responding to service instability (latency oscillation, transient SLO regressions, noisy-neighbor stalls, KV cache avalanches, and multi-tenant degradation). It is intentionally concise so teams can act quickly without flipping through multiple runbooks. Use this as a decision surface: identify the pattern, follow the associated rapid steps, and escalate to deeper runbooks as needed.

When to use this catalog

- Fast-moving incidents where the priority is to restore customer-facing behavior within the first 30 minutes.
- Multi-service degradations where automated routing or fallback toggles can limit blast radius.
- Game day scenarios and tabletop rehearsals as a quick reference for action owners.

Guiding principles

1) Minimize blast radius: prefer targeted mitigations (route, limit, degrade) over global shutdowns.
2) Observe then act: gather a minimal evidence set (traces, P99, token rates, eviction metrics) before irreversible actions.
3) Keep customers informed: if an incident impacts tenants for >10 minutes, publish a short status page note and add periodic updates.

Stabilization patterns (catalog)

Pattern: Latency oscillation (periodic P99 spikes)
- Symptoms: P99 jumps to 300–800ms in bursts for 3+ cycles; throughput sustained.
- Likely causes: asynchronous background batches, intermittent GC on model workers, autoscaler thrash.
- Rapid mitigations (escape-hatch):
  1. Attach live profile: run the tracing hook (obs/trace-link) for the last 10 minutes.
  2. Toggle conservative batcher mode: /api/admin/batcher?mode=conservative -> reduces batch size and prioritizes latency (no config restart).
  3. Pin to lower-seq-length model variant for affected route (route config -> set model_variant=fast-latency).
  4. If oscillation continues, enable per-route rate-limiter at 80% of normal QPS for 15 minutes.

Pattern: Noisy neighbor GPU saturation
- Symptoms: single-host GPU util spikes to 98% while others at 60%; specific tenant latency increases.
- Likely causes: oversized burst jobs, driver-level memory leak, misbehaving private deploy.
- Rapid mitigations:
  1. Identify host via metrics (gpu-alloc / host-id).
  2. Migrate affected reservations: run CLI migrate-reservation --host HOSTID --target pool-safe.
  3. If migration fails, drain the host (drain-host HOSTID) and enable fallback to prewarmed dedicated pool.
  4. Notify infra-sre and open a follow-up ticket with host logs.

Pattern: KV cache avalanche / mass eviction
- Symptoms: sudden spike in cold-start token latency; cache-miss rate > 60%; downstream P95 token latency increases.
- Likely causes: model rollout that changed prefix patterns, cache TTL misconfig change, or eviction due to memory pressure.
- Rapid mitigations:
  1. Re-enable prefix-KV sticky policy (config: cache.prefix_policy=sticky).
  2. Roll back model rollout to previous version for the offending route.
  3. Gradually ramp requests back with canary traffic (10% -> 25% -> 50%).

Escape-hatch inventory (actions you can invoke immediately)

Table: quick inventory of escape-hatches
| Action | Owner | Trigger | Immediate rollback criteria | CLI / Console path |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Route-level rate limit (soft) | runtime | P99 > 300ms for 5m | P99 < 250ms for 10m | Console -> Routes -> Rate limits |
| Switch to fast-latency model variant | runtime | SLO regression + regression test pass | Traffic restored and qualitative checks pass | /api/route/update -> model_variant |
| Batcher conservative mode | serving-runtime | P95 token latency > threshold | P95 < baseline for 10m | /api/admin/batcher |
| Drain host and migrate | infra-sre | GPU saturation on host | Host rebalanced and utilization < 70% | infractl drain-host HOSTID |
| Re-enable KV sticky policy | platform | sudden cache-miss spike | cache-miss < 15% for 20m | Console -> Caching -> Prefix policy |

Step-by-step runbooks (short forms)

Runbook: Rapid route-level throttling (ten-minute stabilization)
1. Trigger: Alert: route.<service>.p99.latency > 400ms for 3 minutes.
2. Evidence to collect (first 5 minutes):
   - P95/P99 traces (jaeger link), top 5 trace spans, and token counts.
   - Queue depth and drop rates from queue-metrics dashboard.
   - Identify recent config changes (deploys in last 60m).
3. Action: apply a soft rate limit at 80% of normal QPS for the affected route.
   - Console -> Routes -> Edit -> Add soft_limit=80% with 15m TTL.
4. Observe for 5–10 minutes. If P99 falls below target, start a slow ramp back (90% -> 100% over 20 minutes).
5. If P99 does not improve, switch model variant to fast-latency and notify product.

Runbook: Noisy-host containment
1. Trigger: single-host GPU util >95% and tenant errors rising.
2. Evidence: host metrics, active reservations, and running job list.
3. Action: mark host as draining, migrate non-critical reservations, re-route latency-sensitive jobs to prewarmed pool.
4. Communication: post on #ops-bridge channel and update status page if >10 minutes.

Customer status templates (short, copy-paste)

Status update — initial (within 10m):
"We are investigating elevated latencies impacting model inference for some customers. Engineers are actively identifying the source and applying mitigations. We will post an update within 15 minutes. Impact: partial for some API routes."

Status update — action (after mitigation applied):
"We have applied a temporary mitigation (rate limiting / model variant switch) which has reduced error rates and latency for affected requests. We are continuing to monitor and will follow with a detailed post-incident note."

Status update — recovery (when stable):
"Service performance has returned to normal. We are running a set of post-incident checks and will publish a short summary and follow-up actions within 48 hours."

Template: customer-facing root cause summary (48h)
- Impact: summary of who was affected and approximate timeframe.
- Root cause: short one-line cause.
- Resolution: actions taken and why they work.
- Follow-ups: planned infra/config changes, rollback/rollforward schedule, and timeline for completion.

Game day and drill guidance

Purpose: validate the escape-hatch catalog under stress, exercise communication cadence, and confirm rollback criteria are understood.

Suggested exercises (1–2 hours each)
- Latency oscillation drill: simulate GC spike on a model worker and practice toggling batcher conservative mode and model-variant pinning.
- Cache-eviction drill: deploy a synthetic traffic pattern to cause cache churn; practice re-enabling sticky policy and ramping canary traffic.
- Noisy neighbor drill: mark a host as saturated and exercise drain/migrate and failover into prewarmed pool.

Exercise checklist
- Pre-run: assign Bridge lead, Evidence owner, and Customer comms owner.
- During run: collect prescribed evidence, make one mitigation, and document timestamps.
- Post-run: 30-minute retro capturing time-to-first-action and time-to-recovery, plus a 1-page remediation plan.

Ownership and escalation matrix

- Bridge lead: first 30 minutes orchestration and status page publication.
- Evidence owner (runtime/op-observability): collects traces, SLO dashboards, and relevant logs.
- Infra escalation: infra-sre on-call for host-level actions (drain, migrate).
- Product/Model PM: notified when model variant or behavior change is required.

Escalation thresholds (examples)
- If incident expected to exceed 60 minutes OR customer-impacting errors > 5% of tenant traffic, escalate to SRE manager and Customer Success lead.
- If more than 3 tenants report degraded service directly, open a Sev2 and engage GTM lead.

Post-incident guidance

1. Evidence capture: attach SLO timelines, sample traces, and commands executed to the incident timeline.
2. Blameless postmortem: follow the postmortem template (timeline, root cause, contributing factors, corrective actions, owners, and ETA).
3. Runbook updates: if an escape-hatch was used, update this catalog with notes on effectiveness and add a section on 'when not to use'.

Appendix: CLI snippets and config quick-reference

- Apply soft route rate limit (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://admin.redwood/api/routes/route-id/rate-limit" -d '{"soft_limit":0.8, "ttl_minutes":15 }'

- Switch model variant (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://admin.redwood/api/routes/route-id/model-variant" -d '{"variant":"fast-latency" }'

- Drain host (example):
  infractl drain-host --host HOSTID --reason "noisy GPU saturation"

Configuration table (example thresholds)
| Metric | Alert threshold | First action | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| route.p99.latency | >300ms for 5m | soft rate limit 80% | runtime |
| host.gpu.util | >95% for 2m | drain host | infra-sre |
| cache.miss.rate | >50% | re-enable sticky policy | platform |

Related pages and links

- Include links to the full runbooks: runtime emergency runbook, infra host recovery runbook, and postmortem template.

Revision history

- 2025-11-02: created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-06-18: added noisy neighbor containment steps (reviewer: Arjun Patel).
- 2027-03-14: expanded escape-hatch inventory and added game day exercise checklist (reviewer: Lina Gomez).

title: dsid_e20c039e79f74814b0442b5ea8eba500__suggestions-guardrails-and-constraints.txt
text:
Optimization Suggestions (Beta): Guardrails, Safety Constraints, and Edge Cases

## Purpose
This document defines **guardrails** and **constraints** used by the Optimize Suggestions system (beta) when generating **batching** and **caching** recommendations. The goal is to ensure that suggestions:
- Are conservative and safe for production workloads.
- Avoid recommending changes that are likely to violate latency/reliability SLOs.
- Are robust to telemetry gaps and known workload edge cases.
- Are explainable in the Console (“why we recommend this”, “what could go wrong”, and “how to apply safely”).

This doc is normative for suggestion generation logic. If a recommendation is blocked by a hard guardrail, it should not be emitted.

## Scope (beta)
In scope:
- **Batching suggestions:** tuning continuous batching parameters (e.g., max_batch_size, max_batch_delay_ms, target_tokens_per_batch) for a specific route/model.
- **Caching suggestions:** enabling or tuning prefix/KV caching parameters (e.g., cache enablement, cache capacity tier recommendations, cache admission policy).

Out of scope (beta):
- Quantization recommendations.
- Automatic application of settings without user action + rollout controls.
- Customer-specific savings guarantees.

## Definitions
- **Route:** A customer-defined API route or application endpoint (often maps to model + prompt pattern + traffic).
- **Suggestion unit:** (org_id, project_id, environment, region, route_id, model_id, model_version).
- **Interactive route:** User-facing requests where tail latency is highly visible (chat UI, autocomplete, agent loops).
- **Batching:** Combining multiple requests into a single forward pass window to improve GPU utilization; typically increases queueing.
- **Caching:** Reusing computation for repeated prefixes/KV states; can reduce cost/latency when prompts share prefixes.
- **Risk level:** Low/Medium/High label shown in Console; defined in the Risk Scoring ADR and copy guidelines.

## Data prerequisites (eligibility gating)
Suggestions are only computed for a suggestion unit if telemetry is sufficient and recent.

### Minimum telemetry requirements (hard)
All must be true:
- **Lookback window:** at least **24 hours** of data (rolling), with staleness <= **6 hours** (compute job time).
- **Volume:** >= **10,000 requests** OR >= **2 million prompt tokens** in the lookback window.
- **Latency coverage:** p50 and p95 latency available (server-side, end-to-end).
- **Traffic stability:** at least **6 distinct hours** with non-zero traffic (to avoid single-burst artifacts).

If any are missing, do not emit suggestions; return “Insufficient telemetry” state to the Console.

### Data quality exclusions (hard)
Do not emit suggestions for a suggestion unit if:
- The route is in an incident/mitigation state (e.g., active rollback, elevated error rate) as signaled by platform incident flags.
- Observability indicates telemetry corruption (e.g., missing model_id/model_version, negative durations, non-sensical token counts).
- The model_version is in canary/experimental state not intended for broad optimization (flagged by model lifecycle service).

### Environment restrictions (hard)
- Suggestions are generated only for **production** and **pre-prod** environments. Do not generate for “dev/sandbox” where traffic is not representative.
- **Tenant isolation:** suggestions must never aggregate across orgs/projects. (Also applies to any caching recommendations—see Security/Privacy guardrails.)

## Global safety guardrails (apply to all suggestions)
### SLO and route criticality (hard)
Do not emit **any** suggestions for a route if any of the following is true:
- The route has an explicit p95 latency SLO <= **300 ms** (low-latency routes are extremely sensitive to batching delays).
- Observed p95 latency <= **350 ms** AND p95 jitter (p95 - p50) <= **120 ms** (already tight; avoid adding queueing variability).
- The route is tagged as “interactive-critical” by customer config or Redwood Console classification.

Rationale: batching/caching changes can shift tail latency and variance; for these routes we require explicit human tuning rather than automated suggestions.

### Reliability / error rate (hard)
Do not emit suggestions when reliability is already degraded:
- p95 of 5xx rate over the lookback window > **0.25%**, OR
- Timeout/cancel rate > **0.5%**, OR
- Recent regression flag is active (latency or error SLO burn within last 6 hours).

Rationale: optimization estimates assume steady-state behavior; recommending changes during instability reduces trust and can worsen incident recovery.

### Confidence gating (hard)
If the system cannot compute a confidence band (due to missing inputs, insufficient samples, or extreme variance), do not emit the suggestion.

Operational rule:
- If confidence is “unknown”, block.
- If confidence is computed but below minimum threshold for the suggestion type (see below), block.

### Change magnitude limits (hard)
Suggestions must remain within conservative bounds:
- Never recommend a parameter change that exceeds **2×** the current setting in a single step (e.g., max_batch_size from 8 → 32 is blocked; must be staged).
- Never recommend reducing max_batch_delay_ms below safe minimums (to avoid CPU churn / scheduling overhead):
  - Streaming routes: min **1 ms**
  - Non-streaming routes: min **2 ms**

If a larger change is theoretically optimal, emit *no suggestion* in beta (we prefer no suggestion over unsafe guidance).

### Rollout safety posture (soft → copy + deep link)
If a suggestion is emitted, the details drawer must include:
- A recommended rollout approach (canary % and duration) and a link to Rollouts tooling.
- A note that savings are **estimates** and not guaranteed.

(UX enforcement is tracked in Console design spec; generation must provide the necessary fields: recommended_canary_percent, recommended_hold_minutes, and primary_risk_factors.)

## Batching-specific guardrails
Batching can materially improve cost/throughput, but it increases queueing and can amplify tail latency under bursty traffic.

### Batching eligibility (hard)
Emit batching suggestions only if all are true:
- **Concurrency/QPS:**
  - Average concurrency >= **4**, AND
  - p50 QPS >= **2 req/s** over at least 6 hours in the lookback.
- **Batchability:** tokenization and model execution path supports continuous batching for the model family (runtime capability flag).
- **Traffic shape:** coefficient of variation (CV) of per-minute QPS <= **1.2** (avoid extreme burst patterns in beta).

If concurrency is low, batching benefits are typically negligible and can harm latency.

### Latency impact bounds (hard)
A batching suggestion must satisfy BOTH:
- Estimated p50 latency increase <= **+5%** OR **+25 ms** (whichever is smaller).
- Estimated p95 latency increase <= **+8%** OR **+60 ms** (whichever is smaller).

If the estimator predicts larger deltas, block the suggestion.

### Maximum batch delay constraints (hard)
Do not recommend max_batch_delay_ms above:
- **Streaming:** 6 ms
- **Non-streaming:** 12 ms

Rationale: delays above these thresholds are frequently user-visible and are hard to justify without deeper customer-specific tuning.

### Token-length variance (hard)
If sequence length distribution is highly variable, batching can create head-of-line blocking.

Block batching suggestions if:
- p95 prompt_tokens / p50 prompt_tokens > **3.0**, OR
- p95 total_tokens / p50 total_tokens > **2.5**

### Queueing sensitivity (soft → risk up-label)
If the route already shows queueing sensitivity, we may still emit a suggestion but must increase risk:
- If (p95 - p50) latency is large (>= **400 ms**) and GPU utilization is high (>= **85%**) → escalate risk by one level.

### Multi-region and routing complexity (soft → emit fewer suggestions)
If traffic is split across regions and the lookback window per-region is below volume minimums, do not emit region-specific batching suggestions.

Rule:
- Require minimum telemetry *per region* for region-scoped suggestions; otherwise block and fall back to global messaging (“need more regional data”).

## Caching-specific guardrails
Caching is most effective when prompts share a stable prefix. Incorrect scoping or oversubscription can create reliability issues.

### Cache safety (hard) — tenancy, privacy, and scoping
Caching recommendations must respect the following invariants:
- Cache keys must be scoped at minimum to: **org_id + project_id + environment + region + route_id + model_version**.
- No cross-tenant cache sharing is allowed, including “global” caches.
- The platform must not store raw prompts in cache metadata. Use hashed/normalized keys per runtime standard.

If the runtime configuration for the target deployment cannot guarantee these properties (capability flag), block caching suggestions.

### Caching eligibility (hard)
Emit caching suggestions only if all are true:
- **Repeatability signal:** estimated reusable-prefix rate >= **8%** of prompt tokens (conservative threshold for beta).
- **Observed cache behavior:**
  - If cache is currently enabled: cache hit rate < **60%** AND eviction rate suggests thrash (see below) OR there is clear headroom.
  - If cache is currently disabled: projected hit rate >= **15%** with acceptable confidence.
- **Sufficient volume:** same minimum volume as global prerequisites (do not relax).

### Cache thrash and OOM risk (hard)
Block caching “increase capacity” or “enable caching” suggestions if memory pressure is likely to cause instability:
- Evictions per 1k requests > **25** and cache memory usage is already >= **80%** of allocated cache budget.
- Any cache-related OOM/eviction storm signal in the last 24 hours (platform reliability flag).

In these cases, do not suggest “turn it on more”; instead, emit no suggestion in beta (future work: remediation suggestions).

### Latency regressions (hard)
Caching suggestions must not predict latency regressions above:
- p50 latency increase <= **+2%** (caching should not slow the median), and
- p95 latency increase <= **+5%**

If enabling caching is predicted to increase tail latency (e.g., due to lock contention or cache serialization overhead), block.

### Prompt variability / personalization (soft → risk up-label + explanation)
High personalization reduces cacheability and can confuse users (“why are you recommending caching if prompts vary?”).

If variability indicators are high, still allow suggestions only when projected savings are strong, but escalate risk and require stronger explanation:
- Distinct normalized prefixes per minute > **0.7 × QPS** (most prompts are unique).
- High entropy in the first N tokens (runtime-provided proxy metric).

UI requirement when this triggers:
- Include “This route has high prompt variability; expected gains depend on stable prefixes (e.g., system prompt and templates).”

### Tool calling / function calling (soft → generally safe)
Tool calling often shares a stable system prefix; caching can help, but request payloads may include volatile tool outputs.

Rule:
- Do not use tool outputs as cache keys.
- Treat tool outputs as part of the non-cacheable suffix; do not assume reuse.

If telemetry cannot separate prefix vs suffix reuse, block (confidence unknown).

## Guardrails for estimate presentation (to preserve trust)
These are generation-time constraints to avoid “too-good-to-be-true” outputs.

### Savings caps (hard)
For beta, cap displayed savings for any single suggestion unit:
- Cost savings percentage: max **35%**
- $/day savings: max **$25,000/day**

If the raw model exceeds these caps, clamp and add a note in explanation: “Capped for conservatism in beta.”

### Assumptions disclosure (hard)
Every emitted suggestion must include the minimum assumption fields so the Console can display a consistent disclaimer block:
- pricing_basis (token price version)
- lookback_window_hours
- traffic_volume_summary (requests, tokens)
- stale_as_of timestamp
- key drivers (e.g., concurrency, reusable-prefix rate)

If any are missing, block the suggestion (avoid partial/opaque suggestions).

## Known edge cases and how we handle them
### 1) Bursty traffic with periodic spikes
Symptom: batching looks great on averages but causes p95 blow-ups during spikes.
- Current handling: block batching suggestions when QPS CV > 1.2 (hard).
- Future: spike-aware modeling and separate “peak-hour” suggestions.

### 2) Mixed workloads under one route (multiple prompt patterns)
Symptom: aggregates hide a low-latency sub-route.
- Current handling: if telemetry indicates multi-modal latency distribution (bimodal p50/p95 across segments) and we can’t segment, block.
- Recommendation: customers should split routes or add route tags; Console onboarding links to “route hygiene”.

### 3) Streaming vs non-streaming mix
Symptom: batching delay acceptable for non-streaming, unacceptable for streaming.
- Current handling: if streaming_share is between 0.2 and 0.8 (mixed) and cannot segment, block batching suggestions.

### 4) Very long context windows
Symptom: caching savings appear huge but cache size becomes dominant risk.
- Current handling: apply cache thrash/OOM hard blocks; additionally block caching suggestions if p95 prompt_tokens > 16k unless cache budget is explicitly high.

### 5) Autoscaling transitions / cold-start dominated latency
Symptom: p95 latency driven by scale-up, not model runtime; batching/caching won’t fix it.
- Current handling: if “cold_start_fraction” > 5% of requests, suppress suggestions (hard) and rely on separate autoscaling guidance.

### 6) Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private differences
- Hosted/Dedicated: guardrails apply as written.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): if telemetry completeness cannot be verified or runtime capability flags are missing, block (hard). Private deployments often have custom settings; we avoid brittle recommendations in beta.

### 7) Recent model version change or rollout in progress
Symptom: estimates based on mixed model versions.
- Current handling: if model_version changed within lookback window and traffic split is > 20% across versions, block suggestions for that route/model until stable for 24 hours.

## Exception process (rare; requires human review)
If a customer account requires suggestions despite a guardrail (e.g., they explicitly want aggressive batching), the correct mechanism is:
1) Do not bypass guardrails in automated generation.
2) Use Solutions Engineering / Applied ML to provide a manual recommendation and guide the customer through a controlled rollout.

Internal request path:
- File an Optimize ticket with workload details and include telemetry snapshots.
- Approvers: Aditya Rao (PM Optimize) + Jonas Weber (Perf/Evals) + Sean Gallagher (SRE) for any exception affecting latency SLO routes.

## Monitoring and regressions
We treat guardrail violations as correctness bugs.

Alerting (owned by Eng Platform + Applied ML):
- If post-apply telemetry shows p95 latency regression > 10% for routes where a batching suggestion was applied (within 24h), trigger an investigation label “suggestions-guardrail-miss”.
- Track “blocked_by_reason” counts to ensure we are not overly suppressing (watch for telemetry pipeline regressions).

Success criteria for guardrails (beta):
- < 2% of applied suggestions result in a sustained p95 latency regression > 8% without a corresponding cost reduction that user deems worthwhile (validated via beta feedback + telemetry).
- Support tickets about “suggestion harmed performance” are triaged within 1 business day and linked to a guardrail update if necessary.

## Change log
- 2026-02-26: Tightened low-latency route exclusion (SLO <= 300 ms); added mixed streaming/non-streaming batching suppression; added savings caps for beta.
- 2026-02-10: Added cache thrash/OOM hard blocks and minimum reusable-prefix thresholds.
- 2026-01-22: Initial beta guardrails for batching/caching suggestions.

title: dsid_2add37caccb641db8f1d608bc5878847__shadow-to-prod-eval-continuity-guidelines-2026.txt
text:
Shadow-to-Production: Eval Continuity & Safety Guidelines

Summary:
This document prescribes the end-to-end process for using shadow (mirrored) traffic and continuous eval outputs to safely promote models into production for text generation and embedding workloads. It connects eval-harness artifacts (workload fingerprints, prompt coverage, quantization evaluation), runtime observability, and automated rollback triggers so teams can preserve quality SLOs while iterating quickly.

Goals:
- Ensure production promotions are gated by real-traffic shadow evaluation + synthetic continuity checks.
- Define concrete metrics, thresholds, and automated actions for safe rollback and triage.
- Provide runbook steps and ownership for degradation investigations spanning eval-harness -> runtime -> model-promotion-service.

Applicability:
- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployment modes that support request mirroring (shadow routing).
- Target workloads: text-generation/chat, embeddings, and reranking.

Key Concepts and Signals:
1) Shadow run: mirror a sample of production requests to candidate model instances without affecting user-visible responses. Shadow traffic should preserve original request headers and sampling ratios.
2) Continuity test suite: a short, prioritized set of prompts derived from prompt-sets-and-benchmarks that exercise long-tail failure modes for the target workload.
3) Response Stability Index (RSI): a composite signal combining token-level edit distance, semantic-similarity delta (embedding cosine), and policy-safety flags. Range 0-100, lower is better.
4) Token Amplification Ratio (TAR): ratio of mean tokens generated by candidate model to baseline. Flags unbounded or degenerate generation.
5) Quantization Delta: measured difference in essential eval metrics (RSI, semantic-score, latency) between full-precision and quantized variants during shadow runs.

Gating Metrics and Thresholds (default baselines):
- RSI: <= 4.0 relative increase over baseline (if >4.0, fail gate).
- p95 latency: no more than 20% regression vs baseline and absolute p95 <= 1.2s for small-chat profiles.
- TAR: between 0.8 and 1.5 (outside => investigate hallucination/verbosity).
- Semantic Recall (embedding cosine on ground-truth checks): >= 0.92 average for retrieval prompts.
- Safety flags (policy classifier): no more than 0.2% absolute increase in high-severity flags.
- Quantization Delta: RSI increase <= 1.5 and latency improvement >= 10% (otherwise treat quantized variant as incompatible for that workload).

Traffic Sampling and Shadow Configuration:
- Shadow sampling rate: start at 0.1% of requests for initial verification, ramp to 2-5% as confidence increases.
- Sampling strategy: stratified by route and prompt-type fingerprint (use eval-orch fingerprint tagging) so slices are covered proportionally.
- Forge requests exactly as sent by clients (including conversation history) but set header X-Shadow-Run: candidate-model-id.
- Storage: persist shadow responses in the eval-orch datastore for at least 30 days for retrospective triage.

Continuity Test Suite (runtime-synth):
- Run 1: latency-sensitive prompts (short queries, token cap 64) x 200 samples. Check p95 and token tail behavior.
- Run 2: long-context prompts (>= 2048 tokens) x 100 samples. Verify KV-cache correctness and output truncation.
- Run 3: adversarial prompt set (from prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/adversarial-noise) x 300 samples. Measure safety flags and RSI.
- Run 4: embedding recall microbench (100 paired queries). Measure semantic score and embedding variance.

Promotion Workflow (high-level):
1) Preflight: run inference-readiness-eval-matrix locally with model candidate (unit-sized synthetic suite).
2) Shadow rollout stage A: mirror 0.1% traffic for 48 hours. Collect metrics and continuity tests.
3) Review: automated report generated by eval-orch summarizing gating metrics; reviewers assigned (owner + applied-ml) must sign off or open a triage issue.
4) Shadow stage B: increase to 2% mirror for 72 hours if stage A passed. Run full continuity suite nightly.
5) Canary (optional): route 1% of live responses to candidate for actual responses with rollback guardrails and customer-scope opt-outs.
6) Promote to production routing if all gates pass for 7 days; otherwise, rollback to previous stable model and open a regression investigation.

Automated Rollback Triggers (examples):
- Any RSI increase >8.0 vs baseline within a 1-hour window.
- Safety flag spike: >=0.5% absolute increase in critical flags in 15 minutes.
- Latency SLO breach: sustained p95 > 1.2x baseline for 30 minutes or p99 > 2.0x baseline.
- Token amplification: TAR > 2.0 sustained for 10 minutes.
- Quantization catastrophic: semantic recall drop > 0.08 absolute.

Immediate Rollback Procedure:
1) Alerting: Pager duty escalation to oncall-model-owner and applied-ml triage@redwood. Notify customer-success if any customer-visible regressions are observed.
2) Execution: call model-promotion-service API to revert traffic to previous model_id. Example: 
   curl -X POST https://internal.api.redwood/v1/model-promote 
     -H 'Authorization: Bearer $RD_TOKEN' 
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
     -d '{"action":"rollback","target_model_id":"model-1234","reason":"RSI spike"}'
3) Preserve artifacts: snapshot shadow response storage slice, collect profiler traces from runtime-collector, and start automated bisect job if enabled.
4) Postmortem: within 72 hours produce a regression triage that includes top failing prompt slices, quantization parameters, and kernel-level profiling.

Investigation Playbook (triage owner responsibilities):
- Step 0: Confirm alert validity (check noise, infra events).
- Step 1: Compare shadow vs baseline slices in eval-dashboard; prioritize high-severity slices with >0.5 RSI delta.
- Step 2: Run hypothesis checks: quantization delta? prompt-tokenization mismatch? KV-cache context corruption? model artifacts mismatch?
- Step 3: If quantization suspected, re-run quant-eval job with --deterministic-seed and capture full logits for 100 seeds.
- Step 4: If infra suspected, attach runtime profiler traces and coord with eng-serving-runtime for kernel scheduling logs.
- Step 5: If model bug, label and route to model-onboarding team for rollback/retrain.

Quantization Specific Guidance:
- Always include a quantization shadow pass in Stage A for any new quant profile. Record Quantization Delta (RSI, latency, memory) in the promotion report.
- Reject quantized promotion when RSI increases >1.5 and semantic recall drops >0.02 for retrieval/rewrite workloads.
- Recommended quant profiles by workload:
  * chat-medium: int8-gptq-8 + group-size=64 (fast path; verify with long-context tests).
  * retrieval-heavy: fp16 fallback preferred; quantized variants must pass embedding-stability audit.

Observability and Dashboards (what to monitor):
- eval-orch/shadow-metrics: RSI-by-slice, TAR, safety-flag-rate, embedding-delta.
- runtime/latency: p50/p95/p99 per-model and per-route.
- stability/rolling: 1h, 6h, 24h windows for RSI and safety flags.
- promotion-service: model-version lineage and active traffic splits.

Example CLI / YAML snippets:
- Run a targeted continuity eval (eval-orch):
  redwood-eval run --suite continuity-short --model candidate:2026-04-01 --out results/continuity-short.json --samples 200

- Shadow routing rule (kubernetes Ingress annotation):
  annotations:
    redwood.io/shadow-target: "model:candidate-2026-04-01"
    redwood.io/shadow-sample: "0.001"

Ownership and Roles:
- Model Owner (primary): responsible for promotion and initial triage.
- Applied ML (secondary): owns eval-harness suites, continuity tests, and quantization pass criteria.
- Serv‑runtime: responsible for tracing, profiler data, and kernel-level reconciliation when latency/throughput regressions appear.
- Customer Success: notified for production-visible regressions and coordinates customer communication.

Risk Register (common failure modes):
- Silent semantic drift due to tokenization mismatch between training and serving. Mitigation: tokenization fingerprint checks in preflight.
- Quantized hallucinations: mitigation: additional adversarial-run sweep and reject quant-profile if TAR or RSI flags exceed thresholds.
- Data leakage in shadow logs: mitigate by PII scrubbing and strict retention policies (30-day default, 7-day for sensitive customers).

Appendix A — Quick Checklist Before Promotion:
- [ ] Preflight eval matrix passed (unit and synthetic).
- [ ] Shadow stage A (0.1%) passed gating metrics for 48h.
- [ ] Continuity test nightly runs succeeded at 0 regressions for top-5 critical slices.
- [ ] Quantization Delta measured and within thresholds.
- [ ] Monitoring dashboards provisioned and reviewers assigned.
- [ ] Rollback playbook tested within the last 30 days (game-day).

Appendix B — Example Promotion Acceptance Table (fill in in review):
| Metric | Baseline | Candidate | Delta | Pass? | Notes |
| RSI (avg) | 2.4 | 3.1 | +0.7 | Yes | within 4.0 threshold |
| p95 latency | 820ms | 900ms | +9.7% | Yes | under 20% cap |
| TAR | 1.0 | 1.12 | +12% | Yes | acceptable verbosity |
| Safety flags | 0.12% | 0.15% | +0.03% | Yes | low absolute delta |

Document Maintenance:
- Owner: applied-ml team (Marisol Chen).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any production regression.
- Next scheduled review: 2026-04-01.

Related resources and links:
- eval-harness: orchestration runbooks and runner CLI (link internal)
- prompt-sets-and-benchmarks: canonical continuity and adversarial suites (link internal)
- model-onboarding: inference-readiness and promotion matrix page (link internal)

Contact and escalation:
- applied-ml-oncall@redwood (primary)
- eng-serving-runtime-oncall@redwood (secondary)

This guideline balances safe promotion speed with robust automated protection. Follow the thresholds as defaults and tune per-product with signoff from applied-ml and product owners.

title: dsid_2227cc62a32547e0a483fd67ac157126__sdk-playground-labs-and-error-injection-recipes-2026.txt
text:
sdk-playground-labs-and-error-injection-recipes-2026

Title: SDK Playground Labs and Error Injection Recipes
Space: eng-developer-experience
Author: Aditi Rao
Owner team: engineering
Status: published
Last updated: 2026-10-12

Summary:
This document provides a compact, hands-on set of playground labs, SDK integration templates, API examples, and canonical error-injection recipes intended for developer onboarding, SDK maintainers, and support engineers. It is optimized for fast experimentation in a local sandbox and for producing reproducible support bundles when escalating issues to runtime or infra teams.

Goals:
- Give engineers a low-friction sandbox to validate common SDK integration patterns (auth, streaming, batching, local cache).
- Provide reproducible error-injection recipes to surface failure modes seen in customer support cases.
- Capture canonical fixes and triage checklists so support and SDK teams respond consistently.
- Define docs-site ownership and release steps for snippets and quickstarts.

Audience:
- Developer experience engineers (SDK owners)
- Support engineers and solutions engineers
- New platform integrators and developer advocates

Contents:
1) Quickstart labs (local)
2) API examples (curl, Python, Node)
3) SDK template layout and recommended config table
4) Docs site operating procedure for snippet updates and release gating
5) Top support issues and canonical fixes (triage + commands)
6) Ownership, metrics, and lifecycle

1) Quickstart labs (local)
Overview: Each lab is runnable in under 10 minutes on a developer workstation. The labs assume a Redwood API key available in REDWOOD_API_KEY and Docker (for the local proxy) if you want to simulate network faults. Use the sandbox token (org-sandbox) for functional testing only.

Lab A: Auth + Simple Generation
- Objective: Validate SDK credential handling and error semantics.
- Steps:
  1. Install: pip install redwood-sdk==0.6.0 (or npm i @redwood/sdk@0.6.0)
  2. Set credentials: export REDWOOD_API_KEY="sk-sandbox-xxxx"
  3. Run example: python examples/auth_gen.py
- Expected output: JSON with tokens_used, model_name, and a 200-level response.
- Failure injection: run with REDWOOD_API_KEY="" to verify 401 handling and telemetry breadcrumbs.

Lab B: Streaming and Resume Simulation
- Objective: Validate partial responses and resume semantics used by front-end clients.
- Steps:
  1. Start local stub: docker run -p 8080:8080 redwood/local-runtime-stub:0.4
  2. Run node streaming example: node examples/stream_resume.js --url http://localhost:8080
  3. Kill the process at token 60 and run again to validate idempotent resume.
- Failure injection: use tc/netem to add 200ms packet loss on loopback.

Lab C: Batching + Local Prefetch Cache
- Objective: Measure latency and unit cost impact of local prefetch + batcher.
- Steps:
  1. Start the batcher: ./bin/local-batcher --config examples/batcher.yaml
  2. Run the load script: python examples/batch_load.py --qps 20 --dur 60
  3. Inspect metrics: curl http://localhost:9100/metrics | grep redwood_batch_latency
- Expected thresholds: p95 < 120ms with batch size <= 8; cost/token reduced by ~18% when cache hit ratio >= 0.6

2) API examples (copiable)
Curl: single-shot generation
```
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-small-2026","input":"Summarize the following..."}'
```
Python (requests): streaming w/ reconnect logic
```
import requests
from requests.exceptions import RequestException

URL = "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/stream"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']}"}
try:
  r = requests.post(URL, json={"model":"redwood-small-2026","input":"..."}, stream=True, timeout=30)
  for line in r.iter_lines():
    if line:
      print(line.decode())
except RequestException as e:
  # canonical retry backoff for SDKs: 100ms, 500ms, 1s
  print("retrying", e)
```
Node (sdk snippet): resumable stream + telemetry event
```
const Redwood = require('@redwood/sdk')
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const stream = client.stream({ model: 'redwood-small-2026', input: '...' })
stream.on('data', chunk => console.log(chunk))
stream.on('closed', () => client.telemetry.event('stream.closed'))
```

3) SDK template layout and recommended config
Purpose: A baseline SDK layout that reduces onboarding time for new language SDKs.
Recommended file layout:
- /src/index.js or /src/__init__.py (public entrypoint)
- /examples/* (playground snippets)
- /test/golden/* (integration goldens e2e-lite)
- /docs/snippets/* (extracted snippets for docs site)
- /scripts/ci/* (smoke harness)

Minimum config table:
| setting | description | recommended default | owner |
|---|---|---:|---|
| batcher.max_size | max queued requests per batch | 8 | sdk-team |
| retry.backoff_initial_ms | initial backoff on 5xx/timeout | 100 | sdk-team |
| telemetry.level | snapshot vs full | snapshot | devx-team |
| local_cache.ttl_seconds | ephemeral prefetch TTL | 30 | devx-team |
| snippet.auto_sync | copy examples into docs site on release | true | docs-engineering |

4) Docs site operating procedure (snippets and releases)
This section defines how snippet changes are validated and released to the docs site to avoid regressions.
Checklist for snippet or quickstart updates:
1. Update snippet in /docs/snippets with a runnable marker and include a smoke test under /test/golden that completes inside CI (30s wall).
2. Open PR with label docs:snippet and request reviewers from devx and sdk teams.
3. CI must pass both unit + golden smoke. Golden run must post a synthetic telemetry event to the staging snippet-harness.
4. Docs release steps (owner: docs-engineering):
   a. Merge PR after approvals.
   b. Run docs-site preview pipeline and verify snippet rendering at https://docs-staging.redwood.ai/snippets/<slug>
   c. Create release note in product-docs/release-notes referencing snippet id.
   d. If change modifies API surface, a feature flag must be set and a 2-week deprecation notice posted on SDK CHANGELOG.
Emergency rollback (if snippet causes production SDK break):
1. Revert merge in the docs repo.
2. Create a Patch release for the SDK with the old snippet embedded as a fallback comment.
3. Notify support and post incident note in #devx-snippet-incidents.

5) Top support issues and canonical fixes
A compact list of recurring issues observed in support tickets, with triage steps and canonical fixes. Use these as the first-pass checklist when assembling a support bundle.

Issue: Authentication failures (403/401)
- Symptom: sudden spike of 401s from a single tenant after a regional failover.
- Quick triage:
  1. Verify token expiry: echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY | cut -d'.' -f2 | base64 --decode || (note: some tokens are opaque)
  2. Check request timestamps vs server logs: curl "https://logs.redwood.ai/query?tenant=...&from=now-15m" -H "Authorization: Bearer $AUDIT_TOKEN"
- Canonical fix: Confirm token rotation window was applied; if rotated mid-deploy, advise client to use retry with 429/401 handshake: 1) fetch new token, 2) replay idempotent requests.

Issue: Streaming partial payload stops mid-response
- Symptom: Front-end sees stream close at ~50–80 tokens with no finalization event.
- Quick triage:
  1. Collect client side socket logs and server stream-ids: identify last sequence id.
  2. Correlate with runtime instance (X-Instance-ID header) and check instance health (systemd logs, OOM).
- Canonical fix: In SDKs implement resumable sequence-id resume: send last_ack and resume_token; if resume fails, fall back to retriable deterministic regeneration with a note in telemetry.

Issue: Batcher latency spikes at p95
- Symptom: p95 latency for generation increases by >200ms after traffic shift.
- Quick triage:
  1. Inspect batch size distribution: curl http://batcher-host:9000/debug/batches
  2. Check cache hit ratio: curl http://local-cache:9119/metrics | grep cache_hit_ratio
- Canonical fix: Reduce max window to 50ms for latency-sensitive routes and promote local cache prefetch for the affected route. Add an autoscaling policy for batcher pool if sustained QPS over commit.

6) Metrics, ownership, and lifecycle
- Runtime for docs updates: docs snippets should be validated weekly in a Golden CI job. Failing snippets generate a pager during business hours only.
- Owners:
  - SDK snippets: devx-sdks (primary), sdk-team (secondary)
  - Streaming examples: eng-serving-runtime (primary), devx-sdks (secondary)
  - Docs publishing pipeline: docs-engineering (primary)
- KPIs to track:
  - snippet_runnable_rate (goal 98%)
  - mean_time_to_fix_snippet_broken (target < 48 hours)
  - support_escalation_rate_due_to_snippets (target < 2%)

Appendix: Useful commands and debugging snippets
- Collect support bundle (local):
  tar czf support-bundle-$(date +%s).tgz logs/*.log metrics/*.prom diagnostics/*.json
- Simulate 10% packet loss locally (Linux):
  sudo tc qdisc add dev lo root netem loss 10%
- Canonical script to replay a failed request with idempotency key (bash):
  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/replay -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -d '{"idempotency_key":"<key>","original_request":{...}}'

Cross references:
- See also: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/multi-model-orchestration-sdk-samples-and-exchange-format-2025
- See also: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook

Document maintenance:
- Reviewed quarterly by devx owners. Major SDK version bumps require snippet smoke revalidation and a docs freeze window of 72 hours prior to release.

If you have questions or want a live walkthrough of the labs, ping #devx-playgrounds or assign to the author.

title: dsid_24870c97df2d4e36aecd062358bc4dbb__slo-resilience-scenario-workbook-2024.txt
text:
SLO Resilience Scenario Workbook and Execution Guide

Summary:

This workbook collects high-value SRE scenarios that exercise SLOs, error budget governance, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, and operational tooling. It is intended for on-call responders, SRE leads running war rooms, and engineering teams planning capacity experiments and runbook validation. Use it to rehearse, run tabletop exercises, and to guide post-incident changes.

Scope:
- Services: model-serving, request-router, prefix-cache, embedding-pipeline, billing-proxy, capacity-orchestrator.
- Environments: prod (all regions), staging (pre-production), shadow clusters (canary).
- Audience: on-call, reliability engineers, product stewards, platform capacity owners.

When to use this workbook:
1) Prior to high-risk releases (model rollouts, autoscaler changes, quantization changes).
2) During quarterly resilience drills.
3) As part of incident retrospectives: validate mitigations in lab before closing action items.

How to read this guide:
- Each scenario includes: triggering conditions, impacted SLOs, error-budget thresholds, runbook steps (rapid mitigation and recovery), telemetry to collect, post-incident verification, and experiment-lab instructions.
- Use the Decision Matrix at the end to choose escalation and capacity actions.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Primary responder (on-call): execute immediate mitigations, own the incident timeline.
- Capacity owner: evaluate capacity maneuvers, run quota/eviction operations.
- SRE lead: coordinate cross-team escalations, declare incident severity.
- Product steward: approve quality-vs-cost tradeoffs and rollback decisions.
- Postmortem author: collect evidence and complete incident review within 5 business days.

Scenario catalog (executables):

1) Multi-region GPU fabric outage (cold failure)
- Trigger: > 30% GPU nodes in region X transition to UNREACHABLE in 5m window; model-serving p95 latency doubles; overall successful request rate drops > 10%.
- Impacted SLOs: request success rate (99.9% monthly), p95 latency (200ms target).
- Error budget action thresholds:
  - Warning: 5% of monthly error budget burned in 30m -> trigger emergency monitoring channel and throttle low-priority tenants.
  - Critical: 20%+ in 1h -> initiate cross-region failover and capacity rebalancing.
- Rapid mitigation steps (ordered):
  1. Verify Hermes alert and confirm node state via capacity-orchestrator: `capctl list nodes --region X --status unreachable`.
  2. Immediately enable burst-absorber: `capctl absorb --policy surge-redirect --target region-Y`.
  3. Shift model routing policy to failover pools: update slo-router policy to `regional-fallback: true` with canary fraction 10%.
  4. Scale dedicated warm pools in region Y by +25% using `autoscale apply --pool warm-pool-model-a --delta 25`.
  5. If external traffic surge persists, throttle non-critical routes (embedding-bulk, async-batch) by 50% via traffic-shepherd rule.
- Telemetry to collect during incident:
  - Per-region GPU health, node counts, queue lengths, and preemption events.
  - Token-level success and error rates by tenant and route.
  - Autoscaler decisions and recent allocation traces.
- Recovery verification:
  - p95 latency returns within 1.2x baseline and success rate returns to >= 99.5% for 30m window.
  - Re-enable throttled routes one at a time and confirm no relapse.
- Post-incident lab reproduction:
  - Use the capacity-sandbox harness: `cap-sim --fail-region X --duration 15m --load-profile spike-50pct`.
  - Validate that `burst-absorber` and `warm-pool` scale up as expected and alert as expected.

2) Latency tail regression after quantized runtime rollout
- Trigger: p99 latency increases 2x after quantization kernel flip; customer complaints for interactive chat increase.
- Impacted SLOs: tail-latency (p99), interactive response SLA (200ms p95).
- Error budget actions:
  - Immediate rollback if p99 breach sustained for 10 minutes and error budget burn > 8%/day.
- Runbook steps:
  1. Confirm deployment tag and kernel selection: `runtimectl show --deployment model-a --field kernel`.
  2. Switch traffic to pre-quantized variant (model-a.fp16) via gradual rollback (canary 5% -> 20% -> 100%).
  3. Pin suspect kernel in model catalog and mark as blocked: `modelctl block-kernel quant-kernel-v3`.
  4. Open a regression ticket to Applied ML + Runtime with reproducible trace, token sampling, and profiler dumps.
- Data to collect: tail latency histograms, kernel-level traceback logs, NVTX timings, memory copy durations.
- Lab reproduction: run `quant-lab --input sample-promptset.json --sequence-length 1024 --repeat 1000 --measure p99` and attach profiler output.

3) Embedding workload microburst causing queue starvation
- Trigger: embedding cluster queue depth > 10k sustained for > 2m with consumer lag rising; embeddings SLO degrades.
- Impacted SLOs: embedding throughput (99% of requests processed within 30s), embedding freshness.
- Mitigations:
  1. Enable backpressure admission control for bulk embedding jobs: `embedctl admit --mode conservative`.
  2. Temporarily promote high-priority tenants to reserved lanes with guaranteed slots (update fairshare config).
  3. If queue cannot be drained in 15m, activate emergency preemption of long-running batch jobs.
- Observability artifacts: sample request traces, queue latency percentiles, tenant-level queue contributions.
- Prevention experiments: implement and A/B the suggested intelligent-batching policy in Optimize for 7 days with shadow traffic.

4) Model quality regression that triggers silent error budget burn
- Trigger: automated evals show a drop in prompt-set accuracy by > 5% vs baseline while service metrics remain green (no latency errors).
- Impacted SLOs: qualitative SLOs tracked in QualityGuard (accuracy / hallucination rate).
- Immediate actions:
  1. Shift traffic to last known-good model variant and enable traffic shadowing for observability.
  2. Quarantine suspect model from catalog and disable auto-rollout policies.
  3. Run quick rollback validation with canary prompts and human-in-the-loop checks for critical tenants.
- Post-incident steps: add new synthetic prompt sets to regression harness, extend eval cadence for that family of prompts to 4 runs/day for one week.

5) Billing-proxy induced throttling that appears as SLO degradation
- Trigger: billing-proxy rate limiter misconfiguration causes 429s on background routes, error budget unaccounted.
- Impacted SLOs: background request success; customer-facing SLAs if cascade occurs.
- Rapid mitigation:
  1. Revert recent billing rule changes: `billingctl rollback --commit HEAD~1`.
  2. Open short-lived exception to allow traffic through for affected tenants, track cost impact.
  3. Add metric guard: rate limiter headroom must be >= 20% of peak observed 30d traffic.
- Long-term: create a pre-deploy validation harness that emulates quota exhaustion.

Standard incident-review checklist (mandatory for every SRE incident):
1. Evidence collection: timeline, traces, top-10 related alerts, and debug snapshots.
2. SLO impact reconciliation: compute exact error-budget burn windows and map to service commits/deploys.
3. Root-cause hypothesis and validated steps reproducing the behavior in lab.
4. Action items: owner, target date, verification steps.
5. Severity and customer-impact annotation for postmortem.

Decision matrix (quick reference):
- If error budget burn rate > 10%/hour: escalate to SRE lead and consider tenant throttles.
- If key SLO degraded and recovery not achieved within 30m: invoke cross-region failover.
- If degradation is quality-only (no infra signal): prioritize rollback of model changes and run quiet rollback validation.

Operational tooling and commands (examples):
- capacity-orchestrator: `capctl list pools`, `capctl scale --pool-name X --ratio 1.25`.
- slo-monitor: query recent SLO burns: `sloquery --service model-serving --window 1h`.
- telemetry-replay: `teleplay --from 2025-08-01T12:00Z --to 2025-08-01T13:00Z --service embedding-pipeline`.
- sandbox reproduction harness: `cap-sim --scenario multi-region-gpu-fail --scale 0.5`.

Post-incident verification rubric (for action item closure):
- Make: change merged, tests added (unit + integration for the failure mode).
- Test: a deterministic replay reproduces the failing behavior in the sandbox and demonstrates the fix.
- Observe: metrics show improvement with no regression to other SLOs for 72 hours in staging shadow and 1 week in prod for critical fixes.

Experiment lab playbook (safe rehearsals):
1. Plan: define hypothesis, duration, and blast radius.
2. Preflight checks: run `telemetry-replay` for baseline windows and save snapshots.
3. Execute in shadow cluster with mirrored traffic: `trafficctl mirror --target shadow-1 --fraction 0.25`.
4. Monitor: slo-monitor + real-time dashboard; hold go/no-go windows every 5 minutes.
5. Rollback plan: pre-prepare rollback runbooks and an automated switch to previous routing with `slo-router switch --to previous`.

Continuous improvement and reliability initiatives:
- Quarterly scenario additions: each team contributes 1 new scenario per quarter focused on their highest risk surface.
- Runbook rehearsal cadence: run one large multi-team drill and two focused single-team drills per quarter.
- Tooling improvements: invest in telemetry-replay fidelity and expand `burst-absorber` policies to include token-aware throttles.

Appendix A — Minimal evidence packet for postmortem:
- Incident timeline CSV (start, events, owner).
- Top 10 query traces (sampled token traces).
- SLO burn graphs exported as PNG.
- Relevant commits and deployment IDs.
- Sandbox reproduction commands and expected outputs.

Appendix B — Example JSON for telemetry-replay command:
```
{
  \"service\": \"model-serving\",
  \"window\": \"2025-08-01T12:00:00Z/2025-08-01T13:00:00Z\",
  \"scale\": 0.5,
  \"inject_failures\": [\"node-unreachable-region-X\"]
}
```

Contacts and escalation paths:
