- On-call SRE: `#oncall-model-serving` (Slack).
- Capacity owner: `capacity-team@redwood.ai`.
- Incident commander escalation: `sre-leads@redwood.ai`.

Document maintenance:
- Owner: eng-sre reliability initiatives lead (Aisha Patel).
- Review cadence: annual review and after every major multi-region incident.
- Additions: submit scenario proposals via the SRE Scenario Registry (internal form link).

End of workbook.

title: dsid_afc1bf975ac941e0ab64f0238e1f038e__chronological-upgrade-timeline-and-customer-notification-protocol-2026.txt
text:
Chronological Upgrade Timeline and Customer Notification Protocol

Overview:
This document prescribes a chronological, role-oriented upgrade timeline for private deployments (VPC and on-prem), and the customer-facing notification protocol that must accompany each phase. It is intended for Release Engineering, Field Operations, Solutions Engineering, and Customer Success when coordinating upgrades that may affect tenant SLAs, network topology, or runtime state.

Goals:
- Provide a single, reproducible timeline for upgrades and rollbacks that balances operator safety and customer transparency.
- Define measurable thresholds and automated gates used to trigger rollback decisions.
- Standardize customer communications and escalation templates to reduce confusion during events.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to private deploy upgrades that touch runtime artifacts (model binaries, runtime shards, KV cache format, networking proxies, control plane components).
- Assumes a pre-existing support contract and a named Customer Success owner per upgrade.
- Assumes telemetry and synthetic checks are available (see acceptance checks table).

Actors and ownership:
- Release Lead (RL): coordinates timeline, signs off preflight, primary decision-maker for go/no-go.
- Field Operator (FO): performs the change, runs operator commands, coordinates rollbacks.
- Solutions/SE: verifies customer-specific traffic shaping and runbook coverage.
- Customer Success (CS): triages customer communications and captures acceptance.
- Oncall/Observability (OBS): monitors real-time metrics and runs regression tests after rollout.

Preflight checklist (minimum pass to schedule upgrade):
1) Signed release plan document with risk classification and backout window (RL).
2) Snapshot and evidence: model/artifact hashes, control-plane state snapshot (FO).
3) Telemetry health baselines: 24h baseline of 95p latency, error rate, and KV cache hit-rate (OBS).
4) Customer readiness: written confirmation of maintenance window and support contacts (CS).
5) Rollback artifacts present: previous model image, previous control-plane manifest, and automated rollback job validated in staging (FO).
6) Acceptance tests: smoke script list and synthetic traffic profile validated against baseline (SE).

Acceptance checks table:
| Check | Frequency | Pass criteria | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 95th latency (token gen) | continuous | <= 1.5x baseline for 30m | OBS |
| Error rate (client-facing 5xx) | continuous | <= baseline + 2% absolute | OBS |
| KV cache miss ratio | every 5m | <= baseline + 10% relative | OBS |
| Token throughput | continuous | within expected throughput envelope | FO/OBS |
| Telemetry ingestion lag | every 1m | < 60s | OBS |

Chronological timeline (recommended template)
Phase A — Planning (T-14d to T-7d):
- T-14d: Release Lead publishes schedule and initial risk assessment. CS notifies customer with a courtesy heads-up.
- T-10d: SE runs customer-specific compatibility checks (networking, KMS/HSM, image allowlist).
- T-7d: Final preflight checklist completed; RL requests formal customer acknowledgement of maintenance window.

Customer notification (Planning):
Subject: Planned maintenance: Redwood private upgrade scheduled [DATE]
Body (short): We plan a maintenance window on [DATE] targeting component(s): [component list]. Expected customer impact: [none | transient latency | brief unavailability]. Primary CS: [name] — escalation: [email/phone].

Phase B — Pre-deployment (T-2d to T-0):
- T-2d: Run full synthetic acceptance suite against a realistic replay for the target tenant. Save results to artifact store.
- T-1d: Operator dry-run in staging that mirrors operator steps for production (FO).
- T-12h: Final go/no-go sync: RL, FO, OBS, SE, CS. RL records decision outcome in release tracker.
- T-1h: Customer reminder: maintenance start in 1 hour with link to status page and ticket.

Customer notification (Reminder):
Subject: Reminder: maintenance window starts in 1 hour — [DATE]
Body (short): Maintenance will begin at [TIME]. No anticipated data loss. If you have high-priority traffic, please notify CS immediately.

Phase C — Deployment (T0 to T+48h):
- T0 (start): FO begins staggered rollout by operator-defined shard. Stagger cadence: 5–10% of tenants or control-plane nodes per batch depending on risk class.
- After each batch:
  - Run smoke acceptance (3–5 min): latency, error rate, kv-consistency.
  - If all checks green, proceed to next batch.
  - If any check fails, pause and escalate. Observe for 10–30 minutes depending on severity.
- Automated gating: CI/CD job will automatically halt rollout if error rate breach occurs and will notify the RL and OBS slack channel.

Rollforward success criteria (during Deployment):
- 30m stable with all acceptance checks green at batch-level.
- No customer-reported incidents >P2 during staged rollout.

Immediate rollback triggers (examples and thresholds):
- Client-facing 5xx increases by >5 percentage points over baseline across affected tenants for >10 minutes.
- 95th percentile latency >2x baseline for >15 minutes.
- KV cache miss delta >25% leading to sustained throughput degradation >20% for >10 minutes.
- Any data corruption or mismatch detected in model artifact checksums.

Rollback decision matrix (simplified):
- If a critical trigger appears within 30 minutes of batch completion: immediate rollback of that batch. FO executes batch backout script.
- If systemic across multiple batches and cannot be isolated: halt rollout and initiate full release rollback (see procedure).

Rollback procedure (operator steps — checklist):
1) Mark release as ROLLBACK in release tracker and notify all stakeholders (RL/CS/OBS/SE).
2) Execute backout job: `rdu operator rollback --release <release-id> --target-batch <id>` (FO).
3) Verify checksum and model artifacts on rolled-back hosts.
4) Re-run smoke acceptance against rolled-back batch.
5) If rollback successful: notify customer with rollback confirmation and follow-up timeline for remediation.
6) Open postmortem ticket and assign to RL for RCA within 72 hours.

Post-deploy observation (T+48h to T+7d):
- T+48h: Full-system synthetic run and customer acceptance validation (SE + CS).
- T+72h: Performance regression sweep; if no regressions, RL moves release to stable and schedules a retrospective.
- T+7d: Close release after final evidence bundle is saved and postmortem (if any) is published.

Customer notification templates (examples):
1) Successful upgrade confirmation:
Subject: Maintenance complete — Upgrade applied to your private deploy [DATE]
Body: The planned upgrade completed at [TIME]. Observability checks show system health within expected ranges (95p latency: [value], error rate: [value]). If you observe issues, open a ticket referencing [release-id].

2) Rollback notification (immediate):
Subject: Action taken: Rollback executed during maintenance [DATE]
Body: We detected [brief reason] and executed a rollback for affected nodes at [TIME]. Impact: [summary]. Next steps: [investigation timeline]. Primary contact: [CS name].

3) Postmortem summary (P3/P2):
Subject: Postmortem: [summary title] — incident summary and remediation
Body: Short timeline, root cause, mitigation steps, and planned preventative actions with owners and ETA.

Operator runbook snippets (commands and short examples):
- Snapshot control plane: `rdu operator snapshot --component control-plane --out /artifacts/$(release-id)-snapshot.tgz`
- Trigger batch rollout: `rdu operator rollout --release <id> --batch-size 10% --wait`
- Force rollback of batch: `rdu operator rollback --release <id> --batch <n> --confirm`
- Evidence upload: `rdu artifacts upload --path /artifacts/<release-id> --tag release-evidence`

Evidence and audit requirements:
- For regulated customers, persist: release manifest, operator commands with timestamps, telemetry window (T-24h to T+72h), and signed customer acknowledgement. Retention: 7 years for financial customers; 1 year default otherwise.

Escalation flow during failures:
1) FO attempts mitigation and notifies RL (within 5m of detection).
2) If mitigation fails within 15m, RL declares incident and pages SRE/P0 channel.
3) CS posts to the customer ticket and triggers customer call if impact >P2.

Checklist for customer-facing readiness before sign-off:
- Maintenance window confirmed and logged.
- Backup snapshots created and verified.
- Rollback artifacts validated in staging.
- Operator runbooks reviewed and practiced within the last 30 days.
- Observability dashboards and synthetic checks configured and smoke test green.

Appendix A — Example timeline (condensed):
- T-14d: Schedule and risk notice sent.
- T-7d: Final signoff and evidence snapshot.
- T-1d: Dry run completed.
- T-1h: Customer reminder.
- T0: Start staggered batch rollout.
- T+48h: Full-system validation.
- T+7d: Release close and evidence archive.

Appendix B — Quick links and references:
- Upgrade runbook (operator): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/upgrade-and-rollback/operator-sentinel-escrow-and-durable-rollback-procedures-2026
- Operator cutover checklist: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/operator-cutover-chronicle-and-customer-communication-template-2026
- Evidence retention policy: /confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/policy-2025

Revision history:
- 2024-09-10: Initial draft (Daniel Park)
- 2025-06-03: Added automated gating thresholds and rollback triggers (Leah Kim)
- 2026-01-14: Expanded customer templates and evidence retention details (Omar Ruiz)

End of document.

title: dsid_220a8ea4b4394a18b1ad7e4af7df35e0__conversational-feedback-loop-labeling-integration-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Conversational feedback loop & labeling integration playbook

Overview:

This playbook describes an end-to-end integration pattern for ingesting conversational feedback from customer applications, enriching and routing it to a labeling hub and model-eval harness, and surfacing high-quality signal into QBR reporting and model retraining pipelines. The goal is to make feedback ingestion reliable, auditable and cost-efficient while providing deterministic lanes for immediate remediation, quality telemetry and curated label sets for retraining.

Scope and intended audience:
- Audience: Customer Success Engineers, Integration Engineers, Observability owners and ML Ops.
- Out of scope: research-only annotation experiments and external crowdworker contracting.

Key owners and operational SLAs:
- Product Owner: Aisha Patel (Customer Success)
- Integration Owner: Marco Ruiz (Solutions Engineering)
- Telemetry Owner: Lina Chen (Eng Platform)
- Labeling Hub Owner: Diego Alvarez (Applied ML)
- Operational SLAs: ingestion availability 99.9% per region; median end-to-end latency (app event -> labeling queue) <2s, p95 <10s for streaming; 100% event storage for 72h, sampled subset retained for 2 years.

Prerequisites and required services:
- ingress-gateway: mTLS or token-auth endpoint customers post feedback to.
- telemetry-gatekeeper: JSON schema validation, deduplication and rate limiting.
- event bus: Kafka (telemetry-events-prod) or durable queue (PubSub/SQS) with DLQ.
- labeling-hub: supports API and web UI for human labeling and enrichment.
- model-eval-harness: nightly batch and online scoring harness.
- telemetry-archive: S3-compatible archive for long-term storage and legal hold.

Logical flow (text diagram):
Customer App -> ingress-gateway -> telemetry-gatekeeper -> telemetry-events-prod (feedback.raw) -> enrichment workers -> labeling-hub (labeling.inbound) -> human labelers/auto-labelers -> labeling-hub.outbound -> model-eval-harness -> eval.results -> telemetry-archive / qbr-dataset

Data contract and schema (required fields):
- event_id (string): globally unique id, e.g. evt_01F4YZ
- tenant_id (string): tenant-abc
- timestamp_iso (string): RFC3339 UTC, e.g. 2026-01-11T16:23:12Z
- source (string): enum {chat-widget, voice, api, webhook}
- feedback_type (string): enum {correction, rating, taxonomy_tag, ignore}
- payload (string): JSON-encoded payload, e.g. '{"correction":"Prefer X"}'
Optional fields: user_id (hash recommended), session_id, original_response (trimmed to 8k tokens), confidence (0..1).

Security & privacy controls:
- PII handling: user_id must be hashed at client or ingress-gateway (default SHA256 with tenant-managed salt) unless contract allows plaintext.
- Access controls: labeling-hub and telemetry-archive must be RBAC-restricted. Roles: viewer, labeler, curator, admin.
- Legal hold: telemetry-archive retention tags; events may be marked retention=legal_hold.

Ingestion examples (cURL):
1) Minimal rating event:
curl -X POST https://ingress.redwood.example/v1/feedback
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
  -d '{"event_id":"evt_01F4YZ","tenant_id":"tenant-abc","timestamp_iso":"2026-01-11T16:23:12Z","source":"chat-widget","feedback_type":"rating","payload":"{\"rating\":0}"}'

2) Correction event with original response (trim to 8k tokens):
POST /v1/feedback
{
  "event_id": "evt_01F4Za2",
  "tenant_id": "tenant-abc",
  "timestamp_iso": "2026-01-11T16:25:05Z",
  "source": "api",
  "feedback_type": "correction",
  "payload": "{\"correction\":\"Use product X instead of Y when context includes Z\"}",
  "original_response": "...",
  "session_id": "sess_9a2"
}

Validation and common rejection reasons (telemetry-gatekeeper):
- 400 INVALID_SCHEMA: missing required field(s)
- 401 AUTH_FAILED: token expired or invalid
- 429 RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED: per-tenant rate control
- 413 PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE: payload/original_response exceeds 64kB limit
- 422 DUPLICATE_EVENT: event_id seen in last 24h

Enrichment and automated labeling rules (examples):
- Enrichment adds tenant_plan, model_version, route.
- Auto-label rules:
  - rating <= 0 -> auto-label=low-quality
  - correction length < 30 chars -> short-corrections queue for curator review
  - banned-content regex match -> escalate to Safety queue

Sampling and retention policy for QBR datasets:
- Deterministic sampling: 10% of feedback events per tenant per week, stratified by feedback_type and model_version.
- High-signal retention: any event auto-labeled low-quality or routed to Safety retained 2 years.

Operational runbook (triage playbook):
1) Alert: labeling-hub throughput drop (LH_Throughput_p95_below_threshold)
   - Check telemetry-gatekeeper: error rates and 429s.
   - Verify consumer lag: kafka-consumer-groups --describe --group labeling-inbound-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka.prod:9092
   - If DLQ growth, inspect 413/413s for oversized payloads.
2) Duplicate-event storm
   - Mitigation: enable dedupe-mode=drop-duplicates on telemetry-gatekeeper, route ingest to fallback buffer endpoint returning 202 while investigating.
3) Suspected PII incident
   - Action: tag suspect tenant with legal_hold, export batch for secure wipe (follow data-erasure playbook), notify Legal.

Integration rollout checklist:
Preflight:
- Confirm tenant_id mapping and auth method (mTLS or token)
- Exchange public keys / JWKS endpoints
- Validate sample payloads against telemetry-gatekeeper staging endpoint
- Confirm labeling workflow and roles list
Canary (1 week):
- Route 1% traffic to feedback pipeline; monitor ingestion success, p95 latency and false-positive auto-label rate
- Weekly sync with Solutions Engineering and CS to tune rules
Full launch:
- Enable full traffic routing, enable stratified sampling for QBR and add tenant to retention dashboards

Model quality & QBR integration:
- model-eval-harness runs nightly jobs joining labeled items with model metadata to compute metrics (precision@k for corrections, conversion lift, false-positive rate).
- QBR outputs: weekly top-10 failure patterns; monthly curated dataset (~5k examples) for retraining candidates; quarterly executive summary with net quality delta and remediation plan.

Example consumer config (JSON represented as text):
{
  "consumer_name": "cs-labeling-consumer",
  "source_topic": "feedback.enriched",
  "batch_size": "50",
  "max_retries": "5",
  "dead_letter_topic": "feedback.dlq"
}

Troubleshooting cheatsheet:
- Ingest 401s: confirm JWT audience (aud) matches ingress-gateway expected_aud; check clock skew > 2 minutes.
- High 413s: clients sending full conversation traces; recommend client-side trimming and summaries.
- Sudden low-quality spike: check recent model-version rollout and latency regressions.

Suggested monitoring dashboard panels:
- Ingest: events/sec, p50/p95 ingestion latency, error rates (400/401/413/429), DLQ growth.
- Quality: auto-label precision (sample-verified), manual label throughput, median time-to-label.
- Business: tenant-level feedback rate normalized by MAU.

FAQ:
Q: Can we accept raw audio feedback?
A: Ingest audio only after transcription by a companion service; mark source=voice and include transcript in payload.

Appendix: useful commands and endpoints:
- Validate sample schema: curl https://telemetry-gatekeeper.staging/validate -d @sample-event.json
- Check consumer lag: kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server kafka.prod:9092 --describe --group labeling-inbound-consumer
- Export suspect tenant batch: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin>" https://telemetry-archive/export?tenant=tenant-abc&since=2026-01-01 -o export.ndjson

Next steps:
- After integration, schedule a 30-day QBR with the CS manager to review weekly failure patterns and agree remediation runway.
- Related docs: telemetry schema guide (ingest schema), labeling-hub operator runbook, data-privacy-and-retention-policy.

title: dsid_e2c43ae0190d4b22b77fd7cef28719c4__runtime-keycache-corruption-gpu-oom-hotfix-runbook.txt
text:
Runbook: Runtime keycache index corruption causing GPU OOMs (runtime-2.4.x hotfix)

## Purpose
This runbook covers detection, mitigation, and rollout steps for a class of incidents where long-running sessions experience sustained GPU memory growth, degraded tail latency, and eventual GPU OOMs due to keycache index inconsistency after journal compaction.

This page supersedes the emergency notes in ENG-424242 by consolidating the confirmed root cause, the runtime-2.4.x hotfix behavior, and operational procedures for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

## Summary (what happened)
Over multiple escalations (Hosted + Dedicated), customers reported sudden GPU OOMs coinciding with:
- Sustained GPU memory growth on long-running sessions
- Increased p95/p99 latency
- Spikes in keycache journal compaction time
- Repeated key index resync events

In affected cases, stale index entries prevented proper eviction. Under fragmentation, the GPU allocator entered a stall pattern (increased reserve/retry loops), leading to runaway reservation for a subset of sessions and eventual OOM.

## Confirmed root cause (updated)
The initial hypothesis (dangling pointers in the merge path) was partially correct but incomplete.

**Confirmed cause (runtime-2.4.0 through runtime-2.4.1):**
A race condition in the keycache journal compaction + snapshot merge path where concurrent eviction and a compaction commit could publish a partially-updated index view. The index version could advance while a subset of segments still referenced pre-compaction offsets, producing a mixed-generation index.

**Why it showed up “cross-environment”:**
Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments manifested at different thresholds because:
- Workload mixes differed (long-tail autoregressive vs. short requests)
- Memory pressure differed (fragmentation tolerance varies by GPU SKU and co-tenant load)
- Some environments had higher compaction frequency due to key churn

**Secondary amplifiers:**
- Long-tail autoregressive requests with large KV footprints avoid typical short-circuit evictions.
- Fragmentation increases allocator compaction overhead; once stalls begin, handle cleanup lags, increasing pressure further.

## Blast radius / customer impact
- High severity when it triggers: request failures due to OOM, degraded throughput, and sometimes traffic migration.
- Hosted: multi-tenant transient throttles and elevated retries.
- Dedicated/Private: prolonged degradation possible if nodes are not restarted or upgraded.

## When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when you observe any combination of:
1) Rapidly increasing GPU memory (allocated or reserved) without matching throughput
2) Keycache index resync loops and/or elevated compaction latency
3) GPU allocator stall metrics increasing (reserve failures, retry loops)
4) OOMs on long-running sessions that do not reproduce on fresh pods

## Signals and dashboards
Primary dashboards:
- Memory fragmentation / arena metrics: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/mem-frag-ENG-424242
- GPU OOM heatmap: https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/gpu-oom-heatmap

Key metrics to watch (names may differ slightly by cluster):
- runtime.keycache.journal_compaction_duration_ms (p95, max)
- runtime.keycache.index_resync_count
- runtime.keycache.eviction_failures
- runtime.gpu.allocator_stall_ms (p95)
- runtime.gpu.memory_reserved_bytes vs runtime.gpu.memory_allocated_bytes (gap indicates fragmentation/reservation pressure)
- runtime.session.handle_leaks (if available)

## Triage checklist (15 minutes)
1. Confirm scope
   - Is it a single model deployment, a region, or multi-region?
   - Identify whether issues correlate with long-running sessions.

2. Confirm symptoms
   - Check OOM logs and allocator stall metrics.
   - Check for index resync spikes and compaction spikes.

3. Identify runtime version
   - Versions at highest risk: runtime-2.4.0, runtime-2.4.1.
   - Hotfix versions: runtime-2.4.2-hotfix (preferred) and runtime-2.4.1-hotfix (intermediate, if already deployed).

4. Decide immediate mitigation
   - If active OOMs: apply emergency mitigations first (below), then proceed to rollout/upgrade.

## Immediate mitigations (no code change)
### Mitigation A: Reduce long-lived session pressure
- Temporarily lower max session TTL (if supported by the serving config) and/or reduce max context length for affected endpoints.
- Preferably target only the affected model deployment(s) to minimize customer impact.

### Mitigation B: Force safe eviction mode (runtime flag)
If the deployment supports runtime flags, enable safe eviction mode to reduce the probability of publishing mixed-generation index views during pressure.

Set one of the following flags (depending on environment tooling):
- KEYCACHE_SAFE_EVICT=1
- RUNTIME_KEYCACHE_SAFE_EVICT=true

Operational notes:
- Safe eviction can reduce throughput by ~2–6% on KV-heavy workloads; treat as temporary.
- If OOMs persist after enabling, proceed to Mitigation C and upgrade.

### Mitigation C: Controlled restart / pod recycling
If allocator stalls are already severe, a rolling restart can restore service while you prepare the hotfix rollout.

Guidance:
- Hosted: follow standard regional rolling restart policy; keep capacity headroom.
- Dedicated/Private: coordinate with Customer Success; do not restart all nodes simultaneously.

## Hotfix / permanent remediation
### Recommended fix version
**runtime-2.4.2-hotfix** (preferred)
- Adds index generation fencing and atomic publish semantics for compaction merges.
- Introduces stricter validation around index segment boundaries.
- Adds a bounded emergency reclaim path to break allocator stall loops.

Notes on earlier hotfix:
- runtime-2.4.1-hotfix reduces incidence via linearized merge fencing, but does not fully eliminate mixed-generation edge cases under extreme churn. Upgrade to runtime-2.4.2-hotfix as soon as feasible.

### What the hotfix changes (operator-facing)
- New metric: runtime.keycache.index_generation_conflict_count (should remain near zero)
- Additional log lines when safe eviction is triggered under fragmentation
- Emergency reclaim triggers only when stall thresholds are exceeded; it is rate-limited

## Rollout procedure
### Hosted rollout (canary → regional → global)
1. Stage
   - Deploy runtime-2.4.2-hotfix to staging.
   - Run replay workload for at least 6 hours (24 hours preferred if incident pressure is low).

2. Canary
   - Start at 5–10% traffic in a low-risk region (historically eu-west-1 was used).
   - Monitor for at least 12 hours; extend to 48 hours if the incident is ongoing or signals are noisy.

3. Regional expansion
   - Increase to 25% then 50% in the canary region.
   - Expand to one additional region.

4. Global
   - Proceed to full rollout once key signals stabilize (see Success Criteria below).

Rollback plan:
- If index_generation_conflict_count increases or OOM rate worsens, roll back to prior stable runtime and enable KEYCACHE_SAFE_EVICT=1 until a corrected build is deployed.

### Dedicated/Private rollout
1. Confirm maintenance window with Customer Success.
2. Upgrade one node first (or one pool) and run a 2–4 hour soak test.
3. Upgrade remaining nodes in rolling fashion.
4. Leave safe eviction enabled for 24 hours post-upgrade if the customer runs KV-heavy workloads, then disable if stable.

## Success criteria (what “fixed” looks like)
- No OOM regressions on historical replay traces or during soak.
- allocator stall metrics decrease materially (target: ≥25% reduction from incident baseline).
- Memory fragmentation improves (arena free-percentiles improve by ~20% within 24 hours on representative load).
- Index resync count returns to baseline; generation conflicts remain ~0.
- Impacted customers confirm restored baseline throughput.

## Failure modes and what to do
1) OOMs persist after hotfix rollout
- Verify the running version actually updated.
- Check if workload exceeds expected KV limits; consider tightening context/TTL.
- Enable safe eviction mode temporarily.
- Escalate to Serving Runtime on-call with:
  - Region(s), model deployment(s)
  - Runtime version(s)
  - 2–4 hour window of dashboards
  - Representative request traces (redacted)

2) Throughput regression after enabling safe eviction
- Disable safe eviction after hotfix deployment and 24 hours of stability.
- If throughput remains degraded, check for unrelated GPU fragmentation drivers (driver version changes, co-tenancy shifts, model swaps).

## Communications guidance
- For active incidents: publish a brief customer-facing status update noting mitigations in progress and an ETA for a runtime hotfix.
- For Dedicated/Private: provide a maintenance window and a rollback plan.
- After full rollout: share a short incident summary and confirm monitoring improvements.

## References
- Primary incident tracking: linear://ENG-424242
- Hotpatch PRs:
  - https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1892 (initial fencing + tests)
  - https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1894 (instrumentation + allocator guardrails)
  - https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1901 (index generation atomic publish + validation)
- Dashboards:
  - https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/mem-frag-ENG-424242
  - https://console.redwood.ai/dashboards/gpu-oom-heatmap

## Changelog

title: dsid_740c89854e31413b9504eef4143307a2__per-minute-session-credit-framework-brief-2026-11-23.txt
text:
Per-minute session credit framework - brief

Overview:

This brief specifies the Per-minute Session Credit Framework (PM-SCF) — a standardized metering and contract abstraction that converts session-duration and fidelity demands into a compact credit unit for pricing, entitlements, and SLO reconciliation. The goal is to make session-based commercial agreements tractable for both developers and commercial teams while preserving predictable economics under bursty, multimodal conversational workloads.

Intended audience:
- Product managers and pricing leads
- Solutions and sales engineers
- Billing & revenue operations
- Runtime and telemetry engineers

Goals and success metrics:
- Provide a single canonical credit unit ("session-minute credit") that maps to runtime cost signals (GPU-time, token throughput, KV cache pressure).
- Enable per-customer contracts that are: auditable (billing events traceable to telemetry), predictable (<=10% monthly variance against the projected spend for typical workloads), and fair (credits align with resource cost).
- Reduce complexity of commercial negotiations by supporting 3 contract primitives: baseline monthly commit, burst buffer credits, and fidelity-adaptive discounts.

Definitions and primitives:
1) Session-minute credit (SMC): the atomic billing unit. One SMC represents the cost-equivalent of a single minute of median conversational throughput for a defined fidelity profile. The SMC is not a time measurement in the runtime; it is a cost-normalized token-time abstraction.
2) Fidelity profile: a label defining resource intensity (e.g., "low-emb", "conv-standard", "conv-high-fidelity"). Each profile has a conversion multiplier to SMCs.
3) Baseline commit: monthly SMC allocation included in the contract at discounted unit pricing.
4) Burst credits: pool of pre-purchased on-demand SMCs at a higher unit cost for transient peaks.
5) True-up: monthly reconciliation comparing actual SMC consumption to baseline commit.

Conversion and calibration model (high level):
- SMC conversion is derived from a workload-weighted runtime cost model using three telemetry signals: average active GPU-seconds per session-minute, average tokens emitted per session-minute, and observed KV cache hit ratio.
- Formula (conceptual):
  SMC = alpha * GPU_seconds_per_minute + beta * tokens_per_minute * token_cost_index - gamma * cache_hit_saving
- Alpha/beta/gamma are tuned quarterly by the pricing analytics team and published as a conversion table.

Pricing tiers and rate sheet (example table):
- Baseline SMC unit price (example): Standard fidelity: $0.020/SMC; High fidelity: $0.045/SMC; Embedding-heavy sessions: $0.012/SMC
- Burst SMC price multiplier: 2.0x baseline unit price
- Minimum monthly commit: 50,000 SMCs (can be negotiated)

Contract clauses (example YAML snippet for legal and billing coders):
  contract_component: "baseline"
  currency: "USD"
  baseline_commit_smc: "50000"
  unit_price_usd_per_smc: "0.02"
  burst_buffer_smc: "10000"
  burst_unit_price_multiplier: "2.0"
  true_up_window: "monthly"

(Embed this snippet into the standard commercial template. It will be converted into billing line items by RevOps.)

Telemetry and enforcement:
- Required telemetry events (minimum): session.start, session.heartbeat (1m cadence), session.end, model.variant, fidelity_profile, session.kv_hit_rate, tokens.emitted.
- Billing will consume the session.heartbeat stream to compute per-session SMCs; implementations MUST ensure heartbeats are emitted at the configured cadence to avoid undercount/overcount disputes.
- Telemetry contract examples:
  - session.heartbeat payload should include: session_id, timestamp, active_gpu_seconds, tokens_emitted, fidelity_profile, kv_hit_ratio.

SLO and reconciliation workflow:
1) Realtime: the runtime exposes a per-route SMC burn-rate gauge to the Console (1m resolution) and alerts when burn-rate deviates ±25% from expected based on the selected fidelity profile.
2) Monthly true-up: RevOps computes actual SMC consumption by aggregating heartbeats and applying the published conversion table; invoices reflect baseline used, burst usage, and any negotiated credits.
3) Dispute process: customer disputes must include raw heartbeat exports for the disputed month. The standardized CSV export format is described in Appendix A. Disputes window: 60 days after invoice issuance.

Operational playbook for onboarding a customer to PM-SCF (numbered rollout steps):
1. Pre-sales sizing: Solutions engineer runs the Session Simulator with the customer’s workload sample to estimate median tokens/min and expected fidelity mix; produces a projected SMC consumption report.
2. Contracting: Pricing selects baseline tier and rate, RevOps adds burst buffer and sets SLA credits for underperformance.
3. Instrumentation: Runtime team enables heartbeat stream and verifies event schema.
4. Pilot (30 days): Customer runs production traffic with a capped burst buffer. Telemetry is monitored daily and an initial reconciliation is produced at day 30.
5. Finalize commit: Based on pilot results, either adjust the baseline commit or migrate customer to a consumption-only pricing plan.

Migration and edge cases:
- Legacy customers on per-token metering can be migrated by running a 60-day shadow conversion and presenting a migration credit that amortizes risk over 3 billing cycles.
- For long-duration streaming sessions (multihour), we cap per-session SMC at 6x per-hour baseline to avoid runaway invoices. Exceptions must be approved by RevOps.
- Offline batch embedding jobs should default to an embeddings fidelity profile; if runtime is run on Dedicated, conversion should use Dedicated-aware multipliers.

Telemetry schema (Appendix A) (CSV export columns):
- invoice_period, customer_id, session_id, heartbeat_timestamp, active_gpu_seconds, tokens_emitted, fidelity_profile, kv_hit_ratio, derived_smc

Rollout plan and timeline (recommended):
- Q4 2026: finalize conversion table, implement heartbeat consumer in Billing pipeline, internal pilot with 3 strategic customers.
- Q1 2027: public launch for new customers (opt-in for legacy customers).
- Q2 2027: telemetry-driven optimizations and quarterly update of alpha/beta/gamma coefficients.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Inaccurate heartbeats lead to billing disputes. Mitigation: require SDK and runtime validation tests and sample export for first bill cycle.
- Risk: High-fidelity burst patterns create unpredictable cost for the vendor. Mitigation: conservative burst pricing and optional soft caps with automated throttles.

Ownership and decision rights:
- Product (owner): finalize fidelity profile taxonomy and conversion policy.
- Pricing & RevOps (owner): rate sheet, contract templates, true-up process.
- Runtime & Telemetry (owner): heartbeat implementation, Console burn-rate gauges, export tooling.
- Legal (owner): contract language and dispute clauses.

Appendix B: Example customer scenario (worked example):
- Customer A: median conversational session 2.5 tokens/sec, average session length 6 minutes, fidelity mix 70% conv-standard, 30% conv-high-fidelity.
- Apply conversion table -> estimated SMC/month = 75,000. Pricing team proposes baseline commit 70k SMC @ $0.02 -> monthly baseline $1,400; burst buffer 10k SMC @ 2.0x -> on-demand buffer.

Action items (next steps):
- Product to publish v1 conversion table (owner: Maya) by 2026-12-15.
- Runtime to deliver heartbeat consumer and example CSV exporter by 2027-01-05.
- RevOps to draft contract clause templates and invoice mapping by 2027-01-20.

Related reading and references:
- Internal: consumption-scenario-simulator design spec, session-aware-cost-tuning playbook, runtime-billing-reconciliation-explainability-playbook.

Document change log:
- 2026-11-23: Created (Maya Thompson).
- 2027-01-10: Clarified heartbeat schema and added worked example (review: Evan Liu, Priya Singh).

title: dsid_d3df5f41e30846509429b17443d7f572__extensible-toolcall-versioning-and-safeguard-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Extensible tool-call versioning and safeguard playbook

Summary

This playbook defines Redwood's standard approach for introducing, evolving, and deprecating tool-call (function/tool) APIs and their schemas across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. It focuses on three goals: preserving customer runtime stability, enabling safe evolution of tool signatures and behavior, and minimizing costly rollbacks when incompatibilities surface.

Context and motivation

- Tool-calls are first-class in our generation/chat API surfaces. They allow model outputs to invoke structured functionality downstream (e.g., search, database queries, external tool execution).
- Tool schemas change frequently during product iteration (new params, removed fields, semantics). Without explicit guardrails, changes can cause production failures, user-visible regressions, or silent correctness issues.
- Private and on-prem deployments require extra caution: runtime-sidecar adaptors and compatibility filters must support graceful pivoting when the control plane pushes schema or behavior changes.

Scope

This playbook applies to:
- REST/streaming generation endpoints that expose tool-calling (hosted and self-hosted).
- Client SDKs that serialize and deserialize tool-call payloads.
- Runtime sidecars/adaptors used in Private deployments.
- Rollout automation and canary policies in the Redwood Console.

Key principles

1) Always additive-first. New optional fields and tools are preferred over changing existing field semantics.
2) Capability negotiation. Clients and runtimes must advertise supported tool schema versions and feature flags.
3) Fail-safe behavior. If a runtime cannot safely execute a tool-call due to schema mismatch, it must fall back to a safe no-op path and emit a clear diagnostic event.
4) Observability and guardrails. Every tool invocation must produce structured telemetry for lineage, validation failures, and user impact scoring.

Roles and ownership

- API Product: decides recommended schema expansion windows and backwards-compatibility constraints.
- Runtime (serving-runtime) team: implements adaptor shims, capability headers, and runtime fallbacks.
- DX/SDKs: provide client-side helpers for capability negotiation and migration warnings.
- Customer Success & Private-deployments: manage communication and upgrade coordination for private customers.

Compatibility model and headers

- All tool-call requests must include a Tool-Version header and a Capability-List claim in the request context. Example headers:

  Tool-Version: tool/search@v1.4.0
  X-Redwood-Capabilities: tool-call=stable,structured-params=v1.4,early-return=true

- The server responds with a negotiated Tool-Version and a Compatibility-Outcome field when the toolbox adapts or downgrades:

  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
  Negotiated-Tool-Version: tool/search@v1.3.0
  Tool-Compatibility-Outcome: downgraded (missing param: bounding_box)

Negotiation rules (ordered):
1. Exact match: if the runtime supports declared version, use it.
2. Minor-compatible downgrade: if runtime supports a lower minor version with identical semantics for required fields, downgrade and record outcome.
3. Safe fallback: if required fields are missing in runtime, return a capability rejection and route to safe fallback path.

Schema evolution lifecycle

- CHANGE TYPE: ADD OPTIONAL FIELD
  - Acceptable: immediate rollout.
  - Action: no tolerance window required. Clients should be resilient to unknown fields.

- CHANGE TYPE: PROMOTE OPTIONAL -> REQUIRED
  - Acceptable: after 90-day deprecation window and client-usage audit.
  - Action: publish migration guide, add server-side soft-reject flag for 30 days (return 422 with migration_hint).

- CHANGE TYPE: REMOVE FIELD or CHANGE SEMANTICS
  - Acceptable: never without clear migration plan.
  - Action: create a staged deprecation ADR, run automated compatibility tests (see Tests & gating), and schedule a phased rollout with canary and customer opt-in.

Runtime adaptors and shims (Private deployments)

- Sidecar behaviour: Private runtimes must ship a sidecar that can perform schema translation for common safe changes (rename, default-injection, minor-version mapping). The sidecar MUST NOT attempt to guess semantics for removed fields — it should reject with a clear diagnostic.
- Shipping a shim: sidecar shim must include a mapping table in YAML, signed artifact, and a checksum. Example shim snippet: 

  mappings:
    - from: tool/search@v1.4.0
      to: tool/search@v1.3.0
      transforms:
        - rename: { from: 'bbox', to: 'bounding_box' }
        - inject_default: { field: 'timeout_ms', value: 1500 }

- Security: shims that alter payloads must be validated by runtime-signing (HSM/KMS) and logged in audit trail.

Testing and gating

- Unit tests: schema-parsers in SDKs and runtime must have >95% coverage for boundary and optional-field behavior.
- Integration test matrix (automated):
  - Client vX + Server vY + Sidecar shim present/absent (matrix permutations).
  - Use our synthetic harness to exercise 10K tool-call permutations and flag any unexpected rejects or silent drops.
- Canary policy: 1% traffic for 72 hours, then 5% for 48 hours, with automatic rollback on these signals:
  - Tool invocation error rate > 0.1% (absolute) above baseline.
  - User-impact score increase > 0.5 (see Observability section).
  - Latency p95 increase > 25% for tool routes.

Operational playbook: rollout and rollback steps

1) Pre-release
   - Publish migration guide and release notes.
   - Add compatibility tests to CI (matrix above).
   - Signal private-deployment customers and schedule maintenance windows if shim installation is required.

2) Canary rollout
   - Enable new tool version for 1% of traffic using runtime routing rules.
   - Monitor the three automatic rollback signals and set alerts.

3) Ramp
   - After 72h with no trigger, ramp to 5% for 48h, then 20% for 24h, then full rollout if green.
   - During ramp, disable automatic pruning of unknown fields in SDKs (so clients surface schema issues).

4) Post-rollout
   - If pushing a version that promotes fields to required, start 90-day deprecation calendar and add server soft-reject.

Failure modes and mitigations

- Silent-accept (runtime ignores unknown required semantics): Requires immediate incident. Mitigation: identify affected routes, force negotiation failure to block malformed invocations, and revert routing.
- Shim-mismatch (sidecar applied an incorrect rename): Treat as data-corruption incident. Mitigation: revert shim, re-run migration test harness, and provide remediation script to affected customers.
- Client that cannot be upgraded: use per-tenant feature flags to continue serving an older behavior for up to 12 months and log a technical debt ticket for product follow-up.

Observability and telemetry requirements

Every tool-call must emit the following structured fields:
- tool.id (string)
- tool.version.requested (string)
- tool.version.negotiated (string)
- tool.compatibility.outcome (enum: exact|downgraded|rejected|shim-transformed)
- tool.validation.fail_reasons (list)
- user-impact-score (float 0..1) — derived from downstream error mappings

Retention and alerting: events are retained at high fidelity for 45 days for hosted customers and 90 days for enterprise customers. Alerts: create alert when tool.compatibility.outcome == rejected AND invocation-rate > 1/min for 5m.

Examples and snippets

- Example client negotiation (curl):

  curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/chat/generate \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \
    -H 'Tool-Version: tool/search@v1.4.0' \
    -H 'X-Redwood-Capabilities: tool-call=stable,structured-params=v1.4' \
    -d '{"messages": [{"role":"user","content":"Find restaurants near me"}], "tools": [{"id":"tool/search","params":{"q":"restaurants"}}] }'

- Example negotiation response: 

  {
    "id": "resp_123",
    "tool": {
      "id": "tool/search",
      "version": "v1.3.0",
      "compatibility": "downgraded",
      "notes": "bounding_box param not supported, defaulted to full-radius"
    }
  }

Tests and automation hooks (CI)

- Add a compatibility job that runs on every schema change PR. The job performs:
  - Schema linting (reject breaking changes without ADR).
  - Matrix-runpermutations using our ephemeral runtime testbed.
  - Generates a compatibility report artifact stored with PR.

- PR gating rule: any PR that modifies a tool schema must include a compatibility_report artifact and a migration.md file.

Related pages and artifacts

- Related runbooks: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/tool-call-fallback-runbook (link placeholder)
- CI job: redwood-ci/tool-compat-matrix (internal pipeline)
- Migration template: migrations/tool-schema-migration-template.md

Appendix: Minimum SLOs for tool routes (recommended)

| Route class | p50 latency | p95 latency | error-rate SLI | notes |
|------------|------------:|------------:|---------------:|-------|
| Inline tool-call (synchronous) | 80ms | 350ms | <0.1% | Default host route
| Async tool-call (background) | 200ms | 800ms | <0.5% | Accepts eventual completion

Review cadence and governance

- API Product and Runtime must review the playbook annually or after any severe incident flagged by Customer Success.
- Any removal or semantic change to a tool field requires an ADR and sign-off by Product, Runtime, DX, and Security.

Contact

- Playing-author: Priya Nambiar (priya@redwood.ai)
- Runtime owner: Jun Park (jun@redwood.ai)
- DX contact: Marisol Ortega (marisol@redwood.ai)

title: dsid_6e8847f7278e4e929393087264a310ab__burst-capacity-audit-events.txt
text:
Dedicated Burst Capacity: Audit Logging Events (Config, Overrides, Administrative Actions)

## 1. Purpose
This document defines the **audit events** required for the Dedicated **Burst Capacity** feature. The intent is to ensure that:
- All **customer-impacting configuration changes** are attributable to an actor, traceable to a request, and available for compliance evidence.
- Any **administrative override** (including emergency actions) is recorded with sufficient context (who/what/why/when).
- Audit logs are consistent across control plane services and are safe to expose to customers where applicable.

This spec is used by:
- Platform Control Plane engineering (event production)
- Security engineering (schema, access controls, retention)
- SRE (incident forensics)
- CS/Support (customer explanations)
- Legal/Finance (contractual statements, dispute resolution)

## 2. Scope
### In scope
Audit events for:
- Tenant-level burst configuration changes (enable/disable, caps/limits, priority tier)
- Policy guardrail changes that affect admission (e.g., max burst ratio, cooldown windows) when modified outside standard release/config pipelines
- Administrative actions and overrides (including emergency circuit breaker actions)
- Permissions and access to sensitive burst debugging tools (who accessed decision explanation, who ran an override)

### Out of scope
- Standard request/response logs for data plane inference requests (covered by existing gateway telemetry policies)
- Per-request admission decisions as a full audit trail (too high volume). Instead, we audit **configuration and override state** and provide sampled/aggregated decision telemetry separately.

## 3. Definitions
- **Tenant**: A Dedicated customer account/environment represented by `tenant_id`.
- **Burst configuration**: Controls that allow a tenant to temporarily exceed reserved baseline capacity via Redwood-managed burst pools.
- **Override**: A non-default change that bypasses or modifies admission behavior outside customer-configured limits (e.g., allow temporary burst above cap, force deny bursts for tenant, disable burst in a region).
- **Actor**: Entity that initiated the change.
  - Human user (Redwood employee, customer admin)
  - Service identity (automation, control plane job)

## 4. Systems that must emit events
| System / service | Responsibility | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `control-plane-api` | Primary authoring surface for tenant burst config | Emits config change events + validation failures when relevant |
| `policy-engine` | Evaluates admission guardrail rules; stores global/fleet rules | Emits policy change and override events |
| `burst-admission-controller` | Enforces admission + fairness; implements circuit breaker hooks | Emits events for admin actions (breaker toggles, forced denies) and access to debug endpoints |
| `console-backend` | Customer-visible surfaces; read-only access paths | Emits events for customer admin actions, and for support impersonation sessions if used |
| `billing-metering-exporter` | Exports burst usage metering (non-audit) | Not an audit producer; referenced for correlation IDs only |

## 5. Audit event requirements (global)
### 5.1 Required baseline fields (all events)
All burst audit events MUST include the following fields in the audit log payload (field names are normative). When a field is not applicable, it must be omitted (not set to null).

**Event identity & timing**
- `event_id` (UUID)
- `event_time` (RFC3339/UTC)
- `event_name` (string; see catalog below)
- `event_version` (integer; start at 1)

**Actor & access context**
- `actor_type` (one of: `redwood_employee`, `customer_user`, `service_principal`)
- `actor_id` (employee id / user id / service principal id)
- `actor_email` (for humans when available)
- `actor_roles` (RBAC roles evaluated at time of action; string list serialized, e.g. "[\"support_oncall\",\"platform_admin\"]")
- `actor_ip` (source IP if available)
- `user_agent` (if from web/SDK)
- `authn_method` (e.g. `sso`, `api_key`, `oauth`, `m2m`)

**Request & traceability**
- `request_id` (control plane request id)
- `trace_id` (distributed tracing correlation id)
- `change_ticket` (e.g. Linear/Jira id) when action requires a ticket; see §8

**Target resource**
- `tenant_id` (if tenant-scoped)
- `resource_type` (e.g. `burst_config`, `burst_override`, `burst_circuit_breaker`, `burst_feature_flag`)
- `resource_id` (stable id; for tenant config use `tenant_id`)
- `region` (if scoped)
- `hardware_class` (e.g. `h100`, `l40s`) if scoped

**Outcome**
- `outcome` (`success` | `denied` | `error`)
- `error_code` (if denied/error)
- `error_message` (redacted; short)

### 5.2 Change representation rules
For change events, include:
- `change_type` (`create` | `update` | `delete` | `enable` | `disable`)
- `before` and `after` snapshots **only for the fields that changed**.

Sensitive values must be redacted (see §7). For example, do not emit raw API keys, internal capacity pool IDs that could reveal fleet topology beyond what is necessary, or any prompt/content.

### 5.3 Determinism + non-repudiation
- Events must be written to the audit store **before** acknowledging successful config writes to the caller (best effort: at-most-once log emission is not acceptable for config changes; see §10.2).
- For asynchronous workflows, emit both:
  - `...requested` when a change is accepted for processing
  - `...applied` when it takes effect

## 6. Event catalog (normative)
Event names follow: `burst.<domain>.<action>`.

### 6.1 Tenant burst configuration
| Event name | Trigger | Producer | Actor | Required additional attributes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `burst.config.enabled` | Burst enabled for a tenant | `control-plane-api` | customer user or Redwood employee | `tenant_id`, `after` (enabled=true), `burst_plan` | `burst_plan` is a packaging identifier (e.g. `standard`, `enterprise_gold`) not a price |
| `burst.config.disabled` | Burst disabled for a tenant | `control-plane-api` | customer user or Redwood employee | `tenant_id`, `before` (enabled=true), `after` (enabled=false) | Emit even if disabled due to incident response |
| `burst.config.updated` | Any burst limit/guardrail updated at tenant level | `control-plane-api` | customer user or Redwood employee | `tenant_id`, `before`, `after`, `effective_at` (if delayed) | Examples: max burst ratio, per-tenant cap, cooldown window |
| `burst.config.validation_failed` | Attempted change fails validation | `control-plane-api` | customer user or Redwood employee | `tenant_id` (if known), `validation_errors` | `validation_errors` should be a short string, not a structured object (avoid nested) |

**Tenant config fields that are auditable (when changed)**
- `enabled` (boolean)
- `max_burst_ratio` (e.g. 1.0–3.0)
- `burst_gpu_cap` (integer GPUs or GPU-slices; specify units in field string e.g. "8 gpus")
- `burst_qps_cap` (if applicable)
- `cooldown_seconds`
- `priority_tier` (`standard`, `silver`, `gold`) 
- `deny_on_slo_regression` (boolean; if this differs per tenant)
- `regions_allowed` and `hardware_classes_allowed` (if explicitly constrained)

### 6.2 Policy guardrails & global limits
These changes are restricted to authorized Redwood roles and typically require an approved change ticket.

| Event name | Trigger | Producer | Actor | Required additional attributes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `burst.policy.rule.created` | New guardrail rule added | `policy-engine` | Redwood employee/service principal | `rule_id`, `after`, `scope` | `scope` as string (e.g. "global" / "region=us-east" / "hardware=h100") |
| `burst.policy.rule.updated` | Guardrail rule modified | `policy-engine` | Redwood employee/service principal | `rule_id`, `before`, `after`, `scope` | Include `reason` when manually modified during an incident |
| `burst.policy.rule.deleted` | Guardrail rule removed | `policy-engine` | Redwood employee/service principal | `rule_id`, `before`, `scope` | Deletions require ticket + reviewer approval (see §8) |
| `burst.policy.slo_gate.updated` | SLO-based gating thresholds changed | `policy-engine` | Redwood employee/service principal | `before`, `after`, `metric_name`, `threshold` | This is highly sensitive; must be restricted access |

### 6.3 Administrative overrides
Overrides are intended to be time-bounded and attributable.

| Event name | Trigger | Producer | Actor | Required additional attributes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `burst.override.created` | Create an override (allow/deny/raise cap) | `policy-engine` | Redwood employee | `override_id`, `override_type`, `expires_at`, `after`, `reason`, `change_ticket` | `override_type`: `force_allow`, `force_deny`, `raise_cap`, `lower_cap` |
| `burst.override.updated` | Modify an override | `policy-engine` | Redwood employee | `override_id`, `before`, `after`, `reason`, `change_ticket` | Any extension of `expires_at` must include explicit reason |
| `burst.override.deleted` | Remove an override early | `policy-engine` | Redwood employee | `override_id`, `before`, `change_ticket` | Record if removed due to rollback |
| `burst.override.expired` | Override reaches expiry | `policy-engine` | service principal | `override_id`, `before`, `expires_at` | Actor is the expiry job/service principal |

### 6.4 Circuit breakers & emergency controls
| Event name | Trigger | Producer | Actor | Required additional attributes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `burst.circuit_breaker.enabled` | Global or scoped circuit breaker enabled | `burst-admission-controller` | Redwood employee/service principal | `scope`, `reason`, `effective_at` | Scope examples: "global", "region=eu-west", "hardware=h100" |
| `burst.circuit_breaker.disabled` | Circuit breaker disabled | `burst-admission-controller` | Redwood employee/service principal | `scope`, `reason` | Must reference incident id when applicable |
| `burst.fleet_safety_cap.updated` | Fleet safety cap changed | `policy-engine` | Redwood employee | `before`, `after`, `scope`, `change_ticket` | Treated like a policy change |

### 6.5 Access to sensitive burst debugging and support tooling
We audit access to tools that can reveal admission rationale, internal states, or tenant configuration, even if no change is made.

| Event name | Trigger | Producer | Actor | Required additional attributes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `burst.debug.decision_explained` | Debug endpoint used to explain admit/deny | `burst-admission-controller` | Redwood employee | `tenant_id`, `region`, `hardware_class`, `explanation_mode`, `redaction_level` | Must not include prompts or customer data payloads; log only metadata |
| `burst.support.impersonation.started` | Support impersonation session begins | `console-backend` | Redwood employee | `tenant_id`, `session_id`, `reason`, `change_ticket` | Only if impersonation is supported; otherwise omit event |
| `burst.support.impersonation.ended` | Support impersonation session ends | `console-backend` | Redwood employee | `tenant_id`, `session_id` | |
| `burst.audit.exported` | Audit logs exported (customer request / evidence) | `control-plane-api` | Redwood employee/service principal | `tenant_id`, `time_range`, `export_format`, `reason`, `change_ticket` | No bulk cross-tenant exports without Security approval |

### 6.6 Feature flags (rollout controls)
Feature flags that change customer behavior must be auditable.

| Event name | Trigger | Producer | Actor | Required additional attributes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `burst.feature_flag.updated` | Burst rollout gate changed (region/hardware allow-list, per-tenant enablement) | `control-plane-api` | Redwood employee/service principal | `flag_name`, `before`, `after`, `scope`, `change_ticket` | Includes kill-switch toggles |

## 7. Data classification, redaction, and customer sensitivity
### 7.1 Data classification
Burst audit logs are classified as **Restricted** because they may contain:
- Customer identifiers (`tenant_id`, account names via joins)
- Operational details (regions, hardware classes, guardrail thresholds)
- Security-sensitive actions (override usage)

### 7.2 Redaction rules
Never include:
- API keys, secrets, bearer tokens
- Prompt text, generated text, embeddings, or user content
- Raw internal pool instance IDs that reveal exact fleet topology (use `region` + `hardware_class` + logical pool name if needed)

Allowed content:
- Tenant id
- Config fields and numeric limits (caps/ratios) 
- Reason codes and short human-entered reasons (must not include customer content)

If a reason string is free-form, enforce:
- Max length 512 chars
- Reject/strip newlines
- Log pipeline must apply basic PII detection and flag suspicious entries to Security (best-effort)

## 8. Change management requirements (tickets + approvals)
### 8.1 Actions requiring a change ticket
The following MUST include `change_ticket`:
- Any `burst.policy.*` change made outside standard versioned deployment artifacts
- Any `burst.override.*` create/update/delete
- Any `burst.fleet_safety_cap.updated`
- Any cross-tenant `burst.audit.exported`

Recommended ticket systems:
- Linear: `ENG-*`, `PM-*`
- Jira (incidents/support): `INC-*`, `INT-*`

### 8.2 Two-person rule (recommended)
For high-risk actions, require an approval workflow and include `approved_by` as a string field (email) in the event payload:
- Global circuit breaker disable in peak hours
- Increasing fleet safety caps
- Creating overrides affecting multiple tenants

If implementation cannot enforce approvals at execution time, document the manual approval in the ticket and ensure the event includes the `change_ticket`.

## 9. Retention, storage, and access control
### 9.1 Retention
- Default retention for burst audit logs: **400 days** (meets typical enterprise/SOC2 evidence needs while limiting risk)
- For customers under contractual audit retention requirements, retention is handled by the platform’s standard audit retention policy; do not implement per-tenant retention forks in burst services.

### 9.2 Storage and integrity
- Audit events are written to the central audit pipeline (Append-only store).
- Storage must support immutable retention windows (WORM-equivalent controls via object lock where applicable).

### 9.3 Access
- Read access restricted to:
  - Security engineering and compliance (broad)
  - SRE on-call (incident-only)
  - Support/CS (tenant-scoped only, with ticket reference)
- All access to audit logs should be audited by the existing audit system (meta-audit).

## 10. Implementation guidance
### 10.1 Event emission points (recommended)
- Emit audit events at the **command boundary** (where the system decides to apply a change), not in downstream async workers.
- For multi-step propagation, use `...requested` and `...applied` patterns.

### 10.2 Failure handling
- If audit write fails, config changes must fail closed for:
  - `burst.config.*` writes
  - `burst.override.*`
  - `burst.circuit_breaker.*`

Exceptions: None for burst controls.

### 10.3 Idempotency
For config updates and override creates, include:
- `idempotency_key` when supported by the caller
- The audit pipeline should deduplicate by (`event_name`, `request_id`) as a safety mechanism, but producers remain responsible for consistent emission.

## 11. Sample audit events (examples)
### 11.1 Tenant burst enabled
```json
{
  "event_id": "2c3f8b8b-3a71-4ac9-9f6d-88e1f2ef0c1a",
  "event_time": "2025-03-12T19:22:41Z",
  "event_name": "burst.config.enabled",
  "event_version": 1,
  "actor_type": "redwood_employee",
  "actor_id": "emp_1842",
  "actor_email": "miguel.santos@redwoodinference.com",
  "actor_roles": "[\"customer_success\",\"dedicated_admin\"]",
  "actor_ip": "203.0.113.10",
  "authn_method": "sso",
  "request_id": "cp_req_01HRQY3C0Y1VJ6S0J5K9",
  "trace_id": "b8d1a8f2a3f7b0b1",
  "resource_type": "burst_config",
  "resource_id": "tenant_9d2c",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_9d2c",
  "region": "us-east",
  "hardware_class": "h100",
  "change_type": "enable",
  "after": "enabled=true; max_burst_ratio=2.0; burst_gpu_cap=8 gpus; cooldown_seconds=300; priority_tier=standard",
  "burst_plan": "standard",
  "outcome": "success"
}
```

### 11.2 Override created during incident
```json
{
  "event_id": "37c0d7b6-9f9c-4c71-a59b-2a1f3c0a2c44",
  "event_time": "2025-05-18T03:11:05Z",
  "event_name": "burst.override.created",
  "event_version": 1,
  "actor_type": "redwood_employee",
  "actor_id": "emp_0319",
  "actor_email": "peter.holtz@redwoodinference.com",
  "actor_roles": "[\"sre_oncall\",\"platform_admin\"]",
  "actor_ip": "198.51.100.27",
  "authn_method": "sso",
  "request_id": "pe_req_01HS9A2P88VZKQ",
  "trace_id": "0fca2d4f3a992d31",
  "resource_type": "burst_override",
  "resource_id": "ovr_7f31",
  "tenant_id": "tenant_4a11",
  "region": "eu-west",
  "hardware_class": "l40s",
  "override_type": "force_deny",
  "expires_at": "2025-05-18T04:11:05Z",
  "after": "force_deny=true; reason_code=FLEET_SAFETY",
  "reason": "Mitigation: elevated non-burst p95 latency; temporary deny bursts while circuit breaker thresholds are tuned.",
  "change_ticket": "INC-1842",
  "outcome": "success"
}
```

## 12. Compliance mapping (reference)
This section helps auditors and internal reviewers understand how these events support common controls.

- **SOC 2 CC7.2 / CC7.3 (change management / monitoring):**
  - Captures administrative changes to burst configs and guardrails.
  - Captures incident-driven overrides and breaker toggles.
- **SOC 2 CC6.x (logical access):**
  - Captures actor identity, roles, and authentication method.
  - Captures access to sensitive debug and impersonation tooling.
- **Customer contractual audit clauses:**
  - Provides a defensible record of customer-visible configuration changes and Redwood administrative interventions.

## 13. Open questions / future enhancements
- Customer self-serve audit export: whether we provide tenant-scoped export directly in Console for Dedicated Enterprise plans.
- Signing audit events at the producer (application-level signatures) vs relying on storage immutability controls.
- Standardizing `approved_by` workflow enforcement for two-person rule actions.

## 14. Ownership
- Document owner: Security & Compliance (Naomi Feldman)
- Implementation owners:
  - Control plane event emission: Ethan Park
  - Policy engine rule/override events: Jordan Lee
  - Admission controller debug + breaker events: Vikram Singh / Sean Gallagher (SRE review)

For questions or to request an exception, file a Security review ticket and link this page.

title: dsid_7527c7e4f8a048c185f5f912b97bcc0c__slo-evolution-capacity-simulations-runbook-2025.txt
text:
SLO Evolution & Capacity Simulation Runbook

Overview

Purpose: centralize the SLO lifecycle decisions and the set of reproducible capacity simulations, so SRE and platform teams can evolve SLOs safely, validate autoscaling and fallback policies, and link simulation results to incident reviews and error-budget actions. This runbook prescribes the policy, tooling, and a repeatable test matrix for Redwood inference services (hosted-api, routing-proxy, model-worker pools).

Scope: hosted inference and dedicated pools. Excludes on-prem Private packaging tests (see eng-private-deployments/runbooks).

Key definitions
- SLO: Service level objective measured as error budget and latency percentiles over a rolling 30d window unless noted.
- Error budget: 1 - SLO (percentage of allowed user-visible failures). Consumed by user-visible errors and latency misses.
- Simulation: controlled load or chaos test intended to exercise autoscaling, fallback routing, cache eviction, and degraded-model behaviors.

Executive summary
- Target primary SLOs: availability (successful requests rate) and latency (p95 for short responses, p99 for long streaming). Example baseline SLOs we validate with these simulations:
  - hosted-api availability: 99.95% monthly (error budget 0.05%)
  - p95 latency (completion<512 tokens, small model): <= 250ms
  - p99 latency (completion>1024 tokens, large model): <= 2000ms
- We run full simulation campaigns quarterly and after any major change (runtime, kernel updates, quantization changes, major capacity changes).
- Simulation results must be attached to incident reviews when relevant and drive either SLO revision, operational tuning, or rollout rollback.

Ownership and escalation
- Runbook owner: SRE - Capacity & Resilience team (primary contact: nadia.chen@redwood.ai).
- Secondary owners: infra-platform (autoscaler), runtime-performance (kernel), product-ops (customer-facing SLA decisions).
- Escalation path: on-call -> L2 capacity engineer -> Runtime lead -> Head of SRE. Use Slack channel #sre-capacity for live coordination.

SLO lifecycle and change policy
1. Propose change: product or platform teams propose SLO evolution with rationale (tradeoffs, observability evidence). Attach before/after expected user impact matrix.
2. Simulation gating: major SLO relaxations or tightenings require an approved simulation campaign (see 'Simulation templates' below).
3. Rollout plan: staged rollout with canary (5% traffic), A/B (50/50 for 24h), and full (100%) with automated rollback if error budget burn rate > 3x in 1h or latency p99 exceeds threshold for 10 minutes.
4. Post-rollout review: collect metrics and attach to incident review if thresholds tripped.

Error budget policy and automated responses
- Consumption accounting: counts both 5xx responses and latency misses defined per SLO rule. Latency miss example PromQL for p95 miss over 30d window:
  - promql: 'sum_over_time((increase(requests_total{job="hosted-api",status!~"2.."}[30d])))/sum_over_time(increase(requests_total{job="hosted-api"}[30d]))'
- Automated responses by burn rate:
  - Burn rate < 1.0: normal operations.
  - Burn rate 1.0-3.0 sustained for 1h: SRE notified, reduce non-critical deploy velocity, enable extra monitoring retention for affected routes.
  - Burn rate >= 3.0 for 30m: trigger immediate mitigation playbook (see 'Mitigation steps' below) and schedule incident review.

Mitigation steps (fast path)
1. Route traffic to fallback models with documented performance profile (call: routectl promote-fallback --service hosted-api --percent 50).
2. Throttle non-essential APIs (admin/debug endpoints) via ingress rule: `kubectl patch configmap ingress-rules -p '{"data":{"throttle": "true"}}'`
3. Increase dedicated pool shards (if capacity available): `infractl scale pool model-worker --shards +2 --priority emergency`
4. If GPU memory pressure high, enable low-memory quantized variant: `runtimectl set-variant --model-id open-llama-7b --variant q4_0 --apply`
5. Notify customers on SLA-sensitive contracts and open incident bridge.

Simulation templates and tooling
- Tools we standardize on: k6 (functional load), vegeta (microburst), chaos-mesh (network latency/partition), and our in-house replay tool 'traceloader' for synthetic prompt mixes.
- Baseline dataset: use anonymized 30-day request corpus from hosted-prod (redwood-internal S3 path: s3://redwood-simulations/baselines/last-30d) with parameterized token distributions.

Test matrix (example)
| Scenario | Traffic multiplier | Model size | Batch size | Target QPS | Duration | Acceptance 
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Steady ramp | 1.0 -> 3.0 | small (2B) | 8 | 1k -> 3k | 2h | p95 <= 250ms, error rate < 0.1%
| Microburst | 5x spike (10s) | small | 1 | 5k peak | 1h (repeats) | autoscaler < 60s to add nodes, error rate < 0.5%
| Worker crash | steady 2x | large (20B) | 4 | 800 | 30m | fallback routing <= 30% traffic, customer impact <= 1%
| Cache eviction | steady 1.5x + cold cache | mixed | 8 | 1.2k | 90m | cache-miss latency added < 300ms

Operational steps to run a simulation (playbook)
1. Pre-checks (run 24h prior)
  - Ensure on-call rota assigned and incident bridge reserved.
  - Snapshot current infra: `infractl snapshot --env prod --name sim-<date>`
  - Notify customer-ops about scheduled campaign (48h notice for Dedicated customers).
2. Staging run (quick smoke)
  - Replay 1 hour of baseline traffic at 0.5x using traceloader. Confirm dashboards green.
3. Execute ramped tests
  - Launch k6 script: `k6 run --vus 100 --duration 2h scripts/steady-ramp.js --out influxdb=http://monitoring:8086`
  - For microbursts use vegeta: `echo 'GET http://hosted-api/v1/generate' | vegeta attack -rate=5000 -duration=10s | vegeta report`
4. Chaos injections (optional)
  - Network latency: `chaosctl create latency --target routing-proxy --latency 150ms --duration 600s`
  - Pod kill: `kubectl -n runtime delete pod model-worker-abc-123`
5. Triage and mitigation (if thresholds tripped)
  - Follow Mitigation steps and stop tests: `k6 stop <run-id>`
  - Record metrics snapshot `promql: topk(20, avg_over_time(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])[15m:]))`
6. Postmortem and artifacts
  - Upload logs and dashboards to simulation run ticket and link to incident review if applicable.

Prometheus alerts and example queries
- Alert: SLO_Latency_P95_Exceeded
  - expr: 'histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="hosted-api"}[5m])) by (le)) > 0.25'
  - for: 10m
  - severity: page
- Alert: Error_Budget_Burn_Rate_High
  - expr: 'increase(errors_total[1h]) / increase(requests_total[1h]) / (0.0005) > 3' (where 0.0005 is baseline error budget for 99.95%)
  - for: 30m

Linking simulations to incident reviews
- Any simulation that trips a page is captured as an incident in the same format as production incidents. Attach: simulation plan, scripts, recorded k6/vegeta outputs, chaos definitions, and dashboard snapshots.
- Use `incctl create --type simulation --title "Sim: <name> <date>" --artifacts s3://redwood-simulations/runs/<id>` to create the review.

Operational tooling and dashboards
- Dashboards to review during simulation:
  - SLO summary (30d window): availability, latency percentiles, error budget burn rate
  - Autoscaler metrics: desired vs actual replicas, scale decision latency, GPU utilization per shard
  - Cache layer: hit ratio, byte throughput, eviction rate
- Runbooks and scripts are kept in git repo: git@github.com:redwood-infra/sim-playbooks. Tag simulation commits with `sim/<yyyymmdd>-<service>`.

Incidents and post-simulation review standard
- If simulation results indicate fragile behavior (e.g., sustained error budget burn), a post-simulation incident review is required within 3 business days. The review should include:
  - Timeline of events (minute-granular), owners, actions taken
  - Root cause hypotheses and evidence (heap profiles, kernel changes, autoscaler logs)
  - Corrective actions and owners with dates
  - If applicable, SLO revision proposal with customer impact analysis

Frequency and gating
- Quarterly full campaigns for each critical service.
- Ad-hoc campaigns gated by major runtime or workload changes (kernel upgrades, quantization profile changes, new autoscaler strategy).

Appendix A — Example configuration snippets
- Autoscaler policy example (YAML):
  apiVersion: autoscaler.redwood/v1
  kind: PoolAutoscaler
  metadata:
    name: model-worker-default
  spec:
    minReplicas: 4
    maxReplicas: 64
    targetGPUUtilization: 0.65
    scaleUpCooldown: 45s
    scaleDownCooldown: 300s

- k6 steady-ramp snippet (JS):
  import http from 'k6/http';
  import { sleep } from 'k6';
  export let options = { stages: [ { duration: '20m', target: 100 }, { duration: '70m', target: 300 } ] }
  export default function () { http.post('https://hosted-api/v1/generate', JSON.stringify({prompt: 'sim-test'}), { headers: {'Content-Type': 'application/json'} }); sleep(1); }

Appendix B — Acceptance checklist before marking a simulation as successful
- [ ] All alerts cleared or root cause documented
- [ ] No unintended customer-visible errors above acceptance threshold
- [ ] Autoscaler actions observed and within expected latency
- [ ] Artifacts uploaded to simulation ticket
- [ ] Post-simulation notes added to SLO change proposal if applicable

Related pages and references
- Service capacity governance handbook (link in metadata)
- SLO escalation guidance (link in metadata)
- Runtime kernel upgrade ADRs

Document change log
- 2024-11-12: Initial published by Nadia Chen.
- 2025-02-28: Added automated rollback criteria and microburst scenario details (reviewers: Liam Patel, Aisha Rahman).

Contact and feedback
- For questions or to propose a simulation: open a ticket in SRE board and tag @sre-capacity.

title: dsid_aad8390c04a64fc5b8fedb656be101a2__workload-placement-decision-matrix-and-examples-2025.txt
text:
Workload placement decision matrix and examples

Summary

This document provides a pragmatic decision matrix and worked examples to help platform engineers and service owners decide where to place inference workloads across Redwood deployment modes (hosted API, Dedicated pools, Private/VPC). It summarizes the key workload signals, placement rules, and a repeatable evaluation procedure. The goal is to reduce subjective calls, speed provisioning, and make placement decisions auditable.

When to consult this document

- New model onboarding requests (PRD -> runbook)
- Product teams considering SLA/latency guarantees or cost tradeoffs
- Capacity planning and budgeting cycles
- Incident triage when capacity constraints require devolution/fallbacks

Decision matrix (short form)

Use the following primary signals to decide placement. Each bullet is weighted (high/medium/low) for the typical tradeoff decision:

- Latency sensitivity: high = p50 < 50ms endpoint response; medium = 50-200ms; low = >200ms
- Peak concurrency: high = >500 qps sustained; medium = 50-500 qps; low = <50 qps
- Data sensitivity: regulated/PII = high; internal-only = low
- Cost-sensitivity: budget caps or startup cost constraints = high; cost-secondary = low
- Model churn: frequent/new-variants = high; stable pinned model = low

Rule of thumb mapping (summary):

- Hosted API: best for low-to-medium concurrency, low data-sensitivity, fast time-to-value, and experimental models.
- Dedicated (reserved GPU pools): best for high concurrency, predictable throughput, and moderate data-sensitivity where SLA-backed latency is required.
- Private (VPC / on-prem): required for regulated workloads, full data isolation requests, or when network egress controls require it.

Decision matrix (detailed)

| Signal | Hosted | Dedicated | Private (VPC/on-prem) | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Latency SLO p50/p95 | medium | high | high | Dedicated and Private support pinned capacity and colocated networking to meet tail SLOs |
| Sustained QPS | <500 | >=500 | >=500 (but depends on infra) | Dedicated has autoscaling/burst policies for queues |
| Data sensitivity | low | medium | high | Private required for regulated data or explicit KMS/HSM needs |
| Model churn / releases | high (fast) | medium | low (slower ops) | Hosted supports quick rollouts, Private deployments prefer controlled rollouts |
| Cost predictability | low | high | high | Dedicated contracts provide committed cost predictability |
| Operational ownership | Redwood managed | shared | customer-managed | Private shifts day-2 ops to customer or integration team |

How to use the matrix (step-by-step)

1. Collect signals: service owner fills the Workload Intake form (see Appendix). Required fields: expected p50/p95, peak qps, data classification, expected token volume, model size, SHAs of model artifacts.
2. Compute placement score: apply weights (latency 30%, concurrency 30%, data-sensitivity 20%, cost 10%, churn 10%).
3. If score > 0.7 -> recommend Dedicated; 0.4-0.7 -> recommend Hosted (with optional Dedicated for burst); <0.4 -> Hosted. If data-sensitivity = high => override -> Private.
4. Present recommendation in an RFC and include a runbook snippet for rollout and rollback.

Evaluation procedure (detailed checklist)

- Owner: service product/ML engineer; Reviewer: platform oncall
- Required artifacts:
  1. Latency SLOs (p50/p95/p99) and error budget (e.g., 99.9% p95).
 2. Traffic profile: QPS distribution, daily/hourly peaks, 30/90-day projections.
 3. Model profile: model name, architecture, size (FP16/INT8), KV-cache expected reuse ratio.
 4. Cost expectations: per-token cost target or monthly committed spend limit.
  5. Security requirements: data residency, KMS/HSM, audit retention.

- Runbook sanity checks (pre-provision):
  - Verify test harness that reproduces 95th percentile latency locally or on canary capacity.
  - Verify model behaves with recommended quantization profile (if any).
  - Confirm fallback path (smaller model / hosted fallback) is implemented.

Example decision scenarios

Scenario A — Chat completion for internal analytics (low sensitivity, medium concurrency)
- Signals: p50=80ms, p95=220ms, peak=120 qps, model = 13B quantized INT8, data = internal
- Matrix => Hosted recommended with a caching layer and request-level batching.
- Implementation notes:
  - Use hosted with recommended batching: batch_size=64, batch_timeout_ms=12.
  - KV cache TTL = 4 hours for common prefixes.
  - Monitor token-cost per 1k requests and set alert if > baseline + 20%.

Scenario B — Customer-facing real-time assistant (PII, high concurrency)
- Signals: p50=30ms requirement, p95<80ms, peak=800 qps, model=30B FP16, data=PII
- Matrix => Private or Dedicated (if customer consents to shared Dedicated with strict tenancy).
- Implementation notes:
  - Prefer Private when legal requires VPC and customer-managed KMS.
  - If Dedicated: reserve 2x baseline capacity (autoscale headroom) and enable burst credits.
  - Set circuit-breaker thresholds: queue_length > 5000 -> degrade to distilled model and route to fallback endpoint.

Scenario C — Experimentation: new open-source model (high churn, low concurrency)
- Signals: p50=120ms, peak=15 qps, model changes weekly
- Matrix => Hosted (experimental) with rapid canaries.
- Implementation notes:
  - Use hosted ephemeral model variants with traffic split 90/10 canary.
  - Integrate automated evals against golden prompt-set and fail on >5% quality regression.

Operational knobs by placement mode

Hosted API:
- Batching: configure per-route suggested batch_size and timeout. Default: 32/10ms.
- Caching: prefix and KV cache enabled by default with suggested TTLs.
- Rollouts: canary splits via Redwood Console.

Dedicated:
- Pool sizing: reserve GPUs based on sustained qps and model per-GPU throughput (measured in tokens/sec).
- Autoscaling: target CPU/GPU utilization 60–75% to preserve headroom for spikes.
