- Targets: integration regressions, mismatched telemetry, streaming edge-cases, and canonical patches (not product feature requests).

When to use this runloop

1. Customer or QA reports an SDK-related outage, degraded latency, or incorrect API surface behavior.
2. Observability detects repeated error cohorts tied to client SDK versions (>= 3 errors/minute sustained for 5 minutes).
3. Developer working on an SDK change cannot reproduce production behavior locally.

Quick summary of the runloop (3-phase)

1) Triage (15–30m): support identifies severity, captures minimal repro, flags telemetry cohort, and assigns an owner.
2) Repro & Fix (1–72h): SDK engineer reproduces, implements fix or mitigation, publishes a canary patch.
3) Rollout & Verify (1–7d): staged release, telemetry validation, customer communication, and retrospective.

Templates included in this doc

- Minimal Repro Template (for triage)
- SDK Bug Issue Template (for engineering)
- Telemetry Event Schema and Query Examples
- Support Handoff Checklist (one-pager)
- Canonical Fix TL;DR format (for Knowledge Base)

Minimal Repro Template (copy into support ticket)

Purpose: capture the smallest amount of information that lets an SDK engineer reproduce the issue. Fill and paste into a ticket.

1) Short description (1 sentence):
   - e.g. "JS SDK v2.3.1: streaming response drops after 12s when using chunked uploads"
2) Severity: P0|P1|P2
3) Affected SDK(s) and exact version(s):
   - JS: redwood-js-sdk@2.3.1
4) Steps to reproduce (minimal):
   - Step 1: npm install redwood-js-sdk@2.3.1
   - Step 2: node repro.js (attach repro.js below)
5) Observed behavior (logs, status codes, stack traces):
   - Paste 10–20 lines of logs, include correlation ids (request_id) if available
6) Expected behavior: one sentence
7) Sample request payload (redact PII): attach as file or inline JSON
8) Telemetry cohort id or sample query output: attach link to dashboard or saved query
9) Customer contact (if external): email and preferred contact window

SDK Bug Issue Template (engineering backlog)

Title: [SDK][library][severity] Short summary
Assignee: SDK owner
Priority: P0|P1|P2

Description: include Minimal Repro Template output.

Acceptance criteria:
- Repro script demonstrates failure in CI and locally.
- Unit / integration test added that fails pre-fix and passes post-fix.
- Patch includes changelog entry and migration notes if API surface changed.
- Telemetry event published on fix then validated in canary traffic.

Testing matrix (example):
| SDK | Platform | Version | Test target |
|-----|----------|---------|-------------|
| JS  | Node.js 18 | 2.3.1 | repro.js script + unit |
| Python | 3.10 | 1.9.0 | integration harness + mock server |

Telemetry Event Schema (recommended minimal fields)

We require a short, consistent telemetry schema for SDK errors to aid rapid grouping in detection queries. The following JSON illustrates the recommended event payload that SDK clients should emit for captured errors (SDKs should map to host telemetry pipeline).\nExample body (send as JSON to telemetry pipeline):
{
  "event_type": "sdk.error",
  "sdk_name": "redwood-js-sdk",
  "sdk_version": "2.3.1",
  "error_code": "STREAM_ABORTED",
  "error_message": "socket hang up after 12s",
  "request_id": "req_abcdef12345",
  "timestamp": "2027-01-12T21:09:05Z",
  "context": {"sequence_length": 1024, "model": "rw-v3-medium", "route": "/v1/generate"},
  "customer_id": "acct_9876"
}

Notes: the top-level "context" may be a free-form map, but the fields in the example are strongly recommended. Ensure PII is redacted prior to emitting.

Saved queries (examples)

- High error rate: count(sdk.error) by sdk_version where event_time > now() - 5m group by sdk_version having count > 3
- Streaming aborts: filter error_code = 'STREAM_ABORTED' and count > 1 in 10m

Support Handoff Checklist (one page)

1) Verify customer-reported reproduction using Minimal Repro Template. If not reproducible, capture network traces / HAR and escalate to engineering with "needs-more-info" label.
2) If reproducible: create SDK Bug Issue and attach repro and telemetry links.
3) Add temporary mitigation: feature flag, server-side throttle, or client default change. Give mitigation a TTL and document in ticket.
4) Assign SDK owner and set a fix ETA.
5) Notify Customer Success and the original reporter with clear next steps and expected ETA.

Canonical Fix TL;DR format (for KB)

- Title: 1 line summary of root cause and affected versions
- Symptoms: bullet list
- Root cause: 2–3 sentences
- Fix: patch version and brief description of change
- Workarounds: immediate action customers can take if they cannot upgrade
- How we validated: telemetry queries + test matrix results

Example canonical fix (short):
- Title: JS SDK 2.3.x streaming hangs due to missing keep-alive in chunked requests
- Symptoms: streaming payloads drop after ~12s, request_id shows ECONNRESET
- Root cause: Node HTTP agent default socketTimeout closed idle connection before next chunk
- Fix: set agent.keepAlive = true in low-level transport, add integration test for chunked streaming
- Workaround: set SDK option {streamingKeepAlive: true} until upgrade
- Validation: canary traffic (5% of production) for 48h, error rate back to baseline

Operational playbook: step-by-step run (example P0)

1) Alert triggers: high error cohort or on-call support page.
2) Triage owner confirms reproducibility within 15 minutes using Minimal Repro Template.
3) If not reproducible, collect HAR, debug logs, and escalate to "investigate-io" channel.
4) If reproducible, open SDK Bug Issue and start a short-lived bugfix branch with scope-limited change.
5) Publish canary package (npm/pypi) with tag `canary-support-<ticket>` and run automated canary job that mirrors customer traffic for 4 hours.
6) If canary passes, cut patch release, publish changelog, and schedule an orchestrated rollout (see Rollout checklist).

Rollout checklist

- Prepare release notes and KB canonical fix entry.
- Coordinate with Customer Success for targeted customer notifications.
- Release strategy: 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over 48–72 hours with telemetry validation at each step.
- If regression detected at any stage, revert to previous version and announce rollback.

Example code snippets

Node (emit telemetry event):
const telemetry = require('rw-telemetry');
telemetry.emit({
  event_type: 'sdk.error',
  sdk_name: 'redwood-js-sdk',
  sdk_version: '2.3.1',
  error_code: 'STREAM_ABORTED',
  error_message: err.message,
  request_id: ctx.requestId,
  timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
  context: { sequence_length: ctx.seqLen, model: ctx.model },
});

Python (minimal repro runner):
# repro_runner.py
from redwood import SDKClient
client = SDKClient(version='1.9.0')
resp = client.generate(prompt='x' * 1000, stream=True)
for chunk in resp:
    print(chunk.text)

CI: sample test matrix stanza (YAML)
- job: sdk_integration_repro
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  strategy:
    matrix:
      sdk: [js-2.3.1, python-1.9.0]
  steps:
    - name: Run repro script
      run: ./repro/run_${{ matrix.sdk }}.sh

KB and repo locations to update

- SDK repo: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js
- DevX docs: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/docs-site/sdk-docs-home
- Support playbook: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/support-top-issues/support-repro-harness-and-triage-guides-2026

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: SDK owner listed in SDK CODEOWNERS.
- Secondary owner: DevX on-call for SDKs.
- Escalation: if a customer-impacting regression cannot be mitigated within 8 hours, escalate to Director of Developer Experience and include incident bridge.

Postmortem & retrospective guidance

- Required for P0s: full postmortem within 72 hours. Include timeline, root cause, remediation, and follow-ups with owners and due dates.
- Run a retro with Support + SDK Engineers + QA to identify tooling or test gaps; add action items to the sprint backlog.

Appendix: useful queries and saved dashboards

- Saved dashboard: "SDK Error by Version" (default time window: 24h).
- Saved query IDs: err_by_version_2027_01, streaming_aborts_2027_01

Contact & feedback

For feedback on these templates or to request a new template for a specific SDK, open a PR in the DevX docs repo and tag @asha-patel.

Document history

- 2026-11-02: initial draft by Asha Patel
- 2026-12-08: added canary publishing guidance and telemetry schema (reviewed by Mei Chen)
- 2027-01-15: finalized rollout checklist and published

title: dsid_2f716c27ad35463fb207f5f7decad25c__fewshot-priming-economics-and-sample-compression-2026.txt
text:
Few-shot priming economics and sample compression guide

Summary:
This guide documents Redwood's recommended approach to designing few-shot prompts and compressed sample sets for production evals. It balances quality (coherence, instruction-following) against unit-costs (tokens per probe, annotation overhead) and operational constraints (throughput, latency for streaming evals). The guidance is intended for evaluator engineers, model-onboarding owners, and probe stewards.

Goals:
- Reduce per-probe token cost by 20–60% without regressing key quality slices (intent accuracy, safety sentinel pass-rate).
- Provide an auditable compression workflow so that downstream continuous evals and shadow deployments use reproducible priming sets.
- Define metrics and an acceptance gate for compressed few-shot sets.

Background and tradeoffs:
Few-shot priming increases model context and improves alignment accuracy on many instruction tasks, but it also inflates token usage and can amplify quantization sensitivity. Compression here means generating a smaller representative set of examples or a condensed priming representation (templates, canonicalized examples, or sketch encodings) that preserves signal for the target slices.

Key principles:
1) Slice-first fidelity: prioritize preserving performance on high-priority slices (billing-sensitive, safety-critical) when compressing.
2) Incremental compression: perform staged compression with an explicit acceptance gate at each step.
3) Telemetry-driven selection: use real traffic fingerprints and evaluator telemetry to pick candidate exemplars.
4) Quant-compatibility testing: run compacted priming through quantized-shadow evaluation to detect sensitivity early.

Definitions:
- exemplar: a single few-shot example used in the prompt.
- compaction: any operation that reduces token footprint of a priming set (e.g., truncation, templating, summarization).
- fidelity delta: observed change in slice-level metric after compaction (positive or negative).

Recommended workflow (high level):
1. Assemble seed exemplar pool from: production probes, human-curated anchor examples, and synthetic perturbations. Target pool size: 500–5k per slice.
2. Compute exemplar fingerprints: token length distribution, semantic embedding, label anchoring, and contextual importance score.
3. Rank exemplars per slice using a hybrid score: w1 * embedding-diversity + w2 * label-coverage + w3 * recency. Default weights: [0.5, 0.3, 0.2].
4. Apply staged compaction strategies (see table).
5. Run micro-canary evals across: float baseline, INT8/INT4 quant-shadow, cached vs cold contexts.
6. Accept/reject with acceptance gate (see Acceptance gate).

Compaction strategies (choose 1–3, apply incrementally):
| Strategy | Typical reduction | When to use | Risks |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Truncate long examples (keep minimal context) | 20–40% | Long narrative examples with low label density | may omit crucial reasoning steps |
| Template extraction (replace verbose spans with slot templates) | 30–70% | Repetitive instruction scaffolds across examples | over-simplification, instruction ambiguity |
| Example summarization (LLM-based abstractive) | 40–80% | Long multi-paragraph demos | hallucination in summaries |
| Representative exemplar selection (diversity-based sampling) | 50–90% | Large exemplar pool with redundancy | misses rare edge behaviors |
| Sketch encoding (compact structured tokens for reasoning chains) | 60–95% | Controlled tasks with repeatable reasoning patterns | requires runtime deterministic decoder |

Config example (YAML) - compress-config.yaml:
---
slice: "account-inquiry"
seed_pool_path: "s3://eval-probes/seed/account-inquiry-v2.jsonl"
fingerprint: [embedding_model: "embed-v3", tokenizer: "cl100k_base"]
rank_weights: [0.5, 0.3, 0.2]
max_tokens_after_compaction: 2400
stages:
  - name: "template-extract"
    strategy: "template-extraction"
    params: {max_template_slots: 3}
  - name: "select-representatives"
    strategy: "k-center-sampling"
    params: {k: 64, diversity_metric: "cosine"}
  - name: "summarize-examples"
    strategy: "abstractive-summarization"
    params: {max_length: 80, model: "summarizer-2b"}
acceptance_gate:
  target_metric: "intent_accuracy"
  delta_threshold: -0.015  # reject if accuracy drops >1.5%
  additional_checks: ["safety_sentinel_pass", "embedding drift < 0.02"]
---

Acceptance gate (detailed):
- Primary metric: slice-level intent accuracy or task-specific correctness.
- Allowed fidelity delta: default -1.5% relative to full-shot baseline for non-S safety slices. For S (safety/finance/legal) slices the allowed delta is -0.2%.
- Checkpoints:
  1. Local micro-canary: 256 probes, compare float baseline (full shot) vs compressed.
  2. Shadow canary: run 2,000 probes against quant-shadow configuration.
  3. Production probe escrow (optional): limited roll-forward on 0.1% of traffic for 24 hours.
- Rollback triggers: fidelity delta > threshold, safety sentinel failures increase by >0.1%, or latency regression > 25ms p95.

Metrics and telemetry to capture:
- token_savings_pct (per-probe)
- fidelity_delta_by_slice (intent_accuracy, topk_coverage, safety_pass_rate)
- quant_sensitivity_score (change from float to quantized on critical prompts)
- exemplar_coverage (percent of original labels represented)
- sampling_entropy (indicator of selection diversity)

Procedural checklist: compress-and-certify (numbered):
1. Create seed pool and store versioned manifest in S3 with sha256 checksums.
2. Run fingerprinting job (embedding + tokenizer stats) and persist results to probe-catalog.
3. Run automated ranking; inspect top-100 exemplars manually for critical slices.
4. Execute first compaction stage (template extraction).
5. Launch micro-canary: 256 examples, run against float baseline. Record metrics and attach run artifacts.
6. If pass, execute second stage (representative selection) and run shadow canary.
7. If shadow canary passes, attach compressed set to promotion PR and request two reviewers (probe steward + model owner).
8. On approval, schedule a 24h prod-escrow roll-forward (0.1% traffic) with observability hooks.
9. If production signals are green, tag the compressed set as promoted and update eval catalog.
10. Archive the original seed pool and link to compressed set for traceability.

Pseudocode: exemplar ranking (simplified)
```
def score(example):
    emb_div = diversity_score(example.embedding, shard_embeddings)
    label_cov = label_coverage(example.labels)
    recency = recency_score(example.timestamp)
    return 0.5*emb_div + 0.3*label_cov + 0.2*recency

ranked = sorted(pool, key=score, reverse=True)
selected = k_center_sample(ranked, k=K, metric="cosine")
```

Acceptance test matrix (decision table):
| Stage | Dataset size | Baseline | Quant modes | Accept if | Action |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| micro-canary | 256 | float | none | delta >= -0.015 for non-S slices | proceed |
| shadow-canary | 2,000 | float | INT8, INT4 | all quant modes within thresholds | proceed to PR |
| prod-escrow | 0.1% traffic | quantized serving | INT8 | no safety sentinel regressions, p95 latency within 25ms | promote |

Ownership and roles:
- Probe Steward: owns seed pool curation and manual inspection (team: applied-ml).
- Evaluator Engineer: owns ranking pipeline and micro-canary execution (team: eng-evals).
- Model Owner: final approval on promotion PR and rollout gating.
- SRE/Observability: ensures telemetry hooks and alerting during prod-escrow.

Rollout checklist for model onboards that will use compressed few-shot sets:
- Add compressed primer reference in service eval-contracts.yaml.
- Include a quant-sensitivity job in CI that runs on PRs (INT8 + INT4).
- Instrument per-route token_savings_pct and fidelity_delta_by_slice to Redwood Console dashboards.

Troubleshooting and recovery patterns:
- If quant_sensitivity_score spikes after compaction: revert to previous primer and run targeted exemplar augmentation for the adversarial sub-slice.
- If safety sentinel failures increase: immediately pause roll-forward, revert serving primer, and open an incident with applied-ml and safety SMEs.
- If latency p95 increases during prod-escrow: evaluate whether decoder complexity from sketch encodings is the cause; prefer template-extraction fallback.

Auditability and reproducibility:
- All compression runs must produce a manifest: {seed_manifest_sha, compaction_steps, random_seed, compressed_set_sha}.
- Store manifests in eval-catalog S3 and link the compressed_set_sha from the model promotion PR.

Open questions and future work:
- Better automated exemplar-to-template extraction that preserves reasoning chains without hallucination.
- Compact sketch encodings that are runtime-decodable across different serving runtimes.
- Integration of exemplar-level explainability signals to prefer exemplars with clear token-level attribution for decisions.

References and related docs:
- See eval-harness throughput/fidelity playbook for aligning micro-canary sizes.
- See quantization-profiles checklist for mixed-precision rollout guidance.

Appendix: quick CLI snippets
- Fingerprint job (example):
  rci eval-fingerprint --input s3://eval-probes/seed/account-inquiry-v2.jsonl --embed-model embed-v3 --out s3://eval-catalog/fingerprints/account-inquiry-v2.jsonl
- Run micro-canary:
  rci canary-run --set compressed-v1 --size 256 --mode float --out s3://eval-artifacts/canary/account-inquiry/micro-2026-03-10.json

Contact and ownership:
- Document owner: Priya Natarajan (applied-ml)
- Reviewers: Marco Alvarez, Diane Chen
- For operational help: ping #eng-evals on Slack and tag the oncall evaluator engineer.

Change log:
- 2026-02-12: created initial draft.
- 2026-03-10: updated acceptance thresholds and added quant-sensitivity_score metric.

title: dsid_fc7c2c3ce16c4b9695190cdb0aa5fe26__adr-shadow-traffic-routing-architecture.txt
text:
ADR: Shadow Traffic Routing Architecture (Inline Mirroring, Bucketing, Fail-Open)

## Status
Published (approved for Phase 1 MVP). Any material changes to timeouts, bucketing inputs, or request capture fields require a follow-up ADR.

## Summary of decision
We will implement shadow traffic by **inline mirroring** a sampled subset of production requests in the **data plane routing path**, sending a best-effort duplicate request to one or more shadow targets while returning the **control** response to the user.

Key properties:
- **Fail-open**: shadowing must never block or degrade the user path. Shadow execution is best-effort with strict timeouts and circuit breaking.
- **Deterministic bucketing**: a stable request fingerprint drives sampling and variant assignment for consistent comparisons.
- **Minimal capture**: shadow request/response artifacts are redacted and retained briefly; scoring happens asynchronously.

## Context
Redwood’s Rollouts framework supports canaries and A/B testing for latency/cost, but customers and internal teams need a safe way to measure **quality regressions** (format adherence, refusal/safety, instruction following, etc.) for model/version/quantization/prompt changes without impacting user-visible responses.

Shadow traffic duplicates a subset of real production requests to candidate variants and scores outputs asynchronously. This ADR focuses on **where** shadow duplication happens (data plane vs offline replay), **how** requests are sampled/assigned, and **what** fail-open means operationally.

## Problem statement
We need a routing architecture that:
1) Produces comparable control vs shadow outputs using real production prompts/contexts.
2) Keeps user-path latency and reliability unchanged (or within a tightly bounded overhead budget).
3) Works across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments with consistent semantics.
4) Minimizes data retention and reduces exposure of sensitive prompt/response data.
5) Integrates cleanly with existing routing and rollouts primitives (variants, policies, guardrails).

## Considered options
### Option A — Inline mirroring in the data plane (chosen)
**Description:** After request admission and route selection, the router mirrors the request to shadow target(s) asynchronously, while processing the control request normally.

**Pros**
- Highest fidelity: shadow sees the same request payload, same headers/metadata policy, and same timing window.
- Enables deterministic bucketing keyed on request fingerprint at the moment of routing.
- Works for “online-only” traffic (no dependence on log availability).
- Natural integration point with routing policies and rollouts objects.

**Cons / risks**
- Any synchronous work on the user path risks tail latency impact if not carefully bounded.
- Requires robust guardrails (timeouts, backpressure, circuit breakers) to avoid resource contention.
- Streaming requests need special semantics to avoid mirroring an unbounded stream.

### Option B — Async replay from captured traffic/logs
**Description:** Capture production requests into a log/queue and replay them later to candidate variants.

**Pros**
- No data plane mirroring overhead if capture is lightweight.
- Replays can be scheduled/regulated to fit scoring capacity.
- Easier to “pause and resume” experiments without touching the router.

**Cons / risks**
- Lower fidelity for requests with ephemeral context (tool results, auth-derived features, time-sensitive prompts, retried requests with altered metadata).
- Adds pressure to retention/storage; higher compliance complexity (more prompt storage by default).
- Harder to guarantee that replay payload matches what the model actually saw (normalization/versioning drift).
- Delayed feedback; less usable for real-time canary decisions.

### Option C — Hybrid: inline capture + later replay
**Description:** Capture a canonical, normalized request envelope inline, then replay later.

**Pros**
- Can reduce immediate shadow target load.
- Preserves a “canonical input” concept.

**Cons / risks**
- Combines the main risks of A (data plane work) and B (retention/compliance).
- Still requires careful decisions on what to capture; mismatches remain likely.

## Decision
Adopt **Option A: Inline mirroring in the data plane** with the following constraints:
- Mirroring is **asynchronous** relative to the user-path response.
- The router enforces **strict resource isolation** for shadow (separate connection pools/queues; bounded concurrency).
- Shadowing is **fail-open** with circuit breaking and backpressure.
- Sampling and assignment use a **deterministic request fingerprint** and consistent bucketing.
- For streaming requests, mirror only a bounded, well-defined portion (see “Streaming semantics”).

## Architecture overview
### Data plane flow (conceptual)
1) Request arrives at Router.
2) Admission checks (auth, quotas, basic validation).
3) Determine control target using existing routing policy.
4) Compute request fingerprint and evaluate shadow policy:
   - sampling decision
   - shadow target set (one or more variants)
   - metadata/header handling rules
5) Execute control request normally.
6) If sampled, enqueue shadow work item (non-blocking):
   - fire-and-forget dispatch to shadow target(s)
   - record telemetry links between control and shadow
7) Return control response to user.

### Shadow path isolation
- Shadow dispatch uses a dedicated internal “shadow egress” queue and concurrency limiter.
- Shadow requests are executed with:
  - lower priority
  - strict timeouts
  - capped retries (default: none; see below)
- Shadow failures are logged as telemetry but never surface to the user.

## Deterministic bucketing strategy
### Requirements
- Stable assignment for a given “logical request” to reduce variance when comparing control vs shadow.
- Privacy-preserving: avoid storing raw prompt text or high-risk identifiers in telemetry.
- Works across regions and deployment modes.
- Avoids high-cardinality explosion.

### Fingerprint inputs (v1)
We define a **normalized fingerprint input string** composed of:
- `tenant_id` (internal UUID)
- `route_id` (stable route identifier)
- `request_type` (chat.completions | responses | embeddings | rerank)
- `canonical_messages_hash` OR `canonical_input_hash` (see below)
- `tooling_mode` (none | tool_calling_enabled) when applicable

Canonicalization rules:
- Chat/messages: normalize to a stable JSON representation (ordering, whitespace) before hashing.
- Remove/zero fields known to be unstable across retries (timestamps, request_id, tracing ids).
- Truncate inputs before hashing at a configured limit (default 8KB of canonicalized text) to bound CPU.

### Hash function
- Compute `fingerprint = HMAC-SHA256(tenant_fingerprint_key, normalized_input)`.
- Use the first 64 bits as `fingerprint64` for bucketing.

Rationale:
- HMAC prevents cross-tenant correlation and reduces risk if fingerprints leak.
- Per-tenant key rotation is supported (see consequences).

### Sampling and assignment
- Use consistent bucketing over `[0, 9,999]`:
  - `bucket = fingerprint64 mod 10,000`
  - sampled if `bucket < (sampling_rate_bps)` where bps is basis points (0–10,000).
- For multi-shadow-target experiments, assign targets deterministically:
  - `target_index = (fingerprint64 / 10,000) mod N`
  - For “mirror to all” experiments, dispatch to all targets but still use a single sampling gate.

Notes:
- This is not a user-level sticky assignment; it is request-level stability. If customers want session-level stickiness, they should pass a stable user/session key (future enhancement, explicitly not required for v1).

### Collision handling
- Collisions are expected to be extremely rare and acceptable at our sampling rates.
- No special collision detection in v1; metrics are computed in aggregate.

## Fail-open behavior (hard requirements)
Shadow traffic must be invisible to end users and must not affect control-path SLOs.

### What “fail-open” means
- If shadow dispatch fails (queue full, timeout, shadow target errors), the control request proceeds normally.
- The router must never wait on shadow completion to respond to the user.
- Shadowing must not consume unbounded resources (CPU, memory, connections).

### Timeouts
Defaults (v1; may be tuned under SRE guardrails):
- Shadow dispatch enqueue: **<= 1ms** budget on the user path.
- Shadow target request timeout: **2s** absolute (configurable per request type).
- Shadow overall work item TTL: **10m** (after which it is dropped and recorded as expired).

### Retries
- Shadow path retries are **disabled by default** to prevent amplification.
- Exception: idempotent request types may allow **1 retry** behind a feature flag, only when SRE confirms no correlated incident risk.

### Backpressure and circuit breakers
- If shadow queue utilization exceeds threshold (e.g., 80% for 5 minutes) OR scoring/telemetry lag exceeds SLO, automatically:
  - reduce effective sampling (e.g., clamp to 10% of configured rate)
  - then disable shadowing for the route if the condition persists
- If shadow target error rate exceeds threshold (e.g., >5% 5xx over 5 minutes), open circuit for that target.

Operational note: exact thresholds are specified in the SLO/guardrails doc; this ADR establishes the principle and required mechanisms.

## Streaming semantics
Streaming requests require bounded behavior to avoid mirroring indefinite token streams and to control egress cost.

Decision (v1):
- Mirror the **initial request** payload (messages/instructions/tools) and request parameters.
- Shadow requests may be executed in non-streaming mode, capturing only the **final completion** (or up to a configured max tokens) for scoring.
- If the control request is cancelled by the client, shadow continues best-effort up to a cap, then is cancelled.

Rationale:
- Quality metrics generally evaluate final output structure/content; streaming chunk-by-chunk parity is not required for v1.
- Non-streaming shadow reduces complexity and cardinality of partial-chunk telemetry.

## Security and privacy considerations
- Fingerprints are HMAC’d and non-reversible without tenant keys.
- Telemetry must not include raw prompts by default. Shadow artifacts are referenced via redacted storage pointers with strict retention.
- Header/metadata mirroring is policy-controlled (default denylist for sensitive headers).

## Consequences
### Positive
- High-fidelity comparisons: control and shadow are derived from the same live request.
- Fast feedback: supports near-real-time monitoring during canaries.
- Clean integration with routing policies and rollouts (single place to enforce sampling, guardrails, and audit logs).

### Negative / trade-offs
- Router complexity increases (must maintain shadow queue, isolation, and circuit breakers).
- Adds bounded CPU overhead (fingerprinting + enqueue) on the user path.
- Requires careful tuning to avoid egress pressure and connection pool contention.
- Per-tenant HMAC key rotation can shift sampling assignments over time; comparisons across rotation windows must be treated carefully.

### Non-obvious implications
- Deterministic sampling can under-sample rare but critical request classes. This is mitigated via segmentation and manual overrides (future: stratified sampling; not in v1).
- If the request includes tool calling with non-deterministic tool outputs, shadow results may diverge due to tool side effects. For v1, shadowing should disable external side-effecting tools or mirror in “read-only” tool mode where supported.

## Rollout plan (routing component)
1) Internal-only feature flag: `shadow_traffic_enabled` (off by default).
2) Enable for a single internal tenant + single route at <=0.1% sampling.
3) Verify:
   - p99 control latency delta within budget
   - shadow queue health, circuit breakers, and telemetry correctness
4) Expand to limited beta (Dedicated) behind allowlist.

## Open questions (tracked outside ADR)
- Stratified sampling support (by route segment, request type, or customer-provided key).
- Session-level deterministic assignment (customer-provided stable key) vs request-level only.
- Shadowing for multi-modal inputs (images/audio) and canonicalization rules.

## References
- SLOs/Guardrails: shadow traffic SLOs and guardrails
- Data model/cardinality ADR: telemetry schema constraints and required dimensions
- Data retention/redaction policy: prompt/response handling rules
- Control plane policy service: shadow policy schema and validation rules

title: dsid_8d3f696ffd48454ca98929e7771a65af__quantization-rollout-observability-and-billing-hooks-spec-2027-04-21.txt
text:
Quantization rollout, observability & billing hooks — design spec

Overview

This design spec describes how Redwood will orchestrate a controlled rollout of model quantization variants while ensuring: (1) comprehensive observability to detect quality regressions early, (2) billing hooks that correctly surface changed unit economics to customers, and (3) customer-facing communication and migration tooling. The spec focuses on hosted and dedicated deployments; private deployments will be covered by a companion ops-runbook.

Goals

- Safely enable per-tenant or per-route quantized variants (8-bit/4-bit) with automatic fallbacks.
- Produce telemetry sufficient to detect quality drift within 30 minutes of rollout changes for any tenant.
- Expose billing events and cost delta estimates in the console and usage exports so customers can decide when to opt-in/out.
- Provide an automated preflight simulation to estimate latency, memory, and token-cost changes for a tenant before migration.

Non-goals

- This spec does not define new quantization kernels or low-level runtime execution optimizations (runtime team responsibility).
- It does not replace contractual changes for SLA/price adjustments; it provides signaling hooks and recommended contract text for commercial teams.

Background and motivation

Quantization reduces memory and compute cost but can change output distributions (fidelity) and latency characteristics. Customers with tight quality constraints need: (1) rigorous observability to detect regressions; (2) billing transparency when unit costs change; and (3) safe rollback and migration pathways. Existing model-variant rollouts handle code-level switches, but quantization introduces unique telemetry and billing semantics that must be integrated with Redwood Optimize and Console.

Key concepts

- Quantized variant (q-variant): A model binary compiled/quantized to a lower precision (e.g., int8, int4).
- Preflight simulation: Synthetic or replayed workload run that produces latency/memory/cost delta estimates and a shadow-quality score.
- Telemetry gate: A set of signals (metrics + regressions) used to automatically pause or rollback a rollout.
- Billing hook: Event emitted when a tenant's effective per-token cost or capacity credit changes due to quantization.

Design overview

1) Rollout model

- Variants are deployed per-route (API route) with tenant-specific policy override. Default policy is tenant-opt-in.
- Rollouts support staged canary: internal canary (eng-prod), external canary (select customers), gradual percentage-based ramp, and tenant-initiated migration.
- Each rollout includes an associated "quantization profile" meta-record: precision, expected throughput improvement, estimated cost multiplier, and known limitations.

2) Observability and telemetry gating

- Minimum telemetry produced for every q-variant invocation:
  - token_count (input + output)
  - latency_p99, latency_p95, latency_p50 (per route, per tenant)
  - kv_cache_hit_ratio (where applicable)
  - top_k_token_prob_shift (approx metric computed from shadow-eval; see QA below)
  - perplexity_delta (shadow vs baseline)
  - deterministic-safety-check-failures (count)

- Derived signals and thresholds (defaults):
  - quality_regression_alert if shadow-quality-drop > 3% on a route over a 30-minute window.
  - latency_regression_alert if latency_p95 increases by > 50ms and p95 baseline was < 300ms.
  - cost_delta_notice if effective per-token cost changes by > 10%.

- Telemetry collection details:
  - Streaming traces should tag invocations with variant_id, rollout_id, tenant_id, route_id, and inferred-fidelity-tier.
  - Shadow-eval: For external canaries and staged rollouts, a sample of requests (configurable, default 1%) are evaluated against baseline full-precision model to compute fidelity metrics off-path. These shadow-evals are sampled asynchronously and do not affect live latency.

- Automated gating:
  - Each active rollout has a gating policy (json). Gate checks run every 5 minutes and compute statistical significance (Welch t-test) between baseline and q-variant on the past 30 minutes. If any gate condition trips, the rollout is automatically paused and an incident-style notification is created with recommended rollback steps.

3) Billing hooks and semantics

- When a tenant receives traffic served by a q-variant, Redwood must:
  a) Calculate the rendered cost-per-token (C_token) used for billing and UI. Default: C_token(q-variant) = C_token(baseline) * cost_multiplier(profile).
  b) Emit a BillingEvent with the following attributes: tenant_id, rollout_id, variant_id, effective_cost_multiplier, timestamp, estimated_monthly_savings (based on last 7 days consumption).

- Billing integration points:
  - Real-time console: display effective per-route cost delta.
  - Ingestion pipeline: BillingEvents feed usage reconciliation and downstream billing batch (daily).
  - Alerts: If the billing delta is negative (unexpected cost increase) above threshold, create immediate PagerDuty alert.

- Customer-visible notices:
  - Console banner when a tenant is on a q-variant for more than 1 hour: "This route is using a quantized variant that reduces compute cost by ~X% and may change output fidelity. See migration details."
  - Billing exports include both baseline-equivalent tokens and effective tokens for reconciliation.

Config schema (example)

- rollout_policy.json (fields):
  - "rollout_id": string
  - "route_id": string
  - "variant_id": string
  - "target_percentage": integer (0-100)
  - "shadow_sample_rate": float (0-1)
  - "gating_policy_id": string
  - "billing_mode": ["pass-through", "adjusted"]  // pass-through uses baseline pricing; adjusted applies multiplier

YAML example:

  rollout_id: qroll-2027-04-21-42
  route_id: /v1/chat/completions
  variant_id: gptx-q8-2027-03
  target_percentage: 25
  shadow_sample_rate: 0.02
  gating_policy_id: gp-quant-std
  billing_mode: adjusted

Rollout steps (operational playbook)

1. Preparation (preflight)
  1.1. Create quantization profile and register variant_id.
  1.2. Run preflight simulation for the customer or tenant: replay last 24h sample calls or run synthetic prompt set to estimate latency/cost/fidelity deltas.
  1.3. Produce a preflight report: expected p95 latency change, estimated monthly savings, shadow-quality-score. Deliver to customer console.

2. Internal canary (multi-team)
  2.1. Deploy to internal canary pool (eng-prod).
  2.2. Observe telemetry for 48h.
  2.3. Approve or abort based on gating policy.

3. External canary (selected customers)
  3.1. Notify customers via console and email (template provided).
  3.2. Ramp target_percentage to 10% for 24-72h.
  3.3. Gate checks run every 5 minutes.

4. Gradual ramp
  4.1. Increase target_percentage in steps (10, 25, 50, 100) with minimum 2h at each step.
  4.2. If gating policy trips at any step, automatically pause and notify SRE/owner.

Observability & dashboards

- New dashboard tiles (Console + internal Grafana):
  - Per-route per-tenant fidelity heatmap (shadow-quality-score over time).
  - Cost delta timeline (estimated vs realized).
  - Rollout health timeline with gating decision markers.
  - Latency distribution overlay baseline vs q-variant.

- Alerts and PagerDuty:
  - quality_regression_alert => P2 (pager duty after 15m sustained).
  - latency_regression_alert => P3.
  - billing_delta_negative_alert => P1 (immediate).

SLOs and thresholds (suggested defaults)

- Shadow-quality-drop tolerance: <= 2% for internal canary, <= 3% for external canary, <= 5% for production ramp.
- Latency p95 increase tolerance: <= +20% or +50ms (whichever is smaller) during canary.
- Detection window: 30 minutes for automated gating; 7 days for billing reconciliation checks.

Testing, QA and metrics validation

- Unit tests: gating policy evaluation logic, billing event emission, edge-case missing telemetry.
- Integration: End-to-end test that simulates a 10k-req/hour tenant with shadow-evals enabled and asserts that: billing events are emitted, preflight report is produced, and that gate trips when intentional regression injected.
- Chaos testing: Inject synthetic noise in shadow-eval metrics to validate false-positive rate.

Customer communication and migration UX

- Preflight report displayed in Console with a single-click "Schedule migration" that triggers tenant-initiated ramp.
- Email + Console templates for external canary invitations.
- Billing FAQ text included in migration flow; template for Account Execs for larger customers.

Data retention and privacy considerations

- Shadow-eval artifacts that include customer prompt/response pairs must be subject to PII scrubbing and retained per Data Retention policies (default 30 days for preflight artifacts; longer only with explicit consent).

Ownership and rollout governance

- Feature owner: runtime-variant-team (primary).
- Observability/gating service owner: eng-platform (secondary).
- Billing pipeline integration: finance-legal (contract), billing-engine (implementation).
- Product comms: product-marketing (external).

Open questions and risks

- Calibration of shadow-quality-score: which metric best correlates to customer satisfaction across varied prompt sets? (Action: run multi-tenant correlation study Q2 2027).
- Should we offer an automated opt-out window that refunds a proportional credit if quality regressions are detected post-migration? (Commercial decision).

Appendices

A. Example gating policy (gp-quant-std)
  - window_minutes: 30
  - sample_minimum: 500 requests
  - metrics: ["shadow-quality-drop", "latency_p95_delta"]
  - thresholds: {"shadow-quality-drop": 0.03, "latency_p95_delta": 0.05}

B. Preflight report sample fields
  - baseline_p95_latency_ms
  - qvariant_p95_latency_ms
  - estimated_monthly_savings_usd
  - shadow_quality_score
  - confidence_interval

Contact and next steps

- Proposed timeline: prototype (Q2 2027), internal canary (Q3 2027), external canary (Q4 2027).
- Action items: design review (this doc), implementation RFC from runtime team, billing-engine API contract, Console UX mockups.

For discussion at the next cross-functional rollout sync.

title: dsid_6e67e8cf2f0a411b826b14c382c783f1__declarative-gpu-feature-flagging-and-iac-guardrails.txt
text:
Declarative GPU feature flagging and IaC guardrails

A prescriptive pattern for managing GPU-related feature flags (scheduling toggles, kernel rollout, quantization profiles) as first-class Terraform artifacts with policy checks, CI gates, and runtime wiring. This doc defines modules, policies, rollout steps, and monitoring contracts to safely enable/disable inference features across hosted, dedicated, and private environments.
Purpose: reduce blast radius and operational toil when changing GPU runtime behavior by: (1) codifying flags in Terraform, (2) enforcing policy-as-code at merge time, (3) providing a repeatable canary + automated rollback flow, and (4) instrumenting observability for safety and cost impact.
GPU runtime changes (e.g., new kernels, mixed-precision switches, KV cache prefetch tweaks) frequently affect latency, cost, and correctness. Ad hoc toggles in code or ad hoc scripts lead to drift, lack of audit, and slow incident response. Treating flags as IaC gives us versioning, reviewability, and a single source of truth that the deployment control plane and SREs can rely on.
- Make GPU-related feature flags discoverable and auditable
- Prevent unsafe flag combinations via pre-merge policy checks
- Provide a low-friction canary rollout path with automated monitoring
- Ensure rollbacks are fast, measured, and reversible
- Keep runtime flag evaluation light-weight and decoupled from control plane

- This doc does not replace application-level feature flags (end-user UI toggles)
- Not a detailed kernel implementation guide — focus is operational control, not kernel dev

Applies to flags that change inference serving behavior or allocation semantics: kernel selection, mixed-precision enablement, prefix/KV caching modes, tenant preemption preferences, and autoscaling aggressiveness. Excludes per-request prompt-level flags and user-visible product feature flags.
High level: 1) Flags are defined in a central Terraform module (gpu_flag). 2) Each environment (prod/dedicated/staging/private) consumes the module and sets values in environment-specific tfvars tracked in Git. 3) A GitHub Actions pipeline runs policy-as-code (OPA checks) + integration canaries (lightweight smoke tests) on PRs. 4) Runtime path: serving control plane reads the consolidated flag state from an immutable configuration store (S3/GCS) generated by terraform apply and served by a read-optimized metadata service. 5) Telemetry tags on inference traces annotate which flags were active.
Recommended Terraform module layout and usage (example):

Module: modules/gpu_flag/main.tf

```hcl
variable "name" { type = string }
variable "enabled" { type = bool }
variable "rollout_percent" { type = number, default = 100 }
variable "owner" { type = string }
resource "redwood_infra_flag" "this" {
  name = var.name
  enabled = var.enabled
  rollout_percent = var.rollout_percent
  metadata = { owner = var.owner }
}
output "flag_id" { value = redwood_infra_flag.this.id }
```

Example usage in env overlay (env/prod/main.tf):

```hcl
module "kv_cache_prefetch_v2" {
  source = "../../modules/gpu_flag"
  name = "kv_cache_prefetch_v2"
  enabled = true
  rollout_percent = 10
  owner = "serving-runtime-team"
}
```

Notes: - All flag names are lower_snake_case and must include a component prefix (e.g., serving_kernel_*, cache_*). - Use rollout_percent to perform percentage canaries at the traffic router layer (see rollout procedure).
Pre-merge checks (run in CI):
- OPA/rego rules ensure: no conflicting flags enabled simultaneously (e.g., kernel_x_v2 + kernel_x_safe_mode), rollout_percent in [0,100], owner is non-empty, and any flag that reduces isolation requires an approved exception.
- tfsec/static analysis verifies there are no secrets in tfvars.
- Integration smoke: a lightweight canary job runs the serving smoke harness against a staging namespace with the new flags applied.

Example Rego rule (human readable):
- Deny if rollout_percent > 0 and enabled == false (misconfigured semantics).
- Deny if name contains "private_" and target environment != private.
1) Create feature-flag TF change in a branch targeting the appropriate env overlay (e.g., env/prod). 2) Open PR with 'flag: <name>' label. 3) CI runs OPA checks + staging smoke tests. 4) Once CI passes, merge to main. 5) Terraform apply runs in GitOps runner and writes a new flags manifest to stable bucket (s3://redwood-config/flags/<env>/<timestamp>.json). 6) Router reads manifest and begins rollout by evaluating 'rollout_percent' (deterministic hashing on tenant id) and activating the flag for the first X% of tenants. 7) Observe for 1h: latency P95, error rate, cost per request, and qualitative QA checks. 8) If metrics breach thresholds (see guardrail thresholds), automatically trigger rollback-conductor to revert the tf change or set rollout_percent back to previous value.

Guardrail thresholds (example):
- latency_p95 increase > 18% over baseline -> alert
- request_error_rate increase > 1.0 percentage point -> alert
- cost_per_token increase > 12% -> alert

Automated rollback policy: the monitoring job can open a hotfix PR that sets the flag back to the previous stable tag and auto-merge under an emergency policy if SRE approves.
- GitHub Actions pipeline jobs: validate, opa_check, smoke_canary, plan, apply (apply runs only in main branch via runner with least-privilege service account).
- Example job fragment:

```yaml
jobs:
  opa_check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: opa test ./policy -v
  smoke_canary:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: ./ci/smoke_canary.sh --env=staging --flag-manifest=./out/flags.json
```

- Secrets and cloud creds: restrict terraform apply runner to dedicated CI machine with ephemeral creds and narrow IAM role: flags:Write to config-bucket, read-only on infra-state, no admin on compute resources.
- The serving control plane uses a read-only manifest derived from Terraform outputs. Manifests are versioned and immutable (content-addressed).
- Runtime evaluation code is simple: lookup flag_name -> {enabled, rollout_percent, metadata}. Hash tenant_id % 100 < rollout_percent -> enabled for tenant.
- Flag evaluation must be non-blocking and default to safe state (disabled) if manifest is unreachable.
- Telemetry: attach flag_version and active_flag_list as tags to traces and span logs to enable post-hoc rollback/traffic-slicing analysis.
Required metrics and dashboards:
- Flag rollout dashboard: flag name, version, rollout_percent, active_tenants_count, applied_regions
- Safety signals: latency_p50/p95/p99 by flag_version, error_rate by flag_version, cost_per_token by flag_version
- Canary healthcheck SLO: smoke_canary must succeed at > 99% per 5m window during rollout

Alerting playbook:
- SEV1 if latency_p95 increase > 30% and > 5% tenants affected -> paging SRE and Serving Runtime owner
- SEV2 for cost regressions > 25% -> notify FinOps and runtime owner
- All alerts should include: flag name, manifest version, tf commit hash, link to PR and runbook.
Flag ownership matrix:
- Definition/Module ownership: eng-infra/Terraform team (primary)
- Runtime wiring and router gating: serving-runtime team (primary)
- CI & policy automation: eng-ci team (primary)
- Emergency rollback conductor: on-call SRE for serving-runtime (primary)

Contacts: aisha.patel@redwood.ai (module lead), ethanc@redwood.ai (OPA & CI), marta.r@redwood.ai (runtime), oncall-serving-runtime@pagerduty.com
For existing ad-hoc flags: 1) Inventory -- run a 2-week discovery job scanning repos and runtime manifests. 2) Create mapping PRs that produce equivalent Terraform gpu_flag resources with rollout_percent set to 0. 3) Run smoke tests and increment rollout_percent in small steps. 4) Deprecate inline toggles and add a blocking pre-merge OPA rule that denies direct changes to runtime flag endpoints without corresponding tf change.

Backfill schedule example: Week 1: inventory and mapping, Week 2: create tf modules and PRs (rollout_percent=0), Week 3-6: staged rollouts and deprecation of old toggles.
Quick rollback steps: 1) If a severe regression is detected, run: `terraform -chdir=env/prod plan -var 'kv_cache_prefetch_v2.rollout_percent=0' && terraform -chdir=env/prod apply -auto-approve` (GitOps runner will prefer hotfix PR flow). 2) If apply is blocked, run the emergency API: `curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/flags/<flag>/override -d '{"enabled":false}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'` (requires on-call SRE token). 3) After rollback, create a postmortem and tag the PR with 'incident:flag-rollout'.
- All flag changes must be auditable via Git history and bucket manifest versions. - Sensitive flags (those that affect tenant isolation or data residency) must be marked with metadata.sensitivity = "high" and require an approved security exception before enabled in non-private envs. - Terraform state for flag modules is stored in the same backend as infra state but with a separate key prefix and read ACL restricted to infra service accounts only.
Conflict detection Rego pseudo-rule: `deny[msg] { input.flag1.enabled == true; input.flag2.enabled == true; msg = sprintf("%v conflicts with %v", [input.flag1.name, input.flag2.name]) }`

Sample flags table (informal):
| flag_name | component | default | owner | sensitivity |
| serving_kernel_x_v2 | serving-runtime | false | serving-runtime | medium |
| kv_cache_prefetch_v2 | cache | false | storage-team | low |
| mixed_precision_global | runtime | true | serving-runtime | low |

- RFC: Flag-as-IaC proposal (internal RFC link)
- Serving Runtime rollout API docs: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-flag-eval.json
- CI templates: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/flag-ci-templates.json
- Pilot with two low-risk flags (kv_cache_prefetch_v2, serving_kernel_x_v2) in staging within 2 sprints.
- Add OPA policies to the central CI pipeline and enforce on all infra repos.
- Schedule a runbook game-day with SRE and serving-runtime to exercise automated rollback.
This pattern intentionally prioritizes auditability and small-step rollouts over speed. For emergency patches we keep an approved escape hatch documented in the runbook_snippets. Please send implementation questions to the owners listed above.

title: dsid_10fb906e0456491b8d35cd516a5448c7__blackbox-api-mirroring-workflow-and-debug-playbook-2025.txt
text:
blackbox-api-mirroring-workflow-and-debug-playbook

Summary

This playbook describes a safe, repeatable workflow for creating blackbox mirrors of production API traffic, sanitizing the captured payloads, and replaying requests against local SDKs, staging stacks, or canary model variants. The goal is to reproduce real-world failure patterns, measure regression risk for SDK/serving changes, and accelerate bug triage without exposing customer PII or impacting production.

When to use

- Reproducing a hard-to-trigger error that only appears under production traffic mixes (multi-route, multi-tenant, variable prompt sizes).
- Verifying that an SDK or runtime change preserves downstream observability (trace IDs, latency distributions, token counts).
- Running end-to-end golden checks against a candidate model or quantization profile.

Prerequisites

1. Ownership and approvals: security and product sign-off for capturing traffic (see Security & Compliance for approvals).
2. A dedicated capture window or sampling rate that keeps production impact negligible. Typical default: 1% request sampling for high-volume tenants; full-capture only with explicit approval.
3. Access to the capture bucket (S3-compatible) and a staging cluster or local harness with the same API surface.

High-level approach

1. Capture: sample and persist a representative request set.
2. Sanitize: remove or obfuscate PII and customer identifiers.
3. Enrich: add metadata needed for deterministic replay (headers, seed RNG hints, model pinning).
4. Replay: run the harness against the target (local SDK, staging endpoint, or canary model).
5. Observe: compare telemetry (latency histograms, error rates, token counts, outputs).

Traffic capture & sanitization

Capture locations and mechanisms (choose one):

- Edge proxy (Envoy / NGiNX filter): captures request/response envelopes and headers. Pros: earliest point-of-ingress, consistent headers.
- Platform gateway (API router): captures enriched metadata (customer_id, route, feature flags).
- SDK-side logging (developer box): for telemetry cases where full body capture is not allowed.

Capturing example (Envoy Lua filter snippet):

# lua snippet (Envoy) - capture headers and body to stdout for an external collector\local function capture(request)
  local h = request:headers()
  local body = request:body():getBytes(0, request:body():length())
  -- emit to a logging pipeline, not stdout in prod\end

Sanitization rules (enforce with automated pipeline):

- Remove fields: user_email, full_name, ssn, credit_card, device_id when present.
- Hash or salt identifiers: customer_id -> sha256(customer_id + capture_salt). Store salt in KMS.
- Prompt shortening: truncate prompts > 10k chars to first/last 1k with a hash placeholder for the middle.
- Skip binary attachments entirely (log metadata only).

Example sanitization command (jq + openssl):

cat raw_capture.jsonl | jq '.request.body |= (.prompt |= (if length > 10000 then (.[0:1000] + "\n...<TRUNCATED>...\n" + .[-1000:]) else . end) | del(.user_email, .ssn))' \
  | openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -salt -pass pass:$SANITIZE_KEY > sanitized.jsonl.enc

Metadata enrichment

Before replay, add fields that help determinism and observability:

- replay_id: uuid4
- original_timestamp_utc
- route_hint (e.g., text-generation v.s. embeddings)
- model_pin (if the capture included a model alias)
- intended_sampling_mode (sync|stream|function_call)

Replay harness patterns

Supported harness targets: local SDK (Python/TS), staging HTTP endpoint, canary-serving runtime.

Core replay modes:

1. Synchronous request-by-request: replay each captured request and persist the result. Useful for correctness and output diffs.
2. Concurrency-preserving replay: preserve timestamps and inter-request arrival spacing to exercise batching and runtime scheduling. Use for performance regressions.
3. Batched trace replay: replay only requests that hit specific code paths (e.g., long-prompt cache misses).

Python replay harness (simplified):

# replay_harness.py (pseudocode)
import json, requests, time, uuid
with open('sanitized.jsonl') as f:
    for line in f:
        rec = json.loads(line)
        rec['replay_id'] = str(uuid.uuid4())
        headers = { 'X-Replay-ID': rec['replay_id'], 'X-Original-Ts': rec['original_timestamp_utc'] }
        resp = requests.post(STAGING_URL + rec['route'], json=rec['request'], headers=headers, timeout=30)
        save_result(rec['replay_id'], resp.status_code, resp.text)
        time.sleep(adjust_interarrival(rec))

SDK integration patterns

- Hook points: provide an X-Replay-ID header and ensure SDKs propagate this to tracing and metrics.
- Deterministic seeds: when the SDK exposes sampling or soft-rng features, allow setting a replay seed from replay_id to reduce nondeterminism in comparisons.
- Output normalization: SDKs should offer a normalize_output() helper to remove metadata such as timestamps, non-deterministic ids, and token boundary differences prior to diffing.

Observability and diffs

Compare the following telemetry between original-capture-derived expectations and replay outputs:

- Latency P50/P95/P99 (ms)
- Token usage distribution (input_tokens, output_tokens)
- Error taxonomy (HTTP 4xx, 5xx, SDK exceptions, model-timeouts)
- Output similarity score (BLEU/ROUGE/embedding-cosine) where applicable

Example diff command (jq + python):

python tools/diff_outputs.py --expected expected_results.jsonl --actual replay_results.jsonl --metrics latency,token_counts,similarity --out diffs/summary.json

Safety, rollout and data governance

- Captured datasets are to be stored in a restricted bucket with lifecycle 90 days then auto-delete unless flagged for retention.
- All datasets must be tracked in the internal capture registry (include name, sample rate, captain, purpose, retention).
- For customer-sensitive captures require explicit legal approval; label those captures in the registry and limit replay to isolated air-gapped environments.

Operational checklist (before you start)

1. Confirm approvals and sampling rate recorded in capture registry.
2. Verify KMS key for salt hashing is accessible and audited.
3. Reserve replay environment with sufficient tokens/quota and model pins.
4. Run a small sanity replay (10 requests) to validate harness and normalize functions.

Post-replay triage workflow

1. Open an investigation ticket with replay_id, sample inputs, and failing response slices.
2. Attach diffs and telemetry reports.
3. If regressions are observed, run targeted replays focusing on affected route/model pins.
4. For SDK regressions: bisect across SDK versions with the same corpus.

Appendix: example capture record (sanitized, single-line JSONL)

{"replay_id": "<filled-at-enrich>", "original_timestamp_utc": "2025-03-05T14:22:11Z", "route": "/v1/generate", "request": {"prompt": "The quick brown fox...<TRUNCATED>", "max_tokens": 256}, "customer_hash": "sha256:abcd..." }

Appendix: portability matrix (recommended replay target by investigation goal)

| Goal | Target | Notes |
|------|--------|-------|
| Output correctness | Local SDK (pinned) | Fast iteration, low cost |
| Performance regression | Staging runtime with same hardware profile | Preserve batching and kernels |
| Production-only scheduling bugs | Canary-serving pool | Must be isolated and monitored |

Ownership and contacts

- Playbook author: Evan Morales (engineering)
- Runbook owner: Observability team (platform.eng@redwood.example.com)
- Security contact: Rina Kapoor (security@redwood.example.com)

Change log

- 2025-03-12: Created initial draft.
- 2025-06-18: Added deterministic seed guidance and replay_id standardization.
- 2025-09-01: Hardened sanitization rules and added lifecycle/retention guidance.

Links and references

- See Security & Compliance: capture-approval-process for approval workflow.
- See eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/replay-harnesses for sample harnesses and perf tooling.
- Tools: tools/diff_outputs.py, tools/normalize_output.py (internal repo)

title: dsid_419fc9cd8d514d8a943e409339b30631__contract-gateway-and-edge-validation-adr-2026.txt
text:
contract-gateway-and-edge-validation-adr-2026

Summary
-------
This ADR records the decision to introduce a Contract Gateway at the edge (the Contract Gateway) that performs: (1) lightweight schema validation and capability negotiation for incoming requests, (2) fast-path routing for compatible requests, and (3) structured downgrade and audit mechanisms for incompatible or degraded requests. The gateway is a small, highly-available service deployed in the edge/ingress plane that standardizes request/response envelopes and enforces deployable validation policy.

Context and motivation
----------------------
- We operate multiple model variants (quantized/FP16/multi-precision) and deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private). Clients currently need to anticipate variant differences leading to brittle client logic.
- Several incidents have been traced to mismatched request envelopes and late-stage validation failures that amplify cost and latency.
- We want an operationally simple mechanism to route compatible requests through a low-latency fast-path to runtime variants while rejecting or transforming incompatible requests at the edge with actionable telemetry.

Goals
-----
1. Provide a single entrypoint that validates canonical request envelopes and capability hints before requests hit serving runtime.
2. Enable deterministic fast-path routing for requests with verified compatibility (sub-10ms extra edge processing).
3. Emit precise validation telemetry and structured error reasons for downstream tracing/evals.
4. Support progressive rollout: feature-flagged validation policies and a clear rollback plan.

Non-goals
---------
- Full payload schema transformation (heavy payload rewriting belongs to gateway adapters downstream).
- Replacing the model-serving contract or long-term client adaptation; this gateway is a compatibility enforcement and observability layer.

Decision
--------
We will implement a Contract Gateway service with the following characteristics:
- Lightweight JSON schema checks and key capability negotiation (e.g., streaming, function-calls, structured-output) performed synchronously before routing.
- A stable metadata envelope that contains: client-capabilities, request-class, route-hints, request-id, and optional client-schema-hash.
- Fast-path allowlist: verified request signatures/hashes or capability proofs that bypass in-depth validation.
- Degradation policy: if validation fails, gateway returns clearly typed errors (4xx with structured reason) or routes to a transform/backfill path depending on policy.
- Telemetry: every decision emits an event to Kafka/telemetry pipeline with fields mapped to existing telemetry schema.

Design details
--------------
Request envelope (example):
{
  "envelope_version": "1.0",
  "request_id": "req_abc123",
  "client_capabilities": ["streaming", "function_call_v2"],
  "request_class": "interactive",
  "schema_hash": "sha256:...",
  "payload": { /* model-specific body */ }
}

Validation rules (summary table):
| Rule ID | Target field | Check | Failure action | Owner |
|---------|--------------|-------|----------------|-------|
| VG-001  | envelope_version | must be 1.0 or 1.x | reject (400) | api-platform |
| VG-002  | schema_hash | optional but if present must match canonical schema store | route-to-transform or reject | model-onboarding |
| VG-003  | client_capabilities | subset of known capabilities | downgrade to non-streaming fast-path | eng-serving-runtime |
| VG-004  | request_class | must be one of {background, batch, interactive} | reject (400) | api-platform |

Capability negotiation
- Clients include declared capabilities; the gateway validates them against the capability catalog. If a declared capability is unknown but non-critical, gateway removes it and records a capability-mismatch metric. Critical unknown capability -> reject.
- For streaming requests, the gateway verifies transport and allowed size/time budgets before handing off to the runtime.

Fast-path routing
- A fast-path requires: envelope_version match, schema_hash match to canonical store, and client_capabilities subset verified.
- Fast-path routing target: cluster label fastpath=true on runtime side. Fallback to default route when any check fails.
- Metric: fastpath_accept_rate (target >= 80% for stable workloads) and fastpath_added_latency (target < 10ms p50).

Observability and SLOs
---------------------
- SLOs (Contract Gateway):
  - Availability: 99.99% (global edge for control plane calls excluded).
  - Validation throughput: handle peak p95 request rates with <5% additional tail latency.
  - Fast-path latency budget: additional p50 < 10ms, p95 < 35ms.
- Telemetry emitted per request: request_id, envelope_version, validation_result, failure_reason (if any), routed_variant, schema_hash, client_capabilities, latency_ms.
- Traces: start trace in gateway and propagate trace context to runtime; add an event for validation decision.
- Error budgeting: validation-rejects per client are counted against client-specific onboarding metrics and trigger alerts when >1% of requests rejected for 5m.

Runtime integrations and infra implications
----------------------------------------
- The gateway is stateless and horizontally scalable. It lives in the edge layer (kube cluster(s) colocated with ingress).
- It needs read-only access to: canonical schema registry (with caching), capability catalog, and route metadata. These are read-through caches with TTLs.
- For Private deployments, the gateway will be packaged as a lightweight sidecar option or an edge-service template with configuration flags (to respect customer network controls).

Security and privacy
--------------------
- Gateway must not persist payloads beyond ephemeral processing except for structured audit events. Payloads that contain PII are redacted before any audit emission (use default redaction rules consistent with data-management policy).
- All config endpoints and the schema registry access must be TLS mutual-auth.

Rollout plan
------------
1. Prototype (2 weeks): implement a mock gateway that validates envelope_version and request_class; capture metrics.
2. Pilot (4 weeks): enable in non-production region; instrument telemetry and run canary traffic for a subset of clients (feature-flagged).
3. Gradual rollout (8 weeks): incrementally enable validation rules; monitor fastpath_accept_rate, validation_reject_rate, and latency budgets.
4. Enforcement (after 12 weeks): begin rejecting with 4xx for high-confidence rules; communicate deprecation windows to SDK teams.

Rollback and mitigation
- Feature flags for each validation rule.
- If gateway causes >0.5% increase in p95 latency across a region for 15m -> disable new validation rules immediately and rollback to previous gateway image.
- Emergency bypass: an authenticated tenant-level header (signed by infra) can route requests directly to runtime; usage of this bypass must be tracked and limited.

Ownership and next steps
------------------------
- Owner: api-platform (primary), eng-serving-runtime (integration), eng-infra (deployment & infra), security (privacy review).
- First implementation ticket: AP-1234 (Contract Gateway basic validation and telemetry).
- Documentation: add a new page under eng-developer-experience/api-examples that includes SDK examples for building compatible envelopes.

Open questions
--------------
- Canonical schema store consistency model for private deployments (pull vs. push sync).
- How to handle encrypted payloads where schema_hash cannot be computed at the gateway. Proposed temporary solution: route to runtime with a flag and rely on runtime-side validation.

References
----------
- Related ADRs and playbooks: canonical-request-schema-and-validation-playbook-2025, adr-protocol-adaptor-and-validation-contract-2026.
- Telemetry schema: architecture-and-standards/observability-standards/typed-telemetry-annotations-and-backfill-standard-2026.

Appendix: example HTTP interaction
----------------------------------
Request:
POST /v1/generate HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redwood.ai
Content-Type: application/json
X-Client-Id: sdk-js-2.3.0

{ "envelope_version":"1.0", "request_id":"req-123", "client_capabilities":["streaming"], "request_class":"interactive", "payload": {"prompt":"Hello"} }

Possible gateway responses:
- 200 -> routed to runtime (fast-path header: X-Routed-FastPath: true)
- 400 -> { "error": "validation_error", "reason": "unknown_capability:function_call_v3" }
- 202 -> accepted for async transform/backfill (policy dependent)

This ADR is effective immediately for new ingress deployments created after the date above.

title: dsid_e47ab3022c9c488d9e4e770f2cf41874__gatekeeper-deployment-safety-config-fencing-playbook-2025.txt
text:
Gatekeeper: Deployment Safety, Config Fencing, and Runtime Contract Playbook

Overview

Purpose:
This playbook defines a layered ‘Gatekeeper’ approach to make deployments and config changes across Redwood Inference predictable and safe. It combines pre-deploy validation, runtime contract enforcement, and automated rollback/mitigation rules so that services (especially model-serving and inference pipelines) can evolve without causing widespread customer impact.

Audience:
Engineering teams that own API surface, runtime components, fleet configuration, and release tooling; SRE/PD teams who run canaries, and product owners who need clear rollback SLAs.

Scope:
- Applies to all API-facing services and inference runtime components: hosted API, Dedicated schedulers, and Private runtime sidecars.
- Does NOT replace per-service release notes or change approval; it standardizes checks and rollback triggers.

Key principles:
- Fail-fast before traffic: stop bad config artifacts at the gate.
- Least-surprise runtime: enforce backward-compatible contracts and optional capability negotiation.
- Observable safety: every gate emits telemetry and a single canonical incident signal.
- Automated but auditable: automated remediation triggers must be reversible and logged.

Terminology:
- Gatekeeper (the pattern): a collection of validations and runtime enforcements applied during deploy and live traffic.
- Fence: a rule that prevents a config, schema or artifact from progressing to the next stage.
- Contract: API/schema/behavioral expectations declared by the service.

Safety layers (summary):
1) Preflight/Lint Gate (CI)
   - Config schema validation (YAML/JSON schema).
   - Static contract tests (OpenAPI/protobuf compatibility).
   - Resource and quota checks against current capacity (see Capacity rubric).
2) Canary Gate (staged rollout)
   - Canary ratio: default 1% traffic for 30 minutes with synthetic tests.
   - Automated health checks and model-quality smoke tests (if inference change).
3) Runtime Fence (adaptive enforcement)
   - Capability negotiation: failing clients are served with a stable fallback.
   - Circuit conditions: enforce early-exit and backpressure thresholds.
4) Automated Rollback/Degrade Gate
   - Triggers for rollback/degrade include SLO breach, error spike, quality regression, or contract violations.

Concrete checks and thresholds (table):
| Gate | Check | Default Threshold | Owner | Action on failure |
|------|-------|-------------------:|-------|------------------|
| Preflight | Schema validation | 0 errors | Authoring service | Block merge |
| Preflight | Compatibility tests | 0 incompatible ops | API platform | Block deploy |
| Canary | 5xx rate | > 0.5% absolute increase | SRE | Pause rollout, investigat e |
| Canary | P95 latency | > 2x baseline | SRE/Service | Abort canary, rollback |
| Runtime | Model-quality delta (eval) | absolute drop > 3 points | Applied-ML | Revert to previous model |
| Runtime | Error budget burn | > 60%/30m | SRE/Owner | Traffic cutback + rollback |

NOTE: Teams may tighten thresholds for high-risk services (see service risk matrix).

Preflight checklist (detailed):
- Lint and schema: run ./tools/config-lint --schema=infra-config-v2.yaml
- Contract tests: make contract-test; includes OpenAPI diff and Protobuf compatibility check.
- Security gating: secrets not embedded; KMS key reference validated.
- Cost guard: estimated GPU-hours and memory footprint reported; alert if exceeds reserved budget.
- Smoke harness: run synthetic request set (prompt-suite-ci) against new artifact in test cluster.

Example CLI snippet (preflight):
$ ./ci/preflight-run --service inference-api --artifact sha:abcd1234 
# returns JSON summary with fields: passed_checks, failed_checks, estimated_gpu_hours

Canary rollout recipe (recommended default):
1. Deploy artifact to canary fleet (tag: canary-<build>) in region-local cluster.
2. Route 1% of production traffic using traffic-router v2 with header-based stickiness.
3. Run automated synthetic prompts every 30s (10 concurrent).
4. Monitor pre-configured dashboards for 30 min.
5. If no triggered fences, increase to 10% for 1 hour, then 50% for 2 hours, then full.

Numbered rollback decision flow (automated + human-in-the-loop):
1) Monitoring detects a fence trigger (e.g., error spike, latency exceedance, model-quality regression).
2) Automation evaluates severity and service tier. If severity >= automated_rollback_threshold, proceed to step 4.
3) Notify on-call, create an incident with runbook link, and pause rollout.
4) Automated rollback: traffic-router shifts all traffic to previous stable variant, sidecars mark artifact as deprecated, and the deploy is rolled back in orchestration system.
5) Post-action: postmortem owner assigned within 24 hours.

Automated rollback safeguards (must be implemented):
- TTL window: automated rollback operations must be rate-limited (no more than 2 auto-rollback events per service per 24h).
- Human override: on-call can veto an automated rollback within 2 minutes of trigger if a mitigation path exists. The override must be recorded with justification.
- Read-only staging flag: rollbacks in private deployments (air-gapped) require manual approval unless the customer opts-in for automated recovery.

Runtime contract enforcement patterns:
- Schema negotiation: responses include x-contract-version header; clients that cannot parse newer fields receive a compatibility view (stable schema renderer).
- Feature toggles: server-side feature gates are fenced by a config hash; older clients are mapped to conservative toggles.
- Graceful degradation: when dependent subsystems are unhealthy, the runtime returns structured partial responses with metadata about missing fields and reason codes.

YAML example: Gatekeeper admission (k8s webhook) config
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: gatekeeper-deploy-fence.redwood.svc
webhooks:
  - name: validate-infra-config.redwood.svc
    rules:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE","UPDATE"]
        resources: ["deployments"]
    failurePolicy: Fail
    admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]
    clientConfig:
      service:
        name: gatekeeper-admission
        namespace: infra-system
        path: /validate-deploy

Observability and SLO instrumentation (must-haves):
- Metrics: deploy.latency_ms, deploy.canary_error_rate, deploy.rollback.invocations, model.eval_delta, contract.compatibility_failures.
- Traces: every deploy should include a distributed-trace span: deploy.flow.<service> linking CI -> canary -> promotion.
- Logs: structured event at each fence with fields {service, artifact, gate, result, actor, timestamp}.
- Dashboards: per-service deploy summary and a team-wide Gatekeeper health board.

Alerting rules (examples):
- P0: deploy.rollback.invocations > 1 for a single service in 15m -> Pager to SRE and service on-call.
- P1: contract.compatibility_failures > 0.1% of traffic in 10m -> Slack @channel and ticket created.

Testing and CI integration:
- Contract fuzz tests: run nightly with a corpus covering major client types. Failure must block production promotion.
- Synthetic prompt-suite: every model variant must include a 200-query smoke set; regression > 2% triggers a fence.
- Chaos tests: periodic simulated canary failures to ensure rollback automation works end-to-end.

Ownership and roles:
- Service Owner: ensures preflight tests and synthetic harness exist.
- SRE: owns canary platform, alerting, and rollback automation.
- Applied-ML: owns quality metrics and model-eval gating.
- Release Engineering: integrates the Gatekeeper checks into CI and provides the promotion API.

Escalation matrix:
- 0–15 min: on-call engineer triages and either approves immediate rollback or pauses rollout.
- 15–60 min: SRE + Service Owner coordinate mitigations and decide on targeted rollback windows.
- 60+ min: Engineering manager and product representative determine broader customer communication and executive notification.

Governance and exceptions:
- High-priority customer hotfixes may request bypass of automated gates via the emergency release process; request must include a rollback plan and acceptance of potential increased monitoring.
- For Private/On-Prem deployments, Gatekeeper automation is advisory by default; customers can opt into automated rollback via contract.

Operational runbook excerpts (quick actions):
- Pause rollout: curl -X POST https://traffic-router.internal/api/v1/pause -d '{"service":"inference-api"}'
- Force rollback: ./releases/promote --service=inference-api --to=stable --force
- Query last fence events: ./infra/events query --filter 'service:inference-api AND gate:fence' --last 1h

Appendix A: Capacity rubric (short)
- Low risk: services with < 500 RPS and no GPU dependency: default gates.
- Medium risk: services with 500–5k RPS or single-GPU models: tightened thresholds (P95 latency x1.5).
- High risk: multi-region ingress, >5k RPS, or customer-facing SLA: require full canary sequence plus staged DB migrations.

Appendix B: Example contract failure message (structured JSON response)
{ "error": "contract_incompatible", "details": "client requested response schema v2.1; server produced v3.0 with unknown field 'internal_flags'", "action": "served_compat_view", "timestamp": "2025-09-18T12:34:56Z" }

Related reading and links:
- See service-starter-kit-safe-config-patterns (infra-standards) for templated config files.
- See prompt-suite-ci-contract-testing-guidelines (model-serving-standards) for model smoke-test patterns.

Revision history:
- 2025-03-12: initial draft by Asha Khandelwal.
- 2025-06-04: added automated rollback safeguards and private deploy advisory.
- 2025-09-18: tightened canary thresholds and added TTL rollback safeguard.

If you have questions or want this playbook applied to your service, file a request to release-engineering@redwood.internal and tag the service in the ticket.

title: dsid_740d08eb30a24bf085d205d92c9694ca__control-exception-evidence-register-template-2025.txt
text:
Control Exception Evidence Register Template

Overview:

This document defines a standardized Control Exception Evidence Register (CEER) and a corresponding template for packaging the evidence required when approving, exercising, and periodically reviewing exceptions to security and compliance controls. The CEER bridges RBAC & auth exception records, audit-log artifacts, data residency/retention constraints, Secure SDLC implications, incident-response hooks, and the compliance evidence workflow used by auditors and security reviewers.

Scope:

- Applies to any formal exception or temporary deviation from documented security controls across Redwood Inference services, including but not limited to RBAC policy relaxations, cross-region data access, altered retention settings, or third-party connector exceptions.
- Intended audience: security reviewers, risk owners, engineering owners, compliance, audit, and SRE.

Key objectives:
