- Simple alert rule example (text description):
  - Alert name: RedwoodHighP95Latency
  - Expression: p95(route="/v1/generate") > 150
  - For: 10m
  - Severity: critical
  - Notify: SRE on-call + delivery lead

Rollback and rollback-test validation:
- Verify the deployment automation can perform a controlled rollback to the previous model/runtime revision. Test plan:
  1. Trigger a canary release to 5% of traffic.
  2. Inject a synthetic error that causes failure-rate > 5% for canary (use traffic rewriter or fault-injection in the runtime test harness).
  3. Confirm automated rollback triggers within 2 minutes and the system returns to the previous revision with no additional errors.
- Commands to validate rollback logs (example):
  - kubectl -n redwood-control logs deployment/rollout-manager | tail -n 200
  - grep "rollback initiated" /var/log/redwood/rollout-manager.log

Checklist for security and compliance signals:
- KMS rotation event logged and validated against the customer key ID.
- TLS mutual auth handshake success rate > 99.9%.
- RBAC test: attempt an action with a role below required privilege and confirm 403 logged and audited.

Operational runbook snapshot (to include in handover):
1. How to surface a late-binding model fallback: CLI example and required flags.
2. How to escalate when trace sampling drops unexpectedly.
3. Commands to increase continuous batching window (if customer desires throughput tuning).

Reporting and handover artifacts (deliver to Customer Success and SRE):
- 72-hour baseline report (PDF): includes latency percentiles, error rates, trace sample examples, and any deviations.
- Runbook excerpt: 2-page quickstart for on-call (paging thresholds, key dashboards, rollback steps).
- Evidence bundle: screenshots/links to traces, example logs, and the Prometheus query outputs used for checks.

Template: 72-hour baseline report (text layout)
- Executive summary (1 paragraph)
- Metric snapshots (table: metric, observed p50/p95/p99)
- Alerts fired (if any) and resolution status
- Action items and owners

Common failure modes and mitigations (observed in previous private deployments):
- Symptom: high p95 latency after adding larger sequence-length requests. Mitigation: pin a quantized model variant for high-seqlen or increase batch size window for low-priority routes. Owner: Runtime team.
- Symptom: missing spans in traces. Mitigation: check tracer agent sidecar, verify sampling headers are preserved across proxies. Owner: SRE.
- Symptom: audit logs not arriving. Mitigation: check forwarder credentials, rotate key if expired, and run log-forwarder debug. Owner: Security.

Appendix A: quick debug commands (examples)
- Check control plane leader: kubectl -n redwood-control get pods -l app=control-plane -o wide
- Show recent high-latency requests (example log query): jq '. | select(.level=="error" and .latency_ms>200)' /var/log/redwood/requests.log | head -n 50

Appendix B: example JSON telemetry mapping (used by delivery automation)
- Example (text): {"metrics": ["redwood.requests.received_total","redwood.requests.latency"], "labels": ["customer_id","route","model_version"]}

Appendix C: acceptance signoff checklist (one-line items for signature)
- All required metrics visible for 24h
- Traces for multi-service path verified
- Audit logs for admin actions verified
- Baseline SLOs validated for 24h
- Automated rollback tested and validated
- Delivery lead: ____________________ Date: ________
- SRE on-call: _______________________ Date: ________

Links and references:
- See deployment playbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-playbook-vpc-onprem-2026
- Observability standards: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards

Notes and change history:
- 2025-11-12: Created by Aisha Raman (initial checklist)
- 2026-02-28: Updated fault-injection rollback test and tightened p95 examples to match runtime v2.8.

Contact: delivery@redwood.com

title: dsid_290001c62e1b4d97a794f5895306b3cf__hybrid-control-plane-reference-architecture-2026.txt
text:
Hybrid Control-Plane Reference Architecture for Private Deployments

Overview

Purpose: This document describes a recommended reference architecture for private deployments that combine a lightweight, customer-hosted control plane (VPC or on-prem) with managed central services operated by Redwood Inference. The design balances security, low-latency local serving, and simplified day-2 operations for customers that require data residency and air-gapped options.

Scope: covers architecture patterns, on-prem packaging options, hardware profiles, day-2 operational runbook primitives, upgrade and rollback strategy, and a customer requirements checklist used during scoping. This is intended for solution engineers, SREs, and customer infrastructure teams.

High-level goals
- Provide deterministic latency for local traffic (SLO: 95th percentile < 75ms for in-VPC inference on 256-token requests).
- Maintain centralized observability and billing while ensuring customer controls over sensitive data.
- Allow safe, reversible upgrades with automated canary/rollback tooling.
- Support both Kubernetes-native and VM/systemd packaging with consistent operational primitives.

Reference architecture (hybrid control-plane)

Architectural components
1) Customer Control Plane (local) — runs in customer VPC or on-prem cluster
- redwood-local-control: API gateway and config agent (HTTPS, port 8443)
- redwood-edge-agent: inference worker manager and local KV cache
- model-store-proxy: optional pull-through cache for model artifacts (only for approved models)
- local telemetry relay: aggregates traces/metrics, forwards to central observability over TLS

2) Redwood Central Services (hosted) — managed by Redwood Inference
- onboarding API and licensing service
- model registry (metadata only; binary artifacts may be proxied)
- billing / quota system (token accounting)
- update delivery service (signed rollout artifacts)

3) Network & Security Patterns
- Private peering or AWS PrivateLink between customer VPC and Redwood control plane endpoints; fallback to mutual-TLS over public egress if peering not available.
- Mandatory mTLS for all control-plane traffic; customer controls root CA in restricted deployments.
- Minimal egress: telemetry, licensing heartbeat, and signed artifact retrieval; data plane (inference traffic) remains local unless explicitly routed.

Deployment topologies (pick one)
- Single-cluster VPC (recommended for cloud customers): Kubernetes cluster + LoadBalancer + Spawned GPU nodepool for inference.
- Multi-cluster edge (recommended for large retail/telecom): small clusters at edges serving local requests, federated to central control plane for policy/rollout.
- Air-gapped on-prem: initial artifact bundle delivered on USB or secure transfer; control plane operates fully locally with optional periodic signed manifest verification.

Packaging options
- Kubernetes Helm (primary): chart name rwd-inference-private, chart versioned with semver. Provides Helm values for: imageRepository, nodeSelector, tolerations, gpuClass, persistenceClass, and database backend.
- Containerd + systemd (edge or appliance): rwd-private-appliance.tar.gz contains systemd unit files, container images, and an installer script (./install.sh --accept-license).
- Bare-metal package: prebuilt Nix/Ansible role for managed installs in regulated facilities.

Hardware profiles (reference)
- Small (dev/test): 1x GPU T4, 8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, 500 GB NVMe
- Medium (production): 2x A10/A100-40GB, 32 vCPU, 256 GB RAM, 2 TB NVMe
- Large (high throughput/low latency): 4x A100-80GB, 64 vCPU, 512 GB RAM, 4 TB NVMe

Storage and artifact strategy
- Models stored as immutable artifacts with hash-based names. Model download occurs to local persistent volumes in /var/lib/redwood/models.
- Recommended retention: keep last 3 model revisions on disk; older artifacts purged by policy.

SLOs and readiness
- Control plane API availability: 99.95% monthly (excluding maintenance windows)
- Local inference worker health probe: readiness within 5s; liveness should restart container if no forward progress for 30s
- Model load latency: 95th percentile < 20s for warm cache, < 120s for cold load from remote artifact store

Day-2 operations (runbook primitives)

Monitoring and alerts (baseline)
- Node GPU utilization: warn at 65%, critical at 85%
- Inference error rate (5xx): warn at 0.5%, critical at 2%
- Model load failures: immediate page to on-call if >3 failures in 10 minutes
- Telemetry heartbeat: alert if control-plane heartbeat missing for >10 minutes

Routine tasks
1) Scaling GPUs
- Kubernetes: update nodepool autoscaler config and label new GPU nodes with nodeSelector gpu=enabled. Verify pod eviction and re-scheduling with readiness probe.
- Non-K8s: add node, register with redwood-edge-agent via ./agentctl register --node-id <id>.

2) Certificate rotation (90-day cadence)
- Generate CSR using local CA or Redwood-managed CA depending on confidentiality.
- For zero-downtime rotation: deploy new cert to control-plane, wait for all agents to re-establish connections, then retire old cert.

3) Backup & restore
- Backup config DB daily (encrypted snapshot to S3-compatible endpoint).
- Test restore quarterly to a staging environment; document time-to-restore target (TTR) <= 2 hours for config DB.

Upgrade and rollback strategy

Principles
- Keep control plane and inference runtime decoupled: image compatibility matrix is required and enforced by the installer.
- All upgrade artifacts are signed by Redwood (verified by local agent).
- Provide canary and staged rollouts with automatic health gates.

Upgrade procedure (Kubernetes Helm example)
1) Prepare: ensure CI-generated release artifact is signed and in artifact registry.
2) Canary: deploy new control-plane chart to 5% of nodes or a dedicated canary namespace. Run regression evals against a smoke prompt set (automated).
3) Monitor: 30 minutes observation window with metrics: request latency, error rate, model load failures, and resource utilization.
4) Ramp: 25% -> 50% -> 100% in increments, with a minimum 15 minute observation window at each step.
5) Complete: mark release in local registry and notify Redwood central for telemetry aggregation.

Rollback procedure
1) If health gates fail during canary or ramp, initiate automated rollback: helm rollback <release> OR agentctl rollback --version <previous>.
2) If rollback fails or repeated issues occur, escalate to Redwood platform support and, if necessary, open a mitigation window (pause further rollouts globally).
3) Postmortem: collect control-plane logs, k8s events, agent heartbeats, and a core dump of the failed process where applicable. Run fail-mode simulation in staging.

Testing and QA requirements
- Mandatory: smoke evals, perf benchmark (p50/p95 latency vs baseline), and token-cost regression check.
- Optional but recommended: shadow traffic test for 24–72 hours before full cutover.

Operational ownership and escalation
- Customer infra owns cluster lifecycle, network peering, and encryption keys.
- Redwood Inference owns control-plane functional compatibility, signed artifacts, and central telemetry ingestion.
- Escalation path: on-call SRE -> Senior SRE -> Platform Eng -> Product Eng. Include contact matrix in customer onboarding doc.

Customer requirements checklist (pre-engagement)
1) Network connectivity: ability to create PrivateLink or allow outbound TLS to x.x.x.x:443 and telemetry.redwood.ai:443
2) KV and object storage: S3-compatible endpoint or permission to use Redwood-provided artifact mirror
3) Host OS and container runtime: Ubuntu 22.04, containerd 1.6+ (K8s), or supported RHEL/CentOS for air-gapped installs
4) GPU constraints: list of available GPU types and counts, NVMe scratch space per node
5) Compliance needs: required encryption at-rest algorithms, root CA controls, and required audit log retention window
6) Maintenance windows and allowed daily outage minutes for upgrades

Appendix: Example commands and snippets
- Helm install (canary namespace): helm upgrade --install rwd-control ./chart --namespace rwd-canary --set image.tag=2026.02-canary
- Agent register (systemd): sudo /opt/redwood/bin/agentctl register --server https://control.local:8443 --token-file /etc/redwood/token
- Backup config DB (example): pg_dump -Fc -h localhost -U rwd_config rwd_config > rwd_config_$(date +%F).dump

Related artifacts and references
- Chart repo: git+ssh://git.redwood.internal/rwd/charts.git
- Artifact signing doc: /confluence/security-and-compliance/running-signed-artifacts-2025
- Onboarding checklist (operational): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/customer-requirements-library/onboarding-checklist-2025

Revision history
- 2025-11-12: Initial draft by Maya Chen
- 2026-02-15: Clarified canary ramp windows and added air-gapped packaging notes (Samir Patel review)

title: dsid_ac57a706f85a4654aa33243672e918dc__tenant-egress-fallback-and-fairshare-throttling-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Tenant egress fallback and fair-share throttling playbook

Summary

This playbook describes the operational procedures, validation tests, and escalation steps for tenant egress fallback and fair-share throttling for Dedicated and Private tenants. It targets customer-success, SRE, and platform engineers responsible for onboarding enterprise customers with unpredictable burst traffic or constrained egress capacity.

Goals

- Ensure predictability for tenant traffic when outbound (egress) capacity is constrained.
- Maintain latency SLOs for high-priority tenants while applying fair-share policies to noisy neighbors.
- Provide a deterministic automated fallback that preserves availability and preserves customer data guarantees.

When to use this playbook

Use this playbook during:
1) Pre-production validation for Dedicated/Private tenant cutovers.
2) Go-live where tenant traffic patterns are unknown or have burst risk.
3) Incidents where egress link saturation, pod/instance ejects, or third-party API throttles cause increased latency or errors.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: Customer Success (Onboarding team) — Amira Patel
- Operational owner: Eng SRE — Diego Morales
- Runtime/Platform owner: Eng Platform — Priya Natarajan
- Pager: #sre-oncall (primary), #cs-help (secondary)
- Escalation: If pager not acknowledged in 15m, escalate to SRE L2 and Customer Success Manager.

Scope and constraints

- Applies to tenants on Dedicated capacity and Private VPC deployments.
- Not for Hosted (shared) tenants unless explicitly configured with fair-share proxies.
- Does not modify customer data retention or encryption policies.

Prerequisites and config artifacts

- Tenant capacity profile created in Capacity Service (capacity-service v2): tenant_id, target_rps, burst_rps, expected_seq_len.
- Ingress and egress proxies must expose the following metrics to metrics-ingest: ingress.rps, egress.bandwidth.bytes, proxy.queue_length, request.latency.p50/p95/p99.
- Fair-share controller enabled in tenant_proxy.conf with the following knobs: max_tokens_per_second, priority_weight, weight_decay_window_ms.
- Sufficient observability: synthetic journey for tenant with end-to-end p50/p95 thresholds.

Validation tests (pre-go-live)

Execute the validation harness below in a staging environment that mirrors production network topology. Document all results in the onboarding ticket.

1) Baseline characterization
- Inject steady traffic at target_rps for 10 minutes. Verify p95 latency < tenant_p95_slo and error rate < 0.1%.
- Required metrics: ingress.rps, egress.bytes/s, kvcache.hit_rate.

2) Burst resilience check
- Ramp all tenant test clients from target_rps to burst_rps over 60s. Observe fallback behavior. Expected outcome: lower-priority tenants receive graceful rate-limiting; high-priority tenants retain >= 85% of baseline throughput.

3) Egress saturation simulation
- Throttle external egress (eg simulate 40% link loss). Verify that fallback to local cache and degraded-mode responses occur: response codes 200 (degraded ok) or 503 (if hard fail) per policy. Verify circuit-breaker triggers at configured thresholds.

4) Fair-share fairness validation
- Run 10 tenants simultaneously with varied priority_weight values. Measure delivered RPS per tenant and verify proportional share within +/- 10% of configured weights.

Pre-Go-Live checklist (must pass all items)

- [ ] Capacity profile uploaded and approved.
- [ ] Tenant proxy config reviewed and committed to config repo (reviewer: Eng Platform).
- [ ] Synthetic journey created and scheduled for tenant.
- [ ] Alerting rules created: high egress utilization (>85%), proxy queue_length > 50, fair-share-imbalance > 15%.
- [ ] Backstop fallback policy documented in the customer runbook (customer-facing).

Go-Live steps (recommended timebox: 60–90 minutes)

1) Golden path smoke (0–10m)
- Verify ingress/routing is pointing to Dedicated/Private capacity.
- Run 2 quick synthetic requests and validate correlation IDs flow through logs.

2) Canary ramp (10–30m)
- Start with 5% of traffic routed to new tenant environment. Monitor p50/p95, error rate, and proxy queue.
- If p95 increases > 25% baseline or error rate > 0.5%, abort canary and roll back routing.

3) Gradual ramp (30–60m)
- Increase traffic by 20% every 10 minutes, monitoring fairness and egress usage.
- Confirm fair-share controller is distributing capacity proportionally.

4) Full cutover and verification (60–90m)
- Update routing to 100%. Keep enhanced monitoring for 6 hours. Document any anomalies.

Degraded-mode behavior and automatic fallback

- Soft-fallback: When proxy queue_length > 75 or egress_bandwidth >= 90% for > 30s, the system applies fair-share throttling and enables degraded responses for non-critical endpoints (e.g., background embeddings refresh).
- Hard-fallback: If requests.latency.p99 > 3x SLO for > 2 minutes, or error rate > 2% for > 5 minutes, fail open to read-only cached responses and notify SRE.
- Customer notification: For hard-fallbacks, Customer Success must send a templated notification within 30 minutes describing impact and mitigation steps.

Automated remediation actions (ordered)

1) Activate fair-share throttling profile (fast path).
2) Evict low-priority background requests for 60s.
3) Route new tenant traffic to lower-cost region if cross-region fallback policy exists and region latency delta < 50ms.
4) Provision burst capacity (manual escalation to capacity team if autoscale cannot allocate).

Telemetry, alerts, and SLOs to configure

- Metrics to send to metrics-ingest: tenant.{id}.ingress_rps, tenant.{id}.egress_bps, tenant.{id}.delivered_rps, tenant.{id}.throttle_rate, tenant.{id}.priority_share_pct.
- Core alerts (severity mapping):
  - P0: egress_bandwidth >= 95% for > 3m (pager)
  - P1: proxy.queue_length >= 75 for > 2m (page + slack)
  - P2: fair-share-imbalance > 20% for > 10m (slack only)
- Suggested SLOs (tenant-level):
  - Availability: 99.95% (excluding scheduled maintenance)
  - Latency p95: tenant-specific (recommended default 300ms)
  - Throttling transparency: any throttled request must return `X-Redwood-Throttle: true` header and include an advisory in response body where applicable.

Escalation matrix and playbook actions

1) First responder (SRE oncall) — Triage, perform automated remediation steps 1–3.
2) If unresolved after 15 minutes — SRE L2 and Customer Success notified; open incident channel and begin stakeholder comms.
3) If unresolved after 60 minutes — Eng Platform and Capacity team pager.
4) If unresolved after 3 hours — Executive escalation and formal incident postmortem.

Incident comms template (short)

Subject: [Incident] Tenant {tenant_id} - Egress congestion detected\\nBody:
- Impact: Elevated latency and partial degradation for tenant {tenant_id}.
- Timeline: {start_time} UTC
- Mitigation: Applied fair-share throttling and evicted background requests; routing adjusted.
- Next steps: Capacity team provisioning in progress; monitoring in place.

Post-incident items and QBR inputs

- Document the root cause, timeline, and mitigation in the incident ticket.
- Recommend capacity or architectural changes: e.g., increase egress pool by N GPUs or enable region-fallback by default.
- Add the incident to the next QBR with the following artifacts: synthetic journey traces, request/response samples with correlation IDs, and fairness delta graphs.

Testing scenarios matrix (examples)

| Scenario | Goal | Expected outcome | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Single-tenant burst | Verify high-priority preserved | High-priority tenant keeps >=85% throughput | Run for 30m
| Multi-tenant simultaneous burst | Validate fair-share | Proportional throughput within +/-10% | Use 10 tenants
| Egress link failure | Validate degraded-mode | Cached responses + advisory header | Simulate packet loss at edge

Appendix: sample tenant_proxy.conf snippet

# Example TOML snippet for fair-share controller
[fair_share]
max_tokens_per_second = 1200
priority_weights = { gold = 10, standard = 5, trial = 1 }
weight_decay_window_ms = 60000
eviction_policy = "background-first"

Appendix: basic CLI checks for oncall

# Verify current queue lengths and throttle rates (run on proxy-host)
curl -sS http://proxy-host.local/metrics | grep tenant.{tenant_id}.throttle_rate

# Force a synthetic request with correlation id
curl -H "X-Correlation-ID: onboarding-123" -X POST https://tenant-ingress.example/v1/generate -d '{"prompt": "smoke test"}' -v

Recovery and rollback guidance

- Immediate rollback: Re-route traffic back to incumbent environment via edge-router config if p95 > 2x SLO during canary.
- Long-term remediation: Schedule capacity expansion, add egress caching layer for large-response endpoints, or adjust tenant priority weights for steady-state fairness.

Document history and change log

- 2026-01-15: Created by Amira Patel (initial draft).
- 2026-03-02: Added automated remediation ordering and telemetry section (reviewer: Diego Morales).
- 2026-08-02: Published with expanded testing matrix and CLI snippets (reviewer: Priya Natarajan).

Related pages and references

- Dedicated tenant cutover safety-net playbook — see related_pages for link.
- Synthetic health suite implementation guide (health-and-qbr).
- Eng SRE capacity profiling guide for tenant planning.

End of playbook

title: dsid_48fa74f556aa4f0c9996b53170693e8f__perf-baseline-dashboards-spec.txt
text:
Perf Baseline Dashboards Spec (Q1 2026)

## Overview
This page specifies the Grafana (and optionally Looker) dashboards and alerting used to report and triage results from the Q1 2026 “Perf baseline & representative workload suite” project.

The dashboards must support:
- Baseline reporting for key metrics (TTFT/TPOT percentiles, throughput)
- Root-cause oriented drilldowns (saturation, queueing, kernel selection, cache behavior)
- Run-to-run comparison and regression attribution
- Direct linking from dashboard → run manifest → traces/logs/artifacts

This spec is intentionally prescriptive: consistent naming, tags, and panel layout are required so that engineers can move between runs, models, regions, and SKUs without relearning the UI.

## Goals
1) Provide a single “source of truth” view for a benchmark run (or run set) including:
- TTFT p50/p95/p99
- TPOT p50/p95/p99
- Throughput (tokens/s, req/s) and concurrency
- Saturation indicators (GPU utilization, KV cache pressure, queue wait)
- Noise/variance indicators

2) Enable regression triage in < 15 minutes for most cases by answering:
- What changed? (runtime build, scheduler profile, kernel profile, driver/CUDA, workload seed)
- Where did the time go? (queue wait vs prefill vs decode)
- Is it capacity/saturation? (GPU busy %, SM occupancy proxy, memory BW proxy, KV cache hits/evictions)
- Is it a kernel selection / fallback issue?

3) Standardize drilldowns and links:
- “Open run manifest”
- “Open trace (Tempo)”
- “Open logs (Loki)” and “Open scheduler debug bundle”

## Non-goals
- Customer-facing benchmark dashboards
- Replacing perf-canary gating output (these dashboards complement gating, they do not define pass/fail)
- Building a general-purpose production SLO dashboard (production SLO dashboards remain in eng-sre; this is for benchmark runs and canary runs)

## Definitions (must match ADR-0172)
All metric names and boundaries must match: confluence://architecture-and-standards/decision-records/adr-0172-benchmark-metrics-and-run-manifest-format

- TTFT (time-to-first-token): server-side elapsed time from request accepted by Redwood ingress/runtime to first token emitted on the server response stream (“first token on wire” at the server). Excludes client read/backpressure.
- TPOT (time-per-output-token): (server-side time between first token and end of generation) / (number of output tokens - 1). For non-streaming responses, measured from internal first-token event to internal last-token event.
- Throughput:
  - tokens/s: total output tokens / wall time, reported per replica and aggregated
  - req/s: request completions / second (for embeddings and non-streaming)

Cache state dimension:
- cold: prefix/KV cache disabled or empty
- warm: prefix/KV cache enabled and warmed per workload definition (see representative workload suite v1)

## Data sources
### 1) Bench results store (authoritative)
- Storage: ClickHouse cluster “obs-analytics”
- Database/table (canonical): bench_results.perf_metrics_v1
- Grain: one row per run_id x metric x percentile x (optional) cohort
- Key columns (expected):
  - run_id, run_group
  - created_at
  - model_id, model_family
  - workload_id, workload_family
  - region, gpu_sku
  - runtime_build (git SHA/tag), runtime_version
  - scheduler_profile, kernel_profile
  - cache_state, streaming_mode
  - metric_name (ttft_ms, tpot_ms, tokens_per_s, req_per_s, queue_wait_ms, …)
  - percentile (p50, p95, p99) or value_type (mean, max)
  - value
  - sample_size

Note: Grafana queries should prefer ClickHouse for percentiles computed from raw samples when available. When only summarized percentiles are stored, clearly label as “reported percentile”.

### 2) Prometheus for real-time canary runs
- Primary: redwood-benchmark Prometheus job scraped from perf-canary and benchmark harness
- Metrics prefix: redwood_bench_* and redwood_runtime_* (bench-tagged)
- Use Prometheus only for “last N hours” canary visibility; use ClickHouse for historical baselines.

### 3) Traces/logs/artifacts
- Traces: Tempo, trace_id stored in ClickHouse as bench_trace_id where available
- Logs: Loki (bench-tagged), run_id must be a log label
- Artifacts: S3-compatible bucket “perf-artifacts” (internal), path includes run_id

## Required tagging / dimensions (contract)
Dashboards assume the following tags exist on every run. If a run is missing a dimension, panels may be incomplete; the run should be considered “invalid for baseline”.

Required dimensions:
- run_id (string, unique)
- run_group (string; e.g., “q1-2026-baseline-freeze”, “nightly-main”, “release-branch-2026.02”)
- model_id (string)
- workload_id (string)
- region (string; at least us-east, eu-west)
- gpu_sku (string; e.g., H100-80GB, A100-80GB, L40S)
- runtime_build (string; git SHA or release tag)
- scheduler_profile (string)
- kernel_profile (string)
- cache_state (cold|warm)
- streaming_mode (streaming|non_streaming)

Strongly recommended dimensions (improve attribution):
- driver_version, cuda_version
- container_image (digest)
- power_mode / clocks_locked (boolean)
- instance_type
- replica_count

## Dashboard set (navigation)
We will publish a small, consistent set of dashboards in Grafana folder:
Folder: “Perf Baselines (Serving Runtime)”

Dashboards:
1) Perf Baseline — Overview
2) Perf Baseline — Run Compare
3) Perf Baseline — Saturation & Queueing
4) Perf Baseline — Variance & Noise
5) Perf Baseline — Kernel/Scheduler Attribution

Looker (optional): “Perf Baseline — Executive Summary” (tables + trends; no deep triage)

## Global dashboard variables (Grafana)
All dashboards must expose the same variable names and defaults.

Variables (type → source):
- run_group (query → ClickHouse distinct run_group; default: q1-2026-baseline-freeze if present)
- run_id (query → ClickHouse distinct run_id filtered by run_group; allow multi-select)
- baseline_run_id (query → ClickHouse; single-select; default pinned to baseline anchor build)
- candidate_run_id (query → ClickHouse; single-select)
- model_id (query → distinct)
- workload_id (query → distinct)
- region (query → distinct)
- gpu_sku (query → distinct)
- cache_state (custom: cold,warm)
- streaming_mode (custom: streaming,non_streaming)

Conventions:
- If a panel is meaningful only for streaming, it must explicitly filter streaming_mode=streaming.
- For comparisons, always compute (candidate - baseline) and (candidate / baseline) where applicable.

## Dashboard 1: Perf Baseline — Overview
Purpose: one-page health view for a selected run_id (or run set), covering core metrics and quick links.

Layout (top → bottom):

### A) Run header (text panel)
Must display:
- run_id, run_group
- model_id, workload_id
- region, gpu_sku
- runtime_build, container_image
- scheduler_profile, kernel_profile
- cache_state, streaming_mode
- sample_size

Also include:
- Link: “Open run manifest”
- Link: “Open traces (Tempo) filtered by run_id”
- Link: “Open logs (Loki) filtered by run_id”
- Link: “Open artifacts folder (S3 browser)”

### B) Core latency percentiles (time series or stat grid)
Panels (stat w/ sparkline where time window supports):
- TTFT p50 (ms)
- TTFT p95 (ms)
- TTFT p99 (ms)
- TPOT p50 (ms)
- TPOT p95 (ms)
- TPOT p99 (ms)

Display requirements:
- Units: milliseconds
- Each stat must show last value + delta vs baseline_run_id when both baseline and candidate are selected
- Include sample_size and run_count in tooltip

### C) Throughput and completion
Panels:
- tokens/s (mean) and tokens/s (p95 of per-window)
- req/s (for embeddings and non-streaming)
- completed requests, error count, timeout count

### D) Quick saturation indicators (single-value + threshold colors)
Panels:
- GPU busy % (if available; else “GPU time / wall time” proxy)
- Avg batch size (decode) and avg batch size (prefill)
- Queue wait p95 (ms)
- KV cache hit rate (if enabled)
- KV cache eviction rate (evictions/min)

Color thresholds (initial; tune after variance calibration):
- Queue wait p95: green < 5ms; yellow 5–20ms; red > 20ms
- KV evictions: green < 10/min; yellow 10–100/min; red > 100/min

### E) Top regressions within run set (table)
If multi-select run_id is used, show a table sorted by worst TTFT p99 and worst TPOT p99, including:
- run_id
- ttft_p99_ms
- tpot_p99_ms
- tokens_per_s
- queue_wait_p95_ms
- kernel_fallback_rate

## Dashboard 2: Perf Baseline — Run Compare
Purpose: side-by-side comparison baseline_run_id vs candidate_run_id and clear deltas.

### A) Summary delta table (table)
Rows (metrics):
- TTFT p50/p95/p99
- TPOT p50/p95/p99
- tokens/s
- req/s (if relevant)
- queue_wait p95
- batch_assembly_ms p95
- kernel_fallback_rate
- kv_hit_rate

Columns:
- baseline value
- candidate value
- absolute delta
- relative delta (%)
- sample_size baseline/candidate

Formatting:
- Relative delta should be colored by perf-regression policy thresholds (see confluence://architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/perf-regression-policy-and-thresholds)

### B) Percentile curves (if raw samples are available)
Panels:
- TTFT empirical CDF (baseline vs candidate)
- TPOT empirical CDF (baseline vs candidate)

If raw samples not available, show p50/p95/p99 only and label clearly.

### C) Decomposition (stacked bar)
Panels:
- TTFT decomposition: queue_wait + batch_assembly + prefill_compute + first_token_emit_overhead
- End-to-end generation decomposition: decode_compute + scheduling_overhead + streaming_overhead

Note: decomposition requires benchmark instrumentation; if not present, panel should show “missing metric” state with a link to ENG-4826.

## Dashboard 3: Perf Baseline — Saturation & Queueing
Purpose: answer “is this a saturation/overload/queueing issue?”

Panels:
1) Concurrency over time (requested vs achieved)
2) Queue depth (avg/max) and queue wait percentiles
3) Batch assembly time percentiles
4) Batch size distribution (histogram-like table)
5) Backpressure/load shed counters:
   - requests_throttled_total
   - requests_dropped_total
   - overload_mode_seconds
6) GPU utilization proxies:
   - gpu_busy_percent (preferred)
   - sm_occupancy_proxy / kernel_active_ratio (fallback)
   - hbm_bw_proxy (fallback)
7) KV cache pressure:
   - kv_cache_bytes_used
   - kv_cache_bytes_free
   - kv_cache_evictions_total

Interpretation guidance (text panel at top):
- Rising queue wait with flat GPU busy often indicates scheduler bottleneck, dispatch overhead, or batch assembly inefficiency.
- Rising GPU busy with rising TTFT p99 indicates saturation; compare to batch size and backpressure.
- High eviction rate combined with long-context prefill can produce TTFT tail spikes even if GPU busy is stable.

## Dashboard 4: Perf Baseline — Variance & Noise
Purpose: make noise visible and prevent overreacting to expected variance.

Panels:
1) Run-to-run variance (box plot) for TTFT p95/p99 by (model_id, workload_id, gpu_sku, region)
2) Warmup effect:
   - TTFT p95 over first N requests vs steady state
   - tokens/s over time
3) Host / placement indicators (if captured):
   - CPU steal %
   - NUMA remote memory ratio
   - GPU clocks (min/avg/max) and clock throttling count
4) Confidence / sample size panel:
   - sample_size
   - bootstrap CI width (if computed)

Required annotation:
- Every panel must support “show baseline freeze window” annotation (vertical region) when run_group=q1-2026-baseline-freeze.

## Dashboard 5: Perf Baseline — Kernel/Scheduler Attribution
Purpose: pinpoint regressions tied to kernel selection changes or scheduler behavior changes.

Panels:
1) Kernel selection breakdown (table):
   - kernel_name
   - selection_rate (%)
   - fallback_reason (if any)
   - associated sequence-length regime
2) Kernel fallback rate over time
3) Scheduler fairness/latency tradeoff indicators:
   - per-tenant fairness index (if benchmark simulates tenants)
   - queue discipline mode (label)
4) Sequence length distributions (from workload definition + observed):
   - prompt tokens histogram (bins)
   - output tokens histogram (bins)
5) Correlation panel:
   - scatter: TTFT p99 vs kernel_fallback_rate
   - scatter: TTFT p99 vs queue_wait_p95

Drilldown links:
- “Open kernel debug dump for run_id” (artifact path)
- “Open scheduler debug dump for run_id” (artifact path)

## Standard links and URL conventions
### Run manifest
- Stored at: s3://perf-artifacts/manifests/{run_id}/run-manifest.json
- Grafana link label: “Run manifest”
- If run manifest is mirrored into ClickHouse as JSON text, also provide “View manifest in table” link.

### Traces
- Tempo query must use:
  - tag: run_id={run_id}
  - optional: model_id, workload_id
- Grafana link label: “Traces (Tempo)”

### Logs
- Loki query must use label selector:
  - {run_id="{run_id}", app=~"bench-runner|redwood-runtime"}
- Grafana link label: “Logs (Loki)”

### Artifacts
- Base path: s3://perf-artifacts/runs/{run_id}/
- Expected artifacts:
  - scheduler.jsonl
  - kernel_selection.jsonl
  - perfetto_trace.pb
  - stdout.log, stderr.log
  - results.json

## Alerting spec (Grafana + perf-canary integration)
Dashboards provide visibility; alerting drives action.

### Alert categories
1) Perf-canary regression alerts (nightly + release gating mode)
2) Benchmark infrastructure health (missing metrics, run failures, unusually high variance)

### Alert routing
- “Perf Regression (page)” → on-call (eng-serving-runtime primary) when:
  - run_group is a release gating group OR regression is severe
  - AND metric breach meets “regression” threshold (not just noise)
- “Perf Regression (triage)” → #eng-perf-triage (Slack) for non-gating nightly regressions
- “Benchmark Infra” → #eng-benchmarking for harness/fleet issues

### Initial alert thresholds (policy-aligned)
Use confluence://architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/perf-regression-policy-and-thresholds as canonical. Until calibrated, implement conservative defaults:

- TTFT p99 regression (streaming workloads):
  - page if candidate/baseline ≥ 1.15 AND absolute delta ≥ 10ms
  - triage if candidate/baseline ≥ 1.08 AND absolute delta ≥ 5ms
- TPOT p99 regression:
  - page if candidate/baseline ≥ 1.12 AND absolute delta ≥ 0.2ms
  - triage if candidate/baseline ≥ 1.06 AND absolute delta ≥ 0.1ms
- Throughput regression (tokens/s):
  - page if candidate/baseline ≤ 0.90
  - triage if candidate/baseline ≤ 0.95

Noise guardrails:
- Do not alert unless sample_size ≥ minimum configured per workload family
- Suppress alerts when benchmark infra health indicates instability (e.g., GPU clocks unlocked + high throttling)

### Alert annotations
Every regression alert must include:
- baseline_run_id, candidate_run_id
- model_id, workload_id, region, gpu_sku
- runtime_build(s), scheduler_profile(s), kernel_profile(s)
- Links: Run Compare dashboard with variables set; run manifest; traces

## Panel naming conventions
- Prefix with metric family: “TTFT”, “TPOT”, “Throughput”, “Queueing”, “KV Cache”, “Kernel Selection”, “Infra/Noise”
- Include percentile in title: e.g., “TTFT p99 (ms)”
- Include cohort in title if filtered: e.g., “TTFT p99 (ms) — long-prefill”

## Dashboard QA / acceptance criteria
A dashboard release is acceptable when:
1) Selecting any run_id from q1-2026-baseline-freeze produces non-empty values for core panels (TTFT/TPOT/throughput) and correct units.
2) Drilldown links resolve correctly for at least 3 sample runs (manifest + traces + logs).
3) Run Compare produces correct deltas and percent change formatting.
4) At least one workload per family (chat streaming, long-context, embeddings) has meaningful saturation panels.
5) No panel uses ambiguous metric definitions (must match ADR-0172).

## Rollout plan
- Phase 1 (Dec 2025): Publish dashboards with core metrics and run header + links. Validate tags and manifest linking.
- Phase 2 (Jan 2026): Add saturation/queueing panels as scheduler instrumentation lands (ENG-4826, PR-21503).
- Phase 3 (Feb 2026): Add kernel attribution panels as kernel debug dump ships (PR-21519).
- Phase 4 (late Q1 2026): Turn on alerting for nightly; then gating mode after a 2-week dry run.

## Ownership and change management
- Dashboard owner (implementation): Sergio Costa
- Standards owner (metrics + tagging): Allison Grant
- Alert routing owner: Aisha Bello

Changes to:
- metric definitions → require ADR update or explicit sign-off in perf standards page
- alert thresholds → require review by eng-sre + perf program owner (Jonas Weber)

## Appendix: Example ClickHouse query templates (reference)
Note: these are illustrative; actual queries live in Grafana panel definitions.

A) Fetch TTFT percentiles for a run
SELECT percentile, value
FROM bench_results.perf_metrics_v1
WHERE run_id = '${run_id}'
  AND metric_name = 'ttft_ms'
  AND percentile IN ('p50','p95','p99');

B) Fetch baseline vs candidate for delta table
SELECT
  metric_name,
  percentile,
  anyIf(value, run_id='${baseline_run_id}') AS baseline_value,
  anyIf(value, run_id='${candidate_run_id}') AS candidate_value,
  (candidate_value - baseline_value) AS abs_delta,
  (candidate_value / baseline_value) AS rel_ratio
FROM bench_results.perf_metrics_v1
WHERE run_id IN ('${baseline_run_id}','${candidate_run_id}')
  AND metric_name IN ('ttft_ms','tpot_ms','tokens_per_s','queue_wait_ms')
  AND percentile IN ('p50','p95','p99')
GROUP BY metric_name, percentile;

## Appendix: Known gaps (as of last_updated)
- Not all runs have trace_id populated; until then, the “Traces (Tempo)” link should fall back to a query by run_id label.
- KV cache metrics are incomplete for some SKUs; panels must tolerate missing fields.
- Some embeddings workloads do not emit tokens/s; throughput panel must switch to req/s when workload_family=embeddings.

text: Embedded Playground: SDK Sandbox Starter Pack ## Summary This page describes the "embedded playground" starter pack for SDK teams who want an in-product, lightweight sandbox runner that can be embedded in developer docs, support consoles, or internal demos. The pack includes: a minimal React frontend, a Node-based backend proxy that enforces rate limits and telemetry, and a recommended deployment pattern for staging and production. Use this when you need a reproducible, observable demo environment that mirrors production API behaviour without exposing raw credentials or unlimited quotas. --- ## Goals - Provide a secure, low-friction way to run SDK code snippets live in docs and support flows. - Ensure parity with production runtime behaviour (timeouts, retries, streaming) for meaningful developer experience. - Bake in telemetry and canonical error handling so support can reproduce customer issues reliably. ## When to use this starter pack - Documentation pages that offer "Try it" interactive examples. - Internal training and onboarding sandboxes for new hires. - Support playbooks where agents need to reproduce a call quickly. - Feature demos that require predictable quotas and no risk of leaking keys. ## What you get in the repo (files & roles) - README.md — setup and maintenance notes. - frontend/ — React app with an embedded code editor and result pane. - backend/ — Node Express proxy, request validation, rate-limiter hooks. - infra/ — Helm chart + k8s manifests for staging and prod. - telemetry/ — pre-configured OpenTelemetry YAML and sample dashboards. - templates/ — HTML snippet and SDK snippet templates for docs. ## Quickstart: Local dev (10–15 minutes) 1. Clone the starter pack: `git clone git@internal:redwood/playground-starter.git` 2. Copy .env.example -> .env and set DEV_API_KEY to a scoped sandbox key (see Access below). 3. Start the backend: ```bash cd backend npm install npm run dev ``` 4. Start the frontend: ```bash cd frontend npm install npm run start ``` 5. Open http://localhost:3000 and paste sample prompts from templates/example-prompts.md Notes: the backend will validate the sandbox key and attach `x-rd-playground=true` header to calls so telemetry and cost accounting are isolated. ## Example: Embedded React snippet (copy into docs) This minimal snippet renders an editor and calls the sandbox endpoint. title: dsid_2a45f178276d4810ba2e6e40050a2aea__compliance-reporting-pack-prd.txt
text:
PRD: Baseline Compliance Reporting Pack (On-demand Exports + Customer Package)

## Summary
The Baseline Compliance Reporting Pack is a standardized, customer-ready set of exports and summaries that Redwood Inference can generate on-demand to accelerate enterprise security reviews and support internal audits. The pack focuses on the minimum evidence that repeatedly blocks deals: audit log coverage and exports, retention configuration, data residency/region posture, and access control/RBAC posture.

This PRD defines the pack contents, customer expectations (what it proves / what it does not), integrations (audit-log-exporter + telemetry), output formats and versioning, and MVP scope for the initial GA.

## Problem statement
Enterprise prospects adopting Dedicated and Private deployments consistently request:
- Proof that Redwood maintains audit logs for key administrative and access events.
- A time-windowed export of audit events for their review.
- Clear retention controls and a reproducible export of retention configuration.
- Data residency confirmation (regions used; where logs live).
- A summary of access control model (RBAC) and administrative access.

Today, Sales Engineering, Security, and GRC assemble these artifacts manually, which is slow, error-prone, and inconsistently formatted.

## Goals (what success looks like)
1) Provide a baseline compliance pack that can be generated in < 30 minutes end-to-end for a standard time window (e.g., last 30 days), with minimal Engineering intervention.
2) Reduce repetitive Security/GRC work during sales cycles by standardizing:
   - Contents
   - Report templates/filters
   - Output formats and naming
   - Evidence checklist
3) Ensure the pack is defensible and auditable:
   - Export is versioned
   - Inputs/time windows are recorded
   - Access to generate/download is permissioned and logged
4) Support Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployment modes with tier-appropriate data availability and wording.

## Non-goals (initial GA)
- Full custom report builder or arbitrary customer-defined report sections.
- “Bring your own GRC” integrations beyond standard exports (JSON/CSV) and a generated PDF/HTML summary.
- Per-field redaction policy framework (handled under logging standards and product logging controls).
- Attestation that substitutes for SOC 2/ISO certificates (we provide evidence artifacts; we do not provide audit opinions).

## Target customers and personas
### External
- Customer Security Reviewer / Auditor: needs evidence, clarity, and repeatability.
- Customer Security Admin: needs configuration exports (retention, access control) and region posture.
- Customer Platform/SRE: wants operational details (availability, where logs live, export mechanics).

### Internal
- GRC Lead (Olga Petrov): owns evidence set, checklist alignment to controls, packaging.
- Security Engineering (Marcus Lin): validates audit event coverage, security of exports, access control.
- Engineering (Kevin Osei, Platform/Control Plane): owns exporter integration and retention config export.
- Sales Engineering / Customer Success: uses pack as standard response to questionnaires and procurement.

## Customer expectations and promises
### What the pack should answer
- “What administrative/security-relevant events are logged?”
- “Can you export audit logs for a specific time window?”
- “What is your retention configuration for key data classes, and can we get it in writing/export form?”
- “Where is our data processed/stored (regions), and does the report reflect that?”
- “Who has access (RBAC) and how do you control administrative actions?”

### What the pack is NOT
- Not a guarantee of absence of incidents.
- Not a replacement for SOC 2 Type II report or ISO certificate.
- Not a record of customer application-level content unless explicitly enabled and within configured retention.

## Pack overview (baseline contents)
The Baseline Compliance Reporting Pack includes the following sections and artifacts.

### A) Executive summary (customer-facing)
- Pack name and version
- Customer tenant/org identifier(s)
- Generation timestamp and requested time window
- Deployment mode: Hosted / Dedicated / Private
- Regions included
- Short narrative: what’s included, limitations, and how to validate authenticity

### B) Audit logging coverage summary (customer-facing)
- Coverage statement: event categories logged and where they originate
- Known exclusions for the customer’s deployment mode
- Definitions:
  - “Audit logs” vs “Request/Response logs”
  - “Actor” (user vs service account)
  - “Control plane” vs “data plane”

Deliverable: PDF/HTML section + JSON coverage manifest.

### C) Audit log export (customer-facing)
- Time-windowed export of audit events
- Must support filtering templates:
  - Admin changes (RBAC/permissions, retention policy changes)
  - Authentication/security events (API key lifecycle, SSO/SAML changes where applicable)
  - Configuration and deployment operations (model pinning/rollouts where in scope)

Deliverables:
- CSV export (preferred for reviewers)
- JSON export (canonical; used for verification and machine parsing)

### D) Retention configuration export (customer-facing)
- Export of current retention settings by data class
- Includes safe defaults by tier and customer overrides
- Includes legal hold state (if present) and change history summary for the window

Deliverables:
- JSON export of effective policy + metadata (policy version, applied scope)
- PDF/HTML summary table

### E) Data residency / region summary (customer-facing)
- Regions enabled for the tenant and where primary control plane data is stored
- Notes on dedicated/private topology when applicable (customer-managed regions/VPC)

Deliverables:
- PDF/HTML summary + JSON region manifest

### F) Access control / RBAC report (customer-facing)
- Roles present and high-level permissions
- Users/service accounts with assigned roles (optionally limited to admins)
- SSO enforcement status (if applicable)

Deliverables:
- CSV/JSON export + PDF/HTML summary

### G) Evidence collection checklist (internal + optionally shareable)
- Checklist aligned to SOC 2/ISO-style controls with “where to find it” pointers
- Owner, frequency, and validation steps

Deliverable: checklist document included in internal bundle; shareable variant must omit internal-only system names where required.

## Integration points and dependencies
### Audit logs
- Source of truth: audit-log-exporter
- Required capabilities:
  - Time-windowed exports
  - Standard templates (field set + filters)
  - Support bundling attachments (e.g., retention config export) into a single package
- Ownership: Kevin Osei (engineering) + Marcus Lin (security review)

### Retention controls
- Source of truth: Retention Policy Service (control plane)
- Must export:
  - Effective policy evaluated for the tenant
  - Policy change history for requested window
  - Legal hold status and hold reason codes (if any)
- Ownership: Ethan Park / Benji Okafor (engineering)

### Telemetry / observability
- Used for:
  - Verification signals included in internal appendix (optional): TTL lag, purge success metrics, backlog indicators
  - Confidence check that retention enforcement is working for the tenant/region
- Ownership: Logan Wright / Caleb Johnson

### Console and packaging
- Primary generation triggers:
  - Console “Generate compliance pack” action (RBAC-restricted)
  - API endpoint for internal automation / Private deployments
- Packaging service assembles artifacts, renders PDF/HTML summary, and stores package metadata.

## Functional requirements
### FR1: Pack generation request
- Inputs:
  - Tenant/org identifier
  - Time window (start/end) with validated max range (MVP: up to 90 days)
  - Region scope (auto = all regions where tenant is active)
  - Template selection (baseline templates only in MVP)
- Output:
  - Job ID + status endpoint
  - Estimated completion time

### FR2: Access control and auditability
- Only authorized roles can generate/download packs:
  - Internal: Security/GRC/SE roles
  - Customer: Org Admin (Dedicated/Private), subject to feature flag
- Every generation and download must itself be written to the audit log.
- Generated artifacts are stored with an immutable manifest and checksum.

### FR3: Deterministic content and versioning
- Pack must include:
  - Pack schema version (e.g., “baseline.v1”)
  - Component versions (exporter version, retention service schema version)
  - Field dictionary for audit export columns
- Backward compatibility:
  - CSV/JSON fields are additive within a major version
  - Breaking changes require a new major pack version

### FR4: Audit log export templates (baseline)
MVP must include at least these templates:
1) Administrative changes (RBAC, retention policy changes, org settings)
2) Authentication & credential lifecycle (API keys, SSO toggles where supported)
3) Access events (admin console access, privileged actions)

Each template defines:
- Event type set
- Required fields
- Default filters
- Output file naming convention

### FR5: Retention export
- Must export effective retention for the following data classes (where applicable by tier):
  - Audit logs
  - Request/response logs (if enabled)
  - Traces
  - Metrics
  - Artifacts (eval datasets) if present in the customer environment
- Must clearly label “not collected” vs “collected but retention disabled/short” vs “collected and retained”.

### FR6: RBAC export
- Must include:
  - Role definitions (name, description)
  - Role assignments (principal, role, scope)
  - “Admin-equivalent” indicator for top roles
- Must support omission of non-admin users for large tenants (MVP: default to admins-only; toggle for full export internal-only).

### FR7: Data residency summary
- Must include:
  - Regions where the tenant is configured to run
  - Regions where control plane config is stored
  - Notes for Dedicated/Private: customer-managed networking and storage boundaries

### FR8: Delivery formats
- Customer bundle:
  - PDF or HTML summary
  - CSV exports
  - JSON exports
  - Manifest file (checksums, timestamps, versions)
- Internal bundle:
  - Everything above plus optional verification appendix (telemetry checks) and internal run references.

## Non-functional requirements
- Reliability: 99% successful generation for standard windows (<= 30 days); failures must be actionable with clear error codes.
- Performance: Export generation should not impact production workloads; adhere to rate limits and use batching.
- Security:
  - At-rest encryption for stored packages
  - Time-limited download URLs
  - Principle of least privilege for pack generator service
- Privacy:
  - Exports contain metadata about actions and actors; must avoid including prompt/completion content unless explicitly configured elsewhere.

## User experience and workflows
### Console (primary UX)
- Location: Security & Compliance → “Compliance reporting pack”
- Actions:
  1) Select time window
  2) Select baseline pack
  3) Generate
  4) Download
- UI must display:
  - Included sections
  - Notes/limitations by deployment mode
  - Generation status and last generated packs
  - “Who can access” explanation

### API (secondary)
- Endpoint group: /v1/compliance-packs
- Operations:
  - POST create generation job
  - GET job status
  - GET download links
- Use cases:
  - Internal automation by GRC
  - Private deployments where customer prefers scripted export

## Data sources and field-level expectations
### Audit log export fields (baseline)
Required fields:
- event_id
- event_type
- event_timestamp (RFC3339)
- actor_type (user/service)
- actor_id (stable identifier)
- actor_email (if available)
- source_ip (if captured)
- region
- resource_type / resource_id
- action
- outcome (success/failure)
- request_id / correlation_id

Optional fields (best effort, additive):
- user_agent
- mfa_present (if applicable)
- auth_provider (if applicable)

### Retention export fields (baseline)
- tenant_id
- policy_version
- effective_at
- data_class
- retention_ttl
- purge_semantics (soft/hard where applicable)
- legal_hold (true/false)
- exceptions summary

### RBAC export fields (baseline)
- principal_id
- principal_type
- principal_email (if applicable)
- role
- scope
- created_at
- last_updated_at

## Analytics and success metrics
Product metrics:
- Time-to-deliver pack to customer (median; target < 1 business day once requested)
- % of enterprise security reviews where baseline pack is accepted without follow-up
- # of manual GRC hours per deal (target reduction)

Operational metrics (SLIs):
- Pack generation success rate
- Median generation time by window size
- Export job failure rate by component (audit exporter vs retention export vs RBAC export)

## Rollout plan
Phase 1 (MVP):
- Internal-only generation for design partners and active deals (GRC/Security/SE)
- Baseline pack with audit export, retention export, region summary, RBAC export
- PDF/HTML summary + CSV/JSON + manifest

Phase 2:
- Customer-admin generation in Console for Dedicated/Private tenants (feature-flagged)
- Expanded templates and improved wording/limitations

GA criteria:
- Documented runbook for failures
- Standard FAQ and customer-facing doc page published
- Security sign-off on content and access controls
- Backward-compatible versioning strategy implemented

## Risks and mitigations
- Risk: Missing audit event types or inconsistent event naming reduces customer trust.
  - Mitigation: baseline template review with Security; coverage manifest; gap tracking.
- Risk: Export contains sensitive internal fields or customer content.
  - Mitigation: field allowlist for customer bundle; Security review required for new fields.
- Risk: Export generation increases load on audit store.
  - Mitigation: rate limits, batching, async job queue, and SRE-defined guardrails.
- Risk: Confusion between audit logs and request logs.
  - Mitigation: strong definitions in summary; explicit “not included” statements.

## Open questions
1) Which RBAC scopes should be included by default for large enterprises (org-wide vs project/workspace)?
2) Should we include an optional “verification appendix” in customer bundle, or keep strictly internal?
3) For Private deployments, what is the minimum supported packaging mechanism when the customer does not allow outbound storage?

## Appendix: baseline pack naming and storage
- Pack name: Redwood Inference Baseline Compliance Reporting Pack
- Version: baseline.v1 (MVP)
- File naming convention:
  - summary-baseline-v1.pdf (or .html)
  - audit-logs-admin-changes-<start>_<end>.csv
  - audit-logs-admin-changes-<start>_<end>.json
  - retention-config-effective-<timestamp>.json
  - rbac-admins-<timestamp>.csv
  - regions-<timestamp>.json
  - manifest-<timestamp>.json

Ownership
- Product owner: Naomi Feldman
- GRC owner of evidence set: Olga Petrov
- Security sign-off: Dr. Aisha Rahman / Marcus Lin
- Engineering DRI: Kevin Osei

title: dsid_7391d231876446669d62d1e3e939f3ab__incident-evidence-orchestration-for-multi-tenant-model-failures-2026.txt
text:
incident-evidence-orchestration-for-multi-tenant-model-failures-2026

Summary

This playbook defines the evidence orchestration, collection, and packaging process for incidents that originate from model-serving failures in multi-tenant environments. It is focused on preserving chain-of-custody, meeting cross-border data residency constraints, and producing artifacts suitable for internal investigations and external audits.

Scope

- Applies to incidents where a model-serving event affects more than one tenant or where tenant isolation may be implicated (data leakage, cross-tenant inference responses, or authorization bypass).
- Covers services: inference-gateway, model-router, kv-prefix-cache, tokenizer-service, audit-collector, and inference-observability.
- Excludes: single-tenant application errors unrelated to model outputs (those follow standard app incident process).

Key goals

1. Collect a minimal, precise evidence set that establishes timeline, root cause signals, and affected tenants.
2. Maintain strong chain-of-custody and tamper-evident packaging suitable for compliance requests.
3. Respect data residency constraints: evidence extraction should avoid copying regulated customer content outside permitted regions.

Definitions

- Evidence bundle: A sealed archive containing logs, traces, config snapshots, RBAC audits, and migration/rollout metadata for the incident window.
- Sealing manifest: JSON metadata listing file checksums (SHA256), collection timestamps, and collecting agent identity.

Roles and responsibilities

- Incident Commander (IC): Security oncall by default; coordinates cross-team evidence work. Owner: security-oncall@redwood.example.com.
- Forensic Lead: Senior SRE or Security Engineer who performs log extraction and sealing.
- Tenant Liaison: Customer Success engineer assigned for tenant-facing comms if required.
- Legal/Escalation: Security & Legal reviewers for high-sensitivity or cross-border incidents.

Immediate triage checklist (first 30 minutes)

1. IC confirms scope and classifies incident severity.
2. Enable immutable logging window on audit-collector for the affected timeframe (see commands).
3. Capture live snapshots: model-router config, routing-table revision, and active model-versions list.
4. Notify Forensic Lead and open a sealed evidence channel (S3 bucket with restricted policy or on-prem vault).

Collection windows and time bounding

- Primary window: T0-1m to T0+30m (T0 = first observed anomalous request/alert).
- Extended window: T0-24h for related telemetry (rate changes, autoscale events, gating changes).

Service-specific collection checklist

- inference-gateway:
  - Gather: request headers, per-request route decisions, tenant-id, request-id, response-id, and partial streaming deltas where applicable.
  - Command example: curl -X POST "https://infra-admin.internal/v1/diagnostics/search-requests" -d '{"start":"2025-11-15T14:23:00Z","end":"2025-11-15T14:55:00Z","service":"inference-gateway","filters":{"tenant_id":["tenant-A","tenant-B"]}}'

- model-router:
  - Gather: routing-table@revision, rollout flags, fallback-model-mapping, kernel-selection decisions.
  - Snapshot config: /etc/model-router/revisions/<rev>.yaml and /var/log/model-router/decision.log

- kv-prefix-cache:
  - Export: cache-hit/miss counters and exact keys evicted or promoted for the window.
  - Note: do NOT export raw cached payloads if they contain regulated user content; instead export key-level metadata and checksums.

- audit-collector and observability pipeline:
  - Export: raw audit events, ingestion receipts, and downstream archival confirmations. Ensure export includes ingestion-offsets to allow replay.
  - Retain: the original signed ingestion manifest produced by audit-collector.

RBAC and authorization evidence

- Capture RBAC decision logs for the window from the authz-service. Required fields: principal_id, role_bindings_snapshot, resource, action, decision, policy_version.
- If JIT (just-in-time) privilege elevation occurred, include activation token IDs and duration.
- For delegated tokens (e.g., model-to-model calls), include token lineage: parent token id -> child token id -> TTL at issuance.

Data residency / retention mapping (summary table)

- Artifact type | Typical location | Allowed export regions | Retention TTL
- ------------ | ---------------- | ---------------------- | ----------
- Request headers (redacted) | s3://audit-collector-regional/ | same-region only | 90 days
- Traces (service-level) | efs://obs-traces/ | cross-region read allowed via ephemeral access | 30 days
- Raw model outputs (customer content) | encrypted regional blob store | region-only, legal approval required for export | 7 days default
- RBAC decision logs | s3://authz-logs/ | same-region; meta-only copy allowed cross-region | 365 days

Evidence minimization rules

- Default: prefer metadata, checksums, and redacted payloads. Only include raw customer content when strictly required for root cause and only after Legal approval.
- Approved redaction patterns: replace customer PII in JSON strings with <REDACTED-PII> and retain SHA256 checksum of original content (stored separately in sealed manifest).

Chain-of-custody and sealing procedure (numbered steps)

1. Forensic Lead performs targeted extraction using read-only diagnostics APIs. Record exact CLI commands used and operator identity.
2. Create sealing manifest (manifest.json) listing files, SHA256 checksums, collector identity, and UTC timestamps.
3. Compute a signed manifest token using our internal HSM key (hsm-sign manifest.json) and attach signature as manifest.sig.
4. Move artifacts into the incident bucket: s3://incidents/<incident-id>/sealed/ and set bucket-policy to block public access and restrict to evidence-role.
5. Log the S3 object versions and retention locks in the audit-collector.

Tamper-evidence and verification

- All artifacts must include a SHA256 checksum listed in the manifest. Verifiers should re-compute and compare checksums.
- Manifest signature verification example: hsm-verify --key-id hsm-evidence-key --signature manifest.sig manifest.json

Packaging & handoff to Compliance/Legal

- When incident is classified as requiring external report or audit:
  1. IC opens Compliance request ticket and attaches sealed manifest.
  2. Forensic Lead prepares a redaction report describing redaction algorithm and checksums for any removed content.
  3. Legal approves cross-border export if needed and authorizes a one-time ephemeral share link (7-day expiry) with IP allowlist.

Forensic query snippets (for on-call use)

- Kibana-like query for cross-tenant anomalies:
  - service:"inference-gateway" AND response.status:[400 TO 599] AND (tenant_id:"tenant-A" OR tenant_id:"tenant-B") AND @timestamp:[2025-11-15T14:00:00Z TO 2025-11-15T15:00:00Z]

- Authz decision extraction (CLI):
  - authz-cli export-decisions --start "2025-11-15T14:00:00Z" --end "2025-11-15T15:00:00Z" --service model-router --out decisions.csv

Escalation criteria (when to involve legal / executive comms)

- Any evidence that tenant data was delivered to another tenant or external endpoint.
- Any cross-border export request where raw customer content would leave its residency region.
- Material customer outage impacting >5% of instances for >1 hour.

Post-incident evidence review (within 7 days)

- Forensic Lead produces a short evidence report that includes:
  - Timeline of key artifacts and hashes.
  - List of artifacts redacted and reason.
  - RBAC policy changes and rollout history tied to the incident.
  - SLO impact summary (latency error budget, token loss, request failure rate).

Retention and disposal

- Evidence bundles are retained for the minimum compliance TTL required by the most restrictive affected tenant. Default retention: 365 days unless a legal hold is placed.
- Disposal steps: remove S3 versions, expire KMS keys where allowed, and record disposal event in audit-collector with proof-of-deletion checksums.

Automation & tooling notes

- Use the incident-orchestrator service to run standardized extraction playbooks; it will populate manifest.json and optionally sign using the HSM.
- Integrate with the legal-approval service to gate cross-region transfers.

Appendix A - sample sealing manifest (example shown redacted)

{
  "incident_id": "INC-20251115-0234",
  "collected_by": "jared.liu@redwood.example.com",
  "collected_at": "2025-11-15T15:05:12Z",
  "files": ["inference-gateway-requests.log.sha256", "model-router-revision.yaml.sha256"],
  "signature": "<attached-manifest-signature>"
}

Appendix B - contact matrix

- Security oncall (IC): security-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Forensics rotation: forensics-rotation@redwood.example.com
- Legal escalation: legal-escalations@redwood.example.com
- Customer success (tenant liaison): cs-liaison@redwood.example.com

Related pages and references

- See: /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/just-in-time-privilege-activation-and-audit-evidence-2025 for RBAC logging schema.
- See: /confluence/security-and-compliance/compliance-evidence/evidence-orchestration-for-model-serving-governance-2026 for policy-level evidence packaging guidance.

Change history

- 2025-11-15: Draft created by Jared Liu.
- 2025-12-03: Forensic extraction commands standardized by Maya Chen.
- 2026-01-20: Legal-approved cross-border gating and ephemeral share process added.

title: dsid_f81901cb01e74214a84c540e6c3a14cf__offline-artifact-delivery-and-model-refresh-runbook-2026.txt
text:
Offline artifact delivery and model refresh operator runbook

Summary

This runbook describes the operator-level steps, verification checks, and rollback procedures for delivering model artifacts to air-gapped or VPC-private Redwood Private deployments and performing a safe model refresh (hot-swap or staged rollout). It covers secure artifact packaging, transport validation, HSM/KMS verification, on-host ingestion, staged rollout patterns, automated health checks, and troubleshooting. Intended audience: field operators, platform engineers, and customer SREs running private deployments.

Goals and SLOs

- Goal: Replace a model bundle in an offline/private environment with minimal downtime and provable integrity.
- SLO: Model refresh completion within the operator maintenance window (default 30 minutes for small changes, 90 minutes for full model swap) 95% of the time.
- Safety constraints: No automatic switch to a new artifact unless all verification gates pass.

Ownership

- Primary executor: Field Operator / Platform Engineer (on-call operator).
- Reviewer/approver: Deployment Custodian (customer or Redwood field lead).
- Backup: Remote Escalation to Redwood Private Deployments team (pager).

Prerequisites and environment checklist

1) Pre-flight (remote before artifact export):
   - Confirm approved change request: CR-ID (vendor or customer) and signed acceptance.
   - Verify package manifest and signed digest are present in the artifacts registry (S3, GCS, or internal registry).
   - Ensure operator has the following: dev laptop with USB-A/USB-C transfer tools, signed access token (expiration >= 6 hours), and the vendor-supplied manifest.

2) Target environment (on-prem or VPC):
   - KV-store (redis) and serving runtime versions must match compatibility matrix (see Compatibility table below).
   - Node-level disk free >= 50GB (recommended) and memory headroom for model load (see resource table).
   - HSM/KMS accessible: either network HSM (for VPC) or local hardware token (for airgapped sites) with operator key escrow details.

Compatibility table (example)

| Component | Minimum supported | Verified for this run | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Serving runtime | 1.8.2 | 1.9.0 | Runtime picks specific kernels for quantized models |
| KV cache format | v2 | v2 | v2->v3 migrations require pre-warm step |
| Model bundle format | rbf-2025-10 | rbf-2026-01 | rbf-2026-01 supports delta patches |
| On-host agent | 3.4.x | 3.4.1 | Feature flag for atomic-swap required |

Artifact packaging requirements

Each model bundle must include the following files at top level of the artifact tarball (.tar.gz or .zip):
- model.bin (binary weights or shard list)
- model.metadata.json (see example below)
- model.manifest.sig (detached signature; signed by Redwood release key or customer-signed key)
- checksums.sha256 (SHA-256 sums of artifact contents)
- compatibility.txt (runtime and kv-cache constraints)

Example model.metadata.json (operator should validate locally):

```
{
  "model_name": "rw-opt-13b-q4_0",
  "variant": "quantized-q4_0",
  "version": "2026-05-01",
  "shards": 4,
  "size_bytes": 14000000000,
  "created_by": "redwood-release-bot@redwood.ai",
  "notes": "delta-patch-ready"
}
```

Transport and delivery patterns

There are three recommended delivery methods depending on customer connectivity:

A) Encrypted network transfer (VPC with egress to secured artifact gateway):
   - Use the internal artifact gateway with TLS mutual auth. Transfer command (example):

   curl --key operator.key.pem --cert operator.crt.pem --cacert gateway-ca.pem \
     -F "artifact=@/tmp/rw-opt-13b-q4_0-2026-05-01.tar.gz" \
     https://artifact-gateway.internal.redwood/api/v1/upload

   - Verify gateway returned upload_id and that server-side checksum matches checksums.sha256.

B) Physical transfer (airgapped sites):
   1. Export artifact from build farm to an encrypted thumbdrive using vendor tooling. Use LUKS or BitLocker with a randomly generated passphrase exchanged via an out-of-band channel (phone or secure chat with OTP).
   2. Maintain chain-of-custody log: operator name, time, thumbdrive ID, CRC of transfer.

C) Shuttle appliance (for large datasets > 100GB):
   - Use Redwood-certified shuttle appliance. Follow appliance manifest signing flow and use the provided transfer client (shuttle-client v2+).

Signature and integrity verification (mandatory)

All artifact arrivals must pass cryptographic checks before ingestion. Steps: 
1) Verify checksums: `sha256sum -c checksums.sha256` should report `OK` for every file.
2) Verify detached signature: `openssl cms -verify -in model.manifest.sig -content model.metadata.json -CAfile release-certs.pem` (or use `gpg --verify` for GPG-signed manifests).
3) Verify manifest fields against a local allowlist (expected model_name, version range, shard count).
4) HSM/KMS verification: if the artifact is encrypted with customer key, run `kms-client decrypt --key-id alias/customer-model-key --input model.bin.enc --output model.bin` and validate HMAC in `checksums.sha256`.

On-host ingestion sequence (safe mode)

1) Quiesce new traffic: set runtime flag `--accept-new-models=false` and drain short-lived requests. This preserves in-flight responses and keeps cold starts predictable.
2) Create a staging directory with unique timestamp: `/var/lib/redwood/staging/model-2026-05-01-timestamp/`
3) Copy artifact to staging and run verification steps from previous section on-host.
4) Unpack into staging and run container-level smoke load: `./bin/model-verify --warm --max-requests 20 --kv-preload` (the agent provides this helper). Expected exit code 0.
5) Validate runtime telemetry: check `model_load_time < 60s` and `initial_memory_rss < 90% of node free memory` in agent logs.

Staged rollout patterns (choose one)

A) Canary (recommended for critical customers):
   1. Add new model to the runtime but keep traffic weight = 0.
   2. Configure synthetic traffic generator to send 1% of production-equivalent traffic (10 qps or min(1% of avg qps, 20 qps)).
   3. Observe SLOs for 30 minutes: latency p95 < 2x baseline, error rate < 0.5%.
   4. If stable, increase weight in exponential steps (1%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%) with 15–30 minute observation windows.

B) Atomic swap (fast path for non-breaking quantization fallback):
   - Perform a single atomic endpoint switch after pre-warm. Requires `--atomic-swap` enabled. Backup snapshot is kept for 15 minutes before garbage collection.

Automated health checks and telemetry gating (must pass before advancing)

- Health checks: `model_ready` metric, `kv_cache_hit_ratio > 0.6`, `latency_p95 < baseline * 1.5`, `error_rate < baseline + 0.25%`.
- Telemetry sources: per-node agent, control-plane trace, and synthetic client.
- Gate: all checks must be green for two consecutive windows to proceed.

Rollback and emergency backout

Immediate rollback (fast):
1) If canary/atomic swap fails, immediately set traffic weight back to previous model (control-plane API call). Example API call: 

POST https://control-plane.internal.redwood/api/v1/models/{endpoint}/traffic-shift
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "from": "rw-opt-13b-q4_0:2026-05-01",
  "to": "rw-opt-13b-q4_0:2026-04-15",
  "weight": 100
}

2) If node-level memory pressure or OOM observed, execute emergency kill (on operator judgement) and restart runtime with previous snapshot: `systemctl restart redwood-runtime && /usr/local/bin/redwood-restore --snapshot /var/backups/model-snapshot-2026-04-15.tar.gz`

Forensic evidence collection (post-failure)

- Save staging directory, `/var/log/redwood/agent.log` (last 5000 lines), and `journalctl -u redwood-runtime --since "-2h" > /tmp/runtime-journal.log`.
- Preserve checksums and manifest, and forward to Redwood forensic bucket (via secured transfer) within the customer-approved retention policy.

Operator checklist (short)

1) Confirm CR and maintenance window.
2) Validate artifact signature and checksums.
3) Quiesce new connections and stage artifact.
4) Run container smoke tests and telemetry validations.
5) Execute canary or atomic swap as per policy.
6) Observe telemetry gates, then ramp to 100% if green.
7) If failure, perform rollback steps and collect forensic data.

Troubleshooting and common failure modes

- Failed signature verification: ensure operator has the correct release-certs.pem. If missing, escalate to Release Engineering.
- HSM decryption timeout: Check network path to KMS, verify operator token validity, and re-run with `--kms-retry 3`.
- High cold-start latency: ensure KV preload completed and increase pre-warm threads `--prewarm-threads` by +2.
- Serving runtime rejects shards: verify `shards` count in model.metadata.json and confirm shard placement in `/etc/redwood/shard-map.json`

Audit and evidence log format (minimum fields)

- operator, timestamp (UTC), artifact_id, transfer_method, signature_key_id, preflight_checks_passed (true/false), canary_result (pass/fail), rollback_invoked (true/false)

Sample audit line (CSV)

operator,timestamp,artifact_id,transfer_method,signature_key_id,preflight_checks_passed,canary_result,rollback_invoked
mtthompson,2026-05-12T11:05:12Z,rw-opt-13b-q4_0-2026-05-01,physical,B2F3-RELEASE-2026,true,pass,false

Related pages and references

- KMS/HSM operator quick reference (internal link)

Appendix: quick commands

Verify checksum:
sha256sum -c checksums.sha256

Verify signature (CMS):
openssl cms -verify -in model.manifest.sig -content model.metadata.json -CAfile /etc/redwood/release-certs.pem -out /dev/null && echo "signature OK"

Unpack into staging and run verify helper:
mkdir -p /var/lib/redwood/staging/model-2026-05-01-timestamp && tar -xzvf /tmp/artifact.tar.gz -C /var/lib/redwood/staging/model-2026-05-01-timestamp && /usr/local/bin/model-verify --path /var/lib/redwood/staging/model-2026-05-01-timestamp
