4) Secure storage: move the archive to the restricted evidence S3 with bucket-policy: deny-delete-unless-role:legal_audit.

Special considerations by deployment type:
- VPC (customer-attached bucket):
  - Ensure export job uses the customer-approved encryption key.
  - Confirm network egress rule allows telemetry export to the bucket; if not, use the edge-proxy relay pattern.
  - Coordinate with customer security contact before moving evidence off-network where required by contract.
- On-prem / Airgapped:
  - Use local-attested USB transfer procedure only after signing and storing checksums in the control-plane ledger.
  - Maintain chain-of-custody paper or digitally-signed receipts for physical transfers.

KV cache and model artifact specifics:
- Rolling back a model that requires a changed KV cache schema requires a two-phase approach: first, restore service to stable model and keep both schema-compatibility adapters active; second, run adapter-based reconciliation across tenants for 48–72 hours before deprecating the old adapter.
- Avoid purging KV epochs until reconciliation is complete. If storage pressure requires pruning, take snapshots and store in the evidence bucket with explicit ledger references.

Interaction with customer requirements and SLAs:
- If rollback affects committed SLA windows, follow the customer compensation matrix and notify Customer Success.
- For regulated customers (finance/healthcare), follow the additional evidence preservation checklist in the Customer Requirements Library (see Related pages).

Runbook snippets and CLI examples:
- Trigger full telemetry sample: rwdctl telemetry sample --scope incident --enable true --duration 2h
- Export evidence: rwdctl evidence export --prefix evidence/rollback/${CUSTOMER}/${ID} --include logs,traces,artifacts --encrypt-kms arn:aws:kms:us-west-2:1234:key/abcd
- Roll back runtime image (canary-aware): rwdctl rollout rollback --service serving-runtime --to-tag v2026.01.10-stable --max-in-flight 2

Post-rollback steps and postmortem:
1) Keep monitoring elevated for 72 hours; collect SLO/quality metrics and compare to pre-incident baseline.
2) Populate postmortem with: timeline, root-cause hypothesis, decision justification for rollback, evidence ledger entries, and remediation action items.
3) If rollback should be automated for similar failures, open a design ticket for a safe-automation RFC and schedule a canary test.

Appendix A — Minimal evidence metadata table:
| artifact | required fields | retention (default) | notes |
| control-plane-snapshot | revision, timestamp, operator | 2 years | include config and feature flags |
| model-artifact | checksum, manifest, provenance | 3 years | include model-card with eval snapshot |
| telemetry-archive | sha256, start/end, redact-policy | 2 years | store redaction policy reference |
| kv-snapshot | shard-id, epoch, checksum | 3 years | required for regulated tenants |

Related pages and references:
- See: customer-requirements-library/private-deploy-acceptance-and-smoke-validation-2026 (telemetry and evidence contracts)
- See: upgrade-and-rollback/private-deploy-evidence-preservation-and-forensic-playbook-2026 (detailed forensic scripts)
- See: day-2-ops/private-deploy-livetail-and-debugging-runbook-2026 (live debugging and elevated telemetry patterns)

Contact and ownership:
- Document owner: eng-private-deployments (oncall@redwood.com).
- For legal/evidence escalation: legal-evidence@redwood.com.

Change history:
- 2026-02-15: created by Priya Malhotra
- 2026-03-01: updated verification checklist and VPC evidence notes (reviewers: David Chen, Aisha Gomez)

title: dsid_87218372cdd24e5584eb9be8609a6447__slo-harmonization-progressive-throttle-handbook-2026.txt
text:
SLO harmonization and progressive throttling handbook: tenant fairness & burst variance

Summary:
This handbook defines a cross-service approach for harmonizing SLOs across heterogeneous inference workloads, handling burst variance without destabilizing the fleet, and implementing a progressive throttling controller that enforces tenant fairness. It combines capacity budgeting, proportional error-budget gating, and a gradual throttling algorithm to preserve critical customer SLOs while preventing noisy-neighbor cascades.

Intended audience:
- SREs and Platform Engineers responsible for multi-tenant capacity
- Oncall responders handling SLO regressions and throttling events
- Product and Customer Reliability partners who negotiate SLO contracts

Goals:
- Provide a repeatable process for aligning individual service SLOs with global capacity constraints
- Ensure predictable, auditable throttling decisions with tenant fairness guarantees
- Reduce incident surface caused by bursty tenants while limiting user-visible degradation

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to Redwood public-hosted inference endpoints, Dedicated pools, and Private VPC routable clusters (where platform-level throttling exists)
- Focus on multi-tenant GPU-backed text generation and embedding workloads with token-based billing
- Not intended for single-tenant Dedicated reservations or external partner on-prem appliances that enforce customer-managed throttles

Definitions and primitives:
- SLO window: 7d rolling for availability and latency; 30d for throughput/quality metrics (unless contract specifies otherwise)
- Error budget (EB): 1 - SLO (e.g., for 99.95% availability EB = 0.0005)
- EB burn rate: current_window_error_rate / allowed_error_rate over evaluation window (typically 1h, 6h, 24h)
- Headroom tokens: reserved capacity (tokens/sec) buffer kept for priority tenants and emergency flows
- Burst variance: measured as coefficient of variation (stddev/mean) over 5m windows of token/sec per-tenant
- Fairshare weight: per-tenant scalar (configured in tenancy registry) used when proportional throttling is needed

High-level approach:
1) SLO harmonization: translate per-tenant SLO commitments into a capacity contract that maps to token/sec budgets and priority tiers.
2) Capacity budgeting: compute baseline capacity, headroom, and emergency reserve. Use predictive shadowing to model expected bursts for the next 72h.
3) Progressive throttling: when aggregate consumption threatens capacity or EB burn thresholds are crossed, apply a staged throttle that is proportional to recent consumption and weighted by fairshare.
4) Observability and review: every throttle action is logged, traced to an oncall page, and included in the post-incident SLO review if EB impact exceeds thresholds.

SLO harmonization procedure (operational):
1. Gather commitments: product teams register SLOs in the SLO registry. Required fields: SLO target, primary metric (latency/error/availability), tenant_id, fairshare_weight, peak_profile (tokens/sec 95th/99th).
2. Normalize metrics: map product-level metrics to platform metrics (examples below).
   - Service latency (p95): service.{tenant_id}.latency_ms.p95
   - Token throughput: service.{tenant_id}.tokens.per_minute
   - Availability: service.{tenant_id}.request_success_ratio
3. Compute per-tenant budget: use 95th percentile peak_profile and multiply by target headroom factor (default 1.2) to produce allocated token/sec budget.
4. Conflict detection: run daily harmonization job that flags when sum(allocated budgets) > available_capacity * (1 - reserved_headroom). Flagged items create negotiation tickets.
5. Escalation: if negotiation fails within SLA (72h for minor, 7d for major), platform enforces temporary proportional reductions (see progressive throttling) until a contract is agreed.

Capacity budgeting details (calculation table):
- Inputs:
  - cluster_total_tokens_per_sec = measured effective token throughput for cluster (e.g., 120k tokens/sec)
  - reserved_headroom_pct = 12% (default)
  - emergency_reserve_tokens = 5k tokens/sec (configured)
- Derived allocations example (text table):
  - available_for_alloc = cluster_total_tokens_per_sec * (1 - reserved_headroom_pct) - emergency_reserve_tokens
  - tenant_alloc_i = min(requested_95th_i * 1.2, available_for_alloc * fairshare_weight_i / sum(fairshare_weights))

Handling burst variance:
- Measure per-tenant burst_window CV over rolling 5m windows.
- If CV > 2.0 for tenant X and tenant_alloc_x > 0.2 * available_for_alloc, mark tenant as "high-variance" and require a burst mitigation policy: lower peak cap OR enable preemptible queueing.
- Preemptible queueing: non-priority requests are queued for up to 10s with token-level hints; queue eviction is proportional to fairshare.

Progressive throttling algorithm (pseudocode):
1) Trigger conditions:
   - cluster_free_tokens < throttle_trigger_tokens (default: 8% of cluster_total_tokens_per_sec) OR
   - global_error_budget_burn_rate > 3x for 1h window
2) Determine throttleable population: tenants with fairshare_weight < priority_threshold OR tenants currently consuming > 110% of allocated budget for 10m
3) Compute proportional reduction R_i = clamp(0, 1, alpha * (consumption_i / alloc_i - 1)) where alpha is ramp factor (initial 0.5)
4) Apply staged ramp: R_i applied at 10s; re-evaluate every 30s and increase alpha by 0.25 each step up to 1.0 if aggregate free tokens remain below target
5) Grace for priority traffic: high-priority tenants see R_i scaled by (1 - priority_discount) where priority_discount ∈ {0.5, 0.7} depending on negotiated tier
6) Enforcement modalities: token-rejection (HTTP 429 with Retry-After), queueing, or shedding non-critical features (feature flags).

Example throttling HTTP response (JSON):
{"error":"throttled","reason":"progressive_congestion","retry_after_seconds":30,"tenant_alloc":"1200 tokens/sec"}

Traceability and audit logs:
- Every decision must produce an immutable throttle-event with fields: event_id, timestamp, trigger_reason, tenants_impacted, aggregate_free_tokens, applied_reductions, operator (auto or manual), runbook_version.
- Throttle-event must be persisted to service.audit.throttles (retention 90d) and indexed for rapid lookup in the Console (throttle-inspector).

Monitoring, alerts and dashboards:
- Core metrics to monitor:
  - cluster.tokens.free (tokens/sec free)
  - service.{tenant}.tokens.consumed.p95 (5m)
  - service.{tenant}.error_budget.burn_rate.1h
  - throttle_events.count and throttle_events.latency_impact
- Alerting primitives:
  - P1: cluster.tokens.free < 4% for 15m -> page SRE oncall, run emergency_capacity_playbook
  - P2: single-tenant EB burn_rate > 10x for 1h -> notify tenant owner and SRE steward
  - P3: progressive throttle active > 30m -> create auto-ticket for product/sre sync
- Dashboard: harmonization view showing allocated vs consumed, per-tenant CV heatmap, throttle events stream, and predictive headroom forecast for 72h.

Runbook: oncall actions when progressive throttling triggers:
1. Acknowledge pager and open a dedicated incident channel (prefix: THROTTLE-<cluster>-<time>)
2. Consult harmonization dashboard and throttle-event details using event_id from alert
3. Evaluate if a manual override is required: check emergency reserve and immediate customer-impacting tenants
4. If manual override granted: reduce alpha or disable ramp for specific tenant(s); record reason and ETA for revert
5. Notify product/CS owners for highest impacted tenants with ETA and mitigation steps
6. Execute mitigation sequence if required (examples below)

Mitigation examples and quick fixes:
- Rapid temporary scale-up: if cloud quota allows, spin up additional serving capacity (make/runbooks/scale-up-quickstart) and set temporary allocation_policy = "shadow-scale".
- Non-critical feature shedding: toggle feature flag to bypass heavy generation paths for top consumers.
- Emergency token credit: apply short-term extra tokens to a priority tenant from emergency_reserve and reduce others proportionally; requires approval from SRE lead.

Incident review and postmortem linkage:
- Threshold for incident review: any progressive throttle that causes >0.5% SLO delta for a paying tenant for >1h or any manual override approved during a throttle event.
- Review artifacts required:
  - throttle-event record, harmonization state snapshot, capacity forecast at time of event, root-cause hypothesis, and corrective actions
- Review checklist:
  1. Confirm trigger pathology (burst vs CPU OOM vs kernel scheduling)
  2. Validate correctness of fairshare weights and allocations
  3. Identify needed product or contract changes (e.g., change SLO window or reserve)
  4. Track action items and assign owner with target completion date

Operational tooling and automations:
- Harmonization job: nightly job (harmonize-slos) that produces negotiation tickets for overcommit scenarios and publishes alloc snapshot to service.storage.allocations/{date}.json
- Throttle controller: kube-managed service (throttle-controller) with leader election; default reconciliation interval 30s; exposes /debug/decisions and /metrics
- Throttle-inspector: Console plugin to visualize throttle-events and runbook links; supports ad-hoc replays against a shadow cluster

Ownership and governance:
- Primary owner: SRE Platform Team (oncall: eng-sre)
- SLO registry and tenant weight edits: Product + Platform joint approval (change request through ticketing system)
- Emergency reserve budget changes: requires SRE lead + Finance approval for Dedicated capacity changes

Change log:
- 2026-04-10: created initial harmonization and capacity budgeting framework (Aisha Kapoor)
- 2026-05-12: added progressive throttling ramp algorithm and queueing guidelines (Liam Chen)
- 2026-06-15: formalized incident review linkage and audit logging requirements (Mariana Ortiz)

References and related pages:
- service-onboarding/slo-registration-template (internal link id: CONFL-8021)
- eng-sre/runbooks/emergency-capacity-playbook-2026 (CONFL-5102)
- eng-sre/operational-tooling/throttle-controller-design (CONFL-7743)
- console/throttle-inspector-design-doc (CONFL-8812)

Known limitations and future work:
- Current model assumes token/sec linearity; non-linear model behaviors (long-context generation, tool calling) need specialized accounting.
- Fairshare weight tuning requires periodic calibration; propose quarterly calibration runs that include product stakeholders.
- Integrate model-quality SLOs into harmonization to avoid prioritizing throughput over correctness.

Appendix: example allocation snapshot (CSV style)
tenant_id,fairshare_weight,requested_95th_tokens_per_sec,allocated_tokens_per_sec,variance_cv
acme-photos,1.0,1200,1100,0.8
notion-lite,0.6,800,720,1.6
research-lab,0.3,400,360,2.8
partner-x,0.1,200,180,1.2

Contact:
- SRE Platform Slack: #sre-platform
- SRE Steward rotation calendar: internal link CONFL-CAL-STEWARD

End of handbook.

title: dsid_975eec8599794dfa9137f62d32617a54__third-party-accelerator-compatibility-and-dependency-matrix-2026.txt
text:
Third-party accelerator compatibility and dependency matrix (compatibility manifest)

Summary:
This page is the canonical compatibility and dependency matrix for third-party accelerators that the runtime supports or plans to support. It codifies driver/runtime/library versions, expected kernel features, known incompatibilities, required CI smoke tests, ownership, and an automated manifest format (JSON) used by our onboarding toolchain. Use this when: planning support for a new accelerator, triaging inference regressions on a new hardware class, or validating release gates before a runtime rollout.

Goals:
- Capture the minimal set of platform packages (drivers, runtimes, libs) required for the serving runtime to deliver production SLOs.
- Provide reproducible test matrix entries used by CI and the hardware lab.
- Surface common failure modes and triage steps specific to each vendor.
- Define rollback and mitigation procedures when a hardware-specific kernel or driver causes regressions.

Scope and conventions:
- This document covers: NVIDIA (CUDA/NVML/NCCL), AMD (ROCm/MIOpen), AWS accelerators (Inferentia/Trainium), Intel/OneAPI-backed accelerators, Graphcore/Poplar, and other partner ASICs where we have lab access.
- Each matrix row includes: vendor, model family, required host kernel ABI, driver/runtime version range, critical libraries, recommended Docker base images, CI test IDs, owner, and known-risk flags.
- Version ranges are inclusive. Entries marked "experimental" must pass the experimental-canary CI suite, not just the smoke suite.

Compatibility matrix (text table):
Note: use this table as a quick reference. The source-of-truth is the JSON manifest in the repository at infra/accelerator-manifests/compatibility-manifest.json.

| Vendor | Family / Models | Host kernel ABI | Driver / Runtime | Critical libs / plugins | Recommended image tag | CI test(s) | Owner | Risk notes |
|--------|------------------|-----------------|------------------|-------------------------|------------------------|-----------|-------|------------|
| NVIDIA | A100, H100 (Tensor) | linux-5.15+ (glibc ABI stable) | CUDA 12.2 - 12.4, NVIDIA driver 535+ | cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL, NVML | redwood/runtime-nvidia:cuda12.4-rt-2026 | ci-accel-nvidia-smoke, ci-nvlink-stress | runtime-hw | NVLink firmware mismatch causes memory teleport errors (see known issues) |
| AMD | MI250, MI300 | linux-5.15+ (ROCm-ready ABI) | ROCm 5.8 - 6.0 | MIOpen, ROCm NCCL-compatible libs | redwood/runtime-amd:rocm5.8-rt-2026 | ci-accel-amd-smoke, ci-rocm-memory-fft | runtime-hw | GPU page table fragmentation risk under high concurrency |
| AWS | Inferentia | linux-5.10+ (aws kernel) | Neuron SDK 2.3+ | neuron-libs, neuron-runtime | redwood/runtime-aws:neuron2.3-rt | ci-aws-inferentia-smoke | platform-partner | Binary ABI for Neuron is sensitive to compiler flags; require vendor-signed kernels |
| Intel | Gaudi/ Habana (Partner) | linux-5.15+ | Poplar / OneAPI stacks | poplar-rt, onednn | redwood/runtime-intel:oneapi-2026-rt | ci-intel-accel-smoke | runtime-hw | Driver installer writes kernel modules to non-standard paths; watch mknod/udev permissions |
| Graphcore | IPU-M2000 | linux-5.15+ | Poplar 2.x series | poplar-plugins | redwood/runtime-ipu:poplar2-rt | ci-ipu-smoke | runtime-hw | High cold-start memory usage; require warmup harness |

(For an up-to-date machine-readable matrix, see infra/accelerator-manifests/compatibility-manifest.json in the infra repo.)

Manifest format (example JSON snippet):
This is the canonical object the onboarding automation consumes. Store one file per vendor-family in infra/accelerator-manifests/.

{
  "vendor": "nvidia",
  "family": "h100",
  "models": ["h100-sxm", "h100-pcie"],
  "host_kernel_min": "5.15",
  "driver_version_range": "12.2:12.4",
  "required_packages": ["nvidia-driver>=535", "cuda-toolkit>=12.2", "libnccl>=2.15"],
  "recommended_image": "redwood/runtime-nvidia:cuda12.4-rt-2026",
  "ci_gate": "ci-accel-nvidia-smoke",
  "risk_flags": ["nvlink_firmware_sensitivity"]
}
(When editing the manifest, increment the manifest_version field and attach the matching lab test run id.)

CI and lab test design:
- Smoke suite (ci-*-smoke): quick boot, telemetry, single-request inference for canonical models, KV cache sanity, and basic memory pressure. Completes in < 5 minutes per node. Required for all PRs that touch runtime scheduler or kernel selection.
- Stress suite (ci-*-stress): multi-concurrency sustained runs, NVLink/PCIe saturation tests, rendezvous N random seeds to detect numerical drift. Runs in ~2 hours across our lab pool. Used for release gating on major driver bumps.
- Fidelity suite (ci-*-fidelity): compares output distributions against golden corpora, quantization toggles, and mixed-precision paths. Used when enabling quantization profiles.

CI matrix YAML example (used by our GitHub Actions):

name: Accelerator Compatibility Matrix
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  matrix-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-22.04
    strategy:
      matrix:
        vendor: [nvidia, amd, aws]
        model_family: [h100, a100, mi300, inferentia]
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Launch lab node (or mock)
        run: ./infra/labctl/launch_node --vendor ${{ matrix.vendor }} --family ${{ matrix.model_family }}
      - name: Run smoke tests
        run: ./infra/ci/run_compatibility_smoke.sh --manifest infra/accelerator-manifests/${{ matrix.vendor }}-${{ matrix.model_family }}.json

Known failure modes and triage playbook (quick reference):
1) Driver mismatch at startup (symptoms: driver load failures, NVML unavailable, crate reports "missing kernel symbols").
   - Commands: sudo dmesg | tail -n 200; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version --format=csv; rocminfo; sudo modinfo nvidia
   - If driver ABI mismatch: pin to the last known-good driver (see infra/accelerator-manifests/last-known-good) and trigger a canary rollout.
2) NVLink firmware mismatch (symptoms: inter-GPU copy hang, elevated kernel errors, OOMs during large KV cache warmups).
   - Triage: check nvidia-smi -q -d LINK; check firmware version table in infra/hardware-inventory/firmware.csv. If mismatch detected: set scheduling policy to avoid cross-socket NVLink paths (see mitigation below) and file an infra ticket for firmware alignment.
3) Host kernel OOPS when loading vendor kernel modules (symptoms: kernel oops, machine reboots, module load stacktrace).
   - Triage: capture vmcore if possible; collect /var/log/kern.log; isolate kernel version and report to partner. Revert kernel update and boot previous AMI.
4) Inference numerical drift after driver update (symptoms: fidelity alerts, increased model perplexity).
   - Triage: run ci-*-fidelity suite on the same commit+driver to confirm; if deterministic, mark driver as blocked for quantized paths and force fallback to float kernels; open follow-up with research and vendor.

Mitigations and operational knobs:
- Scheduler-level mitigation: 'evict-across-nvlink' boolean in scheduling profiles. When true, the scheduler will prefer cross-socket placement only for requests that are tagged as high-throughput and tolerant of additional latency.
- Kernel selection fallback: runtime keeps a per-node kernel-hint file produced by the onboarding manifest. If a kernel path is missing at startup, runtime will: 1) degrade to a compatible kernel plugin (if available), 2) reduce concurrency quota for the tenant, and 3) emit an operational alert with a suggested rollback.
- Container image pinning: all production pools use image digests (sha256) instead of tags. The manifest includes recommended image digests under recommended_image_digest.

Rollback and canary process for driver/runtime changes:
1) Staging validation: the proposed driver/runtime version must pass the smoke and stress suites in staging (staging-lab with 3 nodes) and not regress more than 1% on 95th p99 latency for canonical prompts.
2) Canary: roll to 5% of production traffic in a single region with canary telemetry enabled. Observe per-model fidelity metrics for 24 hours.
3) Rollback criteria: any of the following triggers a rollback: p99 latency increase >10% vs baseline, fidelity regression >0.5% for golden prompts, GPU hardware errors >0.1% of requests.
4) Rollback steps (operator):
   - Set scheduling policy to avoid affected pool(s): curl -X POST $RUNTIME_API/pools/scale -d '{"pool":"h100-rt-prod","target":0.9}'
   - Trigger node drain: infra/labctl/drain_node --node h100-rt-12
   - Re-image node with last-known-good driver image: infra/ami-bootstrap/reimage --ami ami-xyz --manifest infra/accelerator-manifests/last-known-good/nvidia-h100.json
   - Monitor: validate smoke-suite; close incident if green.

Ownership and contact matrix (text):
- runtime-hw (owner): Priya Nambiar, Luis Ortega — Responsible for manifests, smoke tests, and lab coordination.
- infra (owner): Jonah Park — Responsible for AMIs, kernel builds, and lab node boots.
- research/applied-ml: Maya Chen — Responsible for fidelity suite, golden corpora, and drift triage.
- platform-partner: Partner PM / Partner Eng — vendor-specific escalation.

Lab checklist before declaring full support:
1) Run full stress and fidelity suites for 48 hours across 3 nodes.
2) Validate billing/chargeback hooks for the pool (cost attribution).
3) Document warmup and eviction behaviors in the runtime pool README.
4) Add entries to hardware-inventory, include firmware and BIOS versions.

Operational examples and debug commands (cheat sheet):
- Check basic GPU health (NVIDIA): nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY,UTILIZATION,LINK
- Check NVLink details: nvidia-smi -q -d LINK | egrep -A4 "Link"
- ROCm diagnostics: /opt/rocm/bin/rocminfo; /opt/rocm/bin/rocm-smi -d 0 --showtemp
- Container runtime test: docker run --rm --gpus all --privileged redwood/runtime-nvidia:cuda12.4-rt-2026 nvidia-smi -L
- Kernel module info: sudo modinfo nvidia | head -n 40

Appendix A — Example compatibility test case (text):
- Test id: ci-accel-nvidia-smoke-001
- Purpose: Validate A100/H100 basic inference path and KV cache warmup under 8 concurrent workers.
- Steps:
  1) Boot node with manifest infra/accelerator-manifests/nvidia-h100.json
  2) Pull recommended image digest and run containerized test harness: infra/ci/harness/run_infer_test.sh --image sha256:abcd... --concurrency 8 --model gpt-redwood-small
  3) Assert: 95th latency < 200ms, memory growth < 2GB/worker after 30s warmup, no GPU driver errors in dmesg.

Appendix B — How to update this manifest:
1) Edit infra/accelerator-manifests/<vendor>-<family>.json and bump manifest_version.
2) Run ./infra/ci/run_compatibility_smoke.sh --manifest <path> locally against a mock node or in the lab.
3) Create a PR against infra with the manifest and the lab run id attached. Tag runtime-hw and infra teams as reviewers.

Change log (brief):
- 2026-05-12: initial published manifest and CI matrix (Priya Nambiar).
- 2026-08-16: added ROCm 5.8 compatibility entries and stress test IDs (Luis Ortega).
- 2026-10-03: added Graphcore IPU entry and expanded rollback procedure (Priya Nambiar).

title: dsid_007f9c5d6d1f4fb5bfbc8b187a6c0921__node-configuration-baseline-gpu-workers.txt
text:
Node Configuration Baseline: GPU Worker Nodes

## Purpose
This page defines the **baseline configuration** for Kubernetes GPU worker nodes used for Redwood Inference inference workloads (Hosted, Dedicated, and Private when running the Redwood-supported k8s topology).

The goals of this baseline are:
- Ensure nodes are **repeatable** across regions and GPU types.
- Minimize post-provision break/fix by enforcing known-good settings.
- Make node readiness **machine-verifiable** via automated validation gates (Provision-to-Ready).

This baseline is implemented via:
- **Golden GPU images** (drivers/CUDA/NCCL + OS hardening)
- **Terraform/cluster bootstrap** (disk layout, instance metadata, tags)
- **Node validation agent** (DaemonSet) + control-plane readiness state integration

## Scope
Applies to:
- GPU worker nodes in Redwood-managed clusters used for inference serving.

Out of scope:
- Control plane nodes
- Specialized research/training clusters
- Major scheduler design changes

## Ownership and change management
**Owner:** Infra/Fleet

Changes to this baseline require:
1) Update to golden image pipeline and/or Helm values
2) Validation rule updates (if applicable)
3) Staged rollout by region/GPU type

For any change that affects correctness or fleet stability, coordinate with SRE for alerting/rollback triggers.

---

## Baseline requirements (must-have)
The following settings are **required**. Deviations require an approved exception.

### 1) Operating system + kernel baseline
**OS:** Ubuntu LTS (golden image pinned; see image channel policy)

**Kernel:** Must meet the minimum supported version for the image channel. Do not mix kernel major versions within a pool during a staged rollout.

**Kernel modules (required where applicable):**
- `nvidia`, `nvidia_uvm`, `nvidia_peermem` (if RDMA/GPUDirect required)
- Filesystem driver for chosen layout (ext4 or xfs)

**Kernel parameters (GRUB / cmdline) (required):**
- `cgroup_enable=memory` (if not default for distro)
- `swapaccount=1` (if required by kubelet enforcement)
- `transparent_hugepage=never` (preferred for latency stability)

**Sysctl baseline (required):**
- `vm.swappiness = 0`
- `fs.file-max = 2097152`
- `net.core.somaxconn = 65535`
- `net.core.netdev_max_backlog = 16384`
- `net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 16384`
- `net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range = 10240 65535`
- `net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 1048576`

**Swap:** must be disabled.

Validation (automated):
- Swap disabled
- Kernel cmdline includes required flags
- Sysctl values match baseline (within tolerance where indicated)

### 2) Time synchronization
Accurate time is required for:
- TLS/auth token verification
- Distributed tracing ordering
- SLO/SLI calculations for time-to-ready

**Required:**
- `chrony` enabled and configured to use Redwood-approved NTP sources
- NTP drift must be stable (no frequent step changes)

**Acceptance thresholds:**
- Clock offset <= **100ms** (steady-state)
- `chronyc tracking` reports synchronized (`Leap status: Normal`)

Validation (automated):
- Chrony service running
- Offset within threshold at validation time

### 3) Container runtime configuration
**Runtime:** containerd (Redwood-managed version pinned per image channel)

**cgroup driver:** systemd

**Required containerd configuration:**
- `SystemdCgroup = true`
- NVIDIA container runtime configured (e.g., `nvidia-container-toolkit`) such that GPU workloads can request devices via the device plugin
- Image pull behavior aligned with fleet defaults (rate limiting + registry mirrors where configured)

**Recommended (unless documented exception):**
- Disable unbounded per-container log growth; configure log rotation at node level if runtime uses JSON-file logs

Validation (automated):
- containerd running and responding
- NVIDIA runtime/toolkit present
- Basic `nvidia-smi` works inside a GPU test container (smoke check)

### 4) Kubernetes kubelet baseline
**Kubelet must be configured via the cluster’s node bootstrap** (not manually edited post-join).

Required kubelet characteristics:
- **Container runtime endpoint** points to containerd socket
- **Cgroup driver** matches runtime (systemd)
- **CPU Manager policy:** `static` for deterministic CPU pinning on latency-sensitive pools (Dedicated inference)
- **Topology Manager policy:** `restricted` (or per-pool override) to reduce cross-NUMA latency regressions
- **Eviction thresholds:** configured to protect the node and avoid hard OOM cascades

Baseline flags/settings (canonical; exact wiring may vary by distro/bootstrap):
- `--cgroup-driver=systemd`
- `--container-runtime-endpoint=unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock`
- `--fail-swap-on=true`
- `--cpu-manager-policy=static`
- `--topology-manager-policy=restricted`
- `--kube-reserved` and `--system-reserved` set (see below)
- `--eviction-hard` set (see below)

Resource reservation defaults (per node; may be tuned by instance size):
- `system-reserved`: 0.5 CPU, 1Gi memory
- `kube-reserved`: 0.5 CPU, 1Gi memory

Eviction hard defaults:
- `memory.available < 500Mi`
- `nodefs.available < 10%`
- `imagefs.available < 10%`

Node labels/taints (required):
- GPU SKU label present (e.g., `redwood.ai/gpu-sku=A100-80GB` / `H100-80GB`)
- Pool identifier label present (e.g., `redwood.ai/pool-id=<id>`)
- Inference taint (where used) applied consistently to prevent non-serving workloads from landing on Dedicated pools

Validation (automated):
- Node joined cluster and reports Ready to Kubernetes
- Kubelet flags/config match baseline expectations
- Required labels/taints present

### 5) GPU software stack
**Driver/CUDA/NCCL versions must match the pool’s pinned image channel.** Mixed versions inside the same pool are not supported.

Required:
- NVIDIA driver installed and loaded; persistence mode enabled where supported
- CUDA toolkit version aligned with runtime requirements
- NCCL version aligned with fabric/network stack expectations

GPU health signals (required for node admission):
- No active GPU Xid errors at validation time
- ECC error counters below quarantine thresholds (see Quarantine Policy)

Validation (automated):
- `nvidia-smi` reports expected driver version
- GPU count matches expected for instance type
- Health check passes (no critical Xid/ECC thresholds exceeded)

### 6) Disk layout and mount options
The node must provide **stable IO performance** for:
- container image pulls/unpacks
- `/var/lib/kubelet` and ephemeral workloads
- logs and core dumps (where enabled)

Baseline layout (typical for cloud instances; exact device names vary):
- Root volume: OS + minimal runtime dependencies
- Data volume(s):
  - `/var/lib/containerd`
  - `/var/lib/kubelet`
  - `/var/log` (optional; may remain on root if sized accordingly)

Required mount options (where applicable):
- `noatime`
- Ensure sufficient inode counts for imagefs

Required sizing (defaults; may be tuned by pool type):
- Root: >= 200Gi
- Container/imagefs + kubelet: >= 500Gi combined for inference pools with frequent model/container churn

Validation (automated):
- Filesystems mounted at required paths
- Minimum free space available at validation time
- Basic write/read throughput check meets minimum (see validation thresholds)

### 7) Ulimits and process limits
Required ulimits (system-wide baseline):
- `nofile` (open files): **>= 1048576** (soft/hard)
- `nproc` (processes): **>= 131072**

Rationale:
- Prevent file descriptor exhaustion under high connection concurrency and agent sidecars.

Validation (automated):
- `ulimit -n` and `ulimit -u` meet baseline

### 8) Networking baseline
Required:
- MTU consistent with region/VPC standard (avoid mixed MTU in a pool)
- conntrack sized for high concurrency (see sysctl)
- DNS resolution stable (node-local DNS if configured by cluster standard)

If using high-performance networking (e.g., EFA/IB):
- Required drivers installed and link state healthy
- RDMA devices enumerated when applicable

Validation (automated):
- DNS resolution check
- Basic egress check to required endpoints (registry, control-plane, telemetry)
- Optional: intra-cluster bandwidth sanity test (pool-dependent)

### 9) Security hardening baseline
Required:
- OS security updates applied per image channel policy (CVE patch cadence)
- SSH configuration per Redwood baseline (no password auth; keys via fleet automation)
- Host firewall rules as configured by cluster standard
- Audit logging enabled per Security guidance (where required by compliance profile)

Validation (automated):
- Image provenance attestation present (build metadata)
- Required security agents present and healthy (when applicable)

---

## What is validated automatically (Provision-to-Ready gates)
Nodes are only eligible to join serving pools after automated validation passes.

### Pre-flight checks (before node joins serving)
Validated by the node validation agent and/or bootstrap scripts:
- Swap disabled
- Kernel cmdline + sysctl baseline
- Time sync within threshold
- containerd healthy + configured
- Disk mounts present and writable
- Required outbound connectivity (registry/control-plane)

### Post-flight checks (after node joins cluster, before Ready-for-Serving)
Validated after node is schedulable but before it can receive inference workloads:
- GPU health + driver parity (expected version)
- Kubelet configuration sanity (cgroup driver, reserved resources, eviction settings)
- Device plugin functioning (GPU allocatable present)
- NCCL/all-reduce smoke test (only for pools that require multi-GPU fabric validation)
- Lightweight inference/perf canary (pool-dependent; detects obvious regressions)

### Validation artifacts and failure reasons
For each validation step, the system records:
- Step name and duration
- Pass/fail outcome
- Pointer to logs/artifacts
- Canonical failure reason code (used by dashboards and triage runbooks)

---

## Recommended (should-have) settings
These are strongly recommended for fleet stability and performance; they may be enforced later.

- Disable CPU frequency scaling where possible; use performance profile for latency-sensitive pools
- IRQ balancing tuned for high-throughput networking + GPU workloads
- Node-local caching for image pulls where supported by the environment
- Log rotation and retention policy consistent with observability retention targets

---

## Exceptions policy
Exceptions are allowed only when:
- Required by a specific GPU type/region constraint
- Required by a customer’s Private deployment constraints
- Temporarily needed for incident mitigation

Exception requests must include:
- Pool(s) impacted and expected duration
- Risk assessment (correctness/availability)
- Rollback plan
- Validation impact (what checks must be modified)

---

## Quick reference: baseline checklist
Use this as a human-friendly summary; automated validation is authoritative.

- [ ] Swap disabled
- [ ] chrony synced (<= 100ms offset)
- [ ] containerd healthy, systemd cgroups, NVIDIA runtime present
- [ ] kubelet uses systemd cgroups, reserved resources set, eviction thresholds set
- [ ] GPU driver/CUDA/NCCL match pinned image channel
- [ ] `nofile >= 1048576`, `nproc >= 131072`
- [ ] `/var/lib/containerd` and `/var/lib/kubelet` on correct disks with `noatime`
- [ ] conntrack + network sysctls set
- [ ] Required labels/taints applied

## Support and escalation
- Baseline ownership (Infra/Fleet): page the Fleet on-call for provisioning/validation failures.
- If the readiness state machine/API is inconsistent or stuck: engage Platform Control Plane on-call.
- For paging/alert thresholds or SLO concerns: engage SRE (Reliability Initiatives).

For common failure modes and safe remediation steps, see the Provision-to-Ready failures triage runbook.

title: dsid_f879b89567134d049f8c4d19ad9f8f03__cache-metrics-naming-and-cardinality-policy.txt
text:
Cache telemetry metrics: naming + label cardinality policy

## Purpose
This page defines Redwood Inference’s standards for **naming** and **label cardinality controls** for prefix/KV cache telemetry.

These metrics power:
- Runtime and SRE dashboards for cache efficiency and regressions.
- Telemetry aggregation jobs (e.g., “increase hit-rate” recommendations).
- Guardrail alerting (cache-efficiency SLOs).

The goals are:
1) consistent naming and units across runtime, gateway, and ingestion;
2) metrics that are **joinable** with route/model/deployment context;
3) strong controls to prevent **cardinality blowups** and telemetry cost spikes;
4) privacy-safe instrumentation (no prompt content, no raw identifiers).

This policy applies to **runtime-emitted cache metrics** (prefix cache + KV cache) and ingestion-side label enforcement.

---

## Non-goals
- Defining the semantic meaning of hit/miss (see ADR).
- Defining new eviction algorithms or cache policies.
- Providing customer-facing product guidance (see PRD / Optimize copy).

---

## Metric backend expectations
We emit metrics via OpenTelemetry Metrics and export to our Prometheus-compatible backend.

Conventions:
- Counters MUST end with `_total`.
- Gauges MUST include unit (e.g., `_bytes`).
- Histograms MUST include unit (e.g., `_seconds`, `_tokens`).
- All cache metrics MUST share a consistent **namespace** and **label set** as defined below.

---

## Naming conventions
### Namespace
All cache telemetry MUST use the following prefix:
- `redwood.runtime.cache.*` for runtime-level cache events and state
- `redwood.gateway.cache.*` ONLY for gateway-side cache controls (rare; prefer runtime metrics)
- `redwood.telemetry.cache.*` for ingestion/pipeline health metrics (drop counters, enforcement)

### Cache type segment
Include the cache type explicitly:
- `prefix` for prefix cache (prompt prefix reuse)
- `kv` for KV cache (attention key/value reuse)

Examples:
- `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.hit_total`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.miss_total`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.evictions_total`

### Metric name patterns
Use the following patterns to reduce ambiguity:
- `...hit_total` / `...miss_total` for request-level outcomes
- `...reused_tokens` histogram for amount of reuse
- `...wasted_prefill_tokens_total` for wasted prefill accounting
- `...evictions_total` with `eviction_reason` label
- `...pressure_ratio` gauge (normalized 0–1 when possible)

### Units and suffixes
- Tokens: `_tokens` (hist) or `_tokens_total` (counter)
- Bytes: `_bytes` (gauge) or `_bytes_total` (counter, rare)
- Seconds: `_seconds` (hist)
- Ratios: `_ratio` (gauge)

Do NOT encode units in labels.

---

## Required vs optional labels
This section defines the only allowed label keys for cache metrics. Labels outside this list will be dropped at ingestion (see enforcement).

### Required labels (MUST be present)
These labels are required on all `redwood.runtime.cache.*` metrics.

| Label key | Type | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `env` | enum | `prod`, `staging`, `dev` | Required; used for routing + alerting |
| `region` | enum | `us-east-1`, `eu-west-1` | Cloud region; low cardinality |
| `deployment_mode` | enum | `hosted`, `dedicated`, `private` | MUST match control-plane taxonomy |
| `cache_type` | enum | `prefix`, `kv` | Included even when implied by name to simplify queries |
| `model_family` | enum | `llama`, `mistral`, `qwen`, `mixtral` | Use curated taxonomy; see “Model labels” |
| `prompt_len_bucket` | enum | `0_128`, `129_256`, `257_512`, `513_1024`, `1025_2048`, `2049_4096`, `4097_plus` | Required on request-scoped cache metrics |

### Conditionally required labels
Required only for certain metric groups.

| Metric group | Conditionally required labels | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Miss/hit counters | `outcome` OR separate `hit_total`/`miss_total` | Prefer separate counters; if using `outcome`, it MUST be `hit`/`miss` only |
| Miss reason breakdown | `miss_reason` | Only for `...miss_total` / miss histograms |
| Evictions | `eviction_reason` | Only for eviction metrics |

### Optional labels (MAY be present)
These are allowed but must follow the constraints below.

| Label key | Allowed values | Constraints |
|---|---|---|
| `model_id` | allowlisted short ID | Must be from model registry allowlist; no raw version strings |
| `model_version` | allowlisted short ID | Only when needed for rollout debugging; see “Cardinality caps” |
| `route_id` | stable low-cardinality ID | MUST be a control-plane assigned ID (not a URL path); see “Route labels” |
| `route_tier` | `default`, `premium`, `internal` | Helps explain SLO differences |
| `traffic_class` | `chat`, `completion`, `embeddings`, `rerank` | Only if explicitly required by dashboards |
| `sampler` | `full`, `p10`, `p1`, `p0_1` | Emitted by runtime when sampling is applied |

### Forbidden labels (MUST NOT be emitted)
These cause immediate ingestion drops or aggressive aggregation:
- `tenant_id`, `org_id`, `customer_id`, `user_id`
- `request_id`, `trace_id`, `span_id`
- `prompt_hash`, `prefix_hash`, `cache_key` (any per-prompt key)
- `ip`, `email`, `api_key_id`
- any free-form string labels (URLs, error messages, exception types)

Use traces for high-cardinality correlation (see tracing standards). Metrics must remain low-cardinality.

---

## Label value normalization rules
### Route labels
- `route_id` MUST be the control-plane assigned ID (stable across deploys) and MUST NOT encode tenant identity.
- Do not use raw paths (e.g., `/v1/chat/completions`) or customer-defined names.
- If a workload has >500 distinct `route_id` values in an env+region, ingestion will:
  1) keep the top N by volume (default N=200),
  2) remap the rest to `route_id="other"`.

### Model labels
- `model_family` is required and must come from the canonical taxonomy maintained by Platform/Telemetry.
- `model_id` is optional and must be a short, allowlisted identifier (e.g., `llama-3-70b-instruct`).
- `model_version` should be used sparingly. When enabled, it MUST be a short, allowlisted version ID (e.g., `v2025_03_12_a`). Do not emit git SHAs or full artifact digests.

### Deployment mode
`deployment_mode` MUST be one of: `hosted`, `dedicated`, `private`.
- Private VPC/on-prem should still report a region-like identifier (customer region mapping), but MUST be from an allowlist to avoid per-customer regions.

---

## Bucketing standards
Buckets are mandatory for request shape slicing without per-request tags.

### `prompt_len_bucket` (required)
Bucket based on **prompt tokens at prefill start** (after canonicalization, before decode).

Allowed values:
- `0_128`
- `129_256`
- `257_512`
- `513_1024`
- `1025_2048`
- `2049_4096`
- `4097_plus`

Notes:
- Use tokenization consistent with the runtime’s billing tokenizer for the route/model.
- If token count cannot be computed, emit `prompt_len_bucket="unknown"` ONLY for non-prod; in prod this should be treated as an instrumentation bug.

### Histograms
To keep series counts bounded, histograms MUST use the default bucket sets below.

#### Reuse depth / reused tokens histograms
Metric examples:
- `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.reused_tokens`
- `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.reused_tokens`

Histogram buckets (tokens):
- `[0, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096]`

#### Request latency correlation (optional)
If a cache metric is explicitly designed to correlate with prefill/decode latency, use:
- `redwood.runtime.cache.*.prefill_savings_seconds` (histogram)
Buckets (seconds):
- `[0.0005, 0.001, 0.0025, 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]`

Do NOT create new custom bucket sets without Telemetry review.

---

## Canonical metric set (runtime)
This table lists the initial standardized metric names for cache telemetry. Teams should extend within this structure rather than inventing parallel names.

### Hit/miss outcomes
| Metric name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.hit_total` | Counter | Request-level prefix cache hit (per ADR semantics) |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.miss_total` | Counter | Request-level prefix cache miss |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.hit_total` | Counter | Request-level KV cache hit |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.miss_total` | Counter | Request-level KV cache miss |

### Miss reason taxonomy
When `miss_reason` is present, it MUST be one of:
- `capacity` (insufficient space / allocation failure)
- `ttl_expired`
- `policy_disabled` (route or env config)
- `hash_mismatch` (canonicalization/key mismatch)
- `version_mismatch` (model/version incompatibility)
- `unknown`

### Evictions and pressure
| Metric name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.evictions_total` | Counter | KV cache eviction events |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.evictions_total` | Counter | Prefix cache eviction events |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.allocated_bytes` | Gauge | Bytes allocated to KV cache |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.allocated_bytes` | Gauge | Bytes allocated to prefix cache |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.pressure_ratio` | Gauge | Normalized memory pressure indicator (0–1) |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.pressure_ratio` | Gauge | Normalized memory pressure indicator (0–1) |

`eviction_reason` MUST be one of:
- `capacity_pressure`
- `ttl`
- `policy_change`
- `compaction`
- `unknown`

### Reuse effectiveness and wasted work
| Metric name | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `redwood.runtime.cache.prefix.reused_tokens` | Histogram | Tokens reused from prefix cache |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.kv.reused_tokens` | Histogram | Tokens reused from KV cache |
| `redwood.runtime.cache.wasted_prefill_tokens_total` | Counter | Prefill tokens that did not contribute to subsequent decode due to cache misses/evictions (per ADR/definition page) |

---

## Cardinality budgets and hard limits
### Core principles
1) **No per-tenant metrics**. Use tiering or aggregated datasets instead.
2) Every new label MUST justify operational value and pass a cardinality estimate.
3) If you need “deep debug” per-request visibility, use **traces** or sampled logs, not metric labels.

### Hard limits (enforced in ingestion)
The ingestion pipeline enforces:
- Max label keys per series for `redwood.runtime.cache.*`: **8** (excluding OTel-required resource attributes managed separately).
- Max distinct values per label (per `env+region`) for:
  - `route_id`: **<= 200** kept, remainder mapped to `other`
  - `model_id`: **<= 50** (allowlist)
  - `model_version`: **<= 20** per `model_id` (allowlist)
- Max active time series per metric name (per `env+region`): **<= 50,000**

If a metric exceeds limits, ingestion will:
1) drop forbidden labels,
2) remap overflow label values to `other`,
3) as a last resort, drop the metric and emit a pipeline health counter (see below).

### Recommended target budgets (design-time)
Before merging instrumentation, teams should target:
- <10k active series per metric per `env+region` under typical production load.
- <2x series growth when enabling `model_version`.

Telemetry team will request a “budget sheet” for any new label or new histogram.

---

## Sampling policy
Sampling is allowed (and often required) for high-volume cache events.

Rules:
- Sampling MUST be deterministic per request (so dashboards don’t flicker unpredictably) and MUST be recorded via the `sampler` label.
- Counters that feed SLO guardrails SHOULD remain unsampled when feasible.
- Histograms may be sampled more aggressively than counters.

Default guidance (prod):
- `hit_total` / `miss_total`: full (no sampling)
- `reused_tokens` histograms: `p10`
- trace span annotations for cache events: `p1` or lower

If sampling differs by environment, it MUST be documented in runtime config flags and surfaced in dashboards.

---

## Privacy and data handling
- Metrics MUST NOT encode prompt content, prompt hashes, or any stable per-user/per-tenant identifier.
- Prompt length bucketing is allowed and required.
- Any canonicalization identifiers should be handled as:
  - (preferred) counters/histograms without exposing key material
  - traces with sampling and privacy review

For privacy review questions, contact **Marcus Lin** (Security) and Telemetry schema owner (Nadia Rahman).

---

## Ingestion-side enforcement metrics
To make enforcement visible, the pipeline emits:
- `redwood.telemetry.cache.label_drop_total{reason=...}`
- `redwood.telemetry.cache.series_overflow_total{metric_name=...}`
- `redwood.telemetry.cache.remap_to_other_total{label_key=...}`

These are monitored by SRE to detect “dashboard shows zero hits” failure modes.

---

## Change management
### When you add or change a cache metric
1) Open a PR that updates the runtime instrumentation.
2) Update this standards page if you add new names/labels/taxonomy.
3) Provide a cardinality estimate (worst-case + expected) and sampling plan.
4) Validate in staging with ingestion guards enabled.
5) Coordinate dashboard updates and alert rule changes.

### Backwards compatibility
- Renames MUST include a deprecation window of at least **2 releases**.
- Dashboards/alerts must be migrated before old names are removed.

### Exceptions
Exceptions (e.g., temporarily enabling `model_version` in prod during a rollout incident) require approval from:
- Telemetry pipelines lead (Logan Wright) AND
- SRE approver (Sean Gallagher)

Exceptions must include:
- scope (env/region),
- time window,
- rollback plan,
- expected series delta.

---

## Appendix: Example queries (PromQL-style)
### Cache hit-rate by model family and prompt length bucket
- `sum(rate(redwood_runtime_cache_kv_hit_total[5m])) by (model_family, prompt_len_bucket) / (sum(rate(redwood_runtime_cache_kv_hit_total[5m])) by (model_family, prompt_len_bucket) + sum(rate(redwood_runtime_cache_kv_miss_total[5m])) by (model_family, prompt_len_bucket))`

### Miss reasons (topline)
- `sum(rate(redwood_runtime_cache_prefix_miss_total[10m])) by (miss_reason)`

### Detect remapping to `other` (potential cardinality issue)
- `sum(rate(redwood_telemetry_cache_remap_to_other_total[10m])) by (label_key)`

---

## Owners
- Metric schema owner: **Nadia Rahman** (Telemetry)
- Ingestion enforcement: **Caleb Johnson** (Platform/Telemetry)
- Dashboards/alerts: **Allison Grant** (Observability)
- Runtime instrumentation: **Omar El-Sayed** (Runtime)

title: dsid_c143a139d6514ea48af3bc2e5fc53c8d__slo-composition-multi-tenant-models-2025.txt
text:
SLO Composition for Multi‑Tenant Model Serving

Purpose

This page defines Redwood's standard approach for composing, allocating, and monitoring Service Level Objectives (SLOs) across multi-tenant model-serving surfaces (hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private runtime sidecars). The goal is predictable customer experience, fair resource isolation, and measurable unit economics that feed billing and capacity planning.

Scope

- Applies to: text generation, chat streaming, embeddings and reranking endpoints that are served from a shared runtime (multi-tenant GPU pools and multi-variant model deployments).
- Excludes: one-off batch-only offline workloads and single-tenant appliance deployments with explicit per-customer SLA contracts.

Key principles

1) Tenant-first SLOs: SLOs are expressed from the consumer's perspective (e.g., 95th percentile request latency for a customer route), not only internal pod metrics.
2) Composability: Service-level SLOs are built from per-route, per-variant, and infra SLO primitives using explicit weighting and error budgets.
3) Isolation and fairness: Composition must support throttling and fallback policies that avoid noisy-neighbor effects.
4) Cost-awareness: SLO formulas must account for cost amplification (model size, quantization, batch size) so capacity planning and billing reflect true unit economics.

Definitions and primitives

- route: the API surface configured by a customer (e.g., /v1/generate with model=redwood-alpha).
- variant: an individual model binary/configuration (fp16, q4_0, q8_0) served behind a route.
- infra_slo: cluster-level SLOs (e.g., GPU prewarm availability, queue latency).
- tenant_slo: per-tenant observable (latency_p95_ms, error_rate_5m, token_throughput_rps).

SLO composition model (formula)

We define a deterministic composition function that aggregates variant-level observations into route-level SLOs and then into service-level commitments. The canonical form: 

route_slo = sum_i(weight_i * variant_slo_i) + infra_risk_margin

Where: 
- weight_i is the traffic-weight fraction for variant i over a sliding window (default 1-minute).
- variant_slo_i is the measured objective (e.g., p95 latency) for that variant.
- infra_risk_margin is a fixed offset derived from infra_slo violations (see infra interaction).

Example: p95 latency composition

If variant A (weight 0.7) has p95=120ms and variant B (weight 0.3) has p95=260ms, route_p95 = 0.7*120 + 0.3*260 = 162ms.

Per-tenant SLO tiers

We standardize on three tenant tiers for hosted and dedicated customers. Private deployments may map these to contract terms.

| Tier | Commitments (example) | Error budget 
|------|-----------------------|----------------|
| Standard | p95 <= 250ms, available 99.9% (monthly), error_rate < 0.5% | 0.1% monthly 
| Premium  | p95 <= 150ms, available 99.95% (monthly), error_rate < 0.2% | 0.05% monthly 
| Latency-Optimized | p95 <= 80ms, available 99.99% (monthly), error_rate < 0.1% | 0.01% monthly

Note: These are customer-facing commitments. Internally we map them to route and variant objectives with explicit headroom and safety margins.

Infra interaction and risk margins

Infra SLOs (GPU prewarm time, queueing time, streaming packet loss) feed a risk score R in [0,1] every minute. We add an infra_risk_margin_ms = baseline_margin_ms * R to composed latency SLOs. Baseline_margin_ms = 40ms by default for shared pools, 10ms for Dedicated.

Monitoring and queries

Instrumentation must expose the following time series per (tenant, route, variant):
- redwood.requests.latency_ms.p95
- redwood.requests.errors.count (HTTP 5xx, model-runtime-failure)
- redwood.tokens.generated.total
- redwood.queue.wait_ms.p50/p95

Example PromQL for tenant p95 latency (1m lookback):

  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (tenant, le) (rate(redwood_requests_latency_bucket[1m])))

Alerting thresholds (recommended)

- Alert: tenant_p95_exceeded
  - Condition: tenant_p95 > committed_p95 for 3 consecutive 1m windows
  - Severity: P2 for Standard, P1 for Premium / Latency-Optimized
  - Runbook: see runbook id: eng-sre/runbooks/tenant-slo-breach

- Alert: infra_risk_degraded
  - Condition: infra_risk_score > 0.6 for 5m
  - Severity: P1

Operational behaviors on SLO pressure

1) Reactive traffic shaping (automated): when a tenant exceeds error budget and infra risk > 0.5, system applies soft-throttles (rate limit 10% reductions, per-tenant) and moves lower-priority traffic to fallback variants.
2) Canary-aware rollbacks: deployment changes that increase variant tail latency by > 15% must be automatically rolled back (see ADR: canary-mesh-guidelines).
3) Billing impact: sustained tier violations >72h triggers account review and cost-corrective actions (credits, prioritized capacity purchase offers).

SLO spec (YAML example)

  kind: SLO
  tenant: example-corp
  route: /v1/generate
  metric: latency_p95_ms
  objective: 150
  window: 30d
  weights: 
    variants:
      - name: redwood-alpha-fp16
        weight: 0.8
      - name: redwood-alpha-q4_0
        weight: 0.2

CLI integration

To apply a tenant SLO (engineers):

  # redwoodctl is the internal control-plane CLI
  redwoodctl slo apply -f tenant-slos/example-corp-slo.yaml --env=prod

Rollout and validation checklist (owners must complete before going GA)

1) Define per-variant telemetry exports (owner: runtime-team).
2) Configure composition weights and initial infra_margin (owner: eng-sre).
3) Smoke tests: synthetic traffic that exercises 99th percentile flows for 24h (owner: perf-team).
4) Observability validation: dashboards, alerts, and sampled traces available for tenant (owner: eng-platform).
5) Assume-failure drills: simulate node preemption and verify fallback routing (owner: eng-serving-runtime).

Ownership and governance

- Runtime: implementation of variant-level metrics and weight reporting — eng-serving-runtime team.
- SLO system & alerts: eng-sre.
- Billing & cost mapping: finance-legal + product (billing-data-pipeline).
- Policy & tier definitions: product team (final approval).

Runbooks and links

- eng-sre/runbooks/tenant-slo-breach (detailed triage steps)
- eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/fallback-orchestration
- perf-team/simulations/multi-tenant-loadbook-2025

Appendix: Examples and edge cases

1) Cold-start amplification: for routes with >25% cold starts in a 5m window apply an extra cold_start_penalty_ms of 200ms to the composed SLO and escalate to eng-sre.
2) Skewed variant traffic: If any variant weight < 0.05 but variance in p95 > 3x other variants, ignore that variant's p95 and use cluster-median instead (to avoid noisy short-lived canaries impacting route commitments).
3) Private deployments: customers may opt-in to "contractual isolation" where infra_risk_margin is negotiated and removed from public commitments; documentation lives in eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops.

Change log

- 2025-03-12: Initial draft (Maya Patel)
- 2025-06-10: Added infra risk margin and monitoring queries (Ethan Wong)
- 2025-09-01: Finalized rollout checklist and tier definitions (published)

If you have questions or need a tailored SLO mapping for a specific customer, open a ticket with the runtime or eng-sre team and include the tenant_id and intended traffic profile.

title: dsid_a6a2008d9ce14a10bcd8698b19021430__quota-enforcement-shim-terraform-module-and-slo-contracts.txt
text:
Quota enforcement shim Terraform module and SLO contracts

Overview

This document describes the design, implementation, and rollout plan for a small, reusable Terraform module (quota-enforcement-shim) that enforces tenant egress and GPU capacity quotas at infrastructure provisioning time and exposes SLO contract metadata for downstream billing and alerting. The shim is intentionally lightweight: it does not replace the allocator, but it provides deterministic enforcement points for cross-account / cross-region quota policies, a test harness for canary promotion, and integration hooks for billing reconciliation.

Goals

- Provide a single, testable Terraform primitive teams can attach to tenant onboarding and burst orchestration.
- Enforce hard and soft quotas consistently across cloud accounts (GCP/AWS).
- Emit structured SLO metadata and provenance tags to be consumed by billing and telemetry pipelines.
- Enable safe canary promotion of quota changes via CI/CD (Buildkite/GitHub Actions).
- Minimize blast radius: the shim is opt-in per-tenant and can be rolled back via automated TF rollback.

Non-goals

- Not a replacement for runtime capacity allocators or the GPU scheduler.
- Not responsible for chargeback computation (it provides attributes used by billing pipelines).

Architecture and components

1) Terraform module (quota-enforcement-shim)
   - Purpose: attach quota checks and enforcement resources (IAM, service-accounts, deny policies, quota alarms) to tenant landing zone.
   - Outputs: enforcement_ids, slo_metadata_tag, canary_flag_resource_id.

2) Policy adapter (lambda/cloudfunction)
   - Purpose: reconcile desired quota in TF state with cloud provider quota APIs and set soft/hard limits where supported.
   - Runs: on TF apply (invoked via remote-exec or provider webhook) and on a scheduled reconciliation every 30 minutes.

3) Canary harness (CI/CD job template)
   - Purpose: promote changes in small increments (per-region / per-tenant subset) using a staircase canary pattern.
   - Integrations: Buildkite pipeline that runs TF plan/apply in canary mode with smoke tests.

4) Telemetry and billing hooks
   - The module writes an slo_metadata_tag (JSON string) into resource tags and emits a CloudWatch/Stackdriver metric "tenant.quota.enforced" with dimensions {tenant_id, region, policy_id}.

Module interface and example

Table: module variables and short descriptions

- variables: (expressed here as a human table)
  - tenant_id: string - unique tenant identifier (required)
  - quota_group: string - egress|gpu_compute|concurrent_sessions (required)
  - hard_limit: number - absolute limit that must not be exceeded (optional - provider dependent)
  - soft_limit: number - threshold to trigger alerts and throttling (optional)
  - enforcement_mode: string - block|throttle|monitor (default: monitor)
  - canary_percent: number - percent of tenant traffic/capacity to apply change to during canary (default: 0)
  - regions: list(string) - regions to apply enforcement in (default: [primary region])
  - billing_tag_override: string - optional freeform string for billing pipelines

Example snippet (Terraform usage):

provider "aws" { region = "us-west-2" }

module "tenant_quota_shim" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-infra/tf-modules.git//quota-enforcement-shim?ref=v1.2.0"
  tenant_id = "tenant-42"
  quota_group = "egress"
  soft_limit = 1000 // Mbps
  hard_limit = 2000 // Mbps
  enforcement_mode = "throttle"
  canary_percent = 10
  regions = ["us-west-2", "us-east-1"]
  billing_tag_override = "team-redwood-enterprise"
}

Behavioral policy matrix

- enforcement_mode = monitor -> write slo_metadata_tag, create metric, do not modify cloud provider quotas.
- enforcement_mode = throttle -> attach rate-limiting sidecar or quota policy when supported (e.g., Cloud NAT throttle rules / GCP egress gateway config).
- enforcement_mode = block -> attach deny policies where provider supports explicit denies (used only for extreme enforcement and requires legal & security approval).

Canary promotion workflow (step-by-step)

1) Developer opens PR bumping module usage and changes soft_limit/hard_limit/canary_percent.
2) CI runs unit tests on module (terrafmt, tflint, terraform validate) and an automated static policy check (OPA).
3) Buildkite pipeline: run TF plan in canary mode for a small tenant cohort and create a plan preview artifact accessible to SRE.
4) Smoke tests: run a 10-minute traffic replay against the canary region and verify: telemetry emitting, no unexpected 403/500 errors, slowdowns within SLO.
5) If smoke tests pass and telemetry indicates < 0.5% error delta, promote to additional cohorts using a staircase (10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with manual approval gates at each step.
6) Rollback: if any step fails, pipeline runs an automated TF apply reversing the change and creates an incident with pre-populated diagnostics.

Testing and CI requirements

- Mandatory checks for every PR using the module:
  - terraform validate & plan (diff must be explainable)
  - tflint & terratest suite (unit tests for provider interactions mocked)
  - OPA policies: ensure no module can create global-blocking deny without security tag
  - Integration test: ephemeral tenant created in a sandbox account, module applied, policy adapter run, telemetry validated

Operational runbook (oncall steps)

1) Alert: "tenant.quota.enforced.failed" -> primary oncall (infra) paged.
2) Triage: review last TF plan artifact, enforcement resource IDs, and provider API error codes.
3) Quick remediation: if enforcement caused unexpected blocking, set module enforcement_mode=monitor in the TF workspace and apply rollback.
4) Reconcile billing: trigger the billing export job to reindex slo_metadata_tag values and run the reconciliation script with the affected tenant_id.

SLOs and alert thresholds (consumable by monitoring)

- Enforcement success rate: 99.9% of TF applies that include quota-enforcement-shim should complete without provider error. Alert on < 99.0% over 1 hour.
- Canary stability: canary cohort must show < 1% increase in 5xx errors and < 5% tail latency increase during promotion window. Alert and auto-rollback otherwise.
- Telemetry emission: every enforcement apply must emit at least one metric point within 5 minutes. Alert if missing for > 10 minutes.

Billing reconciliation contract

- slo_metadata_tag contents (JSON string): {tenant_id, quota_group, enforcement_mode, applied_at_iso, module_version, policy_id}
- Billing pipeline job consumes slo_metadata_tag and creates billing rows. If enforcement fails mid-apply, module must write a "pending":true flag. Billing job ignores pending entries and notifies billing-ops channel.

Ownership and rollout

- Primary owner: infra/terraform-team (owner on call: Diego Alvarez)
- Secondary owner: infra/sre (oncall rotation)
- Rollout phases: sandbox -> staging (1 month) -> select customers (2 months) -> GA

Migration notes for legacy tenant-onboarding

- Legacy onboarding scripts must be updated to include the module in their TF root. For tenants where legacy automation cannot be updated immediately, use the policy adapter in read-only mode to generate reconciliation reports and gradually adopt enforcement.

Backout and disaster recovery

- TF rollback is the primary backout mechanism. The module provides an automated revert plan that targets only the enforcement resources added by the module.
- If provider APIs are unresponsive, run the offline reconciliation script to generate a safe-state plan that sets enforcement_mode=monitor for all affected tenants and applies it once the API recovers.

Telemetry and dashboards

- Dashboard widgets: enforcement success rate, canary error delta, enforcement latency (time between TF apply finish and metric emission), billing import lag.
- Saved queries: last 24h failed applies by region, list of tenant_ids with pending flag > 10m.

Risks and mitigations

- Risk: provider quota APIs are inconsistent across regions. Mitigation: module contains provider adapters and defaults to monitor mode for unsupported regions.
- Risk: mis-tagging could cause billing misattribution. Mitigation: strict tf tests verify slo_metadata_tag schema before apply.

Open design items

- Standardizing canonical metric names across clouds (work in progress with telemetry team).
- Formal SLA with billing team for reconciliation time window (proposal: 2 hours).
- Auto-approval logic for low-risk promotions (future work).

Appendix: CLI snippets and troubleshooting

- Create a canary plan locally:
  TF_WORKSPACE=staging 
  terraform init 
  terraform plan -var='tenant_id=tenant-42' -var='canary_percent=10' -out=canary.tfplan
\- Apply the plan:
  terraform apply canary.tfplan

- Re-run reconciliation lambda manually (AWS):
  aws lambda invoke --function-name quota-policy-adapter --payload '{"tenant_id":"tenant-42"}' /tmp/output.json

- Quick check: verify slo tag is present on enforcement resource:
  aws resourcegroupstaggingapi get-resources --tag-filters Key=slo_metadata_tag,Values="tenant-42"

Contact and escalation

- Slack channels: #infra-terraform, #infra-oncall, #billing-ops
- Pager rotation: infra oncall (see rota linked in team wiki)

Change log

- 2024-05-10: Draft created by Maya Chen.
- 2024-09-02: Added canary staircase and metric contract after SRE review.
- 2025-02-12: Updated TF module source reference and CI requirements per Diego's review.

Related pages and references

- Tenant quota playbook (internal): /confluence/eng-infra/gpu-fleet-and-capacity/gpu-tenant-credit-buckets-and-granular-throttling-policy.json
- TF module registry guideline: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/tf-module-publish-safety-harness-and-contract-tests.json

title: dsid_416438990a294f56911b40e22070c886__runtime-experiment-signal-catalog-2027.txt
text:
Runtime experiment signal catalog and hypothesis matrix

Purpose
-------
This document centralizes the signal definitions, collection guidance, and hypothesis matrix for runtime experiments across Redwood's serving stack. It is intended for engineers running controlled performance experiments, A/B rollouts, profiling campaigns, and benchmark suites. The goal is to reduce ambiguity about which telemetry to use for which kind of experiment and to standardize evaluation heuristics and rollback criteria.

Scope
-----
Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private runtime variants. Focused on: request path telemetry, kernel scheduling metrics, KV cache signals, batching utilization, and cost-attribution signals used by Redwood Optimize and runtime autoscalers. Not a replacement for incident runbooks; where an experiment reveals an incident, follow the incident playbooks in oncall_and_incident_response.

Quick summary (one-line)
----------------------
Use this catalog to: (1) select 3–5 core signals for hypothesis acceptance, (2) set primary/secondary thresholds, (3) follow the step-by-step experiment run, and (4) export the result to the benchmark suite for regression tracking.

Signal catalog and rationale
---------------------------
Each signal below includes: name, cardinality (per-request / per-slot / host-level), sampling guidance, expected distribution shape, primary/secondary use, and recommended alert thresholds for experiments.

1) request.latency_ms.{p50,p95,p99} (per-route, per-model)
- Cardinality: per-request aggregated by route/model/region.
- Sampling: full for release-level A/B; 10% for long-running smoke experiments.
- Distribution: heavy right tail; expect multiple modes if mixed sequence lengths.
- Use: Primary for latency SLO experiments.
- Experiment thresholds: delta(p95) <= +10% relative for canary acceptance; delta(p99) <= +20% triggers manual triage.

2) kernel.queue_depth_avg (per-device, per-kernel-type)
- Cardinality: device,kernel-type (attention, ff, matmul).
- Sampling: continuous at 1s resolution.
- Distribution: near-zero for elastic workloads; spikes indicate contention.
- Use: Secondary signal to explain latency regressions.
- Thresholds: sustained > 50% of peak slot count for >30s => consider reducing concurrency or increasing slots.

3) kvcache.hit_rate (session-id, per-model)
- Cardinality: session-level aggregated to route/model.
- Sampling: computed on write-window (1m).
- Distribution: dependent on prompt reuse; typical baseline for chat products is 0.35–0.85.
- Use: Primary when testing prefix caching or warmup strategies.
- Thresholds: drop > 15 percentage points relative -> expect token cost increase; auto-fallthrough if paired with latency increase.

4) batch_utilization_pct (executor-pod, per-1m)
- Cardinality: executor-pod.
- Sampling: 10s rolling window.
- Distribution: multi-modal depending on client batching.
- Use: Primary for cost-efficiency experiments; correlate with tokens/sec.
- Thresholds: sustained < 20% while throughput stable suggests misconfiguration (e.g., slice size mismatch).

5) kernel.exec_time_ms.{mean,95th} (per-kernel-type, per-device)
- Cardinality: kernel-type, device.
- Use: Diagnosing scheduling vs kernel inefficiency.
- Thresholds: > +25% mean vs baseline => flag for kernel rollout hold.

6) memory.gpu.free_mb and memory.gpu.fragmentation_pct (node-level)
- Use: Safety signals for private/on-prem experiments; fragmentation > 60% + free_mb < reserve -> OOM risk.

7) cost.per_token_usd (route, model_variant)
- Use: Primary for Optimize-driven experiments.
- Calculation: (infra_cost + reserved_amortization) / tokens_generated.

Instrumentation and collection guidance
-------------------------------------
- Services and names: rdx-runtime-dispatcher (ingest), rdx-kernel-agent (device-facing), rdx-kvcache (session store), rdx-metrics-aggregator, rdx-benchmark-runner. Tag metrics with: service, cluster, region, model, model_variant, route, experiment_id, canary_group.
- Metric format: Prometheus-style timeseries with labels above; export to metrics pipeline with 10s scrape where possible and 1s for kernel-level counters.
- Logs: include structured JSON request events with fields: request_id, route, model, seq_len_in, seq_len_out, kernel_hints, start_ts, end_ts. Example: 

```json
{
  "request_id": "r-7f3a2c",
  "route": "chat-default",
  "model": "open-vicuna-13b-quant-v2",
  "seq_len_in": 64,
  "seq_len_out": 128,
  "kernel_hints": "sharded-attn",
  "start_ts": "2027-02-10T15:12:03.123Z",
  "end_ts": "2027-02-10T15:12:03.379Z"
}
```

Benchmark config and expected artifacts
--------------------------------------
When converting an experiment to a benchmark, include a config file. Minimal example (YAML):

```yaml
benchmark_name: kvcache-warmup-vs-none
model: rdx-llama-30b-q4
routes: [chat-default]
workload_profile: production-sampled-2027-01
duration: 30m
concurrency: 64
metrics: [request.latency_ms.p95, kvcache.hit_rate, batch_utilization_pct, cost.per_token_usd]
export_to: perf-db://benchmarks/kvcache-warmup-vs-none-2027-02-10
```

Expected artifacts:
- raw telemetry (prometheus histograms + traces)
- per-request logs (parquet)
- experiment summary (markdown) with stat tests (see below)

Hypothesis matrix and statistical evaluation rules
--------------------------------------------------
Use the following convention for experiment outcomes: Primary signals (1–2) must meet acceptance thresholds; secondary signals should exhibit no regression beyond soft thresholds.

- Hypothesis example: "Enabling async kvcache prefetch will reduce p95 latency by >= 8% without increasing cost per token by > 5%."
- Primary signals: request.latency_ms.p95 (delta <= -8%) and kvcache.hit_rate (delta >= +6 percentage points).
- Secondary signals: cost.per_token_usd (delta <= +5%), kernel.queue_depth_avg (no sustained >75% saturation).

Statistical rules:
1) Use bootstrap resampling over per-request latencies; report 95% confidence intervals for deltas.
2) Accept only if delta and CI both exceed the acceptance threshold in the favorable direction.
3) For cost signals where variance is high, cap sample variance by stratifying on seq_len buckets: [0-64, 65-256, 257+].

Experiment runbook (step-by-step)
--------------------------------
1) Define experiment_id and register in the experiments board (team-wiki experiments index).
2) Select the core signals (max 5). Mark primaries.
3) Create benchmark config and a dedicated metrics dashboard with experiment_id filter.
4) Run warmup: 10 minutes at 25% target load to populate caches.
5) Execute canary: 5–10% traffic for 30 minutes.
6) Collect telemetry and run stats pipeline: 
   - Command: rdx-benchmark-runner analyze --experiment-id EXP123 --save-summary ./summary.md
7) Evaluate acceptance per hypothesis matrix.
8) If accepted, escalate to rollout plan (see rollout checklist). If rejected, capture triage notes and create a follow-up profiling ticket.

Rollout checklist and safety gates
----------------------------------
- Gate 1 (canary acceptance): primary signals meet thresholds; no kernel exec_time regression > 25%.
- Gate 2 (stability hold): run 2h at 50% traffic with continuous monitoring; no alerts fired.
- Gate 3 (full rollout): ramp to 100% over 3 steps (50%, 75%, 100%) with 10–20 minute hold per step.

Rollback criteria (automated and manual)
---------------------------------------
Automated rollback (preferred): any of:
- request.latency_ms.p99 increases > 40% for > 2 minutes.
- kernel.queue_depth_avg sustained > 80% for > 60s and accompanied by increase in request errors.
- memory.gpu.fragmentation_pct leads to OOM events.

Manual rollback: triggered by oncall if triage finds systemic regression in model quality (see eval signals) or client-facing error rates > 0.5% over 10m.

Tracing and attribution guidance
-------------------------------
- Ensure each request carries experiment_id, route, and model_variant. Span composition should include: dispatcher -> scheduler -> kernel-agent -> kvcache.
- For expensive experiments, enable 100% traces for canaries for 5–10 minutes to capture tail behaviors.

Examples: short triage checklist for a regression
------------------------------------------------
1) Confirm metric delta with raw per-request data (avoid dashboard smoothing artifacts).
2) Check kernel.exec_time_ms by kernel-type to see if new kernel hints caused regressions.
3) Inspect kvcache.hit_rate and warmup windows; check prefetch logs.
4) Run microbench: single-request microbench with the failing profile using rdx-runtime-local-runner.
5) If kernel-level, annotate a kernel snapshot and assign to kernel-team for kernel rollout revert.

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- Document owner: runtime-performance guild (alias: #runtime-performance).
- Primary engineering owner: Aisha Patel (aisha@redwood.example.com).
- Secondary owners: Marco Chen (kernel), Dana Ortiz (profiling/telemetry).
- Pager: runtime-oncall (see oncall rotation page).

Appendix A — canonical metrics queries
--------------------------------------
PromQL examples (simplified):
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{route="chat-default",experiment_id=~"EXP.*"}[1m])) by (le))
- kvcache hit rate: sum(rate(kvcache_hits_total{model=~".*"}[1m])) / sum(rate(kvcache_requests_total{model=~".*"}[1m]))

Appendix B — experiment result template (markdown)
--------------------------------------------------
- experiment_id: EXP123
- hypothesis: text
- primary_signals: list with baselines and deltas
- secondary_signals: list
- raw_artifacts: link to perf-db
- statistical_summary: link
- verdict: accept | reject | inconclusive
- triage_notes: free text

Related pages and references
----------------------------
- Runtime profiling playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025
- Benchmarking suite guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/mixed-workload-slo-simulation-suite-2026
- Autotune framework: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki/runtime-autotune-framework-spec-2026

Change log
----------
- 2026-11-15: created by Aisha Patel (first draft).
- 2026-12-21: added bootstrap rules and cost stratification (reviewer: Marco Chen).
- 2027-02-10: updated thresholds and rollout ramping guidance (reviewer: Dana Ortiz).

End of document
