title: dsid_3e2ab70470a54953ab43cb113ac009e8__preflight-private-deploy-acceptance-checklist.txt
text:
Preflight acceptance checklist for private GPU deployments (on‑prem / VPC)

Summary
-------
This page is the canonical preflight acceptance checklist for Redwood Private GPU deployments (customer VPC or on‑prem installations). It is intended for SRE, Private Deployments, and Customer Engineering during handover to customer operations. The checklist covers hardware and capacity validation, network and egress patterns, Terraform/IaC gating, CI/CD smoke tests, runtime validation, security controls, and operational runbook readiness. Use this checklist to validate a deployment before the customer goes live or before we handoff day‑2 operations.

Scope
-----
- Applies to Redwood Private deploys that include GPU inference nodes, the Redwood control plane connector, and optional on‑prem artifact registries.
- Not a replacement for customer regulatory audits; use as an engineering acceptance gate.

Quick acceptance criteria (pass/fail)
-------------------------------
- All infra resources created by the deployment IaC converge without errors.
- GPU fleet nodes attach to the control plane and report healthy KV cache metrics for >15 minutes.
- Networking tests (TLS egress, PrivateLink / VPC peering, and NAT path) pass.
- Baseline perf smoke test: 95th percentile token latency <= declared SLA for the model tested.
- Security: audit logging enabled, KMS integration validated, and secrets rotation experiment passed.

Preflight checklist sections
---------------------------
1) Hardware & firmware verification (owner: infra‑ops)
   - Inventory: verify serial, model, and firmware for each GPU host. Acceptable GPUs: A10G, A100‑40GB, or equivalent as agreed with customer. Record device IDs.
   - Firmware/BIOS: platform firmware within supported revision range (example: BIOS >= 2024.06.1).
   - Drivers: CUDA >= 12.2, NVIDIA driver >= 537.x. Ensure driver modules load at boot.
   - NCCL and cuDNN: versions pinned in the image manifest.
   - Health probes: SMART pass for NVMe, ECC error rate < 1e‑6 over last 24h.

2) Networking & egress (owner: cloud‑networking)
   - Subnet allocation: tenant subnets match IaC vars (see Appendix). No overlapping CIDRs with control plane.
   - DNS: internal DNS entries for control plane connectors resolvable from each host.
   - Egress path: verify NAT or proxy rules allow outbound TLS 443 to the control plane endpoints. Use curl/openssl tests outlined below.
   - MTU: confirm MTU >= 9000 if configured for RDMA/GPUDirect; otherwise validate MTU 1500 path.
   - Firewall rules: ports allowed: 443 (control plane), 22 (maintenance, bastion restricted), 123 (NTP) — see table.
   - Latency and bandwidth: run iperf3 to the egress gateway; target >= 500 Mbps sustained per host for model pulls during startup.

   Example CLI checks:
   - DNS resolution: dig +short controlplane.redwood.example.internal || fail
   - TLS handshake test: openssl s_client -connect controlplane.redwood.example.internal:443 -servername controlplane.redwood.example.internal 

3) Terraform / IaC acceptance (owner: infra‑iac)
   - Plan validation: terraform plan must show no diffs after apply in acceptance environment.
   - Policy checks: run OPA/Conftest where policies must pass (no public s3 buckets, IAM least‑privilege checks).
   - Remote state: state backend healthy and locked during apply. Test cross‑account lock/unlock.
   - Module pinning: all modules referenced by version tags; no local path overrides in final PR.
   - Integration smoke script: run ./ci/acceptance/run_iac_smoke.sh — expect exit code 0.

4) CI/CD and image promotion (owner: infra‑ci)
   - Image provenance: image manifests signed and digest matches manifest in IaC variables. Verify with cosign: cosign verify --key k8s/key.pub registry/repo:tag.
   - Canary deploy: promote to a 1‑node canary pool; validate startup logs and health endpoints for 30 minutes.
   - Rollback test: exercise the automated rollback by triggering a failing healthcheck and confirming the orchestrator demotes the canary and restores previous image.

5) Runtime & serving smoke tests (owner: serving‑runtime)
   - Control plane registration: nodes must register and report "READY" state in the fleet console within 5 minutes.
   - KV cache warmup: seed and read back a KV object; validate cache hit ratio > 50% for a warmup synthetic.
   - Baseline model test: run generate endpoint against the deployed small model (e.g., opt‑1.3b quantized) with these checks:
       * correctness: outputs not truncated or garbled for a 200 token prompt.
       * latency: P95 token latency <= 120ms (adjust based on declared customer SLA).
       * throughput: sustain 10 RPS for 5 minutes without errors.
   - Streaming & chunking: validate streaming responses are delivered in <= 200ms chunks for first token.

6) Observability & telemetry (owner: eng‑platform)
   - Metrics: host_exporter, nvml_exporter, and runtime exporter enabled. Confirm required metrics exist:
       * gpu_utilization, gpu_temperature_celsius, host_cpu_steal_pct, token_latency_p95, inference_errors_total
   - Traces: distributed tracing headers propagate through control plane; sample traces are visible in Jaeger/OTEL backend.
   - Logs: centralized logging configured (stack: Loki or ELK). Verify a 15‑minute log retention pipeline for critical logs.
   - Alerts: default alerting rules present for node_down (5m), gpu_overtemp (1m), token_latency_p99_exceed (10m).

7) Security & compliance (owner: security)
   - Secrets: verify KMS integration (AWS KMS / customer HSM) and that secrets in transit are encrypted.
   - RBAC: admin, operator, readonly roles mapped to customer groups. Validate one user in each role for testing.
   - Audit logging: API calls and node registration events forwarded to audit log sink and retained per SLO.
   - Pen test quick check: run the container CVE scanner and confirm no critical CVEs in the runtime image.

8) Operational readiness & runbooks (owner: private‑deployments)
   - Runbook completeness: runbooks exist and are linked in the customer runbook index: node‑drain, kernel‑panic, network‑partition, kv‑cache‑evict.
   - Escalation path: defined oncall list, pager duty rotations, and primary/secondary oncall prepopulated.
   - Playbook drill: run a short table‑top for a node failure with the customer and record gaps.

Acceptance matrix (required checks)
--------------------------------
| Area                | Check (pass criteria)                                     | Responsibility       |
|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|----------------------|
| Hardware            | Firmware and driver match manifest; SMART OK              | infra‑ops            |
| Network             | DNS, TLS, MTU, and egress path verified                   | cloud‑networking     |
| IaC                 | terraform plan/apply converges; OPA policies pass         | infra‑iac            |
| CI/CD               | Image signed; canary and rollback behavior validated      | infra‑ci             |
| Runtime             | Nodes READY; P95 latency within SLA for baseline model    | serving‑runtime      |
| Observability       | Metrics, logs, traces present; alerts firing in test      | eng‑platform         |
| Security            | KMS, RBAC, audit logging validated                        | security             |
| Ops readiness       | Runbooks exist; oncall assigned; drill completed          | private‑deployments  |

Operational rollout procedure (numbered)
-------------------------------------
1. Kickoff validation meeting: confirm owners and signoff checklist sections.
2. IaC apply in preflight namespace (tagged: customer‑acpt). Confirm remote state stable.
3. Promote image to canary pool (1 node). Monitor for 30 minutes.
4. Run runtime smoke tests and collect telemetry for 15 minutes.
5. If canary passes, promote to 10% of nodes. Run 1 hour soak tests.
6. If soak passes, promote remainder in rolling batches while monitoring replication of latency and error signals.
7. Post‑promotion: run full suite of security checks and handoff meeting for day‑2 ops.

Rollback decision criteria (examples)
-----------------------------------
- Latency regression: sustained P95 increase > 25% vs baseline for 15 minutes.
- Error spike: inference_errors_total increase > 50% absolute or >5x rate for 5 minutes.
- Node crash loop: >3 restarts in 10 minutes for the same node.

Post acceptance tasks
--------------------
- Tag the IaC commit with "customer‑acpt‑YYYYMMDD" and close the deployment runbook.
- Export a final telemetry packet (metrics + 1h of logs) and attach to the customer artifact archive.
- Schedule a 1‑week follow‑up QBR with product and customer engineering.

Appendix A — Example Terraform variable table
-------------------------------------------
| variable_name                 | example_value                         | notes                                    |
|------------------------------|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| tenant_cidr                  | 10.58.0.0/22                           | tenant isolation; must not overlap vpc   |
| gpu_instance_profile         | redwood‑gpu‑a100                       | referenced in node pool module           |
| controlplane_endpoint        | controlplane.redwood.example.internal | used by connector service                |
| image_manifest_digest        | sha256:abcd...                         | must match cosign signature              |

Appendix B — Useful commands and scripts
----------------------------------------
- Run IaC smoke: ./ci/acceptance/run_iac_smoke.sh --env customer‑acpt
- Check node status: ./scripts/node‑list.sh --env customer‑acpt | jq
- Run perf smoke: ./scripts/perf_smoke.py --model opt‑1.3b --rps 10 --duration 300
- TLS test: echo | openssl s_client -connect controlplane.redwood.example.internal:443

Related artifacts & links
-------------------------
- Private deploy architecture reference (internal): /confluence/eng-private-deployments/deployment-guides/private-deploy-architecture-reference
- Runbooks index: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/day-2-ops/runbooks-index
- IaC policies: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/policy-as-code-gpu-tenant-guardrails-and-opa-admission

Ownership and contacts
----------------------
- infra‑ops: infra‑ops@redwood.example.com (primary: Marcus Li)
- cloud‑networking: network‑eng@redwood.example.com (primary: Rachael Nguyen)
- infra‑iac: iac‑team@redwood.example.com (primary: Priya Menon)
- serving‑runtime: runtime‑team@redwood.example.com (primary: Tomas Alvarez)

Revision history
----------------
- 2024‑10‑15: initial draft by Ava Thompson.
- 2024‑12‑12: added KMS/HSM validation steps and perf thresholds (reviewer: Marcus Li).
- 2025‑01‑20: updated CI/CD canary timing and added telemetry export step (reviewer: Rachael Nguyen).

title: dsid_ac6177124d354bbabf73eaed89989734__audit-log-coverage-regression-runbook.txt
text:
Runbook: Audit Log Coverage Regression (Missing Sensitive-Action Events)

## Purpose
This runbook describes how to respond when Redwood’s audit logging coverage regresses (e.g., a newly added/changed admin endpoint or workflow no longer emits a required audit event, or emits an event that fails schema/taxonomy requirements).

Coverage regressions are treated as security-impacting quality issues because they can break customer detection/investigation workflows and SOC2/ISO-aligned evidence expectations.

## When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when any of the following occurs:
- The Audit Coverage dashboard shows a drop in observed coverage for one or more `event_type`s.
- An alert fires for missing expected event types for a sensitive action.
- Support/Solutions reports a customer issue: “action happened, but we don’t see a corresponding audit event” (common in Private and Console workflows).
- CI begins failing due to new/changed code paths missing required audit fields or using an unregistered `event_type`.

If the issue is that events are being emitted but not delivered/exported (ingestion backlog, exporter failure, high drop rate), use the **Audit Log Pipeline Incident Runbook** instead.

---

## Definitions (quick)
- **Sensitive action:** An action listed in the sensitive actions taxonomy that requires an audit event (RBAC, credential lifecycle, policy/routing changes, retention/residency changes, audit export config, Private install/upgrade/rollback/config apply, etc.).
- **Coverage regression:** A sensitive action occurs (or is exercised by tests/synthetic) but the expected audit event is not observed OR is observed but invalid (wrong `event_type`, missing required fields, schema validation failure).
- **Producer:** The service/tool that emits the audit event (API Gateway, Control Plane, Console backend, Private installer, policy engine, exporter normalization layer).

---

## Severity and handling guidelines
### Default severity
- **SEV2 (security-impacting)** if:
  - A required sensitive-action audit event is missing in any production tier (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) for GA surfaces, OR
  - The regression affects multiple tenants/projects, OR
  - A customer SIEM export pipeline is known to be affected.

- **SEV3** if:
  - The missing event is in a gated/feature-flagged preview surface, OR
  - Impact is limited to internal environments / pre-production.

### Escalation triggers (page/incident)
Escalate to on-call / incident process when:
- Coverage gap coincides with pipeline symptoms (ingestion latency spike, drop-rate alerts).
- The missing event is for high-risk actions (RBAC changes, API key create/rotate/revoke, audit export destination changes, retention/residency changes).
- A regulated enterprise customer is blocked (Support ticket tagged: “security review”, “SOC2 evidence”, “Private”).

Primary escalation channel: `#eng-security` and `#eng-platform`. For incident coordination: `#incidents`.

---

## Required access
- Observability dashboards (audit coverage + event validation failures).
- Ability to query audit events (by `event_type`, `service_name`, `deployment_mode`, `tenant_id`, `request_id`).
- Read access to service repos / CI logs (for lint failures and test output).
- Linear/Jira access for creating/triaging work items.

Owners to contact if access is blocked:
- Dashboard access / telemetry: Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman
- SRE / alerts: Sean Gallagher, Rafael Mendes
- CI enforcement tooling: Sahana Iyer

---

## Quick decision tree
1) Are audit events being emitted but not delivered/exported?
- Yes → Use **Audit Log Pipeline Incident Runbook** (delivery issue).
- No / unknown → Continue.

2) Is coverage drop limited to a single `deployment_mode` (e.g., Private only)?
- Yes → Likely producer parity gap (Console/Private installer/control plane differences).
- No → Likely shared library/schema/taxonomy change or a producer regression across modes.

3) Does CI/lint fail for audit logging in the relevant repo?
- Yes → Likely missing required fields or unregistered `event_type`. Fix in code + add test.
- No → Likely code path exists but event emission not called or behind an unexpected branch/permission check.

---

## Triage checklist (do these in order)
### Step 1 — Identify exactly what is missing
Capture the following (paste into the ticket/incident):
- Expected `event_type` (from taxonomy)
- Action/workflow that should generate it (endpoint + UI path + installer command)
- Affected deployment mode(s): Hosted / Dedicated / Private
- First observed time (approx) and whether it correlates with a deploy
- Example tenant/project (if safe) and the actor type (user, service account, system)

Common signals:
- Coverage dashboard tile: “Expected vs Observed by event_type (24h)”
- Alert name: `audit_coverage_gap_detected` or `missing_sensitive_action_events`
- CI failure name: `audit-event-required-fields` or `event-type-registry-check`

### Step 2 — Confirm it’s a coverage regression (not an ingestion delay)
Run these sanity checks:
- Check audit ingestion latency for the same window.
- Check drop-rate metrics and exporter error rate.
- Check whether other unrelated event types are flowing normally.

Rule of thumb:
- If **many event types** drop simultaneously and ingestion latency spikes → delivery issue.
- If **one/few event types** drop while overall volume is steady → coverage regression.

### Step 3 — Reproduce (preferred) or isolate via traces
Pick the lowest-risk environment where you can reproduce:
1. Staging or dogfood tenant
2. A private test fixture environment (if Private-only)

Reproduce the sensitive action and capture:
- `request_id`
- `trace_id`
- `admin_action_id` (if present)
- HTTP route + method
- Actor identity context (user_id / service_account_id / impersonation)

Then search audit events by correlation id (example query patterns):
- `request_id:<id> AND event_type:*`
- `admin_action_id:<id> AND schema_version:v1*`
- `trace_id:<id> AND service_name:<service>`

Expected outcomes:
- No audit event at all → missing emission.
- Audit event exists but invalid → schema/taxonomy mismatch.
- Audit event exists but wrong actor/target semantics → producer bug (still considered a coverage failure for acceptance).

### Step 4 — Identify the producer and route to the right owner
Use the workflow to map to a producing system:
- Control Plane (tenant config, RBAC, API keys, policy/rollouts): **Ethan Park** (lead), Benji Okafor
- API Gateway (admin endpoints, quota overrides, auth policy enforcement knobs): **Amara Diallo**
- Console backend (admin workflows, export config UI/BE): **Dylan Brooks / Chloe Martin**
- Policy engine (routing/policy changes): **Jordan Lee**
- Private installer/upgrade tooling: **Vivek Kulkarni** (PM), engineering owner via `redwood-private-installer` rotation; ping `#eng` with “private-installer” tag
- Exporter normalization/schema tagging: **Kevin Osei**
- Telemetry coverage dashboard/alerts: **Logan Wright**
- CI enforcement/lints: **Sahana Iyer**

Routing instructions:
- Create a Linear ticket under **Engineering / Security & Platform**.
- Add label: `audit-logging` + the relevant subsystem label (`control-plane`, `console`, `gateway`, `private-installer`, `exporter`, `policy-engine`).
- Assign directly if clear; otherwise post in `#eng-platform` with the captured repro + correlation IDs and request an owner within 4 business hours.

### Step 5 — Correlate with a change
If possible, tie the regression to:
- A specific deploy (service release timestamp)
- A PR merged recently touching:
  - auth middleware
  - routing changes
  - RBAC checks
  - new endpoints
  - refactors around request context propagation

If you find the likely PR, link it in the ticket and tag the author + service owner.

---

## Mitigation options
Choose based on impact and feasibility.

### Option A — Hotfix to emit the event (preferred)
- Add the missing audit event emission on the sensitive code path.
- Validate against schema v1 using the shared schema validator.
- Ensure the `event_type` is registered in the central registry.
- Add unit/integration tests (see “Adding enforcement tests”).

### Option B — Emergency rollback
If a deploy is clearly responsible and impact is high:
- Roll back the offending service release.
- Confirm coverage returns to baseline.
- Open follow-up ticket for forward fix (do not rely on rollback long-term).

### Option C — Temporary exception (last resort)
If immediate fix is not possible and risk is understood:
- File an exception request per the audit logging exception process.
- Include explicit expiration (default max: 14 days) and mitigation (manual review, added monitoring).
- Note: Exceptions are not acceptable for the highest-risk actions without Marcus Lin + Naomi Feldman approval.

---

## Verification (what “fixed” means)
A fix is complete when ALL are true:
- The sensitive action reliably emits the expected `event_type` in the relevant deployment mode(s).
- The event validates against schema v1 (no required-field omissions).
- Actor attribution is correct (including impersonation context where applicable).
- Correlation fields are present (`request_id` + `trace_id`, and `admin_action_id` when produced by Console/admin workflows).
- Coverage dashboard shows the event type returning to baseline and no “expected vs observed” gaps for at least one full deploy cycle.
- Regression prevention test(s) are merged and passing in CI.

For customer-reported issues:
- Provide Support with:
  - the `event_type`
  - the fixed version/build
  - a short confirmation statement that duplicates are possible due to at-least-once delivery and should be deduped by `event_id` (if relevant)

---

## Adding enforcement tests (how to prevent recurrence)
### 1) Register or confirm `event_type` in the central registry
- If a new sensitive action was introduced, add its `event_type` to the registry.
- Ensure required fields match taxonomy requirements (e.g., actor + target + diff summary for config changes).

### 2) Add unit tests at the producer
Minimum:
- Test that the code path calls audit emitter with:
  - correct `event_type`
  - non-empty `event_id`
  - `schema_version` set to `v1` or `v1.x`
  - required fields present (actor, target/resource, timestamp, service_name, deployment_mode, tenancy fields)

### 3) Add integration/E2E tests for the sensitive action
Use the standard harness (see Linear ENG-4834) to:
- Execute the sensitive action via API or UI-backend call.
- Poll the audit sink/test collector.
- Assert an event exists with the expected `event_type` and validated schema.

Recommended assertions (keep stable to avoid flakes):
- Must match: `event_type`, `service_name`, `deployment_mode`, `actor.type`, presence of `request_id`.
- Avoid brittle assertions on dynamic text. Prefer structured diff summaries when available.

### 4) Ensure CI coverage gates are updated
If the regression came from a new endpoint/workflow:
- Add the endpoint/action to the “sensitive actions coverage list” used by CI gates (where applicable).
- Confirm the audit lints are triggered on the owning repo (ENG-4831 patterns).

### 5) Update coverage expectations (telemetry)
If dashboards track “expected vs observed” from a static list:
- Add the new expected `event_type` so a future missing event pages early.
- Owner: Logan Wright / Nadia Rahman.

---

## Common root causes and fixes
- **New admin endpoint added without instrumentation** → add audit emitter call + test.
- **Refactor bypassed middleware that injects actor/source_ip/correlation** → restore context propagation; add regression test for actor + `request_id`.
- **Console workflow calls a backend mutation that isn’t classified as sensitive** → update taxonomy and ensure backend emits the event (do not rely on frontend-only logging).
- **Private installer parity gap** (hosted emits, private doesn’t) → instrument installer command execution and capture operator identity where available; ensure schema alignment.
- **Event emitted but dropped by validator** (missing required field) → fix producer payload; ensure redaction rules don’t blank required fields.

---

## Communication templates
### Slack (internal)
Post in `#eng-security` and `#eng-platform`:
- “Coverage regression detected: missing `event_type=<...>` for action <...> in <deployment_mode>. First seen <time>. Repro request_id=<...> trace_id=<...>. Suspected producer=<service>. Linear=<link>.”

### Support handoff
- “Identified missing audit event for <action>. Fix merged in <service>/<version>. Expected `event_type=<...>` will be present with `schema_version=v1`. If customers see duplicates during retries, dedupe by `event_id`.”

---

## Owner checklist (post-incident / post-fix)
- [ ] Add/confirm E2E coverage test for the workflow.
- [ ] Ensure event type is in registry + taxonomy.
- [ ] Confirm dashboards/alerts include the new event type if applicable.
- [ ] If customer-impacting: add a brief entry to the internal release notes and link the Support ticket.

---

## Appendix: What to include in the Linear ticket
Title:
- “Audit coverage regression: missing `<event_type>` for `<workflow>` in `<mode>`”

Description:
- Expected event_type + taxonomy link
- Steps to reproduce
- Correlation IDs (`request_id`, `trace_id`, `admin_action_id`)
- Observed behavior (no event / invalid event)
- Scope (which tenants/modes) and severity
- Suspected owning service and recent changes

Attachments:
- Redacted sample audit events around the repro window (do not include secrets; follow redaction rules)

---

## Changelog
- 2026-02-24: Added enforcement test section and clarified routing table for Private installer and exporter normalization.
- 2026-02-10: Updated severity guidance and correlation ID capture requirements.
- 2026-01-31: Initial published runbook.

title: dsid_bffe5847565845288976fe42ea7cb6d9__token-bundle-flex-enterprise-metering-2026-08-20.txt
text:
Flexible Token Bundles & Enterprise Metering: Packaging and Migration PRD

Overview
--------
This PRD describes a new packaging and billing initiative: Flexible Token Bundles (FTB) and Enterprise Metering (EM). The goal is to provide predictable unit economics for mid-market customers while offering usage elasticity for enterprise customers that prefer metered invoicing. This doc covers product requirements, billing model specifics, console and API changes, migration plan for existing customers, rollout milestones, acceptance criteria, and ownership.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
- Feedback from sales and CS: customers want both predictable credits for self-serve teams and a clear metered invoice for enterprise procurement.
- Several pilot customers reported underutilization of large reserved packages and sticker shock for unpredictable burst usage.
- The new offer should reduce billing disputes and accelerate enterprise procurement cycles while preserving PLG motion.

Primary goals
-------------
1) Deliver a Flexible Token Bundles product that:
   - Allows customers to purchase bundles of tokens with optional auto-topups.
   - Supports token expiration controls and enterprise-level rollover rules.
2) Deliver Enterprise Metering that:
   - Produces a detailed per-route/per-model invoice with daily aggregation and line items suitable for enterprise procurement.
   - Supports minimum monthly commitments and credit reconciliation.
3) Minimize migration friction for existing reserved-capacity and credit customers.
4) Ensure clear SLO/usage behavior mapping so customers can predict latency & cost tradeoffs.

Success metrics (first 6 months)
--------------------------------
- 20% of ARR-new bookings via FTB or EM in Q4 post-launch.
- 30% reduction in billing-support tickets related to usage disputes for pilot accounts.
- 10% increase in retention for customers who convert from one-off credit purchases to FTB.

Customer personas
------------------
- Growth-startup engineer (self-serve): wants simple bundles, reasonable rollover, clear console UX.
- Platform/ML team at mid-market: wants predictability, invoiceable commitments, and console telemetry.
- Enterprise procurement: needs per-day metered line items, signed contract SKUs, and flexibility for overage handling.

Product requirements (must-have)
--------------------------------
1) Purchase experience
   - Web console flow: choose bundle size (10M / 100M / 500M tokens), optional auto-topup threshold (10% / 20% / 50%), and rollover policy (none / 90-day / unlimited up to cap).
   - API/CLI endpoint to purchase bundles: POST /v1/billing/bundles {"bundle_tier": "100M","auto_topup": "20%","rollover": "90d"}.
2) Token accounting
   - Tokens consumed are deducted from bundles first, then charged as metered usage if auto-topup disabled.
   - Bundles are consumed per-customer (org-level) with per-route attribution in telemetry.
3) Enterprise Metering invoicing
   - Daily aggregation of usage by: date, model, route, region, effective price tier.
   - Produce invoice-ready CSV and JSON payload that maps to procurement-friendly line items.
4) Contract and minimum-commit support
   - Allow sales to create contract-backed pricing with a minimum monthly commitment and overage multiplier (e.g., 1.2x list price).
5) Console visibility
   - New Billing > Bundles dashboard with: remaining tokens, rollover window, projected burn rate, alerting thresholds, and next auto-topup ETA.
6) Billing & Finance controls
   - Audit trail for bundle purchases and auto-topups (who, when, payment method, invoice id).
   - Support for manual credit adjustments and reconciliations.
7) Security and compliance
   - Preserve existing PII/tokenization of payment methods; support export of billing artifacts with retention aligned to finance policy (7 years).

Non-functional requirements
---------------------------
- Availability: billing API 99.9% monthly uptime.
- Latency: bundle purchase endpoint 95th percentile < 300ms for authenticated requests.
- Data freshness: daily metering export must be available by 06:00 UTC for the previous day.

Design: billing models and examples
----------------------------------
- Flexible Token Bundle (FTB) structure
  - SKU: ftb-10m, ftb-100m, ftb-500m
  - Unit price example: ftb-100m = $650/mo (base example), per-token effective price = $0.0000065
  - Auto-topup: when remaining tokens <= threshold (e.g., 20%), system creates topup purchase for same SKU and posts an invoice.
  - Rollover: unused tokens flow into a 90-day expiry pool, then expire. Customers can upgrade to unlimited-rollover capped bundles for enterprise SKUs.

- Enterprise Metering (EM) structure
  - Daily line items aggregated by model+route.
  - Sample CSV schema (text table):
    date,model,route,region,tokens_consumed,effective_price_per_token,amount_usd,contract_id
    2026-08-01,redwood-v2-base,chat,us-west-2,1,200,0.000007,0.0074,CTR-12345

Pricing examples and overage behavior
------------------------------------
- If an organization has a 100M FTB and consumes 120M tokens in the billing cycle:
  1) If auto-topup enabled: system purchases a 100M topup at list price at the moment of threshold trigger (creates invoice).
  2) If auto-topup disabled: excess 20M charged as metered usage at the per-token overage rate (e.g., 1.0x or 1.2x contract multiplier).

Console and API changes (developer-facing contract)
----------------------------------------------------
- New API endpoints:
  - POST /v1/billing/bundles -> create bundle purchase
  - GET /v1/billing/bundles/{bundle_id} -> bundle status and remaining tokens
  - GET /v1/billing/metering?start=2026-08-01&end=2026-08-07 -> daily aggregation export
- Console additions:
  - Billing > Bundles page: purchase flow, bundle list, auto-topup settings, manual topup button, CSV export.
  - Alerts: webhook and email notifications for 10% remaining, topup success/failure.

Telemetry, analytics and instrumentation
---------------------------------------
- Metrics to emit: bundle_tokens_remaining{org}, bundle_auto_topups_total, bundle_rollover_expired_total, metered_daily_tokens{org,model,route}.
- Events should include invoice_id, purchase_method, and contract_id for EM customers.
- Dashboard updates: per-org burn-rate forecast (7-day), top 5 routes by token consumption, and reconciliation view for finance.

Migration and coexistence strategy
----------------------------------
1) Existing credit customers (one-off credits): offer opt-in to convert credits -> FTB at pro-rated rates.
2) Reserved capacity customers (Dedicated): expose a bridge where dedicated commit remains but can optionally enroll in EM reporting for consolidated billing.
3) Phased migration: pilot with 10 customers for 8 weeks; collect feedback and iterate.
4) Data migration actions: create bundle records that reflect existing credit balances; mark legacy credits as deprecated but readable in console for 90 days.

Rollout plan and milestones
---------------------------
- Phase 0 (Aug 2026): API design finalized, mockups complete, legal & finance alignment.
- Phase 1 (Sep 2026): Implement backend accounting, basic console UX, internal pilot with finance and CS.
- Phase 2 (Oct 2026): Customer pilot (10 customers), automatic daily exports to finance, sample invoices.
- Phase 3 (Nov 2026): Public beta for new signups, limited self-serve purchase.
- Phase 4 (Dec 2026): GA for FTB; EM GA early 2027 after invoicing edge-cases resolved.

Acceptance criteria
--------------------
- Functional: create bundle, consume tokens from bundle, trigger and process auto-topup, export daily EM CSV, and generate invoice-ready files.
- Non-functional: bundle purchase latency < 300ms p95, metering export available by 06:00 UTC daily, billing API 99.9% uptime.
- Operational: pilot accounts report <= 2 billing discrepancies in the 8-week pilot window.

Security, compliance, and finance controls
-----------------------------------------
- All billing artifacts stored in finance S3 with restricted access.
- Audit log entries for any credit adjustments; require two-person approval for adjustments > $5,000.
- Support for SOC2-required retention of billing logs and exportability for audits.

Open questions and tradeoffs
---------------------------
1) Topup granularity: should topups be same-SKU only or allow mixed smaller increments? Tradeoff: UX simplicity vs. flexibility.
2) Rollover policy complexity: unlimited rollover increases liability and accounting complexity.
3) Overage multiplier: fixed vs. tiered by contract size. Finance prefers tiered multipliers.

Ownership and stakeholders
-------------------------
- Product lead: Aisha Patel (owner)
- Engineering lead: Marcus Chen
- Finance owner: Priya Rao

title: dsid_6e438f9d76c74fc1ae20b20329ef7a2b__package-compatibility-license-audit-playbook-2026.txt
text:
On-Prem Packaging: Binary Compatibility, SBOM, and License Audit Playbook

Summary:
This playbook defines the required checks, automation, and escalation steps for on-prem packaging artifacts shipped to customers. It covers binary compatibility verification, Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) generation and verification, license scanning and audit gating, and runtime compatibility validation for Redwood Private deployments.

Scope:
- Applies to all on-prem packages, container images, and single-file runtime artifacts created by rbuild and the redwood-package-service intended for customer air-gapped or VPC-private installs.
- Excludes ephemeral test images used only in CI test clusters (those are covered by the CI test plan).

Goal and exit criteria:
- Every released artifact must have a reproducible build trace, SBOM, and cryptographic signature.
- No high- or critical-license violations allowed. Medium-risk license findings must have documented business approval.
- Runtime compatibility tests must pass on the declared target host matrix before release.

Definitions:
- Artifact: Any binary, container image, or package (RPM/DEB/tar.gz) intended for customer deployment.
- Build trace: Deterministic list of inputs (git hash, build script, base image digest, toolchain versions) to reproduce an artifact.
- SBOM: Software Bill of Materials (SPDX v2.2 or CycloneDX 1.4).

Pre-flight checks (CI/CD gate - enforced):
1) Reproducible inputs captured: git commit, build container digest, rbuild flags.
2) SBOM generated via syft: syft <artifact> -o spdx-json > artifact.spdx.json
3) Cryptographic signing: cosign sign-blob --key $COSIGN_KEY artifact.tar.gz 
4) Checksum verification: sha256sum artifact.tar.gz > artifact.sha256
5) License scan: grype artifact.tar.gz -o json > grype.json; no HIGH/CRITICAL allowed.
6) Vulnerability threshold: no CVE with score >= 9.0 in image layers that are not patched or whitelisted.

Packaging steps (recommended procedure):
1) Create build environment via rbuild with pinned base image digests (do not use :latest tags). Example: rbuild build --commit $GIT_SHA --base-image "gcr.io/redwood/base@sha256:..." --output /artifacts/myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz
2) Generate SBOM: syft /artifacts/myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz -o spdx-json > /artifacts/myservice.sbom.spdx.json
3) Run license scan: grype /artifacts/myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz -o json > /artifacts/grype.json
4) Sign artifact and SBOM: cosign sign-blob --key $COSIGN_KEY /artifacts/myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz; cosign sign-blob --key $COSIGN_KEY /artifacts/myservice.sbom.spdx.json
5) Publish to staging registry with digest pinning and set immutability tag policy.

SBOM generation and verification:
- Format: Prefer SPDX JSON v2.2 for all on-prem artifacts. CycloneDX allowed if produced by a toolchain requirement.
- Content requirements: component name, version, supplier, checksums (sha256), file-level relationships, and build environment metadata.
- Verification step (post-build):
  a) Verify SBOM checksum matches artifact: sha256sum -c artifact.sha256
  b) Validate SBOM schema: jq -e . < artifact.sbom.spdx.json >/dev/null || exit 1
  c) Cross-check SBOM components against grype findings to ensure no conflicting entries.

License scanning and audit gating:
- Primary tool: grype (config: policies/license-policy.yml).
- Policy: block releases with any HIGH/CRITICAL license issues (GPLv3 with static linkage, AGPL where distribution triggers server-side obligations, or proprietary licenses with incompatible terms).
- Medium license issues: require a documented exception with legal and product sign-off in the release ticket.
- Manual audit: For any package with non-standard licensing, run a manual license review template (see Appendix) and attach to release ticket.

Compatibility matrix and runtime validation:
- Maintain a published compatibility matrix file (compatibility-matrix.yml) with host OS, kernel versions, glibc, container runtimes, and minimum GPU driver versions. Example matrix rows:

  | Component         | Supported OS      | Kernel        | glibc | Container Runtime | Notes |
  | myservice         | Ubuntu 22.04 LTS  | 5.15.x        | 2.35  | containerd 1.6+   | requires userns-remap off |
  | r-deploy-agent    | RHEL 8.9          | 4.18.x        | 2.28  | docker 20.10      | SELinux permissive required |
- Runtime validation suite (run as part of release pipeline against a matrix):
  - smoke-start: start service, check health endpoint /healthz within 60s.
  - kv-cache-load: run a short workload to validate KV cache warmup within 120s.
  - quantization-check: run a deterministic sample inference and validate output checksum against baseline.
  - gpu-driver-probe: verify NVIDIA driver & CUDA version when GPU images included.

Upgrade and rollback considerations (on-prem specific):
- Upgrade artifacts must include a migration plan file migrations/README.md with step-by-step schema and config changes.
- Backwards compatibility policy: minor releases (<major.minor.patch>) must support config v1. If there is a breaking change, mark with MAJOR and require customer opt-in.
- Rollback artifacts: every release pipeline must publish the previous successful artifact and keep it available for 14 days in the staging registry.
- Emergency rollback steps (customer-facing runbook snippet):
  1) Stop new service: systemctl stop redwood-myservice || docker stop myservice || kubectl scale deploy/myservice --replicas=0
  2) Pull previous artifact by digest and restore: r-deploy-agent install --digest sha256:<previous_digest> --keep-config
  3) Run runtime smoke tests and finish with /healthz green.

Automation and CI checks (enforced in reforged CI):
- Build pipeline gates: reproducible trace, SBOM present, signatures, grype policy, and runtime smoke tests.
- Periodic scheduled checks: weekly re-scan of published artifacts for new CVEs and license changes; results create a security ticket if findings exceed thresholds.
- CI failure policy: any gate failure blocks merge to release branch; release engineer triages within 2 business hours.

Escalation and ownership:
- Packaging owner: eng-packaging (primary: @priya.nandakumar@redwood.ai).
- Security reviewer: eng-security (oncall: @elena.kuznetsova@redwood.ai).
- Legal reviewer for license exceptions: legal-team (triage: samir.patel@redwood.ai).
- Customer-facing issues: customer-success and solutions-eng are notified automatically via release ticket watcher.

Audit evidence and compliance artifacts to attach to release ticket:
- artifact.sha256 and artifact.signature (cosign)
- artifact.sbom.spdx.json (SPDX v2.2)
- grype.json (license/vuln report)
- compatibility-matrix.yml entry used for validation
- migration README if applicable

Appendix: sample commands and manifest examples
- Checksum and verification:
  sha256sum myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz > myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz.sha256
  sha256sum -c myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz.sha256

- Cosign signing example:
  export COSIGN_KEY=/keys/cosign.key
  cosign sign-blob --key $COSIGN_KEY myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz --output-signature myservice.sig
  cosign verify-blob --key $COSIGN_PUB myservice-1.2.3.tar.gz --signature myservice.sig

- Minimal packaging manifest (rbuild-manifest.yml):
  name: myservice
  version: 1.2.3
  base_image: gcr.io/redwood/base@sha256:abcdef1234567890
  toolchain:
    go: 1.20.5
    gcc: 11.3
  sbom_format: spdx-json
  sign_with: cosign

- Example SBOM (SPDX fragment):
  {
    "spdxVersion": "SPDX-2.2",
    "dataLicense": "CC0-1.0",
    "SPDXID": "SPDXRef-DOCUMENT",
    "name": "myservice-1.2.3"
  }

FAQ and common failure modes:
- Failure: grype detects GPLv3 statically linked dependency. Action: build a non-static variant or replace dependency; if unavoidable, file legal exception.
- Failure: SBOM missing file-level checksums. Action: update syft invocation to include file metadata and re-run packaging job.
- Failure: cosign verification fails for customer environment. Action: confirm cosign public key distribution and re-sign artifacts with customer-shared key if required.

Revision history:
- 2025-11-12: Created (Priya N.)
- 2026-01-08: Added compatibility matrix and automation section (Marco D.)
- 2026-02-03: Clarified license policy and added rollback runbook snippet (Elena K.)

Contact & owners:
- Eng Packaging: eng-packaging@redwood.ai
- Security oncall: eng-security-oncall@redwood.ai
- Legal: legal@redwood.ai

title: dsid_ffa8f7ac269544a3aeb517fc0f57b24c__observability-shift-left-capacity-onboarding-manual-2025.txt
text:
Observability Shift-Left: Capacity Onboarding Manual

Overview:

This document defines the "observability shift-left" approach for capacity onboarding at Redwood Inference. Shift-left means integrating production-grade telemetry, SLO/error-budget alignment, and capacity forecasts earlier in the lifecycle — during service design, CI, and pre-production load validation — to reduce onboarding time and post-launch incidents.

Goals and scope:

- Reduce time-to-safe-launch for new tenants and services by 30% through standardized preflight checks and telemetry templates.
- Ensure every onboarded workload has clear SLOs, a mapped error-budget policy, and baseline capacity forecasts prior to production traffic.
- Provide runbooks and automation hooks for predictable ramp, measurement, and rollback.

This manual applies to: new model tenants, major model-version rollouts, new public API routes, and capacity-sensitive feature launches. It does NOT replace service-level runbooks (these remain the responsibility of service owners).

Key principles:

1) Instrument early: teams must add the recommended metrics/traces at code review time, not as a post-launch task.
2) Preflight parity: telemetry and deployment topology in staging must mirror production for the load profile being validated.
3) Error-budget policy by design: SLOs and error budget rules are defined and automated before first traffic.
4) Guardrails over guesswork: use synthetic canaries and CI-driven load validation to catch scale regressions pre-deploy.

Roles and responsibilities:

- Service owner (Product/Feature team): define functional requirements, SLO candidate values, and approve rollback conditions.
- Platform SRE (Onboarding lead): run preflight checks, validate telemetry, run synthetic load tests, and sign off on capacity forecasts.
- Observability engineering: provide dashboards, alert rules, and telemetry validators; own golden queries.
- Capacity planning: convert traffic forecasts into capacity commitments and autoscaling profiles.

Preflight checklist (mandatory items before production traffic):

1) Telemetry and tracing
   - Metrics present: request_count, request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), request_errors, token_consumption_per_request (for model-serving), kv-cache-hit-rate.
   - Tracing enabled for request path with sampled spans for llama/model and routing decisions.
   - Metrics exposed to Prometheus-compatible endpoint and pinged by telemetry validator.

2) SLO and error-budget mapping
   - Candidate SLOs documented (availability and latency buckets). Example: availability 99.95% (5xx and timeouts) ; p95 latency <= 350ms for short-text route.
   - Error budget policy: throttles, automatic fallbacks, and escalation contacts.

3) Capacity forecast and autoscale profile
   - 90-day traffic forecast with 95th and 99th percentile burst estimates.
   - Autoscaling policy (min/max nodes, scale step, cooldown) and expected cold-start penalty documented.

4) Synthetic and stress validation
   - CI job that runs a 30-minute synthetic canary with production-shaped distribution.
   - Failure injection scenarios validated (backend timeout, NVMe failure, node eviction).

5) Observability dashboards and alerts
   - Pre-built per-route dashboard exists and renders in <15s.
   - Alert thresholds configured for SLO burn rate, CPU/GPU saturation, and queue build-up.

Example SLO table (to be included in service PR):

| SLO name | Metric | Target | Measurement window | Alert action |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| API availability | 5xx + timeout rate | 99.95% | 30d | Pager at burn-rate > 2 |
| Embed latency (short) | p95 request_latency_ms | <= 350ms | 7d | Auto-fallback to smaller model |
| Token throughput | tokens/sec per-node | >= 12k | 7d | Autoscale + add reserved nodes |

Telemetry validators (example Prometheus queries and golden checks):

- Request rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="myservice"}[1m]))
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="myservice"}[5m])) by (le))
- Error rate: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="myservice",code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="myservice"}[5m]))

Preflight automation (CI hooks):

1) ci/telemetry-check: validate presence and formatting of required metrics and labels.
2) ci/synthetic-canary: run short synthetic load with expected distribution and assert SLO candidates are met in staging.
3) ci/chaos-smoke: run a 5-minute fault injection (timeouts, GPU preemption) and ensure graceful degradation and fallback triggers.

Sample TPS-to-capacity conversion (example calculation steps):

1) Baseline p95 latency L_p95 and tokens per request T_r.
2) Target throughput per node = (1 / L_p95) * headroom_factor (0.6 for mixed workloads).
3) Required nodes = ceil( forecast_peak_tps * T_r / throughput_per_node ).

Operational runbook: onboarding flow (step-by-step)

1) Service owner files "Capacity Onboarding PR" containing: SLO candidate table, telemetry sample (prometheus labels), initial forecast and autoscale policy, and test plan.
2) Observability engineering runs ci/telemetry-check and returns findings.
3) Platform SRE schedules a 2-hour synthetic run in pre-prod and collects logs/traces.
4) If SLO candidates fail, iterate on model/config and re-run canary.
5) Once green, Platform SRE publishes a "Launch Readiness" note with signed capacity commitment and auto-scaling knobs.

Escalation and rollback policy:

- If burn-rate > 4 within a 1-hour window, SRE on-call should engage platform capacity pool and initiate burst capacity policy.
- If sustained SLO violation > 6 hours, execute rollback to last-known-good model version and open an incident (Severity P1).

Alert definitions (examples):

- SLO burn-rate alert: burn_rate(SLO_requests) > 2 for 15m -> Pager.
- GPU saturation alert: avg_gpu_utilization > 85% for 5m -> Slack + on-call.
- Queue latency alert: request_queue_latency_p95 > 2000ms for 2m -> Runbook stage 1.

Example observability config snippet (YAML) to include in service repo:

telemetry:
  prometheus_endpoint: /metrics
  metrics_required:
    - http_requests_total
    - http_request_duration_seconds_bucket
    - request_errors_total
    - gpu_utilization_percent
  labels_required:
    - service
    - route
    - model_version

Launch verification checklist (post-launch 72-hour window):

- Hourly review of SLO dashboard for 72 hours.
- Compare synthetic canary performance vs live.
- Confirm autoscale events match predictions and no significant cold-start penalty.
- Customer-impacting errors resolved or mitigated within policy windows.

KPIs and measurement for onboarding efficiency:

- Mean time to onboard (MTTO): measurement from PR creation to signed launch readiness. Target: <= 8 business days.
- Post-launch incident rate (first 14 days): target < 1 major incident per 20 launches.
- Telemetry coverage score: percent of mandatory metrics present at launch. Target: 100%.

Appendix: common failure modes and mitigations

1) Telemetry gaps: add fallback exporters; enable service-level push gateway if scrape is blocked.
2) Unexpected token spikes: enforce per-tenant rate limits and queue shaping in gateway.
3) Slow cold-start: pre-warm nodes during launch window and use warm-pools for reserved capacity.

References and links:
- Capacity governance handbook: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-capacity-governance-and-error-budget-handbook-2025
- Onboarding checklist: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/capacity-onboarding-checklist-for-new-model-tenants-2026
- SLO definitions and burn-rate calculator: /confluence/eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/slo-oncall-escalation-and-capacity-triggers-2026

Contact and ownership:

For questions, reach out to Platform SRE (onboarding@redwood.ai) or Observability engineering (obs-eng@redwood.ai).

Revision history:
- 2025-03-12: Initial draft by Maya Chen.
- 2025-06-20: Added telemetry validator queries and CI hooks (reviewed by Luca Martinez).
- 2025-10-02: Updated launch verification checklist and KPIs (finalized after Q3 onboarding retro).

title: dsid_6f86af4dec28405ba3cfbf6ed2b5c206__runbook-optimize-quality-gate-failures.txt
text:
Runbook: Optimize Quality Gate Failures (triage, mitigation, rollback, escalation)

## Purpose
This runbook covers operational response when **Optimize quality gates** fail, flap, or time out. It is intended for SRE oncall and incident commanders during beta/limited production rollout.

Quality gates are mandatory evaluation checks required before applying Optimize recommendations (batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization profile changes) to production traffic.

This runbook focuses on:
- Triage steps (what failed, where, why)
- Distinguishing **real quality regressions** vs **eval flakiness / infrastructure issues**
- Safe mitigations (pause/rollback/disable) and when to use overrides
- Escalation paths and required artifacts

## When to use this runbook
Use this runbook when any of the following occurs:
- A production or staging rollout is **blocked** due to `quality_gate_failed`.
- Gate run pass rate drops sharply (potential system issue or a regression).
- Gate runs exceed expected runtime (timeouts / capacity constraints).
- Customers report “change blocked by quality gate” and claim it is a false positive.
- Oncall receives alerts for spikes in gate failures or flakiness.

## Definitions
- **Gate run**: A single evaluation execution comparing baseline vs proposed config (smoke tier and/or full tier).
- **Baseline**: The currently active production config for the route/model (or quantization baseline selected per model family + GPU SKU).
- **Proposed config**: The Optimize-recommended config diff pending apply/canary.
- **Smoke gates**: Fast subset evaluation intended to complete quickly and catch obvious regressions.
- **Full gates**: Broader prompt set coverage for higher confidence.
- **Flake score**: Eval-harness signal indicating run-to-run variance or instability.

## Severity guidance
Use the following severity guidance for operational handling:
- **SEV-2**: Gate system failure blocks multiple rollouts, or widespread timeouts across a region; customer impact likely (blocked deploys, delayed cost savings) but production inference quality is stable.
- **SEV-1**: Gate failure correlates with live production quality incident (customer-visible output degradation) OR a bypass/bug allows Optimize changes to ship without gating.

## Ownership / escalation (who to page)
Primary:
- **SRE Oncall**: Coordinates incident and mitigations.

Escalate based on failure class:
- **Applied ML / Evals** (gate metric validity, prompt set issues): Jonas Weber, Karthik Iyer, Selene Huang
- **Eval-harness / integration** (timeouts, retries, artifact generation): Olivia Grant
- **Runtime safety** (config diff correctness, unsafe combos): Noah Patel, Sofia Ivanova, Omar El-Sayed, Grace Kim
- **Rollout controller** (promotion blocked, rollback hooks): Hannah Rivera, Jada Williams
- **Release engineering / CI capacity** (GPU scarcity, job scheduling): Connor O'Brien, Sahana Iyer
- **Product** (customer comms, override approvals): Aditya Rao, Paula Mendes

If uncertain: page **Sean Gallagher** (SRE lead) or **Allison Grant** (observability/alerts).

## Quick start (first 10 minutes)
1) Identify scope:
- Is this a **single route/account** or **system-wide** (multiple routes/models/regions)?

2) Pull the gate run details:
- Gate run ID
- Route / model / region
- Config diff type(s): batching, cache, quant profile
- Tier(s) executed: smoke, full
- Failure reason code(s)
- Flake score + number of retries
- Artifact links (per-suite results)

3) Decide initial posture:
- **If system-wide failures/timeouts:** treat as infra/system issue; prioritize restoring gate pipeline (avoid mass overrides).
- **If localized failures:** treat as likely true regression or prompt set sensitivity; proceed with regression triage.

## Where to look (dashboards, logs, traces)
### Dashboards
Use the “Quality Gates” dashboard:
- Funnel: proposed → gates started → passed → applied
- Failures by reason, config type, model family
- Gate execution latency (p50/p95) and timeout rate
- Flake rate / quarantine rate

### Key metrics (common names; confirm in dashboard)
- `redwood.optimize.gates.run_count` (tags: route, model, region, tier)
- `redwood.optimize.gates.pass_rate`
- `redwood.optimize.gates.fail_rate` (tags: reason)
- `redwood.optimize.gates.flake_rate` (tags: prompt_set_id, suite)
- `redwood.eval_harness.job_latency_ms` (tags: suite, region)
- `redwood.eval_harness.job_timeout_rate`
- `redwood.optimize.gates.block_apply_count`
- `redwood.rollouts.promotion_blocked_count` (reason = quality_gate)

### Logs
- Optimize service logs for gate orchestration: filter on `gate_run_id` and `state_transition`.
- Eval-harness logs for the corresponding job IDs.

### Traces
- Look for the distributed trace spanning Optimize → eval-harness trigger → result aggregation.
- Common choke points: artifact upload, result parse, retry storms.

## Triage decision tree
### Step A: Classify the failure
1) **Quality regression (likely real)**
Typical signals:
- Stable infra metrics; low timeout rate.
- Failure reasons like `metric_regression_exceeds_threshold`, `rubric_score_drop`, `task_success_drop`.
- Consistent failure across reruns; low flake score.

2) **Eval flakiness / prompt set instability**
Typical signals:
- High flake score; pass/fail flips across reruns.
- One or two suites dominate failures; others are stable.
- Known “hard case” prompts in the failure list; large variance.

3) **Infrastructure / capacity / regional issues**
Typical signals:
- Elevated eval-harness latency/timeout in a region (e.g., eu-west).
- Many runs failing with `timeout`, `artifact_upload_failed`, `insufficient_capacity`, `job_evicted`.
- Correlated with GPU scarcity, queue backlog, or object store errors.

4) **Config diff validation / safety checks**
Typical signals:
- Failures before eval starts: `invalid_config_diff`, `unsupported_combo`, `baseline_not_found`, `quant_baseline_mismatch`.
- Consistent immediate failure after proposal creation.

### Step B: Take the appropriate action
Proceed to the matching section below.

---

## Case 1: Suspected real quality regression
### Goal
Prevent degraded outputs from reaching production traffic. Keep rollouts safe and ensure clear evidence for owners.

### Immediate actions
1) **Block promotion / freeze apply** (if not already blocked)
- Confirm rollout controller has halted promotion for the affected canary.
- Ensure Optimize “one-click apply” remains blocked for this proposal.

2) **Do not override by default**
Overrides are for exceptional cases and require evidence + approval (see override policy).

3) Collect required artifacts
- Gate run summary (baseline vs proposed)
- Per-suite metric deltas and failing prompts list
- Model/version, hardware SKU, quant profile IDs
- Route traffic characteristics (context length distribution if available)

### Investigation steps
1) Validate baseline correctness
- Confirm baseline is the currently active production config for the same route/model.
- For quant changes: ensure baseline selection is correct for model family + GPU SKU.

2) Check whether regression is tied to a specific config type
- Batching changes: look for long-context or high-concurrency sensitivity.
- Cache changes: look for prefix/KV cache correctness or eviction policy impacts.
- Quant changes: look for long-context degradation, specific token ranges, or decoding instability.

3) Re-run full gates once (optional)
- Only if the run did not show flakiness and infra is healthy.
- Do not loop reruns; avoid burning GPU time.

### Mitigation / rollback
- **Preferred**: Keep proposal blocked; ship no config change.
- If a change was partially applied (should be rare):
  1) Trigger rollback to baseline via rollout controller.
  2) Verify traffic is fully back on baseline config.
  3) Add a temporary “deny apply” policy for that config diff signature if the same recommendation keeps reappearing.

### Escalation
- Page Applied ML (metrics/threshold interpretation) and Runtime owner for the specific knob.
- File a regression ticket with:
  - gate_run_id
  - route/model/region
  - config diff
  - failing suites + prompts
  - artifacts links

---

## Case 2: Eval flakiness (false positives / unstable suites)
### Goal
Avoid blocking safe optimizations due to unreliable evals while maintaining safety.

### Identification checklist
- Flake score above policy threshold.
- Pass/fail flips across reruns.
- Failures cluster in a single prompt set or suite.
- High variance in rubric scoring or task success under identical config.

### Actions
1) Confirm rerun policy was applied
- Eval-harness should perform limited automatic reruns and aggregate results.

2) Perform a controlled rerun (one time)
- Rerun the same tier (smoke/full) once.
- If the result flips, treat as flaky and proceed to quarantine.

3) Quarantine the flaky prompt set/suite (admin action)
- Quarantine at the suite/prompt-set granularity with a reason code and expiration/owner.
- Ensure quarantine is visible in the gate results UI and audit logs.

4) Apply temporary policy adjustment (only if needed)
- Prefer quarantine over relaxing thresholds globally.
- If many routes are blocked, consider switching certain config types temporarily to smoke-only *with explicit approval from Product + Applied ML*.

### Escalation
- Page Applied ML (Jonas Weber / Selene Huang) to:
  - confirm suite health
  - adjust suite sampling or golden outputs
  - recalibrate variance assumptions

### Customer support note
If a customer reports a false positive:
- Provide the gate run summary and explain quarantine/rerun process.
- Do not recommend override as the default workaround unless approved.

---

## Case 3: Infra/capacity/timeouts (gate pipeline unhealthy)
### Goal
Restore gate pipeline reliability quickly. Avoid widespread overrides that defeat safety.

### Identification checklist
- Spike in `job_timeout_rate` or p95 eval latency.
- Fail reason codes: `timeout`, `queue_backlog`, `insufficient_capacity`, `artifact_upload_failed`.
- Concentrated in a region (commonly seen: eu-west).

### Actions
1) Confirm scope
- Is it one region, one suite, or global?

2) Mitigate load
- Temporarily reduce concurrency for eval-harness jobs in the impacted region.
- Prefer shifting eval execution region if supported (per integration contract) while keeping baseline/proposed identical.

3) Fix the underlying bottleneck
Common fixes:
- Increase eval GPU pool capacity / adjust scheduling priority.
- Resolve object storage / artifact upload errors.
- Reduce retry storms (cap retries; add jitter/backoff).

4) Communicate expected delays
- Notify Product/Program (Aditya Rao, Talia Benson) if gates will block rollouts beyond the SLA.

### Escalation
- Page eval-harness owner (Olivia Grant) and Release Eng (Connor O'Brien / Sahana Iyer).
- If regional: involve Infra/SRE for that region.

### Temporary policy option (last resort)
If the gate system is broadly down and customers are blocked:
- Temporarily pause Optimize auto-apply globally.
- Allow manual config changes **only** via change management workflow and with audit logging.
- Document duration and follow-up actions. Do not disable enforcement without VP Eng approval.

---

## Case 4: Pre-eval validation failures (config diff / baseline issues)
### Goal
Stop invalid proposals early and prevent repeated noisy failures.

### Common causes
- Unsupported knob combinations for a model family/hardware SKU.
- Missing or mismatched baselines (especially quantization baseline selection).
- Schema drift between Optimize and eval-harness contract.

### Actions
1) Verify rejection reason
- Look for `invalid_config_diff` or `baseline_not_found` in Optimize logs.

2) Confirm schema/version compatibility
- Check whether Optimize and eval-harness contract versions are aligned.

3) Block repeated proposals
- If a specific recommendation keeps being generated, add/adjust static validation rules to prevent proposing it.

### Escalation
- Runtime safety architect (Noah Patel) for unsafe combos.
- Control-plane integration lead (Ethan Park) if baseline resolution is broken.

---

## Rollback / disable procedures
### A) Rollback an applied optimization (if it made it to canary or beyond)
1) In rollout controller, select the impacted rollout and trigger **Rollback to baseline config**.
2) Confirm:
- Promotion is halted.
- Traffic percentage returns to baseline.
- Error budget / inference quality signals stabilize.
3) Create a follow-up ticket to prevent re-recommendation (validation rule or recommendation suppression).

### B) Disable auto-apply (recommended safety lever)
Use when gate system is unstable or a specific recommendation class is suspected unsafe.
- Disable auto-apply at the route or account tier.
- Keep one-click apply enabled only if gates are healthy and passing.

### C) Disable Optimize recommendations for a route (surgical)
Use when a customer is repeatedly blocked and work is ongoing.
- Disable recommendation generation for the route (temporary).
- Record reason and expiration.

### D) Override (exception-only)
Overrides must follow the exception policy:
- Time-bound expiration
- Named approver
- Required evidence (gate artifacts and rationale)
- Audit log entry and follow-up task

SRE guidance:
- SRE oncall may facilitate the process but should not act as the default approver.

## Evidence checklist (attach to incident / escalation ticket)
- gate_run_id(s) and timestamps
- route, model, region, account tier
- config diff (sanitized)
- baseline identifier and quant baseline selection details (if relevant)
- failure reason codes
- flake score, rerun counts
- artifact links (suite outputs, prompt IDs)
- screenshots or links to dashboard panels showing failure spike

## Post-incident / follow-up checklist
- Was enforcement correctly defense-in-depth (Optimize apply + rollout promotion)?
- Did alerts trigger appropriately (no noise, no missed detection)?
- Were timeouts within expected bounds? If not, file capacity/scheduling follow-ups.
- Were flaky suites quarantined with clear reason codes and owners?
- Were any overrides granted? Confirm expiration and follow-up tasks are tracked.
- Update this runbook with new failure modes or improved queries.

## Appendix: Common failure reasons and interpretation
- `metric_regression_exceeds_threshold`: Likely real regression; validate which metric/suite.
- `rubric_score_drop`: Check variance; may be flaky if close to threshold.
- `task_success_drop`: Usually higher-confidence; treat as regression until disproven.
- `timeout`: Infra/capacity; correlate with regional latency.
- `artifact_upload_failed`: Infra; often object store or permissions.
- `invalid_config_diff`: Schema/validation; fix recommendation generator or validation rules.
- `baseline_not_found`: Baseline resolution issue; block proposals until fixed.

## Appendix: Known patterns (as of limited production rollout)
- Quant profile regressions can appear only on **long-context prompts**; ensure suites include long-context coverage for the affected model family.
- EU-West timeouts typically correlate with eval GPU pool saturation; reduce concurrency and coordinate capacity.
- Flakiness clusters are often suite-specific; quarantine is preferred over relaxing thresholds globally.

title: dsid_405145c78ec0427399173a33ffc7a9ae__economic-priority-governor-and-degradation-scenarios-2026.txt
text:
Economic Priority Governor and Degradation Scenarios: design & runbook

Overview

Purpose: This document describes the Economic Priority Governor (EPG) — a scheduling policy component that combines token-cost signals, per-tenant budgets, SLOs, and priority tiers to make admission, throttling, and graceful-degradation decisions in Redwood's serving runtime. It includes design rationale, policy examples, a rollout/test plan, observable contract, and a practical incident/runbook for when degradation modes trigger.

Audience: runtime engineers, SREs, product owners for Dedicated/Private tiers, and on-call responders.

Summary of behavior

- The EPG takes as input: request priority, tenant token-budget metadata, model variant cost estimate, current per-GPU/KV cache pressure, and SLO health signals.
- It evaluates a scoring function that yields one of: allow, delay (micro-burst queue), degrade (route to cheaper model variant or quantized path), or reject.
- Degradation modes are tiered and reversible; the governor records decisions and exposes a decision trace for postmortem.

Design goals and constraints

1) SLO preservation: keep p95 latency and error-rate SLOs for high-priority users where feasible.
2) Cost predictability: prevent runaway cost from low-priority or uncontrolled workloads.
3) Graceful degradation: prefer fidelity stair-step (model->quantize->cached-response) rather than blackholing traffic.
4) Observability: each decision must emit a DecisionTrace event with inputs and reason codes.

Decision inputs and data model

- request.priority: enum (urgent, interactive, background)
- tenant.budget_window_usd_per_hour: numeric (configured per-tenant)
- model.variant.cost_per_ktoken_usd: numeric (runtime catalog metadata)
- gpu_utilization_pct: rolling 30s average
- kvcache_hit_rate: rolling 1m average
- slo_health: derived boolean from SLO engine (true=healthy)

Scoring function (high-level)

score = w_p * priority_score + w_c * cost_risk - w_s * slo_headroom + w_r * resource_pressure

Interpretation: lower score -> more aggressive degradation. We tune weights (w_*) via A/B simulation experiments documented below.

Policy configuration (example table, expressed in prose)

- admission_thresholds: numeric thresholds for allow/delay/degrade/reject decisions. Example: allow if score >= 0.7, delay if 0.5<=score<0.7, degrade if 0.2<=score<0.5, reject if score<0.2.
- degradation_order: [model_variant, quantize_profile, cached_prefix, approximate_rerank] (applies in sequence)
- preemption_policy: immediate for urgent over background; background requests can be preempted after 120ms of queuing.
- budget_burn_rate_limit: per-tenant burn-rate cap (e.g., 3x hourly average). Exceeding triggers soft-degrade, repeated exceed triggers strict reject.
- safety_gates: absolute p95 latency floor (e.g., 800ms) — if exceeded for 3 consecutive 1m windows, governor shifts to stricter degrade mapping for all non-urgent traffic.

Configuration example (YAML snippet)

policy:
  admission_thresholds:
    allow: 0.7
    delay: 0.5
    degrade: 0.2
    reject: 0.0
  degradation_order:
    - model_variant
    - quantize_profile
    - cached_prefix
    - approximate_rerank
  preemption:
    urgent_over_background_ms: 120
  budget_controls:
    max_burn_multiple: 3.0
    warning_window_minutes: 10
  safety_gates:
    p95_latency_floor_ms: 800
    sustained_window_minutes: 3

Operational observables (metrics, logs, traces)

Emit and dashboard these metrics at tenant and cluster level:
- epg.decisions.allow_total, delay_total, degrade_total, reject_total (counters)
- epg.degrade_by_type{model_variant,quantize,cached} (counters)
- epg.budget_overage_count (gauge, tenants currently over budget)
- epg.decision_latency_ms (histogram)
- request.p95_latency_ms, request.p50_latency_ms (runtime request metrics)
- cost.estimated_usd_per_minute (cluster estimate)
- slo_health (boolean per-service)

Each decision should also produce a DecisionTrace JSON attached to the request trace with fields (flattened key/value in logs): decision, score, inputs:[priority,cost_estimate,budget_headroom,gpu_util,kv_hit], applied_degradations, reason_code.

Runbook: incident flow when safety_gates trigger

Purpose: step-by-step actions for on-call to restore SLOs, assess cost impact, and roll back unintended degradation.

1) Alert symptoms and triage
  - Pager triggers when cluster-level p95 > 850ms for 3 consecutive minutes AND epg.degrade_total increased by >200% vs baseline.
  - On-call examines: cluster GPU utilization, epg metrics, per-tenant budget_overage_count, and DecisionTrace samples.

2) Initial mitigation (fast)
  - Temporarily widen admission_thresholds (allow->0.6) for 5 minutes to favor throughput over cost while diagnosing: CLI: redwoodctl epg set --path /policy/admission_thresholds.allow --value 0.6 --team runtime --ttl 300
  - If widening reduces p95 under floor, keep open and continue root-cause. Otherwise revert.

3) If broad widening is unsafe, quick-targeted mitigations:
  - Pin high-value tenants to reserved capacity (switch routing policy to dedicated pool) via routing API. Example: curl -XPOST $ROUTER/api/v1/route/pin -d '{"tenant":"acme","pool":"dedicated-us-west-1"}'
  - For top offending tenants (by DecisionTrace), apply temporary per-tenant throttle: redwoodctl tenant throttle --tenant-id <id> --qps 10 --duration 15m

4) Deeper diagnosis
  - Replay DecisionTrace logs via the EPG simulator (see Testing and simulation) to reproduce policy decisions.
  - Check for model catalog mis-priced variants (cost_per_ktoken drift) and measurement anomalies in cost model.
  - Confirm KV cache hit-rate; low hit-rate may force model re-exec and drive up cost.

5) Restore & follow-up
  - Roll back any ephemeral policy changes using redwoodctl epg rollback --reason "post-incident".
  - Open postmortem referencing DecisionTrace correlation ids for affected requests.
  - If mis-pricing found, publish corrected model cost metadata and run full canary.

Testing and simulation plan (before rollout)

1) Unit tests: deterministic scoring inputs -> expected action (allow/delay/degrade/reject). Store cases in the scoring test matrix repo.
2) E2E EPG simulator: a lightweight harness that replays real request traces and asserts that SLOs, cost, and per-tenant budgets behave as expected for policy parameter sweeps.
3) A/B rollout in sandbox (recommended matrix):
  - 5% traffic with canary weights for 24h across three traffic shapes: interactive-heavy, background-batch, and bursty-chat.
  - Measure p50/p95 latency, epg.degrade_by_type, and cost.delta_usd/hr.
4) Chaos tests: inject KV cache TTL expiration spikes, and GPU slow-path latency increase to validate degradation order and safety gates.

Simulation commands (examples)

- Start simulator with historic trace: ./epg-sim --trace traces/2026-02-22/interactive.json --policy policy/epg-canary.yaml --report reports/canary-interactive.json
- Run parameter sweep: ./epg-sim --sweep policy/param_grid.yaml --out reports/sweep-summary.csv

Rollout plan and gating

- Stage 0 (dev): unit tests + simulator run (green)
- Stage 1 (canary): 5% production traffic, 24–48h. Must show no >2% regression on p95 for urgent tier and cost delta within expected band.
- Stage 2 (regional expansion): 25% traffic for 48h with alternate hardware templates.
- Stage 3 (full): 100% with gradual scale over 6h and a 1h fallback window.

Acceptance criteria (example)

- Urgent-tier p95 change <= +2% versus baseline.
- Background-tier cost reduction >= 10% in high-burn traces without increasing urgent-tier p95.
- DecisionTrace sampling success >= 99%.

Known risks and mitigations

- Mis-priced model variants: mitigate by batching a catalog refresh job and adding canary tags on cost changes.
- DecisionTrace overload: sample at 1% by default; increase when debugging but watch storage cost.
- Tenant UX regressions: add visible headers in API responses when degraded: X-Redwood-Degraded: quantized-profile-3 so customers can failover.

Operational ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: Runtime Scheduling team (on-call alias: runtime-scheduling@redwood.ai)
- Escalation: Eng SRE (pager: eng-sre@redwood.ai) -> Head of Runtime (Marco Ruiz)
- Change approvals: runtime-architecture SIG and Security review for policy changes that expose tenant metadata.

Appendix A: example DecisionTrace (flattened log line)

timestamp=2026-08-02T14:12:33Z decision=degrade score=0.34 priority=background cost_est_kusd=0.003 tenant_headroom_usd=2.5 gpu_util=92 kv_hit=0.21 applied=[model_variant:fast-quant,quantize:8bit] reason=budget_burn_high trace_id=abc123

Appendix B: quick CLI reference

- Inspect current policy: redwoodctl epg get --path /policy --format yaml
- Set a temporary threshold: redwoodctl epg set --path /policy/admission_thresholds/degrade --value 0.25 --ttl 600 --author "oncall"
- Revert latest change: redwoodctl epg rollback --last 1 --author "oncall" --reason "mitigation"

Appendix C: simulation test cases (human-readable table)

1) Interactive low-cost: high urgent fraction, low average sequence length -> expect allow rate >95% for urgent tier.
2) Bursty batch: many background jobs arriving in bursts -> expect degrade for background and stable urgent p95.
3) Cache-thrash + expensive model: low kv_hit + high model cost -> expect degrade to cached_prefix or quantize earlier.

Related work and references

- runtime-architecture/runtime-decision-graph-and-observed-behaviour-catalog-2026 (decision trace schema)
- benchmarking-and-perf-suite/model-variant-selection-cost-latency-tradeoff-matrix-2024 (cost heuristics)
- profiling-playbook/causal-latency-attribution-and-signal-enrichment-playbook-2027 (latency attribution)

Change log

- 2026-03-01: Drafted initial design (Anika Sharma)
- 2026-06-15: Added runbook mitigations and CLI commands (Marco Ruiz)
- 2026-09-12: Updated safety gates and rollout gates after canary results (Sana Patel)

title: dsid_a6cabb5d64cb486fbffc0de9fa863937__runtime-resource-annotation-taxonomy-2026.txt
text:
Runtime resource annotation taxonomy and signal enrichment

Summary

This document defines a canonical taxonomy for resource annotations used across the serving runtime, plus the enrichment pipeline that turns raw telemetry + config into scored signals used by the scheduler, admission controller, and autoscaler. The goal is to standardize names, types, semantics, and operational practices so that components can interoperate without brittle ad-hoc mappings.

Motivation

- Multiple teams (scheduler, kernel mapper, autoscaler, Observability) require consistent, machine-readable metadata about model-serving resources (GPUs, shards, model variants, containers, and requests).
- Inconsistent annotation names caused mismatches in fallback routing and incorrect prefetch decisions during Q3 incidents.
- A small, well-documented set of canonical fields reduces cognitive load for owners and speeds rollouts of policy changes.

Scope

- This taxonomy applies to: GPU nodes, runtime shards, model-variant instances, session tokens (provenance), and request classes.
- Out of scope: long-term billing tags (managed by Finance) and user-level semantic labels (managed by product teams).

Core principles

1) Backwards-compatible: existing annotation keys must continue to be supported; new keys should have clear deprecation paths.
2) Idempotent enrichment: repeated enrichment runs should produce identical signals for the same inputs.
3) Typed and validated: each key has a strict type and acceptable value range.
4) Explainable scores: any composite score must be reproducible and accompanied by its component weights.

Canonical annotation table (summary)

| key | type | description | primary consumers | default/notes |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| resource_type | string | one of [gpu-node, shard, model-variant, session, request-class] | all | required |
| affinity | string | affinity class: one of [high, medium, low] used for co-location heuristics | scheduler, autoscaler | default: medium |
| eviction_priority | integer | 0 (never) - 100 (highest) eviction ranking, lower = safer to evict | scheduler, runtime | default: 50 |
| kvcache_hotness | float | 0.0-1.0 locality score for KV cache reuse | kernel-mapper, scheduler | computed by enrichment pipeline |
| kernel_hint | string | preferred kernel execution path (e.g. attention-sliced-v2, fused-mlp) | kernel-mapper | optional |
| fidelity_profile | string | fidelity target: [max_quality, balanced, cost_saver] | autoscaler, rollout | impacts quantization and fallback policies |
| estimated_tps | float | estimated tokens-per-second capacity for this resource | admission, autoscaler | derived from microbenchmarks and telemetry |
| thermal_headroom | float | 0.0-1.0 available thermal headroom; <0.2 triggers soft-limits | scheduler, SRE | pulled from node sensors |
| model_variant_compat | list | list of variant ids this resource is compatible with | orchestrator | canonicalized to short ids |
| provenance | string | origin id of last configuration change | all | helps audit and debugging |
| isolation_class | string | [best_effort, strict, dedicated] determines multi-tenancy isolation | scheduler, infra | default: best_effort |
| prefetch_hint | string | [none, small, aggressive] KV prefetch strategy expected | kernel-mapper | influences warmstart behavior |
| billing_bucket | string | internal billing categorization | billing, finance | optional, tie-breaker only |

Full field definitions and validation rules

- resource_type (string, required): must be one of the canonical values. Reject unknown types during ingestion and route to owner for classification.

- affinity (enum): used by the placement policy to express co-location sensitivity. Implementation note: treat affinity high as an additive score +30 in placement ranking.
