- Token cost drift: alert when 24h rolling avg per-token cost > 15% change vs 7-day baseline.
- Cache miss rate: alert when aggregate prefix miss rate > 8% for 2m or when a single prefix accounts for >40% of misses.

Monitoring and dashboards:
- Dashboard tiles required: p50/p95/p99 token latency by route, per-route token-per-request, cache hit ratio, KV read ops/sec, GPU utilization, per-tenant token cost distribution.
- Alerts: create SLO-driven alerts in Prometheus/Alertmanager and route to inference-oncall. Example alert expr: (sum by(route) (increase(kv_cache_misses[2m])) / sum by(route) (increase(kv_cache_reads[2m]))) > 0.08

Preflight checks (run before a rollout that touches TER or prefetch behavior):
1) CI verification: run unit and integration tests for TER control logic and canary harness.
2) Canary workload: deploy to a single low-risk region with synthetic traffic matching the production token-distribution.
3) Load sweep: run a token-cost sensitivity sweep (0.1x, 0.5x, 1x, 2x) and validate that p99 latency and cache hit ratios remain within thresholds.
4) Telemetry sanity: ensure the new metrics (prefetch_backpressure, ter_decision_count) are emitted and consumed by dashboards.

Terraform / IaC pattern (example):
- The TER has two IaC artifacts: a feature-flagged config (Terraform) and a canary deployment (k8s manifest) with a traffic shadow.
- Config example (Terraform variables):

```
variable "prefetch_enabled" { type = bool default = true }
variable "prefetch_max_concurrency" { type = number default = 32 }
variable "prefetch_ttl_seconds" { type = number default = 300 }
```

- Recommended module layout:
  - modules/ter/config.tf (feature flags + constraints)
  - modules/ter/policy.yaml (policy map for tenant classes)
  - modules/ter/ci_canary_pipeline.tf (integrates with buildkite and promote workflow)

Kubernetes canary deploy fragment (text example):
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ter-controller-canary
  labels:
    app: ter
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ter
        canary: "true"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: ter
        image: registry.redwood/ter:v2025.10.2-canary
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "2"
            memory: "4Gi"
```

Traffic shaping and CI/CD rules:
- CI pipeline must include a safety gate job that runs a 30-minute synthetic session workload and asserts: p99 < threshold and cache hit ratio delta < 2%.
- Promotion to prod requires: two successful canary windows separated by at least 15 minutes, signoff from runtime or infra-sre reviewer, and a feature-flag toggle to allow rollback.

Runbook: Incident response flows
1) Symptom: sudden p99 token latency spike for interactive routes (>325ms)
   - Immediate check: use the latency dashboard to determine if spike is global or single-region.
   - If single-region and GPU utilization > 85%: run 'ter scale' (see commands) to increase hot-pool size.
   - If miss rate increased > 8%: inspect top 10 prefixes with highest misses. If a single tenant/prefix responsible, temporarily throttle that tenant via tenant-rate-limiter and open ticket to tenant-owner.

2) Symptom: per-token cost jump (>15% vs baseline)
   - Check query complexity and model version rollouts (release-notes). Verify no recent model-promotes.
   - If caused by increased KV reads: reduce prefetch aggressiveness (decrement prefetch_max_concurrency by 30%) and enable conservative burst-credit policy.
   - If unexplained, switch affected routes to a cheaper quantized model variant via smart-routing fallback.

3) Symptom: KV-cache cold-miss storm
   - Identify time window and compute cold prefixes: query 'kv_miss_top_prefixes' metric.
   - Kick prefetch seeding job for top prefixes: run prefetch-job CLI (see below) with immediate=true for top-20 prefixes.
   - If prefetch jobs fail due to API throttling, reduce batch size and stagger jobs by 30s.

Command references (CLI examples):
- Scale TER hot pool (region):
  - terctl scale --region us-west-2 --pool hot --delta 4
- Prefetch seeding job (one-off):
  - terctl prefetch --prefixes file://hot-prefixes.json --ttl 600 --concurrency 16 --immediate
- Inspect top miss prefixes:
  - promql: topk(10, sum by(prefix) (increase(kv_cache_misses[10m])))

Safe rollback checklist (if TER changes regress cost or latency):
1) Flip feature flag: terraform apply with prefetch_enabled=false (dry-run first).
2) Gradually scale down canary and rollback images to previous stable tag.
3) Re-run the CI synthetic test, validate telemetry.
4) Postmortem owner and timeline: runtime-team assigned within 24h.

Operational playbook for scheduled warmups (daily business hours):
- Schedule: 15m before the start of major tenant traffic windows (configurable per tenant).
- Job: prefetch-seed-top-100-prefixes --ttl 900 --stagger 5s --concurrency 8
- Verification: check KV read rates and hit ratio improvement within 3 minutes.

Cost accountability and FinOps signals:
- Each TER decision includes a cost-annotation tag (ter_decision_cost_estimate) used by billing pipelines.
- FinOps SLO: per-tenant variance dashboard and weekly token burn report. Any > 20% spike triggers a review.

Post-incident retrospective and changelog requirements:
- For any incident that triggers oncall paging, create a short incident summary in /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/incidents with: timeline, root cause, mitigations, and three action items (owner + due date).
- Changelog: update modules/ter/policy.yaml and add release note with the exact terraform diff and the canary window timestamps.

Appendices
A) Metrics list to emit (minimum):
- kv_cache_reads, kv_cache_misses, kv_prefetch_requests, ter_decisions_total, ter_prefetch_latency_seconds, route_p99_token_latency, route_token_cost_per_request

B) Example policy fragment (YAML blob) to be stored in module config:
```
policies:
  interactive:
    prefetch: { enabled: true, concurrency: 24, ttl_seconds: 300 }
    burst_credit: { window_seconds: 60, max_tokens: 1000 }
  batch:
    prefetch: { enabled: false }
```

C) Quick links (internal):
- Runtime kernel rollout: /confluence/eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build/quantized-kernel-canary-matrix-and-ci-deployment-protocol.json
- Cache consensus design: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/kv-cache-consensus-and-warmup-coordination-runbook.json

If you have questions or want this runbook adapted for Private deployments (air-gapped HSM/KMS constraints), reach out to the owner (Alden Chen) or open a PR against modules/ter in the infra repo.

title: dsid_63efbaf30eb54ef09df0a93f53e36606__service-account-breach-response-and-forensic-runbook-2026.txt
text:
Service Account Compromise: Response & Forensic Runbook

Summary:

This runbook describes the end-to-end response, containment, evidence collection, and post-incident controls for a confirmed or strongly suspected compromise of a service account used by a model-serving component (API gateway, inference worker, or CI/CD service account with deploy permissions). It explicitly maps actions across RBAC containment, audit log extraction, data residency and retention considerations, SDLC gating for model rollbacks, and evidence packaging for compliance audits.

Scope:
- Applies to service account compromises that affect model-serving flows (hosted, dedicated, or private deployments).
- Includes compromises where credentials were exfiltrated, API tokens misused, or short-lived tokens were abused.
- Excludes purely human user account compromise (see user-account-breach runbook).

Goals:
1. Contain active abuse within 30 minutes of detection.
2. Preserve forensic integrity and chain-of-custody for all evidence.
3. Minimize service disruption while ensuring compliance with data residency and legal hold requirements.
4. Enable safe SDLC-mediated rollback or redeployment of models and infrastructure.

Roles & Ownership:
- Incident Commander (IC): Security On-Call (primary).
- Containment Lead: Platform SRE.
- Forensics Lead: Security Threat Ops.
- RBAC Remediation Owner: Identity & Access team.
- Legal/Privacy: Legal counsel (notified within 1 hour for cross-border data).

Severity Triage (quick check):
1. Active exploitation impacting customer data or production inference paths -> Sev-1.
2. Credential exposure with no observed exfiltration but high privilege -> Sev-2.
3. Suspicious token usage (failed auth patterns) limited to internal test environments -> Sev-3.

Immediate containment checklist (first 30 minutes):
1) Acknowledge and assign IC.
2) Rotate all tokens/keys associated with the service account using KMS/HSM. Commands:
   - AWS (IAM): aws iam update-access-key --access-key-id <key> --status Inactive
   - GCP (service account keys): gcloud iam service-accounts keys disable <key-id> --iam-account=<sa>@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com
   - KMS rotation for model-encryption key: terraform apply -target=module.kms_key.rotation --auto-approve
3) If the service account is used by multiple services, temporarily revoke its active bindings (remove from instance profiles, deployment accounts).
4) Apply temporary emergency RBAC policy: create a time-bound deny policy for the account. Example (pseudo):
   - deny: model-serving:invoke on resources: inference/* where principal = service-account-123 until +2h
5) If rollback is required, engage Platform SRE to divert traffic to a stable variant or fallback model.

Audit logging & evidence collection (preserve chain-of-custody):
- Evidence goal: a minimal tamper-evident package containing raw logs, derived artifacts, and a signed manifest.
- Sources to collect (ordered by priority):
  1. API gateway access logs (timestamped, request ID, principal ID).
  2. Inference worker logs (stdout/stderr, request IDs, model version, sequence lengths).
  3. Identity provider events (token issuance, key creation, role assumption).
  4. KMS/HSM rotation and access logs.
  5. Host/instance syslogs around the event window (±30 min) with process lists.
  6. CI/CD audit entries for deployments and config changes.
  7. Network flow logs (VPC flow logs) and firewall logs if available.

Minimum evidence manifest (example):
- manifest.json (SHA256 of each artifact)
- gateway-raw-logs-20260210T1030Z.gz (SHA256: ...)
- idp-events-20260210T10Z.json.gz
- kms-access-log-20260210.log.gz
- collection-script-output.txt
- chain-of-custody-signed.txt (signed by Forensics Lead)

Audit queries (examples):
- Query gateway logs for principal usage in last 24h (Splunk):
  index=gateway source=access_logs principal=service-account-123 | stats count by status_code, uri_path, user_agent
- Query IDP for ephemeral token issuance (Elasticsearch/Kibana):
  POST /_search
  {"query": {"bool": {"must": [{"match": {"principal":"service-account-123"}}, {"range": {"@timestamp":{"gte":"now-1d"}}}]}}
- Extract KMS access entries (CloudTrail):
  aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=ResourceName,AttributeValue=arn:aws:kms:... --start-time 2026-02-09T10:00:00Z --end-time 2026-02-10T12:00:00Z

Preservation & retention rules mapping:
- If evidence contains customer PII or regulated data, mark for legal hold and set retention to the maximum of: legal hold OR standard 7-year evidentiary retention.
- Default forensic evidence retention: 3 years (unless legal hold or regulatory override).
- Audit log snapshot for incident package: immutable storage (write-once) + checksum.

Data residency considerations:
- If logs or artifacts cross geographic borders during collection (e.g., centralized logging in a different region), capture a locality manifest showing origin and storage location for each artifact.
- If affected tenant data has residency constraints, restrict copies of raw inference payloads to region-specific forensic buckets and notify Data Residency Officer.

RBAC remediation & hardening (next 24–48 hours):
1) Re-assess least privilege assignments for the compromised account; reduce permissions to the minimum required for its role.
2) Replace long-lived keys with short-lived workload identity tokens (e.g., OIDC tokens signed by internal STS) and set TTL <= 1 hour for production workers.
3) Implement JIT activation for any privileged roles the account had (timebound entitlements).
4) Schedule a policy review to evaluate whether the account should be split into narrower-purpose identities.

Model rollback / SDLC gating (if model or serving code implicated):
- Criteria to trigger rollback: evidence of model tampering, unexplained parameter/config modifications, or deployment activity matching compromise window.
- Rollback steps (controlled):
  1) Freeze current deployment channel (prevent new rollouts).
  2) Promote last known-good build from artifact repository (hash & manifest checked by Forensics Lead).
  3) Run smoke tests in isolated staging and verify inference outputs against golden prompt set (use Redwood Optimize quick-eval harness).
  4) Gradual traffic shift (canary) with strict telemetry enabled and auto-fallback to stable model on anomalies.

SDLC gating requirements post-incident:
- No redeploy of model-serving code or model artifacts until: forensics signed-off, RBAC remediated, and patch applied. Use code-review checklist items: dependency pinning, reproducible builds, provenance manifest attached.

Communications, legal & compliance notifications:
- IC to notify: CTO, CISO, Legal, Privacy, Platform Lead within 60 minutes for Sev-1.
- Customer notification: follow legal counsel guidance and regulatory notification windows (GDPR: 72 hours if personal data breach).
- Internally: use encrypted incident channel with access limited to responders.

Evidence packaging & transfer for audits:
1) Create immutable archive (signed tar.gz) with manifest and checksums.
2) Record chain-of-custody entry: who collected, when, commands used, storage location (S3 URI or equivalent), and signing key id.
3) If transferring to third-party forensics vendor, use an approved NDA & secure transfer (SFTP + PGP signature).

Post-incident: remediation and lessons learned (within 7 days):
- Run a root-cause analysis and document measures taken.
- Update RBAC policies in the central policy repo (PR with reviewers: Identity & Security).
- Add a regression test to the evaluation harness to detect the same indicators of compromise in future (prompt set + golden outputs).
- Schedule follow-up audit of similar accounts and run automated entitlement scans.

SLOs & measurable thresholds used in this runbook:
| Objective | Threshold | Owner |
|-----------|-----------|-------|
| Contain active abuse | 30 minutes | Platform SRE |
| Evidence package prepared | 6 hours | Forensics Lead |
| Legal/Privacy notified (Sev-1) | 60 minutes | IC |

Appendix A — Collection commands (examples):
- Compress and checksum logs:
  tar czf gateway-logs-20260210T1030Z.tgz /var/log/gateway/access.log* && sha256sum gateway-logs-20260210T1030Z.tgz > gateway-logs.sha256
- Query Postgres audit table for role grants:
  psql -h postgres-prod -U auditor -c "SELECT * FROM role_grants WHERE principal = 'service-account-123' AND granted_at >= '2026-02-09'::timestamp;"
- Sample Splunk search to pull request payloads (redact PII on export):
  index=inference source=worker_logs principal=service-account-123 | table _time request_id uri payload | eval payload=redact(payload, "PII") | outputcsv evidence_payloads.csv

Appendix B — Forensics checklist (tick-box):
- [ ] IC assigned and timeline recorded
- [ ] Service account tokens rotated and emergency deny applied
- [ ] All relevant logs exported and checksummed
- [ ] Evidence manifest created and signed
- [ ] Legal/Privacy engaged and hold decision documented
- [ ] RBAC permissions reviewed and hardened
- [ ] SDLC gating confirmed before redeploy
- [ ] Postmortem scheduled and action items tracked

References & related policies:
- Identity & Access Management standard (RBAC model) — see ../rbac-and-auth/authorization-logging-and-deprovisioning-guidance-2026.json
- Audit event schema & retention — see ../audit-logging/event-schema-contract-and-retention-runbook-2025.json
- Forensic preservation & legal hold — see ../incident-response-security/forensic-log-preservation-and-legal-hold-playbook-2025.json

Change history:
- 2026-02-10: Drafted by Aisha Patel (Security).
- 2026-02-18: Added KMS rotation and data residency bucket guidance after review.
- 2026-03-01: Finalized and published after tabletop exercise outcomes.

title: dsid_b22a699a20f34b7aaf17c7d7e98f564b__slo-lease-and-temporary-capacity-grant-procedure-2026.txt
text:
SLO Lease and Temporary Capacity Grant Procedure

Summary

This runbook defines the SLO Lease model: a controlled, auditable procedure that temporarily grants additional capacity or relaxed SLO enforcement to a product/team for a bounded window. The intent is to provide predictable, low-friction operational support for planned experiments, burst traffic events, and carefully-scoped migrations while protecting platform-wide stability and multi-tenant fairness.

Why we need an SLO Lease

- Many production changes are time-bound (launch windows, migrations, marketing spikes) and require transient exceptions to normal SLO enforcement or capacity allocations.
- Existing mechanisms for emergency capacity (ad-hoc admin quotas, manual throttle lifts) are ad hoc, lack audit trail, and risk race conditions across tenants.
- SLO Lease provides a structured path with approval, telemetry guardrails, automated enforcement, and post-lease review.

Scope

- Applies to hosted and dedicated inference tenants managed by Redwood Inference.
- Covers temporary increases to concurrency, burst capacity, priority token bands, and controlled SLO relaxation (latency tail allowances, elevated error budget allocation).
- Excludes permanent capacity changes and SLA re-negotiations (handled by capacity reservations or sales/enterprise workflows).

Definitions

- SLO Lease: Time-boxed permission allowing a consumer to exceed normal resource allocations or error budget limits under specified conditions.
- Lessee: The team or product requestor receiving the lease.
- Lease Governor: The owning SRE oncall or capacity owner who approves/oversees the lease.
- Lease Window: Start and end time for the grant.

High-level policy

- Maximum lease duration: 72 hours for burst experiments without exec approval. Longer leases require justification and product/SRE leadership sign-off.
- Maximum additional capacity: capped at 2x baseline concurrency for public tenants, and 3x for dedicated customers with reserved headroom agreed in contract.
- Every lease must include: purpose, owner, concrete rollback criteria, observability plan, and a post-lease audit.

SLO Lease Request Procedure (one-click + manual steps)

1) Request initiation (lessee):
   - Fill the SLO Lease request form (internal UI or CLI). Required fields: service, tenant id, lease window (UTC start/end), requested delta (concurrency/priority/tokens), objective (launch/migration/load test), expected traffic profile, owner (oncall contact), and automated rollback criteria.

2) Automated pre-checks (system):
   - Verify current platform load: local cluster CPU/GPU utilization < 85% and platform-wide spare headroom >= requested delta.
   - Simulate projected pick-up using recent traffic histograms. If simulation predicts >15% SLO degradation to impacted services, the request is auto-deferred to manual review.

3) Lease Governor review (SRE):
   - Verify that observability hooks exist (synthetic canaries, trace sampling, cost estimate).
   - Confirm ownership and rollback playbook.
   - Approve, approve-with-conditions, or deny. Decision must be recorded with reasons and TTL.

4) Execution (automation):
   - Upon approval, orchestration creates a scoped policy: new quota, dynamic routing weights, and a telemetry-scraping job.
   - Enforcement pieces: admission-controller patch, priority-queue token update, and real-time dashboard link posted to the lease request thread.

5) Active monitoring (lessee + SRE):
   - SRE oncall monitors lease health dashboard for the first 30 minutes at 1-minute resolution.
   - Alert thresholds: 5xx rate delta > 0.5% AND p99 latency increase > 25% triggers auto-revoke.

6) Lease termination and audit:
   - At lease end (or on auto-revoke) automation reverts policies and captures a lease runbook artifact: metrics snapshot, decision log, and owner confirmation of rollback.
   - Lessee files short post-lease note within 48 hours summarizing outcomes and learnings.

Approval Criteria (decision table)

| Criterion | Acceptable Range | Action if outside range |
|---|---:|---|
| Platform spare headroom | >= requested delta + 10% | Defer to capacity team; deny automated approval |
| Projected impact to top-10 tenants | <= 2% SLO degradation | Manual review required if >2% |
| Observability coverage | Synthetic canary + traces for affected routes | Block if missing |
| Rollback automation | Must exist and be tested | Block if untested |
| Security / data path changes | None or reviewed by security | Security review required |

Note: The table above must be used by the Lease Governor during manual reviews.

Oncall Runbook: Steps for SRE when a lease is active

1) Acknowledge lease request in the oncall page and subscribe to the lease thread.
2) Verify automation applied the intended quota delta (CLI check):

   rwictl lease status --lease-id=<ID> --format=json

   Expected fields: applied:true, start_ts, end_ts, delta_concurrency, rollback_query_link

3) Open the live lease dashboard (link auto-posted). Focus metrics: p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, headroom ratio, cluster GPU utilization, and tenant throttling counters.

4) First-30-minute checks (manual):
   - Confirm synthetic canary steady within 10% of baseline.
   - Confirm total platform headroom drift < 5%.

5) Escalation criteria (immediate action):
   - If 5xx rate delta > 0.5% AND p99 > 25%: trigger auto-revoke and page product owner + SRE manager.
   - If cluster GPU utilization > 95% for 3 consecutive minutes: initiate emergency backpressure (see emergency backpressure CLI below).

6) If auto-revoke triggered: follow rollback verification steps (below). Open incident channel if root cause uncertain.

Rollback verification steps (automation + manual validation)

- Automation reverts quotas/policies. Confirm via CLI and telemetry:

  rwictl lease revert --lease-id=<ID>
  rwictl quota list --tenant=<TENANT_ID> | grep <TENANT_ID>

- Validate telemetry returns to baseline in 15 minutes. If not, escalate to SRE lead and open incident.

Telemetry queries and dashboards (examples)

- Canary success rate (PromQL):
  sum(rate(canary_success_total[1m])) / sum(rate(canary_run_total[1m]))

- Tenant 5xx delta (PromQL):
  (sum(rate(http_requests_total{tenant=\"<TENANT_ID>\",status=~\"5..\"}[1m])) - sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~\"5..\"}[1m])) * tenant_traffic_fraction)

- Headroom ratio (internal metric):
  1 - (cluster_allocated_capacity / cluster_capacity)

Automation and sample manifests

- Lease Request JSON (example):

  {
    \"tenant_id\": \"tenant-42\",
    \"service\": \"text-generation-prod\",
    \"start_utc\": \"2026-06-10T08:00:00Z\",
    \"end_utc\": \"2026-06-10T14:00:00Z\",
    \"delta_concurrency\": 100,
    \"owner\": \"eng:search-team\",
    \"rollback_criteria\": {
      \"p99_latency_increase_pct\": 25,
      \"five_xx_delta_pct\": 0.5
    },
    \"observability_hooks\": [\"canary-heuristic-01\", \"trace-sampling-1000/10min\"]
  }

- Admission controller patch (YAML snippet):

  apiVersion: rwi.platform/v1
  kind: LeaseOverride
  metadata:
    name: lease-tenant-42-20260610
  spec:
    tenant: tenant-42
    deltaConcurrency: 100
    targetServices:
      - text-generation-prod
    revertAfter: 6h

Audit, post-lease review and KPIs

- Within 48 hours the lessee must publish a short post-lease audit note capturing: whether rollback criteria fired, actual cost delta, lessons learned, and whether a follow-up permanent capacity request is required.
- SRE team will sample 10% of leases for quarterly audits focusing on cross-tenant impact and governance adherence.
- KPIs to track: lease success rate (no auto-revoke), avg time-to-revoke, percent of leases with complete observability, and cost delta per lease.

Security and compliance notes

- No lease may alter data residency configurations or bypass encryption. Any request that affects data paths must include a security reviewer and be marked \"restricted\".

Edge cases and guidance

- Overlapping leases: If two leases would in aggregate exceed accepted headroom, automation serializes approvals and notifies both lessees.
- Unresponsive lessee: If lessee owner does not respond during active alerts, the Lease Governor has authority to revoke.

Open runbook checklist (copy this during a live lease)

- [ ] Lease request verified and approved
- [ ] Automation applied and validated
- [ ] Synthetic canary present and green
- [ ] 30-minute watch completed
- [ ] Owner acknowledged progress updates
- [ ] Rollback tested and available
- [ ] Post-lease audit scheduled

Appendix: FAQ and examples

Q: Can we extend a lease mid-window?
A: Yes, with a new request and shortened automated pre-checks; Lease Governor must approve extension. Maximum cumulative extension limited to 72 hours without exec approval.

Q: What happens when a lease is revoked automatically?
A: Automation immediately reverts policies and posts metrics snapshot. Oncall must validate the revert and open an incident if metrics do not recover within 15 minutes.

Contact and ownership

- Primary owner: SRE Capacity Squad (sre-capacity@redwoodinference.internal)
- Runbook author: Maya Chen (sre)
- Escalation: PagerDuty: SRE oncall -> SRE Manager -> Head of Platform

Related pages and references

- See capacity governance handbook for reserved capacity flows and enterprise contracts.

Change log

- 2026-01-15: Created by Maya Chen.
- 2026-03-02: Added automated pre-check simulation step and PromQL examples (reviewer: Diego Alvarez).
- 2026-06-01: Updated approval caps and added extension guidance (reviewer: Priya Kapoor).

title: dsid_ff22d0b9c78c435b9a5d0ccb567b28ca__multi-region-gpu-preemption-mitigation-and-network-failover.txt
text:
Multi-region GPU preemption mitigation and network failover playbook

Operational runbook for detecting, mitigating, and recovering from GPU node preemption events and associated cross-region network failures. Covers detection rules, automated mitigations, manual fallback steps, Terraform/IaC rollback patterns, CI/CD rebuild guidance, and post-incident analysis checklist.
Oncall SREs, Infra Engineers, Platform Engineers supporting GPU inference pools, and Runbook responders.
Applies to all production GPU inference pools (named: gpu-inference-pool-{region}), cross-region routing (cross-region-router), and private VPC peering connections used by Redwood Dedicated and Private customers. Not for single-node dev clusters.
Primary: infra-sre (pager: #infra-sre on PagerDuty). Secondary: platform-gpu (slack: #platform-gpu). Key on-call engineers: Maya Chen (author), Omar Patel. Emergency escalation: Eng SRE manager - Lena Novak.
1) Alerts: node-preempt-count > 3 within 10m for any region -> Severity P1.
2) Cross-region packet-loss > 2% for 5m -> Severity P1.
3) API error rate for "gpu-inference" route > 1.5% above baseline for 10m AND latency tail (p95) increase > 2x -> Severity P1.
4) Alerting sources: Prometheus rules (gpu_node_preempt_events_total), Cloud provider preemption notifications, Route healthchecks (cross-region-router-health), and Redwood console per-route SLA dashboards.
5) Runbook trigger: Any P1 alert related to preemption+network triggers this playbook.
- Enable graceful eviction hooks in node-manager: ensure podCheckpointing = true and kv-cache persisted to external store.
- Pre-warm reserve capacity: terraform module variable reserve_gpu_count per region (default 2).
- Autoscale policy: maintain min_replicas >= floor(0.2 * requested_capacity) during business hours.
- Use preemption-aware instance types where possible (spot fallback via on-demand burst).
- Batching policy: reduce preferred_batch_size to lower p99 tail during degraded network.
- Cache policy: enable prefix-KV caching and set cache_ttl=300s for non-critical models.
Step 0: Announce incident in #incidents with summary and RFC ID.
Step 1: Verify Affected Regions: run: 
  - kubectl --context=prod-<region> get nodes -l accelerator=nvidia -o wide
  - ./infra/tools/check-preemptions.sh --since 10m
Step 2: If preemptions concentrated in one region, trigger cross-region-router failover: 
  - Open Redwood Console -> Routing -> cross-region-router -> set policy to 'manual-failover' -> route primary -> secondary (region B).
Step 3: Scale up reserve in target region (region B) using Terraform apply (short window): 
  - cd infra/terraform/modules/gpu-pool; terraform plan -var='region=region-b' -var='reserve_gpu_count=3'
  - terraform apply -auto-approve -target=module.gpu_pool["region-b"].reserved_instances
Step 4: Drain affected nodes gracefully: 
  - kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
  - Verify persisted KV-caches are recovered on new pods.
Step 5: If network (VPC peering/TGW) shows packet loss, enable regional egress routing via backup transit gateway: terraform apply -var='enable_backup_tgw=true' -target=module.network_transit["region-b"]
Step 6: If CI/CD deploys are failing post-failover, rollback last deployment using release tag: 
  - ./ci/release rollback --service gpu-inference --tag v2025.01.03
Step 7: Communicate: update customers on status page and affected quotas.

1) Validate BGP/peering state: aws ec2 describe-transit-gateway-attachments (or gcloud equivalent).
2) Switch to backup route table: aws ec2 replace-route-table-association --association-id <assoc> --route-table-id <backup-rtb>.
3) Reconfigure NLB health check thresholds to 2 consecutive successes / 10s during failover for quicker recovery.
4) If DNS-based routing used, reduce TTL to 60 and update CNAME to point to regional endpoint.
4a) Example: aws route53 change-resource-record-sets --change-batch file://failover-dns.json.
5) Verify egress to S3/Artifact storage over backup path: curl -v https://s3.amazonaws.com/redwood-artifacts/healthcheck.txt
- Always use -target for emergency short-lived changes to limit blast radius.
- Use terraform workspace per-region (workspace: prod-region-a).
- For reserve capacity changes, prefer module input changes over resource creation. Example variable override: reserve_gpu_count.
- Patch flow: create PR in infra/terraform with plan output, set tag 'emergency' for oncall review.
- Reconciliation: after incident, convert -target changes into full planned PR to be merged and applied in normal cadence.
- Example snippet: 
  module "gpu_pool" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@repo/infra/modules//gpu-pool?ref=v1.9.0"
    region = var.region
    reserve_gpu_count = var.reserve_gpu_count
  }
- If nodes come back with different GPU drivers, rebuild golden image: trigger pipeline gpu-image-build (Jenkins job: infra/gpu-image-build).
- Quick rebuild command: ci/pipelines/trigger.sh --job gpu-image-build --ref release/gpu-driver-540
Post-incident checklist: 
1) Reconcile terraform emergency changes into mainline PR.
2) Audit metrics: preemptions, p95 latency, packet loss, and per-route error rates.
3) Run regression evals against production prompt-sets for impacted models.
4) Update runbook with timeline and root cause hypothesis.
5) Schedule blameless postmortem and assign action items (owner and due dates).
6) Verify SLA credits and billing adjustments if customer-impacting.
7) Update capacity models and adjust reserve_gpu_count if needed.
Metric | Threshold | Immediate action
-----|-----|-----
node_preemptions/min | >3 in 10m | Trigger P1 playbook and reserve scale-up
cross_region_packet_loss | >2% for 5m | Route failover to backup TGW and enable backup NLB
gpu_inference_error_rate | +1.5% over baseline for 10m | Investigate model-level fallbacks and rollback last deploy
region_capacity_utilization | >85% sustained for 15m | Autoscale reserve + alert to capacity planning
NLB_unhealthy_hosts | >1 per AZ | Increase health check sensitivity and bring reserve instances online
-- Check preemptions: ./infra/tools/check-preemptions.sh --region region-a --since 10m
-- Terraform reserve increase (targeted): terraform apply -auto-approve -target=module.gpu_pool["region-b"].reserved_instances -var='reserve_gpu_count=3'
-- Drain node: kubectl drain ip-10-0-45-12.us-west-2.compute.internal --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120
-- Route53 DNS failover change batch (failover-dns.json): {
  "Changes": [
    {
      "Action": "UPSERT",
      "ResourceRecordSet": {
        "Name": "gpu.redwood.ai.",
        "Type": "CNAME",
        "TTL": 60,
        "ResourceRecords": [{
          "Value": "gpu-b.region-b.redwood.ai"
        }]
      }
    }
  ]
}
-- CI rollback: ./ci/release rollback --service gpu-inference --tag v2025.01.03
Dashboards: infra/gpu-preemption-overview, infra/cross-region-latency, console/per-route-slo. Important panels: preempt_count (by region), node_restarts, cross_region_packet_loss, gpu_utilization_by_pool.
Alert runbook links embedded on dashboards for one-click incident creation.
Title: Multi-region preemption + network failover YYYY-MM-DD
Summary: <one-line summary>
Impact: <customer-facing impact and duration>
Timeline: <HH:MM - events>
Root cause: <hypothesis>
Mitigations performed: <actions>
Service impact: <routes, models, customers>
Action items: <list with owners and due dates>
Attachments: plan outputs, terraform diffs, logs, traces (links)
- infra/terraform/modules/gpu-pool README
- infra/tools/check-preemptions.sh
- consoles: Redwood Console -> Routing -> cross-region-router
- Dashboards: infra/gpu-preemption-overview
- CI jobs: infra/gpu-image-build (Jenkins)

This playbook emphasizes minimizing customer impact by combining automated defensive controls (reserve capacity, graceful eviction) with targeted Terraform interventions and safe CI/CD rollbacks. After any use of -target or emergency var overrides, make a full reconciled PR to ensure state drift is eliminated.

title: dsid_55a170818d7f48ca90f565bcdbaae5c9__incident-bot-playbook-rehearsal-cli-runbook-2026.txt
text:
Incident-bot Playbook Rehearsal CLI (Dry-Run Executor) — On-Call Runbook (2026)

h1. Overview
The *Playbook Rehearsal CLI* allows responders to validate incident-bot playbooks end-to-end in a controlled *dry-run* mode. Rehearsal executes the same step ordering, condition evaluation, and integration wiring as a live run, but prevents production mutations by enforcing strict side-effect policies.

Use rehearsal to:
* Confirm step ordering and guardrails before production changes.
* Validate that playbook queries/conditions work against realistic telemetry.
* Produce an auditable report of intended actions (including simulated API calls).

h1. What Rehearsal Does (and Does Not) Do
h2. Does
* Executes playbook steps using a *safe dry-run executor*.
* Replays sanitized telemetry (logs/metrics/traces) from a snapshot to validate queries used in conditions.
* Substitutes *mutating* requests with simulated responses and records the “intended” state transitions.
* Writes audit events for who rehearsed what and when (no secrets persisted).

h2. Does not
* Perform live production mutations.
* Persist secrets, raw customer payloads, or secret placeholders.
* Bypass network restrictions without explicit admin policy.

h1. Prerequisites
* You have incident-bot CLI access for your org.
* The org has the rehearsal feature enabled.
* You have (or can generate) a sanitized snapshot appropriate for the playbook.

h2. Feature Flag / Enablement
Rehearsal is gated per-org behind feature flag: *playbooks.rehearsal_cli*.

Notes:
* Org admins enable the flag in the org control-plane.
* Admins may optionally provide a policy file that allows specific non-mutating endpoints (see “Network Policy”).

h1. Quick Start
h2. Rehearse with a stored snapshot
Command:
*incident-bot rehearse <playbook-id> --context snapshot:<snapshot-id>*

Example:
incident-bot rehearse pbk_service_failover --context snapshot:svc-checkout-2026-03-12

h2. Rehearse with a short live sanitized capture (low risk)
Command:
*incident-bot rehearse <playbook-id> --live-snapshot --duration 120s*

Example:
incident-bot rehearse pbk_latency_mitigation --live-snapshot --duration 90s

h2. Output formats
* --output human (default)
* --output json
* --output compact-summary

Examples:
incident-bot rehearse pbk_service_failover --context snapshot:svc-checkout-2026-03-12 --output json > rehearsal-report.json
incident-bot rehearse pbk_service_failover --context snapshot:svc-checkout-2026-03-12 --output compact-summary

h1. Safety Model
h2. Side-effect prevention
The executor blocks production mutations by default.

Rules:
* HTTP methods POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE are treated as mutating unless an integration explicitly marks the call as safe-to-simulate.
* Mutating calls are replaced with deterministic simulated responses.
* Read-only calls are permitted only if they match the active network policy (default is deny-by-default for external calls).

h2. Network policy (updated)
Rehearsal no longer uses an ad-hoc CLI allowlist. Instead it accepts an admin-managed policy file:
* --network-policy <path>

Policy file (YAML) supports:
* allowed_hosts
* allowed_paths (optional)
* allowed_methods (default GET/HEAD)
* deny_patterns (regex)

Example:
incident-bot rehearse pbk_service_failover --context snapshot:svc-checkout-2026-03-12 --network-policy ./rehearsal-network-policy.yaml

h2. Secrets handling
* Snapshots must be sanitized.
* The CLI fails fast if a snapshot contains secret placeholders (for example, tokens that match internal secret marker formats) or if a playbook references a secret directly.
* If you see a failure referencing “snapshot hygiene”, do not bypass it—regenerate the snapshot via the sanitizer.

h1. Snapshots and Telemetry Replay
h2. Snapshot sources
Rehearsal accepts:
* Stored snapshot IDs (recommended)
* Live-sanitized capture for short windows (use only when needed)

h2. Where snapshots live (updated)
Sanitized snapshots are stored in the org snapshot bucket and referenced by ID (the CLI does not require direct bucket access).

Operational notes:
* Snapshots are retained per org policy.
* Snapshot IDs are logged in audit events; snapshot contents are not.

h2. Telemetry replay behavior
The replay harness injects events into an isolated in-memory store for query evaluation. It uses accelerated timestamps (not real-time) to keep rehearsals fast.

h1. Expected Output / How to Interpret It
A rehearsal report includes:
* Playbook ID and revision
* Snapshot context
* Step-by-step results (pass/blocked/simulated)
* For each integration call:
  * whether it was executed (read-only), simulated (mutating), or blocked (policy)
  * request summary (sanitized)
  * simulated response summary (if applicable)
* Intended state transitions and guardrail triggers

Tip:
* A “blocked” step is usually a policy configuration issue or a playbook step that attempts a mutation without a simulation template.

h1. Common Failure Modes and Fixes
h2. Error: Feature flag disabled
Symptoms:
* CLI returns “rehearsal not enabled for org”.

Fix:
1) Ask the org admin to enable *playbooks.rehearsal_cli*.
2) Retry the command.

h2. Error: Snapshot hygiene check failed
Symptoms:
* CLI reports secret placeholder detected or “sanitizer assertion failed”.

Fix:
1) Regenerate the snapshot using the approved sanitizer.
2) Confirm the playbook does not reference secrets directly.
3) Re-run rehearsal.

h2. Error: Network call blocked by policy
Symptoms:
* Step fails with “blocked by network policy”.

Fix:
1) Confirm the playbook should be making the call in rehearsal.
2) If safe/required, ask an admin to update the *network policy file* (do not use one-off allowlists).
3) Re-run rehearsal with --network-policy.

h2. Error: Simulation template missing
Symptoms:
* Mutating call has no simulator response template and step fails.

Fix:
1) Add or update the integration simulation template for the endpoint.
2) Re-run rehearsal.

h1. Operational Guidance
h2. When to use rehearsal during an incident
* Before applying a new/updated playbook in production.
* When validating a high-risk step ordering change.
* When conditions depend on complex queries that are easy to misconfigure.

h2. Performance expectations (updated)
* Small snapshots: typically seconds.
* Large snapshots: may take 1–3 minutes depending on event count and query complexity.
* If a rehearsal exceeds 5 minutes, switch to compact-summary output and validate that the snapshot isn’t oversized for the scenario.

h1. Audit and Compliance
Rehearsals emit audit events including:
* actor (user)
* playbook ID and revision
* rehearsal context (snapshot ID or live capture metadata)
* policy mode (default/explicit network policy)
* high-level outcome summary

No secrets or raw snapshot payloads are stored in audit logs.

h1. Escalation / Ownership
* Primary owner: Incident Automation (incident-bot) — Eng SRE
* Security review questions: Security & Compliance (AppSec)

If rehearsal blocks incident response and you need urgent help:
1) Capture the rehearsal report (json output preferred).
2) Page the on-call for Incident Automation.
3) Include the playbook ID, snapshot ID, and the blocked endpoint summary.

2026-03-18: Updated enablement guidance (flag renamed to playbooks.rehearsal_cli) and replaced CLI allowlist with admin-managed --network-policy. Clarified snapshot storage and replay timing behavior.
2026-03-01: Initial publication of rehearsal CLI runbook covering dry-run executor, snapshot hygiene, audit events, and common failures.

title: dsid_ec5f65a05e8a4dc690e0dc61a116b937__commercialization-playbook-optimize-conductor-fidelity-addons-2029-02-09.txt
text:
commercialization-playbook-optimize-conductor-fidelity-addons-2029-02-09 Overview: Purpose: This playbook describes the commercialization strategy, product packaging, pricing mechanics, and launch operations for Redwood Optimize 'Conductor' and its associated Fidelity Add‑Ons. It is intended for product managers, sales engineering, pricing, and GTM teams coordinating the cross-functional launch and early commercial expansion. Scope: - Redwood Optimize Conductor: orchestration and policy engine that executes model selection, batching, and cache coordination across multi-variant deployments. - Fidelity Add‑Ons: per-tenant optional bundles that trade unit-cost for output fidelity and latency guarantees (e.g., Fidelity Shield, Deterministic Routing, Hot-KV Retention). Background: Redwood Optimize has matured from an internal optimizer into a modular commercial product. Conductor is the central orchestration component customers adopt to achieve cross-model cost targets and fidelity SLOs. Early adopters requested licensed fidelity controls (to lock outputs, pin KV caches, or preemptively allocate reserved micro-burst capacity). This playbook turns those capabilities into GTM-ready SKUs and outlines rollout controls to balance revenue with operational risk. Objectives: 1. Launch Conductor with a clear baseline SKU and three additive Fidelity Add‑Ons that are easy to sell and instrument. 2. Provide deterministic billing primitives so finance and customer success can reconcile cost savings vs charges. 3. Define rollout guardrails (canary segments, quota limits, automatic rollback criteria). 4. Establish success metrics and playbooks for onboarding, escalations, and migrations. Target customer profiles: - AI-native startups that require predictable per-route fidelity for PLG growth. - Mid-market teams optimizing inference spend across dozens of model variants. - Enterprises with contractual fidelity and latency guarantees for regulated workflows. Value propositions (by persona): - Engineering: single API to express fidelity policies with runtime enforcement, reduces fragmentation of in-house schedulers. - Platform/Infra: lowers average cost per token via cross-model KV reuse and safe batching while enabling tiered SLOs. - Finance/GTM: productized add‑ons that capture value from customers who trade cost for reliability. Product definitions and SKUs: (Use the table below as canonical SKU description for contracts and billing systems) SKU | Short name | Unit | Description | Default inclusion ---|---:|---:|---|--- OPT-CONDUCTOR | Conductor | monthly seat / tenant | Core orchestration engine, includes policy primitives, telemetry, and basic autoscaling integration | Included in Optimize core tier (or add-on for hosted customers) FID-SHLD | Fidelity Shield | percent-of-usage crediting + surcharge | Guarantees top-k stability for route prompts (measured by response re-rerun similarity). Applied as billing multiplier when limits exceeded. | Optional add-on FID-ROUTE | Deterministic Routing | per-request overlay credit | Routes requests to deterministic inference lanes with reserved KV warmers. Charges per-request for deterministic lanes. | Optional add-on FID-HOTKV | Hot-KV Retention | GB-month + per-surge fee | Increased KV cache retention and pre-warming for tenant-specific prefixes to reduce cold token latency. | Optional add-on Pricing models and examples: - Conductor baseline: charged as fixed monthly tenant product fee plus a small per-route decision token charge (0.1 cents per policy decision). - Fidelity Shield: charged as usage multiplier (e.g., +15% to tokens billed under shielded routes) with a monthly cap. Optionally sold as a firm per-route SLA price for enterprise customers. - Deterministic Routing: sold as micro‑SKU per-request overlay (e.g., $0.002 per routed request), measured on routed count. - Hot-KV: charged as tiered GB-month (0–50GB = $X/GB, 50–250GB = $Y/GB) plus pre-warm operations fee for bursts. Example billing snippet (JSON for billing system ingest): { "customer_id": "acct_123", "sku": "FID-ROUTE", "period": "2029-02", "units": "4350", "unit_price_usd": "0.0020" } Packaging guidance and recommended bundles: - Starter Optimize: Conductor included with limited policy rate (5k decisions/day), no add‑ons. Ideal for trials and PLG users. - Scale Bundle: Conductor + Fidelity Shield (discounted when purchased together), includes 100k policy decisions/day and 5GB Hot-KV. - Enterprise Fidelity: Custom pricing with deterministic routing SLAs, reserved KV capacity, and a seat for SRE integration. Includes implementation support and 6-month usage refund SLA for failing SLOs. Contract & legal notes (clauses to include in the exhibit): 1) Fidelity SLA definitions: define measurement method, sampling windows (30m), and remediation credits (pro-rated product credit). 2) Data residency on Hot-KV: specify whether KV storage is tenant-isolated and encryption at-rest policy. 3) Capacity overrun: automatic throttling vs paid pre-warm option. 4) Termination and migration assistance: outline export format for cached KV prefixes and policy definitions. Operational rollout and guardrails: 1. Staged rollout phases: a. Alpha (internal + 2 customers): manual enablement, close SRE monitoring, 24/7 on-call for first 2 weeks. b. Beta (selected customers, <20 tenants): feature-flagged in console, billing in sandbox only, success rep onboarding. c. GA (public purchase): backfill documentation, default quotas applied, support SLAs live. 2. Canary segmentation rules: - Start with non-critical routes that account for <5% of tenant token volume. - Disable add-ons automatically if error rate delta > 0.5% or average latency increase > 60ms sustained over 10 minutes. 3. Automated rollback triggers (runtime): - Policy decision runtime exceptions > 0.1% across requests for 5 consecutive minutes. - Memory pressure on KV nodes > 75% for > 5 minutes. - Billing meterfeed anomalies (negative credits or >200% spike) trips a hold on add-on billing pipeline. Onboarding playbook (step-by-step): 1. Pre-sales: run the Conductor readiness assessment (see Appendix A). Capture route shapes, expected qps, model variants. 2. Sales engineering: configure a sandbox tenant, pre-seed Hot-KV prefixes for sample workflows, and run the fidelity ramp test. 3. Customer success: run a 3-week migration plan: - Week 0: training and policy authoring workshop - Week 1: alpha traffic on non-critical routes - Week 2: scale to 25% route volume and validate metrics - Week 3: full cutover and closeout checklist 4. Finance: verify billing metering events in staging and confirm invoice mapping (SKU IDs, units). 5. Post-launch: 30/60/90 day QBR cadence to confirm ROI and potential upsell to Enterprise Fidelity. Monitoring, observability, and telemetry contracts: - Minimum telemetry emitted per policy decision: decision_id, timestamp, route_id, policy_version, decision_latency_ms, model_selected, kv_hit (boolean), tenant_id. - Cost dashboards: tiles for cost delta vs baseline, per-route fidelity charge accumulation, Hot-KV usage by GB. - Alerting thresholds (suggested): - fidelity-policy-latency > 200ms (P3) - kv-evictions-per-minute > 5 (P2) - deterministic-routing-drop-rate > 0.1% (P1) Metrics of success (KPIs): - Adoption: percent of Optimize customers purchasing ≥1 Fidelity Add‑On in first 90 days. Target: 18%. - ARR uplift: incremental ARR from Conductor + Add‑Ons within 12 months. Target: $4M. - Cost delta: average net cost savings customers realize vs baseline serving. Target: >=15% for Scale Bundle customers. - Operational stability: <2 rollbacks per quarter across all customers. GTM sequencing and collateral: - Phase 1 collateral (Beta): technical whitepaper, decision sample code, SRE runbook, and feature video. - Phase 2 collateral (GA): pricing sheet, 1-pager for sales, prepared contract exhibits, training for AE/SE teams. - Enablement: self-serve quickstart (console wizard to enable Conductor and 14-day Fidelity trial), sales playbook for enterprise negotiation play. Escalation and incident playbooks (high level): - For fidelity regressions (customer-reported quality drop): immediate ingress to 'fidelity-incident' Slack channel. Triage steps: gather decision samples, roll back to previous policy_version, open a priority incident with SRE. - For billing anomalies: freeze add-on billing for affected tenant, notify Finance and CS, run detailed meter reconciliation. Rollback and migration considerations: - All policy changes are versioned. Customers can request a rollback to the previous policy_version; retention of decision logs for 90 days is mandatory for forensic analysis. - KV export format: newline-delimited JSON of prefix -> serialized-value, with a provided CLI (redwood-kv export --tenant --prefix

). Include rate limits on exports (max 50MB/min). Launch checklist (must complete before GA): - [ ] Legal exhibits drafted and approved by Finance & Legal. - [ ] Billing SKU mapping implemented and tested in sandbox. - [ ] Console UI for add-on enablement complete and QAed. - [ ] Telemetry and alerting dashboards deployed. - [ ] On-call rota for first 30 days assigned. - [ ] Customer-facing technical docs and quickstarts published. Ownership and contact matrix: - Product lead: Maya Chen (Optimize) - Engineering owner: Samir Patel (Conductor runtime) - SRE: Elena Rostova (Hot-KV reliability) - Sales Engineering: Liam O'Connor - Finance/Billing: Priya Natarajan Appendix A — Conductor readiness assessment (template): 1) Route inventory: list top 10 routes by token volume. 2) Model variants: list models and quantization profiles currently in use. 3) Latency SLOs: per-route 50/95/99 percentiles. 4) KV usage: prefix list, average size, cache hit rates. 5) Peak shaping: expected burst factor and duration. Appendix B — Sample policy (YAML): policies: - id: route-qa-stability match: route == "qa-annotator" decision: mode: deterministic-routing fallback: best-effort kv_prefixes: ["qa:annotator:v1"] fidelity: shielded Frequently asked questions (FAQ): Q: Can customers trial Fidelity Add‑Ons without immediate billing? A: Yes — we offer a 14-day trial for Fidelity Shield and Deterministic Routing for up to 5k routed requests. Finance will not invoice trials and usage is metered only for internal validation. Q: How do we measure fidelity for SLA disputes? A: We use a deterministic rerun sampling methodology (sample size 1k reruns over a 30m window) comparing normalized output similarity. Exhibit defines threshold and sampling frequency. Q: What are typical migration risks? A: Hot-KV scaling, unexpected policy decision latency due to large policy trees, and billing mismatches. Follow the onboarding playbook and staged rollouts to mitigate. Notes and open questions for product committee: - Consider a continuous discount curve for multi-add-on purchases (currently left for pricing ops decision). - Validate Hot-KV tiered pricing against observed storage durability costs. - Define a mechanism for partial refunds when fidelity SLAs are missed (credit vs usage rollback). Document history: - 2028-12-05: Draft created by Maya Chen. - 2029-01-10: Internal review with SRE and Billing teams. - 2029-02-09: Update to pricing examples and canary rollback triggers after beta learnings. Related artifacts and links: - Implementation runbook (engineering): /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/conductor-deploy-runbook - Billing mapping spec: /confluence/finance-and-legal/contracts/billing-sku-mapping-2029 - Telemetry schema: /confluence/eng-infra/observability/optimize-telemetry-schema End of document.

title: dsid_50a4b1f84e9c4174869135fc11d35144__annotator-calibration-for-longcontext-streaming-eval-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Annotator calibration for long-context streaming evals (playbook)

Summary

This playbook describes the end-to-end process for calibrating human annotators used in long-context, streaming-style evaluations. It covers selection and priming of annotators, creation of streaming-specific judgment tasks, inter-annotator agreement (IAA) targets, drift detection, telemetry required, and automated remediation steps. The goal is to ensure that annotation quality meets the fidelity requirements of production-facing long-context features (e.g., multi-turn chat with >8k tokens, streaming function-calls, and KV-cache sensitive prompts).

Why this matters

- Long-context streaming evals amplify small annotation inconsistencies because judgments depend on earlier context and partially observed responses.
- Low annotator calibration increases variance in eval metrics and can mask regressions introduced by quantization, KV-cache changes, or prompt rewrites.
- Well-calibrated annotators reduce false-positive regression alerts and speed up triage in the regression playbooks.

Scope

- Applies to internal and partner annotation vendors used for streaming, long-context, and multi-turn eval workloads.
- Does NOT replace safety or legal review for user-sensitive data; see privacy-first-shadow-eval docs for sensitive pipelines.

Owners and escalation

- Ownership: Applied ML — Evaluations (primary), Runtime Reliability (secondary)
- Day-to-day steward: Ivy Chen (applied-ml)
- Escalation: If IAA falls below thresholds for two consecutive weekly sweeps, notify the Evaluations oncall and open an investigation ticket (SOP ID: EVAL-AUD-34).

Definitions and success criteria

- Judgement unit: A single streaming session fragment: includes the conversation prefix up to the turn, the partial response (possibly streaming), and the intended evaluation prompt instructions.
- IAA (Krippendorff's alpha for ordinal labels; Cohen's kappa for binary): Target >= 0.7 for ordinal 3+ labels, >= 0.8 for binary pass/fail for production slices.
- Annotator latency: Median annotation time per judgment unit \u003c= 75s for full 8k-token session fragments (instrumented).
- Drift window: 7-day rolling metrics. Significant drift if metric moves >2.5 standard deviations from baseline.

Prep: tooling and data setup

- Create streaming judgment tasks in the Evaluator UI with the following config fields:
  - session_id (string), prefix_tokens (int), response_stream_chunks (list), expected_behavior_tags (list), quality_sentinels (list).
- Telemetry to capture per judgment unit (minimum):
  - prefix_token_count, response_token_count, stream_chunk_count, chunk_interarrival_ms, annotator_id, annotator_latency_s, annotator_confidence_score, gold_label_id(optional), anchor_probe_flag.
- Provide annotators with a streaming playback widget that can: pause/replay by token range, show temporally-aligned function-call traces, and reveal metadata (model version, quantization profile, KV-cache state).

Calibration procedure (step-by-step)

1) Seed-phase (10 hours ceiling) — establish initial calibration:
   a) Select seed probe set: 500 judgment units across the top 10 production slices (mix of short, medium, long contexts).
   b) Each candidate annotator labels the full seed set.
   c) Compute IAA and per-slice confusion matrices.
   d) Pass criteria: overall IAA >= 0.7, no production slice IAA \u003c 0.6. Those who fail receive focused retraining and re-test on 100 new seed units.

2) Anchoring-phase (daily run, ongoing) — keep annotators anchored to golden examples:
   a) Inject 5–10% anchor probes each day (randomized) with previously adjudicated labels.
   b) Track anchor agreement by annotator (daily) and by slice (rolling 7-day).
   c) Auto-suspend annotator from live tasks if anchor agreement \u003c 85% in a rolling 48-hour window.

3) Drift detection and triage (weekly):
   a) Compute per-slice metrics: label distribution, average annotator confidence, median annotation time, anchor-agreement, and IAA.
   b) Flag slices with any of:
      - IAA drop \u003e= 0.1 absolute vs baseline,
      - anchor agreement \u003c 85%,
      - median annotator latency increase > 2x baseline (could indicate task confusion).
   c) Triage steps (ordered):
      1. Re-run a 100-probe adjudication on the flagged slice.
      2. If adjudicated labels disagree with current anchors, create a re-anchoring batch and notify steward.
      3. If disagreement is between annotators only, schedule focused retraining and a 50-probe retest.

4) Continuous quality regression guardrail (integration with eval harness):
   - For every model promotion or quantization change, require a shortform shadow evaluation against an anchored probe set (min 1,000 units) where annotator anchor agreement must remain within +/-2% of baseline.

Guidance for long-context specifics

- Context trimming: Provide explicit priming guidelines to annotators on how to mark relevance when past context exceeds 16k tokens; allow annotators to mark earliest token ranges they used when judging.
- Streaming partial-response judgments: Use a 3-stage label flow: preliminary-pass (after first N tokens), mid-pass (after chunk M), final-pass (full response). Capture timestamps and final label must be used for scoring.
- Function-call fidelity: Expose function-call traces inline; ask annotators to rate (0–2) fidelity of function semantics and argument completeness.

Example task template (JSON snippet)

{\n  "task_id": "stream-annot-0001",\n  "session_id": "s-53042",\n  "prefix_tokens": 6200,\n  "stream_chunks": ["chunk-1", "chunk-2", "chunk-3"],\n  "instructions": "Rate helpfulness (0-3) after full response. Mark if any earlier context changed your judgment.",\n  "anchors": ["anchor-123"]\n}

Automation and dashboards

- Required dashboards (Grafana/Looker):
  - Annotator Health: per-annotator anchor agreement trend, median latency, tasks_completed/day.
  - Slice Quality: per-slice IAA, label distribution delta, anchor coverage.
  - Shadow Promotion Gate: pass/fail for promotions; show detailed diff of anchor labels.

- Alerts (PagerDuty for Evaluations oncall):
  - P1: Overall test-suite IAA \u003c 0.65 for 24h -> create incident.
  - P2: Any production slice anchor-agreement \u003c 80% for 48h -> run triage playbook.

Adjudication and dispute workflow

1. If two annotators disagree on an anchor probe, route to an adjudicator (senior annotator) with context and both judgments.
2. Adjudicator records decision and rationale in the adjudication UI (required).
3. Update the anchor set if adjudicator verdict differs from current anchor; create re-anchoring job for impacted annotators.

Training materials and shrinkage planning

- Create a 60–90 minute calibration module covering: long-context priming, streaming playback usage, function-call traces, and example edge cases.
- Maintain a rolling pool of 1.5x annotators for critical slices to absorb shrinkage.

Rollout checklist for a new streaming eval (pre-launch)

1. Confirm instrumentation captures stream_chunk timestamps and annotator metadata.
2. Run seed-phase with at least 8 annotators and reach pass criteria.
3. Create anchor set (min 500 judged units) and enable automatic injection.
4. Configure dashboard and alerts.
5. Run a dry-run shadow promotion with a known-good model to validate guardrail thresholds.

Failure modes and mitigations

- Symptom: sudden spike in median annotation time. Mitigation: sample recent tasks and check for task UI regressions or unclear instructions.
- Symptom: IAA collapse only on very long contexts. Mitigation: split tasks into two judgment types (context-summarization + judgment) and re-assess.

Related artifacts and links

- Streaming playback widget design doc: /confluence/eng-developer-experience/api-examples/streaming-playback-widget-design (internal)
- Anchor probe manifest schema: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/evaluator-interchange-format-and-federation-spec-2026
- Regression triage playbook: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/model-regression-forensics-playbook-2026

Appendix: Minimal telemetry schema (CSV header)

session_id,prefix_token_count,response_token_count,stream_chunk_count,chunk_interarrival_ms,annotator_id,annotator_latency_s,annotator_confidence,label,anchor_flag,model_version,quant_profile

Contact

For questions or to request re-anchoring support, contact Ivy Chen (applied-ml) or file a ticket in the Evaluations backlog (component: eval-anchors).

Revision history

- 2026-01-12: Created (Ivy Chen)
- 2026-02-03: Added automation alerts and failure-mode mitigations (reviewers: Asha Gomez, Liam O'Neill)

title: dsid_639dd0469ca34277a35642bf3a09d3e9__probe-correlation-matrix-and-explainability-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Probe correlation matrix and explainability playbook

Summary

This playbook documents the standard process, tooling, and interpretation guidance for computing probe correlation matrices and producing probe-level explainability artifacts. The goal is to accelerate root-cause triage for multi-probe degradations, make correlations auditable, and produce human-friendly explanations that feed into regression triage, quantization decisions, and rollout gating.

Motivation

When multiple probes or slices begin to degrade simultaneously, on-call and evaluation engineers need a systematic way to: 1) measure how probes co-vary, 2) identify probe groups likely driven by the same upstream cause, and 3) generate explainability signals (feature importances, counterfactual probes) that guide mitigation. Ad-hoc correlation checks and scatterplots slow investigations and produce inconsistent conclusions. This playbook standardizes the pipeline, thresholds, and remediation handoffs.

Scope

- Applies to automated probes and hand-curated slices used in evaluation harness and continuous shadow validation across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- Focused on categorical and numeric probe outputs, classifier scores, embedding distances, and metadata dimensions (tenant, model_variant, quant_profile, kv_cache_hit).
- Excludes raw model logits analysis; that is covered in runtime-profiling runbooks.

Ownership

- Primary owner: Evaluations & Applied ML (evaluation-harness team)
- Secondary consumers: Model-onboarding, Oncall/Eng-SRE, Product QA
- Pager handoff: If correlation analysis returns a causal hypothesis with confidence >= 0.8 (see scoring below), notify the oncall channel #eval-triage and open an incident with tag "probe-correlation".

Key definitions

- Probe: a named test or metric (e.g., fewshot-coherence-english, longcontext-kv-dropout, financial-entity-redaction).
- Correlation matrix: NxN matrix reporting pairwise Spearman rho, Pearson r, and Kendall tau between probe signals over an anchored time window (default 1h / 24h for production triage).
- Explainability artifact: per-probe contribution vector (feature importance) computed by a lightweight surrogate model (tree-based SHAP or permutation importance) that uses telemetry and context features.

Data pipeline and inputs

1) Input windows: default windows are 1 hour (fast triage) and 24 hours (stability analysis).
2) Signals ingested: probe_score, probe_count, stderr_of_score, median_latency_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, quant_profile, model_variant, tenant_id, request_size_tokens, top_k_entropy.
3) Aggregation granularity: 5m buckets; higher fidelity available on request.

Standard procedure (step-by-step)

1. Kickoff
   - Trigger: automated alert (multi-probe degradation or SQC breach) OR manual triage request.
   - Command to start pipeline (CI runner):
     
     ./eval-tools/compute_correlation.sh --window 60m --granularity 5m --probes "probeA,probeB,probeC" --out /tmp/corr_run_$(date +%s).tar.gz

2. Data extraction
   - Pull probe telemetry from eval_telemetry_v2 (BigQuery) using the provided SQL template.
   - SQL snippet:
     SELECT
       bucket_start,
       probe_name,
       AVG(probe_score) as mean_score,
       SUM(probe_count) as total_count,
       AVG(latency_ms) as mean_latency,
       ANY_VALUE(model_variant) as model_variant
     FROM eval_telemetry_v2
     WHERE probe_name IN (@probe_list)
       AND bucket_start BETWEEN @start AND @end
     GROUP BY bucket_start, probe_name

3. Matrix computation
   - For each pair of probes compute: Pearson r (for normally-distributed numeric signals), Spearman rho (rank correlation for ordinal signals), and Kendall tau (robust rank correlation).
   - Also compute p-values via permutation tests (n=2000). Store both raw and adjusted p-values (Benjamini-Hochberg).

4. Explainability artifacts
   - Build a surrogate model per probe using the same telemetry features (random forest, 100 trees, max_depth=6). Compute SHAP values to rank features correlating with probe score shifts.
   - When sample size < 200, use permutation importance to avoid overfitting.

5. Cluster and hypothesis generation
   - Convert correlation matrix to adjacency graph using threshold T_link=0.6 (Spearman rho) and q-value < 0.05. Run community detection (Louvain) to find probe clusters.
   - For each cluster, produce a prioritized hypothesis list composed of common top SHAP features and shared metadata tokens (e.g., quant_profile=q8_4, kv_cache=false, tenant=payment-service).

6. Scoring and triage decision
   - Hypothesis confidence score = weighted sum: 0.5 * mean_cluster_rho + 0.3 * common_feature_agreement + 0.2 * p_resource_change (derived from infra telemetry).
   - If confidence >= 0.8 -> declare likely common cause; invoke rollback/canary freeze per rollout policy.
   - If 0.5 <= confidence < 0.8 -> create an investigation card and schedule shadow re-run with targeted injections.

Thresholds, SLOs, and alerting

- Default thresholds:
  - T_link (Spearman rho) = 0.6
  - p-value q < 0.05 (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted)
  - Minimum overlapping buckets between two probes to consider pair = 10 (5m buckets; 50m total)
  - Minimum samples for surrogate modeling = 200
\- Oncall SLOs for first analysis artifact: 30 minutes from alert -> first correlation matrix and explainability report uploaded to artifact store.

Interpreting the outputs

- Correlation matrix file: CSV with columns [probe_x, probe_y, pearson_r, spearman_rho, kendall_tau, p_raw, p_adj] and an accompanying heatmap image.
- Graph view: nodes = probes; edges weighted by spearman_rho. Strongly connected components suggest shared cause.
- Explainability summary per probe: top 5 features with mean SHAP and directionality (+/-). Look for shared features across probes (e.g., model_variant=v2.1, quant_profile=q8_4).

Common interpretation pitfalls and mitigations

- Shared upstream traffic shifts (tenant bursts) can create spurious correlations: always check tenant_id and request_size_tokens as potential confounders.
- KV-cache cold-starts appear as synchronized latency spikes: verify kv_cache_hit_rate before concluding model degradation.
- Quantization-only effects may produce small but consistent shifts across probes; use the quant_shadow regression tests before rolling back quant changes.

Remediation runbook (short)

1. If confidence >= 0.8 and cluster indicates single model_variant: open an Ops-Change with rollback recommendation to previous stable model (include artifact id and time range).
2. If confidence indicates infra cause (e.g., reduced GPU_mem_available): coordinate with SRE to scale or migrate.
3. If evidence suggests probe definition drift (probe metadata flags): move probes to a maintenance state and schedule re-annotation.

Example artifacts and filenames

- corr_run_1612345678.csv (correlation matrix CSV)
- corr_run_1612345678_heatmap.png (heatmap PNG)
- explain_probe_fewshot-coherence-1612345678.json (per-probe explainability vector)
- cluster_report_1612345678.md (cluster hypotheses and remediation actions)

CLI and code snippets

- Quick correlation (Python, high-level):
  from eval_tools.corr import CorrelationRunner
  runner = CorrelationRunner(window='1h', probes=['fewshot-coherence-english','longcontext-kv-drop'])
  runner.run(output_dir='/tmp/corr')

- Example permutation test command:
  python -m eval_tools.stats.permutation --x probeA.csv --y probeB.csv --n 2000 --out pvals.json

Configuration table (default values)

| config_key | default | description |
|---|---:|---|
| correlation.window | 1h | Primary triage window |
| correlation.granularity | 5m | Aggregation bucket size |
| correlation.n_permutations | 2000 | Permutations for p-values |
| explain.surrogate_model | random_forest | Surrogate used for SHAP calculations |
| explain.min_samples | 200 | Minimum samples to run surrogate |
| cluster.link_threshold | 0.6 | Spearman rho threshold to form graph links |
| cluster.community_algo | louvain | Algorithm for cluster detection |

Note: table above is presented as text. Each config is also stored in /infra/configs/eval-corr-defaults.yaml.

Outputs, storage and retention

- Artifacts saved to GCS path: gs://redwood-eval-artifacts/corr_runs/YYYY/MM/DD/<run_id>/
- Retention policy: essential artifacts (cluster reports + explainability summaries) retained 2 years. Raw matrices and images retained 90 days unless flagged for long-term audit.

Integration points and automation

- The correlation runner is integrated with the eval-harness CI and automatically attaches the primary artifacts to an ongoing incident when confidence >= 0.8.
- A scheduled daily job computes 24h matrices for critical probe sets and publishes a stability digest to #eval-digest.

Checklist before promotion or rollback

1. Re-run correlation and explainability on a shadow cohort that isolates the suspected confounder (e.g., single-tenant or single-quant-profile).
2. Run the probe-level replay harness (shadow re-run) for at least 1000 samples or 1 hour, whichever is longer.
3. Validate surrogate model explanations are stable across seeds (SHAP variance < 0.1 normalized).

Appendix A: Example CSV row (correlation matrix)

probe_x,probe_y,spearman_rho,p_raw,p_adj
fewshot-coherence-english,longcontext-kv-drop,0.72,0.0004,0.0021

Appendix B: Troubleshooting tips

- If correlation computation exceeds 15 minutes: reduce permutation n to 500 for fast triage, mark results as low-confidence.
- If surrogate model fails due to high cardinality categorical features: apply feature hashing with 64 bins.

References and related artifacts

- See /applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness/eval-mesh-and-workload-fingerprinting-2026 for upstream fingerprinting guidance.
- See /applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/probabilistic-blame-model-and-hypothesis-library-2026 for automated blame assistance that consumes this playbook's outputs.

Document change log

- 2026-01-15 Maya Chen: Created initial playbook and pipeline templates.
- 2026-02-10 Priya Nair: Added community detection clustering and scoring formula.
- 2026-03-02 Diego Martinez: Updated retention policy and SLOs for artifact delivery.

title: dsid_2a4ecf1699c944aaa31b92d3f2efb874__dependency-latency-attenuation-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Dependency latency attenuation playbook and operational pattern catalog

Overview

Purpose
This playbook codifies a set of operational patterns, configuration defaults, and rollout procedures for attenuating latency volatility introduced by downstream dependencies (datastores, feature services, model shards, third-party APIs, and hardware-accelerated kernels). It is intended for service owners, SREs, and runtime engineers who own end-to-end request latency SLOs.

Scope
- Applies to all Redwood production services that contribute to user-facing inference latency (edge proxies, request routers, model-serving frontends, and orchestration layers).
- Covers patterns for fault-tolerant latency control: time budgets, graceful degradation, hedging, caching, pipelining, rate-limiting, and backpressure.
- Does NOT replace per-service runbooks; it is a catalog and prescriptive default.

Why this matters
Downstream variability (GPU preemption, noisy neighbor I/O, upstream control plane spikes, external API throttling) is the most common root cause of bursty P50/P95 regressions. Consistent attenuation reduces incident volume, simplifies incident severity classification, and lowers token-unit cost by avoiding expensive emergency fallbacks.

Key concepts and definitions
- Attenuation: The deliberate insertion of control logic at call-sites to prevent downstream tail events from disproportionately affecting user-observed latency.
- Latency budget: Per-stage allocation of the end-to-end SLO (e.g., request_end_to_end_slo = 1200ms; model_infer_budget = 800ms).
- Elastic degradation: Graceful reduction of quality or feature set when budgets are exceeded (e.g., switch to cached answer, shorten context sent to model).
- Fast-fail vs Hedge: Fast-fail returns immediately with fallback when a call exceeds a short local timeout; hedging issues a parallel second request with higher cost to reduce tail latency.

Operational patterns (catalog)
1) Tiered time budgets and local timeouts - For every external call, require a documented latency budget and a local enforcement timeout that is a fraction of the allocated budget. Example: model shard call with allocated budget 400ms => local enforcement timeout = 320ms (80%). - Enforce time budget using language-level cancellable contexts or request-scoped cancellation tokens. - On timeout, emit an event with dimensions {service, route, caller_component, budget_class}.

2) Graceful degradation strategies (quality vs latency trade-offs)
- Prefer deterministic, low-compute fallbacks: prefix cache lookup, shorter prompt template, condensed user input, or canned response where correctness requirements allow.
- Degradation hierarchy (preferred order): in-memory cache -> local LRU prefix-match -> approximate reranking (cheap embedding) -> lower-capacity model variant -> canned/generic result.

3) Hedging policy (parallelism with guardrails)
- Use hedging only for requests where P95 tail materially affects UX and cost is justified by user impact.
- Default hedge policy: issue second request at 1.5x local budget when the first request hits 60% of its budget. Cancel slower request on first successful response.
- Hedge budget must be accounted for in cost forecasting and feature gating.

4) Client-side and gateway admission control
- Gate incoming traffic based on dynamic backpressure signals: outbound queue depth, active GPU utilization, and per-tenant cost throttles.
- Admission tiers: standard, degraded (reduced throughput), and blocked. Transitions must be recorded as events and tied to alerting.

5) Smart short-circuit and fast-path routing
- Short-circuit to cached outputs or lower-cost variants when request matches known patterns (exact prompt hash, frequent query). - Maintain a short-lived in-memory bloom filter for hot prompt-hashes to reduce cache-miss cost.

6) Circuit breakers and progressive retry policies
- Circuit breaker states: CLOSED, OPEN, HALF-OPEN. Open when error rate or latency breach exceeds threshold for 2 consecutive minutes. Use exponential backoff with jitter for retries and a guarded probe in HALF-OPEN. - Retries: only for idempotent idempotency-keyed requests. Maximum retries = 2; backoff base = 100ms.

7) Backpressure propagation and capacity-aware batching
- If downstream lag or GPU backlog exceeds threshold, upstream components should pause non-essential work and inform routers to reshape traffic (batch windows, fewer concurrent streams). - Implement a priority queue where control-plane and critical SLO traffic are preemptive.

8) Observability and signal taxonomy
- Required metrics at every call site: latency_histogram_ms, p50/p95/p99, error_rate, timeout_rate, active_inflight, retry_count.
- Required traces: end-to-end trace with spans for caller, network, dependency, and client-side cancellation. Include budget allocation tags: budget_total_ms and budget_consumed_ms.

Recommended defaults table (apply unless service-specific justification documented)
| Parameter | Default value | Rationale | Guardrail |
|---|---:|---|---|
| End-to-end SLO (interactive) | 1200ms | Target for chat/interactive inference | SLO must be declared in service profile |
| Per-stage budget (model inference) | 800ms | Typical model infer central budget | Budget must be validated under synthetic load |
| Local enforcement fraction | 80% | Protect downstream step for cancellation overhead | Must be >60% and <95% |
| Hedge trigger | 60% of local budget | Avoids unnecessary parallelism | Hedge only enabled via feature flag |
| Max retries | 2 | Limits amplification | Retries only for safe idempotent paths |
| Circuit open threshold | 5% error_rate or p95 > 2x budget for 120s | Fast protection from cascading failures | Requires ops review to adjust |

Instrumentation checklist (must be present in PRs that change call sites)
- Add local timeout and cancellation handling.
- Emit budget-start and budget-end events.
- Tag traces with budget metadata.
- Add metric for fallback_usage_count.
- Add alert if fallback_usage_count > 1% sustained for 10 minutes.

Runbook: detection -> mitigation -> post-incident steps
1) Detection (alerts)
- Alert: model_infer_p95 > 1.5x declared budget OR fallback_usage_count spike > 1%
- Pager: for sustained breach > 10 minutes or if customer-facing errors increase.

2) Mitigation (first 15 minutes)
- Triage owner (service-oncall) verifies recent deploys, config changes, and upstream incidents.
- Immediately enable fast-path degradation flag (pre-approved per-service) to switch to cached or smaller-variant model.
- Reduce admission rate to degraded tier by 25% if p95 remains high after 30s.
- If degradation ineffective, engage infra to scale GPU pool or shift traffic to a different region/replica.

3) Longer-term remediation
- Run synthetic replay with golden prompt set to reproduce tail.
- If root cause is a third-party API, apply aggressive caching and adjust circuit thresholds; consider on-ramps for SLA-bound customers.
