- Provide plan quota targets (sustained RPS + burst guidance) for customer-side token-bucket settings.
Migration objective:
Move from the customer’s legacy endpoint (e.g., https://api.cleardata.ai/v1/llm) to Redwood API endpoints while preserving reliability and enabling safe rollback.

Current Redwood endpoint (recommended):
- Non-streaming: POST /v1/responses
- Streaming: POST /v1/responses (stream=true)

Note: Older references may mention /v1/generate. That endpoint is supported for backward compatibility in some environments, but /v1/responses is the default for new integrations and has the most consistent behavior across SDKs.
h2. Implementation checklist (high level)
1) Acquire API key
- CS provisions a staging key tied to the customer account.
- Confirm environment separation: do not reuse staging keys in production.

2) Sandbox test
- Make a single non-streaming call and validate:
  - HTTP 2xx
  - request_id present
  - model_id matches expectation
  - token counts are returned/observable

3) Dual-write gateway (recommended where feasible)
- Route traffic to both:
  - Redwood (new) and
  - Existing LLM endpoint (old)
- Log-only for the secondary path (do not return to user) to compare latency, errors, and output characteristics.

4) Canary traffic split
- Start at 5–10% for at least 48 hours.
- Increase in steps: 10% → 25% → 50% → 100%.
- If customer insists on a faster cadence, 24-hour steps are allowed only if tracing-based rollback hooks are enabled.

5) Telemetry
- Capture per request:
  - request_id
  - latency (client + server, if available)
  - token usage
  - model_id
  - customer correlation id (if available)

6) Rollback plan
- Immediate fallback to old endpoint on:
  - error rate spike, or
  - sustained latency regression vs agreed thresholds, or
  - unexpected model_id mismatches.
- Rollback should be executable without redeploy (gateway flag preferred).
h2. SDK setup (recommended defaults)
Use these as starting points; tune after benchmarking with representative prompts.

h3. Timeouts
- Connect timeout: 2s
- Read timeout:
  - Streaming: 45s (updated from older 30s guidance to reduce false timeouts for long generations)
  - Non-streaming: 20s (updated from older 15s guidance to accommodate longer outputs)

h3. Concurrency
- Max in-flight requests per process: start at 8
- Typical safe range after validation: 8–16 depending on prompt length and average max_tokens

h3. Client batching
- If using the Redwood SDK batching layer, keep the default batch window of ~25ms unless you have strict latency SLOs.

h3. Idempotency
- For retryable non-streaming POST requests, include an idempotency_key.
- For streaming requests:
  - Prefer stream resumption when supported (stream_id / cursor semantics).
  - Avoid blind “restart from scratch” retries unless the operation is explicitly idempotent and the customer experience tolerates duplication.

h3. Headers and tags
- Always log request_id.
- Tag requests with a stable integration identifier (e.g., "cleardata-stitch-adapter") to isolate traffic during canaries and incident triage.
h2. Retry and backoff guidance
h3. What to retry
Retry on:
- Network timeouts / connection resets
- HTTP 429
- HTTP 502 / 503 / 504

Do not retry on:
- HTTP 400 / 401 / 403 (except 429)
- Validation errors (treat as integration bugs)

h3. Backoff parameters (recommended)
- Strategy: exponential backoff with jitter
- initial_delay: 250ms (updated from older 200ms guidance)
- max_delay: 5s
- max_retries: 6 (updated from older 5 retries to reduce customer-visible failures on brief throttling events)

h3. Streaming retry guidance
- Streaming requests should not be aggressively retried from the beginning.
- Preferred approach:
  - reconnect and resume when stream resumption is supported (stream_id/cursor)
  - otherwise surface an ergonomic error to the caller and allow the application to decide whether to retry.

h3. Idempotency note
- If the application cannot guarantee idempotency_key uniqueness per logical request, it should disable automatic retries for non-streaming calls to prevent duplicate outputs and confusing UX.
h2. Rate limiting patterns
h3. Client-side limiter (recommended)
- Implement a local token-bucket limiter per process keyed by API key.
- Configure:
  - capacity = burst allowance (example starting point: 20)
  - refill rate = sustained RPS target (CS supplies plan-specific quota targets)

h3. Behavior on 429
- Back off client-side for a randomized window (2s–8s) in addition to exponential backoff.
- This reduces thundering-herd behavior during shared throttling windows.

h3. Route-level protections
- Apply per-route concurrency limits for heavy generation calls (long max_tokens / long contexts).
- Consider separate pools for streaming vs non-streaming to prevent long streams from starving short requests.
h2. Operational checks for endpoint migration
Before routing >50% traffic to Redwood:
- Verify metrics parity vs old endpoint
  - latency (p50/p95/p99)
  - error rates
  - token counts for a representative prompt set
- Validate output quality
  - run a fixed prompt set through both systems
  - review deltas with the customer
- Confirm cost and throughput expectations
  - validate sustained QPS and peak burst behavior against plan targets

Automated health checks CS can run (if enabled):
- 2xx ratio and 5xx/4xx trends
- token usage delta per request type
- model mismatch alerts (returned model_id differs from expected)
h2. Network allowlisting / IPs
- By default, customers do not need to allowlist specific Redwood ingress IPs for outbound calls to the Redwood API.
- If the customer environment requires strict egress allowlisting, follow the Security page: confluence://security-and-compliance/network/egress-and-allowlisting-guidance.
- Important nuance: static IP ranges may differ by region and can change as infrastructure evolves; prefer domain-based allowlisting when possible and follow the current Security guidance rather than copying IPs into customer runbooks.
h2. Minimal code samples
These snippets are intentionally minimal; wrap them with your organization’s retry + rate limiting utilities.

h3. Node.js (minimal)
const { RedwoodClient } = require('@redwood-inference/sdk');

const client = new RedwoodClient({
  apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY,
  timeout: 20000,
  connectTimeout: 2000
});

async function generate(prompt, idempotencyKey) {
  return await client.responses.create({
    model: 'redwood-large-v2',
    input: prompt,
    idempotency_key: idempotencyKey
  });
}

h3. Python (minimal)
import os
from redwood import RedwoodClient

client = RedwoodClient(
  api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY'],
  connect_timeout=2,
  read_timeout=20
)

def generate(prompt, idempotency_key=None):
  return client.responses.create(
    model='redwood-large-v2',
    input=prompt,
    idempotency_key=idempotency_key
  )
h2. Rollout tempo and thresholds
Default canary windows:
- 48 hours minimum per ramp step
- Target thresholds during canary:
  - error rate < 0.5% (aggregate)
  - stable p95 latency vs baseline

Optional faster cadence:
- 24-hour steps permitted if tracing tag + rapid rollback hook is enabled.
- Use stricter on-call readiness (customer + CS) during the first 24 hours of each step.
h2. Ownership and support
Customer Success (CS):
- Owns canary planning, ramp schedule, and success criteria.
- Coordinates staging/prod key provisioning and integration readiness.

Engineering Support (as needed):
- Assists with SDK-level issues, retries, streaming resumption, and performance tuning.

Escalation trigger examples:
- sustained 5xx rate increase
- repeated 429 spikes after client limiter deployed
- unexplained model_id mismatch alerts
h2. Changelog
2026-09-12
- Updated default endpoint guidance to /v1/responses (non-streaming and streaming).
- Updated recommended read timeouts (streaming 45s, non-streaming 20s).
- Increased recommended max_retries from 5 to 6; initial backoff from 200ms to 250ms.
- Updated sample model from redwood-large-v1 to redwood-large-v2.
- Added explicit note on allowlisting guidance and avoiding hard-coded IPs.

2026-08-04
- Initial publication consolidating SDK setup, migration steps, retries, rate limiting, and canary metrics used for ClearData Stitch adapter rollout.

title: dsid_54f01021e9a94a2380c145269639b4c1__operator-runtime-seeding-and-traffic-mirroring-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Operator runtime seeding and traffic mirroring playbook

Summary

This playbook describes a validated, operator-driven process for seeding runtime state and performing live traffic mirroring in on-prem / VPC private deployments. The goal is to enable low-risk model and config rollouts, reduce cold-start impact, and give operators a deterministic path for verification and rollback without impacting production tenants.

Scope and audience

- Audience: Field operators, deployment engineers, SREs responsible for customer private deployments.
- Scope: Seeding model artifacts, KV cache warmup, prefix-caching strategies, routing-level traffic mirroring (1:1 and 1:n), observability thresholds, and safe rollback steps. This playbook applies to both single-tenant and multi-tenant private control planes where an operator has access to the runtime operator API.

When to use this playbook

1. Initial customer activation where model artifacts must be preloaded to avoid cold token latencies.
2. Model swap or quantized artifact rollout where output quality and latency must be validated with mirrored live traffic.
3. Capacity-driven cutovers (moving tenant traffic between proxy fabrics or during hardware migration).

Prerequisites

- Operator CLI/console access to the private control plane and runtime operator endpoints.
- Signed model artifact available in the artifact repository and accessible to the runtime image signer.
- A canary tenant or test tenant that mirrors production traffic (recommended).
- Observability hooks enabled: per-route latency p50/p95/p99, token throughput, KV cache hit ratio, error rates, and regression hooks for quality check (BLEU/embedding drift or custom eval).
- Out-of-band communication channel with customer NOC and an agreed maintenance window (if required).

Topology and patterns

We support two common mirroring topologies:

- Sidecar mirror: Proxy duplicates incoming request headers/payloads to a mirrored runtime instance in parallel. Useful for per-tenant verification without changing routing.
- Egress-shim mirror: Upstream router sends a sampled fraction of traffic to the mirror cluster using routing weights. Useful when sidecar injection is expensive.

Example diagram (text):

Client -> Ingress Proxy -> (primary runtime) -> responses
                      """"""""""""""
                      -> Mirrored runtime (read-only, seeded artifacts) -> logging/metrics

Operational principles

- Mirrored runtime must be read-only and never acknowledged as authoritative for production traffic.
- Seeded KV/cache state should be treated as advisory; operators must track cache TTLs and seeding age.
- Traffic mirroring must be limited to a safe sampling fraction when doing first-time validation: 0.1% -> 1% -> 10% -> 100% progression model.

Step-by-step: Runtime seeding

1. Verify artifact integrity
   - Confirm artifact signature and checksum (sha256) against the artifact manifest.
   - CLI: runtime-operator artifact verify --artifact-id <ARTID> --sha256 <SUM>

2. Stage artifact to runtime image
   - Upload artifact to local artifact cache and mark as staged for tenant/cluster: runtime-operator stage --artifact <ARTID> --tenant <TENANT_ID>

3. Warm model weights and KV cache
   - Strategy A: Prefetch model weights into local GPU memory using runtime preloader: runtime-preload --artifact <ARTID> --nodes all --batch-size 1
   - Strategy B: Replay representative prompt corpus (10k prompts representative of production traffic) against mirrored runtime in isolated mode to populate KV cache. Use replay tool with throttling to avoid CPU/GPU contention: replay-tool --corpus /data/rep-corpus --rate 50/s --target <MIRROR_ENDPOINT>

4. Verify memory and readiness
   - Check readiness endpoint and GPU memory occupancy: curl -sS http://<node>/runtime/health | jq .gpu_memory_mb
   - Expected: model resident and readiness==true.

Step-by-step: Traffic mirroring (safe progression)

1. Create mirror policy (dry-run)
   - Define an objective: quality-signal threshold (e.g., embedding drift < 0.05, top-1 rerank alignment > 98%) and latency budget (p95 < baseline + 50ms).
   - Create mirror policy in operator: runtime-operator mirror create --from-cluster <INGRESS> --to <MIRROR_CLUSTER> --sample-rate 0.001 --mode read-only --filter "route:/api/v1/chat/*"

2. Observe for 1–2 maintenance cycles (30–60 minutes)
   - Collect metrics: mirrored latency p50/p95/p99, cache hit ratio, model output divergence (see Quality checks). Do not escalate traffic.

3. Increase mirror rate stepwise: 0.01 -> 0.1 -> 1 -> 10 -> 100
   - At each step run the quality regression checks and ensure observability gates are satisfied before moving to the next step.

Quality checks and gating

- Metrics to compute every 15 minutes:
  - Latency delta: p95_mirror - p95_primary <= 50ms
  - Cache warmness: KV cache hit ratio > 60% after seed phase
  - Output divergence: embedding cosine distance median <= 0.04 vs baseline, or task-specific metric (F1/BLEU) regression <= 1.5%
  - Error rate: 5xx rate mirror <= 0.5% absolute increase over primary

- Automated gate example (pseudo-rule):
  - IF latency_delta_p95 > 100ms OR error_increase > 1% OR output_divergence > threshold -> AUTO-PAUSE mirror and notify operator channel

Observability and logs

- Required dashboards: Mirror-Latency, Mirror-Quality-Drift, KV-Cache-Occupancy, Mirror-Errors. Dashboards should include per-tenant and per-route breakdowns.
- Trace tags: add tag mirror=1 and seed_age=<minutes> to all mirrored requests for trace correlation.
- Logging: mirror runtime must emit request-id, model-artifact-id, seed-checksum, and decision flags.

Rollback and fail-open behavior

- Mirror-only operations are safe by default (read-only). However, if the mirror runtime exhibits consistent regressions, follow the rollback checklist:
  1. Set mirror sample-rate=0 and mark mirror policy paused: runtime-operator mirror pause --policy <POLICY_ID>
  2. If the problem is a bad artifact, mark artifact revoked and trigger failover to previous artifact: runtime-operator artifact revoke --artifact <ARTID>; runtime-operator rollback --artifact <ARTID_PRIO> --tenant <TENANT_ID>
  3. If operator cannot revoke artifact immediately, isolate mirror cluster at network level and drain mirrored pods.

Escalation path and ownership

- Primary owner: PrivateDeployments Engineering (oncall: private-deployments-sre rotation)
- Escalation: contact Platform Reliability -> Product -> Customer Success (template message included below).

Operational checklist (table)

- Pre-seed checklist:
  - Artifact signature verified
  - Observability hooks enabled and dashboards accessible
  - Canary/test tenant configured
  - Maintenance window agreed (if >10% traffic)

- Seeding checklist:
  - Model weights resident on GPU across nodes
  - KV cache hit ratio observed improving > 40% within 1 hour of replay
  - Readiness endpoints green on all seed targets

- Mirroring progression checklist:
  - Stepwise sample rate documented and approved
  - Quality gates green for 30 minutes at each step
  - Rollback plan validated and contact list confirmed

Example configs

Mirror policy (YAML example):

---
apiVersion: redwood/v1
kind: MirrorPolicy
metadata:
  name: tenant-123-mirror-1
spec:
  source: ingress-proxy
  destination: cluster-mirror-ten-123
  sampleRate: 0.01
  mode: read-only
  filters:
    - pathPrefix: /api/v1/chat
  annotations:
    owner: private-deployments
    ticket: PD-2345
---

Seed replay config (example JSON lines):
{
  "corpus": "/data/customer/tenant-123/rep-corpus.jsonl",
  "target": "https://mirror.tenant-123.internal:8443/v1/stream",
  "rate": 25,
  "duration_minutes": 120
}

Operator CLI snippets

- Stage artifact: runtime-operator stage --artifact art-2026-06-03 --tenant TEN-123
- Start seeded replay: replay-tool start --config seed-replay.json
- Create mirror policy: runtime-operator mirror create --from ingress --to mirror-ten-123 --rate 0.01 --filter "/api/v1/chat"
- Pause mirror: runtime-operator mirror pause --policy mirror-abc123

Troubleshooting cookbook (common failures)

1. Slow p95 on mirror after seed:
   - Symptom: p95_mirror >> p95_primary even after seed phase
   - Actions: verify GPU memory residency, reduce batch-size, validate kernel/quantization mismatch between clusters. If mismatch, revert to previous artifact.

2. High output divergence:
   - Symptom: embedding drift > threshold
   - Actions: run off-line evals on seeded mirror with the same prompts used in production sampling, compare top-k outputs. If drift persists, revoke artifact.

3. KV cache not warming:
   - Symptom: cache hit ratio remains <20% after replay
   - Actions: ensure replay corpus covers prefixes and conversational back-and-forth; increase replay diversity and duration; confirm that caching keys and prefix hashing match between primary and mirror runtimes.

Templates and communication

- Customer notification template (short):
  Subject: Planned runtime seeding and verification for <customer-name> (window: <start> - <end>)
  Body: We will perform routine runtime seeding and staged traffic mirroring to validate a model refresh. Production write path will not be impacted. If you observe regression, contact NOC at <contact>.

- Incident template (if rollback):
  - Summary, start time, affected tenants, action taken (mirror paused, artifact revoked, rollback initiated), next steps, owner contact.

Post-mortem data to collect

- Replay corpus used, sample rates and step timings, metric deltas (latency, error, divergence), kubernetes pod events, GPU memory profiles, and request traces with mirror=1 tag. Preserve artifacts and checksums.

Ownership and contact list

- Private Deployments Engineering (oncall): private-deployments-sre@redwood.internal
- Runtime artifact team: artifacts@redwood.internal
- Observability: telemetry@redwood.internal

Appendix: Quick reference commands

- Check mirror metrics: telemetry-cli query --dashboard Mirror-Latency --tenant TEN-123 --range 60m
- Verify artifact checksum: runtime-operator artifact verify --artifact art-2026-06-03
- Pause mirror quickly: runtime-operator mirror pause --policy mirror-abc123

Notes and rationale

This playbook codifies a minimal-risk pattern that balances operator autonomy with automated gates. Seeding avoids the large latencies common on first cold-infer request; mirroring gives a realistic signal for quality without impacting production. The safe progression and gate rules are conservative by design and should be tuned with specific customer SLAs and workload profiles.

title: dsid_a15105ac05894880910c15c92024b8b3__observability-driven-onboarding-runbook-2027.txt
text:
observability-driven-onboarding-runbook

Overview

Purpose:
This runbook defines an observability-first approach to enterprise onboarding for Redwood Inference customers. It standardizes the telemetry contract, synthetic acceptance checks, escalation paths, and QBR handoff artifacts used during a customer go-live and the first 90 days of production.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private deployments and to Hosted customers with enterprise SLAs.
- Covers telemetry-onboarding, pre-cutover validation, day-0 to day-14 stabilization, and QBR handoff.

Owners and Primary Contacts
- Customer Success (owner): Maya Chen (maya.chen@redwood.com)
- SRE / Platform escalation: Arjun Patel (arjun.patel@redwood.com)
- Serving Runtime SME: Sofia Martinez (sofia.martinez@redwood.com)
- Account Executive (commercial): Liam O'Connor (liam.oconnor@redwood.com)

Acceptance gates (must pass before route to production)
1) Telemetry contract validation (required)
   - Metrics: request_count, request_latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, token_consumption_total, kvcache_hit_ratio, active_connections_by_tenant
   - Traces: 95% of generation requests produce a trace with span for model-select and runtime-exec
   - Logs: structured request_id on all runtime logs with severity mapping (INFO/WARN/ERROR)

2) Synthetic scenario pass (3 independent runs)
   - Latency synthetic: 95th percentile end-to-end generation under 2.5s for the workload profile
   - Accuracy synthetic: pre-agreed prompt set map-of-outputs >= customer baseline (see "synthetic-prompt-set" artifact)
   - Failover synthetic: simulate a model-variant fallback and verify successful completion within 3s of fallback trigger

3) Cost and quota sanity check
   - Token burn projection for first 30 days within agreed threshold +/- 30%
   - Adaptive-rate-limiter integrated and returning 429s with observability tags when saturating

Telemetry contract: implementation checklist
- Instrumentation owners must ensure metrics emit at the tenant/request granularity. Required labels: tenant_id, region, model_name, route
- Preferred exporters: Prometheus (metrics), OpenTelemetry (traces), JSONL to S3 for long-term logs.
- Retention: 90d metrics, 30d traces, 365d logs (customer may opt for shorter).

Prometheus example queries (copy into onboarding dashboard)
- Total requests by tenant (30m): rate(request_count{tenant_id=~"TENANT_ID.*"}[30m])
- 95th percentile latency (10m): histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[10m])) by (le))
- KV cache hit ratio: sum(rate(kvcache_hit_total[5m])) by (tenant_id) / sum(rate(kvcache_lookup_total[5m])) by (tenant_id)

Synthetic health checks and dashboard layout
- Dashboard sections: Overview, Latency & Throughput, Token Economics, Failure Modes, Instance Health, Rollout & Canary Status
- Widgets to include: p50/p95/p99 latency heatmap, request rate by tenant, token burn by route, cache hit ratio trend, recent errors table (parsed with error codes), live traces sample panel

Pre-cutover procedure (Day -3 to 0)
1) Day -3: Telemetry smoke test
   - Verify data arriving in Grafana and alerting pipeline.
   - Run the baseline synthetic suite; document results in the onboarding ticket.
2) Day -2: Load profile run
   - Ramp to expected steady-state TPS for 30 minutes, then peak to 2x for 15 minutes.
   - Confirm autoscaling/queueing behaves as expected, confirm no token anomalies.
3) Day -1: Canary rollout
   - 1% of traffic routed to the new tenant config. Monitor the canary for 60 minutes.
   - Check for errors, latency, and cost deltas. If any SLO breach detected, abort and roll back.
4) Day 0: Full cutover
   - Schedule 60 minute maintenance window. Notify stakeholders (email template provided below).
   - Enable full route, run post-cutover synthetic suite after 15 minutes, and validate telemetry contract.

Stability operations (Day 0–14)
- Daily cadence: 09:30 PST standup (CS + SRE + Runtime) for first 7 days, then every-other-day till day 14.
- Check list for standup:
  - Any SLO alerts fired in last 24h? (yes/no, link to alerts)
  - Token burn variance > 20%?
  - Customer reported LLM output quality regressions?
  - Any escalations initiated?

Escalation matrix and SLAs
- P1: Production-wide outage for customer's tenant (affects > 90% requests)
   - First response: SRE on-call (15m), followed by CS lead (30m)
   - Escalation: Paging to Engineering runtime leads at 60m, exec-brief within 2h
- P2: Severe degradation (p95 > target or error rate > 5%) for a single route
   - First response: CS + SRE (30m), resolution target 4h
- P3: Functional bug with workaround (non-blocking)
   - Response: Assigned support engineer within 8 business hours

Escalation contact table (use internal contact channel first, then email if needed):
- SRE on-call: PagerDuty roster (use paging code "RI-SRE-CUST")
- Platform lead: arjun.patel@redwood.com
- Runtime SME: sofia.martinez@redwood.com
- CS Lead: maya.chen@redwood.com

Communication and customer comms templates
- Pre-cutover notification (email):
  Subject: [Redwood] Scheduled go-live window for <tenant_name> on <date>
  Body: Short summary, expected window, primary contacts, rollback criteria, monitoring link (dashboard URL).

- Incident update template (customer-facing):
  1) What happened (concise)
  2) Impacted customers/tenants
  3) Mitigation steps taken
  4) ETA for resolution or next update

Rollback and safe-fail procedures
- Automatic rollback trigger conditions (examples):
  - p95 latency increase > 2x baseline for > 10 minutes
  - error rate > 5% sustained for > 5 minutes
  - token burn projection exceeds agreed cap by > 50% within next 24 hours
- Rollback steps:
  1) Use routing control to switch traffic back to previous deployment (CLI example):
     redwood route set --tenant <TENANT_ID> --route <ROUTE> --target previous
  2) Re-enable canary at 5% and rerun synthetic
  3) Open a post-rollback ticket and schedule a root-cause analysis (RCA) meeting

Postmortem and RCA handoff criteria
- Trigger an RCA when any of the following occur:
  - P1 incident
  - P2 incident that required > 4 hours to resolve
  - Any customer quiet-go-live rollback within first 14 days
- RCA ownership: SRE + Runtime + CS representative. Deliverable: written RCA (timeline, root cause, corrective actions) within 5 business days.

QBR handoff and artifacts (first QBR after go-live)
- Dashboard snapshot exported with:
  - Latency/Throughput trends since go-live
  - Token economics and cost delta vs projection
  - Error and degradation timeline with RCA links
  - Synthetic suite pass/fail history and prompt-set differences
- Customer Success playbook for the QBR:
  1) Review contract SLOs and whether we met them
  2) Share operational highlights and any outstanding risks
  3) Agree on quality/regression plan (if any)

Runbook annexes (copy into onboarding folder)
- Synthetic prompt set template: synthetic-prompt-set-v1.json
- Grafana dashboard JSON: onboarding-dashboard-template.json
- Prometheus alert rules: onboarding-alerts-rules.yml

Troubleshooting checklist (quick steps during an incident)
1) Identify affected tenants and routes: run request_count PromQL filter by tenant_id.
2) Check instance health and oom/killed events on nodes serving tenant.
3) Inspect traces to find whether slowdown occurred in model selection or runtime execution.
4) If KV cache hit ratio dropped significantly, flush affected prefix cache and monitor.
5) If error codes 5xx dominate, scale burst pool or reroute to fallback variant.

FAQ
- Q: What if synthetic checks pass but customers report poor output quality?
  A: Open a quality triage ticket and escalate to Applied ML; attach failing prompts and model version. Consider A/B rolling back to prior model variant.

References and links
- Onboarding dashboard template: //grafana.redwood/internal/dashboards/onboarding-dashboard-template
- Telemetry contract spec (internal): /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/telemetry-contract-spec
- Canary playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/canary-rollout-playbook

Revision history
- 2026-11-02: Created by Maya Chen
- 2027-01-12: Added synthetic failover scenario (reviewer Sofia Martinez)
- 2027-02-14: Added PromQL examples and expanded escalation matrix (reviewers Arjun Patel, Liam O'Connor)

title: dsid_b1bd1000cfe94cf5a023306c0f03658d__enterprise-observability-contract-harmonization-playbook-2026.txt
text:
Enterprise Observability Contract Harmonization Playbook

Overview
This playbook defines a repeatable process for harmonizing observability contracts across enterprise customer telemetry sources during onboarding. Harmonization reduces integration friction, ensures consistent SLO/SLA mapping, and shortens time-to-QBR readiness. Use this guide when integrating any new Dedicated or Private customer with custom telemetry, third-party agents, or legacy instrumentation.

Goals
- Provide a minimal required signal set for Redwood feature areas (ingress, request lifecycle, model inference, billing tokens, and error taxonomy).
- Define canonical metric/event names and recommended labels/tags.
- Specify retention, sampling, and privacy controls for regulated customers.
- Prescribe validation checks, ownership, and escalation points.

Scope
Applies to: Dedicated and Private customers onboarding into Redwood's monitoring and customer-facing SLO/Uptime reports. Not intended for ad-hoc product experiments.

Owners and stakeholders
- Customer Success (CS) — primary onboarding coordinator, responsible for acceptance criteria.
- Observability (Platform) — implements collectors, forwarders, and ensures schema conformity.
- SRE/Infra — verifies SLO mappings and alert routing.
- Customer Engineering — integrates customer telemetry; point-of-contact for schema questions.

Required signals (canonical contract)
The table below lists the minimum signals required to support production monitoring and QBR metrics. Provide all signals as either metrics (time-series) or structured events with the specified fields. If a customer cannot emit a field, mark the exception in the onboarding ticket.

| Signal | Type | Required fields / labels | Purpose | Acceptable fallback |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ingress.requests_total | metric (counter) | tenant_id, route, region, ingestion_type | Throughput and quota accounting | aggregated by tenant only (if per-route not available)
| request.latency_p50/95/99 | metric (histogram) | tenant_id, route, model_variant, sequence_length_bucket | Latency SLOs and perf trending | p95 only for initial acceptance
| inference.tokens_generated | metric (counter) | tenant_id, model_variant, prompt_hash | Inference economics, cost attribution | per-tenant token counts
| response.error | event | tenant_id, request_id, error_code, error_category | Error triage and classification | aggregated error rate by tenant
| kvcache.hits / kvcache.misses | metric | tenant_id, model_variant, prefix_cache_key | Cache efficiency and cost reduction | sample logs with cache-hit boolean
| billing.request_cost_usd | metric | tenant_id, billing_cycle, cost_type | Chargeback & QBR cost breakdown | estimated cost model from Redwood side
| telemetry.pii_exposure_alert | event | tenant_id, request_id, detection_ruleset_id | Data privacy monitoring | periodic sampling with redaction

Privacy and regulated accounts
For customers with data residency/regulation constraints (HIPAA, GDPR, FINRA):
- Never forward raw request/response text. Use hashed prompt IDs (prompt_hash) and token counts.
- Provide a privacy filter sidecar pattern: upstream collector masks or removes fields labeled pii_sensitive before forwarding.
- Retention: default 30 days for raw structured events, 365 days for aggregated metrics. For regulated customers, support options: 7/30/90-day retention tables.
- Document the KMS/HSM key ids used for redaction and provide evidence of encryption-at-rest and in-transit.

Sampling and cardinality guidance
- Low-cardinality tags: tenant_id, region, model_variant, route. Avoid user_id or free-text prompt content.
- For high-cardinality fields (prompt_hash) use bucketing: keep only first 8 characters of hash and limit distinct values per tenant to 10k/day.
- Sampling strategy: 100% for p95/p99 latency and error counters; 1–5% for raw example traces (for debugging) unless customer permits more.

Onboarding acceptance criteria (checklist)
1. Schema alignment: Customer telemetry emits all required signals with matching field names or mapped via an agreed adapter.
2. Ingestion validation: Observability platform ingests at least 7 days of representative traffic or synthetic replay.
3. SLO mapping: Latency and availability SLOs mapped to tenant dashboards.
4. Privacy gates: PII redaction and retention windows verified.
5. Cost mapping: Token & inference cost metrics available and reconciled with billing estimate.
6. Alerting: Alert rules for latent p95, elevated error_rate (>0.5% sustained 10m), and telemetry pipeline dropouts.
7. QBR readiness: Data populated for the last 30 days for the QBR template (see QBR readiness checklist).

Detailed onboarding procedure
Step 0 — Pre-engagement\- CS collects: customer account team, legal constraints, expected qps, list of models and regions in scope.\- Create an onboarding ticket in JIRA with "observability-contract" template and assign Observability engineer.

Step 1 — Schema discovery (2–3 days)\1. Run a short discovery call with Customer Engineering to list existing telemetry endpoints and formats (Prometheus, OTLP, Datadog, custom logs).\2. Ask for sample payloads (anonymized) and a list of current tag sets.\3. Produce a mapping document within 48 hours with fields either matched or flagged for adapter implementation.

Step 2 — Adapter & transport (1–2 weeks)
- If the customer uses a homegrown format, Observability team builds an adapter (Fluent Bit/Collector pipeline) to translate to canonical names. Document the adapter config as YAML in the ticket.
- Configure TLS and API key exchange. For Private deployments, confirm VPC peering or TLS proxy endpoints.

Step 3 — Validation (3–7 days)
- Run synthetic traffic that covers: high throughput, long sequences (>1024 tokens), and failure modes (timebox exceed, model OOM).
- Verify metrics: counters increase, histograms report expected buckets, events contain required fields.
- Execute the validation queries below and record results in the ticket.

Validation queries (examples)\- p95 latency by tenant: SELECT percentile(latency_ms, 95) FROM request_latencies WHERE tenant_id = '<TENANT>' AND time > now() - 1h\- error rate: SELECT sum(errors) / sum(requests) FROM (SELECT count_if(response.error = true) as errors, count(*) as requests FROM requests WHERE tenant_id = '<TENANT>' AND time > now() - 10m)

Step 4 — SLO mapping, alerts and runbooks (2–5 days)
- SRE maps the onboarded metrics to Redwood SLOs and creates runbook stubs. Example SLOs: request availability >= 99.95% monthly; p95 latency < 300ms for short sequence routes.
- Create alerts: (1) p95 latency increase > 30% over baseline for 10 minutes; (2) sustained error_rate > 0.5% for 10 minutes; (3) telemetry ingestion missing for 2 minutes.

Step 5 — Handback and QBR prep (1–2 days)
- CS verifies that all QBR metrics populate correctly for the prior 30 days.
- Produce an "Observability Acceptance" sign-off artifact with: mapping doc, adapter config, retention policy, SLOs, and runbooks.

Rollback and remediation steps
- If validation fails, revert the adapter config and pause ingestion for the tenant while preserving raw payloads for investigation (no raw text forwarded for regulated accounts).
- Escalation: Observability -> SRE -> CS -> Legal for PII incidents. Use the major-incident template in escalation-playbook.

Common integration patterns and sample configs
1) Prometheus scrape adapter (yaml):
- job_name: "redwood-tenant"
  static_configs:
    - targets: ['collector.local:9100']
  relabel_configs:
    - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_namespace]
      target_label: tenant_id

2) OTLP to Redwood-forwarder (cli example):
- otelcol --config /etc/otel/config.yaml --exporter.redwood.endpoint=https://telemetry.redwood.ai:443 --auth.token=<REDACTED>

3) Minimal JSON event example (privacy-preserving):
{
  "event_type": "response.error",
  "tenant_id": "acct-2b7f",
  "request_id": "r-9f1a",
  "error_code": "MODEL_TIMEOUT",
  "error_category": "timeout",
  "timestamp": "2026-02-15T14:03:22Z"
}

QBR readiness checklist (for CS owners)
- 30 days of latency, error, and cost metrics available
- Dashboards pre-populated and linked in the QBR template
- Cost attribution validated against billing estimates 
- Two example incident summaries (if any) with remediation notes
- Privacy and retention policy documented and agreed

Templates and artifacts to attach to the onboarding ticket
- telemetry-mapping.csv (field mappings)
- adapter-config.yaml (collector/exporter config)
- acceptance-signoff.md (one-pager with signatures from CS and Customer Engineering)
- slo-definition.json (SLOs and objectives)

References and related pages
- Observability onboarding checklist (internal link)
- QBR telemetry storyboard and action plan
- Escalation templates for PII or SLA incidents

Appendix: common troubleshooting commands
- Check ingestion pipeline: curl -fsS https://telemetry.redwood.ai/health || echo "pipeline down"
- Verify metric existence (example time-series store): SELECT count(*) FROM metrics WHERE name = 'ingress.requests_total' AND tenant_id = '<TENANT>' AND time > now() - 1d

Revision history
- 2026-01-15: Created by Maya Chen
- 2026-02-20: Added privacy gating guidance and additional validation queries (reviewers: Jasper Liu, Leah Martinez, Arjun Patel)

Contact
If you have questions about implementing the contract or need an adapter review, contact the Observability on-call channel (#obs-oncall) and assign ticket to the Observability team.

title: dsid_4a35f075919f4c13bfe0fb6fd3169e3d__kernel-state-redistribution-and-rollforward-sop-2026.txt
text:
Kernel State Redistribution and Roll-Forward SOP

Overview
======
This runbook documents the standard operating procedure (SOP) for redistributing kernel-managed execution state across GPUs and performing a roll-forward recovery when a traditional rollback (reinstating an older model or kernel bundle) is unsafe or unavailable. The focus is on minimizing customer-visible latency and preserving KV-cache / session-consistency while satisfying SLO guardrails.

Scope and when to use this SOP
-----------------------------
- Applies to sharded and single-GPU kernel topologies that maintain volatile execution state (KV caches, per-request scratch, compiled kernel state).
- Intended for incidents where:
  - a kernel variant becomes unresponsive or corrupt mid-epoch and a rollback would cause unacceptable latency/regression, or
  - partial state loss affects a subset of shards but continuing execution with reconstructed state is preferable to global fallback.
- Not for: full-node hardware failures with persistent disk loss (see node-replacement playbook).

Ownership and escalation
------------------------
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime Oncall (team: eng-serving-runtime).
- Secondary: Kernel/ Scheduling Squad.
- Pager escalation: if the runbook cannot bring request-service back within 5 minutes, escalate to SRE lead and declare P1.

Success criteria
----------------
- Target: 99% of in-flight sessions either complete without user-visible error or are gracefully migrated to a compatible fallback within SLA.
- Safety gates: token-consistency checks pass, KV cache rehydration success rate >= 95% for affected sessions, no silent divergence of session outputs after roll-forward.

Prerequisites and fast checks (0-2 minutes)
-------------------------------------------
1) Confirm incident classification: kernel corruption vs performance regression.
2) Check SLO dashboards: tail latency 95/99 quantiles, error-rate spike.
3) Run quick telemetry queries:
   - kernel_process_health{kernel=\"X\"} over last 2m
   - kv_rehydration_failures{shard=~\"affected.*\"}
4) If hardware-level alerts present (ECC, nvlink down), consult hardware runbooks — do not proceed with roll-forward.

High-level steps
----------------
1) Quiesce new admissions to the affected kernel cohort (2 channels):
   - Set admission controller tag: \"redistribute-only\" for experimental routes.
   - For high-severity incidents, flip canary routing rule to divert new traffic to fallback pool.
2) Mark kernel shards for snapshot extraction.
3) Extract consistent snapshots with lightweight freeze and copy protocol (see snippet).
4) Verify snapshot integrity and generate redistribution plan.
5) Perform state redistribution (shard relocalization) in parallel with live rehydration probes.
6) Monitor session consistency checks and release admissions once thresholds met.
7) Post-incident audit and write-up.

Detailed procedure (play-by-play)
--------------------------------
1) Quiesce and force admissions policy (operator, 0-1 min)
   - Run: 
     ```bash
     # route new traffic away from kernel-X cohort
     rctl set route --cohort kernel-x --policy divert --target-pool fallback-pool
     rctl tag cohort kernel-x set redistribute-only=true
     ```
   - Expected result: new requests are diverted or annotated so redistribution does not need to handle them.

2) Snapshot extraction (operator + kernel-scheduler, 1-3 min)
   - Goal: capture consistent KV cache and minimal execution metadata without halting in-flight generation.
   - Implementation pattern (incremental freeze):
     - Apply per-shard soft-lock: sets `frozen=true` for snapshot epoch.
     - Drain micro-batches for 200-500ms to allow deterministic cache flush windows.
     - Emit snapshot artifact to object-store: `s3://runtime-snapshots/<incident-id>/shard-<n>.tar.gz`
   - Example command (controller):
     ```yaml
     # snapshot job manifest (pseudo-yaml)
     job: snapshot-extract
     cohort: kernel-x
     epoch: 2026-03-01T12:34:00Z
     shards: [0..7]
     mode: incremental
     ````

3) Validate snapshots (kernel-scheduler, 1-2 min)
   - Run integrity checks: size sanity, checksum (sha256), schema validation.
   - Telemetry queries to confirm snapshot completeness: `snapshot_manifest_complete{incident=\"<id>\"}`
   - If any snapshot fails validation, mark shard for targeted re-extraction.

4) Redistribution planning (scheduler + operator, 1-3 min)
   - Build plan: mapping from source shards -> target GPUs. Consider affinity, NUMA, memory headroom, and thermal state.
   - Example planning table (human-readable):
     | source_shard | target_node | target_gpu | mem_headroom | reason |
     |--------------|-------------|------------|--------------|--------|
     | 0            | node-a      | gpu0       | 18GB         | underloaded
     | 1            | node-b      | gpu1       | 12GB         | hot-swap

5) Roll-forward redistribution (parallelized, 2-8 min)
   - Steps per target shard (automated operator actions):
     a) Allocate ephemeral slot on target GPU with `prewarm=true` to compile kernels and reserve KV memory.
     b) Stream snapshot artifact into slot and perform in-situ rehydration.
     c) Run deterministic probe (seeded micro-batch) to validate cache coherence.
     d) Promote slot to live routing (gradual weight ramp).
   - Example CLI (pseudo):
     ```bash
     runtimectl allocate-slot --node node-b --gpu 1 --slot-prewarm --labels redistributed
     runtimectl stream-snapshot --src s3://runtime-snapshots/<id>/shard-1.tar.gz --dest slot://node-b/gpu1/slotA
     runtimectl probe-slot --slot slotA --probe-seed sha256:abc123 --timeout 10s
     runtimectl ramp-route-weight --slot slotA --from 0 --to 100 --duration 30s
     ```

6) Consistency and divergence checks (continuous during roll-forward)
   - Checkpoints to observe:
     - per-session hash equality for deterministic probes: `session_output_hash{session=~\"migrated.*\"}`
     - KV miss ratio for migrated sessions should be <= 3% after 60s of promotion.
     - Token-level latency regression: tail p99 for migrated cohort must not increase more than 25% relative to baseline.
   - Abort criteria: any deterministic probe mismatch, KV rehydration failure > 5% for > 2m, or sustained p99 > 2x baseline.

7) Cutover and release (finalize, 1-2 min)
   - Once targets pass probes and metrics are within thresholds:
     - Promote routing weight to 100%.
     - Remove `redistribute-only` tags and re-enable normal admission.
     - Emit event: `incident.<id>.rollforward.complete` to the incident channel.

8) Post-incident and cleanup (10-30 min)
   - Deallocate ephemeral prewarm slots.
   - Archive snapshots with retention policy: keep hot snapshots 7 days, cold snapshots 90 days.
   - Create incident audit: attach snapshot manifests, metric timelines, and decisions.

Emergency roll-forward (when snapshots incomplete)
--------------------------------------------------
- If snapshot extraction fails for a shard but continuing service is required, we may perform a partial in-memory reconstruction:
  1) Identify compatible donor shard (same model variant, recent epoch).
  2) Copy best-effort subset of KV entries: high-frequency keys first (top-10k by recency).
  3) Mark reconstructed shard as "best-effort" with stricter monitoring flags.
  4) Notify product and CS if reconstructed sessions are customer-visible.
- Safety note: this step increases risk of subtle output divergence. Use only under explicit P1 authorization.

Telemetry and dashboards to monitor during procedure
--------------------------------------------------
- Essential metrics: `kv_rehydration_success_rate`, `probe_output_match_rate`, `cohort_p99_latency`, `admission_diversion_rate`, `slot_compile_errors`.
- Suggested dashboard panels (table):
  | panel | description | alert threshold | owner |
  |-------|-------------|-----------------|-------|
  | KV Rehydrate | % success per shard | <95% -> warn | Kernel Squad |
  | Deterministic Probe | match rate | <99% -> alert | Scheduler |
  | Tail Latency | p99 cohort | >1.25x baseline -> warn | SRE |

Configuration snippets
----------------------
- Example admission policy (JSON):
  ```json
  {
    "cohort": "kernel-x",
    "policy": "divert",
    "target_pool": "fallback-pool",
    "annotations": {"incident_id":"INC-2026-1234","redistribute_only":"true"}
  }
  ```

- Snapshot job manifest (CLI form):
  ```bash
  runtimectl job create snapshot --cohort kernel-x --epoch 2026-03-01T12:34:00Z --shards 0-7 --mode incremental --out s3://runtime-snapshots/INC-2026-1234/
  ```

Safety concerns and fallbacks
---------------------------
- Rolling forward can mask deeper data-corruption bugs. If divergence persists post-rollforward, perform a conservative rollback to last verified kernel variant and notify security/product for deeper investigation.
- Maintain legal/compliance trace of snapshot artifacts—treat as sensitive if they contain customer prompt-derived identifiers. Follow security-and-compliance retention policy.

Runbook decision matrix (quick reference)
----------------------------------------
- If kernel unresponsive but memory intact -> attempt roll-forward.
- If nvlink/PCIe errors or ECC -> stop and engage hardware replacement.
- If snapshot integrity fails across >50% shards -> fallback to global model variant rollback.

Postmortem checklist
--------------------
- Collect: snapshot manifests, controller logs, probe outputs, compile errors.
- Quantify customer impact: sessions affected, requests timed out, cost of emergency slots.
- Action items: schedule root-cause analysis, follow-up kernel tests, and a small-run chaos test to validate the snapshot/recovery path.

References and related playbooks
-------------------------------
- Eviction Rewind and State Reconstruction Playbook (link in related_pages)
- Kernel Safety Net and Rollback Playbook (link in related_pages)
- Runtime snapshot storage and retention policy (internal infra docs)

Appendix: Common debugging commands
----------------------------------
- List cohort slots and state:
  ```bash
  runtimectl slot list --cohort kernel-x --verbose
  ```
- View snapshot manifest and checksums:
  ```bash
  aws s3 ls s3://runtime-snapshots/INC-2026-1234/ --recursive
  aws s3 cp s3://runtime-snapshots/INC-2026-1234/manifest.json - | jq .
  ```
- Force a targeted probe against slot:
  ```bash
  runtimectl probe-slot --slot slotA --probe-seed sha256:abc123 --retry 3 --log-level debug
  ```

Contact and escalation list
---------------------------
- Serving runtime oncall: paged number and Slack channel (#runtime-oncall)
- Kernel squad lead: @Rina Shah
- SRE manager: @Ava Patel

Document history
----------------
- 2025-11-12: Drafted by Diego Morales
- 2026-01-15: Reviewed by Kernel Squad and SRE; added emergency reconstruction section
- 2026-03-01: Finalized gating thresholds and published

title: dsid_f8a8d8e60b01406d9a90cc5a24048564__request-stitching-and-session-coalescing-spec-2026-09-29.txt
text:
Request Stitching and Session Coalescing Design Spec

A design specification for combining related request fragments into coherent inference sessions ("request stitching") and opportunistically coalescing concurrent tenant sessions onto shared backend resources to reduce per-token cost and KV-cache churn while meeting latency SLOs and tenant isolation constraints.
Overview

This spec defines Request Stitching and Session Coalescing: two coordinated features intended to reduce redundant KV cache warmups, increase effective GPU utilization, and lower per-token costs for multi-request conversational workloads. Request Stitching means merging logically related partial requests (e.g., multi-turn fragments, document-chunked prompts, or streaming deltas) into a single served session when semantics and safety rules allow. Session Coalescing means routing and packing concurrent short-lived or low-fidelity sessions from multiple tenants onto a smaller number of backend model sessions when policy permits.

This document covers goals, constraints, high-level design, API/contract changes, configuration examples, SLO and telemetry requirements, rollout plan, testing and backwards-compatibility considerations, and ownership.

Motivation

- Many customers send bursty conversational traffic composed of short partial updates. Each update causes KV cache overhead and repeated kernel scheduling.
- Cold KV cache population is a top driver of tail latency for LLM conversational workloads and increases per-token GPU time for short requests.
- Dedicated short sessions waste context window compute and reduce packing efficiency.

Goals

1. Reduce average per-token GPU time for conversational workloads by 10–30% for qualifying traffic classes.
2. Maintain per-route p95 latency within existing SLOs (default p95 < 250ms for interactive tiers) for requests eligible for stitching/coalescing.
3. Preserve tenant isolation and auditability; coalescing must never allow cross-tenant data leakage.

Non-goals

- This spec does not change fundamental billing semantics. Billing implications are surfaced as warnings and telemetry; commercial pricing changes are out of scope for the initial technical rollout.
- We will not implement cross-tenant prompt content sharing; session coalescing only shares runtime state when explicitly permitted by policy (see "Affinity & Privacy").

Key concepts and terminology

- Stitchable request: a request identified as semantically mergeable with previous open session fragments by the client or router heuristics (e.g., 'append', 'stream-delta', 'followup').
- Session affinity key: an opaque key used to bind an incoming request to an in-memory model session (can be tenant-level, route-level, or client-provided).
- Coalescing window: a short time window (e.g., 50–500ms) during which compatible short sessions may be co-located onto a single backend session.
Design overview

1) Stitching Model
- API contract: new optional field in generation/chat payload: "stitch_instruction" (enum: none, append, replace, merge_safely) and "stitch_id" (string).
- Server behavior: when stitch_instruction != none and a matching open session (stitch_id) exists, router will route the fragment into the existing session's stream of tokens rather than creating a new KV context.
- Safety checks: compatibility validation includes model family compatibility, pinned model version, request temperature/fidelity thresholds, tokenization alignment check, and per-tenant policy. If validation fails, fallback to normal routing and emit a telemetry event.

2) Session Coalescing Model
- Coalescing is driven by a policy expression attached to tenant entitlements: "allow_coalesce: true|false" and an operational predicate: {max_context_fidelity, max_token_budget, allowed_model_variants}.
- The router maintains short-lived coalesce pools per region and model variant. Eligible sessions are placed into a pool for up to the configured coalescing window. When pool scheduling triggers, the runtime will instantiate as few backend sessions as feasible and map multiple logical sessions into the runtime with strict per-session boundaries enforced at the prompt/result layer.
- Coalescing will not share raw prompt text in-memory across tenants; instead, the runtime uses a multiplexing layer ensuring per-session token isolation in compute kernels and maintaining separate KV namespaces.

3) Affinity & Privacy
- Affinity levels: 
  - tenant_affinity: only same-tenant requests may be coalesced (default for regulated customers).
  - route_affinity: same tenant + same route (stronger isolation).
  - cross_tenant_shared: cross-tenant coalescing allowed only when tenants opt-in and have identical model fidelity constraints.
- Coalescing is disabled automatically for routes with PII classification, high-sensitivity labels, or when KMS-wrapped keys require dedicated HSM-backed sessions.

4) KV and Cache lifecycle changes
- Each logical session maintains a virtual KV namespace id. Backend runtime preserves separate KV keys per logical session to avoid contamination. To reduce duplication, runtime implements "sparse prefix reuse": when two sessions share an identical recent prefix, the kernel re-uses precomputed attention artifacts but still enforces namespace separation.

API changes and examples

- New optional fields for generation/chat API (HTTP/JSON):

  {
    "stitch_id": "string (optional - opaque)",
    "stitch_instruction": "none|append|merge_safely|replace",
    "coalesce_preference": "auto|tenant_affinity|route_affinity|deny",
    "session_ttl_ms": "integer (optional)"
  }

- Example: appending a chunked document: 

  POST /v1/generate
  {
    "model": "rwd-llama-70b-econ-v1",
    "stitch_id": "doc-12345-chunk-1",
    "stitch_instruction": "append",
    "input": "First chunk of a long document..."
  }

Operational configuration table

| Setting | Default | Purpose | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| coalesce_window_ms | 100 | How long router holds eligible sessions to attempt packing | eng-platform |
| max_coalesce_per_backend | 12 | Max logical sessions per backend runtime instance | eng-serving-runtime |
| stitch_validation_timeout_ms | 30 | Timeout in router for compatibility checks | eng-platform |
| tenant_opt_out_label | "no-coalesce" | Tenant label to disable automatic coalescing | customer-success |
SLOs and telemetry

- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for coalesced and non-coalesced paths must be tracked separately. Baseline SLO: coalesced p95 <= non-coalesced p95 + 40ms.
- Cost: track GPU-ms per-token and compare coalesced vs baseline per tenant segment.
- Correctness: monitor stitch-fallback-rate (number of stitch attempts that fell back to normal routing) and stitch-reorder-rate (cases where appending changed logical response ordering). Acceptable initial thresholds: stitch-fallback-rate < 5% and stitch-reorder-rate < 0.05%.
- Security: audit logs for any session coalesce actions, including affinity decision, participating tenant IDs, and decision reason.

Rollout plan

1) Canary (2 weeks): opt-in internal tenants + a small set of low-sensitivity beta customers. Metrics: latency, GPU-ms/token, fallback-rate. Blocker criteria: coalesced p95 worse than baseline p95 by > 60ms for > 10% of requests.
2) Beta (6 weeks): broader self-serve opt-in for customers with normal sensitivity. Provide UI toggle in Console and API flags. Add billing telemetry but no pricing changes.
3) Default-on for host/standard (3 months): flip default to on for non-restricted tenants; provide a 30-day notice and migration guidance.
4) Enterprise mode (parallel): for regulated tenants, provide dedicated per-tenant coalesce pools with tenant_affinity enforced.

Migration and compatibility notes

- Existing clients not sending stitch fields operate unchanged (stitch_instruction defaults to none).
- Customers that currently expect strict per-request billing may observe a small shift in cost-per-token telemetry due to reduced overheads; we will surface this in the Console under "Cost Insights -> Session Coalescing".

Testing matrix

- Unit tests: router decision logic for stitch compatibility, pool placement, TTL expiry.
- Integration: runtime isolation tests validating KV namespace separation under heavy coalesce packing (simulated multi-tenant traffic).
- Perf: synthetic conversational workloads with varying fragment sizes to validate GPU-ms/token improvements and tail latency.
- Security: adversarial mixing tests ensuring no prompt leakage across tenant boundaries.

Instrumentation and dashboards

- New dashboards: 
  - "Session Coalesce Overview" (global coalesce rate, average pool fill, avg coalesce window time)
  - "Tenant Coalesce Health" (per-tenant cost delta, fallback-rate, opt-out status)
  - "Stitch Errors" (reasons: model mismatch, pin mismatch, validation timeout)

Ownership and runbooks

- Owners: 
  - Product: Priya Nair (strategy + customer communication)
  - Eng Platform: Evan Brooks (router/policy)
  - Serving Runtime: Lina Gomez (runtime multiplexing, KV semantics)
- Runbook outlines: failure modes and mitigation. Examples: 
  - If coalesce backend saturates -> throttle new coalesce pools and revert to non-coalesced routing. Notify oncall and adjust coalesce_window_ms down by 50%.
  - If stitch_reorder_rate rises above threshold -> temporarily disable stitching for affected routes and create hotfix that forces strict session ordering.

Open questions (for review)

1. Billing model: should we expose a "coalesce credit" for customers who opt-out but want to pay for dedicated runtime? Recommend cross-team sync with Finance.
2. Deterministic replay: how do we guarantee exact response replay for stitched sessions when a fragment was merged and later trimmed? Proposal: store a lightweight fragment log per logical session for 48 hours.
3. Opt-in UX: should the Console provide per-route default and per-route overrides or a single tenant-level toggle?

Appendix: CLI/Debugging examples

- Inspect router decision for an incoming request:
  $ redwoodctl debug router --request-id=abcd-1234
  Decision: stitch_attempted=true, stitch_id=doc-12345-chunk-1, decision_reason=compatible, pool_id=coalesce-us-west-3-42

- Sample telemetry event (JSON shown for diagnostics):
  {
    "event": "stitch_attempt",
    "request_id": "abcd-1234",
    "stitch_id": "doc-12345-chunk-1",
    "decision": "fallback",
    "reason": "model_mismatch"
  }

Related work and references

- See runtime KV cache lifecycle document for sparse prefix reuse algorithm.
- Prior PRD: Predictive Batching & Cost Optimizer (2026-03-01) for performance baselining.

Summary and next steps

If approved, engineering teams will begin implementation in the router and runtime multiplexing layers per the rollout plan. Product will prepare documentation, migration notes, and Console toggles for customer opt-in. Finance and Sales will be engaged to review billing implications before defaulting this behavior on for any customers.

title: dsid_889c7133415f4af18de26f7d4c28a515__per-route-fidelity-budgeting-prd-2028-04-12.txt
text:
Per-Route Fidelity Budgeting PRD

Overview:

This document defines the product requirements for Per-Route Fidelity Budgeting, a mechanism that allows customers to declaratively allocate a quality (fidelity) budget to API routes or endpoints. The feature enables fine-grained, per-route tradeoffs between latency/cost and output quality, with automated enforcement and observability. The goal is to give platform operators and product teams the ability to set and monitor fidelity expectations per application route, reduce unexpected cost spikes, and enable graceful degradation when resources are constrained.

Why this matters:

- Teams frequently mix high-fidelity features (e.g., long-form generation, code synthesis) with low-fidelity tasks (e.g., classification, short responses) on the same account. A single global SLO or model selection often leads to either excessive cost or poor UX.
- Per-route fidelity budgeting provides predictable unit economics and safer rollouts for features that require different quality profiles.
- Enables product-driven SLAs: product teams can prioritize critical routes (payments, moderation) while economizing on lower-priority API surface area.

Goals (must have):

1. API primitives to declare a fidelity budget per route and a fallback policy.
2. Runtime enforcement that selects model/variant/quantization profiles to meet the declared budget, with transparent logging of decisions.
3. Console and API-level telemetry showing fidelity, cost, latency, and quality regressions per route over time.
4. Backward-compatible defaults so existing customers see no disruption.

Goals (nice to have):

- Integration with Redwood Optimize to automatically suggest budgets based on historical traffic.
- Auto-adjust policies that increase fidelity during low-utilization windows and decrease during capacity pressure.

Non-goals:

- This PRD does not define new token-level billing models. Pricing implications are described as guidance only.
- Not addressing multi-tenant fairness isolation (covered by tenant-aware PRD).

User personas:

- Product manager (PM) building a chat experience: wants to ensure critical user flows get high-quality responses while keeping costs manageable.
- Platform engineer: needs programmatic controls and auditability for routed decisions.
- SRE: needs observable impacts on latency and capacity under stress.

User stories:

1. As a PM, I can set a fidelity budget (0-100) on my route /chat/assistant so that the system prefers high-quality variants within budget.
2. As a platform engineer, I can define a fallback policy: (a) degrade to lower-CPU quantized model, (b) switch to short-answers mode, or (c) return 503.
3. As an SRE, I can see per-route cost, mean latency, and quality score (from canary evals) in the Console and query them via API.
4. As an admin, I can get alerts when a route exceeds its fidelity budget for N consecutive days.

Functional requirements:

FR-1: Route Configuration API
- Expose a new RouteConfig object (see example) that supports fields: fidelity_budget (int 0-100), fallback_policy (enum), target_latency_ms (int), priority (enum low|normal|high).
- RouteConfig can be applied via: Console UI, REST endpoint, and Terraform provider.

Example API payload (JSON):

{
  "route": "/api/v1/chat/assistant",
  "fidelity_budget": 80,
  "fallback_policy": "degrade-quantized",
  "target_latency_ms": 250,
  "priority": "high"
}

FR-2: Runtime Decision Engine
- At request time the router evaluates: route config, current capacity state, model performance profiles, and historical quality for the route.
- The decision engine selects a model variant (e.g., redwood-7b-fp16, redwood-13b-8bit) and execution profile (batching, kv-cache reuse) designed to keep expected quality above the budget while minimizing cost.
- All decisions must be logged with reason codes (e.g., MODEL_SELECTED, BUDGET_EXCEEDED, CAPACITY_PRESSURE).

FR-3: Policy Enforcement and Fallbacks
- If the system predicts that the fidelity budget cannot be met without violating latency SLOs or capacity constraints, it follows the configured fallback policy.
- Supported fallback policies: degrade-quantized, short-answer, reduce-context-window, return-503.

FR-4: Telemetry and Observability
- Instrument per-route metrics: fidelity_score (0-100), estimated_unit_cost_per_1k_tokens (USD), p50/p95 generation latency, model_variant, decision_reason.
- Console dashboard: multi-tenant view with time-series charts and ability to slice by model variant, region, and customer tier.

FR-5: Acceptance and Quality Validation
- For routes with fidelity_budget >= 70, require daily canary evaluation against a reference prompt set with pass/fail thresholds (configurable).
- If a model/variant causes a quality regression, auto-trigger rollout pause for that variant for affected routes.

Non-functional requirements:

NFR-1: Backward compatibility
- Default routing behavior remains identical for routes without RouteConfig.
NFR-2: Latency overhead
- Decision engine evaluation must add < 3ms median overhead to routing.
NFR-3: Scalability
- Support 50k route-config lookups/sec with 99.9% availability.
NFR-4: Security
- RouteConfig changes must be RBAC-protected and audited.

SLOs and metrics:

- Fidelity-compliance SLO: 95% of requests for routes with declared fidelity_budget must meet/ exceed the declared fidelity band (three-day rolling window).
- Cost containment: for routes with budget <= 50, average per-token cost should be <= 70% of baseline high-fidelity model.
- Decision-latency SLO: decision engine p50 < 3ms, p99 < 10ms.

Telemetry definitions (table):

| Metric | Unit | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| fidelity_score | 0-100 | Aggregated quality score from eval hooks and automated labelers |
| unit_cost_per_1k_tokens | USD | Estimated cost after model selection and batching |
| model_variant | string | Selected model variant id |
| decision_reason | string | ENUM describing why variant was chosen |

Security & compliance:

- RouteConfigs are considered configuration data: store encrypted at rest.
- Access requires config:write scope.
- Audit log entries for every change and decision event must be retained according to retention policy (default 90 days, enterprise option to extend).

UX and Console mockups (text):

- Console Route Settings page: fidelity slider (0-100), dropdown for fallback policy, target latency input, preview of estimated monthly delta in cost.
- Dashboard: per-route sparkline of fidelity_score, stacked area of model_variant usage, alerting card showing budget breaches.

API and SDK examples:

- REST: POST /v1/routes/{route_id}/config
- SDK (python):

from redwood import RoutesClient
config = {
  "fidelity_budget": 60,
  "fallback_policy": "short-answer",
  "target_latency_ms": 200
}
client.routes.update("/chat/summary", config)

Quality evaluation hooks (example):

- Customers can attach a small prompt-set id that the platform runs daily when a variant is used in production. Results feed fidelity_score.

Pricing and packaging implications:

- Introduce a Premium Fidelity Add-on: accounts may opt into fidelity guarantees that enable paid priority on model capacity and more aggressive cache warming.
- Default behavior: no change to per-token billing. Pricing tiers/options to consider:
  - Free/Standard: self-managed fidelity budgets; best-effort enforcement.
  - Premium Fidelity: SLA-backed fidelity compliance, faster fallback activation, dedicated capacity.
- Guidance for sales: include fidelity budgeting as part of Dedicated capacity conversations where predictable unit economics are required.

Rollout plan and milestones:

1. Phase 0 (2 weeks): Design, API schema, and data model discussion. PRD review.
2. Phase 1 (8 weeks): Build RouteConfig CRUD, Console controls (alpha), and simple runtime hook that logs decision_reason without enforcing fallbacks.
3. Phase 2 (8 weeks): Decision engine integration and enforcement, telemetry, and canary evaluation framework. Internal beta with 3 customers.
4. Phase 3 (6 weeks): Console dashboards, alerting, rollout to GA, docs, and sales enablement.

Rollout gates:

- Gate A: Decision engine latency < 3ms in load tests.
- Gate B: Canary evaluation pipeline stable and producing fidelity_score within expected variance.
- Gate C: RBAC + audit logs implemented.

Backwards compatibility and migration:

- Existing routes without configuration use current routing rules.
- Customers may bulk import configurations via CSV/Terraform. Provide a migration tool that suggests initial budgets based on historical per-route quality and cost.

Open questions / trade-offs:

- How to quantify fidelity objectively across diverse tasks (chat vs code)? Proposal: adopt per-route prompt sets for evaluation and allow customer-supplied ground truth when possible.
- Pricing model: whether to charge for Premium Fidelity as a flat add-on vs per-request markup. Recommend trials during beta to observe elasticity.

Owners and contacts:

- Product lead: Aisha Chen (product)
- Engineering lead: Liam O'Connor (eng-platform)
- SRE Lead: Meera Patel (eng-sre)
- Research/Applied ML: Diego Rivera (applied-ml)

Appendices:

A. Decision reason codes (example): MODEL_SELECTED, BUDGET_MET, BUDGET_EXCEEDED, CAPACITY_PRESSURE, FALLBACK_ACTIVATED

B. Sample alert thresholds:
- fidelity_breach_route_critical: fidelity_score < (budget - 10) for 6 hours -> pager
- fidelity_trend_degrade: fidelity_score down 20% over 7 days -> email + slack

C. Terraform snippet (example):

resource "redwood_route_config" "assistant" {
  route = "/api/v1/chat/assistant"
  fidelity_budget = 75
  fallback_policy = "degrade-quantized"
  target_latency_ms = 300
}

Document history:
- 2028-04-12: Initial draft authored by Aisha Chen
- 2028-04-15: Updated with telemetry definitions and rollout plan after engineering review

title: dsid_9b3ead802ba243248b7cd32da6091240__stakeholder-synthesis-playbook-long-tail-regressions-2026.txt
text:
Stakeholder synthesis playbook for long-tail regressions

Summary:

This playbook defines a lightweight but rigorous process for identifying, containing, and synthesizing stakeholder-facing artifacts for long-tail regressions — recurring, low-to-medium impact SLO regressions that surface intermittently across tenants or routes and persist for days to weeks. These regressions are often noisy, hard to reproduce, and frequently involve multi-component interactions (routing, cache, model variants, autoscaling). The goal is to shorten MTTI (mean time to identify), standardize evidence packaging for product and customer stakeholders, and create a repeatable operational cadence to remove ambiguity from customer communications and postmortems.

Sections:
1) Detection & classification
2) Immediate containment runbook (first 30 minutes)
3) Evidence pack: what to collect and how to store it
4) Stakeholder synthesis and messaging templates
5) Longer-term remediation and game-day plan
6) Ownership, rotation tweaks, and success metrics

---

## 1) Detection & classification

Short intro: Long-tail regressions differ from high-severity outages. They often present as subtle SLO drift, tenant-specific p99 spikes, or periodic increases in error rate for a subset of routes. Classify the event quickly to size the response.

Classification matrix (use this to choose containment actions):

| Class | Symptoms | Initial priority | Typical owners | Example threshold |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| L1 — transient noise | single-region p95 latency +10% for <2 hours | low | service owner + oncall | p95 > baseline*1.1 for <2h |
| L2 — long-tail regression | repeated tenant p99 spikes, elevated error % for multiple days | medium | service owner + infra + product | p99 > baseline*1.25 across 6+ occurrences in 48h |
| L3 — emerging systemic pattern | multiple services or regions show drifting SLOs | high | cross-functional page + incident lead | global p95/p99 degradation > 20% or sustained for 4+h |

Notes: baseline = rolling 30-day median for that route/tenant. Use alert aggregation to group correlated signals across tenants and models.

## 2) Immediate containment runbook (first 30 minutes)

Objective: reduce customer-visible impact while preserving evidence for root-cause analysis.

Step-by-step:
1. Acknowledge and classify the signal in the alerting system (PagerDuty). Tag event with "long-tail" and affected tenant(s).
2. Triage owner (oncall) runs quick query to scope: top 10 affected tenant IDs, affected routes, model version, and regions (commands below).
3. If tenant-impacted, engage tenant success/customer success per comms matrix.
4. Apply non-invasive mitigations first: widen autoscaler min capacity by +10%, apply temporary rate-limit backfill, enable prefix cache bypass for suspect model variants. Document each action in the incident chat.
5. If mitigation resolves visible symptoms within 15 minutes, continue monitoring for 2h and begin evidence pack assembly; otherwise escalate to L2 and run the escalation checklist.

Useful queries (examples):
- kubectl logs -l app=redwood-serving --since=30m | grep <tenant-id> | head -n 200
- curl "https://ops-api.redwood/v1/metrics?route=<route>&window=60m" | jq
- SELECT tenant_id, p99_latency FROM metrics.route_aggregates WHERE window='60m' ORDER BY p99_latency DESC LIMIT 20;

Escalation: If >10% of a service's tenants are impacted or the mitigation increases error rate elsewhere, invoke cross-functional page and attach the quick-scope output.

## 3) Evidence pack: what to collect and how to store it

Purpose: Provide a consistent bundle for postmortem analysis and for customer-facing summaries (helps legal, compliance, and CS). Store the evidence pack as an artifact in the incident S3 bucket: s3://incidents/long-tail/YYYYMMDD-<incident-id>/evidence.zip

Minimum evidence checklist:
- Incident metadata file (incident-id, owner, start/end timestamps, classification)
- Top 100 request IDs (with timestamps) and full request/response traces (Jaeger links or trace blobs)
- Request payload examples for each affected tenant/route (sanitized)
- Model version and model routing policy snapshot (models.json)
- KV/prefix cache hit/miss snapshot and eviction logs for the window
- Autoscaler events (scale-up/scale-down) and GPU utilization graphs (CSV)
- Representative logs from: serving runtime, router/proxy, autoscaler, and model loader (last 24h)
- Alert and notification timeline (raw PagerDuty/Slack messages)
- A short reproduction attempt log: commands tried and their outcomes
- Temporary mitigation actions applied and timestamps (who applied them)

Metadata file example (plain text, one line per key):
incident_id: LT-20260301-42
classification: L2
start_ts: 2026-02-26T14:05:00Z
detected_by: anomaly-detector-v2
owner: ashapatel@redwood.ai
affected_tenants: [tenant-671, tenant-254, tenant-194]

Retention: evidence packs for long-tail regressions are retained for 540 days. Mark packs required by legal as restricted in the index.

## 4) Stakeholder synthesis and messaging templates

Purpose: Rapidly produce clear, non-technical and technical messages for customers and internal stakeholders. The synthesis has two parallel outputs: (A) Customer brief (concise), (B) Internal synthesis (technical + evidence pack link). Both must be produced within 48 hours for L2 events.

Customer brief template (use for affected tenants only):
Subject: Brief update — intermittent increase in latency for [service/route]
Hello <CustomerName>,

Summary: Between <start_ts> and ongoing, we observed intermittent increases in latency for <route> which may have affected some requests. We have applied temporary mitigations and continue monitoring. We have not detected data loss.

What we did: temporarily increased capacity and adjusted routing to reduce impact.

What we're doing next: collecting traces and running a targeted game-day to reproduce and fix the root cause. We will share a technical summary within 5 business days and a final postmortem within 21 days.

Who to contact: <CS rep name> (cc) — for urgent concerns reply to this message.

Internal synthesis template (deliver to product, infra, security):
Title: LT-<id> synthesis — short description
Owner: <owner team/email>
Start: <start_ts> — Observed by <detector/alert>
Scope: top affected tenants, routes, model variants, regions (attach evidence pack link)
Immediate mitigations: list of actions + timestamps
Initial hypothesis: succinct bullet list of working theories
Next steps: planned deep-dive, responsible owners, timeline
Impact summary: measurable customer impact (requests failed, latency deltas, affected SLAs)

Always attach: evidence pack S3 link, top 10 traces, and relevant dashboards. For any L3 escalation, use the full incident comm template in the incident-runbook index.

## 5) Longer-term remediation and game-day plan

If a long-tail regression cannot be eliminated within 72 hours, schedule a dedicated remediation sprint with the following cadence:
- Day 0–3: triage and reproduce attempts; expand evidence pack if needed
- Day 4: postmortem skeleton and product sync — 1 hour cross-team meeting
- Day 5–14: remediation sprint (2-week window recommended) with weekly syncs
- Post-sprint: full postmortem and follow-ups tracked as ACTION items in the RCA board

Game-day scenario (run quarterly for long-tail readiness):
Objective: practice diagnosing tenant-scoped latency regressions with noisy autoscaler and cache churn.

Setup checklist:
- Choose two teams: Incident Response (oncall + infra) and Stakeholder Comms (CS + Product).
- Seed synthetic tenants with malformed model routing metadata that triggers a slow fallback path (test cluster only).
- Configure alert nebulizer to send intermittent p99 spikes for the seeded tenants.

Exercise flow (3 hours):
1. Detect — alert triggers for seeded tenants; oncall triages and applies standard containment actions.
2. Evidence pack — participants practice assembling required artifacts within 45 minutes.
3. Stakeholder synthesis — craft customer brief and internal synthesis within 60 minutes.
4. Debrief — 45-minute retro. Record observations as runbook updates and add checklist items to the runbook.

Success criteria: evidence pack completeness >= 90%, customer brief accuracy (validated by CS), and reproduction attempt documented.

## 6) Ownership, rotation tweaks, and success metrics

Who owns this playbook: Eng: Incident Response Working Group (alias: ir-wg@redwood.ai).

Oncall rotation tweak suggestions for long-tail sensitivity:
- Add a 24-h "long-tail shadow" to each weekly rotation: a secondary oncall who reviews longer-running anomalies mid-shift.
- The long-tail shadow rotates weekly and is responsible for ensuring evidence packs are assembled for any L2s detected on their watch.

Success metrics (tracked quarterly):
- Mean time to evidence pack (MTTEP) — goal <= 48 hours for L2 (current baseline: 96h)
- Fraction of L2 events with customer brief delivered within 48h — goal 90%
- Reduction in repeat regressions caused by the same root cause within 90 days — goal 50% reduction

Appendices:
A) Quick escalation checklist (one-line actions):
- Acknowledge -> run quick-scope -> apply non-invasive mitigation -> collect traces -> open incident artifact -> notify CS -> escalate if unresolved

B) Postmortem skeleton (to paste into the incident tracker):
- Title:
- Incident id:
- Timeline (concise):
- Impact (customers, SLOs, duration):
- Root cause (hypothesis + evidence):
- Contributing factors:
- Resolution steps:
- Action items (owner + due date):
- Evidence pack link:

C) Customer comm template (full sample):
Subject: Intermittent latency affecting requests to <route> — update
Hello Acme Team,

We wanted to inform you that we observed intermittent latency increases for requests routed to <route> between <start_ts> and <end_ts/ongoing>. Our monitoring indicates ~X% of requests for your tenant experienced p99 latency above our typical threshold. We do not believe any persisted data was lost.

Immediate actions we took:
- Increased temporary capacity for the serving pool
- Adjusted routing to prefer the latest model variant with healthy cache behavior
- Increased diagnostic tracing for your traffic

Next steps:
- We're collecting traces and will share an initial technical summary within 5 business days and a final report within 21 days.

If you need a meeting sooner, your CS rep <name> is available to coordinate.

Thanks for your patience,
The Redwood Inference Ops Team

D) Evidence storage and index naming conventions (reference):
- Path: s3://incidents/long-tail/YYYYMMDD-LT-<seq>/evidence.zip
