- Index entry format: <incident_id> | <start_ts> | <classification> | <owner> | <s3_path>

E) Runbook edit checklist (for playbook maintainers):
- Verify queries work against staging/production telemetry (update if schema changed)
- Confirm evidence S3 policy is valid and access audit logged
- Update customer brief language with legal/CS once per quarter

Related pages and references:
- incident-comm-and-postmortem-framework (for full postmortem templates)
- observer-lifecycle-and-incident-runloop-for-llm-serving (tracing & observability guidance)

End of document.

title: dsid_385e7a324ffd4a1f91ab08d80e4554cf__tool-call-invalid-json-streaming-us-east-2025-02.txt
text:
Incident Review: Tool-call argument JSON malformed in streaming (us-east)

## Summary
On 2025-02-12, a configuration canary in us-east introduced malformed JSON in tool/function calling arguments for a small subset of streaming requests. At least one dedicated customer escalation (HelioPay) reported strict JSON parsing failures.

## Customer impact
- Symptom: `tool_calls[].arguments` contained trailing commas or invalid escaping
- Primary impact: customer tool router failed to deserialize arguments; resulted in request retries and error spikes
- Affected: streaming-enabled tool calls with arguments spanning multiple deltas

## Detection
- External: customer escalation via Support (SUP-1842)
- Internal: increased 5xx rate in a dedicated tenant route; no automated alert existed for JSON validity

## Timeline (UTC)
- 2025-02-10 23:00: canary enabled `tool_args_delta_coalesce_v2` in us-east
- 2025-02-12 15:10: customer escalation reported malformed JSON
- 2025-02-12 16:05: rollback of `tool_args_delta_coalesce_v2` completed
- 2025-02-13 09:00: CS published workaround guidance

## Root cause
The streaming delta coalescer appended separators when joining tool-call argument fragments and did not correctly handle the end-of-object boundary when a fragment ended with a comma token. This produced an extra comma immediately before `}` in rare chunk boundary cases.

## Mitigation
- Rolled back the canary flag in us-east
- Provided customer workaround guidance (disable streaming for tool calls; validate + retry)

## Corrective actions
1. Add end-of-tool-call JSON validation in the serializer path
2. Add metric: `tool_args_json_valid_rate` per region/model
3. Add alert when valid rate < 99.9% for 15 minutes

## References
- Jira: SUP-1842
- Slack: #support ts=1739293321

title: dsid_10ddfbb0b28b40c48848fa05804a3717__authorization-and-travel-matrix-templates-2026.txt
text:
Authorization and Travel Matrix + Operational Templates

Overview:
This playbook consolidates authorization patterns, approval matrices, change-management steps, data handling rules, procurement and vendor onboarding flow, and travel approval templates into a single operational reference. It is intended for cross-functional use by hiring managers, finance, IT/security, engineering managers, and program owners.

Goals:
- Provide a single source of truth for who can approve which requests and at what thresholds.
- Reduce approval friction by standardizing templates and SLA expectations.
- Improve audit readiness through explicit ownership and retention rules.

1) Access & Permissions Matrix
Summary:
Provide role-based access patterns for common systems (G-Suite, AWS, Redwood Console, Dedicated Admin, Private Deployments). Use least privilege and just-in-time access where feasible.

Matrix (summary table):
- Role: Employee; Systems: G-Suite (basic), Redwood Console (read); Default approver: Manager; Approval SLA: 2 business days.
- Role: Developer; Systems: Internal Git repos, Redwood staging; Default approver: Team Lead; Approval SLA: 2 business days.
- Role: Production Operator; Systems: Redwood Dedicated, Prod infra; Default approver: SRE Manager + Security Reviewer; Approval SLA: 1 business day.
- Role: Vendor Contractor; Systems: Scoped VPN, Redwood Console (limited); Default approver: Contract Owner + Security; Approval SLA: 3 business days.

Request patterns and required artifacts:
- New access request: justification, expiry date (30/90/180 days), data classification label, risk level.
- Emergency elevated access: pager/incident link, time-boxed (max 8 hours), post-incident review required.

2) Change Management (applies to infra, runtime, API contract changes)
Principles:
- Small, reversible changes are preferred.
- Critical-path changes require canary rollouts and automatic rollback hooks.

Change types and approval flow:
- Standard (non-production code/config change): submit change ticket, peer review, CI green => deploy to staging. Owner: author.
- Major (schema/API breaking, infra scaling changes): design review doc + ADR required, signoffs: owning product manager, infra lead, security, and at least one reliability reviewer. Schedule change window and define rollback.
- Emergency (P0/P1 incidents): follow incident runbook. Post-mortem required within 7 days with remediation plan.

Change SLA & gate checks:
- All Major changes must have an ADR published >= 72 hours before scheduled rollout.
- Canary duration: minimum 30 minutes or 10k requests, whichever is longer.

Checklist (pre-deploy):
1. Testing matrix completed (unit, integration, perf).
2. Monitoring dashboards updated.
3. Fallback path defined.
4. Rollback playbook attached.

3) Data Management and Handling Rules
Classification labels: public | internal | confidential | regulated.
Rules by label:
- Public: no restrictions.
- Internal: storage in internal buckets only; default encryption; retention default 2 years.
- Confidential: restrict to VPC-only storage; access via approval matrix; retention per data owner.
- Regulated: follow region-specific retention, encryption with customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM), audit logging for all access.

Required documentation on data usage:
- Data processing description (purpose + retention).
- Data flow diagram (plain-text or ascii) showing ingress/egress.
- Owners and contact info.

4) Procurement, Expenses & Vendor Management
Procurement thresholds and approval matrix:
- Low-touch purchases: <= $2,000, team budget owner approval.
- Mid-tier: $2,001 - $50,000, require Finance manager + approving director.
- Large / Capital expenditures: > $50,000, require Finance Director + Legal + Exec sponsor.

Standard vendor onboarding steps (checklist):
1. Vendor risk assessment (security questionnaire).
2. Contract review by Legal.
3. Finance set-up and PO issuance.
4. Access scoping (least privilege) and expiry.
5. Quarterly vendor reviews for critical vendors.

Expense rules:
- Per-diem caps and country-specific rates are in the Travel section.
- Receipts required for all expenses >= $25.
- Personal charges on company cards must be reimbursed within 14 days.

5) Travel Policy (operational template + matrix)
Booking and approval flow:
- All travel: submit travel request in Travel Portal with itinerary, cost estimate, and business justification.
- Approvers: Manager approves travel; for international travel or expense > $5,000 require Finance review.
- Travel Safety: Security must review travel to high-risk regions (>moderate advisory) before approvals.

Per-diem and allowable expenses (examples):
- Meals: up to $75/day domestic, $120/day international (region-adjusted).
- Lodging: reasonable mid-market hotel; use corporate negotiated rates where available.

Emergency and Duty of Care:
- Employees must register trips via Travel Portal. Security team monitors travel advisories. In case of evacuation, contact Security Ops immediately (security-ops@redwood.com).

6) Templates and Sample Artifacts
Included templates (copy/paste-ready):
- Access Request form (fields: requester, system, role, justification, expiry, manager).
- Change Request checklist (fields: change type, risk, rollforward/rollback commands, test plan).
- Vendor Onboarding intake form (vendor name, contact, data access required, security posture summary).
- Travel Request template (itinerary, objectives, estimated cost, manager approval).

Sample Access Request (plain):
- Requester: Jane Doe
- System: Redwood Dedicated - prod-metrics
- Role: Read-only
- Justification: Support quarterly latency study
- Expiry: 90 days
- Approver: Team Lead (signoff)

7) Ownership, Audit, and Review Cadence
- Policy owner: Finance-Legal (primary), Security (co-owner for access/data policies).
- Review cadence: full policy review annually; access matrix audited quarterly.
- Audit artifacts retention: access approvals and vendor agreements stored 7 years.

8) Incident and Escalation Paths
- Unauthorized access detected: notify Security Pager, revoke affected credentials, conduct time-boxed investigation (48 hours).
- Failed change causing outage: escalate to Oncall SRE, initiate rollback; postmortem published to eng-oncall within 72 hours.

9) Quick Reference: Approvals and SLAs
- Standard access requests: 2 business days.
- Production operator access: 1 business day + security review.
- Vendor onboarding baseline: 10 business days (assuming questionnaire returned).

10) Appendix: CLI snippets and policy links
- Example: create temporary access ticket (internal CLI):
  rw-ops access request --system prod --role read-only --expires 90d --justification "latency study"

Related pages and references:
- See: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/incident-process/ (incident runbook)
- See: /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/ (RBAC standards)

Contact and escalation:
- Policy owner: Maya Chen (maya@redwood.com)
- Security co-owner: Priya Natarajan (priya@redwood.com)
- Finance contact: Alejandro Ruiz (alejandro@redwood.com)

Change log:
- 2026-01-15: Document created.
- 2026-06-20: Added emergency access pattern and JIT guidance.
- 2026-10-03: Updated travel per-diem and vendor onboarding SLA.

text:
Runtime fidelity sprint handbook: profiling, kernel interactions, and rollback protocols

Overview

This handbook describes the goals, lab protocol, measurement artifacts, and safe rollback procedures for a 'fidelity sprint' — a focused engineering sprint whose objective is to change or validate runtime fidelity (model variant, quantization, kernel variant, batching policy, or routing policy) without regressing customer-facing SLOs or quality metrics. It is intended for engineers, SREs, and applied ML practitioners who run experiments across the serving runtime.

Why a fidelity sprint?
- Reduce regressions: small behavioral changes in kernels, quantization, or batching can introduce subtle regressions in output quality or latency distribution.
- Reproducibility: define a repeatable lab protocol for new kernel rollouts and quantization profiles.
- Operational safety: codify rollback and guardrails that preserve availability and cost targets.

Scope
- Applies to changes that affect inference fidelity or execution internals: kernel variants, quantized weights/ops, KV-cache prefetch hints, scheduler admission policies, batching heuristics, and model-variant routing.
- Does NOT cover: API surface changes, control-plane-only feature flips, or customer-facing configuration changes that don't change execution fidelity.

Owners and stakeholders
- Sprint lead: owner of the change (name + pager) — typically a runtime or applied-ML engineer.
- QA / Evals: applied-ml team responsible for the prompt-suite and regression gates.
- Oncall SRE: responsible for rollout monitoring and rapid rollback steps.
- Product owner: for business risk decisions when rolling out to Dedicated/Private customers.

SLOs and acceptance criteria
- Latency SLOs: 99th percentile tail latency increase <= 10% relative to baseline for the same workload mix.
- Error budget: no more than 5% additional errors (5xx or runtime timeouts) during canary windows.
- Quality gate: prompt-eval pass-rate delta <= 0.5% absolute (for high-sensitivity tasks) or <= 2% for low-sensitivity tasks.
- Cost delta: per-token cost increase <= 5% (unless explicitly approved).

Labs and environment matrix (table)
- The lab matrix documents target hardware, kernel variants, and fidelity settings we exercise:

| Environment | GPU type | Kernel variant | Model variant | Typical sequence lengths | Notes |
|-------------|----------|----------------|---------------|-------------------------|-------|
| local-lab-rt | A100 80GB | v2-lowlat | fp16 | 32-128 | dev-only, limited concurrency |
| perf-lab-1 | A100S | v2-default | int8-q | 16-256 | synthetic replay of production traces |
| canary-region | T4/GPU | v2-explicit-prefetch | fp16 | 8-512 | small % of real traffic |
| dedicated-staging | H100 | v3-kernel-tiling | int8-q | 64-1024 | reserved for enterprise smoke tests |

Prerequisites (checklist)
1) Baseline capture: collect a 24-hour production trace and compute baseline SLOs and per-route token distribution.
2) Eval prompt set: ensure there is a labeled prompt set for at least three sensitivity tiers (high/medium/low).
3) Telemetry hooks: feature flags, kernel parameter tags, and tracing for kernel decisions must be enabled.
4) Canary plan: percentage targets, ramp schedule, and alert thresholds declared in the sprint ticket.

Experiment procedure (numbered steps)
1. Prepare artifacts\   a. Build the kernel/quantization artifact and tag with semver: kernel:vX.Y.Z-fidelity-sprint\   b. Generate a benchmark spec (JSON) that includes: route list, concurrency shape, sequence-length distribution, and sample prompt corpus. Example: {"routes": ["chat_v1","completion_short"], "concurrency": "Poisson(8)", "sample_corpus": "gs://redwood-evals/fidelity-sprint/"}
2. Run lab smoke tests (local-lab-rt)\   a. Execute unit-level smoke with trace replay: ./scripts/replay_trace.sh --trace=24h-baseline --kernel=kernel:vX.Y.Z\   b. Validate memory, no OOMs, and kernel logs for warnings.
3. Microbenchmark suite (perf-lab-1)\   a. Run throughput and tail-latency suite: python tools/bench_runner.py --spec fidelity_bench.json --out /tmp/bench-results.json\   b. Record: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU UTIL, kernel occupancy.
4. Offline quality evals\   a. Run the labeled prompt-set through both baseline and candidate artifacts: eval-runner --baseline s3://... --candidate s3://... --metrics rouge,bert-score,exact_match\   b. Produce a delta report and flag prompts with >X% change for manual review.
5. Canary rollout\   a. Start with 0.5% traffic in canary-region for 30 minutes. Monitor SLO and eval signal.\   b. If green, ramp to 2% for 2 hours, then to 10% for 4 hours.\   c. During each window, run shadow-mirroring to capture full outputs for offline eval.
6. Production ramp and final validation\   a. Only after meeting acceptance criteria for two independent canary windows do we proceed to full region or Dedicated rollout.\\n
Monitoring and telemetry (what to watch)
- Latency heatmap per route and per-sequence-length bin.
- Kernel decision rate: % of requests using new kernel vs fallback.
- Error types: kernel-timeout, OOM, scheduler-rejected, model-internal-errors.
- Output divergence fingerprints: fingerprint ID match rate between baseline and candidate outputs (approximate hash equality).
- Cost signals: per-route GPU time, kernel time breakdown, and billing samples.

Alert thresholds (sample)
- p99 latency increase > 12% for >5m -> page_oncall (P1)\- error-rate increase > 5% for >5m -> page_oncall (P1)\- eval-pass-rate drop > 1% absolute for high-sensitivity prompts (manual review) -> escalate to product + applied-ml

Rollback procedure (runbook)
1) Automated rollback trigger \   - If any P1 alert above fires during canary, the system must automatically flip routing to baseline kernel variant for the affected cohort.
2) Manual rollback steps (if automation unavailable)\   a. Oncall runs: curl -XPOST https://controlplane.internal/api/rollout/rollback -d '{"target":"kernel:vX.Y.Z","reason":"p99-latency"}'\   b. Confirm traffic reverts using: k get routes --selector fidelity-sprint=true -o wide\   c. Validate telemetry: confirm p99 returns to baseline within 3x of mean reversion time (typically 2 minutes).
3) Post-rollback actions\   a. Create a hotfix ticket, attach all trace artifacts and eval failure cases.\   b. Hold a 2-hour warroom with applied-ml and kernel-owner to triage.\\n
Quality analysis guidelines
- For each flagged prompt, capture: input, baseline output, candidate output, token-level alignments, and logits (where available).
- Use the scoring rubric: 1=identical, 2=minor wording difference (acceptable), 3=meaningful semantic change (requires escalation), 4=hallucination/regression (blocker).
- Tag each prompt with sensitivity and business impact.

Kernel scheduling interplay notes (short guide)
- Batching tradeoffs: larger batches improve throughput but increase latency tail for short-sequence requests. During fidelity sprints focus on sequence-length-aware batching (max_batch_size per-seqlen-bin).\- Preemption: enable preemption for priority traffic to avoid head-of-line latency for interactive routes. Validate preemption counters don't inflate kernel switch rate by >3x.\- KV-cache prefetching: for long chat sessions, prefetching reduces token latency but increases memory pressure. Add memory headroom checks and a soft cap of 80% GPU memory for prefetch cache.

Benchmarks and artifact naming convention
- Bench artifact names: fidelity-bench.{kernel_tag}.{model_tag}.{gpu}.{date}.json\- Always store raw traces, aggregated metrics, and the prompt-evaluation delta report in: gs://redwood-bench/fidelity-sprints/{sprint_id}/

Reporting and post-mortem
- After the sprint complete (success or rollback), the sprint lead must produce a 1-page summary with: baseline vs candidate summary table, failure cases, root cause hypothesis, and recommended next steps. Attach raw artifacts and the canary ramp timeline.

Appendices
A) Example benchmark spec (JSON)\\{
  "sprint_id": "fs-2026-07-23",
  "routes": ["chat_v1"],
  "shapes": [{"concurrency":10, "seq_len":64}],
  "duration_minutes": 60
}\\n
B) Quick commands\- Collect runtime traces: ./tools/capture_runtime_trace --duration 60 --out /tmp/trace.json\- Run bench: python tools/bench_runner.py --spec /tmp/fidelity_bench.json --kernel kernel:vX.Y.Z --out /tmp/results.json\- Trigger rollback (manual): ./scripts/rollback_kernel.sh --target kernel:baseline

C) FAQ\- Q: Can we skip shadow-mirroring during canary?\   A: No — shadow outputs are the primary artifact for post-rollout quality analysis.\- Q: Who signs off a Dedicated customer rollout?\   A: Product + Customer Success + Security (if private deployment).

Document maintenance
- Owner: Maya Chen (runtime). Update cadence: before every major kernel release or every 6 months.
- Record of changes: last major revision consolidated monitoring thresholds (2026-11-30).

Related links
- Runtime profiling guidelines: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/runtime-profiling-playbook-guidelines-2025\- Rollout orchestration: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/runtime-feature-flagging-experimentation-contract-2026

End of handbook
